Obviously, if you are looking at this, you take your game seriously. This is a great complement to your golf arsenal. I combine this with my normal gps to get very accurate. Personally, you are still going to want something to measure front / back of green's to know how far you need to "clear" something and your absolute max distance, but this is nice to lock in on closer exact yardage. title: Great product
text:
I needed a simple way to illuminate a small unlighted closet. The closet is an odd shape so the ability to spread the light around by using three small lights instead of one large light was perfect for me. Initially one of the three lights did not work, but later I figured out the light sensor of this unit was seeing the light emitted by the other two units and inhibiting its operation (the unit will only turn on if it senses motion and darkness). I repositioned it and now all three work perfectly. I took the advice of other reviewers and did not use the supplied adhesive tape and instead used 1" 3M command removable strips. Even with the 4 AA batteries installed, only two 1" strips were needed to hold the light to a wall (read on about a ceiling mount)

The unit has a mounting plate where you can attach the adhesive strips, and then slide the light on to the plate. This will make it easy when eventually the AA batteries need to be replaced. Along with the adhesive strips, the vendor provided screws to more permanently install the mounting plate if desired

For 2 of the three units the mounting plate did not engage the light firmly and it was loose. As I had put one on the closet ceiling and gravity was not helping to hold the light to the plate, I had to put another 3M strip on the light itself and adhere it to the ceiling to insure it did not fall off. If not for this little flaw this would have need a 5-star product. Overall though it did the job for my situation

title: Bose = Superior comfort, lightweight
text:
I'll be directly comparing to the Bose AE2W bluetooth headphones..

Comfort/Build Quality:
Bose = Superior comfort, lightweight, better build quality
Sony = Uncomfortable after a while, a little chunky, heavier, decent build quality, wish they used better pads

Audio Quality:
Bose = Great sound stage, okay wireless sound quality (Limited to SBC codec), not a lot of bass, if any..
Sony = Good sound stage, fantastic wireless sound quality (SBC, AAC, and AptX), medium to a lot of bass

Controls:
Bose = Better controls on headset to change volume, answer a call, etc. but weird you have to remove the module to go wired - very intuitively placed controls
Sony = Crappy, non intuitive controls on headset.. Although once you get used to their location, not bad but it feels like you're going to push the headphones off your head when you use buttons/volume control

OS Integration:
Bose = Amazing iOS integration, you get a battery meter on iOS, volume changes on the headphone change the phone volume as well, .. It's a unified volume system.
Sony = Crappy seperated volume controls.. Your device volume is treated seperately from the headphones. For example, if your phone is set to a medium or low volume.. You will turn up your headphones and still realize it's not loud enough.. What I end up doing is putting my phone to max volume then adjusting the Sony headphones to desired volume. This is probably killing the battery of my phone faster.

Noise cancelling:
Bose = Has none.. But being over-the-ear blocks out a fair amount of noise but these headphones are completely USELESS on an airplane (tried multiple times).. You have to run your device at max volume/headphones at max volume to hear anything.
Sony = Haven't gotten a chance to test these on an Airplane yet but when NC is turned on, it definatey helps a bit in the office but it doesn't cancel out people's voices.. Only constant sounds like the AC running.. I expect them to knock down engine noise/wind noise of an airplane pretty well though. If you're serious about noise cancelling, you should get the Bose QC25s (wired). If you're trying to find a DO-IT-ALL pair of headphones, i think the Sony are the only ones you can buy on the cheaper side..

Price:
Bose = 250
Sony = 170-180ish

If money is not an object, maybe take a look at the Beats Studio Wireless/Parrot Zik 2.0, both nearing $400.

Keep in mind Beats Studio Wireless will not work when battery runs out (even over wired). Parrot Zik 2.0 DO work after battery runs out over wired according to preview reviews.

Summary.. since the Sony are about $70 cheaper than the Bose, I say if you can cope with them being a little uncomfortable, the Sony offers better sound quality and more flexibility with added Noice cancelling. I am a Bose fanboy and still recommend these only because they are more modern, hopefully one day Bose will do noice cancelling and bluetooth together with better codec support for better sound quality.

title: Great! Better than "5-up" pages, in my opinion
text:
These PrintFile brand photo sleeves are excellent quality and work perfectly.

This product (Printfile 35-8P) holds the 8 photos (four on each side) so they are all in "portrait" format. Contrast that with Printfile's 35-10P (couldn't find an Amazon link), which holds 10 photos (five on each side) so that 3 are "landscape" and 2 are "portrait", per side.

I have some of each style, and I've decided that I like the 35-8P (this product) better even though it holds fewer photos. My wife and I are not skilled photographers; rather more of a point-and-shoot type. We shoot photos in both formats, but most of our photos are in landscape format. With the 35-8P sleeves, while we'll have to first turn the binder 90-degrees to comfortably view landscape photos, we won't have to keep turning the binder often, as we would using the 35-10P sheets.

If you have total freedom of the order of your pictures, you may have better luck, but I found it difficult to load the 35-10P pages -- it seemed whenever I needed to fill in a portrait slot, I didn't have one, or I had 4 portrait ones I wanted all on the same page, etc.

I have number of different Printfile brand photo and negative sleeves, and I've been extremely happy with their clarity, ruggedness, and design.

Here are some sizes. The 35-10P page is somewhat larger, which could matter for your binder or if you plan to use index tabs in some way.

Printfile 35-8P (this product):
Total overall height: 11"
Total overall width: 9 1/2"
Width from center of holes to outer edge: 8 13/16"

Printfile 35-10P:
Total overall height: 11 5/16"
Total overall width: 10"
Width from center of holes to outer edge: 9 1/2"

title: Does not function in repeater mode because of LACK OF INSTRUCTIONS
text:
I'm actually shipping this back to Amazon. I read all the reviews before buying it and was sure this would fix my wifi woes. My primary router is located at one end of my house and my office and bedroom are located way over at the other end. I have only good to fair reception down at the far end, not enough for most applications. I've solved that issue for now by running a 100' ethernet cable down to the far end, and have the computer wired in by ethernet. However, this means I can't move from room to room, and my android phone has a poor connection as well. I bought the Asus ethernet adapter/repeater to boost the signal down at the other end of the house. According to the reviews I read, that's what this is capable of.

It looks kind of futuristic, and I was kind of excited to see it when it arrived and get it out of the box. I've been dealing with the wifi connectivity issues for a while, so was really looking forward to FINALLY getting that resolved. So, when it arrived, I got it out and, uh.... where are the instructions? It's packaged with a "quick start" guide only. No user manual. No detailed instructions on how to use it. Hmmmmm..... that was the start of my problems. So they figure you should go online to get the user manual there. That assumes you've got connectivity. But let's assume connectivity for the moment..... There were no instructions anywhere on the Asus website on how to get this thing to function in repeater mode. What it CAN do, quite well, is to receive wifi and to transmit that, via an ethernet cable, to any device that isn't wifi capable (or in my case, isn't receiving a wifi signal) so that's the "adapter" mode. And the receiver capability is truly impressive! It got a much, much better signal from my primary router down at the far end of the house than any of my wireless devices can, and transmitted that just fine to my computer via an ethernet cable. The problem is that that doesn't solve my problem. I already have an ethernet cable I can plug in to my computer. I don't need something to boost the signal and still be hard-wired. (for that, I could spend another $10 on another 100' of cable and run it down to the bedroom)

So I called up Asus technical support. They agreed. Yup, it sure was a problem that there were no instructions included in the box. Yup, there aren't any instructions on their website either. They were going to have to walk me through it on the phone. OK, so I spent about 45 minutes with a tech support person who freely and repeatedly told me he had no experience with this device and kept putting me on hold to go ask his supervisor who knew more about it. When I asked if someone who DID know more about the product could help me, he said he was required to keep helping me, because that's how they expected him to learn the product line. After 45 minutes of this, we completely exhausted what he was able to tell me, and he finally handed me off to someone else. We'd gone through all the configurations and installation, etc. After another 15 minutes, I had to leave to go pick up my kid. (hard deadline) It took forever to get these folks to understand that I needed the device to work in repeater mode (wifi broadcast), not adapter mode (hardwired to my laptop). It also took forever to get the tech to understand that my ethernet cable was already directly plugged in to my router and I didn't need to plug it into a jack in the wall. ("Yes, even though the router is at the other end of the house. It's a 100' long cable.") OK, so at the end of all this, what I had was a really fantastic antenna that could pick up the weak wifi signal and transmit it via ethernet cable. If that's what you need, the Asus is a fantastic antenna. What it could NOT do, was to take the ethernet signal (yes, plugged directly in to the router) and broadcast that as a wifi signal at the other end of my house. I tested the wifi signal with 3 different laptops and 2 androids. Sitting right next to it, not one of them could pick up a wifi signal from the Asus device. It was simply not transmitting any signal.

So MAYBE the device is capable of functioning as a repeater if configured properly. I will never know, because they don't provide an instruction manual or instructions of any kind, and their tech support team doesn't understand the product or know how to get it to work in repeater mode either. I put it down out of frustration a month ago, plugged my ethernet cable back in, and I'm now at my deadline for returning it to Amazon for a refund and I don't have time to mess about with this any more. Overall, a very disappointing, frustrating, expensive experience. Amazon at least, makes returning it FAR easier than I thought it would be. Just pop it back in the box with a packing slip and they'll send UPS to my house to collect it tomorrow or the next day. Thank you, Amazon, for making the return so easy.

title: Only one flaw
text:
The music quality is superb out of this little thing. I have the Sennheiser HD 448 and they sounded waaay too flat before but now it has that extra bass and then some. I will update once I try out my yet to arrive Audio Technica A700x on this but I can't see myself rating the udac2 anything other than a 4/5. Why? The thing heats up like crazy, EVEN WHEN NOT IN USE! If it's simply plugged into your USB port and the computer is on, the udac2 starts heating up whether or not the udac2 is actually on. I'll simply have to unplug it when not in use but you'd think there'd be some way around this in the design itself.

UPDATE: Ok I've been able to test them with both of the aforementioned headphones and...there's no way I'll be able to go back to my desktop jack. The quality out of these things is just superb. I've read around and there are some very technical complaints about the udac2 such as those by "NwAvGuy" and most of it goes over my head. HOWEVER, after looking around I think this really is the best bang for the buck in this price range. The Fiio E10 seems to be in league with the udac2 with sound quality (possibly better) BUT this seems to be displaced by inferior build quality! I absolutely would not be able to withstand a faulty jack, hissing, or deterioration with time as users have complained, though this is just what I've heard and I do not have the E10.

I spoke earlier about the heat issue and having to unplug the udac2 when not in use was a hassle, but I've exploited this to my advantage by chance. My non-headphone setup is a 5.1 system but the udac2 becomes the default sound device as soon as I plug it in and goes back to the 5.1 system when I unplug it (NOT turn it off, unplug). I leave my headphones plugged into the udac2 24/7 so there's still only just 1 connection I need to make to get it going (the USB). Now, as I've adapted and taken advantage of the heat issue's outcomes, it doesn't exactly excuse the fact that there is a heat issue! I've read that this is because of there not being enough power from the USB port (even though I'm using the back port of my more than powerful enough desktop), the suggested remedy has been to get a USB hub but really, the udac2 should just come with a power supply instead of making the unit itself heat up. I'd overall give this a 4.5/5 and can't recommend it enough. I'm no audiophile (or a really noob one) but I like good sound and I don't want to sell my kidney for it. $120 well worth it.

title: Fantastic Pro Camera
text:
I purchased this camera to use in my event videography business. My first shoot with it was a big car show. I spent about 4 hours taking beauty shots of the cars. I can't even describe how happy I was using this camera, it was such a breath of fresh air.

My own cameras have always been consumer grade, but I have also used professional cameras in my line of work, everything from big shoulder cams to P2 and DV prosumers. This XA10 is my favorite by far! First off, my favorite shooting mode is 24p native. This is a mode that no other camera I've held has offered. Since it's the only mode that allows me to put full 1920x1080 progressive footage on BluRay (interlacing is of the devil!), just that alone makes the camera worth way more than it's reasonable price tag! For instance, with my little consumer camera, I had to choose between 1080 30i or 720 60p, so of course I always used 720p, despite the lack of resolution. And the expensive P2 cam at work I played with (way more expensive than the XA10!) doesn't even shoot at full 1920x1080! It gave me a silly resolution like 1280x1080 with a long pixel aspect. (I can't remember if that's the exact resolution, but I do remember going "UGH! WHY?!" when I saw the footage.) I was blown away by the quality of the XA10. I took some test video of my cat. The background was beautifully out of focus, she was in perfect focus, and you can count the strands of hair on her. It's really amazing and is hard to explain what a difference the full HD, progressive, film mode, and 24Mb bit-rate does for the picture clarity. The sensor in the camera is superb and makes the colors really pop off the screen. The film mode gives you that film motion blur that has eluded video cameras since the dawn of time.

Now that my format rant is out of the way, I'll talk about the features and usability. Some people have complained about the touch screen and understandably so. I haven't found it problematic, though. I've been able to learn it (a little difficult at first) and use it easily. It also has a face recognition auto focus, which I've been impressed by. It catches faces easily and tracks them well, even in pictures. You can tap the screen to tell it where to lock onto and it can be anything, not just faces. I used it several times at the car show to lock onto a specific car so that others were out of focus. One time where I really enjoyed it was when I zoomed in tight on something, tapped to focus on that object, then zoomed out slowly until another object came into the foreground. Then I tapped the new object on screen and it focused on the new one in the foreground. I was able to do it all while handling the camera and zoom, so I thought that was real slick.

People have also complained about the rattling audio switches on the XLR panel. Mine does the same, and yes it is a problem that should be fixed, but as for me, it hasn't given me trouble while shooting. You really have to shake the camera to get them to rattle.

I was hesitant to go for this camera at first because of how small it is. I was afraid it would be shaky just like my consumer camera. But so far, size has turned out to be this camera's plus. Carrying it around and shooting for 4 hours straight, doing a lot of moves and gliding it into interiors and panning around, proved that a big camera would have tired me out quickly. Handling this camera was a breeze, especially with the handle. I found myself constantly switching between the strap and handle for different shots. I haven't had much trouble with camera shake, partly because it's a solid camera (the mic adds some weight too, so it's not so light that I can't control it), and partly because of the good stabilizer. That's another feature I've enjoyed. There's a button on the LCD that you hold to activate the powered stabilizer. It makes the shot so smooth that it looks like it's on a tripod. You have to be very careful not to move too much or it'll jerk the picture around, but it has a shake indicator that shows how much you're shaking it, so just hold your breath and keep it as still as possible, and the stabilizer does the rest. Very good when you're zoomed in all the way on a small object. For instance, I could stand a good few feet away from a car, zoom all the way in, hold the stabilizer button, and get a tripod-steady shot that was so close, you could see the mileage on the car.

A few other things about this camera I like are:
- Very fast exposure adjustment
- Very fast and accurate auto-focus
- Manual focus ring that feels good when you use it
- Good mechanical insulators between the shotgun mic and the camera
- Zoom control is very good, allowing you to get really slow, smooth zooms

A few things that bug me about it, but aren't big deals:
- Viewfinder doesn't angle up which makes it hard to use at all.
- I was disappointed to find that you can't do simultaneous recording to internal memory and SD card. If you want to do back up recording, you need 2 cards and you can't even use the internal memory. Since I don't want to buy another card, I'll just keep using the memory I already have and hope I never run into a situation where I need the backup.

Also, don't even bother with the battery that comes with the camera, it lasts less than an hour. I recommend this battery kit instead:
http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0049VMMZ2/ref=oh_details_o04_s00_i01
Just one of these batteries last 4 hours with a 48v mic running.

That's about all I can think of. Bottom line, if you need a budget prosumer camera, this is the one!

title: For Android and i-Devices only
text:
Of late, I've been having fun turning a desk light on and off remotely through my husband's i-device with Monster Central's Power Control. As with the X-10 systems of some renown (that have been around for some years now), Monster Central lets you control some (expandable) quantity of electrical lights and appliances in your home remotely. But where the X-10 family includes both handheld (on premises) remotes and all flavors of software controllers both trendy and arcane, Monster is just going with two phone and tablet platforms: Android and Apple. If you have an iDevice or a Samsung Galaxy Tab, with this product, you are all set. If it's a PC or, say, an Amazon Kindle Fire that you want to use to control Monster Central, at least for now, it's no go.

I know this because I spoke to support at Monster myself in recent days, while trying to figure out how to sideload the Monster Central Software for Android onto my first generation Kindle Fire, with no handy Android device on my person to fascilitate this transfer. (Answer: I don't think it can be done. At least not without putting my trust in some unknown and unauthorized third party source online, and I'm not really even sure if the original software -- were it attainable from *authorized* sources -- would play nicely with my Kindle.)

I tried to explain all this to the Monster support rep - about the older Kindle Fire and its customized Android 2.3 Gingerbread OS and the intransigence of the Google Play store when it comes to trying to get Android software for a sorta-but-not-strictly Android device...but when the rep turned out to be -- well, polite, enthusiastic, but less conversant with the topic than even my own tech-clueless self - that's when I knew I was up spit creek, pardon my faux expletive.

I realize that Monster is somewhat the new kid on the block when it comes to this kind of product, and don't expect them to have an app for everything going back to the first Palm Pilot, but some kind of desktop solution to alternately control their product would be strategically wise, if they really want to break into X-10's well-staked-out territory. Reports of the desktop computer being dead are greatly exaggerated! (And don't even start with me as to why I don't have an iPhone or an android phone - I'm cheap and tend to keep things -- like phones or first gen Kindles -- until they break.)

Hubbie won't keep the software on his phone for long. Perusing the Android site for the Monster Central software, we noticed that permissions for the software include giving over to Monster the right to take pics with your device's camera, at will and without advance notification. "Well, no," says husband, "I don't consent to that." And I don't blame him. I honestly lack the imagination to even guess why Monster might feel the need to reserve such a permission for a home automation app.

You can download the product manual and promotional information from the Monster website, but currently that's pretty much it for online support. I guess that's an "if (we) build it, they will come" approach to marketing, and certainly enough enthusiast sites have sprong up for X-10 over the years, that the expectation isn't entirely a bizarre one. But overall the impression I'm left with is that Monster is only dipping a toe here in the kiddie pool, unconvinced as to whether there's room for them in the home automation market, and unwilling (as yet) to invest in making the software available for a wider range of computing products, mobile or otherwise.

title: Very Happy
text:
I installed this product in a 2005 Mustang GT convertible with the Shaker 1000 audio system (pictures above). I wanted to keep the factory radio because I was happy with the sound and use my iPhone for all my in car infotainment anyway. I use the Pandora and SiriusXM Apps for music and the Adam Carolla and Stitcher Apps for my podcasts. I use the free Waze App for navigation. I also like the automatic volume adjustment with vehicle speed in the factory unit - a useful feature in a convertible! Ford does not sell a dedicated iPhone cable that works through the factory head unit even though there is an Aux button on the radio. This product got positive reviews and seemed to do everything I wanted so I decided to give it a try.

The installation took one afternoon by myself. I got the instructions on how to remove the radio from Crutchfield - they will give this to you for free if you purchase any car audio equipment from them or you can pay $10 for them without another purchase. As recommended in another review, I used 2 splitters (1-male-into-2-female RCA connectors) so that I could use both the iPhone cable and the Aux headphone jack inputs. I did not want to cut into my wiring harness for 12V power so I used a fuse tap (also pictured above) in an open fuse location for power. This resulted in an "always on" power supply, even when the car is off (as opposed to the power just coming on with the car's ignition). I was worried that this might put a constant power drain on the battery but it does not appear to do so as long as the switch is off and the iPhone is not connected. I ran all wires in split corrugated tubing to protect them and went pretty zip-tie happy to make everything neat. I would recommend removing the trim panel on which you are going to mount the switch and/or aux input jack and drilling the holes from behind. My drill skipped a little bit on the hard plastic and made a few scratches. The iPhone holder I used is a ProFit Bravo minigrip (model BR-200BG). It is held on with a 3M adhesive pad that is not supposed to leave a mark when you remove it. I think it looks nice and holds the phone securely. It is also fully adjustable.

I am very happy with the final result. I have uploaded pictures of my install if you are interested. It looks nice and the only exposed wire is the iPhone connector by necessity. It charges the phone and all audio plays through this cable without the need for a second cable plugged into the headphone jack on the phone. I did not have to adjust the output level on the box. It is about as loud as the radio (but who really listens to the radio anyway, right? Isn't that why you are buying this thing in the first place?). I'm not an audiophile but the sound is super clear without any static at all using either the iPhone cable or the Aux input. I use a 3GS iPhone and it is fully compatible. My wife has a 4S iPhone which I have not tried yet but certainly can if anyone is interested.

Overall I am very happy with this purchase and the ease of installation. It was hundreds of dollars cheaper than a new stereo and gives me exactly what I wanted - iPhone and Aux input capability. Only time will tell how durable it is as some of the lower rated reviews report that their unit failed after 6-9 months. I'll certainly addend this post if mine fails. I would recommend this product to anyone who is looking for an inexpensive and pretty easy way to add a line-in to any factory (or aftermarket) car stereo. Good luck!

title: Outstanding
text:
The Good:

-I have 6 of these units installed around the exterior of my house, paired with a Ademco/Honeywell wireless base (using a 'chime' feature, not a standard ear piercing alarm), going on three years now with not *one* problem, other than ones I've created myself.

-Very sturdy product: I accidentally ripped one off the side of my house with the back of my trailer and it went right back up with no problems other than my feelings of stupidity.

-Very reliable. I was concerned about false alarms in the middle of the night, but after several years we have only had several that have been easily correctable. In one instance my next door neighbor was setting it off when he got in his car in the morning (so not really a 'false' alarm), and we have one detector that picks up car headlights from a particular driveway at a particular time of day, which I would adjust the sensor if it happened more than a couple of times a year. The batteries are still going after three years, although battery life depends on usage, which ours don't get much activity.

-Peace of mind. It feels nice to go to bed at night knowing that I will know the instance someone gets within 40 feet of my house, which gives me time enough to put my clothes on and arm myself in case I need to protect my family. And they do have tamper alarms, so the alarm will sound if you don't have them activated and someone tries to rip one off the wall (hopefully you are at home if that happens).

The Bad:

-Programming these into a base unit is not for the faint at heart. The detector itself is very straight forward in its control mechanisms, and also easy to install on the wall, so not a knock on this product, but you are still signing up to program a base unit if you buy one of these. Different units can present different experiences, but it usually isn't simple with most 'professional' units. It took me most of a day to install six external units (plus a couple of inside units) and setup two base units, but this isn't an issue just pertaining to these detectors, so be prepared to spent some time getting them set up the way you want, regardless of what you end up buying. Just know with these, once you get them setup and work out any intricacies they usually work great.

-They are *expensive* compared to other units, but you get what you pay for. I watched a friend who bought some cheaper units that were 'easier' to work with and then subsequently spend months and many sleepless nights trying to get his to function properly to no avail and then finally give up on them. These are designed for outdoor use and they just work.

The Ugly:

-As with most things you have outside, they can get nasty (e.g. bird poop, sun fade, other miscellaneous gunk), so clean them up once or twice a year and try not to put them in direct sunlight. I put a piece of heavy duty plastic over the top crease/crack and that seemed to help on the top (which is where most of the gunk accumulates, granted, I live beside a busy road which creates a lot of dust/dirt, so you may not find it necessary).

***Update March 2020*** Overall this has been a solid system for 10+ years with very few problems. After 8-9 years I've had 2 out of 6 units stop communicating with the base for no obvious reason, even though everything appeared to check out fine (batteries, base re-enrollment, different locations, sniffer success), which had to be replaced, but I'm still going to keep using these units as they have given me so few problems.

title: Excellent monitor after making one single adjustment
text:
When I first received this monitor, I was extremely pleased with every aspect of it. Brilliant colors, and no dead or odd pixels at all. It appeared perfect, until I viewed an all-black screen to test the backlight bleedthrough. There, I noticed that both right-hand corners had some noticeable bleedthrough, which was pretty upsetting considering what I paid to have a brand-name display. Also, after about a half-hour of trying out a few games, I noticed that my eyes were starting to hurt, and my girlfriend walked by and remarked, "How can you stand it? It's so bright, I can only look at it for two seconds before I have to look away!"

I then went to TFT Central, where I read a very thorough review of this monitor. They mentioned that the monitor comes factory pre-set at 100% brightness, with a luminance of 300 cd/m2, which they said was far too bright. They recommended setting the brightness down to 18%, which would bring the luminance to 121 cd/m2, which they consider optimal. A setting of 18% seemed very radical to me, and I had severe doubts, but I tried it, and after only a few seconds, it seemed just perfect, and still does. My eyes no longer hurt, and my girlfriend agrees that it looks "just right" now. Also, that setting also resulted in the elimination of my backlight bleedthrough problem. That single adjustment has resulted in a perfect monitor for me. So please keep this in mind, as I was considering returning the monitor because of this.

My previous monitor was a Samsung T240, which was capable of "only" 1920 x 1200, so I was worried that the jump up to this 2560 x 1440 monitor would be too much for my GTX570 video card to handle as far as gaming. So I tested it with a few modern games at 2560 x 1440, while leaving all other in-game settings as they were, and did notice a framerate drop, but not nearly as severe as I'd feared. I lost an average of around 30% frames per second, but some in-game tweaking could bring that back, although I probably won't do that since I'm still getting around 40 fps in most modern games (such as "Bioshock: Infinite" and "Ghost Warrior 2") with most settings cranked fairly high. It's not *quite* as smooth as I'd like, but everything is still very playable as-is. That said, I wouldn't want to play modern games at 2560 x 1440 with much less than the aforementioned GTX570 (or ATI equivalent), as I think the GTX570 is about at the low end of what I'm comfortable with for that resolution. Of course, you could always lower the resolution in-game, but I swear, once you've seen "Bioshock: Infinite" running at 2560 x 1440 with most options set to high, you'll have a hard time turning it down to anything lower. It looks glorious!

One drawback for some people might be that the stand for this monitor is quite large. I was a little concerned about this when I ordered it, but I've found it not to be much of a problem, as the two "front" feet stick mostly far to the sides (as opposed to foreward - see photos), thus still leaving me plenty of deskspace for spreading out papers. I did leave the shorter back foot sticking a bit off the back of my desk, increasing the deskspace in front. And it's still very stable. This monitor is never going to tip over.

Also, I was very pleased that Viewsonic included every cable for every hook-up the monitor supports. One thing I did wrong was assume I could just use the same DVI cable I'd been using with my other monitor for this one. When I did, I got an extremely bad picture. Turns out you NEED to use the DVI-D cable that comes with the monitor. The one that came with my other monitor was a DVI-I cable, which will not work properly with this monitor. Don't worry though. The included DVI-D cable will plug right in to your DVI port on your videocard. So details like including every cable you might possibly need was a big selling point for me. There's nothing like hooking up a piece of tech in the middle of the night, only to find out you can't use it for lack of a simple cable. No such worries here, as they've included them all. A CD with drivers is also included, but not necessary, as they were found online, and installed automatically. The only thing I used the CD for was to view the pdf manual.

So overall, I am extremely happy with this monitor. I bought the Viewsonic brand based on my positive experiences with them in the 1990's, and it appears they still know what it takes to make a great one. The only thing that really puzzles me is why in the world they chose to ship these out with the brightness set at 100%. Other than that however, I can find no fault with this excellent monitor.

For a gaming PC, media center or just about anything you should go with a either a bigger 7200 RPM or an smaller SSD for the same price.

BTW, I gave 3 stars just people read this review but the product doesn't have any flaw by itself. We have 4 old WD raptors in a Terminal Server for 60 users on RAID 1+0 and they are very reliable (4 years 24/7 with a heavy load).

title: So far, so good!
text:
I purchased this router, after some google research, to replace a suspect D-Link DIR-655. I have a small home network with a Windows 2008 R2 server (also serving as my NAS with 48TB of storage), 3 Windows 7 workstations and an older XP laptop which is used both wired and wirelessly. The problem I was experiencing was very, very slow slow broadband connection speeds, both for downloads and uploads. After much experimentation I came to the conclusion that the culprit was the D-Link router, so I replaced it with the ASUS RT-66U.
Setup was as simple as it gets; I just followed the standard of powering-down and disconnecting the cable modem, replacing the D-Link router with the ASUS route, powering them up in sequence and finally connecting and booting my main workstation. Since the default IP for the ASUS router matches my private lan, there was, in fact, little to do, aside from setting up the DHCP server range for the workstations. My server, and network printers have static IP's, so no extra effort there.

My broadband speeds have been both stable and improved by nearly a 100x factor. Given the large files that I both tend to download, and upload, the improved speed is very, very welcome. While the D-Link router would occasionally render similar performance, it seemed that every couple of days I would have to disconnect and reboot both the modem and the router to get reasonable performance, which would then slowly deteriorate. Releasing and renewing the DHCP lease from the cable did not usually achieve good results, only the diconnection and rebooting seemed to accomplish what I wanted. In the 72 hours that the ASUS router has been online, performance has not waverd.

Pros:
Features I especially appreciate:
Download and Upload bandwith management: Whle the router comes with a default automatic managment of file download/upload bandwidth management, there is the option to set your own parameters, allowing the user to improve download/upload speed or give precedence to other web activities (gaming, streaming, etc.).

RF Broadcast power: The user can increase the signal strength of the wi-fi broadcast (within the limits of FCC requirements). By increasing the signal from it's default to 80% of maximum, I found that my 5 year-old laptop indicated maximum signal, and speeds up to the 54Mb/s for my 2.4GHz reception three stories down and diagonally across my home through floors and walls. Pretty impressive. I don't have any faster wi-fi devices, so am unable to test that performance.

There are a number of other features which I don't need at this time, including the ability to use USB-attached storage as a NAS, as well as the VPN server, the guest network capabilities (a quick look indicates this could be useful for a Bed and Breakfast, guesthouse or small motel, etc.), parental control, and their AiCloud apps Android and iOS devices.

Cons:
Price? Though I feel I got my money's worth YMMV.

Bob

title: Fantastic camera in a tiny package
text:
I have been a Nikon user for many years, but I wanted something small to take places where my D90 would be too large and bothersome.
I got the Olympus OM-D EM-5, just to try it out. I intended to sell it if it didn't meet my quality expectations.
Well, it turns out I'm now selling the D90.

Image quality:
The OM-D produces images that are just as good in terms of colors and sharpness as the D90.
It has a tad less dynamic range, but better high ISO performance.

Video:
Much better than the D90. That isn't saying much, because the D90 is not know for its great video capabilities.
It shoots HD up to 1080i and can focus while filming (an iffy proposition, but there it is).
The 12-50 kit lens was made for video. The power zoom mode is silent and smooth (the manual zoom mode is better for stills).
I don't care much about video but it might be important to you.

Autofocus:
Same as the D90!
That blew my mind, because I had never seen a mirrorless camera come close to the focusing speed of a DSLR.
The OMD is a tiny bit faster in some cases and a tiny bit slower in others. Most of the time the difference is imperceptible.
In any case, it is blazingly fast.

Continuous Autofocus:
Decent, but not as good. I never use continuous focus, so for me this is a moot point, but if you shoot sports it might matter to you.

Viewfinder:
The electronic viewfinder is a joy to use. It is crisp and clear even in low light.
I can set it to show me the blown highlights and crushed shadows so I can adjust the exposure BEFORE taking the picture!
With the DSLR I would have to "chimp" by looking at the photo after it was taken, adjust, take another photo, adjust, etc.

Configurability:
You can configure three buttons in the camera (plus one in the 12-50 lens) to access the functions you use the most.
The dials are also configurable. For the rest of the functions you have the "Super Control Panel".

Touch Screen:
I'm a button guy and usually hate menus, so I thought I would have no use for the touch screen, but the "Super Control Panel" works very well.
At the touch of a button you bring up a screen with the most important settings.
Touching each setting selects it and then you can use the dials or arrows to set their value.
It very fast and easy. No menu digging. Almost as good as the D90's dedicated buttons.
(BTW, you do have to dig into the menus to enable the Super Control Panel. For some dumb reason, it is disabled by default.)

Size, Weight:
This camera is amazingly small and light. Especially compared to the Nikon D90.
If you put the minuscule Panasonic 14mm pancake lens on it, it may even fit in a large pocket.
I find it very easy to handle, but people with large hands could have problems.
The camera feels very solid and well built.

Neck Strap:
I hate neck straps. I really, really hate them.
For this camera, things are worse than usual.
The neck strap attachment clips on the camera dig into your palms and are uncomfortable when you're holding the camera.
I removed the clips and attached a wrist strap instead. A camera this small and light is better with a wrist strap anyway.
Someone already posted a photo of this in the Amazon listing so you can see what that looks like.

Mysterious Noise:
As reported in many reviews, the image stabilization makes a mystery noise. It is really more like a very faint whisper.
You can only hear it in a very quiet room, and then just barely. It is not an issue.

Conclusion:
All in all, I find the Olympus OM-D to be equivalent to a consumer-level DSLR, but in a much more convenient package.
But the most important factor is that this camera is fun to use.

title: More trouble then its worth. It's like a trainer and a nutritionist that doesn't listen to you.
text:
I got the fitbit one to exercise and keep track of my food intake. This tries to do both, but doesn't really do either.

My Complains with the exercise monitoring:
1) Driving adds steps and stairs climbed. Which increases my daily calorie burn, which is not going to be accurate because of this. I drive my car almost everyday, which means my fitbit log is going to be off almost every day. I can go into the dashboard and erase the steps/stairs added while driving, but this is incredibly tedious, especially when I driving multiple times a day. There should be a pause or hold button, but there isn't one. You just have to go into your dashboard manually every time you get in your car. And I'm usually too busy working or doing some errands to make a note that says from 12-1230 I drove to work, etc... Could be fixed with simple hold option, but there isn't one so they get dock'ed one star.

2) Calories burned shows way too much. It shows sitting down and watching t.v. as an activity of burning calories. Sitting does not burn any more calories then sleeping, but with fitbit it adds calories burned. While that might make me feel good in the short term, I would rather it be honest and accurate. Another issue is I'll put it in at the beginning of work, and log it at the end of the day and it will say I burned 5000 calories that day. On top of that it will say my daily calorie burn naturally is 2000 calories. That is not accurate. I've talked to my doctors and they have told me that it is way off. Fitbit asks for your weight and age. Doesn't take in account height, muscle mass, water weight or your actual specific caloric burn. It just generates it for you. If there was an option to add these features or adjust what my actual calorie burn is according to my doctors I wouldn't complain, but it forces you into a group. Again a simply feature that could be fixed.

3) Doesn't really keep track of weight lifting and calories burned from that. Yes you can put in the dashboard that you lifted weights for an hour, but it will just show calories burned at that time, not what calories your burning from adding muscle. It's especially annoying when you lift for an hour and half and your exhausted and then you get little reminders saying get up, or that you're behind, when you're not.

4) Can't be used with running or elliptical. If you put it on your waist or on your ankle the calories are way off, so you have to take it off when you exercise, and again remember what you burned, or how long you did what. Which is fine if I just run at the same speed for an hour, but if I'm changing speeds/incline it's not going to be a set number. And again, like a lot of my complaints, if I have to remember or make a note of my calories or how much I just exercised, whats the point of the fit bit?

My Complains with food log:
1) The food menu on the dashboard has a lot of pre-measured nutritional information. This is great when I'm going out to eat, or I buy something prepackaged. I can just look it up, and put it in, but when I cook something myself, I have to type every bit of nutrition information in manually because the choices they give are off. I.E. I'll cook eggs that have no sodium and low calories, but the option for scrambled eggs shows higher calories and lots of sodium. I don't know how they can fix this, but the fact that I now have to type down every little bit of information after every meal is a pain, and what happens if I forgot a meal, or I'm too busy to type it. It's basically not doing anything that a pen and paper doesn't already do for me. Also when you start typing in your food it starts to autofill and at least half the time it deletes what I wrote and I have to put in the information again. Maybe if the foods were accurate or typing in food was easier I wouldn't be bothered by it, but it's just another annoying detail.

2) Food Groups Matter- Fitbit just puts in calories eaten, not what type of foods. 2000 Calories from healthy protein, fruits and veggies is different then eating 2000 calories from ice cream. In terms of fat/sodium/sugar often times the healthier food eaten is shown as being worse then the unhealthy food. I.e. A hamburger with 600 calories might show less sugar/sodium then 600 calories from fruit and veggies. This is crucial when trying to loose weight/maintain energy. I wish fitbit would have an option to show healthy foods eaten from unhealthy ones. If there was a food pyramid or pie chart that separated it into categorizes that would be so helpful. That it kept log of dietary fiber, sugar, fat, carbs, protein and separated into those categories (MAYBE BY WEEK/MONTH INSTEAD OF JUST DAY) instead of just a very broad calories eaten. And again I can do this manually, but if I'm doing it manually, whats the point of having a fitbit?

Fitbit Dashboard/Program Complaints:
1) The stupid badges are pointless. I'll put my fitbit on at work and after work when I get home an log in and it will show I walked 23,000 steps and get the badge. Yay, way to go me, but I didn't get any stairs climbed today. So I get a frown face.
A) I'm an adult- a frowny face/smily face is not going to get me to exercise and B) When I've walked that many steps, done that much distance, much more then I needed, I don't need to climb stairs. Overdoing one, cancels the other out. But instead I get the little reminders and faces. Wish there was a button that said leave me alone until tomorrow, or something. Also would be nice if there were other badges, like pushups/situps/crunches, instead of just steps/distance/stairs.

2) Doesn't keep track of measurements. Waist, arms, thighs, chest. I've lost size in these areas, but my weight shows the same. I just wish it did that as well. Would have been a nice feature.

3) Also wish it kept a log of alcohol/caffeine. I'm trying to decrease my coffee intake, and it would be nice to use fitbit to do that. Not something I expect from fitbit, but it would have been nice.

So a lot of my complaints are things that can be adjusted manually in the fitbit dashboard, but if I have to adjust all these things, and then pull out a calculator or measuring cup to keep track of everything, whats the point of having a fit bit? A pen and paper would be easier at that point. I would give a higher rating, but a lot of these problems could be fixed relatively easily, and yet the makers of fit bit aren't doing anything about it. Maybe giving them badges would motivate them to do these...

title: Pay Attention to Antenna Placement
text:
The Leaf Ultimate combines the thin Mohu Leaf antenna with a integrated signal amplifier. The antenna itself is a thin sheet of laminated plastic with black and white sides, to match decor, and two pre-punched holes for hanging the antenna from a wall. It comes bundled with black and white push pins and adhesive velcro strips to offer two different ways of mounting the antenna on the wall. I chose to use the push pins to minimize potential wall damage. They worked well.

Also included in the box is a well-written instruction manual, a separate "quick review" sheet, an ample length of coaxial cable for connection and a wall power adapter. The antenna's amplifier terminates in a USB connector, so it can be powered off of a USB port on a TV set or other device; in my case I used a Tivo. If a USB connection isn't available, the supplied power adapter is the other option.

While the antenna is somewhat omnidirectional, it is important to experiment with wall placement before committing to a location. A foot or less placement can make a different in signal strength. Some TV sets, and other devices (such as my EyeTV USB TV tuner) have signal strength meters to help with set up. It is worth looking to see if this is the case with your TV set or other device. Having someone watching signal quality while another person moves the antenna is extremely useful.

I own both the Ultimate and a Regular Leaf antenna. The difference between the two rests in signal strength. I was able to get a few additional channels with the Ultimate over the conventional Leaf. However, stations that are prone to signal dropout will not necessarily work better with the Ultimate - as I found with a couple of channels that I watch. It improves things, but does not necessarily alleviate signal dropouts completely. On my EyeTV I can see that signal strength is definitely improved, and signal quality modestly so for marginal channels - including one particular channel that I simply couldn't get before. But - that being said - this same channel still suffered from dropouts that made watching a frustrating experience. I should add here that your mileage may definitely be different - it depends on things such as terrain, location of towers and so forth.

Is the Leaf Ultimate worth the extra money? I think it might be, because I do see some improvement in the channels I watch all the time. I can say that this time around, I did spend much more time on antenna placement than with my original Leaf antenna, and that alone may have made some of the difference. But at the end of the day - I have used a lot of different indoor antenna solutions (including one I built out of coat hangers - look it up on the internet - MAKE has an article on how to build one) and the Leaf works as good as any of them, and is much more aesthetically pleasing.

title: Cable is Mis-labelled - Uses 28AWG instead of 24 AWG
text: A number of reviewers have stated that this cable is not good for powering devices.  An an electrical engineer I purchased a number of these for a current project.  I found out the same thing.  The voltage drops by about 1 volt across this 6 foot cable.  I disassembled one of the cables to find out why.  The problem is the the Red and Black wires for power and ground are the same 28 gauge wires used for the D+ and D- signals.  The outer jacket of the cable is labelled the same as most USB cables.  It indicates that the D+ and D- pair is 28 AWG and that the other two conductors are 24 AWG.  This is not the case at all and is false advertising.

title: 'Near mode' is of questionable value - $100 more - and why no XBox 360 support?
text:
All of this is AFAICT based on working with both the Kinect for Windows sensor and XBox 360 sensor in VS 2010.
Other developer comments and corrections are welcome.

I feel Microsoft is trying to convince developers that the 'near mode' is somehow qualifying the Kinect for usable input from users at normal laptop or desktop distances in the Windows environment, buts its ability there is very much in question.

-The near mode doesn't mean you can get skeleton data at closer distances, just DEPTH data. Depth data without associated skeleton data is of limited usage. For skeleton data your best bet is to turn off near mode and stand 4-5 feet away *exactly like the XBox 360 sensor*.

-Keep in mind that near mode is a *separate mode* and a compromise - the 'too far' distance is more limited in near mode :|

-It's $100 more than the XBox version for no reason I can discern. Even Microsoft states that the XBox 360 was capable of depth info at these distances in the correct light. The adjustment they made for near mode must have been incredibly trivial.

-It doesn't work with the XBox 360, which yes *is* important for developers if you only want to buy one device but also do R&D into production Kinect interfaces of any kind (which I recommend you do before programming with Kinect). Again, I don't know why they did this, except to sell an extra Kinect to developers. Its otherwise identical in every respect and its normal mode works exactly the same way as the XBox 360. Microsoft would have had to deliberately broken XBox support, or *just not really tried at all*.

text:
When we remodeled our family room, I installed 2 CAT5e cables from a network patch booth (closet) to the AV rack location where all networked AV devices and a cable modem sit. Our firewall/router sit in the upstairs and this is why I needed two network cables, one for the cable modem to the firewall (WAN), the other for the firewall to the AV devices (LAN).

Later when we installed a DirecTV DVR, I found it would accept a phone line connection to display caller ID on the screen. But we did not have a phone jack near the AV rack. I considered a possibility to remove floor trims to install more cables, which of course would be the last thing to do.

I found this product and installed one in the network patch booth to combine a network connection and a phone connection and another behind the AV rack to split the connections. Voila! My daughter was the first to notice the caller ID display and the display made her say "Cool!"

An ignorant reviewer complains there's no RJ11 connector. Yes, that's true. All connectors are physically RJ45, but an RJ11 plug fits in an RJ45 jack, so there's no problem and this actually leaves some enhancement room. I wish it had clear "NETWORK" and "PHONE" markings instead of "A" and "B," though the difference is obvious if you look at the spring contacts. I also wish the RJ11 side supported two pairs of single lines for even more aggressive use of the existing wiring.

title: Solid beginner's turntable
text: I'm just a 17 year-old, wannabe audiophile. I love the sound and experience of listening to vinyl records. This budget turntable is what has gotten me started, and what a great budget turntable it is. Seriously, this thing is bottom-dollar. You're not going to find a useable turntable for less then this. At about 100 bucks, I really think this was an amazing deal. At the same price you can get a junky all-in-one Crosley or Electrohome, but you're not getting a complete or accurate depiction of what the recording was intended to sound like. Since each stereo component has to be dirt cheap, those turntables are awful quality. Still somehow they remain popular. I've used and heard these at friend's houses. They put out weak sound, and you're not going to hear the wonderful warmth that vinyl can provide. You might as well stick to your low bitrate digital files if you plan on buying one of those. This turntable will provide you with a much more satisfying listening experience than a Crosley or digital files however. It never skips when tracking. My friend's Crosley skips constantly. I really think for 100 bucks, this thing puts out fantastic quality. Since this has a built in phono amp, you basically have all you need to plug into any home stereo system. I hook this up to my dad's Bose receiver and I can tell it sounds fantastic. Bose isn't a true hi fi company, despite what they want us to believe based on their prices, but its still a quality system. I also enjoy listening to the Audio Technica with headphones. I use my Bravo V2 hybrid headphone amp with my Sennheiser HD 598 headphones plugged in (both of which I highly recommend, but of course sound is subjective especially with headphones I believe). I think I can hear even more detail with this setup. Bottom, if you're on a short budget like me, this the turntable to get. I think you will be satisfied. By the way, you could upgrade your cartridge down the line and further improve sound quality.

title: Reasonbly Good Value for the Money with Yamaha's Consistantly Reliable Quality
text:
As usual, Yamaha gives you good value for your money. This radio can play CDs, connect to remote devices through Bluetooth (one device at a time), has a dedicated dock for an iPod and has an auxiliary input for a wired connection. It is not as loud as a Bose WAVE but the color of the sound can be adjusted at low, mid and high frequency ranges with the remote; overall the sound quality is better than the Bose WAVE. It has an alarm clock and adjustable back lighting for the display on the radio it self. The sound it puts outs out is clean and clearly audible. I am able to pull in radio stations quite easily with out constantly fiddling with the antenna (I live in a large metropolitan area with near a landing approach for an airport). You can automatically scan for radio stations and store the ones you want as presets.
I have two remarks to say about this appliance. The first is that although you can scan for radio stations and set up presets, the remote does not have a key pad. Consequently you cannot key in a specific radio station and you can not choose one station to go to from you preset list. You have to go through the stations sequentially whether your are tuning or picking from your preset list. (I kick myself for not picking up on this before I purchased the device.)
The second is that although you could connect an Airport Express to the auxiliary input and and use Apple Airplay to remotely listened to music, I think that Yamaha should have WiFi enabled the radio since it is also doubling as an amplifier and speaker system for other types of audible media. Yamaha has fallen short in this area in general. I have a stereo system (not a home entertainment system) that includes a receiver, two sets of speakers, a CD player and Blue-ray player, all made by Yamaha. Only the Blue-ray player is networked (Ethernet) enabled and i haven't actually used that capability yet.
For these reasons I will give it a three. What they provide you all works and works well, but I feel Yamaha didn't provide quite enough for convenience and for the current "connectivity" environment that is out there. Had they included these other two features, this radio would have been a "grand slam". As such it is an "off the wall" type double. A keypad on the remote would have gotten it up to a four, maybe a four and one half. You could easily do worse with your money and the product is good enough to take the time to write this review. For a desktop system that is close by at hand, this is the one to buy.

title: One great remote!
text:
At the end of April I received an promotional email from Logitech indicating if I were one of the first fifty people to respond I would receive a free Harmony Ultimate Remote. I replied right away and sure enough I received the remote. All Logitech asked in return was to use the remote and provide feedback on it. Here are my impressions so far.

The Harmony Ultimate is a new universal remote from Logitech and is a big step forward from the Harmony Touch which was introduced last year. The Ultimate and the Touch share the same body and button layout. What sets the Ultimate a part from Touch for me are the updated menus, the ability to assign multiple commands to the same physical buttons, the mobile apps for ISO and Android OS and the RF functionality with the included Hub.

There are many changes to the menus on the Ultimate which remove some of the major complaints with the menus on the Harmony Touch. One issue with the Touch was the placement of the "Help" button on the top of the touch screen. When using the transport buttons on Harmony Touch my thumb would often touch the Help and it would be launched inadvertently. Another annoyance was that I would have to drill into the menu to bring up the swipe functions. It seems that Logitech has listen to User's recommandations and has designed the new menu on the Harmony Ultimate to be more logical and User friendly. The Swipe function now has its own dedicated arrow which launches the Swipe function by dragging the arrow up from the bottom of the screen with your thumb. The Help function has been moved to the main menu and removes the accidental hijacking of the remote's functions by simply resting your thumb below the transport buttons. The remote also vibrates when one of the soft buttons on the touch screen is selected.

One of the biggest complaints with the Harmony Touch was the limited hard buttons to control the remote. Not having a physical buttons for the skip forward and skip backward functions was for most a deal breaker. All non hard buttons on the Touch were housed with in the remote's touch screen or menu and required the User to divert their eyes from what they were watching and look at the remote to key enter a command. This was fine for all advanced functions that were not needed by the User for general operation. To remedy the lack of hard buttons, Harmony has provided the ability for the User to designate two commands for each hard button. The User can now assign a short tap for one command and a long tap for another for the same button. This new functionality allows the operator to assign a short tap to the" >>" button to control the Skip forward and a long tap for the fast forward operation. This repurposing of the hard buttons expands the hard buttons available for the User to assign and removes the need to divert the eyes from the screen. So now the User has two methods to skip forward and backward; use the swipe on the screen or a set up the dual tap method on the remotes physical buttons. Using either method is very easy and doesn't detract from the User's experience with the Ultimate. It should also be noted that the updated menu and dual button functionality will be available to the Harmony Touch as a firmware update sometime this summer according to Logitech as will the RF functions as well.

The Ultimate also has a mobile app which turns your smart phone into a remote with the included Hub. This is good step forward and is very similar to the Harmony Link that was out a couple of years ago that worked with Smart phones running IOS and Android and also with expanded operations on the IPad. However if you used the Link in combination with the Harmony One for example, the system would be out of synch and would cause chaos with your equipment. The new Harmony Ultimate Hub handles all the work of synching the equipment between the IPhone and the Ultimate remote to ensure smooth operations. I have only used the Iphone and IPad and have yet to try the Android app. There is currently no IPad app, however the IPhone app works on the IPad though it is some what basic compared with the old Harmony Link application that is available for the IPad.

The new RF capabilities really set this remote apart from the other IR remotes that Harmony or other manufacturers have. The ability to have your equipment behind closed cabinet doors or in an AV closet is great. I no longer have to point the remote at the equipment or worry about line of site when executing a command. The Ultimate allows you to make configuration changes on the fly within the remotes own menu. You can also use the web application to make configuration changes to the remote and synch all change whether completed on the remote or the web GUI without connecting the remote to the computer. This is very convenient.

I currently have several Harmony remotes that include the 676, 510, 650, Harmony One, Harmony Link, Harmony Touch and now the Harmony Ultimate. I have always recommended the Harmony line of remotes to my friends and have used the Harmony One as my standard to compare all other remotes to. When the Harmony Touch was introduced last year it had a very good build quality, but there where things that just didn't measure up to the Harmony One. The lack of skip forward and skip backward hard buttons for instance. The awkward touch screen and the somewhat confusing menu made it hard for me to recommend it. The new Ultimate has changed that and I find myself wanting to use it more and more. It is for these reasons that would recommend this remote. The new web application is also much better and allows the User to carry multiple Harmony remotes with in the same User profile.

Hope this is helpfull

text:

The network wireless works fine and it's nice, but the apps aren't consistent across iOS and Android as some features are available on one but not the other. I like to fall to sleep using Pandora, but I can't use their app to send music to the speaker and have to rely on Polk's app. That means I can't set it to turn off in an hour like I can on Pandora's app. Overall this feels like a work in progress rather than a fleshed out idea (though I'm sure it'll get better in time). No opinion on the PC/Mac side of things as I haven't explored that.

Build Quality wise it's great. It's a stout feeling speaker and I have no complaints here.

Sound Quality wise it's a full sounding speaker, definitely has more bass/mid-bass than you'd expect for something this size (you won't be feeling it though). Unfortunately whatever design decisions they made to get that must have affected the vocals. Voices seem to have more bass than they should and overall are hidden behind the rest of the music. Idina Menzel's voice in Frozen's "Let it Go" isn't the featured part of the song as it takes a back seat to the instruments. A good EQ might be able to help with this, but I haven't had luck getting one to work with iOS or Android. I also have hard time finding a volume level that's right for going to sleep to.

Ultimately these aren't bad speakers, they just aren't for me. I prefer my old Klipsch iGroove SXT and will likely be returning the Omni S2 in favor of it.

title: Great "Stick" But Lose The Condom!
text:
Its a nice small design with the exception of the thick "rubber condom" they put over it. Yeah, some people will like the "fluids" resistant design so they can practice "safe transfer". I carefully pulled the "condom" off of it (a tiny bit of glue inside) and I'm left with a nice slim "stick" with a sturdy clear case, the same size as their Xporter design! Nice! I can still pop it back in its "condom" for that extra safety, you know, when those unexpected moments hit you out of the blue! Speed? Sure, I'll drink to that. Here's a sample on my little Acer Netbook with USB 2.0 ports. Did you hear what you just read? USB 2.0 ports, not 3.0 ports.

Crystal Disk Mark benchmark test
Seq-read/write
1000MB---29.12/13.75
512k---30.04/0.675
4k---5.772/0.007

Real World
800MB AVI Video File
58 Seconds = 13.80 MB/S

So, pretty decent transfer on USB 2.0 ports. No doubt on 3.0 ports the speed would be whatever it would be. For the price you can't get much quicker (or safer) than this! If you want a "quickie" and would like to practice "safe transfer" then this is your ticket. Cheers, mate!

UPDATE Oct 28,2012:
I just transferred a 2.7GB ISO file of Windows 8 to the stick. The ISO file has 2,089 files, 868 folders, approx 2,760MB (2.7GB) and it took exactly 2 minutes 45 seconds. That's 16.7MB/S! Pretty good for being on a USB 2.0 system. So a USB 3.0 stick definitely makes a big difference on a USB 2.0 system as the same ISO file transferred to my Patriot Xporter 128GB USB 2.0 stick took 6 minutes which is about 7.7MB/S.

Sheesh.

These are awesome headphones; the design is chunky, robust and minimalist. I get a lot of compliments on them. The sound is pretty good and decent. Good enough for listening to music at work/bus/train, etc and blocking out unwanted noise.

Now the only con: The "turncables" do not last very long. They deteriorate very fast, even if you are gentle with them. I used to own the Plattans before investing in these Zinkens and I had issues with those as well. The cables/jack lose their connectivity, the sound is affected and so is the microphone. But at least with the Zinkens, you can REPLACE THE CABLE, which you cannot do with the Plattans. So I suggest to everyone deciding between the Plattans and Zinkens, to save up money and get the Zinkens because it will be worth it. Recently my Zinkens cable/jack stopped working, but I was able to order a new cable (through the UrbanEars website) for 15 bucks (shipping included!) and now they work like new! At least you don't have to throw out the entire headset (as I did with my Plattans)!

One suggestion to all: If you place your Iphone/Music Player in your pocket with the headset on and Zinken/Plattans plugged in, it WILL wear down the jack (the connector) on the cord. I've come to notice this only recently. Bending, moving, etc... will put stress on that jack. It's my only logical conclusion, so I suggest you only carry and/or wear your Iphone/Player while enjoying your Plattans/Zinkens or any earbuds for that matter!! It took me a while to make this connection (pun intended), but I truly believe now it will place less wear and tear on the cables and last longer. title: The real reason to avoid this one
text:
Most negative reviews of screen protectors mention issues with bubbles, trapped dust, misalignment, etc. 99% of it is user error. Some people have even stupidly installed the protective film that is meant to protect the actual screen protector in the package. If the screen protector isn't installed correctly, it will look bad. This applies to all of them, and the majority of the screen protectors on the market are equally difficult (or easy) to install. When reading reviews of any screen protector, look for those that discuss the following:

Fit -- how well is the screen protector customized for your device? Some of them are designed to have small border of "unprotected" space around the screen. Some include a cut-out circle to be applied on top of the home button. Others may not have a cutout for the front face-time camera. And some of them are just plain misaligned (but be wary of lone reviewers who say this. It's often a result of improper installation)

Clarity -- Speaking in terms of just the clear screen protectors (i.e. no special features like anti-glare, privacy, mirror, smudge-proof, etc), it's important to take note of multiple reviews that talk about distortion of the display. This is most important on a retina screen. You're already going to be sacrificing at least SOME clarity when you put a screen protector on your iDevice's retina display, but there are some "clear" screen protectors out there that produce more distortion than necessary. Some of them have issues with the "orange peel" effect, where the screen, while clear, has the look of a textured surface (like an orange) that distorts the view. Other screen protectors have issues with reflecting an absorbing light, creating a rainbow effect when held at certain angles. Keep in mind, though, that it's usually only noticeable in certain harsh lighting environments, so take note of reviews that mention rainbow distortion in multiple lighting conditions.

Feel -- How does your hand (and stylus if you use one) glide across the screen? No screen protector will feel just like your ipad's bare screen, but it shouldn't add too much extra resistance. I've seen screen protectors in the past that made those rubber capacitive styli squeak across the screen. HOWEVER, take note of the following: Most, if not all, screen protectors are packaged with thin plastic films that protect the front and back (adhesive side) of the screen protector itself. After installation, when you peel off the front film, a lot of them will leave behind a little bit of sticky residue. This residue will make the screen protector have a lot of friction, and it can even make the rainbow effect look more intense. But, this residue can be removed relatively easily with eyeglass cleaning solution and a small amount of force with a microfiber cloth. It might take a few "sessions" to fully clean it. I mention this fact because a lot of negative reviews are written in the heat of the moment, in anger. Oftentimes the reviewer took the screen protector off his device after only a couple of hours. As odd as it sounds, screen protectors seem to need some "settling time" before they can be truly evaluated.

Scratch Resistance -- The point of a screen protector is to protect your device's bare screen from abrasions, but it's an exercise in futility to use a screen protector that scratches so easily under normal use that you have to replace it every month just to see your screen again. A plastic screen protector will scratch, but some more easily than others. Personally, I use a screen protector because I'm not always a delicate little angel with my electronics. I also like to be able to do a quick spray and wipe down without worrying about rubbing particles of dust, dirt, crumbs, etc. into the iPad's not-as-scratch-resistant oleophobic coating. I need a screen protector that can withstand that abuse over a reasonable amount of time. Most of them will.

Touch Response -- most screen protectors are going to reduce the screen's sensitivity to a capacitive stylus. The screen responds to your touch, and a stylus relies on your body contacting the stylus's conductive material making contact with the screen. Add to that another layer between your touch and the digitizer on your ipad, it's inevitable. How much it affects your stylus depends a lot of the quality of the stylus (the amount and quality of conductive surface on the stylus itself), as well as the thickness of the screen protector. Under no circumstances, however, should you ever put up with a screen protector that causes a noticeable reduction in responsiveness to your touch. Most of them are fine in that regard.

Having said all that, I'll preface my review with one more thing: I have a lot of experience installing screen protectors. I've installed them for friends, family, clients, and myself. With most of these screen protectors, there's one simple fact: The product package does not include everything you need to do a proper, successful installation. Save yourself some headache and go to Youtube to find proper instructional videos.

But the issue with this screen protector is that it's prone to scratches on an almost comical level. No other screen protector I've encountered, including the cheap $2 ones that don't even come in a branded package, are this prone to scratches. It looked like a 1-year-old first-gen ipod nano after about 2 days of normal use. If you don't get the reference, let's just say it was pretty scuffed up.

The short and sweet of it is this: This writeright screen protector installs and looks just like the other static-clings on the market, but it is fragile to the point that it should be recalled.

And I realize my review of the actual product was shorter than my intro. I just felt the need to add some credibility to my comments.
