title: Great video recorder... once you get it working!
text:
I bought the Hauppauge 1445 HD-PVR Gaming Edition to record video from my XBox 360. It works great, but after a day of struggling with the device and being ready to rip my hair out, hopefully I can give you some details and save you from similar frustration.

The box comes with everything you need to get started: the Hauppauge itself, an AC adapter, a component cable capable of connecting any of the current-generation gaming systems (PS3/360/Wii), a male-to-male component cable for passthrough to your TV, a USB cable for connecting to your computer, and a software disc. Keep in mind that you'll be doing all the capture on a computer; this device does not have an integrated hard drive, or the ability to add one.

I specifically bought the gaming edition so I could get the included multi-device component cable, because aside from my Wii, I hook everything up via HDMI. If you're buying the gaming edition for the green light on the device... go ahead. If the color of the light doesn't matter to you, DON'T buy the gaming edition. I made the mistake of believing that for five extra dollars, I was going to get a high-quality cable, despite being an analog signal split between three possible input connections. After plugging the cables, I realized my mistake. There was ghosting, what some might call the "halo effect", around everything. It was most pronounced around text. This effect appeared at 720p and 1080i resolutions, and also appeared in recordings, proving that the problem was with the cable itself and not with my setup. 480i and 480p had no ghosting issue, so if you're planning on recording Wii only, you can make do with the included cable. I had to go out and buy a dedicated cable for my XBox 360. I'd recommend you do the same, and stick with the cheaper "blue" model.

After that frustration, the biggest problem was getting the damn thing to actually work. I connected all the cables and the USB cable as instructed, popped in the disc, and installed the device drivers and the ArcSoft ShowBiz software. I launched the ShowBiz capture module, and ... no video! I had all the correct inputs selected (Hauppauge device, component input, rear stereo audio), and the preview window showed nothing. Trying to capture video despite that yielded an error when stopping the capture. I must have changed literally every device and format setting, trying to find whatever quirk in my settings was causing the issue. I even installed the drivers and software on another computer to see if it was my laptop's fault. As a last resort, I visited the Hauppauge website and downloaded the drivers from the Support page. After updating my drivers... lo and behold, the preview video was there! Why the included drivers didn't work from the get-go, I have no idea. What's even more confusing is that it wasn't included as a suggestion in any of the troubleshooting documentation I could find, nor did the driver changelog suggest that it was solving any problem in my setup. So, I spent the better half of my day just getting the capture set up and getting quality video going.

I'm happy to say that following those issues, the device works flawlessly. Once you start capture up, the device lights up bright to let you know that it's busy at work, encoding the video and transferring it to your computer according to whatever settings you have set. There's no lag on the TV itself, despite the Hauppauge being in-between. The video as well as the audio will be played back on the computer with a bit of a delay though, but you can feel free to mute your system while recording happens to avoid the distracting audio. You don't really need a powerful system to capture video, because all the encoding is done on the Hauppauge itself (editing is a different story). You have a large range of mbps/sec qualities to choose from, whether you want to bitrate to be constant or variable, and whether you want stereo sound to be encoded as AAC or AC3. In addition, you have a range of output formats to choose from, including .TS, .M2TS, and .MP4. These are organized according to whichever device you plan to use to play the media back (AVCHD, PS3, and XBox 360, respectively). I recommend recording in .TS format, regardless of what device you'll use. .MP4 has audio sync issues, so avoid using that format.

I cranked mine up to the highest variable bitrate and AC3-encoded audio at 720p in .TS format, and it cost me about 1.6GB for a 20 minute video. Not too shabby! I haven't compared various bitrates and their effect on file size, but you can probably make your space go a lot farther with a bit of experimentation. The quality was great; what I saw on my TV was what recorded, with no audio hiccups or stuttering of any kind.

If you're planning on doing some trimming of your videos, and maybe adding some transitions, basic effects, or text, then ArcSoft ShowBiz will do the trick for you, complete with the ability to upload directly to YouTube. For me, I needed something with some more options (no fade through black, ArcSoft? Really?). I used AVS Video Editor, which has a much more robust set of options, and best of all, takes your .TS format video without a fuss. Be warned that it will include a watermark upon publishing if you don't buy the full version. Unfortunately, you likely won't be able to "cut out the middleman", so to speak, when capturing video. AVS couldn't capture video from the Hauppauge, so I'm stuck with capturing the video with ArcSoft ShowBiz and opening up the video in AVS. I can't say for sure if any other Windows-based video capture software will work, but I had no such luck. Those of you using a Mac or Linux, there are third-party solutions out there to get you rolling. I haven't tested them yet, so I can't tell you what type of experience you'll have.

Overall, the Hauppauge HD-PVR does a great job of what it's supposed to do: Capture high quality video from your game console or other component video device and provide an acceptable set of editing and uploading options. I took off one star for the initial frustration and the poor-quality gaming cable. Once it's working, it does a great job of what it promises to do.

Happy recording! If you have questions, feel free to leave a comment on the review.

title: Refurbished Dell Latitude D620
text:
I truly give this a 3 1/2 star rating. I'll tell you the Pros and Cons, and what the computer is and isn't made for. I wanted a new Laptop for the online marketing I do since I thought my Toshiba A205 was done for. The shipping from ABCcomputers was fast and everything they said the computer was, was valid information. I was ready to go back to Windows XP OS with the Dell, but decided to install Vista in it instead. The battery and charger worked very well to my surprise lasting well over 2 hours and there were very few cosmetic scratches. Yet the one thing that I cannot get over about the computer was how dim the screen was. I have doubts that all Dell D620 screens come that dark, but it seems as though it's always on a power saving mode for battery life like a typical laptop. It's a slight annoyance, but I believe I can live with it, and I can say this was the greatest of all problems I had with the computer.

ABCcomputers described it as a powerful laptop despite it's 1GB RAM memory, 1.65GHz Dou Core Processor and only 80GB HDD memory. To my surprise it was a work horse! Here's the twist, I replaced the 80GB Seagate Hard Drive with an 128GB Solid State Drive in the Dell and could start maybe 10 applications all at the same time including 3 web browsers with practically no application effecting the others performance. Here's another twist; when I found out what was wrong with my Toshiba (a newer computer than the refurbished Dell), I switched the Solid State Drive to the Toshiba that had 2GB RAM, and 1.85 GHz Duo Core Processing. In this experiment, I found the applications sometimes load a few seconds slower than instantly like in the D620. I actually encountered some freezing of applications I had to force close in the Toshiba. This never happened when the SSD was in my Dell D620! I still kept the SSD in the Toshiba because of how bright and wide screened it was over the Dell. Besides, the SSD works good enough in the Toshiba.

The computer's processing seems very good with it's original Seagate Harddrive. I really don't know what you can ask for more out of a refub Dell from 2006. This Dell's focus was primarily as a business computer so Word Processing is ideal. I was planning on upgrading the Dell even more by putting in 4 GBs of RAM as it only has 1GB. Before anything my main focus is getting that backlighting brighter as Fn + the UP arrow key does not do the trick. I'm sure that would cost at least over $100, and right now that's too much of an investment out of this secondary computer. At the same time the computer can only use 3.5GB out of the 4GB of RAM because of the BIOS blocking it or 32 bit OS you're using. Either one is the case but I'm not %100 sure. The D620 is not a light computer even though the screen width is just 14 inches wide. They made it pretty sturdy with a Strike Zone feature that probably helps keep your hardware and cpu denying damage.

It's not at all a Gaming PC. A video card / whole new motherboard has to be put inside of it just to recognize a newer Microsoft game. So, sorry gaming geeks, you'll have to pay probably another hundred dollars if you wanna play Skyrim and your other favorite games. Gaming wouldn't be exceptional anyway, since the screens brightness isn't top resplendent or enchanting.

Concluding my own personal story, I now have a secondary laptop that I'll probably just store files on such as music for I Tunes, and maybe in the future video file, and probably do some web browsing. I think its a good PC, but I would like to know what others feel about their Latitude's backlighting. Comment because I wanna know. It's a decent computer, but I think it would be well worth the $200 if it didn't hurt my eyes to watch lol. Other than that problem I would recommend someone buying this computer and upgrading it as they go making it a super computer like I did.

title: Poor quality/keeps resetting/lackluster customer service
text:
1/13/2013: I had to come back and lower from 2 starts to 1 star. Western Digital's router has now recieved the spot for my worst electronic investment ever. It neither routes or stores data very well.

I'm on my 3rd replacement router from Western Digital and I've found the following:

1. You can not transfer large volumes of files to it. I was trying to use this as my network "NAS" for backups, and when trying to transfer anything more than around 50GB's of data to the router causes the network to crash about half way through the transfer. So much for using this for backup

2. Performance - This is advertised at 450mb would would translate to at least 45MB per second transfer rates. I just upgraded 2 computers one with an SSD drive and the other with a 7200RPM drive, and the fastest throughput I can get is 11 or 12MB's per second. Yes, I know there is overhead and performance limitations of the hardware connected...but give me a break, it should be doing at lest 25MB's per second.

3. Crashes constantly - I will say that each router they send me seems to be getting better. First router would crash and I would have to reset the box every other day or so, the second one was about once a week. My third one hasn't yet and it's been about 5 days, but I still have problems with transferring larges amount of data to it.....seems to always brings this router down.

I wish I could go back in time when I made this purchase and did my research, but unfortunately this product hasn't been out THAT long so there wasn't a tone of review. This goes down as my WORST ELECTRONICS PURCHASE EVER and I've been buying electronics for over 30 years. WD, you completely lost me as a customer on this one. Thanks for nothing.

Dan

I've been a fan of Western Digital for years purchasing several of their hard drives in the past and with a Linksys router on it's last leg, thought I would try out this new combination.

I was delighted at first which lasted a couple of months, but the one thing I noticed was I was having to reset the router about once a week as the entire network would stop working. This increased in frequency till I finally called WD support to have the router replaced. Now I'm sitting here with a replacement router and it's giving me the same exact issues. Having to restart the router already twice in the last 5 days.

The only thing that makes this even worse, is when I was sent the second router they promised to send it out the day I call, and after calling in a week later to find out where my router was I found out it had JUST been shipped out.

Western Digital has both let me down with their product quality and their customer service. After being a customer for years, this is enough to make me never want to purchase another product from them.

title: Holy Schiit this sounds good!
text:
I have been looking for a very good DAC that didn't cost an arm and a leg. I was very close to pulling the trigger on the Emotiva XDA-2 when I started reading about Schiit. The Modi was the answer for my set up.

I will be running the Schitt Modi through a vintage Fisher amp rated at 30 watt per channel. I will be using Fluance SX6 speakers and will eventually add a sub.

Shipping speed was average and seemed slow but, I was just eager to get it. The packaging is spartan and no frills. It was the unit in a plastic bag, in a box with a single insert sheet on how to set up the USB version which is what I got. There were also four little vinyl feet to put on the bottom of the unit. These are very cheesy and you would be better served by going out to get some nice felt or rubber feet at the local store. They really got cheap with this Schiit.

So, onto the unit itself. The build quality is excellent. The fit and finish is tight and looks very good. The front is plain with just the Schiit logo on the left and a bright LED on the right. To my dissatisfaction, it's white and annoying. If they could do it in blue it would be much more pleasant on the eyes so, maybe they will read this and make them blue or give you the option in choosing a color.

Hookup was straight forward. I dug a USB cable out of my box-o-cables and then plugged in the Logitech Z-3 speakers through the RCA outs on the back of the unit with an adapter cable that accepts a 3.5mm jack. That was it! In less than 60 seconds, I was listening to music.

A minor nit pick is that Schiit could include a USB cable. You can order one from them at an additional cost which really is Schiit-y of them to charge for it. They seem really chintzy about little extras. I understand they are trying to keep the cost down but, come on guys - hook a brother up! :-)

As a quick, initial test, I just ran my amplified Logitech Z-3 2.1 speakers through the DAC and even with those speakers, the improvement in sound was very noticeable. I have never heard them sound so alive until I hooked up the Schiit Modi. The sound stage was widened considerably which opened up a bouquet of dynamics that had never seen the light of day because of all the noise and poor sonics from the stock sound card.

I started my testing with The Desert Rose Band tune called "Darkness On the Playground". The acoustic guitar rang clear and the slide guitar was well defined. The subtle cymbal play was crisp and noticeable where as before it had been buried in a muddled mush pile. The bass was snappy and well timed with no thrash at all.

Next up was Lou Reed's "Turn To Me". The opening guitar piece just flew out at me and was very well defined. Reed's vocal timbre was spot on by the time the rest of the instruments kicked in.

Here is a list of what I listened too.
The Desert Rose Band - Darkness on the Playground (Streaming via Grooveshark)
Lou Reed - Turn To Me (Streaming MP3 over LAN)
Motley Crue - On With the Show (streaming via Grooveshark)
Motley Crue - Toast of the Town (streaming via Grooveshark) The opening riff on this tune was amazing. It sounded so raw and in your face.
Sheryl Crow - Waterproof Mascara (streaming MP3 over LAN)
Rush - Fly By Night - (compact disc via PC) I suspect this CD was not mastered very well originally because the whole recording sound heavily compressed. It did not sound good to me.
Rush - Spirit of the Radio (compact disc via PC) This was crisp and well defined the sound stage was very good. Vocals sharp and uncompromised.
Norah Jones - Don't Know Why (streaming MP3 over LAN) Smooth and neutral with well defined timbre in Norah's voice. The upright bass was clear and bouncy with good clarity. The high notes she hits hit me so smoothly.
Willie Nelson - Always on My Mind (streaming MP3 over LAN)
Crosby Stills Nash and Young - Woodstock (streaming MP3 over LAN)
Boston - Rock -n- Roll Band (streaming via Grooveshark) Wow! Wow! Wow!

My conclusion - The Schiit Modi throws a wide and full sound stage. The sound produced is clear and concise with out feeling compressed at all. On only one recording did the sound seem muddled and compressed however, this seemed to be isolated to that disc. Even streaming music off the internet sounded excellent.

For $99 plus shipping ($109) you cannot go wrong. I do think that Schiit is a bit cheap with the packaging, the little feet and the lack of any accessory (USB cable). The little feet are terrible. The LED light is wicked bright but, hook up is straight forward. If you are looking for an audiophile DAC on a budget, this just may be the ticket for you.

title: ASUS  + DD-WRT = Good
text:
The first RT-N12 I received was DOA, but was sold as "like new." Sounds like several people have had this experience. Second time around, I went with a new one for 10 bucks more. I am comfortable with DD-WRT firmware, and would not even give ASUS' firmware a chance after reading the reviews on it. Some claim they have fixed their problem, but why bother when DD-WRT is going to be so much better anyway?

A lot of the problems I read on this site in the one star reviews seem like the kind of problems that DD-WRT would help. One downside is that with the small memory size, only the "mini" build will fit on it. For most home users this is a non issue, but if you want to run OpenVPN or another fancy application on your router you need to move up to at least the RT-N16.

If you are unfamiliar/intimidated by third party firmware, don't be too put off by most of the terse warnings on DD-WRT's website. Earlier routers were much easier to brick than these more modern ones, ASUS included. Its still best to follow instructions step by step. There's more margin for error than they'd have you believe, in my opinion. For a $40 router, if you are unhappy with its performance under stock firmware, why not give it a try? In fact, why not give it a try on whatever your current underperforming router is? It might just save it and you won't need a new one!

title: Great New Mouse
text:
Was originally hoping to pick up a Razer Ouroboros over the Christmas season, but those sold like hotcakes, and are back-ordered until God knows when. Loved the Ouroboros design, customization, and the dual 4G laser. Thought that thing was so cool.

Since I was looking for one of those to no avail, I started looking for a new mouse. Had a Deathadder, but had been looking for a wider mouse with more buttons and stuff.

After a lot of deliberation, I ended up on this one. Even though it wasn't wider than the Deathadder, I thought it was cool and pretty much had everything I wanted in my new mouse.

It was packaged as other Razer mice are; nothing special, but a nice touch. Took this thing out of the box to find it was smaller than I anticipated, but I loved the design. The matte finish and the sleek curves looked so awesome in person. Put this thing my hand, and it feels as good as it looks. It was so comfortable. I have large hands and I was kind of surprised that it was so comfortable, but the matte finish and rubber finger grips on the side are a big part of that. The LED's also look great, coming from a blue on the Deathadder, but I really wish I could change the color.

Performance wise, I am currently using a SteelSeries QCK mouse pad. No problems and this thing moves so smoothly and accurately across the pad. I run the mouse around 3500-4000DPI, and its really smooth. No jumps or anything. No complaints. The left side buttons are little hard to use for me, without implementing a claw grip or some hybrid grip. Not a big deal for me, as I don't need to be lightning quick pressing those. They weren't really designed to be easily be used by your ring or pinky finger, so that's fine.

I had a bit of trouble with Synapse 2.0 installation, because the Deathadder converted kept stopped working. Unplugged the Deathadder, and no more problems. Works well, but it is a little annoying that this stuff has to be on the cloud and I can't just use the legacy drivers that were beyond simple to use.

Overall, this is a great mouse, and the price point is just about right. For those who complain about the price, try to find an ambidextrous mouse, with LED lights, dual 4G lasers at 8200DPI, great design, and a fantastic finish for $70. You can't, because they don't exist!

Connectivity always seemed to be a pain as we'd spend the first 15 minutes of every ride trying to get everyone paired, so I was excited to upgrade. Unfortunately the build quality of the 20S is too poor to recommend. Either wait for an update or look elsewhere.

Positive:
The technology is great. Easily pair to other riders, very clear communication over quite a distance and if you go out of range it reconnects you as soon as you're back in range. Speakers are great as is the microphone and audio quality. The app is simple but effective. All the technology is great and if this review ended here I'd give it five stars.

Problems:
Build quality is terrible. The exterior case came loose within the first four hours of riding making me concerned that the outer shell was going to fly off and at the least the interior was now totally exposed to rain. All the little holders where the screws attach had broken. So I super glued it and kept going. After another couple hours I found I was constantly losing all sound. I stopped and found the little tab that holds it in place on the docking station would no longer 'click.' No matter how hard I slid it down onto the holder it would not latch so I could only get sound by riding holding the unit onto the dock with my left hand - not the best motorcycling technique. So, now I have a $250 intercom that only works while I'm squeezing it hard and riding one handed. From their forums I learned this was a common problem.

Since it's a $250 worthless device right now I should probably give it one star, but the technology was really good before the plastic parts gave up.

UPDATE - Sena support did get back to me and replaced the unit. It doesn't look like anything has changed so I expect the same problems will eventually occur so I'm only taking the unit out of the cradle when absolutely necessary and being very careful to compress the unit to take the stress off the clip that holds it in place while releasing it. I loved the ability to quickly take the unit off and on with the previous version to make it easier to keep it from being stolen or exposed to weather, but the better technology of this newer version is way better. So it's a five for intercom/phone usage, two for the parts attaching it to the helmet and the screws that hold the case together.

title: It's August, 2012... Surely They've Fixed This?
text:
Yeah, no. They haven't. Like many here, I suppose, I read the reviews for this unit thinking that surely Logitech must have worked things out by now. Having used a Harmony for years, I was used to the crappy software and non-intuitive updating process. Surely I would fare better than the rest of these nattering complainers! Yeah, no. I didn't. Not only have they not worked out the problems, from everything I am able to gather on the web they seem to have released this product then just sort of... forgot it even exists?

To be fair, the setup was about as easy as I expected, which is to say, not easy at all. I already have Logitech's horrifying remote software installed for my Harmony 880, I'll just plug in the new remote, fire that up and click on the "New Remote" button. Hm. Yeah, nothing happens. OK, so it's Harmony, but the Harmony software doesn't work for it. Brilliant. The instructions say you have to go to myharmony.com, so fine. I'll do that. I've read the reviews... this is going to be fun. Not.

So hey, I went to myharmony.com expecting troubles and surprise, surprise... I got them! No harm no foul, right? What problems, you say? Well, you have to have an account and your login is your email address, so the first thing I did was go back in my email and look up what email I had been using previously. I attempted to retrieve my password using this email address so I didn't have to create a new account. Error message: "there is no email matching that on file." Sigh. OK, so I'll create a new account. I attempt to use that email address as the login when creating the new account. Error: "that email has already been registered." Really? No, seriously. Really??? Sigh. OK, I'll use a completely different email and create an account. :(

Once I managed to create an account and login, I am told I have to install... software. You don't say. Software. Like the software I have installed for my 880? So, you can't update... you can't... REALLY? OK, so by this time, I'm just like WHATEVER. I gave up. Perhaps I should have done this sooner, because at this point things got a bit easier. After installing the new software, setting up your devices and activities is not only easy but it is a much more intuitive endeavor than it ever was using the software for my 880. Would I have preferred it if Logitech had any idea about usability and I was able to port the data over from my 880? Sure. But whatever, at least if they make you do it again, they make it a somewhat nicer experience. Hey, maybe this is going to work out after all! Link detects your wifi... password... Link is connected to your wifi... you're all done! Great!

So I take it to the living room and set it up by my AV center and I'm actually pretty jazzed! The light goes green... all set! I download the app to my iPad and prepare for the awesomeness. The app comes up and asks you to select your unit from the list... mine appears as "Living Room." I click it, I see the email I used, and it asks me for the password. I enter the password and... get that spinny thing. And you know, it's taking a really long time. It's taking the kind of time that you can just feel in your bones is going to end badly. And so it does.

ErrorCode: 2 ErrorDetail: FAIL

FAIL. In all caps. Not even kidding. This amused me briefly, until I realized that this was the end of the line. This is it. End of line. I went through all the suggestions. Reboot the Link, uninstall and reinstall the app. I even tried using the wrong password just so I could get a different error message. But when I go back, use the right password and try to get this useless hunk of plastic to work, the result is always the same: ErrorDetail: FAIL. No explanation. No exposition. No nothing. It literally just flat-out doesn't work. At all.

So, like many users here, I will be returning this unit. I suggest you heed my warning and not bother blowing the hundred bucks in the first place.

Finally, I would like to say: it's fairly criminal that there aren't a dozen or more units that function like this one is supposed to to choose from in 2012. How hard can this be? IR remote controlled by iPad via wifi - this really shouldn't be so difficult. And yet, I bought this unit despite the crap reviews precisely BECAUSE there is literally NO ALTERNATIVE! I find that pretty shocking.

The Circular Polarizer filter is by far my most favorite filter of the bunch. I was able to remove reflections from the streams. Also there was times the sun hit the leaves in a certain way which reduced the colors drastically. With the filter i was able to bring back those colors. I also noticed it made the sky have a darker more blue look to it.

I dont shoot indoors much so I havent been able to test the FLD filter. But knowing its in my bag makes me feel ready for when that time comes.

Pros - UV filter protects my lens, CPL Filter reduces light reflection and helps with color contrast.

Cons - I want to buy another set for my other size lenses

For the price its a great value. The peace of mind is worth it alone.

title: Don't BUY, not worth the headaches
text:
Bought my Win8 laptop and one of these devices and after messing with it for an hour found out through Netgear support that it needs a firmware update to work on Win8. Netgear can't tell me when this will happen so it's useless at the moment. Not happy that they can't get this done quickly. So at this point can't tell you how well it works because it doesn't.

Updated 4/30/2013
If I had to do over, I would not buy the PTV3000. I have gone around and around with different drivers, firmware, etc. Sometimes it works and the next day it doesn't. Right now I am on Firmware 2.21.15, latest WiDi version 4.0.18.0, Latest Intel WiFi version 15.6.1, running Win 8 - 64 bit, Intel i5, 8 Gig Ram, Win Exp Index of 5.8 and a broadband connection with Fios of 50/20 with an actual tested WiFi speed of 20/30 on an N Router.

Problem is when I connect Widi, it takes forever, then I watch my Wifi Signal drop by 1/2, my D/L speed drops to 1, it works for a while until finally the PTV quits and goes back to square one and the WiDi app still shows connected. After that, I have to reboot, because the WiFi dies on the vine.

I don't know if its NetGear, Intel, or my Ultrabook, but at this point it all stinks. I have been having issues since November and 90% of the time it doesn't work and the 10% of the time, it works half @$$.

If I was a regular computer user versus a hacker type, I would have thrown the PTV3000 in the garbage in frustration. So far I have only gotten as far as thinking about it. I don't like letting the tech beat me, but I am going to give up again for a while until they get this problem (if they can) fixed.

In my opinion Netgear hasn't got an answer because I truly believe they and Intel still haven't figured it out completely. Yes it may work for some of you, but my experience so far has been complete crap. If you have the latest drivers of everything after all these revisions it should work by now.

text:
I purchased the U-Board for several reasons. The first was that I wanted to raise my MBP to the same height as my 23" ACD. PROS

CONS
- At this price, I expected workmanship to be higher quality. It's not.

title: Outstanding product, very highly recommended !!
text:
Looong time back I bought the Bose TriPort IE which I still love for its simplicity. Later, by chance I got a hand on the Shure SCL4.

The Shure SCL4 has served me well for the past.
But after 6 years of usage I consider to upgrade.

My selection was between

- Sony XBA-H3
- Westone 4R
- Shure 535 or 530
- Ultimate Ears UE900
- Bose QuietComfort 20i

I read about the issues typical earphones have.
- weak cable connections
- insufficient noise isolation
- easy to break

I felt like the XBA-H3 is a solid built (with one exception that can be fixed).
The included ear pads should be replaced.
They don't even deliver the level of noise isolation I got used to from my Shure SCL4 from 6 years ago.

So a bit of the quality gets "lost" because of the standard seals that come with it.
First thing I swapped towards thicker foam ear pads.
So I used Shure's extra thick foam pads and adjusted the center hole so it fits on the Sony.

Size: Compared to typical in ear phones the XBA-H3 feels clumsy.
This is of course to accommodate the 3-way driver unit.

Sound quality: With a 3-way driver unit installed it should not come at a surprise that the Sony delivers the sound of a big headphone in a compact portable package. The XBA-H3 even compares to big headphones like the Audio Technica ATH-AD1000 that I use at home. So the XBA-H3 really doesnt have to hide.

Long time listening: Surprisingly it doesnt get burdersome listening 4 or even 8+ hours (flight).

Other: Sleeping with these in the ears might be an issue due to their size.
When you turn the head you might press against the earphone.

Conclusion:
I believe you will be hard pressed to find anything better in the current marcet.

You really have to listen to it to believe it.
The headphone produces an incredible amount of details.

Sony delivers two accessory cables with the earphone.
One cable with 3 contacts and one with 4 contacts (and build in mic).
So you can use it on your stereo as well as a headset on your phone.
Also included is an accessory pouch and 4 size of ear pads.

Outstanding product, very highly recommended !!

One thing is sure, other makers really have to step up their game now ... ;-)

title: Big step backwards in ergonomics and general utility
text:
I have owned 6 different Logitech Harmony remotes, and thus far, have liked or loved them all.
This new unit, although it looks very fancy, has a big touch screen display, works very well in both RF and IR mode, and has a generally pleasing form-factor, is a big step in the wrong direction in terms of daily use.
First, the battery life is absolutely horrific. If you don't plan on storing the remote in the charger (I don't have an electrical outlet near my seating position), then plan to get about 2 to 3 days of intermittent use out of the remote before it completely dies without warning and needs a full recharge. Not having the option to use alkaline batteries is a big detriment here, but even the rechargeable harmonys I've had have been vastly superior to the battery life of this unit.
Second, the ergonomics feel very awkward in the hand (to me). Too bottom heavy, too wide and thin on top and just not easy to navigate and use with one hand.
Third, the touch screen is very sensitive so I find myself constantly brushing against the screen or having a leg or hand barely come into contact with the remote and, thus, altering function, changing input and channel, etc.
Finally, the layout of controls, although simpler and more consolidated, does not fit the pattern and button layout of any previous harmony product. In my opinion, it is not as intuitive and easy to manipulate.
I hate to say this, because I am a HUGE Logitech fan (have owned dozens of their outstanding problems througout the years, without complaint), this my most loathed of all tech/electronics purchases of the past 3 years....I rue the day I met thee, Logitech Harmony Ultimate!
By the way, I'm in my early 40's and have been a highly competent technophile my entire life, so these comments are not left by someone who remembers the Great Depression and thinks that Email is the newfangled witchcraft that will surely usher in the days of the apocalypse.

title: narrow field of view, purchase of wide angle lens neccessary
text:
I was in the market for a new consumer camcorder after my Canon HV20 HDV camcorder passed away. I really liked the HV20 but its zoom lens had a severely limited field of view at the low end of the zoom range (~45mm equivalent) that required purchase of a wide angle add on lens (Canon model costs >$200). I had to carry around this lens everywhere I wanted to record indoors in smaller rooms or outdoors group activities. Otherwise, the narrow field of view would have required a distance of at least 15-20 feet from groups of 3-5 people to get everybody into the picture. In most indoor settings distances such as these are difficult to achieve, especially in small rooms.

When testing new Canon m40 and m50 series models I was shocked to learn that the lens had the same FOV range as the old HV series, probably using the same lens ! I ended up purchasing a Panasonic HC-V700k that has a fantastic zoom range and image stabilization, starting at 28mm equivalent going to a useable (!) 46x, ideal for both close indoor and outdoor shots. The drawbacks are that it allows 60i/p only, and I am not so impressed with low light sensitivity, but otherwise the HC-V700 is a fine camcorder. I am sure the Canon m40/50 models have better color and low light sensitivity, but it is disappointing that Canon leaves their customers with such a limited lens option on its new mid-budget consumer camcorders that are otherwise much improved.

title: A featured packed fantastic computer for the money
text:
I didn’t buy this computer on Amazon but fell compelled to write a review anyway. I bought this computer to replace my 2011 HP G7 which abruptly died without any hope of repairing it. I was attracted to the specs, specifically the i3 processor, 10 point touchscreen, and excellent battery life. The aluminum lid and inside portion looks and feels great, the Dell logo is metal also.

Pros:

- The battery life they claim is actually about right, which is amazing because every manufacturer seems to lie about it. With moderate use and the screen brightness at 80% I got 6 hours 53 minutes, with the brightness at 100% it dropped by a hour. The screen brightness out of the box is set below 80% so I am sure it could get the 7.4 hours they advertised.

- The processor, as mentioned, is an intel i3. Unfortunately, this chip is the 3rd generation Ivy Bridge and not the 4th generation Haswell. Having a 2012 chip in a 2013 laptop isn’t that big of a deal due to the low price of this computer. The Haswell processors are very expensive and can only be found in higher end computers. The i3 in this unit is very fast and can cold boot Windows 8.1 in only 16 seconds.

- The screen is good quality when compared to other sub $430 laptops. The ten point touchscreen is very responsive - I’m surprised at how responsive it is.

- It has 2 USB 3.0 ports and 1 USB 2.0 port which usually is the other way around on lower priced laptops.

- It has a “spill resistant keyboard” and also bluetooth

Cons:

- The computer only comes with 4GB of ram which I suppose is OK for light use. But if you plan on having a over a dozen tabs open and also running other programs at the same time you should really upgrade it. The good news is that a ram slot is open already because Dell put in one 4GB chip instead of two 2GB chips. I ordered an extra 4GB chip so I can max out the ram.

- The very top part of the screen is sightly not tucked under the bezel, I'm hoping that this is a one time defect. I ordered a replacement.

- The laptop is 100% silent except for the fan which always makes a humming sound, even if the computer is idling. I'm also hoping this is a one-time defect but I don't know.

- The video card is intel's “HD Graphics 4000,” which means you cant do more than light to lightly moderate gaming. It should work well with most business applications, though.

- It does not come with a SVGA monitor port, only HDMI out.

Overall, I am very pleased with this laptop. It would be great if Dell included some additional features such as a fingerprint reader, SVGA monitor port (which would permit me to use my two 19” external monitors on my desk), Blu-ray drive, Windows 8 Pro, and a better GPU. Most of these features are premium so they really aren’t a deal breaker when considering buying laptops in this price range.

I would encourage anyone who wants a quality touchscreen Windows 8.1 laptop that has phenomenal battery life and a fast processor to buy this computer. The quality feels very good and the aluminum is a nice touch for a laptop in this price range. You really cant do much better in the sub $430 market.

title: Only works if you pay for monitoring
text:
I travel extensively for work and bought this camera to keep tabs on my house while I'm away. Sadly, I had to return it.

The camera was extremely easy to set up and the night vision is awesome! It could clearly see the far side of the room which is about 30' away. However, one thing they don't mention in the literature is that the motion detector is sensitive to light and will read light changes as motion. This means that every time a cloud passes your window (or over a skylight) an e-mail is sent telling you that there is motion in the house. This wasn't an issue during the 30 day free trial of paid monitoring. However, once the free trial expired, I was getting 30-40 emails per day for motion alerts.

When I contacted Dropcam, they told me they were aware of the problem and that the only way to solve it would be to purchase the monitoring package which would give the ability to set zones around the windows that the camera would ignore, thus eliminating the false motion alerts. After paying $200 for the product, I didn't want to be held ransom for another $200 per year to make the camera work right. Since I purchased the camera through Amazon, Dropcam told me there was nothing they could do except replace the camera with a new one which they admitted would have the exact same problem.

The situation was further exacerbated by the fact that the camera worked correctly for the first 30 days … meaning that Amazon's return policy had expired by the time the free monitoring trial had ended. Thankfully, Amazon agreed to return the camera anyway.

Long story short …
- Product only works as advertised if you pay the annual monitoring fee.
- Motion sensor send false alerts if you have windows in your room.
- Poor product support by the manufacturer.

title: Outstanding value!
text:
My expectations were tempered when I ordered this item, as it sounded nearly too good to be true. But after a month of using the battery and the wall charger, I can highly recommend this package. The battery charger will reliably charge the battery in under 2 hours from empty. The DC input and fold-away plug are a huge bonus when traveling. The battery itself seems as good as the original Sony which came with the camera, and it lasts longer (slightly larger capacity rating). I did have to insert battery into the charger several times at first, in order to loosen up a particularly snug contact which made the battery tough to eject from the camera. However, a couple trips into and out of the charger allowed the battery to then slide into and out of the camera as expected.

The screen protectors are decent quality and easy to apply. Not the best I have used, but they definitely beat scratching the display. I haven't noticed any real degradation of detail or color, although since they are not a matte finish, glare is still present.

title: Works flawlessly
text:
I know this is going to sound nuts, but I currently have 5 hard drives and 1 optical drive plugged into all 6 ports on my motherboard and I was looking for expansion to install a cache SSD drive, specifically, the Crucial Adrenaline. When I got the product, it looked very cheap and was a little surprised, but installing the cache SSD into the Apricorn Velocity Solo and booting up was easy and without any issues.

The only thing I should warn people about is that if you plug in a drive which contains your backup, like mine initially was connected to a hard drive that contains my system backup, and I used a CD to initiate backup process, it wasn't able to read the hard drive. But in normal operation, it worked flawlessly. The only other irritating thing is that, now "Safely remove drive" is always present due to this, not a huge problem, but its quite irritating when I remove removable drives. I can't test the speed as I'm using this on a PCIe X1 1.0 as my motherboard is pretty old by today's standard and do not have all the latest things like PCIe 3.0 or PCIe x1 2.0. However, SSDs are known for their speeds, cache SSDs are no different. Even though I'm using the Velocity Solo on a PCIe x1 1.0, the SSD speed is still very fast.

My system before installing the Velocity and cache SSD, booted up to a useable state where I can scroll in firefox took almost 9 mins, after the installation, my computer was up and ready in less than a minute, allowing me to fully surf the net to be exact. I wouldn't hesitate to recommend this or get another one to use on another computer.

title: Not a replacement for Sony VRD-MC6
text:
I ordered this to replace my malfunctioning Sony VRD-MC6 (which is no longer in production and is going for an obscene markup these days).

I use portable DVD recorders for my job as a professional legal videographer. In order to maintain a reasonable work flow, I record directly to DVD while out on the job. This recorder has at least two major marks against it (I didn't keep it long enough to see if there were any other issues).

1. It will not allow you to pause or stop during a recording and then resume recording to the same disk. As soon as you hit "stop" it begins formatting the disk. There did not appear to be any "pause" function.

2. Formatting takes a very long time.

This device will not work for situations where you need to be able to stop and resume recording and do not have a lot of time to wait for the long formatting process before switching out disks when you do stop it.

I give it two stars because the device will probably work well enough if you are just dubbing something from start to finish and are not on a schedule.

I returned it and bought an older Sony VRD-MC5. There is clearly still a market for portable DVD Recorders (given the high markup on the Sony's), and Pegasus might have found a comfortable niche selling a comparable product. Unfortunately, while this may look like the Sony recorders, it doesn't come close to performing like one.

title: Need patience and two 19mm spring pins to make this work!
text:
Apparently Garmin doesn't read these reviews, and whoever responsible for designing this wrist strap kit should frankly be fired. First, no instructions. This is annoying, but the least of your worries -- the lack of 19mm spring pins is the real problem.

Here are the installation steps: (1) The two plastic connectors connect to the watch (they only go on one way). Put the connector on and then use 2 of the 4 straight tension pins included to pushall the way through connector and watch. The pins, however, are extremely difficult to push through (you'll be tempted to get a ball pin hammer out!). I bent one trying, but finally after much cursing they went in. The tool doesn't help with this, you need to press it against a hard surface and just push.(2) place the strap under the watch with the "buckle" on top and the velcro on the bottom, face up. You'll see now where the loops attach to the connectors on the watch. (3) Here's the frustrating part: you'll need two 19mm spring pins -- if you use the 2 other plain tension pins that came with the set it's not going to work (some complain of the pins falling out). Cunningham's review mentions this but I thought maybe Garmin finally put the right pins in the package. I figured I could cannibalize another watch to get 19mm SPRING PINS if I really did need them. Yup, I needed them. I think it is ABSURD that you'd have to either have the pins at the ready or spend $4.75 on them. (You can buy them on Amazon). GARMIN SHOULD INCLUDE IN THE KIT EVERYTHING YOU NEED TO INSTALL THE BAND! But they don't. That's the reason for my 3 stars. Once I got the band on I liked the end result in terms of the better fit on my small wrist. But this "project" was more frustrating than it should have been, and if I didn't have the 19mm spring pins I would've been furious. You've now been warned!

title: Good Overall Player
text:
I purchased a secondhand Pioneer DVL-919 recently. Mine is the champagne coloured one that is made in Japan.

When I accidentally damaged my Panasonic LX K700 LD player, I needed a replacement. Although I also have a Blu-Ray and DVD player, I still have a fairly large collection of laser discs which would cost a bomb replace with Blu-rays and DVDs. My first purchase was a Pioneer Laserdisc CD Karaoke CLD-3760KV. The sound was good but the picture quality was not up to my standards so I bought the DVL-919. I am truly happy with it!

On the LD side, the picture quality is good. I had also subsequently bought a Pioneer CLD Elite 99 and a HLD X9 laser disc players. In comparison, the DVL-919 picture quality is not as good as these 2 high end players. But the image quality is still good compared to the players that are not the 'Elite' or high end ones.

Of course, you cannot compare LD image quality to a DVD or Blu-ray image as there is a 30-year difference in technology. That's like comparing apples and oranges! Side change is very quick. You can 'pause' to a scene and see the picture rather than get a blue screen like other models.

DVD picture quality is also good. Despite what you may read on the online reviews that combination players are not that good, this is not the case here. The DVD image is good.

In my opinion, sound quality is where the LD is till better than a DVD or Blu-ray due to the compression and size difference between them. The player has the following features which ensures that the sound is great when playing LD or CD:

1. Video Noise Reduction
2. Virtual Dolby Surround (certified by Dolby Laboratories Inc.)
3. DTS (Digital Theater System) Digital Audio Output Terminal

I have no problems with the remote. It's big and fits into my large hands. Has a display dimmer if you want to dim or not see the LED display. Has a light switch you can activate if you are watching a movie in the dark. Maybe the arrangement of the buttons could be more user friendly but this is just a minor issue with me.

Only other issue is that this model is bigger than most LDs and I have to place it over my amplifier in such a way that the front sticks out a little. Again, just a small issue with me and not a big deal.

Also, do not believe the rumours that it can play both NTSC and PAL LDs. I found that out the hard way and now have 3 PAL LDs I cannot play! The DVL-919 can only play the NTSC LDs. The European version, the DVL-919E is the one that can play PAL Laser discs. However, this was my mistake for not doing a bit of research earlier.

Overall, A good player and I would recommend it. It can play LD, DVD and CD with a great sound quality. So, what more can you ask for?

title: Must have for the GoPro line of cameras
text:
Well, I have been through several action cams and I must say that the video quality on the GoPro Hero series has been the best. I have pretty much settled in to the Veho MUVI HD line and the GoPro Hero3 Black edition.

The only thing the irked me about the GoPro was the exclusion of an LCD preview screen. Now, granted for many uses and LCD screen is well....useless. But there are those times when having the screen is the difference between the perfect angle and wasted SD Card space and time.

How would you like to get home just to find out that you had the camera at an angle that looked just goofy?

On to the screen....Well, it's pretty simple really. You snap it on the back of the GoPro (like many other of the accessories for this cam) and you are off. What does it allow for? Well, the obvious is the ability to preview what you are shooting and also to review what you have shot. The other, VERY important advantage is the ability to navigate the menus (something that I feel the Veho MUVI HD NAILS!!!). The screen turns this otherwise daunting (ok maybe not daunting, but pretty cruddy) task into a few touches here and there. Oh yeah, and the waterproof casing for the screen works remarkably well in terms of responsiveness through the membrane.

The main disadvantage that I see is the battery life reduction. Ok, the battery life on the GoPro is already not too awesome, but with the screen it gets worse. Again, remember what this camera is for and you will be fine.

title: Good but flawed, fragile and expensive - a cash cow for Sony
text:
I bought this camera Dec 2012, and have used it in a variety of circumstances. If I had it to over again, I would not buy it.

I generally like the camera. Its small and light, and fairly efficient. It turns on quickly and captures images quickly. Its a great camera to carry daily and capture the things you would miss. The image quality is very good.

For reference, I normally use/used Nikon D800, D700, D3s, Hasselblad H3d-31, H4d-40, Phaseone P65+. Compared to those the focus is much slower but the weight is much less. I also have a Canon G11 for a pocket camera - which is paintfully slow to record each image. So the Sony is a pretty ideal 'every day carry camera', albeit with a wide angle view on everything.

I read the blog reviews by Steve Huff, Lloyd Chambers, and Ken Rockwell. I pretty much agree with all of them, but feel Steve loves the camera, the other two liked it but ultimately rejected it. All point out the good image quality, but Ken pointed out there is a slight greenish tint - I agree but its somewhat subtle and can be compensated for in lightroom but colors still don't look quite right. Lloyd felt the camera didn't have a comfortable ease of use even after weeks of usage. I don't think its too bad, but there is a huge ton of menu options to wade through. I think everyone agrees that it can be slow to focus, but generally I don't think its too bad - it might take 5 seconds to rack back and forth to get the focus at twilight or in darker situations. The focus peaking feature is very helpful and I wish professional cameras had this - but still some of my images were not sharp using this, so not sure what is up with that.

There are several things very significantly negative about this camera in addition to those issues. First of all its fragile. I dropped a D700 3 feet onto concrete and there was no damage at all. The sony was around my neck on a very short neck strap and as I bent over to pick something up, it swung left to right, knocked something, and the glass over the LCD shattered. I was unhappy about that, but it worked fine and thought I would just live with it. Then two weeks later the focus system went out - and it was impossible to focus using auto focus or manual focus.

The second problem is that Sony is unreasonable. I took the camera to a Sony store and they said the focus problem was clearly a warranty issue since the camera was only 3 months old. However, the Sony repair center said that the entire warranty was void. They presented me with a bill for $950 to repair both the focus problem and the cracked glass.

By comparison, I have had $3000-$5000 Nikon's repaired by Nikon for never more than $225. I have had two $12,000 used Hasselblad's repaired by Hasselblad for about $450 each. I have personally put a Schott glass screen cover on a Nikon D3s for $20 and there were instructions for removing it by heating it up to losen the glue. And in years of photography I have never seen a glass screen crack or break before this despite all kinds of abuse in the field. So $950 for a repair on a new camera point and shoot is just out of control. Its more than the price of a new Sony Nex-6 or Nex-7 (and keep in mind the problems were not with the expensive RX-1 sensor - they were with mundane parts of the camera). They also refused to fix just the focus problem without fixing the cracked glass. Essentially they had a set of rules that were all to their benefit and I had no options at all. So this camera has now cost me $3500 for the camera alone. It might cost me more if I buy hazard insurance, or a heavy duty leave-on case that takes away from the qualities of being small and light.

A third negative is that Sony charges astronomical fees for every accessory with this camera. Want a charger for your battery? Thats a fee. You want a lens shade for the lens, $200. You want a view finder, $450. Everything about this camera is out of control in price. The feeling I have, is that this camera is geared toward rich people with big pockets, and Sony is out to fleece them as much as possible - as evidenced by the out of control accessory prices and out of this world repair costs - and how easily they voided their warranty.

I am nervous to use this camera now that I see how easily it breaks. I also read another reviewer who mentioned the lack of weather sealing. We know the focus system is subpar. Yes, it has the same size sensor as the $1800 Nikon D600, but why exactly is this simple camera with a lack of pro features so expensive?

I would also say that dealing with Sony's support staff was no piece of cake. I spent over 4 hours on the phone over 10 days - either on hold or shuffled off to another person. A supervisor promised to ask an engineer if the cracked glass was related to the focus problems that developed later, and would call back in "an hour" - that hour turned out to be 10 days. I have had much better experiences with Nikon and Hasselblad tech departments - getting clear answers with a lack of hold time.

If I had it do over again, I would buy a Fuji, and wait a year for another company to come out with a full frame mini.

text: I'm an avid DIY'er, after much research and reading the reviews on this product I decided to purchase..bad idea.  I followed the directions to the "T" and overcharged my system.  What the manufacturer's don't mention is that when your A/C is running the condenser is cycling off while recharging; this gives a faulty reading to the fill level that's coming from the condenser.  Now what used to be somewhat cool air is warm, there's a chemical smell coming from my A/C vents while it's running, the condenser no longer cycles off which leads me to believe it may be going out or definitely is going to need to be evacuated, and I'm going to be out more money for taking it in for repairs.  If you've done your own recharge before, you should be okay.  If not, beware, have someone with experience teach you before taking the plunge yourself.  Also the pen light that came with the kit did not function.  Wouldn't recommend it.

title: Not all bad
text:
This is my second N9. The first one I received had pretty bad backlight bleeding so i rolled the dice and exchanged it for a new one. I've had this tablet for about 1 week now. I use it everyday so here are my thoughts and concerns.

First off, 2 issues:
LED Backlight bleed - this second unit had a lot less backlight bleed than the first. There is just a tiny bit in the top left side if you hold the tablet in landscape orientation with the camera on the left. I'm not saying that this is acceptable but backlight bleeding is a common issue with LED screens. It's not enough to bother me but I'm still on the fence about returning this unit and waiting for Google/HTC to release a v2 or just wait for the next batch. Got a couple weeks left to send this back to Amazon.

Heat - I also experience the warm spot right near/under the camera but that's probably where the CPU and GPU are located so yes, typically those spots will get pretty warm. It's not crazy hot though where it will warp or wear the plastic backing. I had the tablet running for 5 hours the other day and it never got uncomfortably hot. I think my phone gets more hot and more uncomfortable than the tablet. As I feel this is an issue, I'm hoping that with some software updates they can improve this (if that is possible)

Things I like:
Lollipop - it's smooth, it's great, it's a huge upgrade from Kit Kat. I love the card system. It makes multitasking so much easier. I also like how the UI looks flatter and more simple. Just makes everything a bit more clean looking. Also nice to be able to get updates right away with no bloatware and extra crap that's not needed.

Design - I like the simple design. The tablet feels great in my hands, it's not too heavy, the design looks sophisticated while not being flashy (like the Samsung Tab S with it's gold rim). I appreciate the buttons being capacitive rather than physical buttons. That way the home button is always between my hands (keeps it out of the way when I play games in landscape)

Speakers - I know people expected more out of the HTC Boom sound but I actually think they do pretty well for speakers on a mobile device. It's a lot better than any other ones that have speakers on the back or bottom where when you lay it down it sounds muffled. With this, I can actually have some decent sound when listening to Pandora while I cook in the kitchen. Also, when watching a movie, it's nice having the sound in stereo pointing at me rather than to the sides or the back.

Everything else about the tablet is meh. Camera, never expected too much out of it. Display, it's nice but it's not breathtaking like Samsung's AMOLED (which is just super saturated). Battery life is pretty good but I don't think it's what they listed on their spec sheet.

Overall, I think the tablet handles well. If you want a pure Android experience, this is the tablet to get. Form factor is about perfect and I prefer a 4:3 ratio for the display. I don't mind the black bars while watching a movie or Netflix, I actually like it since the controls are in the black area.

Now, like all the other people, I'm still debating about returning this device (hence the 3 stars) and waiting or testing my luck again for a non defective unit. Any advice would be great.

title: Noise cancelling is LIGHT years behind Audio-Technica
text:
Full disclosure: I own Audio-Technica ATH-ANC7B headphones, which I purchased on Amazon in 2012, two years prior to when this review is being published. I used them so much that I took advantage of the warranty replacement due to loss of hearing in one ear after one year. And another year later, the seam has ripped so the yellow foam in one ear cup is sticking out. Everything still works flawlessly, but the inside of the left ear cup looks quite ghetto.

After that, I figured I'd give another brand a try because there are a few things about the ANC7B I don't like -- horrible sound leak AND hissing with noise cancelling turned on; the NC switch eventually needs to be jiggled to the perfect spot or the left ear doesn't play sound; and the low battery repeating audio signal comes on 3-4 hours before the battery is dead and is _extremely_ annoying.

-----

The Good:

The Solitude fixes all of that:
- There is zero hiss with the noise cancelling turned on.
- There is no sound leak, as far as my partner could tell.
- And the NC switch is easy to toggle without feeling like it will cause problems later on.
- I don't know about the low battery warning, but the manual says it only comes on 30 minutes before the battery dies.

Even better, the Solitude XCS feel great. They're MUCH lighter than the ANC7B headset, and I have to admit more comfortable too.

Minor bonuses:
a) The packaging material and booklet makes you feel like you're buying a premium product.
b) The inline microphone cable is a nice bonus too. (The ANC7B now comes with an option to buy a microphone cable too, but that was not available when I purchased them in 2012.)
c) The volume control on the headset could be useful for some. For me, I'm accustomed to just using my phone's volume buttons, so I don't think I would use this feature much.

-----

The Bad:

Unfortunately, the noise isolation on the Solitude is downright awful. With the ANC7B, just putting on the headphones with nothing playing immediately muffles A LOT of external noise. It fully encloses your ears and could certainly be used as noise cancelling earmuffs without even an audio source connected.

The Solitude XCS feels almost no better than on-ear headphones, rather than the noise reduction that you would EXPECT from headphones that enclose your ear. There's barely any depth to the foam area, and with no audio playing, there's almost zero external sound reduction.

-----

The Ugly:

Now this is the really disappointing part. The noise cancelling is LIGHT years behind the ANC7B. I purchased the Solitude XCS specifically because it is rated for 18 dB attenuation whereas the ANC7B is rated at 20 dB. I guess those 2 decibels are larger than they seem, because the noise cancelling is a ***WORLD*** of difference. I literally was switching between both headsets on my desk back and forth and turning on the noise cancelling and the difference is night and day. It really is a huge difference, extremely noticeable when you own both pairs, one right next to the other.

Even worse, there is a noise cancelling feature, and a volume amplifying feature (to increase the volume). However, turning on the noise cancelling does NOT amplify the volume! Why not??? It's already using battery power, why the heck wouldn't it increase the volume??? That makes absolutely zero sense whatsoever.

Turning on the noise cancelling on the ANC7B also amplifies the volume by quite a significant amount, making it a godsend for air travel. The fact that the Solitude doesn't do this renders the Solitude useless for air travel in my opinion. Removing the jet engine noise is one thing, but I still prefer to boost the volume to drown out all OTHER external noise except for what I'm listening to. In fact, at home, with noise cancelling turned on and maximum volume, I could still hear external noises. With the ANC7B, the world was on mute.

-----

Summary:

I am extremely disappointed in the noise isolating and noise cancelling performance of the Solitude XCS. If this is your first foray into noise cancelling headphones, or you just don't care about noise reduction (but then why are you considering buying these?), then the Solitude XCS are a decently nice pair of headphones, especially for the price (though the ANC7B can be found Used - Like New or Very Good for not much more than the Solitude). These are decently nice, but not in comparison to the ANC7B. I'm giving it 2-stars instead of 1 because of the premium feel of the headphones and packaging, and the fantastic weight/comfort.

However, if you're spoiled by any other high-end noise cancelling headphones like I am, then this review is for you, and I think you'll be very disappointed like I was.

I have already returned the Solitude XCS.

However, and this might surprise you, I will NOT be purchasing another Audio-Technicas, because of the annoying issues listed at the beginning of this review. I was trying to save some money by going cheaper, but I've learned that good noise cancelling costs money. I'll never purchase a cheaper headset than my ANC7B. I'm considering getting the Bose QC15, or possibly a higher level of Audio-Technica.

I'm looking for a the best noise cancelling headphones that don't have hiss, sound leak, and preferably don't cost $250 like the Bose QC15. But, if that's the price, I might just have to pay up. Anyone have suggestions?

-----

TLDR:

Solitude:
++ No hiss
++ No sound leak/bleed
+ Lighter
+ More comfortable
+ Better noise cancelling switch / less prone to cause issues over time
~ Volume control on headset
~ Mic on cable
-- Worse noise isolation/reduction
--- Terrible active noise cancellation
--- Volume is NOT amplified while noise cancellation is enabled (this is baffling)

Audio Technica:
+++ Significantly better active noise cancellation
++ Much better noise isolation
+ Volume boost (amp) while noise cancelling is enabled
- Heavier, not as comfortable
-- Noticeable hiss when NC is turned on and nothing is playing
-- Horrible sound leak/bleed with NC turned on
-- Low battery warning is very annoying
-- NC switch is tough to toggle and also prone to breaking; eventually needs to be jiggled into the perfect spot or the left ear won't play sound

title: The HDHomeRun instructions you might want for use with Linux
text:
This thing produces amazing picture and sound quality even with weak signals. Of course, if the signals are really weak in your area (see TVfool), you'll need an antenna placed where it can detect the signals, and with enough gain to boost them to a level suitable for an antenna preamp. Once that's done, you should have no problems getting amazing video and audio from this overpriced project box with a couple of silicon tuner ICs and leds inside. If anyone else made a similar product, they'd have to compete and the price would drop to about $30.

You'd think that SiliconDust would spend some of their obscene profits on documentation for Linux. Windows installation is automatic, so no Windows documentation is required.

After flailing about for a couple of days, I discovered that the necessary software (hdhomerun-config and hdhomerun-config_gui) can be installed automatically on a computer running Ubuntu, via the Synaptic Package Manager, which itself might first have to be installed via the Ubuntu Software Center. Ubuntu Software Center installs only the GUI, which oddly doesn't facilitate recording - just tuning, essentially. However, I'm not certain that Synaptic Package Manager installs the VLC player, which is one of the few players that can play the HDHomeRun's output directly. So I suggest installing all of the software first via Synaptic, and then checking for the VLC player. If it's not present, then install the GUI software via Ubuntu Software Center - it will install only what Synaptic didn't. Or you could get a degree in programming, and do it manually.

Then, by entering some simple commands (outlined below) into command-lines in terminal windows, you can save the HDHomeRun's output directly to your hard drive with no conversion to another format, so the recordings are also amazing, but they consume a lot of disk space. (By the way, the xfs format is the most efficient for recording and deleting those potentially vast ts files, so you might want to create a partition for your Videos directory and give it the xfs format.)

The HDHomeRun can be connected directly to PC's, and this paragraph describes how this is done with a computer running Ubuntu 12.04. (Connecting the HDHR to a router would be simpler, if you had a router.) In Windows, this setup is totally automatic, but in Ubuntu, it's only partly automatic. In Ubuntu (as with Windows), you have to first connect the signal and power to the HDHomerun, and connect it to your PC. Then you open the System Settings ("gear" icon on left of screen) and select Network, select Wired, and then set the on/off button to On. Then, you click on Options, then IPv4 Settings. Then, in the Method box, select Link-Local Only, and Ubuntu will automatically establish a connection to the HDHomeRun. The exact procedure will vary between some versions of Ubuntu, but I assume there will be some resemblance. If the HDHR and your computer ever have difficulty establishing a connection, after having established connections previously, go into System Settings/Network/Wired and verify that the port is turned on. Sometime clicking on Rescan in the HDHR control panel helps.

At this point, you should be able to fire up the HDHomeRun GUI by clicking on its icon on the left side of the screen (assuming you let the Ubuntu Software Center and Synaptic Package Manager install the HDHomeRun software, as described above). You should also be able to find channels and view them via the VLC player. (If scenes with motion appear "smeared," this could be due to the VLC player's difficulty with de-compressing the amount of compression used by that station. One fix is to record it and convert it to another format before viewing.) YOU CAN ALSO SAVE THE PROGRAM YOU'RE WATCHING to Downloads by clicking on the Record button, which can be made to appear by clicking on View in the main menu, and selecting Advanced Controls.

The VLC player produces smeared/pixelated video when playing some programs, because some high-definition programs are difficult to decode "on the fly" due to the amount of compression used in encoding them. Although I can't rule out other solutions, one solution that works very well for me is to save the program to disk, and convert it to a format which is easier to play. A "transcoder" program called Handbrake performs such conversions very simply, and with excellent results. You just need enough space on your drive for the source file and the output file.

As far as I know, VLC doesn't facilitate recording both tuners' outputs simultaneously. Its documentation doesn't say anything about recording, and there's nothing about recording with VLC on the internet either (or at least there wasn't until this was published), other than a passing remark about the hidden Record button.

However, there is a way to record the outputs of both tuners simultaneously without installing any more software. It requires typing (or copying/pasting) text into the Linux command-line, which is accessed by pressing Ctrl-Alt-t. Pasting into the command line in done with Ctrl-Shift-v.

First, set each tuner to the desired channel, and note that each tuner has the same ID#, followed by -0 or -1 (displayed in the GUI). Then open two terminal-windows, because once you start a recording process in one window, you won't be able to enter any more commands into it.

Then decide where you want to put the recordings (.ts files) and change the directory (folder) to that directory by typing cd Downloads or cd Videos (or whatever folder you want to use) into the command line, and pressing Enter. (Note: the cd command is case-sensitive, so that "videos" is not the same directory as "Videos.") Then decide what you want to name the files. In the first, terminal, enter the following command:

hdhomerun_confg ID# save /tunerN filename.ts,

where ID# is the tuner's ID#, N is 0 or 1, and filename is the file where you want to save that tuner's output. (These commands can be found in the HDHomeRun Development Guide, which can be found by Googling the title.)

That should start the recording process for that tuner, and the terminal-window will start filling up with dots to indicate recording in progress.

To record the other tuner's output, do the same thing in another terminal-window.

To stop EACH recording, click on the ID# of the associated tuner in the GUI "control panel," click on Stop, and then close the associated terminal-window.

Once you're done recording, you can close the terminal windows, open the VLC player, and open the recording you want to watch.

Those who want to automate recording to a degree similar to that of programming a VCR should consider HDHomeRun Recorder. The official page can be found by Googling "hdhomerun_recorder" (with the quotation marks and the underscore). As of this writing (12/12), the best set of instructions I've seen on installing and using it is contained in the Michigan Telephone blog, also evidently written by a programmer.

title: When radio dies, dealing with XM customer service requires medication
text:
I'm on my third XM Onyx. The first one died after 2 years, but had been a nice little radio till then. I purchased a replacement, but after 2 weeks the screen went blank. I called XM about it, and here's how my day went:
When I called customer service, I gave them my account info and was put on hold. The Customer Service Rep answers, asks for account info, puts me on hold again. The hold music is scratchy keyboard, like a warped 78 record. When she comes back on line, she tells me I have to talk to "Advanced Service Rep," and--you guessed it---puts me on hold.
I wished I had a copy of WAR AND PEACE because I had time to read it.
The Advanced Service guy finally come on the line, asks for account info then says, "Please hold while I look up your account." His hold music is also scratchy keyboard but more grating. When he comes back, Advanced guy says I have to talk to someone in "E-commerce," because "They can get you a new radio."
Okay, I'm getting closer, I think. The E-commerce agent asks for account info, puts me on hold, then comes back on and says, no, I wasn't supposed to call her. "Dial this number," she says. I dial it and I'm BACK to the Customer service voice loop. I could have read three chapters by now. This rep eventually sends me back to an "Advanced Service Rep" and I wonder if I'm an unwitting subject in some macabre experiment.
This guy (after asking for my account information) says I must go back to E-commerce. "No!" I cry out desperately, "No, no--I've already been there, they say you have to help," and he says, "I don't know why they told you that, you need to talk with them, here's the number." I ask to talk with a supervisor. He says he is the supervisor, and to call the number he gave me. I decide that the next mystery novel I write will include a murder in a call center.
This E-commerce person at least has better "hold" music. A jazzier tune, less staticky, with vocals: A woman singing "I want to move to Italy." I got hear the whole song. Twice. E-commerce eventually comes on the line and asks for--surprise, surprise-- my account info. Then I'm back on hold (no lyrics this time, but three unnerving electronic notes repeated over and over and over). I start plotting out the murder mystery in my head. The killer might even get off because it's clearly a justifiable homicide.
"So you say your radio is broken," E-Commerce says, waking me from my slumber. "Would you like another one? Can I have you repeat your account information?"

I realize then that it's the call center itself that is the antagonist in my novel-to-be. They're driving customers to the brink of madness. Perhaps they are Taliban operatives, and "customer service" is actually a terrorist plot. What messages have they imbedded in that infernal hold music?
E-commerce finally promises a new radio. I'm not even sure I want it now. What subliminal messages might it relay when I'm listening to Dr. Billy or Ted Talks?
And why do I have this sudden desire to move to Italy?
