title: The PN60E6500 is well worth the extra $200
text:
The product photo for these TVs (the 550 series) shows a matte, anti-reflective screen. This is misleading. The 550 series does NOT feature an anti-reflective screen. It has no anti-reflective coating at all. It is as reflective as glass, and consequently not the best choice for rooms with windows.

Amazon's product description for the 550 series is identical to its description for the next model up (the 6500 series). Reading the two descriptions, a reasonable person will conclude that the only difference between the 550 and the 6500 is the type of stand that the TV sits on. In particular, both TVs are said to feature a "Real Black Panel" and both screens are shown with the same matte finish. So why not get this TV (the 550) and save $200?

Here is the crucial difference: This TV (the 550) has the basic "Real Black Panel," which Samsung describes as an "advancement in software technology that provides deeper and darker black levels for bolder hues, higher contrast, and smoother, clearer picture quality." In other words, the basic "Real Black" is purely a function of software, not of anti-reflective coating.

The 6500 on the other hand has "Real Black Panel Pro," which Samsung describes as "An advancement within the panel structure of the plasma and a software improvement that depicts blacker blacks, bolder color, higher contrast and exceptional picture quality. This technological improvement provides the most cinematic viewing experience available." In other words, it has the software as well as the anti-reflective coating that distinguishes the high-end Samsungs. Amazon mentions that the much pricier 7000 and 8000 models have "Real Black Panel Pro," but neglects to mention that the 6500 has it too.

Again, it depends on the lighting situation in the intended room, but in most situations, the 6500 is well worth the added expense.

title: has nice features; only accommodates one oversized plug
text:
Despite having 5 surge protectors in active use in my office at the moment, I haven't actually been able to test this against a real power surge... nor am I likely to do so for purposes of a review. That said, here are some highlights:

Pros:
* Easy-to-read light tells you whether your power strip is grounded or not (first time I personally have ever seen that feature on a power strip)
* Has a recessed on/off switch, so it's a little more difficult to bump on accident (although I still have to turn all my plugs at a 90 degree angle to the floor because my cats like to step on them, and this one does click on/off fairly easily)
* Low-profile plug where the power strip plugs into the wall - helpful for tight spaces behind desks, and the cord juts out to the bottom/right at about 45 degrees, so you can actually use this in the top spot of a normal paired outlet without blocking the lower outlet

Cons:
* Only supports one large plug (and you can see from the picture the direction the rest of them have to be oriented). Honestly, this is a huge drawback for me since normally 1/2 to 1/3 of the plugs I use need a little extra space.

Neutral:
* Includes child-safety covers that aren't easy to open/close, but easy enough with the metal end of an plug
* Includes one phone "input" and two "output" spots (although I use VOIP and a wireless phone, so it's a non-issue for me)
* $75,000 for coverage to damaged equipment SOUNDS like a great thing, but ultimately is probably more marketing than anything else, because it has a ton of caveats, like:
......... After damages, you have to ship the surge protector AND all damaged equipment to Belkin at your own expense
......... The damaged equipment you ship in MUST be accompanied by a receipt showing what you paid for it (so if I've lost the receipt for my years-old Dell, and don't have a receipt at all for the machine that was a gift from my husband's office, I'm out of luck)
......... ALL wires (even internet/modem) leading into equipment must pass through the surge protector
......... Belkin may chose to repair instead of replace, and then you have to pay for cost of shipping to/from the repair center
......... Doesn't cover damage due to _low_ voltage conditions (like brown-outs)
......... They won't just give you $75K; they'll only give you "fair market value of the damaged equipment OR original purchase price of the equipment, whichever is less" (and not incidental costs like lost business while your machine was out of service)
......... All damage claims must be made within 15 days from the date of the Occurrence

so the warranty isn't bad per se, but quite a hassle, and maybe not as impressive as you might originally assume.

title: Used to be good, now....
text:
After reading several reviews of WiFi range extenders, I settled on the Amped Wireless SR150. I needed to extend the WiFi over an additional 30 foot range. It has done the job. From the source WiFi, I can download at 10 Mbps. At the Amped WiFi, I can download at 7 Mbps. So, there's a slight degradation from the source, but it is not noticeable for steaming movies or surfing the internet. All in all, this product did the job that it promised. It has extended my WiFi throughout the house. I have unplugged and plugged in this device several times and I have yet to have any issues. So, I must recommend this if you're looking to extend your WiFi.
~~~~~~~~~~
UPDATE (3/29/13)
All in all, this product works. However, there are instances when this product resets for no apparent reason. This can happen when it stays on for long periods of time or when you turn off the source and then turn it back on. Usually, I'll just turn off both devices, and the turn them back on in a specific sequence (source first then the WiFi extender). That usually does the trick. Yet, I'm not inclined to try any other extender. It still seems to work for me 80% of the time.
~~~~~~~~~~
UPDATE (7/5/13)
This is my final update. After over a year of dealing with this extender, I have to say that it has become a problem. It no longer can connect to my home network. I have rebooted it, updated the firmware, turned it off and on. All to no avail. So, the life of this product is little over a year. I don't think that it's worth it. So, I can no longer recommend this WiFi extender.

title: Submerged in the Hudson River for 2+ weeks!
text:
My wife and I purchased this camera for our honeymoon to Mexico just about 3 months ago. We went in the pool, and swam in the underground rivers and it worked great! Our only complaint at that time, was that some pictures showed spots on them because of the water on the lens but otherwise, we were impressed. We were able to figure out most of the different features quickly just by going into the different menus and looking around.
Fast forward, 2 months, and we go river tubing with our friends. My wife wanted to take a silly picture of me but in the meantime, lost track of the camera and it fell to the bottom of the river. The area that we were in was about 4 feet deep and the current was moderate. Needless to say, we threw our hands up and said oh well. After we got home, my wife wrote to the local tubing companies letting them know that she had lost the camera. Two and a half weeks later, we are notified by one of the tubing companies that they believe they found our camera. We pick it up and it was indeed the same one! It was under the water for at least 2 weeks. Short of a few scratches, the camera worked like it did when we first took it out of the box. title: Best universal remote I've ever used
text:
My brother just got a new blu-ray, but the universal remote for his cable box that is about 6 years old does not support it, so I got this remote for him. At first I tried a $10 Philips universal remote (same brand as the blu-ray player), but for some reason the blu-ray was the only device that the new remote would not work with. It even had a learn button to copy the infrared signal from other remotes, but even that function wasn't working correctly for his blu-ray remote.

This remote is easy to set up. Just go to myharmony.com and register. It asks for an email but that just acts as your username. I have yet to receive any emails from logitech. Once you enter your devices' make/model, you can further customize the preset commands for anything that is missing, or reassign buttons you never use with different features if your remote has more buttons than the Harmony remote, such as a DVR.

I played with this at my house with a Hitachi TV, Pioneer receiver, Motorola DVR, and Windows Media Center before taking this to my brother's house and setting it up for his Samsung TV, Philips blu-ray, Onkyo receiver, and Scientific Atlanta DVR. It worked with all of the devices. The only issue is remembering the custom assignments if you reprogram a button.

Cons - Compared to other universal remotes I've tried, there are very few cons. I would say the software could be a little more open. You can set the volume controls to work with a device other than which device is selected on the remote. For instance, we have the volume set to always control the audio receiver. I would says a con in this regard is that you cannot do this with any other function. I would like the play,stop,ffwd,rew,etc. buttons that control playback to be set to the DVR whether the TV or cable box is selected, but it's not really that big of a deal.

The other con I would say is that the remote does not have a "learn" function like the other cheap remote I tried. Logitech is proud of their comprehensive database of remote commands for so many different devices, but for the rare occasion (I haven't experienced it yet) that there is an error, it would be nice to just be able to copy the command directly from the original remote.

Other than these two very minor concerns, this is a great remote. I might purchase another one for myself because even with my DVR's universal remote, there are still functions for which I must keep the original remote handy.

I hope others find this review useful.

Thanks!
Amy

title: Overhyped, but technically fantastic lens!
text:
I've been using this lens for a couple of days now, and from a technical/objective standpoint, it's an optically fantastic lens and a great value compared to its direct competition. Subjectively, however, the lens has a very edgy quality to it that at times can feel a bit uninspired, clinical, and lifeless.

As a point of reference, I'm a wedding/portrait/event photographer who has owned a good number of different fast primes and the typical assortment of zooms a wedding photographer keeps handy. My current kit consists of the Sigma 35, Canon 85 1.2, 24-70 2.8II, and 70-200 2.8II, mounted on a pair of 5D Mark III's, and a Sony a7r, which I use to mount my Canon lenses.

Overall the professional reviewers are on point when they say that this lens is a technical marvel. The amount of detail this lens is able to resolve at its widest aperture is a technical feat that few lenses outside of the $4,000 Zeiss Otus are able to best (though the Sony FE 55 1.8 comes very close as well). In terms of resolving power, Sigma set a goal to leap-frog Canon and Nikon and set its sights on the Otus....a goal which they largely succeeded at reaching, at a quarter of the price of the Zeiss.

That said, any good portrait photographer will tell you that there's more to an image than how sharp it is, and more to a lens than its ability to resolve detail. Though sharpness is one of the few characteristics of a lens that we can objectively quantify, at the end of the day, its only one of the many criteria one should consider when evaluating a lens. After shooting with this for a couple of days and letting the initial elation with how sharp the lens is wear down, I started to notice that much like the Sigma 35, the Sigma 50 seems to lack the tonal depth and richness of Canon's L primes....particularly in rendering the subtle gradient shifts on skin tones exposed with a soft light. I often switch back and forth between lenses during shoots, and have found that the Sigma will more readily expose specular highlights, washing out skin-tones compared to my Canon lenses at an equivalent exposure.

Also, the Sigma 50's bokeh while much smoother than the Sigma 35, lacks the silky quality of the Canon's primes...particularly the Canon 85 1.2 and 50 1.2 (which I owned for a while). Granted much of this is an inherent function of lens design...chasing resolution by over-correcting the spherical aberration in the 50 1.2, and the fringing that plagues the 85 1.2 can lead to harsh rendering of focus areas when dealing with a complex background. Compared to longer focal lengths which will blur background elements into an indiscernible blur of color, the beauty of shooting at the 50mm "normal" perspective is the ability to keep background elements in the frame to provide context to a photo, while blurring out distracting elements smoothly to keep the viewers attention keenly on the subject. The Sigma 50 is able to provide this particular 'look', however the Canon 50 1.2, while not nearly as sharp, excels at providing a silky smooth backdrop to frame behind your subject.

This is completely subjective of course, and my point isn't to that Canon's approach definitively is better than Sigma's. The point again is that there's more to a lens than raw resolving power alone, and not to get caught up in the hype (engineered by Sigma) when making your decision.

That said, all subjectivity aside, again the Sigma is technically a spectacular lens. I haven't yet decided if its right for me and am flirting with ideas of working a trade for a 50L, while the Sigma is still a hot commodity in short supply. I most certainly appreciate the lens for what it is, however, and what Sigma set out to do with it. Not quite a 5 star lens for me, but a very strong 4.

title: ViewSonic PJD6243
text:
Our reliable and well-used Infocus LP650 finally died and we did a thorough review of all current projectors initially settling on the ViewSonic PJD6243 due to: 1) brightness 2) price 3) HDMI 4)low ambient noise level 5) long bulb life 6) availability of an "eco" mode that did not seem to diminish overall brightness very much. Upon receiving the unit and setting it up in our conference room, we found that it was clearly louder than the old LP650 even though the advertised noise specs were more favorable. We tried the "green" eco mode to see if the fan noise would subside, but heard no appreciable difference in the volume. On the plus side, the projector was brighter and clearer and produced a larger image - but the extra noise was a deal killer for us since we also do speakerphone conference calls in the same room and the fan noise was loud enough to be picked up by our phone speakers.

We know that this newer DLP technology runs hotter than the older generation stuff, so we expected some more noise as a result. This unit, with its small size, appears to require more air volume to keep it cool and the acoustic design was just not adequate to keep it quiet enough for us. We have ordered another brand (BenQ MW712) which is more expensive but with better noise specs and hope that it delivers.

If you have a larger conference room or plan to use this in a noisier environment like a classroom, it would be a good choice.

title: Great idea and it may work nicely but during setup
text: Great idea and it may work nicely but during setup, I've noticed a couple of quirks worth mentioning.  FIRST, note that this unit mounts on a *single* wall stud so you have no room for error in terms of where (horizontally) on a wall you put it.  Since studs are typically framed every 16" inches, you can only put it on a wall at 16" increments.  SECOND, when pushed against the wall, the M200 sits approximately 5" off center from the base so you need to account for this in determining if the stud you plan to use is going to sufficiently "center" your TV.  What this basically means is that, assuming you want your TV to be centered on any given wall, you must have a wall stud that is nearly exactly 5" off center of your wall or your TV will not be centered on your wall.  The silver lining is that the M200 pivots so that the base can be to the right or left of center. But, still, you'll need a stud that is 5" away from where you want your TV to be centered.  Fortunately for me, the back of my wall is my furnace room and it's not sheet rocked so I'm just going to add another 2x4 stuff exactly where I want the M200 base to go.

text:
This is a wonderful receiver that has plenty of features for both the novice and advanced user. I bought this to update my older Yamaha with no HDMI connectivity. Pretty much stayed with the same brand, as I was very pleased with the previous receiver's performance. Just needed more connection options, and the network abilities for streaming music are a plus.

I have it hooked up to the following:
42" Panasonic Plasma
Samsung Blu-ray player
Comcast DVR box
Roku 2 XD
Nintendo Wii
Soon to add an XBox 360 Kinnect
Speaker system consists of Front: Polk Monitor 40s Center: Polk CS 1 Rear: Polk Monitor 30s Sub: Polk PSW 10

Everything is connected via HDMI, except for the Wii, which had to use composite. Set up was an absolute breeze, as was the speaker calibrartion with the YAPO Mic. The GUI is really nice in that it over lays onto whatever you're watching. The getting started guide gives you all the basics, and If more instruction is required, they include the manual on CD. I'll admit that I'd prefer the manual be printed, but if it helps keep costs down and maybe save a few trees, then no big deal.

The only minor complaint/issue I came across during setup was that I no longer could use my component set up for the Wii. Since the component inputs are coupled with either digital coax or optical, you can't use them with the Wii, because there is no matching audio input. On my previous receiver, the component inputs were labeled DVR and Cable/sat & there was a corresponding audio input. It would have been nice to maybe have a 3rd set of component inputs paired with composite audio inputs. Again, this is minor, as the receiver does have all composite inputs (labeled AV 5), so you're not totally out of luck. I would have deducted 1/2 star, if I could, but I'm not willing to take a full start off for that. I did find a component to hdmi adapter for $30, so i was able to work around it.

The sound on this thing is tremendous and video looks supurb. Yamaha just seems to get it right. I've had friends who have tried other brands and most have had video problems at one point or another. I've had this receiver for 4 months, and no problems what-so-ever. It just plain works.

Over all, I would highly recommend this to anyone looking to dive into home theater for the 1st time, or just updating/upgrading their current system.

title: Good "smart" HDTV
text:
This was not only my first HDTV purchase ever, but my first TV purchase, period. I'd managed to live with hand-me-down and garage-sale TVs up til now, but I decided I wanted something nice for a change. I don't subscribe to cable or satellite television, so I wanted something that had some built-in "smart" capabilities. I also wanted something that wasn't going to break the bank. I really dislike 3D content, so I decidedly did NOT want a 3D TV. Finding a nice TV that has smart features and *isn't* 3D is getting harder and harder. For the most part, this TV has fit the bill, and I've been happy with my purchase.

I thought about putting together a list of pros and cons, but that didn't really seem to work too well with this particular review, so I've listed some general notes below:

-- PICTURE QUALITY
In a word, excellent. Granted, I don't have a whole lot to compare it to, but it's one of the best I've seen. Blacks are good, as are whites. Images are nice and crisp when viewing HD content.

-- TURNING OFF TRUMOTION
The one thing that gave me a real headache with this TV was figuring out how to turn off the TruMotion setting. I know some people are really jazzed about the 120 Hz view and the lack of motion blur, but to me, it made everything look like I was watching a soap opera. (Don't know what I'm talking about? Google "soap opera effect.")

So I turned it off. That was easy enough: Settings -->' Picture '--> Picture Option '--> TruMotion '--> OFF. There, fixed! Or so I thought. It fixed it for the TV input. But then I started watching something on Netflix (via the app on the TV), and the dreaded soap-opera effect was back!

It took me several days of online searching and talking to friends before I figured out that you have to REPEAT THIS process for EVERY SINGLE INPUT. (e.g. Input '--> HDMI 1 -->' Settings '--> Picture '--> Picture Settings '--> TruMotion '--> OFF.) And for the built-in apps, like Netflix, you have to start a video, then go the QMENU -->' Set Video -->' Picture Option '--> TruMotion -->' OFF.

Once you've set it for each input and app, though, it does stay defaulted to that. So at least you only have to do it once, not every time you start a new video. I found no online documentation ANYWHERE that specified this, though, so I thought it was definitely worth mentioning in this review. Hopefully it will help someone else.

-- SOUND QUALITY
Not as great, though not as bad as some flat-panels I've heard. You can turn it up as loud as you want, but after about the half-way point on the volume scale, there's not much difference. It's the same way with my parents' LG HDTV, which is a few years old. I solved this problem by hooking up an external home stereo system ([[ASIN:B003B8VBJ2 Sony BRAVIA DAV-DZ170 Home Theater System]]) and bypassing the TV's built-in audio altogether.

-- "SMART" FEATURES
The "smart" features were one of the selling points for me. When it comes down to it, though, I only really use 2 of them - Netflix and Hulu Plus. Some of the reviews (and comments on reviews) suggested that this unit might have an Amazon Instant Video app. It does not. Let me repeat: THIS TV DOES NOT HAVE AN AMAZON INSTANT VIDEO APP. And from what I can tell from various sources online, it never will. No idea why, since there are other LG HDTVs that do. This one just isn't one of them. One user suggested that it just required a firmware update. My firmware is up to date, and there is still no Amazon app. Sorry, people. It just doesn't exist.

EDITED 11/25/2013: I updated the firmware recently, and I can confirm that this TV DOES now have an Amazon Instant Video app. Finally!!

The "premium" apps this TV comes with (or at least, the ones mine came with) are:
-- Vudu
-- Hulu Plus
-- MOG
-- AccuWeather.com
-- MLB.TV
-- Netflix
-- CinemaNow
-- YouTube
-- NHL
-- vTuner
-- Associated Press
-- Facebook
-- Picasa
-- Google Maps
-- Twitter
-- Viewster
-- Amazon Instant Video (as of Nov 2013)

The LG app store is a joke. Forget finding anything you would ever want, much less be willing to pay for, in that store.

The online browser is also a joke. If you have to view a website on your TV (e.g. a network television website or Amazon Instant, etc. to view a video), your best bet is to hook up a computer via HDMI. Don't bother trying to do it with the built-in browser. It may work, but it won't work well, and it will be a painful experience. Trust me, I tried.

The YouTube app is pretty weak. It works, but it's less user-friendly than even the mobile YouTube website. Good luck finding anything specific.

The Netflix and Hulu Plus apps work well enough. They're not as user-friendly to navigate through as their respective websites, but that's to be expected, and I've found that it's easy enough just to queue up things on the computer first, and then play them from the TV apps. That saves you a lot of annoying "typing" with the magic remote.

I haven't tried any of the others. I see absolutely no reason why I would want to view Google maps, Associated Press content, Twitter or Facebook on my TV. I don't watch sports, so the MLB.TV and NHL apps are of no use to me. I have no idea how well they work. I'm a pretty loyal Pandora user, so I haven't tried MOG. I just plug in my iPhone to my stereo system when I want to listen to music.

-- SMART SHARE
It works, but it's not very user-friendly, in my experience. I was able to connect my Win7 laptop to the TV without much difficulty, but it's virtually impossible to search for a particular song or album or artist via the Smart Share interface - browsing seems to be the only option, and that can be a real pain when you have a LOT of music/videos/etc. to scroll through.

Streaming music seems to work just fine, but streaming video resulted in a lot of lag, and I've got a great WiFi network set up here. Anything over about 480p just doesn't really stream well on this TV, in my experience.

It also seems to lock up the TV frequently, requiring you to turn it off and on again before you can do anything.

-- THE "MAGIC" REMOTE
Many people have complained that this thing is annoying. I don't have a problem with it. It's like a Wii remote: you wave it around, and the cursor on screen follows your movement. There aren't a lot of buttons on it, though - volume up/down, channel up/down, Home (which takes you to the main app/input selection screen), Back (which exits out of the screen you're in), a scroll wheel that serves as channel up/down when you scroll and an "enter/select" key when you press it, a Help button, and an Input button.

Since I don't have cable TV, I don't have a lot of channels to scroll through when I'm watching actual television, so the lack of a number pad doesn't bother me. But I would find it annoying to have to use a different remote or manage to figure out how to bring up the on-screen number pad if I had hundreds of channels at my disposal and wanted to go to a particular channel instead of just scrolling through them all.

The remote sometimes takes a moment to register, too. I've found that you have to wave it around for a second or two before the TV realizes you want to do something and brings up the cursor. I frequently have to recalibrate it, too, by waving it around in a figure-eight motion, to get it to actually recognize my motions.

-- SIMPLINK
Works nicely. It was pretty easy to hook up my home theater system so that it turns on and off automatically with the TV.

-- THE INPUTS
The inputs all seem fine, and they're plentiful. I don't have that many devices that needed connecting - a DVD player/home theater system and occasionally my laptop (when I want to watch something on Amazon Instant Video or something on another website). It's easy to swap between inputs.

-- THE OUTPUTS
It's a little annoying that this TV only supports digital optical audio out, with no other analog options, but I guess it's not really unexpected, given the cost of the system. It hasn't posed a problem for me, but it's something to be aware of if you have an older stereo system that doesn't support that kind of input.

-- THE PHYSICAL STRUCTURE OF THE UNIT
I was actually pretty impressed with this. I'd heard horror stories about how unstable and top-heavy HDTVs could be. I bought the 42" and have it mounted on the stand that came with it. It feels pretty sturdy to me. I have cats who seem to think the space between the back of the TV and the wall is the perfect hiding place, and while I definitely do not approve of them being back there (and make them move every time I witness it), they haven't even nudged it.

The swivel feature is also useful, since I have it positioned at one angle when I'm watching alone, but want it angled more to the left when there are more people watching, due to the position of my sofa. Swiveling the TV on the stand doesn't feel unstable at all, which I was a little worried about initially.

-- PRICE
The price on this unit is excellent. You won't find a lower price anywhere, and if you do - even if it's after you've already made your purchase (as long as it's within 14 days of delivery) - Amazon will honor it, per their "TV Low Price Guarantee" (http://www.amazon.com/gp/help/customer/display.html?nodeId=200556860). I purchased this unit at $749, and by the time it shipped, the Amazon price was already $20 lower. They reimbursed me the difference, which was really nice. I see now it's even cheaper. While there are some quirks with the system, this is an unbeatable price for a great TV.

title: Really great design - with one unfortunate design decision
text:
First of all, I have been a long-time universal remote user since the inception of the "ahead of its time" Pronto Neo which had a great concept but suffered through implementation through to our Harmony 900 in the living room and the Harmony One in our bedroom.

Out of the box, I loved the feel of this remote. It's considerably lighter, but not too light - it feels well-balanced and has a much more ergonomic fit. I grip this remote and I feel like I have full range of control, unlike the 900 which is a bit on the large side (I have small hands so the 900 is occasionally annoying).

If you have owned a Logitech remote and you're replacing it with this one, the new website which helps you program it makes it a breeze. My Harmony One settings transferred flawlessly to this remote. I even added a setting with relative ease, although I do miss the functionality and greater range of control offered through the 900 software. That said, for a casual user, this is by far their most user-friendly iteration yet.

But here is what I loved most about my setup experience. I discovered that I had the wrong HDMI input setting for the feature added to the remote. Normally, I'd be shouting expletives at this point because my 900 would require me to sit at the PC, make the changes, download the settings, and then TRY AGAIN. Not this remote - I was able to change the HDMI input setting directly through the touch screen menu with a couple of simple swipes and it was fairly self-explanatory. I would venture to say that my parents could probably use this thing without my help.

The touch screen is as responsive as a smart phone and it didn't take long for me to navigate through the various menus to change backgrounds, change icons for various settings (my wife likes to watch Netflix on the PS3 in the bedroom a lot - lo and behold, a Netflix icon for the "PS3" activity setting!), activate the number pad if I want to manually input channels, etc. The colored buttons on the bottom react just the way that they do on a typical DVR remote.

In the remote setup menu, you can even enter your zipcode, identify your satellite/cable provider, and actually program your favorite channels on your remote based on this data so you can look at CNN, TNT, AMC, or other popular channels by tapping an icon on your remote.

Functions like play, stop, and pause are on top along with fast forward/reverse. But now we come to my gripe. We watch a LOT of movies...would it have hurt the design team just to add a 1/4" for next/previous chapter buttons??? They are available as soft buttons, true, but I find myself using those functions more often than fast forwards/reverse. Personally, I was pretty disappointed by this and I rated at 4 stars (wish I could do 4.5).

Otherwise, it's a great remote! I highly recommend it. I also love the vertical charger which the remote sits in a manner that ensures full battery contact unlike the 900 charger which leaves room for potential error in placement (and no charging).

I'll be happy to entertain any questions through comments. Apart from my gripe (and it's really 4.5 stars at that), I love it.

title: Highly reccommend to a friend.....
text:
This is the first LED TV I have owned. I have had a 51" Samsung, and a 42" Panasonic (Smart), and those were both Plasmas. I now am using a 47" Vizio, and it is an excellent TV. I will put it in my LR. The new TV is back in the Den area.

One thing I have noticed over the years, if you want certain features, you must buy a smart TV, just to get different sound outputs, and more inputs. It seems just about everyone buys the Smart TV, so they can set up the Wi-Fi apps. I bought this TV strictly on the new full array and all the improved LED enhancements. Also, its refresh rate, and the sound outputs. I had been wanting an LED for a long time, and this was one of the best I could find in my price range, and I am not disappointed.

I have mine set up differently than most folks on here. In fact, never read about someone setting it up like mine. The key to my system, is my receiver/amp. The amp has 5 HDMI inputs, and only 1 HDMI output. So, I have everything hard wired thru my amp. I have my Blu-ray player going into 1 HDMI input, and my Broadband cable (Charter) at 30 Mbps, going into another HDMI input, and currently, that is all, but I do have my cassette deck going into an audio input.

I do not have cable TV, or Satellite as I can get 19 channels over the air for free, just use a small cheap digital antenna, and run it straight into your RF input, and the TV will scan for channels and remembers them. The picture quality in HD over the air, is as good as Blu-ray or Netflix. I belong to both Netflix, and Amazon Prime, so I can just switch to the HDMI input my Computer is on, and then I'm online, on the big screen. I no longer use a computer monitor. But you must upgrade your graphics card that came with a PC, to handle the big screen. And it must have an HDMI output on the new graphics card.

So, it's all in one back here. I love the set up. Only thing I lack, is good speakers. I'm using an old Sony 5.1 stereo surround sound. Which is much better than the TV speakers. My amp is a Yamaha RX-V475. 2013 model year, with future tech built in. But, back to saving for now. I might go for speakers next fall, but for now, this is nice.

I would highly recommend this TV to a friend, or anyone who needs those Smart Apps (wireless). I'm a retired electrician. I prefer to hard wire most stuff. I do like my wireless rain gauge and temp gauge, and the solar lighting for my Flag at night.

In the LR, I will have the 19 free channels, and also have a combination DVD/VCR player and another Blu-ray player in there.

title: The New PaperWhite is a Home Run!
text:
I have owned every e-ink kindle since the 2nd generation, and after being slightly disappointed with the touch due to its inability to handle the number of books I have archived, I was really looking forward to the paperwhite. I received the paperwhite yesterday, and I was not disappointed at all. In fact, "thrilled" would be a better description! I really believe this to be what the kindle was meant to be all along.

The menu is much more intuitive, and the display is really spectacular, in my opinion. I noticed that some people commented on there being 4 brighter spots along the very bottom of the screen, but I did not find them to be a distraction at all. I only used the text to speech feature once on my earlier kindles, and so I cannot honestly say that I miss having it in the new kindle paperwhite.

For me, the best improvement after the lighted screen is the fact that books are now shown with their covers in similar fashion to the kindle fire, as opposed to a text list. I find that it is so much easier to organize my books into collections with the paperwhite, and it is so much nicer when looking for a particular book.

I feel that the touch screen is more responsive than the touch screen on the kindle touch. It is much more consistent and solid in its response and does not miss what I am trying to accomplish. That, combined with the fact that the menu is better organized and more intuitive makes this kindle my absolute favorite.

All in all, I believe that Amazon has hit a home run with the kindle paperwhite.

I also have the TDK A33 (my girlfriend's actually). It is a great speaker, especially for the size. But the KMC-3 is the one that truly shocked me (and my family) when I first used it. Massively full sound, even at low volumes.

One more thing: People complain about the eight D cells. But at least they're REPLACEABLE. This beast won't turn into a brick one day due to non-replaceable batteries.

My advice: If you're already looking in the $200 range, you owe it to yourself to audition this before you buy. And yes, it makes the much ballyhooed $175 Logitech "Boom" (with its non-replaceable battery) seem like a toy in comparison.

I am happy with this headset. Its light weight, comfortable to wear, battery lasts more than a day even after heavy use, has long range of usage and has better audio quality. I am using it for normal use (listening to music, Skype calls on laptop and as hands free device on smartphone) as well as for video editing. Audio quality is not to the point of studio quality but stands in par in most situations. Microphone works great but picks up wind noise and also it is little bit soft (Not a major issue). I switch headset between my phone (NFC enabled) and laptop (non-NFC enabled) quite easily. It will not connect to both of them simultaneously. It takes around 45 min to charge it completely. When battery is low, audio quality is poor and you will also see indicator light change. You can't use it while charging and also you can't use it with audio cable when its completely discharged. That function would have been nice. For this price, this is more than I could ask for.

Hack: To switch from NFC enabled phone to non-NFC enabled Bluetooth laptop. (Pair your headset to the laptop at least once)
1) turn your phone's Bluetooth OFF.
2) Turn-off and turn-on head set. This removes previous connection protocol from it.
3) On your laptop, try disabling and re-enabling Bluetooth. Upon re-enabling Bluetooth, laptop searches for previously paired devices (headset). Head set will be found and connected (You will see notification on laptop screen and audio notification in head set). If this doesn't work try next step.
4) Hibernate your PC, and wake it up (Win 8 takes less than 10 sec to do this). When PC wakes up, it looks for previously paired devices. Head set will be connected and you will see notifications.
5) These steps usually work but occasionally they don't. In such situations, delete paired devices from your laptop settings and repair the headset. This should fix the problem.

Let me know if there is any better way.

title: Quiet but not the best quality
text:
I bought this a little over a year ago because the shrill clicking of a standard mouse was driving me crazy. This mouse is definitely much quieter. There is still some sound, but it is quite soft and 'dull' rather than the loud and shrill click of a standard mouse.

However, after just over a year of frequent use (probably 60+ hours a week between work and personal use) the left mouse button is beginning to lose its sensitivity. I have to click much more firmly before the mouse registers the clicking.

It's actually first mouse I've ever had wear out on me. So, it loses a star for that, but here I am to buy another... Hopefully the next one holds up better.

EDIT: It's now 11 months since I purchased the second mouse and the second one has developed the same issue with poor responsiveness. So these definitely seem to have a limited lifespan.

5 stars for performance when new, but only 3 stars overall since it appears to only last about a year for me.

I'm too stingy to spend $30 every year on a new mouse. So I'm off to try a different quiet mouse and hopefully find one that's more durable.

title: Now I Am Happy!
text:
Review Overview
- I am very satisfied with my purchase of the Caféjo's My French-Press.
- It is intelligently designed for convenient function and compactness.
- The way I am using my Caféjo's My French-Press.
- Product solves a practical need of portability and service on the road as well as at home.
- Product supports the use of k-cups, pods, and loose ground coffee.
- My conclusion and recommendation.

Review Details
Caféjo's My French-Press has proven to be an excellent addition in our home and busy lifestyle. This product does exactly what I have been looking for. I love it when a product comes along that solves a need or one of my highly desired "wants" and this one did both superbly. Additionally I am impressed with its smart design and parts that fit and interlock well with each other. For example, the multi-use design of the plunger doubles as an incrementally marked measuring cup and used for heating water or milk directly in the microwave. The plunger also sports a built-in handle for pouring the brewed coffee into a coffee mug. The air sealing gasket on the plunger appears to be fabricated from a material that has excellent sealing and cleaning properties yet still plunges smoothly. The "stem" of the Caféjo attaches nicely to the collection cup which is designed with a pouring spout. This allows coffee to be poured without having to disassemble the unit. All of this makes using the Caféjo's My French-Press a breeze. Here's how I use it.

1. Fill the measuring cup portion of the plunger with 8 ounces of water then heat it in the microwave until it just starts to boil. Microwave ovens vary but this takes about two minutes. I let the water come to a boil as it will cool down to the 195 degrees or so that I like to brew fairly quickly.

2. While the water is heating I pop the k-cup in and lock it into place in the Caféjo and set the unit directly on top of my favorite coffee mug/tumbler to dispense directly into it instead of using the collection cup. It is at this point that the k-cup is punctured by the Caféjo on the top and bottom at the same time. Although handy I do not use the collection cup at all because I have cups and glasses that the Caféjo fits on top of and is perfectly stable, like they were made for each other. If interested here are two of the tumblers types I use.

[[ASIN:B005PQK7KM Smart Planet EC-46 Double-Wall Glass Coffee Travel Mug, Red]]
[[ASIN:B003LJX0O0 Trudeau Xpress Ceramic Tumbler, Chocolate Colored Lid and Grip]]

3. When the microwave's two minutes are up I carefully retrieve the hot water and pour it into the Caféjo unit, insert the plunger (it's the cup I just heated my water in) and slowly plunge for about 30 seconds, or...slower if I want a stronger coffee. Done.

I have been enjoying the Keurig for some time now so while I was on a seven-week business trip I missed my k-cup hot drink types (e.g. coffee, tea, hot chocolate, cider) and conveniences and the different varieties of blends and flavors. For the duration of my trip I used a small 4-cup drip coffeemaker yet I still wasted more coffee than I actually drank. So I am delighted now that I can pack my Caféjo when I travel or even when I'm just over visiting my parents or other family and friends.

This unit is very compact to use, to travel with, and to store and its cleanup is a snap. Another nice touch is that the kit includes all three of the most popular adapters; those being the k-cup, the pod, and loose-ground to accommodate for my favorite bulk ground coffees too. This is much appreciated as I still like to grind my own beans to control flavor as well as ensure freshness, plus the freshly ground coffee makes me feel a little bit pampered too :)). I have found that bulk/bagged coffee is usually less expensive than k-cups which run from about $0.39 all the way up to a $1.00 or more for each k-cup depending on what and how much is purchased at a time. BTW at about $0.41 one of my most favorite k-cup coffees is [[ASIN:B007Y59HVM San Francisco Bay Coffee Fog Chaser One Cup for Keurig K-Cup Brewers, 80-Count]].

In conclusion I'm very pleased with this product. So much so that I am gifting these for Christmas presents this year. I can highly recommend this product for its quality and service for anyone and especially those folks who don't want or cannot spend the hefty prices for the electric single-cup units, or those that just want to "keep it simple", or for those who need portability, or those who want versatility, and especially for anyone wanting all of the above. I hope my review has been helpful to you.

title: Decent value. Easy to use. Sound quality improved by equalization. See below for measurements.
text:
These A100's are compact and sound okay, especially if you apply equalization. See below for the equalization parameters I used.

I have a Dell monitor with its accompanying Sound Bar. I used to have relatively high-end computer speakers but at some point I started to value compactness and simplicity over sound quality, hence I got the Sound Bar with the monitor. But eventually my pendulum swung the other way and I decided I wanted better quality, but keep simplicity, and not take up a lot of desktop space.

I gave these AmazonBasics A100's a try because they're so inexpensive, I figured even if I didn't like them, I wouldn't mind having spent the very little money on them that they cost. Plus, I figured, they couldn't sound worse than the Sound Bar.

I love the fact that I can plug the USB power cable into the back of the monitor, alleviating some cable clutter behind and under my desk.

The sound quality slightly exceeds that of the Dell Sound Bar. Both have the nice feature that even when the volume is cranked up, if there is no signal, they don't produce much audible hissing noise. Plenty of cheap speakers audibly hiss when turned up, but not these.

My ASUS Xonar DGX sound card (http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B007TMZ1BK/) has an equalizer in the driver, so I decided to measure the frequency response of these A100's and the Dell Sound Bar, then compensate for each. Here's the compensation based on the frequency response I measured for the A100's:

Frequency in Hz , Amplification in dB:
30 , +20
60 , +20
120 , 9
250 , +3
500 , -6
1000 , +1
2000 , +4
4000 , -14
8000 , +1
16000 , +10

I applied that amount of amplification per channel using the Asus Xonar DGX Audio Center. The improvement is night-and-day better.

(If you really want to dial in the compensation better than the GUI sliders let you, you can manually edit the text in the config file directly. It's here: C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Roaming\ASUS\Xonar DGX Audio Center\cmicnfp.ini. The units are logarithmic, where 1310720 corresponds to 20 dB, and the bands 0-9 correspond to the frequencies listed above.)

I applied the same procedure to the Dell Sound Bar. The main difference is that in the 120 Hz band, the Sound Bar response was also below what I could measure. The upshot is that more of the audible frequencies in the Dell were uncalibratable, compared to the A100. So, even after equalizing both, the A100's sound better than the Dell Sound Bar.

As you can infer from the chart above, the A100's do not generate much pressure in the extreme low (<=60 Hz) and high (>= 16 kHz) frequencies. That's what you should expect. It would be extraordinarily difficult for such tiny speakers to generate a lot of bass, and without separate tweeters, I wouldn't expect the extreme high-end to sound very crisp.

Obviously this is a lot of effort to go through for $14 speakers. I did it out of curiosity more than dedication to making these speakers work for me.

The next step up I would take would be a drastic leap from these: Probably AudioEngine A2+ or Vanatoo Transparent One, which cost literally an order of magnitude more money, and take up significantly more desktop space. Not a fair comparison with the A100's. So this was a fun little exercise before diving into spending real money.

In summary, these speakers are worth what they cost, and you can get a heck of a lot more out of them if you apply equalization -- which some sound cards offer.

title: First Smartphone - Not too bad.  Not Perfect.
text:
Preface: I have waited a long time to enter the smartphone realm. I have been computer savvy for over 20 years and I didn't see the need to get into smartphones until reliable 4g became the norm.

I have had this phone for about 6 months now. I know it's the II. I bought this because some of my friends have the I and it was really the only one worth getting with a slide out keyboard at the time of my purchase.

The phone is fast. Good processor on 4g with good signal and it's like surfing from my desktop with good cable internet. The display is great too. I can view HD content and it looks fantastic, not that I would spend much time video watching on a phone; though I have had friends watch HD movies I have brought on my phone (hefty internal memory without the need for an extra SD card) and they enjoyed the quality of the screen in addition to the audio provided through the simple micro RCA plug. You plug in your favorite headphones, ear-buds or external speakers and you'll have great sound.

The standard battery has to be charged daily even with minimal use. This was new to me as my previous phones would go for days without needing a charge. I really only use my phone for web surfing for about 30 mins a day at most with a few texts and the occasional phone call.

The surface is very very slippery! I cannot state that enough! Without a case you'll be dropping this thing often and probably have a very hard time sliding the keyboard open (almost impossible with one hand for me.) A case solved this for me [[ASIN:B0067MGGCQ OEM Samsung Stratosphere I405 Droid Shell Combo w/ Holster & Kickstand]] Of course, a case is a smart buy even if you don't find the slide difficult.

It has taken me a long time to gain proficiency with the keyboard. My last phone was the ENV3 and it's compact keyboard with small buttons are a dream to type on. While the larger buttons and spaces between them on this phone may suit some people I really dislike it. Even after 5 months I still cannot type as fast as I can on my old ENV.

I replaced my 1st Strat2 after having problems with the speaker. I found out that the battery cover was pressing on the speaker making it not work. The replacement I was sent didn't come with a battery cover so I don't know if I simply have a defective one. I ended up slipping a tiny piece of rubber under the cover near the speaker and I haven't had any further problems.

title: Comfortable, crazily high bass. Mic DOESN'T Work [Appears to affect a lot of people] but Razer appear to not care too...
text:
Its a Razer product which explains the high price and so it is also expected to come with high value and quality.

The very first thing I noticed about the headphone is that my laptop doesn't detect the existences of the microphone on it. And a simple Google search about the issue will review to you that a very large amount of customers out there suffer from the same issue. While fixes exist such as buying an USB sound card etc I strongly doubt any customer paid a large amount of money for a quality product only to know he is needed to buy an extra product to make it work. Contacting Razer support is also disappointing because the guy actually suggested that buying an external USB Soundcard would solve the issue, and I was really disgusted by that reply.

Of course the key aspect of a headset would be
1. the sound quality
The sound quality for the Kraken Pro is great for gaming, clear sound output for gaming use, very nice to listen to gunshots, sword fights sound so personally I like the sound output of this headset a lot.

However if you are looking for this headset to be multipurpose and enjoy listening to your music a lot. This is an extremely terrible piece of crap. Excessive bass on the headset, way too excessive almost comparable to Beats and I listen to music through a GoVibe Magnum which increases the bass and with the Kraken you really don't feel like listening to music anymore. If you like Rock of Country, clear voice style, don't ever get this headset. If you are considering music as an important part of your Kraken's daily routine, be prepared to drown in pure bass of your music, because It's all about that Bass, No Treble, Literally.

2. Comfort
The headset is among the more comfortable headset I have worn. Long gaming session = no problem at all. Most headset even from Razer tend to strain the lower part of my ears which becomes really uncomfortable beyond around 1.5 hours but so far this headset as been great.

The way the microphone is place is also really awesome, easy to keep and carry around when you don't need it.

title: Wow, this is a great system!
text:
I have to start off this review by stating that I originally purchased from Amazon the Yamaha YHT-495BL. The seller, Electronics Expo, was sold out of the 495BL and they upgraded my order - free of charge - to the YHT-595BL. This seller is great to step up like this and they shipped it right away. It arrived two days early, too. Great work.

Now on to the product itself. I've had about five hours with it so far (which isn't a lot, I know), but I am so impressed with the sound quality. I was smiling ear to ear as Casino Royale came to life. My original system was a 10 year old Sony Receiver with 5.1 Surround Sound. The Receiver was starting to go, and I think the Sub was on it's way out as well.

SET-UP: The Yamaha 595BL is an easy system to set-up. Everything worked the first time plugging it in (except for one thing which is state below). I hooked up the Playstation 3 and Direct TV via HDMI (taking advantage of the FIVE HDMI ports). The picture quality of both look fantastic as always (no change as far as I can see on the 50" TV), and the sound is crisp and clear. The YPAO Microphone is slick, as I put in the middle of the room and let the system measure the sound. Changing the levels is easy, too, as I thought the front speakers were too loud as compared to the center channel.

THE SOUND: Once the levels were set correctly, Casino Royale sounds great. At first, before I changed the levels, the music was louder than the dialogue, and even louder than some gun shots, as Bond was going after the bomb-maker in the opening action scene. After changing the levels, I started it over, and it was right where I wanted it. And, the subwoofer - I love bass, and this one rocks! It's about half the size of my old Sony, but sounds so much better. I even finished Casino Royale and started Quantum of Solace, and the sound effects of the opening car chase were awesome. Can't wait to re-watch Inception, Transformers, Harry Potter, and other movies.

THE REMOTE CONTROL: Since I have my whole system set up through the receiver, the Yamaha Remote can now be the universal remote. I had been using a five-year-old Sony Remote Commander that was big, bulky, and required many button presses. Now, with the Yamaha Remote, if I want to switch back and forth from HDMI 1 (PS3) and HDMI 2 (DirecTV) I can do so with one button press - no more hitting the TV Button, then the Input Button, the scrolling up and down on the TV to select the device (which could be up to four button presses). I will say, there are a lot of buttons on the remote, and it is intimidating to look at; but, the only ones I need are the inputs at the top, and the setup button and the arrows near it in the middle.

THE SPEAKERS: The construction seems solid and the size is great! What's even better is the outstanding sound quality that comes out of them. The sub is small, yet powerful.

I-POD INTERFACE: Love the USB at the front of the Receiver. I plugged it in to try it out with my iPhone, and you can select music, videos, iTunes U videos, and more. When you bring up music, you can do so by artist, playlists, and more. The screen even shows the album cover while the tracks are playing.

FM RADIO: The only thing I've had difficulty with is the Radio, and I can't figure out why. I have the FM antenna plugged in, but it won't hold a signal. I read that you can change the "MODE" so I'll try that. UPDATE: after reading on the owner's manual disc, I did try hitting the "MODE" button on the remote. One press of the button changed the FM mode to Mono, and the FM station is coming through great with no static whatsoever.

OWNERS MANUAL: Just as the other 1-Star Review states, the owner's manual is on a disc. I would prefer to have it in paper right in front of me so I can read detailed information. But, overall, it's no biggie.

I have to say, I feel bad for the other review of this product from January 2, 2012. If the speakers had reversed polarity, it's my amateur opinion that those speakers were wired wrong in the factory. That's too bad. Also, I have switched back and forth between many of the inputs (HDMI 1 -> HDMI 2 -> HDMI 1), and I have not experienced the problem that is described in that review. However, I've only had it operating since last night.

My first impression is that this system is outstanding. I'm very impressed with it's overall quality of sound, bass, size, setup, features, options, etc. This is my first Yamaha product, and I hope it lasts as long as my Sony system did. If it does, I'll be very, very happy.

Again, thanks to Electronics Expo for stepping up as they did to take care of my order.

title: So far so great
text: Bought this half way across the world about month ago. Not too worried about the warranty and returns because the price is so good, and it is Panasonic, right? Not from some run-of-the-mill nameless manufacturer. Got it for $189 when it was listed at $199 (I suppose Amazon dropped the price to nudge me to buy), and it is now $319.99. The video camera is palm-size small and feels very light. This is important when you need to hold it for a long period of time while shooting some scenes. Unlike my previous video camera, which required mini CD-R, this works off SD cards (must be class 4 and above though), which is readily available and don't cost much either. The only negative is that it doesn't come with a carrying case so I am carrying it around in the bubble-wrap from the box. The built-in lens shutter is a nice touch. I can say bye bye lens caps, which was so common in video cameras, and frankly so last century. I've taken a 45 minute video of myself delivering a lecture, which was the main reason I bought this cam, and it has turned out well, both video and audio. The battery consumption was only 1 bar out of 3 bars that I started out with and the file size was about 2.3 gb (set to the second highest resolution of the cam). I am sure that scenes with greater motion will consume more battery power and memory consumption will be more. But this is my assumption. My only complaint is not with the camera but the software that came with it. I could import the still pictures, but not the videos. By the way, the still picture resolution and color are nothing to shout about. Maybe I have not read the full instructions in the manual, but who reads manuals nowadays? So I did it the old-fashioned way. Windows-Explored the SD Card and copied the video file out to my PC. Overall, very satisfied with this product, so far.

title: Better than Zagg! Less than half-price!
text:
I was wary of purchasing something other than a Zagg shield but after purchasing several Zagg products in the last few months and noticing that the quality has significantly decreased I decided to give ArmorSuit a shot. I'm very glad I did. Installation is so easy. Make sure the screen is clean, spray the front of the screen protector before removing it from the backing, spray your fingertips, and back of the screen protector. After that just put it on your iPad and squeegee the excess application spray out. If you mess up, gently peel it back and start over. Took me about 10 minutes. Bubbles and any other imperfections come out after a few days. If for whatever reason you need to readjust the screen protector you can do that too! Just spray your fingertips and gently work the corner of the screen protector up, reapply the application spray, squeegee, and you're golden!

I've has this on since March and have been thoroughly impressed with the quality and durability of these shields. In fact I've been so impressed that now my entire family has these on their iPads and iPhones. It heals quickly, the customer service from these guys is top-notch, and you save money! Seriously, stop reading this and hit 'Add to Cart'.

title: Great so far
text:
I haven't tested the RAM using MemTest or a similar utility, but since installing it, my system has been fast and stable (which, in itself, is a good sign). So, from a hardware perspective, all is well so far.

I will say, though, that I don't enjoy being required to adjust my BIOS to take full advantage of a component like system memory. I've been building computers for years, and RAM has always been a plug & play type of component in my builds, unless one intends to overclock (which I don't). And you DO need to adjust your BIOS in order for this RAM to perform as it was intended. It took a bit of research to be sure I was making the correct adjustments, but once I did, all was well. So far, it's been worth the effort. But I would have preferred some detailed instructions and best practices included with the chips. If not for my fellow reviewers on Amazon (thank you, all!), I would not have know I needed to do this.

My other caution to you is this: be sure these chips will fit in your case. Because of the attractive heat dissipaters, these chips are higher than the average stick of RAM. I have a very large, spacious case, but my CPU cooler is massive. The RAM just squeaks in behind the CPU cooler, but with almost no room to spare. I couldn't install any more of these chips if I wanted to because of their height.

But all in all, I am very happy with my purchase!

title: After 8 Months...
text:
I received this eight months ago. I hesitated to write a review earlier because I really wanted to see how this cover would work in the long run for my iPad 3. I had a few covers for my iPad 3 before I received this one. While this cover is just OK, I was even unhappier with the other covers I had. I have never had an Smart Apple cover for this iPad. While this cover acts in the same way as a Smart Cover in some respects, it has some shortcomings of its own.

Here are my thoughts:

1. Nice outer material and black color is ideal. The black color hides oil and dirt buildup that naturally comes from hands over time.

2. The gray inner color is NOT ideal. I have found that dirt accumulates on the soft, suede-like material and the color allows it to show. A few days after I got the cover, I had dusty hands from some handyman work I was doing. I needed to check out a YouTube video with dusty hands to see what I needed to do with the handyman work. I have never been able to completely get these dust marks off ever since.

3. Over time the cover does not close as tightly as it once did. The elastic strap has stretched a little more than it did at first. This prevents the magnets in the cover from touching the right spot on the iPad 3 to put it to sleep. The cover sits cockeyed now. The result is that the screen stays on, drains the battery, heats the unit, and I am left with a dead iPad the next time I go to use it. This is the biggest issue I have with this cover. It no longer reliably puts the unit to sleep and drains the battery dead without me knowing.

The cover was great for the first 4-5 months. However, now it just drains my iPad unless I am neurotic about making sure that it is in sleep mode. To make sure it's asleep, I find myself peeking under the corner that doesn't have the magnet (which makes the iPad sleep). Seems unnecessary and I am looking for a new cover.

title: Comparison to Triple Fi 10
text:
My audiophile journey started with a cheap pair of Koss in-ears (poor fit and boomy bass), followed by Etymotic ER6i's (accurate but anemic bass, boring sound signature, horrible microphonics), Ultimate Ears Super Fi 5 Pro (decent bass, but still not exciting enough in the treble region), Ultimate Ears Triple Fi 10 (boomy bass, sibilant treble, poor fit, but despite all of that my favorite in-ears to date).

My review will focus on a comparison of this IEM to its predecessor the Triple Fi 10 (which I will refer to as TF10 from now on), and will hopefully help you decide whether it's worth it to invest another $400.

Form: UE900 fit is 100% better than the TF10's. The tips no longer protrude straight out from your ears, it now feels more like a custom IEM and "sits" on the inner part of your outer ear. It also lies flush so that you can actually sleep on your side with these on. In addition, the barrel where the sound exits is much smaller on the UE900 and appears to be 1 medium-sized channel and 1 tiny channel rather than the 2 large channels of the bulkier TF10. With any of the stock silicon tips (S, M, L) the TF10 would slip out of my ear simply because the barrel was as large as my ear canal. The stock Comply T500 foam tips allowed the TF10's to stay in my ears and form a nice seal, but the tradeoff was the treble and high-mids became muffled/veiled. The barrel of the UE900 is much smaller and both silicon and foam tips (Comply Ts500) stay in my ear canal without slipping out.

Sound: There is so much debate about whether driver burn-in exists. Maybe the driver changes its signature or maybe you adjust to the sound, the end result is the same: you listen to these headphones over a period of time and see whether you like it or not. Right out of the box the UE900 retain the "exciting" sound of the TF10's. The TF10's were somewhat harsh in the highs (with silicon tips), very veiled in the mids (with foam tips), and boomy in the lows (sometimes headache-inducing). My least favorite aspect of the TF10's were the mids. With vocal songs I felt like there was always a curtain between my ears and the voice no matter how deeply I tried to insert the TF10's. The UE900's has less harsh highs (I haven't cringed much yet), more prominent mids (though still slightly veiled in comparison to my Sennheiser Momentums), and a 20% reduction in bass quantity (but more comfortable to listen to). In summary the UE900 has a gentle U-shape frequency response rather than the sharp V-shape of the TF10's. The UE900 manages to maintain an exciting sound and appears to be more resolving so now I am actually hearing more details in some of my songs. Keep in mind that the UE900 accomplishes this all with the stock Comply foam tips.

Durability: As I have only recently received the headset, I can't evaluate how the plastic housing of the UE900 or its braided cable will hold up over time.

Accessories: Not a huge factor in purchasing an IEM. It has a nice magnetic-hinged glossy plastic box, a carrying case, 3 different sizes of comply Ts500 tips, and I think 4 different sizes of silicon tips. It comes with an Apple compatible blue braided cable plus a backup black cable without any remote (a nice touch, as my TF10 cable broke within 1 year)

My music preferences lean toward pop, techno, vocal, and alternative rock. My sources are Galaxy Nexus GSM, Lenovo X230. No amp required.

Summary: As an overall package the TF10 was a 15% upgrade over the Super Fi 5. With the infinitely better fit and slightly upgraded sound quality, I feel the UE900 is a 30% upgrade over the TF10.

title: ASUS K200MA  Nice, but a bit sloooooowwwwww ........
text:
ASUS K200MA. I want a small portable laptop for travel, and a few years ago, bought a refurb netbook with 1GB RAM, 320GB HDD. Even though I easily upgraded the memory to 2 GB, it was painfully slow, probably due to the Atom processor. This seems to be the better solution, so I've ordered one from Amazon today; seems like almost the same price I paid for the refurb crappy netbook several years ago. I choose this over Chromebooks, and a similarly prices Acer, and the high priced MacBook. I have an external CD/DVD RW that I purchased for the netbook, and rarely use. On my travel, I don't need a CD/DVD. The Chromebook might do it for me, as I use google drive a lot, but I thought, what the heck, you might as well have a full featured PC & software along so there's no compromise. The Acer machine had a good price, but I didn't want to lug around a 15.6" monstrosity for travel. The HDD slowness shouldn't bother me too much, because my 15.6" home PC has about the same relative specs for a device 5 years old. I'll have to get used to Win 8, but you all took some of that fear away. I'll get this in about a week, put it thru its paces, learn a little about Win 8, and post a review after I know more. Thanks again for helping out with the selection.

UPDATE: 8/13/2014 - I've used this for several weeks, not constantly, but enough to know a few things:

1. Win 8 is not so bad. Just toggle back to Win 7 if you don't like the "blocks". Win 8 is not particularly intuitive, but how much do you want to spend for an iMac?
2. My main computer is a 2008 HP 15.6" laptop with 4 GB memory, 320 HDD, and AMD Premium dual core processor. It is a LOT faster than this 4 GB, 500 HDD, Celeron "turbo" machine. I can only attribute the difference in speed to the Celeron processor. Seems to take way too long to load my ISP home screen, and to change between emails. So, I'm a little disappointed, I expected better. But, not disappointed enough to send it back. It is the right size for me, great capacity, great screen resolution, OK battery life, top quality in all other respects. There are cheaper machines out there, with better processors, but generally 15.6" screens, not touch screens, and I don't want to lug those around for travel. So, I think it'still four stars, maybe three unless you need lightening speed.

title: Excellent sound, but with a few quirks
text:
The Sony STR-DN840 delivers great sound quality out of the box. I was surprised that it made my speakers sound better than my other receiver. Out of the box set-up was simple. If you've used other receivers, this one is no different. Before fine tuning it, I just turned on my TV and started watching. The sound quality was excellent. I felt like the sounds were clearer than with my other receiver.

I ran into issues during the auto customization part. Sony provides a little microphone so that the receiver can automatically adjust the speakers to your seating position. During this process, I receiver an error saying that my speakers couldn't be detected. This made no sense to me since I could hear the test tones being played on my speakers. I tried several times to no avail. I can only conclude the the microphone was defective. I was however, able to calibrate the speakers using manual calibration. This wasn't a huge deal to me since I like to customize things myself anyway.

Pairing the receiver with my Nokia N9 was very easy. I can easily stream music from my phone to the receiver. Streaming from my Windows 7 machine has proven difficult. The receiver isn't listed as a device on my network. Digging deeper, I can find that it is on the network, but I can only access the device's page and not actually control it. Logging into the receiver from my computer brings up a bare bones page, but there is the option to update the receiver. When I click to update the receiver, it asks me to choose a file. I can't find the file anywhere though and there are no instructions on how to obtain it. It's been a frustrating process.

On the other hand, I'm really looking for a receiver that can make movies and games sound great. On that, the device delivers. It delivers better sound quality than other receivers I have used. For me, streaming from my computer to receiver is a nice to have feature. The sound quality is more important. This receiver offers all of the options I need for great sound with 7.2 channels and a decent number of HDMI ports. Many of the receivers at this price point offer 5.1 channels at a lower wattage. This receiver also prepares you for the future in that it offers a 4k pass through. I don't yet have a 4k TV, so I can't comment on how well it works, but it's nice to know that this receiver is 4k ready.

Despite its quirks, I still give this receiver a 4 star rating. It delivers on the most important aspect of a receiver - the sound quality.

title: Good for on-the-go.  Doesn't really replace a home desktop though.

The keyboard dock is great but it's far too top heavy and can fall off the base quite easily. Not very optimal for a guy who likes to lay down while typing. My biggest gripe was the lack of hard drive space. Only 32GBs of space (17 after Windows installation).
I sold it later and got a real computer.
This tablet is great for those who'd like the portable true Windows experience. Great for those who use spreadsheets and don't like the current tablet offerings. It's also a very cool device.

My recommendation: This device is not meant to replace a laptop. At least not for me. Mediocre keyboard kept me from using the device as a true portable laptop. Great addition to a main PC device. Better than any price comparable Android tablet just because it runs Windows operating systems.
It's quite the business savvy machine. Recommended for those who need to do businesses on the go.

title: Does Not Work With Windows 7
text:
I purchased this cable as an extension for a web camera. Upon plugging the cable in (just the cable itself, no device attached at the other end) Windows 7 recognizes the cable as an "unknown device" and attempts to install drivers to support it. Every time windows attempts this I receive the following error: "Device driver software was not successfully installed. Please consult with your device manufacturer for assistance in getting this device installed." The cable is unresponsive both before and after this message appears and will not recognize any device attached to it.

I thought that this might simply be an issue with my laptop so I gave the cable to my brother who tried it on his desktop (also Windows 7). He had the exact same issue. He is a comparatively tech-savvy guy and could not get the cable to work for the life of him. Perhaps it is a Windows 7 issue? Hard to troubleshoot as no instructions or software requirements are included with the product. There are no driver downloads on the manufacturer's website. I am thoroughly disappointed with this - getting a cable to work should not be this difficult! I am going to follow up with the seller to find out what may be wrong. I will report back if I can get the issue resolved.

I also purchased a Plugable brand 10 meter cable (http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B004AGX4YO/ref=oh_details_o01_s00_i00)which functions perfectly well on both my laptop and my brother's desktop. The Plugable cable also required a driver installation but it installed automatically, without error, the first time I plugged it in. I am happy with the Plugable cable as of now.

text:
Summary - Great deal if you can get them for under forty bucks, don't expect Bose Quietcomfort functionality at this price.

We flew to Australia and back recently and I wanted to make sure my wife was comfortable on the trip. My sister had strongly recommended a pair of noise cancelling headphones for the long trip so I pulled the trigger on these - from the specs and reviews they had a lot of the other sub $100 NC headphones beat.

We were quite happy with them, though you really have to understand a few things. First, the headphones are somewhat lightweight with relatively lightweight ear cups and foam. Heavier foam would help noise isolation, but would also make them more bulky and hot. Second, the NC feature works for some types of noise better than others. If you sit in front of a 20" box fan on high, the NC is amazing! For a loud blender, not so much. It really works well for lower frequency "Thrumming" type noises that you get in a car, train, or airplane.

I use them now at the office where there are things like fans and air duct vibrations. I've tried the Bose headphones, and while they are definitely nicer (I'd guess they are about 20% more comfortable and block/cancel about 30% more noise), they definitely are not 10x as nice!
