title: The perfect tool for centralizing all your peripherals
text:
Docking stations have been a popular computer component for centralizing peripherals while maintaining a clean work place. Plugable has made the Plugable UD-3900 USB 3.0 Universal Docking Station as the complete docking experience.

Package Contents:
* Docking Station
* USB 3.0 Cable
* DVI to VGA Adapter
* Power Adapter
* CD (Driver and User Manual)
* Quick Installation Guide

Accessories:
The USB 3.0 cable is 39 inches and has a thick gauged wire. It is better constructed than most other USB 3.0 cables I have used before. The DVI to VGA adapter is matt black with two hand tightened screws at the side to add functionality to VGA monitors. The power adapter's cord is approximately 68 inches, with a 2 x 4 x 2 inch large brick at the end. This power adapter is much larger than any other adapter in my surge protector that may have issues with neighboring outlets.

Specifications:
Ports and Connectors-
* To Computer: 1x USB 3.0 Port (Type B female connector to match included cable)
* USB Ports: 2x USB 3.0 Ports (in front) | 4x USB 2.0 Ports (in back)
* Ethernet: 1x Gigabit Ethernet Port (10/100/1000 Base-T Ethernet RJ-45 connector)
* Video: 1x DVI-Port (24 pin + 5 pin Female Connector) with DVI-I to VGA adapter, 1x HDMI Port
* Audio: 1x Microphone (3.5mm stereo audio in), 1x headphones/speaker (3.5mm stereo audio out)
Power-
* Power Adapter: Input: AC 100-240V, 50-60Hz, Output: DC 5V/4A
* Power Mode: Self-powered

Hardware:
The device is rather compact and light at 8.5 x 5 x 4 inches, 13 ounces. Unlike the [[ASIN:B00GQQO8FA HooToo HT-UD01 USB 3.0 Universal Docking Station]]], that is a horizontal design, this is a vertical one. The major difference between the two is that the peripheral ports are all spread apart, with two USB 3.0, one headphone, and one microphone ports in the front, four USB 2.0 ports at the top of the back, followed by Ethernet, DVI-I, HDMI, USB 3.0 male, and power adapter ports. Because of the vertical design, this also takes up a lot less space on my desk, further allowing me to have a cleaner workspace. At the left and right have vent holes for heat and "DisplayLink: Plug and Display" text at the bottom, and on the front is a Blue LED for power and Green LED for USB connection. The bottom has a fairly large flat base (4.5 x 2.5 inch) to stabilize the vertical design. Overall, I like this design, as it feels right. I wouldn't change the placement of any ports or design.

Minimum System Requirements:
* Intel/AMD Compatible Dual core CPU at 2.0 GHz or higher.
* Windows XP 32-bit, Windows Vista 32/64-bit, Windows 7, or Windows 8 32/64 bit, Mac OS 10.8.3 or higher (Linux not supported at this time for DisplayLink USB 3.0 generation products)
* 1GB of RAM
* USB 2.0/3.0 port
* 30MB of available Disk Space

The minimum system requirements basically any operating system (except Linux, which only support DisplayLink's USB 2.0 drivers), processor, and hardware that is made within the last decade. I really like the wide compatibility with their products, as this can be used with even budget-friendly computers without video cards.

Software and Setup:
Before plugging this device into your computer, install the software from the either the included CD, or if you prefer the most recent drivers, from "displaylink.com/support". This is, without a doubt, a very important point. If you do not install the drivers prior to plugging this into your computer, then you will have Windows or Macintosh attempting to automatically install drivers, which will have the device malfunction until the proper drivers are installed.

If you have a monitor connected, then the DisplayLink icon will display with the following menu:
* DisplayLink Manager
* Check for Updates...
* 2. Plugable UD-3900
- Screen Resolution
- Screen Rotation
- Extend to (Left, Right, Above, Below)
- Extend
- Set as Main Monitor
- Mirror
- Off
- Optimize for Video
- Fit to TV
* Audio Setup
* Video Setup

The overall software for this device is very straight forward and intuitive, which is great for anyone that is new to multiple monitors.

Testing:
Once you have installed the software, all the peripherals (including monitors) will be successfully connected to your computer. I tested this on my desktop, which uses a i7 2600K processor and AMD HD6950 graphics card. Although this software is geared toward laptops, it is an excellent addition to my desktop. I also like that I have the option to easily switch over my keyboard, mouse, wireless adapter, and external hard drive to a surface tablet (Not RT) or laptop without needing to move any peripherals from my work station. I also want to note that the peripherals responded as soon as this was plugged into my desktop, and maintained connection even when my desktop restarted and was going through bios settings. This may be an expected outcome but isn't the same outcome that the same similar HooToo product produced.
I then tested fit of the ports in the front and back. The USB 2.0 Ports, Ethernet, HDMI, and DVI-I ports fit perfectly, but the USB 3.0 ports in the front have a tight fit. I don't know if this was intentionally done or not by Plugable.

I benchmarked the USB 3.0 ports with my Brinell 1TB USB 3.0 External Hard drive, using CrystalDiskMark, and found the following results:

Read: 88.50 MB/s
Write: 89.19 MB/s

Although this is lower than my average results of 116 MB/s Read, and 94.15 MB/s Write, it is very close. This product has satisfied all necessary concerns for a docking station.

Final Thoughts:
I think this docking station is the complete package. My only wish would be to have extra USB 3.0 ports, but the existing USB ports accomplish the goal of centralizing all my main peripherals. I would recommend this to users for both desktops, and laptops, who want to centralize their peripherals and have a cleaner work place, and is why I give this product a rating of 5 out of 5 stars.

Pros:
+ Centralizes USB, Audio, Video, and Network peripherals into a clean environment; Gives opportunity for easy switching from a desktop to laptop (or vice versa) with one USB cord.
+ USB 3.0 port was benchmarked and tested very closely to expected results.
+ Ability to connect up to two monitors.
+ Compatible with almost any computer hardware within the last decade, and most Windows and Macintosh platforms.

Cons:
- Not compatible with Linux (Limitation of Linux drivers).
- Only 2 USB 3.0 ports (Although this may be enough for most people, and if not, getting a USB 3.0 hub would solve the issue)
- Fit of USB 3.0 ports is very tight.

I was provided a sample in exchange for a thorough and honest review.

title: IF you have shielded cable, you might prefer this over the APC version, at essentially the same price.
text:
Unlike the APC version of this class of device, this unit at least appears to provide a shield connection, so that if you are using shielded cable, the shield current will be passed through the device. I have not yet disassembled one of these to see how the shelf connection is connected up, so it may just all be voodoo. The presence of the insulating grommet around the ground lead causes me to infer that the shield is connected to the metal case of the unit, and that the ground may well be "connected" via a PCB-etch spark-gap, like the APC version.

If this is the case, and you are using shielded cable, you should keep the case away from contact with ground.

Probably.

The unit (or mine at least) came with a total lack of meaningful documentation, so who knows?

Of course, my network was installed in the '90s , when even CAT-5 was a bit of a novelty. So unfortunately I have no shielded cable, so I guess I have no particular motivation to find out. Yet.

By the way, my sample has no "in" vs "out" markings, and sure enough, it doesn't matter. Works either way.

So does the APC version, by the way, even though it does specify. That is probably just to minimize tech support calls about how to hook it up.

I knocked of a star for the total lack of documentation. IMHO all such devices should come with an accurate schematic diagram so the design philosophy can be determined.

title: Not spectacular, but decent enough.
text:

There's really only one really big 'problem' with it, and that's this: I use an antenna for OTA television reception. No cable. Sometimes, the signal comes in weak, which causes the typical digital blocky image breakup.

Under VERY rare circumstances, the TV will glitch up as it struggles to render the weak image... and suddenly the audio will SHOOT UP to full volume while emitting garbled noise. Even worse, the TV *locks up* while doing this, and my only recourse is to scramble for the power cord to kill it.

It scares the absolute living HELL out of me every single time. To be fair, it's only done it perhaps three times over the course of ownership, and 99.9% of the time it's completely fine. Unfortunately, this third-ever instance of this problem is what caused me to look around online (and write this) and see if there's a firmware update or something, but sadly, I'm on the latest version.

If it wasn't for this bug, I'd be completely happy with the TV. :/

UPDATE: Around late 2014-2015, this TV started developing an issue where the screen image would narrow down to a single pixel row, or go blank entirely. Audio still works. Nothing else. If I power cycle the TV, it works fine again. There is no rhyme or reason to this. I've had it happen within 5 minutes of using the TV. And sometimes I can go 6 to 8 hours with no problem.

title: Really?  That's as loud as they go?
text:
Like others that have reviewed these, I REALLY wanted to like them. I ordered them despite the reviews (from people I should have trusted) saying the volume was too low. I found all the other reviews of adequate or fine volume to be encouraging and hoped I'd experience the same.

I have had Sennheiser products before, as well as Bose QC 15 and Shure in-ear. All of them blow these away in sound quality, and mainly, VOLUME. The headphones are VERY nicely built and VERY comfortable. But I'm sorry, that just can't possibly be as loud as they go?

Yep, it is. No matter what source I plug into wired or hook to via bluetooth, the maximum volume is so low it's just not enjoyable. I want to USE these things on a plane, in the gym, walk around town in them, but it's impossible, because you can't get the volume loud enough to hear your source at a decent level let alone drown outside noise. And the SRS and Noise cancelling are just worthless, making the already low quality sound even lower in volume.

Trust me, I really want to love and keep these. I spent an entire night googling "hack bluetooth volume" and "hack Sennheiser volume" - I even want to write to Sennheiser and ask them where the parental control lock is so I can turn it off, because I can't believe they released these with THAT as the maximum volume. Seriously, please tell me there is a firmware upgrade or a way to connect to these and override the poor default max volume setting and I'll keep them!

I want to like them so badly I spent the rest of the night going back and forth between these, the Bose, and my just newly purchased Beats Wireless. Trust me, I do not want to like these piece of crap built Beats Wireless bluetooth headphones. They aren't as comfortable nor as nicely made as the Sennheiser. But I can hear them damnit! The volume is night and day different between the Beats (and the Bose and others) and the Sennheiser. The Beats at half volume blow the Sennheiser away.

Please Sennheiser, tell me how to hack into these and fix the volume and I'll keep them. Otherwise, I have to return them and wear these crappy Beats that I can at least HEAR.

I am a DJ and music producer/remixer, so I know sound quality, but sound quality is no good if you can't get decent volume!

title: Agree that the earphone design is stupid and defective, but they sound good.
text:
Got these for $60 on sale, and it is surprising that such a well-known company would make such design flaws.

Here are the good things:
:
1. Batteries are replaceable and rechargeable.
2. Sound is very good to excellent. They sound better than my TV's speakers.
3. Reasonably comfortable to wear.
4. Nice charging station.

BUT HERE ARE THE BAD PARTS:

* 1. Earphones are not cups. They are flat and nearly smooth. Do not bend forward or they will slip off. Ridiculous. One way to reduce this defect in design and manufacture is to reverse the phones. They won't be flush on your ears, and they won't sound as good, but more pressure will be applied to your ears reducing the chance of them falling off. Mine have fallen off many times from just looking downward. The headband tension is unfortunately not adjustable. The hand band thus could be too tight or too loose for some people.

* 2. The flat foam covers come off too easily. It's just a slight rotation and they are not held in tightly.

* 3. On Off switch is too close to volume switch

* 4. Although the range is about 150 feet, quite impressive, when going for than 30 feet from the transmitter there is a regular rhythm annoying chirp. Fine tuning doesn't help.

* 5. Sennheiser should have added a MUTE circuit. If the earphones are turned on and the TV is not, there is loud static through the headset.

Sennheiser should redo the ear foam and provide free replacement units to all HDR120 users. These are recommended for the sound quality and comfort.

This review should technically be cross-referenced to the HDR-120 + RS-120 since it was purchased with the charging station, but the criticisms remain the same.

title: UltraPro 72mm Variable NDX Fader Filter ND2 - ND1000?
text:
I ordered this from Fanta (through Amazon) and it was about 2/3rds more expensive than here. The edge of the ring says Vivitar Series 1. It says nothing about 'UltraPro'. So I'm uncertain I'm reviewing the identical product or not. Yes, there are index marks on the ring. More importantly, the forward most part of the ring is 5mm MORE than the part that threads into your lens. This means you won't be able to install/remove the hood for your lens with this installed. If you leave the hood on, it's going to make installing this most awkward and difficult without cross threading or scratching the lens.

I believe Vivitar's reasoning, however, was to avoid vignetting by making the outer-forward portion of this filter bigger. I, myself, found the swivel ring turns easily and smoothly. It's made of metal and optical glass. The threads seem well machined and don't stick, unlike some of its plastic Chinese cousins. If this is the same unit as the more expensive 'UltraPro' I just purchased from Fanta through Amazon, I wish I'd purchased from this vendor as I bought 3 (67mm, 72mm, 77mm). I'm a bit nervous/leery of sending it back under Amazon's 30-day return policy simply because I found a much better deal. I could save $46 if Amazon would accept them back--but perhaps they ding customers for returning items that aren't straight up 'defective'?

HOW IT WORKS:

I've played around quite a bit with linear polarizing filters and circular (CPL) ones. Wikipedia has a wonderful animated diagram explaining how CPL's work. Essentially they're a combination of a straight up linear filter stacked on a quarter-wave linear polarizing filter. The combination (with the simpler linear filter being the first the light hits) creates a kind of helix spiraling light beam pattern that doesn't defeat the functionality of modern digital cameras with their phase focusing and light metering systems. You can check on my explanation by holding the CPL up to your eye and looking at a pair of polarized eye-glasses with a little illumination behind them. If you hold the CPL in the same orientation it would be mounted on your camera, no matter which way you rotate the CPL, the light on the far side of the polarized glasses will still be visible through it. BUT, if you reverse the direction you look through it and THEN rotate the CPL, you'll see the polarized eye-glasses change from transparent to 'black'. That's because the straight linear portion of the filter is now the ultimate arbiter of how the light will be polarized before it gets to your eye. In its more normal orientation, however, it is the quarter-wave plate that is the final arbiter.

So I tried the same thing with this variable NDX, and guess what? It behaves much the same way as the CPL with one important difference. If I hold the NDX in its normal orientation, leaving it wide open (minimizing any 'darkening'), it matters not which way or how much I rotate it while looking at the test polarized eye-glasses mentioned above. If I reverse it (leaving the NDX wide open), I get the very same effect described above when examining the polarized eye-glasses. However, the CPL doesn't (at least on its own) DARKEN the image when I rotate its elements relative to one another. The variable NDX does! How can this be? My guess is, unlike the CPL, the NDX doesn't use a quarter-wave plate as one of its elements. I don't think it uses two simple linear polarizing elements either. I think it uses a linear polarizing element stacked on a plate with a much smaller perpendicular wave plate than one-quarter. Perhaps it's 1/16th, I don't know. But in any event, it's small enough to effectively remove almost all the light when the two elements are rotated 90 degrees to one another. This approach might allow the phase focusing and metering of your digital camera to continue to function even with a variable NDX on it.

Them's my thoughts and I'm sticking to them until someone offers a more plausible explanation. I hope you appreciate the physics of my explanation as understanding light mechanics may help you be a better photographer. This is worth owning although admittedly I'd like to own it for 3/8ths less that what I do. I haven't tested it for aberrations/artifacts. But having the dynamic range of a video camera overwhelmed and the white balance screwing up the color saturation is a pretty serious 'aberration' in its own right.

title: Decent phones, but lacking in detail/presentation
text:
I heard quite a bit of buzz about these before I purchased them. My friend (a protege of mine who is getting into producing dubstep and the like) got a pair (of the KNS-6400) and I had a chance to check them out and was impressed. I auditioned them further at guitar center off of an ipod and they responded extremely well to some skrillex and DJ Tiesto. I picked up a pair that same day. I've had them for about 9 months now and realized (a few days ago) I wanted a second reference set of phones. Again, Guitar Center had a great deal on a set of Audio Technica ATH-M45s. Picked those up (they were the white ones) and noticed that listening to the Audio Technica's (as much as I had liked the KRKs up to this point) opened up gobs more detail and richness in each of the recordings I auditioned. All of the songs I had mixed on the KRKs were excellent sounding on the Audio Technicas (the KRK's always tended to translate rather well for mixing duties) but I noticed a immense amount more bass depth and detail and a higher degree of "immediacy" from the Audio Technica's. Things were simply more exciting sounding... somehow.

First song I tried mixing on the Audio Technica's (ATH-M45s) turned out way better than I had anticipated. Pleasant surprise.

There's an interesting trade-off here for the KRK KNS-6400 that I've noticed from my experience in using the amount of headphones I have over the years (I've owned a lot of phones/headphone amps/interfaces). The KRK's seem to strike a tonal balance that is conducive towards mixing that will translate very well across playback platforms. I've written a good deal of songs through the KRKs and they always tended to sound very "even" on any system I tried them on (with the exception of managing low-bass, this was actually somewhat problematic). In comparison, the Audio Technica ATH-M45s made it easier to really enjoy mixing (sounds just felt more real and alive) but caused the overall mix balance to apparently suffer a bit (at least upon a couple initial comparisons with reference songs). It gets even more interesting though, because the more I listened through the KRKs to the song I just finished mixing on the Audio Technica's, the more I actually started to prefer the tonal balance of my own song to that of reference commercial pieces that I typically use in comparison. For as many years as I've spent mixing, I've come across strange scenarios like this on a somewhat frequent basis that are especially confounding.

What I think it boils down to is this. The KRK KNS-6400s are really decent phones. They allow for very accurate mix balancing in terms of the scope of frequency spectrum (expect problems in the low-bass where they lack definition and extension). However, they don't make mixing all that exciting. The can definitely do the job and if the level of detail is what you want then they could very well be a great fit as they have for many other people. But something about what I was able to accomplish with the Audio Technica's was so much more immediately satisfying in terms of crafting an end-product from both a production and mixing perspective that I can't really look back. The KRKs do (in direct comparison) actually sound a little hollow I suppose. I don't think what I'm describing is really a factor of frequency response per say. I could see how people would really like this set. I can also see how you might come to the same conclusion as I did. I never had that "wow" moment with the KRKs where I was so impressed with a mix that I just sat there wondering how it ended up sounding so good when (by all considerations) it really shouldn't have. The KRKs always just sort of delivered what I generally expected from them.

I prefer being pleasantly surprised. Other phones have done that for me. The KRKs will make an excellent second reference set however.

title: Makes me love the ASUS T100
text:
I read all the reviews for the Asus T100 before buying, and like most others, I felt it was a great value except for the annoying, shiny, fingerprint-magnet surfaces. So I bought the Skinomi TechSkin for it. I had absolutely no problem installing it and had it on, pretty close to perfect, in under 30 minutes. I do have a lot of experience installing similar products though. Right now, the screen looks kind of grainy, but that should clear up completely within a day or so. The result is excellent. The Asus T100 looks so much better, and NO fingerprints ANYWHERE. I am very happy with both products. I will be posting this same review to the Asus T100 page.

Edited to add: I've just read some of the other reviews in which people got discouraged with the screen protector and discarded it. This is a shame. It actually goes on very well if you wet it sufficiently and slide it into place. Have a paper towel ready to blot the excess as you squeegee the bubbles and liquid out. It is really easily moveable for quite a while afterward. I got it into place and used a blow dryer to speed up the drying, as per the instructions. My best advice is to dampen your fingers with the included solution before peeling it off its backing, and don't be afraid to moisten the whole screen protector. It doesn't have to be dripping, but definitely coated. Squeegee out the bubbles and excess and then slide it into position. You won't be disappointed. It reduces some of the glare, and almost all of the fingerprints. I hope this is helpful.

It would constantly have to be rebooted and connections were constantly lost. Could not get a connection in the basement and NO BARS outside on iPhone or iPad. Purchased it and had it set up within minutes. No Brainer Setup - I call it. No tech support, no problems whatsoever. Placed it in exactly the same location as my other routers - WOW - FAST RELIABLE CONNECTIONS!! I Finally got what I paid for. Thanks Apple. I get powerful connections even outside and down the street almost 100 meters away!! Full bars connection ANYWHERE inside my home with iphone and ipad. Other computers that are wireless have much stronger throughput connections and reliable. Been a month now and NO LOSS OF CONNECTION!!! Oh and no flashing crazy little lights waking you up(if you put it in bedroom)just a soft glow from a green light(which you can swith if you want it for connection status light)I think I sleep with a little smile on my face now. title: Not bad
text:
Upon arriving in beautiful California for a long vacation, I dropped my Canon S90 -- a miraculous point & shoot, legendary for its picture quality. Stunned, I dropped into the nearest retail store & bought a quick make-do replacement. I chose the Elph 110 HS because it had the widest aperture of all the offerings (f2.7) & was the most pocketable. I prayed that our vacation pictures would be decent.

After 10 days of putting the Elph 110 HS through its paces, I think I'll keep it. The color quality is wonderful. The camera meters well. The image sharpness varies: soft in the corners, and not as sharp at wide angle or tele. The best images are mid range; at 2 feet to 25 feet, the Elph 110 is as sharp as anything from the S90. You need to pay strict attention to where the camera is focusing as the auto settings latch on to strange things. Make sure to switch between macro, mid & distant focusing. I was happier using SuperFine compression & custom color settings, bumping up the sharpness, contrast & saturation a bit, and shooting in P (Program) mode where I could control the focus. Auto has its uses, and for quick snaps, it does a good job. The flash set just the right amount of fill flash. I was especially pleased with my flash shots. My low light pictures turned out fine with additional flash or slower shutter speed or a white balance adjustment or a little exposure compensation, and I didn't have to bother using higher ISO settings. It is marvelously portable, slipping into pockets, purses, small fanny packs & eyeglass cases with ease. Battery goes from empty to fully charged in two hours.

The camera has good capabilities: exposure lock, focus lock, flash exposure lock, exposure compensation, Canon's ample array of color effects, good white balance settings (including custom white balance), a good drive mode, and can even take photos in square format (I like!). It has Stitch Assist for panoramic shots. Long Shutter mode allows for shutter times up to 15 seconds & is easy to use. There is a grid display option.

Settings: Less useful ones are toy camera, fish eye (wish it were a true fish eye), posterizer, soft focus, miniaturizer. There is a snow setting, but no sunset setting. There is no sports/kids/pets or otherwise high shutter speed setting. Supposedly in auto the camera can detect children or babies & automatically switch to drive mode. You can print a single image from video, but I can't attest to image quality. Face ID (the camera can "memorize" faces) might be useful if you have kids, but I can't see using it much.

Cons: There is much menu diving, especially to do the work arounds for tricky shots. I couldn't get Tracking AutoFocus to work well. No RAW and no choice of color space. The histogram display is post-shot only. It blows out highlights like crazy, but so did my S90. I confuse the shutter button with the on/off button sometimes, again just like my S90.

In short, it's a better than average camera that can do a lot. If you are patient in setting up the work arounds to compensate for the lack of a Manual setting, you can get the trickier shots. I wish the sharpness were more consistent across various types of shooting. But if you just want a camera for family/friends snap shots, the sharpness is excellent for that kind of photography.

title: Great sound and battery life, watch out for the sensor
text:
I bought the Voyager Pro HD for use with my iPhone 4s. The sound quality and battery life are excellent. Make sure you try a couple of the earpieces to get the best fit, because this is important to sound quality, comfort, and apparently reliable operation of the sensor.

In my experience, the sensor is very reliable at detecting when the headset is off my ear, but also makes the mistake of assuming the headset is off my ear way too often. If you go to the support site, you will find that holding the headset by the mic end for several seconds (off your ear) is a simple way to recalibrate the sensor.

On the iPhone 4s, the symptoms of sensor error (which they don't tell you in the manual or on a support call) are:
1. Siri doesn't respond to a 2 second press of the Call button
2. The iPhone uses its internal speaker for audio on calls rather than the headset even though the headset is shown as connected
3. While playing music, the sound cuts in and out as you walk or turn your head

I hope that Plantronics will address this issue with a software rev. At minimum, it would be nice if there was a button press or combination that would force the headset to assume it is on your ear.

Meantime, I like this headset but was very frustrated at having to diagnose this issue myself. I hope this review prevents others from going through that frustration.

title: Nice, but defective
text:
I really liked this case/keyboard combination. It's only marginally bigger than a case without a keyboard, something one might miss just looking at the photo. Even if you never use the keyboard, it's still a nice case.

Mine was defective. 8 of the keys didn't work at all. For some reason Amazon won't let you exchange this item, so I just returned it and ordered another one. The replacement worked OK.

Here are some strong points:

- Sturdy case
- Rechargeable keyboard, uses same charging cable as Kindle
- Totally solid stand for landscape viewing. It will not wobble or collapse.
- Magnet-triggered automatic sleep/wake when you open and close the case
- Magnetic attached keyboard that's easy to remove, but stays in place.
- Elastic holder for a stylus.
- Kindle fits firmly in case with no chance of slipping or falling out.
- Cut-outs allow access to the ports and speakers.
- Setup documentation is clear and easy to follow.
- Good protection for the Kindle.

On the negative side:

- The tuck-in tab that closes the case fits rather tightly, making it difficult to insert. The replacement keyboard was easier to insert.
- The keys are pretty small.
- If you hold down a key for a fraction of a second longer than necessary, it will repeatttttttttttttt.
- No provision for a vertical standing position.

Hint: If you are holding the Kindle in the case and not using the keyboard, you will fold the front cover behind the Kindle, which means that your fingers are grasping the back are pressing the keys. So just remove the keyboard which is just held on with a magnet when holding it this way.

All of that said, I found that I really don't have much use for a keyboard, and I ended up using a different case that was a little more slim.

title: Decent for the money
text:
I bought this as a stand-in for a record player of my mom's that she had lent to someone and never got back (and still hasn't). For the money I paid for it (on sale for $50 or so) it's a decent record player, and you'll be hard pressed to find another with a built in receiver in this price range. The sound when hooked into external speakers is pretty good all things considered, but it's not going to hold up well against anything more expensive.

Construction wise I haven't had any real problems in the several months I've had it, from the looks of other reviews I guess I got lucky in that respect. It plays smoothly and has an auto-stop feature and a raise/lower lever (which is great if you have shaky hands like me), it even has a little 45 adaptor tucked away in the corner which I thought was nice. It's also cool that it plays 77 rpm records, even though most people don't have those (I only have one out of about 200 or so records). As far as the sound quality goes, I don't have anything to compare it to directly, but I've definitely heard better, even my ipod hooked through the same speakers sounds better most of the time.

My biggest problem with it are the built in speakers, which while horrible to begin with, refuse to turn off when I plug external speakers in, so you still end up hearing them regardless of whether the switch on the back is on or off (which only seems to turn off the headphone jack). This results in a tinny, crappy sounding version of your music playing alongside your regular speakers which is incredibly annoying and takes away from the music. The mp3 ripping is a joke, it ends up at about youtube sound quality. The max volume is also pretty low, and without any sort of EQ settings besides a bass boost button, it's really varies in sound quality between records.

title: Claimed response time not correct
text:
Acer's manual and marketing details state the monitor has a 2ms response time, however I see ranges from 9-17ms from my testing. Their manual doesn't state weather this measurement is for white->back->white or grey-to-grey, so I tested both.
I also tested "display lag" and saw numbers from 11-22ms depending on weither v-sync waiting was turned on or not. My methodology was to use a 1000 fps video camera and a micro-controller hooked up to the PC. The PC would trigger a light on the micro-controller and simultaneously present a new frame of data to the monitor. Using the recorded video footage I could measure the time between when the micro-controller light turned on and the monitor initially displayed the first scan line of new data. I could also see when the full display was updated with new frame data. I used 1080p resolution at 120hz for testing and 127/255 gray levels for g2g. My video card was Nvidia GTX 480. More specific timings:

no-vsync white->black->white/2 = 13ms average
no-vsync white->gray->white/2 = 14ms average
vsync white->black->white/2 = 10.6ms average
vsync white->gray->white/2 = 11.2ms average

title: Good Value
text:
I have a Speck case for my Nook Simple Touch, and it has about the same quality; the stitching, aesthetic feel, and durability. I would say that this is even better in quality because it has real leather and is cheaper.

Usability: 9/10

I would give the usability a 9/10. It has 4 angles, and all of them seem to work well. There are holes for the speakers, and you'd think that there would be a disruption since some angles could block the speakers. This isn't the case. It's designed to make a little room, so the sound is never obstructed when you put it in all the different angles. The installation was very easy since you just push in all the corners. The only bad part is not being able to use the micro USB port in all the angles. This is bad if you're using a controller to play the game since you have to rest it on the micro-usb cable to make it work. I don't blame Blurex for this. It's Acer's problem since they put the micro-USB port on the bottom. Blurex would have to put holes in the case to make the USB usable in those angles. No one would want to buy a case with 3 holes on the cover. You can access all the ports and charge it when it's closed.

Aesthetics: 10/10

The aesthetics are good. The case feels very solid. It does add some weight onto the tablet, but it doesn't bother me. I'd rather have a heavier case than a very light one. The leather feels nice. It's smooth, but has a grippy texture. It's not as grippy as the back of the A510 backing, but that's made of synthetic plastic and not leather. Even the corners, that hold the tablet, feel very solid.

Overall: 10/10

That USB problem isn't a huge issue. The price is good at $20, and there aren't many other cases for this tablet right now. It's a good deal considering my Nook Speck case was the same price, and that was smaller and didn't even have leather.
I'd give it a 10/10 overall in terms of quality, aesthetics, and value.

title: Where have you been all my life!
text:
I've been trying for quite some time to get a decent network connection to some electronics in our basement from our modem/router on the second floor. I've tried various wireless access points in different locations, repeaters, and so on, but I've never been able to get decent throughput on a wireless connection. I've also tried powerline ethernet and got extremely poor performance from that approach because it is critically dependent on the physical layout of your electrical system when the nodes aren't on the same circuit, and our situation isn't compatible with the requirements in that respect.

Enter ethernet over coax cable. Fortunately we happen to have the right cables in place to make the connections from upstairs to the basement, and lo and behold, it works wonders. I'm getting 4-5 times the throughput using ethernet over coax compared to the best wireless performance I've seen. The marketing blurbs say something about 270Mbps but I believe that is somehow related to the theoretical maximum of the media. The actual real-world limit is lower due to the 100Mb ethernet port on the device. At any rate I now get ~80+Mbps throughput on drag-and-drop file transfers from our linux pc upstairs to a Windows pc in the basement, compared to something like 16-20Mbps over wireless.

Setting the system up was plug and play, and I was very impressed with the Actiontec package, which included literally everything I needed, including two cat5e patch cables, two coax patch cables, and even a splitter, which came in handy. The system coexists well with our over-the-air TV, which comes in from an outside antenna on the same coax as the ethernet. Note that according to the documentation it does not work with most satellite systems. All in all I am very happy with this product, and highly recommend it.

title: Paperwhite
text:
I truly love my Kindle Paperwhite. This is my second Kindle but its really my first. I purchased an original Kindle a few years back and my wife decided she really liked it. Hence I never really saw my Kindle after that. Add my son getting his hands on the original and suddenly dad's Kindle was his in name only. I considered getting a second Kindle a while back, but then I learned about Paperwhite's pending release and decided to wait a bit. I had an iPad with the Kindle app, so I wasn't really concerned about the wait. I am glad I waited, as Paperwhite is everything I was looking for and then some.

I like the backlit screen. In fact I was somewhat disappointed when my original Kindle did not have a backlit screen. I can now read in a poorly lit, or unlit room, and not need a lamp. The screen is still the same size, but the device itself is small enough to fit in one hand or my back pocket. Thus I can essentially take my Paperwhite anywhere. The e ink, or whatever they call it, is still far superior to reading from my Kindle app on my iPad. A while back I saw Amazon's Jeff Bezos on an interview show and he said then there is room in the world for both tablets and e readers, and that statement still rings true. Of course the playing field has changed a bit as Amazon has entered into the tablet market, but I do prefer reading the Kindle rather than seeing my own mug in the screen of my iPad.

I purchased the Paperwhite case, which will be a separate review, and I strongly recommend the case for anyone who takes their Kindle out of their house. One drawback is the lack of color ink, but perhaps someday Amazon will find a way to combine e ink and color. For this reason the photography books I buy are better read from my iPad (reflection of my face in screen acknowledged) than the Paperwhite, but that is life. I also subscribed to some digital content magazines and the iPad's color screen again makes the experience more satisfying, but for general books, the Kindle Paperwhite's e ink is more pleasing to my reading experience.

There are several e readers available, but I'm an Amazon fan so I prefer Kindle to any others. I've never owned any other reader so my review is biased, but I'm not made of money either, so my decision to stick with Amazon is also based on economic realities. Paperwhite offers many of the features the competitors offer and it has the Amazon name behind it, so it is part of the original e reader product line. I (actually it was my wife who bought it for me) own the special offers variety and the nice thing is for the $20 I could have the annoying ads removed. Thus far the ads have not irritated me to the point of spending the money, but it's nice to know I can get rid of them should I chose.

In closing I just want to say that I'm glad I got the Paperwhite and if you are an e reader fan, I recommend you buy one as well.

title: Not for external drive use on USB - misleading product description
text:
I bought this WD Red drive to provide backup for my large (data) desktop. I use Windows backup. I paired the drive with a StarTech USB 3.0 enclosure and a Koutech USB 3.0 PCI card (each of which worked fine. I can't say enough positive things about Koutech support, BTW). Tested it for reads and writes: very fast. Then I tried to run backup, and Windows backup failed. Without belaboring the many phone calls and hours of research on the web, the problem is a combination of Microsoft Win 7 inability to handle 4K logical & physical sectors with WD's failure to provide microcode to emulate 512e sectors for this drive. (NB: Windows 8 does support 4K sectors). After a number of emails back and forth - over several weeks - I finally wound up with WD level 2 support who informed me that the drive was intended as an "internal drive" with the implication that I was unreasonable to try to use it as an external drive. Of course, WD markets this as a (and has an approved enclosure list for) NAS drive when it's connected via ethernet. When I queried what a NAS drive was if not an external drive, I was told that it was the USB attachment that created the problem. BTW, level 1 tried to blame the enclosure first, then the USB card, then my motherboard... anybody but them.

The good news is that the drive is fast attached as I have it via USB 3.0 and if there were not a specific problem with Microsoft Windows Backup (or some other critical application), it would be fine. The real problem is the marketing language and lack of cautions from WD about a well-known and well-documented problem.(If you want more detail search for "Windows 7 Backup error 0x8078002A" or "4k sectors and windows backup.") Despite what you may read about potential solutions, the WD Quick Formatter cannot find WD Red drives when USB attached. Further, Level 2 WD support assures me that there is no microcode in the WD Red drives which can be used to emulate 512 sectors, so there is no solution.

As for now, I have switched backup programs, hardly my favored workaround. But it took so long for WD to get back to me and finally give me a definitive answer that my 30 day window to return the drive passed.

As long as you are dealing with applications which are not sensitive to 4K vs 512 sectors, the drive is fine. If there is a dependency, pass it by.

title: The Trials and Tribulatons of OTA TV
text:
I recently retired, began to live on a reduced income, and watched my satellite TV subscription increase to nearly $120/mo. So I cut the cable. I've lived in the same house for 43 years. It was built in 1902. The walls are plaster over lath and wire, which can be a problem for indoor reception except near windows. There are two translators located at opposite ends of the valley, 3 and 9 miles from my house. Large trees, and a barn block some signals. The translators are low power, between 1 and 2 watts. In the 1970s I used a large mast with a huge, high gain antenna that was boosted and had a power rotator. It was a great pain in the bippy. My first satellite dish had been mounted on a power pole, but tree leaves broke up the signal when the wind blew. I put up a 12 ft. pole 25 feet away and a tech mounted a new dish to it, but coupled with the old cable on the power pole. I bought two of these RCA antennas and mounted them where the satellite dishes had been, pointed them at the translators, uncoupled the old satellite cable connector and connected the cables to a combiner. Voila! Free digital TV.

The antennas work just fine, but I discovered that not all tuners are equally sensitive. When attached directly to my TV, the TV tuner read signal strengths in the 70s to 90s. When attached to our TiVo DVR the picture was still good, but the signal strengths are in the 50s and 60s. TiVo has a bogus explanation for this that I'll skip for this review. If you're connecting cables to splitter/combiners outdoors, remember to use cable fittings that have O-rings in them to keep water out. If you live in a rural area served by mountaintop TV translators, you won't get a program guide on your TiVo unless you bother them consistently to convert the normal broadcast channels to the translator frequencies. Even though the translators are low power, and I'm running about 100 feet of RG-6 cable, there is no need for a booster. Sometimes a signal booster can overpower your signals and pixelate them.

I hope this helps someone - I did have to do a little heavy pruning of a large Douglas fir and the top of a lilac bush to get an unimpeded line of sight to one of the translators. Due to my wife's work schedule, we needed the TiVo DVR. We added a Roku box and a Hulu Plus subscription. We already had Amazon Prime for shopping and a high speed DSL connection for our computers. I hooked up a small computer to one of the HDMI jacks on the TV and we can get most everything we want to watch now. The cost of the DVR and Roku will be easily paid for by savings. The TiVo and Hulu subscriptions run about $23/month. This is far cheaper than $120/mo. for satellite. I must be honest and say that I have to fiddle around more to "dial up" what we want to watch, especially with online content. I do miss plunking down and using just one remote. However, the savings really add up fast.

title: Despite the high price tag, it's worth it.
text:
I've used Logitech's squeezebox units and roku's soundbridge units and found them both lacking. I was frustrated with the setup, the errors, the lack of continued support (nice when you pay $300 for a unit and they just don't really update it much), and the need to run applications to leverage the full functionality. I still have my squeezebox but it's mainly used as a bedroom clock now.

So when I discovered Sonos I was a bit skeptical. But I looked into the platform more and decided to give it a shot, and I'm so glad I did. I'm in love with this device, plain and simple. It hits all the right points: it's easy to use and set up (took me less than 10 minutes), it has all the main music sources, and has great support.

The device sounds amazing too. My favorite aspect though has to be that it just works. No errors about not being able to connect to the server, no issues with wi-fi dropping, nothing. It responds almost instantly to whatever I ask of it and does it every time. It's just amazing how well it works.

That said, it's not perfect. My main complaint is that the unit is completely reliant on a smartphone or tablet for functionality. Aside from volume control on the unit there's nothing else you can control without a smartphone or tablet. It makes me miss the remotes from the competing products as well as a display on the unit. If I'm moving around I don't want to have to pull my phone out of my pocket and unlock it to see what song is playing, and I don't want to have to do the same just to skip to the next track. I can understand the lack of a display to a degree, it may ruin the overall design of the unit, but a simple RF/IR remote with volume and play controls, maybe two context sensitive buttons (e.g. thumb up, thumb down in Pandora) would really elevate this device to perfection to me. To some extent I get that it's not included because of the way Sonos works as a whole home music situation, but they're smart people and should be able to figure a way to make it work (a switch from unit to zone on the remote even?). And while I'm aware of the Sonos Control it functions no different than my phone (aside from a lock screen). I just want a simple button based remote like that on a Squeezebox, Apple TV, Roku, etc etc. Maybe in a future hardware unit.

As a note, I bought this as a Bundle that included a free bridge. A bridge is almost essential if you don't have another Sonos product. As a note first, for those complaints that Sonos isn't wireless - it is. You simply need to have one of the Sonos components wired in and the rest of the units can connect to it wirelessly. Simply put their wireless in their own network but need a physical connection to your own network through at least one unit. That's the point of the bridge, a cheap unit to hide away.

Pros:
++Sounds amazing
++Easy to use/setup
++Great list of music sources
++Works flawlessly
+Looks good
+Use Android/iOS phone or tablet as a controller

Cons:
-Price is a bit high, especially if you need to get a bridge
-No dedicated remote or display

Very pleased and planning to add more units once I move to a larger apartment.

title: Good camera, but here are things you should know
text:
I like this camera. It's a little heavy, but seems to be well-made and durable. It looks sharp, and of course it has the Zeiss lens. I like the quality of the photos that I have been getting from it. I think I will keep it for a long time.

However, there are some things that you should know before getting this camera. First, there are virtually no instructions or user guides in the box. There is a bare-bones guide that tells you (in several languages) what the various parts of the camera are, but as far as a discussion of the features of this camera, forget about it. Sony does have an on-line guide "CyberShot User Guide", but you're going to have to Google it to find it, because Sony's website is so fragmented and incomprehensible that it's unlikely that you will find it easily.

Second, be advised that the highly-touted WiFi feature to upload your images to your computer is very difficult to use. It is not automatic, meaning that every time you want to upload images to your computer, you've got to go through a manual process. It is a very clunky process, and it takes a long time to upload images wirelessly. The process has failed on me several times and I don't know why. The USB cable upload process is much better than the WiFi feature. Similarly, uploading to a smartphone has never worked for me (iPhone). It simply does not work.

There are a couple of proprietary applications that Sony touts to process images (PlayMemories and one other (I forget the name of it)). Be advised that these applications are designed for Windows, not Mac. Sony has adapted both applications for Mac, but you're going to have to look hard for them on the Sony website (try Googling them), because Sony's website and tech support are such a mess. If you have a Mac, you're probably better off just importing photos into iPhoto and forgetting about the Sony software.

I realize that "real photographers" probably don't need much hand-holding to use this camera or to process their images. If you've got Photoshop and know how to use it, all the other software is unnecessary. Similarly, the various features of the camera are second nature to adept photographers. However, for the rest of us (weekend users, etc.), it seems to me that Sony could have at least included a guide in the box to refresh our memories (aperture control, shutter control, etc). It would have cost them virtually nothing. Let's face it, folks, this is a $750 camera. Would a $1.00 color brochure have been asking too much of Sony? My little $200 Canon point-and-shoot had a full-color guide in the box when I got it several years ago.

I give this camera a solid 4 stars, but I give Sony a very generous 2 stars. This balances out to 3 stars, in my opinion. The camera is really nice, but Sony is clearly not ready for prime time in the consumer camera market.

title: DisplayPort 1.2 and Daisy Chaining- What you need to know
text:
I bought three of these monitors at the same time, as well as 3 DisplayPort 1.2 cables (I TRIPLE checked this because of how I wanted to configure the system). My setup is somewhat unique, so this review is primarily for those that want to have a single displayport 1.2 cable driving all three monitors in a daisy chain setup. The idea is relatively simple: Your graphics card output going into monitor 1 input. Then you connect a cable on monitor 1's displayport OUTPUT to monitor 2's displayport input. Repeat for up to a total of FOUR monitors. Sounds like an easy way to rid yourself of wires and have a clean setup right? Well, here's my experience.

Some background. This monitors are revision A01, my graphics card is a Gigabyte 7870. It has two mini DPs, a DVI out and am HDMI out. I used the supplied adapter from the graphics card for a mini DP to full sized DP, then hooked in the Cables Matters Displayport 1.2 cable to my first monitor. I daisy chained the other two according to Dell's instructions. BY DEFAULT the Dell's DisplayPort 1.2 capability is OFF. With it off you will definitely get no signal in a daisy chain configuration, from any of the monitors. To fix this, on monitor 1 (the monitor with the direct input from the graphics card) touch the menu button directly to the left of the power button. Make sure the monitor registers your touch- you will know if it does because the monitor will display a message saying it has no signal and you can select a different input by clicking the menu button. Once the menu comes up with different inputs, make sure the DisplayPort option is selected and HOLD the green checkmark button for approximately 8 seconds. A menu will come up asking if you would like to switch to DisplayPort 1.2. Make sure enable is selected and click the green checkmark. Repeat these steps on each monitor EXCEPT the last monitor in your DisplayPort daisy chain configuration. This one should stay in DP 1.1a mode.

Alright! So now everything is set up correctly and it should be smooth sailing from here on out right? Well.. not in my case. I experience a plethora of issues: one of more of the monitors will flicker, one or more of the monitors not coming on at ALL, one of the monitors will randomly shut off while the other two work properly and wont reinitialize. Essentially what it feels like to me is that the monitors aren't able to adequately send the signals to each other. I can't tell if this is a throughput issue, some type of handshake issue, graphics card drivers issue, etc. It's somewhat confusing honestly; in my experience all three monitors will initialize and display (albeit in a mirror mode NOT an extended mode) before Windows loads. My theory is that post-Windows, the signal sent to the monitors is displayport 1.1. The monitors don't seem to have a problem sharing a displayport 1.1 signal and displaying in mirror mode, but what's the point of that? That's not why people are getting three monitors! We want monitor extension, eyefinity, etc. When Windows loads, I THINK that the graphics card switches to DP 1.2 mode. So it appears like its a Windows issue or drivers issue but I think its a DP 1.2 issue. This could be two things. A cable/throughput issues or a monitor issue. AMD software has a displayport troubleshooting program, and when I can get all three monitors to actually work and display, the displayport program shows a total bandwidth of 20gb/s and each monitor is taking approximately 4.5 gb/s. So that says to me that its not throughput.. which leads to the only thing left.. the monitors themselves.

I believe these monitors have a serious issue with DP, specifically 1.2. I think DP 1.1a works fine.. but if you want to daisy chain you are REQUIRED to use DP 1.2 because of the throughput limitation of 1.1a. In this monitor's current state, I would not recommend this type of configuration. You can still use the HDMI inputs or the mini or full-sized DP (make sure 1.2 is turned off) and everything should work fine.. but for the sake of this review, I wanted to speak directly to the issue of DP 1.2 and daisy chaining.

I will update my review after I get my setup hooked up via HDMI for all three monitors. My plan is to use two Mini DP to HDMI adapters and hook two monitors up using that configuration, and my third monitor will simply be an HDMI connection from my graphics card to monitor.

So should you be concerned that this monitor doesn't really function properly in DP 1.2 mode? Only if you MUST run a daisy chain configuration. The main difference between DP 1.1a and 1.2 is throughput. You need that extra throughput to send enough signal through the cable to allow all three monitors to get a "chunk" of data. 1.1a cant push enough data through the cable, so you can't daisy chain. DP1.2 is also needed for high resolutions, for the same throughput reasoning. More data, more throughput required. The dell is a 1080P monitor so that's not an issue.

title: Perfect for what it was designed for
text:
We have two Jambox products: the regular Jambox and the Big Jambox. We first bought the regular sized Jambox and then bought this one for outdoor parties in the backyard or when we camp. The size is a bit bigger than you might at first expect but the sound is great, the battery really lasts, and the Bluetooth range is fine. We've even had the phone inside and this outside with no problem (up to a point of course).

What really separates this from the smaller version are:

1. This one has bi-directional communication with the device it is paired to. In addition to the volume up and down controls, you can pause a track, skip forward or skip back.
2. The sound is much bigger. If you max the sound on the smaller version (which is great for what it was designed for) you get some distortion and across the spectrum the bass isn't as deep. While this certainly isn't a deep base device, both the low and high notes are great for it's size and it can go much louder without distortion.

From a charger perspective it is nice that you can charge it either with the included 1/8th" (?) charger and jack, or by plugging in a small USB cable (I use the same charger and jack as my Galaxy phone). I haven't timed how long it take to charge but it seems about 1/4th the running time (if you play it for four hours I'm guessing you can charge it in about an hour).

We've had this outside for parties up to about 60 people and camping groups of perhaps 30 people, and it has been great. Is this the same as putting your full-size speakers to the windows or using wired outside speakers? Of course not. But, again, for the purpose they have got to be the most convenient and quality option I've seen or tried.

One note on color: We bought white because it was on sale at about 25% less than the other colors. The obvious thought is a white speaker designed to be used outside is going to get ugly fast. So far we haven't had an issue. I've wiped it down several times since where the buttons are (top and side) and the low-profile rubber feet on the bottom can pick-up dirt. I might feel differently in a year or so but for now I'd probably go for the savings and still buy white if I had to do it over again.

Overall, good product at a fair price and great for what it was designed for.

title: Well-done knockoff of old favorite
text:
Back in the days before USB (which still exist in most industrial automation) every engineer needed a handy RS232 breakout box to diagnose handshaking and Tx / Rx line reversals.

Those boxes were pricey, but well made. This box appears to be a decent knockoff.

Switches are provided to isolate each line independently, an array of jumper sockets allows you to reroute signals for proper handshaking. LED's show status.

Cons:
1. the serial line powered LED's are VERY dim, and they are on/off only, not tri-state (Off=floating, grn=-v, red=+v)
2. there is no place in the device to store the jumper wires, use a zip-lock bag or you will lose them

title: This really improved the speed of my Mac Mini (2007 model)
text:
I have a 2007 Mac Mini, running 10.6.8 Snow Leapord, that had begun to slow down over the last few years, especially when a Time Machine Backup was running. Boot up times were about 2 minutes, so I purchased this 128 GB SSD drive, installed it, partitioned it, restored my backup from Time Machine and my Mac Mini now runs like it did (maybe faster) than when I purchased it in 2007. My Mac Mini boots up quickly and is ready to use in 30 seconds. I have a 1.83 GHZ core 2 duo processor and 2 GB of memory. The Mac Mini fan is not running as much either, so this drive is putting off much less heat than the old mechanical drive the Mini originally had.

There are videos on youtube showing how to dis-assemble the Mac Mini (search for "mac mini upgrade ssd"). To make removing the cover easier, I took a 4 inch wide paint scraper, sharpened the blade with a grinding stone, and then wore gloves to avoid a cut while removing the cover. Watch the videos, because removing the cover, small screws and antennas inside the case are a bit tricky if you are not comfortable with that sort of task and you could damage your Mini and void your warranty too.

You DON'T have to enable a feature called TRIM (search for "SSD TRIM" to see what this is) for the SSD but I did. It is not a requirement! AND from what I read, TRIM support became available in 10.6.2 (and my not be available if you have an older version of OSX). But if you want to enable TRIM support...then read on.
TRIM support is detailed at the link below. I can't say how much faster TRIM support made the Mac, because I didn't notice any difference as the Mac was blazing fast anyway, but the article below said TRIM could extend the life of the drive. Notice the article below is for OSX Lion, but these commands still work for OSX Snow Leopard.

[...]

If the article above has expired, then search for "mac mini ssd upgrade IOAHCIBlockStorage" and you will surely find more instructions. If when executing the commands to enable TRIM, you get an error message stating that it did not recognize ".{9}", don't despair. I got that several times, and it is due to the fact that text editors and word processors will sometimes change characters like ' to " or change ' to ` when displaying text. Those are very subtle differences that the eye won't see, but a computer operating system will choke on. If you run into this, just search for another article on the internet with the same instructions, or contact me and I will send you the commands that work.

title: Works Well if Expectations are Reasonable plus Review Update to 5 stars much later
text:
I am glad that I read reviews on a lot of these before I ordered this one. So many had poor reviews and I wanted to get a signal pretty far from the main router. I did not expect much even considering the good parts I read about this one. The house where the main router is has a concrete foundation underground and the house is a combination of brick and stone. There is a small studio on the same property but far which is also stone. As it was, I could get one bar on wireless but not actually surf the net.

With this repeater/range extender I've had decent luck given what these are for. I get at least 3-4 bars most of the time on my laptop and better on my Kindle. I can usually check mail with little problem and load most pages fine even with heavy graphics. It is slow sometimes but I expected that.

For watching video on Netflix or Youtube I can get a decent playback about 75% of the time with a couple of laggy moments. Captioning doesn't stay caught up very well, but I had worried that I might not be able to view movies at all so I'm still happy with this. I tested it for a while before writing the review to see how it would be over time and it's still going well.

I had to update after having this for a long time and have updated to 5 stars. Performance at first was as described above and I knew any shortcomings were due to the heavy stone walls. I decided that I needed a stronger signal, so I moved the extender outside the house and put it in a ziplock bag, expecting it to die quickly. It is NOT intended for outdoor use. However, it has now been through snow, rain, blistering hot sun, wind, dust and it still works like day 1. Plus, having it outside allowed me a much stronger signal in the studio across the property. It's only right to raise the rating after all that. I bought another one for a friend as well, for indoor use, and hers works fine. Changed to highly recommended.

title: Best cheap option for gaming, but apparently Lenovo has quality control issues.
text:
I bought this laptop about a week ago and I am actually considering returning or if possible asking for a replacement that solves my issues. As far as ratings let's get into it by listing the Pros and Cons

**List of Pros**

Gaming performance 4/5
So far one the games I've tried, this machine has performed like a champ. No real complaints here. Also, considering I'm upgrading from a 5 year old laptop, this machine is greater than anything I have ever experienced.

Battery life 3/5
I guess this could be both a pro and a con for this laptop as the time that the battery lasts really depends on what you are doing at the time. If you are just doing schoolwork, the battery could potentially last up to 4 hours. If you are playing games, it will last about an hour at the most. Still, this is much better than my previous laptop so big points for that.

Camera 4/5
The 720p cam
era on this laptop is decent, but much better than what I am used to. The images are grainy, however the is no lag on the camera. I guess for most people this might me a problem, but it is good enough for me.

Windows 8.1 4/5
I think windows 8.1 is one of those things that can be considered both a pro and a con. There are a lot of things I miss about windows 7, but let's face it, Windows 8.1 is much more efficient at both gaming and energy consumption. However, I hate that damned Metro interface, especially since this isn't a touchscreen computer.

"Ultrabay" ??/5
I know this is definitely a pro, but it seems that Lenovo isn't really offering readily accessible Ultrabay accessories so i'm not 100% sure if i'll be able to add another graphics card or not. As you know, this computer, the y410p comes with an optical bay drive in the computer instead of the second graphics card. I am not sure how much this will affect gaming performance but I guess i'll find out soon.

Keyboard 5/5
The keyboard is definitely a strong point on this laptop. It feels very responsive and tactile for both gaming and typing in general. However, in my experience, while gaming it tends to get a little hot over the WASD keys which kind of makes it undesirable to use during gaming. The back-light is configurable to have two levels of brightness in a red lava color. I haven't had it out in public, but i'm pretty sure it would stand out. Overall, it's a very strong keyboard.

Ports 5/5
I am SO glad that Lenovo decided to include so many different kinds of ports on this laptop. Three USB ports (one 3.0), HDMI, VGA, Ethernet (missing on most slimmer laptops nowadays), Audio and microphone jacks, 1 Kensington Lock, and 1 SD/MMC/MsPro Card slot.

**List of Cons**

Build Quality 2/5
Casing / Body
Upon receiving this laptop, I was surprised at the low quality of the overall build. The lid as well as the bottom are both made out carbon-fiber, which,to the touch actually feels quite durable, but I guess we'll see how it holds up the first time I drop it.
The thing that stands out to me the most and probably is the most undesirable thing about the aluminium palm rest is the seemingly jagged, abrasive ridge that hurts your wrist if you slide your hand over the edge of the laptop. On my previous laptop, a nicely built Sony Vaio, the ridge was smooth to the touch and your wrist or hand could just slide off the laptop naturally. However, on this laptop it goes from smooth aluminium to jagged edge really quickly.

Sound 4/5
The speakers on this laptop are louder than any I've ever tried. But, once again, that might not be the best thing, as loudness doesn't always translate into quality. I've found that when I play certain song at max volume it actually makes the speakers wobble creating a distorted sound and basically ruining the sound quality of the song. A perfect example of this is the song "Years" by Alesso. When it plays the first part of the song, the piano part, you can hear the wobble distortion sound, ruining the first part of the song. Now, I've noticed that maybe ~75% songs are able to play without distortion at max volume so I can't take too many points off, but it is something to be aware of.

TouchPad 2/5
The touch-pad on this laptop is probably one of the worst touch-pads I have ever used on a laptop. However, if you are going to do any serious gaming or media editing, you'll probably be using a mouse so this is a moot point. However, for just general use laying in your bed or something, I found the touch-pad a pain to use. The material that they used seems to be some kind of matte plastic instead going with my personal favorite -- frosted glass -- which was used on my Sony Vaio. I have heard that you can download drivers from Synaptics website to make the TP work better, but I have not yet tried this.

Weight 3/5
This laptop is definitely on the heavier side, although not too heavy where it's going to break your back or something. IT weighs 4.8 pounds without SLI and without the power brick and 5.5 with the power brick.

Verdict 3/5
All in all, for the price I paid $819 + $59 tax so $879 (bought it directly from Lenovo's website), there is simply no laptop that I could find that squeezes more parts, ports, etc into a gaming laptop for around that price. So this is definitely a good deal for the money, and it blows my previous laptop out of the water, but the various design flaws like the sharp edges, sometimes faulty speakers, and below average touch-pad bring the overall score down. About the edges, I am considering calling Lenovo and asking about whether I can get it replaced for a laptop that doesn't have that issue, as I could probably live with the other shortcomings.

***EDIT***
I ended up calling lenovo and returning this laptop after finding out that the edges are apparently a design flaw and both the y410p and the y510p have that problem. I ended up going with the [[ASIN:B00JLJICZG GIGABYTE P34Gv2-CF1 14" Gaming Notebook]] which is much more expensive but also a lot slimmer and has better build quality. In the end, I picked quality over price.

title: Exceeds Expectations
text:
I was skeptical about purchasing an indoor antenna given my location, 2nd floor apt. bldg. surrounded by trees and other apt. bldgs. and only 1 window option to place the antenna. I purchased this Terk FDTV1A antenna a Phillips Indoor Amplified Uhf/vhf/fm/hd antenna for comparison. The Phillips did not detect a single channel and, initially, the Terk only picked up 4 channels (and only when using the amplifier & placing it in the widow well). However, I was not interested in any of those channels.

I decided, on a whim, to try a cable splitter and attach the antenna and my Sony HD TV to the cable jack on the wall. To my utter surprise I now receive ABC (which, from my research, most indoor antennas cannot receive) as well as CBS and the local broadcast channels that I received before. I still don't receive Fox or NBC :(

To be completely honest, at times, the reception IS intermittent depending on the weather/cloud cover but, overall, I'm very pleased with this antenna. Especially given that I contacted a website mentioned in one of the Amazon reviews for these antennas (can't remember which review) that did not even recommend an indoor antenna for my location LOL.

I do believe that my location is my biggest obstacle with this antenna and am confident that with fewer obstacles I would pick up nearly all channels with this fantastic antenna!

Thanks to ALL who took the time to post detailed reviews about this antenna! Your opinions and experience are invaluable to future buyers of products!

title: SURPASSES EXPECTATIONS
text:
Just got it today, have played with it for a few hours. Bought it for the advertised reasons: My TV, a Vizio M470SL, produces great video quality but the sound is generally uneven, and specifically voices are muffled and tend to be drowned out by bass, so I had to constantly raise or lower the volume when switching between channels or inputs, or even during the same program, to find a balance between audible dialogue on the one hand and sound effects that would not shake the room on the other hand. Sometimes, it just wasn't possible to strike this balance, which meant that I'd have to choose between missing elements of dialogue or getting blown away by the rumble and fury. (Please note that this is typical of LED and Plasma TVs in general -- I do not mean to imply that Vizio's TVs are any worse in this respect than other brands, and if you like to watch TV at very high volumes anyway then it probably wouldn't be a problem for you.) The Solo solves this problem quite effectively. I have tested it on several cable channels and types of programming, a dvd player, a blu ray player, the Onlive gaming service I use through the Vizio Costar (which is a great addition for dedicated Androidiacs out there or for anyone who wants a functional browser -- i.e., Chrome -- on their TV), and played music through a few different apps -- the Solo sounds excellent with all of these. Of course, type of input should not make a difference in sound production or quality since the Solo connects to the TV with an optical cable (Bose includes one with the Solo, as well as some other type of cable, component I think, so you don't have to buy one).

Also love that there are no visible wires strung about my living room as was the case with my previous 5.1 system, a respectable Sony that cost almost twice as much as the Solo, but to my ear the Solo outperforms it too without all the complex, fragile, and ugly-to-look-at wiring.

As for the quality of the sound, I am actually stunned at how much of an improvement it provides over my TV speakers. Voices are not just clear but realistically resonant. John Goodman in Season 4 of Damages and Alan Rosenberg in The Guardian, two guys with lively and resonant voices, never sounded so good. Dolly Parton's numbers in Best Little Whorehouse were fantastic, although not even Bose can do much for Burt Reynolds.... It's not just voices, however. All sounds give the impression that you'd receive if you were actually present to the action on the screen. Watching Reds and Giants game right now, for example -- when a pitch hits the catcher's mit, you here that snap-on-leather sound just as you would experience it in the stands, rather than the lifeless thud sound that registers on the TV speakers. I watched Prometheus with my TV speakers about a week ago and thought the sound was really impressive until I watched again the first half hour of that movie with the Solo just a while ago and realized that I had missed out on a lot -- and a movie like that is a good test of the Solo's primary purpose, because somehow it allows you to fully experience the full range of audible material without drowning out the dialogue, so that not once did I feel the need to raise or lower the volume. My last comment on the sound quality is about the bass it produces, which is qualitatively different than the kind of base from my old speaker system. I am not sure how to describe it -- the Solo produces plenty of bass (I can feel it in my body) but it isn't harsh at all, rather somehow gentle and richer with a lot of depth.... It's tangible without shaking the room -- I guess that's the bottom line.

Absolutely worth 400 bucks, which incidentally you can pay in easy installments if you buy it for the same price on the Bose site. The customer service is excellent too. Obviously old people who can't hear well and therefore have to crank the volume on their TVs to hear what Jessica Fletcher or the Golden Girls are saying would benefit greatly from this device. It's not just for the hearing-impaired, however. I am in my early 30s was motivated to try this out just because I was so tired of having to play the volume controls to find the right balance. Anyone who shares that frustration would really like the Solo, I think.

title: great price, not so great item
text:
I ordered the kindle fire when it was the deal of the day for about $60 less than the regular retail price. I wanted a cheap case to go with THE FIRE and felt as if I needed to find one fairly quickly so that I would not risk the deal of the day selling out. (It eventually did).

I found this case and it was about the price of a cheap fast food lunch.
I probably should have known better, but what is done is done- I ordered the cheapest case I could find.

My first impression of this case was actually quite favorable. It looks great. It also feels nice and solid.

However, the real reason that I purchased this case is for protection for my Kindle Fire.

In order to describe my problem with the case, I will need you (the reader) to think of this case like a hardback book.

The spine of this book (this case) was created to hold lets say 200 pages, but the actual number of pages (THE FIRE) is closer to 220, therefore the book (this case) will not shut completely over the pages (THE FIRE).

Think of it like trying to place a PEN inside of hardback book near the spine and trying to close the book. The result is a buldge at the spine leaving a gap on the fire where there is no coverage for the screen. Because the case does not fit flat over the fire's screen, if you were to place your case in your purse or bag, you are asking for trouble as the gap is large enough for items to get inbetween the top of the case and the screen.

I have used a rubberband to secure the top of this case until a replacement (different item) arrives in a few days. For the price of this case, the rubberband thing might be acceptable for some- for me it is not!

I did NOT attempt to contact the seller regarding this issue. At this price point (under $5.00) , I believe that the return shipping would be more trouble than it is worth.

So two stars for the look and feel of this item, and negative one star for the coverage for your Kindle Fire, leaving a net result of the ONE star that you see above.
