title: "Will You Still Need Me, Will You Still Feed Me, When I'm 64?"
text:
OK, I admit it. They say that 60 is the new 40. Unfortunately that doesn't work with technology. I've tried to keep up but I find myself becoming a little more like my wife. She just wanted a cellphone to take and make calls on. I preferred and appreciated the extra features and apps and was willing to learn them. Now I find myself just wanting a great TV picture (and sound) without all the bells and whistles like 3D, video streaming, and everything else that requires extensive research and understanding to use.

So, based upon my willingness to 'own up' to being behind on the current TV magic, knowing that a few problems have cropped up for customers buying direct from Amazon (and the problem of repacking and return shipping), and knowing my propensity for seeing Murphy's Law in action, I decided to buy this TV locally. When I did, they matched Amazon's $2,199 price. So I paid the extra $250 to have them deliver the set and integrate it into my home theater unit. That way they would take care of the unit's return if it was faulty, jostled in shipping, or dropped by one of the techs when he was stung by a wasp while bringing it up the front steps.

It turned out that there was nothing faulty with the TV, but watching the two guys setting up and calibrating the set saved me a tremendous amount of time and frustration. Since it took two of them about three hours to set it up, it probably would have taken me weeks. Until recently I never understood why my father always wanted to keep things simple and easy. It seems like everything we buy (cars, phones, computers, appliances, etc.) come with a 400 page manual--or require you to go online and read the information there. I'm pretty much burned out on that, so much so that I MIGHT stop buying certain things because of the college courses I need to take to use them.

Sorry. Another result of aging is the meandering thoughts encountered when trying to explain myself. Back to the TV. I had a Samsung LED unit for the last four years that had a great picture but also a propensity for burned out pixels. A $500 repair solved that problem and relegated the set to a junior level in the basement. (See, there I go again.) I love the picture on this TV. I have been watching the Tour de France at night and thoroughly enjoy the spaciousness and clarity of the picture. Blu Ray movies 'pop' on this set. Switching back and forth from an HD channel to the same analog feed shows the tremendous difference between the two. My home theater unit supplies a wonderful listening environment so I haven't used the TV speakers. Most people probably don't.

So I'm very happy with this Sharp TV. I have owned Sony, Mitsubishi, Hitachi, and Samsung units but of course the picture quality has come a long way since I bought my 70" rear projection set in 1981. If you are not completely comfortable with setting this TV up, STRONGLY consider hiring an expert to do it for you. Younger people will laugh at this suggestion, but you know what I mean.

title: Great Antenna
text: Bought mine while in Arizona last winter and was picking up 17 stations 100 miles away, had it attached to my ladder in back of motor home. title: Great device with lots of potential (some limitations)
text:
Great device with a few bugs, but lots of potential.

I frequently go with Boy Scouts to areas where cell phone communication is not available. My main purpose for purchasing this device was for emergency communications. During our last camp (week long in Wyoming), was used several times to order supplies from people coming later in week and to pass general messages. Luckily was not needed for emergency, but was nice to have. I did not have problems activating device like other reviewers. While it mentions that it may take some time to send and receive, when using device, I discovered it had capability to manually check for messages, so when you send a message, you can check more frequently, often getting turn around in just a few minutes. When left alone, however, sometimes would go many hours without getting signal and there was no warning or notice of this, making it unreliable for incoming emergency messages (trouble at home).

Pros:

* Two way communication - This amazed everyone at camp and I was soon the go to person to send messages home.
* Ability to link to a smart phone (easier to message)
* Ability to send and receive messages without phone (while this is harder to compose, it is nice if phone not close by or battery ran out).

Cons:

* No warning when no signal. While I generally had a good connection, when device left alone, sometimes after many hours, would notice it had not connected since l looked at last, but no warning or notification that device was not connected. Status light only flashes red when it can't send a message.
* Phone app does not have capacity to manually check for messages, look at time since last satellite connection, need to do that from device
* Not great features as stand alone GPS. Cell phone app can show location maps and where message were sent from, but no good map view on device (that I could find).
* Message sent has lot of unnecessary verbiage, often confusing recipients: "See XXX's location: [...] [actual message here] Delorme-Always inReach" . Would be nice if option to send without location (not always necessary) and Delorme signature.

Overall this is a great device, with a lot of potential. I love the ability for 2 way communication. There are some limitations, some of which are likely overcome with firmware updates in the future.

Update June 2014
After a year with this product, I am lowering my review to 2 stars. Above review is still accurate, great to have two way communication when out of cell phone range, BUT, now to get basic features as a GPS device, you must buy the new Explorer module. Come on folks, can't your current users get a device that functions as it should. This should be available through a firmware update (mine is up to date), so if this changes I will update my review. I am not spending $400 to get basic GPS functions this device should have come with (and available on any cheap GPS). I will stick with my Garmin Oregon and if needed buy a newer Garmin before another Delorme.

title: Very Cool, but Functional, Next Gen Camera
text:
Excellent next gen camera – particularly for a semi-amateur/semi-pro (with emphasis on the semi-amateur) like me.

Acts as a replacement for a basic DSLR for most uses, but with the benefit of being able to effectively refocus after the fact. This is my third camera, and I have yet to use my DSLR since this arrived.

Ability to shift perspective cool, but not a key use for me.

Optical zoom and wide lens offer both zoom and macro lenses all-in-one.

Perspective shift and refocus most valuable for shots with subjects at varying distances. Clearly of most value in daylight.

Primary limiting trade-off: If you have no need for post-capture refocusing, perspective shift, etc., and want the highest possible fixed resolution, you can get higher resolution static pics at present from a high end DSLR.

Biggest benefit so far: allows me to capture shots of my son’s cross country meets – particularly in the home stretch -- and then send separate photos to the other parents with each of their children in focus despite being at varying distances from my son (and therefore out-of-focus in a static DSLR shot) at the time of capture.

Overall Rating: Excellent new technology. Above expectations. Cool form factor (which at the same time can also be viewed as a limitation for our existing investments in other lenses). Fixed resolution trade-offs particularly worth it for uses with multiple subjects.

title: Best price to performance walkaround lens
text:
I was skeptical about this lens because frankly, I thought you had to have a big piece of glass to have a decent, sharp lens. I'm not really too keen on my 50mm f/1.8 lens; build quality and image quality is "ok" but not stellar. Also, I favor the 35mm angle of view on a full frame camera.

When my 40mm f/2.8 STM lens arrived, all those concerns disappeared. It doesn't quite turn my 5D Mark III into a chunky "point and shoot" camera, but it almost does. I love keeping this lens on the camera. The small size of the glass means I'm much more comfortable *not* using a glass UV filter, which I typically put on all my lenses to protect the glass. in terms of bumping or scratching the glass, it's a much smaller target.

I love the small size, which makes my big bulky camera a lot less noticeable. I love the metal mount, which very firmly attaches to the camera body. I also love the smooth, damped action of the focus ring, a nice surprise I was not expecting. Manual focus depends on having the meter active; in other words, the ring is not directly attached to the focus mechanism, so turning the focus ring even in manual doesn't always automatically change the focus. But mainly I am using this as an autofocus mid-wide angle lens.

Having f/2.8 on this lens means great low light performance with the 5D Mark III. It's quite sharp even wide open. Tests I have seen show much sharper image quality than either the 50mm f/1.8 *and* the 50mm f/1.4, which was a big surprise. The "Shorty Forty" competes with L glass in terms of sharpness, while being one of the cheapest lenses in the lineup. Basically, this is a lens I could keep on my camera almost all the time, unless I wanted to jump up to 85mm or down to 16mm, which is what I have. I am actually selling my big, bulky Samyang 35mm f/1.4...with the 40mm I just don't need it anymore. I'd rather have 2 cheap Nikon manual lenses with Fotodiox Pro adapters for the same price.

Another great feature of this lens is how close you can get to the subject and still focus; it's not a macro lens, but you can get right up on something and get a good, sharp shot. If you really wanted macro in a lens close to this focal length, the 50mm f/2.8 Macro is supposed to be quite sharp also. But, you get a lot less angle of view with that one.

I will say, the lens was intended to be used with the new Canon Rebel T4i to give videographers live autofocus. I think that's a mistaken game plan. Either amateur photogs will use a cheaper camera or pros will not need it, preferring manual focus for video. I owned a 60D but sold it to get the 5D Mark III. I don't plan to go back to crop sensors any time soon, so STM is not a feature I can comment on.

But if you have a full frame camera, this is a no brainer. Keep it on your camera and I bet you'll a) use your big full frame camera more often and b) use your 50mm lens, whatever it is, a lot less. 40mm is a great compromise between the "classic" photojournalism focal length of 35mm and the "standard" focal length of 50mm. I wouldn't do a lot of close up portraits with the 40mm due to distortion, except for kids, since that makes them look even cuter.

Just buy it, and enjoy your sharp images and also how easy it becomes to keep your 5D in your coat pocket, satchel or cargo pants pocket so it's more convenient to use. It also makes it a lot easier to carry on a neck strap.

While on Maui, I was able to capture about one hour of good snorkeling video and pictures before the camera failed.  There was no evidence that water leaked into the battery/SD Card compartment so water probably leaked elsewhere on the camera - a defect that should be covered by the warranty.  I sent the camera in for repair assuming the warranty would cover the repair work. I have had the camera about 30 days.  Today, I received a phone call from the Panasonic Exchange Center requesting $180.00 to repair the camera.  They told me the camera leaked and that it was my fault by not following the proper use procedures - no warranty protection.  Basically there was no recourse to the accusation that I was at fault and that the problem was likely caused by defective material or workmanship regarding Panasonic.  So beware if you purchase this camera, the warranty is mostly worthless and if you plan to use the camera underwater buy an addition waterproof bag (Aquapac) or case - kind of defeats the purpose of buying a water proof camera doesn't it.  I am not paying $180.00 for the repair and we will never again purchase another Panasonic product.

title: Not for novices, and not intuitive even for advanced photographers
text:
My mother told me she wanted a camera with a viewfinder, but she didn't want anything too bulky. So I thought this camera would be a godsend. Instead, it has infuriated her and even leaves me (a photography enthusiast) scratching my head sometimes.

The bad news:
The viewfinder is VERY small. I get it -- it's a small camera. But if they made the camera just a BIT taller, they might be able to squeeze in a slightly larger (and therefore vastly more usable) viewfinder. The camera doesn't need to be thicker for the viewfinder, just taller. As it stands, the viewfinder is only useful in emergency situations when it's too bright outside to see the LCD screen. You would not want to use it regularly to compose shots.

The camera's software interface is not intuitive at all. You really have to work at it to understand how to adjust it properly. The camera needs a dedicated flash on/off button and a dedicated burst mode button. Many point-and-shoot cameras have these, so I don't think it's asking too much. These functions should not be buried in menus.

The button that is used to go "back" in menus is also the Delete button, so people may be reluctant to use it. Not intuitive.

I realize the 1/1.7" sensor is larger than most P&S cameras (which is good), but couldn't they at least make a 10X or 12X zoom? 7X just feels a bit too limited.

I tried the camera in shutter priority mode, but it never warned me that the photo would be underexposed because of setting the shutter too fast. It did not show me the corresponding aperture and ISO settings as I adjusted the shutter speed. This does not encourage beginners to get out of Auto mode.

I tried to set up the WiFi to send photos to my mother's PC, but because she had a space in her Windows username, I could not set it up because the camera does not allow you to enter spaces when typing in text (I confirmed this limitation with a Panasonic rep). The only suggestion was to change the username in Windows so it no longer had a space in it.

My mother doesn't see very well even with her eyeglasses, and she has a hard time reading the screen let alone using the viewfinder. And because the On/Off switch is located closer to the edge of the camera than the shutter button, she says she finds herself accidentally switching the camera off when she's trying to frame a shot.

The good news:
Once you learn where things are on the camera (which isn't easy), it does take very nice photos for a point-and-shoot. It's quite quick to focus, and it suppresses noise well up to ISO 800. You can even get away with ISO 1600 if you don't mind a little noise...but I wouldn't go higher than that unless it's an emergency. But that's pretty good for a P&S camera.

The burst mode is lightning quick -- once you dig through the menus to find that setting.

It has a viewfinder, and it fits in a pocket. I can't think of too many cameras that can do that.

title: bright enough for a bright room, apart from that, meh.
text:
ok for an led tv, but the software stinks and the tv is underpowered in terms of processor.

when people tell you the smart TV functions are slow, believe them. if you are used to using roku or fire, this will seem like it's going backwards. it can take 30 seconds from when you click an icon before the service comes up, assuming it does load, which is not always the case. then, the buffering is incredibly slow as well and hangs up all the time. i can get it to just load and play a netflix movie maybe one time in 3. if i switch to roku, using the same wifi and net connection, it's 5 seconds to buffer and the movie is on. the whole setup on this tv is wonky.

it also took me a full hour on the phone with the samsung techs to get smart tv to work at all even after updating the firmware when i got the TV. it's just a lousy design and it's woefully underpowered and has too little memory.

i do not like the picture either, but then, i hate all LED tv's and the over-saturated, fake, world of warcraft looking images they provide. (though i use a wolf projector in the theater and a plasma in the bedroom, so my expectations are very high). despite the claims of great movement, it also still has motion artifacts in action scenes. it seems to be about as good as any of the led tv's (they nearly all use the same panels), but i think the whole genre stinks, so, take my views on picture with a grain of salt if you like led tv's (as some seem to).

honestly, i would never put up with a tv this bad apart from one thing: i need the brightness and in that, it excels.

i'm using this in my gym which has a ton of windows and the glare is just too much to use a plasma if you want to be able to see it.

the sound is OK, though, like any of these new panel TV's, you really need an external audio system.

the only reason i am keeping it is that there is no tv with a good picture that works in such a bright room and i am using roku anyhow. if you want an actual smart tv, this is NOT it.

title: Digital out with iPad and a Coax DAC
text:
I wrote to Peachtree Audio support to find out if this thing would work with the iPad and Apple camera connection kit. Peachtree Audio completely ignored my friendly e-mail. I was a little offended by this. I mean, not even a "sorry, can't help you." Crickets. (EDIT: Peachtree Audio did eventually respond to my e-mail about 5 days after I sent it. Kudos to them. I'm glad I gave their product a good review)

Nevertheless, I bought this thing to find out if it would work. What I need to do is connect my iPad to my amp's coaxial input. The iPad, in case you're not aware, can output sound digitally via USB if you stick the apple camera connection kit in the iPad's connector. This gives you a USB slot that will pump your music to a DAC or amp that accepts USB. Some DACs work with the iPad, some don't. Generally, if your device doesn't require a special driver, it will work with the iPad. If you have a DAC or amp with coaxial input but no USB, you'll have to convert the USB signal to coaxial. Enter the Peachtree Audio T1.

The Peachtree Audio T1 *does* work with the iPad. But since it draws too much power for the iPad to run it, you'll need to put a powered USB hub into the chain. Any powered USB hub should work. All it needs to do is provide some extra juice to run the T1.

The T1 itself is simple, compact, and seemingly well made. It has a slightly rubbery exterior with a USB slot and blue LED on one side and an RCA coax output on the other. The sound quality is perfect... I can't tell the difference between this and any other digital signal, even after close listening with my Sennheiser HD600s. This is how it should be.

So what I have, using the Peachtree Audio T1 and the iPad connected to my home system, is access to all the music on my computer using iTunes home sharing or iTunes match, plus most of the other music in the world using Spotify, Pandora, etc. plus Youtube, HBO GO, Netflix... anything that makes sound on an iPad can now route digitally through the superior DAC in my amp.

Even though Peachtree ignored me, I'll give them the benefit of the doubt; maybe my e-mail got lost in the ether. (EDIT: as mentioned, they did not ignore, the are just a little slow). This is a good, solid product at a fair price and it creates a total win for my entertainment system. Plus, it's made by a known company instead of some obscure seller on e-bay peddling something sketchy looking.

If you need to convert a USB audio signal to an S/PDIF RCA signal, and you don't really need resolution higher than what's audible by dogs and men, this thing does the trick nicely.

This would be a five star rating if the item shipped with a USB cable. I suspect it doesn't because some people are deluded into thinking they need a very expensive high end USB cable. See my comment appended hereto.

title: Pleased with the MH40 so far, but they fell off my head...
text:
The MH40 came handsomely packaged. After removing the shrink wrap, you slide the box out and then open it like a book to find the headphones.

The headphones sit in a dense foam, at the center of which is a round leather box inside which you find the two cables.

When I first plugged in the cables with the iOS controls, those controls didn't work and I thought I had a dud. But reseating the cable resulted in the controls working. And they have worked each time since. I haven't tried the other cable yet.

About the controls - they aren't raised on the cylinder that hosts them, so you can't tell by tactile touch that you're clicking the intended button. I would like them to address that. With my Etymotic hf3, I can feel that I am clicking the button and know which button I am clicking without looking.

The mute button on the right can works wonderfully - you click it and the audio is muted. I don't it believe it mutes your microphone when you're on a call if that's what you're thinking.

About the sound - there is debate whether you need to break in a pair of headphones. Given that there may be a break in period, I will reserve judgement on the sound for the moment. But I will say that I feel like I am not getting enough volume out of the MH40 - I have been listening to them at or near full volume much of the time. I know the listening experience is going to be different from in-ear monitors, but I have had to set the volume higher than I would have expected.

About noise isolation - I wore the MH40 while walking around outside, and I was much more aware of the hustle and bustle around me than I would have been if I was wear in-ear monitors. I wouldn't use these headphones outdoors, so this isn't a real world application - at least not for me. But it does speak to the noise isolation you can expect from the MH40.

About the microphone - I did a couple of phone calls with the MH40, and though I forgot to ask the other parties how I sounded, they were able to hear me - no complaints.

About comfort - my head isn't huge, and it isn't small. I have worn them most of today, and the MH40's are reasonably comfortable. My ears do feel a little pressed, and a little hot, and I have had to adjust them a few times. They aren't as comfortable as in-ear monitors, but I don't expect them to be. Still, given that I have been able to wear them most of the day says something positive.

About the build - the workmanship on the MH40 is just fantastic! It feels and looks well constructed! I could not be more pleased! I got the tan leather / stainless steel, and it s a beautiful combination! I wonder if I would not have been more pleased with the black leather / gunmetal finish.

About the carry bag - I am not going to use it. I don't plan to travel with these headphones, but I can see how someone who would travel with them would appreciate a hard case.

About the leather case for the cables - the lid doesn't come completely off but is attached to the box. I'm concerned about how that joint will do after being opened and closed again and again.

I will follow up on the sound after a break in period.

Update 1: There has been questions about the weight of the MH40. I'm sad to report that when I was sitting, I looked down, and the MH40's tumbled off my head. Not cool! Maybe they need to include a chin strap with these?

title: Well, you decide
text:
I'm a tinkerer. I like android, and I'd never buy an apple product for all the BS lawsuits they've done to android phone tablet OEMs. As such, I can handle roadblocks and problems with ease. Unfortunately, most can't. So here is my gripes and observances so far with the device; some annoy me, and some will just cause it to be returned for most people:

HARDWARE

1. Some complain about the top right hand corner, being able to push the glass in. I can, but very little, so that's really nothing to me.

2. The bottom left of the screen has a little light bleed. Visible when the screen is all black.

3. It doesn't seem to register finger taps as well as my HTC Sensation does.

4. The wifi keeps sleeping or something. So it keeps throwing a "No connection error" while the wifi comes back. Never had an issue like this with my phone.

SOFTWARE.

1. I go to use Netflix, and it just closes. I try to update the app, but it doesn't offer an update. Wait, the description at the play store says if I can't update it, click here to install it. It downloads an apk for me to install, thus requiring the install of 3rd party sources. Now it opens.

2. The "My Library" has a serious flaw. I can't tap on any links in epubs (same issue with the Transformer 300). That's a big show stopper. And the page animations are very choppy. So I installed FBReader instead. Then I associate any epubs I download with that.

Here's the weird part: I can't disable it to just get rid of it. And this obviously is ICS. Even on my phone previously preinstalled apps you couldn't remove can at least be stopped and removed from the app list (I know that from people who upgraded from 2.3 to 4. I don't run carrier crap and thus was in control via a 3rd party ROM since day one). Not here. Now I realize there might be a reason for it, but still.

3. Using Hotmail. The email app has no built in settings for it, nor did it work for me doing it the exchange server route. Ended up using the app. Why it isn't a non-issue like my dad's 2+ year old ipod touch is beyond me.

4. Has a newspaper app. Activated the free trial, then tries to load a newspaper. After waiting about a minute, it disappears.

There are good things about this device. Problem is, I know the average person could care less. Some of it is Asus' fault, and some of it is Google. But I have a feeling that most people (read: people who shouldn't own electronics, apple or otherwise) will get frustrated and return it.

I know that with my know how I can get it to work much better than any ipad ever will, so I like it.

UPDATE: The dock gives it a nice touch, so I upped it a star.

title: Will Transfer Your Commercial VHS Tapes too!
text:
These units are advertised as great for converting your home movies, and stuff you recorded on tape. Yes,that is true, but these units are good for your COMMERCIAL vhs tapes as well.

I had HUNDREDS and HUNDREDS of vhs commercial vhs tapes. There was no dvd format when I first started buying movies. As movies I really loved came out in dvd format, I replaced the tapes, but I had SO MANY.

I actually priced getting them copied to dvd, but the cost was $20 per tape. Even then, I doubt that the business would have copied my commercial tapes. One day, I found this unit!

MOST of my tapes were able to transfer. So many I had purchased before copy-protected was introduced. Of course, the transfers had to be done in real-time. In those days of the big push to get them copied, I had two units going almost non-stop. I would leave for work with two movies copying, come home and begin again. FYI, I went through all of the tapes first and put them in pairs - two movies which would complement each other on one dvd.

It took an entire summer, but I managed to get all of the movies transferred, with some exceptions. No Miramax or Disney tape would copy, some Warner Bros would not copy and a few others here and there, but stacks and stacks and stacks of commercial vhs tapes DID copy and copy beautifully. Even all 58 hours of my I Love Lucy video club vhs tapes transferred perfectly.

I will say that the weakest link in these units is the vcr. I blew out two, however, remember, I had them going literally every hour I was awake and home. I kept those units as the dvd players still work great. However, I quickly replaced them with new units to get everything copied.

There are pros and cons of having tracking vs no tracking. The no tracking units track better, however when I came upon a tape with tracking issues, it sure was nice to have the tracking option to clean up the picture. If I had to choose one, I would get the one with the option to adjust the tracking.

I had one unit with a tuner and the rest without. For dubbing those old commercial tapes, I found the ones without the tuner work best. There were many times the one with the tuner would give me an "unable to copy" notice, but when I took the same vhs tape to a non-tuner unit, it copied perfectly. In addition to this occuring with a number of commercial tapes, I found this especially the case with my own personal tapes of things I copied from HBO years ago. No dice on the tuner unit; all systems go on the non-tunered one. So, go with the unit with no tuner.

With these Magnavox dubbing units, I was actually able to copy most of my commercial vhs tapes. They did beautiful transfers and made it possible for me to hang on to these films. Replacing all on dvd was simply cost-prohibitive. In addition, so many of the movies I had on tape have never come out on dvd (Isadora with Vanessa Redgrave, Finnegan Begin Again with Mary Tyler Moore and Robert Preston, The Rolling Stones 25 X 5, the Beast of IRS and so many 80's bands video compilations, ALL of Live AID, starting with the Australia stuff that began in the wee hours our time, tapes and tapes of music videos, when MTV really showed music videos - I could go on and on.)

I actually accomplished this several years ago, but just never wrote a review. I know there have to be some people out there holding onto to vhs tapes, but not knowing a way out - here it is!

And, you can also convert dvd to vhs, but only if it is a non-commercial, non-copy protected dvd. I had taped and burned a couple of shows to dvd and a friend asked for a copy. When I tried to copy the dvd on my computer software, I found the original disc had errors. So, I copied the dvd to tape and then burned the tape back to dvd. VERY labor-intensive and would only do this for a really good friend, but it can be done with this unit.

If you are still holding on to commercial vhs tapes, give this a shot. It sure worked for me. In fact, it STILL works. I still have a stand-alone vcr, which I regularly use to tape movies and documentaries I like, but not enough to buy the dvd - and burn those tapes to dvd.

title: The Best Radio They've Ever Made
text:
I've been an XM radio subscriber for over a decade...since 2002 as a matter of fact. I've had many radios over that time. This is easily the best radio they've ever made. And it's not even close.

The good:
- It has 20 presets; two banks of 10. I've found that to be more than enough.
- Screen is bright, easy to read, and organized.
- TuneStart. This alone is worth the purchase. After the radio has been running for a few minutes, whenever I tune to a station in my presets, it starts at the beginning of the song. It makes scanning around for music a far more enjoyable experience. You'll never again find a song you want to hear and only be able to catch the last 30 seconds.
- TuneMix. Start this mode and your radio will play one complete song from a random preset. After the song ends, it'll change to another channel and play another complete song there. It works with most music channels and it's an easy way to listen to a mix of all your presets. The best part of TuneMix is the ability to skip a song you don't want to hear and simply jump to the next one.
- Supports the Xtra/2.0 channels that only the newest XM radios can tune to. These channels have far better sound quality than the regular 1.0 channels.

The bad:
- If you're an audiophile, XM may frustrate you. The standard 1.0 channels often sound compressed. The 2.0 channels sound much better, however.
- Plug and play radio. The plus is that you can install it yourself. The downside is that since you're doing it yourself, it won't be as clean of an install as if the receiver was built into your car. Doesn't bother me, but I could see some people wanting something more integrated.
- FM Modulation. The FM transmitter can be weak. The signal is further degraded if you have multiple devices plugged into other outlets in your car (e.g. my iPhone charger). Luckily there is also an option for a direct connection via an AUX port.

Overall:
This is a fantastic radio. There's a few shortcomings but they aren't the fault of the radio itself. If you want SiriusXM, this is the radio to choose.

title: Works well, but you'll need more juice to fully recharge your Kindle Fire
text:
I have tested this product ([[ASIN:B005ZSSBYY Opteka BP-SC4000 Solar Powered Backup Battery and Charger]]) and found it to perform exactly as advertised:
- It is able to sustain an output of 5V 1A continuously, and
- The internal battery has a measured capacity of 4000mAh.

The solar-charging function works, but at 250mA peak current, it will take at least three sunny days to fully recharge the internal 4000mAh battery. It is best to recharge the internal battery in advance using an USB port or AC adapter (not included), and only rely on solar panel to provide a trickle charge.

The battery status indicator is non-linear. That is, each one of the four LED bars does NOT represent 25% of charge. According to my measurement, this is the actual representation during discharge:
4 bars = 87 - 100% full
3 bars = 73 - 86% left
2 bars = 58 - 72% left
1 bar = 1 - 57% left
0 bar = empty

You can use the USB output to recharge almost any USB devices. There are 10 adapter tips in the package, including mini-USB, micro-USB, plugs for various cell phones, even one for Nintendo DS. However, if you're looking for a backup battery pack for your [[ASIN:B0051VVOB2 Kindle Fire]], you really should get one with a higher capacity battery. Here's the reason why:

The Kindle Fire's internal battery has a capacity of 4400mAh. To recharge it using an external battery pack requires a two-step conversion process: First, the 3.7V from external battery pack is boosted to 5V at the USB port. Next, the 5V is stepped down to around 4V to recharge the tablet's internal battery. Even if each conversion step is 85% efficient, you still lose 28% of energy in the process (0.85*0.85=0.72). That's why you always need 1/3 higher capacity than the device you want to recharge.

If you only expect to use this Opteka backup battery to recharge your Kindle Fire up to 2/3 full, then this is still a good choice. Otherwise, look for a battery pack with a rated capacity of 6000mAh or more.

[Update on Dec 3, 2012]
During my summer vacation trip, the SC4000 proved to be a life-saver. On many occasions, I have used it to rescue other battery-powered appliances such as camera, cell phone, GPS and media player. For that I'm satisfied with this product.

[Update on Dec 7, 2012]
I just noticed there is another similar product sold here at Amazon:
[[ASIN:B005FNL0J2 EZOPower Universal USB Solar External Rechargeable Backup Battery - 3000mAh]]
It looks identical to the SC4000 except for battery capacity. Use caution when you shop.

title: It's wafer thin...
text:
Viewsonic makes quality video projectors and computer monitors, but isn't known for its computer products. The ViewPad E100 might change that a bit. It features a bright, color accurate display with good resolution in a very light, thin package. Speed isn't great when used with my Sprint mobile hotspot, but the E100 does get the job done for Web surfing (although don't expect smooth video streaming). In a nutshell:

PROS:

1. Lightweight, attractive design

2. Very good, bright screen image with rich color rendition and crisp image quality

3. Responsive touch control

4. Android OS, with access to apps via Amazon App Store

5. Kindle access

6. Clear speakers

7. Easy navigation

8. MicroSD card slot for memory expansion up to 32GB

CONS

1. Slightly flimsy construction - the frame creaks when the E100 is handled, and the back cover feels very thin.

2. 4GB RAM is fine for a few apps but can't handle many running at once

3. Slow for some Web applications.

4. Battery life isn't stellar.

All in all, for a budget tablet to be used mainly for casual Web browsing, game playing and e-book reading, the ViewPad E100 does what I want it to do (although better video streaming would be sweet, but that might be the fault of my Sprint Web access device). The image quality is quite good for a tablet at this price point - as one would expect from a company specializing in monitors and projectors - and makes using the E100 a pleasure. It's a good beginner's device, so approach it from that angle if you decide to give the ViewPad a go.

title: I need a secure strap. I sometimes run while snapping photos.
text:
I just moved up to a "big girl" DSLR: [[ASIN:B00894YX2U Canon EOS Rebel T4i 18.0 MP CMOS Digital Camera with 18-135mm EF-S IS STM Lens]]. As I take a lot of photos where I literally have to run out ahead of the action, I must have something better than the usual shoulder strap.

I recently saw a lady skiing with a camera bearing a huge telephoto lens hanging down by her side. I can only guess that she had the exact same Joby strap. (It looked like the same one to me, anyway.) I should have asked. UPDATE: I have skied with my camera hanging from this strap. Didn't really get in my way.

I have read the one and two star reviews from the true pros, who use cameras even more expensive than mine, and who do photo shoots more frequently than I. I respect their experienced perspective on this product, but I love this Joby camera strap for my level of photography.

So it arrives and I take it out of the box. It was super-simple to attach the strap to the camera. It took me a little while to take the plunge and crank on the tab that allows the strap to adjust. I am always afraid of breaking something made of plastic by not understanding how it should move. After that moment of truth, I was able to adjust the camera strap to fit my rib cage. The camera feels very secure hanging from the strap.

The instructions in the box didn't help much. It was helpful to flip over to YouTube and watch a couple of videos of the strap in action. When you raise the camera, you need to move the strap at the same time, pushing the extra over your shoulder. One person said this would be too much friction over the course of the day. Time will tell. I can feel a little friction on the side of my neck. If it really bothers me, I might cover the shoulder strap with microfleece. I'm good at sewing.

Overall, a very nice experience right out of the box. I'm sure I'll have my camera at the ready more often because of this strap.

title: Fantastic FM Transmitter
text:
For a while I was using a Belkin 50 dollar piece of garbage that was wired, had no controls for a phone, and transmitted terrible quality. I lived with it for a little while and eventually stopped using it altogether and went to CD's (I know, right?).

Not only is this product priced very reasonably, it's aesthetically pleasing and works like a champ in conjunction with my Samsung Galaxy Nexus 4G smartphone through Bluetooth. Plug it into your car and bend the firm, stiff chord to your most comfortable angle, and leave it there. It includes a small, discreet power button on the ball at the end of the plug, so you never have to take it out of the lighter, but it wont be drawing any current and, ergo, wont damage your battery.

Pairing it is a snap; simply hold down the blue phone button on the left hand side for a few seconds and it will start to flash, at which point you can whip out your phone, find it via Bluetooth, and connect (no password or anything of the sort, it connects right away). Once it pairs successfully it has a slight beep to let you know, and both phone buttons are solidly lit (and stay that way, as do the 3 other buttons circling the knob at the top).

The 3 buttons at the top are self explanatory; play/pause, next, previous. They work through both aux input and Bluetooth, providing your device supports it (most if not all Androids do, and I believe all iPhones should as well, but blagh). The knob has 2 functions; station and amplification. Simply turn it to change what station your broadcasting to, and push it down and hold for it to select whichever one it finds to be the most abandoned and therefore broadcast the best. If you just press it down for a moment, you can adjust how much it amplifies the volume it's receiving. One problem many FM transmitters have is the volume is too darn low, and most do not have a way to change that; this one does. You have a selection of 1 through 30. The instructions recommend 25 (which I've found to be the best). Anything above that and it will be amplifying it to the point where you will have distortion and it wont sound nice at all. Ironically, it doesn't come out of the box at the 25 setting (at least, mine didn't), so be sure to check that upon arrival -- if it's very low volume, that's likely the 'problem'.

And finally we come to the hands-free feature, which is just great. Too often have I been on the highway and gotten a phone call, which requires me to shuffle around while driving, attempting to wrestle my phone from the kung-fu grip of my pocket, hoping I move fast enough to not miss the call - no longer a problem. It comes with dual mics (that's right, two microphones...) that sound great and have no echo, despite the fact the sound of the call is being transmitted through the car stereo. Call quality is great; of course that's highly dependent upon your phone. It plays it's own tone when it sees a call coming through; simply press the blue phone button on the left to answer the call and when you're finished, press the red (unless the other person hangs up first, in which case you need to do nothing). This will also resume your music.

To wrap up this rather lengthy review, this product is built well, provides the best FM quality music you will be able to get, and looks just darn awesome. Thinking about it? Go ahead...get it. :)

title: Just added two more Motorola radios to my cache
text:
I've been a happy Motorola FRS radio customer for years. I purchased my FRS radios before consumer GMRS radios were even available in mass retail. My 'old' FRS radios still work, but our family has expanded and I wanted to add a couple more radios to our cache of outdoor adventure gear.

I'm happy with the MT350R radios. We use when skiing, so I'm happy they're weather-proofed. We also use the lanyard loop and wear under our jackets, so I'm happy weather-proof means (to me) sweat-proof under a coat. I like the rechargeable batteries, with the option of using alkaline batteries. These offer options for turning on lots of beeps and noises, and I shut all of that off because I just don't find it to be that useful. I also tend to stay on the lower-power FRS channels and avoid the higher-power GMRS channels, not only for battery savings, but because 35-miles just isn't very realistic. Whether using low- or high-power channels, line-of-site communication with the other radios in our party is all you get. If you can see where the other people are -- waiting at the bottom of the slope, at the top of the next ridgeline, your belayer on a climb, etc. -- then these will work well. But, they can't transmit through mountains.

These do exactly what I need, and I have no regrets about this purchase. The color shown in the photo appears more orange, which is what I wanted. The actual product color looks like school-bus yellow.

title: Works well and is easy to use, but incomplete instructions
text:
I just got a new computer and wanted to transfer all my documents and settings. I know I could have transferred everything to a hard drive and then transferred those files to the new computer, but a friend recommended this highly so I thought I would give it a try.

WHAT I LOVE ABOUT IT:
1. Very easy to use. Just plug the cable in the old computer and then plug the other end into the new computer and follow the very simple instructions on the computer (but, wait...didn't you say incomplete instructions??? Wait...I will explain later!)
2. Transferred not only the files but the settings as well. I had a lot of shortcuts on my old computer and they were in the same location on the desktop on the new computer. Basically, the old desktop and the new desktop have the same exact shortcuts in the same place.
3. Didn't transfer old programs (I knew that already), but told you what programs you needed.
4. Entire iTunes library tranferred without a hitch. A couple of years ago when I bought my old computer, transferring my iTunes library from the even older computer was a real hassle and I lost alot of music.....using the easy transfer cable made it hassle free.
5. Plugged it in overnight and in the morning (I had almost 500 GB of files to move), everything was transferred.....nice, nice, nice.
6. Before you transfer the data from one computer to another computer, the program allows you to choose which files and folders you wish to transfer. There are even advanced settings that allow you to migrate programs (I actually migrated a few free utilities with success!)

EVERYTHING WAS SO EASY....... BUT---
It comes with a free download of Bravura. I was confused as to whether I needed to download it. They provide incomplete information (even on their website). I didn't download Bravura and am still unsure as to what Bravura does....I wish they had more detailed information.

But still, a fantastic product--so simple and easy to use. I wish this had been around the last time I upgraded computers. Definitely worthy of five stars!!!

title: A muddy-sounding expensive upgrade to the previous model
text:
Additional comment, 14 May 2014: it seems that one person has found my review helpful, and 7 have not. Please don't be shy, leave comments. I'd love to know what I missed out, or if you're just Bose fans trying to 'down vote' me.
Additional, 22nd December 2014:
I've added some headlines to the review to help you find the info you want. If you care most about the sound, skip to 'HOW DO THEY SOUND?'. I also tweaked a few paragraphs and tightened them up.
------

A WARNING

Bose like to re-name and repackage their headphones frequently. These are slightly revised, renamed AE2 headphones. I went through three pairs of these headphones over five years: [[ASIN:B00009MK3T Bose TriPort Around Ear Headphones (Old Version)]]. Each time they were an identical product, but branded differently. They were the predecessor to the [[ASIN:B008YUNHK8 Bose® AE2i Audio Headphones (White)]] cans, and the Soundtrue headphones are a slightly tweaked and rebadged version of the AE2i model.

FEATURES

What immediately grabbed me about these headphones is the removable cord: the reason I went through three pairs of the TriPorts in 5 years is that the cord frayed (under light but regular usage) on every one. Compared to the AE2i cans, the Soundtrue headphones are $50 more expensive. That's a big difference. It gets you the removable cord (which is hopefully cheap to replace directly from Bose) so their longevity should be increased and may lead to less replacements down the line. I cannot state strongly enough how the biggest weak point in the TriPorts was the bell wire-thin cord that tangled and frayed so easily. This removable cord, previously only seen in Bose's cans at the $250+ range, is a big upgrade.

The cord also has an iPod/iPhone/iPad/Mac friendly microphone/remote control cluster on the cord. It feels weird, after using Apple's own headphones, to have these controls on the left rather than the right, but these cans have only one cord and it goes into the left cup. I'm sure I wouldn't notice after a couple of days. It's convenient, if you use a Mac and spend a lot of time in GoToMeeting or Google Hangouts (like I do) to have volume controls on the headphones. That said, the controls on Apple's own headphones are very obvious and tactile. These are mushy and hard to find by touch. I had no problem finding the up control but kept missing the down control.

I can't say that this removable cord with controls and mic are $50 worth of upgrade, and if you use a PC or an Android device, the controls will not be fully compatible. Let's move on.

As with the old TriPorts, these headphones are incredibly light and comfortable. I have no doubt they could be worn for eight hours without hurting the head or ears, just like the old pair. This pair also fold (in one direction only) for stowing, which might be convenient provided you have a large, flat area to store them. I prefer the Sony's more traditional folding inwards of the cups to the Bose folding flat. Your mileage, as always, might vary.

So we have a very light, comfortable pair of headphones with a removable cord and a price placing them in the upper region of the beginner audiophile's budget. Let's have a listen!

HOW DO THEY SOUND?

This review will be making comparisons with my memories of five years usage of the previous TriPort model and my current Sony headphones [[ASIN:B008A87W46 Sony MDR7506 Professional Large Diaphragm Headphone [Electronics]]], which usually sell on Amazon for about $80 and are often considered to be the best headphones for $150 or under. The old Bose pair had a rounded off top-end, slightly boosted bass and a prominent midrange that made for a pleasant, warm sound. I used these headphones up to eight hours a day without fatigue. The Sony pair are clear, well-separated and don't boost any frequency. At first they seem to lack bass, especially coming from the old Bose pair, but it's a very natural sound, albeit sometimes less involving. I loved the old Bose and feel the same about the Sonys, which are helped by that $80 price tag.

This is where it all falls down, and quickly. I have a standard suite of tracks I use to test speakers and headphones and I have used them on the Bose TriPorts, the Sony monitors, some JBL Roxy headphones, a pair of $300 Polk bookshelf speakers, a pair of Pioneer floor standers, a Yamaha 5.1 surround kit and a few different iPod dock speakers. They are chosen for a reason: they represent my listening habits and allow me to quickly judge if I'll be able to use the product for a long period of time.

First up, 'So What' from the mid-90's Mastersound 24kt gold CD of Kind of Blue by Miles Davis. Separation should be good and each instrument distinct. The Bose have boosted the bass and blurred it into the midrange. Instantly, instruments began to bleed together. It's not Beats levels of overwhelming bass, but it's not a great start.

Now a real challenge: the Japanese reissue of the Agharta album by Miles Davis. This is a tough one: numerous instruments playing funky grooves with many overlapping textures and sounds: the keyboards are frequently ear-piercing; a drum machine was used for texture, not drum patterns; Pete Cosey played a table of small instruments alongside his guitar. This is unusual, dense, complex music and the sound engineer added huge amounts of reverb to the sound, just to make it tougher to handle. The old Bose smoothed the sound a little without harming the mix; the Sony pair represent it faithfully and naturally; these SoundTrue headphones fail to distinguish the rhythms, textures and notes played. Although not *terrible* I would not class them as doing a good job here.

So if bass is this pair's forte, lets's try '3 hours' from Emika's self-titled debut album. This track has so many sub frequencies it could make your teeth rattle. On the other hand, if your phones/speakers can't separate the bass frequencies and directions, it'll feel like a subwoofer blasting in-between your ears. I expected the new Bose to fail here, but they did better than I expected. The bass was not so strong as to change my body's biorhythms, but neither was it clear enough to distinguish every different bass frequency. I give them a pass on this track, but only just.

A real challenge for most phones, and my first endurance test, is 'Getting Up' from the Q-Tip album, The Renaissance. This song is all bass and high-end. The old Bose made it bearable, even pleasant to listen to. The Sony's do pretty well with it, but their transparent nature means they don't smooth the inherent harsh production. This track put me off the Dre branded Beats for life. Like their predecessor, the SoundTrue's round off the top-end, making it more bearable. Sadly, unlike the previous pair, they boost the bass and mid-range, making this song as difficult to listen to as the Beats phones did, just in a different manner.

Onto R&B/Soul: 'Q.U.E.E.N.' from Janelle Monae's last album, has lots of bass, horns and guitar with soul to spare. It swaps between singing a rapping. It's a great song, but the Bose phones boost that bass line too far. It makes the track feel funkier, for sure, but all those wonderful details in the bass/midrange are being lost. I would classify this as a pass, but only just.

My final track is 'I Wish I Was' from the 2006 Twilight Singers album, Powder Burns. The Bose have a lot to live up to here: hearing this track on the old TriPorts was my 'wow' moment. Those cans revealed elements to this song I had never previously heard from other speakers or headphones. The song moves from quiet and subtle to a bombastic, wall-of-sound chorus, with some gritty guitar lines heralding the change. This song really benefits from good midrange representation, but needs the bass for those loud parts. Things started off well, all the subtle details were revealed, as with the previous Bose pair. The intensity builds, and things sound a little muddy as that scratchy guitar kicks in and then... the bass overpowers the entire song. It was unlistenable and extremely unpleasant on the ears. I actually took true headphones off in horror. When I went back to corroborate what I had heard, it was no better: the bass rolled into the mid-range and destroyed the sound of the song. Just horrible.

CONCLUSION

1. These phones cost more than their predecessor, but have a removable cord and (Apple only) controls and mic on the cord.
2. They are incredibly lightweight and easy to wear.
3. They round off the top-end, and abnormally boost the bass and mid-range.
4. The bass and mids bleed into one another.
5. This content bass/mid bleed makes these headphones very fatiguing to listen to, and as stated above, sometimes downright unpleasant.

I can't recommend these headphones. They might work as a gateway drug for Beats users who want to step away from 100% obliterating bass to a combination of obliterating bass and midrange, before they move on to more natural sounding headphones, but I can't recommend them to anybody else, especially when the Sony studio monitors sell for $100 less.

title: The Almost Perfect Tablet
text:
The Nexus 7 is the ultimate tablet. I know that there are people who will adamantly disagree with me for different reasons, but for me this is it. What I want in a tablet is something that I can use for e-reading, web browsing, e-mail checking and game playing. Lots of devices can do these things, but none of them can do it better than Google and Asus' Nexus 7.

The size of the tablet is what appealed to me in the first place. I had owned an iPad 2 before, and while I liked it and appreciated it for all it could do, it was simply too big for me to comfortably hold in one hand while I was riding on the bus or sitting at home. When I want to read a magazine, comic book or book, I want something that I can hold in one hand for long periods of time. While the Nexus 7 isn't a light as a Kindle, it is extremely easy to hold in one hand. This is partially due to the size and weight, but also, perhaps almost equally due to the fantastic build quality and materials. The back of the device, as has been mentioned many times over, is rubbery/leathery and just feels good and is nicely textured and there is almost no risk of accidental slips.

The speed of the device is one of the reasons why I was so attracted to getting it in the first place. I have a mid-range Android phone and a mid-range laptop, and for once I wanted something that could do everything snappy, zippy and just...well, fast. The Nexus 7 does that in spades and then has some oomph left over for multitasking unlike any Android device I've ever used, including the Samsung Galaxy S3.

Video quality is superb and it streams HD-quality movies from sources like Netflix, as well as all the movies and TV shows I have on my home server, which I stream via Plex and watch on the Plex app. Loading books and comics and everything else I could think of was just a matter of creating a folder and dragging and dropping. The open Android market, compared to other ecosystems, has a player and an app for almost any file format you can think of, and the Nexus 7 makes reading PDF's, e-books and magazines a quick, painless and beautiful affair.

Gaming on the Nexus 7 is also fantastic. I have installed several games from the Tegra Zone, just to test out the graphics, and they are unlike anything you've seen, except, save the current generation iPad (and, even then I would argue that they are equal).

The thing I love most about Android -- specifically after Ice Cream Sandwich, and even more so with Jelly Bean -- is the widgets. I don't like having countless apps clog up my home screens. That's what an app drawer is for. On my Nexus 7 I have apps on two pages -- the first, main home screen and a screen dedicated to games. The rest of the pages, including most of the first home screen, is dedicated to widgets. I use widgets for Gmail, Google Now, Google Keep, Evernote, Drive, Calendar, Twitter/Facebook, Google Currents, Pulse News and several more. They make opening apps unnecessary at times, and display the information I need to know without jumping between apps.

This device gets my highest recommendation, and the only reason it is not 5 stars is because I had an issue with build quality in a previous Nexus 7, and had to get a return/exchange on it -- though this was not the fault of Amazon, and I believe was just due to the individual seller I purchased from.

Get one now, and enjoy everything a tablet should be.

title: Have a USB 3 Port First
text: I don't have any real scientific proof to back my review, only personal anecdotal stories.  I purchased one of these to use back and forth between a few desktops and laptops.  Only one of those laptops have a USB 3 port, the other and the desktops are only USB 2.  As for the hard drive itself, I've never had it not work, lose data, corrupt, etc.  My data has been safe and sound on it despite my multiple connections, and for the most part, speed via the USB 2 connection is sufficient (although much better through the USB 3).  My experience comes from the drive's impact on my desktops and laptops.  On all my USB 2 devices, I can't boot properly with the unit plugged in and powered on.  Its a case of the BIOS looking to see if the device is a bootable device, but the size of it just bogs the system down.  On the USB 2 laptop and one of my desktops, keeping it plugged in has caused stability issues with Windows 7, sometime making the explorer freeze up for extended periods of time, sometimes Windows just powers off unexpectedly.  I blame the drive only because if I don't have the drive plugged in all day, those units don't display these issues. I've had no issues with the USB 3 enabled laptop.  So, the long and short of it is that I still regularly use the drive, I'm generally happy with the purchase, but I find that I keep it unplugged from my computer when I don't actually need the data.  A bit of a pain, but doable.  I would not, however, get another one of these drives for any unit that did not already have a USB 3 port.

title: Didn't like at first, it got better. UPDATE on warranty service!!!
text:
At first I didn't like this mouse till I got used to it. I hate wireless anything (Mouse, keyboard, etc.) because batteries hate me and die at the worst times but this is one of the last wired trackballs around. So I gave it a chance.
Bad points are the ball comes out at the drop of a hat and the 3 points that the ball rotate on get clogged with dirt and you need to clean often. Luckily the ball comes out easy so it's not to bad.....
Once you get used to the ball (I used to put the Logitech in my lap and put my hand on it, this is awful large for that!) and hovering your hand over it and custom set the buttons it works pretty good.
WARNING! This comes with no software disk, you have to get it off the Kensington website yourself BEFORE plugging in the track ball. Otherwise it was smooth sailing.
UPDATE!!!! The unit finally started to fail after almost 3 years of getting knocked on the floor. I use it in my lap to get pressure off my carpal tunnel wrist and can't tie down the cord because of that. I drop it or get it tangled in my leg and it hit has the floor over a hundred times.
Like all of these eventually the wire where it meets the unit gets a bad connection and it fails.
I sent them a complaint and they sent back I needed to send them the serial number off the bottom AND a copy of the receipt. It can't be done by email, you have to do it off their webpage. You can send a copy of the receipt scanned by uploading on their website. They also have a 800 type number that's open during Pacific time Monday to Friday.
I sent in the copy of the scanned receipt (Uploaded off their webpage) and they just sent me a free, no charge replacement WITHOUT having to send them the old one. They just said to toss out. I kept the ball.
The ball falls out easily but you need to clean out the cavity occasionally because the crud builds up and the ball gets hard to move. On the plus side the ball is almost the size of a tennis ball so if you knock it over it's usually easy to find.
If you use your computer a lot and like a trackball that has 4 buttons that you can set yourself for their functions (With the Trackball Works program) this should be a good unit. I definitely have gotten my $72 (It was more expensive in 2012 and I paid for shipping extra) out of it and I got a brand new replacement on the 5 year warranty.

title: Going to fit just about anything you need and look totally sexy while doing it!
text:
Chose this case for only a few reasons. After doing mountains of research I could safely conclude that tons of cases will fit my full board, a large graphics card, and a few hard drives. Many cases out there have some crazy 8 or 10 extra drive bays, which just seems excessive in most cases (pun intended). This was one of the few cases that had a concealed and aesthetically pleasing front. I didn't want 8-9 drive bays sitting unused in front covered by an ugly mesh screen. The cases they make now days are massive and many full size cases will fit everything one needs. I had about 7 or 8 cases I was deciding between. All were well reviewed, solidly built by reputable companies so it really did eventually come down to, "what do I feel like taking up half my desk and how will it look". A better case won't make your hard drives faster or your video card work any better.

Other notes: Fan control is more useful than I thought. I keep the fans on low and it's nearly dead silent (my cases is about 2 feet from me ON the desk)

- Only slight "problem" I can find: My Coolermaster Hyper TX3 does only have about 3/4 of an inch left for clearance until it meets the side of the case. The area I'm referring to is screen over and has mounts for, I believe, a 200mm fan. I wasn't planning on and haven't bothered to put a fan there but just from looking at it maayy possibly not fit. Wasn't really a big concern as there is PLENTY of airflow in this case especially if you throw in a front 140mm (as I mention later, the green LED is so worth it :D ) and being that it's covered by a clean looking grill it still provides nice ambient airflow right to the top of the cooler (putting my hand up to it right now I can definitely feel a solid, cool breeze coming from it)

* I had started to consider which case came with more fans until I stopped being lazy and realized fans were $10-15 dollars and not something I want to judge a case by. I decided to grab a green LED NZXT 140mm for around $14 for the front. The side fans kick out a ton of air but a straight front fan to create a good air flow direction definitely helps and the green LED definitely helps the sexyness even more :)

*USB was definitely a concern. Would have liked ~4 on the panel (front or top, whichever case you look at). I have a Razer Keyboard that supplies me with an additional port and have a USB hub ($10-$20 a lot of places) that I have kind of "mounted" conveniently on my desk. That takes care of that problem.

Final thoughts.
It sounds kind of superficial but I did HOURS of research trying to find out which case was "better" or the "best one". Eventually I realized that unless you are running 8+ drives, 3+ video cards, some crazy liquid cooling, and just an insane amount of hardware, there are 25+ cases on the market from good companies that are going to do exactly what you need. If I was going to have a massive box of metal and plastic on my desk, why not pick the one that looks the best while serving my (and 95% of peoples) needs. Sexy as hell, very solid design, and excellent airflow. Gaming for 5-6 hours straight (don't judge me) my CPU, with fans on lowest setting, has never touched over 40 degrees Celsius and my GTX 780 has never budged over ~33 degrees. Thought about going liquid cooling but with this guys' fans on low, I can feel the air flow in my room change this thing is moving so much air. Save your money on liquid cooling and put it towards your Graphics card or a larger capacity SSD. Hope this helps, happy building!

the camera

title: Loving it !!
text:
Just like most folks, I was trying to make some space on my computer desk and putting a desk mount is the best way to do it. I needed a single arm mount as I don't have dual monitor requirements. There is not much price difference between a single mount vs a dual mount monitor though.

The design is pretty sturdy. I have a 22" monitor and this mount holds it without any issues. Putting up the mount on the desk should be much easier than what I experienced, mostly due to bad instruction manual. Rather then giving every step, they have showed the end result. Be careful when you put screws on the back of your monitor. There are separate ones for curved vs flat back monitors (that was my fault, not the manual's). The only problem that I see with the mount it is its tilt (which is +/- 15 degrees). The bolt that controls the tilt can be made better. It was extremely hard for me to tighten it up for the monitor to stay level (at zero degree tilt). The manual says to attach the swivel to the back of your monitor after you have attached it to your desk, which is fine. But you are absolutely going to need another hand if you try to do it that way. The other easier way is to bring the height to the lowest point, tilt the swivel to face the desk (as much as possible), and then attach the monitor to it (its so much easier this way).

I knocked off one star for the bad manual, and slight issue with the tilt bolt. Other than that, its a great buy for a single monitor mount.

title: Works with Droid Razr Maxx - after some fooling around
text:
I needed a breakout adapter so that I could plug an external microphone into my Droid Razr Maxx to use it like a tape recorder, and this seemed to fit the bill. When it arrived I plugged the adapter in, then plugged in the headphones and microphone. Hit record, and . . . nothing - the phone was still only picking up sound from the built-in mics. Was it the wrong adapter? Did the Droid headset jack have a different wiring?

After some research (including checking the adapter wiring with an ohmmeter) I discovered - like one of the other reviewers who has a Macbook - that you need to plug the mic and headphones into the female splitter jacks first, then insert the StarTech adapter 4-pin plug into the phone. The phone needs to detect what kind of device is plugged in before it will route the signals properly. Once I did this, I had no problem using the external mic to record with. Now my phone acts like a fairly decent digital audio recorder.

I'd have given this five stars - good build quality, no problems with audio noise - if the manufacturer had simply enclosed a note saying "plug in the adapter after you plug in the mic and earphones". A frustrating experience, but at least I learned something new about the Droid Razr internals.

I read reviews from the Rockford Fosgate 12" [[ASIN:B004UFHXNI Rockford Fosgate P3D4-12 Punch P3 DVC 4-Ohm 12-Inch 600-Watt RMS 1200-Watt Peak Subwoofer]]subwoofer (by the way there was a very little magnet on it) and decided to buy it when everybody said it was awesome and deep bass. I even had my super clean Pioneer amp for it and it was still hitting hard and rough. That wasn't clean. So what I am starting to see is that everybody's opinion is skewed or perceived differently. One guy thinks its clean and nice but to the other it may be rough and annoying because of different perceptions.

I did not enjoy the other Fosgate, I even tried Kicker and they were still on the rough end. JBL actually has a nice product here. I have not tried the lower end woofers for the car but based off what this one produces, the other JBL lower models may produce good bass.

Don't be fooled by other reviews.

This was my setup running at about 500-600 watts RMS. This subwoofer is rated at 700 watts RMS.
