title: Incredible Budget Netbook
text:
If you are someone who is looking for a computer that can game, and you're on a budget, look no further then the Acer Aspire One AO722-0473 Netbook.

But, I'm guessing you would prefer more detail then that.

First, I want to address what's bad about this laptop. Which, honestly, for this price is not much.

Now, my biggest problem with this laptop is the fact that it is a gigantic fingerprint magnet. Both the screen and top cover will gather fingerprints faster then you can blink an eye, and you will find yourself wiping the screen and cover off far more then you would prefer.

Another is the fact that there was inaccurate information given about the size of the hard drive on this thing. It is advertised as a 320 GB hard drive, but I received a 284 gig hard drive. I expect a bit of fluctuation, but a whole 36 gigs missing is a huge annoyance. But, even if you receive one of these with that size of a hard drive, it should be more then adequate for your needs.

Next is that it doesn't come with a bluetooth card, but I don't use bluetooth devices so it's not an issue. Anyways, it is easily fixed with a USB dongle that according to other reviewers is ~25 dollars.

Last, but not least, is the weak processor. The 722 uses the AMD Dual Core C-60 Processor, mine has Turbo CORE technology that gets it up to 1.333 GHz, but the base version has 1 Gigahert period. Now, the reason I have a problem with this is because I am a gamer, and I actually game quite a bit on this computer. I meet the minimum requirements for most modern games across the board, except the processor, which is to weak to play them.

But, that's it for the bad. Now for the good, which far outweighs what is bad.

One of the best things about this laptop is the fact that it has a full-size keyboard. I'm a writer, and this really makes my day. I can drill away and type without making many mistakes because this keyboard is so easy to get the hang of. It also presents all of it's functions in an easy fashion. All you need to do is hold down the function button and hit one of the F keys with a picture on it. All of the pictures clearly explain what they do, so this makes it very easy to disable to touchpad while you're typing so that you don't accidentally hit it with you're palm or mute the sound when you're in a quiet public area.

Second, I have seen reviews that say the speakers on this thing are bad. That just isn't the case, they output audio quietly, but they are sufficient for my needs. I do wish they were a bit louder, but just because they're a little on the quiet side doesn't make them bad. It doesn't distort my audio, and while music and other things are quiet, they are at least clear. Anyways, you are usually carrying netbooks around to use in public areas, which you would of course want headphones for anyway.

Third, this thing is light. I can toss it in my bookbag or just carry it around and hardly notice it's there. It's also very thin, so it can actually fit in my overstuffed bag.

Fourth, and best of all, this netbook comes with Windows 7 Home Premium, NOT starter, which is rare for netbooks at the price.

Fifth, this netbook comes with a full LED LCD HD 11.6" screen. The average screen size for netbooks is 10.1", and I can definitely say that the extra inch comes in handy and makes it easier to see and read things on the screen. The screen is vibrant as well, but my biggest problem with it is that there isn't a very wide range of brightness settings. So if I want to make it really dark while I'm trying to sleep and leaving it on to do something, I can't. Luckily, I can just configure it to stay on while I close the cover. So, it's not a huge deal. Especially when the picture on it is very good.

Sixth, this computer is extremely speedy thanks to it's 2GBs of DDR3 SDRAM. I can do full HD video streaming without a hitch, and standard definition still looks good. I've watched both movies and TV Shows both locally on the computer and streaming and I can't find a huge problem with anything. Sometimes HD video streaming will skip a frame, but it's never a huge deal. I don't have Netflix, so I unfortunately can't share my experiences with it.

Seventh, and most important for me, is the fact that this thing can game very well. The biggest problem doing this is the fact that it has a weak processor, so it'll meet the requirements of most modern games, but if they are processor heavy games, then they are going to lag. Luckily, games that aren't very processor heavy play just fine. Here is a list of games that I have played and my experiences with them:

Sins of a Solar Empire: 30 FPS, slight dips occasionally, can lag a little while in combat

Diablo 2: Lord of Destruction: ~60 FPS without disruption

Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic: ~25 FPS with frequent lag, still playable, but huge lag in larger battles and you won't be able to pass becoming a jedi because it becomes unplayable at that point

Age of Empires 3: ~30 FPS, dips frequently, a slight bit laggy during combat. But completely playable.

Age of Empires 2: Age of Conquerors: ~60 FPS without disruption

Star Wars: Galactic Battleground: ~60 FPS without disruption

Max Payne: ~60 FPS without disruption

The Sims 3: ~25 FPS, dips frequently, still playable but a slight bit laggy

Deus Ex: ~60 FPS without disruption

Guild Wars: ~30 FPS, constant dips

Call of Duty 4: ~20 FPS, barely playable in SP, lags pretty badly during the more intense set-pieces, MP pretty much unplayable

League of Legends: ~25 FPS, fully playable, dips occasionally

As you can see, most of the older titles play fine. If their slightly newer or more processor heavy like KOTOR, then you're out of luck. But if you just want to game on the go, it shouldn't be a problem.

Eighth, the webcam is sufficient, but strangely doesn't come with the ability to video capture. It looks okay, but it won't ever keep up a constant stream. By constant I mean a full 30 FPS stream, it takes a second for your hand to appear like 3 times while you wave past it. But, I haven't used it (although Skype is pre-loaded onto here), so it's not a huge problem for me.

Ninth, the touchpad is good. I don't use it much, as I'm more of a mouse guy. Anyways, I can't game with a touchpad. The only problem I have is that it isn't sensitive enough and for some reason is placed farther left then it should be. If I accidentally leave it on while I'm typing, my palm will brush it and I may accidentally delete my work. Thank god for the undo button. Anyways, it's multigesture so it's good. I like the scroll bar on the right side of it.

Tenth, the wireless card is great. I get great download speeds on it that I never got with my old computers Ethernet card, it let's me take full advantage of my internet connection and that's always nice. I've always been touchy with gaming on a wireless connection, but this wireless card makes sure it works.

Finally, the computer comes with a nice amount of ports. 3 USB 2.0 ports, 1 HDMI output, 1 VGA output, a headphone jack, a microphone jack, an Ethernet insert, and a insert for your charging cable. It doesn't come with a CD drive, but since this is a netbook, this is expected.

In closing, this computer is great. Especially for a gamer like me who's been out of the PC market because of the expense of computers. I will be buying the RAM upgrade, but the computer runs perfectly fine without it. It's also great for people who type a lot thanks to it's full size keyboard. So no matter what kind of person you are, be it gamer or someone who wants it for more Office purposes, this will be more then enough to do what you want. Even if you just want to watch movies or TV shows. It's also at an unbeatable price, even if you buy it at the MSRP.

*This review was assembled from 2 and a half weeks experience with the laptop

Thanks for reading, make sure to say I was helpful, :)

title: Unreliable
text:
I've been printing shipping labels with this printer almost every day for over six months. Based on that experience, I would dissuade anyone who wants to use this printer for a similar purpose from buying it. This printer does a poor job of printing shipping labels for two main reasons.

The first problem is poor paper tray/loading performance. To print a shipping label, I'll insert one sheet of label paper into the top of the print tray. What often happens is that it'll pull two sheets of paper at once and print part of my labels on the top sheet, and part of it on the sheet underneath it. So then I have to throw out two sheets of paper and start over again, wasting paper and ink. This happens far too often.

The other problem is the poor quality of the print. Vertical lines look broken up into several segments because the print heads are poorly aligned or some similar situation. This causes the barcodes on my shipping labels to look very bad, and makes me wonder if they scan correctly. This is in draft quality. If I try to print the labels in standard quality, they come out even worse, with blotchy ink smudges all over the barcodes. And I get these results even after doing everything HP tech support instructs me to, like cleaning and aligning the print heads and resetting the printer.

These problems seem to be inherent to the printer design rather than being a case of a bad sample because I had to invoke the warranty service from HP to exchange the printer. My original printer and the replacement that HP sent me had identical problems.

That's too bad that this printer is such poor quality, because it has the exact features I'm looking for--a basic, economical inkjet printer without fax or scanning capabilities but with WiFi and separate cartridgees for each color. If anyone can let me know of another printer with those same features but better quality, please let me know!

title: Good after a little handiwork to fix the charging problem.
text:
I picked up one of these recently and was able to fix the charging problem by replacing the battery. The light uses one rechargeable LIR2477 button battery, which you can find online for about $4 to $5. (Amazon doesn't currently list any, unfortunately.) The repair itself requires a soldering iron, a small philips screwdriver, and the replacement LIR2477 battery. I also used some short pieces of wire and electrical tape, since my replacement battery lacked solder tabs.

The light has 3 screws; two are visible, and one is hidden beneath the rubber pad at the bottom. Once the screws are removed, the casing comes apart easily to reveal the battery. The positive and negative sides of the battery are connected to metal tabs, which are then soldered to two points on the adjacent circuit board. After the tabs are desoldered from the board, the battery pops right out. It's probably a good idea to notate/photograph the connections to verify that the replacement battery terminals are connected properly.

If the replacement battery has tabs, you can just solder it in place. My replacement didn't come with tabs, so I soldered two short pieces of wire to the circuit board and taped each end to the corresponding side of the battery. This has the added bonus of making battery replacement easier in the future.

title: A few problems, but great support and overall a good choice
text:
This was the second model of 8 inch frame I tried, after buying and returning a Philips that I bought at Walmart (see my review of that elsewhere on Amazon). This whole category of product, at least at this price point, does seem to present some reliability issues, so it requires some patience and perhaps also some luck.

There is Good News (mostly) and Bad News (a little) about this frame. The Bad News is that the first one I received had a faulty power cord, such that if you so much as breathed on it the frame turned off. The Good News is that Micca's technical support was right there with a replacement cord. Once I got that, I plugged in a usb chip with about 200 photos on it, to get it set up as a present for my elderly mother so she can just plug and play. That worked great, but I wanted to add and delete some photos, so I went through that process a few times until I got the selection just right. Then when I played them on Random a problem cropped up where the frame seemed to pick a "favorite" photo that showed very frequently, the other 199+ not so much. Once again Micca's technical support, even though it was a weekend, was right there with helpful suggestions. Together we finally figured out that all my adding and deleting had corrupted my usb chip. I reformatted that, re-pasted the photos, and now it works just great.
What I learned is that the software in these frames is not as robust as the software on a computer. You have to treat them gently. You should start with a nice clean usb chip, newly formatted and completely empty. Do your adding and deleting on your computer, and then copy the final product to the chip when it's all done. For me, at least, that gave great results. The photos are clear and sharp and the viewing angle is excellent, much better than the Philips I started with which was unviewable unless you stood directly in front of it. It can do a lot of stuff like music and video that neither Mom nor I have any interest in so no opinion about that. For viewing photos and simple operation, this is a winner. At this price point, this is the frame to get.

title: This review is for the Lumix ZS19 which is the same as this camera but without GPS
text:
I want to preface that I am not a professional or very dedicated photographer. My review is for people like me: love photography, use mostly scene settings, some manual tinkering (aperture and shutter speed priority) and love to take scenery and wildlife pictures. I am in the market for a smaller camera to take to my hikes/travel etc. to replace my Lumix FZ28 which was stolen on my recent trip to Costa Rica. I already have a Nikon D5100 which I love and takes great pics, but it is just to heavy and bulky to take along. I purchased both a Canon SX260HS and a Lumix ZS19 to try out because both their specifications seem comparable and I trust both brands. I took pics side by side with these two cameras, and here are my observations:
1. color: panasonic colors were generally cooler with more green/blue vs. the canon's warmer colors (yellowish tones) for the same scenes and lighting
2. the HDR features of the Lumix are amazing for high contrast/bright background.
3. the zoomed pictures for the Lumix were clearer (less blurry) than the Canon's (I took pictures of a power tower and some distant hills in the late afternoon light)
4. the most important consideration for me was the ability to focus. I took pictures of flowers and foliage and the Lumix clearly outshone with the feature of the touch screen (I could tell it to focus on a particular petal or detail just by touching the image on the screen) whereas I ended up with a lot of out of focus pictures with the Canon.
Note that I did not try the GPS feature of the Canon since it is not that important to me.
In conclusion, even the expert reviews talk about a better image quality of the Canon SX260, I decided that for my purposes, I prefer the images that the Lumix ZS19.
I am going to return both cameras today and order the Lumix ZS20 instead (because of the promotion, the price of the ZS20 is the same as what I paid for the ZS19, so the GPS feature is for free!!!)

title: Exceeds expectations
text:
Installed this antenna to replace the DISH. I needed an antenna that was small enough to fit in a cramped attic and being in a fringe area was unsure if any antenna would work. Stations are 40 miles away but in one general direction. After much research on line and looking at other antennas I decided on this one. Once hooked up, combined with a Wingard 8700 preamp, I get 38 stations all with a solid respectable signal.

Very pleased with the number of stations this antenna grabs from 40 miles, especially in an attic. There are two VHF stations, one low and one high, I didn't think I would pick up at all. While the antenna did pick them up, marginally if at all, there was much pixelation. I was surprised to see Channel 6 come in at all and channel 12 came in OK but not great. I attached some telescoping antennas to form a horizontal dipole antenna using some rabbit ears and now get 4 to 6 bars of signal from these stations.

Awesome antenna, especially for an attic, even in a fringe area that picks up not only UHF but VHF as well. The VHF is better improved with slight modification in my situation. While I have no antenna to compare it too it was purchased after much research and well pleased with the decision. If thinking about getting this antenna don't hesitate.

This was the most frustrating experience, with lots of incompatibilities, and when I got it to work the odd time, trouble with rewinding or fast forwarding. Oh, and the picture quality was crappy which I thought was just caused by the quality of the videos I ripped from my DVD's. Anyway, I got tired of fighting with my blu-ray and looked and saw the Amazon Fire TV had a DLNA player available within it, and I didn't see a ton of complaints from people trying to get it to work. I already have a smart tv with apps for Amazon VOD, and Netflix so I didn't need another provider for these services and only really cared about the DLNA client, and since this was only $99, I'd give it a whirl.
Setup was a breeze, it came already tied to my Amazon Prime account. The hardest part (seriously) was finding the HDMI port on my tv. I had it up and running within 5 minutes of starting the install, and where my Blu-Way wouldn't work with most of the media servers I had tried to set up (Router, NAS Drive, Windows 7 Server) this worked seamlessly with all of them and would play all the formats I had. And my god...the video quality playing my DVD rip was seriously 10 times better than it had been on the Blu-Ray. This was a bonus I was not expecting. And nice things like FF and RW worked as they should. I am very happy.
Another thing I wasnt expecting was to switch from my smart tv interface for Amazon VOD and Netflix to using the Fire TV interface. FireTV is much faster to move through the menus and I think the video quality is even better than it is going through my tv apps. I don't know why, but it looks like it is. The voice search runs perfectly as well. So, all in all. This was a killer purchase. It met all my key needs for playing my network video files, plus I got benefits from it I was never expecting in terms of better access and video quality on Netflix and Amazon VOD. title: A Lens that can be enjoyed by both lens snobs and frugle photographers alike
text:
Obviously there are a ton of reviews already written about this lens. Normally I wouldn't even bother throwing my $0.02 in but having owned all 3 of the current Canon 50mm lenses I felt there might be something I could add to the conversation.

I started with the nifty-fifty, the 50/1.8 ver 2. It was good optically but the AF was useless in low lighting and it was built like a toy. I used it for about a year until the front element fell off one day for no apparent reason.

Next I got the 50/1.4 and I truly fell in love with it. Because 50mm is my favorite and most used focal length (and because I'm a bit of a snob when it comes to lenses) I thought it would be a good idea to invest in the 50L so that's what I currently own.

I adore that 50L but truth be told if it was lost, stolen, or broken tomorrow I would replace it with the 50/1.4 and wouldn't feel that sorry for myself. I suppose that's the highest compliment I can pay the 50/1.4. It's sharp, its AF is quick, and unless you're shooting directly into the sun without a hood the color and contrast are fantastic.

Of course it can't shoot at f/1.2 but to be perfectly honest, I rarely shoot the 50L wide open and isn't all that sharp at f/1.2 anyway. It's a luxury I could live without.

The only significant advantage of the 50L is the build quality. The 50L is built rock solid. It could be used as an effective paperweight during a hurricane and you could probably bludgeon to death any potential muggers with it if you were so inclined. The 50/1.4 is by no means is as fragile or cheap as the 50/1.8 but you'd have a hard time using it as a weapon. It's strong enough to handle day-to-day professional use but it leaves a little to be desired. Of course if for some reason it does break down, you can replace it 3 more times for the cost of one 50/1.2L.

This lens, along with the 85/1.8 are probably the biggest steals you can find in the Canon or Nikon lineups. Like I said, I'm kind of a lens snob but I would have no qualms breaking out one of these on a shoot. If you need a 50mm lens, buy it.

title: Ignore the reviews from those who clearly don't understand what a double-conversion online UPS is!
text:
Online UPS's offer the ultimate in power protection. Unlike other types of UPS's (Standby or Sinewave) your equipment is ALWAYS isolated from line power. Power from the electric company goes into a charging circuit which charges the batteries. This is a very simple, robust circuit that is not sensitive to power problems. All it does is charge the batteries.

Then, an inverter circuit uses battery power to generate perfect, pure 110V AC power for your equipment. Non double-conversion UPS's don't work like this. They feed line power to your equipment, and if there's a power problem then, and only then, will it start converting battery power to AC, The inverters in those UPS's are not designed to run 24/7 like the inverters in online UPS's. Your equipment will be exposed to all sorts of power glitches that can slowly cause damage and other problems like data corruption.

The truth is that only online UPS's provide the type of protection most people THINK they are getting with lesser UPS's.

Now, about this unit specifically....it's well made and a bargain at the price.

The nature of ALL online UPS's is that they are very heavy, and because it's constantly charging and inverting, the fans run all the time. There's no such thing as a silent online UPS.

title: Good price but process was a little confusing
text:
I ordered the protection with just days to go before the first year was up. But the Prime delivery was on time and I registered without incident. Here's a few things that someone else may want to know.

1. The protection covers the 13" MacBook Pro Retina model. The fact that it covers Retina is not made clear in the product description.

2. When I received the Amazon purchase confirmation email it said "Your protection plan service agreement will be sent via a separate e-mail by your seller." The protection I purchased was sold by Amazon so it wasn't clear what the "seller" reference meant. But worse, it made it sound like I would receive the agreement or at least the registration number in an email. I received no such email. I did receive a physical box on the day promised and that had the registration ID. Now having completed the entire process I think it means that when you get the registration information delivered and then register you can get the confirmation in an email which is what happened. See next item.

3. By going to the Apple web address that came in the boxed instructions I was able to navigate to the Apple page where I entered my registration id and the serial number of my MacBook. No problems encountered. The completion message said I would be sent a Protection Plan Certificate by regular mail or email--the choice was mine. I chose email and the certificate arrived within about 10 minutes.

It was a bit nerve racking for me because I let it go until the last minute. If there was a glitch that would have been a problem. There were no glitches in the end and I am a happy camper.

title: Great features. The best I've tried.
text:
Bought for my 70 year old mom so her kids may more easily share photos with her. This unit has so many features it is hard to know where to start.

Screen Quality
So, so. Adequate in most use cases but this would could be improved by having a 1024 x 768 resolution or better. Typical photo frame angle of view which is to say it is average.

Ease of Use:
The wireless feature worked great and pretty easy to set up. I did the setup and I am technically proficient with this kind of stuff. The remote definitely helps with day-to-day use as trying to remember the order of the buttons on the back of the unit to navigate menus and settings will not work unless you are doing so constantly. The manual could definitely use some improvement. It did not cover use of some of the features very well if at all. For instance, setting up and using the Internet radio required some trial and error but I did eventually figure out how to listen to a station or two. Same goes for the weather feature. I don't think my mom would be able to manage some of these "extra" features and probably doesn't really care to anyways.

Comments on Features Tried:
The radio worked after playing around a bit. This is probably the least documented feature. Still not entirely clear on the best way to set the station and obviously this thing is not going to be great audio quality and isn't meant to be. But if you would like some background music or something to listen to NPR or something it will work for that. Just not that great if you need to be changing channels all the time. More of a set it and forget it kind of thing.

Grabbing pictures from several web photo sites was relatively easy to set up (on the website). I tried Picasa and flickr with no real issues.

Emailing photos to the frame seems to be one of the more documented and easier things to do. Just go to their website and setup an account (very easy) and pick your email address which goes through their servers (for instance you email address might be your.name@mypixstar.com). Then you can send pictures to it directly (via their servers). I think the documentation said there is a 20MB per email limit so you can email several photos at one time. You can view the photos via the online account that have been sent to the frame and manage things there much easier than using the frame itself for management. Things like deleting photos, etc. are much easier to do online. The online interface is not great but it gets the job done and is relatively simple. There are settings that adjust what happens when an emailed photo is received like just accept all without prompting and play a sound when this happens, accept only from a list of senders (entered online), show a notification screen on the frame that shows who it is from and prompts for acceptance into the slide show, etc. There is an overlay feature that can be enabled/disabled that will overlay the sender's email address and the email subject line on the photo when displayed. It seems to get in the way of the photo a bit more than I'd like so I have disabled this feature.

Weather
Online you can enter one or more cities for the frame to display a screen of weather information like the next two or three days forecast temps. If your city is not among the choices on their website (my Mom's wasn't) you can request them to add whatever cities/towns/areas you want. The response to this was very fast. The screen displays randomly (if your frame is set to display randomly) and updates several times a day.

Online Management
You can manage most settings and other aspects of the frame online and this is definitely the way to go for those things that can be set there. Things like file and folder management are relatively straightforward. Since I know my Mom's account password I can remotely manage the frame for her for some aspects of it that aren't quite so obvious. You can change slide show settings like which folders will be included (only emailed photos, only web albums, all). One caveat to this is that the online settings can't be changed when the frame is offline. It does show on the main screen whether it is online or offline. I wish there was a way to wake it up remotely. I set my Mom's frame to come on at 10am and turn off at 10pm but for some reason it often shows offline when I view her account via the website. Haven't asked her if she is physically turning it off and on of if she isn't touching it.

Support
Tech support for the frame is fantastic. Not sure what size of operation this is (I get the feeling it is small) but responses to all of my tech support requests (via email) were extremely fast. Often just minutes and they were very active in trying to help figure out a photo rotation issue I was having which ended up being a Google Picasa photo export issue and not anything to do with the frame. Extremely impressed with the tech support. There is also an online feature to request new features for the frame and a means for online account holders to vote for requested features. I requested a couple of features and while they were not able to implement them due to limitations in the hardware or software system, they did respond very promptly to the feature request. The only downside is this online feature is not the easiest thing to find (there is a red "Feedback & Support" tab attached to the extreme right side of the web site that I somehow didn't see for quite some time although it is blatantly obvious now that I know it is there. Just not the usual place for the Support link for a website. The other downside is that the voting, blog and feature request doesn't seem to have a lot of activity (not a lot of voting or feature requests). If more people with this frame actually used this feature I can't help but think that it would improve by leaps and bounds much more quickly.

Pros
Feature set. More features than you can shake a stick at. If you like playing with features, this is the frame for you.
Tech support response and feature request options are great. It seems like they aim to please with tech support and adding features.
Of the several photo frames I've tried over the years this is the one to get if you can afford it.
Easily email photos to frame.
Grabs pictures from online web albums like Picasa, flickr, Google+, facebook, shutterfly and many more.
Supports grabbing photos via DLNA from folders shared on your home computer or laptop (I didn't try this).
2GB on-board memory with SD card slot for additional.

Cons
Web site interface and frame interface are not the greatest but there are a lot of features and functionality here and they get the job done.
Screen resolution at 800x600 is not the greatest but beyond 3 or 4 ft, greater resolution probably wouldn't help.
Not available in other sizes. 10.4 inches sounds big but it really isn't if viewed more than 3 or 4 feet away. Depending on where it will be placed and the viewing distance that results, this could be a problem. Would be great to see a 15 inch version of this.
Pretty expensive for a photo frame.
Printed manual is not as good or helpful as it could be.
Manual not available online (that I could find).

Unknown
Reliability. Been in use for a couple of months with no issues. My luck with a variety of different photo frames in the past was not good. I think they all eventually died within two years.

title: Just as good as a Ciniq but with limitations
text:
I needed a Cintiq replacement (mine's was broken during transit from Korea). I also used a YiYnova MSP19 last year and was not too happy because of the line that streaks across the screen while drawing (still a decent alternative and I believe the YiYnova MSP 19U has no issues after the driver update). I was skeptical at first because of the low price and a few things I heard online about the product but I am impressed. The pressure sensitivity is spot on, the pen is accurate, the screen don't get hot while drawing, and the film that covers the screen makes it feel like writing on paper. The resolution looks good and it actually has a similar feel (almost) as the Cintiq. The 19 in screen is plenty of real estate to do artwork. I used it so far in sketchbook pro, ZBrush, and Photoshop and it worked fine (after fighting with the drivers on Windows 7). The pen feels natural in your hand and runs smooth across the screen. Once you get it working right, you will have a lot of fun with it (12 hours of use and loving it).

The part that keeps it from being as professional as the Cintiq is the drivers, the software, and the pen. The drivers are not fully compatible with window 7 and 8. The pressure sensitivity don't work on Win 8 (they are working on a fix and is set for March release hopefully). In Windows 7, you have to uninstall all Wacom drivers for it to work. This makes it hard if you want to use a regular tablet just for practice. On a desktop, it's easy to extend the screen and work it independently, but under a laptop, I couldn't get this to work. You have to mirror the laptop (still working on it maybe it's me messing up).The express key buttons don't work under Windows 7 or 8. I will give an updated review when I get them working (I'm currently talking to customer service). The screen is not as bright as the Cintiq but it's still looks crisp enough to be a professional grade. The pen don't have an eraser feature so artist need to either program the express keys (mines don't work at the moment) or manually switch, which can be annoying sometimes. The software package (it has no real use) has a cumbersome look and feel to it.

Overall, I am pleased with this product minus the small imperfections (the buttons, drivers, and pen). Once they fix the small stuff, then this will definitely be a professional grade tablet (it already is if you can get past the small stuff). I believe they will fix the small stuff so I highly recommend it. I will give an update with any fixes that they give me (the customer service is awesome!) so I can help make things painless for whoever buys it.

Update: I figure out how to get the tablet to work on the lapetop. This is controlled by Windows Tablet PC utility under systems. Once you start the setup, press enter until you are on the tablet screen (works like a champ). I found some working drivers for the express keys at bosto.trixbrix (it seems I can't add a link to this post so just add dot com to the end of the link and go to the support section). Everything works great. The only thing that needs to be fixed is the pressure sensitivity and compatibility for Photoshop in windows 8 (sketchbook pro, Corel painter, ArtRage, ToonBoom, and ZBrush works good). That is the only issue left. My rating for this item and all the hassle is a 3 1/2. If everything worked out of the box it would get a 5. I'll update as I get use to it.

title: Erratic Toshiba Elan Touchpad Makes this unusable
text:
This laptop cannot respond to a taps consistently or reliably. Double-Tapping a track-pad is a much easier gesture than physically clicking the lower right corner.

The Elan trackpad (Smart-Pad) in this Toshiba S55 cannot be used so that you can count on it to respond with your first or second or third or more attempts at double tapping.

In a Word Document, doing a tap and drag across a sentence or paragraph to highlight text takes multiple tries. Then double tapping to bring up a context menu to copy or cut highlighted text doesn't work with ease. It takes many tries at double tapping for the Elan to respond by bringing up the context menu.

Tapping to drag a window to another area of the desktop also doesn't respond. Often you need to tap the desktop then tap the window then double tap the window to engage dragging. Same goes for re-sizing a window.

Double-tapping the desktop is most difficult; double-tapping the windows 8.1 new Start Button to bring up its context menu is even more difficult.

Problems with the Elan "Smart-Pad" used in not only Toshiba's S50 line but also its S70 are complained about in Toshiba's Community Forum going back at least 8 months. Toshiba hasn't update its Elan driver since March 2014.

Using the same pressure tap will get different results. When you are able to get the trackpad to respond repeatedly, then pause for a while. It will again be unresponsive.

This is one compromise I cannot make with a laptop. This makes this laptop unusable.

You may find, as I have, that no matter how you configure the "Smart-Pad" in Mouse Settings through High or Low Sensitivity, palm sensitivity and others, this trackpad is horrible. Unlike this Toshiba's, trackpads in Macbook Pro, Acer V5 and Logitech T650 work well. If they can do the job than there's no reason this Toshiba's shoudn't either. The Elan and its drivers in this laptop, for lack of a better word, suck.

You'll be much happier with another product where you don't have to fight with the trackpad all day long ( and with this Toshiba's battery that day can be as low as 2 hours)

title: Great when it works.
text:
Well, first I'd say that when this camera works as expected, it's awesome-- great picture, great functionality, great helmet / surface mounts. But while the hardware side is excellent, the software side flat out sucks.

Since purchasing the camera a couple weeks ago there have been 2 major firmware updates for the camera and 3 software updates for the Android app. One of the firmware updates added the ability to turn the camera on / off via wireless (great!) and to view footage / images on the camera from your phone (also great!).

On the downside, the camera's wireless DOESN'T TURN OFF when you turn off the camera. . .WTF??

So what this results in is no less than 3-4 episodes of me showing up at the top of a hill for a mtn bike ride or stepping off a dive platform to find out that the battery was dead since the wireless had been ON the whole time, draining the battery. Read the gopro support forums-- this is a well known issue, with most users saying, "just remove the battery!" as if that's a solid solution to a stupid software glitch.

Furthermore, make very certain you spend the extra $$ on a very reputable, high-speed memory card. For a long while I was baffled by the camera working fine for a while, then shutting itself off for no reason, in the middle of filming, in the middle of an activity that doesn't lend itself to messing about with a camera. I came to learn that this was due to the camera exceeding the write speed of the memory card. Once that was resolved, we have had no more issues.

So altogether I have to give this camera a 5 star rating for the hardware, and a 1 star for the software-- leaving it with a middle of the road 3 stars, since (hopefully) gopro will get their software shop in order and get these issues resolved.

The next problem was with pairing between android and Inreach unit which I found the solution with a "power start" by holding
power and tracking buttons simultaneously.(not in owners manual).The inability of the Delorme Inreach to reliably receive text messages from my remote location was disappointing to say the least.I expected the inreach to work simply and reliably as does my spot messenger but I found it to be cumbersome and very finicky in actual use.I tired of solving a new issue each time I tested the unit.Delorme claims the unit sends and receives text messages but in reality my experience was negative on most all counts!Battery life was very poor using 4 sets of lithium batteries during my testing.
I returned the Inreach to Amazon for a refund and received a very fair credit to my account.

title: Amazing tablet
text:
I had actually heard about this product from tumblr. Some people were mentioning this tablet mainly for the price. With the tablet, you REALLY get your moneys worth, and I mean that in the best of ways.
My first ever tablet was awful. I might as well of used a mouse. My second ever tablet was a wacom bamboo fun. Wacom is very, very expensive, but usually they are pretty good quality. I thought it was pretty nice and it suited my needs. When I drew with it, I still had issues though, and drawing on the computer with it never felt as easy as with a pencil and paper. I just thought that was how it was with all tablets.
I heard about this one, and firstly about the price. When I did more research, everyone was saying how it operated better than the bamboo tablets.
And I have to say, it does. It out performs it in terms of smoothness, and pressure sensitivity. And it lags a lot less too. I like the size of it (it's pretty big) but then again, some people may not like that.
Some people complain about the batteries that the pen takes, but it only uses one triple a battery at a time, and it lasts a long time. The biggest issue I had was with installing the driver and software. It took me an hour to figure it out, but I'm not tech savy.
The key is to delete anything from a preexisting tablet on your computer, and maybe change the download settings on your computer. If the tablet doesn't work with a certain drawing program or the pressure sensitivity doesn't seem to be working, it's not the programs fault, it means the driver hasn't installed.
I had the issue of the pen working, but not the sensitivity, and someone tried to tell me that it was paint tool sai (an art program), and that they weren't compatible, but this is not true. It all has to do with the driver. Hopefully no one else has this issue.
Overall though, I'm extremely pleased with this product, and would recommend it over the wacom bamboo tablets.

Pros: Large, amazing pen sensitivity, pen stand, feels sturdy, hotkeys are super useful, price is fantastic
Cons: Pen takes batteries, size may be an issue to some, installing the driver is a pain (at least for me) and the program seems a bit outdated

I only needed to transmit a continuous 12 Mbps lossless (meaning any lost packets would interrupt the feed) and it couldn't even do that. I would not buy this crap again. It's cheap and I doubt it would pass Cat5E standards. I'm returning these things.

These are really cheap cables with bad, uneven twisting which at this length makes for a lot of problems when you have interference (such as a power cable, overhead fluorescent lights, A/C or powered speakers).

Couldn't use them (50ft along some minor interference points, 1 powered speaker, power cables, 1 800MHz 10mW RF transmitter (a RF remote control)). They feel shoddy and the plastic can be squeezed easily and the twisted pairs can be pushed flat with fingers, the molding around the connectors is badly finished and the internal wiring itself cracks (you can feel them cracking) when run around even an obtuse corner in a purpose-built cable gutter, I doubt it's copper, the wires themselves look like aluminum (they are a silver color).

title: Awesome!

The T.V. is a 55" smart LG LCD. I disconnected the old speakers, hooked up the Energy 5.1 Take Classic Home Theater System to the amp, (the speakers do not come with an amp) ran the surround test and inserted the movie Independence Day. At a conservative volume, I watched and felt the spaceship move over the moon. The bass was phenomenal! I skipped to the Empire State building blowing up and I was there. I almost felt the rush of air emitting from the explosion! The next movie was Jurassic Park and when the boy is watching the ripples in the water glass when the T-Rex was approaching, I was watching the same thing in my coffee cup. The mid-range is exceptional co-existing amicably with the tweeters. Even at low volume, the details are present and when there is silence in the movie, there is silence. Soundtracks are slightly muted as to not interfere with the dialog. Setting the amp to 7.1 dramatically increased the rear speakers but the "wow" factor belongs to the 8" sub. Forget the high-end systems such as Bose. Believe me; these speakers are worth the price and then some. If there were a 6 star rating, I would have selected it. Fast delivery too.

title: Good but. . .
text:
I looked at a lot of televisions at a bunch of stores, did some research, looked at prices and ended up purchasing the Sharp LC-60C7500U. The picture is very good but suffers from a problem I noticed in a lot of large wide-screen TVs: The details in faces tend to be sort of wiped out and featureless, like everyone is wearing pancake stage makeup. This is highly dependent on the source, too, and doesn't always happen. But it happens enough to be mildly annoying. I find that the 240 Hz (augmented to 480 Hz by Aquamotion) accentuates this flaw, so for most viewing, I turn all this stuff off. I was watching a nature show about leopards and the spots were kind of swimming around as the Aquamotion tried to blend the pixels to hide any jitter. I also usually turn off automatic contrast control. It makes the screen get noticeably brighter or darker, depending on the scene, and is, again, mildly annoying. However, for watching sports or other fast moving sources, these features work great.

The sound is very good, with enough bass that I usually don't feel the need to run audio through my stereo system. It doesn't get very loud, but loud enough for viewing. Since it is advertised as 35W, it seems they could have put some speaker terminals in the back to allow secondary speakers, but apparently no one does this.

As mentioned before, I find myself adjusting picture quality a lot. This will surely taper off as I get more used to what settings I like, but for the time being I have to keep the TV remote close by. One thing I am finding that has to be adjusted is zoom and stretch. You can pick which format you want, but you can't simply turn it off and rely on whatever the source provides. So when I switch from TV to DVD, I have to fiddle with the controls to make the screen look right, depending on the movie. "The King's Speech" requires one setting, while "Casablanca" requires another.

Overall, I'm pleased with my purchase. In retrospect, I could have purchased a 55" and been just as happy, but I'm not bringing this one back.

UPDATE 1/16/14
I have gotten used to the controls now and find that I am happy leaving the Aquamotion 480 on all the time. I don't know if I just got used to it or what but I don't notice any pancake makeup look any more. I still leave the auto contrast off.

There have been a few times when I turn the TV on and the picture is fuzzy. I turn it off for a few seconds and turn it back on and it's fine. Overall, the picture is really crisp.

Another minor annoyance is that the audio and video get a second or so out of sync sometimes. This is at least, or maybe entirely, the fault of the cable DVR, because hitting pause and then play fixes it. I just don't remember ever seeing this on my old TV. And actually I watch enough sports, where the camera is pointing to the field, that I rarely see this.

UPDATE 2/14/14
I had only watched a few movies on this TV until recently and there is a major bug. As I mentioned earlier, in DVD mode the stretch feature cannot be turned off. You have the choice of Stretch (picture is bigger than screen), Widescreen (left and right of picture go past the borders of the screen), Black Bars (squeezing picture between two vertical black bars on left and right), and Smart Stretch, which I don't understand. I had watched a movie in Smart Stretch and it appeared to be OK. Then I recently watched "Doubt" and found that Smart Stretch distorted the picture so that all the people were squashed vertically. I put it on Stretch and that cured the squashing but extended the picture beyond the borders of the screen. Neither of these is acceptable. I sent a request for technical support to Sharp and here is the response I got:

"Thank you for contacting Sharp Electronics Corporation.
There is not a way to turn off the view mode the view mode ensures that the TV and the device can be changed to be in sync."

In other words, we don't care and we're not going to do anything about it. You'll have to diddle with the controls every time you want to watch a movie.

I assume that all Sharp TVs have this bug so I would caution anyone to check this before buying any Sharp TV. Had I bought this TV to watch movies I would have returned it.

UPDATE 6/8/14
I was constantly annoyed by the color in movies. I could tell it had something to do with black level, but no amount of adjusting could fix it. Then one night as I was messing with it again, I ran across a menu that said, "black level high" or black level low". It was set on low. I switched it to high and voila! Problem solved. I have no idea why Sharp would set something like that as a default, but then I don't understand why there is no setting for watching movies without stretch, either. That's still a major annoyance and would prevent me from buying this TV if I had it to do over again.

title: Solid DLNA renderer implementation
text:
This review primarily speaks to the DLNA renderer and internet streaming features of AVR 2650. Before I dive into this I want to say that I am completely satisfied with this receiver and (other than some of the minor internet streaming issues I describe below) my only complaints are that (1) unlike my old H/K AVR 125, it does not allow you to associate different speaker configurations with different sources (I prefer to listen to music in 4.1 configuration, with center speaker off, because I am generally moving around while listening to music and prefer for it to be non-directional) and (2) the remote is NOT pretty and does not make it particularly easy to scroll through available sources.

Now let's address DLNA and internet streaming:

My main goal was to stream the output of my computer (PC) soundcard (using a DLNA server like Jamcast) or the output of foobar2000 player installed on my computer (using foo_upnp plugin) to the Hi-Fi system in the living room one floor down (wired connection using powerline adapters). I prefer to manage my playlists at the computer and just stream them to the living room HiFi system. Plus this allows me to use the DSP chain on my computer (e.g. cross-fading, replaygain volume adjustment, etc) and serve the final digital stream to my HiFi system. This is called a "DLNA infinite stream" because it's not streaming discrete files. I don't care about navigating the individual songs stored on my PC or NAS using the device's interface (I can imagine it would be a pain to navigate a large music library using ANY device without a keyboard).

My secondary goal was to use this device to play internet radio streams without involving a PC.

My experience with AVR 2650:

DLNA streaming: I have tried dedicated network players made for this purpose and adorned with various bells and whistles (Cambridge Audio NP30; Grace Digital Wi-Fi / Ethernet Radio Tuner GDI-IRDT200). Neither of them worked for DLNA infinite streams. I was pleasantly surprised to find that AVR 2650's DLNA Renderer implementation was SOLID, and it played LPCM infinite streams without a problem (both virtual soundcard mode of Jamcast, and Playback Stream Capture feature of Foobar2000 + foo_upnp)! Although it lacks the impressive listing of accepted formats of the dedicated players mentioned above (which are anyway half-truths at best as evidenced by the above issues), AVR 2650 streams LPCM and MP3 reliably. That is all I really need, since all the decoding of all audio formats happens on my computer, and the final stream is then sent to the receiver as LPCM.

Internet radio: the receiver does NOT shine in this department, but it does implement basic internet radio functionality. The online interface for managing your "preset" internet radio stations is not nearly as clean and easy to use as the one for Squeezebox Touch. Of course selecting which stream to play is also not as simple as the Squeezebox Touch. AVR 2650 won't play non-MP3 radio streams, so AAC and AAC+ and others are not supported. It does not show the title of the currently playing track, only the name of the station. But you should not really expect your receiver to be an all-around internet music player. The internet radio implementation will always depend on the commitment of the manufacturer to maintain and improve the internet portal for managing your presets. And that commitment will always be tenuous at best. Unless we come up with some kind of open XML standard for managing internet radio presets, thereby relieving the manufacturer of this responsibility.

So the bottom line is for internet radio you should just get the Logitech Squeezebox Touch.

title: Now we're really having fun
text:
TL;DR: Yahoo! BUY! Otherwise, let me entertain you...

Last year, I fenced my lot in, a 6 foot high fence you absolutely cannot see though. Our driveway goes between the fence and a small outbuilding onto the alleyway behind our home, resulting in a completely blind entry into the alleyway for us. To compound the problem, I have a large pickup and have to back out -- I really have *no* idea what's going on in the alleyway. And of course, there are some jokers who randomly fog up and down the alley at ludicrous speed. The problem was begging for a solution before my truck, which I really like, took a serious hit.

I already had a backup camera and 2-input monitor (one input unused) in the truck, so here's what I did:

I mounted two cameras on the side of the outbuilding, parallel to the alleyway, one pointed each way. I fed this to an inexpensive video combiner also purchased here at Amazon (VideoSecu Office Home Security Camera CCTV Color Surveillance Video Quad Splitter Processor 1EY), which I set to dual split mode, which forwards two cameras in one frame, with the two images stretched vertically, side by side. Which looks decent in a widescreen monitor, btw, although it is admittedly somewhat distorted. This, in turn, I fed into the product here, the 2.4 GHz transmitter, mounted at about head height on the inside of a wood wall immediately adjacent to my exit from the driveway.

Then I mounted the receiver in the truck, high up in the rear seat area of the cabin. I fed the received video to the previously unused input on the monitor, made sure power was coming from a circuit that was hot only when the ignition was on, and that completed the install.

Now, whenever I am near the outbuilding, which essentially means any time I am backing up even over by the house where I park, I can get a clear view up and down the alleyway before even sticking an inch of the truck body out there. My risk of being t-boned went from a dice roll to zero in one move. Just imagine the difference in stress. Did I mention I really like my truck?

So... we also have another vehicle, a car, that the lady of the house generally drives. I thought it would be good if she could see what was going on as well, although she drives out vehicle-front first and can see a little bit anyway. So I got her a monitor like mine, bought a second 2.4 GHz rx/tx unit from this page, and installed the receiver in her car. I was taking a chance that there was only one channel involved (so that the 2nd receiver would also hear the first transmitter), but that in fact turned out to be the case.

So now she can see what's going on as well, and again, our risk is lowered. I stored the 2nd transmitter as a backup. Then I bought a third set so as to have an RF monitor in the shed if and when I mess with things in there, and again, stashed the transmitter as a spare for the spare, as it were.

The only thing that didn't go perfectly is that in her car, I was sort of forced to mount the receiver low and under the dash as she really didn't want wires all over the place, nor was I prepared to do surgery on the headliner. This puts a lot of metal between the receiver and the desired signal, and indeed, the signal is not very strong in her car. I'm considering doing something more like getting a little mini-coax and hacking the antenna up by the windshield. I'll add to this part of the review if I get around to that.

Let me clear, though: I consider this problem not in any way a fault in the rx/tx units, just a problem I caused by mounting the receiver low and near all that metal.

The wiring... meh. I would have liked to see a little heavier wiring for the power supply. Those wires are thin! And speaking of the power supply, what I used in the outbuilding was a 2.5 ampere linear power supply that feeds the cameras, the switch/combiner, the in-shed receiver, and the transmitter. I'm a ham radio operator (amateur radio) and I really can't tolerate all the RF noise the typical el-cheapo switching power supplies, such as the ones that came with the security cameras, generate in the normal course of operation. So the 2.5 amp linear supply takes care of everything with ease, and there's no RF noise at all.

I have not observed excessive heat at any of the three receivers, or at the transmitter. A little warm, that's all. Reception (and therefore transmission) is extremely stable and reliable, and quality of the signal is perfect when within a reasonable range for my application, which is 20 feet or so in any direction. I use an old CRT video monitor along with the receiver in the shed; I rarely have occasion to turn it on, though.

Word to the wise: Note that because the units do get a little warm, we know they're consuming a few watts of power, even without measuring. You really want to connect them only to +13.8 VDC circuits that are active only when your vehicle is running and the alternator is producing charging current. Otherwise, you run the risk of going to start your engine after a few days break and... nothing. Dead battery. I hate it when that happens. I don't think you'd like it either.

Anyway, these are great, flexible products that can really kick up the safety for you and yours, and I highly recommend thinking about what more you can accomplish outside of just making a backup camera wireless, especially since it's pretty easy to run a video cable for that application. That switcher combiner I mentioned can do a quad combine with four cameras, and you can feed that to the transmitter. Four cameras, all displayed at once via one monitor input. Give you any ideas?

Cheers!

title: Never thought I'd mouse with my right hand again
text:
It's been over 10 years since I had to start mousing with my left hand. Any time I tried using my right for longer than a few hours, then pain in my wrist and forearm would set right back in like it never left and stay for hours and sometimes days. Now with the same trouble starting in on my left wrist, I was genuinely concerned. Initially, I was looking for a trackball and in the process saw a recommendation for Evoluent. I'd never seen or heard of a vertical mouse before but the concept seemed brilliant. What better way to get the pressure off of the flat of the wrist than to rotate the wrist?

Because my left has been giving me so much trouble, I decided to go with the right-handed model and take a chance that it wouldn't fire up the pain again on that side. I can honestly say that I've been using it now for weeks with NO PROBLEMS!

Pros:
1) I can mouse without pain!
2) Fits my hand perfectly - make sure to pay close attention to the sizing chart.
3) Stylish, if VERY different.
4) The macros are SWEET and can be a real time saver.

Cons:
1) It’s a bit too hard to grip for my taste. When mousing, if you get to the edge of your pad, you want to pick up the mouse and move it over. The instructions tell you to tilt it and drag it, but I found that to be annoying. You can't exactly grab it and lift it up as it will slip from your grip if you don't apply finger pressure (which triggers clicks you don't want). I solved the problem with a bit of bat grip tape. I put a small strip along the thumb rest and another strip along the palm side. I can now grip it easily between my thumb and palm and move it or lift it as I choose.
2) If you can't handle people poking fun at how it looks, get something more traditional and suffer the consequences. The most common comment is "it looks like a pencil sharpener". Don't care though - it's WORTH it.

Can't express how happy I am to have found this product. I highly recommend it to anyone suffering from wrist or forearm pain from traditional mousing.

title: Perfect bluetooth headphone starter set.
text:
The Soundbot SB270 bluetooth headphones are my second set of bluetooth headphones.
The first pair of bluetooth headphones I purchased were the LG 730 Tone+ headphones, which are excellent.
[[ASIN:B009A5204K LG Electronics Tone+ HBS-730 Bluetooth Headset - Retail Packaging - Black]]
However I would actually recommend these SB270's first for anyone looking for their first set of bluetooth headphones, for a few reasons.

Primarily, price. With a promotional code, I was able to get these headphones for just a little over $20. The LG's cost around $50. For the price of one LG headset I was able to get two of the SB270's, one for me, one for my wife. Mine are the black and red, my wife's are the silver and white. Both function excellently.

Secondly they have almost all the same functions and features of the LG's, with a few extras, such as the capability to plug them in with a 1.5mm jack, and multi-touch controls.

How do they compair to the more expensive LG 730's?
Sound and volume wise, they're comparable. I think the SB270's may be a bit louder than the LG's actually, but that would make sense since the LG's are earbuds, and the 270's are on-ear headphones.
The 270's have very nice sound, comparable to mid-range wired headphones. I have a nice pair of wired headphones that wrap around the neck, paid about $30 for them, chose them specifically because they had a good range of sound output, and were sturdy so they could handle movement, etc. The SB270's sound like that wired set, which is good.

The LG's, sound better. The LG headphones have very crisp, clear sound, the highs, lows, and midrange are all nice and clear and don't blur together.
The SB 270's sound isn't quite as crisp and clear as the LG 730's, BUT, it's not so far off that I would call it a deal breaker. The 270's still have great sound, they seem more geared toward mid-range though. The bass isn't bumping, but it's not absent either. Headphones are never really known for having great bass anyway, considering these are at least comparable to a good priced wired set, I'm satisfied and wouldn't complain about it at all.
Soundwise I'd say the SB270's are comparable to a mid to high range pair of wired headphones, while the LG730's are firmly in the high quality range.

Design:
These are two completely differently designed pairs of headphones. The LG's are earbud style with a base around your neck, the SB270's are padded over the head on-ear style headphones. Both are comfortable and lightweight and the freedom to move around without chords is amazing.
The LG 730's have a few more bells and whistles, but both headsets have the same basic functions. When playing music you can pause or start a track, fast forward, rewind, skip tracks, change volume, etc. and both headsets can do phone calls with built in microphones.
The LG headphones do provide voice prompts to tell you when the headset is on and what the battery level is though (Low, Medium, High). The 270's do not, you don't really have any easy way to judge the battery level while using them. But considering they have a 12 hour battery life, it hardly matters unless you intend to wear them for an entire day.
The SB270's have touch controls though, which are interesting. Once you get used to them they're pretty quick and easy to use, and you can do all the normal functions, without even needing to touch a button, which is pretty cool.
The LG 730's have an actual on/off switch, which I like. You know for sure whether or not the headset is on or off because you physically slide the switch into position. With the SB270's you have a multifunction button, which must be pressed or held down to turn on/off the set or go into pairing mode. I know this is common with a lot of bluetooth devices these days, but the certainty of the switch is a plus for me.
The SB270's have a plug so you can use them with traditional wired devices. This is a HUGE plus. I bought some bluetooth adaptors for my computers, and I do prefer the mobility and freedom wireless bluetooth provides, but having the ability to plug the headphones into older devices that aren't capable of connecting wirelessly is a major advantage that the LG's don't have. If you wanted to use those with an older device you would have to buy a plug in bluetooth converter, which can be expensive and bulky in itself and kind of defeats the purpose of a mobile portable device.
Being on-ear headphones the only issue I've found with wearing the 270's so far is that your ears will get warm. Great in Winter, not so much in hot weather, this is the only factor I've found so far that would make me want to limit how long I wear them. Otherwise the padding is soft and comfy, they're lightweight and adjust easily so I've had no problem with them. They also won't pop or slide out of your ear like an earbud might with enough movement.

The reason I got these headphones in the first place was because my LG headphones actually started to die. I've had them for several months now, during which I used them quite a bit, I wear them and listen to music almost constantly at work, which means my headphones are working almost 10 hours a day. The LG's never died or ran out of power once during that time, but the left headphone started to go out. It still works, but only at about a third of the power it used to, and with no bass at all.
I was disappointed considering I spent so much on those headphones, and then one of the earbuds just went out like that. Granted it gave me a lot of use and sounded and worked great the entire time, but I expected more reliability and durability than that.
When it came time to look for a replacement I did my research and the SB270's quickly became the forerunner.
Ultimately, the sound isn't quite as crisp as the LG's, but it's not so far off that I really care or notice all that often. Considering the price, and extra options these headphones have that the LG's dont, and the fact I really never used the voice notifications on the LG's anyway, I would definitely recommend these headphones for anyone looking for a starter set.

Save your money, buy a pair of these, try them out, if you really like it and decide you want something with better quality sound, then save up and buy yourself a real quality pair of bluetooth headphones with some serious bass and high range, but be prepared to go to $100 or more. The LG 730's are nice, but not so much nicer than these that they justify the extra $30 I think.
I listen to music all the time, and I do try to get the best sound and value I can for my dollar and right now, I think these are it.

Update - I went out for a walk today and it started raining, when I saw that it was starting to drizzle I wondered whether or not the rain drops would mess with the multi-touch panel on the headphones. It didn't. The headphones held up just fine, and the rain didn't mess with the multi-touch panel at all, no unwanted pauses or skips. So, while I wouldn't recommend using electronics like these in the rain, rest assured if you do get caught in a sudden downpour, the headphones won't mess up or have any issues.

title: Contant Traveler's Friend
text:
Well, I'm not a "road warrior" but I am on my 9th flight so far this month (as of Oct 20, 2013) and that's not too unusual. I don't use these headphones for anything other than my "travel docket" so I don't know about their performance for a workout, but I can tell you without hesitation, that on a plane (prop or jet turbine) or in an airport they are excellent headphones.

Sound quality on the units from my MacBook Pro is as good as any other headphones. I get, slightly decreased bass response, but overall enjoyable and they are plenty LOUD. In fact, I had to crank my MBP system volume down to 2 (2 clicks above mute) or else the headphones were too loud. Even without the ANR engaged, they help to isolate a lot of the environmental noise on the ground.

Now, in flight they are amazing. Granted, I've never owned a $300 paid of ANC headphones but these do an amazing job of blocking out the engine noise and making my flights (even on that last prop plane jump from CLT to CHA) a lot more enjoyable. When in flight, I can keep my iPhone volume output on about 4-5 (out of 10, so let's say "the middle") and hear the music clearly. Two months ago with my over-the-ear $160 headphones I had to crank the volume almost all the way up and still had trouble hearing things.

As for the headphones durability, I haven't had any of the problems other users have experienced, but I do really take good care of my stuff (i.e. I "baby" my gear) but I haven't had to change the battery since I bought the headphones, so they've so far performed on over 20+ hours of flight time from one battery. And that's a good deal, to me :-)

All in all, this is the best $99 investment I've made in my "travel gear" and I am thrilled that I did!

title: Does exactly what it says on the tin!
text:
There's really very little to complain about with this Western Digital My Passport 2TB. It plugged straight into my 2009 iMac (and worked at USB 2.0 speeds) and worked just as well on a Sony Vaio Z series at USB 3.0 speeds (after formatting to NTFS).

There are a couple of things that let the drive down, and they are as follows:

1.) It's really, really plastic. The silvery color is going to look pretty bad (if you're an aesthetics-type person), so be sure to be gentle with it or pick up a third-party case for traveling around.

2.) It's quite a bit bulkier than the standard 2.5" notebook drive + enclosure. This is due to Western Digital using a 15mm drive in here versus the "standard" notebook drive thickness of 9.5mm (or 12.5mm with larger disks). It's not a huge device, but you definitely notice it's "there."

Overall, though, it works quietly, efficiently (it uses Western Digital's "Green" line of disks inside), and I've had absolutely zero problems with it. And for a hard drive which is designed for storage over speed (yes, it's USB 3.0, but it's only a 5400rpm disk), you can't say fairer than that!

4.5 stars out of 5.

title: Excellent Tablet/Phone With Excellent Features - A Very Detailed Review
text:
For months I have been enjoying the P5100 tablet/phone (in the White color). So here is my detailed review on this very special tablet with phone/data/WiFi capabilities. Even with the Tab 3 10.1 available, I find I still love this model because of the PHONE/DATA/3G capabilities as it has been a lifesaver on the road as I use this for a tablet and a phone. *Note that in many ways, this tablet is a better choice than the Tab 3 10.1because of the fact of high ratings and the fact that it has a phone/data for just a few dollars more than the Tab 3 10.1 WiFi only.
At the end of this review, I will give you a checklist that will help you decide whether to purchase this Tab 2 Phone/Tablet or the Tab 3 WiFi Only Tablet that I believe may help you with your decision on whether to purchase this phone/tablet or not...

PROS:

- Biggest Pro - This phone/tablet is UNLOCKED and will accept ANY GSM Sim card. (It is the regular sized Sim not the micro Sim. To fully test it out, I removed the activated Sim from my Tab 2 7.0 (P3100) I decided to upgrade to this device as it is so much larger and just use the P3100 for WiFi and tablet use only. Now I am a big WiFi user (95% to 99%of the time), so I use WiFi in order to save on data. So I rarely need to turn on data (so I have a very data amount each month), but nice to know with this device, I can have data when no WiFi is available when traveling.

- With Archived Adobe Flash that I downloaded and put into Maxthon Browser, I can watch videos on the internet as well as Amazon videos. (Ask me in the comments if you need help with installing Archived Adobe Flash).

- Printing on the Tab 2 - I installed Cloud Print from Playstore (free) and print anything I want using the Tab 2!
- Screen clarity/crispness/detailing: For me, this tablet renders SUPERB clarity, crispness and great details on every screen, whether on the internet or in a app or program! Colors are very VIVID!

- Sound Quality - This tablet has Stereo speakers (located on each side of the tablet). I listen many times to music or videos using the on board speakers and they are adequate. However, I purchased a pair of Sony Headphones for just $15 here on Amazon and now listen to music with them and the sound is awesome! (There were no headset to use the phone inside the box, however, I purchased a Samsung phone headset on Amazon for about $10 and they work great for phone calls.
- Phone Call Quality - Whether using a headset or speakerphone, the call quality is PERFECT. Have never had any static, the sound is plenty loud and never had any dropped calls!

- Music Quality - SUPERB! This tablet comes with a stock music player, which does a fine job of making playlists, finding songs, the usual things you use a player for. However, if you are wanting to SYNC your music from MS Windows Media Player (an easy way), then you will need to get the app from Playstore called Winamp. It is great and so easy to use. You may want to check it out.

- Video Quality - Wonderful!!!! he stock video player is just so so...Now I am a techie that is kind of picky so I use the app called QQ Player from Playstore--this plays every type of movie type I tried(even old old ones that would not play in the stock player)...Now if you install the archived flash, and do it correctly, you can view internet videos (except Amazon Videos). I recommend JUST Maxthon browser because it plays every video I tried so far where other browsers did not do so well...

- Reading/Creating/Editing Word, Excel, Text Files and much more on this tablet: This comes with a OK app for reading Office documents, however, I prefer Kingsoft Office which is a free app from Playstore. It is the best I have ever tried and I am very picky about so called Office programs. It is very compatible with MS Office as it reads, edits and creates Office files and reads PDF files, and it has more features of any other Android Office program that I tried. This app is a MUST have for tablet owners in my opinion.

- Speed (Overall) - In apps, programs and on the internet and watching videos, I give this tablet a high mark in my estimation! I give it 4.98 out of 5 stars as it is fast and works like a champ.
- Overall Score (even with minor cons below) I give this a 4.98 out of 5.

CONS
1) The MAJOR CON with this tablet (and most international devices) is that there is NO US WARRANTY. For the WiFi Only version of this tablet (without phone and data part), there is a US Warranty, so keep this in mind before you purchase.
For me, I purchased this knowing about the No Warranty. Yet, I have found in my experience, that if a device is going to fail or misbehave, it will usually do it within the first 30 days. (For me, it is very rare for any device to fail me after 30 days. Being a techie though, I just keep a device one year (sometimes two years)and then I get the newest device with newest OS.

2) No Jelly Bean (yet), but I read where the Tab 2 with 3g will soon be getting Jelly Bean OTA (directly on the device).

---Checklist That Will Help You to Decide Whether or Not to Purchase This Device---

If you can answer YES to FOUR or more to below statements, then highly consider this device:

- You HAVE TO Data for places where there are NO WIFI HOTSPOTS - this is so important.
- You are looking for a device with a STANDARD SIZED Sim card, not a micro one.
- You need an ALL IN ONE DEVICE: Tablet/Phone/3G data for carrying ONE device instead of two or more.
- You need a 10.1 screen that is crisp, bright and colors vivid, this will may an excellent choice.
- You can accept the fact that the OS is 4.03, Ice Cream Sandwich (however, I read where 4.2 Jelly Bean will be available and the roll-out is starting soon for this device via OTA (directly on the device).
- You like the fact that this tablet with phone and data is available new for 410 dollars (white version) or 385 dollars for the black version (this is just a little more than the Tab 3 10.1 costs for a WiFi only).
- You like the fact that this device has very high ratings at 4.4 stars vs the Tab 3 10.1 at UNDER 4 stars.
- You can live with the fact that the Tab 2 line accepts a propriety (wider) USB charger (which are available on Amazon and other stores) rather than a standard micro USB port for the Tab3 line (however, the Tab 3 line's port requires a 2AMP charger, not the old type 1amp charger).

Since I am a techie person, if you are to have any questions about this tablet, please ask me in the comments below and I will answer.

title: Bargain Priced Fully Featured WINNER
text:
Make no mistake, Lenovo produces a solid fully featured highly-ranked laptop for... peanuts.
The G500, with an Intel Core i3-Ivy Bridge dual-core 2.5 GHz processor, 500GB HD, 2 - 3.0 USB ports, 4 GB of DDR3 RAM, with Win 8 as native OS, and more, the G500 matches anything in the 2013 game up to twice the cost. I did kick my RAM up to 8GB since I use Adobe Photoshop CS6.
This G500 will get 'r done! You can pay a bit more for the i5 processor model but you will not gain much/enough.
I have had computers since 1990 and Windows from 3.1 (with a few Big Mac's along the way) and I am here to promise that if you give Win 8 64-bit a chance, you WILL fall in love with it. I did. No manual. Look Ma, no hands. Just toured and learned. Quickly. I predict that if you liked Win 7 you will really take to 8. Really. And moving into Win 8 and setting my network, adding devices, etc., it was a SNAP! Even more effortless than in Win 7.
Lenovo support is excellent, both online and through telephone contact.
The only drawback, for some, might be the weight, generally slightly heavier compared to most lappers. This is due to overbuild and should NOT be considered a minus.
The design is exceptional, contemporary, and stylish sort of... in a Chinese way. Lenovo has been around for many years (began with IBM) and you'd be surprised at how much Lenovo there is today in other brand computers.
I could go on and on heaping praise on Lenovo and this G500 but I will bet that IF you do your research and compare, you'll grab this or another Lenovo model pronto.
Now go do your homework.
And to the nitpickers, yes, this is a late 2012 model.
Not to worry.
UPDATE 11.11.2013
Still liking this lapper VERY MUCH. And slowly getting used to the Win 8 first big service pack I (or 8.1)installed a few weeks ago. Norton AV 360 had a brief conflict but they provided a patch that cured a short-lived evil; no other problems so far and none anticipated. Everyone I talk to about Lenovo and their product line, from rank beginner to experienced expert, agrees that Lenovo's recent number two ranking in the cluttered world of laptops IS well deserved.
A shout out to all you past, present, and future vets; THANKS for your service.
UPDATE 11.30.2013
This economy laptop continues to please, amaze, and run fast and smooth just like the big expensive guys.
Win 8.1 still a winner in my experience.
I pinch myself when I look back in disbelief and realize I have no more than 300 dollars invested. Like the old Timex, my G500 keeps on ticking and also like the Timex, if it fails, I can toss it.
Happy Holidays.
UPDATE 7.20.2014
Still providing an excellent experience. Reliable. Durable. Liking Win 8.2 much more over time; this OS is turning out to be quite stable.
