title: Why You Need Skinomi
text:
I love Skinomi screen protectors and have used them on my cameras and cell phones for several years. I know how to apply them successfully on small screens, so I thought I would take a chance on my new Kindle Fire HDX 8.9 inch tablet. I bought two, in case I screwed something up on the first application (which I did), but I learned from my mistakes and the second went on perfectly. Here is what I learned:

1) Work next to a bright light that will fully illuminate the surface of the device. Dust is the enemy, not air bubbles. Air bubbles can be removed and the small ones disappear as the film dries, but dust is forever. Therefore, it is IMPERATIVE that no dust be on either the device screen or adhesive side of the screen protector. I cleaned the screen with the supplied cloth and spray water/soap solution, then used a clean synthetic camera lens brush to remove every speck of dust.

2) Thoroughly mist the exposed screen with the solution, mist your hands and fingertips, remove the opaque back from the screen protector, mist thoroughly and QUICKLY, then immediately turn the screen protector sticky side down, so no dust will attach to it. Line it up with the screen as best you can and lay it down. The water/soap solution will allow you to slide the protector around the screen until it is aligned correctly. Then use a credit card to push bubbles to the edge of the screen protector for removal. Small air bubbles will disappear as the protector dries, but trapped dust will not, which is why it is so important to make sure there is no dust on either the screen surface or the adhesive side of the protector.

3) Let it dry. The screen protector will be set in a few hours and all the bubbles will disappear in a day or two. Any remaining bubbles are trapped dust, which takes us back to steps one and two. The sooner you can get a misted screen protector onto a dust free, misted device screen, the more successful you will be.

Skinomi does not reduce touch screen sensitivity at all and feels smooth to my fingertips. It does not distort vision or viewing quality. It is TOUGH and has averted many disasters for me with dropped phones, etc. It adds tensile strength and prevents the scratches that allow gorilla glass to weaken, crack and shatter. BTW, dust scratches screens, as it is composed of the same silica that glass is made from. Metals are softer than silica, so gorilla glass protects from keys, knives, screwdrivers, etc., but it is no match for the microscopic scratches made by dust, and THAT is why you need a screen protector. A scratch free screen will remain strong and crack resistant, especially if the protector is Skinomi, with its Lifetime Guarantee.

title: Decent Cloud Camera
text:
Having owned quite a few DLink Cameras over the years here are some pointers before you start installation:
1) Create a MyDlink.com account.
2) Download the setup.exe for your respective camera from the support link on that site. This is only a utility to configure the camera, and will not install any items on your pc.
4) Connect the camera to a physical network cable, not wireless, at this point. Run the setup.exe

Many network devices have an admin webpage, if you can locate the DHCP address, however I advise not to do this. Running the setup.exe will save you some headaches and additional steps (including linking the camera to mydlink for cloud use). The setup.exe will handle:
-scanning the network for your camera
-setting an admin password
-setting up your device to use a wireless network (it will scan for your Wireless Name and you can specify the password)
-link this camera to your mydlink cloud account so you can use a mobile phone (android, iphone), or remote PC, to browse this remotely.

One of the nice features for mydlink is it works without the necessity to open any additional ports on your network or require a running PC connected to the device. I find the dlink app through my wife's iphone ideal for the occasional check in when we are on vacation or out of town. When we show friends/family they are impressed enough to purchase similar dlink models. I currently have 8 cameras running on my mydlink account.

Another common issue I see often are the cameras have a focusing lens on the camera that may not be intuitive or noticed during installation. This focusing ring can be adjusted by turning it clockwise or counter clockwise. Once the camera is configured, using the steps above, I would adjust this where needed. I have found quite a few skewed one way or the other that made the picture out of the box unacceptable but became clear once adjusted.

There are other cameras on the market, including HD versions, but I have found these cameras a good value. The mydlink feature is one of the reasons I select D-link over the other models. Please keep in mind that the max resolution is 640*480. Good for monitoring areas for activity or changes, but not enough to read text (ie license plates) or specific details that would require an increased resolution (ie facial features from a distance).

title: A little disappointing
text:
I purchased this item recently, on the basis of a review in MONITORING TIMES, September 2012. Some of the Amazon reviews seemed fantastic, but I would have considered giving this one a One-Star rating, except for the low price and some redeeming qualities (See below):
FIRST, the good News: The radio is small and light, truly shirt pocket sized. It appears to be reasonably well made, considering the price class. It picks up local stations well. I've been using it to listen to an FM station that I listen to nearly all the time; there are some other high powered FM stations much closer to me, on frequencies as close as 1.4 MHz. away and they do not interfere, which I can't say for some other inexpensive radios!
NOW, the bad news: Tuning is stiff, with a little backlash; and backlash only gets worse with time, it will increase the more the tuning knob is used, but this probably won't be a problem in my case as I listen mainly to just one FM station. I have tried it on the AM broadcast brand, and it picks up several from Anchorage, about 60 air miles away, but the ones running lower power (5 KW.) don't come in nearly as well as the ones running higher power (50 KW.) As for short wave, forget it; I realize that propagation conditions have been poor to mediocre lately, and a lot of SW BC stations have gone off the air; it's kind of a dying medium, but some of us old diehards still like to listen to what we can find still on the air. With the built-in antenna, I couldn't pick up anything on SW on any of the bands, trying it every day for several days. (I was using another receiver to find the strongest stations on the air and make sure they were on the air.) Using a clip lead connected to a 10' length of wire inside a wood frame house to give better reception enabled me to JUST pick up a few of the strongest SW stations, but not well enough to comfortably listen to them.
IN SHORT: Just about worth the $20, if your expectations aren't too high. Either the one I got is on the low side, performance-wise, or else the folks who gave it Five-Star reviews didn't have very high expectations. I made the mistake of throwing away the original packing materials, otherwise I'd have returned it for a refund, but it looks like I'm stuck with it ; I'll use it when I take my dog for walks, using a pair of earphones (not supplied, but then I didn't expect them to be, at the price).

title: Disappointment -- get the Logitech C920 instead!
text:
I wrote this review for the Logitech C920, but since it compares it head to head with the Creative Live! Socialize HD camera I owned before it, I'm including the review here too:

I owned this Creative camera for about 6 months until I was lucky enough to upgrade from Windows to Mac, which this camera didn't support. Because the Creative camera had other issues (a weird circular spot that appeared in all photos and videos, likely a hardware/sensor/lens issue), I was able to return it and was on the hunt again for a better camera, this time preferably with Mac support.

I then turned to Logitech and I ended up in countless of angry threads online about the fact that the Logitech C920 didn't have support for Mac, something its predecessor the C910 had. Well, I ended up getting the C920 anyway because I didn't like the idea of buying the previous generation, and Logitech's own support reps on their site even mentioned in a thread that the support in C910 wasn't that great anyway. And everyone seemed to rave about the picture quality of the C9x0 in general, so I thought I'd take a chance.

And boy did the C920 exceed my expectations! Yes, there is no Mac support in the sense that there is no way to modify any settings like white balance, brightness, saturation, gamma, etc.... but the reality is, you don't need it. This camera adjust perfectly to *any* lighting condition! I've used this in daylight, during nighttime with an incandescent energy light bulb, and even in the darkness with the cold light from my big 24" monitor lighting up my face. Regardless of light source, the camera just adjusts perfectly and generates skin tones that don't want me to cover up my face in late night meetings with my colleagues overseas. The Creative camera made my face completely blue unless I had several lamps on in the room to compensate for the harsh monitor light.

Another thing that the Logitech does far better than the Creative is auto-focus: on my Creative camera, the auto-focus seemed to live a life of its own, and it often got stuck near-sighted. The trick then was to put a piece of paper in front of it and then suddenly remove it, (hopefully) causing the camera to re-focus. It worked about half of the times. The Logitech camera, in comparison, gets the autofocus right every single time, and focuses more quickly too.

So, although you can't modify any settings if you're on a Mac (no problem if you're running Windows), I can still highly recommend the Logitech C920 camera as it adjusts perfectly, and generally has stunning image quality. I do *not* recommend the Creative camera -- stay away from it!

title: Appealing effects, but has problems
text:
I used the Darbee for about 10 days, and after being initially skeptical, I was impressed with the image enhancement abilities of the device. That said, I found that it had three problem areas:

1. It would not process 3D signals reliably. The symptom was that it would lose lock and blank the image momentarily, repeating every 3 to 5 seconds, on some source material. FYI, the 3D format was "checkerboard", which may now be obsolete, but its the only format that works on my "3D-ready" DLP.

2. On some source material, there were repetitive audio dropouts, about 1 or 2 per second.

3. On initial power up and handshake to the TV, the result was virtually always a "green screen", sometimes a "magenta screen".

The third problem had a work-around: switching the HDMI input to re-sync, but that was an annoyance. The first two problems were deal-breakers, and the Darbee was returned for a refund. I think all three issues are HDMI sync related, rather than signal processing related. But since HDMI is the only way in & out of the device, Darbee needs to make it work with any HDMI devices, which may be easier said than done. I don't know if my experience is common to other users, but I'm disappointed to have to return it. Maybe when I get a newer TV, I might try getting another one.

text:
Well, there are the obvious things that are good about this cable:

What I didn't expect was that it would save me from my own stupidity. One day, I set my laptop on top of a small basket, since it was convenient. Next thing, cat walks by, brushes against it, and BAM - over goes the laptop, landing squarely on the headphone jack in an almost Olympian effort to bust something inside my computer.
I walk over, expecting disaster - instead, the cord has snapped cleanly, with about 3mm of it sticking out the side of my computer.

They made the minitoslink tip/head with a sort of fat base, slipped the fibre channel up into the connector tip, then formed the connector shroud around the base of the connector tip - perfect design, kudos! It lets the cable be built strong, but not so strong as to break the computer; and yet allows the miniToslink tip to be sturdy enough that you don't end up with it trapped inside the port.

The shroud is of course cracked (I mean, it had a laptop lever itself about it), but was even able to slip the miniToslink tip back onto the bare fibre cable and loosley fit it back onto the shroud - obviously falls apart easily, but is a workable temporary fix until a new one arrives.

title: Don't Expect Your World to Change
text:
The cable does increase transfer rates but by nowhere near the 10x advertised rate. I backed up my PC using the backup software that came pre-installed on the PC. The software makes an image of the PC's drive that, in this case, is about 70 GB compressed. I made two backups to the same Goflex drive on separate days using first the USB 2.0 cable and then the USB 3.0 upgrade. The resulting transfer rate increased from approximately 12MB/s using USB 2.0, to 31MB/s using USB 3.0. That is an improvement of about 2.5x. I've read that this has more to do with the limitations of the rest of the systems than it does with USB 3.0. Examples would include the transfer rates of the disk drives themselves, the software, and even the CPU. Overall, I'm happy; for not much more than twenty bucks I less than halved the time it takes to backup my PC. It's difficult to complain about that.

My only complaint with the cable is the fact that you cannot remove the cable from the adapter. This makes it impossible to fit the portable drive into its carrying case without removing the entire adapter. Then you have to store the adapter separately. If Seagate did that only to save money, boo to them; I would have gladly paid more for a removable cable. So for that, it gets 4 stars. Still, I'd call it a must-have upgrade for any Goflex USB 2.0 drive. I'll be buying one for my other drive.

Kudos to Seagate for the upgradable drive concept. That's a five star concept.

To put the whole thing into perspective: the original IBM PC XT came with a 10 MB drive. That was a mind boggling amount of space. It held all of your software and data. With today's 31 MB/s transfer rate, you could have transferred the entire contents of 3 of those drives in less than 1 second. That is awesome.

title: Not bad
text:
NEW EDIT: I withdraw "not a bad power supply". I blew the pass transistor tonight pumping 3A into a near short for an extended time. Definitely a stress test, but still within the specs! Taking it apart to fix it, I notice three things: 1) There is NO thermal shutdown circuitry at all. No wonder the transistor blew. 2) The thermal transfer between the transistor and heat sink is atrocious. Just a little, quite thick, pad. No paste at all. 3) The main filter capacitor, despite being a decent brand (Nippon Chemi-Con) was near failure, drawing a ton of DC current and getting quite warm. (Dropped to just one star because operating a device within its advertised specifications should never break it.)

Not a bad power supply. The knobs and banana jacks are a bit iffy, but not horrible. Single-turn pots, but easy to adjust voltage by single digits. Current is a bit harder. I didn't have the grounding problem that someone else reported, but I suspect something was shorted in his (the internal assembly is atrocious; I wouldn't be surprised). Nice displays and backlights. Good, solid transformer, pass transistor, heatsink, etc. I wouldn't mind a load switch and a CC set button, but for an $80 power supply, I can overlook it.

Voltages according to my B+K 2712 (±0.1%,5dgt DCV, ±2% DCA): set 00.0, 02.0, 04.0, 08.0, 16.0, actual 0.0037, 2.0067, 4.047, 7.997, 15.972. Short-circuit currents: set 0.00, 0.10, 0.20, 0.40, 0.80, 1.60, 3.00, 3.13 (maximum), actual 0.000, 0.100, 0.201, 0.406, 0.801, 1.602, 2.994, 3.114. Ripple according to my old analog 'scope: 1mVpp at 10V with no load; 7mVpp with 100mA load; 5mVpp with 1A load.

EDIT: The drift on this thing at voltages under about 3V is really bad. If I set it to a voltage in that range and watch it with a voltmeter, the voltage drifts around a few tenths of a volt in either direction constantly! It stays solidly at the set voltage above that, though.

title: So much for being good for gaming....
text: I bought this laptop about a year ago with the intention of having a computer for school and casual gaming.  At first it worked fine, nothing overly impressive over my previous laptop, but it functioned about the same.  Then, about six months ago, it started overheating, and when this laptop overheats, it automatically shuts down, which is really frustrating when you are in the middle of playing a game.  As of this date, the only game I can play for more than 20 minutes without the computer commencing a thermal shutdown is solitaire.... It also overheats when I watch netflix and have more than three tabs open.  To help reduce this, I have the laptop precariously balanced between a stool and the arm of my couch.  I discovered that HP, in their infinite wisdom, did not install a venting fan, and instead thought an auto overheat shutdown would be a much better way of preventing heat damage.  The only ventilation it has is a small vent on the left side and a perforated panel on the bottom-left corner of the laptop.  Bottom line, if you just need a computer for checking e-mail and typing essays, you can buy another laptop for half the price, because that is all this thing is good for....

I noticed the Guest Network on this router is completely missing. It does not appear anywhere and there is no way to configure it. I put in a call to Netgear and they are looking into the situation and I will receive a call from the ticket being elevated to senior technicians. The tech I had took over my computer and agreed it was missing. Well, purchasing a brand new router on the day it was released can have glitches in the firmware but the whole guest network missing? I await the senior tech's call.

5-29-2012 - As of this writing I have not received the call from the senior technician that I was promised. I have also noted that the wireless range on the G network is very restricted next to the WNDR4500 that I still have. I swapped the routers back and forth to confirm this and each time the G network range on the R6300 was far less than on the WNDR4500. I have very reluctantly sent back the R6300 since these two issues make it a deal killer. The WNDR4500 is operating wonderfully and I intend to keep it until another generation of A/B/G/N/AC is released and the firmware issues are settled. I really like Netgear products and I have 5 of their 8 port gigabit switches and I have loved their past routers. They made a misstep in releasing this router before it was ready for the consumer. The firmware is in great need of an upgrade since the wireless guest network is missing and the range of the G network is so abysmal. I will still look at Netgear products but I will not be the "first on the block" with a brand new device again since thorough testing does not seem to be done before release. Long live the WNDR4500!

title: Wish it was a good night lens
text:
This is a wide, fast lens, and in daylight shooting, it excels. However, at night, with stars and dealing with the broad range of brightnesses found in the night sky, it pretty much falls flat on its face. Wide open, where it gathers the most light and offers the most creative dark-regime options, chromatic aberration puts purple rings around bright lights (like bright stars) and anywhere away from the center of the lens, the coma is not just present, but extreme: You'd think you shot a sky full of crescent moons. I shoot auroras and other similar subjects, and this lens is simply unable to render stars correctly until it is stopped down so far that the 1.4 rating becomes completely irrelevant.

Aside from that, in daylight, I found the focus speed to be acceptable on my 6D, and also repeatable -- generally focus is hit first time and the pictures are fine. Color depth is excellent, and you can do the whole collection of usual daytime tricks with a 24mm lens and they come out just fine. It came with a lens hood. It's kind of heavy, lots of glass in this design, but I didn't find that disruptive. I intend to keep it for its daylight performance, but I'm still on the hunt for a good, wide night lens.

Bottom line, if you shoot the night sky... it just doesn't do a good job. If you're a daylight / bright regime shooter, this may be just the lens for you.

title: Pretty but not reliable
text:
Something got lost between the idea and the execution. One would think this is a great tool after reading the major reviews, but it comes up short in just too many areas.

Much of the cost is from the high visibility display that can be seen in brightest sunlight. Garmin got that part of "HUD" correct.

But all it does is tell you when the next turn is. That turn can be 10 miles away. There will be an arrow pointing to either right or left and "10 Miles" on the screen. Nothing to indicate you will be going straight for that length. Not intuitive at all.

There are small arrows at the bottom of the HUD to indicate how many lanes on your road and what lane you should be in to make the turn, regardless of how far is it.
My unit consistently shows an incorrect number of lanes. A 2-lane highway can show 4 lanes and one of my freeway sections with 6 lanes shows 3. Several areas in an area I travel daily are simply incorrect and if someone followed the lane markings and arrow directions would be lost in no time. There seems to be no easy way to pass on a map correction to Garmin. This is a problem with the Garmin app, not the HUD - but still...

Finally, the distances are not accurate. I can be making a turn at an intersection and the HUD might show 100 feet to go before that turn.

This is all fixable with better software and I hope Garmin gets to work on it.
For now, it's simply not accurate enough to use in a place I've never been to before.

**Update**
It sits on my dashboard and I don't use it. I suspect when Garmin issues some updates might give it another try.

To make a long story short, when I got the terminal and was walking toward the luggage area, I happened to discover that i had not zipped up the case. Both zippers for the camera compartment were fully unzipped. If it had not been for the 2" still closed, I am certain that the camera would have fallen out at some point while I was gathering together my possessions, retrieving my computer case from the overhead compartment, and making my way with my computer case and carry-on bag to the terminal from the back of the plane.

title: Fun times making it work.
text:
I bought this box mainly to finally get some use out of the usb 3.0.
I've owned it for less than a week
I had issues with this box from the start.

Issue 1
The power supply is inadequate, and can't handle the 4 1.5 TB seagate drives I had in it at the beginning. Sometimes it would stay powered up when I turned it on, but most of the times it would immediately power it's self off. I swapped the seagate drives with 4 hitachi drives that don't draw as much power when they are spinning up. So that "fixed" the unstable powering on issue.

Issue 2
After booting to windows it kept saying I needed to format the drives, several times for each drive. Eventually it would recognize the drives as having data and work properly. I browsed the help forum for mediasonic products, other people had this same issue, nobody there had an answer aside from either using a usb 2.0 port, or the esata port. I fixed this issue for myself by disabling legacy usb 3.0 support in my motherboard bios.

Issue 3
If I have the power sync mode set to put the device to sleep when I power down my computer, the next time I turn my computer on windows recognizes the drives just fine, but sees them as being empty. No fix for that I could find aside from not using that power sync mode. I suppose I could see if this power sync problem goes away if I connect with the esata port instead of the usb 3.0. But I would have bought the cheaper box if I wanted to use the esata. I am now using the power sync mode where it powers off when I shut my computer off, so I have to turn the probox on every time I turn on my computer.

I've wasted about 5 hours of my time, updated drivers, bios, chipset, read forums & I took my computer apart twice to swap drives around.

title: Despite some minor flaws, it's the best head-unit I've ever owned
text:
This replaces a Kenwood 6190HD and as a DIY car audio enthusiast for 20 years, this has been a delight. Among my favorite attributes are:

- excellent garmin POI database and fast route calculation
- Pandora integration is slick (bookmarking artist/album, thumbs up/down, browse playlists, etc)
- separate EQ settings for different sources (handy for streaming audio vs connected media)
- tweaker's dream: EQ, DSP, crossover (e.g. set a tweeter size, then apply flat attenuation to the treble. SO much better than trial and error with jumpers in your component crossovers)
- reverse tilt screen
- two USB inputs (I had to get creative with past headunits as I have an iPod and USB drive)
- usb drive support is quite good (I like to organize my folders to make finding music easier while driving.. something you can't do with an iPod)

Cons:
- I'd have preferred a 5-band parametric EQ (minor quibble, as the graphic EQ is quite excellent)
- only one reverse tilt setting for the screen
- as mentioned in other reviews, there's no way to hide unused sources and clean up the main menu UI (or more importantly, the sources cycled when you use the steering wheel controls to step through them)
- usb drive support could be MUCH better (though I know of no head unit that does it better). This is more of a complaint around head-units in general - iPod connectivity and bluetooth smartphone integration seem to be where all of the real effort an innovation are going, so those of us who prefer high-quality audio on a connected non-apple device are left with few options. Easy improvements include: support for exFAT and/or NTFS filesystems, building persistent index files for large libraries, increased limits on file/folder count, etc.

Overall, this has been the most headache-free HU I've had. If you want fast/excellent GPS navigation, dirt-simple smartphone integration, and excellent sound quality, EQ, and DSP, then this is an unbeatable package overall.

title: Great, but buyer beware!
text:
Problems
Quality control issues by Philips. I had to go thru four pairs of these to find two good ones. The other two were unbalanced, meaning the right channel being quieter than the left. The right side was 30% quieter on the first pair, and 20% quieter on the second pair with problems. This is not much, and it is difficult to pinpoint for a casual listener, but for a premium headphone is inexcusable. After realizing the unbalance I went and measured in order to come with the numbers. This issue gave the impression the headphones were not detailed.
Nevertheless I realized the potential of these headphones, and the immensely pleasurable sound, and persevered until I gathered a really good pair.
The second problem is related to what you are using to drive these. A cheap amp like a Fiio E10 simply does not work because it destroys the bass by making it boomy and diffuse. I think muddy is the word. You will need an amp with very low output impedance, or a decent player.
I am using them with a Sony NWZ-S754, and I cannot put them down. They work quite decent with a Sansa Clip + as well.

On the plus side
The Philips Uptowns are good for all kinds of music.
When used with the Sony NWZ-S754, the amount of nice treble detail, and articulated deep bass, the forwardness of mids is amazing. They color a bit the sound in the most pleasurable way. The sibilance is absent, women voices are not crushed, a piano sounds like a piano, and the soundstage is nice. Indeed superb headphones. I have a Beyerdynamic 880 and they gather dust now. The Beyers are possibly more accurate, but they sound boring to me now because they don't come even close to the Philips in the detail department. Nothing in the price range comes even close. I should say they have angled drivers, wow!

In case you decide to buy them you have to be careful that you get a good balanced pair (!!!!), use a proper source, and you will be satisfied.

title: I can call it BAD MEDIA -- after buying over 600 of these...
text:
I used Verbatim until they started making media in India, then I noticed an obvious increase in PI errors and failures with Nero DiscSpeed. I also do a data verification when I burn a disc.

Everyone said to go to Taiyo Yuden, so I did.

The first 200 boxes of these I got were great, very low PI errors and failures, no coasters. PI failure around 2-3. Then I bought another 200, they were both awful, very high rates of errors and failures, around 8-12. Then I got another box of 100, they were decent, failures around 5-6 sometimes the error rates were high enough that I'd throw away the disc after running a check on it, just using my own judgment. I got another 100 in the mail today and they are the worst I've seen yet, failures around 10-20. That's not good media, not even average media. That's worse than Verbatim from India, worse than TDK from Radio Shack.

I don't know what brand I'm going to next; I just know experience has taught me, regardless what EVERYONE else says, this media is average at best, and highly overrated. After buying over 600 discs, I'm not sure how many coasters I've had that didn't verify, but the quality is very variable, very unpredictable. I should note - I've tried all of these on 2-3 different burners while doing this, the trend held regardless.

title: Amazing Gaming Monitor!!  Absolutely recommended!
text: I've been in the Market for a 120Hz (This one is 144Hz) monitor for some time now.  But I was a little concerned about the amount of money required to purchase one.  After a year of reading reviews and watching videos on various products I saw this monitor being referred to as one of the best you can get.  I watched a lot of videos and read a lot of reviews about this very exact model.  So I finally decided to spend the cash and purchased it.  Let me tell you it is worth every penny!!!  If you are on the fence on whether or not to sink the money into a high refresh rate gaming monitor, do it now!  You will not regret it at all.  I had no idea what I've been missing out on all this time.  It really is night and day coming from a traditional 60Hz monitor.  This monitor is incredible.  The build quality is top notch, and I love the little remote it comes with to cycle through the menu.  I find most monitors these days are going to a touch type button layout, and I've never found one that is simple to use or is 100% responsive to my touches. The detachable remote on this monitor makes setting up profiles and adjusting settings a lot easier.  The menu system isn't perfect tho, and cycling through some settings takes a little more time than I would like it to.  The colors on this type of monitor are good, but if color accuracy is something you absolutely must have you will have to look elsewhere.  Viewing angles are okay as well, but it is limited compared to other monitors.  I've never understood why that is such an important stat for some.  Unless you have an audience watching, you will be sitting directly in front of the screen anyways.  Mine also came with no dead or frozen pixels so I was extremely happy about that.  The stand is very adjustable and can be positioned to any angle or height most people will need, I also like that is has a hook mount on the back to store away Headphones when not in use.  I don't play many FPS these days but decided to break out TF2 again and this monitor has gotten me interested in playing them once again.  Other games such as Crysis look amazingly smooth.  But you do have to have a gaming rig beefy enough to get those frame rates high enough to take advantage.  But honestly if you have the amount of money required to sink into this monitor, you probably have all those bases covered.  When I made the jump from all CRT to LCD 10-12 years ago I never did realize what I was missing out on when it come to smoothness and video response/lag.  I've read the 24" version is just as good.  So if your on a budget I would recommend purchasing that one if size isn't a big deal for you.  BenQ has done an awesome job with this one.

title: A Gaming Computer for a Bargain Price.
text:
A textured and comfortable finish is on the lid. The keyboard is laid out with set-in keys and is can be easily cleaned. The keyboard boasts an IceCool palm rest, and does help keep the keyboard from becoming uncomfortably warm. The fan must be impressive, as it only becomes a bit warm during heavy gaming. The screen supports 720p HD, but not the full 1080p. However, there is an HDMI port that can be used to connect to a full 1080p TV to fix that. Overall, a very sturdy computer.

However, the speakers are not that great, and I recommend purchasing separate speakers.

A hybrid of NVIDIA and INTEL processors, this computer can run high-end computer smoothly at high settings. I tested the gaming capabilities on Amnesia - the Dark Descent, and it ran almost completely high settings, though it SSAO should be set to medium to prevent lagging issues. It can also run Dead Space 1 and 2 at their highest settings with no hiccups. It may lag with Anti-Aliasing enabled, though older games like Half-Life 2 do not suffer from enabling it at the highest AA settings. It also runs PCSX2 games pretty well, and at the highest of 2x Native resolution without lag. However, enabling the hardware anti-aliasing causes slight slowdown (5-10 frames at the lowest AA setting) at 2x resolution and a few garbage graphics appear.

IMPORTANT: The 750 hard drive is divided into two partitions, one that hold the OS and general files (279 GB) and one that holds general files called DATA (394 GB, I suggest using DATA for heavy-duty files like music, videos, and games). REMEMBER: programs like iTunes and gaming services need to be in the same partition as the music and game files they will be using. I tried placing all the music files into the DATA hard drive and using iTunes's, which was in OS partition, directory settings to try to pick them up from the DATA partition. It didn't detect them for some reason.

Also, there is the NVIDIA settings program that junctions the NVIDIA processor to certain programs. Choosing the automatic option will just allow the program to choose between running a program with the high performance, but battery-draining, NVIDIA processor, or the slower integrated processor. I suggest leaving most to auto, but programs that run games should be set to high as a default for a considerably more enjoyable experience. Just right-click either the game or the service that runs it and the NVIDIA settings tab should be under the drop-down menu. Find and add the program to the given list and set it to the high processor and not the integrated option.

Among the flaws I could find were the brightness and color settings (it can be quite bright), but just use the color management program to calibrate the screen and/or use the Intel HD Graphics settings to set brightness, contrast, and color profiles. Also, there is some bloatware that Asus leaves behind, but a few are important, like LifeFrame, which is vital for webcam adjustments; research each carefully. Also, the mouse can be a bit touchy sometimes, and you might want to buy a separate USB mouse.

title: I love the equipment, but the monthly service fee is a rip-off
text:
I am a huge foan of home automation and have been looking for a while for a solution that I can install at our lake house to allow remote monitoring of the property during our absences. A local contractor told me that he had just got done installing the new Schlage system in a client's home so I decided to give it a whirl.

I'm going to summarize my experience and focus on a key point later in this review:

Hardware experience:
-You will not be blown away by this camera. There are many other available webcams that offer wifi camera monitoring with better quality (some w PTZ capability)
-The ease to which this equipment comes together on the Schlage Nexia system is really nice and highly recommended for the less than technically savy person.
-Be prepared to pay a $12.99/month MINIMUM fee for the Nexia service to allow you to monitor the camera or interact with any other Nexia-enabled device in your house.
-The camera is NOT an outdoor camera and this limits the practicality of installing this in remote places. Most people want to have the exterior doors covered.

My biggest gripe about this setup was not about the hardware as I found the Schlage hardware to be on-par with a lot of it's counterparts in the DIY price-range. It's the monthly Nexia service fee which is a minimum $12.99/month I could not get over. I couldn't bring myself to pay a monthly bill to via a webcam that I was providing internet service for.

***THIS IS IMPORTANT!!!***
What Schlage doesn't tell you is that the Nexia gear will work Vera from micasaverde.com and with Homeseer found at homeseer.com both allowing the same functions and no monthly fees! Please, before you sign up for another monthly contract, check out these two websites as I found it offered basically the same functionality without having to pay for service.

Again, the hardware is great, but I would highly recommend you setup the equipment on one of the free services out there in lieu of paying for monthly service.

title: Correcting Misinformation . . .
text:
(UPDATED) According to other reviewers Garmin is now providing software to access the recorded video, which can be accessed by plugging the unit into your computer. You may also download it from http://www8.garmin.com/support/collection.jsp?product=010-01311-01 . (Thanks D. Kerman).

1. There is no provided software. (Which isn't a problem.)
Quite simply, Gamin includes no software to access recorded files. Instead the Dash Cam 20 interfaces with your computer much the same way as a digital camera would. Garmin includes a short usb data cable, which you can plug directly into your computer, or you can remove the included microSD card and insert it into the provided microSD to SD card adapter, or use your own SD card reader. Note: The Dash Cam 20 does not include an SD card reader. That said, many Macbook Pros and pc laptops have a built in card reader. No matter how you access the card's data, it will appear the same as any flash drive. Access the drive, and navigate through the "Garmin" and "Video" folders to find your recorded videos. Note: Simply accessing your recorded videos through a card reader will not affect the formatting of the card, and Garmin does not use proprietary formatting.

2. The Dash Cam 20 will work with a Mac.

Now, if you're using a mac and you try to open a file, you'll be presented with the following error message:
"The document "VDO_0001.avi" could not be opened. A required codec isn't available."

That's not so much Garmin's fault as it is Microsoft's and Apple's. AVI files were developed by Microsoft . . .

Now, should Garmin have picked a different file type? Probably. Can you still open it? Absolutely. You're going to need to download a free piece of software called VLC. Just think of it as the software Garmin should have included. A simple Google search for VLC will take you to the correct site: "VideoLAN - Official page for VLC media player". Click the big Download VLC button and open the .dmg file that just downloaded. Drag the VLC icon to the Applications directory and we're almost done. Next right click on any .avi file in the videos directory and click "Get Info". Click the small triangle next to "Open With" and choose VLC. Finally, click the Change All button. You're done!

Now when you double click on any .avi file you'll be able to watch them without any problem. Note, the first time you open a file, you may get a message stating: "'VLC' is an application downloaded from the Internet. Are you sure you want to open it?" Obviously, you need to click Open. If you're concerned about downloading software from the internet do a little Googling, you'll see that VLC is a very safe and trusted piece of software.

3. You can "export" video files with embedded GPS data.
Saving video files from the memory card is just like manipulating any other files on your computer. If you want to save a video, just select it and drag it off the card to some other folder. It's that simple. GPS data is automatically printed onto the video. It's worth pointing out that the GPS data does not exist as a separate file. Therefore, it is not currently possible to drop GPS data into some mapping program to trace your driving routes.

4. The Garmin Dash Cam 20 does support 32 GB SDHC 10
I bought the [[ASIN:B009QZH7BU SanDisk Ultra 32 GB MicroSDHC C10/UHS1 Memory Card with Adapter (SDSDQU-032G-AFFP-A)]] and it works just fine.

A final thought or two for now . . .

The included suction cup mount kind of sucks. It's just like every other Garmin suction cup mount, however it just doesn't work that well in my 2004 Chevy Silverado with this dash cam; it just takes up too much space. Depending on your application it may be fine, but I was going for a more permanent and discrete appearance. In fairness, that's hard to do with a suction cup mount. After searching I found the [[ASIN:B002T0EK64 i.Trek Sticky Mount for Garmin Nuvi (Black)]]. It's perfect for my application. It's much smaller than the suction cup mount and allows me to mount the dash cam right along the top of the windshield tucked next to my rearview mirror.

Note: One reviewer stated suction cup mounts are illegal in 13 states. Windshield mounts are actually illegal in over half of all states and the District of Columbia, and others put certain restrictions on where things can be mounted. I would suggest a Google search if you're unsure of the laws where you live.

Overall, I'm quite happy with this purchase so far. Are there cheaper alternatives? Absolutely! The thing is, I was looking for one with speed indication that is stamped on the video. That information is just one more relevant piece of evidence that will be useful in the event of an accident.

title: Will this be the beginning of the hybrid router/NAS movement?
text:
I just set this up to replace an E3000 as the main router. The reason for doing so is that the 5GHZ radio on the E3000 is flaky and doesn't reach my master bedroom. The router is placed at the front of the house in one bedroom with my master bedroom on the other end of a 2000 sq ft house. It's not a large distance as the house is rectangular so it's 50 feet at most, but there are walls in between. The 5GHZ radio was an epic fail on the E3000.

I'm happy to report that this unit solves the issue of the 5GHZ signal death. The signal is now stronger than the 2.4Ghz signal of the E3000. I routinely receive full to half bars on my Ipad on the 5GHZ spectrum in my bedroom where I had none before. This means that I will not have to put money on the AC68U which I suspect will cost at least $50 more for the external antennas. Unless you have a gigantic house, there's no need to get its big brother. As far as I know, the only difference between this and the AC68U are the external antennas and the extra stream radio that requires an equivalent adapter to use. In other words, not worth it as you will be hard pressed to reach the theoretical 866 Mbps of this router.

The unit has 256MB RAM with dual core ARM A9 processors (similar to the earlier Ipads). I have to say that the web interface is much faster than what I was used to. Youtube no longer freezes when it stream (but I still need to test further). However, streaming 1080P video from my HTPC to my Samsung TV the video froze twice. I use the E3000 as a client bridge with its 2.4ghz radio to the AC56U, which then transmit that signal by 5GHZ radio to the TV. I will have to test some more because it should not be freezing at wireless N signal. I may switch out a different router other than the E3000 because I suspect it's not the AC56U that's causing the issue. The E3000 has always been flaky even with DD-WRT.

The RAM usage indicate only about 50MB on usage with 200MB free. With that kind of headroom, I hope that Plex Media Server finally offer up a version for routers. I believe that dual core 800MHZ CPU is now fast enough for routers to become a poor man's NAS (the Marvell of the low end NAS are basically faster clocked A9's). Yes, the router does come with its own DLNA and download software, but it's not good. I will be looking to replace download master with transmission when I have time.

This unit is basically the fastest consumer router on the market so far with full unlocked dual core and 256MB RAM. If it ever offers software package installs like the NAS units currently do, it could finally usher in the hybrid Router/NAS market. Do it, Asus!

I will update this review with issues and its reliability later as I continue to use it. For its main purpose of increasing range along with offering fast and reliable connections, it's a five star router.

Update 8/1/13: Well, I just realized that although AC is good enough for 1080P streaming, N is not. Since My TV is wireless N 5GZ, and not AC, I will instead be using a wired connection between the router and TV. I may have to buy another AC56U to create a media bridge if I turn the AC56U into a NAS... but that would be expensive. Which brings me to my next con. This router is great for the coverage but AC speed is useless if you don't have AC clients. Additionally, the ASUS is too expensive to be used as client bridge. I will be looking to the cheaper brands AC routers with DD-WRT support for use as client bridges.

title: A good budget tablet-- just don't drop it!
text:
I've had this tablet for a little over 24 hours so these are my first impressions...

The Coby Kyros MID9742-8 is part of Coby's 3rd generation of Android tablets. I also have one of their 2nd generation tablets, the MID7022-4G, a 7" capacitive touchscreen tablet running Android 2.3, but I wanted a bigger screen. The 9742 is an upgrade in many ways:

* larger screen (9.7" vs 7")
* higher resolution (1024x768 vs 800x480)
* more memory (1GB vs 512MB)
* more storage (8GB vs 4GB)
* newer version of Android (4.0 vs 2.3)

The processor is clocked the same (1Ghz), but instead of the old Telechips ARMv6 chip used in the 7022, the 9742 uses a newer Allwinner A10 ARMv7 chip. It's still not a powerhouse, by any stretch, but clock-for-clock the newer ARMv7 chip is more powerful. For example, my old 7022 can't run Netflix without the video looking like a slideshow. The new 9742 can run Netflix with only the occasional hiccup.

The Allwinner A10 CPU used in the 9742 uses a Mali-400 MP GPU (same as is used on the Samsung Galaxy SII), so it should be able to run pretty much any current game, though I haven't tested it in this regard yet.

I can confirm what another reviewer said, that com.adobe.flashplayer_111115007.apk works to install and run Adobe Flash. I found this version for download at 1mobile.com. This was the first one I tried and it worked so I didn't test any other versions.

As others have mentioned, Coby tablets do NOT have access to the Android Market (now called Google Play) nor does it come with any of the Google apps (GMail, Maps, Talk, Voice, etc). Instead, the 9742 comes with a GetJar app, but the selection is pretty thin there. You can download the Amazon App Store app, though, to get Netflix and Angry Birds. You can also download apps from other sites like the aforementioned 1mobile.com where I found Adobe Flash and a few other apps that weren't available on the Amazon store.

The only big downside to this tablet for me is that it feels pretty flimsy. The screen side is nice and rigid, but the backside is made of very thin plastic. You can feel it flex beneath your fingertips with minimal pressure. And occasionally you can feel/hear a creak along the edges when you grip it, like the two halves don't quite fit together. True, the thin plastic body contributes to the tablet only weighing a pound-- about 30% less than most other 10" tablets-- but I think I'd take a little extra heft in exchange for an aluminum or thicker plastic body. I don't have much confidence it would survive a fall.

All in all, for around $230 (as of April 2012), I think the Coby MID9742-8 is a good value. I wouldn't pay any more than that for it, though, since you can a get dual-core Acer A200 tablet for around $300 (again, as of April 2012).

UPDATE (May 3, 2012): After having the tablet for over a week it turns out that I've been unable to get any version of Adobe Flash to work properly. They seem to install, and sometimes they will load in the browser and start playing videos, but they all inevitably crash within minutes, hanging the browser and requiring a force stop within the "Manage Apps" settings menu. From searching various Android forums on the web, this seems to be a common problem among Allwinner A10-based Android 4.0 tablets. I'll update again later if I can find a working version.

I've had this laptop for about a day, and so this is by necessity a first impression; I'll update it later once I've had it longer.

The build quality is superb. I'm not sure if there's any metal in this, but it's high-quality plastic with an attractive finish. The images don't really show that the visible surfaces when the lid is open are a shiny brushed gunmetal gray. It looks and feels good. The shiny closed lid is also good-looking, but picks up fingerprints like crazy. Not really a big deal for me.

The keyboard is perhaps the best laptop keyboard I've ever used. The keys are dished and fairly long-travel, and are probably as close to the feel of a separate, desktop keyboard as is possible to get on a laptop. The keyboard layout is reasonably full, though there doesn't appear to be any way to send a BREAK without remapping. This is only really a concern for software developers using the standard keybindings in debuggers.

The screen, as others have said, is beautiful. Samsung's a big maker of laptop displays as well as monitors and flat-screen TVs, and this laptop is a great advertisement for their quality. It's bright, desktop-like, with great color and clarity.

The graphics chipset is capable of running World of Warcraft on 'Ultra' graphics settings at 60fps+, even in 40-per-side battlegrounds and 25-man raids. That's about as demanding as I get with graphics, and it's wholly up to the task. There are more expensive laptops with the more powerful NVIDIA GeForce GFX 675MX or 680M chipsets out there, but none of them are this affordable, and most of them make worse compromises in terms of weight, size, heat and looks.

Don't mistake, this is a big laptop. However, its styling hides its bulk quite effectively, and the wedge shape means it's comfortable to type on. It's also substantially smaller and lighter than the Alienware 17" offerings, let alone the 18" behemoth.

I thought before getting it that the rotary mode switch on the side was a gimmick, but it's actually quite useful. The settings for each mode are very customizable, and the modes are well-chosen to match common laptop usages. Certainly a lot easier than digging in Control Panel to switch between power modes!

When not in Game mode, this laptop is also admirably subtle. It doesn't scream 'Gamer Laptop!' unless you want it to, unlike most alternatives. You could take this into a sober business meeting and not draw too much attention.

If I had to carry this around every day, it'd probably be too heavy, but my personal laptop usage is as a movable desktop replacement, and this fits the bill. It can be easily packed up and moved, but it needs a substantial backpack and you certainly feel the weight.

For my needs, this is the perfect machine. The only real criticism I could lay on it is that it would be majorly improved by having SSD options, but I suspect the next revision of the hardware will. It does have a small caching SSD onboard, however.

Strongly recommended for the demanding user seeking a desktop replacement with no compromises on computing power and wanting something a bit more subtle than an Alienware.

title: An exceptional diamond in the rough
text:
Coming into buying this pair of headphones I was looking initially at getting either the Ultrasone 780 or the Audio Technica ATH M50, but after checking out some reviews decided to go with these.
I was not disappointed.

Build quality:
The HM5's are made of rubberized plastic with brushed metal ear-cup covers, pleather ear pads and headband cover, fabric headband padding and a metal headband support ribbon. The cord is a removable, dual mono design with a screw-on 3.5mm to 1/4" adaptor. It also comes with a HUGE but very well padded travel case. The materials all feel very high-quality and are appropriate for its price. The only exception to this is the headband padding which compressed down after a few months. 4/5

Looks:
I like the way the HM5's are styled, that said, they are FAR too large to wear around town without looking like a bit of a dork. 3/5

Comfort:
The pleather ear pads are thick, supple, and very comfortable. The clamping force was a bit high out of the box, but settled down quickly. Some other people have complained that their ears get sweaty after extended use. I have not had this problem in the slightest, but I also live in cold Chicago. So that might have something to do with it. I would have given these a 5/5 for comfort, but the headband padding did not stand up well over time and compressed into the sort of U-shaped well that it is held in. This means the headband digs into my head uncomfortably and has to be moved every hour or two. 4/5

Sound quality:
Here's where these headphones really shine. The HM5's have a wonderfully neutral frequency balance, but still have a tight, punchy bass that never feels weak. The sound clarity is exceptional, however, it is slightly too warm to really achieve the cold precision of analytical headphones. That said, the warmth really gives these headphones a lush sound that doesn't get harsh, even at high volumes. You can really distinguish every little detail in your music and the high fidelity makes it easy to place sounds three-dimensionally. It really comes in helpful in games like Far Cry 3 where you often hear animals or enemies you can't see and need to be able to find quickly. The soundstage is rather large and airy too, better than almost any other closed-back headphones in this price range. Some people have pointed out that its driver design kind of rips off the Sennheiser HD650's. However, this is actually a huge complement as the 650's are $480 and are considered to be some of the best headphones on the market. 5/5

Conclusion:
These headphones are exceptional sounding and beat most headphones at and even above its price range. A seriously good deal. Overall: 5/5

title: was a little afraid that for the price it wouldn't be a good tv. Wow
text:
Picked this tv up for $219, was a little afraid that for the price it wouldn't be a good tv. Wow!!! It is amazing for the price, IMO.

I use it as a computer monitor and there is no ghosting/motion blur at all with any games I play on the PC. The Sims 3 looks stunning on it! Don't let the 60 hz refresh rate fool you - it does just fine with games. I was using a 22.5 inch Asus LCD monitor, with 2 ms seek time, and this tv performs just as well as that one did.

The sound is about average I would say, it's not terrible but also isn't great either. I'm planning to hook it up to my surround system with the optical audio anyways. Honestly, not many LED's have great sound these days. I have heard much, much worse sound than this TV has.

Picture is clean and crisp. There are plenty of settings to adjust to your liking, and I was amazed at how sharp this tv can get if you turn up the sharpness. The colors are absolutely perfect, and if you check site's that do in-depth reviews, you will see that this tv does an amazing job at the price range it's in when it comes to color spectrum calibration and black levels.

The black levels of this tv are amazing, it gets about as pitch-black as you can get. Like professional reviewers have said though, it does not get as bright as some other tv's do and isn't quite as vibrant. It's really dark in my computer room though, so this doesn't affect me at all. Might be something for you to consider if you plan on having it in a bright room.

Overall, this tv is exactly what the professional reviewers say it is - one of THE best tv's you can get for under $500, period!

title: Good quality wire with a few flaws.
text:
First I want to say that this is true 12 AWG wire, so you get what you pay for. However, working with this wire is frustrating as hell.

The wire isn't clearly marked, or "striped" to which wire is which. Other brands have a stripe going down the entirety of one wire to differentiate positive and negative, whereas this wire has very small writing on one of the wires every few inches. When you're working in a poorly lit and cramped environment, the last thing you want to do is hunt for the writing.

The separator between the two wires is also very difficult to tear due to its thickness. I found that many times when I went to tear the two wires apart that I would end up ripping the insulation off one of the wires. I resorted to using a knife to separate the wires but even that was a pain.

My third complaint is partly my fault, however it was still an annoyance. The shielding is so thick to the point where it makes stripping wires difficult without cutting a good deal of wire. I ended up having to restrip my wires many times because of this.

All in all you do get quality copper that is 12 AWG just as stated, but I wish I bought speaker wire from Monoprice instead. I had some left over from a previous install and working with that versus this is night and day.

title: Excellent Performance - Great Value
text:
Having been a 3+ yr heavy user of the first gen Audio Technica noise cancelling headphones until they broke (one of the ear speakers cracked), I veered into other brands of noise isolating earbuds (Sennheiser, Etymotic, Polk & Sony) because of other features such as iPhone controls & compatibility, high end sound quality, or the structure of the earbud itself. While those products all have their own merits, noise isolating will never equate to noise cancelling for me. I travel extensively year-round and found that once I switched away from a headset, I really enjoyed the freedom earbuds bring to sleeping positions in an airplane seat, to the compact storage in my carry aboard, for the quick in and out of my bag when getting seated on a plane, and that I don't look like a studio DJ on and off the plane. For those of you with hair on your head still (and ladies, of course), earbuds won't leave you with dreaded headphone hair mushed down in that ear to ear strip across your head.

The Quietpoint technology that is built into these is identical to their headphones, but of course have none of the bulkiness and noise leakage associated with an over-the-ear product. With the Audio Technica ANC headphones, the noise leakage is enough that people immediately nearby will know your playlist by the end of a flight. Not so with the earbuds, and that was a huge plus to avoid raised eyebrows and awkward glances on those days when you just needed volume and bass. Even in an office environment where I need to cut the background clutter of the HVAC and other low frequency noise, these are comfortable to slip in and just turn on the ANC with no music. Huge benefit in that environment. Many flight attendants are overly serious about all that on-off switch stuff and tend to single out ANC headphone users for special attention to have the noise cancelling off for arrival and departure. With these, you're relatively anonymous and won't get the same condescending third grade speech to make sure your headset is off (and yes, of course you should always turn them off as requested).

Battery life is around 10-12 hours of use for me. The music can be heard with or without the ANC on, and a dead battery does not prevent you from listening to music. My iPhone has enough sound equalizing adjustments that I can pick the right one (Settings>Music>EQ in OS 5.1.1) that accents the bass or treble as needed. The sound quality in these is very pure and if I had to be critical, perhaps just a bit short on the bass. But that is being really picky and I recognize that to get that bass in an earbud you'd have to head north of $200. I use the included foam earbuds exclusively with these as they best conform to my ear canals with no wobble or slippage moving around, even on hot muggy days.

The noise cancelling unit is 32" of cable (about 16" is split) from the earbuds and then there is another 22" of cable to the connector. This is plenty of cable for nearly everyone. At 6' tall, the noise cancelling unit is at my waist with enough generous slack to turn my head and no binding sitting or standing. The included bag is a bummer here, but I use a variety of Gary Waterfield products (sfbags.com) to keep everything tidy and stored anyhow. The included earbuds are 3 sizes of silicone (S, M, L) and a single size of the durable form fitting memory foam.

As a pilot who has used their aviation headsets for years, I will always concede that Bose makes better noise cancelling technology...for a significant premium. If you are an earbud fan or thinking of shedding the headset, until Bose starts making noise cancelling earbuds and you're ready to spend 4x as much (street value) to achieve that extra 5%...this is a simple choice.

title: Dual MONITOR dream come true!
text:
My job is very complex. I have to have a lot of power (CPU, RAM and HD)) and love the use of two monitors. I have used a dual monitor setup for years, but my love and work related use of photography and graphic design pushed me into searching for better quality. Once you go to a dual monitor system there’s no turning back. Multi-tasking takes on a whole new dimension.

These monitors came plug-in-play out of the boxes. I will point out that the HDMI cable was missing- but I can get over that. Plugged one into the DVI and one into Video (cause my HDMI cable was missing) outlet and ‘BANG! Set up the right and left side properly the rest was history. Clarity and color is stunning. The monitors rise and pitch! The controls are on the front, but who messes with those when they are set. They are lightweight, but not cheap. They swivel as advertised. Going with a dual system requires a little real estate on the desk. They seem to operate with Windows 8.1 very well. I am not a gamer, but I do have a great system sporting a fast Intel i7 with 32GB RAM and a TB of HD. On a slow day I have WORD, Outlook, MS Expressions, FileZilla, Windows Explorer, Internet Explorer, Firefox and Adobe Photoshop going on the desktops. If I get busier I add WordSearch, Adobe Lightroom, a huge proprietary accounting software system, Windows Media playing in the background along with multiple windows of Browsers and WORD Documents. Absolutely a symphony of applications and power never failing under the name of ASUS! The monitors handle it all without a hiccup. Animation, movement and display is never skewed or compromised, which most of these issues do more with power then graphics but it does make a difference.

The color calibration is spot-on. What I see is what is printed! I am more than happy. I would recommend these to anyone. IPS is what is says it is. This is a real great price especially if you need some heavy weight Photo processing equipment on a tight budget.

Cons: None! None that I have honestly found.

title: Amazing TV if you get a Samsung Panel + Calibration Settings.
text:
I purchased this TV a week ago upon exchanging my Toshiba 32L2400U for wobbling purposes. I needed a TV that I can game on my desk with consoles/PC and use as a PC monitor. I was a bit weary because of the panel lottery that is involved here (or at least was in the past with this TV). I got the UU02 panel and checked the service menu to find that it stated "32Axxxxxx". According to multiple sites, if the TV shows an "A" in the service menu after the number then it is indeed a Samsung panel.

The default "Standard" and "Dynamic" settings are honestly horrible, but after messing around with calibration for about a week, I can say that it is an amazing picture TV for gaming. This TV supports 4:4:4 for using it as a PC monitor and has a special PC mode after renaming the input to "PC".

Here are my settings I use for gaming. This should honestly give you the best picture for your TV. These settings should be just as good if you are using it for movies/TV.
NOTE: these are settings done on a Samsung panel, so it probably won't look the same on another panel.

Movie mode also has the best right-out-of the box settings. While the other two modes look terrible out of the box. Thus making Movie Mode the easiest to configure. The only reason to use Standard is if you want the auto backlight dimming. This basically makes the darker scenes appear more like it actually would and thus darker. Note that for these settings, you need Standard Mode. Movie Mode will not look the same.

UPDATE - 10/14 After much more advanced customizing, I've come to a conclusion that the default offsets seem to be off just a bit. The picture as a whole seems to have way too much blue background. I did a few adjustments with the color and offsets that should provide a more realistic and better color view. I will continue to update this if I adjust anything else.
Mode: Standard
Backlight: 18 (This is personal pref and will be different depending on where the TV is at)
Contrast: 90
Brightness: 46
Sharpness: 12 (Another personal pref, wouldn't recommend anything above 20)
Color: 48
Tint: G52/R48

R-Offset-25
G-Offset-24
B-Offset-21
R-Gain-14
G-Gain-21
B-Gain-25

Gamma:-1

title: Very Good "Tough" Speaker
text:
The Fugoo Tough Bluetooth Speaker is a very good option if you are looking for a ruggedized Bluetooth speaker. It delivers very good sound from all directions. While its overall volume will not blow you away, it is loud enough for small parties and get togethers. The pairing is easy and it is very easy to operate. The downside is that it does not come with a remote (it is optional) and there are no dedicated controls on the unit to switch tracks (you have to hold the center button along with the plus or minus button). The price is on the high side (though certainly lower than the Bose products) so the inclusion of some of the accessories such as the remote, would go a long way to adding value.

*** Positive Points: ***

- Good Construction that feels rugged and is water resistant
- Small size but with great sound quality
- Multidirectional speaker placement allows a full room of sound
- Good Battery Life
- Voice guided operation such as a voice to tell you it is on or connected.

*** Negative Points: ***

- While Bass is present it is less than other speakers such as the SoundFreaq Soundkick or Bose setups
- Less overall volume than some other portable Bluetooth speakers
- Power Button and indicator lights are hidden on the side of the speaker
- Does not achieve the stated 40 hours, at least not with 50-70% volume levels
- In order to shift tracks you have to hold the center button along with the plus or minus button. It would be better if it had dedicated buttons
- Optional remote should be an included accessory
- Pricey

title: sound quality is amazing. I'm not a big fan of Beats and ...
text:
First, sound quality is amazing. I'm not a big fan of Beats and have always purchased Bose headphones over beats because well, they're usually about the same price, and Bose sound better. Beats may look nicer, but I'm buying for sound, not look. I was skeptical buying these due to their high price tag and not being able to give them a listen first, but I'm blown away as to how well they work. Most in ear headphones that promise crisp sound and deep bass usually need a tight seal in your ear or else they sound like a tin can. As soon as you begin to sweat, they keep falling out or breaking that seal. These are the first headphones i've used that do no need that tight seal to sound amazing. They just do, no matter what, and have the hook around the ear so they don't fall out.

They are also extremely comfortable. To me, they are nice and light and don't begin to hurt my ears. These are the first bluetooth headphones I've had where I can actually leave them in comfortably the entire time I'm at the gym.

As for people stating they have audio/video sync issues.... I understand the concern as I watch tv shows on my tablet to get through cardio session. However, the audio video sync is perfect using a galaxy note 10.1 2014 edition running plex for videos. I'm not sure this issue has been resolved previously, or if my setup just works, but there's no delay whatsoever.

As of now, I don't have any complaints about these headphones with possibly the exception of the price tag. It's a heft price, but if you keep trying different $30-$60 bluetooth headphones, you'll end up paying that price anyway, plus i'm using it as a bluetooth headset for phone calls while driving (since Illinois has hands free laws). So 2 birds....well worth it. Now, if they could just manage to eliminate the cord between the two...

title: The best wide-angle lens for canon
text:
I've been photographing weddings for about 8 years now and I've been through my share of lenses. There are currently three lenses I carry with me at all times: The 50 1.2L, the 70-200 2.8L and this one, the 28 1.8. It's the only non-L lens I ever shoot with.

Let me preface this by saying that I'm not a wide-angle guy. I like 50-85mm for almost everything I do, and 28mm is about as wide as I'll go. I used the 24 1.4L for about 2 years as my wide angle prime and I ended up selling it. It was hard to get in focus and it seemed to have some aberrations and other flaws. On top of that it was $1,600.

I sold the 24 1.4 and have used the 28 1.8 ever since. I don't regret that decision one bit. If you're looking for a professional level lens for under $1000 (under $500!) then get this. It's a no-brainer.

My only gripe is with the quality of flare you get shooting into the sun. I try to work in flare as much as possible to give portraits and other pictures interesting looks. The flare pattern on the 24mm 1.4 was really great. It was smooth and beautiful. On the 28mm you can have some weird patterns and shapes which sometimes look like teardrops. It's not terrible, but sometimes you have to clone out some weird stuff.

Pros:

Great sharpness
Very little distortion
Lightweight but built well
Inexpensive

Cons:

Manual focus isn't a smooth as an L-Series
Flare isn't as pretty as the 35L or the 24L

title: Wonderful Product Hampered With Poor Setup Instructions
text:
April, 2014 - I am a Version FiOS and Mac user. Version provides my internet and cable TV services. All of the Coax cables in the home are connected to our FiOS router. In summary, this is a wonderful product with bad setup instructions. Fortunately, Amazon's reviewers have provided the required setup instructions.

In my situation, the WiFi in the bedroom was slow and unreliable. I finally got tired of waving my MacBook Pro around in a vain attempt to get a stronger signal and decided to do something about it. I read the Amazon customer reviews on the Actiontec Ethernet to Coax Adapter ECB2500C. I chose the line splitter method of connection. Other methods might work, but I know this one works.

I purchased the following items:
Actiontec Ethernet to Coax Adapter ECB2500C
RCA Two Way 3 Ghz Bi-Di Splitter
3ft Coaxial Cable
50 feet of Cat6 Snagless Ethernet Patch Cable

Connecting the Actiontec Adapter:
Unplug the Coaxial TV signal cable from the wall, and attach the new 3ft Coax cable to the wall outlet. Plug the other end of that cable onto the single side of the splitter. Plug the coax cable from the cable box (the one that used to plug into the wall) into one of the double side splitter openings. Now using the coax cable that came in the Actiontec box, plug one end into the Actiontec adapter and the other end into the double side splitter. Now plug in the Actiontec adapter's power brick.

Connecting the Mac:
Turn off your Mac's wireless connection. Turn off your MacBook and plug in the Ethernet cable. If you have a modern MacBook, you will need a Thunderbolt to Gigabit Ethernet Adapter. Turn on the MacBook. Open System Preferences, select Network, click Ethernet connected on the top left of the network screen. Click advanced on the bottom right. Click Renew DHCP lease. Click OK, this takes you back to the Network Panel. Now click Apply and close the network screen. You are now connected.

Actiontec Management:
You have a wonderful product that is handicapped with horrible instructions. Read the comments from Amazon's users and update your instructions. Also provide pictures of how to connect the box in different situations. Provide instructions for people with Windows and Mac's and perhaps Linux. Provide instructions for FiOS and other cable users. This is a wonderful device, it deserves wonderful setup instructions. I did not rate the product down because Amazon users provided appropriate instructions.

title: Lexar shoots and scores
text:
I just ordered two of the 128 GB and two of the 32 GB to go along with two 64GB cards I have.
First, why so many cards and different sizes?
Well, it depends on what you are doing at the time you are taking the photographs.
Last night, I did the photography for a colleagues play that he and his students were putting on and I ended up having to switch cards and still almost ran out of space in four hours (I took a lot of pics of the whole show)... could have probably used the 128 GB.
I also travel a lot and take a lot of nature photographs on two or three week backcountry excursions so I would definitely use the larger cards for that, not being able to dump the cards as often as I would like.

Now, for the cards themselves.
These cards are simply fantastic. I've used them for about two months in my two cameras (the one I specifically bought them for was my new Nikon D-810, but they work just as well in my older olympus body). No transfer errors, no write errors (probably the most important issue to me) and they are fast (I haven't been able to overrun the buffer yet, more than likely because of the card speed). I shoot almost everything in RAW format (full frame) so with the 64 GB card, on the Nikon body, I can store about 780 RAW images so the more cards, the merrier. If you choose to store images in jpeg, you can store a hell of a lot more, depending on the resolution you choose.
I use an external card reader (USB 3.0) on my laptop and a built-in reader on either of my other two computers and pretty much the transfer rate and the read-write speed is the same on either of the computers.
I wouldn't call them cheap but for this type of thing, cheaper isn't necessarily better, especially storing a large number of photos.

text:

title: Remote ruins the whole device
text:
I have had Google TV since the day the Logitech Revue came out. I bought two of these Co-Star boxes. One was to replace the Logitech Revue and the other to add Google TV to another TV in the house. My cable provider (Bright House) has given me two different brands of cable boxes. One is a Cisco box and the other is a Samsung box. Both use the same remote control model and those remotes are interchangeable. During initial set up, I programmed the co-star remote to work with those boxes using the on screen wizard. It didn't take long for me to discover that critical buttons for basic operation of the cable boxes were either improperly mapped or non functional with the co-star. Specifically the back, red, yellow, blue, and green buttons didn't work. The red, yellow and back buttons are heavily used buttons with Bright House boxes and critical for basic operation. Other buttons and the track pad had varying levels of pressure required to work. Sometimes you barely have to press the button and others you have to mash it down. This made it very difficult to use the product.

The custom UI Vizio employed is confusing and at times intuitive. The built in DLNA player does not play MKV's while Logitech's Revue does.

I contacted Vizio support via chat the first time about the button mappings issue. The person responded that I need to contact the cable box manufacturer to get the correct codes. I did so only to have them tell me I need to contact the remote manufacturer (Vizio) to determine which code the remote uses to work with their devices. Bright House also indicated I should contact Vizio. So I re-engaged vizio support via chat and phone. They again told me that they could do nothing about it. During a google search on the problem I ran across a Google TV support page which had an Google TV andriod engineer who indicated that Vizio had control of the remote key mapping loads for their product (sorry I didn't keep the link but will update if I locate it again).

Point of this story is, the remote doesn't work very well if at all. It's poorly designed and difficult to use. It may not even be compatible with your cable box, and support isn't going to help you if you have a problem. The Logitech Revue (Gen 1 Google TV) and the Sony Internet Player (Gen 2 Google TV) both are superior devices to this one. If you are looking for a reason to hate Google TV this is the product to get. If you want a positive experience stay away from this device.
