title: Best value UWA, provided you get a good copy
text:
I owned multiple copies of this lens, having switched between Nikon and Canon bodies. My take on the pros and con are as follows:

Pros:
+ Price/value - the least expensive autofocusing ultra-wide angle (UWA) lens for crop sensor. If you have a good copy it's competitive with the Nikon 10-24 or Canon 10-22.
+ Sharp if you have a good copy - the center is sharp wide open and the corners catch up around f/8 to f/11
+ Good colors/contrast - I found pictures from the 10-20mm to have better contrast and more saturated colors straight out of camera than the Tamron 17-50mm, a lens that pairs well with this lens at around the same price.
+ Solid build quality - no wobbly parts, tightly constructed, and internal focusing (no extending/retracting parts when focusing). The zoom and focus rings both have a solid feel to them.
+ Fast and almost silent autofocus
+ Comes with a 5-year warranty, padded case and hood (Canon only provides 1 year and no accessories for their non-L lenses)
+ Takes 77mm filters - no vignetting even with non-slim frame filters

Con:
- I've mentioned "if you have a good copy" several times. I've tested 5 copies of this total and 3 of them showed some degree of de-centered elements, two obvious. If a glass lens element or group of elements is not aligned or slightly tilted inside the lens, the effect can show up in pictures. The effect is that one side (left, right, top or bottom) will be blurry and out of focus while the other side will be sharp and in focus. To be fair, this isn't a problem limited to this lens - there are copies of the $2000 Nikon 14-24mm or the $1700 Canon 16-35mm that have this problem. The problem does seem more pronounced in UWA lenses, probably due to the large angle of view. How do I test for decentering? Shoot a flat subject (a brick wall, a row of trees or even a grass lawn) but make sure the lens is facing completely perpendicular to the subject. Shooting at a non-90 degree angle will naturally cause one side to be more out-of-focus, especially at wide apertures. If the lens is decentered, it will be most apparent at its widest length and aperture (in this case, 10mm f/4) because the most glass is exposed to the sensor. View the image at 100% on the computer at the sides of the image. Usually most lenses have one side slightly sharper than the other, but if one side is obviously blurrier than the other then it can be a problem in your real-world shots. It's a shame that quality control and manufacturing tolerances have not caught up to eliminate this problem and I've heard that it can be quite time-consuming to fix a decentered lens.

In short, I recommend this lens for its pros but advise you thoroughly test it out when you get it.

title: Cool looking camera that is water resistant
text:
This is my 3rd Sony camera and I have always bought a waterproof housing kit to go along with my cameras. When I saw that the T series was waterproof I decided to make a trip to the Sony store and check it out.

what I needed:
Zoom while video-recording
macro shots - like taking a photograph of your fingerprint if you wanted too
Something sleek and compact - this comes in many colors but I got the black one.

That's pretty much it. I'm not a pro-user. I have a toddler so in addition to carrying all his toys and diaper things I didn't want to lug around a big DSLR.

Pros:
Small, sleek design
Waterproof - when you have a kid, you want to get in on the action with them. I went to a water park and wasn't worried about getting my camera wet.
Optical zoom while recording
With a very fast mover toddler I make use of the multiple frame bursts. You can take up to 10 photos in one instant and when you review it, you tilt the camera and it goes from frame to frame. Pretty cool to see your toddler dancing and you're controlling the speed and the direction he's going in the images.
You can adjust which "buttons" are shown on the LCD screen. Because I use the frame burst feature quite a bit, I added it onto my home screen so I can access it easier.
There are some features where you can make the background fuzzy and focus in on only a certain part of the photo. The image looks like it was taken with a DSLR camera.

Cons:
Takes some time "processing" the image after I finished taking a pic. I think I was using the "intelligent" mode though.
It also takes some time when you can actually scroll through the pics. You have to wait til the page loads and it takes some time. It's kinda irritating.
You can only force flash when you're in certain modes.
The pictures you take during the video are not so good quality.
The touchscreen doesn't compare to the iPhone.

I wish Sony would install some time lapse software and color selection (e.g. take a photo in black and white but select out one or two colors so a red rose and everything else i black and white).

Other than the slowness of the camera I think it's great if you're looking for a rugged camera and if you have a toddler =)

I will definitely buy another waterproof Sony camera after this one.

title: Very good, but watch out for inconsistent quality control!
text:
I used this headset with my iPhone 4S, and waited to put it through its paces with my iPhone 5 before submitting this review. Thankfully, this headset works just great with the iPhone 5.

One of the neatest features with Jabra headsets (including this one) is the ability to monitor the device's battery life without any third-party apps on the iPhone. A little battery bar appears at the top of your screen next to the Bluetooth symbol on your iPhone, which is a really, really handy way to see how much life your headset has left.

Call quality with this headset is excellent, but this excellence comes with some caveats. I have in my possession three Jabra SUPREME headsets. All of them have very different qualities to the person on the other end. My wife can tell me if I'm using headset A, B, or C in a "blind" test. One of the SUPREME headsets is utterly useless, and my wife complains I sound like I'm talking into a bucket. The other two are reasonably similar, but one of them has the edge. Thankfully, it's this one.

Jabra support has been reasonable to deal with regarding getting the bad one replaced, but even then, - let me reiterate, - all three are different. We hope to see some tighter quality control from Jabra in the future to wholeheartedly recommend this headset.

That said, if you can get a good one, you'll be very satisfied.

4 stars out of 5.

title: Excellent headphones, great value
text:
I fly a lot and I've used the Audio-Technica ATH-ANC7B headphones on several trips and around the house since buying them. The noise cancellation performance and audio quality is very good and I think they are an excellent value. They also work without a battery, although the frequency response seems to be noticeably different.

Before I bought these headphones I used a pair of Shure in-ear monitors which provide excellent passive noise attenuation. I've gotten used to using the Shure IEMs for extended periods of time after many years of travel but the Audio Technica ATH-ANC7B headphones are more comfortable for me and I'm sure they would be much more comfortable for most people. The noise attenuation and the sound quality of the ATH-ANC7B's seems to be about the same to me, i.e., very good for both sets of headphones.

The Audio Technica website says that the ANC7B's earcups were "redesigned for greater comfort with generously cushioned padding and a shape that fits easily over any ear". I read some complaints about the size of the earcups for some other Audio Technica headphones which led me to choose the ANC7Bs - I find anything that presses against my ear lobes to be very uncomfortable after a very short period of time. I found that the ANC7Bs are just large enough for my ears - they are completely comfortable for me to wear but if they were any smaller (or my ears any larger) they would definitely be uncomfortable. I tried on a pair of Bose QC-15 headphones after I received the Audio Technica headphones and the Bose headphones definitely feel larger and more comfortable to me.

The headphones come in a relatively flat, attractive hard case. I can fit the case inside my suitcase or computer bag without any difficulty or any fear of damage. The headphones come with adapters for 1/4" and dual-plug airline jacks plus two straight 1/8" cables for connecting the headphones to the audio player. The case has a small pouch attached to the inside of the case that can hold those items plus a spare battery.

The final thing I'll mention is that the other headphones I considered buying were the Bose QC-15 headphones and the less expensive ATH-ANC25 and ATH-ANC27 headphones. . After agonizing about it a little I decided to take a chance and buy a pair of used ATH-ANC7B headphones from Amazon Warehouse Deals for about half of what a new pair would have cost and about 1/4 of the price of the Bose headphones. Amazon said that there might be slight cosmetic issues but the headphones I received appear to be in perfect condition. After my experience with these headphones I'll definitely look at used options that are available for other products. I couldn't be happier with how things turned out.

title: Amazing device
text:
I have been waiting for an awesome tablet worthy of purchase for awhile now. The Asus Transformer Infinity T700T is exactly what I was looking for. I considered getting the 64GB model, but ended up getting the 32GB model shipped overnight, along with four accessories including protection and a 64GB class 10 microSD, for about the price of the 64GB model alone.

I can only give 4 stars however, as the Infinity does seem to have some type of bottleneck or other kink in its internal memory. This is evident by low i/o scores in quadrant, even though the device still ends up with a respectable overall score. Hopefully Asus will be able to address this issue with software and firmware updates, although there is speculation that the hardware used is to blame. Some enthusiasts are exploring utilizing the microSD instead of internal storage, so perhaps even if the hardware is the culprit, a solution may become available.

Otherwise the device is amazing. Web content is very well suited to a 10" handheld touchscreen; forums, images, videos, shopping, email and more all translate beautifully to the slate. Magazines and books look very nice as well, though I prefer eInk for text only books. The screen is very smooth and responsive.

The software was not modified heavily by Asus, a few limited additions and tweaks were included, and are easily deactivated if so desired. Things like a customized notification panel and brightness settings fall into this category. The included branded applications are similarly easy to deactivate. These include a file manager (which is awesome, especially for us nerdy types), a notebook that handles writing and drawing (interesting so far, as a digital notebook has been a desire of mine for some time now), a cloud storage system with 8GB from Asus, and of course the gratuitous media and application store, among others.

Many complaints of Android tablets take the form of "but the applications!", though a collection of millions of applications does not occur overnight. Android is great in that with some determination and patience, one can make whatever application they desire, no 'Store' required. Those of us who are unwilling or unable to write their own applications need not fear, the more Android tablets are out there, the more developers will release tablet optimized programs.

I did cover the Infinity with a Skinomi clear full body protector as soon as I received it, which disappears nicely over the first few days and seems to be a great anti-scratch layer. I have found myself thinking that the screen protector should have come in matte finish though, as the gloss is wicked with glare reflections. I then put the Infinity in a rooCase multiple position folio case, which is great for preventing larger stresses such as bumps, as well as providing a stand that changes to fit the situation. The Jot Classic stylus does seem to stutter across the Skinomi occasionally thus far. I have considered gluing a small bit of lint-free cloth to the disk on the Jot, though this will negate some of the precision the stylus offers.

The 64GB class 10 microSD worked immediately. Others have previously reported problems with cards larger than 32GB, though this appears to have been resolved. I believe that it was formatted exFAT upon arrival.

title: Live up to a high standard, though imperfect
text:
I recently developed a liking for headphones and wanted to try out the 7506, having the impression they were sort of a long-standing classic pair. I also read an extensive report claiming them to be the best pair of over-ear headphones in the $150 MSRP range.

I haven't owned them long enough to say much about durability, and they may have not had enough time to "burn-in" (I'm not confident myself of the importance of burn-in, but it seems to be a widespread-enough idea that I do give my headphones a short burn-in), but so far I agree that they are a great pair of headphones. They have a much more even or flat response than any popular pair of headphones to be sure, but my primary comparison is my go-to pair of Sennheiser 380 Pros. They are both phenomenal sounding. The best way I've found to describe the difference is that the 380s lean just slightly towards the lower frequencies, and the 7506s towards the brighter side. The 380s have a wider soundstage, as well (probably because of the larger ear cups and distance between the speakers and your ears). As a result, there were some songs that felt more rich from the 380s...but some songs that felt more exciting from the 7506s.

The 7506s have a relaxed fit, and the pads are quite soft. They will likely make contact with your ears, and I do feel some fatigue after extended listening. I have a very big head and typical sized ears, which is why I opted for the 380 Pros as my first pair...the ear cups are massive, very large and deep, and make no contact with your ears, but the headphones are heavier and grip tighter, so instead of any ear fatigue you feel a fair amount of warmth. The 7506s have padding on the speakers themselves, as well, inside the ear cup, so the contact with your ears is padded. They are lightweight and don't grip too hard. The headband is comfortable, though I noticed it tends to grab my hair more than I'm used to.

I don't like the coiled cable, though it is more lightweight than the one on my 380s, so it's a bit more manageable. I also don't like that the cable can't be removed, and therefore not easily replaced.

The ear cups don't swivel side to side very far, but can flip all the way around, and are on a hinged arm. You can sort of push them up against the headband (with the two ear pads together) to make the set pretty compact, and there's a basic storage bag that they'll fit in. They're fairly mobile.

I also noticed that the best place to grip the cups as you put them on or take them off is covered with the same thin material that's on the ear pads. It makes me think this will probably wear out fairly fast, but that's sort of a nit-picking detail.

I'm fairly new to the audio scene and don't pretend to be an expert, but hopefully this can give a wide audience an idea of what these headphones are like. I give them 4-stars for a satisfactory, but not exceptional, product. You are getting what you pay for, but in my opinion, not more.

I'll probably update this review once I've used them a bit more extensively.

Additional comments:

I've now owned these for nearly 4 months, and have used them quite a bit.

They aren't so great for using at my DJing jobs. While their mobility helps, they don't produce massive volume, and they don't isolate all that well. This makes it a bit hard to listen to songs in advance before including them in my set, with the music blasting from my system.

They are, however, unquestionably, the best flat-response audio I've ever heard in headphones. No range is neglected or favored. When I mentioned earlier that they make some songs more "exciting" than my 380 pros, I was hearing the crispness these songs bring to audio, particularly in the mids and trebles, where other headphones couldn't seem to be bothered. I was listening to some vocal-heavy music (ie Sam Smith) the other night on another pair, and was just feeling unsatisfied...then I switched to the 7506s, and suddenly the vocals came alive. Vibrant, deliciously crisp, presented on a silver platter. Where my 380 pros still make some dance beats and music that shines with the bass cranked up more punchy, the 7506s just can't be beat in showing you the music in its pure, raw form.

Another update:

These continue to shine as magnificent headphones. I continue to be more impressed the more I learn about audio. I'm going to bump my rating to 5 stars. Of the headphones I own, these are the most satisfying as far as sound is concerned. I do feel like the comfort could be better, but it's not drastic enough to deny that last star. They also, as I mentioned, aren't ideal for DJing, but since they aren't advertised/meant for such purposes, I won't hold this against them either.

title: Great Network-Ready AV Receiver
text:
I've owned this AV receiver for a couple weeks now and am quite happy with its performance. I opted to network it by connecting it via Cat6 cable to an 8-port Gigabit network switch, which is then connected to a universal WiFi adapter that is connected to the 5-GHz band on my dual-band WiFi router. I have been able to stream Pandora, Internet radio (vTuner), and audio/video via AirPlay from my MacBook Pro with iTunes without issue.

I can confirm that the user interface experience is a bit dull (e.g. grey, no on-screen keyboard, etc), but it functions well enough, so I can't complain. I have other devices (e.g. Roku 2) with better interfaces that I'll likely continue to do most of my streaming from. The HDMI overlay setup menu is an independent mode, but I'm not sure why others are finding that to be a fault as I would not want a video stream to be playing in the background while I was trying to read the white text of the setup menu and make changes.

I was a bit disappointed to learn, after getting the AV receiver networked, that it is unable to update its firmware automatically. Instead, it detects that a new firmware version is available (after checking over the Internet) and then provides you with instructions for downloading the update from a computer and applying it with a USB thumbdrive. As a result, the primary purpose for networking the AV receiver is to enable AirPlay support.

The ControlApp works great on my Android smartphone running the "Gingerbread" (v2.3.4) version of the OS. After detecting the AV receiver, it downloads a small update to the app, which permits you to control the volume (using an on-screen dial) and toggle between the input sources. I find that I can use either the included remote control or the Android app interchangeably, without having to toggle anything on the AV receiver itself.

I use "Direct" stereo mode with some fantastic Pioneer floor standing loudspeakers with MCACC enabled. The audio output to the speakers has been incredible. I am hearing things in HDTV streams that I've never heard before.

I have a Wii connected to the Composite input and can confirm that 1080p up-sampling works without a hitch. Sometimes there is some very subtle flicker along the bottom/top of the image, but it seems to go away after a minute or two. This is an up-sampled image, so its graphical quality is not improved, but simply made compatible with the HDMI output provided to my TV.

I also have my non-HDMI Xbox 360 (in HD mode) connected to the Component input and can confirm that 720p/1080i passthrough is supported. Unfortunately, 1080p passthrough is not supported over the Component input (aside: I've verified that my Xbox 360 can support 1080p resolution by connecting it directly to my HDTV). When attempting this feat, sound was successfully played, but no image was displayed on my 1080p HDTV. After my initial disappointment, I have resolved to use my Xbox 360 in 1080i mode.

My remaining devices (Cable Box, Roku 2, and PS3) are connected via HDMI and work flawlessly. I have noticed that switching input sources is not instantaneous. The delay (usually less than 5-sec) is compounded by my HDTV going into "Searching for Signal" mode whenever a switch is made. I have an older HDTV from 2007, so newer TVs that "find" signals faster will likely have reduced delays between switched feeds. From everything that I've read, my observed delay is pretty typical of AV receivers switching between concurrently executing audio/video sources and has much to do with the amount of processing enabled. This performance is not a deal breaker for me, as I'm usually using a particularly input source exclusively for some period of time before switching to another. I have no need to rapidly bounce back-and-forth between input sources.

I am very pleased with this product and look forward to being able to test its 3D passthrough capability when affordable consumer devices begin to appear on the market in the coming years.

text:
April 2014 Update.

As one of the first purchasers of this tablet, I have now been using it several months. This update was actually motivated by an action by Dell. I have moved it up to 4 stars, and replaced my initial negative experience with this update as I feel the product as it ships today no longer has the negative aspects that the "first adopters" like myself experienced. Give me a version with 128GB and a wacom and you will have a 5-star product.

title: Almost worthy successor to the MX-2, Matricom just raised the bar kindof BUT some bugs still
text:
UPDATE (12/01/14):
After using for 3 days would probably would give it 2.5-3.5 stars due to several 'bugs' and minor annoyances that hopefully Matricom can fix in next update soon.

Shutdown NOT the same as Power Off (-0.5):
Before I explain more, please note that I think when you "shutdown/turn off" you're not truly powering off the device like on the MX-2. The only way I've found so far to "recover from soft brick" like while updating from preloaded firmware to 1.1, is to first try shutting down, then remove the power cord, wait 20 seconds, then re-insert power chord. Other reviewers or people having issues should try this, but maybe wait 20-30minutes even while screen went black, coz it appears something working in background, at least in the meantime.
In future, can "shutdown" = "turn and power completely off", i.e. you shouldn't have to physically disconnect power chord everytime

Remote 'too' sensitive & needs play/stop button (-0.5):
Even though i still use wireless keyboard and xbmc/kodi apps on tablet/phone, the 2 out of 3 times you use the included remote it does "skip" or double press almost any of the keys. It does take some getting used to, and still not huge, but can Matricom maybe tweak and make button press commands slightly less sensitive in next update? Probably people are used to the old remote which required the thumb strength of the hulk and the persistence of serial stalker!
Also, too late for me, but if Matricom gets a chance to update/modify the hardware of the next remote, please include a dedicated Play/Pause and Stop button at least.

Couple times, had to 're-enter' wifi settings(-0.5):
I've had to re-enter wifi credentials on two separate occasions. It's only happened twice so far, but dont recall having this issue on mx-2 (except for the last firmware 1.2 update, side note- I recommend rolling back back to 1.19 on MX-2), but hopefully doesn't happen again. Some people are experiencing some issues with the ethernet plug, i personally can't speak to that, but if that's the case then Matricom may have found the holy grail of electronics by making the ethernet connection more buggy than wifi!!!

USB hub(-0.25-5):
mentioned previously this box only has 2 USB2.0 instead of the 4 USB ports on MX-2. I tried one USB hub (unpowered) to no avail, however, it wasn't the greatest USB hub and fairly economical, but seemed to work with my old laptop fine. Again, maybe I need to try a good hub with separate power connection (more cables) if wanting 3 or more USB devices plugged in at same time (DVD/Blu-ray, HDD, wireless keyboard, flash drive etc).

Menu screen(-0.25-5):
coupled with the included remote, my wife struggled to click on the "media" icon and browse through some of the other apps. I think in next firmware update Matricom should update firmware.

Overview:
The box has potential, but away from the hype, needs some firmware and software updates very soon (please make sure testing of new firmware is done thoroughly beforehand) and make the whole setup and icons more intuitive. Please include Kodi/XBMC logo and the ability/option to go straight to kodi/xbmc next time.

I would recommend holding off on ordering this just yet, but if Matricom's track record is anything to go by, there should be updates within a couple months and most get resolved, then definitely get one, minus the hassle!
Other reviewers giving 1 star is unfair, even at this stage, movies, shows, music is smoother on this than the MX-2 and the picture quality is better (true 1080 this time).

ORIGINAL REVIEW (11/28/14):
I have tried several media/tv boxes in the past couple years, and prior to this G-Box Q I had the Matricom MX2 which was easily the best of the bunch at the time, even with the "kindof 1080 but not really true 1080".

I had high expectations on this box, and there were ideally a number of things i wanted Matricom to fix from the flaws/issues with the MX2. But let's start with the negatives, get those out the way, of which in this case several are non-issues to me but may be a 'hassle' to others...

Cons:
- No clear Guide/Instruction Manual as to how to set it all up etc which may be a concern to some who rely on guides/instructions manual. (Not an issue to me, as software, skins etc can change so much and is so configurable, a quick google search, yahoo or forums have plenty of recent walkthrough guides with pics etc)
- Two less USB ports this time ('only' 2 instead of 4 on the previous gen MX-2) *Might* be an issue to me and others especially if you have at least two plugged in with peripherals, particularly wireless keyboard/remote and HDD. I am not sure if a USB would work to increase number of USB ports or if its worth it, I dont think so. Another reason if you have an external DVD/Blu-Ray drive, you would have to choose which two of the three you need plugged in at same time.
- USB is 'only' 2.0 i.e. no superspeed USB 3.0, so plugging in an external HDD or storage device if on USB 3.0 wont run at its max speeds. Again, may be an issue for some wanting max speeds transferring/streaming data if required, not really for me.

Pros:
1) Cleaner, more professional package, compared to previous version, light years ahead (see pic for comparison)
2) Remote Control much better, simpler & cleaner, HOWEVER, buttons may now be too/over-sensitive, but compared to previous one, i don't mind better sensitivity (the last one was annoying when the "OK" button would need to be firmly pressed repeatedly, but not an issue with this one). Plus I and many others use XBMC/KODI apps on their tablets/phones anyway.
P.s. The remote control requires 2 AAA batteries (not included)!
3) Pre-packaged software a lot cleaner, similar kindof to PS3/PS4 menus, I think it can be configured and tweaked, but haven't tried, and i'm ok with it currently, might change in a couple weeks/months
4) Hardware is so much smoother, a LOT less buffering, quicker menu responses, i'm guessing between the faster CPU, GPU, memory and internal storage, should be able to stream consistently quicker - this is probably the overriding benefit.

SETUP:
First time, i was concerned, it seemed to get stuck when it was auto-updating both/either the firmware and android OS and my TV screen went black. i left for about 30 minutes and restarted the TV but couldn't tell if it was going to be ok. I first tried turning off power with remote, but no luck, then I bit the bullet and unplugged the power, waited 10 seconds, reconnected and seemed to be ok, had to go back to settings screen click on "install update" icon after it had downloaded and we were "ready".

Step two, is setting up XBMC/KODI. There are many sites and guides but a couple v good and clear step by step ones with pics are the "xbmc hub" (becoming kodi), 'tvaddons' and the various wikis. there are simple guides that require a few clicks and searching and dont require much customization, helpful if its your first time or are unsure, then there are more complete. So far Kodi and the work of the xbmc/kodi community is very impressive. Hats off to all the developers for simplifying it, I know a lot of hard work has gone into it, especially in last 12 months.

Step three, you can install apps from play store and tweaks, but honestly, use it almost entirely for watching movies, streaming news and add-ons.

Honestly, for the price and checking out the competition, even if you have a "Smart" (lol) TV or other device, this has become essential, and am very tempted to now by another one or two, for my other tv and as a gift.

SUMMARY:
Very good, for the price and quality I don't think you can beat it, once you get it setup and use it for a couple days or so, you will not turn back. a few minor things that may or may not be issues to everyone, but for me the benefits far outweigh anything, and very pleased with the improvements over the previous model.

title: So far, so good!
text:
I go through so many of these things--it's my observation that headsets designed for mobile phones around the $20 mark are generally disposable garbage. But for lack of choices the last time I went to buy a pair, I purchased this set.

I really like them so far. I've had and used them daily for two months. As others have reported, sound quality is good. In general, I find the clip-over-the-ear style of headphone to be more comfortable, and slipping them down to my neck when I need to is a breeze. Plus, if you have long hair, it's much easier to keep them clear of your hair. Just slip them under your hair around the back of your neck, then lift them up to your ears. Easy. Hair's not messed up.

Do watch yourself with the mic and drinking beverages. :P I've nearly drown mine in tea a number of times, but the mic is flexible and still achieves good sound with it moved far afield of your intended beverage.

The plastic from which the set is constructed is flexible and less apt to break (I've had others made of brittle plastic that didn't even last a month), BUT I must say I have never used the hinges for folding them up. (I didn't even know they were hinged until I read these reviews!) That's probably important, since that seems to be what breaks for most people. So if you don't need to fold them up, don't. They'll likely last longer.

I'm going to buy another pair for a friend who has the same woes with disposable headsets, and tell him the same thing I'm explaining here about not folding them. But I will say, if/when this pair breaks, I'll be damned if I buy another $20 pair of headphones for my phone. :)

First, the tripod doesn't need instructions unless you've never seen a tripod before!
Second, the panel clips are difficult to work with until you realize that that they 'clamp down' facing center flat against the panel. You'll need to be sure to push the center locking pin on the clamp completely though both panels or the panel and tripod support. Once you have the clip completely though lock it down.
When you clamp the clip you'll see the center lock. Make turn to secure it in place.
The clamp is very tight but necessary, after all you don't want the clips to be anything but tight. -You don't want the panel to fall from the tripod and possibly get damaged! -

title: Wonderful tablet!
text:
This tablet is awesome. I bought it for school primarily, but I now use it for just about everything. It almost replaces my laptop! I use it to take notes, read books or papers, grade papers, watch videos, listen to music... really for everything. It's large but once you get used to it, it seems totally normal and then typical 10" tablets look tiny. The S-pen is amazing! I take notes all the time using the S-pen with handwriting detection, and my handwriting isn't perfect. Occasionally it guesses wrong and I have to rewrite it, but overall it works enough to be more efficient than using a Bluetooth keyboard. I also like to draw and the S-pen is fabulous for that with the write drawing app (e.g., Sketchbook Pro). It is incredibly precise, moreso than any stylus I've tried--and I have tried many. I don't really need a new phone but my next phone will probably be a Samsung Galaxy Note (whatever is new by the time I need one) because my experience with the S-pen on this tablet has been so positive. Multitasking is useful but it would be nice if it worked with more apps. Occasionally when I'm multitasking the handwriting detection will start acting up, rebooting the tablet fixes it though.

The only downside to the 12.2 inch tablet is the lack of accessories. The only nice folio case I could find for it had a very tiny keyboard, which was unfortunately a deal breaker for me. The case with the best keyboard isn't a real folio case and doesn't offer much cushion or protection for the tablet.

A note to other owners: several months after buying this tablet I did have some issues. The tablet started crashing a lot and was agonizingly slow. I contacted Samsung about it and they said I could send it in for warranty repair, which I really didn't want to do. I ended up removing the microSD card I was using with the tablet and viola, problems fixed. It stopped crashing and ran like new again! Not sure exactly why this happened but if anyone is experiencing these symptoms and sees this review, maybe it'll help you.

title: Great Laptop... Until I sent it in for repair
text:
I bought this laptop new in July as a college graduation present from my parents. I was incredibly happy with the laptop... at first. I was excited to be able to game (play WoW at reasonable FPS for raiding and little latency; exciting for a little machine!!!). I had to laptop for just over two months and a USB port stopped working. After an over-the-phone attempt fix to see if it was a software problem, I had to mail the laptop in. I was guaranteed repair and having it hipped back in 5-7 business days. Over 3 weeks later, I finally received my laptop from the repair center complete with a damaged inner box where the repair center dropped the laptop. (There was a box packed in a box, so it couldn't have been from shipping.) Taking the computer straight out of the box, the track pad did not work properly which was not an issue I had when I sent it in. After calling Samsung they apologized about the broken track pad and the time it took to repair, but insisted they do not quote times for repair.... Okay, fine, you had one misinformed customer service rep. The agent I was dealing with them told me I needed to return the laptop again and I would "get it back when I got it back." Apparently, according to this agent, Samsung policy is that the repair center gets three attempts to take their time and return the laptop to you and it's not until after the third time that they offer refunds or exchanges. With the help of Amazon, I ended up getting a full refund, but I would not have been able to by myself. I will *never* purchase nor recommend another Samsung product nor laptop to anyone, ever; You've been warned about their "repairs," customer support, and faulty laptop repair policy.

PS- Thank you Amazon for helping me correct the issue so I could have a college graduation laptop that brings me smiles, plenty of gaming, and isn't a Samsung.

title: Read the description very carefully as it can be misleading.
text:
I just purchased this product from Amazon. In reading the description of "Sony 150 Expanded Long Range..." I thought these were better than the Sony MDRRF985RK wireless headset selling for $73.99 (today on Amazon) and some $4 less at our club discount store. So, I made the Amazon purchase and I also bought the $69.99 ones at our club store.

Upon receipt I thought I would compare the sound, range, etc. Will, I didn't even plug in the Amazon ones selling for twice as much as they are in fact the same, MDRRF985RK wireless headset. Normal list price is $109.99, but as I mentioned they can be purchase for a lot less. The Amazon "bundle" includes a dbTech Digital to Analog converter ($29.99 in prime) for TVs without an analog converter. OK, now I understand the bundle description. Amazon's description with "Expanded Long Range" makes it sound like these are a better headset when in fact they are the same product. Amazon's price for the MDRRF985RK is $73.99, add in the $29.99 converter (if you really need it) and this totals $103.98 if purchased separately, which is a lot less than the $139.95 Amazon wants for the bundle. I should add that I have returned this "bundle" to Amazon and will now purchase another headset by itself as the sound is very good compared to my old Advent wireless headset. Additionally, changing frequencies with the auto-tune is great. The volume adjuster is somewhat difficult to locate, but a spot of hot-glue nearby will solve this concern.

Oh, about the "expanded" 150' range. This is the normal, typical range for the MDRRF985RK. Which I found not to be the case in my house as I moved from room to room. However, in the same room with the transmitter they work great, even near my wireless PC and phones. Hence, the 3-star rating.

Anyway long story short I contacted AmScope customer support and they agreed to swap out the 5X eyepiece for a 20X eyepiece ... making my microscope identical to this model.

I was happy with AmScope customer support, they were prompt, courteous, and effective. (You do have to deal with technical support through email however.)

I am very happy with this microscope for use with SMT electronics. Allows enough room between the objective lens and the board to get in a probe, or soldering iron to do work.

Like most binocular microscopes, you have to carefully adjust the distance between eyepieces (simply move them), and then focus on your subject with your right eye only, then with your left eye only, adjust the left eyepiece to get a clear picture in your left eye. (After that you only need to use the main focusing knob to focus on your different subjects). Once done, the view is nice and clear through both eyes. For the money, can't beat it.

The version of the microscope I received was slightly different than that pictured. My microscope has a long flexible metal "boom" that comes up from the base, allowing you to position the light as you prefer. The light is not halogen, but a very bright LED .... Runs cooler than halogen, and (in theory) should last a whole lot longer than the halogen bulb. For my purposes, the light is plenty bright.

Another reviewer complained about vibrations in the view... (Perhaps he was doing some sort of time-lapse photography or something.) ... Anyway for my purposes, I find the stand to be sturdy. When I place my eyes up against the rubber eyepiece "thingies", I find no problems with "view vibration".

title: Not ready for "Prime Time".
text:
This product works great, as long as you don't attempt to store any data on it. And I'm not being sarcastic.
The device has a browser based configuration front-end, which stops working after about 1 TB of data is stored. At the same time, the cloud aspect also become inaccessible, making the unit basically useless. On the local LAN, the stored files are still accessible, but no cloud access.
I found that, after a reboot, the configuration access works for about 40 seconds, not enough time to do anything important, then it's "Page not found".
Western Digital support had me reboot, system restore, reformat, change RAID types, hard reset, etc. Nothing worked. I returned the unit and got a refund, but had to pay for shipping. That sucked!
I purchased the Seagate Business Storage NAS 16TB. About the same price as the Western Digital. So far it is working perfectly. I will write a separate review.
I won't condemn the Western Digital Corp., or this particular product. I may have simply gotten a lemon. But the problems exhibited, appear to me to be firmware related. I hope they resolve the issue, but I would NOT recommend this product to anyone.

Update:
I read some of the other negative reviews (someone else said "Not ready for primetime", interesting), and had one suspicion confirmed. When copying a large amount of data, the system gets busy indexing, and becomes inaccessible, but does eventually come back to life after a few days or weeks. Anybody else see a problem with that? Seems like that would be easy for WD to fix. I can say, as a Software QA person, that a company that does not fix the little bugs will nerver fix the big ones.

title: Nice little pouch and it ships fast.
text:

To my surprise I received this item to the USA in 4 working days on a Saturday. So bravo to the seller for the quick shipment.

Now on to the product review.

After putting in my 3 ND & 3 Grad-ND P-series filters, there is one more spare spot for a 7th filter. On top of that, I can, as the picture shows, store my cokin filter holder in there as well. The dividers inside are held in place by velcro which can be adjusted easily. The only thing I couldn't fit in there was the sun-visor attachment, but I think I can live with that.

The pouch is nice and compact and sports a flap, held also by velcro, to attach to your belt. I personally like the small compact size, as opposed to another model I bought for the bigger Z and X-series filters.

The material is very nice, seems like it will hold up to some wear and tear, however, in looking over the stitching, I am concerned that some of the stitch work will eventually come undone. This shouldn't be a problem, I am sure when that happens, I can get it sewn back together.

There is enough space inside to access the filters and the material inside is soft so it won't scratch your filters. At the bottom of the removable fan-fold filter holder there's a strap that I had to adjust as I felt it was too tight, and it didn't need to be, because the filters still are secured. The top of the fan-fold also has an elastic-strap as well to lock the filters so they won't fall out by accident. It seems there are plenty of safe-guards to prevent your filters from falling out.

The zippers themselves seem quite good. Since I recently got this, I've found the zippers on my unit to function well (as intended). I will update this if anything does go awry.

For the most part, I am very impressed with this item that came from China. I am giving this a 4 out of 5 stars, as the stitching seems it might fall apart and doesn't seem very durable. Other than that, I think it will hold up to some good use over the years.

If hooking up the TV to a 5.1 system or a Sonos soundbar or something then I might have considered a series which was a bit thinner, but we knew this would be a standalone item, and hence why these inbuilt speakers are so pleasing for us.

I personally like the Samsung Smart interface and how easy it is to set up.

One feature we were really surprised by and made it a wow moment for us was "screen mirroring" from an Amazon Kindle Fire to the TV.
We download shows to our Kindle Fire (of which there are loads of free stuff when you have Prime! - Love Amazon Prime!) and then can play them through our TV as they "wirelessly detect" each other. Its kinda like having a built in Chromecast but with more content possibilities and then you get great other features like xRay information during playback of content ( this is a Kindle Fire/Amazon Instant Video feature - but is so cool mirrored on this TV!)

This works super will for us as we have this TV at our cabin which has no wireless or cable and so our plan was to hook up a DVD player. Now we don't even need the DVD player and so just have a beautiful looking and sounding screen on the wall and no messy wires and devices attached.

title: Great for Movies!
text:
Great for movies, but not much else, unfortunately. Get this if you're a fan of Windows 8.

Some background: I received an Insignia Tablet with the Google Android operating system on it last year for Christmas and I love it! I have only three issues with Android: 1) It doesn't have Office, 2) it can't print and 3) the pop-up keyboard isn't the easiest to type on. For these three reasons, I found myself using a desktop PC for many things and wished I had a better tablet solution.

I thought this Acer Aspire Switch 10" was the solution... but, no. This PC/tablet does have Office, a removable keyboard, and it can print to a wireless printer. It also has a larger, high quality screen to watch videos, which is quite nice. The real problem with this device is the Windows 8x Operating System. It's HORRIBLE! To me, it's a half baked operating system on top of Windows that's not integrated. Here are some examples:

1) It locks up - no surprise there. It's Windows.
2) The pop-up keyboard doesn't automatically pop-up when in Windows, making it a pain to use. It pops-up as expected in the "tablet like" interface.
3) If you don't want to use a Microsoft mail product (which I don't), the tablet interface launches a web browser for email. When you're done, it doesn't automatically bring you back to the tablet interface where you started, further evidence of non-integration.
4) When I watch Netflix movies using the Netflix app, it interrupts me every time going into Windows telling me I plugged headphones in. Then because the Netflix app isn't integrated, I have to manually go back to the tablet interface and launch it again.
5) It's not a real tablet so app choices are limited. I have apps on my Google device that I'd like to continue to use and they're just not available.

My guess is if I wanted to spend hours and hours figuring out how to configure it, I could find a fix to these issues, but I don't. I'd much rather use a real tablet interface. This needs to be more integrated to be a viable solution.

If it were possible to install Android or ChromeOS or some other flavor of Linux on this hybrid tablet, I'd give that a try, but nowhere online have I found anyone having success doing this. If you get this Acer Aspire Switch 10", you are locked into Windows 8, and all that entails.

title: The Little Travel Router that Can
text:
Impressed. I find the ZONET zsr4174we router quite easy to work with and surprisingly flexible. In particular, it's PPTP VPN feature is compatible with the popular HideMyAss VPN service to enable NetFlix access outside of the USA. It WiFi connects to my Apple TV 2012. Here's how.

Plug a live Ethernet cable from your router into the ZONET. Use the ZONET's hardware mode switch to select Wireless Router. Pause for the reboot. Use the ZONET's web page (Wireless N SSID, 192.168.2.1, admin/admin) setup to specify the following along with the usual router setups (change admin/admin password, provide a WiFi passwod, change SSID, whatever). For Apple TV 2012 device, use "WPA2 - Personal" security mode with AES encryption algorithm. If you screw up the Zonet's settings, you can reset the router by holding down the mode/reset button for 30 seconds.

1. PPTP Server: <some HMA PPTP ip server address>
2. User Name: <your HMA username>
3. Password: <your HMA PPTP password (not your web login password)>
4. MTU: <use the default>
5. Address Mode: <select Dynamic>
6. MPPE: <must be checked>
7. It should automatically connect to the HMA server. Check the Status page to verify.
8. The ZONET is now a VPN connected wireless router. Just point your device at the SSID.

I haven't found any firmware updates but then I don't have any issues.

title: Let me clear some things up
text:
First, this review is based on value, what you get for your money. Is it the very best bracket made? No. Is it worth the money? Without question. Now, let's clear some things up that others have written. Someone wrote that he has a 7D and there is no room between the camera and the vertical bracket for his hand, even at the farthest setting. Either ephoto changed their design since his review or he's laughably unqualified to write a review. I have a 60D which is nearly identical in size to the 7D and and it fits perfectly and comfortably when mounted in the middle position where you see the camera mounted in the picture. I then moved it to the farthest setting (as he indicated he had) and I could fit my arm in the space between the camera and the bracket. It's about 4.5 inches of space. People also complained that the arm is loose. What? Tighten the nut that holds the arm which is designed with washers that act as spacers to hold tension for such adjustments. It would have taken less time to do that than write your review. If you ask "Why should I have to adjust or tighten anything?" BECAUSE IT WAS $20! Twenty very well spent dollars. In addition, it holds the camera steady without twisting. This done by the camera being tightened down onto a rubberized pad. (My Manfrotto bracket has a horrible problem with loosening and twisting). Lastly, I use it with my 60D with a Pocket Wizard TT1 AND zone controller mounted on the hot shoe and it fits perfectly with about half an inch to spare below the top bracket. I did have to adjust the height by loosening the screws on the side and sliding it up to the tallest setting (again, as it was designed to do). Also, all the aforementioned adjustments took me less than 30 seconds. It literally took longer to get the tools out than it did to adjust the bracket to suit my needs.

In a nutshell- After exhaustive research and months of waiting to pull the trigger- I could not be happier!

The hardest part of the repair job was removing the original cracked screen. It sprayed tiny glass shards everywhere while I pried it off so wear eye protection. Some latex gloves are a good idea too. It took about 20 minutes of gentle prying around the perimeter to get it off. Blowing a hot hair dryer on the edges seemed to make the glue softer and easier to unstick. Amazingly, the old screen still worked after it was removed (before I unplugged its ribbon cable) while completely shattered. The other slightly tricky part was removing the home button from the old screen and getting it lined up properly on the new screen. I ended up having to place the button assembly on the contacts in the iPad so it would adhere to the screen in the right spot once the screen was stuck back on. Overall, a repair that can be done at home with minimal tools. There are some good videos on youtube that show the whole process so check those out before you decide to purchase.

Back in November 2011 I decided that 7" tablets were the sweet spot for me, roughly the same size as a paper back novel, and about the same weight, I was going to get a Dell Streak7 but Dell discontinued it, so I ended up buying three Samsung Tab 7.0 plus in early 2012, I was quite happy with them, until I dropped mine just about a year later and broke the glass - the 7.0 plus has been discontinued, so I replaced it with the Tab2 7.0, the subject of this review.

I'm a wee bit disappointed that it does not have 5GHz WiFi, but I can live without it, the same goes for the flash on the rear facing camera, and delighted to find that the Tab2 has much better battery life than my old 7.0 plus - I have no idea if this is OS or hardware related as the 7.0 plus is running Ice Cream Sandwich, and the Tab2 7.0 is running Jelly Bean - but with the 7.0 plus I could easily drain the battery in a couple of hours and had to remember to disable the WiFi when not using it, the Tab2 in contrast has been running with the WiFi on for over two days on the initial battery charge.

Well - after six months with the Tab2, I am out of storage space - my not so favorite app, Zinio, for reasons best known to them (and despite promises to do so) won't let me store magazines on the SD card and filled up my storage.

I dragged out the old Tab 7.0+ and found a genuine Samsung digitizer on ebay and fixed it - the colors on the old 7.0+ are much more vivid than the Tab2.

title: The perfect size and an excellent tab for the price
text:
I've used my Galaxy 3.0 tablet for 2 weeks, every day, and I couldn't be happier. I find the screen to be great, very sharp and very responsive, and am not having any issues with rapid discharge - in fact I have been able to go 2+ days on one charge as long as I let the tablet sleep when I am not using it. I purchased one of the cases that put the tablet in sleep mode when the cover is closed, and this may be hapling with battery life. So far I have not watched videos much but I have spent lots of time on the internet, listening to music (through earbuds) and on youtube and with multiple apps open at the same time.

I often edit documents and photos on the tab and am very happy with its performance. OTG capability is a must for me as I use my tablet as a laptop replacement when I travel and I need to be able to transfer files from SD cards and USB drives. File transfer and uploading/downloading to the internet are all very fast, much faster than my previous android tab, which was a relatively new and very well-rated 10-inch tab from a different manufacturer. I have a Motorola bluetooth keyboard which works beautifully with this Samsung tab (all the keys work properly with no resetting).

I am finding the 8-inch size to be perfect for me, just big enough for all the "work" I do (file and photo editing) and for watching videos but small enough to be very easily transportable. It is also a perfect size for reading (eg using the Kindle app), and the tablet has a "reading mode" setting that is easily accessible that optimizes the screen for such apps.

A few caveats - I use a Samsung Galaxy phone and so am used to the Samsung interface and am a fan of it. I like the external buttons and I love that my phone and tablet interface so well. Also, I have small hands so am not bothered by small buttons or form factor. I am not a gamer so do not use my tab with those apps.

I am very happy with my purchase.

title: So far, pretty good with IMPORTANT information about restore process
text:
If you don't read my review PLEASE JUST READ THIS!

If you do the Operating System Restore process using the Lenovo Software, DO NOT USE AN EXTERNAL HARD DRIVE THAT ALREADY HAS DATA ON IT. The process will wipe the hard drive clean of all other data. (And there was no warning before hand. Real bummer.) They recommended using an external hard drive at the beginning of the process saying it would be more stable but who would have thought it was gonna take the entire 2T bite hard drive over and wipe it clean. To create restore disks, you will need either an external DVD burner and a few DVDs (it's a little over 8GB of data that will be transferred over) or, as I later found out, you can also use a blank 16GB USB Flash drive.

OK so, I got mine from Computer Upgrade King. Pretty decent guy to deal with.

As you read this review, bare in mind that I got mine 4 days ago and am still testing it out.

UPDATE: It's now been a few weeks that I've been using this laptop and I am updating this review as I come across things I encounter.

The look and feel of the laptop is sturdy.

LENOVO SUPPORT
I have been relatively happy with their support. 24/7 tech support but I just discovered, after a call about bluetooth (I could not access the software so I could not pair my new headset) that their tech support is only for hardware issues and that Tech support for software issues is a paid service. May be so with all the companies but this is the first time I had it explained to me that way. Anyhow, I did some more digging and found my fix. I went to Lenovo to see if there was a driver download for Bluetooth and there was. I installed it, rebooted and that was what I needed. Easy peasy pairing my headset (which, by the way was a Targus TA-44-HP-BT in case your interested.)

PERFORMANCE
My machine came with 4GB Ram and the AMD- A4 5000 process (1.5GHZ). I have to say I wasn't crazy about it getting choked up a few times. I read reviews of others complaining about this but, I didn't understand how that happened with 4gigs of ram installed. But this is my first experience with a Windows 7 OS and it's "bazillion" services and processes running in the background so that may be part of the problem. At one point when I opened Task Manager, the CPU usage was at 100% or fluctuated between 60% and 100% and the Ram used was 3 1/2 gigs and just Windows Update was open along with the Lenovo System Software. I couldn't do anything but wait. I actually disabled Windows Update for now and, so far, no choke ups. I'll update on my own time schedule, not theirs. But all this had me concerned so I called the tech support and the guy told me about hitting the F10 key at boot up which opens up a whole array of diagnostics. I ran the battery of tests (some tests take hours so be aware of that) and I passed them all. Another nice feature from Lenovo. So, if you're expecting this thing to perform like a "work horse" that can run a few programs at a time, it will definitely depend on which programs and the resources they require.

KEYBOARD
I really like the keyboard. As good as an old Dell laptop I had which was my standard for a laptop keyboard. Slightly indented so it cradles your fingertips a bit. And it's not cramped at all as I expected being a small laptop. Everything is so well placed that I was typing in the dark. Well, everything but the FN key. Why they put the FN key where the CTR key goes is a mystery to me. But there is a fix if you check out the manual. You can swap them.

CUSTOMIZATIONS
I was surprised at how many customizations they offer to you. It's in the boot up process. Check out the manual for that. Really nice options for a tweaker.

SOUND
Sound through the speakers is loud as laptops go so, if listening to the spoken word, it will do fairly well. But forget about thinking that it having Dolby means it's gonna sound good with music. Very light on the bass and thin sound through the speakers. I am not happy with the sound coming from the headphone jack (or the Bluetooth Headphones) when listening to music or movies. I was spoiled by my Toshiba Thrive. The Thrive had a warm, full sound coming from the head jack so this will be something to get used to.

VIDEO
Once again, I have a Toshiba Thrive tablet and it has a great HD screen so that was my standard. I watched an HD movie last night on the Lenovo and it was equally as good.

SCREEN
I thought the screen colors were a bit washed out but, what I discovered is that, in order to get the best viewing experience color wise, the screen has to be tilted back somewhat more than I expected.

WEBCAM
Couldn't get any specs on the webcam so I was concerned it was gonna be pretty low in the mega pixels department but was surprised that it wasn't awful. It does allow for low light recording which is good for me since I record mostly at night. It's fairly decent in my opinion as onboard webcams go, picture wise that is.

MICROPHONE
I am not happy with the mic though. There is a background noise in the audio that is very annoying. The poor placement of the on board mic is the cause. Instead of it being on the lid of the laptop right next to the Webcam, it is placed under the keyboard, right under the CTRL key. I put my ear to the laptop and it's the same sound I hear in the audio recordings. Either the spinning hard drive or the fan. (What were they thinking???) Anyhow, I reduced mic boost to zero and the mic volume to 40% but it didn't help much. The noise was still there in the recordings. Not really heard through the speaker playback but if you listen to the recording with a headset you can hear that winning sound. So, I thought an external mic would solve my problem but, as I later discovered after a tech call to Lenovo, with combo jacks (The x140E has only one jack for both mic and headset), the combo jack will recognize an ordinary 3.5 microphone jack as a headset and not as a mic. You need a special microphone with a compatible plug (don't know what that is called) or an adapter/splitter that will allow you, not only to plug an ordinary 3.5mm mic in and have it recognized AS a mic but allows you to plug in both (mic and headset) at the same time.
They sell an adapter here at Amazon for about 8 bucks by StarTech.

Another fix: use a USB mic. But, I suggest you plug it in to the USB port on the right hand side away from the noise.

I am doing my best to be objective in my review. What I mean by that is: the 2 things I GOT the Laptop for was making Webcams and watching Movies and there were matters concerning both these things that I am not happy with (aka mic noise and not so great headphone sound output). But the overall Laptop has many good qualities. It all depends on what you're planning to use it for.

text:
I tried (over three days - which may not be enough time) the following:

- NoiseHush BT700-12267 Freedom Bluetooth Headphones with Mic
- Sony MDR10RBT Bluetooth Wireless Headphones
- Bose AE2w Bluetooth Headphones
- Nakamichi Bluetooth Headphine BT304

I wanted bluetooth and over the ear for noise isolation.

The NoiseHush were the best for sound (I listen to jazz and classical) in terms of clarity of highs, mids, and lows. However, the sound stage seemed much narrower than the others. This is particularly the case when listening to classical. The headphones were the cheapest feeling of the four. The adjustments moved too easily and I was constantly fiddling with them mid-listen to sit back on my ears. They had a light, overly-plastic feel throughout. I am not sure they would stand being tossed into a briefcase or backpack. The ear cups were too round to cover my (medium-sized) ears. The blue light indicating that they were connected was so ridiculously bright and its location on the front of the ear cup made it reflect in my glasses. As a result, every 5 seconds I saw a two pulse intensely blue flash. Covering the led with black tape did nothing as the light leaked through the thin plastic of the ear cup. The engineers really screwed this up.

The Sony MDR10s were the most expensive of the four and I expected to get what I paid for. This was true to some degree. They were the best design and used the best materials. Solid, heavy, and the feeling of quality! They were also super comfortable and sealed the sound out the best of all the headphones. No distracting blue flashes on these headphones. The kicker is, however, that in "somewhat blind" side to side to side to side sound tests, the Sony always came out on the bottom. I know! Everyone claims these sound so great. To me, they lacked the crispness, separation, and energy of the other three. It was not a matter of the others having overly enhanced highs. These lacked clear highs. Again, if you look at my musical preferences, highs are WAY more important to me than lows. That said, the MDR10s also lacked a full mids and lows, too. It was a bit like I had tissue stuffed between the drivers and my ears. Not kidding here.

The Bose AE2w headphones were the most comfortable of the group. Just of enough band tension to keep them sealed against my skull and large openings for my ears. They were not as good at sealing out ambient sound as the Sonys which is entirely related to the thickness of the padding. Given how much I paid for these, I was surprised by how much cheaper feeling these were (no only compared to the Sonys, but also to the Nakamichis). They were better constructed than the NoiseHush, but as I implied above, this is not saying much. The Bose really did have a well-balanced sound. Not thrilling, mind you. The Bose sound interpretation was pleasant, but not thrilling. Not sure what it is about them. I think that perhaps there is not enough separation between the highs and lows. Everything converges on the mids. It's not like the muffled, blurred sound of the Sony's. You can hear the sharpness of the violins, but at the expense of the bass and drums. Within the same movement, it can be too bass and drum heavy. It seems like the Bose phones can only concentrate on one thing at a time. Really odd.

The Nakamichis were shockingly well put together. They came in the cheapest packaging (plastic see through "box") hanging on a plastic tab. Nothing that would give you confidence that these were quality products. (Nakamichi needs to hire a designer to work on this as presentation is huge with the buying public - think Bose and Beats) They were not as comfortable as the Sony or Bose options, but they were also only one third the cost. I have to remove/adjust them to give my skull a rest after one hour of listening. I did not have to do that with the Bose or the Sony headphones. The padding seems to be a bit harder than the Bose and Sonys. That said, the ear cups are large enough to accommodate my ears easily. The seal, therefore is decent. It does not isolate you from the dishes being done, but you can't hear the sound of Minecraft coming from my son's iPad when he is sitting next to me. It may seem counterintuitive, but despite not being noise isolating, there is very little sound leakage. The sound is perfect for what I listen to. There is superb separation among all the elements in the orchestra and the sound stage is super wide making it feel like the music is around you instead of centered in your skull. Now don't get me wrong, these don't give me the spine tingling feeling of my Klipsh in-ear phones, but I also don't have to deal with the pain (figuratively) of a wire or the pain (literally) of stuffing foam into my ear canals. Given the choice, I gravitate towards to the Nakamichis for the balance of: sound, comfort, and convenience. Either way, I will admit that it does feel great to remove headphones after listening for awhile. It's a bit like how good it feels when you stop banging your head against the wall. Though I haven't done that in some time.

So, there you have it. Hope this helps.

title: Great headset for the budget minded
text:
The steel series Siberia v2 headset packs a lot of quality for the money. I picked this headset up on Cyber Monday for $50, along with an Astro Pro Mix amp. My review of this headset will contain both the use of the astro mix amp, and without.
So I want to keep this more focused on gaming, since this is a gaming headset. I can't tell you how angry it makes me reading reviews on gaming headsets where the reviewer is just talking about how great or terrible it sounds listening to classical music, when all you want to know is how well it performs while gaming! I will include a bit about music, but I won't wax on about it.

So I've previously owned Turtle Beach x1, TB x3 (wireless), and Tritton AX pro headsets. I can say with great confidence these blow all of them combined out of the water! I also have experience using the Astro A40, and Sennheiser PC360s (Currently called the G4ME One) both with Astro Mix amp. Far and away the Mix amp with PC 360 is the best setup I've ever experienced (For gaming).
-------------------------------

Siberia V2 without mix amp tested on PC with AC Unity, Battlefield 4, and Left for Dead 2:

*Good sound stage for positional Audio. Caught a few people sneaking up on me, but got caught a lot when a lot of sound was happening. Could not tell whether enemies were up high or low, but could hear them walking all around me.
*Kind of quite compared to what I am use to, but still loud enough to make gaming enjoyable.
*The Lows are very dominant, but not overwhelming. They Handle the blends of highs mids and lows all happening at the same time, without the sounds all bleeding together, or cutting out like some headsets (Astro A40).
*Microphone works well, and friends noted that I sounded allot clearer and louder than before (which sometimes isn't always good)
*Very Comfortable once broken in. Can wear them for hours and hours. I was worried about the ear pad material making my head sweat, but it doesn't. Before they were broken in, they clamped to my head and pressed together a bit too hard, but not much of an issue now that they are broken in.
------------------------------
Siberia V2 With Astro Mix amp tested with Battlefield 4 on Xbox 360, and PC with AC Unity, Battlefield 4, and Left for Dead 2:

*Great sound Stage for positional Audio. Noticeably better than without the mix amp (I run with the clean EQ). With some Juice, these things BANG! I could hear people or zombies sneaking up on me allot easier with other sounds banging in the headset. In battlefield, I could hear people running all around, And had an easier time telling where enemies were. Still had the problem of not being able to tell if they were high or low.
* The lows were still more dominant, but the mids and highs sounded much better! No bleeding or smearing tones at all. Everything was very well defined, but the bass being more dominant, sucks sometimes for FPS gaming. Was awesome for Assassins Creed Unity. Makes it way more cinematic, and thus more enjoyable.
*Microphone, of course, no difference.
------------------------------
So the Headset by itself is good, but pump a bit more juice to it, and add Headset virtual surround, and they come to life! This is the least expensive headset I've ever purchased, but the best sounding. Forget Triton, forget Turtle beach. Comparing to the other High end sets in the Astro A40s, and the Sennheiser PC360s, I would say this is an incredible bang for your buck headset, but not the go to for a highest quality audio setup.

Compared to the Astro A40s:
*They sound way better overall. Better sound stage, better defined tones, however... With the Mix amp, The A40s barely edges out the Siberia V2 for positional queues, which I believe is the biggest factor for FPS games. The A40 however does have issues with allot of sounds happening simultaneously and the Highs are very dominant. So if there is an explosion, footsteps your tracking, gunfire and friends talking, it all sort of blurs together and sounds god awful. The Siberia V2 handles everything very well, and keeping everything better defined. Dollar for Dollar between the two, plain and simple.. Siberia V2 all the way.

Compared to the PC 360s:
Without the mix amp, I definitely prefer the Siberia V2. With the mix amp, however.... The PC 360 wins by a large margin. The only thing the PC360 doesn't do as well is bass. But for gaming audio, too much bass can make you audibly blind for seconds at a time, and that's just when someone will sneak up and take you out. The PC360 with mix amp is hands down the best audio system I've ever experienced in gaming. Handles all sounds perfectly defined, and you can hear if something or someone is dropping in on you, or something from any direction, as well as how far away that sound is. It's absolutely amazing! Sorry for rambling there, I'm just a big fan of that configuration. But you're talking a $330 ($200 for the headset $130 for the Amp) config vs $180.

Sound Stage: 7/10
Overall sound: 8/10
Comfort: 7/10

Finally, the music review section. Audiophiles who review gaming headsets against listening to music will love this detailed review:

It sounds good.....
(lol) Hip-Hop and Dub step are the standout genres, especially with an amp.

Hope this helps someone out, who was in my position of wanting to find a quality headset for gaming audio, across multiple platforms, but didn't want to break the bank. If you have any questions or would like further information, write me a comment and I'll get back to you.

title: More than just a personal speaker
text:
There are two things that I immediately noticed when I tested the review sample that I received: (1) the controls are on the bottom of the speaker, and (2) it's louder than other speakers in its size and price range.

As for the placement of the controls, it isn't an issue for me because I usually control the volume level and track skipping from my phone. Regarding the volume it's capable of putting out, it's more than just a personal speaker. I can stream music to the speaker in my kitchen and hear it clearly in my living and dining rooms. That's pretty loud.

The heart and soul of a speaker is the sound quality and this one is very good in that category too. It has good frequency response across the high, mid and low bands, but emphasizes the mids, then the highs and finally the low end in that order. While the bass is surprisingly prominent for such a tiny speaker it is not the dominant frequency band. The mids and highs are very clear and you can hear nuances in music in those frequency bands better than the bass.

One final thing that I love is the ease of pairing and connecting. As soon as you power it up and scan for it from your phone or other device it shows up in the list of available devices. A simple touch of the device name on your screen and it pairs and connects. If you want to use the aux port (the 3.5mm one for headphones) all you need to do is press the button on the speaker that has a bluetooth and phone logo for three seconds and it switched to aux port mode.

I test a lot of speakers and this is one of the better ones I've come across. Not only does it perform, but I like the styling, which counts for something. It's an easy five stars the way I rate, which factors price, ease of use, performance and sound quality. This one has it all.

title: TTL didn't work on E-30; zoom motor noisy, then stopped working
text:
I have been a photographer for decades, and when I saw the low price for a Vivitar dedicated flash, I jumped and got one. But this Vivitar isn't the Vivitar I grew up with, having passed through other companies, a bankruptcy, and then being purchased by low end accessory maker Sakar.

A dedicated "through the lens" (TTL) flash works by having the camera and flash talk to each other over pins in the flash socket. When you trigger a shot, the camera instructs the flash to fire a low-power "pre-flash". The camera senses the light from this this low power pre-flash and decides how much power will be needed to get a proper exposure. The camera sends this information to the flash, opens the shutter, and tells the flash to fire for exposure. This pre-flash and exposure flash happen so fast that you can't detect them as individual events, but they do happen.

My copy of this flash blew out a lot of photographs with massive overexposure, most of the time it was acting as a regular "dumb" flash and not a true TTL. Since I was at an event using it, I stopped using it as a dedicated flash and used it in manual. Shortly after, the zoom function stopped working.

I sent this back and ordered from Amazon a Metz mecablitz 50 AF-1 TTL, and it has worked flawlessly for well over a year and at least 10,000 shots. It was a little more expensive, but I haven't regretted it for a minute.

Maybe my Vivitar was just a bad copy, but it felt so cheap and flimsy I wasn't willing to find out.

title: NOT for wide-angle
text:
All variable ND filters create an x-pattern at full darkness; this you can find all over the Internet, and on the accompanying caution sheet Hoya includes. But what you may not learn so easily is that this tendency is exacerbated by wide-angle lenses. If, like me, you want an ND filter for landscapes, well, I hope you are content to shoot your landscapes at telephoto ranges because this just won't cut it at anything wide.

I've uploaded some pix to clarify, though you'll see right off I didn't put much time into making them as good as a magazine review. Sorry. Shooting with a Canon 5D3 and a 24-105 zoom, I found the filter very effective at telephoto lengths. The one I've posted above, at 93mm, is pretty good. I didn't have a nice uniform object to shoot and the clouds confuse the issue, but overall it's a pretty good shot at about 8 stops down from the very lightest area of the filter. That's what Hoya promises, and it delivers.

But at the other end of the range, at 24mm, the problems began. I uploaded an extreme example just to show you how bad it can get--of course, no one expects a variable filter to be useable at full darkening; that's just not the technology. But you can see where the darkening tends to be, and maybe that'll help you find it in the other shots. I can't tell you where on the zoom the problems began, but I'd guess 40mm would be pretty safe. I'm shooting with a full-frame camera, BTW. At 24mm, I could get maybe 5 or 6 stops of darkening that were useable. Maybe. The real problem began when I switched to a 17-40mm lens. 24mm on that lens was much worse; a significant X-pattern. Even at 40mm there was some darkening but at 17mm, wow. Useless. At that same area of 5-6 stops, the darkening was significant. To go any farther was pointless. As is, for me, owning this lens. It's going back today.

This was my first variable ND filter, so I can't say whether it's any worse or better than the competition. My main complaint is that it's not useable for the wide-angle landscapes I shoot, and I can't say if any others would be better or worse. Oh yeah--another minor issue is that the Canon lens cover won't fit over this filter like it will over a B+W or other filter. Again, I can't say if others will be better. . .though come to think of it, that's not a problem with my B+W polarizer.

I'd like to add that the seller, Gigabargain, was super about this return. No questions asked, full refund. And the shipping was fast, too; I suspect they'll always be faster to the West Coast than the big New York stores. I highly recommend them.
