title: Screen Issues
text:
Straight out of the box the screen had clumped together stuck black pixels and the LED blobby light leakage even at midilevel illumination. I called Kindle support and requested a return for a new replacement. However the service rep said Amazon couldn't guarantee that I wouldn't get a refurbished unit! Given that the unit arrived to me defective, and I didn't see this as a warranty issue (I used it for just a handful of minutes) I then requested a refund instead with prepaid return shipping. Based on the fair number of other buyers who have reported screen problems, my hypothesis is that Amazon's quality control is amiss. The screen on my unit did not look like the evenly illuminated product advertisement photos.

I have the Kindle 3g keyboard and Fire models and was looking to add the Paperwhite, but the screen issues and bureaucratic, poor customer service has turned me off from buying this model from Amazon. I had previously seen demo models at local retailers that looked fine and would bought local, but they were out of stock at the time. I'm now undecided whether to further pursue purchase of this model. In the past the level of support received from Amazon has been good. But in this instance it was too much of a hassle and resulted in the sale being lost.

title: 5 stars for CPU, 3 stars for CPU cooler
text:
The CPU itself is great! I overclocked it to 4.2 Ghz, and my gaming DIY PC was a star! The integrated graphics without the drivers are horrible. But installing the drivers makes all the difference: 1.0 (without drivers)->6.7 (with drivers) on the Windows Experience Index (rating from 1.0 to 7.9) for graphics and gaming! It was even better than my ATi Radeon HD 6450! (It scored 4.4 and 4.6, for Aero and Gaming, respectively)

But the CPU cooler was the only con. And it was a biggie. I can take Intel's side in saying most people don't like the risk of overclocking. But then again, this is an unlocked CPU that was meant for overclocking!

The temperatures were 35 Celsius idle, 70 Celsius while gaming, at 3.4Ghz (Turbo Boost was off). But going to 4.2 Ghz meant 65 Celsius idle, and 100+ Celsius doing simple browsing! Of course, I turned the PC off immediately and never used it again until I installed a different Cooler Master CPU cooler.

Though I recommend the CPU, I think you should order a Hyper 212 Plus or some other CPU fan with it.

EDIT: Even though the included fan was bad, the Rocketfish one I ordered was even worse. Due to this I am changing my review to 5 stars.

EDIT2: Actually, the fan is pretty good if you don't use the CPU in the background (antivirus and BOINC). The temperatures are 10 Celsius lower than with BOINC running.

text:
I was about ready to abandon the air rifle world, because my Diana 54 with a 'good' Weaver scope just wouldn't do better than about 1-1/2" groups at 25 yards. Yes, I know the manuals all say you need to use an airgun scope because of the double kick, but the Weaver never gave me any indications of being less than solid. I thought my gun was simply inaccurate.

I decided to give the gun one more chance and splurged on a Umarex 3-9x44 scope with the one-piece locking mount. I wouldn't have believed the possiblities. I just finished sighting the gun at an indoor range and was able to put three touching holes into a 25 yard target. That's pretty tight for little .177 holes in my opinion. Just say I'm thrilled and finally believe in the accuracy potential of the lowly pellet gun, or at least the RWS model 54.

Incidentally, I sighted in three guns. The Umarex scope shined relative to a Cabelas's Pine Ridge and another Weaver. It's a very nice scope for the money with outstanding clarity, and a very nice short-range parallax adjustment. Looking forward to playing with the Night Vision functions. I'm not sure if that's a gimmick or value add, but it's certainly not a drawback on this scope and base combo.

I recommend this add-on to anyone interested in tapping the accuracy potential of their air rifle. I was shooting Gamo Red Fire pellets.

title: So far, so good.
text:
Anyone that's scared of Windows 8, please take your fears elsewhere. This review is about the product purchased. And that said, there's an immediate flaw - as another reviewer mentioned (after I purchased it, naturally, I realized this) the product details are incorrect. This model does NOT come with the liquid cooling system, one of the main reasons I was willing to drop nine-hundred bucks on a system here. Thanks, HP. And thanks, Amazon for the quality control on your descriptions. Serious let down.

However, you'll notice the 4 star rating. I only knocked a star off for the sham job I experienced with the lack of cooling system. Beyond that the hardware is absolutely bangin. This comp is a beast as is. In less than 10 seconds it boots, I can log in, and skip to the desktop with all of the startup programs loaded. That alone is seriously worth mention.

As expected, the video card is absolutely garbage, so plan on replacing it. If you're buying a rig like this, you're buying it because you want high-end graphics. Word to the wise, there are no pre-bought systems out there that come with a good graphics card! So that's not a knock on the comp itself, but rather a fact of life. I paired it with a GeForce GTX 660 (amazing value for the price) and had no trouble installing it even though it's an elephant of a video card. The system picked it up right away and installed all the correct drivers. I still recommend checking the drivers at the NVidia site though. Newer is always better when it comes to drivers.

Skyrim was my bench test. Loaded the game onto the comp and overclocked it, modded to absolute hell and back, and I can play it on Ultra settings for hours without skipping a beat. For those who don't know what that means, it means that this computer can seriously handle anything you can throw at it.

It's a long term purchase, and aside from the ill-advised product description, it is exactly what you'd expect from a system approaching a grand. In hindsight, I'd still buy it. But I won't go so far as to say I'd buy it again, because I already own it, and then I'd have two, and that would be one too many.

Good deal.

title: It COULD be a great lens... but this lens will EAT YOUR DUST!
text:
I loved this lens when I first bought it. I own a Canon 5d MK II which I use for both professional photography and professional video production. In fact, I loved this lens so much that I went and bought the Rokinon 85mm, too. Then IT happened. And IT changed my perspective on the Rokinons. I use to share the sentiments held by most of the reviewers here on Amazon, but there is one big flaw in this lens, and it should be taken into consideration before you pull the plug and buy one.

Okay... I'll get right to the point. My first Rokinon 14mm started out great but somehow got dust inside the lens between the lens elements after only 3 months of use. At first I thought I could blow it out with compressed air, but had no such luck. I had a commercial shoot that week that required my Rokinon 14mm, so in a pinch, I bought ANOTHER one. I chalked up the last problem to bad luck. Unfortunately, after owning the SECOND Rokinon 14mm for only a month, the same thing happened. When the lens is stopped down to f2.8 it's impossible to tell that there's dust in there. But when you push the lens to f8, f11, f16, or f22 and point it at a light background, it becomes glaringly obvious that there is dust INSIDE the lens. The ROKINON LENSES NEED BETTER SEALING. Now I know that not all lenses provided by even the major manufacturers are fully weather sealed. But I've found that the Rokinon 14mm is much more susceptible to dust than any other lens I've owned (weather sealed or not). The same thing has happened to the last two $400 Rokinon lenses I've purchased and I will be purchasing no more from this manufacturer. It's just not worth the risk. I know it's a tempting purchase. When you consider that the Canon 16-35mm L is over twice as much money, the Rokinon seems like a great deal. But I believe the Rokinon is too much of a risk unless you plan on shooting in a sterile environment and avoiding the outdoors completely. Believe me, it's worth waiting and springing for the Canon 16-35 which is weather sealed. For the price I just paid for my now two defunct Rokinon 14mms, I could've owned a used weather-sealed Canon 16-35mm.

My primary background is directing. I am a working commercial director that has directed national television along with many national commercials and one feature film. I am also a cinematographer. Even shooting high profile jobs, I'm always searching for cheaper filmmaking options and ways to reduce budgets. I love independent filmmaking and all the work-arounds and problem solving it entails. I love finding cheap equipment that somehow rivals the big players in the business. So I was extremely excited to discover the Rokinons because as a cinematographer, they made sense to me. Why not make a lens cheaper by tossing out all the fancy electronics, automatic apertures and autofocus features that I don't need anyway?? Why not just focus on the glass itself and nothing else? The Rokinon glass is very nice for the price. Aside from the extreme barrel distortion, I thought it was the best ultra wide angle lens you could find for the money. Unfortunately, this lens needs to be sealed better. It doesn't necessarily need to be completely weather sealed, as some of my other favorite Canon lenses aren't weather-sealed and seem to do just fine. The Rokinon just needs BETTER SEALING.

It's no fun to spend $400 on a lens that becomes useless in a month. And in my line of work, where deadlines are harsh and stress can be high, two strikes means the game is over. This lens will EAT YOUR DUST and that is not a good thing.

title: Eventually seems to be fine
text:
I ordered one of these cards in preparation for a long trip. When I got the card I put it in my camera and took several photos and everything seemed fine as I reviewed them. The next day when I went to look at the images, I discovered they had disappeared. Thankfully they were not very important, so I formatted the card and shot a bunch more images to try and replicate the problem but everything seemed fine. A few days later after shooting several hundred more images, I noticed that several photos were showing as corrupted and I was unable to download them. Thankfully I was able to use a file retrieval program to retrieve the corrupted files. After contacting the seller, I arranged to get a replacement.

When the new card arrived, I tried everything I could imagine, shooting almost 2000 images, swapping out to other cards, turning the camera (Canon 7D) on and off and pulling the battery, but the card seemed to be fine, so I headed out on my trip. About 600 photos into the trip, I noticed more corrupted images. Thankfully I had a few older SanDisk cards that I managed to get by on for the rest of the trip. When I returned, I contacted Sandisk and they led me through some techniques to try to solve the problem, but a few weeks later more files were corrupted, so I returned the card and got a replacement. It seems that the third time was the charm as I haven't had any corrupt files since then.

I have been a long-time SanDisk customer and am glad they replaced my faulty cards, but I am disappointed that I had to go through two bad cards in a row before finally getting a card that works. For an Extreme product, I expect much better quality control than this.

title: Great Board so far!
text:
Built my dream computer over Christmas holidays using this board w/i7-2600k CPU, 16 gigs Corsair Vengence memory, OCZ 120 SSD Vertex 3 boot drive. So far no problems. I plan to overclock from 3.3 mhz to 4.5 mhz in next week or so now that I know everything is stable. Installed in Antec P280 case (quiet). Using a Zalman CPU cooler and ATI HD5870 graphics card. Runs cool and quiet. Went with OCZ 850 Gold power supply - overkill, I know - but got it on sale & w/rebate. Very efficient PS. I'm a graphic designer and don't play games on computer (yet)... Running Win 7 Pro 64bit to take full advantage of memory.

Didn't really need the /Gen3 model board but was only $20 more - I've found that after about 3 yrs, enough has changed that you might as well do a new build. The Gen3 makes the PCI slots upgradeable to the faster PCI 3 standard which is not available yet. I'll probably never use it prior to new build, but for $20 got the Gen3 model anyway.

Also didn't really need the Z68 version. P67 would have been fine since I am using a dedicated graphics card. Z68 lets you use onboard cpu graphics & dedicated graphics card. Again, price difference wasn't that great, so decided to go with the newer board. P67 model allows for easy overclocking. H67 model allows for onboard graphics option, Z68 does both. I assume if you are buying a MB that you have a graphics card. So if you want to save money go with P67 board.

Manual seems better than most... good details. I haven't read too much yet. Nice to have 4 Sata 3 (6gig) drive capability. Right now I have all drive 8 drive connectors full (only 1 Sata 6gb drive) - but plan to upgrade drives with new hybred Sata3 6gig drives when drive prices come down. Would like to have 10 drive connectors, but 8 is still good (4 Sata 2 & 4 Sata 3s). Lot of USB (2 & 3) connectors plus internal USB 3 connector is nice for case front USB 3 ports.

Board is nicely laid out, memory slots far enough away from CPU that didn't have any problem with Zalman 9700 CPU cooler hitting memory. CPU avgs 25 C temp with fan running at a quiet speed of 1800 rpm. System stays at a cool avg 28c temp. GPU 51c. So board is quality made with good heat dispersement.

Bottom Line: good quality board. Easy to overclock. Good documentation. Good online help. Lot of connectors (drives & USB). Probably don't need Gen3 for future proofing yet to come PCI 3 cards. Probably would have been just as happy with a P67 card for $20-$30 less. But since the board is something you don't replace often (opposed to drives), I am glad I went with this board - even though it was about $40 more than I needed to spend. If you are like me and reviewing lots and not sure what to buy... get this board, you will not be sorry.

title: Objectively great image quality, fantastic value
text:
Measured using XRite i1 Display pro.

First off, calibration settings (Standard mode):
- Gamma 1 (most important setting)
- Contrast 50 (Update: Contrast 44 for virtually perfect 2.2 gamma tracking, reduces Contrast ratio to 3100:1 which is still great; with Contrast 50, it tracks 2.1 linearly which is arguably a good thing for a *VA panel due to the slightly darker center cone of viewing)
- Color: R100 G99 B99
- Brightness appropriate for environment; at night I use 0 with ambient lighting behind the display (*strongly recommended to greatly reduce eyestrain* with any display)

Results:
- great gamma tracking to 2.2
- grayscale deltaE under 1 average, no obvious tint (particularly no green tint, which was awful on my Asus VG236H before calibration)
- roughly 3600:1 (!!!) static contrast
- color accuracy (to the usual Rec 709 / sRGB color space) is pretty good but not great, dE 3.7 for primaries & secondaries. Saturation sweep shows no compression thankfully. Blue is the most inaccurate with dE of 4.3 at 80% saturation and 5.4 at 100% saturation, it's skewed toward magenta (purple)

Color accuracy isn't good enough for pro use but color *saturation* is very good and it's accurate enough. I can't emphasize enough how much more important the static contrast is than perfect color accuracy for general image quality (and even among pros, some argue for the highly improved dynamic range over IPS being more important than marginally more accurate colors). The colors are close enough to hardly be noticeably 'off' (I can hardly notice even after applying the ICC profile calibration), but try watching any show or game or whatever (basically anything) next to a high quality IPS (e.g. a top notch tablet display like an iPad 3+ or Nexus 7) to compare and it will spoil that panel for you. You have been warned.

Pros:
- fantastic IQ per above, better than basically any TN or IPS/PLS for virtually any price due to *VA contrast
- no calibration instrument needed for good gamma and other image accuracy, just use my settings above (this is a big deal for a monitor at this price)
- overdrive (AMA) 'Advanced' mode does its job fairly well for a *VA panel
- useful OSD adjustments available especially for this price range
- has standard 100mm VESA mounting holes
- PWM not used to control backlight brightness
- effective (and not overly dirty-looking) anti-glare coating

Cons:
- responsiveness is clearly a weak point. AMA 'Advanced' setting is recommended and good enough for me, but might bother some, YMMV. Do not use "Premium", it overshoots like crazy. If you've used any typical IPS from the past few years, 'Advanced' is a bit slower than that.
- why is the frame glossy? WHY BENQ, WHY??? GRRRRRR. Very cheap-looking glossy plastic everywhere
- control buttons are somewhat unintuitive, and there is no shortcut button for brightness.
- stock gamma is set to 3 when '1' is clearly the most accurate; Picture modes other than 'Standard' are pretty useless (this is par for the course for pretty much all monitor manufacturers)
- backlight could dim a bit lower ... but at least it doesn't use PWM
- ships with VGA cable instead of DVI (again, wtf, why Benq why????)

Conclusion:
Highly recommended for any general usage (including gaming, photos - as explained above) unless you're sensitive to the average/poor motion performance.

Updated review on 8/5/2014 with minor changes to calibration settings

title: The bee's knees
text:
I purchased this to add hands-free calling and music streaming capabilities to a stock 2010 Honda Accord base stereo. I had some reservations after being burned on other products that I've tried, but this one works exactly like I had hoped. For the record, I'm using this device with a Samsung Galaxy Nexus running stock Android 4.2.2.

Design: The power and 3.5mm jack are on the same cable and split with about 10 inches of individual wires after the "Y". If your AUX jack and 12V plug are further apart than that, it could be an issue. Luckily, the 2010 Accord has a spare 12V plug in the armrest cubby adjacent to the AUX input. If the AUX input was on the stereo (most cars), I would have had to use the forward 12V plug and remove my phone charger. Small potatoes, yes, but it's a big difference in the amount of wire clutter you could have around your dash.

Strong positive in comparison to other products: the microphone is fantastic. It clearly picks up my voice with minimal background noise, even when on the highway.

The forward/backward buttons on the top ring of the device work great and are easily found despite their small footprint.

The sticky pads used to mount the device seem to work well after about a week's worth of use in California summer heat.

The face of the device doubles as the main button - short push activates bluetooth streaming from an open music app and a long push activates the voice dialing feature in Android.

Only one gripe: the volume difference between music and phone calls is huge...calls come through very quietly sometimes, regardless of the volume settings on my phone. If I press the volume up rocker on the phone, sometimes the call volume jumps up to where it should be. I'm not sure if this is a device or phone issue.

Overall, I am very satisfied that I (finally) ended up with a solid hands-free device for my car that works predictably. For the price, it is a steal.

title: Great, but not as good as the SHQ1000/28
text:
As a very satisfied owner of the SHQ1000, I was sad to see them finally go (after 10 months of fairly heavy usage). So I went online to buy another pair and stumbled upon the newer model, the SHQ1200. I noticed that the reviews for this were generally lower than that of the SHQ1000, but I went and ordered them anyways.

I can say first off that these are great earbud headphones for the price, however, there are some things that potential buyers should know before making a decision. Compared to the SHQ1000, the cable is about 8 inches shorter, which could be a deal-breaker to some. The audio jack is also a right-angle connector instead of the straight one used in the SHQ1000, which is good for me since it seems more durable (however it's not that the jack connector in the SHQ1000 wasn't durable). I was also disappointed to find that it didn't come with a cable cinch to "zip up" the cables so they weren't separated so low, however I'm sure you could just use the clip that came with it if you really had to (same one that came with SHQ1000 by the way).

The audio quality is at least on par with the SHQ1000. I did notice that they weren't quite as loud as the previous model (about 90% as loud as the SHQ1000s), and that there was slightly more bass in the newer model. Other than that, they're both largely the same. They both feel exactly exactly the same in the ear even though the speaker on the SHQ1200 is slightly bigger. I was also easily able to use the rubber covers from the SHQ1000 on the SHQ1200 and vice versa.

In conclusion, if you're looking for a good pair of earbuds for a good price, look no further. You'll find what you want either in this model, or in the old SHQ1000 model. After about a week of usage, I'd have to say I still prefer the old model, however these are quickly serving up to still be a great replacement.

UPDATE: After 2.5 years, the left speaker died. It appears to be a dead speaker and not the right-angle connector that's usually a weak spot on headphones. They were definitely worth the money, and I'll probably stick with Phillips for my next set.

title: I cannot find any compelling reason why you shouldn't buy these speakers right now
text:
I'll start this by destroying my credibility. I am not an audiophile, and this is my first surround sound system worth the name. I did, however, do a massive amount of research before buying these. This is going to be long, so the TLDR on this is:

These are great speakers for the price, and will probably be more than adequate for the needs of anyone who is not an audiophile. They are also better than many $600-$800 sets in terms of frequency response curve and general sound reproduction. They will not have the same build quality or design aesthetic as these premium sets, but look fine, and are made well. You won't regret buying these unless you have much more exacting standards than the average person, and even an audiophile would be satisfied with these as a second room/vacation home setup.

So, the rest:

I was originally settled on the Energy Take Classic 5.1 set. (which has become the long standing gold standard of affordable 5.1 speaker sets)
[[ASIN:B001202C44 Energy 5.1 Take Classic Home Theater System (Set of Six, Black)]]
But, a price bump on those right when I decided on them led me to do some re-shopping. After reading and watching the CNET review on these, I started looking in to them seriously. I suggest you check out that review.

These speakers are actually the replacements to the Monoprice 9774 5.1 system. The reason those were replaced was due to a patent lawsuit because they were exact clones of the Energy Take Classic 5.1 speakers. Nearly identical form factor, Identical internal components, and most interestingly, identical performance and frequency response curve. But over $100 cheaper than the average price of the Energy speakers. So that wasn't going to last, and it didn't. For a while there, they were hands down the best speaker per dollar that could be purchased. These Monoprice speakers are just enough different to dodge another lawsuit. The surprise is that in some respects, they are better than the speakers they replaced. The consensus seems to be that they provide a more satisfying over-all sound than the Energy Take Classic. I can't speak to this because I'm not in a position to directly compare them. But everybody that has seems to agree that these are either equivalent or better. The fact that they're cheaper doesn't hurt one bit.

Another advantage is that if you want to add two speakers and make this a 7.1, Monoprice actually sells you two more matching speakers for about $80.

[[ASIN:B00IACEN3A Monoprice Premium Home Theater Satellite Speaker - Black (110800)]]

Energy only sells the satellite speakers for their set as a package. And though exactly matched speakers in a 7.1 isn't mandatory, it certainly makes it easier for your receiver to blend.

These are a recent purchase, so I can't speak to how long they will last. I can say they sounded great to me right out of the box, and the spring connectors were super easy to use.

Important notes:

Break in Period: Don't blast these things full volume until you've been using them for quite a good little while. A couple of weeks of regular TV watching should do it. This type of speaker needs time to loosen up and mellow out. Skipping this step is a really good way to permanently damage your sound quality. They're actually supposed to sound even better after being broken in, as well.

Subwoofer Cable: if you order these, you need to get a shielded RCA splitter subwoofer cable. (one male connection that splits to two male connections) It will actually run ok off of a single RCA into the white input, but spend the extra $6 and do it right. They're all over amazon. I almost took off a star for them not including this, but I just couldn't make myself do it. The speakers themselves are just too solid.

Speaker stands: A lot of people make the obvious (and incorrect) assumption that the Monoprice speaker stands will fit these Monoprice speakers perfectly. (go figure!) They don't. They work, but only if you mount the speakers upside down. I ordered some that are on the way. If those work out, I will edit this review.
Edit: They didn't really work out. I'm using them, but they aren't ideal.

Anyway, you should just go on and buy these unless the Energy Take Classic set is at one of the periodic low dips to $250 range. At that point they become a serious contender because of a 3 year warranty vs the 1 year that Monoprice offers. (or if you have a fascination with gloss black finishes) But that's about the only things that distinguish them from these. AND they might actually not sound as good.

FYI - there are some known problems with the dust covers tending to have the little plastic bits break off inside the speaker when you try to remove them. So, if you want to use these without the dust covers, slow and steady wins the race. I intend to leave mine on, but it is something to be aware of.

title: Not PC Friendly.
text:
It took me a couple of evenings' hard work to connect it to my PC, so let me help you. To connect it to your network, follow the instructions that come with it --or go to the PIONEER site to find the manual: So far so good. Then, if you don't already have iTunes on the system, download it from the Apple download site. Launch iTunes, and click on the Airplay button (or, click on Help -search for Airplay). The Airplay button is a small button next to the volume control slider on the top left side of the screen. A pull down menu will guide you to select speakers. You can select Single, or Multiple; then the speaker, or speakers you want to stream to. Single, and one external speaker, will stream monaural to your external speaker. Selecting Multiple, and two speakers (one of which can be your computer speakers), will output one of the stereo channels to each.

The Pioneer speaker will time out and turn off, if there is no input stream for it. To avoid this, follow the instructions that come with it (on a yellow sheet supplement) that tell you how to turn on the Quick Start Mode (at turn on, press ON until the blue light goes steady, then press the INPUT button for three seconds). This will keep the speaker on stand-by for as long as the media player stays on (holds onto the port). But then, off it will go again (sorry, folks!)

Now, if any one can figure out how to stream through the Microsoft Media Player, please let me know. There is a simple way, I understand, if you use Windows 7 (use the Send to, button at the top of a playlist window.) But, I am running Vista. So... Help, please! Problem is, iTunes does not play WMA files... My classical library holds over 1000 CD's, and I don't want to have to convert them to mp3.

Performance:

My network connection is excellent. I made the wireless connection through an old NETGEAR router running only g (802.11g protocol); and connected this router to the rest of my home network via Ethernet cable. I avoided hanging it (the speaker) on the main wireless router of the network because that one runs n, and I don't want it to be switching to g just for the speaker (the speaker runs only on a g network.) The relative disadvantage of g, in this case, is range. You must keep the speaker close to the router, i.e., closer than you would with n.

Would I buy another one? No. If you plan to put one in each room of your house, think again. Every time you want to stream music, you will be running from room to room to restart each one manually! This is not, a set once and forget speaker.

Sound is adequate for what you pay (reviewing the XW-SMA1), but just barely. I have to knock down the mid-range by 24dB (using the iTunes equalizer) to get what I consider flat response. Of course, this is subjective --and no, there is no problem with my hearing, I had it tested recently... The response appears to be peaking between 250 and 500Hz. I find this disappointing, Mr. Pioneer chief engineer Andrew Jones: You are too preoccupied with your woofing, and I want to hear brilliant strings!

Dynamic range is good. No discernible distortion at top power.

Signed: A 72 year old audio aficionado.

title: Dang Samyang! (Rokinon)
text:
I was looking at DxOMark's lens ratings based on resolution, and was surprised to see a Samyang 85mm f1.4 (specifically on a Nikon D800 body) was in the top 5 of all lenses tested. It actually tied a Carl Zeiss lens. Samyang sells their lenses under several brands - I know Bower and Rokinon are two, there are others. I found the 85mm under the Rokinon name with the Nikon AE chip for $250 barely used so I went ahead and got it.

I love this lens - it may be the sharpest lens I've owned, but also the bokeh is super nice and pleasing to the eye. The lens is fairly hefty and build quality feels very solid. It is manual focus only, but for the ridiculous low price for an optic of this quality I can live with it. Plus the Nikon version with the chip in it will trigger your focus confirmation light in the viewfinder when you are in focus. I planned on using this for portraits anyway - so I can live without AF.

Watch your depth of field until you get used to it. It's not really a fault of the lens but more just what happens with a lens of this focal length. 85mm at f1.4 is going to have a crazy shallow depth of field. I do this on purpose with portraits a lot - very nice effect on individual portraits. This lens is pretty darn sharp even wide open at f1.4. There is some barely noticeable vignetting wide open that is easily corrected in post. Also my Nikon D600 tends to correct it if I shoot jpg instead of RAW.

Don't hesitate to buy this lens. This may be one of the best camera related purchases I've had. I'm now looking at some of their other lenses.

title: Fantastic little machine!
text:
This was a gift after my VAIO, which I hated, finally quit. It's only been two days, but I'm in love with this little machine! The size and weight were exactly what I was looking for and the touchscreen is an added bonus for the price ($259 w/Prime). The keyboard is smaller than the standard size I'm used to, but it isn't an issue for my clumsy fingers. I don't find the keys hard to press and they're sturdy enough that I don't feel like they'll be broken easily. The screen isn't too difficult to read in the shade, but it does have a gloss that easily reflects light. Indoors there is no issue with glare.

This computer is user friendly, but is taking me time to get used to. I've been a longtime Vista and XP user. I don't keep up with technology but have familiarity with Windows and haven't had a problem figuring out how to do what I want. As a graduate student I spend a lot of time on Office, which this machine doesn't include. Google Drive is easily accessible, however. I have yet to work on projects but can tell that the touchscreen is going to help with browsing research and navigating screens, plus it's fun to use! I don't think there would be any interference with the keyboard if a user prefers to use the touchscreen predominately, which I'm finding I prefer to the touchpad.

The only minor concern is the touch pad, which sounds hollow when tapping. Maybe I need to adjust the pressure I use, but it's a bit noisy when tapping. My review gives 4 stars for the issue I encountered with a setting that restricted the use of the keyboard. The fix came from Google and hasn't been a problem, but it was disconcerting.

title: Works Well with My Old Western Digital Drive
text:
I recently rebuilt an old computer, installing a new Western Digital 1 TB hard drive in place of the old WD 320 GB drive. But the old drive was still fine for backups, and this Vantec enclosure is keeping it in service.

Installation was reasonably straightforward, although -- as many others have pointed out -- the LED "drive activity" cable is a bit difficult to connect since there isn't much room left for it once the drive has been attached. But patience and persistence are all you need. The accompanying instructions didn't show the orientation of the LED cable plug (apparently this information is printed on the circuit board but obscured by the installed drive), so I just took a chance on that. Fortunately, I got it right (I would not have relished opening up the case again to reverse the connector).

In operation the aluminum case seems pretty warm to me after an hour or so, but I haven't seen any signs of malfunction. Since I don't intend to run this drive except when making backups, I'm not too concerned about the heat.

For complete system backups, I use both Acronis True Image and Windows 7's built-in imaging program (the latter is an excellent tool that is not well publicized). I was glad to discover that my Vantec eSata device was recognized by the boot-up rescue disks that I created for both of those imaging programs; if it had not been, a complete system recovery from an image file would have been difficult at best.

title: Decent performance- but note:
text: The main reason someone would buy an antenna like this would be because your local TV stations are still using the VHF (hi or low) bands to transmit the new digital stations. Most converted to UHF when they went digital. If your local stations stayed at VHF (usually because they were too cheap to upgrade their hardware), you can't use the standard 'HD antennas' that are everywhere, compact, and sometimes even cool looking. Alas, the only way to collect VHF is with a giant antenna. Don't be fooled- many of those small antennas say they'll work at VHF... that's true kind of like using a coat hanger technically 'works' it just works really badly. This antenna actually works decently at both VHF and UHF- about as good as any of the larger antennas. If you compare the gain of this antenna to a larger one in both VHF and UHF bands you might see a 1dB difference, but that really won't matter- or rather, if that little bit matters, you probably can't use an antenna to watch that fringe channel reliably anyway. So ultimately I'm happy with this antenna, and if your local stations cross into both UHF/VHF bands and you're not in the boonies, you probably will be too.

title: M6204 poor product, poor software
text:
I purchased a refurbished M6204 mp3 player very cheaply, and it turned out to be expensive at the price. Where to start... how about the defective rca easyrip software that stopped functioning after only one day and no long recognized that the mp3 player was connected to the usb computer port? I removed the software three times and reinstalled it three times. It was still non-functional in regard to putting music files into the player, although it could be used just for ripping music onto the computer. However, after much online searching for help, I learned the software can be bypassed and one can use Windows Media Player for both ripping and synching to the player.

But then there are two main problems with the player itself. I ripped music from CDs I had purchased. About 1/5 of these albums will not play in the mp3 player for some unknown reason. The error message claims that the player does not support the format, although the format is only wpa or mp3 and is supposed to be supported, just like all the other ripped album files that function perfectly. Two albums that were giving me this problem worked fine after I had reinstalled them. However, another three albums didn't. When one attempts to delete these non-functioning files, the player freezes up after informing you that the delete was successful. If you wait long enough, you're ultimately able to shut it down.

As for getting any kind of support for this product, don't hold your breath or you'll be sorry. There IS no decent support. If you long for headaches and endless stress in your life, the M6204 will help you achieve both. Guaranteed.

The speakers itself sounds really good, surprisingly good for the size. The subwoofer completes the whole sound package. And the price is a great value for what you get. The problem is the subwoofer needs to be placed near a wall or corner for optimal sound - as specified in the user manual. However when one does so, the remote control is useless. The remote has to be pointed at the front of the subwoofer. In hindsight, something I probably should have realized when looking at the pictures. The remote control was a must-have for my application, so I decided to return the item.

Here is where Amazon Customer Service failed me. I was not able to self-service a return and was given this information when I tried: "For safety reasons, items that are classified as hazardous materials or use flammable liquids or gases cannot be returned to Amazon.com. Customers should dispose of hazardous materials according to Local, State and Federal regulations. Customers should contact their local government or local waste company for directions on how to dispose of Household Hazardous Waste." WHAAAAAAAAT? My only guess is the speaker magnets are considered a hazard(?)!

After chatting with the Amazon Chat service, I was directed to speak to large item return department (these speakers arrived in a 24x24 inch box) to handle hazardous returns. They were not able to return my item because it's been tagged as hazardous and they were not able to explain why/what was hazardous about it. (Now I am a bit worried - I don't want this thing in my house!). I explained the Amazon product page does not state this item cannot be returned nor does it state its a hazardous item.

Nonetheless Amazon would not take this item back, and offered me a partial return. I accepted out of frustration did not want to spend more time chasing this down. So BUYER BEWARE!!!! No returns on this mysteriously classified hazardous item!!!!

title: Two bad experiences
text:
Many others have commented on the features and some deficiencies of this Acer V5 touch laptop, so I am not going to comment on those, but I will highlight my experience about the quality and reliability of this laptop.

I was in the market for two 'average use' family laptops, so a Windows 7 laptop would have mostly sufficed, but after seeing the Acer V5 touch laptop at a warehouse retail chain, and reading many of the reviews here at Amazon, I decided on buying the V5. I was prepared for the deficiencies because the V5 showed more promise with its features that were important to me (3rd gen i5, backlit keyboard, 15.6" screen, touch, good form factor, price and a fast wi-fi).

The first unit worked fine for about 3 weeks before it started giving minor trouble with wi-fi (will not 'wake up' after sleep or standby). Although a nuance because I had to reboot it every time this happened, I continued using it. I installed a few additional software so I could use this with my Canon printer and Netgear ReadyNAS. Soon after, the behavior of the laptop started changing with erratic slow-downs (e.g. CPU = 90%+ for the Task Manager process etc.) and freezes. I was still not convinced this was a bad laptop and questioned the driver and Windows 8 compatibility. This, until the screen stopped responding to touch. With no other option to fix the touch, I restored the laptop to factory settings thinking one of the drivers could have caused the touch screen to fail. The full restore to factory setting took almost 7 hours but still no response to touch. I packed it up and returned it to the store.

The second unit which I am currently using is already showing wi-fi connectivity issues - connection stays dropped after waking up from 'sleep' or standby. Sometimes, wi-fi will not connect even after restarting. The erratic slow-downs do happen on this one but much less than the first unit. While the wi-fi problems are worse on this unit (and some erratic slow-downs), the rest of the features work well. The only new software I have installed are, to access my Netgear ReadyNAS and small utilities like 7-zip, VLC, Google Drive etc. The other annoyance with this unit is the 'dongle' for using Ethernet 'wired' connection. The dongle is used between the Ethernet connector and the laptop for wired network connections. It just seems to delicate around where it connects to the laptop, that I fear it may break soon. It slides into the laptop easily but seems to get stuck when removing. BEcause of the wi-fi issues, the wired connections is slowly becoming my favorite but then it reduces the mobility of the laptop and also makes me use the touch features much less. I plan to call Acer support soon to help resolve the wi-fi issue.

I will update if I run into other issues with the second unit.

Update 01/01/13: My wi-fi completely stopped working. It would not detect any wifi network nearby. I contacted Acer support via their Chat support (fast response - even on New Years Holiday). Support advised me to reset the BIOS to factory settings and if that doesn't fix the wi-fi, they advised a restore of the OS (Windows 8) to factory settings. This sounded easy enough and my wifi started working soon after a BIOS reset (I did not have to do an OS restore). The BIOS reset is fairly easy - 1) Access the BIOS using F2 as soon as you power up. 2) Reset to default settings using F9 3) Save the BIOS setting using F10. I will wait for a few more days of reliable use, before modifying the rating.

Update 01/15/13: The wi-fi has become more predictable and less troublesome, probably because there are other troubles which have now surfaced (unfortunately, because I wanted to like this laptop). One thing to note, when the wifi does not 'wake up', then disabling/enabling the wireless adapter resets it. Other times, I have to remove my wireless network from the configuration and it resets the wifi - it does prompt for the WPA2 key again which I have now memorized. The two other problems I have now started seeing are: 1) Abrupt disappearance of the mouse pointer (requires a restart to get it back again). 2) The machine almost never shuts down 'cleanly' - on shut-down, it shows a garbled screen for about 30 seconds and then brings up the ACER welcome screen (BIOS) as if it is restarting. I will call Acer one last time to resolve these which I am sure a full restore should be able to resolve. The problem is that I do not know when the problem will restart after a full restore. This may be going back to the store...

Anyone has better suggestions for a reliable Windows 8 'Touch' laptop or maybe I will stick to my old Mac for now until some Win 8 touch laptops establish reliability.

The purple is a little more to my liking on this vs the mCover but both are pretty accurate in the photos. I actually have side-by-side of both in the user photos as well.

So - it's going back for the lack of protection. Otherwise, it would be worth the price.

title: Pa-per-white\ n (1806): a polyanthus narcissus bearing clusters of small very fragrant pure white flowers
text:
Apropos of nothing, I like the rather literary name given the latest iteration of the Kindle e-book reader. It has a nice poetic ring to it, as the name Kindle itself does. No doubt Amazon had this "pure white" flower in mind when naming the device, as it ostensibly might nicely describe the brilliant new display. In the case of my first Kindle Paperwhite this was sadly not the case. The display appeared with not only the obvious artifacts from the four LED lights at the bottom of the screen, but there were these visibly distracting striations of the slightest shades of pink and green, a kind of pale blotchiness across the entire display. In addition, the text did not appear consistently black and crisp, but rather washed out and gray in varying degrees. Mine was not the Kindle Paperwhite described and depicted on Amazon's website. I immediately signed in to Amazon to read the hundreds of customer reviews and was shocked to see the huge number of customers who were experiencing the same problem. There were the understandably indignant one-star reviews, but even the vast majority of the four and five-star reviews acknowledge these screen issues, (although most of these customers apparently felt they could live with the Paperwhite's idiosyncrasies). Okay, so I decided that maybe I could "live with" these defects along with everybody else. After all, the Paperwhite was not without some redeeming qualities. I am an avid reader and huge fan of the Kindle, having owned every model, save the first. Each new model, at least in my mind, has been an improvement over its predecessor, (despite the minor learning curve of mastering each new model). I should also mention that I am a devout follower of the church of Amazon, and blindly refused to believe that Mr. Bezos was intentionally misleading his flock. So I picked up my Paperwhite and gave it a real go.

Alas, the display issues were too glaring. I was feeling bamboozled. Where was the "truth in advertising" here? We were not getting the product we paid for as advertised! I called Amazon Customer Service, mentioning the issues of which so many other customers were complaining. Surprisingly, the agent claimed to be unaware of such complaints, (right, uh huh), but none-the-less promptly issued me a replacement which arrived on my doorstep less than two days later. The replacement did offer some improvements. The text appeared noticeably sharper, with blacker blacks, etc. The odd color banding across the display was still there, but less glaringly obvious. The shadowing at the bottom of the screen from the LEDs was still there, but what is one to do? I wasn't expecting miracles. But I decided that I could live with these anomalies such as they were. Nothing is perfect in this world, right? I've read many coffee-stained pages throughout the years, got through many worn-out, yellowed old hardcovers, and beach-worn and summer battered paperbacks. And truly, never has a book's physical imperfections ever lessened my enjoyment of reading it. The Kindle is a brilliant invention (despite its flaws), a machine that to my mind has changed the way we read (the dictionary always at hand, the translator, the ability to archive highlights, its compactness and lightness, the ability to browse a bookstore at whim). The Paperwhite's optional, handsome leather cover is also miracle of invention (highly recommended); open it and you are brought back to the last page read (on the Kindle sans ads); close it and it is put to sleep, wireless off. Very cool.

As for "truth in advertising"? The biggest disappointment here is just that. There is none. And why should I be surprised? There isn't much difference between the photographs of the Kindle Paperwhite touted and sold on Amazon, and those photos of perfectly prepared, mouth-watering cheeseburgers foisted on us by McDonalds and the like. Has any burger ordered come close to looking like the burger pictured in those ads? But herewith lays my beef with Amazon. I thought they were better than that.

Oh boohoo, right? I'll keep my Kindle, flaws and all, because I like it enough. Clearly Amazon has a few quality control issues to iron out with the Paperwhite, and maybe someday they'll get it right, (I am almost tempted to shell out for the extended warranty on this one). And maybe someday, all of us who blind-faithfully purchased the new Kindle from Amazon will get a humble apology.

title: I can now watch DirecTV on two TVs with only one DVR!
text:
This does exactly what I wanted. I have a DirecTV DVR connected to my [[ASIN:B0019LX84E LG 42LG70 42-Inch 1080p 120 Hz LCD HDTV]] in the lounge and wanted to also send the output to the [[ASIN:B003GDFJUO VIZIO XVT323SV 32-Inch Full HD 1080p LED LCD HDTV with VIA Internet Application, Black]] in our bedroom.

To do this I switched everything off, took the HDMI cable from my DirecTV, unplugged it from the LG TV and instead plugged it into the input on the splitter. I then used a new 3ft HDMI cable to connect the first output on the splitter to the LG TV, and a 25ft HDMI cable to the Vizio in the bedroom. Powered everything on, and like magic the DirecTV was mirrored on both TVs. As both TVs are 1080p I get the best quality.

I also have a [[ASIN:B002IC0YL8 Logitech Harmony 900 Rechargeable Remote with Color Touch Screen]], so we can now watch DirecTV in our bedroom and still be able control the satellite box via RF, watch recording, pause live TV etc. This setup gets the wife approval stamp! Of course you can't watch different channels in each room - to do this I'd need to buy an additional receiver for the bedroom, but that's not a big deal. This costs about $400 less than getting DirecTV's Whole Home DVR with additional DVR and Home Cinema setup (which is also needed if you wish to network both DVRs). If you don't have the Harmony 900 RF remote, I think you can purchase an RF remote for the DirecTV DVR.

Some points to note:

- The output to both TVs is the lowest resolution either TV can handle. For example, if one TV is 720 but the other is 1080, then the output to both will only be 720.
- Remember you need an additional short cable to connect the splitter to your original TV. I forgot and had to order one on Amazon!

title: Complete Assembly!
text:
I bought this item because i had an internal hard drive for an old Dell, and wanted to use it externally for my iMac. After reading reviews I was slightly skeptical of assembly. I chose this one, though because it was the cheapest I could find for a 3.5 drive. Either, I could figure out assemble or if i couldn't i would manage without the back on.

After receiving the item and opening the package. I started to assemble. There are 6 screws, four that allow the drive to stay in place and two that you use to screw the back of the enclosure on. After placing drive in enclosure i randomly placed screws to hold in place. Then two screws left did not allow me to place back of drive on. I then said oh well.

After a few days I went back to the drive and noticed that there were 2 screws that were different from the other four! After seeing the difference in the screw heads I realized that those two were meant for the back of the drive and behold, I was able to COMPLETE ASSEMBLY and back was able to be screwed on!

If you are going to order this enclosure pay close attention to the difference in the screws.

Side Note: I never built an enclosure before with an internal drive. At first I got frustrated because i thought i needed cables to connect the internal drive to the enclosure (as with placing it in the old Dell). You can just place drive in enclosure without extra-cables. I had a Doh moment.

thanks for reading.

title: works well despite the low cost
text:
I was milling over external storage options and saw this enclosure. The low cost set off a red flag, but I had an unused 10 GB drive from a dead laptop and thought the device was worth the gamble.

The enclosure ships with a handy pouch, a small phillips screw driver, a usb cable, and a couple of case screws. My unit, at least, didn't come with any instructions though it's fairly easy to figure out how to install the drive.

The board / IDE connector is a bit flimsy, so heavy handedness might cause an issue when installing the drive. The cable has two leads that plug into the PC; without instructions, I wasn't sure if both needed to be connected or not but found that one lead would only illuminate the led while the other seemingly powered the drive and the led.

Once hooked up, my PC saw and identified the device right away - a 2.8 GHz Pentium 4 with Windows 2000. To test out the device, I formatted the drive, added and deleted a few files and folders. There were no problems, so I proceeded to test the speed; I copied about 2 GB worth of various length files, and that process completed in under 3 minutes.

I've used the device a few times, and so far, it's been pretty reliable. I'm happy with the performance and portability - the low cost was nice bonus. For those on a tight budget with an existing drive, this device may be a viable alternative to an external usb drive.

title: Simple to Use and Can be also used as a quick Disconnect from web device!
text:
Simple to use and does what I wanted, and also a great low price!

This switch allows you to plug in your PC and then with a simple push of a button change to a different internet connection, or plug in your internet connection and control which PC has connection to it, it's an A B Switch for ethernet ports, simple as that.

Why would anyone need to switch internet connections I don't know, LOL.

That's NOT how I use it. I plug my PC into the output and my internet connection into one of its inputs ( either A or B side) doesn't matter which side. Then i leave the remaining Ethernet input connection empty!
So by connecting it this way, it effectively converts this "A" "B" type switch into a simple on/off switch for quickly disconnecting the attached PC from the internet.
I find this much easier than fiddling with cables in the back of the PC.
When would you want to disconnect from the internet? That's up to you. Some people might prefer to only connect when checking e-mail, or doing an update or web search and be disconnected the rest of the time when working on the PC, watching movies or listening to music, whatever you use the PC for other than internet access to be safer against being hacked.
Or like me, I basically just disconnect when I see suspiciously large amounts of internet activity that I didn't initiate or after a reboot to prevent some virus' from sending out data to connect to certain servers etc... and once I feel it is fine and nothing suspicious is occurring then I press the button to connect to web again.
I love how easy this switch makes that process, no wires to mess with and no relying on the computer software itself to disconnect because it might be compromised by a virus to prevent disconnecting or might have froze up and not accepting any commands from the user. This is when having a quick and simple physical way to disconnect from web comes in real handy.
And at this low price it is so worth having on every PC in your home. I will order another now.
:)

title: Here is a calm account of why I sent mine back.
text:
I purchased one of these and ended up sending it back.

First, my primary motive for buying the device was to provide a way have all the features of a regular Kindle (which my wife has and uses most every day) and add the ability to view movies and play games.

1. It had only 8 gig of memory. This is supposed to be a multi-media device! There are SD cards out there with 32Gb that cost a bit over $30.00 and have the Amazon.com brand name on them! Are you kidding me? This device cannot have more than 8 gig of memory and that isn't expandable? Kindle text readers have 4 gig, and that's a lot for text, but the Fire has 8 gig and is supposed to be a media repository? C'mon! How long until the 16 gig version makes this one obsolete, and the 32 gig version makes THAT one obsolete, etc.

2. For a little more money (OK, about $150.00 more) I can get a full fledged 64 bit Windows 7 computer called the Acer Aspire One. I can install the Kindle reader on that machine; download my Amazon video libary to a multi-hundred gig hard drive; access the Internet in the way I'm accustomed to; and even do productive work! Yes, that's almost twice what the Kindle Fire costs, but still we're talking about $350.00. That's a few dollars more than a water and sewer bill here here in the greater Seattle area! If you can't pay your water bill you likely can't or shouldn't be buying a Fire anyway. The Kindle Fire is for playtime only. As a child I was warned not to play with fire, and now there's a device called "Fire" that's good only for playing. (I ended up purchasing an Aspire One and it did all I discribed but had the display fail in a week, but that's another review.)

3. Oops, this thing uses WiFi only and there's no 3G! What made the text Kindle's miracle machines is not only the revolutionary display for reading text, but the 3G feature that meant you could download book from most anywhere. Now with the Fire we're back to the WiFi hotspot carp again. Am I near a hotspot? Do I want to have WiFi at home when all my other computers are on a fast and reliable hard wired gigabye CAT-5 network? Do I want to be using WiFi on this machine at public WiFi hotspots not knowing how secure those hotspots are? Not really a selling point there. Hear that "pac-man dying sound"? That's me when I found out after buying the Fire that it has no 3G access. So this really isn't a build on the Kindle we know and love, it's a different platform that happens to share the same brand name. I started to feel a bit "burned" by the Fire after the sheer lack of connectivity and futureproofing hit home.

4. I've got a home network with six Windows PC's. I am very accustomed to that platform. Why do I need a completely different device that works a completely different way. I can type rather quickly just fine. Why do I need a device that limits me to moving my fingers across a piece of glass. How do I take care of that piece of glass. Installing my own screen protector was a not-very-epic but time consuming failure. Now the screen is protected, but now despite my best efforts I've got tiny air bubbles between the glass and the screen protector which allows me to rub my fingers back and forth across a screen for no reason since I can type just fine thank you. The original Kindle is a techinal marvel for literates; this "Fire" is a computerized toy for idiots (ok, maybe I'm not as calm as when I started this review). My only caveat is that if you get some games on it and give it to your kid, s/he might stay quiet long enough to get some work done, which in some situations might be worth the price of admission to the Kindle Fire user community.

So...er...that's why I sent it back.

title: Do not buy drives with 1 Year warranty!
text:
I used to buy Seagate retail drives exclusively for their 5 year warranty. This one came with only 1 year warranty. Well, I could not tell Seagate losses due to floods but I'm sure they made much more due to inflated HDD prices. Now they are dropping down warranties to increase their bottom line and consumers are getting products which likely to die after warranty expires. I owned a lot of Seagate drives - 200, 300, 400, 750, 1.5T, 2T, 3T. But I'm really disappointed in Seagate move to 1 year warranty. It must be a sign of Seagate quality going the drain in the name of increased profits. Otherwise they would market (as they used to) their famous 5 year warranty over competitors.

Just recall famous MAXTOR 120GB drives - they all had flawed design and were dying after 1 year. So there was a reason Maxtor slashed both warranty period and prices on their drives. Now Seagate is repeating the same trick and I'm not going to waste my money on them.

Here are few things I can tell after using hard drives for years in my own setup:

- They all will fail - sooner or later. So backups and redundancy is a must.
- Think about warranty period as the hint on when drive will most likely to fail.
- 1 year of warranty also means that you will loose 100% of your storage investment when drive fails next day warranty ends.
- You can still sell your old working drives.

And here is my optimal setup, which allows me to minimize storage cost, downtime due to individual drive failure and to ensure data preservation:

- Local raid setup with data integrity check - to minimize downtime due to drive loss and avoid silent data corruption (bitrot).
- Local raid backup - to minimize recovery due to accidental deletion and multiple drive loss in raid.
- Remote backup - to minimize data loss due to theft, flood, fire.

So I'm buying other manufacturer's drive with 3 years warranty instead to secure my storage investment for 3 years. Good luck with your drive to last beyond 1 year!

title: Excellent Laptop
text:
I have many years of experience in the IT field and this is hands down the fastest and most reliable laptop I've ever used. Ever since Alienware came out with their PCs and laptops, I've wanted one, and I'm glad that I waited for this 4th generation of the Alienware M17xR4 (it is M17xR4, not AM17xR4 as listed). What sets this laptop apart from the rest is that it has the latest 3rd generation Intel i7 quad-core CPU technology, which is a significant improvement over the previous i7 chips. The transistors are smaller (22 nanometers instead of 32 on Intel's 2nd gen i7 CPUs), and they're built in 3D, which translates to improved power efficiency so that the battery will last longer and will not cause as much heat as before, and obviously an increase of speed in games, videos and financial applications.

The screen looks great, very high resolution, and the speakers are Klipsch ProMedia which is a high-end brand, and that means the sounds are crisp and clear. No need to worry about the sound not being loud enough as on some laptops, this will make the majority of music and movie fans very happy. I've had laptops which required externals speakers to be able to hear movie dialogue, so it's nice to see that some thought and effort went into the audio hardware. Includes 7.1 digital audio out using HDMI out connection or an S/PDIF optical port. The sound card is Creative's latest, Creative Sound Blaster Recon3Di High-Definition 5.1 Audio with THX TruStudio Pro Software, so you're getting the best of the best.

I bought mine with the nVidia 2GB GeForce GTX 660M GPU, which is just a month old, came out around the same time as this laptop was released, as well as Intel's 3rd gen i7 CPU. What's great about the 660M video card is that it's very fast yet uses much less power than all other high-end GPUs (Graphics Processing Unit), which means that it'll use less power/battery and won't make the laptop as hot as the bigger, faster and more expensive cards. I went with this one specifically because I've used numerous laptops of different brands and most of them tend to get very hot after hours of usage, especially if gaming, whereas this GPU stays pretty cool and the laptop doesn't get much more than warm after playing games like Diablo 3, StarCraft 2 and Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 3 for hours at a time.

Plenty of ports for external devices, including HDMI 1.3 input and 1.4 output, (4) USB 3.0, firewire, eSATA (3 Gbps), 3 auto-sensing jacks for line out (1 headphone), microphone jack, mini-display port, VGA port, and a 9-in-1 media card reader. It also has an Intel Centrino Wireless-N 2230 Wi-Fi card with Bluetooth 4.0, and of course your standard 10/100/1000 Mbps NIC for wired networking.

If you like using Skype or similar programs for video conferencing, then you'll dig the built-in 2.1 Megapixel full HD camera with dual digital microphones, which records high quality videos and superb sound.

The exterior of the laptop is made of a soft touch finish which feels like velvet, and it looks great. The only downside with it is that it is highly susceptible to smudges, especially from greasy finger prints, which can be a pain to clean, but it's not too bad.

I'd say hands down the coolest feature of this laptop is the highly customizable keyboard and lighthing which allows for, get this, 512 trillion different combinations! The keyboard itself can be split up into 4 different colors, and each section can be set to solid, morph or flash. Solid just stays as one color, morph will gradually change from a range of colors that you choose and the flash option flashes the colors like a Christmas tree light. There are numerous pre-defined color schemes from basic to advanced, and you can create your own custom schemes or even modify the existing ones. It's not just the keyboard that you can change, however, you can also change the front two lights that are on the left and right beneath the keyboard, then there's the Alienware letters below the display, the touchpad, the alien head (whose flashing eyes functions as the HDD activity indicator) and the media touch-control panel. This is all controlled by the Alienware Command Center, which has options for controlling the touchpad, keyboard and a host of other features. Also, the keyboard is fairly large which is great for me because I have big hands, and this was an important deciding factor when I bought this laptop because I can't stand typing on smaller laptop keyboards since I always tend to accidentally hit the wrong keys, but fortunately that's not the case with this one. It's comfortable to type on and feels similar to typing with a regular sized desktop keyboard.

The media touch-control panel is practical and feels futuristic, which only requires a light touch to use. You can control your music and movies from here, including the volume, basic playback functions and the DVD eject button.

The DVD or blu-ray player, depending on which model you buy, is slot loading, meaning there's no annoying slide-out tray to deal with, which is how most car CD players are these days.

The Alien Autopsy software allows you to restore your system from a back-up image that you'll have to create, which should be made as soon as you log in for the first time, that way you'll have your factory defaults saved with no chance of software corruption.

Upgrading the RAM and HDD (Hard Disk Drive) is very easy for those used to upgrading PCs and laptops, but shouldn't be too hard to learn for the novices. There are 4 RAM (memory) slots, 2 are on the bottom and 2 are underneath the keyboard. The 2 slots on the bottom are filled, so if you want to upgrade you'll have to follow Dell's user manual for removing the keyboard and the top plastic cover surrounding the keyboard. The RAM can be upgraded to 32 GB, which is far more than even most desktops/towers. If you do decide to upgrade the RAM, just make sure that the memory sticks are the same speed, size, type and preferably brand, otherwise you can run into the BSOD issue (Blue Screen of Death as it's known in the IT world). There are 2 HDD slots, one's filled, the other's empty and it's right next to the main one. To get to the HDD, simply unscrew two small screws underneath the battery, then slide the bottom cover towards you (with battery end facing north) and from there you can easily see where the HDD go.

There are some very cool wallpapers and Windows login backgrounds that come with the laptop, including an Alienware theme pack. What's cool about Alienware is that it's not just a gimmick with its alien theme, they make some of the finest laptops on earth. Top quality components with a neat style and a highly customizable lighting design, definitely a laptop that will attract attention at LAN parties, airports or at the office. It is a bit on the heavy side coming in at just under 10 lbs. (the technical details again are inaccurate which lists it as 18 lbs, which is probably the shipping weight but it doesn't specify this), but that's to be expected for a laptop this size.

There's a metal plate on the bottom that's used for laser etching your name or slogan to personalize it, but since this is through Amazon you'll have to take it to an engraver if you wish to get this done, normally this is done when you buy it directly from Dell/Alienware. This is a nice touch.

The thermal cooling system is excellent with two large vents on the bottom of the laptop that draw air in to cool the system then there are two large vents on the back left and right that blow the hot air out. The laptop is incredibly silent and you will only hear the occasional loud sound of the fan during intense gaming when it will increase the fan speed to expell excess heat, but these instances are few and far between, for the most part it is one of the most silent laptops I've ever used, and I've worked on most of the various laptop brands.

Oh and the battery life is incredibly impressive, I get 5.5 hours of battery life on a full charge, high-capacity 9-cell battery. That's with the 660M GPU, of course, if you get a faster/bigger video card it will drain the battery life much quicker because they use much more power/higher wattage.

This is a great desktop replacement, in fact I've barely used my main tower since I purchased this laptop. It comes with Windows 7 Home Premium 64-bit edition, which supports up to 16 GB of RAM. You'll have to upgrade the OS if you want more RAM, which isn't necessary for the average user or even gamer. It's a solid build, has pleasent aesthetics and a comfortable feel. This is a laptop that's built to last. My next PC/laptop purchase will definitely be an Alienware.

title: Terrible when it really counts
text:
I purchased the WD7500 less than a year ago in order to backup several years of data CDs, DVDs, a desktop, and two laptops. The speed was great and connectivity was a breeze. Then the drive failed. I did not drop it, did not immerse it in water, and only traveled with it (from home to school or work) on two occasions. Moreover I had never filled the drive to capacity. The failure occurred while I was watching a video presentation I had stored on the drive.

To date I figure it is not a physical failure, however my computer "savyness" will not help. You see, Western Digital, in order to limit customers' use of the drive, included a native USB port and a proprietary connection. This prevents a customer from removing the enclosure and installing the drive into a laptop or desktop.

Although the drive is advertized and labelled as SATA, the secondary connection is not a SATA connection. Therefore when this drive fails, and it will (just read various boards on the Web) you could not just slip-off the enclosure and tie it into a computer to try and diagnose the problem or retrieve your data. Worse yet, the proprietary connection means that regular data recovery services will charge more (I have had quotes ranging from $350- $2,000) to retrieve the data (if this is possible).

Since the drive is still under warranty, WD will replace it, but will do nothing about recovering the data. They do, however, have a list or preferred data recovery specialists to whom you can take the drive.

Unfortunately, other portable HDD manufacturers are doing the same. Your best bet is to buy a bare drive, a separate enclosure, then combine the two to make your own portable drive.
