title: An entry level studio headphone at a mid-range price
text:
For starters, I'm no audiophile. Sure, this is a typical cliche of how people will begin their reviews, but it's still the truth. I simply love my music. I own/have owned so many different brands/sizes/types of headphones, monitors, and stereo speakers that I've certainly become picky about my liking towards certain models. Whether I'm in the mood for rockin' out with some colored home stereo speakers or relaxing at my computer desk, with the desire to listen to music the way it's meant to be heard, I've got speakers and headphones for every occasion.

Frequently, I purchase store returned products at deep discounts, which is how I came about finding these headphones. I knew prior to purchasing them as a store return that they had a manufacturing defect. The right speaker was defective right from the start, so everything else about the headphones were still new and still in it's wrapping. Unfortunately, this is an issue KRK has been dealing with for years; poor quality control. I've owned Rokit 5's, 6's, and 8's, and half of them had manufacturing defects from the get-go (required "warming up" before they would get louder). But because KRK has made itself known as one of the most popular brands in music monitoring, people continue to buy 'em.

Upon dissasembling the right headphone to see the issue, I came to conclusion that the coil inside the speaker wasn't wrapped tightly enough and was pressing against the top of the clear plastic that covers the speaker itself. So when you pressed down on the clear plastic itself, the speaker would begin playing again. I wasn't going to do anything about it, so I removed the speaker.

I had a pair of Sony MDR-V55 DJ headphones hanging around where the chassis was broken, but the speakers still worked. They are NOT studio monitor headphones, but I figured since the 2 used the same size (40mm) speaker, I would take 1 speaker (initially) from the Sony's and put it in the KRK's to be able to compare the sound quality side-by-side. This is where I was surprised...

Both the Sony and KRK speaker were extremely close in sound. By this, I mean that the lows both hit at about the same level and the mids were both fairly flat. However, the Sony did have a bit higher treble. I mention this because the Sony's are DJ headphones, NOT studio headphones. DJ headphones are meant to be colored, loud, and inaccurate. On top of this, the Sony headphone MSRP is $79.99 while KRK is @ $199.99. By no means am I supporting or promoting Sony; however when you are looking for a studio headphone, you aren't looking for inaccuracy. Like I mentioned, the only difference I heard was a more accurate treble in the KRK speaker. Also, the KRK could withstand more power before becoming distorted. And of course KRK is known for enhanced bass in both their headphones and speakers.

I eventually changed both speakers from the Sony to the KRK chassis.....

By no means does the KRK sound bad, just not as accurate as everyone thinks they are. I also own Beyerdynamic headphones which I absolutely love. The bass is tight and far from pounding like the KRK does. Then again, they are also in a different price class, so I guess its like comparing apples to oranges.

As for build quality (chassis wise), I'd say the KRK is on par for other entry level monitor headphones in it's class. It is mostly made up of plastic, with a chrome ring around the outside cups and a stamped-on KRK logo in the center. Thought the plastic itself doesn't seem very cheap as it doesn't seem like it will break unless you try to break it. For example, the MDR-V55 was made of fairly cheap plastic, which broke, and lacked comfort too. However, Sony also isn't a brand to be looking in to if you're looking for studio headphones anyways. These KRK's actually are somewhat comfortable; a little tight, but manageable for maybe a couple hours at a time. As another reviewer had mentioned, the (stiff) foam on the headband actually becomes noticeable and slightly irritating after wearing it for a little while.

What the KRK 8400 studio headphones do have going for them is their clean and sleek design, great portability, and pretty comfortable ear pads. It does come in a nicely packaged box with a quality leather carrying bag and thick audio cables. However, another peeve that I have with these is how KRK decided to go with a non standard 2.5mm to 3.5mm jack. It's nice that the cord is detachable, but it's a hassle that you don't have the option of using the quite common 3.5mm to 3.5mm cord. Just don't lose the cable!

Though I think these deserve a 3.5(ish) out of 5, I decided to give them the benefit of the doubt. I gave them a 4 because it seems not many other people are complaining about manufacturing defects, and they are selling much lower than their original MSRP; especially when bought used. I think these are worth it if you can score them for under $100. If you have a slightly higher budget than that, I'd recommend looking at a different brand as you can a decent pair of mid level studio headphones for a bit more (used, most likely).

title: Deceptive Tumi / Amazon Add-a-bag
text:
I purchased this item from Amazon - and it was NOT as described - probably partly due to Amazon and partly due to Tumi's shady practices - specifically the practice of revising product specs without changing ANYTHING on the product's UPC code/model #, etc.

In particular, the Add-A-Bag feature - which I specifically was looking for and is described on Amazon as having. The backpack I got from Amazon did NOT have the Add-A-Bag sleeve. I happen to be near a Tumi store, and I went to the store - they had the same bag WITH the Add-A-Bag sleeve. Same UPC code, same everything, except the Add-A-Bag. This is a Tumi-owned store. And the reps there said yes, Tumi has a habit of making product changes mid-stream, and this was such an instance. Same price. Not same product physically, but as far as Tumi goes - it's the same. This is just plain slimey practice for such an expensive item.

Not only that, they make it slightly different cheaper for their OUTLET stores but call it the same thing. (I will give them credit though - the model # is slightly different - a letter is added at the end to distinguish the Outlet product.] The Outlet product doesn't have the same zippers or trim. Inferior.

So back to the non-outlet product as described here on Amazon and at the non-Outlet Tumi store: the bags that actually do have the add-a-bag: not very good. Horribly designed add-a-bag: the opening at the bottom is barely big enough to get even a Tumi-branded handle through. And all but impossible to get nearly any piece of luggage's handle to go through (Kirkland, Samsonite, etc.). I tried. If the Tumi backpack is completely EMPTY and you do it *just right* it might fit - but once you put stuff in the Tumi backpack, forget it. title: A good Sat Nav for a trip to Europe
text:
Nice Sat Nav for a recent trip to Europe. I purchased the Western European maps, and loaded the countries we planned to visit. For the most part, it worked really well.

Pros:
1. Large display is really easy to see
2. Traffic data does actually work in the countries we visited, where it could get the FM signal
3. Routing from point A to point B was not difficult; the UI is fairly intuitive

Cons:
1. There is an odd loop you can get stuck in when you attempt to see the actual route you'll be taking, and at times I wanted to toss it out the window because there was not easy to find "back" button to simply return me to the route in progress
2. It power-cycled itself while we were in the middle of a route, for reasons unknown, at least 5 times (during the course of three weeks)
3. The keyboard annoyed me because even though I don't have gigantic fingers, I'd frequently try to press a letter and get the one above instead
4. The teeny, tiny little roads that it favored in Ireland were super narrow, lacking a white center line, and somewhat unnerving to drive on as one had to pull off to one side in order for oncoming traffic to be able to pass. Attempting to set the unit to "Don't make me drive on one-lane roads" mode proved impossible. I imagine there is a setting for that, but after two weeks we gave up trying to find it. That meant plotting a course from one city to the next just to be sure we would not have to drive on death-defying narrow roads in the pitch dark while it was raining.

I'll definitely take it with me when I go back, and I'm glad we had it on our recent trip.

title: Good replacement for Comcast-supplied equipment
text:
I've only had this in use for about 12 hours, but so far it works extremely well. This review will be most helpful if you are a Comcast subscriber.

I ended up buying this combined cable modem/router after I made a mistake by unplugging the Arris Docsis 2 cable modem I had been renting for years from Comcast and installing the new "Technicolor" Docsis 3 (higher throughput) modem/router sent to me. I have my own small network consisting of a Netgear 3800 router in the den with an older Netgear wireless access point in another room (cabled to the 3800), and I wanted to continue using the wireless system I had instead of switching to the Technicolor's router Wifi, which does not get good reviews for range or stability. To use your own wireless router (the 3800 in my case), the Technicolor has to be placed in "bridge" mode by a Comcast rep so that it does not also assign IP addresses, avoiding conflict with the 3800, which is also assigning IP addresses via DHCP. Well, it turns out that the Technicolor won't stay in bridge mode very well, and just a few minutes after everything was working, the Technicolor defaulted back to router mode, and poof!, all internet access through my 3800 was lost. Thinking that a retreat back to the Arris was warranted, I called Comcast back to get the Arris re-connected to my account and re-activated, but there was no turning back- for whatever reason, the tech could not get the Arris provisioned properly again (and he tried multiple times). So I looked at the Comcast compatible equipment list, and spotted the C3700. After purchasing it at a big box store due to time constraints, I connected to it via network cable with a computer, typed in 192.168.0.1 in a browser window, and used the supplied username/password to go into the management pages. I was able to find the screen where the router functions are disabled with a single click (can't remember which screen now, but the pdf manual available online has clear directions) to put it into "bridge" mode, then called the Comcast billing people and asked that the new cable modem be added to my account and activated. It took about 10 minutes for this to happen- I knew I was close when then the computer I had connected to the modem's top network jack gained internet access. I then reset my 3800 by turning the power off, then on again, let it boot up until the wireless lights came on, then connected the C3700 with the 3800's WAN jack (the WAN jack is marked with yellow on the 3800). After about 30 seconds, the 3800 obtained an IP address from Comcast (the C3700 was now bridging and had no server functions), and I was able to gain access to the internet from all computers via the 3800's WiFi channels. I did not test the C3700's wireless capabilities, but would expect them to be good based upon my previous experience with recent Netgear Wifi routers.

A few suggestions:

1. If you are going to buy your own modem/router versus rent one from Comcast (or any other company for that matter), try to buy the same brand of modem as the router you want to use. This avoids one vendor from blaming the other for any problems you have. I was lucky, and didn't have problems, but if I did, Netgear would have been obligated to help me.

2. If you call tech support at Comcast and you get someone who is simply unable to help, politely end the call and try someone else. I got some incorrect information from several techs, but once I found someone who was knowledgeable, I understood that it was impossible to ensure that any of the Comcast stores would have a particular replacement modem available after a potentially long wait in line (you can't call them directly), and I decided it was time to buy my own modem.

The C3700 does not support telephony, so if you want to keep your phone line through Comcast, you'll have to find another unit. I hear they exist, but I didn't investigate very much where to get one. The solution I am using is to install an ooma box, and port the Comcast home number to ooma. ***If you go this route as well, don't cancel your Comcast phone service until you get the home number transferred!***

I like the Netgear use interface, and I have had no problems with the Netgear Wifi router models 3800 and 3700 in use after several years of use. I am hoping that this C3700 modem follows in the same footsteps. The C3700 does generate considerable heat, so it needs to be given plenty of ventilation space. I subtracted one star because the documentation in the box is inadequate (the PDF online), and if someone is buying a modem/router they might not have access to the internet to get the pdf online to figure out what to do next.

Update 6/29/14: I started using the unit as a wireless router and had excellent signal strength, but after about 2 months of use, I was getting up to 6 or more disconnects from the internet each day, including some problems with drops from the 2.4 and 5 GHz networks. The connections would be restored after I cycled the unit using the on/off button at the bottom back. I called tech support and was told to do the following, which helped somewhat:
1. Go in to the router (192.168.0.1) from a browser when connected to the unit with a network cable (through a switch is OK), then choose the "Advanced" tab in the Genie home screen, then "Setup" to the left, then "Wireless Setup"; change the channel for the 2.4 GHz network to 11, and the channel for the 5 GHz network to 153. Click to apply the new settings.
2. On the left-hand side now choose "Advanced Setup", which should be the last choice in the list, then "Advanced Setup" then "Wireless." Change the "CTS/RTS Threshold" to 2306 for both the 2.4 and 5 GHz networks.

Update 7/11/2014- Continued to have problem with dropped wireless channels, primarily 2.4 GHz, and after trying to solve the problem without success by allowing the Netgear Genie firmware to automatically switch channels away fro conflicts without success, I had to call tech support, and got a replacement authorized. I paid for overnight shipment at about $30, and got the unit on the second day. Irritating- you can't ship the old unit back in the same Fedex box because the pre-paid return slip is ground versus priority, so there's some added cost for a box if you have to buy one at Fedex. So I reinstalled my networks in the new unit, and it seems to be somewhat better, although I am still getting some drops daily.

SUGGESTIONS FOR NETGEAR- 1. Please fix the bug that resets the year to 1970 for all log entries after a power cycle, until the time stamp is regained. 2. The logs do not contain enough detail to really help much in troubleshooting- I can't tell if my wireless signal is dropping unexpectedly due to a router issue, or if I am getting some nasty interference from surrounding wireless networks, or none of the above. Maybe I just don't know the Genie software well enough, but I need to know when attached devices drop off the network, and when internet access is lost.

AUGUST 2014 Update- well, the drops continued and a Comcast service visit found the cable signal to be good. The tech could not find a problem, so I got charged $60 for a service call. That was the last straw- I don't know if Comcast's signal is dropping or if I got a second bad Netgear unit, and had no way to figure it out. I switched to ATT Uverse and have been very happy so far- no internet drops whatsoever in a week and the wireless signal from the Motorola NVG589 modem-router-wireless radio actually covers the entire house, better than my Netgear WNDR 3700 or WNDR 3800 or C3700 ever did. However, for those of you really tired of wireless problems, I heartily recommend you think about using a commercial-grade wireless access point by a vendor such as Ubiquiti. I have been fighting poor wireless coverage for years and I'm ready to shell out some money for quality equipment. I have a Ubiqiti access point on its way from Amazon. Once I get it installed, I'll do a review.

title: EXCELLENT, EXCELLENT.
text:
I got this as a gift for Christmas, and I can confidently say that this was one of my favorite gifts of all time! I'm kind of a hobbyist and am using a Canon XS. The kit lens that came with the XS was good, but I wanted a wider aperture. Once I put this lens onto my camera and learned how to use it properly (still learning, of course ;D), I didn't want to put my kit lens back on. And I haven't yet.

Pros
****
-Price - This is a FANTASTIC lens for the price. Of course, I don't have a handful of lenses to compare this to, but I can confidently say that what I got from this lens was definitely worth the price. As a student, and as a hobbyist, I couldn't justify having myself, or anyone else, spend a lot on a lens for me. Sure, the f/1.4 might be better, and sure, I'll get it eventually, but I don't have an extra $200 to spend at the moment, since I don't have a full time job. In the end, I might be paying more to get this lens first, and then buy the better one when I'm actually employed, but I simply can't afford the 1.4 right now. If you're NOT on a budget, then by all means, dish out the extra for the f/1.4. Also, you can sell this 1.8 on ebay for a really good price if you choose to upgrade later, if it makes your decision any easier.

-Sharp and clear! Sooo nice. Just remember that if you shoot at f/1.8 and decide to halfway depress the shutter to focus and then recompose your shot, your results might not be as sharp. This isn't really a fault of the lens, but the fact that you're shooting at f/1.8.

-Wide aperture: SO lovely. It's excellent for portraits, or whenever else you might want to isolate your subject from the background. It CAN be a tad soft wide open, but it's not a huge issue for most people, especially since this is an inexpensive lens. And if you're a professional, you probably won't be looking at this lens anyways. On the plus side, the softness wide open can be nice for portraits.

-Eats light for breakfast. This lens is fast. You can shoot in lower light conditions, compared to the standard kit lens.

-Light and compact!

Cons
*****
-Plastic construction: Not a huge issue for me. I honestly don't think it feels cheap, but I'm not a pro and have not used many lenses. It might feel cheap in comparison to those, but for someone who upgraded from a kit lens, it's fine. Just be careful and hope you're lucky? I haven't had mine fall apart yet (or get stuck to my camera, as several reviewers had issues with), so my fingers are still crossed. I've had this for 5 months so far. Also, I feel like most people know this, but don't fidget with the focus ring if it's on AF.

-Loud AF: Whrr whhhrr whhhrrrrr. You won't be hiding in bushes, getting sneak shots of people anyways, right?! It's not a huge deal, but sometimes, the AF is so loud as its struggling to focus in lower light situations, I just want to put the lens out of its misery and set it to manual. But it's really not a deal killer for me. I'll let the whirring noises make my presence known!

Side Notes
**********
There's no zoom, but it's a prime lens, so that's a given. Learning to move yourself (or your subject ;D) can lead to interesting results, compared to standing in place and letting zoom take care of everything for you. Moving from my kit lens to this lens made me feel a little naked at first, but I don't miss zoom.

You can get up to around 1.5 feet distance from your subject. I keep wanting to get closer, so this is something I'm trying to get used to.

Also, I use a Canon XS, so with the 50mm, things feel a little "tight" since the XS isn't a full-frame camera. The 50mm on my XS is more like an 80mm on a full-frame camera.

It might be tricky to get shots of people in small spaces where you can't back up enough to get enough of them in the frame.

Anyways, if you're on a budget or are a hobbyist, this lens is a great buy. Especially if you're moving from a kit lens, you'll be amazed at what this little guy can do. =D

title: Good Choice For Intermediate To Advanced Users
text:
The Good:
+ No software required on PC
+ Supports latest Wi-Fi standard
+ Solid Connections
+ Detailed Admin Interface

The Bad:
- Terse setup instructions
- No NTFS support
- Default settings leave vulnerabilities

Overall:
The Buffalo AirStation Extreme is a good choice for intermediate to advanced users, but novices may be frustrated and left vulnerable.

Setup: I would not recommend this to first time networking users unless you are fairly technically savvy. The instructions that come in the box are bare bones although Buffalo tried to make this a user-friendly product. It comes with both SSIDs pre-configured along with admin passwords on a pullout card on the bottom. While this makes things easier in theory, you will need to change the default admin password. Your SSID passwords are unique, but I changed mine to something a little easier to work with.

NAS/USB: I have an external USB that I previously attached to my old router, and it is formatted NTFS. I couldn't get the AirStation to see the files, and it only recognized a small partition. When I pulled up the help page, it said that NTFS file systems are *not* support. I worked around this by connecting it to the desktop and sharing it. However, this is not ideal, as this can be kludgy with Linux machines.

Use: In order to take advantage of the AC speed, your device has to work with 5 GHz frequency Wi-Fi. Even though it is not capable of fully utilizing the AC speed, I wanted to hook up my Roku HD. It can only connect to 2.4 GHz networks. What's interesting is that there are a lot of variables that factor into video performance. The software on your streaming device impacts performance. I have Netflix on my Roku and my Blu-Ray player. This is where the detailed admin screens for the AirStation are useful.

I had my Blu-Ray player connected to the AC SSID while my Roku was on the lower bandwidth N SSID. The Blu-Ray player only pulled data down at around 1 Mbps; however, the Roku pulled 20+ Mbps. Needless to say the playback is much better on the Roku in spite of the fact that it was on the "slower" network. The moral of the story is that there are a lot of factors that affect performance. It is not enough to have a super fast router, but it is helpful to have a router capable of diagnosing the problem. It is also good to be on the latest/faster standard as you will be future-proofed for a good while.

Conclusion: It has a few quirks, and it might not be the easiest for novices to use. However, the Buffalo AirStation Extreme has some good features, and it will be a top of the line device for some time. I recommend it to intermediate to advanced users looking for an upgrade with an eye to the future.

title: Inconsistent performance
text: I never write reviews. But I feel I must review this product in order to help with the stress it has caused me over the past 2 months. Let me state for the record that I love this device when it does what it is supposed to do. When it performs as advertised it is fantastic and is perfect for my needs (I run 15-20 miles per week). SO...it's a great product in theory. The problem is that it works as advertised AT BEST 50% of the time. There are a couple primary problem areas that I have had and it seems as other reviewers have also had. 1. It's ability to sync with the satellite is inconsistent. Even though I run in the same general area every day I can only count on it connecting to a satellite if I have first synced it and downloaded my previous run. I therefore have to sync the watch after every day I run in order to maximize the chance it will connect to the satellite. (I will say that you can still use it with fairly good results with a nike+ shoe pod). 2. The actual syncing and uploading of runs is problematic. Almost every time I try to sync it says "couldn't connect to NikePlus. Try Again". Usually, after a few tries and some unplugging and replugging the watch it will finally connect. Sometimes...like at this very moment when I write this review it refuses to connect even after 30+ minutes of trying again. 3. When I finally get my workouts uploaded the GPS mapping feature only sometimes yields results. It seems like the percentage on this last problem has actually improved over the past 2 or 3 weeks, but taken as a whole these main problems are not what I expect when they represent the basic functions I paid to get when I purchased this sports watch. I hope Nike fixes these bugs soon. Maybe the next iteration of SportWatch GPS will do what its supposed to do a higher percentage of the time.

title: Fake, do not buy
text:
I should have packaged this back up and sent it right back as soon as I opened it, but I'd waited a long time and the kids were desperate to watch movies on the big screen so against my better judgement I put this thing into my projector.

First of all it's an obvious fake (Look at these pictures I took comparing it to the OEM lamp that I removed from the projector: http://imgur.com/x6iLgwZ). The fit is awful. There's a plastic clip over the metal housing that is just out of place enough that it doesn't doesn't slide into the projector the way the OEM one does! The black plastic connector (which is brown on the OEM lamp) is very brittle and broke off while I was installing it. I had to salvage the connector from the OEM lamp to complete the install.

After getting it installed the projector starts up and seems to work fine. However, it is considerably dimmer than the OEM bulb. The PT-AE8000U is known for its incredibly high lumen intense vivid bright image and we've come to love and enjoy watching movies on it. But once we started up a movie on this replacement bulb the vivid brightness was gone. There is also a strong odor of burning plastic now emanating from the projector and it seems to be putting off more heat than usual.

It's better than nothing while I wait for a genuine OEM replacement lamp to arrive. Hopefully it does not burn my house down.

title: Effective and useful
text:
Theoretically, this looks like a great product - lets you quickly attach / detach a GoPro from most places. I used to have a problem with the amount of fiddling needed to mount a GoPro with the standard mounts.
In practice, it's pretty good - the clamp is large enough to fit most places, the mounts are secure, and the spring is hard enough to make sure it doesn't slip off. It does have a problem with vibration, though - the length of the arm means that even the slightest looseness in the point where the arm attaches to the clamp, means the camera will gently rock / sway enough on a moving platform to be noticeable in the video.
Other than that, it's a great add-on; probably the best and most useful all-purpose mount you can have, other than a headstrap mount.

title: Map upgrading is impossible with my iMac
text:
I was delighted with this GPS after I bought it from another retailer when my Garmin (bought from Amazon) Nuvi's screen failed after 3 years of very heavy use. I needed a working GPS in a hurry since I was on vacation some 2000 miles from home in unfamiliar territory.

On the plus side; The screen is large and easy to read and it provides all the details I need in a GPS.

Right from the start, however, I have been unable to upgrade the maps. Roads I travel frequently have been improved/re-routed and I'm tired of driving through the wilderness with all the recalculated route announcements chiming every few miles.

I, and others who are far more computer-savvy, have failed to get anywhere updating this and so I'm now looking at a Garmin replacement (my 4th Garmin, the first 3 of which still work fine) some 8 months after buying it. I don't see another TomTom in my future purchases.

Definitely one to avoid if you expect the company to honour their sales-pitch of "free map upgrades".

title: Poor Sony Warranty/Repair Service
text:
The camera is a good product, but if you have problems, the warranty customer service is TERRIBLE! My battery door would no longer stay closed. I sent it back and didn't hear anything for a month. When I called the rep told me I needed to give him the serial number, so he could track it down. He verified that they had received it, but couldn't find it. I asked him why it was my responsibility to find the serial number, which is on the camera that is at your facility. He told me that would be the quickest way for him to track it down.

I told him that was poor service and that I would be joining the myriad of others who have left scathing revues on Amazon.com about Sony's repair service. He said, "Well, those were just written because we didn't meet their expectations." I told him that my expectations were not met either. He then told me that I would hear back from Sony about my camera within 48 hours. I asked him to let me speak to his supervisor and he said he was as high as it goes. I told him I was sure he didn't own Sony and asked again to speak to his supervisor. He told me I would hear from someone within 48 hours. I asked him to give me his name repeatedly, but he finally just hung up on me. During the entire conversation I could hear people laughing and carrying on in the background. I could hear jokes being told to each other. This just adds to the incredible lack of professionalism provided by Sony repair.

title: Very comfy, nicely made, sounds -um- OK
text:
Now, did I need another set of headphones, considering that I have probably 20 phones for each ear? I guess I must really like headphones.

What attracted me to these were the many comments about how comfortable they are and indeed they are. Instead of adjustable sliders or such, these use a very stretchy inner band. It and the ear cushions are super soft and plush. And the 'phones are light. Add that up and yes, these are very, very comfortable.

The soft cushions are surprisingly good at isolation. So while I would think these are good for exercise, I would not recommend them for biking or anything where you need to remain aware of your environment. Perfect for on the treadmill at the gym if you don't like conversation.

The cord is fabric-covered which resists tangling. They come from only the left cup, meaning even less tangling (since they don't meet under your chin and can't get all twisty).

The cable is about two inches long, with an extension cable to connect it to your device.

How about the sound? That's where these fall down. The sound is not bad, but not good. They seem to have pretty good range but are very boomy in the mid- and low-tones. Some music sounds great, some sounds out of balance. They sound like $25-$40 'phones to me. Distortion is OK and the sound is clean enough that I don't think they would be very hard to wear for a while if you can overlook the boominess-- and the comfort would make them a great choice for long listening.

But good sound -- isn't that what headphones are about? Disappointing, given how comfy they are.

Overall: These would be a great set if they sounded better, but for times when you don't need an audio experience, these are great in every other way.

title: For the price, and expected use it blows everything else away
text:
I'm using a Chromebook as a supplemental computer for writing and heavy web browsing, and it's an incredible deal for the price. Most others have explained the Chrome OS well, and the limitations of such. I accepted them when I decided to buy it, but I wasn't expecting how high quality it was.

It's literally a $250 11" macbook air in terms of style. The build quality is very good, with large keys, a responsive trackpad, and a decent screen. If you are used to netbooks and low-end laptops like I am, you'll really be surprised at how solid it feels. The screen is very crisp for text, although the viewing angles are slightly odd. Rather than too dark, it seems too washed out at sub-optimal angles. For the price though this is one solid piece of gear.

What's also surprising is how fast and responsive it feels. It awakens instantly from sleep, and boots from powerdown to log-in in about six seconds. Tabs open quickly, and saving JPEGS to the SSD literally was instant. While watching full screen video from Hulu worked well, with no stuttering, the display felt only average, with slightly washed out colors and muddy edges.

The power brick is tiny, and from initial power on to use took all of five minutes. It really doesn't feel like something that is based on a tablet chip, and if you are okay with not being able to use dedicated programs, it works very well. It's possible to use the web for a tremendous amount of things, like basic photo and video editing, as well as lite productivity software through Google Docs.

The only downsides I have had is that there are no buttons on the trackpad. While right clicking is absurdly easy (just click with two fingers slightly spread apart instead of one) selecting large blocks of text is a little less so. I also had one game's sound not work well, and saving to Google drive didn't work on one photo app; instead, I had to save locally. Considering how many benefits counterbalance this, I can give it five stars easily.

This is probably the perfect computer to give to a senior; it just works at what it does, has no security issues and is far better built than the price would suggest. It's also an ideal computer if you want something portable do to light work on; small, good battery life, and nimble enough to do work on. Some issues you would think aren't even any. Yes, without an internet connection it's useless, but your average laptop or home computer is almost never without it, and the internet makes up a majority of the average user's use. You can't do Netflix on this one, due to the CPU, but given its poor streaming library, I don't miss it.

I recommend it, and I'm really loving it now. It's nice to be surprised above your expectations for a product, and this one does so.

title: Not a good baby monitor solution
text:
Returning this science project to Amazon. Here's why it doesn't work for us as a baby monitor:

-- Uses .5 mb of upload bandwidth per camera for HD video and audio. We have DSL, which only gives us ~1mb of upload available at any time.

-- Does not allow "real time" monitoring. This was the biggest disappointment, and Dropcam doesn't make this clear IMO. There is no direct Dropcam to phone/ipad/computer monitoring via wi-fi. The video/audio streams out to the Dropcam web site / cloud, then you download the stream to your device. We saw lag times of 2-8 seconds depending on the device; not acceptable for baby monitoring.

-- Portability issue. When I shut down the Dropcam to move it to another room, it wouldn't boot back up and go back online. It dropped in and out and continuously lost the connection. I tried a number of solutions, but it seems the camera needs to be re- set up each time it is disconnected from power.

-- If internet goes down, you have no camera. Rare that this happens, but it happens.

I'll be looking into doing a wireless IP cam with the IP Cam Viewer Pro app as an alternative to this DropCam. The whole thing just struck me as overhyped, made-in-China, not ready for primetime.

FYI: Users have been asking for real time connection via wi-fi for more than a year on the Dropcam support site, but Dropcam responded that they want everything to go through the cloud. Too bad.

title: Works fine, but usefulness is limited

This product is two pieces of plastic (the lens mounted in a holder), so there's not much to say about it. It's simple and does what it's supposed to.

However, it's advertised as a solution for all your white-balance problems. That's simply not true. At best, it beats "auto" mode. The problem is that it measures the incoming light spectrum, which means you have to have your camera set at subject's location pointing back toward where you intend to take the photo, and have the zoom set as wide as possible to get the best sampling of the incoming light.

In many cases that's impractical, and it's still an approximation anyway since light will be hitting your subject from 180 degrees. You're better off with a good white/gray reference card.

title: C. Crane CC-2 Radio Fail
text:
I ordered this radio in order to listen to AM radio at its best. After reading the many positive reviews and weighing them against the negative ones, I felt it might be a crap-shoot. Well, unfortunately, the radio arrived in an open box with no instruction manual. Although I was able to download the manual from the C. Crane website, I had an uneasy feeling that the radio might have been a return from another purchaser. Otherwise the radio was in good condtion, wrapped in it's protective thin foam bag.

After connecting the radio and doing a little listening in the FM band (not overly impressive... many stations sounded distorted even after fine-tuning) I switched to the AM band and did some critical listening for about 3 hours. I moved about my home testing the reception against an old Sony SRF-80W (an interesting radio in its day) and found absolutely no difference whatsoevere in this expensive radio's ability to capture the signal better or clearly.

Fortunately, I also ordered the Sangean PR-D5 based on reading the CC-2 radio's reviews. WELL! It appears that either the CC-2 I received is defective or the Sangean PR-D5 is a superior radio all around. Again, I moved around various areas of my home (this time with three radios) comparing the ability of the radios to capture the AM signal. There is no contest... the Sangean PR-D5 was clearly a winner over the CC-2 and was a big improvement over the Sony SRF-80Ws ability to capture clean AM in certain areas of my home.

I really wanted to like the CC-2 being that it has so many other nice features but it's AM quality was very, very subpar. Also, the FM sounded distorted in a number of stations; as if the high frequencies were over saturated.

The weight and quality of the radio felt very good, though. I suspect, as others have mentioned in previous reviews, I may have received a defective radio. I am not willing to chance ordering another of these, however, especially since it's quite pricy. I'll keep the Sangean PR-D5 and be happy that I saved more than 50% of the CC-2s cost.

Needless to say, this radio is going back. I'm gald Amazon has a great return policy.

title: Outstanding value!  (I have both the 39" & 50")
text:
I bought the 39" version to use as a computer monitor a couple months ago and liked it enough with it that I decided I wanted another. Rather than get another 39-incher, I chose the 50" because I'd read some reviews that suggested it had a better panel and could actually do 120Hz gaming (the 39" drop frames). Given that they have the same 3840x2180 resolution, the 39" has a higher DPI, thus everything is smaller and crisper than a standard 24" 1080p monitor, while the 50" has a DPI pretty much the same as a 24" monitor. Yes, both do need to have their out-of-the-box settings tweaked, but once you've done that, the image quality is actually quite nice.

Since getting the 39", my 2460x1600 30" monitor has been feeling quite neglected. At the same viewing distance as the 30", the 39" is probably the largest size I'd want for a computer monitor. The 50" is viable as a monitor IF you have a deep enough desk so that you can position it further away. The 39" can be a little finicky syncing. The 50" has always synced flawlessly. The 50" also has better viewing angles. 3840x2180 @ 30Hz is just fine for desktop work. 1920x1080 @ 120Hz is wonderful for gaming.

In short, you can't beat either of them for twice the money. I'm glad to have both and am actually considering getting another 50" for a special project.

p.s., Seiki, how about an equally good, bargain priced 8K panel? One can always hope!

title: Excellent bang for the money
text:
What can I say, got 5 pairs of the ATH-T400 yesterday - one for me, rest as gifts. Purchased 2 and tested one and immediately went back to the store and got 3 more. Really didn't expect great sound (or lack of it) at this price range. More expensive headsets would be a diminishing return on your dollar which is typical on all audio gears, but this is a good starting point. Each of the 2 round tubing for the headband has a steel spring inside, not all plastic, so should give years of service unlike both of my Sennheisers with both bands broken within 2 years.

Very comfortable except it gets a little warm inside the ear-cup - Its closed, not open air. But still better than my first Koss with liquid filled ear pads and headband too tight - your will sweat in that Koss for extended use but it had pretty good sound then. Exterior sound isolation is good and you won't hear the doorbell or your neighbors lawnmower when the music is on except listening to classical during silent passages.

Very efficient, 105 db/mW. Almost anything could drive it at good sound level. Had to turn the sound volume way down even on my anemic build-in motherboard audio output jack.

Frequency range 15-23,000 Hz. Better than your ears. That only tell part of the story, what you really wanted to know is the frequency response plotted on graph paper indicating the deviations relative to dips and peaks throughout the audio range and how smooth the response is. No distortion figure S/N ratio provided either nor transient respond. You don't expect any technical detail at this price range and was not provided. Lets say it sounded pretty good: highs were crisp, mid-range smooth and lows were tight. Transient response were good too so was seperation. I listen to vocals, jazz, pop, light rock and a little classical and opera. Would not know if its any good for hard rock, metal or any sound requiring very deep base and very high sound pressure.

Decent headset for the money.

title: Excellent radar detector
text:
I was looking for a cheap solution to cover myself from any speeding tickets or red light cameras. I picked up this Cobra for $40 based on my price bracket. It had the sleekest looks out of all the detectors in the same price range. It comes with a 6' 12v lighter socket cable and a suction cup windshield mount that holds the detector with velcro. I found that the adhesive on the backside of the velcro wasn't so great and ended up using industrial strength double sided tape instead. I had the detector mounted directly behind my rearview mirror, but low enough that the rear sensor can pick up radar from behind. I ran the power cable through my a-pillars and into the ceiling trim for a nice, clean look. I've tested the strength and reliability of this detector personally using a variable speed limit sign mounted in my company parking lot; this detector easily picks up the sign from over 500 feet away, regardless if I'm heading towards or away from it. Yes, like ALL DETECTORS it goes off when it sees automatic doors or other devices that throw electromagnetic energy. This is why when you're driving around the city it'll go off seemingly at random when there are no police present. Please educate yourself on how detectors work if you think this is abnormal. Furthermore, not EVERY police offer drives around with their radar on, many flip them on while driving past suspected speeders. The best way to not get a speeding ticket is simple - don't speed. If you have to, be aware of your surroundings and use the detector as a second, not first, option.
I'd highly recommend this little guy for anyone looking to spend around $40-50 for a great detector.

title: ...and the problems are back
text:
Review Update 12-17-13: The issues with recovering a forgotten password for the uPro website have returned, and what's worse, Callaway has announced that they are discontinuing support of the device as of 31 December 2014. The device will still work, but the website (such as it is) will be taken down, and no updates will be available. Too bad, really.

*******************************************************************

Review Update, 7-4-13: I logged on to try uploading a couple of new courses -- provided I could remember my password for the uPro site -- and to my delight I found that the folks at Callaway have fixed the "lost password" issues I had trouble with in the past. Clicking on the "Forgot your password?" link gets you an e-mail with a temporary password, and when you log in with that password the site pops you to a page where you can enter a new password. Voila! I updated my password to something that I can (hopefully) remember, uploaded the Pro Mode for a couple of courses I am will be going to in the next few weeks, and I was done. It was dead easy.

*******************************************************************

The actual overhead imagery which is available in the Pro mode on the Callaway Golf UPro MX+ golf GPS unit is amazing, providing true-to-life images of the golf course that is light-years beyond the cartoon images available on most GPS devices. That being said, however, the unit provides plenty of usable data in the standard mode - distance to front and back of water hazards, bunkers, greens, etc. I would like to see the distance to the corner of a dogleg added to the information available, though -- distance to the front of the green on a 495-yard par-5 doesn't help me much when the fairway bends to the right about halfway, but I don't know the distance to the corner.

I found navigating a course with this device to be fairly simple, though a more complete instructions booklet would be beneficial -- I had to figure most of it out on the fly. Entering scores was simple, but when it came to uploading the info in order to analyze stats I ran into a problem. I had forgotten my password to the Callaway UPro website, and their online system for recovering a password flat-out didn't work -- it kept sending me to a page where I could sign up for an account. If I tried to sign up for an account using my existing e-mail address, the system gave a message saying that there was already an account for that e-mail address (as you would expect it to do...), but I was never given the option of resetting my password for that existing account. Sending an inquiry to their Help desk returned a message telling me that I would receive a response in approximately 5 days, which is absolutely unacceptable. That was 2 weeks ago, and I am still waiting for a response from them.

Without account access I was prevented from downloading more "Pro" mode course data -- so there goes that functionality, and w/o that distinguishing characteristic, the UPro MX+ is no better than a dozen other units on the market, some of which are a good bit less expensive. Until that issue is resolved, the unit is sitting in a drawer -- where it's doing no one any good...

title: Need an alternative
text:
After using it for a week, I cannot confirm NETGEAR AC750 is great or decent because maybe I didn't utilize the 802.11ac protocol. Since I paid ~$70, at first, I thought it must perform better than my original cisco RE1000 but instead what I really paid for the dual band at both 2.4GHz and 5.0GHz. As for range extender, it worked as described and extended the range and I got strong signal to every corner of my house but signal strength isn't everything. However for the throughput, it came far less than what I thought. I was a little frustrated considering this product has such good review and thinking that for this price must be a decent product then I researched some more and realized that the repeater would have minimum of 50% throughput loss because there loss between the repeater and router then loss between repeater and my PC. For casual use this is fine but then again for casual use I am also satisfied with a $20 - $30 range extender which what I currently have. I hoped that the dual band (which matched my router) would give me better option since at 5GHz, I would get better throughput for more bandwidth than the 2.4GHz. However, 5GHz is only good for a short distance as it increase distance with wall/duct interference, the signal and throughput decreases so this is pretty much useless over long distance.

So I did a little test one saturday morning (less traffic times, just in case my neighbors and I are using the same channel) with the throughput data below:

Control/Baseline:
PC in the same room as router (TP-LINK TL-WDR4300) connect to router's WiFi (located upstairs, 2nd floor, on one side of the house)
29.97Mbps Download
28.92Mbps upload

Router's WiFi: @ 5GHz, PC using WiFi directly connected to router in living room (located downstairs, 1st floor, on the other side of the house)
19.12Mbps Download
27.77Mbps Upload
NETGEAR AC750: @ 5GHz, connect to range extender in living room
8.49Mbps Download
14.31Mbps Upload

Router WiFi: @ 2.4GHz, Wi-Fi directly connected to router in living room
20.55Mbps Download
23.63Mbps Upload
NETGEAR AC750: @ 2.4GHz, connect to range extender in living room
11.35Mbps Download
10.35Mbps Upload

From the data above, at 5GHz, there is loss due to the distance and interference between the separators (walls/floor). By connecting directly to Wi-Fi of the router (showed the base loss of transmit thru walls): Download speed, I have a loss of 36.2% for directly to router WiFi; Upload speed, I have loss of 4.0% for directly to router WiFi. The actual loss in the same room for the difference using NETGEAR AC750 divided by directly to router's WiFi: Download speed loss is 55.5% and Upload speed loss is 48.4%. That is significant amount of loss considering I have signal loss to the Range extender and total loss from the original signal more than 80% with full bar of signal!!!!

At 2.4GHz, in principle, the range should be better than the 5GHz but the bandwidth is lower. By connecting directly to Wi-Fi of the router (showed the base loss of transmit thru walls): Download speed, I have a loss of 31.4% for directly to router WiFi; Upload speed, I have loss of 18.3% for directly to router Wi-Fi. The actual loss in the same room for the difference using NETGEAR AC750 divided by directly connect to router's WiFi: Download speed loss is 44.8% and Upload speed loss is 56.2%. This actually performed better than the 5GHz and again I was getting full signal bar strength with a loss of more than 70%!!!!

In short, there loss between the repeater and router also loss between repeater and my PC so the best case scenario is 50% loss as mentioned before and shown in the data. Using the signal from this range extender, I am getting more than 70% loss. To make matters worse during high traffic times or when the signal is unstable (e.g. when neighbors and I are sharing some of the same channel), I've been getting 1Mbs Downloads and upload. I mean sure, it was easy to setup and user friendly or whatever but I'm not paying for pretty packaging. I need a solid/real solution of slow throughput and this doesn't work!

As a result of low throughput, although I have extremely good signal, from the NETGEAR AC750 (~$70), I returned it and found a much better solution with the TP-LINK AV500 powerline kit (~$40). The only disadvantage is that it's not dual band with the missing 5GHz band but the throughput is so much better than the NETGEAR AC750 (results below) plus TP-LINK AV500 is $30 cheaper. Here there's a loss from one room to the other through the ethernet cable of 6.0% Download and 2.8% Upload. When setup with WiFi of TP-LINK AV500, I have a loss of 20.3% Download and 9.7% Upload. With this, I get the best of both world: strong WiFi signal strength and excellent throughput! I know it's not a fair comparison that I'm not comparing apples to apples but don't be fooled, signal strength isn't everything. This powerline kit is much better than the NETGEAR AC750... why spend $$$$, just think of the possibilities of a powerline extender for a home network with cheap routers!

Control/Baseline
PC connected to the paired TP-LINK AV500 in the same room as the router
28.61Mbps Download
28.69Mbps Upload

PC connected to the paired TP-LINK AV500 in the living room using ethernet cable
26.88Mbps Download
27.90Mbps Upload

With TP-LINK AV500 in the living room connected through Wi-Fi
21.41Mbps DownLoad
25.18Mbps Upload

title: It would take pages to tell you how much I love this computer!
text:
I waited until I had used this computer for at least a month before I wrote a review. I wanted to list every feature I love about it but no one wants to read a book here in reviews so I will do my best to keep this short. I was intimidated by all the hate for Windows 8 but I really like it! If you have ever used a smart phone or a tablet you will have no problems with Windows 8, don't let people scare you. I hardly ever use the start screen but it's super easy to do so. I can click the window key on my keyboard, I can tap the window button at the bottom of the monitor screen or I can use the super easy sliding charm bar to the side. Once on the start screen I simply tap the desktop icon and I am in my familiar world I am used to.

If I want to see all my stuff I used to get to from the start menu, I just drag upwards and a taskbar pops up with Apps button. On that screen I can see all the folders/icons I am used to, like control panel and my computer etc. The whole start screen was fun to set up. Before I bought the computer I watched 2 tutorials on youtube using my old computer. I highly recommend JAGtutorials. He made it SO easy to learn so I knew just how to rearrange the tiles and pin stuff to my desktop taskbar the way I like.

I made myself customized themes with background pics from my flash drive. Super easy to set up preferences which is important to me so I feel at home. I opened up Google and found Chrome. As soon as I downloaded, it automatically brought over every single bookmark and theme and preference I have setup already. I have been using computers since Windows 3.0 and this was by far the easiest transition EVER.

As for the hardware. I thought I would dislike the mouse since it's shaped a little funny, sort of a bullet instead of the Logitech shape I'm used to, and the wheel works a little stiffly. I got used to it quickly and I don't even notice the difference now. If the wheel is a little choppy for scrolling I use my fingers on the touch screen. Then if the place I need to touch is too tiny for a fingertip I click with the mouse. Perfect marriage of either/or for every situation. I will share a hint. On some websites it's like the mouse click wasn't working but if I tapped with a finger, it worked. Seems like some sites still have some things that must have a tap and some things need a mouse click. So just try both before you get upset. I can understand why people using Windows 8 without a touch screen might encounter problems.

I LOVE the keyboard! I like the sleep button (shaped like a little moon)for when I walk away from the computer (this way I can have screen savers turned off, which I prefer). To wake it up I just touch the button on the back of the right top corner of the monitor and it comes up super fast. The keys are just right. Not too stiff, not too sensitive and just the right size for me. There are even volume control buttons so I don't have to use the cursor to bring up the speaker icon which takes longer, as you know if you ever needed to change volume fast. I like the size and I like the wireless so I can lean back and put the keyboard in my lap if I want. LOVE.

I used my external hard-drive through the USB port. No problems. I hooked up an external optical drive to rip a CD into Amazon MP3 Player. Worked fine with no setup required. I love the sleek white case. I love how easy it is to move it around from room to room if I need to. I love the 20 inch screen. It's so crisp and after working on a small netbook the pictures seem very clear and large on this monitor.

The only Con in this whole process was not with the product itself. It was with Kaspersky security which comes with the Sony. I mention this just to help everyone else out. If you decide to keep the protection and you pay for it, ALL YOU NEED is the activation code. Don't try to download and install a new copy like I did. Just click on the Kaspersky icon, type in your code and you are good to go, with a year of excellent malware protection.

All in all, I spent six months researching a computer that would fit my needs. I started with the hybrid laptops and worked my way through other options with all the pros and cons for each. I could not be happier with this Sony Vaio. It is close to perfect, better than any other computer (of the many and varied computers)I have owned to date. (although I do still have a soft spot for that ancient Packard Bell with Windows 95 on it)... =)

Google has spoiled me by offering lots of services which gets bundled with iOS and stock android devices, initial few days were bit difficult to get adjusted to Fire OS environment but after a week of usage i found ways to handle Fire OS device.

Performance - No lags while operating any apps or browsing sites of watching movies. Fire HDX seems to have enough horse power to deal with all my daily usage. great. good job amazon.

title: Excellent headphones for the price. COMFORTABLE++++++++++++++++++++++++
text:
ABOUT MY PAST HEADPHONE EXPERIENCES:

I haven't had too many quality headphones in the past, so I don't have much to compare this pair into, but these are still great headphones for me.

I have had B&W P5, earlier version of Bose AE (I think it was called triport back then), and couple of Sony headphones on $100 price range. Audiophiles would probably have much negative to say about all those headphones, but I think that they all have been good consumer level headphones. I have also had over 20 pairs of different IEMs, but I don't think that they are comparable to full size headphones. However, I also have had Bose IEMs (oldest version & MIE2i), and I dislike their sound very much, so I'm not too biased to praise Bose for no reason either.

I would pick Bose AE2 over any of the headphones that I have had in the past. They are super comfortable, and the sound is also very good. Sound is very subjective term, but I like the sound of Bose AE2 more than any of those headphones I had in past. Sure B&W P5 probably had more extended sound range, but their sound was somewhat fatiguing, so I couldn't listen them for too long periods of time at once. Bose Triport had more powerful bass than AE2, but they weren't as comfortable. All Sony headphones I have had, or heard, have been good also, but something in AE2 is still better for me to choose them over Sonys.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

ABOUT BOSE AE2:

I'm not an audiophile, more like casual listener who likes to have somewhat good sound. I use these headphones mostly for music, a little bit for casual gaming, and sometimes for couple of Youtube videos.

Biggest bonus in Bose AE2 is that they are very comfortable, more comfortable than any of headphones I have ever tried on my head. They are light weight, and very easy to wear even for a full work day. Also they are easy to drive, so the sound is good always when plugged right into your devices headphone jack, there is no need for external amps or other tricks.

Soundstage is pretty wide in these, which I like very much. Instrument separation might not be top notch, but still very good. Bass doesn't go strongly to subwoofer level, but it is always present and pleasant to listen to. Highs doesn't go to the highest notes either, but that also makes these easier to listen to, because at least for me strongest highs might cause headache sometimes. Midrange is excellent, and vocals are always clear while listening these headphones. They respond to EQ fairly well, so you have an ability to tune sound more to your liking. While listening to these headphones, I can assure that sound never fatigues you, and you can keep listening as long as you like.

I would totally recommend these for casual headphone users, and modern music listeners. This headphones are totally worth their price tag.

title: I got it at Best Buy.
text:
I didn't buy this on Amazon ... Ssshhhh, I got it at Best Buy ... Sorry, AZ, needed it immediately, and there's a Best Buy down the street from me. As far as funcionality, it DOES work, but suffers from some usability "issues." First thing you should know ... plug it into the computer USB slot first, while it is still empty. THEN, insert your SD card. At that point, the computer should detect the card after a couple seconds. This is how it worked on my Mac. Can't speak for Windows PC operation. When I inserted the SD card into the reader and then BOTH items at the same time into the computer, nothing was detected. So, I removed both, and plugged in just the empty reader, followed by the SD card, and then computer detected sd card. Pay attention to the tiny blue LED. If it is blinking, DO NOT remove the reader or the card. It means it is processing. If you see a steady blue light, it means the reader can be removed, BUT ONLY once you have clicked on the EJECT button in your computer operating system.

As far as design, it's clunky. The USB stick is inserted perpendicular into the computer like a regular USB. But the slot in the side of the USB stick is located such that the SD card is inserted perpendicular into the reader! Kind of awkward. The USB reader stick is a bit wide, preventing neighbor USB slots from being accessed by other devices.

Besides these relative limitations, the reader DOES work.

title: Great keyboard that does not feel like a small keyboard
text:
I received this Bluetooth keyboard from Anker and have been testing it for a few days. My first impressions are very positive. The keyboard is more similar to a laptop keyboard (short key depressions) and is about the size you would find on a 12 inch laptop. That sounds small but believe me, using it feels fine. I don't think people who dislike small keyboards will dislike this. For comparison, I propped it up on my 15in Dell Notebook and the actual keys were only slightly smaller (about 2mm each I would guess). Typing on it feels natural and normal, so although it's in a smaller form factor, I wouldn't say it feels you are on a small keyboard.

Pairing was easy enough, turn on Bluetooth on the device, scan for devices, press the connect button on the back of the keyboard, the device will give you a code to type in and away you go! I paired it with my Google Nexus 7 and it was pretty effortless. I then tried it with my Samsung Galaxy S3 and it insisted on changing the input method from Swifkey X (the replacement onscreen keyboard I use) back to the default Samsung one. Not that big of a deal as it's easily changed back... but I do wonder why the Nexus 7 didn't require that? It's important to note that I think this behaviour is down to the devices and NOT the keyboard itself. I'm also certain it could be overcome like nearly all things with Android.

I've not used it when hooked up to a PC but the keyboard appears to have a layout that is more similar to Mac than PC... examining it closely though, it appears to have all the keys for Windows as well, so I doubt it would be an issue. (Ctrl, Alt etc all there, Command would take the place of the windows key if I'm right, I'm not sure).

Getting on to the things I like about it:
+ It feels natural to use - does not feel like a small keyboard
+ Seems to "just work" - not done any fancy setup to get it going, litterally just plopped it down, connected it and started typing.
+ Uses rechargable batteries fine.
+ Makes typing larger amounts of text on Android a lot easier. You will be suprised how much of a diffence this makes.
+ There are media keys (e.g. Play, Pause, Next, Previous, Sound etc...) on the keyboard (but see below about Function keys)
+ I typed this whole review on it. I think this proves you can type till your heart's content.

Things that I'm neutral about:
* Would prefer a built in charging circuit that supports MicroUSB... better still, a way to use it as a wired keyboard with MicroUSB
* You need to find a good way to carry this safely if you want to take it with you. I would be concerned about the keys (although the on/off switch stops accidental keystrokes being sent).

Things I would like to change
- Honestly, I really do not prefer to have a function (Fn) key on the far left, I like Ctrl there. I also prefer for function keys to be dedicated keys, not ones I have to press Fn to activate. This is a preference and all keys are perfectly usable, and function keys are not present in most Android applications. The keys are media keys for the most part (see above)

title: Microsoft should have taken a top-down hardware approach sooner!
text:
Work
I am greatly impressed with the Surface Pro. As a web developer it allows me to ACTUALLY WORK on the go. I can fire up visual studio, the adobe suite, IIS, etc and go to town. It does everything a laptop does with the added benefit of being as portable as a tablet. This weekend I attended two Azure all-day boot camps. My surface shined through allowing me to sit unplugged for 6.5 hours straight while developing, taking notes (even using the stylus!), etc. It gave me 0 troubles.

Gaming
I was actually really surprised at how well Surface managed at gaming. I didn't expect it to and didn't buy it for that purpose but it was able to handle games like Skyrim and Guild Wars 2 on respectable graphics level with good frame rates. I was playing GW2 on custom med-high graphics and riding in at about 40-50 frames. Not bad imho for a device this size and for the battery life you can get. The battery life playing GW2 was about 4.5 hours.

Rumors/Negatives
A lot of the reviews you read about this talk about heat or battery life being a negative aspect. While the battery doesn't last 8 hours like your typical tablet it lasts far longer than a laptop. I think the second release of surface with Haswell chip will do a lot to bring 8 hour battery life to the Pro. As far as heat it does get a little toasty while running resource intensive programs such as a video game but otherwise it remains nice and cool. I've rarely made the fans even have to turn on. The reason for both of these "negatives" is because the i5 processor this baby has that lets you run you x86 apps.

Wishes for v2
Haswell chip for prolonged battery life, option for 256GB SSD, option for 8GB ram. Honestly I understand why they went 64/128gb for sizes but for most people the 64 is not nearly enough. I would have gladly paid an extra 200-300 bucks for 8GB ram and a 256GB SSD even if it meant a reduced battery life to 4 hours. Hopefully with the combined power reduction of the haswell chipset and ever-decreasing cost of memory/storage we can see these options in the inevitable Surface Pro 2.

title: Motorola SB6141 DOCSIS 3.0 Cable Modem...
text:
My New Hampshire ISP is Comcast. My previous modem was a Comcast-leased Arris TM402P DOCSIS 2.0 dinosaur which I regularly got about 25 MB/second DOWNLOADS and 4 MB/second UPLOADS with the Comcast "Performance" level service. I purchased this Motorola SB6141 predicated upon the numerous favorable reviews I read here and on other mail order and technical web sites.

Based upon advice in other reviews, I contacted Comcast directly via telephone to assist me with the install process. Before initiating the actual install I upgraded from their "Performance level to their "Comcast Extreme 50" level service. If you have VOIP telephone service ensure you're on your cell phone when making the install call as you'll lose your internet connection for a few minutes during the install process as you work with their customer service rep. Comcast will ask for the modem make/model # and the HFC MAC ID which is located on the bottom of the modem, in the quick install instructions and on the box.

Comcast will ask you to disconnect your router during the initial modem power-up and boot process. The modem will go through a series of re-booting processes as Comcast uploads their boot log on to your new modem. Expect many flashing lights followed by changing colors, etc. All normal. After about five minutes of this process the service rep asked me to connect my wireless router to check the internet connection. We achieved success on the first try. All in all, a VERY easy install.

Now for the fun part: I have performed three different speed tests since the install was complete an hour ago. None has shown less than 120 MB/second DOWN and 25 MB/second UP. I saw as high as 132 MB/second DOWN when pinging the New York node. That folks is simply amazing.

For all those whining in other reviews regarding the "too bright lights" my advice is to get over it. When you get older like me you'll appreciate all the bright lights and big letters you can get. Trust me on this! I prefer the white external color of the SB6141 over the rather ominous black Comcast-leased dinosaur modem.

I most strongly recommend this modem based upon my explanation above.

title: great for people who dont mope and complain about small stuff
text:
I am using this for both home and work. I have just finished testing it 4 times. I am seeing no difference in speed in Mbs between this and a direct wifi connection. (yes if you hook up directly to the router it is going to be faster than wifi... this is a given) I am only seeing a difference here of .03 mbs between direct and the signal booster.

The product was easy to set up with all the information it came with, and for the price I love it. now if it looses connection here and there so be it. I boot on my computer every day as do most, if I have to boot this on everyday then its not much of a problem for me. People, if you are so damn lazy that you cannot reconnect something when there is a surge in the net or a drop in speed then just get a 100ft cord and have everything hardlined.

The product does everything as promised and is better than I thought it would be.
- capability to secure the extender with password
- keeps with speed of normal wifi connection
- easy to set up
- easy to change settings if you have a mild computer knowledge

THE DISCONNECTION ISSUE: the problem from what I have found resides not in the product but in the pull of bandwidth or lack of bandwidth. If you have devices hooked directly to your regular wifi that are allocating a large amount of bandwidth then 1)the extender will go slower because it is working on less 2) the extender can loose signal because there is not enough signal being sent back and forth for it to make a connection. I suggest bringing the extender in the same room, hooking it up and running a speed test (google it) on both the extender wifi and your regular wifi. If you find that in the same room there is a drastic difference try first resetting your extender to factory and starting over... if that doesnt work, then its time to contact the company.

THIS IS AN EXTENDER NOT A BOOSTER THERE IS NO SUCH THING: this device extends the useable signal that comes into either your modem or your wifi device, it does not boost bandwidth, the device to boost bandwidth is called money, you call your ISP and give them more of it and you get faster internet(more bandwidth). Occam's Razor states the answer with the least amount of assumptions is usually correct. If the device looses signal, check your modem see if it had a signal disruption or if you are pulling all the signal to another device, or if your neighbor is. The device will either work all the time or be faulty and never work. (BTW I work in IT hardware)
****UPDATE**** If you are having disconnection issues go in the advanced settings, you know the place that you already messed with (not knowing what you were doing) and lower the beacon intervals down to 20-100, this seems to be an issue with multiple devices that use a non automated interval speed (because people mess with them. Also helps with the bandwidth issue that some people are complaining about!! *this problem exists with person who bought it, not the company or software. If you want a professional super duper awesome extender/repeater for VOIP/real-time... then go piss the $200 plus on it... you will probably have the same issue's but this one is thirty bucks!

title: These do work with Klipsch Promedia Ultra 5.1 speakers
text:
I should start by saying I do have a pair of speaker stands that Klipsch used to sell for the Promedia speakers. These Atlantic speaker stands are almost identical to the ones offered by Klipsch. One exception is you probably could buy two sets of the Atlantic stands for the same price of one set of the Klipsch stands. The only other exception is how the speaker attaches to the stand. With the Klipsch's stands the speaker adapter just screws straight to the adjustable pole.

This is the instructions to mount Promedia Ultra speakers to the Atlantic stands. First step is to unscrew the feet from the Promedia speakers. Follow the instructions that come with the stands up to the point of attaching the wire management guide. Use the wire guide labeled as "D2". With the wire guide screwed down to the square mounting bracket use a screw labeled as "I-a" with washer label as "H" and insert the screw between the two wires of the guide from the bottom. You may have to spread the wire guide apart a little bit to fit the screw through. With screw "I-a" and washer "H" between the two wires of the guide, insert "I-a" into the threaded hole on the bottom of the Promedia speaker and screw tight. The wire guide is not very stiff, but it will hold the Promedia speaker just fine. I wouldn't recommend using any speaker wire larger than 16awg as the screw holding the speaker to the wire guide will be the way. When attaching the speaker wire to the Promedia speaker that has the spring clips you will have to move the wire guide a little bit to the side, again the wire guide is fairly flexible.

title: OK... but not great
text:
Just bought a Sony DSC-RX100 and spent ridiculous amount of time comparing numerous camera cases both in-store and online. Bought the Apex 30 because of Lowepro reputation (owned other Lowepro cases in past) and what appeared to be rugged construction. Having received the case I can only rate it as OK.

Pro:
Good size to comfortably fit RX-100, couple of batteries, SD card, maybe a filter later.
Well built, but nothing that special. Like rubber bumper on bottom in case of drop.

Con:
Zipper not that smooth. Also zipper catches on orange fold at internal pocket often.
Cumbersome design where second pocket is internal to same pocket as camera. 99% of time you just need your camera.. but 100% of time you need to move internal flap out of way to reach camera makes camera compartment cluttered. Better to have a second zippered pocket for accessories.
Thin shoulder strap seems cheap and I assume uncomfortable after long day of dragging camera around.
Construction really not that much more rugged than other cases (other than rubber bumper).
Hard to clip shoulder strap to rubber band type side attachments.

Not bad but not as good as I expected.

After much research and comparisons, I felt the Case Logic DCB-302 case (http://www.amazon.com/Case-Logic-DCB-302-Compact-Camera/dp/B003F7DWH8/ref=cm_cr_pr_product_top) was the clear winner for the Sony RX-100. title: Warning ! Read about the LX PRO & CONS
text: Of the current 29's available now the LX is in the top 3. However there are problems with all units, which are easily fixed. First go directly to Cobra and read all the TSB's tech service bulletins as most  can be done yourself IF you even feel you need to. Like increasing talkback volume.  You most likely will have to fix the VR6 pot for SWR as it comes way too sensitive, I had to turn mine clockwise to the 5 0clock position to set warning to come on at 2.8 roughly it was coming on at 1.6-1.7.  There are some that have intermittent mike problems and this has to do with SWR and your antenna, after I fixed the VR6 pot its never happened again.  As far as sound quality this is the best 29 we've heard and even better that alot of the radios on the market today. There is tos of room for upgrades just make sure you research first and  go with one of the CBRT recommended sponsors.  There are way too many hacks out there that can ruin this radio, its not like the other 29's.  I feel all these small problems are nothing compared to some other radios and there isnt a radio for under 200 that wont have a little quirk. I recommend atleast a 4' antenna, as with all radios, they are only as good as the antenna. The whip 102" or a 5' firestick is real good, you will want an SWR of 1.4 at a maximum. My whip has me at 1.2 and that is like doubling your power. DO NOT CHEAP OUT on the antenna, always use brand name parts not knock off, all it took me was one off brand spring to ruin the whole setup and fry a final, switch to the firestick spring and all was fine. When the spring flexed at highway speed it lost all continuity and spiked SWR over 3. Cheap china metal as usual , I didn't look carefully. Without pulling out a soldering iron this LX can do 25watts Some are doing more when tuned exactly to factory specifications. The weather feature and alarm are awesome, really help my job.  I suggest researching CBtalk forum before buying any radio.

title: Reboot Loop Cure
text:
I purchased this DVR in February 2011 and it worked fine until March 6, 2012, when I ran into the same reboot loop issue as so many others. Otherwise the DVR is fantastic. I get over 40 over the air channels in Tampa, FL for free (several in HD), and the ability to record whatever I want with a fully functional program guide. Compare this to the $80+ dollars per month I was spending on DirecTV (for my non-HD receiver), and even though this unit appeared to be lost it was still worth the $300 purchase price. I like the DVR so much that I would have purchased another, but being the do-it-yourselfer that I am I read all of the blogs about this problem to see if there was anything I could do to remedy.

Most of the commentary has simply been that the receiver is a piece of junk and it sucks - not many suggested solutions. I did read about a few people that were able to get the DVR to function properly by powering off and then powering back on, but this did not work for me.

So here's what I did that brought the DVR back to life:

1) Unplug ALL connections for 10 minutes.
2) Plug in the power and the video out to the television. I am using the component connectors Y/Pb/Pr and RCA audio cables, not the HDMI connection. Do not plug in the internet connection or connect the antenna in.
3) After I did this I was able to press the menu button on the DVR remote to bring up the DVR menu on the TV. I navigated to reset factory defaults and reset the default settings.
4) Then I connected the antenna in and used the setup wizard to restart the DVR. The DVR then worked fine, just like before the reboot loop error.
5) Reconnected internet after wizard finished.
