title: Very nice but a couple minor flaws - suggest newer model (a57, a65, etc)
text:
I've had this camera a bit over a year now. Did not buy from Amazon but hanging out here more often as a Prime member so finally adding a review. A bit about me: been using DSLR's about 3-4 years, first started out using Olympus 4:3rds system with the underappreciated E330 (the first and for quite some time only "true" live view DSLR that maintained phase detect autofocus while using live view). So in that sense the Sony SLR and SLT offerings were interesting to me when I decided to leave my newer E-30 and the 4:3rds system entirely for greener pastures.

I did look at Nikon and Canon, as of course the '900 lb gorillas' of the imaging world. But I guess I'm a natural contrarian. I am neither 'good enough' nor prolific enough (nor $$$ enough) to even look at full frame, so I only considered slightly larger crops than 4:3rds but still, crops. For the price, and coming into a new system with no legacy glass to worry about, the Sony a55's good reviews and feature set appealed to me. I actually bought it without even being able to see through the EVF as the store I went to didn't have a charged battery for the sample unit (d'oh!).

At this point I've used it about a year and realized that in terms of image quality it provides about everything I could hope for. Colors are rich, detail is superb (16MP is more than plenty for just about anything, although a few of the newer Sony and competitor offerings are starting to beat that), etc. Functionally the camera is very nice as well. I'm not a super-hi-ISO shooter so rarely go above 800, and with proper RAW processing 800 is quite noise free, which is good enough for me. The EVF is a bit of an adjustment - it can look a little 'gritty' even though it's quite high resolution because it is sequencing thru the colors, so if you move your eye really fast you may see a bit of rainbowing effect. If the EVF is 'gained up' (shooting in dimmer light) you will see a bit slower updates and sometimes a little tearing through the EVF. I suspect it might be droppin the frame rate to 'stack' sensor snapshots so to speak. But that occurs in lighting where a typical crop SLR's optical viewfinder would be dimmer, if more 'optically pure', so that's a trade I was willing to make.

Ergonomically the design is great, but a bit small for my hands. (I'm a fairly tall guy, 6' 1.5", 230#ish, long fingers) Compared to my Olympus E-30 (my second DSLR) this seems like a lightweight toy.

So, to specifics:

Likes:

1. EVF data overlay. Digital level gauge, Exposure/Aperture metering, live histogram options, and (sometimes, see Dislikes #1 as well) the "what you see is what you get" nature of the EVF since it gains the image to try and show you your current exposure settings.
2. Review in EVF. Can't do this with an optical viewfinder. Without removing your eye from the viewfinder either autoreview or if you manually hit the review button, you see the image you just shot. Great for shooting in dark environments or semi-private ones (say at a graduation ceremony) where you don't want to light up the rear screen to see.
3. SETTINGS in EVF. The "Function" button lets you tap, use the cursors to move up/down/left/right, roll the front wheel to pick a given setting within a group, tap function again to exit back to shooting mode (or just half-press shutter). All without removing eye from viewfinder.
4. Continuous phase-detect autofocus no matter whether you are shooting fast or slow, from the rear screen or viewfinder, "live" view or "traditional"...the SLT makes it all completely the same. Yes, the transparent film "costs" a tiny bit of light which will affect extreme high ISO shooting. I bet most people's UV filter costs the same amount....its immaterial.

[Overall, you see the top 4 "likes" are all related to the entire EVF vs. OVF tradeoff of the SLT design.]
5. The EVF tunnel sticks 'out' a bit which is nice for not mashing your nose against the back. I suffered a lot of that with my older E-30.
6. There is user-accessible fine tuning of the AF module (do a google search). You're just adjusting the position and angle of the module - not doing any per-lens calibration - but it's better than nothing.
7. Lightweight
8. Good set of AF points and fast AF response. Nothing groundbreaking I'm sure, but quite sufficient. Any focus I've "missed" has been clearly personal limiitations and skill, not because "there wasn't a point there"
9. A lot of the so-called gimmicky features are pretty nice. In-camera panos (I especially like that you can do this panning the camera body 'up' or 'down' with the orientation in portrait mode for a better shaped pano). Twilight portrait and night multi-fire stacking modes.
10. Articulated screen is good, personally I'd say a 'requirement' of any camera that claims to offer live-view like features. I especially like locking it turned in toward the camera to avoid nose grease prints when shooting a lot, or to protect from extreme sun and minor rain. (I would not recommend the Sony a35 only for this reason: no screen articulation)

Dislikes:

1. This is the only feature that's kind of limited my compositional or shooting ability, and is strongly related to "like" #1. The EVF does a 'what you see is what you get' autogaining of the image to help you see the shot as it will be taken. While normally this is great - for studio photographers using radio poppers or others using 'manual' flashes, it has a strong flaw. (In my case, I shoot underwater, with the camera in a housing and external, non-TTL strobes.) In short: if you are shooting with manual settings because you know you have a flash, but the *camera* does not know a flash is attached (manual sync, not communicating with the camera although it may be mounted on the hotshoe), the EVF 'helpfully' gains the image down to below visibility to warn you the image will be vastly underexposed. Unfortunately it's wrong, but the camera doesn't know that. AF points still work and will light up with a half-shutter press...but you're framing sort of blindly. That kind of sucks. BUT - while I'm taking a star off of this camera for that reason - Sony has realized this flaw and fixed it in their newer cameras (a65, a77, presumably a57 that just got announced). They now have the option to disable the EVF brightness link to settings and just reproduce at about the current conditions. This one feature has caused me some problems, so for those of you looking now (March2012 timeframe) for a used or end of stock a55, be aware of this one difference.
2. Articulated screen hinges from the bottom. Sometimes gets in the way on tripod plates. Side articulation might be a tad better. The a77's "wishbone" articulation is better still.
3. As I said body is a tad small for me. Others might really like it a lot.
4. Does occasionally overheat (after taking >250 pics on a single battery in +100 deg weather and blinding sun at a wildlife park...but still, I'm not sure my Olympus would have done that). Those taking video have also noted this in other reviews but I don't do much by way of video so haven't experienced that myself.
5. Wish the AF points could be "grouped" e.g. not just "all" or "pick any one" but also "all", "left, middle, or right grouping", or "pick any one".
6. Wish there was a dedicated (or even programmable) button for turning on/off the inbody stabilization. I do have a hard time remembering to disable it for tripod shots and re-enable it after, or forget to re-enable it after using a long Sigma lens with in-lens stab (150-500mm for example).
7. The video button is kind of easy to hit accidentally sometimes. I think it should require a longer press or maybe hit video then hit shutter. I'm sure those who do video all the time might totally disagree with this one though. :D

Final summary: Note that this review is being written in March 2012, with newer SLT offerings out there. Would I buy this camera again if I had it to do over again a year ago: yes. I do like it. Would I buy it *today*? Perhaps no...but only because I'd be buying a newer model a65 or a77 because of "dislike #1" above. NOT because of anything else wrong with the a55. So for those of you curious about EVF who don't think that one issue would influence your shooting, I'd say an a55 would be a good purchase. The 16MPIX is plenty, the AF is still quite functional, ergo and feature set is fine, and you'll save a few bucks vs. the newest bodies. 4-stars, no regrets, and although I'd like to upgrade myself for that one feature I probably won't soon (underwater housings are body-specific and upgrading a body means I also need to convince the wife I need a new $1400ish housing...going to have to wait a little while for that ;D )

title: Innovative design - Excellent gadget and camera bag
text:
This backpack surprised me in several very positive ways.

First, the construction seems solid. I'll update this review after more use, but for now it appears at least comparable to other backpacks in this price range. The padding, however, far exceeds any other backpack I've used, including several "road warrior" class Targus and IBM bags. There is no question that my gizmos are well-protected in this thing!

Second, the storage is arranged more uniquely than the photos led me to believe. The laptop compartment is comparatively cramped - enough room for any 15" laptop or some of the smaller 17 inchers, with effectively no room to spare for anything other than a few documents or a tablet. Do not buy this expecting to squeeze a textbook or even a thick spiral-bound notebook in with your computer unless you travel with something really thin like an ultrabook.

What you get in return, however, is massive, deep, and flexibly reconfigurable padded pockets in the two main storage areas. Enough room for most of your camera gear in the bottom bay and all of your computer accessories in the top bay. Side pockets accommodate all the trimmings - ID, pens, flash drives, water bottles, and the like.

The end result is a comparatively smaller backpack with large amounts of safe, secure storage. Love it so far!

title: The Grinch Brought This One for Christmas.
text:
Wow. One of the worst electronic devices we've ever gotten. Looks cute, doesn't work. Once it either shuts down automatically (after 30 seconds) or you manually turn it off, the on light stays on and burns the battery. Then it will not turn back on unless you open the battery compartment and shut it again, effectively wiping the camera memory. The battery latches that keep the battery door closed are tiny cheap plastic and broke in minutes, thus not holding the door shut, thus not letting it start up. So that it can freeze up again in 30 seconds. The quality of the pics are, well, wow, just as bad as the physical construction of the camera. My 5 year old was a good sport about it, and tried to use it. When the battery compartment broke a few minutes later, we took the batteries out and she said she'd use it as a pretend camera.

Wow. What a horrible Christmas morning experience with this item. We didn't make too much of a deal about it so she wouldn't worry either. But we'll be sending this pink blob of plastic nausea back and getting her a V-Tech camera first thing in the morning when the stores open. She still wants pink.

Stay away. Stay very far away. As a matter of fact, stay far away from this company, "Sakar", which needs to have someone in the company care about quality control and, what's more, English grammar in their documentation. Ew.

Sanrio should also vet the companies who use their cute logos as well, an experience like this can ruin our image of Hello Kitty.

title: Great Value for the Price
text:
I needed a portable music player that I could take to my garage while I'm working there on the weekend, or use during power outages (I am stationed overseas where that happens all too frequently). I was primarily looking for something that would play MP3s on a SD card or USB thumb drive. Unfortunately, the "name brand" offerings were not at all what I was looking for, at least at a reasonable price. I saw a lot of boom boxes that still had cassette players (the 80's called and they want their technology back!), CD players that may or may not play MP3 CDs, and maybe an "Aux” input but that was it for the most part. Then I came upon this item, which seemed to have all the features I was looking for at a fairly low price. My only question was, "Who the heck is Naxa???!!” I had never heard of the brand before but decided to take a chance, given the low price and mostly positive reviews.

My gamble paid off. I have had this player for 4 months now and I am quite pleased with the purchase. It does everything I need it to do. It accepts a variety of media (SD card, USB thumb drive and MP3 or Audio CD) in addition to the AM/FM radio. The sound quality is actually much better than I expected at this price point. I agree with other reviewers that the volume is limited but it gets loud enough for my needs (and for those that still have kids in the house, that may be a good thing!). The digital display shows the MP3 tag data, although it scrolls through it a bit slowly and of course, no album art. Still, it's far better than displays I have seen on more expensive models.

A couple very minor gripes (resulting in a 4-star grade instead of 5 stars): I'd be happier if the radio function had a digital tuner but a manual tuner is almost unavoidable at this price point. Also when playing MP3s from SD or thumb drive, the player does not "remember" where you left off if you have to turn it off or switch to another mode. That might be a concern for someone using audio-books or other extended-length tracks (e.g. Podcasts). Not a problem in my case.

I’ll also mention that I use the player on batteries almost all the time. My first set of 8 "C" batteries (Energizers) lasted for 4 months with somewhat sporadic use (once or twice a week). Decent, I suppose, but I was hoping for less battery drain. Maybe my expectations were too high, though. By the way, other than the digital display getting dim, there is no “low battery” warning.

To sum it up, for a very low price you get reasonably good performance and lots of flexibility as far as playable media. You are not going to get an audiophile experience but to get that, you'd need to pay much more (and possibly get fewer features). All in all, you can count me as a highly satisfied customer and I would recommend this item to others.

title: Did not work with iPad, Samsung offered zero help.  I found a workaround...
text:
I had high expectations for this product, but I would never recommend this to anyone who wants to use it with an iPad / iPhone. This device is NOT plug and play. To get it to work, you can only use a Windows PC that has WiFi. So, desktop PCs are out of luck.

The funny thing is you need a Windows based PC with WiFi only to run their setup program. After that, the device isn't actually designed for desktop PCs. You can't stream content to Windows PCs, so why require one to use it? By contrast, although it lacks the DVD drive, the Seagate Satellite lets you stream content right out of the box, with anything that can connect to it.

I called Samsung twice and essentially was told they are still working out the kinks and had no way to help me. They said they had some resources on their web site, including a PDF of the book (which is just a worthless sheet already in the box), and some videos. I asked what the videos showed and he told me he's never seen them because Samsung doesn't allow their employees to stream videos, even when they are from their site. So, essentially they don't train their staff at all and they can offer no advice.

I can only assume that if they actually sell any of these, the buyers must be using something other than an iPad to play the content, because out of the box, it doesn't work. The software, the setup programs and the instructions are poorly written and if you can get past that and complete the setup, it still doesn't work.

I eventually found a work-around. After reading online that their device has a DHCP server, that lets you use this as a router (assuming you plug your existing LAN into it), and that it often conflicts with other devices, I decided to try something before sending it back. I changed the device to a static IP, and I picked a number in the 192 .68 .1 .9, then used 255 .255 .255 . 0 as the subnet and left everything else blank. Viola... it worked, but how on earth would they expect anyone to figure that out?

Let's hope they update the firmware and software again to make it right. Until then, buy this only if you are good at puzzles.

title: From a professional Installer
text:
I have purchased and programmed around 50 or more of these remotes. Once you learn how to program it, it really doesn't get any better. There are other remotes out there that are easier to program, but most of those require a computer connection each time you need to make a change. This is where the MX-350 differs. I couldn't tell you the amount of times I've needed to make a quick change or tweak an existing macro, but this allows you to do that on the fly. Don't get me wrong, I've programmed a number of those other remotes too and they are VERY nice to look and an (most) function just as well.

EVERYTHING you need to know about this remote is found in the included manual. It allows for pre-programmed codes for your standard components (DirecTV, TV's, Cable box, Blu Ray Players) but it also has a "learning" mode that allows you to program ANY IR component (with a remote). For example:

I have a lot of movie files on my computer. I purchased a Micca Speck Media Player recently to allow me to connect an external HDD to my TV and play those files. Of course, that component didn't have a pre programmed code, so I simply went to setup mode and then to "LEARN". Face the remote together and push the corresponding buttons and you're all set!

It allows for 10 separate devices to be programmed and also allows for the prementioned, Macros. A "macro" (if you don't know), is the ability to "ONE button push" to select an activity. Say you want to "watch Blu ray". You can program the remote to auto select different inputs, channels, and/or turn on/off selected components during the process.

The remote also has a nice "punch" feature. This allows you to simple "punch" the volume/channel button from one device remote to the other. Say you're watching TV through a surround sound system. You don't want the volume on the control to control the TV volume. So you just "punch" the volume from the "Surround" remote to the "DirecTV" remote. Or whatever component you're watching at the time.

The ONLY thing I don't like about this remote that the other remotes offer is recharging. This remote requires 4 AAA batteries to function. These WILL last a long time, so it's not like you have to replace them everyday. The remote also includes an internal battery that saves all programming in case the batteries do go out. That way you WILL NOT have to reprogram it.

Hopefully this review helps you you make a decision. Feel free to leave a comment or ask a question. Also, if this review has helped you, PLEASE click the "yes" link after the review. Thanks.

title: Great sound quality; a little complicated
text:
The sound quality on this machine is amazing.

It is kind of hard to set it up. You use a microphone (included) to get the acoustics of the room. This is pretty normal. Then you have to set the sound field to match the source video or audio. That's not so standard. Denon, for example, can automatically detect what the source is putting out and adjust automatically. It took a while to figure out what lined up with what, but once I had it all sorted out, I was a very happy camper.

The range of audio, high to low, is very impressive. The bass is amazing. Naturally your speakers will play a role in this, more so than the receiver will, but with the right speakers this unit is pretty amazing. 7.2 strikes me as odd. There is only one audio channel that goes to the subwoofer, so the same sound is sent to both. Humans can't audiolocate subsonics, so there isn't much surround quality involved.

It supports both WiFi (with a good antenna that sticks up from the back) and Ethernet. As with any device, Ethernet will give you the more reliable connection.

It supports Blutooth, which is kind of cool. I use it to stream Audible books from my Kindle Fire. It's very easy to set up.

It supports passive HDMI, which is really nice. You don't have to have everything turned on if you don't need it. When the system powers itself down, which it does if it is inactive for two long -- say if you leave a video or disk paused -- the screen barely flickers.

It does not yet have support for Sirius, which is disappointing, but it supports other services, such as Pandora and, of course, Sony's own Music Unlimited service.

text: Everyone complains about how slow this pc is--and it is like molasses. Next, get rid of Norton and get a lighter anti-virus. Also, the touchscreen is frustrating--disable it by going to control panel, device manager, human interface, and disable the first HID device.  Finally, after all the deleting, run a registry cleaner like "CC". We did this and the pc now runs 5X faster and is "normal" for a little notebook processor.

title: Great pair of binoculars!
text:
What a wonderful set of binoculars. The image is very bright and clear. The image stabilization is a charm to use. The optics are superb.

I compared these binoculars to a cheap ones that I have. I could not believe the difference. After seeing through these binoculars, I think the cheap binoculars were pretty much unusable. I was squinting to see anything from those cheap binoculars. With these canon binoculars, it is as if the binoculars don't exist.

When you look through these binoculars, it is as if you can forget that you are looking through a binoculars. You feel like you are looking at a big round screen, with perfect display. There is no eye strain at all. The brightness of the final image seems more than what my naked eye can see. The image lights up when you see through these binoculars.

I use it for bird watching, and when you look at any bird, it is as if you are watching it's colors for the first time. The view from these binoculars is just so much more bright and vivid, compared to what I can see with my naked eyes.

And rightly so. The amount of light reaching these binoculars is, let's say 42*42/(5*5) times more than my eye - assuming my eye can dilate to 5mm. I am just making some extremely wild guesses here, but I think that the amount of light that gets into these binoculars, is some thing like 60 times what can go in my naked eyes. Of course, some light is lost in optics, and a good amount of light is lost because you are only looking at a smaller part of that light (the smaller field of view compared to naked eye). However, the final view is still bright and crisp, at least as much as I could possibly imagine seeing with naked eye if I could get up close. Beautiful optics light up the scene.

When image stabilization is pushed, it is as if the entire view just freezes, and the movie starts. You forget about the binoculars, and just enjoy your view.

I have used these binoculars for night start gazing as well. I have heavily polluted skies, but with these binoculars I can view many more stars. The orion nebula looks beautiful with these binoculars. I am absolutely new to astronomy, but I think I saw jupiter and it's four moons distinctly using these binoculars. Also the moon is just breathtaking with these binoculars. You can see all the craters, and the terminator (the line between dark and lighted sides of moon), and many surface details in full clarity with these binoculars.

Quality makes all the difference.

I would also like to note that the actual hooks do not stay in place very well. I thought, maybe, the reviews I had read prior to placing my order were simply outliers (from a statistical perspective). The material feels cheap and, again, too flimsy to merit any decent rating. I used this product to help with gym and basketball sessions.

Honestly? I found myself re-adjusting them more than anything else; whether that would be dribbling, shooting, lifting, stretching, etc. I considered this option as a pragmatic and, financially sound, option instead of buying brand new headphones with an in-line mic to stay on securely during exercise.

Needless to say, I will never buy these again. I hate one-sided reviews because it sounds like I'm just hating on the product... But unfortunately this is how the story has unfolded. PHENOMENAL concept, HORRENDOUS execution.

P.S. This was used for the iPhone 5 and its new ear bud design. I will more than likely be buying the Klipsch Reference One headphones with in-line mic and controls because, quite frankly, I hate the Apple ear buds and I am extremely dissatisfied with this Earbudi product. Any amount of sweat will make these clips slip off of your ears. The design of where the hooks meet the clips is underdeveloped.

Do yourself a favor and avoid this product at all costs, even if it's only $10. I'm glad that it was only $10 because I can live with that mistake. I'm going to find new headphones that will fit securely ASAP though.

What I thought was a pretty good deal for Alpine speakers was, in fact, a poor choice. I tried these out for a few days with my Kenwood stereo (50 Watts x 4) and found that they started clipping at about 80% of full volume. title: Anker Batteries for HTC Evo 4G Work Fantastically!
text:
This is a really great deal. I have a 1 1/2 year old HTC Evo 4G. I love the phone but the battery life has left something to be desired. With the duration of the charge on the original battery getting shorter and shorter, I decided to get the Anker batteries.

Living in the D.C. area, I use 3G/4G and GPS a lot, especially while I'm driving. So I've been putting the batteries through the ringer. The main thing with these to remember is to follow the instructions provided with the charger.

Make sure to drain the batteries all the way (until your phone isn't able to reboot anymore) before charging them up again. And don't charge for more than 8 hours. Do that 4-5 times and you'll notice a significant difference in how long they last!

So far, everything has worked out really well. The charge on my original battery was lasting between 4-6 hours. With the Anker batteries, I only need to recharge every other day now. I'd definitely recommend Anker!

title: recording volume too quiet
text:
I have used this microphone for over 2 years recording lectures at the school, and it finally gave up on me. From the beginning, we had a "love-hate" relationship. One one hand, I really like the idea of shielding the noise of my keyboard, and focusing the mic mainly on the class instructor. That purpose worked well. However, the mic had several flaws:

1. the recording level was very low (tested both on DELL and Sony laptop). People bringing a stand-alone voice recorder to class usally achieved a much clearer recording. On my recordings, I had to crank up the volume to the max upon replay to make out anything the instructor said.

2. The metal cap of the mic got loose and started to fall off after 1.5 years. I had never treated this thing harsh.

3. The center of gravity is not in the center of the mic's base. with a USB cable, this mic does not necessarily point into the direction you are trying to aim for. Getting it to point to the exact middle of the classroom always required moving cables around a few times.

4. A couple of times the mic would draw too much current from my laptop, and USB required me to use a cable with two USB connectors, to draw sufficient current. This forced me to always carry a special cable with me, in case there was again a usb power surge.

Overall, I don't think I will ever settle for this model again. It's just too clunky and user-unfriendly designed, though the idea is excellent. I wish there was a follow-up mode to overcome these issues.

title: Great Deal - Great TV
text:
I started by joking with my wife that I wanted a 70" TV. It was ludicrous, we thought. Then I started looking at LCD TV's. I knew I didn't want/need 3D, so that eliminated a bunch, and I knew I wanted at least 60". I looked at Sharp, Samsung and others, but not at Vizio. I'd been warned that they were "cheap" and didn't look as good.

Then, the joking got serious, and I started honestly looking for a 70" TV. When I realized my mounting area was exactly the size for a 70", we went for it. The only choices were Sharp and Vizio. Sharp had four different models, all of varying reviews. Didn't want 3D, didn't need this, didn't want that - and the prices were all $2K or more. Still a steep jump for us. Then there was this Vizio...

I started reading more and more reviews - Vizio was stacking up well against Sharp. And the price was $500 less!! Finally, we jumped and went for the Vizio. Ordered it from Amazon and a week later, two very polite guys showed up in a truck and carried it into my living room. I used the mount I purchased off Amazon and with the help of a buddy, hung it on the wall and hooked it up to the Yamaha surround system I also got on Amazon. BOOM!! Instant home theater (and the biggest one on the block) for under $2K. (Thanks, tax return!)

I am an audio visual person by profession - and I must say I have been very impressed by the picture of the Vizio. Looks great!! Easy to use - easy to navigate. I wish the remote had backlighting, but for the price I paid, I'm not going to complain. I got the 5 year warranty for another $150 or so and I am confident that I'll have 5 years of great viewing ahead of me. Love the TV - picture is crisp and clear and the HD is awesome. The price is doubley awesome. I paid as much for my 70" as my buddy did for his 42" three years ago.

GREAT DEAL!! GREAT PICTURE!! GREAT TV!!

title: By far the best lifelogging camera on the market
text:
I am a cognitive scientist/psychologist active in the Quantified Self movement, and I have had my Narrative Clip since early May (I bought it through their site). I am a huge fan of this camera, as long as you understand the limits to the technology. First, the great. It passively takes one photo every 30 seconds, so your entire day is captured (and can be uploaded to Sweden, if you choose). Most of the pictures aren't interesting (like most of life), but there are always a few interesting photos every day. Personally, I choose one picture from every day and write about it - what was happening, who was there, etc. as a part of my research. The pictures from the Narrative are not "posed" and so you can view (and review) a POV of your life as you live it. To have even one picture from every day of your life is incredible.
What could be improved? Several things. It falls off pretty easily, and can be easy to misplace (and hard to find), so you have to be pretty OCD about where it is at all times (although most lifeloggers are pretty OCD anyways). I wrote my email on a label and attached it to the back. Ideally, cameras could be delivered with this information already inscribed. The camera does not work well in low-light conditions, but it isn't absolutely horrible in low-light either. It doesn't work if it is being jostled around, so I can't wear it when I run. Ideally, the camera should charge and upload photos wirelessly too, but this is probably coming in a future iteration.
In sum, this is an amazing camera from a brilliant design team. My only regret is that I didn't have one to chronicle my children growing up.

title: Excellent Padded Leather "Rotational" Case With Automatic Wake/Sleep Feature
text:
This MARWARE REVOLVE CASE for the 8.9" Kindle Fire HD has a hard interior frame that grips the tablet securely--once you click the tablet in, it won't be falling out again by accident! (But if you need to remove the tablet from the case, it comes out fairly easily.)

The genuine leather cover is smooth (with some visible but attractive grain) and is lightly padded. A narrow elastic band holds the cover closed as needed. This case should provide good protection if your tablet is carried in a bag or tote with other items, is lightly jolted, or is dropped for only a few inches. (I don't think that anything will protect a large tablet from damage if it is truly dropped.)

The case has a built-in stand that solidly supports the 8.9" Kindle Fire at three different viewing angles, in either portrait (vertical) or landscape (horizontal) orientation. An interior frame rotates to change the orientation, but it takes two hands and a bit of effort to change from landscape to portrait, or back. (The same is true of other "rotational" tablet cases that I've looked at.)

A tab on the interior frame fits solidly into one of the three deep slots in the cover to change the viewing angle. The frame holds the viewing angle firmly without easily allowing the tablet to fall flat. However, the viewing angles are rather steep, so that only the third slot provides a comfortable viewing angle for me in either portrait or landscape orientation. (I mostly use my tablet on a tabletop, with a stylus, so need a fairly shallow viewing angle.)

An automatic wake/sleep feature turns the big tablet on or off when you open or close the cover. (When the tablet turns on, you must swipe the "unlock" ribbon, or the tablet will turn off again.) This wake/sleep feature works with both landscape orientations (with the camera on the left or on the right), which is important if you frequently rotate the tablet from portrait to landscape and back.

The wide elastic band inside the front cover had me baffled--until I read the product description to find it what it is for. However, this "hand strap" does in fact work very well for holding your weighty tablet in portrait position for reading if you don't have a flat surface available for the stand.

Overall, this is an excellent high-quality case. It's expensive, but if you want the rotational feature and/or a padded leather cover (both features add some bulk), it's a good choice. Another very nice, less expensive case that I like a little better because it has a wider selection of shallower viewing angles, is the [[ASIN:B009X0167Y Marware Vibe Standing Case for Kindle Fire HD 8.9", Black]].

title: Perfect for star gazing with binoculars
text:
Love this product. When using heavy astronomy binoculars, you really need a good solid tripod. What I love about this one is that with the Paragon-Plus mount, the binoculars sit away from the tripod making it easier to get "under" your binoculars to look up at the sky. Further, due to the parallelogram design, you easily adjust the height for taller and shorter viewers. I had this set up at the Adler Planetarium during the transit of Venus last month. A huge line of people formed to view and this feature made it so easy to adjust the the height for all of the various viewers. One reviewer noted the screw attachment between the mount and tripod, there is actually a small set screw underneath that you tighten with an included allen key. This makes it more stable, but I do agree that this is placed in an inconvenient location. It is difficult to manage in the dark, so set up before nightfall if you can. The tripod is a nice heavy duty support structure. However, I did have to adjust the clamps with an allen wrench to tighten them. Before doing this, they would slide down while viewing. It was not hard to adjust, but just be aware that them may come to you a bit loose.
Lastly, if you like me, do not have Orion binoculars, you CAN still use this mount. However, go to their site and purchase the adapter. ([...]) if that link does not work, try searching for model number 07589. This little adapter changes the angle that your binoculars will attach to the mount. My binoculars mount from underneath and the mount is designed to mount from the side. The adapter replaces the angle bracket included with the Paragon-Plus and changes the angle of the binocular attachment. I do wish this was included, it costs around $30, but it necessary if you have other binoculars. If you haven't bought your binoculars yet, you can save this cost by looking at those with the same attachment as Orion's.
Overall, I am very pleased with this tripod and mount.

***Edit:
A question came through recently about the connection of the tripod to the mount. So I thought I would add some pictures. There is a large thick plate at the top of the tripod portion with an embedded standard 1/4" screw connection. This is NOT a quick release. In fact it does not move at all. All of the moving parts are on the top portion of the mount. The top portion is a parallelogram assembly (that keeps the binos level) with a counter weight to balance the weigh of your binos. So the trickiest part of attaching this is balancing the weight of this thing while attaching it. There is a large round connection point. In the image you will see the Orion logo along the side of this. This entire round connection rotates. So what you do is place it on top of the tripod screw. Hold it steady, and then rotate the large ring (with the Orion) logo until it is fully engaged and tight. I also did a quick video of this rotating portion. You can see it here: (...)

So, it is tricky to get this connected the first time, but once you get the hang of it, it is quite easy to do. Just be sure to hold the top portion steady with one hand and then rotate that large ring (with the logo) at the bottom. It will work just fine. Hope that helps.

title: Great Value Purchase, Sturdy Construction, Nice Sound
text:
Overall this is a great little system. I highly recommend it for anyone who loves to hear their old records in a nice simple fashion. Obviously if you're an Audiophile you'll use a more proper turntable (Audio Technica, Pro-Ject, etc.) to fully enjoy the richness and depth of vinyl, but for those wanting to hear their old 45's and those classic garage sale LP's in a basic no-frills manner, this is a quality choice.

The system is designed to play the standard 3 speeds of records, each with the lid closed to eliminate stray sound. Some advice: give the turntable some speed time playing 45 or 78 rpm records. This gives the turntable a push to work through the "drag" of the lower 33 rpm speed. Initially, my 33 rpms were sluggish on this turntable, but after some time at higher speeds, they worked just fine.

Obviously the speakers will not blow you away, but they are still very good. There's not much bass as you would imagine, but the sound is strong and at higher volumes there is no crackling or distortion. I would put the sound on par with most "jam boxes" we grew up with in the 80's and early 90's. The radio dials are easy to operate (you have standard FM, FM Stereo and AM to choose from). This will come in handy listening to sports on the radio.

Cosmetically it has a nice antique feel. Nice wood finish and stylish controls. Everything is easy to operate and within 5 minutes of removing it from the box I was spinning my classic 45s from Genesis, Ambrosia, Hall & Oates and more. If that's all you need, something simple and easy to use, I highly recommend this.

Long live vinyl my friends!

title: Dream Deck
text:
Would have purchased this from Amazon, but was unsure of my installation skills. They have the best price. Anyway, my dealer installed this for me and included it with my extended warranty. Beat that best buy! This deck is phenominal. The major gripe I have is all the additional cables and modules you need to purchase to utilize all of its features. the basic unit comes with iPod cable, but no video from iPod. You must purchase the upgrade cable, but I've heard that you lose usb connectivity with it. Soooo, make your choice. The deck looks elegent and clean in the dash, complimenting any vehicle. Wish Pioneer could have incorporated a volume knob in the design, but that's a preference I learned to live without. the hard buttons are smallish, but that just adds to the beauty of the design. Screen buttons are a good size. Where this unit really shines is the UI. Everything on screen responds to touch and has a function.
The learning curve is medium, so reading the manual helps, but once you start really using it, all of it makes sense. there are atleast two different ways to get to whatever media you have, all intuitive and logical. the touch screen responds like you'd expect, and there is a calibrator for your convenience. I've never needed it so far. I've had this deck for about four months, and I am very pleased with it. Ipod integration and control is very well done, with minor song listing mistakes. That could be the iPod,(i.e. some songs are not in alphabetical order)not correctly organizing songs, but they can still be found. Don't recommend driving while song searching,just by the way touch screens are designed. Actual buttons make driving and stereo handling much easier. Bluetooth works like it should. Cell phone connection takes seconds and most of your phone features will be available. Phone mic works well. Callers tell me they hear me fine and vocals come thru speaker and unit displays call I.D. on screen. Bluetooth music works well with it's typical hangups: music compression, creating less quality sound and volume. Occasional signal cycles causing breaks in music, but are tolerable if craving that favorite internet radio station, rhapsody or pandora. If you use a bluetooth earpiece for music listening then you understand.
HD radio(included) is real nice. Almost CD quality music from radio, plus more stations. I did't get backup camera hookup, but the camera is around $60. Sirius or XM radio requires an additional module, about $100.00 each, plus monthly subscription. Nah. DVD playback is good, but the safety lockout can sometimes be a pain. they have a bypass for it, but my dealer was legally bound to instal unit according to federal laws. another shop may install parking brake bypass for you. I don't think driving and watching movies is logical anyway. I've got a dvd player for the back. Navigation is another $100.00 or so module, but I bluetooth that from my phone thru deck. Easy. Pioneer did this deck right. Last years deck was alright, but this one is what all other companies need to learn from. I would highly recommend this deck. Even better than some high end factory units. Just be ready for a price shock if you want all of its features.

title: Great design, questionable wireless and software
text:
A lot of people got this mouse for World of Warcraft and frequently commented that it took some adjustment to get used to it. I do not play World of Warcraft. I bought this mouse for Guild Wars 2 and had played it less than a week when I got it. So, basically, I took to the mouse without a problem. I mapped 1-4 to my F1-F4 keys and 5+ number keys as usual. It actually makes the game a lot more fun and even after only a few weeks, playing without it felt slow and limiting. It works great for other games too - basically, it can enhance any game that uses a lot of buttons.

The mouse has both wired and wireless modes - the end of the charge cord either plugs into the mouse underneath the wheel or a cradle (which also acts as a receiver in wireless mode). A switch toggles between them. Battery life is okay - nothing compared to my Logitech M510, which I got in June and is still on the original battery (though that's not a gaming mouse). Wireless on the Naga Epic works for about 8-12 hours and charges in either the cradle or in wired mode. Thankfully, the mouse cord is plenty long for those times the battery is drained and the game session is not over - it's long enough for me to use on the couch. Although the software has an auto shut-off setting after a few minutes of activity, I have found that the battery drains if I do not set the switch to wired. At least there is a charge meter in the Razer Synapse software.

I do have issues with the software and wireless mode. I've had issues where the mouse simply stopped working without a reboot, or started going haywire without a pair. I had to reinstall the Razer Synapse drivers because it simply refused to recognize my mouse, asking that I pair a device. The Razer Synapse software in general seems questionable - I don't much see the appeal of a "cloud-based" driver solution, but I guess there are use cases where this would come in handy.

The build quality otherwise feels good. The mouse has a nice texture on the surface and all the buttons feel appropriately clicky. The mouse comes with a set of 3 side panels to adjust how it fits your hand so it shouldn't be hard for anyone to find a shape that they like. The mouse also lights up in various sections (around the wheel, near the palm rest, and the buttons) and the colors can be customized in the software.

Overall, I really like this mouse, and I would easily give it 5 stars were it not for the issues around battery drain, driver software, and wireless. Yes I can use wired all the time but if I wanted to do that I could have saved a lot of money by going with the regular Razer Naga.

title: Terrible 5GHz WiFi, poor routing
text:
The NETGEAR website technical specifications page for the C3700 (N600 Cable Modem Router) list this device as having support for 802.11ac WiFi. This is not the case; the technical specifications page incorrect per NETGEAR support. Furthermore, this router does not allow you to choose certain DHCP ranges (e.g. 192.168.1.0/24), WPS cannot be disabled, and the "readyshare" usb and DLNA servers cannot be turned off. Finally, the 5GHz 802.11a/n range is HORRIBLE. I literally cannot access it from more than 15 feet away. (In contrast, a Apple Airport Extreme easily covers my entire home with 5GHz signal.) The 2GHZ 802.11b/g/n range is fine, but the router occasionally just disappears, reappearing on it's own after about 30 seconds.

On the plus side, it does seem quite energy efficient, providing both WiFi and cable modem services at only 12V 2.5A input. It also connected to Comcast very easily.

title: Cheap way to get good video of your family
text:
I've been taking movies (8mm film, VHS, HI8, MiniDV, and now SD) for 40 years and I whish you could see the improvements the way I have. Yes, I can take better video with my high MP still camera (if I have the time to set it up), but this little camcorder is a very simple, foolproof way of videoing the family with vastly better quality than it used to be. 1.5MP is NOT enough to attain true HD (as anyone who has done their research should know) so it's an interpolated HD picture, but I think a very good one. There are three ways to show the results of your efforts in HI DEF: 1; get a mini/HDMI cable and direct connect to an HDMI equipped HDTV, 2; get a HI DEF TV with an SD card reader that can play AVCHD files (my Panasonic does that, and I'll bet a JVC will also), or 3; edit clips in the camera and backup and create a DVD (on a computer, using normal DVD discs with the simple supplied software which is loaded on the camcorder along with the full users guide) that will play on a BluRay player at 1080i (interpolated) connected to your HDTV. You can also play LOFI with the supplied AV cable. I may never get all of the hours of earlier video from past decades to easily storable DVD's backed up on HDD the way I can do with this setup right out of the box. If you want perfection, pay megabucks, spend a bunch of time and have at it. If you want to preserve memories that you can relatively easily see in near HI DEF, this is a really cheap way to go. My first portable VHS recorder and cable connected video camera (10 lbs, I bet) cost me over 2 grand in the 1970's. Think about that for a minute! Less than 1/3d the quality at 10 times the price!! Gotta go now and buy a bigger battery and a charger that doesn't have to be connected to the camera. It's worth it.

Two more points to ponder. 1. if you are going to be doing much high power zooming, invest in at least a monopod, or better yet a fluid smooth tripod. At 40x zoom it's virtually impossible to hold the camera (even with a pretty good stabilization system)steady enough to have smooth video. I know of no camera, regardless of price for which this is not true. 2. Also at high zoom, the image sharpness diminishes significantly. The same flower that filled my screen close up had more detail than it did when I backed up far enough to fill the screen at full zoom. Again, I'm not reducing my 5 star rating as one cannot expect perfection at this price point. If you can afford it, there are higher MP camcorders in this series with better optics, but they cost more and for general family videos, I'm quite happy with the overall quality. I'm particularly impressed with the way it handles low light conditions. I guess that's three points, and enough for now.

title: Great camera, but pay attention if you have more than 1,000 images on your SD card ...
text:
This camera is fantastic in all regards, except for two issues

1. I don't like the pop-up flash. My G9 has the flash on the front, I don't understand why this camera now requires you to open the flash to use it. There is no point. It slows down shooting quickly and adds a moving part to potentially break.

2. If you take more than 1,000 photos you cannot transfer them to your computer using the built-in Canon wi-fi!

That's right - if you have over 1,000 images on your SD card, you cannot wirelessly transfer them. I was also unable to connect my camera to my computer with a USB cable. You MUST remove the SD card, and use an SD card reader to transfer your photos! My desktop PC doesn't have that slot, so I am forced to use my laptop.

Now, this may not be a big deal for many users, but in my case I store all my photos on a network attached server. Therefore, I would prefer all my photos are sent to that server right away. By having to put the SD card in my laptop, my laptop will then be monopolized by the huge amount of data being sent over wi-fi, so I cannot use my laptop for an hour or two while photos transfer as the network connection is saturated.

I would far prefer my camera upload photos itself, like I have setup for my Android phones, tablet, and other cameras with Eye-Fi SD cards. That way I can use my laptop while file transfers are handled elsewhere on the network. Uploading videos is also excruciatingly slow, even on a 5GHz wi-fi connection.

Anyway, I think that is a pretty stupid design or limitation, considering I am using a 32 GB SD card and can easily shoot thousands of pictures in a few hours, and you'd think Canon would have designed their camera for that. I have been using Eye-fi cards and other devices with wi-fi and none have that limitation or are as hard to configure. I gave up after spending 8+ hours and 10+ attempts to get the Canon software to work, where Eye-Fi and Android can all be setup in minutes.

For reference, this is what happens:

1. Install the Canon software.

2. When prompted to plug in your camera via USB cable, the camera says "Communication error" on the screen, and your computer will not recognize the camera.

Canon's website says this:

> Message: Communication error

> An excessive amount of images (approx. 1,000) on the memory card prevented printing or image transfer to a computer. To transfer the images, use a commercially available USB card reader. To print, insert the memory card directly into the printer card slot.

title: Best thing since sliced bread!!!
text:
The Samsung Win 7 tablet is fantastic!!

No I am not an employee - just a happy user who has has found the solution to every day computing problems. I have wanted a light portable powerful computer for years - this is close to being perfect.

I have a dual life - I am an engineer with 45 years experience in the computer industry. I love technology as long as it works. I am also a musician. I need to be able to write notes that include graphics - ie music - and I need to be able to store lots of pages of sheet music for when I rehearse or perform.

For the past 3 years I have used an HP touchscreen laptop - nice but heavy, and poor contrast on the screen. The Samsung solves my problems.

Yes the Samsung is expensive - but nothing else does the job. The Ipad is a great concept, but it is a mere toy compared the the Samsung, and not suitable for real every day work for college students or businessmen. You cannot sit in a meeting or a lecture and write detailed notes on an Ipad; anyway you still need a laptop to complete the days work. The Samsung can replace your laptop.

Most days I need to write or type notes, and also I need to have access to the full power of Office 10 for all my other computing tasks. With the Samsung and Onenote, the handwriting input is close to perfect, and if you need a keyboard, the bluetooth optional model is small cheap and effective.

Some complain about the size. For me I need a screen this size. I want to display a full size sheet of music, or a full 8x11 or A4 page document. On the Samsung the display is clear, bright and totally useable in most environments. the 9" and smaller tablets are simply too small for many real world applications.

After 10 weeks daily use, I can say that for my applications (I don't play games or watch videos) I get about 5 hours of use from a charge, a 30min 'refresh' at lunch time gives me an extra 2 hours each day. My system has not shown any sign of adverse wear - hopefully the case issue that others have noticed had been rectified.

Currently I am running the Win 8 consumer preview - excellent for touchscreen users!

At present I own 2 other laptops - I will replace these with tablets within a year.

I completely fail to understand why many Tablet reviewers - like PC magazine - do not include this product in their listings. It may be a little specialized, it may be a little expensive - but wow - it works!!

Whats wrong with it? - well, I would love to be able to be able to replace the battery, or get 10 hours daily use. I would like to have a place to keep the stylus. Nothing too serious.

title: Lenovo has made the perfect tablet for me!

I researched many tablets on Amazon & other websites, finding the best overall price here on Amazon.

The live sky apps are very easy to read on the 10 inch screen.
I'm very impressed with the built in stand, although the bottom could have been slightly heavier to stop the tablet from tipping when angled lower.
The system runs fast enough & pages load quite well, I'm astonished at some of the past reviews about speed & screen clarity.

I'm most impressed with the battery life, quoted at 18 hours.

Pricewise, this Lenovo Yoga 10 sells below the cost of the Samsung & Asus models but performs as well if not better.
Update, 3-18-14: I was showing this tablet to a friend of mine, brought it home & the power button was broken.
I couldn't power it up but Amazon did refund me without question & I purchased an Asus Transformer, which was just returned this week due to slowness, screen freezes and poor GPS.

title: Nice projector -
text:
This little sony is a nice unit.
It is a short throw projector meaning it only needs to be about 3 feet from the screen for a big BRIGHT 70" image.
At this distance ambient light does not cause many problems.
Do you have DIRECT sunlight from big windows ??- go with standard HDTV or get blinds or choose a different room, or really -just don't watch tv. A standard tv will still be washed out in direct sunlight but visible compared to a projector.

The best set up is a darker room which you control the light. (this is the rule for any video viewing - Standard HDTV set or a projector -the less ambient light the better - less eyestrain and improved picture= better overall experience)

For instance -I have this projector set up in a windowless room (otherwise known as a garage).
The projector is 7 feet away from the screen giving me a large 130" image. It is HD (720) but you can see pores and nose hairs with ease. I sit 15 to 16 feet away. I do not miss the 1080P. Thought I would but the image is bright and clear and it really does match my 46" Sony Bravia in terms of picture quality, sharpness and overall color saturation. But at 6 times the size.

I have 3 fluorescent lamps (60W each) in the room and 2 sets of track lighting. It is well light and warm feeling.

The track lighting is LED - which is a directional light and does not diffuse light in the same way incandescence bulbs do.
These lights do not bother the picture or wash it out. They may be a distraction to your naked eye but have no real effect on the image. I just dim these to the appropriate level.

The 3 other lamps I have in the room can wash the picture out a bit. I would say it cuts the quality by 60% with all three on.
Turn off 2 of them and only have one 60w lamp on in the room (enough to read, play cards, etc) and the picture quality goes up to 90%.
Turn down the lights to movie theatre darkness level and it is completely immersive, or 111%. Thats right - it goes to eleven.

Also good to note -projected on a textured white wall it is amazingly decent. Like watching SD. But go splurge for some white blackout fabric for about $15 bucks at a fabric store (-Joanns Fabric) This is the fabric they line blackout curtains with in hotel rooms. No light passes through it and is kinda stretchy fabric. The HD image pops on this. No it is not as good as some high end screens, and I have had great luck with some reflective paints, but go with this option -Its cheap, easy to do and works as well as $100 to $500 screens. I got a roll 55" tall and 9 feet long for $14. A roll this size should not be more than $30 even on eBay.

YES you can see PIXELATION- if you are 13 inches from the screen. I can see pixelation on my 46" Sony too at that distance.
Stand 2 feet away and it is as crisp as it is from 16 feet. I found pixelation to be a non issue with this Sony.

So in conclusion - for about $400 used- pick this up.
Great picture - can be 60" to 130" - no loss of HD quality. You will see lots of new things you never noticed before.
The mono speaker is decent for watching the news etc. -but use a surround sound system.
Fan noise will not bother you unless you watch a bunch of silent movies. It is barely audible 7 feet away from my head.
I have a Vornado heater in the room and as quiet as it is - it is louder than the projector.

I was worried about fast moving scenes blur (sports -college football is my religion, video games etc) - there is no motion blur. It is crisp and quick. Colors are dead on and just look natural - black levels are acceptable, but honestly you could pay double to triple and not get as good a picture. 90% of viewers are going to really like the image.

Playing Call of Duty Ghosts is immersive on a different level than playing on a smaller set. You don't scan the screen left to right trying to take in everything- (you can have this problem if you sit too close) - Instead you just take in the entire image and the players are life size on screen. Looking forward to Titanfall. Racing games will make you sway in your seat.
Kinect is fun too and a short throw projector is the way to go so you don't get any shadow image of yourself on the screen since the projector can be closer than you are to the screen.

Movies - the unit really shines. This projector has the same aspect ratio as if you were sitting in a big movie theater, meaning it encompasses your field of view just like in a theater. Again, you will see detail and notice things in movies you never saw before.

If you are in the market -buy this. If you are not in the market for a projector, get there. It is an inexpensive upgrade that is very fun and practical to boot.

title: Recliner Folio for iPad Mini
text:

Pros:
* Great cushioning, device has ample padding when the case is closed.
* Unique inside cover grooves allows multiple viewing angles (landscape view only).
* The stand part never touches the surface you put the case on so the inside doesn't get dusty/dirty as much.
* Elastic strap will keep the case closed should you drop it.

Cons:
* There's nothing that allows you to prop the device up in portrait view (maybe I'm spoiled by my first case?)
* I didn't find the grooves comfortable when holding it one handed. In fact the first time I tried using the grooves to hold it one handed, I dropped the entire thing.

title: Go with Alpine, You Won't Regret It
text:
I purchased these speakers to replace my stock speakers in my '94 Toyota 4Runner. I thought I was screwed for front end sound in my truck because due to the '94 4Runner design, the speakers are placed in the dash and 4" speakers are the biggest the dash can hold.

But holy crap to these little guys deliver. First of all they're pretty cheap, and I was amazed at the sound that these little 4" speakers can crank out. The tweeters cover the highs extremely well, and the speakers behind them cover mids really well. However, don't expect much bass out of these guys. I had to turn the bass down pretty low on my deck in order to let these guys get up to higher volumes without blowing them out or producing a less-than-stellar sound. But I have two 12" Alpine SWR-12D4 Type R's in the back, and so I got all of the bass I could ever need from those.

Alpine makes a fantastic product. I wanted the best for my custom sound system, and so I went with Alpine for everything. I have zero regrets. These two speakers combined with my 12's and an Alpine CDE-122 deck gave my truck an incredible sound system.

NOTE - These speakers don't come with any sort of adapter to mount them. My 4Runner already had plastic housings for the old stock speakers with mounts built on to it, and I had to modify the mounts myself to mount these speakers.

title: Decent sound, somewhat portable, and looks to be waterproof (but time will tell)
text:
This speaker is marketed as usable for the outdoors. Since it is bluetooth, it's compatible with any number of devices, so there is no limit to the amount of music playable on the speaker (limited really to whatever you have on your tablet or phone).

A bit of a technical discussion

The speaker is fairly large compared to many portable bluetooth speakers, but it is small enough to fit in the corner of your trunk if you wanted something for a picnic. The size also helps a bit with projecting the sound, but not significantly (and it should be pointed out that the speaker does allow for directional use (like in the corner of a patio). The sound quality is consistent with speakers in this price class. Generally speaking, the base is a bit limited, but the music is clear and does not sound overly tinny for any of the musics that I've tried on the speaker. To evaluate the speaker, I played rock, jazz, blues, and classical. For music with a "full sound", one might be a bit disappointed, but you'll have to leave this price point to do better. Also, very notably, the music does not sound crackly. This means that the amplification internal to the speaker is a good design, uses good parts, and probably will suit the needs of most reasonably discerning listeners.

The speaker is rechargeable, so this in itself is going to limit the maximum sound output. So, the listening area is going to be about the size of a normal patio, and effective only if there isn't significant other background noise. So, it may not be great for something noisy like the beach, but in all honesty, not much is that runs on batteries or is rechargeable. Also, the speaker can be paired with another for stereo (other speaker sold separately). I didn't evaluate the speaker for this capability, but I have found some problems with this feature in the past with other speakers.

A bit on the use of the speaker ...

The controls for the speaker are accessible and easy to use. I had no trouble connecting via bluetooth to the speaker (with my Android tablet), and have found that in general other Android devices such as my phone work equally well. The weight of the speaker is not excessive (something around 1 pound) and easy to carry around. My own plan is to use this as an outdoor speaker, but only the test of time will determine if the speaker holds up under weather conditions.

The iLuv brand has captured a fairly large portion of the market for household items speakers, clock radios, listening devices, and other common items. I put them towards the middle of the market in terms of quality and price.

title: Garmin GPS Map 421S
text:
This is my second fixed chartplotter, the first one was a garmin GPSMAP 172, which i really liked but was too old, the plastic around the rear socket was collapsing due to a 7 year sunlight exposure.

I had to buy a SD card with the charts from my region, which were pretty expensive, but i knew that anyway.

The sattelite acquisition is very fast even when cold. The screen is also clear allowing good view from multiple angles.

I don't like so few buttons and i don't like the screens. I miss the "road" one from the 172MAP.

When approaching a waypoint, lets say a small fishing reef, or when a very precise arrival to drop an anchor is needed, i realized the unit was a little bit confused even with "track up orientation". Sometimes I find myself circling the waypoint because the pointing arrow simply doesn't show off or do not indicate the exacty location (0 ft distance). Conclusion: it (the pointing arrow) is not so large and intuitive like the one i had on my previous GPS. Don't get me wrong, of course i can put the boat on the waypoint, but it is not as easy as it was with my first GPS, mainly at night when the human eye looses depth of field and rate of turn awareness because of the lack of external visual reference.

Simply you cannot edit the numbers to show the pointing arrow in a fixed manner together with the other data (SOG, distance to point, ETA, etc), rather you have to wait that it pops out in the chart when your cross track error reaches some value (i suppose).

So, in some cases is hard to put the boat "spot on" the waypoint.

For this price point, we consumers could have a better product, with more buttons. The navigation between the screens is time consuming, the user always have to go back to the HOME screen in order to access other charts. I miss the PAGE button!!!
I don't know if i made myself clear.

I would not buy this product again.

title: Affordable, Sharp, and well build; sadly has one major flaw
text:
PROS:
-Prosumer build quality (much better than the average Nikon consumer stuff)
-Very affordable, especially for a UWA zoom
-SHARP! very sharp
-Excellent zoom and focus ring feel
-Internal zooming and focusing (this is surprisingly nice, especially if you have never had an internal zooming lens)

CONS:
-Extremely high chromatic aberration/color fringing in the edges (not extreme edges, just outside of the center.
-Flares very easily (this is common to other UWA zooms though but its something to keep in mind)

First, I will say that this lens is SHARP! if you like sharpness and care about nothing else, just get this now and don't worry about it. It is also really well built; it zooms nicely, the focus ring begs to be used (especially due to the clutch mechanism it has), it looks rather nice physically, etc. Color rendition is also rather nice and in line with what Nikon produces.

This lens has 1 major problem though; it has extremely high Chromatic aberration. This may not be a huge deal breaker to some users, but if you shoot high contrast images with bright lights, you will certainly notice the CA. The copy that I received had such bad CA that on some of the test shots that I did with this lens the colors around the edges were visibly shifted to a purply-looking mush (it sounds much worse than what it actually was, but it is certainly noticeable). Due to this problem I had to sadly return the lens (and I mean it when I say sadly, as I really wanted to keep this guy).

So would I recommend this lens? I would, to someone on a really tight budget. This leans is awesome, it feels leagues ahead build quality wise than lenses that are much more expensive than this. It is also sharp and produces some nice images. However, if you can afford to fork over some cash, I would try to get a lens that has a bit better optical performance, especially since CA is such an annoying thing to fix (fixable, but nonetheless annoying) and is certainly an issue that cripples this lens... Seriously, if Tokina fixed this issue I would be willing to pay around 1k for this lens, its that nice.

title: Solid 2.4GHz wireless performance, factory firmware could stand a change
text:
My trusty old DIR-655 radio started failing under heavy use (P2P + streaming audio), probably due to heat, so I picked one of these AC1450s up at a local outlet rhyming with Bosco.

Hardware wise this router is a killer deal, since it is effectively the same as a $180-200 R6300, with functions limited in the factory firmware. The warehouse price is very good for a dual band AC router with these specs.

Despite what you may read in other reviews, Netgear has a firmware upgrade as of early Oct 2013: V1.0.0.14. You can only get it if you download the image from Netgear support, it WILL NOT show up in the router's "check for upgrade" function. Mine came with V1.0.0.8 IIRC.

This is actually a very easy router to set up if you like your hand held. Theoretically you are safe using the factory SSIDs since Netgear claims to assign individual values to each router, like a serial number. I still changed to my personal WLAN definition.

I first used my AC1450 as a client AP hanging off my DIR-655 with radio disabled, so the AC1450 provided all wireless access. The 2.4GHz range on this device is a lot better than my draft N DIR-655; I have permanent WiFi clients in detached buildings and the 1450 provided an extra 10% signal strength. However, some clients report connecting at lower rates than the DIR-655 (215Mbps versus 270Mbps). I am willing to live with the tradeoff since my AC1450 WLAN is more reliable, with fewer dropouts than my DIR-655 WLAN. Thus far my AC1450 has served multiple P2P torrents simultaneously with multiple media streams (audio, video, even HD) fine without hiccuping. I also keep a wired VoIP phone bridge connected and the telephone service has stayed stable without any special QoS rules.

I have no 5GHz clients and so performed no 5GHz WLAN tests, on N or AC. However, it is completely normal for 5GHz range to fall short of 2.4GHz range, another point to consider when reading some reviews. Check smallnetbuilder <dot> com for details.

Where the AC1450 falls short in my opinion is with the factory firmware features. I haven't needed to manipulate QoS rules yet but the interface seems really klunky. I have also found no way to set up IP filters to bar incoming probes from known scripters and hackers. Both functions are easy to do with my DIR-655. I also mentioned that a firmware update was certainly available from the support website, but the factory load did not detect it.

I'm hoping that someone figures out how to load DD-WRT or OpenWrt on this thing to enable a whole boatload of great functions at relatively low cost, but thus far I'm willing to live with the factory firmware.

title: Excellent TV(s)
text:
I am really pleased with this TV, which I have used for about two months -- so much so that I recently bought the XVT323SV version (not 3D). These TVs replaced our much loved Sony WEGA 32" and Panasonic 27" analog tv's, which work perfectly.

I decided on these particular Vizio models pretty much based on the PIP/POP feature, figuring that the mostly favorable reviews of the picture and other features would apply to me too. My assessment of various TVs at Costco, Walmart and Fry's led me to believe that the Vizio seemed at least as good as the comparable competitors. Good thinking, it's true, so far.

There are many outstanding characteristics of these TVs that have been noted by other reviewers. Picture is fabulous, sound is excellent (for a TV). The PIP/POP feature works very well (you need a second source). I have used Amazon Instant Video, YouTube, Pandora and some Google apps so far. Google apps are underwhelming.... There are lots of other apps available.

In my research for a TV with PIP, I viewed/downloaded User Guides for all the major TV manufacturers and I commend Vizio for having pretty much the best User Guide by far.

The Remote for these TVs pairs nicely with your cable box or Tivo so that the remote can control device features when using the Input that the device is on. Very nice feature. However, like many devices, some features that I use are buried too far in the menu, so I usually use my jp1 Remotes to pull the features I need to the jp1 remote buttons, no menus needed. This works well on the Vizios.

Overall, I am very happy with both of these TVs. My only lament in the switch from analog to digital technology is the time lag of changing channels/"re-rendering" the picture, slowness of PIP swapping and the terrible Closed Captioning performance by HDMI/Cable Boxes. (I have the Cox SA8240 HDC cable box, which also has terrible PIP performance to go along with bad CC, also buried in the Cable Box menu, the Cox Remote CC button doesn't work at all--jp1 to the rescue, again).

Thank you Amazon! ...and to UPS for hand delivery to my front door.

title: cheap quality, cheap sound
text:
ATTN: if you care at all about sound quality of records, DO NOT BUY THIS RECORD PLAYER. I purchased this record player because my old one (a Fidelity, which I highly recommend if you can find one!) stopped producing sound. Where I live it is incredibly difficult to find a decent record player at any shop, so I searched day and night on Amazon before finally settling on this Crosley brand of record player. It was decently priced, it had good reviews, and had all of the capabilities I needed for a record player (playing records). When it arrived, I immediately noticed the poor quality of the wood chosen to construct this record player. It's seriously like plywood or something. I also noticed that the lid didn't even close all of the way, probably because the wood quality sucks. I then noticed that the metal arm that opens and closes the lid was also poorly made, rickety, and also kind of sucked at both opening and closing, its only job.

Worse yet, the needle is a cheap plastic. It'd be nice for it to come with a diamond needle if the customer is paying almost $140. It's not that hard. I put on a record, and from the built-in speakers alone, the sound was tinny, almost ear-wrenching depending on what you're listening to. It's not a smooth, stable, and balanced sound. However, the speakers do produce a lot/loud sound, which is potentially the only positive thing I could ever say about this record player. I have a pair of Bose speakers I hooked up to it, hoping it would make the sound less washed out, but it only just made it louder and still washed out and tinny. It's like playing CDs. If you want to hear clear, crisp, processed sound, buy a CD player and some CDs. I haven't spent this much money on both this record player and my collection of records to have the exact same effect as if I were listening to iTunes. Truly disappointing. I don't think I'll be buying any new records for a few years until I can wear out this piece of junk sitting in my living room.

I'm disappointed in this company, and I'm disappointed in the people who reviewed it as a good record player. I'm disappointed that a moderately-priced record player (at least according to Amazon's products) would be so astonishingly poor and, honestly, that it's even on the market for people to buy. It's taken my enthusiasm out of record-listening and perhaps, most of all, I'm disappointed in myself for going this route.

Once again: if you enjoy listening to records for that certain record aesthetic, both old and new music, please do not buy this record player. I made a mistake and you will, too, if you drop the money on this abysmal box of wood.

title: Beware the proprietary hard drive format!  Can't be replaced if it fails...  But Amazon RULES
text:
UPDATE: Amazon stepped up to the plate and took the product back with a full refund. They were under NO obligation to do so under the terms of purchase and I had originally contacted them just asking for help getting a response from ASUS. No back and forth. Just a very polit e-mail with a return shipping label. This was well and above what was hoping for. So two takeaways 1). DON'T buy a notebook with proprietary parts - especially from ASUS. 2). DO buy from Amazon. Great end to what had been looking like a bad story.
------
SSD hard drive failed after only a month or two of use (see description below). I start to look into replacing it and discover that the UX21 has a totally proprietary drive size/shape/format and you CANNOT BUY A REPLACEMENT DRIVE AT RETAIL. So if you decide to buy one of these, you are totally at the mercy of ASUS if your hard drive goes bad (as SSD drives often do).

That would also be OK if ASUS was willing to replace it themselves, sell you a replacement drive, or even answer their e-mail. I have been waiting for two weeks now and can't get a peep out of Asus (the only communication from them so far is a "customer service survey" which is ironic given I have received no service so far).

The customer service problems and the early drive failure might just be my bad luck, but I would have NEVER bought this machine if I had known that I could not swap out a part as prone to failure as a SSD hard drive. Do yourself a favor and avoid this sort of risk.

PROBLEM: The hard drive on this machine is failing. Getting "blue screen of death" in Windows. I also run Ubuntu Linux and getting intermittent shut-downs with "I/O error at sector XXXX" reported as the system fails. Most recently the PC has started to boot up into the BIOS screen and not recognized the internal hard drive as a boot option. My best guess is the SSD drive has failed (after only a month or two of use).

text:
