I actually bought the Optoma HD141x and they sent me the Optoma HD26 instead. My HD26 had an issue with the software become unresponsive and I sent it back. The BenQ just dropped down to $700 dollars around that time and it was kind of a no brainier. Amazon gave me one day shipping free on the return if I ordered the BenQ at the same time so I would get my money returned a bit faster.

Not only are the colors vastly more accurate and more finely rendered which makes the entire picture look significantly better, but the motion is far smoother on the Benq AND the brightness level are more even. Contrast ratio be damned, blacks look better on the Benq when actually watching movies and whites are less prone to being overexposed in order to get the correct overall brightness and that is even with ambient light. The smoothness of the motion is a big deal that I don't hear as many people bring up vs the color issues. The Optoma HD26 definitely produced far more rainbow effect for me, though it was generally only an issue in the menu system of my Roku/Plex. The BenQ actually by comparisson produces almost zero rainbow effect for me, even when I try by looking away and back the screen quickly. With the Optoma looking away and back the screen would reliably produce rainbow effects. My father had the same exact experience. This also means the BenQ can produce a larger image with less eye strain than the Optoma and with the more accurate color wheel and brightness there really is not comparison here.

At 700 dollars the Benq is the only 1080p projector to think about for anything other than all day TV watching in which case an LCD or LED projector might suit you better. If you have so much ambient light that your cranking up the Optoma HD26 brightness, your picture quality is probably rather horrible compared to what it could be by simply working out a smarter way to manage light. Even installing cheap electronic curtains might be a better idea that just trying to fight brightness with brightness.

Summary of benefits of Optoma vs HD26

Way better overall picture on any film vs the Optoma which may require you to tweak settings a lot to get anything even close to what the BenQ does out of the box. That will mean changing colors for certain movies to make the look right. For a gaming projector you may not care, but for movies you will.

The remote on the BenQ is significantly better quality and generally more useful though the Optoma is sufficient.

The BenQ has a true sleep timer which does not have to be set each time like on the Optoma which has to be set per each instance of use (irt resets to zero when the projector is turned off. The sleep timer has a nice reminder to tell you it's going to sleep if you don't press any button the remote to tell it not to, great for falling asleep watching tv in the living room.

The BenQ has smoother motion and produced far less rainbows for both myself and my father. This is significant even if you don't see rainbows because nobody wants much blurryness in their action scenes, especially on a 100+ inch screen.

The BenQ's brightness and contrast seem more accurate. WIth the Optoma some movies were more washed out in some scenes and shadow detail overall was not as good. This may lead you to want to adjust brightness for certain movies far more than the Benq AND perhaps even more importantly the uneven brightness will lead to more eye strain.

The few benefit of the Optoma.
It has three simple adjustable feet that will never break. The BenQ has single plastic front foot that would break if it was adjusted a lot, like most portable projectors.

The Optoma will probably produce less eye strain in 3D, but the picture will probably still be somewhat inferior, so for those looking to play games in 3D for hours at a time the Optoma may be the better choice but the motion blur would personally turn my to the BenQ even for gaming and 3D for me is something I use a couple times a year at most for the WOW factor, usually to show off to other people. I prefer zoning out of the huge screen and all the details I could not see before vs being disoriented by the device tricking my eyes depths perception, a strategy that will probably always produce eye train. Until was have holographic 3D we are basically hacking our eyes and brain to fake 3D and I don't think most people really like that for any extended period of time.

The Optoma has cheaper bulbs, but not by enough that it should be a significant deciding point. If you want cheap bulbs because you plan to use this thing 16 hours a day then get an Epson LCD with the 100 dollar bulbs or one of the newer LED projectors. Or just wait a year or two because LED projectors are going to take over, I have little doubt about that. Optoma is already released their first batch and I suspect the next generation of LED projectors is going to start to threaten non LED projectors as being the top consumer projectors.

The Optoma throw range is more adjustable and it can zoom out and image shift left, right, up and down. The BenQ can only zoom in, which is virtually useless and it has no image shift, just keystone. While image shift and zoom are things you want to avoid I can't help but think BenQ could have easily added this to their firmware.

As far as noise goes. I could care less, it's a living room, and even if it wasn't the surround sound more than covered up the fan noise. I didn't notice the fan of either projector whlie watching movies nor did the BenQ strike me as loud even with the stereo off or turned down, but again that's a living room, not a theater room. If you went to the trouble of building a theater room .. why put an Optoma in it when it will certainly produce a less accurate picture by almost anyone's account.

Yes, I did tweak the Optoma setting as per several recommendations on the internet and there just is not sweet spot that can produce a reliably accurate picture like the BenQ can right out of the box, no less after you tweak it and the BenQ pulls away in quality that much more. I think it's a more solid and better made unit as well with better software and a better remote.

I guess I'm officially a BenQ fanboy now, but consider the quality of the product I see nothing wrong with that.

The Optoma was my first projector and I was initially impressed with the huge clear and quite sharp picture. It might be the Optoma produces a sharper picture, but I did not have the time or desire to run them side by side. However sharpness is highly overrated and too much sharpness is not good for watching films, on the other hand accurate colors and brightness are paramount as well as smooth motion and the BenQ appears to win easily. The near complete lack of rainbows for myself and my father is a huge and mostly unexpected plus. The very noticeable lack of motion blur in the Plex menu and movie action scenes was also a welcome surprise.

In the end though I'm happy my HD25 occasionally froze up because it gave me 60 hours or so of time to test out the Optoma in many conditions while also still getting free return shipping since it was both the wrong product AND it was not working entirely right. As far as the freezing goes, I think it probably just needed a firmware reflash because it ran fine when it first started up and I don't think the defect effected image quality because the issue I have with it I've read many other have, particularly the problem with some skin tones looking like spray on tans.
The main military guy in Avatar is a good example of where I could not get a realistic skin tone out of the Optoma no matter what, there just does not seem to be enough fine detail in the color to produce the variations needed for realistic color production. It's almost like colors are averaged on the Optoma, like they are run through some crappy instagram filter. On The Dark Knight serious I constantly had issues with some areas being too dark and some being too light and while that's still a little bit the case vs an LED screen, it's not usually noticeable, but that's why you need to control light, so you can get your shadow details in the picture vs having it washed out or having uneven brightness isues which will cause eye strain. Remember contrast is great, but too much contrast between light and dark = eye strain. You want the subtle and accurate control the BenQ can provide, rather than the brute force light cannon approach that Optoma uses.

The BenQ exceeds my expectations and having seen the two I would not hesitate to pay 100 or 200 more for this projector vs the Optoma. Your investing in a whole setup and everyone wants to keep costs down, but skimping on the projector is not the way to do it. The Optoma is not bad, but there is almost no situation where I would not pay more for the Benq having now owned both projectors for over 60 hours of use.

Hopefully my next projector will be an LED and we can all stop worrying about bulb life, heat, noise, rainbows and motion blur.

The only thing I actually miss is the digital zoom out function which is nice for certainly odd sized movies or perhaps non HD action movies, which is basically almost no movie I watch anyway. I would probably mostly use it for real old movies where the resolution is bad and there is no HD copy, but the zoom out still leaves the light footprint of the full sized picture, so it would be of limited use. Of course I would prefer a lot more optical zoom, but that's not an option for any projectors in this price range and picture quality. The higher refresh 3D glasses support would be nice, but honestly I don't see myself using 3D enough to care and sacrificing picture quality for better 3D makes just about zero sense to me. I don't fully trust wireless enough to care about that option on newer models. I don't need the projector to be any brighter, even in ambient light I run it in film mode. On an overcast day with the windows wide open I can press User2 preset and it bumps up to ambient conditions and I always run it on eco. If direct daylight comes in the room however the image will be washed out, which is the case for any projector given enough windows or direct beams of sunlight hitting your screen (any light beamed on the screen will due a lot of damage to your image quality even from a light that might shine in from another room if it hits the screen just right). No projector alone can look that good in full daylight, so don't think an Optoma HD26 is going to work in daylight well just because it claims higher lumens (which it does not really deliver once adjusted). The only way to get daylight projection is with expensive screens that try to reflect more light back at the viewer without killing the picture, and of course they do hurt the picture some, but it can be done, we have the technology! It's just probably cheaper to install remote controlled curtains and just think how impressed your friend will be!

So.. that's it folks. Get the BenQ or just wish you had, those are the choices in the sub 1000 projector world. If you see rainbows with this thing at least try reducing screen size because you will have to spend 2-3 times as much for an LCD projector that can produce a picture this good and if you see rainbows with this then you probably will also with the Optoma. You can try to get used to it, but comparing to two I can now see that I was getting eye strain from the Optoma, even with a smaller picture size than the BenQ. You really don't want to spend all this time and effort on a projector setup to realize it's giving you significantly more eye strain than your LCD or LED television did or to potentially have to make the screen significantly smaller to compensate which may mean changing your mounting plans, though the larger zoom adjustment on the Optomas will help with placement and adjusting screen size more the fact that it produces more eye strain and a less accurate picture more or less negates any advantages the Optoma may have.

title: Piece of crap
text:
Main computer use is word processing, web surfing and minor computer based art and photo manipulation. Acer Aspire V5 was purchased after a HP laptop died after three years of rather heavy school use. Main selling points were 4 megs of RAM, 500 meg hard drive and the $340 price at Staples.
In the six weeks between the HP dying and my purchasing of the Acer Aspire V5 I sampled a few tablets with the idea that they could adequately replace the HP, I had various issues with each of the tablets but the death knell for all of them was connectivity issues with my printer and their small RAM and hard drives. However, after dealing with this Acer for over a month I feel I would have been better off sticking with the Microsoft Surface.
Yes the Acer V5 has 4 megs of RAM, unfortunately the processor takes the speed down to around 1 meg, I had a Gateway 12 years ago that was faster, in all aspects, than this Acer V5. I had to spend a three days scrubbing the bloat ware which was using 90-95% of of the CPU, after uninstalling the mountain of Acer crap it is now running with around 70% of the CPU free, from time to time, however, it starts running slow and shows that 90+% is in use and has to be restarted before it will clear its cache. On top of the memory space issues it also has trouble handling wi-fi signals, connecting isn't an issue, neither is staying connected, where it has issue lies is with the computer accepting that there is in fact internet access. Again, restarting is the only thing that resolves this issue once it starts. On top of those issues I kept getting virus warnings, straight out of the box, from McAfee and Norton both. Downloaded AVG just to make sure and AVG informs me that Windows has been installed incorrectly and is causing a false virus signal.
Other issues consist of, touch pad unresponsive to tapping and the scroll is horridly placed (entire right hand edge of touch pad) for a right handed user. The SD card reader is located under the right hand side of the device, an SD card can be inserted without flipping the lap top over, extracting it however is essentially impossible. The SD card reader is slightly recessed and upside down (the nail slot on the card cannot be accessed), if this was a self ejecting slot this would not be an issue, but its not. The first time I used the card reader it took half an hour and a pair of tweezers to remove the card. I will not be using that slot again.
All in all I've found the Acer Aspire V5 to be a wonderful, if lightweight and somewhat expensive, paper weight. The chances that I will be purchasing another Acer product in the future are very slim, I didn't expect a super machine, but I did expect something faster and more reliable than a computer I had over a decade ago.

title: HP 2511x is a definite LED-monitor winner
text:
I've been on the hunt for a good reasonably-priced LED monitor for a while (I won't start on this...), something that I will find to my satisfaction in its features and picture quality. I think I've found it. I mainly came to the decision based off the rating ratios, and with the knowledge that even highly-rated items can sometimes lead to disappointment. This one seemed to have the highest proportion of 5-star ratings, and it did have much of the features I was looking for: LED, >23", GLOSSY, few complaints about color and viewing angle, and high customer satisfaction based on ratings. There are actually very few LED monitors out there that are glossy, and I'm so glad this one is a glossy screen. I'll let you know that on my initial purchase, I was sent a unit that was somewhat of a disappointment. The screen overall looked good, but for some reason, the contrast at the top appeared to be darker than the contrast on the lower half the screen. This is ASIDE from the usual TN monitor viewing angle issues that usually has to do with color. Interestingly, the contrast issue was such that the top did also produce a more pinkish tint. It was kind of annoying even sitting 5 feet away at eye-level. I queried several reviewers and looked through what customers have noted, and it didn't seem like anyone had this problem. Some also reported pretty even colors throughout when sitting in front. I gave it a shot and had it exchanged, without any clue if the next unit would have the same issue (e.g., was it just me who was picky?). Lo and behold, my 2nd unit looks more like the one people are giving 5 stars! The contrast top to bottom is MUCH more even, without that pink tint at the top, and the whites look VERY GOOD throughtout the screen, much improved form the last unit. (Currently? The white appears 95-98% even across the screen at 4 feet away or more, and one may detect an extremely subtle pinch of off-white/yellow if you sit closer or if you scrutinize the screen for 1 minute). Unfortunately, this means that not all units are made the same, but I'm glad I finally ended up with a unit consistent with reviews AND satisfies my expectations for a monitor in this price range. So here I go with an outline of my review:

PROS
- Excellent screen size for daily student use. I can sit back much further with less strain on my eyes and posture while still getting great viewing range at eye-level. Given that the resolution is 1080p, 23" might be good for DPI, but 23" is slightly on the smaller range, and I wanted a larger screen size coming off of my 21" previously. 27" would have been a good size, but then DPI would have been less attractive. It's a delicate balance here, and 25" is JUST right, for me.
- Excellent contrast and brightness. I use about 80% and 80%. For reported 250 cd/m2 on this screen, even 80/80 is brighter than my "300 cd/m2" of my Dell Studio XPS 16 screen (which inspired me to find LED monitors).
- Very good viewing angles for its class. TFT-TN monitors will always suffer the same issues, but not all suffer the same extent. I've definitely seen many models/many different brands that have varying degrees of viewing angle satisfaction. Yes, if you lean off center side to side, the further end will start to have a light yellow tint. But let's say you are watching a film/video, and u stand maybe off to the side a bit--you can still see what is going on and you may not even notice much distortion in color/contrast unless you really stare at the screen with scrutiny as you come to the center. If it hasn't bothered me, I don't think it will bother most users who are buying monitors of this class. Believe me, I've seen pretty bad ones.
- White is more white, black is more black. The "LED white" is one of the main reasons to upgrade from a regular LCD monitor. The white is very good especially when you are on center at least 4 feet away. The black is a pure, deep black and smooth and consistent throughout the screen. No backlight bleeding, by the way! Makes black-background webpages and movies very neat to look at.
- Excellent color representation for its class. As you may know, TFT-TN monitors will still have the issue with viewing angles. On center, the left and right are pretty symmetrical and similar/same as the center. Top to bottom, with colors that are not back, you will notice a gradual gradation of color as you scan top-to-bottom, but that is typical, and the issue is actually less on this monitor than on many others I've seen. Only IPS monitors can resolve this, if you're really demanding that. I'm not really complaining. :)
- Sharp and crisp. Text at 80% contrast and 80% brightness is excellent. That's all.
- Easy-to-use buttons. The buttons are actually located on the underside of the screen with labels facing you. The functionality is pretty easy to figure out and not complicated. There's a function to turn off the Power light if you choose to, but I like to keep it on, as it has a nice neon-teal color to it. When activating the monitor from sleep, there is virtually no waiting time for things to show up except for monitor-based prompt menu that says which plug is detected (disappears in 2 seconds or so).
- Stable base and support. Just in case people wanted to know. The monitor will only shake a little when you're touching the buttons or handling the monitor with your hands. Otherwise, it is very stable.
- Glossy. I'm a fan of glossy screens. I won't go into a battle between matte vs. glossy, because both have its pros/cons. I favor glossy over matte because: 1) In any lit room or with windows or whatnot, all my matte screens I've used experience complete screen washout. You basically can't make out anything because the light reflecting off the surface is diffuse and goes across the entire surface. However, with glossy, I've never been bothered by reflections, and even in bright lighting situations, the most you get is a reflection of that source, but it is localized and does not wash out the whole screen. Plus, I probably just subconsciously adapt to it and maybe move my head over 1 inch or ignore the light completely. 2) Glossy in any lit room seems to provide better clarity and richness in color/contrast. (In complete darkness, matte vs. glossy appear pretty much the same.)

CONS
- It's not IPS, but hey, it's got deep black that is consistent throughout. For $230 (when I bought it), this is one of the best in the TN class that I've seen, and met my expectations. The viewing angle descriptions I described above.
- Does not rotate and does not have vertical adjustment. Minor complaint, but I have my monitor on a stand so I can keep it eye-level. It would have been nice to have such features though.
- You may get lucky and get a good unit. But you may also get something slightly disappointing. If you suspect that there may be some flaw or fault to your unit, it's probably not you or your eyes--it's the monitor. Amazon helped me with the exchange process very easily, and now I am absolutely happy with my new unit. This is a quality control issue that likely applies to any product you choose, no matter how good they reportedly are. But if I were you, I -would- believe the 5-star ratings, and you should get a unit that meets those standards.
- This is very picky, and I'm sure most people won't notice, but if you are within the range of 1-5 feet from the monitor and you look away the monitor but keep it enough in your peripheral vision, you might see subtle indication of flickering off to your peripheral vision esp with white background and dark text/lines. Not a biggie, I think it's normal for LEDs to do that (although my Dell Studio XPS 16 WLED screen does not). Just to be clear, there is NO OBSERVABLE FLICKERING when viewing directly at this HP monitor.

I tried to include commentary about features or issues that I did not see any other viewer describe. For instance, few will talk about the vertical viewing angles at eye-level, which for me is a bigger issue than side-to-side viewing angles. I'll just you know that this is the best TFT-TN monitor I've been able to find so far that is glossy and LED. You can expect high-quality from this product, and I hope I've been able to help you in making a decision when searching for a monitor of this class to purchase. My rating is CONFIDENTLY 4.9/5 for a good unit, and I'm not counting off too much for viewing angles, as I'm not trying to compare to IPS class monitors. Anyway, enjoy!

FYI, at the time of writing this review:

5 stars: 63 (75%)
4 stars: 19 (23%) - includes issues that even as someone as picky as I am can live with.
3 stars: 1
2 stars: 0
1 star: 1

5-stars + 4-star ratings = 98%
Pretty impressive.

text:

This new one retains most of the design from the first one, but not the build quality. title: In Love...Good sound and Amazingly light
text:
I did a lot of research and reached out to my musician brother before selecting which headset I wanted for Xmas. Well I got this one!!! :)

Wireless - love being cable-less, it is taking a tad to adapt to it though, I keep catching myself "being careful" with the cables lol when there are none.

Sound - superb, I am not an expert but I love the sound, it is clean. It comes with 3 EQ settings that can be adjusted. In addition, you can just download an EQ application from google play and control the levels from your phone.

Earphones - it comes with 3 sizes earbuds. I feel the medium ones are the ones that make the best seal for me. are light and comfortable, I hardly feel them. I am able to move my head drastically to one size and the other w/o being worried about the cables pulling or snapping.

Calls - In a home setting with a kid, some light music in the background and all...I was able to hear the caller clearly and the caller said they could hear me clearly and no background noise bothering. When pressing the call button you can just say "Call...so and so" or say the number you want to dial. It basically searches your contacts and displays in your screen the name and number options, pretty neat.
Neck ring - it is very light, I can't believe I can hardly feel it. When the vibrate is on and call comes in, it feels like a subtle vibration and almost tickles.

Buttons - so far they feel pretty easily accessible. Hold volume - tells you the battery state e.g. "battery high", Hold volume + tells you "vibrate on/off".

Retracting - you just press the button on each side. I like to hold the earbuds when they are retracting rather than just let them snap, just trying to take care of my investment lol. Hubby did get an extended warranty on them just in case, since they have the retractable system and all.

Tone & Talk app - just downloaded it to pair the device, which can be done manually also, have not played much with it so far but I saw you can have your sms and social media messages read to you.

Cons:

title: "Wow" image quality, perfect for enthusiast who shoots everything
text: I am coming from 6-7 years of using a Canon T2i + 18-135, 85mm (and occasionally a pro friend's L lenses) and mastered the manual side of the camera. I could get some great pictures out of that camera but clearly was ready to invest in something nicer, particularly for indoors -- while the speed light and getting a custom white balance setting helped, I still didn't love any indoor shots...with 4-6 mos of winter, that's important to me. I researched and hemmed and hawed, and actually decided to buy the Nikon D7100. To my great surprise, I could hardly get a shot from this popular camera that was better than my T2i. In fact, it had way worse noise at higher ISOs, the controls were much more cumbersome and the revolutionary focusing system, well, didn't give me sharp pictures no matter what I did. So, I sent it back and went with my original plan, the 6D. The very first thing I did was shoot indoors with no light and I was shocked at how this camera performed! It will grab the absolute tiniest bit of light available and illuminate beautifully and SHARP! I have pictures with 8000-12600 ISOs that are gorgeous with no editing. The auto white balance is almost dead on: I always had to take a custom white balance shot with the T2i, and haven't had to yet with the 6D. The wireless function is very handy: I shot a picture in RAW, edited it on the camera, connected to my iPhone and emailed it and shared to FB. The recipient replied, "Wow, this looks like it came out of a magazine." Completely bypassing hooking up my external drive, downloading, etc etc was great. The HDR setting for heavily backlit subjects is really fun (but don't move!). I could go on and on, the real reason to get this camera is the image quality, it's just amazing. You can't take a bad picture with it. I've loved the time spent really learning photography with the T2i, and now with my toolbox of go-to techniques, I look forward to getting "wow" from picture after picture! The 24-105 is great, and I'll probably add the 70-200 f4L (no IS, since I have a monopod) to take pictures of kid's soccer and my husband's RC airplanes. So far playing around with the 6D, I get exactly what I need for action shots. Don't miss the pop-up flash at all. The handful of times I fill-flashed I didn't really like it anyway. There are several ways to overcome shadows/backlit subjects in this camera and I have absolutely not needed flash indoors at all yet and if so will just use the speed light. Can't put this camera down. Just love it!

title: Lasted just over 2 years: internal plastic lens eventually started burning
text:
When I initially got this, I and my family loved it. The short-throw system was great for our basement, allowing more flexibility in placement, and allowing reasonable use of XBOX Kinect. I didn't want to get a regular LCD or Plasma because it would be more difficult to install and to dispose of when it ultimately dies. We were satisfied for gaming and videos.

The problem with this particular projector was after about 20 months of use, we started seeing a light brown spot in the projected image. It was almost unnoticeable at first, and I thought it had to do with the lamp reaching the end of it's normal life. It turned out not to be related to the lamp. I went through the expense of ordering and replacting the $150 lamp, but the brown spot was still there, and both growing and getting darker.

After doing some research, it turns out Optoma uses an internal plastic (not glass) lens as part of the optics system. The problem lens is not the lens you see on the outside, but is the lens closest to the lamp inside, which is placed in such a way to be most susceptible to damage from heat from the lamp. This lense "preps" the light before going through the final lens system. The problem lens is permanently fixed to the projector case and cannot be removed or replaced. On Youtube an Optoma Gametime owner who had this problem took apart his projector, and shows clearly the lens that eventually starts cooking. His lens actually melted (mine only started browning before we replaced it with a different brand of projector).

From research on the net many people, it turns out, have had this problem with this projector. The first year or two is fine, but then you first notice a light brown area in the picture. This spot eventually grows and becomes more noticeable. The more brown the spot is, the more susceptible it is to heat damage, so the problem starts slowly, but towards the end, you see the brown getting deeper and darker.

There doesn't seem to be an incentive for Optoma to fix this, as customers are happy with the projector for the first year, and many people buy this particular projector because of both the positive reviews (usually written shortly after buying), and the admittedly great price point. But if you really expect more than two years of satisfactory use, beware.

Our projector lasted just over two years, without unusually heavy use, although occasionally the kids would use it over long periods of time on free weekends. They aren't permitted to game during the week, but I'm OK with occasional long gaming sessions on weekends. It is specifically use over long periods of time that eventually leads to the internal plastic lens getting cooked and browning. This probably wouldn't happen if Optoma used a (?more expensive?) glass lens internally. If you only use the projector in 2 to 3 hour sessions, this problem might not occur.

So if you only expect to use the projector occasionally - say as a business user - and never for long periods, then it might be fine. But if you are a gamer, or have kids who are gamers, who could occasionally use the projector for periods like 6 hours or more, you might be disappointed by the relatively short life of the product.

If you are like me and expect a TV or projector to last 5 years, I do not recommend this product. I have given it 2 stars, because it was worry-free for only about 2 years - but with a lamp-replacement, I really think it should have lasted 5 years.

title: Calorie burn count seems accurate for walking and jogging--Motivational
text:
I owned an earlier version of this and unfortunately misplaced it. If I hadn't been offered this one through Amazon Vine chances are I would have bought it.

What I like--

For me, it is accurate in reflecting the number of calories I use through activity--if said activity is walking or jogging which most of my activity is. If I keep track of my calories I get a pretty close estimate of how much weight I will lose (or not lose). It allows me to avoid thinking I am more active than I am. The fact that I can really get a very good estimate of calories out as well as calories in is really very helpful.

You can use the info provided at the web site to get a good idea of how many calories you personally burn doing different activities.

This device does motivate me to be more active. That does translate into weight loss.

The computer interface works fine for me (I have not used this with a mobile device).

What I don't like--

I swim and this is not waterproof.

While the calorie count seems on the money (as it is reflected in weight loss) I don't find the step count accurate.
After the first three months you have to pay for a subscription to the web site or the thing is totally useless.
You only get one arm band strap with this. You will obviously need to change it, so plan to buy several. You will have to order them ($13 each). The one that comes with this is for a medium size arm. Okay for me, but some people will definitely need the small or big size. (Check measurements at the web site.)

Some people are really not going to love the look of the thing either on a bare arm or under a shirt. Personally I don't. (And under a sweater my arm looks really odd when I wear this.) And to get an accurate count of your calorie burn for a day you do have to wear it all the time, at least when you are awake.

Overall, here's the main point. For the most important thing the device does--count calorie expenditure--it works fine and I have lost some weight with it. So I recommend it.

text:

Further because of the softness and the absence of a click, you always bottom out at every stroke: the feeling is rather harsh and definitely not pleasant for the fingers, I fear I may develop carpal tunnel syndrome. Please notice that because of its design, the key travel ends abruptly like what you get with two pieces of hard plastic clashing, there is no gradual end of the key travel such as with the rubberdome. To make the pressing nicer I even tried to put on the silencing rings of the cherry mx, but they don't work on this type of keys, you have to take it as it is.
What I like about this keboard: the construction, the "thumping" sound, the tactile precision (all better than the rubber dome because there is no key-wobbling), the PBT keycaps are nice and better than common plastic keycaps.

title: Goodbye Buddy
text:
Obituary
===========
Buddy, the Canon D10 camera, that has been an integral part of my Gadget family, and had captured numerous nostalgic moments of friends and family in picnics and outings, died this 14th of Jan, 2012 in the waters of Baga Beach, Goa. He was roughly 3 year old since purchase, and was suffering from gross misuse of its durability specifications.

First in the line of Waterproof cameras from Canon, Buddy the D10 was a champion since it came out, it won many review battles and side by side comparisons, and it though looking like a fat kid on the block next to his ELPH brothers, it was always humble and never complained.

I still remember, the excitement when I heard of its release, the specs, the robustness and its waterproof nature, which for me was a time to put my Old Faithful, the Canon S2IS to rest.

I live in Mumbai, India, which enjoys 4.5 months of good rain, including which there are 8 good months of riding season for a motorcycle enthusiast, and numerous weekend getaway places for 1 day or 2 day rides. There are hundreds of seasonal waterfalls and streams which become picnic spots just during these 4 months, and there are numerous beaches on the 500km stretch from Mumbai to Goa. While the S2IS was good overall, the D10 was 100x more suited for such conditions. Now I had been considering a waterproof jacket for the S2IS for quite some time, but it was such a compromise.

Unavailable in India, I had to ship it from states, and because the warranty wasnt valid in India, I hesitated to "test" the waterproof nature for about 2 months Infact, I gave it to a close friend who was going on his honeymoon trip to Mauritius, in hope that he'd do it, but he chickened out too.

We finally tested it in a bucket of water, and woo hoo! The joy I felt, a digital device performing under Water, it was like Magic!

Buddy was a great hit in all parties, we'd set it up on a Mug of Beer, pretending to use it like a tripod, and bang the table slightly so that it falls into the Beer. The people in neighbouring tables would shriek, the waiters would apologize and Buddy would stand up, and take a bow. :)

The D10, then became a regular companion, and never said no to whatever test it was put to. Here's a list of its adventures:

1) Motorcycle ride to Khardungla, the highest motorable road, temperatures of -10C, jittery terrain over 3000Kms, where it fell from a Motorcycle going 60kmph over rocks and snow.
2) The 40+ waterfalls around mumbai
3) Muddy waters of Beaches near city.
4) Clean swimmingpools of Gym, and the waterparks
5) Awesome beach waters of Goa, Pattaya, Maldives
6) Sands of Rajasthan.
7) 2 Holis - the color festival of India
8) Numerous dunks in Water, Beer, Whisky, Vodka, Soap water and what not

The D10 was a favorite of kids and elderly alike, you could leave it with anyone and not worry about it, and they'd return it with a smile. With a sturdy scratch free glass, it never needed a blower or a filter. You could WASH it or wipe it with a cloth, and it'd be ready!.

In broad day light, the D10 was in its natural element, you just point it, it took good photos. Oh, the color's it'd capture!
In dim-light or indoors, it'd struggle, you know its an outdoorsy camera.

It was the most "taken-for-granted" thing in my bag, something which I never did worry about taking care of, and after a lot of misuse, it finally took its last breath when some water creeped in. I knew it was dying for some months, because the autofocus was getting hazy after the numerous falls (we did demo the 4 ft shockproof nature to several people). It died taking shots of me and friends, in one of the finest beaches of India, it had a good life.

I have upgraded to a 600D after its demise, and I eagerly wait for the D20 to come out. For whatever greatness a 600D has, if the D20 is better than D10, there's no better "dont worry about it" gadget that you can handover to friends and family.

Goodbye Friend, you'll be missed and fondly remembered.

title: Decent product, bad packaging
text:
Since my Kindle is new, I was gifted with a free month trial of Amazon Prime. As such I got this Kindle cover at a 72% discount off the retail price. Which is, incidentally, about all the product is worth. If I'd have paid full retail, I would have been pretty upset. Most third-party accessories for these kinds of electronics are sub-par and this is no exception. The leather-look vinyl on the outside is thick and appears rugged. The soft material inside is smooth, and doesn't make my skin crawl like microfiber does. The closure is hidden magnet, which actually works well to my surprise. There is a cheap elastic pen loop on the side that is useless. It's way too big to hold a stylus (mine fell right through it), so I assumed it was for a pen - which would be great if this was a Daytimer - but nobody I know uses a pen for a Kindle.

My biggest complaint about this cover is that it was shipped with a little stuffed "mini suit" on a keychain that I believe is meant to be a screen cleaner...maybe? It's about 3/4-inch long, with shiny plastic on one side, and microfiber on the other. It's really too small to be functional, and I would have been much happier if the cover had NOT been shipped with it, as when it was packed, it was done so that the metal of the keychain jammed permanent indented holes in the cover of the vinyl. What a horrible idea.

There are a couple redeeming qualities:

1) The stand aspect is FANTASTIC. It has a sturdy flap on the back that holds the cover back, with the cardboard folds in the perfect spots, providing a very sturdy stand for landscape hands-free viewing. The same flap folds around the back of the Kindle in portrait view so - unlike other products reviewed in this line - you can read the Kindle like a paperback with the cover folded behind it comfortably flat, unlike a hard edged triangle in your hand. Again, the folds are in the perfect places.

2) The cover holds the outside edges of the Kindle all the way around. Some e-book covers hold the Kindle in the cover with cheap elastic straps. I think that gives the product a cheap look, not to mention, unsafe. This cover holds the Kindle snugly, all the way around for a perfect fit. The bottom framing is a bit big, as it does interfere a tiny bit with navigating the bottom of the touchscreen, but it's certainly not a huge annoyance. The access openings are perfect.

3) The best aspect of this case, which I think is the most unique - and the only reason it got that 4th star from me - is that the Kindle doesn't slide in through the top, or the bottom, risking the possibility that it might - someday - slide out (not that it could anyway, it's held pretty snugly), but it slides into the cover from the INSIDE of the cover at the spine, complete with a velcro tab that tucks behind it to hold it in place, and is hidden when the cover is otherwise in use. All that and it STILL folds perfectly for both portrait reading and landscape hands-free viewing.

All that said, despite the shoddy-looking PU Leatherish cover with indent holes on the front, the function of the case makes it worth $10. Unless I desperately needed a cover, I would be hesitant to pay more than that for it based on looks alone. In fact, despite all the positives, had I seen this in a store with that retail price tag on it, I would never have spent money on it. A slight improvement in design material could probably improve the perception of this cover 100%.

Oh yeah, and either pack those stupid little keychains in bubble wrap, or in a separate envelope, or throw them away altogether. Damaging your product with a stupid advertising gadget is just a waste.

title: Amazing!
text:
This ArmorSuit is great. I bought it for my Kindle Fire - even though the Kindle Fire is supposed to be very abrasion resistant, I wanted to have extra piece of mind. I read a bunch of reviews on this and other products. In spite of the abundance of negative reviews, I decided to give it a try anyway. The positive reviews outweighed the risk, in my mind.

I'm so glad I did! I just applied it two days ago. I watched the online video a couple of times in advance to be sure I understood how to apply the product. My husband noticed that the people in the video don't use excess pressure when applying the ArmorSuit, and that they mention not doing so. I followed the instructions, and application was a cinch. It didn't take long (maybe 5 minutes), and it was easy to do. According to the directions, one should NOT turn on the appliance at least overnight, and preferably for 24 hours. I waited the full 24. The finish is great! A couple of small bubbles that were there yesterday had disappeared by this morning, and the protector is very nearly invisible. I don't think that anyone would even see that the Fire had a screen protector on it unless it was pointed out.

I had a couple of air bubbles on the edge of the black part of the screen that were a little bigger that I didn't see until later (my fault, not ArmorSuit's) or I would have squeegeed them out. I have a feeling that even those may disappear or lessen over the next day or so. I could always peel up the ArmorSuit and re-apply, as there was plenty of solution left. I'll probably just let those go, as they're not at all a bother to me and are exceedingly inconspicuous.

When we saw how clear the finish was, and how easy it was to apply, it made us want to buy one of these for every one of our devices! We may just do that.

Great product! Very happy!

*******
UPDATE-LATER THE SAME DAY

ALL of the bubbles are GONE. I'm amazed, and a little bit "weirded out." This stuff is unbelievable. The screen looks great. I took some pictures of it and will post them in the customer photo section.

title: The media this unit is really meant to stream is your cash back to Amazon
text:
Pros: small, quick response with the remote and decent graphics
Cons: upon searching, this unit directs you to content you must pay for (example below), less intuitive then other such devices to operate (unless you simply want Amazon content), MAC addresses should be printed on the outside label for those who use such things for setup.

I've owned and operated many of the other streaming appliances, this one was purchaed expressly to know more about the voice commands, I have an aging family member that would benefit from this. The voice command is pretty cool, I notice that most everything I searched for needed to be paid if I wanted it. That seems a bit odd as I have Prime, Netflix and Hulu plus so I played further. I loaded Netflix and found House of Cards. While at the point where I could simply press select and a show would begin streaming, I decided to ask the Fire TV for Kevin Spacey. It quickly came back with several movies and House of Cards...if I selected House of Cards now I would be charged 2.99 to view content I already have the rights to. I did the same with a movie on Netflix and had the same result.
I then engaged the parental controls, simple enough that would prevent my loved one from paying for content that is already paid for; the issue now is most everything needs a password to use. It also didn't say if it was paid content or the price, once you type in your password away it goes and the charge happily goes on your Amazon Bill

This product needs lots of work, it also needs a gut check from the suits at Amazon. I'm going to keep the unit to monitor the progress of a very negative shift in program delivery.

I got tired of viewing my magazine via Next Issue and Zinio with the iPad and having to enlarge every page/article, etc. With the SGNP, i don't have to do that anymore and I don't feel "old" visually ;-) This tablet is not heavy, it is thin and comfortable to use, especially the faux leather backing.

The S-Pen is awesome and I can cut out important articles, photos from magazines I read and save them in scrap book for follow-up at a later time. I'm still learning new features every day and loving it more like a kid in a candy store ;-) I have brought pens from Bamboo and Adonit Jot Script Evernote Edition Stylus to use with the iPad 4thGen and the Bamboo was the better of two but they both sucked! S-Pen is by far much better with SGNP - just wish the pen size was a little bigger to make it more comfy to use but it is manageable.

Only drawback is that the Samsung cover is still not available at this time of my review, including an extra travel charger/cable. Samsung needs to do a much better job in making sure that the accessories are available at the same time the tablet is sold.

You can't go wrong with this tablet and the price is a good value with the extras that come along with this device from Samsung.

title: Best travel LED projector for the price
text:
I got this projector mainly for traveling and for big screen movies in the house. It's VERY portable and comes with convenient carrying case for travel. Startup<5sec, cooldown<2sec, only uses 60w power, LED life will outlast me most likely. The 500 lumens and 720p video quality at 15000:1 contrast is perfect for any room that is dim or moderately illuminated. Don't expect it to look good in the middle of the day with windows open letting light in but in a dark or dim room it will blow you away!!! Color is outstanding and there are many settings to tweak it to your liking. It is such a small unit that you can't expect good sound quality and that's why I use a Big Jambox or plug into surround sound speakers if I want a true experience.

As for connectivity, the WIDI is AWESOME and will mirror my laptop in HD with ease (I have 2nd gen i7-2670 w/ HD3000 and GT555m Optimus). My 1.5TB external hard drive plugs directly into the projector via usb and will play content in every format that I've tried so far without the need of a computer (except 3d formats must come from a computer). Standard HDMI for gaming. Has other inputs that I'll never use.

3D works great with Stereoscopic player software (settings: layout=SENSIO Hi-Fi 3D; viewing method=software pageflipping) and SainSonic DLP link glasses. Computer output must be 1024x768 @ 120hz (so essentially a 576p resolution in 16:9 movie aspect but still looks extremely sharp and crisp)

Cons: charger weighs more than projector, that's it.

I highly recommend especially if you move around a lot or travel or have a dark room that needs a large 100" screen.

title: Good idea, but could not get it to work consistently
text:
I have a movie library on a portable USB hard drive. My idea was to use this device as a mobile media server that I could access wirelessly (even if there wasn't an internet connection available). For example, my goal was to plug the router in my car outlet and create a moving wifi network during long trips. My kids could then stream movies from the router (with USB hard drive attached) to their ipads and not have to worry about taking up the precious disk space on the ipads themselves. The extra USB port could even serve as a charger!

As expected, setting up the router was fairly straightforward. It's the no frills web interface that you find with most routers. I got the wifi network configured/protected pretty quickly. I even had it connected to an existing wifi network in my home without any problems The last step was setting up the app on my iphone, and again, that was pretty easy. I went to the app store, downloaded the app, and had the app talking to the router in less than 5 minutes.

The problem I had with the device was streaming movies (which was my main goal). When I connected my portable USB drive to the device, I can see the media on my iphone. When I tested the streaming capability, I found that the device would consistently hang. I never found a pattern. Sometimes it would work fine for 30 minutes before locking up or sometimes it would hang in just 10 minutes. When it did hang, the only way to start streaming again was to reboot the router.

I contacted tech support, and I give them credit for working with me to troubleshoot the issue. I even enabled the logging capabilities to see if I could get more detailed information about the issue. After a few rounds of back and forth, they came back and said they noticed something in the log files and said that usb modems are not supported. As best as I can tell, the USB hard drive I was using somehow presented itself as a USB modem, which of course made no sense. I gave up after that and returned the device.

My best guess is there was some compatibility issue between the device and the hard drive I was using. Unfortunately, I already had the hard drive for awhile (which had tons of content on it), and it was more expensive than the router. Basically, the router was the easier thing to return. Also, I could not find any documentation on what was compatible on the manufacturer's instructions or web site. I desperately wanted it to work, and was willing to get another hard drive that was supported. However, I was not going to risk buying another hard drive and run into the same issue.

title: All I hoped for
text: I did a lot of research before making this purchase, which was to replace a very disappointing point and shoot Nikon.  I had been waiting for the price on DSLR cameras to come down to a level where it made sense to make the leap.  I realized during the research process that every camera I considered buying or have used in my life, I still compare to the sweetest camera I own, which is the Pentax ME Super, circa 1980.  So I was interested and excited to find this Pentax/Ricoh entry level DSLR, at a very competitive price compared to similar Canon and Nikon models.  And I was really happy that my old and very nice Pentax lenses were compatible and could be used on this camera in manual mode.  The first time I picked it up I knew I had made the right decision. I was finally holding a real camera  --beautiful balance and feel, a crystal clear optical viewfinder.  Boy, had I been missing the ability to hold the camera up to my eye and frame a photograph.  The standard lens that comes with the camera is a cut above  --amazing bokeh effect even in autofocus mode.  I won't give a technical rundown because others have done a fine job, and much better than I can.  I will say that the only issue I was concerned about was the 16 megapixels, when other entry level DSLRs have 18 or 20.  I've been completely happy with my photographs, however, and frankly wouldn't want the data storage issues with super-high megapixel files.  The Pentax K-50 is a great buy for anyone looking to get into a DSLR and its features and quality may make it the only camera you will ever need.

title: Amazing product, just right for me
text:
I was pleasurably surprised when Amazon emailed me their offer of a free 30 day trial of the new Amazon Kindle Fire HDX 7”. To tell the truth, I have been meaning to buy a similar reading device with tablet capabilities and couldn’t figure out whether to buy the Nook HD, the Kindle Fire HDX or the Sony Experia Z Ultra. Of course it’s a matter of money. I am not made of the green stuff and even a $300 expense is big enough for me to think three times before buying something first in order to try it out. I read all the reviews, all the personal experiences put out by people, but still, it isn’t the same as having the thing at home to play around with.

This way works the best – they sent the 32GB version that I had chosen in less than 3 days.

From the moment I got the package in my hands, I was in love. It is simply great – it does (almost) everything an IPAD does at a fraction of the cost.

First, the cons – as I am sure there’s ample information on the pros.

1. The camera is ONLY on the front – there is no camera behind the screen. Makes skyping and taking pictures just a tad harder. Not a dealbreaker though, given all the other great stuff this little tablet does.
2. The page turning is by swipes only. When you are tucked in a cozy comforter on a cold night, you sometimes wish for right/left buttons – again, a minor annoyance.
3. The weight – it’s a tad heavier than the Sony Experia Z Ultra. But honestly, if losing weight means spending $400 extra, I can do without it!
4. The included charger is really slow – I spent the extra money for the power charger. Only I didn’t spend $19.99 on Amazon – I got it on eBay (new) from China, for $5.22, free shipping. Still waiting on it, but its guaranteed to arrive in a couple of days. Works for me!
5. I am an Amazon Prime buff – in fact Prime content is the prime reason why I chose the Kindle. It works great – only your ‘watchlist’ shows perhaps a quarter of what you have saved. If there is a way to see the entire watchlist, I haven’t discovered it (yet).
6. The carousel is annoying. It pops up unbidden whenever the Kindle’s turned on. I don’t need to display exactly what books and movies I have purchased and would have preferred if there was a way to discreetly tuck them away only to be brought out when I wish.
7. Browsing emails on yahoo can sometime be frustrating – scrolling is immensely difficult as the tablet, to me, seems too sensitive – whether I use a stylus or my fingers, it tends to pop open the email instead of allowing me to scroll thru the list.
8. Downloading movies is not too cool – takes too long and if the Kindle powers off, there you go. Lost the portion that you had already downloaded and need to restart.

That’s the lot of semi-bad news, if you can call it that. To me, it’s all stuff I can live with, nothing major. Here’s the positive stuff:

1. It is GREAT to watch a movie or a show on. The picture (we have a high-speed broadband Wi-Fi) is crystal clear; there is NO dithering or wait time as the video caches. It’s like watching your own personal wrap around widescreen. You might think the size would be too small, but when you do watch it, the screen’s placed close enough to your face comfortably and it actually seems like a much larger screen. Like I said, GREAT definition and clarity.
2. The sound’s amazing – clear, sharp and realistic. Even without headphones, it’s powerful enough to give true surround effect and loud enough to make my wife complain. With headphones, you don’t disturb anyone and the immersion is complete. BTW I bought JLabs Jbud J5 ear buds with this after doing some R&D (read my review if you wish – I even bought an extra pair for the wife) and it’s a perfect match right off the top. Tailor made for the Kindle Fire HDX.
3. Reading books is easy, except that a couple of left/right/page turning buttons wouldn’t have hurt. The light levels’s just right and if a white page glares at you, voila, make the screen black, the letters white! Bunch of choices in terms of fonts (publisher’s font included) and one can size them up or down as required.
4. Browsing – the silk browser is really great. Fast, no nonsense stuff.
5. People talk about the ‘offers’ as annoying – I find it extremely entertaining. Not just are the products good (no TV infomercials here) but also the entire ad experience is VERY unobtrusive. Flick it off whenever you wish and go back using the tab.
6. Navigating the Kindle is great (except perhaps the carousel feature which I didn’t like). Downloading documents and files, pictures etc is really fast, movies, not so much as explained in ‘Cons’.
7. Best part is its portability. The 7” is slightly too big to slip into the back pocket of my jeans and a jacket pocket is required. However if you do sort out the carrying issue, it’s great to have along and works everywhere there’s Wi-Fi.
8. I took the Boingo Wi-Fi on the go service and so far haven’t had too much trouble with it. Of course it’s not as fast as it’s touted to be and there is a tendency to hook you to the nearest network instead of the dedicated Boingo network, but hey, whatever works. I am not that finicky. It takes a bit of time to get hooked, but once it does, it’s a strong link and stays hooked unless you move a few blocks.
9. The case and paraphernalia. I definitely wouldn’t recommend spending $50-60 on the recommended sleeves and cases. I bought the Fintie faux leather package and for $20 approx, got a nice collection of stylus, sleeve, extra USB cable and some other small stuff. Works even better if you just buy the Fintie case for about $9.99. You definitely need a bigger case to stuff all those bits and pieces though – the charger, USB, stylus, headphones etc. I also bought a screen protector and a TPU Gel soft skin cover to be used in parallel with my Fintie case as added protection. It’s a tighter fit, but works perfectly.

All in all, it’s a GREAT purchase and I am loving it. Will be happy to answer any specific questions that anyone has. I, for one, am a VERY HAPPY customer.

title: Nice piece of kit
text:
The Onkyo sounds great. Looks great. The price is right. What's not to like?

I honestly was not expecting to hear anything particularly different from the 20 year old (?) Sony 5 disc I have and still use; they're both digital, after all. Still.... I'd recently replaced a similarly aged receiver that died (with an Onkyo TX-8020). And I'd purchased a new pair of speakers (Polk RTi4) to use while I repair an older pair. The only thing that I hadn't "upgraded" was the CD player. So I thought, "why not?".

It was a good decision.

I have no idea why it would be possible, but... imaging, transients, presence all seem better with the C-7030. It's the little things. I can now pick out a foot tapping in a Diana Krall album and the "twang" of the double bass in her backing musicians. The "resinous" sound of bow on string in Corelli Concerti; the "percussion" sound of James Taylor's finger picking technique. The sub-woofer seems more precise. Cymbals now seem to "ring". Nice.

One thing that I don't appreciate quite as much is that low frequencies now seem a bit over-emphasized. Mostly in "modern" music. It may be that I'm now hearing what was on the disc all along. Dunno. But in some cases it's a bit over the top. Still, it's easy enough to deal with (turn down the bass).

The headphone connection seems fine.

I haven't used the digital output or the ability to control the unit from an AVR. Those capabilities are not of concern to me.

If you're looking for a single disc player, are willing to spend little bit extra for quality, but don't want to drop $500+ on a Marantz 600x or equivalent, give the Onkyo C-7030 an audition. It might meet your needs.

Amazon was offering the best price I could find. Delivery was prompt, though the box was a bit battered and the closure tape was loose on one side.

text: For the price, it is really hard to beat this case. You get a full tower, with tons of hard drive space (2.5 inch anyway) and great air flow. I  really like the fact that you can move the hard drive by back, or competely remove it with just thumb screw removal. The case is matte black so you wont see smudges and finger marks. There are 4 usb 2.0 and 2 usb 3.0 ports on the top of the case, which is nice. Don't really see that many in that spot. The glass on the side is smoke colored which is nice if you want to see into the case, but not have too much light blaring out of it. There is a decent amout of cable space on the back side, but I think it could have been a half inch thicker. Very small gripe though as my rats nest of cables fit behind there with only little bit of squeezing. What is great about the back side is there is space to mount 2 more 2.5 inch hdds. The dual psu space is quite nice, but I bought it to put the radiator for a h110i in the top. Which brings me to really my only con of this case. There is barely enough room up top for a rad and a cd/dvd drive. And definitely not more than 1 if you are putting in a rad. It will work if you are only using a 120 or 140 rad no problem, but if you are using a 240 you can only use it with fans in push or pull, not both. A 280 rad will not fit with a cd/dvd installed. Also, with a cd/dvd rom in you can only install 120 mm fans in. 140's will not fit. However, that brings me to another big pro of this case. You can fit a massive radiator in the front of the case. It will house up to a 360 rad, in push or pull, and push/pull, and it still leaves room for a huge video card. I have a 7990 which is 12" long, and it fits (barely) with a 240 rad in push/pull.  Over all, this case would get 5 stars if it was about 3 inches longer for the extra room at the top. But still, a very very solid 4 stars! I am very happy with this case.

title: Obviously YMMV, but my experience is good
text:
4-stars because of higher than preferred cost. Otherwise, exactly what I was hoping for.

Clearly, some people have had bad luck with this antenna. Keep in mind that HDTVs may skimp on their tuners because it is assumed that people will have a cable-box with HDMI output. I'm not saying this is necessarily the case with all of the problems that people have had, but it IS possible. Certainly going from an amplified antenna to a passive antenna will change how the signal looks for the TV's tuner.

That said, I got one of these for my Mother who lives on the third-floor of an apartment complex in Cary, NC. She is very picky about the design of her apartment and I chose this antenna because it could be mounted just about anywhere. I stuck this antenna to the window of her apartment where her curtains cover it up usually. I'm very happy with this antenna. She can receive all of the local channels in Cary which broadcast from the WRAL tower; additionally she receives the 3 ION channels, 3 PBS channels, and even the CW channels 20.1, 20.2, 20.3, and 20.4 all of which come from different towers, the Greensboro tower as much as 60 miles away. She also gets many religious channels, spanish channels, and the Home Shopping Network.
My only complaint about this antenna is that it is a little expensive. You could probably get the same performance from a less expensive antenna. However, and I stated, I chose this because of interior design considerations.

My experience was good. The TV this attached to, and which I believe has a pretty robust tuner, is the Toshiba 26" LCD HDTV with Built-in DVD Player (26cv100u).

title: Almost Perfect
text: This boombox is truly the best sounding portable you can buy, VERY loud and clear, as good or better than a shelf system, but it has some minor drawbacks that you should know before you buy. What I dislike most are the 5 EQ presets, which are worthless, I can barely tell the difference between them. And there are no infinite bass/treble adjustments on this radio. They should have either installed a user adjustable EQ or 2 knobs just for mid & treble (the 3 level sub control works GREAT to give you just the right amount of bass for your tastes). Secondly, it has a built-in aux input cord for your mp3 player (smart), BUT, the gain is lower than the CD/radio input (dumb), so you have to turn up the radio's volume considerably higher for mp3s. You would think that the factory would design the aux input to have the highest gain, since the headphone output of all portables tends to be on the quiet side. Third, the gaudy styling and unnecessary red neon sub ring. Sony apparently thinks it's edgy and cool, but none of the consumers think so. It's not so much the color scheme, but the styling that's offensive. I think if they'd put this radio's proven electronics into a more sleek sophisticated boombox housing, similar to the old "executive micro" systems from a decade or so ago, they'd really have a winner. Fourth, the miniscule, non-backlit LCD readout is unforgiveable. Someone at Sony should have been fired for signing off on that. You have to tilt the radio up and practically use a flashlight and magnifying glass to get any info from it. Luckily once you get the hang of using the operational buttons on top of the unit you'll probably never have to look at it. And finally, the price: it's the best sounding boombox but it has a price to match, higher than some shelf systems. I bought mine from Amazon's open box / clearance center, so that can save you some money.

title: Read This Before You Buy ASUS
text:
This is my first review ever and I do not take lightly leaving a negative one, but while I like the features of the N56VM very much, before you purchase an ASUS laptop you should know just how bad their customer service is. My experience with the company has culminated in my being without the machine at the critical moment and having to spend an extra $400 to buy a hasty replacement, not to mention wasted hours on the phone and a lot of stress.

I purchased the laptop almost three months before I needed to take it out of the country for a long period of time. I thought this would give me time to vet the product and, sure enough, a month or so before I had to leave the LCD screen failed and I had to send it back. It was repaired and returned to me. Then, a few weeks later I had my first blue screen and Windows failed. After spending hours on the line with their tech support, it was determined that the hardware was at fault and the laptop would have to be sent back for another repair.

At this point I emphasized that I was leaving the country shortly and MUST have the laptop back very soon. Even though it was the holiday season, if ASUS was serious about customer service and making good on a faulty product, it was entirely reasonable that the laptop could be repaired and returned in time. Failing that, they could refund so that I could purchase another machine.

Unfortunately, as the tech support person informed me, ASUS has no customer service department. Evidently customer service is not their priority. Instead, the tech personnel, who were unfailingly polite but completely emasculated when it came to authorizing anything but rigidly proscribed procedures, could only give me one option: send it in and hope for the best.

When I asked to speak to a supervisor the tech person could only send the phone call off into a region unknown to them and hope someone would pick it up. Finally I was able to speak to someone on the 'escalation' team who authorized an expedited delivery to the service center in California (overnight instead of three-day) but told me he was unable to speak to anyone at the service center and that he didn't even have their phone number, or the phone number for ASUS corporate headquarters, for that mattter.

Something that I noticed is that the more advanced the motherboard is, the more one star reviews it gets. So there are a couple of things I want to comment on.

There is no memory controller on the motherboard. The memory controller is part of the CPU and that is also true of Intel systems. Search for the term "memory controller" at AMD's support site. They have some nice charts and a lot of information about their CPUs. If you're planning on overclocking RAM with a Phenom II, you probably won't like what AMD says about that. Another thing about RAM is that some of it just does not work well with some motherboards and CPUs. I suspect that Asus would prefer that you use their QVL but if you visit the sites of whichever brands of RAM that you like and ask questions in the support forums, the RAM manufacturers will point you to their products that they know will work with your motherboard/CPU.

title: The Continuing Converting of My Elders
text:
I discovered eReading about a decade and a half ago when I used my Handspring Visor to read a Jeff Deaver novel in bits and pieces while at the bank or with the kids at McDonald's Playland. It was a perfect combination of an author who writes short chapters with a small screen device while not having to carry around a big book. Over the years I moved from PDAs to dedicated eReaders, finally getting a Kindle two years ago. Lucky me. And I have been evangelizing in my big family ever since.

The Kindle Amazon delivered here in Canada was the Kindle without Special Offers. It was smaller, lighter and, to my eyes, a bit better screen-wise than my Kindle 3 aka Keyboard. But, alas, it wasn't for me. It was for my aunt Liz, a favourite amongst my multitudinous aunts on my mother's side. She's a mystery lover and so am I. I had many, many mysteries I could put on her machine, given my years of collecting them for my various devices. So, I got her up and going and reading immediately. FIVE minutes of instruction and she told me to go away.

She surfaced yesterday to thank me for the gift and then immediately went right back to reading. Her second book. In three days.

She's 80, soon to be 81. And right now, I wonder if the house was burning whether she'd go back for Uncle Tom or the Kindle first. It's up for debate. Just as it has been for my mother (eReader for sure) and the other aunts and cousins and nieces and one uncle.

The Kindle solves a LOT of problems, especially for older folks who find books heavy and awkward. The ability to increase font size helps overcome other difficulties. And the recharging is so sporadic, one aunt wonders whether it would ever need recharging.

Now, I'm wondering when, or IF, Aunt Liz will ask me about buying the latest Connelly, Sandford or Cussler. It's coming and I'm ready to spend the two minutes needed to show her.

title: Great model. Better image than new crop of cams
text:
I own this c510 and also the new c920. I was surprised to find that the c510 actually has a clearer image (on Skype) than the c920 on Skype, even though the c920 claims 1080p in Skype HD (gimmick). Sure, the newer cams record better video for Youtube uploads, but when it comes to Skype -- and I'm not sure I understand why -- the c510 image is sharper than the c920. I think the internal compression of the newer models actually degrades the image sent to Skype, but that's just a guess. The newer cams such as c525 and c920 will work better to put you in Skype HD mode if you have a slower computer because they have internal processing, though. That is a downfall of the c510. It uses your CPU more and really needs a faster dual or a quad core cpu to go HD mode. If you have an older, slower computer, don't get the c510. But when it does have a faster computer, it seems to provide a sharper image.

The c920, which is the flagship model, is a nice cam, but the whole "1080p" claim on Skype is a gimmick. It only gives you a wider picture, but not a sharper one. I actually found myself zooming-in because the wide picture sets your face back too far with the c920. That just degrades the image anyway, because the zoom is a software zoom. Save yourself some money and don't get that camera. I have mine up for sale on craigslist.

I will also note that after owning over 12 webcams, I am a fan of "fixed-focus" cameras like the c510. They do a better job of giving you a clear image all the way across the screen. Also, the better fixed-focus cams do better in low light.

title: Excellent upgrade for my Challenger
text:
I have a 2012 Challenger with the 6-speaker Boston Acoustics audio package. One of the factory speakers had blown, so I elected to replace my front door speakers with a set of these. The difference is pretty stark.

Since my factory system is amped, I have no idea what these speakers sound like on their own, powered only by a factory unit, but with them connected to an amp, it genuinely sounds like my car has a sub in it. It doesn't. And they can get LOUD without distortion. My ears gave out before the speakers did.

Bass is deep and rich, and sounds great across a variety of music, including pop, rock, hip-hop, and (yes, I checked) even EDM. The audio signal is split before it ever reaches the speaker, so there was nothing at all for the tweeters to do. I wound up turning the tweeter's gain switch to 0, because a little hissy noise was sneaking through, which is to be expected in a 2-ohm circuit.

Installation was fairly painless. The Challenger has a shroud that also serves to aim the speaker up and toward the center of the car, and the Infinity's enormous magnet just barely fit. The speaker's mounting cage didn't, however. I used a heat gun to soften and re-mold the shroud, but it wasn't going to work, so I used the included baffle to lift the speaker about a quarter of an inch over the shroud and the speaker fit the shroud easily. I did have to replace the screws that mounted the speaker to the shroud, since the ones from the factory were now too short, but I had a set of stainless screws the right size already. If you're adding these speakers to that car, make sure you have some 1.5" pan-head sheet metal screws or you're gonna have a bad time. I also used a pair of Metra 72-6514 speaker harness adapters (available here on Amazon) so I didn't have to cut and strip the factory speaker wiring.

For this particular application, I could've spent a little more and gotten some Kappa-series speakers from Infinity, but why? If I had the base audio system in my Challenger, then the added processing power would easily be worth it, but for replacing the stock door speakers on the BA system, this was the better bang for my buck. Or boom, as it were.

title: Worst build quality slingbox produced.  Dont waste your money.  If you do make sure you get a warranty.
text:
I been a longtime sling customer since the 1st day the sling app came out for the iphone appstore back in 2008.
The idea of watching all my shows, sports and everything else on my iphone or laptop anywhere in the world sounded great. I bought a pro-HD slingbox back in 2008 and still works perfect with no probs.
Got a 2nd slingbox this year, the slingbox SOLO model to be able to view my parents dish network programming also.
Well within 3-4 months this one stopped working. It will not power on at all, completelly dead and when I tried to restart it or hit reset it it smelled like burned rubber. So I think it probably shorted out. Many people have discovered that the capacitors installed on the SOLO bulge up about 1 year or even months after purchase, rendering them and the SOLO useless. I didnt bother openning it up or trying to fix it, I shouldnt have to do any of that to a 3 month old electronic device.
I didnt even use it that much. Less than an hour of usage per week if that. Sometimes didnt even connect for weeks, just here and there.
Anyway I read bad reviews about it stop working for many others within 1-2 months and many other issues so I spend the $16 on a squaretrade warranty.
Im very glad I did. Figures it died within months so all I had to do is send it back and squaretrade send me an amazon gift card for the original purchase plus 5% bonus. So Im planning on buying the new Slingbox 350 with that giftcard. Also a 3 year warranty just to be on the safe side. I heard they improved the quality on those new builds so Im crossing my fingers.
I love the sling experience and how I can watch my programming anywhere but if these boxes that cost hundreds of dollars each only last a few months then its worthless. And I dont want to chase the manufacturer all the time to repair or replace my unit and be without use for weeks. I also heard slingmedia customer service is terrible so I didnt even want to attempt contacting them. I just want it to work for at least a few years with no probs. Is that too much to ask Sling?
Im very happy with my original slingbox pro-HD, knock on wood it worked and works great for many years so far but I dont want to spend $300-350 for another one.

So in other words stay away from this Slingbox SOLO model. Do not waste your money or time on this junk. Try the new 350 or 500 model or the old pro-HD model.
And spend the $15-25 on an extended warranty on it. It is well worth it with these unless you want to keep buying new ones every year or having to deal with Slingmedias rude customer service reps wanting to charge you $30 just to talk to you or $100 to fix it if you're out of the 1 year warranty.
