So I purchased a more powerful, super clean amplifier that was better matched with the specifications of these speakers. They sounded MUCH better and didn't seem to require as high a volume in order to sound good. Still not great, but very good. Then about 3 months later one started distorting more and more. I would EQ my way out of it and scoop the sound for the frequencies (lower mids) the right speaker didn't seem to like. It really put a cap on my volume which really isn't that loud anyway. No problem, I can live with it. The distortion started getting worse at lower and lower volume over time. Then, the left speaker started distorting at volume which even the bad (right) speaker could handle.

VERY disappointed. When you pay this much for speakers, you expect not only high fidelity but durability. I live in a hot climate but every other brand I have used seems to tolerate the same climate conditions.

Don't put your money into Focal Polyglass!

text: This is a great product.  I've always wanted to do time lapse, but never wanted to get into all the mechanics of it.  Who wants to tie up an expensive camera and risk it getting damaged or "permanently relocated?"  Brinno makes time lapse stupid easy.  It is almost a miracle in the palm of your hand.  I read the manual, set up the camera and did a great first video of carpet being installed in my game room.  Here's all it takes:  Position the camera, select the capture interval, turn the camera on, record the event, turn it off, let the Brinno do its thing (image processing), pop out the flash card, slip it in the computer.  iPhoto loads it -- BOOM!  You've got a time lapse movie.  It saves as an AVI, but when you load it into quick time (as in play it in quick time) it automatically gets converted into a .mov.  It's that easy.  No assembling in post (as with the GOPRO unit).  Seriously, this thing makes time lapse as easy as taking a snap shot.  Image quality is very good.  Size is shockingly small -- in the palm of your hand.  Light weight.  I was even pleased with the packaging -- rivals that of apple products.  This is truly a user friendly device. title: One of the best hybrid laptops
text:
The speed of this laptop is amazing! I'm a light user. I only really use this laptop to surf the net, youtube, email, play around with photos, watch movies and maybe play the occasional game or two (nothing too graphic intensive). And I find this laptop works very well for my usage.

I've read various reviews on the fan being too loud and coil whine which made me a little reluctant to purchase but luckily I had no issues with mine which was manufactured late January this year (2013). The fan I would say is a little louder than my older laptop but nothing as drastic as people saying they can hear it from meters and meters away. Mine sounds more like it's working harder/spinning faster than my older laptop it seems. I know Lenovo did provide a optional fix which can slow down the rpm and delay the fans at the expense of a warmer machine which I have not yet tried as the fan isn't bothering me too much.

This laptop already had the partition issue that a lot of people were complaining about fixed and had roughly 100-105gb of desk space out of the 128gb SSD with 70-75gb free out of the box.

This laptop is great for those who will mostly use their laptop in laptop mode but want the flexibility to use it in tablet mode when the need arises. In tablet mode, I find the keyboard at the back to be a little weird having owned an iPad and being use to the smooth back. This is fixed with the use of the slip which can be purchased separately and it does work well. Only con is that it instantly makes the tablet mode bulkier than it already is. Tent mode is great for in bed watching of movies on the laptop. Presentation mode is not something I've had to use yet so can't provide many comments.

The touch screen is responsive for my usage. Love the size of the touchpad and it's multi-gestures (zoom in/out, scroll) which is very convenient for me. Hate the small shift button which I always seem to miss... but I assume with enough practice I will get use to the keyboard.

All in all, a beautiful machine. The only one that really caught my eye out of all the touch screen laptops currently available.

It doesn't even have a clock on the front display.  Nor does the display show you the runtime that has elapsed during the movie.  (However, it has a menu where you can access things on screen such as runtime elapsed while you are watching the movie.)  What it is supposed to do, it does well.  Even the Smart features work well and are easy to use.  I usually rent out of Redbox for my movies, but one time I did downstream a 3D movie from one of the Apps, and it works quite well. title: For $200 you just can't go wrong!
text:
I read about this on a tech site and saw that it was just $179 on the Microsoft Store, so I took the plunge. My old 2007 heavy MacBook Pro has all kinds of work done to it to keep it chugging away, but I wasn't looking to directly replace it, just for something really lightweight to use on the sofa while watching TV (or not watching it if it's not all that interesting).

It's a fantastic purchase for the money. It is lightweight, easy to use, and as long as you're not looking for something to run Call of Duty or Photoshop on without any issues, it's perfect. Perfect for web browsing, writing the odd Google Doc or watching a bit of Netflix. And that's all I need it for. Heavy-duty stuff like editing videos I will use the MacBook. But for everyday activities, this is great.

It's hard to find fault with something as good as this when it only cost around $200, but if I have to find some things I don't like, it's mainly things that would increase the price of the device! Such as no backlit keyboard, which makes typing in a dim room at night slightly more tricky. The fact that the proprietary charging plug doesn't have any easy way to inform you if you're inserting it the right way up or not (I've used a little sticker). I do dislike the odd metal 'grip feet' that protrude from the bottom of the screen at the back - I can hear them scraping along my coffee table. What on earth were Asus thinking with those things?? Wish they weren't there, they don't seem to serve any purpose other than grip the surface a little, but grip and scratch? Not such a great solution.

But I do like the netbook. It's fast, and learning to use Windows 8.1 is certainly a learning curve, but I'm getting there. I do like the new Start screen despite its negative write-up in the tech press, and the apps load quickly and work well. And if I want to switch to the full traditional desktop experience, I can in a cinch. I'm not sure why Windows 8 has been slammed so much, it's pretty easy to get your head around the major stuff.

A solid purchase for full on Windows for an amazing price. Very happy customer (of the Microsoft Store - sorry Amazon!) :^)

UPDATE: Thanks to another user pointing this out, the power plug DOES actually go in either up or down. It seemed to go in easier one way and not the other, but I can confirm it doesn't matter which way up the plug is. Good news. Also, after using it for a few days, I cannot believe how long the battery lasts! Three nights of setting up and fiddling and browsing and finally I put it on charge yesterday as it was down to 10%. Excellent.

title: Buffering Blunder
text: I first owned a SMP-N100 and for the most part was satisfied except for occasional buffering issues. About 6 months ago, I bought a Sony television on clearance from a big box store and was pleasantly surprised that the TV included a SMP-N200.  Naturally, I saw it as an opportunity to upgrade my existing player.  Keep in mind that the player is located less than 15 feet from my router and a non-structural wall.  I quickly noticed that Netflix was buffering much more than the N100 and other services were also worse.  I called Sony technical support and a couple days later mailed the player in for evaluation and possible replacement.  A week or so passed and a new N200 arrived.  I hooked up the player and connected wirelessly.  To my disappointment, the Netflix buffering was still terrible.  I then ran a powerline Ethernet connection between the router and the N200.  After connecting, I saw no improvement.  Earlier this month (Oct 2013), I bought a Sony BD Player with wireless connectivity support. I installed the player and set it up as wireless.  In a heartbeat, the buffering disappeared and I had no issues with any content!  As soon as I chose the N200 as source, the buffering returned.  I guess it's possible that I got 2 bad units?  This morning I tried the N200 again and experienced the same results.  I'm pretty sure the unit has been discontinued.  That's good.  The world is a better place.  As a side bar, I also have a Roku that's about 2 years old.  In the same spot as the N200, it works fine.  Bottom line, if you're looking for a streaming player, there are a lot better to be found that the Sony SMP-N200.

title: Awesome Upgrade!
text:
After my Signet Marine depth sounder on my sailboat started continually flashing 18.8, I had to decide; fix this circa 1987 product for at least $150, or swap the whole thing out. I am glad that I decided to swap to the Garmin Echo 200!

Rather than just showing a number, the Echo 200 shows me the bottom contour, and fish! I mounted the transducer inside my hull with silicone glue, to hold the transducer in place. The included 30' cable was barely enough to enable me to mount the transducer near the old one, at the leading edge of my fin keel, and to mount the transducer at the binnacle on my 35' sailboat. I could have mounted the transducer further aft (I have seen some mounted behind the keel), but I want to know the depth BEFORE I run aground. So far, the transducer ACCURATELY shows depths of up to 100', which is all that I need. I am sure that the depth would read higher if I mounted the transducer outside the hull, and that it will read higher once I get out of Narraganset bay.

I love the quick release mount, and the wider screen. I have used the unit in dual frequency/split screen mode, and this makes it really easy to see subtle changes in the depth contour. This would be far more difficult with the echo 150 or 300 unit. I also like that if I want to see numbers only, the unit will show me depth, water (actually hull) temperature, and the DC system's voltage. I have set the voltage alarm so that it goes off at 12.5V, so that I know when to stop sailing, and start the motor.

title: Excellent for converting camcorder and VHS tapes to digital
text:
My apologies for this long review. Hopefully, though, it will be useful to someone.

I'm writing this review from the standpoint of someone looking for a video transfer product to convert camcorder and VHS tapes into digital files for preservation and editing. If you going to use this product to record a gaming session, or to convert high-def video, please see the many other reviews here.

I've spent some time the past 2 weeks comparing competing products for transferring home videos into digital format on my Windows 7 PC for long-term preservation and so that I can edit the videos on my PC. I tried or considered three different products including this Hauppauge HD PVR, and one high-end video transfer company, all on the same Hi8 analog video cassette with a family video that is 15 years old. Along the way, I have gotten some familiarity with the various technologies available today for transferring magnetic tapes into digital form. I found out some interesting things, and thought I would share them, in the hope that it might help others.

First, and you probably already know this, if you have any video memories on magnetic video tape, you want to get them transferred into digital form onto your PC or DVD or Blu-ray as soon as possible, before the video badly deteriorates. This especially includes regular VHS tapes, Video8 tapes, and normal Hi8 tapes, all of which are analog formats and are particularly susceptible to deterioration starting after about 10 years. Somewhat less susceptible to deterioration are Digital8 (which is also recorded on Hi8 tapes) and MiniDV tapes, because those are digital formats. But even for digital tapes, it is still magnetic tape which deteriorates over time, and you need to get those videos off of there. Seriously, at the risk of sounding like a doomsayer, if you have precious memories on magnetic video tape, you need to transfer that video off of those tapes and into digital form as soon as possible, or risk losing them forever. It's not hard to do, and you'll sleep better at night when you get it done!

In my case, I have a bunch of precious Hi8 family video tapes recorded on a high-end Sony consumer camcorder between 10 and 19 years ago, and I am rescuing these Hi8 videos a little on the late side. I wish I had started this project 5 years ago instead. These tapes are still watchable, but they have developed some lines and drop-outs and "hiccups" and digital artifacts. With multiple playback retries, I can fortunately still coax out fairly high quality from these tapes.

A quick note: Digital8 and MiniDV video tape camcorders have USB ports on them for digitally transferring your videos to your PC or Mac. If this is your situation, there is NO need to purchase one of these video transfer products (like Hauppauge HD PVR). You will get the best quality, by far, by using a USB cable to connect your camcorder to your PC or Mac, playing back your video in the camcorder, and using any of a whole bunch of different inexpensive software products on the market that will allow you to capture video from the USB port on your computer. This way, you are getting the digital video in its original form, which is great. You will get worse quality if you use a video transfer product that captures the video off of the video ports on the camcorder, because the camcorder is converting the digital video into analog, then the video transfer product converts the analog back to digital (not ideal, for sure).

So, for the rest of this review, I will assume you have analog magnetic video tape (like VHS, Video8, or normal Hi8), in which case you need a video transfer product like this Elgato Video Capture or something similar.

A note about video resolution: The analog video tape formats (VHS, Video8, and normal Hi8) all have native video resolutions less than 640x480. All of the video transfer products on the market record the video from these formats at either 640x480 or 720x480. It doesn't really matter which of these two resolutions the product records at. The point is, all of the video transfer products record at higher resolution than the original video, so you are capturing all of the resolution of the original video when you do the video transfer, which is good.

A note about overscan lines at the bottom of captured video: As documented all over the Internet, when capturing digital video from an analog video source like an analog magnetic video tape, you will end up with some additional fuzzy lines at the bottom of the captured video. This is totally normal. When played back on a regular TV, these overscan lines are usually chopped off because they appear "below the bottom of the screen," but the digital capture grabs them (including with the Hauppauge HD PVR). To get rid of those lines, you can crop or zoom in slightly when you do your video editing. Interestingly, the Elgato Video Capture device (see below) automatically does a minor zoom on all captured video to remove those fuzzy lines.

A remark about video editing: Two of the products below (Elgato and Hauppauge) produce video files that use H.264 compression. This is an excellent video compression standard for viewing, and is supported by just about all video editing software. However, if you are going to do significant video editing, you may want to use some video conversion software to convert these video files to uncompressed or MJPEG-compressed AVI or MOV files for editing. (There are many inexpensive or perhaps even free software packages that will do this conversion.) The problem with editing H.264 compressed video files directly is that the extreme compression, which crosses video frame boundaries, can cause problems for video editing software, resulting sometimes in digital artifacts or out-of-sync audio in the final edited video output. An uncompressed or MJPEG-compressed AVI or MOV video source file avoids these problems.

A word about using an outside company to make a high-quality transfer of your analog video tape: A search of the Internet reveals many companies that will transfer your video tape into digital form, and send the digital files back to you on a fairly inexpensive USB hard drive that you can supply yourself or that they will sell you. Some of these companies are better than others. A few of these companies are very high-end, using expensive video transfer equipment. I used one of these very high-end video transfer companies, using their most expensive Premium service, to transfer the very same 15-year-old Hi8 tape that I also tried at home with the video transfer products below. I discovered that the transfer done by the outside company was significantly WORSE (lots of lines through the video and tracking problems) than what I was able to do at home with the products below. I don't necessarily think this is the fault of the video transfer company. At home, I was able to use the very same Sony Hi8 camcorder to do the transfer that I originally used to shoot the original video tape. My suspicion is that, especially for older analog video tapes, it helps to use the same camcorder for transfer as you used to shoot the video originally, so that any idiosyncracies in tracking or video head alignment won't be as much of an issue. Just food for thought.

Anyway, as noted above, I have done an experiment over the past 2 weeks, transferring the exact same 15-year-old Hi8 tape to my PC using the high-end video transfer company (above), plus two different video transfer products at home (Elgato and Hauppauge, below), and I also considered a third video transfer product (Blackmagic, below), to compare the pros and cons of each of each approach. Here's what I found out:

[[ASIN:B0029U2YSA Elgato Video Capture]]: Gets the best reviews on Amazon for a relatively inexpensive product for video transfer on both Windows and Mac. It captures video at 640x480 resolution, which means it grabs the full resolution and more of VHS, Video8, and normal Hi8 tapes. This worked great on my 64-bit Windows 7 computer. I just downloaded the latest driver and software from the Elgato web site, installed them both, and I was ready to go. It's incredibly easy to use. It connects to any USB 2.0 port on your computer. There are really no settings; the software guides you through the very simple process, and it transfers your video to your computer as an MP4 file. In case you are curious, the MP4 file it writes uses H.264 compression at 640x480 resolution and (basically) 29.97 frames/sec (standard NTSC) and a video data rate of between about 1100 kbps and 1500 kbps, depending on the complexity of the particular video you transferred. The audio in the MP4 file is AAC format at 48 kHz 16-bit stereo with an audio data rate of 128 kbps. When capturing a 2-hour video, I ended up with an MP4 file that was 1.5 GB in size. This Elgato product scores big points for ease-of-use. However, the video quality, while quite good, is not as high as the Hauppauge HD PVR (see below), because of the heavy video compression the Elgato uses to make a relatively small MP4 file with fairly low data rates. If you look closely at the captured video from the Elgato product, you will notice some minor squares of slightly distorted color at times, where the video has been over-compressed. Also, as noted above, the Elgato Video Capture automatically does a minor zoom on all captured video to avoid the fuzzy lines at the bottom of the captured video. On the plus side, this saves you the step of doing that zoom yourself in video editing. On the minus side, it is cropping all 4 sides of the video slightly, which might not be what you want.

[[ASIN:B0018LX0DY Hauppauge HD PVR]] (this product): The Hauppauge HD PVR exists in two very similar versions, the [[ASIN:B0018LX0DY Model 1212]] and the [[ASIN:B005P5UMVM Model 1445 Gaming Edition]], but the functionality of the two models is identical when capturing video from analog video magnetic tape. (I used the [[ASIN:B005P5UMVM Gaming Edition]].) Although designed for high-def video capture, it's by far the best product I tried for standard-def video capture as well. This product gets excellent reviews on Amazon, and rightfully so. It works out of the box on Windows (including 64-bit Windows 7, which I use), and also supports the Mac with separately downloadable software. When transferring standard definition video, the Hauppauge product captures video at 720x480 resolution, which means it grabs the full resolution and more of VHS, Video8, and normal Hi8 tapes. Like the Elgato product, the Hauppague is very easy to use, though the software give you a few recording options, unlike the Elgato. The Hauppauge connects to any USB 2.0 port on your computer. It gives you a choice of recording video in three different formats: .TS, .M2TS, or .MP4. It doesn't matter much, choose whatever format is most convenient for you; most digital video editing applications can handle any of these formats with no problem. In all three cases, the output file uses H.264 compression, is 720x480 resolution, 29.97 frames/sec (standard NTSC) and a user-selectable video rate between 1 Mbit/sec and 13.5 Mbit/sec. I chose 5 Mbit/sec, and ended up with a crystal-clear video capture with a variable video data rate of 20 kbps (MUCH higher data rate and much lower compression than the Elgato, which means a clearer picture). The audio is AC-3 format at 48 kHz and a data rate of 384 kbps (again, much less compression than the Elgato, which means the Hauppauge perhaps yields slightly higher audio quality). If these technical details sound confusing, it's not important. The point is, the video capture from the Hauppauge product is significantly higher quality than from the Elgato, at the expense of significantly larger output files, and like the Elgato, can be edited with most video editing software. (A 2-hour video capture on the Hauppauge gave me a 5 GB file, as opposed to the 1.5 GB file from the Elgato for the same video tape.) Note that, like most video capture devices, the Hauppauge gives you the full captured video frame, which means you end up with some fuzzy lines at the bottom, as explained above. You can eliminate those fuzzy lines during editing with a crop or minor zoom.

[[ASIN:B003WSQTWU Blackmagic Design Intensity Shuttle]]: This is the cream-of-the-crop for video capture. It comes in either a [[ASIN:B003WSQTWU USB 3.0 model]] for Windows or a Thunderbolt model for the Mac. It captures both high-def and standard-def video in full, uncompressed format, so there is no loss of video quality for compression. For true archival quality of your video memories, this is the Rolls Royce option. However, there are two trade-offs to obtain this quality. The first is that your uncompressed video takes a LOT of disk space. The second, and more important, consideration is that you need a computer that can handle the extremely high data rate coming from the Blackmagic device (since the video is uncompressed). If you run Windows, you need a high-speed computer using an Intel x58 based motherboard, a true USB 3.0 port, and the latest USB 3.0 drivers. Most computers don't meet this requirement, even when they have a USB 3.0 port. There is a list of officially tested motherboards on the Blackmagic web site. My 1st-generation Dell XPS 17 laptop (which has two USB 3.0 ports) does not meet this requirement, so I can't use the Intensity Shuttle, and thus I haven't tried it. Though not officially listed as a supported system, there is a YouTube video called "Intensity Shuttle and Dell XPS Laptop From Scratch - Tutorial" that explains how use a SECOND-generation Dell XPS 17 laptop with the Intensity Shuttle if you re-install Windows 7 and strip down the software running in the background to the bare minimum. Many people who want to use the Intensity Shuttle will buy or build a computer specifically for this purpose. If you don't already have a computer that is compatible with the Blackmagic Intensity Shuttle, and you aren't willing to invest to purchase or build one, or you don't need the full uncompressed archival quality video that is captured by the Intensity Shuttle, go with the Hauppauge or Elgato products, above.

I hope this comparative review is helpful to someone. Good luck, and good for you for transferring your precious older analog video tapes!

title: Works fine, supports Windows 7, but might be more expensive than your needs
text:
I just received this RocketRAID card today. I tried it out, and did some tests, comparing it to the less expensive and less functional [[ASIN:B001MWHI0U LaCie 130823 eSATA PCI Card]], which I have been using for about 6 months.

NOTE: The thrust of this review is comparing this RocketRAID card with the cheaper LaCie card, because I have now used both.

Here is what I found out:

This RocketRAID card works fine. It has official Windows 7 drivers (both 32-bit and 64-bit) available on the company's web site, even though the Windows 7 drivers were not on the CD-ROM included in the box (not a big deal either way). It has two internal SATA ports, and two external eSATA ports, all of which support the SATA II standard (maximum speed of 3.0 Gbit/sec), and is backward compatible with SATA I (maximum speed of 1.5 Gbit/sec). The RocketRAID card includes two internal SATA cables and two external eSATA cables. In addition to the standard slot bracket, the RocketRAID includes a low-profile bracket that you can use instead, if your PC requires it.

Even though the RocketRAID card has two eSATA ports and two SATA ports, you can very easily and inexpensively convert one or both of those SATA ports into eSATA ports instead, so that you have up to 4 eSATA ports for 4 external eSATA hard drives. To do this, just buy any SATA-to-eSATA bracket, like the [[ASIN:B000NPKGH4 StarTech 2 Port SATA to eSATA Slot Plate Bracket (ESATAPLATE2)]] (which is the one I bought). Just plug the SATA cables from the extra bracket into the SATA ports on the RocketRAID card, and you're done. Note that if you do this, it will occupy two slot (bracket) positions on your computer, rather than one, where each slot position provides two eSATA ports.

When you turn on your computer, this RocketRAID card does something a little odd. As part of the boot-up sequence, it shows a full-screen status display, while it "scans" for hard drives connected to it. This takes quite a long time, at least for eSATA drives (which is what I tried it with). I didn't time it, but I would guess it took maybe 30 seconds to get past this status screen, with three eSATA drives plugged into this card. Almost all RAID and SATA and similar cards display some sort of identifying information when you boot the computer, and will usually pause for a few seconds, but what's odd about this card is the very long time it takes for this. Not a big deal, though, unless you are rebooting your computer a lot. Also, I have to confess, I didn't try doing a normal reboot; I did a Windows shutdown followed by a power on, several times. It's possible the status screen doesn't take that long pause on a normal reboot, I don't know.

I compared the performance of this card to the [[ASIN:B001MWHI0U LaCie 130823 eSATA PCI Card]], which I have been using for about 6 months. It is true that this RocketRaid card provides two SATA ports in addition to its two eSATA ports, which the LaCie card does not. Also, RocketRAID supports SATA II (3.0 Gbit/sec) rather than the older SATA I (1.5 Gbit/sec) that is used on the LaCie card. In addition, unlike the LaCie card, the RocketRAID card allows you to configure your SATA and eSATA drives into a RAID configuration.

However, if you are just going to use the RocketRaid card to provide eSATA ports on your PCI-based computer, and you don't need RAID, and you are connecting to normal 7200rpm external drives or slower, go with the LaCie card. First of all, the LaCie card supports eSATA drives that use SATA II, even though it's only a SATA I card, because the SATA II standard is backwards-compatible with SATA I (I use eSATA drives that are SATA II with the LaCie card, works great). Secondly, both SATA I and SATA II are faster than the effective transfer speed of a 7200rpm hard disk (I confirmed this in my own tests, and on the Internet you can also find many other people who have done this real world test), so for a normal 7200rpm external drive (or slower drives), you get the same performance from either the RocketRAID card or the LaCie card. Plus the LaCie card only pauses briefly during boot up, unlike the RocketRAID card that pauses for a long time (see above).

If you read Amazon reviews of the LaCie card, you will see a number of reviewers who point out that there are no Windows 7 drivers for the LaCie card available on the LaCie web site (unlike the RocketRAID card). However, it turns out you can download the Windows 7 drivers (both 32-bit and 64-bit) for the LaCie card from the web site of Silicon Image, the company that makes the chipset for the LaCie card (see my review of the [[ASIN:B001MWHI0U LaCie 130823 eSATA PCI Card]] for details on how to download the Windows 7 drivers for that card). The LaCie card works great on Windows 7 (I've been using it with 32-bit Windows 7, but there is also a 64-bit Windows 7 driver available.)

The LaCie card only provides 2 eSATA ports, whereas the RocketRAID card can provide up to 4 eSATA ports (if you combine it with a SATA-to-eSATA plate, see above). However, you can use two LaCie cards in the same computer to get 4 eSATA ports (this is how I have my computer configured), it takes up the same number of effective slots (two), and buying two LaCie cards is cheaper than buying this one RocketRAID card.

Again, though, if you need SATA ports in addition to or instead of eSATA ports, or if you want RAID capability, or if you have a use for the extra speed of SATA II (which has no real world speed advantage over SATA I for a 7200rpm external hard drive, see above, but could be useful for other purposes), this RocketRAID card is a good choice.

A couple other notes:

If you aren't familiar with PCI vs. PCI Express (PCIe), it's important to note that this is a PCI card. Despite their similar names, PCI is totally different from PCIe. The PCI bus went out of fashion around 2005 (plus or minus), so this card is definitely for PCs that are fairly old. If you aren't sure whether your computer uses PCI or PCIe, check the specs for your computer (if available) or look at the slots on your computer and do an Internet search to see the difference in appearance between a PCI slot and a PCIe slot, to determine which type of slot your PC has.

Q: Why buy an eSATA PCI card in the first place? A: If your external hard drive has a choice of different ports on it (for example, the [[ASIN:B004PNXR44 Western Digital My Book Studio II - 6 TB (2 x 3 TB) USB 2.0/FireWire 800/400/eSATA Desktop External Hard Drive]], which offers USB, eSATA, FireWire 400, and FireWire 800 ports), definitely use the eSATA, FireWire 800, or (if available) USB 3.0 or SuperSpeed USB 3.0 interface. eSATA, FireWire 800, and USB 3.0 all run at effectively the same speed for the purposes of an external hard drive, because these interface standards exceed the effective transfer speed of a 7200rpm external hard drive (see above). USB 2.0 and FireWire 400 run slower -- in real life, with a 7200rpm external hard drive, and the usual hardware/software overhead, USB 2.0 and FireWire 400 run at about one-third the speed of the other three interfaces. It is this speed difference that makes it worthwhile to get an eSATA (or FireWire 800 or USB 3.0) card for your PC, if your external hard disk supports one of these faster standards, and if your PC doesn't already have one of these ports on it.

title: Stopped working and is not 8500mah, but at least it's not a chinese counterfeit
text:
I used this for a while in my FS700, but only as a backup since it stays at 100% for a while and then suddenly drops to 50% and without warning will often drop to near 0%. It had an ok battery life while it lasted maybe even close to a real F970 6600mah battery, but after a while (maybe a year) it stopped charging past 60%, so between that and the camera's inability to effectively tell how full the battery was I took it out of the rotation since I was a bit worried one of the cells went bad or something.

I decided to take the battery apart and see what was wrong with it and since I was curious since I've taken 3rd party batteries apart before and found them half full of metal weights where cells should be. Anyway inside there at least weren't any weights and it was full of 6 18650 3.6V cylindrical cells that are marked 2200mah. Of course these must be 2S3P so if the markings on the cells are accurate (and those are often over-estimated as well) this battery at best is 7.2V 6600mah, definitely not 8500mah as advertised... If it didn't stop working.

Overall I guess maybe I got a bad one so at least these aren't the worst chinese batteries to take a chance on since they acutally have real li-ion cells inside, but don't expect 8500mah, and don't be too surprised if they start dying much more quickly than real Sonys.

title: A VERY Bad experience...BUT SEE THE UPDATE at bottom of review
text:
Purchased the Onkyo TX 8050 receiver on May 4 and 66 days later on July 10 it stopped working. It would keep turning off 3-5 seconds after being turned on. I tried unplugging it, waiting 30 seconds and then replugging it, and also doing a factory reset as per the manual, but neither worked.

Called Onkyo and they told me to bring it to the nearest repair shop which is 20 miles from my home. Being disabled, that is a very difficult thing for me to do. Then I called Amazon and explained the situation. I also suggested to their rep, Marty, that since I'm a Prime member and spend $100s of dollars with them every month perhaps they would extend a courtesy to me and exchange this defective unit for a new one since it's only about a month past their return cutoff.

After 15 minutes of going round in circles on the phone with Marty, I was 'politely' told THEY WOULD DO NOTHING and that I would have to get the defective receiver to an Onkyo repair shop.

It seems to me that an exception could have been made in this case. I would have been better off purchasing the receiver from my local Best Buy or Sears. At least I would have been able to drop it off at their local store for warranty repairs. A much easier procedure.

This left a very bad taste in my mouth and I will have second thoughts about purchasing electronics from Amazon in the future.

UPDATE: 7/25 took the receiver to a repair shop for warranty repairs and when I told them that it keeps turning itself off after a few seconds, they said that the problem is a bad circuit board and that there is a 'service bulletin' from Onkyo about this problem. They also said that they would replace the circuit board and that the problem should not reappear.

Keeping my fingers crossed...

UPDATE: 8/25. I've had the receiver back for about 3 weeks now and all is well. It's got all the features you could want ie. Sirius, Rhapsody, last.fm, Spotify, Pandora and more. I love the fact that you can drive 2 sets of speakers so that the surround sound is amazing. Plenty of power to drive both sets of speakers at obscene levels. Tuning AM/FM stations is a bit of a chore if you don't use the remote, but other then that (and the repair episode)I'm very pleased with this Onkyo. Rate it 4 stars now.

The reason I didn't change the 'master' review to 4 stars is that I, and probably most people, don't read the 'in between' reviews. I read the 5 star and the 1 star comments. A 4 star review would get skipped over, I think, by most people and I wanted those interested in this receiver to read this review to see what my experiences were.

UPDATE: 1/9/13. Still pleased with the Onkyo...no more problems so I've updated the rating to 3 stars. If I hadn't had any trouble with the unit it would rate 5 stars.

title: Excellent Center Speaker! Very Good Value
text:
Bought this item as a Christmas gift for use in the living room home theatre. Already have Bose mains, Polk rears, and Sony sub with a Pioneer receiver and Samsung LED TV. Was previously using an old Radio Shack center speaker. So really needed a good center channel speaker to complete the whole set up. Also wanted a really good center channel since most, well all, of the sound from HD TV comes through the center channel. Background on myself, I am a self-proclaimed audiophile with a very good ear. I am also an Engineering student looking to get into audio engineering, so I know a lot about this stuff and had good experience with it. So the speaker itself.

Design: This is JBL. You can expect only the highest quality in build design. When I first got the package, I was surprised at it’s size. I knew it was a 6” woofer and I have 6.5” mains for my hifi so I should’ve been expecting the size, but when you put 2 of them in one enclosure it gets pretty big. It was also pretty heavy which is good. It will be solid and have no resonance because of this. We had to do a little adjusting to accommodate the speaker in the entertainment center and it sits a little lower than I would like, the couch armrest obstructs it ever so slightly and I was worried it would affect the sound, but it doesn’t at all and when I’m actually sitting on the couch, I’m angled far above the armrest so it’s fine. So just be prepared to accommodate a rather large speaker. The enclosure is poly-filled which is a must and definitely a testament to the quality of the speaker since you don’t see that in cheaper items. It comes with 2 woofers like all center speakers, but it also comes with 2 tweeters. It is basically a standard 2-way design with an extra tweeter for high and ultra high frequencies, making it a 3 way design. I would have much preferred to have a dedicated midrange driver instead of an extra tweeter. This is because the midrange of the most critical of all frequencies and where most sounds are. And since vocals are almost exclusively in the midrange and relegated to the center channel, a center speaker would take great advantage from this.

Sound: I though the sound might lack with this extra tweeter and not a midrange driver, but let me tell you, the sound is superb. The highs a re very crisp and detailed, the midrange was clear and concise, and the lows were tight and not over-emphasized. Voices in TV shows and movies are very clear and I can understand every word. Also, the JBLs are nice and loud. The previous center speaker’s sensitivity was significantly lower than the rest of the system and I often had to turn the volume way up for talking parts and way down during action scenes. The JBL’s sensitivity are much more matched and so the dynamics of movie scenes are much more natural and I don’t have to mess with the volume at all. The tweeters are coupled to JBL’s proprietary EOS waveguide. This really does help propagate sound. I notice that the sound from sitting a couple feet in front of it on the couch and being in kitchen some 20 or 30 feet away sounds to be almost the same exact volume. The EOS acts like a horn in this manner by directing sound and giving it a long throw. But since it’s not quite a horn, it doesn’t sound as directional or “in your face” as horns do and offers a wide dispersion. So overall, the sound is really, really good. JBL delivers again with great sound at a great price. The build quality and design is excellent. I don’t foresee having any problems with this speaker for a long time. This thing is a steal for the Black Friday deal I got it at. It’s totally worth the retail price as well. Don’t pass this one up for something else because you will just not find anything better for the price. Rated 4 instead of 5 stars only because the retail price seems a little steep, but get it on sale and it's beyond 5 stars.

title: Flawless on the Mac!
text:
I bought this drive to consolidate my DVD backups and reduce my disc collection by a whopping 80%! I found the drive for a better price on a site with an egg in the name. I put this drive in a Vantec USA NexStar DX External USB 3.0 Enclosure which I highly recommend. (See user photos above.) My computer is a 3 year old MacBook Pro running Mountain Lion and I use Toast 11 with the Blu Ray add-on for my burning software. I use the Verbatim 97457 25 GB 6x Blu-ray Single Layer Recordable Discs. So far I've burned about 6 disc's with zero verified disc failures. I've read about 20 DVD backup discs without error and I can copy all 4.7 GB onto my computer in about 6 minutes. My computer is limited to USB 2. I expect the speed to be faster when I upgrade my computer to USB 3.

So far I'm very happy with this drive. It been flawless with reading and writing. It does get quite loud when it spools up to full speed but no louder than any other optical drive I've used. The actual hardware burning is the fastest part of the burn process for me. I encrypt my disc's which take forever (about an hour) since it's 25 GB at a time! The physical burning currently takes about 22 minutes and the verification process takes another 15-20 minutes. This is on an older computer with USB 2. I expect my speeds to improve when I update my computer. Your mileage will vary greatly depending on your system.

The combination of enclosure / drive / software has been flawless! It's a true plug and play scenario on the Mac platform. No software drivers needed. All the hardware and software play nice and I've never once had a single issue with drives not being found or discs not being able to be written or read. Everything works exactly as it should.

text:
I've had this for about a month now an absolutely love it. I had an old Samsung soundbar but just didn't get the sound I wanted around the room. We have this in a fairly large living room with high ceilings so it's a big room to fill with just a soundbar. I looked into HTIB solutions and even bought one of the rear "wireless" speaker systems from Sony. The wireless speakers are not truly wireless and need a plug and wires that plug into a receiver. So they are semi-wireless. This Fidelio is truly wireless for the rear/side surround. Audiophiles will probably rip the sound quality but for me it just works great. Our kitchen is attached to our living area so I place one in the kitchen and one behind the couch on our staircase to get a different surround setup. You'll have to play with the best places to put the wireless speakers but it's great for sports and for movies. And when I just want regular TV, I put the detachable speakers back up to charge and get better sound that I had before with my Samsung bar.

An alternate use of this is for anyone with hearing issues as you can put one or both of the speakers right next to you and you are able to hear in a noisy room. I have kids so I sometimes just grab a speaker and put it next to my head on the side table and I can hear just fine with kids running in and out of the room. Or, if the kids go to bed and we want to hear the TV but not have it up too loud, this is a great use as well. You can put it right by you and still hear the TV with the volume much lower than if if was up in the front of the room. The performance has been great and I just love this product so much as it's so easy to setup and use and just blends into the room no matter where you put the detachable speakers. I even can take the speaker outside if I'm using the bluetooth for music as the range reaches that far for us.

On battery life, I haven't run them down yet. Usually get through a full evening of watching football and they still have not run out.

If you don't want the headache of trying to deal with wires for a really good surround experience this is definitely the product for you. I'm pretty picky with this stuff and I highly recommend if you're looking for the best sound avaialable with the easiest setup available. Great, great idea. I guess that's why it won an innovation award at the Consumer Electronic Show (CES).

title: Great for birding
text:
I love them, love them, love them!! On the other hand, most birders who have tried them hate them. Which group will you fall into? This review is intended to help you decide.

I personally carry the 10x or 12x for normal birding. I'm shorebirding I'll carry the 15x. 12x is good compromise of both.

My view: I feel they are the best birding bins out there, by which I mean better than the $2500 super-high end optics, and better than the $1200 Canon IS birding binoculars. These binoculars present a very different trade-off between strengths and weaknesses compared to "normal" high-end birding binoculars, so it takes a while to get used to them.

When people try them for 10 seconds they feel cheap, bad and strange. It isn't until you've gotten used to them over a few days that you start to appreciate that they are different -- and better -- than normal binoculars.

Negatives: They don't feel like "normal" binoculars: they are much lighter are differently balanced. The color distortion and light-gathering are both noticeably worse. Pressing the stabilizing button takes some getting used to. Their close focusing distance is quite poor.

Positives: ability to use higher magnification than you can with regular binoculars. Stabilization. Light weight. Low cost. Don't need to carry a scope. Great low-light performance.

The bottom line is that the normal comparison metrics of color, distortion and light-gathering don't capture the reality of how useful these guys are in the field. Here's a better way to compare binoculars. Give it a try the next time you have a chance to try IS bins. Pick a really distant bird or object. Try to focus on tiny details, such as counting exposed primaries. Try it with your Swarovskis or Leicas. I assure you that you'll see more and better with Canon IS binoculars. The reason is simple: the human brain needs time to process images, and if there is any vibration then any image smaller than that vibration distance is effectively invisible. With hand-held binoculars, there is always some amount of vibration.

If there is any wind (which can cause tiny vibrations in your hands) or motor vibration such as on a boat, of other vibrations (like from passing cars or pedestrians), then there is no comparison and the IS binoculars will win by a mile. In those conditions I can often make out fine details on birds that my companions can barely see let alone identify.

There have been several situations in which I've been scanning a flock looking for a difficult bird together with dozens of people using high-end scopes. For example: find the Black Noddy at 100-200 yards among the thousands of Brown Noddies; find the American Golden-Plover at 150 yards among the hundreds of Black-bellied Plovers sleeping with their heads tucked. You get the idea. With these binoculars, I regularly am the first to find the bird and it sure isn't because of superior skill. That's pretty amazing when you consider that it's 10x binoculars going up against $5000 scopes with top birders behind them. The reason it happens is that I can see more than they can, period.

Another test to try is to look at something at night. In theory the low light-gathering of these IS binoculars should make them far inferior to high-end bins. Not so. Stabilization becomes even more valuable in low-light situations because the brain needs more time to process in low-light situations. The result: I can easily make out fine details on an owl at night that my partners CAN"T EVEN SEE, let alone identify using their binoculars.

As an aside: 90% of serious bird photographers consider Canon IS camera lenses to the best tool available. They are. Why then are stabilized binoculars not held in the same esteem? I think the binoculars deserve the same level of respect as the camera lenses.

title: Worked great for 20 minutes and then the capacitors failed. Buyer Beware.
text:
This is my first Samsung HDTV and I have to say it was great when it worked for the first 20 minutes.
After picking it up at Best Buy I drove home to set it up. Placing the stand on the TV was rather simple, but even after installing it, the stand felt somewhat flimsy. Not a big deal for me.

Powered up the TV and went through the setup steps; again very simple.
Plugged my brother's PS4 into the TV and started gaming on it. Picture and sound quality was very nice, there were a few problems with the Samsung's auto dimming settings, which made the picture look very dark, but I was able to find the option rather quickly and turned it off.

So everything was going fine for about 15-20 minutes and then the picture when completely black... then turned back on... then went black again. Thinking it was maybe a faulty HDMI port I switch ports and switched the source to the second port. No go.
Tried switching out the HDMI cable with another one. Again no go. I then figured out (after seeing the Samsung symbol appearing after the blackouts) that this seemed like a power issue.

Tried turning the TV off for a bit. This seemed to help for a few minutes after turning the TV back on, but after 5 minutes or so the power started switching on and off again.

Turns out this is an issue A LOT of Samsung TVs have and is caused by the types of capacitors Samsung uses. For most people it seems to occur soon after the warranty runs out for the TV. I guess lucky for me it happened after the first 20 minutes.

[...]

Will be returning this unit for a full refund and will probably steer clear of Samsung TVs until this issue is addressed.

I just got this yesterday, so this is not a final review. I wanted to highlight some hook-ups that might be of interest:(update adds computer)

I hooked a Samsung ET-H10FAUWESTA adapter from the phone to the projector via a HDMI cable. The adapter was powered by the phone's charger. This worked fine with a wide variety of material. I wanted the projector to use for demonstrating Google Glass, and it will do the job.

2. Bluray Player
Hooked a older LG bluray player to the projector and watched part of an Indiana Jones DVD.
This also worked fine.

3. Roku
The supplied Roku stick, of course, worked well with the projector. It takes about a minute, or so, to boot up with the Roku, but after that things are pretty snappy. By the way, I installed the Roku Android app on my phone and was very pleased. The remote functions are even more simple than the physical remote, but I was able to stream photos and videos from the phone to the projector. That's very nice indeed.

4. Windows 8 Hybrid Computer
I hooked up an Acer Iconia w500 tablet, running Windows 8, to the projector. When I did it right, everything worked right. The trick was as follows: hook the HDMI cable to the projector and tablet with both units turned off. Turn the projector on, then turn the tablet on. The computer automatically detects the projector and boots up in dual screen(extended). The projector is showing an extended view of the desktop. I didn't get it to show the Start screen, but I have not had a chance to work on it. Another good use for the projector.
--------
As everyone notes, the projector is not HD: its 480p. Its decent enough if you sit about 3x the diagonal screen size away from the screen. I was pleased that the input formats I tried were scaled without any intervention on my part. Yes, the speaker is tinny, but headphones work very well. The focus control is very touchy.

I suggest you go to the 3m web site and download the pdf file for the user guide. There's a lot of good information there that is not in the box. For example, the projector down-converts inputs up to 1080i.

I'm very pleased with the 3m as of this early look. I'm already spoiled by looking a 60 inch display, even if it is SD.

title: very useful for those concerned about energy savings or safety...
text:
QVS Single Outlet Switch is a handy device to control power to an electrical load. A red pilot light type switch, provides a visual indication of whether the switch is off or on. For those that are concerned about energy savings or safety, this switch can be extremely useful.

Designed for ungrounded devices, the switch only has two slots, with no provisions for a grounding prong. When plugged into a standard duplex receptacle, the switch is small enough to permit access to the other half of the receptacle outlet. You may not be able to plug in an oversized power supply, but most normal cord plugs can be accommodated.

I have several of these switches, and the device seems to be fairly sturdy, and well constructed. I have had seen pilot light switches fail, but this one seems to operate very smoothly without a lot of pressure on the rocker mechanism, so I hope that this doesn't happen with the QVS. The switch is UL listed, rated at 15 amps, and is sealed, to prevent the user from tampering with it.

Until and unless some kind of failure occurs, I would recommend the QVS switch over the [[ASIN:B002DNGAZ6 General Electric Handy Switch]], the [[ASIN:B000MXMH6U Leviton 1469 switch]], and the more expensive and longish [[ASIN:B005MYN3OO Belkin Conserve switch]], none of which has a pilot light. The only thing that is inconvenient, is that the QVS switch is currently an "add on" item.

I love this case for my Acer Chromebook. The Chromebook fits perfectly, and the suction cup feature works very well—I open the case, it opens my Chromebook. The 'eggshell' base where my Chromebook sits, held in place by two elasticized corner straps, is very well padded. The 'eggshell' design funnels away heat from the bottom of the device.

This case is extremely well-constructed. It's padded and reinforced all the way around, but without adding unnecessary, unwanted weight. Just handling it you can tell it's a quality build. The exterior has a fully-gusseted, zippered side pocket that expands to about 2-inches—great for a mouse, cables, charger, and a lot more. The bottom of the case has two non-slip skids for use on, say, an airplane tray table, as well as a clear window pocket for ID, which aids the quick identification of 'my' case.

The adjustable webbed shoulder strap comes with a shoulder pad attached, so there's no need to hunt one down for an additional buy unless you want something thicker. The strap easily clips on and off the case with heavy duty 'dog leash' style clips. There is also a built in, retractable, carry handle that makes the case easy to grab without using the strap.

While this case does also fit my 11-inch HP laptop, the laptop's textured lid and back-facing camera negates the use of the suction cup feature. This case is really tailor made for a Chromebook, and it serves that function extremely well.

title: A triumph in design and image quality
text:
My VT50 arrived a little over two weeks ago and I feel that I'm now familiar enough with it to write a review. This review is for the 55" model.

The VT50 replaced my 50" G-Series Panasonic plasma from 2010. While I liked it just fine, it was a tiny bit too small, had a bezel that got uglier over time, and suffered from floating blacks, which was very annoying since my primary use of the display is watching Blu-Ray content in the dark. I had been anxiously awaiting the release of the VT50 - so much so, that I ordered one without seeing it first, reasoning to myself that if I didn't like it, then I wouldn't be satisfied with any TV this year.

The VT50 arrived. Once unpacked and set up, I marveled at the TV before I even turned it on. Was this TV really made by Panasonic, the company known for being helplessly behind the competition is terms of industrial design? The svelte single sheet of glass design is beautiful. The VT50 takes the design introduced with last year's clunky VT30 and trims it down to perfection. The bezel is much smaller than Samsung's E7/8000 and much more attractive in my opinion. It features a nice silver trim around the edges and a classy stand with a silver/black gradient. I can see how the silver edge might be a problem in a very bright room, but I really like it.

But design is secondary, isn't it? Picture quality is why anyone buys a flagship model and the VT50 more than delivers. Panasonic has made major improvements over 2011 models, with a new driving method, redesigned panel, and improved filter. Once initial set-up is done, the TV defaults to standard mode, which looks awful - dull and lifeless with egregious line bleed. Thankfully there's an easy fix - this a THX certified display, and new for 2012 Panasonic includes two separate THX modes for 2D viewing - THX Cinema and THX Bright Room. These modes look great out of the box. THX Cinema is what I mainly watch with, although I sometimes use Bright Room mode, albeit with contrast scaled back to 80. Compared to the THX mode on my last Panasonic, the mode here is much improved and lacks the greenish push that I noticed before. I think rather than try to eyeball it, since I'm not a calibrator, I'm going to leave it in THX mode sans any adjustment and pay someone to calibrate it later this year. Compressed satellite HD actually looks surprisingly great, image processing is top notch here and is good at masking artifacts from less-than-stellar feeds. Definitely better than my old Panny. The picture also has a characteristic that is hard to describe - perhaps "smoother" is the word I'm looking for here; it just looks incredibly natural and effortless in subtle color transitions and gradients. I suppose that can be attributed to Panasonic's claim of improved shades of gradation.

The real test, however, was when I turned off the lights and fired up the Blu-Ray player. The home menu on my Sony Blu-Ray player is a light gray, which is great for testing panels for flaws in uniformity. Knowing problems with banding, blobbing, and splotching Panasonic had with last year's model, I nervously inspected every part of the panel. No anomalies to be found, whew. I pressed play and ended up sampling a variety of content, and the VT muscled through all of it with incredible prowess. The black level here is impressive - I've seen a VT30 in the dark and this rightfully trounces it. I've also seen an E8000 in the dark and it can't get quite as dark as the VT. Letterbox bars blend into the bezel. Thanks to the deep, dark blacks the VT50 is blessed with incredible contrast. Images have an abundance of pop and lifelike depth, and recall the tangible realism produced by later-generation Pioneer plasma panels. Motion is natural, cinematic, and artifact-free when the 4:4 pulldown 96Hz mode is engaged. I do not notice any flicker either. It should also be noted that I have watched enough on it to verify that the image is rock-solid - no floating blacks, fluctuating brightness, no distractions. Just a beautifully rendered, film-like image that pulls you in.

3D performance: Using THX Cinema 3D mode, the 3D image looks great. This is the first 3D TV I've owned but I've seen plenty of 3D on other flat panels and some projectors. 96Hz is unavailable here. Great sense of depth and minimal crosstalk, although I do notice some in higher contrast scenes. This can be somewhat remedied by switching from 60 to 48Hz mode, but it introduces some annoying flicker. I tested using Blu-Ray content like Ultimate Wave Tahiti 3D, Hugo, Tron:Legacy, Arabia 3D, and the Adventures of Tintin 3D. 2D>3D conversion is still unimpressive, even after making 3D adjustments, but I suppose it's not too bad considering the display is doing the conversion on the fly. Not a big deal. Please note that Panasonic does not include glasses in the box for North American sets this year. Yeah, it's a bummer, but the good news is that this year Samsung's cheap SSG-4100 glasses are fully operational with the VT50. I own a pair and a pair of the official Panasonic-made TY-ER3D4MU glasses, and performance is identical, although I find the Panasonic glasses have bigger lenses and are more comfortable.

One thing I did not test much is the Viera Connect platform. I poked around a bit, and it seems largely identical to the interface on my BDT310 Blu-Ray player but with the addition of the web browser. Since the VT50 has a dual-core processor it is quite a bit snappier loading apps and navigating between them, however. Panasonic includes a touchpad remote to make web browsing easier but I found it a bit awkward to use, and while the web browser is decent, I don't see myself ever using it. I don't want to browse the web on my TV, but for those that do, it's not bad.

So while I generally try to shy away from giving products five-star reviews, I have a hard time finding anything bad to say about the VT50. The only thing I can really knock it for is the anti-glare filter - while it's incredibly effective, it does compromise the vertical viewing angle of the TV. I'm assuming it functions by absorbing ambient light from above and below the panel and rejecting it, resulting in a darkened image from above or below. The horizontal viewing angle is not compromised, so I certainly don't think it's worth taking a point away, especially considering that neither I nor anybody I know watches TV sitting below the screen or standing above it.

All told, the VT50 is, simply put, the best plasma Panasonic has ever made, and represents more than a minor improvement over the VT30. Panasonic has set the bar not only for themselves, but has left Samsung in the dust this year. While Panasonic focused on drastically improving image quality this year, Samsung seems content with making minor improvements while adding a camera and frustratingly stupid gesture control to their plasmas. Highly recommended!

title: the Shoulder Rig I've been waiting for!
text:
This "PRIME Video Shoulder Rig Kit by Phototgraphy & Cinema" is a solid product, all knobs and screws are solid and tight, looks great, nice weight...not to light or heavy. it's worth every penny I spent and then some.

The "FREE" Swiss Rods and Friction Arm adds more than $100 bucks worth of value to this value-packed offer. I tip my hat to this company for operating with a sense of integrity. In a world where we hide behind the words, supply and demand, which usually means, we'll charge you what ever we want to charge, even if it's an 800% mark up from what it cost us to design, make and distribute. But, Kamerar has given me a new faith in companies that actually price their products with price points that the average consumer can feel good about investing in. When it comes to any type of accessory, you don't seek them because they are necessary but because they help you do a better job or they make it easier for you to accomplish your task. In the video industry, especially since the popularity of the DSLR-Video products...for some odd reason the accessories cost "WAY" more than the gear. You spend 3-grand for a decent camera and a shoulder rig (designed especially for the camera) costs you 4-grand...WHAT? Isn't that like buying the cake for $8-bucks but the icing, the knife, napkins and the plate will cost you $200-dollars...I don't know what's happened in the last 15 years...but when I make most purchases in the accessory departments, I leave feeling cheated...BUT NOT WITH THIS PURCHASE!

I purchased this for a Panasonic GH2, I know the camera is small but I have Canon and Alpha/Minolta lens adapters and I do a lot of shooting with a Canon 70-200mm 2.8 lens and that lens is almost 3 times heavier than the camera...so I badly need stabilization when going hand held, not just for steady shots but that lens gets heavy after 5 minutes. So this not only does what I intended it to but I also put my Sony EX3 on this rig and it worked nicely...go figure, a $10,000 camera set up on a $250 shoulder rig....hmmmm, I think this must be illegal...at least in America...LOL!

I feel fortunate for waiting until now to get a full shoulder rig. I looked at this rig for over a month, I purchased their Matte Box (SOCOM-BOX 4x4) a few months back and was so blown away by the quality, craftsmanship and price that I went to the web site and couldn't believe my eyes. Things in the video business is going really slow for me this year but the prices @ Kamerar are so affordable that I could afford to purchase products even while things are slow...knowing very well that when things pick back up, I'll have new gear that will improve the overall look and feel of my creations. And for that reason alone I give this product 5-stars! Affordability, seems to be a concern of the past, but this company proves that you can get great quality products without spending an arm and a leg.
I live in Dallas, so this (KAMERAR) being a company in Texas if I had purchased this shoulder rig from their web site I would have had to pay extra for taxes...by finding this @ PRIME on Amazon for a few dollars more I get friction arm and 2 swiss rods...this was a WIN/WIN...I think. I can't speak for Prime or Kamerar, but I love this transaction...plus free shipping and handling (I received this in less than 5 days and the item was securely packed in a tight box with custom gray soft-foam)...man, feels like Christmas in April.

OK, so people won't think I'm involved with this company or getting paid to leave this comment...there is one thing that I don't like about the rig, the "SILVER" (Aluminum) 15mm rods, they also have a strange texture, not smooth like my other rods...all of my other rods from previous rigs are black, so cosmetically I'd prefer black rods...(all of my newer tripods are black) but hey, I'll purchase a pair of 30cm and 40cm black rods with the hundred bucks I saved with the free rods and friction arm...(on a plus note), the rods that come with this rig have the ends that allow you to connect rods together to extend their length.

Thank you "PRIME, PHOTOGRAPHY & CINEMA, AMAZON.COM" for this incredible offer!

p.s.
Even though I purchased a friction follow focus from Jag35, 6-months ago...I've got my eye on your follow focus :o)

title: JVC HARX700 Superb Audiophile Sound for under $40!!!
text:
Bottom Line: Impressive sound for so little $$$. Use of EQ will make these headphones sound spectacular. Well built. Headband can become tight.

Pros: 50mm drivers. Capable of really deep warm bass, distinctive mid-range and clear highs. Well constructed. Beefy cord. Looks much more expensive than actually is. Don't require an amp to drive. Makes me want to listen to them.

Cons: Must use EQ to get the best sound. Headband can feel a little tight after several hours of use, so a little bit of ear/head fatigue. Wish there's a way to adjust the band so it wouldn't clamp down as hard.

I do sound engineering as a hobby and have listened to many different headphones and speakers in my lifetime. I also own AKG K270 and Yamaha HS-80M Monitors to use as reference. I would say that while these JVC can be used as monitor headphones, they are much more enjoyable as a pair used for casual listening. It's analogous to eating comfort food--while they may not be the best or correct thing out there, they just feel so good to listen to. While monitoring equipment are good and serve a purpose, they are not always great to listen to.

Out of the box, these sounded fairly balanced and clean, but a little "reserved", no particular frequency seemed dominant. After 12 hours of continuous music pumping through, these cans sounded a little more open and more details in the music were noticeable. I listen to a wide variety of music, and these headphones can handle pretty much everything I threw at it without distortion. I was particularly looking for good bass response in a pair of headphones, and these didn't disappoint. I listened to the following pieces using my iPhone and my Dell desktop using the EQ that's available in the iPhone or WIndows Media player.

Saint-Saens Symphony #3 "Organ" by Murray/Badea. Thanks to Telarc, this is a killer recording to test any piece of audio equipment. Without EQ applied, the recording sounds just nice and balanced with very good sound stage. Once I applied the EQ, it blew me away. It was like listening to this recording through a giant pair of OHM Walsh speakers. Once the organ came in at the slow section of the 1st movement, I felt the warm organ pedal notes and the accompanying vibration. The recording with EQ sounded really rich and sumptuous. The different instruments came through quite well. Just gorgeous!

One Truth by Globus (Immediate Music). This is a song by a group that produces a lot of music trailers for action movies. This is a pumped up recording with vocals, orchestra, drums, choir, and a lot of bass to get one's attention. I was expecting mucho distortion through the headphones, but the JVC handled the piece just fine, even with EQ applied. The drums were punchy, the bass super deep and tight without sounding boomy,

It's My Life by No Doubt. Another One Bites the Dust by Queen.
These recordings have good punchy bass lines. Again with EQ, the bass shone, very nice and tight without boominess. There was more silkiness to Ms. Stefani's voice which I didn't think was too distracting.

Rest by Gemma. This is a song with solo vocals and piano and trumpet. The JVC brought out many nuances in the singer's voice that I did not notice before. Very silky sounding.

Conclusion: A diamond in the rough! The JVC HARX700 is just spectacular to listen to when proper EQ is applied. Without EQ applied, it is still well-balanced and precise, not leaning towards any frequency range. The headband can feel tight after long use. If the headband's compression was adjustable or if it was made of formable material, it would be perfect. I would definitely purchase again. Highly recommended!

text:
UPDATE: Some problems have been encountered. SEE ADDENDUM.

As a user of the Engenius EUB362 b/g and Alfa b/g USB adapters, I felt it time to move up to Wireless N. Part of this involves being a good citizen. In a hotel/motel with an N installation, bandwidth is conserved if everyone on the network runs N.

With Windows 7, there has been a tendency to avoid the expense of providing a wireless client, and just let Windows manage the connection. I sorely missed the excellent client programs provided by Engenius and Alfa. What a surprise to find that this adapter, which comes in such a plain little box, has the best client program I have ever seen! For most purposes, it is no longer necessary to separate scanning programs such as "inSSIDer", because this client program provides such complete info, with marvelous graphic displays.

The unit works fine without the client program, but I was a bit mislead by the bright blue pilot light. It turns out that this light glows even if the radio is turned off. If you choose not to use the client program, it can be turned on in System-->Device manager-->Network Adapters-->802.11n USB Wireless LAN Card-->Advanced-->Radio On/Off-->Value (Enable/Disable). With the client program, the on/off is right up front.

The radio chip is made by Ralink, [...] , but I have been unable to determine exactly which one it is. It would be interesting to know, because although all current Ralink offerings are either either 1T1R or 2T2R configuration, they may have made a 1T2R in the past. Knowing whether one antenna is primary influences the choice of advanced antennas.

With the assumption that it is 2T2R, the 1000 milliwatts is divided between the two antennas, 500MW to each. This is the first adapter over 500MW that can run off one USB port, at least for a Thinkpad. I cannot vouch for other brands. An unusually thick, high quality USB cable, covered with soft, flexible rubber, reduces power loss that occurs with thin gauge wire.

The power division division, and the use by Wireless N of spatial diversity, suggests that the user may wish to keep his old 1T1R g and n adapters around for use with exotic antennas, such as a "cantenna", flat panel, parabolic, or Yagi types. In the past, users have remarked that Wireless N offered less range, but greater constancy out to the limit of the range. But for anyone who uses the ubiquitous "rubber duck" antennas, such as the ones supplied with the unit, or larger ones, it is doubtful that there is anything better.

To ensure maximum life of the RF amplifiers, attach both antennas before plugging it in. As of the date of my purchase, 10/17/2012, the driver/client program supplied on the mini-CD is the one I used, and it does not have to be replaced by a download. The disk was remastered on 7/24/2012.

Addendum: Three adapters were purchased. The first tested works perfectly. The other two do not. Both fail to obtain an IP address from the router, exhibiting the "169.254..." adr which is Windows shorthand for error.

All three adapters negotiate the link with the access point, an aged Linksys WAP54G. All three adapters show strong signals, with no malfunctions noted by the client app. However, only one adapter obtains an IP address. The latest software from Ralink, dated 42/12, does not change this. In the next week, I'll work through this, so watch this space.

title: Extremely poor QoS for any gamers

Whenever running a download that takes a noticable amount of bandwidth (not even using bittorrent however), upload will be severely affected.  What this means is that your Ventrilo, or even performance in online games will be severely affected.  For example, when playing an MMO, everything from the server will behave normally (aka mobs will hit you just fine) but your own character will not perform any of your actions (because your upstream is being severely limited).  Trying to manually set their port range and increase their priority has a negligible effect on performance.  I intend to return this router since, for this kind of price, I expect its QoS to perform close to flawlessly.

title: A point and shot megazoom camera with interesting features and decent telephoto performance.
text:
On the plus side:

- This camera gives you the opportunity for shots you can't get with other cameras that have lower zoom factors and image resolution.

- Has on-board memory that permits shot taking w/o an SD card

- Comes with a grown-up camera strap, not some puny cord that dangles it off your wrist

On the minus side:

- Camera size requires full sized camera strap.

- No viewfinder. Display can be hard to see in bright sun or glare.

- This camera lacks many controls features of many cameras in same price range: External mode selector, direct aperture or shutter speed control, or manual focus.

- Camera does not auto-detect its orientation and rotate the picture when you hold the camera in portrait position.

Overall:

This camera would disappoint any photographer they thought they'd be working with a real Nikon and not Nikon Lite. As a point-and-shoot camera, the L810 employs specialized technologies like face recognition, wink-activated shutter, and BSS (Best Shot Selection) to do the work of getting a decent exposure. These technologies give you a decent exposure, but sometimes with less than fine image quality.

Many of those features are designed around the idea that people will be in most of your pictures. When it's in the EasyAuto mode, its go to settings are those of the Smart Portrait mode. Although it doesn't rotate pictures based on the way you hold the camera, it will rotate the picture to align it with any face it detects.

Other reviews have recommended reading the manual to get best use of this camera. I second that. For example It's not likely you'd notice that setting the ISO number in the Auto (NOT Easy Auto) mode turns off anti-shake feature. This will give you better image quality in lower light settings where you're using a tripod, but the only way you'd know about this, and other special modes, would be by reading the manual.

One of the bits of advice you get from manual is to take another picture. This has worked for me. Most of the time if auto-focus has selected the wrong subject, trying another shot has produced better results

With batteries, this camera weighs in at just under a pound. After adding in a camera case and a spare set of batteries, its size and weight are more than I'm willing to carry with me every day.

The L810 has individual buttons for each of the three modes: still shots, video, and viewing. They are easy to reach, but have enough separation to avoid hitting the wrong one. Despite some practice, I still don't have the hang of working the video button so that I'm recording when I want to be recording, and only then.

Internal memory supports a decent amount of on-camera editing. For example, you can crop and resize pictures, but some testing I did showed that the camera reprocesses the new image to create it in a standard size. I don't know know much this reprocessing, done even for a simple crop, effects image quality, but I feel more comfortable doing this with desktop software.

The L810 display shows you when the camera is operating in optical zoom range, and when it has switched to digital zoom. I've found it easy to work with. The optical/digital switching mechanism has an unusual feature: selecting a lower image resolution extends the range of the optical zoom.

The L810's telephoto performance and high megapixel rating extend the range of pictures you can show without having to point out and explain "Right there is a bird that was . . ." But, as with every camera, the most important lens for taking good pictures is the one in your eye.
