title: Big Promises, Little Results
text:
I've had the Revue for over a year now, so this is more of a "long term use" review. I'm not going to go through a list of all the features; you can find that in the item description and it would be redundant. This is my experience with the product, and how well (or not so well in many cases) the product works.

At first I was very excited to have easy access to Netflix, internet browsing, and whatever other apps I could find. Setup was easy and I was able to control my entire entertainment system easily (any universal remote could make the same claim though). Netflix buffering was a bit slow compared to my Xbox, but I didn't have to pay for Xbox live to use it on the Revue. Internet browsing was painfully slow however. It was nice when I wanted to check something out very quickly; no laptop startup and I could even put the TV in picture in picture mode, so worthwhile trade. However, Hulu doesn't work with it, and until recently neither did HBO GO. Although HBO GO does work currently, it was prone to buffering problems which didn't happen on my Xbox, iPad, or laptop.

However, about 6 or 7 months into ownership Logitech released an update. I figured it would smooth out some of the issues, and make it a bit easier. Unfortunately, this update reduced the device to a glorified remote. It felt like someone slammed the parking brake. The Netflix app took a terrible amount of time to load, and even then the quality was reduced in most movies. I tried on my laptop and Xbox, both functioned perfectly. Eventually every movie refused to play. Chrome acted like it was on AOL dial-up, and even the tiniest bit of flash caused sites to crash. This was somewhat alleviated by turning off apps ability to run in the background, but only slightly.

The user experience also suffered greatly with the removal or changes to little efficiency features. In the original version you can set up hot keys for super quick navigation. They were completely customizable and made switching back and forth from apps and TV simple. Control-C and I'm in Chrome, TV button back, Control-N over to Netflix and so on. That feature went out for a clunky menu system that takes multiple buttons just to switch to a frequently used app like Chrome. Sure, a small feature, but when compared to the original method this was a let down. Even something like the picture-in-picture took a hit. It was nice to browse around the web (slowly) while having TV play in a smaller screen, and it was easy to move the smaller screen so it didn't cover up the portion of the page I was viewing. But alas, this now requires multiple menus (like everything else) and isn't worth my time.

Unfortunately the Revue has become more of a universal remote than anything else; and a large, clunky one at that. It simply is too slow and frustrating for me to use anymore.

title: Incredible Garmin!
text:
*I'd originally ordered this off amazon but cancelled b/c the ship date was like a month and a half away. I see now that they've got other dealers lined up to get these delivered much sooner. I found mine at one of these other dealers but ordered through their site*

I've owned the Forerunner 101, 305, 310XT, 405, and now this. I have to say, it's the best one yet. But...it's different. At first, I wasn't sure I would get used to it and I fretted over all the reports of bugs. But, a week out, I've pretty much got everything figured out and like the Fenix 2 more every time I use it. I'd not been able to get my 310XT to upload workouts for some time, despite every reading tip and fix imaginable online. It made it a race-only GPS for me. I run ultras so I needed that battery life. But for day to day, I just used my iPhone then Galaxy S4 w/ a gps app. But the Fenix 2 makes things soooo much easier. Battery life is flat out incredible. This is the first GPS I've had that I can actually wear daily as a watch! I love information overload so I have worn a Casio Pathfinder "ABC" watch for years. This is the first thing to get it off my wrist.

After a few beginner's hiccups learning the syncing process, I've had very little trouble uploading my data. And the best thing, usually by the time my workout is uploaded and I've finished reading over my workout, the battery has charged back up to 100%! I was a bit skeptical that the Fenix 2 was going to do everything well, but so far, so good. The heart rate monitor strap Garmin issues now is much improved. And combined with the other accelerometer-based measurements the Fenix 2 records, you get lots of great info on your training. For someone that runs as much as I do, the "recovery time" estimate that the Fenix 2 gives after each workout seems a bit amusing (you really want me to rest 49 hours after running 5 miles?). But other than that, you get good, gimmick-free data. Over all, I'm very happy I decided to splurge on this watch. The only con I can think of is the screen/bezel seems a little soft. I just ordered a screen protector since I plan to wear this watch/gps daily.

text:

After opening the package, I plugged in the mic and opened Audacity to do some test recordings. Simply put, I was amazed at the sensitivity of this microphone!! It not only picked up my voice very clearly, but also picked up the crickets chirping outside my open window.

The audio was clear, and had very little noise. Testing the mic in-game worked flawlessly. My voice came through to other gamers clear as day.

title: Bridge 'em Danno
text:
I've had it running for a few days now, and it is a great value for the price.

HOWEVER - the folks at Medialink need to come to terms with how the majority of their potential customers are using this device; as a BRIDGE, NOT a Router. Let me explain.

Most of us have a cable company (ISP) router/modem combination installed and running. Most ISPs no longer provide separate modems and routers because their costs aren't necessary. So most of us, Medialink, are going to do what you call a "Router To Router Configuration." Before I go any further, let me thank you for hiring technical writers who took the time to do a good job of explaining how to accomplish this task. And thanks to the tech writers for their efforts. (Here's an "RTFM" for them!)

This so called "Router To Router Configuration" is probably the configuration that the device ships to most of the time, so why is it buried on page 48 of a 117-page User Guide that customers probably download from (typically as a last result before returning the product to) the manufacturer? (You can also dig the User Guide out of the "setup" disk.)

To make it work, customers connect the LAN of the ISP's router to the LAN of the Medialink; thus actually extending the ISP's router's LAN, through bridging, not routing. Otherwise they'd be setting up two different networks and would have a great deal of difficulty getting the new network to connect to the internet.

Medialink, you can improve the customer setup experience if you simply add another of your nifty "Quick Installation Guide" for what you call the Router To Router Configuration. You don't have to demean your product by changing the name of the configuration but you could mention during the instructions that customers are bridging the ISP router's LAN to the Medilink's LAN with a LAN to LAN connection.

Actually, it's so easy that customers don't need to worry about setting up or using the Medilink's WAN port. Customers can turn off Medilink's DHCP server and other routing functions; just concentrate on the security and operation of the wireless side of their new device.

title: The best Dedicated e-ink Reader So Far
text:
I will start by saying I am a voracious reader. I sometimes read 2 or 3 books in a day if I am on vacation. I also love books, real books. I always took my current book with me, and at least one back ups. (Because what if the first back-up is bad?) I finally decided I would try an e-reader. Especially for long road trips, and my bus commute.

It took me months to decide which e-ink reader to buy. Lucky for me, my employer provides e-reader content to the public, and one of the departments I work in acts as frequent phone support for patrons having problems. Before I made my decision I had access to many e-readers and tablets. Not just look at it - but to checkout for a night. This includes the biggies, i-Pads, Nooks & variations of those, Kindles, Sony, and more. I decided right away I didn't want a tablet - I have other devices to fill that need.

I finally decided on the Kindle Touch, although it took a while to decide between a Kindle and the other available e-reader with a lit screen. I am on the computer constantly, and wanted to avoid yet another glowing screen in my face when reading. My husband bought me a Kindle Touch (3G, Wi-Fi)in July. I was very pleased with it, and it quickly became my constant companion. I probably would not have purchased another e-reader so quickly but I really wanted a Paperwhite. I read a lot at night, and on the bus in less than ideal conditions. I ordered the Paperwhite a week after it was announced.

A week before my Paperwhite order was shipped I heard about the issues with the light, and carefully looked at all the videos and and descriptions available, and decided I needed to see it in person.

I am VERY pleased with the Paperwhite after using it for a week. (3G, Wi-fi, no special offers) I love being able to adjust the lighting level depending on conditions, and the screen is much crisper than the Touch. No more lighting problems, and my husband loves it that there is no more nightlight while he is trying to sleep, and I'm reading late.

The only time I saw a faint pink or blue reflection on the Paperwhite screen occurred when room lighting was quite dim, and the Paperwhite screen was at medium-low level. It was not a problem for me, and when I turned the Paperwhite light down a notch it vanished. The black smudges at the bottom of the screen that appear in very low lighting conditions are not bothersome to me, and don't infringe on the text. I have seen them on the other brand of e-reader as well.

I got the Paperwhite version without special offers, most people don't mind them, but I do. I don't mind the book suggestions at the bottom. I have heard you can opt out of those as well, but I probably wont, as I'm always looking for something new to read. I ordered 3G because sometimes we go places without wi-fi, and WHAT IF I RAN OUT OF BOOKS and had no way to get more! I can tell you, my husband would prefer that never happened.

Personally I would recommend the Paperwhite to almost anyone looking for a dedicated e-reader. Is it absolutely perfect? No, but it's as close as it gets right now. Hopefully Amazon will bring back the TTS for those who want it, as well as the audio capability. I don't miss either one, but I know those who would. I can see someone with visual issues, including migraine sufferers, possibly having a problem with the blue/pink screen issue in low lighting. I would take a look at it in person before making up your mind.

I have to admit, I hesitate now to read 'real' books. Something I never thought would happen. It's like becoming one of the Pod People. Haha. They are so heavy, taking them on the bus is a pain, and now with the Paperwhite, I can have as many books with me as I want, in a format that is lighter than a single paperback.

UPDATE May 2012
After using this reader for over six months I have to add that I can't imagine NOT having it. I have not had a single problem, except once when I downloaded too many books at once and ended up having to turn it off and on - but it rebooted without an issue. I much prefer it over my husband's Fire (which is perfect for him - but that's another review...) and still over any of the other e-readers we have to play with at work. I have never seen the strange blue/pink screen again, either.

title: Frustrating and Unreliable
text:
I had a frustrating experience with The Amped Wireless unit, which was highly unreliable. It would 'hang' at least once a day and would have to be reset by pulling it out of the outlet and plugging it back in. This meant that I typically had to reconnect the devices that relied on it (Fire TV, wireless speaker, tablets). It was also incredibly slow at times, and even at its best, didn't provide coverage for the entire house (which is not that big).

While the setup wasn't overly complicated, it wasn't exactly plug-and-play either and necessitated that you connect it with a cable to a laptop first. Further, the device doesn't just extend your existing network, but creates a secondary network called [yournetwork]_RE. Since this network was often unavailable, my devices would connect back to the original network, which of course is slow since it's not amplified, which was the reason I bought the Amped Wireless in the first place. I then had to adjust all my devices to forget the original network, which some of them refused to do, so I always had to check which network I was on when the internet connection was acting up. I used the Amped Wireless for about 6 months and then gave up on it.

I replaced this device with a TP-LINK and it has been night and day - that device automatically paired with my wifi with the push of a button and seamlessly extended it. No secondary network; it simply amplifies my existing network, which is what I would expect these devices to do. It has been completely reliable since then and my wifi is now FAST throughout the entire house. Having seen how well this works, I regret waisting $70 on the Amped Wireless, which I can now only sell back for a trade-in price of $12. My advice would be to stay away.

title: Happy
text:
It's becoming a common sight to see boxy action cams sticking out awkwardly off people's helmets, mounted to chest straps, etc. In purchasing Sony's new AS30 I was hoping to find something capable of being a little less bulky and a little more subtle. I want to capture video of my adventures, but where the cam is something I can bring along without having to sacrifice any major attention away from the activity itself, and where it isn't completely obvious to anyone who comes within my vicinity.

I can say that, after a couple days mountain biking with my new AS30, I've not been disappointed.

Now, the cam only included a couple of sticky mounts in the box, and those don't really do it for me. The included mount let me position the camera sticking straight up off the top of my helmet, which works well enough, but between the shape of the camera and mounting it in that position, combined with the extra centimetre of height due to the mount itself, it doesn't really meet my desire for a degree of subtlety. I chose to forego the included mounts altogether, and used some double sided sticky tape and a zip-tie to lash the included waterproof case directly to the side of my helmet. This worked great, and I did it so that I was still able to easily remove the cam from the case in order to change batteries and retrieve the SD card.

I have been reasonably impressed with the size and weight of this new model. I think one would have to be rather fussy to take issue with the weight of this cam when mounted on top of their helmet, as I almost didn't notice it. The weight is noticeable when mounted on the side of the helmet, but I find it tolerable, if still minorly annoying, but which is a small sacrifice I'm willing to make to have it down where it's at least little less protruding.

Using Sony's "PlayMemories" Android app to live stream video from the cam was a significant aid for fine tuning the angle while I mounted it, and easily allowed me to copy videos to my phone for viewing or sharing. You can use your phone to start/stop recordings, but I prefer the physical button on the camera for that, and generally left the Wi-Fi turned off in order to extend the battery life and recording time. The one feature I haven't been able to find, either on the app or the cam interface itself, is the ability to delete unwanted videos or accidental recordings in order to reclaim space. I haven't tried the desktop software, but as a Linux user, I was happy to see that the cam connected over USB as a regular mass storage device, though I still found it much quicker to use a USB3 card reader to transfer videos to my PC. The cam also lists a setting where it can be continuously powered via the USB connection.

The large easy-to-find (even with gloves) physical record button on the back of the cam can be used to almost instantly power the unit on and begin recording with a single press, or to resume recording again if the auto-shutoff hasn't yet engaged. The camera makes distinct noises which allowed me to recognize when recording was started or stopped. Right off, I was able to spend my time riding without constantly having to fiddle around with the cam.

I'm happy with the picture quality, which I expect compares well with other cams currently in this class. I am very impressed with the excellent low-light ability of this camera, which far outshines the few other action cams I have owned previously. The image stabilization works well, though it comes with a noticeable cost to the visible details during segments where things get really bumpy.

I didn't manage to drain the battery on either of my first two outings, so that seems to be working as advertised so far. I really love that I can just bring along an extra battery or two and easily pop them in for a whole day of filming.

Overall, I think it really comes down to how you want to use it, and if it's shape and mounts are suitable for your intended uses, but I would happily recommend this cam based on my experiences so far.

title: Good choice
text: The speakers sound very good, as most people seem to agree.  But the rotating cam locks are not perfect.  I installed two speakers, one in the dining area and the other in the kitchen.  The kitchen speaker is underneath the second floor, but the other one is open to the attic.  After it was installed, I ventured into the attic and found that one of the cam locks had caught the slack speaker wire underneath it.  So make sure the wire is out of the way if you have a lot of slack in it.  The second time I went in the attic, I found that one of the cams wasn't tight, and when I pushed it around it fell into position.  I went back downstairs and tightened the screw.  The other speaker isn't accessible from the back so I can't check that one, but it seems to be okay.  The cam locks can also be a little confusing to tighten, because they seem to swing out counter-clockwise.  It seems like you should turn the screw counter-clockwise, but they do tighten up by turning the screw clockwise.  A sticker on the packaging (which seems like an afterthought) also tells you to tighten the screws by using a power drill on the "torque 2" setting.  I do appreciate being given a finite number for tightening.  However, I was dismayed that Polk doesn't offer guidance on what to do about installing the speaker in an open attic.  I was more concerned about dust and insulation getting on the back of the speaker, as opposed to air leaks, etc., so I made an enclosure out of two Owens Corning pink project boards from Home Depot.  You can use foam board adhesive and drywall screws to hold the box together.  I made mine about 11 x 12 x 24 inches, but Polk recommends a minimum of .6 cubic feet.  Their website has subwoofer box plans, and .6 is equal to 15 x 12 x 11 inches.

title: Poorer reception than with standard dipole wire antenna.
text: I purchased this product to hopefully improve reception of the public radio station here in Dallas, the tower for which is not that far from my home, but the signal for which is somewhat weak and occasionally scratchy.  Unfortunately, this product did not help things at all -- it worked no better than the dipole wire antenna that came with my receiver.  Moreover, although placement is everything with an antenna, the cord on this one is too short to really move it around and try to get a better signal.  Thus, the antenna is now in the trash -- it not only didn't help with the station that I wanted to receive, but it provided inferior reception of other stations that always came in strongly.  I ended up buying a rabbit ears antenna from Radio Shack and it works great, and takes standard coaxial cable, so can be placed anywhere it is needed.  I do not recommend this product.

title: Phenomenal Sound
text:
I lost my Bose QC15 on plane so was in market for a new pair of earphones. For $300, the QC15 is cheaply constructed and the sound is relatively flat and uninspiring. So, I tried the TTRs and Dre Beats noise canceling headphones at an airport electronics store. I was blown away. The TTRs are just incredible across a diverse range of music including ARmin van Buuren, BEP, BassHunter, Flo Rida, Metallica, Tiesto, Taylor Swift, and Ozzy. Yes, I wanted to try them across the full spectrum. I still can't believe the sound is coming from these headphones and my iphone4. The phones come with adapters, travel case, a long cable, and a shorter one with Mic. Without a doubt, the TTRs blows away the QC15 for sound and makes the Dre Beats seem like a muddy replication of bass. The Dre's also seemed really cheap. When you open the TTRs from its nice case, you realize that you actually get something for $300 compared to the plastic construction of the Bose. Solid metal construction with custom leather earphones covers. I highly recommend the TTRs to any audiophile. I did adjust the iphone's EQ to be Acoustic setting which worked across all the music mentioned above.

There are some downsides which is reason they only get 4 stars. Since I primarily purchased the TTRs for business travel, the noise cancelation is not that great. In fact, I would argue that they add noise. A slight and low crackling/static popcorn popping sound is heard from the left channel (where the noise canceling circuitry is located) which is directly caused by the EMI from the 737's engine. I walked up and down the airplane aisle and it got louder as I near the engines. This occured when I placed the music on pause and only listened to the TTR's noise canceling attempt. The QC15 are far superior in this regard but they too crackle but just upon take off and landing. So, if you like to listen to nothing or listen to music softly, the TTRs are not for you as the popping will drive you crazy on the plane. Lucky for me, I watch movies and listen to music at a higher volume where the crackling is unnoticeable. As far as comfort, the TTRs are fine for 3hr trips but I'm afraid that longer trips they may be too tight or heavy. They are new, so the jury is still out. I'll try them on a 10hr flight on 747 next month so I will update this review if noise and comfort is otherwise noted as above. Lastly, the TTRs are bigger, although a nice travel case is provided, they are almost twice the size of QC15s in height even if they fold. This doesn't bother me since I have a backpack, but they will simply not fit in a typical briefcase or roller bag/brief.

If your a frequent traveler on planes, TTRs may not be for you. But overall, the amazing sound for movies and music along with the solid construction, warranty, the TTRs deliver better than life sound and certainly better than the tin-sounding sound from the QC15.

Last point is that I ordered them from Amazon store which was a mistake. The first pair I received was faulty on the right channel. Tried to return to the IZone deals Amazon store but they were very unprofessional and wanted me to drop another $40 to send to some unknown address in Canada. Are you kidding me? So, I simply sent them to Marley and I had a new box/pair back in 4 days.

title: Great hardware, drivers/software and support leave a lot to be desired
text:
I will say that Intel has created something with good hardware that seems robust. This is where the compliments end. The get an idea about how substandard Intel's driver/software support is, just head over to the NUC forums. you'll see a large collection of problems that are either unsolved, or have workarounds involving spending more money.

I'll go over the cons in no particular order (on Win 7x64, Crucial memory and SSD):

-Default BIOS settings don't work for most common configurations. Searching online for NUC installation will yield more results than it should.

-Mini HDMI and DisplayPort. Really? Why? The vast majority of purchasers end up having to purchase an adapter.

-Multi-monitor configuration: I use dual monitors, when I press their power buttons to leave my workstation for a bit, then power them on, ALL programs move to the primary and resize to a small box (probably 800x600). Intel's brilliant suggestion is to buy different mini-DP/HDMI adapters, I did, no fix, and now no reply on forums. Basically, they refuse to fix the behavior. First time I encountered this with ANY multi-monitor setup. A workaround I discovered on my own involves: Lock the workstation > Hit the Switch users button (not intending to switch users) > Power off monitors. When you return, power up monitors, log in, and windows appear in their original position. It's less of a workaround, and more of a daily reminder to spend even more money on a non-NUC solution.

-Gigabit ethernet port: When hibernating, then powering back up, the port won't work until you disable it, then re-enable it. Tried many settings, including disabling power savings.

-Mystery freezes: Power is still on, but nothing on monitor. When doing a hard reset, nothing in the Windows event log. I don't know if this is hardware or software, it doesn't happen often.

-DP/HDMI audio sometimes stops working. I can always get it working again by disabling/re-enabling the hardware.

-Can't use headless without spending more money. See Intel NUC forums. An issue was opened in Nov-2013 using it headless and with TeamViewer, with no resolution! 11 pages of comments and almost a year later, with no real solution. The tagline on their forums is: "An ideal engine for digital signage, kiosks, home theater systems, and intelligent devices for small spaces, or anywhere else you can imagine.". The truth is the exact opposite. If you ever think you need to remotely manage it, look somewhere else.

-Did I mention horrible drivers/software? Intel's common suggestion for users is to try the latest version (understandable), then beta software, then try older versions. It's shocking to see how often they ask people to revert to old versions.

Intel almost struck gold with this product, until they started writing software and "supporting" the software. It's a big shame. I think Intel is a phenomenal company, but this product is anything but. My star rating reflects what the product should be out of the box (comparing it to any other quality barebones system), and their software/drivers. Software/drivers = 1 star, as it works with enough workarounds. Hardware = 4 stars, as it's high quality, but you're forced to spend more money on adapters.

Like many others on Intel's forums, I originally intended to purchase multiple units, but not anymore. I've built more than 30 systems in my life, never have I encountered as many frustrating drawbacks to a product.

title: A nice little unit.
text:
Stylish, stout, holding 6 TB of data, and costing approx $500. Well-built; there is nothing flimsy apparent in this construction. Cooling fins are all over it, and they add to the beauty of this design. Continual long-period use leaves the unit only slightly warm.

Complaints from others are noise and the big blue eyeball, but the noise, IMO, is not much, and the blue magoo can be disabled or made part time if you find it bothersome. And it might be if you do critical photo editing in a darkened environment. A simple note card taped over it also works. It's an upright unit, taking minimal desk space.

More importantly, this replaces a Western Digital unit which had interfacing problems with Apple's OSX 10.9, the "Mavericks" version. This LaCie does not have intermediating programming, just side software allowing some options for its use -- like disabling the blue light.

Also, I recommend this unit to anyone who has an older computer to connect. Newer drives seem mostly Thunderbolt-connected, and I'm not sure about compatibilities. Older computers usually have USB 2 or Firewire connectivity. This LaCie has USB 3 (back-compatible with 2) and Firewire 800 (back-compatible with 400) connections.

title: As good as my L glass
text:
Okay, I'm not talking build quality, nor am I talking aperture. I have a 35mm L and a 24-105mm L and they are both astounding lenses. But I shoot on a crop body camera (7D) and wanted to get a bit more wide and not so much long. On my 7D this lens translates into 24-136mm. It feels almost as well-made as my L glass, but it is WAY less bulky. I needed a shoulder strap with the above-mentioned lenses, but with this, well, it's fairly easy to hand hold. I use a padded wrist strap.

Image quality is outstanding. So close to L quality that I can't see the difference unless I set up laboratory-type situations. If you need to do that, you have WAY too much time on your hands. This, IMHO, is a pro-level lens that you can carry around with you and will cover everything from landscapes to portraits. Macro? Hm...not so much. I have a dedicated macro lens for that.

Suffice it to say that this lens makes a perfect carry-around lens on a crop body camera and will make a very cool wide to middling lens when I upgrade to full sensor.

Why only 4 stars. I've only spent a few hours with the lens and am in honeymoon mode. We'll see how she looks in the cold light of day.

title: Works well!
text:
I like to do a lot of reading at my desk so this portable plastic fold-up stand by AmazonBasics comes pretty handy. I also own the AmazonBasics Mini Travel Stand but the Portable Fold-Up one has the advantage that the notches where the tablet is inserted do not partially obstruct access to the soft keys at the bottom of my Samsung 7-inch tablet screen the way the mini travel stand does.

The stand comes with a 1-page instruction sheet but you may miss it (as I did) because it's tightly tucked between the cardboard holder and the box. Even without the instructions, it doesn't take long to figure out how the stand works. When it is folded up, it measures 7 inches long by 1 inch wide and it is 1 1/2 inches thick. Unfolded, the feet open up to 6 inches apart. The hinged back allows you to adjust your tablet to a comfortable viewing angle. The notches and the side of the hinged back that prop the tablet are rubberized, as are the bottoms of the feet so as to avoid scratching the surfaces the stand touches.

I feel the Portable Fold-Up stand provides more stability than the mini travel stand. However, when I'm on the move I prefer the mini one because it folds up flat and I can slip it inside the carrying sleeve along with the device. I think both stands are good accessories to have as they nicely accomplish the purpose of freeing your hands when using a tablet.

The guy said Asus does not perform call back services.  He told me if this phone is disconnected, I have to call them and wait on the line of callers again!!  I asked the same questions to him, if they would replace my computer or send a repair man to my home.  He said they do not replacement and asked me the situation and all my information.  So I told the same information for the second time.  After that, he told me to send the computer in and it is the only way they cover manufacturing warranty.  If he told me the answer from the first, I would not have wasted the time on the phone!!!  Now, we will wait another 2 to 3 weeks for the repair. The 24-105mm f/4L IS USM is a versatile lens on my 1.6 crop body camera; great for cityscapes, closeups of flowers (although not a Macro), sports and outdoor portraits.  The images are very sharp when hand held with excellent color, and tack sharp in the mid focal range when used on a tripod.  The USM focusing ring is near silent, fast and accurate.  The image stabilization allows for sharp images when shooting hand held. The F/4 aperture is fast enough for most daytime outdoor lighting environments (dawn/dusk).  This lens is of high quality materials and construction (feels great on the camera and when handling).  Operation is smooth and precise, typical of Canon L class lenses.  This is a great general purpose lens, however, if you want to take photos in low light without flash, wide panorama landscapes and long telephoto sports this is not the lens for you.  But then, there is no single lens that has that broad capability.  The 24-105 is expensive in the absolute, but if you do research on lenses you will find it is a real value.  This lens is worth the money, every penny.

title: Mandatory accessory for all GoPro users!!
text: AMAZING INVESTMENT if you own a GoPro!!!!!!!  In fact, if you own a GoPro then this accessory is a mandatory one.  I use this mount on the back of my hand and take amazing video while scuba diving, cave tubing, bike riding, skiing, and hiking in the mountains.  In fact, this strap works better and costs less than the actual wrist strap.  Also, while on the back of your hand, you will always have the camera out and ready for the spur of the moment videos you might need.  To use this on the back of your hand, you begin by placing the soft foam side on the back of your hand.  Bring one strap around the outside of your hand, over your palm, and behind your thumb then secure it.  Next, bring the other strap around the inside of your hand between your thumb and index finger, over your palm, to the outside of your hand and secure it.  Now tighten the straps, but not too tight because you will realize that when you hand is in a fist, the straps tighten (and you will always want to shoot video with your hand in a fist otherwise your fingers will be in the video).  Once the GoPro is snapped in place, use the quick-release vibration plug to secure the camera.  Also, you can tether the GoPro to the straps, thus making it near impossible to lose the GoPro.  And there you have it, a cheap and easy hand mount that can be used in the water, on a hike, in the snow, etc….

title: Amazing Little Tablet for $80
text:
First tablet and purchased as a gift. Let me begin by saying the manufacturer is light on documentation. What's there isn't bad, but everything you need isn't there.

This is a WiFi only tablet and does quite a bit to make setup easy... except. Isn't there always an "except"? Finding the tablet's MAC address can take a few minutes. Figuring out how to enter WiFi data will take another few minutes. There is practically -0- documentation on this crucial process.

There is also no information stating that the WiFi connection has to have an open SSID and that if using WEP, the tablet will on ly work on WEP 1, don't bother with WEP 2, 3, or 4... it will just waste your time.

Having said that, if the tablet will work with a network using a non-transmitted SSID, some other WEP config, etc. I cannot confirm or deny... it's what I had to do to make things work and again, there is little to no documentation on this process.

The actual operation is great. It took a half hour or so to get used to, but it's a first tablet. The unit speed is complained about in reviews elsewhere as is it's lack of "3-D graphics", but it is being used to supplement a laptop, not replace it, and is primarily used to surf the net, watch YouTube, read docs, etc. It is a great $80 investment.

Battery life so far has been about what the specs indicate... 4.5 hours or so, but battery life can be extended quite a bit when reading pdf's, watching video locally, etc. if you turn off the WiFi. Just remember to turn your WiFi back on before you try to surf again, etc.

Can't say enough good about this little tablet. I may buy another one or two and just keep 'em around the parlour for folks to use.

title: Finally a true wireless Remote Release
text:
[[ASIN:B005PCDSBQ RFN-4s Wireless Remote Shutter Release for Nikon DSLR with MC30 Type connection (Nikon D200, D300, D300s, D700, D800, D800E, D1, D2, D3, D3x, D3s, D4) - Transmitter and Receiver Set]]

I have been searching for a wireless remote release for quite awhile.

Have tried many ebay products from China, but they're 1)very bulky, 2)uses expensive batteries(on receiver as well as transmitter, 3)these mounts on hot shoe, you'll have to remove receiver unit in order to use flash(either built-in or SB900), 4)supposed to screw into 10 pin connector and stay there, but they always need to be re-tightened again and again. They just don't last long at all, the wires get snapped inside cable, making bad connection! The batteries came with remote out-lasted the remote, what a joke.

I've even tried one made by Vello Freeware(bought from BH), paid $35, the exact same thing happened.

This RFN-4s for Nikon 10 pin from Korea, truely an ingenius invention!
Receiver unit doesn't even require battery - drawn from camera's own battery(very little) and transmitter requires 1 ordinary AAA battery. On top of that receiver STAYS on the camera tightly screwed into 10 pin connector, and it's out of the way.

Before I buy this product, I worried about the antenna on the receiver, but it turned out to be rubber-like material, does't look and feel like it is going to break at all.

I have been using this RFN-4s on my D800 for about 6 months(edited Dec 25th, 2012), loving it. Worth every extra pennies I spent on this remote release(this unit is quite expensive, but it actually works as it should). So far, I have all good things to say about it nothing bad about it other than its hefty price. I would say, you get what you pay for. Try it yourself and forget about another remote release.

title: The Greatest Sound for the Greatest Number of People!
text:
I like reading reviews here that are short and simple, so let's get down to business.

These headphones rock. If there was ever a balance between fun without drowning out the entire audio spectrum in any particular leaning, these are the best headphones to groove with. EDM, hip hop, R&B, pop, these genres really shine, and they get my feet tapping and moving.

They are not going to be your best bet for analytical headphones, as the bass emphasis and coloration result in a slightly recessed midrange, so those listeners of primarily jazz and classical, I would suggest looking to more balanced offerings such as the Sennheiser Momentum or the Beyerdynamic DT1350.

But that isn't to say that it plays those genres terribly (in fact it can be fun), simply that there are better headphones to offer a better and more accurate presentation. But in my experience, there's no other headphone that moves me musically like the Crossfade M-100. Its near-indestructable quality, comfort pending your ears aren't too large (as I've heard on head-fi, but most people I've had audition them thought they were extremely comfortable), and its sound make for an excellent portable headphone, even fun to listen to at home if you don't mind a bit of extra bass. These headphones are Fantastic Baby!

For more, go to head-fi.org and read my (and more experienced audiophiles) lengthier review

title: Outstanding cable for the price... that was received in WELL under the estimated delivery time to boot.
text:
I am writing this with the assumption that you know there are other options out there, and that Sennheiser makes one of them.

When I bought this cable, I was coming off of my second 4 foot cable (for my HD558's) direct from Sennheiser. As everyone knows, the stock cable is WAY too long for anything but home theater use, so I immediately replaced it back in 2011 when I got these cans. Usually I love everything they do, just about to the point of fanboyism. I do not approve however, of that cable replacement they sell...

Both cables I have bought from them (the 4 ft model, for the HD558) have torn in the exact same place... just under the earcup... from VERY minimal use, as far as removing and installing goes. I travel maybe 6 times a year, halfway across the country, and i remove the cable when I do... Yet both of those have torn in that SAME spot, right next to the locking end. And WHY? Because it is all soft plastic there, a decision I never understood.

Fast forward to buying this cable:
I knew when I bought it that it was either going to be great, or a total stinker... And wonder no more, it's a keeper.
The braiding is tight and attractive. The terminals are heavy and feel durable. The locking end has a textured hard plastic (maybe aluminum?... not magnetic at all) grip, which makes it easy to install AND remove. They even had the foresight to put springs on the outer terminal end of the cable, to keep pressure off of that area... something that would otherwise will kill a cable good and early. I have NO worries whatsoever, after a few days use, as to whether this cable will hold up for years to come.

In short, I could not be more pleasantly surprised.

For those wondering, audio quality is indistinguishable from the Sennheiser brand cables. I live in AZ, and the cable arrived in under a week, when the estimate was more like a month. I am sure tha can fluctuate based on time of year and your location.

This is definitely the cable you are looking for.

P.S.:
If I had ONE gripe, it's that the cable wants to curl a bit when you move. I am using it with devices that are close to me however, so it has not posed a problem. If you are someone who stretches out the cord a bit, this may be irritating for you.

title: Good cheap travel notebook (well, Chromebook).
text:
Update: after using this Chromebook for a couple of weeks. I've learned a few new things.
a) There are tons of hidden/experimental features for you to play around with. Just enter about:flags in the browser. Be careful though.
b) You can install a basic Ubuntu interface and hot-swap between the two OSes, but I find myself using the Chrome OS all the time.
c) It's really nicely built. I really like the design of this cheapo Chromebook.
d) Google updated their Chrome apps for offline usage!

******************************************

Let's keep this simple.

Pros:
- Very cheap. I bought a used/very good one directly from Amazon Warehouse for $145+tax. That's at least 50% cheaper than the cheapest 10" tablet.
- Nice looking laptop. Very clean design with round edges.
- Light as well. I can see myself carrying this around with one hand easily.
- Decent-sized and responsive keypad. This is easily a deal-maker.
- Nice and big trackpad. Supports multi-touch.
- Chrome Web Store has plenty of apps to do whatever you want.

Cons: (let's keep in mind that this is a $150-200 notebook)
- Screen lacks contrast, saturation and has a rather narrow viewing angle.
- Trackpad is just nice, not great. Limited multi-touch gestures.
- A little slow. Maybe it's ChromeOS, maybe it's the hardware. But doesn't run as smooth as I'd like it to.
- Just web apps. But hey, it's a Chromebook. I just wish the button in taskbar didn't say "apps" when they're really just links to websites.

Overall, I feel that this is a great product from Samsung. And assuming you'll always have internet whenever you use it, this will be a great traveling companion.

title: Very good, but has its downsides compared to the LG version
text:
I had a pair of the LG bluetooth wraparound headphones/headset for about a year and thoroughly loved them. When it came time to replace the LG set (one of the wires became frayed), I looked around to see what else was available. I settled on this model because it's battery life and design seemed superior to the LG HBS-730. Also, it looked to be a better design around the neck than the LG.

Here are the Pros & Cons I've found with this headset compared to the LG:

PROs:
1. It fits better and doesn't spin around on my neck. I'm a 15.5" neck, and it's somewhat tight on the sides. I think a 16.5" would be the largest the less-than-flexible frame would handle comfortably. The frame, while not very flexible, sits where you place it and doesn't move around. For instance, when exercising, the LG would frequently slide to one side and then start to fall. I don't see this happening with the Motorola Buds.

2. The cords attached to the ear pieces are much sturdier than the LG, and flat. I doubt they will be breaking as my LG wires did. Also, the way the cords are attached to the frame itself allows the length of the cord to be adjusted much easier than the LG.

3. The ear pieces fit much better and actually stay in. Getting the LG ear pieces to stay in was a constant battle!

CONs (please note I consider these to be minor overall, but still need to be mentioned):
1. The overall sound level is lower than the LG. When I first bought the LG, I thought it was too loud, but eventually became accustomed to it. Now, the Motorola Buds seem to quiet.compared to the LG.

2. Sound quality: The LG headset sounded a little better with music, but the Motorola Buds have a set of Equalizers on them. The only problem with the Equalizers are that the differences are subtle and they are not named (it just says "Equalizer changed"), so when you find one you like, there's no way to know, later, whether you're still using the same one.

3. The Buds are missing some little features that make the LG a good headset (not just headphones). For one, there is no vibration feature with the Buds, so you have to keep the earpiece in at all times, which can be looked down upon in the office or at social gatherings. Also, the girl's voice that is used by the Buds does not enunciate. When you connect to your device, she says "You are now connected", but it really sounds like "You are n---- connected"...it took me a minute to realize she was saying NOW and not NOT.

I hope I have been detailed enough to answer any questions you may have about these. I know, overall, I am very happy with them, but there will be a few features of the LG I will still miss from time to time.

title: Hard to ask for more
text:
It's hard to choose a pair of headphones on looks, specs, or reviews. This pair taught me you can't go on brand, either. I recently owned the lower-end model in JVC's family, the "Flats", and found them too true to their name, with flat, boring sound that sucks all joy out of listening. But just a few more bucks buys these HA-S650s, which can claim both better specs and a more vibrant personality. The trebles have more crispness, the bass has punch, and the sound is more pleasing all-around.

Sound quality is of course subjective, so FYI my personal bias is about halfway between that of an audiophile and a typical American: I like that "power" sound but also accuracy. I'd say these JVCs blow away those pathetic $200 Beats headphones on both counts.

These headphones get the details right, too. Specs are pretty good (8-26,000 Hz range, 112 dB sensitivity), thanks in part to bigger-than-average 36 mm drivers. They look good, and they're light (3.6 oz). The headband's made of high-quality steel, and the earpieces fold flat. They clamp around your ears with a good amount of force, though they get a bit hot when used while exercising. Finally, the MSRP is $70 -- pretty reasonable considering Pioneer/Yamaha/Onkyo/Denon/TDK think they can charge $150 for something similar -- and the actual Internet price seems to be more like $30. If there's a better pair of headphones under $50, I have yet to hear them.

EDIT: I'm dropping to four stars because the cord doesn't last very long for active users. It seems like every 2-3 years, these headphones lose sound in one ear, forcing me to buy a new pair.

As of 2018, this model has been discontinued.

title: Fun Device - Does What I Want and Need
text:
I got this as a Christmas gift and I was so excited to try it out. In the past, I have used the Weight Watchers Active Link which is very limited in its ability due to the fact that it only tells me how many Activity Points I earn-- this is WW language only.

So I opened the Flex, charged the small device as I read the instructions, fitted the correct wrist band and went on my way. I wear the Flex 24/7 with a once a week exception. About every 7-days, I remove it at night to get a full charge. Every other night though, I wear it.

I considered trading it in for the Force so I could get the wrist wear-ability and the stair/flight counter but the Force has its charge port in direct contact with the skin and is not rated as high for water resistance due to its design. My husband and I do a lot of "fun runs" and muddy 5k things such as the Dirty Dash and Warrior Dash and are training for the Tough Mudder this year and really wanted to make sure we bought a device that could withstand the elements.

That being said, I have caught my wrist band once in the last two weeks trying to free itself from my wrist. I had on long sleeve Under Armor and I was pushing my sleeves up to wash my hands. The two materials caught up and the wrist band lost the fight. Thankfully this was because I was messing with it. But since I have read numerous reviews about people's bands detaching without notice, I will be reinforcing my wristband during the fun runs come spring and summer. I figure it will be easy to place a sweatband over the Fitbit, or loop something through the holes on the band other than the clasp that comes in the package.

I have gone to the track to test out the distance accuracy. My Fitbit tells me I have walked a mile before I have actually walked a mile. Usually, I get about 5/6 of the way through the mile. I don't know if that is simply my device, an inaccurate measurement of my stride or that my stride is simply not consistent throughout the day. Just be mindful that this is more or an estimate than a truth until you test it out for yourself.

Over all, I am very happy with this product. I don't have an iPhone or newer Samsung but if you do, look for the opportunity to wirelessly sync your Fitbit while on the go. Currently though, I find that waiting until I am near my dongle (at home or on my Surface while away) is just fine by me! I highly recommend this product to people who want to get more data than your average pedometer or smart phone app. If you like the wrist wear-ability, this is the one for you--nice on the budget at only $99 (ish) and dependable.

Purchased from: Best Buy DEC13/JAN14
Comes with charging unit, small band, large band, wireless dongle and instructions. Also, your basic membership on fitbit.com is free and reports really great features you don't have to sign up for more than once. Plus optional paid options on their site for training tips and other such tools.

Pros: The flex is light, comfortable and really not very noticeable for me (I wear on my non-dominant hand). This product is VERY water resistant so far (shower, pool, sweat, rain, etc). Love the color out of the box. Onetime payment for the device without monthly charges is wonderful. Battery life lasts at least a week (probably more but I charge once a week). Sync happens automatically within 20 feet of the dongle.

Cons: The lime color is already discolored from my clothing and I have only been wearing it for two weeks. This product does not count flights of stairs like the One or the Force does. No option to clip this device on other than in the wrist band. May need reinforcement to stay on during obstacle races and other similar training exercises.

Turn the Kindle upside down so that the side with the light rests on your work surface and the bottom is lifted at a bit of an angle. Push down with your thumbs near the bottom corners until the Kindle is far enough out of the case then detach it completely with a finger.

Summary of stars I am giving:

- FAST Shipping from CMVision
- As advertised the IR range, and pattern is like a flood light
- Size - easy to mount and Conceal
- Spare male connector Y connect 2 IR to 1 PowerSupply 1Amp
- all work as expected

I am giving 6 Stars instead of 5

Note from all who ordered and stated did not work or future buyers.
This are 850n IR LEDs. Most camera should work to increase Night vision. Do the test by
grabbing one of your IR TV remote, not a RADIO remote like the Direct TV brand. At night, or very low light, point remote across the camera or towards the camera. If you see a small light like a PEN flashlight coming out off the remote while viewing your camera output, get this one!

If nothing, this will not work for you!
Hope this helps.

Update: 07/18/2014
All of my CMVison IR Illuminators a still working after 2 1/2 yrs. Probably because I am using a 1/2 = .5 AMP 12V power supply.

Update: 04/23/2017
Finally, one of the original IR CMVision purchase originally in 2012 had to be replaced a couple of months ago.
It is not because it died but the upper section of the LED array is now dim but still putting out a red glow but weak.
After further investigation. The cause is not the IR Illuminator but the power supply which is 12V .5A (500ma).
The plastic housing is discolored and bulging. After checking the output of the power supply, it putting out 16V at 900ma. This is the issue.
The power supply cause the damage on the IR.
Both are replace. IR is now a spare

title: Don't ever take it apart!!!
text:
I've had the Blackrapid straps (2 of them) for a couple years now, purchased from Blackrapid. First of all this is not a miracle strap. Under most conditions it works well enough and is better than the usual neck strap. If you have Manfrotto quick release plates on all your cameras and lenses, the strap attaches quickly and easily--and is more secure than the attachment that comes from Blackrapid. That little chrome thing is a risk, as it will gradually turn and come unscrewed. Plus, you only have one, which means if you change lenses or camera body, you have to unscrew the thing and move it.

Important. When you get the strap, be sure and analyze the threading of the strap through the adjuster, since you get no assembly instructions with the strap. Better yet, make a diagram and put it away. If you ever take this thing apart, you'll be glad you did, because the threading is not at all intuitive. Blackrapid has a video on disassemble/reassemble but it moves quickly, has few closeups, and is of a black strap shot on a black background. Very hard to see.

In use, it is not nearly as slick as BlackRapid's videos would make you believe. And in some situations, having the camera slung along your side causes you to bump things with the camera, lens, or flash, putting either the thing you bump or the camera at risk. Finally, if you use a sling bag, you'll find this strap interferes with it, and there you are with two things that by themselves are time savers, but together, they're a big mess.

I've seen a knockoff of this strap called Carry Speed. It comes with a secondary safety strap. A good idea. It's also cheaper. Another good idea.

title: Great experience with this product...lots of details below!
text:
NOTE: I am adding this comment ahead of my original review below because after 3 months of use my case broke (the plastic surrounding the iPad cracked). I have not attempted to contact Belkin yet, but this has shaken my faith in whether this case will withstand long term use.

--------------------------------------------------------

I have used this keyboard case for about 25 hours now. I have had NO problem with setup, use or fit / physically aspects of the product.

I have long used robust protective cases on my iPads, but never one with a keyboard. I have preferred cases which off full coverage of the back and sides of the unit, which this Belkin product does.

Installation was literally a "snap", and removing it from the case is a bit harder, which is fine because I don't want any concern about the iPad "popping" out.

Bluetooth pairing was simple...the case appears on the list, and you simply select it. No pairing code is required.

Opening the closed case takes just a bit of effort, because the magnets holding it closed a fairly strong. Personally, i prefer it this way, because I don't want it flying open on its way to the concrete!

There is no "on / off" switch to save power on the keyboard, but it isn't required because the keyboard automatically powers on and off depending on whether it is locked in one of three convenient magnetic slots when opened. The slots have just the right balance of magnetic pull so the iPad feels secure, but is easy to remove to close and go.

Speaking of keyboard power, it has it's own USB charge cable. They recommend charging it before first use, but i used the keyboard out of the box for 6 hours with no difficulty. PLUS, once fully charged the keyboard offers 160 hours of use between charges! That's about 3 weeks with my standard usage, which is super.

Bluetooth functionality seems flawless so far. When I place the iPad in one of the mag slots, the keyboard instantly powers on (indicated by a tiny blue LED on one side. There is no discernible delay between opening the iPad and being able to use the keyboard.

I like 99% of the keys present on this keyboard. First, the good news - it has a standard QWERTY layout, and i was immediately touch-typing with no trouble, with a high success rate.

Arrow keys are present, which is helpful both in my IT work, and in navigating pages of text. Also present is a dedicated "home button" key, which is super cool because your hands never need to leave the keyboard to exit apps, double-tap for app switching, etc. It is located conveniently in the upper left corner of the keyboard, where the "ESC" key normally resides.

Also, there is a function key which allows tertiary use of the top row of number keys (for instance FN 1 brings up the iPad search screen, FN 2 brings up the onscreen keyboard, and FN 5 is Paste).

The thing I don't like about the keyboard is the absence of two essential (in my IT work) keys - ESC and CTRL. I called Belkin to see if there were hidden keyboard combinations which might send these characters to an application, but they said no. My work around is to simply hit FN 2, briinging up the onscreen keyboard, which has the keys I need, then press FN 2 again to return to Belkin use. Not much of a problem.

I do wish they had a more extensive user guide for keyboard combinations, because I have discovered through trial and error that pressing ALT-R creates a registered trademark symbol - ® - and there are many other symbols available. It will require experimentation to figure them out though.

Also, the iPad does not perform either auto-capitalization or auto-correct when using this keyboard, which could be considered good or bad. Essentially you just have to treat it as a normal workstation or laptop keyboard.

If you want to use the iPad in "flat mode" you just fold the key board to the back of the unit and off you go. The keyboard auto-powers off in this circumstance, so it no longer interacts with the iPad screen when you are "pressing keys" on the back of the iPad.

The aluminum finish model is a bit slippery on the front, but fortunately Belkin incorporated a leather area that covers that back / bottom of the case which serves several important functions; you can grip the iPad and case more firmly when carrying it, and it provides a soft pad when using the iPad so it does not slip or jar when being placed on the surface.

Te case is a bit heavy, weighing about 15 ounces. Since I am used to heavier protective cases, this is no trouble for me. This brings the combined weight to 2.5 pounds on my iPad 3.

A note about pricing - I saw what I thought was the same keyboard on the Belkin website for $30 less than I paid at Best Buy. After some investigation I found Belkin has two different prices for this keyboard, depending on it you order the black or aluminum finish. I bought the aluminum style for $129 at Best Buy, which was the same price Belkin listed. The black finish is $99, but was not stocked at Best Buy, but was available on belkin.com.

title: Attractive superzoom with lots of connectivity
text:
This is the updated model to the WB250, minor changes here not dramatic. The hand grip is gone on the previous model, replaced with a "pleather" (pretend leather) texture. The main appeal of this type of camera is how you can connect to other devices, making sharing photos and videos quite simple. Hence the "smart" title. Samsung have really embraced this aspect, more so than many makers.

My summary of some good and bad points about the camera

Pros:
+ Good price for a fairly well featured compact, excellent value
+ Handy 21x zoom range 23 - 483mm equivalent in 35mm, that's a nice wide angle and a good telephoto reach
+ 3" 460K touch screen control on the LCD panel it's quite good visibility wise and responds with good accuracy to touches (touch to focus and menus)
+ Image quality is pretty good in daylight fairly sharp images suitable for reasonable sized prints better than many compacts in this price point
+ Fully loaded with connectivity NFC, and wifi with apps available to download (iOS and Android)
+ Battery life isn't bad about 280-300 shots on average
+ Full manual controls on the mode dial (PASM) Max shutter speed of 16 seconds in M Mode (not bad for night shots)
+ Full HD video quality is quite sharp and decent for a compact

Cons:
- Uses micro SD cards, not normal SD cards
- Images in low light are a bit "mushy" I would avoid the highest ISO 1600 setting, though can get away with smaller prints
- Photos can blow out in the highlight end (white out sky effect) dial in a bit of - negative exposure compensation to help here
- LCD hard to see in harsh lighting
- Battery charged in camera (via USB port) probably a non issue for most, you can pick up an external charger

Additional notes:
Flash pops up on the top part of the camera, though re-charge times are not super fast but adequate.
Metering and white balance are ok most times, but you might want to dial it back a bit in harder light

You have your usual selection of tons of auto effects and filters to play around with. Images out of the camera are quite sharp and in good light better than many rivals at this keen price point. I personally find Samsung's default values a bit "pumped" and contrasty for my own tastes, but you can adjust this in camera to suit your own needs.

Samsung Smart Camera App can be downloaded and you can control the camera via that and auto share (facebook and other sites). They even have a baby monitor app so you can use the camera to send an alarm to your phone or tablet if the baby is crying.

Personally I don't need all these features, but you might..so it's there if you want it.
A nicely made, easy to use and well featured camera, if you want decent images, a good zoom range and desire the NFC and wifi aspects, then the WB350F is a good buy, Samsung have really improved a lot in recent years and this is one of their better efforts

What Corsair ships is a kit with two individual type 'A' USB 3.0 cables that the user must snake through grommets at the rear of the PC case, the cables then connected to two USB 3.0 ports at the chassis rear I/O panel. The USB 3.0 specification with its higher data speed means shorter maximum allowed USB 3.0 cable lengths. Corsair's solution with its longer USB 3.0 cables snaked to the chassis rear I/O panel reduces what's left for total USB 3.0 cable lengths for the user to connect cables to the USB 3.0 ports at the top/front of the Corsair Obsidian 800D PC case.

text:
When I bought this adapter I decided not to heed the negative reviews, hoping that the problem was less frequent than reported. I was unfortunately in the wrong. Props to this adapter for being initially easy to install and having a fast connection speed, but it putters out after a few months of use. Perhaps I'm the one that has the problem, however, so I'll be detailed in my description of how I tried to diagnose and fix the problem in case anyone is thinking about buying this and better knows how to resolve the issue I had.

A few months in my adapter would infrequently stop receiving a signal, leaving me without connection. I used safe eject to remove the device and re-plug it into the same USB slot. Problem solved for a time, but it would eventually have the same problem. I'd fix it the same way, but the loss of function became more and more frequent, until a few days ago it started working for 30 seconds before disconnecting again.

I looked up the adapter in my device management window and found that it was reporting Windows Error 43, which in short means the driver or device itself had a problem and so the computer doesn't recognize the device at all. I tried many of the suggested methods found on support forums, including a simple reboot, uninstalling the device drivers and then putting the device back in, and finally powering down the computer, pulling all USB devices, booting up and reinserting all USB devices one by one to see if they were recognized. The fatal error is that the device's driver are actually onboard the adapter itself, so if the device is failing the driver is inaccessible via the device. It didn't matter which USB slot it was in, same problem, but my wireless keyboard, mouse, external hard drive, phone charger and mobile preamp all worked no matter where they were plugged in.

Then I decided to test it on a different computer (the one I'm using to write this) and it didn't recognize the device. I downloaded the driver from the manufacturer's website, double checking that it was the correct device and OS, but when I went to install it the OS failed to recognize the adapter which was plugged in. After all of this it's clear to me that the device itself is faulty, and I'd strongly urge potential buyers to consider other options. I'm currently trying to start a local business and my lack of internet access has crippled the process. Don't skimp, buy something quality.

TL;DR - After rigorous attempts to make this faulty device work, I just had to accept that it was junk.

title: Missed it by that much!
text:
I bought this device so I could switch my keyboard, mouse, and monitor between my desktop and my laptop. I particularly wanted a switchbox that supports DVI since both of my video sources use that standard. I have to say the unit's video performance has been perfect, I am able to run both computers at 1920 x 1080 and there have been no problems during boot, etc. The mouse switching has also been flawless even though I use a mouse with extra programmable buttons.

The keyboard, however, has been a problem area. I use a (brand new) [[ASIN:B004SUIM4E Microsoft Natural Ergonomic Keyboard 4000]].

To start with, when the keyboard is routed through the KVM, Windows sees it as a generic HID-compliant device, not the specific device. This means that Microsoft's utility software for the keyboard doesn't work, so the row of extra buttons at the top of the keyboard is useless. Further, when I type rapidly, the KVM drops keys and gets confused. For example, if I hold the down-arrow key to scroll, the KVM will often beep and act as if it is switching sources. The screen goes black for a few seconds and then comes back.

I found it pretty hard to live with the dropped keys. Not only does this cause needless spelling mistakes, it also causes keys to repeat when the KVM loses the "key up" event, so you end up with long runs of letters.

I exchanged my original KVM through Amazon (a completely painless process, by the way) but the new box had the same problem.

You may well ask why I gave this device four stars despite what has been a fairly serious flaw from my perspective. It's because I discovered an incredibly simple workaround for my problems: I plug my keyboard into one of the KVM's "generic USB device" ports instead of the dedicated keyboard port. Since I did that the box has worked flawlessly. No keys dropped, and the keyboard's extra buttons work fine. Of course I can no longer switch between computers using keystrokes or use any of the KVM's other fancy features (rotating automatically through the computers, etc.) but I don't really need those capabilities. The KVM is right under my monitor so I can easily switch using the button on the front of the unit.

Other reviewers have apparently had no keyboard problems so your mileage may vary. It might be that I type faster, or differently. The KVM may just not like my Microsoft keyboard. Still, I wanted to pass along my experience (and my workaround) to other potential buyers. As long as I don't use the KVM's dedicated keyboard USB port the switch is perfect for my needs.

title: Works Great... Try these steps before you give up.
text:
If it doesn't work for you don't give up too easily, try these steps

Initially it didn't' seem to work on my iPad 2 when I tried to upload photos via a USB flash drive.

But after reading the advice in the comments here, this is what got it working perfectly for me.

1. The switch on the side has to be on set to the correct setting (USB or SD)
2. If a notice comes up "This acccessory is not supported by iPad", click 'OK'

Additionally, the photos have to be :
3. in a folder named DCIM.
4. named in an original format from a camera: DCS_001 or IMG_001
5. have to be numbered consecutively. ( DCS_001, DCS_002, DCS_003 .... etc...)

Photos were not recognized when they were :
A. named with a number or a regular word(s), for example: "2", "Sam", or "Ruthie at the beach".
B. not in the DCIM folder
C. not numbered in consecutive order.

title: Excellent, but some things to watch for
text:
This is an excellent router that works very well for me. It is very easy to use and set up. I highly recommend it. It has every feature you could want. There are a couple of issues to watch out for however.

I suspect that some (not all) the connection problems people are having in these reviews are actually due to their laptop wi-fi cards, if those cards are Intel brand. I discovered that there are a lot of complaints about Intel cards. The main problem seems to be that they won't connect after you come out of sleep or hibernate. UPDATE - as of early 2015 Intel seems to have fixed this in their latest drivers.

Also, if you use the USB ports with a USB 3.0 device, pay attention to your 2.4 ghz channel and watch for strange behavior. A program like "inSSIDer" can help you see what your router signals are doing. The USB 3.0 devices work in the same frequency range as the 2.4 ghz wi-fi signal. This creates interference with the router signal and can cause all kinds of problems like dropouts, disconnections, etc. I have also observed that the interference forces the router to switch to 20mhz bandwidth, which cuts the data rate in half. There are many other reviewers here that report this issue.

This is an issue that seems to be affecting many of the latest routers with USB 3.0 ports, not just this one. Much of the problem seems to be poor shielding in the routers and also in the cables and the devices that attach to them. If you Google "USB 3.0 + wi-fi interference" you will get plenty of hits. The 5 ghz band is not affected. But your guests may need the 2.4 ghz band. See update #2 below.

Another thing I learned is, if you are using a USB external drive in a Samba share, format it in Linux based ext2 or ext3 format and not NTFS. With NTFS you will see weird problems like missing files that are actually there. Again, this is an issue with most routers, not just this one. This is because the router's operating system is Linux. NTFS is a foreign language to Linux and requires a driver. The driver seems to be a third party driver also used in other routers and is the culprit here. I have firmware version 3.0.0.4.374.1317 as of this writing.

Windows does not support ext2/3 so you can't format your drive with Windows. This also means that you can only read from or write to the drive through the router. Look at "GParted" (free) software as your first stop for formatting. Since reformatting my drive to ext2 the weird problems with NTFS completely went away. Also see update #3 below.

UPDATE #1: I have encountered another USB file issue using the ext2 format. I have run into an issue where after copying files to the drive, some random files are tagged as "read-only". There doesn't seem to be a pattern to this. So if you try to delete a large folder with lots of other files and sub-folders, chances are you will run into a "read-only" file and the directory tree remains down to that file. You have to manually go in and un-check the "read-only" property for each file before you can delete it. I have Googled and found this issue reported elsewhere. It doesn't appear that ASUS has done a very good job as a whole with the USB functionality in their firmware. No updates are available to fix these problems, as of January, 2014. I suspect this portion of the code is canned and used in all their routers, resulting in possible problems on all their other models too. I am just now switching to FAT32 format to see if it works better. See update #3 below.

UPDATE #2 --- New USB 3.0 SETTING!!!: I just ran across a new setting I hadn't seen before. It must have slipped in on one of the firmware updates. It is called "Reducing USB 3.0 Interference". It is in the "wireless/professional tab/2.4 ghz" section, at the bottom of the list. According to the pop-up it either decreases 2.4ghz performance or decreases USB 3.0 performance, depending on which you care more about. It seems to be an attempt to address the USB 3.0 interference issue.

UPDATE #3 --- I have discovered that it is a myth that you cannot format a FAT32 drive larger than 32 GB. You just can't do it from within Windows. If you use third party software such as "GPartEd" you can format a FAT32 drive of any size. I have done this to a 128 gB drive, so I know it can be done. Formatting in FAT32 seems to have solved all the problems listed above. It has worked flawlessly for me now for 6 months. FAT32 seems to be they format to go with.

ASUS SUPPORT: Finally, let may give a broader remark about ASUS support, forget it! They are useless. If I were rating their support separately I would give them 0 stars. Over the past 15 years I have opened numerous support tickets with ASUS Support, including about the above issues. They have a perfect record. They have never responded to a single one of them, nothing, ever, zero, nada. I guess they go into a black hole somewhere. They also make it very difficult to report problems with their products.

title: Great complement to a flat panel TV
text:
Summary - excellent product; we'd give it 4.5 stars, marked down slightly for subwoofer power / volume, roll off of very high frequency sound and fiddly wall mounting (we'd rather have a positive bracket).

Installation and set up. The speakers were well packaged and protected which ensured that the product arrived safely from Amazon. The excellent and detailed instructions, in six languages, made the set up very easy straight out of the box. It is important to follow the step by step 'plug in and power up' sequence as described. You can review the User Manual online at the Energy website before purchase.

Shelf mounting (not used in our case). Two curved, self adhesive, legs are provided to stick to the underside of the soundbar. They looked as if they would complement the overall size and shape of the soundbar, but I wonder how effective the adhesive is over time.

Wall mounting. A thin cardboard template is provided to assist wall mounting. Energy require at least 1 inch of space between the soundbar and the TV above; take this into account when deciding whether this will work in your room. The mounting is via two slots in a molded feature that stands proud of the rear of the soundbar. Mounting hardware is not provided - the slot is just OK for a maximum 5mm shaft screws with a 10mm head. The template is not quite accurate; the two screw holes on the template are about 1mm longer than the actual soundbar attachment slots (28.18 inches/715.77mm). Note that this dimension does not correspond to standard drywall stud spacing. The major issue with this style of mounting (slotting the soundbar over pre-positioned screw heads in the wall) is the juggling necessary to ensure that the screws stick out just enough to ensure a tight fit to the wall. The soundbar power wire has an in-line transformer similar in size to that for a laptop. Take this into account when planning your layout. The optical cable provided by Energy is 1.8m long. All connections plug into a central indentation in the back of the soundbar. This indentation is at the bottom half of the soundbar, so if you have to then run the wires upwards towards the TV, they must be squeezed in a tight radius and through quite a narrow gap between the back of the soundbar and the wall. Take this into account when planning your installation.

Subwoofer positioning. There is one left side firing speaker and a rear port. The power cable is approx 68 inches long. The integration of the subwoofer sound is soft and subtle; and it is relatively tolerant to placement. We found that it does have to be turned up quite high using the rotary volume control on the rear, and that the last 1/8th turn of the volume control appears not to be very linear. The family room is 16ft wide by 20ft (which extends into a kitchen / breakfast room another 22ft).

System integration. The soundbar and subwoofer hooked up to each other easily. We chose not to integrate the soundbar volume control into the TV remote, as the TV remote does not have the '3D' sound button (and so we'd need two remotes anyway). The optical connection worked perfectly - excellent, easy set up and instal.

Appearance. High quality moldings with a matt black finish. Looks better than the online photos. It is larger than most of the soundbars that you see in local stores (40 inches wide by 4 1/8 inches high), and complements the 55 inch Panasonic nicely.

Sound quality. This sounds better than anything else I've heard in a store. Overall it is warm and slightly 'midrangey'. The very high frequencies are softened, and this becomes most apparent with music in DVDs where, for example, symbols and high frequency content is somewhat muted at the top end. The sound is well controlled, imagery is nicely focused and the '3D' effect is noticeable, albeit not a true surround sound. Pressing the button to go to the '3D' effect also includes a shift in sound balance. As mentioned above the subwoofer needs to be turned up, but then our room is quite large. The integration of the subwoofer sound is very good and any 'side to side' imbalance from the side firing speaker is masked by this. We do feel that the subwoofer could use more power to fully use the 10inch speaker though. Overall the sound is excellent, and the built in soundbar amplifier can go quite loud with no sign of excessive strain. It is not, of course, a true substitute for a quality receiver and separate surround sound speakers.

Installed with:

Panasonic TC-P55GT30 plasma TV
Oppo DVD player

Reference sound system - Rotel / Bowers & Wilkins 2 channel HiFi system in another room.
