title: Like it but have an issue -Edited
text:
Had to edit my review. Still really like the idea of a chromebook however i'm experience problems with mine. It randomly shuts down. I've posted in googles chromebook forum but haven't gotten an answer that helps. I've ran a Chrome OS recovery which installs a fresh copy of Chrome OS on your computer. It shut down 5 mins after that. I thought maybe it was overheating on my lap - covering the exhaust port and fan but it shut down on a table a couple days ago and last night in the middle of a movie. Both time the vents were completely clear. Have read 2 other reviews that have this problem. Might just be faulty hardware and I got an unlucky one. Not sure but I will have to take this back. Don't know if I will purchase another.

This is my first chromebook. If you know what a chromebook/Chrome OS is capable of will not be disappointed.

I've been using it for a couple days now so I'll give you a breakdown of what I like about it

Screen- 11.6 is alot smaller than I'm used too. That being said its not a bad trade off for the portability of this device. Its a TN screen so colors are not that great but also not bad, I've seen 400-500 dollar laptops with worse screens. I compared the chromebook with the ISP panel and it was so much nicer of a screen but I did not like that chrome book. I actually like the matte screen. My last 2 laptop were glossy so I thought i might not like this one but thats not the case. Remember the price of this laptop I can't complain at all about the screen

Hdmi out - I've hooked this up to my 55" samsung tv via hdmi. The picture was amazing. Just make sure you don't choose mirror displays. that will send the 1366x768 image to the tv. Choose the other setting and it will send a full 1080p signal to your screen. I tested playing movies from either usb port, the sd card, and the actual hard drive on the computer and all worked perfectly.

Webcam- just average. In good lighting its a decent image. Medium light starts to get grainy. Low light pretty bad.

Audio- sounds great with headphones, speaker volume is more than enough with my Grados. Built in speakers are very good as well, better than my last 2 laptops which is odd since the speakers here are on the bottom.

Battery life - have been getting 7-8 hours just as advertised. I really find this incredible, my past laptops were 3 hours at most

wifi- works great. I needed an ethernet port which this did not have. I purchased a usb to ethernet adapter from amazon. It was cheap and works perfectly. Tried it in both usb ports and is automatically detected and worked in both.
[[ASIN:B00BJOZNV2 Sabrent USB 2.0 to Network 10/100Mbps Ethernet Adapter]]

sd/usb ports - all work and quickly, dont' have any usb 3.0 devices to see how much quicker the usb 3 is.

keyboard- i like the small keyboard. can reach any button easily while typing. doesn't feel cheap. the full screen button and the buttons around it are a little "clicky". There is some flex in that area of my laptop which causes that sound. If I push down slight on the plastic above those keys they sound just liek the rest. The tiny flex in the plastic is what is causing the sound , the keys work fine. Some buttons are gone from a regular laptop or keyboard but there are short cuts to each of these missing keys. Just have to look them up - example no delete button but alt+backspace functions as a delete button.

Trackpad- is sensitive and responsive. Click feels solid, but i find that i really click anymore just tap it. Since the laptop is small the track pad is on the small side. Sometimes when I'm scrolling down I run out of track pad. I just have get used to it and two finger scroll a little quicker and then it brings me to the bottom of the pages i'm reading.

So for 199 I really think this is an amazing machine. If you know what Chrome OS is capable of then you won't be disappointed with this. At first I didn't know how I would manage without downloading the programs I have on windows but it seems in this day there is a web based program for everything you need to do.

My only issue is Toshiba just came out with a chromebook CB35-A3120. It has a 13.3 inch screen (supposedly better colors, glossy screen). Two 3.0 usb ports. It is 279 plus tax so its almost 50% more than this model. I've not seen one in a store yet but I might consider getting that instead depending on when I see one in person.

title: Works, but is tricky and finicky.
text:
Note: many reviews here have the features of the AC3 and AC9 mixed up. This review will strictly cover the features of the AC9 only.

First...when I got my AC9's, they didn't work. The AB800 showed a red light and wouldn't trigger even though all the lights on the AC9 and the FlexTT5 were green and happy. To fix this, I upgraded my TT5's to what is presently the Beta firmware (6.5.3). To do this, start the Pocket Wizard utility, hit the gear icon on the bottom left, select the center tab and say you want optional and beta firmwares, then upgrade. Once I upgraded, things started working. It's possible that simply resetting your TT5 to factory defaults will do the trick so try that first (I didn't because everything looked correct).

Despite being grouchy and unpredictable, I like my Flex TT5's mostly because of Hypersync. This has allowed me to shoot my 1D cameras with Canon flashes at 1/500th with only a slight band at the bottom. This shutter speed is fast enough for using fill flash in basketball to get good color on courts that have awful pink/lime green color shifting lights.

But what happens when you need a more powerful flash? Alien Bees are great but with the sync cord they're just dumb flashes which means you're back to the slower X-Sync shutter speed. Replace the cord with a Flex TT5 (which must be set to "basic trigger mode") and things get worse: the radio delay slows your shutter speed even more. In my case that drops the maximum shutter speed from 1/300 to 1/200. So much for using Alien Bees for fill flash.

Fortunately that telephone jack connector on your Alien Bee allows products like the AC9 to control the flash in wonderful ways giving you Hypersync and even High Speed Sync functionality. It really works. It somehow gives you full power flash at a higher shutter speed (in my case 1/500th) and even more surprising gives you a lower power flash at even higher shutter speeds just like the HSS mode on your Canon flash. Although the power drops off as you would expect, I was able to shoot at 1/3200th without seeing a shutter curtain. Since your Alien Bee is already a powerful flash, the remaining power at these higher shutter speeds is very respectable and could be used for fill flash in many more sunlight conditions than a Canon flash.

But... like all of Pocket Wizard's recent products you know that they can act funny and need to be tested with great caution after every setup or they may trick out on you. The AC9 is no exception. The correct procedure is to turn on the flash, then turn on the TT5. That works sometimes but other times I get a green/red light on the flash. I've found that recycling the power on the flash or the TT5 gets it going.

Another setup problem is the power level. The AC9 lets you adjust the flash power level via the camera's flash exposure compensation (FEC). This is very handy but might be a little confusing. Since the flash is not using TTL metering, the setting isn't really compensating for any exposure so it appears to just replace the sliding power control on the back of the flash -- +3 stops is maximum power (full right) and -3 stops is 1/32th power (full left). The problem is after setup, the flash power level doesn't match what the camera says it should be. I've found that I have to change the power setting on the camera, take a shot, then set it to what I want and take another shot.

Like all of Power Wizard's recent products, the AC9 does amazing things and adds tremendous value to your Alien Bee but it has bugs that need to be worked around after every setup -- you can't just plug everything in, turn everything on, and expect it to work the way it's supposed to. For event photography, this adds unnecessary stress if you're running late or need to make some last minute changes.

And it's totally unacceptable that these didn't work at all right out of the box.

title: Pretty nice, durable and good sounding set of cans.
text:
OK, I had these headphones for more than a while now. I can now give my honest opinion. I have many sets rangingfrom Bose, Audiotechnica, Skullcandy, Sony, Seinnhenser, even Beats. From in-ear, over-ear, on-ear. The following is what I look for in a pair of sound cans (in no particular order).

1. Build - I must admit that when manufacturers say "Unrivaled durability" I can't help but to roll my eyes till I get a headache. When I first opened them and felt them, I was surprised as to how hefty they felt. They screamed quality and the metal part on the sides (what hold the cups) seemed like they could take a beating. I was not about to do the "flex test" however, one day I slammed my bedroom door on them and they took the hit like a champ! There you go.

2. Style - I bought the ones that are dark Gray with silver sides. These are very nice looking headphones. They look sleek and the metal sides accentuate the band giving it an elegant air. They're matted so they will not display fingerprints like glossy ones.The cups do not look too big and they're nicely shaped. I will say, however, that the Revo's beauty mostly shines when one is close enough to appreciate them. They are very subtle and not a fashion statement (Beats).

3. Comfort - The Jabra REVOs are very comfortable. The plush memory pads on the earcups adjust nicely to the contours of the ear. They do have some weight though. So that means that after a 1.5-2 hours they will begin to be noticed. Also, this headsets are meant to be used in activities so they fit a bit snug. If you wear glasses this may be a factor as fatigue behind the ears develop rather quickly (at least for me).

4. Sound - This will always be the benchmark for any headphones; the make or break factor. I am happy to report that these bad boys did not disappoint me. Although the bass was a bit emphasized, the highs and mids were present and distinguishable. They are not to the level of say, Audiotechnica or Seinnheiser, but I do enjoy them often. Mostly when I want to have an involved sense of bass.

Overall, I would not recommend them for the original price at $200. However at $120-$140, I'd pick them up. One thing that may not be of interest to many is the ability to connect a second headset to the other cup and share the sounds. I love this as my son and I like to share videos we find on the fly, without taking off the sets. The cord is nice, but I replaced it with another as they build static and transfer sound feedback. Not a big deal but I had to mention it.

Hope this lengthy review helps anyone in making a decision they feel good about.

title: Too tall to use with my CPU heat sink
text:
This RAM installed and worked well, but each chip has its own heat sink which makes each module very tall. If you are using a stock Intel heat sink / fan, this isn't a problem at all because there is no overlap so both the heat sink and RAM will fit fine. If you are using a bigger, more powerful heat sink / fan (for example, I decided to go with the Cooler Master GeminII S), then you won't be able to use all 4 modules in this 16GB set.

The Cooler Master GeminII S heat sink overlaps the 4th RAM slot, and because this RAM is so tall it won't fit underneath, making it so you can only use 3 out of the 4 modules. Since I wanted to use the Cooler Master GeminII S and also wanted a full 16GB of RAM, I replaced this set with the Kingston Technology HyperX 16 GB Kit, which uses a lower profile heat sink that fits perfectly under the Cooler Master.

title: Value for money and a good product
text:
I read a lot of reviews on amazon for different IPAD 2 screen protectors. I finally selected AM amFilm screen protector. My selection was bang on. I received the product earlier than the est.delivery date and in good packaging condition.

Now regarding applying the film on the ipad which seem to be the issue with most buyers/reviewers here and in other brands. I applied the film in under 5 minutes !!. There is a technique of applying the film which I learnt from one of the staff at a apple store in Houston. I used that technique and lo, I had just couple of bubbles which easily cleared using the bubble remover card provided.

The technique is - hold the film at the edges in a U shape and start applying from the centre of your ipad. Use the camera and the ipad button at the centre to make the first alignment. Then holding at the edges, press the film on the ipad screen beginning with the middle part of the screen and keep pressing with the film downwards(in U shape) and in outward direction. If you see a bubble while applying, then retract a little and press again. You should not get any bubble. If you do so it would be towards the edge of the screen which can be eliminated with the bubble removing card that is provided.

Now more about the product. As it says it is a clear(invisible screen) which it is and the advantage is that the IPAD screen looks as bright as one without a film. The downside is that if you have a sticky finger then scrolling would not be that smooth.
I do not have a sticky finger so I am good there.
Scrolling would be smooth on a matte finish film however the downside there would be that you will miss the clarity and brightness of the IPAD screen.

Overall I got 2 films for $9 and feel it is a good deal.....
Hope you like this review and helps in making your decision :)

title: It works great in my skylight.
text:
I had previously purchased an Antennas Direct DB2 antenna that initially worked great. However, at certain times of the year, especially during windy or stormy weather and solar flare activity, the reception on a few channels would fade in and out. It was very disconcerting. But because of my confidence in the quality of products from Antennas Direct, I decided to upgrade to the DB4e to see if the problem could be resolved.

When I received the DB4e, I mounted it in my skylight (see photo), in the spot where the DB2 had been. The DB4e is more than twice as large as the DB2, so I wasn't sure if a skylight installation was going to be practical at all. If it did not work well there, I would have reluctantly mounted it on the roof, where I'm certain it would pick up even more channels.

Well, it works great in the skylight and my reception has never been better. I now get 119 channels on my living room TV and 130 on my bedroom TV (I have no idea why they don't pick up the same number of channels, but they don't). I am 21 miles away from the transmitters. The signal strength on 90% of the channels is 92 or higher, while the lowest signal strength on the very weakest channels is still over 75. More importantly, unlike the DB2, the diagnostics on my TV indicate "0 errors," along with very impressive "signal to noise" ratios. I have not noticed any fade or wavering in any of the diagnostics at all. If I ever do notice it, I will update this review.

UPDATE: I've owned this antenna for over 2 years now and the only problem I have had with it is occasional momentary drops out with channel 7 in L.A. From what I understand (not being a techie) Channel 7, 9, 11, and 13 are the only L.A. stations whose physical channels are the same as their channel numbers, making them VHF signals (see list below). All of the other station's physical channels are in the UHF range, which this antenna is specifically designed for. I've never noticed any dropouts on any of those channels. The very rare dropouts on channel 7 do not happen frequently enough to coax me into mounting the antenna onto the roof, and the only other dropouts I have ever encountered have been very rare in duration (1/4 second or less resulting in a very temporary deterioration of the picture) on channel 9. Both can be explained because this is a UHF antenna. Be that as it may, my 5 star review still stands. END OF UPDATE.

One other note, the DB4e comes almost fully assembled. All you have to do is remove a couple of rubber bands and cardboard used for internal packing, install two metal sleeves and tighten their respective screw/bolts/nuts, and connect the coaxial cable. That's it. It could not have been easier.

I highly recommend it!

The button thing is normal, being used to different placements, it is not a fault of the mouse. I will not give the name of my previous mouse for many years because I don't like to publicly down another product name with my personal problems encountered, since it is only a percentage, and not a 100% total problem.
I highly recommend this mouse if you are an FPS gamer (BF3,BO2, Arma II, ect) You will not be disappointed. The sniper button, unce used to is a killer-raised my scores. Downloading and installing firmware should be done while plugged in a USB 2 port as recommended, then you can swithch to USB 3 if you want- no problems encountered there.
OK, just buy it! If you are a FPS gamer, otherwise I would recommend the M70 meant for multible macro, and having more user buttons. The M60, after a months use has encountered 0 problems, raised my kill/death ratio, made my gaming experiance more comfortable during long hours, gave me more confidence due to the precision, instant DPI and sniper button usage and precise laser tracking. Amazons price is as low as you will find, plus the advantage of their excellent support which I rarely had to use-never had to ask for RMA throughout the years from them as the products they shipped were usually faster than advertised, exactly as advertised, perfect condition, unbeateable price.

title: Hi-Fi from your computer
text:
If you are looking for an amplifier to crank the music to your head phones this is a product for you. If you are looking for a rich and satisfying hi-fi music experience this is a product for you.I will take the rest of this review to describe the latter.

I have always found it hard to describe a specific audio component itself as the total listening experience is going to be as good as the weakest component you have. So first...

If you are looking for a true hi-fi experience playing music from your computer I would first recommend that you invest in an external DAC (Digital to Analog Converter). The DAC in your computer is not real good. There are three components you need to achieve quality Hi-Fi from your computer: 1) headphones; 2) an amplifier; 3) a DAC.

My rig is: HRT Music Streamer II DAC, Audio-Technica ATH-M30 Headphones, and the Little Dot I+ Tube Amplifier.

Before buying the Little Dot my musical experience was very, very good with my headphones and external dac. But, once you catch the Hi-Fi disease you realize the sound can even be better. Being the owner of a Fisher 500B tube receiver I began a search for a headphone tube amplifier so I could have the same warm sound that tubes deliver.

After reading the reviews of others and researching competing products I settled on the Little Dot I+. I can say that this is is one of the best purchases I have ever made.

First things first, if you buy this amplifier and use it with the tubes it comes with it is, frankly, little more than an amplifier. If you replace the tubes (referred to as rolling) with a nice set of tubes you will be blown away.

Rolling the tubes involves plugging a new set of tubes into this amplifier. As you can see from the product picture the tubes are external so this is something anyone can do. If you google tube rolling and little dot you will get information on tube rolling. If you are not one to research everything in detail I will give you the cliff notes version and my experience.

I have used GE JAN5654W (GE makes different versions of the 5654 tube so make sure you get this version!) and Tung-Sol 6AK5. Both are spectacular. The GE JAN5654W are the best value (I paid $18 for five). eBay has a number of stores that specialize in selling tubes. The Tung-Sol 6AK5 cost me $24. I have also read that the Voshkod 6ZH1P-EV, the Mullard M8100 CV4010, and the RCA 5654 Black Plate are also good tubes.

The bass and treble are excellent using the GE JAN5654W or Tung-Sol 6AK5 tubes. The detail is also phenomenal on both. You will hear things in the music that you have never heard before. The soundstage is superb as well. For example, listening to Fleetwood Mac the Chain the drummer, Mic Fleetwood, sounds like he is directly behind you. The midrange is fantastic. Singers like Diana Krall and Adele are a joy to listen to. Both of these tubes provide a rich and warm musical experience that only tubes can provide. If I had to pick I would give a slight edge to the Tung-Sols. But listening is pretty subjective.

One word of warning. Once you experience true hi-fi sound it is hard to go back to an MP3 player plugged into headphones or ear-buds. I let a co-worker listen to my setup and for the rest of the day he did not listen to his music. Even my wife who is not the music fanatic I am gets a smile on her face when she listens to her music though my setup.

---
Added 1/28/2014

I have now tested the following tubes with this amplifier:
-GE 5Star 5654
-Voshkod 6ZH1P-EV
The 5Stars are very nice and a value at $16 (included shipping) for 5 through eBay.
The Voshkod's from yen audio set me back $40 for the pair. They are spectacular. They are my new favorites.

title: The best drive for the money
text:
I feel like many of the highest rated reviews are giving bad advice, so here's my 2 cents. I believe that this is the best ssd for the money. I am writing this review near the end of 2012, and in the future this will probably change. The price on this drive will probably drop over the next year, making it an even better value, then at some point better drives will come out and reduce it's value.

People are just looking at the sequential writes and saying that because this drive doesn't have the best sequential writes, it's not a good buy. This is not a good way to evaluate a drive.

If you head over to anandtech's web site, they have some nice benchmark comparisons. I like their light workloads bench, because it gives a numerical representation of the performance an average user will experience.

You will notice that this drive has one of the highest scores for this light usage benchmark. The only other drives that score that high cost significantly more.

What Samsung did with this drive was to focus on giving the user the best experience for the money. No it's not the absolute best drive for super heavy duty applications, but it's not intended for servers, it's intended for average users.

The 830 was no doubt a great drive, but the 840 is even better, and it can be produced for much less money. For the average user, who is just browsing the web and listening to some mp3's, maybe playing some games or watching a movie, this drive is the clear choice. It will give that user almost the best performance possible, while costing less than almost every other ssd.

I would highly recommend that anyone who doesn't already own an ssd purchase one of these, preferably the 250 gb model as it gives the best bang for the buck. You will not be disappointed, it is the best upgrade you can do for your computer. It will breath new life into any computer and extend battery life on any laptop.

I personally have a 120 gb ocz agility 3 (6gb/sec) in my desktop and would really like to upgrade to this. Even though this ssd has a slower sequential write speed, the overall performance increase I would see is 50-60% and I would also increase my available storage by several hundred percent. 250 gb ssd is so much better than 120 it's not even funny. I try to keep my usage to 50-75% and that only let's me have 3 to 5 games installed at a time. If I upgraded I could likely install 12 to 15 games at the same time.

Overall I am very happy with this laptop and all of this is coming from somebody who occupies his time building high end gaming computers. Keep reading if you are interested in technical jargon, if not have a nice day :)

Technical Jargon:
-Intel Smart Response Technology is what makes this laptop so snappy when compared to other laptops with only a mechanical hard drive. It is actually a fancy name for RAID 0. Inside the laptop is a 30GB SSD that is raided with the 500GB 5400rpm HDD. The software that is installed under the OS learns what programs and files are accessed the most, exactly like superfetch. Those files are cached on the SSD which effectively speeds up the response time of the computer. Though this is not near the performance of using all solid state drives, it is far snappier than any single 5400RPM drive. I would say that it compares favorably to the Western Digital Velociraptor line of mechanical HDDs.

-The reason that I did not give this laptop 5 stars is due to Dell's horrible technical support. After talking to 5 different characters that barely spoke English I discovered that not one knew where I could find the RAID drivers that were needed for the clean Windows installation. After the first technician hung up on me to "do research" I had already found the drivers on both the Intel website and the Dell website. They were also hidden in an obscure folder on the disk that came with my laptop.
This folder was named with 5 seemingly random numbers and letters, like the rest of the driver folders. I continued to talk to technicians to see if it were possible for me to get the correct answer from them and reached the conclusion that it was not. This was after "elevating" my ticket several times, being hung up on twice and after being told I would be called back in 1/2 hour when I in fact after 2 hours did not get called back.

-I truly wanted to rate this laptop at 1 star, but that would have been due entirely to the horrible customer support and not a fair assessment of this light, powerful and sleek laptop.

title: Pellet Stove Backup Power Supply
text:
I originally bought the APC Back-UPS XS BX1000G 1000VA Tower UPS ($125) to protect and provide emergency power for our pellet stove. Once I got it I determined with APC Tech Support help it would not be good for this purpose. So they recommended this one instead because it can handle AC Motor loads and does not change the sinewave that can damage AC Motors. This one though is a great deal more expensive and heavier. However I watched for a "Warehouse Deal" and got this for only $160.00 almost 1/2 of retail plus it included shipping. Hooked it up and it works perfect, "plug and play".

For those that do not know - a pellet stove requires an exhaust fan to run in order to extract smoke to the outside. If your pellet stove is in the burn cycle and the power goes out, chances are smoke will backup in to the house. With this connected it works flawlessly and allows me to shut down the stove and not have any smoke problems. If the power outage is short term it can run the pellet stove for about 40 minutes without AC Power. There are specific systems out there that will run much longer but they are 4-5 times the money and will not power the auto igniter. With this one you don't even know it switched over... I would highly recommend it. Also if you are in a place with long term power outages you can use a generator to provide constant power to the UPS which in turn will smooth out the current and provide exactly what the stove needs. Generators have such a fluctuating current and voltage they can damage the electronics in a pellet stove (as well as any other sensitive electronics). This stops damage from happening.

Also on a side note - for one money we now have our computers protected and will be protecting our TV and related electronics as well.... all around a great piece of equipment for little money!

title: Great When it Worked
text:
This heart rate monitor was fantastic when it worked. After 3 months, and just under 300 running miles logged, it began giving erratic indications i.e. extreme highs and low readings and then would stabilize at about mile #4 in my run. At approximately 400 miles logged with the monitor, it stopped working completely. I reviewed the instructions, searched the web, and here are the corrective actions that I have taken: replaced the battery twice (unit is only 6 months old), cleaned and adjusted the battery contacts inside the compartment as one self-help website suggested, used water, spit, and monitor/ultrasound gel as suggested, and I even tried moving the sensors to my back as another reference suggested even though the monitor worked just fine on my chest for 3 months prior, and thoroughly inspected the O-Ring that seals the battery compartment even though the problems began well before I ever opened it. I have contacted Garmin for a replacement and hope that I just got a unit that came from a bad production lot.

I have read where others have not had any problems which leads me to believe that there may be a production/manufacturing Lot or Batch problem. I hope the replacement that Garmin is sending works for the 1.5 to 2 year expected lifespan of a heartmonitor. High mileage runners (75 to 100+ miles per month) should expect a heartmonitor's lifespan to be in the 1.5 to 2 year range. The other half dozen or so heart rate monitors that I have owned and run with have lasted in that range. The subject monitor here came with my Forerunner 310 and is identical to what is listed in the advertisment.

Good Points: I found this monitor to be very comfortable, easy to take on and off and easy to clean post run. I recommend it and hope that the whatever is going on with some of them, as referenced by the large percentage of negative reviews, runs it course.

Giving Garmin the benefit of the doubt with 3 stars.

title: Sufficient, but not great
text:
For the price, it's a nice radio. It has good sound, good reception, and the USB/SD card feature is handy. But a few little things make this radio a little bit annoying, too.

Small annoyances include the brightness of the display and its readability. It seems to have glare on it no matter what angle the sun or dome light is at, and the blue display is rather dim, so you have to cover the display with your hand just about any time you want to read it during the day. The controls themselves are not too bad, but not entirely intuitive either.

One of the big irritations is that the default display when you are using the USB feature is a slow, cumbersome crawl of the file information. You cannot change the default display to clock, which would have been a reasonable option. You are stuck with a 10 second display of the track number and time, followed by an often inaccurate, slowly scrolling list of the artist, the folder, and the file name. If you press the display button, the clock does come up, but only for 5 seconds. If this unit is replacing your stock radio which housed your car's only clock like mine did, this is especially annoying.

Another irritation is that the random feature is not random. On a road trip, I joked with my wife that the radio really enjoyed file 383. But the joke stopped being funny when I realized that every time I turned on the radio and hit random, it went to file 383. I started keeping track, and it was always the same songs in the same order. Even when I skipped 10 files forward or back, it would play the newly selected song, then go right back to where it was in the "random" list. I did find that if you turn random off then back on again, it would go to a new list, but this, too, was always the same. So your choices are to either hear the same songs over and over, reorganize your memory stick, or turn random off and back on one additional time every time you want your files shuffled. Like I said, the joke stopped being funny.

Overall, for a cheap replacement radio, it has a good number of options, installs easily, and has good sound. Unfortunately, the little irritations add up every time you use the radio, and it leads to car frustration very quickly. If even a few of these were fixable, I'd heartily recommend this radio for anyone. But as it is, unless you are a patient person who just needs cheap USB/SD capability, this radio might not be for you.

UPDATE: After less than 3 months in the car, the trim on the faceplate is peeling off, the buttons are loose, and the USB port has broken on the inside. I've never had a stereo fall apart like this before. I would highly recommend a different kind of radio since it looks like I'll be replacing this one.

title: Imperfect, yet irreplaceable. You can work around the drawbacks.
text:
I've been using these wireless SleepPhones for a year, and can't do without them. I'm sensitive to sounds and even light snoring drives me out of my mind. Soothing sleep music plus the muffling effect of the headband helps block it all out -- but the thought of tossing and turning with wires wrapping around my neck wasn't appealing! Bluetooth to the rescue.

As others have said, this product feels a bit slapped-together, an ingenious but kludgy solution. Recharging is especially annoying; you practically have to disembowel the thing to charge it, and I'm kind of amazed mine still works after doing that hundreds of times. But it does work, and there's simply no comparable product on the market.

The key thing to know: **Do not set your device to play continuously all night long.** If the headphones run out of power, they don't just shut off. Alas, a loud recording speaks straight into your ears, awakening you to tell you it is powering down. (Huge, huge design flaw, please fix!) But frankly, it's probably not a good idea to play music continuously all night long anyway, right? Just set your device to a timer or sleep mode and let it stop after 45 minutes or an hour. If you wake up during the night you can start it again.

title: Charger Not As Advertised
text:
The 1-star rating isn't for the product, it's for Amazon. Like several other people I ordered what I thought to be a compact travel charger with retractable plug as advertised by Amazon. Instead, I received one with the BC-TRV model number but with a power cord. The carton had been opened, instruction sheet was missing, and one of the 4 metal battery charging connectors was bent. It was obviously either used and returned or Amazon was selling factory "scratch & dent" rejects. But why the power cord? I proceeded to spend a good deal of time trying to find out if it was an actual Sony product or a fake. I could find no such Sony product with a cord on my web searches. Finally I contacted Sony support and received the following...

"Thank you for contacting Sony Support. I understand your concern regarding the power cord supplied with the Travel Charger. The BC-TRV released in the U.S and Canada has retractable power plug. However, the model released outside North America has power cord included. Based on the information you've provided, it appears that the unit you received was a non-U.S model. Please check the power specifications before using it. Note: BC-TRV was released in USA on 2/15/2010. Thank you for understanding."

Sure enough, I went to the Sony-Hong Kong website, typed in BC-TRV and there it was...charger with power cord. So why is Amazon advertising a domestic (retractable plug) charger and selling international (power cord) product? We'll never know. Some people may actually prefer the corded version. The power specs were ok and I could have used it, but its not what I wanted/expected. Maybe Amazon should advertise both. But they didn't. What they did only caused confusion and distrust in purchasing from them in the future.

Having said all this, I give them 5-stars for ease of exchanging the product. I did receive the correct charger but haven't used it yet. Hopefully it will work fine. Bottom line...this should never have happened.

title: Excellent GPS - but test it well before keeping it
text:
9-4-12. I bought my first Garmin nuvi 2595LMT 5-Inch Portable Bluetooth GPS Navigator with Lifetime Maps and Traffic device because my Garmin nuvi 650 is 5-years old and would not accept the full US maps due to small memory size. The first nuvi 2595LMT unit was very slow to load, draw and update maps. It was also very inaccurate as to matching an address correctly, although the coordinates were correct (e.g., my home was indicated as 1000 feet away from where the address is). Applying all updates and running Garming diagnostics only improved it by 50%. I had delayed buying a new GPS unit until resolution of the Light-Squared (LS) FCC decision concerning whether the proposed LS network would interfere with global positioning systems - effectively making them useless.

9-24-12. The Garmin Repair advised to return my first unit to Garmin for a "rebuilt" unit replacement. For $242, I don't think so. I returned it to Costco where I got it and bought another identical unit. The new unit performs perfectly - fast and accurate - as it is suppossed to do. Map loading is about 15 seconds; route calulations (25 mile city area) completed in 7 seconds; undates as I drive are less than 2-3 seconds. All the features appear to work, but I haven't tried them all yet. Initial accuracy for my home to map location is only off by 200 ft, but that should improve as the unit is accessible to the GPS satellites for a few hours. The satellites are 23,400 miles from earth in fairly stationary orbits. The mathematical calculations that a GPS unit has to perform are really incredible and this unit does them very fast. At the moment I'm delighted with my second and "good" performing unit, but I detracted 1-star because of the quality control issue with the first one.

I recommend that anyone buying this unit thoroughly test it before the 30-day amazon.com return policy expires. If it isn't working excellently, return it for another one.

title: Solid Camera for the Informed
text:
First, you must know what you are getting into when you buy/use this camera.

WHAT IT IS NOT: this is not a DSLR replacement for use at high ISO's, it will not replace a top end video capable micro-4/3 camera or similar (ex. GH2/GH3), it's AF is not as fast the Olympus OM-EM5, It's sensor is smaller than m/43 but larger than the average point & shoot and other bridge cameras. It is NOT for pixel-peepers.

NOTE/CAVEAT: If you have a body with a serial number starting with the numbers 21 or 22, this is an old production unit and will most likely have the noted (in other reviews) sensor blooming and lens issues. I have a SN 23X.... (replaced by Fuji with a new camera) and it is perfect for these two issues.

WHAT THIS CAMERA EXCELS AT:
1) Good ISO performance for sensor size up to ISO 800, 1600 useable.
2) Excellent MANUAL zoom, silky smooth. Note, it does have a rubber gasket you can hear (internally) if you put your ear up to it - this is a good thing.
3) Optics are sharp, contrasty and the lens alone is worth the price IMO. f/2.8-5.6 is nice for the range.
4) The FPS is nice an speedy if you need it
5) Shoots full HD, but does not have full manual control, but for most causal video people this isn't an issue. If you are a video enthusiast, look elsewhere.
6) Great Fuji auto-white balance
7) Great Fuji colors
8) Full manual control on the photographic side of the camera
9) Weather sealed to a certain level - although not completely. Ex. There ARE seals in the lens, battery door, connection port door, SD card door, ,etc. I cannot confirm seals internally around knobs. The Canadian Fuji site called it sealed, but the USA site does not. Keep this in mind.
10) The body, while large, is a joy to hold and use, high quality feel vs. the cheaper plastic cameras
11) The EVF is great IMO - nice and large, comparable to my old Panasonic GH1
12) Nice built in flash that is pretty powerful for its size (good to about 20') with excellent exposure

Overall, if you are a photo enthusiast who KNOWS how to get the most from a camera and is willing to learn this camera inside and out it can be very rewarding and is in a class of it's own overall. BUT, if you are looking for a more consumer oriented fun bridge with some better video, look at the Panasonic FZ200 or step up to micro 4/3.

For daylight shooting, this beast is excellent and I do not miss my DLSRs at all. It's AF is quick to lock (with the newer serial numbers IMO) and I've successfully used it for action as well. Overall, for what you get for you money, I don't think you can go wrong. YES, you can get better IQ with a DSLR body. But the tele lenses you will get are slower on the short end (f/3.5) and will put the cost higher in the end if you want to keep cost down. Sure, you could match the DSLR to a nice 70-200mm f/2.8 lens and it would smoke the X-S1, but those lenses are $1000+. For the PACKAGE, it's a great option.

This camera is not the only camera I shoot with, for ultimate image quality, I prefer my Fuji X100 which is a stellar performer. I've shot with many high end DSLR's and some of the best glass around and that's the background for this review. For what it is, the X-S1 is very nice!

title: Great value, but this lens is not for everybody.
text:
I've only spent an hour or so testing this lens, but so far I'm quite happy with it.

But be realistic, this is NOT an "L" class lens, nor is it "fast glass"! For $100 (in round numbers), however, it is fairly decent.

First, be sure to order an adapter that fits YOUR camera to go with it. For my Canon T3i, I got a fotodiox product, which has worked fine.

Also, as you may wish to keep the adapter attached to your lens for convenience, get yourself an extra cover for the back of Canon lenses (cheap!), or whatever brand of
camera you have. The back cover that comes with this lens will NOT fit your adapter!

I've gotten nice, shsrp, even impressive images on this overcast day in the Washington, D.C. suburbs, but focusing IS a bit difficult. You might want to focus with the "Live View" screen, if that lets you "zoom in" even further to nail that focus.

I probably would not recommend this lens for trying to get your kid's winning soccer goal or pan after race cars unless you are really good with your focus. The Depth of Field is too shallow and your exposure is governed solely by the shutter speed, which won't be all that fast in most cases and will vary as you turn in relation to your light.

But if you want to get stationary or relatively slow moving objects, you'll be fine.

I've gotten a couple of decent handheld shots with support for my elbows, but using a sturdy tripod and a remote shutter release (or timer) is advisable.

No appreciable spherical or chromatic aberration that I've noticed, but I haven't shot under a wide range of conditions yet. A hood might be a good investment if you're going to be out in the bright sun.

For the price, it is hard to beat.

title: Small camera, big image quality
text:
The Fuji X-M1 sits in the entry segment of the X series models but this one has the unique X-Trans CMOS sensor (the X-A1 has a normal bayer sensor) in other areas though these models are the same (controls/functions etc)

Being an entry model there are a few compromises here, firstly the most obvious one is the lack of viewfinder, secondly controls have been streamlined over higher end models and this doesn't feature the newer on sensor phase detect autofocus of the X-T1 (contrast AF here) despite this the camera still manages to achieve a very small size (very similar to the X10/20 compacts in fact slightly smaller) and it has most of the important requirements aspiring shooter might want.

I've been testing the camera extensively for a while now and made up a quick fire list of some of the better points and weaker areas of the camera. The camera is a good one overall though like most cameras does have some areas that could be better.

Good points:
+ Excellent image quality easily as good if not better than equivalent rivals (with a similar sensor size) Tonality is very appealing and attractive (very subjective but I like it)
+ Huge latitude in raw files both highlight and shadow end with outstanding low light performance very minimal noise
+ Build is solid despite being plastic feels well put together no poor joints or creaking at the seams
+ Full manual controls quite good customisation and menus
+ Autofocus is good for accuracy in most cases (it's reasonably quick though can't match DSLR's for speed)
+ Start up is quick and the camera is responsive with no signs of lag
+ Fairly good buffer around 10 shots raw and about 31 jpegs at full resolution, able to take some advantage of faster cards too
+ Continuous shooting rate of 5.6fps is decent (note the points about AF)
+ Large clear 3.0” LCD is the same aspect ratio as the sensor (3:2) and sharp with a 920k resolution as well as partially articulated (up and down positions) option to brighten it up for daylight shooting (it's a bit reflective though quite clear in most light)
+ Battery life is quite good for a compact sized camera (I got about 390 shots per charge) flash use will shorten this
+ Q menu is well laid out and avoids trips into the main menu system for most common settings
+ Fn button can be user set, C position on the mode dial allows for a memory of settings to be stored (shame it is only one)
+ Hot shoe allows the use of dedicated flashes or other accessories, built in flash extends a decent bit though power is a little low (GN 7)
+ Consistent metering and white balance required little intervention for most shooting
+ Excellent flash exposures (though will increase the ISO if you let it a little too much)
+ Manual focus “peak” is useful though could use more colours (red/yellow)
+ Video is acceptable for a consumer level camera reasonable details and resolution and decent microphone quality, limited options though (you can set aperture before you start but not adjust it during recording) see cons on “moire”
+ Good in camera raw conversions you can adjust quite a few settings too (this creates jpegs from raw files but it's handy to have)

Weaker areas:
- No viewfinder, and no option to add one, no AEL button (Fn can be programmed for this)
- Continuous autofocus/tracking is weak (cannot re-focus after the first shot on cont AF) not a good choice for sports/action shooters (though with pre-focus techniques and some skill it might work)
- Raw not available for ISO 100 or above ISO 6400 (jpeg only)
- Jpegs overly contrasty by default and don't exploit the dynamic range of the sensor (adjusting the shadow/highlights to -1/-2 helps quite a lot) tendency to crush blacks
- Macro button fairly pointless (would be better to have a Fn 2 custom button)
- Battery/memory card slot is covered when on a tripod you can't change either (poor location)
- Card write light covered by your thumb
- Video shows moire and false colours when repeating patterns are in footage
- No dedicated button for ISO (you can set the Fn button to this), movie button cannot be re-programmed
- No “sweep panoramic mode” and no level gauge both are strange omissions, black and white doesn't have the filters either (red/yellow etc)
- 3 scene modes on the mode dial are wasting space, better to put them all in the SP setting (where the other scene modes are) This area would be better reserved for extra user settings
- “Top” control dial is a bit easy to move (can mean exposure compensation is engaged by accident)
- Flash exp compensation buried in the main menu cannot be assigned to the Fn1 button
- Wi-fi has limited use you can send images to devices (even a pc if the software is installed) you can Geotag images too, you cannot control the camera via the Fuji remote app which is disappointing. No option to turn this off (which could conserve battery power)
- No electronic shutter (full mechanical) though it's not obtrusive sound wise

Notes:

If you don't have any lenses the “kit” 16-50mm F3.5-F5.6 is well worth getting I've done a separate review on this lens it's very good optics wise and offers a nice wider angle field of view (equivalent to 24mm)

Unlike some compacts there is no built in memory so you'll need an SD card
Raw files average at around 24MB, which is on the large side for a 16mp camera

Video:
You have a choice of only two resolutions 1920 x 1080 @ 30fps this is for some reason limited to 14 minutes time
1280 x 720 is also @30fps but recording time is 27 minutes.
AF is available in continuous though it does fine don't expect miracles esp in lower light or tracking it's not unsatisfactory for this type of camera though. Moire and false colours are an issue so this isn't going to really suit very serious video shooters, but it does fine for quick clips.

The supplied strap is a thin “pleather” type affair it does the job (same as the X10/X20 cameras) but a fabric one is preferable.

Dynamic range modes:
There are Auto, 100%, 200%, 400%
The camera will raise the ISO levels up to ISO 800 for DR 400%, (and ISO 400 for DR 200%)
In most cases DR Auto does a good job, but DR 200% is fairly safe too the camera won't show massive noise problems at all even at ISO 800.

You do get some useful "one touch" controls if you press and hold the following buttons in:
DISP/BACK: this engages the "quiet mode" this disables the sounds/flash if raised and the AF assist light
Q Button: Brightens the LCD to high levels for use in harsh sunlight
Menu/OK: This locks the 4 buttons around the Middle Menu button (and disables the video button) to stop accidental button presses

When the X-M1 first arrived last year it was fairly expensive and that might have put people off trying one, however fast forward about to the present time it's now at levels similar to budget DSLR's. In terns of what's on offer this is a solid offering, but bear in mind that the main advantages of this are the smaller size compared to a DSLR, it can't offer the same autofocus performance and that's an important point for moving subjects, also the size advantage tends to disappear once you use larger focal length lenses (which are no smaller than their DSLR equivalents) Look at what you needs are. If you're a heavy phone user and want a big step up in quality, the sensor in this camera will destroy even the most expensive phone camera, with ease.

There is a 27mm f2.8 pancake lens which when paired with this body makes for a very compact machine (albeit with a fixed focal length) I've yet to test that lens but it's an option for some if you want to keep the size down.

The biggest attraction is probably the sensor which is very capable and responds well to raw processing, it's certainly a huge step up from a tiny sensor compact in image quality. Even premium compacts will fall behind this, but bear in mind when paired with the 16-50mm lens you don't have very good close up ability and the lens is slower esp the telephoto end. If you shoot a lot of macro or close up photos a premium compact with a fast lens might be a better choice.

On the other hand if you are into experimenting a little you can acquire a lens adapter and though manual focus and aperture control you can mount and use many lenses (there is an M mount Fuji adapter available and lots of third party ones for other lens mounts) this means that even if you are invested in an SLR system you could find a use for this body with your lenses. For newer users or those keen to keep the size down this is a very viable alternative to a DSLR, but it's not for everyone (action shooters) Grip wise a little small here I find a DSLR more comfy to hold for longer periods, everyone is unique though small suits some better than others.

Couple of odd points firstly leaving out the sweep pano and some of the newer film effects (and B&W filters) strikes me as strange considering the target market for the camera, it's also a shame to see no electronic level gauge this featured on the X series compacts. Controls are fairly logical though would benefit from an additional Fn button to program, you also can't turn off the “guide” which might annoy some more seasoned users (this describes the scene/modes on screen) Wi-fi is under exploited and Fuji could look at this not having remote control of a Wi-Fi camera is puzzling. The rear control dial is in an unusual location and takes a while to get used to, it also can be pushed for some settings as well as rotated.

At the default settings jpegs are a bit harsh for my liking (too much contrast and dynamic range is a bit weak) adjusting the shadow/highlight tone helps no end. It's also worth experimenting with the DR settings to get the best out of the camera. If you are working with raw then the X-Trans CMOS has some impressive latitude in both ends able to recover highlights and pull shadows aggresively without a major impact on images. Either way jpeg and raw shooters will be impressed with the camera

I would like to see a few things tweaked and maybe Fuji will get around to adding a sweep pano and some more film modes. The lack of viewfinder is a shame too even a basic one would be welcomed (or the option to add one) it’s down to personal use on that with lighter smaller lenses the lack of viewfinder isn't a massive loss (it's certainly easier to hold a camera stability wise with a viewfinder), but it becomes awkward if you start to use heavier or longer focal lengths.

Overall the X-M1 is a very decent offering and certainly likely to appeal a lot more at this price level, despite the flaws it's a capable camera and more than able to hold it's own image quality is as good as you can get with an APS-C sensor.

title: Ask Seller if it's Retail version or OEM version
text:
The main reason I wanted to write this review was to help people and give them a heads up on the packaging- Depending on who the seller is, you may get an OEM version of this product (no software, cables, etc), or a retail version (includes software, cables, etc). This information can make or break some people's decision to purchase this or not. It does not matter whether or not amazon.com fulfills the order or not. I ordered the first time through "green source technology" (aka IT Frontier on their seller page). It came with the drive only. No instructions, manual, etc. The order was "fullfilled by amazon.com" with prime shipping. I was expecting the manual and software becuase some of the reviews stated it came with it. So I returned it. I decided to give it another shot and order again when I noticed it was available again. This time it was being sold by "Genesis Trade" (Aka E-society according to their seller page). This time it was the retail version that included software (powerdvd which plays DVDs blu rays as well as burning software) and the cables and manual. So the lesson is- contact the seller to make sure you are getting the OEM or retail version. I hope this helps some people as I know this makes a difference to some people.

In terms of the player itself, I am very happy. Very fast reads/writes although I don't recomend this if you are using it as an external drive with an enclosure. To me, the speeds became obsolete going through USB so if you do that, may as well get a lesser drive if you are not going to use it to full capabilities anyway. I am not a big fan of the power dvd/cyberlink software it came with as it comes with a lot of annoying opt ins for advertisements (email info on their products), prompts to upgrade to later versions for more money, etc. The actual interface and play capability is okay. I am also more used to the arcsoft media players software interface also but that may be personal preferance. One thing to note is that you don't need any software for the drive to be reckognized and installed by Windows 7. It will read discs right away. (software needed to play media though). I have a feeling that different sellers may have different software included with the drive as well which goes back to the first lesson learned (contact seller if you need to know exactly what's in the box).

One other tidbit for the less than 1% that this may matter to- if you are using the included software to watch blurays, it won't work if you have a multi screen Eyefinity setup. You need to disable the eyefinity first and then watch the blu-rays. It is possible that upgraded versions of this software may have this fixed.

I hope this information helps.

title: Great iPod Alternative
text:
I bought this particular player because I was tired of being tied to the Apple ecosystem. Anytime I wanted to put new songs, videos, playlists, etc on my old iPod I would be prompted to download iTunes, sync with iCloud, check out the newest U2 album, pledge allegiance to Steve Jobs and check in with all the various other services that come with Apple. It was frustrating, annoying and all I wanted to do was plug in my device, drag a recently downloaded song to it and be on my way.

Enter, SanDisk's Sansa Clip. This device, similar to the Android counterparts of Apple's iPhones, just works and comes without all the extras that you don't need. The device came with a disc of Rhapsody that you are encouraged, but not required, to install but I opted to stick with the music player already installed on my PC and it worked just fine. You plug the device in via the USB cable provided, your computer will recognize it as a flash drive or within the music player you have and you just drop in your mp3s. Easy peasy and you don't have to go through all the unnecessary prompts and/or software updates that bother you with Apple products.

Other things worth mentioning:
User Interface - I was worried that the screen and menus would be a little too old-school-y for me, but it really is nicely done. The screen is responsive and decent enough quality for what is needed. I don't know why I worried about this, but I did initially before purchase. I'm pleasantly surprised, currently.

Built-On Clip - This was a big plus. The clip built on the back is invaluable to me, as I use this purely for the gym and/or running. I had to buy separate cases and bands for my iPod, but this is usable out of the box without any accessories. Big plus.

Battery Life - Because the screen is lower-key than the iPod Nano's I used previously, the battery is able to last MUCH longer. I've honestly not had to charge it yet and I've had it for about a month now, using it 4+ times a week for an hour or so each session.

Lock Screen - This device has a built in lock functionality that is nice for unintentional song changes and battery saving. Just need to long-press the home button and away you go. This is part of the reason I've gone a month without charging.

That's about all that comes to mind at this point. Again, this is a great, no-frills device that is absolutely perfect if you're looking for something to play music and only play music. It just works.

title: Nice Keyboard
text:
I'm typing this review on this keyboard. It is very nice once you get used to the key arrangements and the feedback. Coming from a long time on regular keyboards, it took me a little while to get used to a mechanical keyboard again. My only major gripe with it is that some of the keys touched each other when it first arrived and I had to bend some of them a bit to keep them apart.

If you are mostly a mouse clicker, the following nitpicks won't affect you much. If you use Emacs, Photoshop or use extensive keyboard shortcuts for anything else, the following may prove worth noting.
1. The spacebar isn't just shorter than normal, it isn't centered. The 4.5-key width bar is easier to get use to if you tab out spaces with the left thumb, whereas right thumb-ers might need to search a bit initially. To give you an idea, the bar's right end is flush with the N key. (Typical keyboard spacebars are 6+ keys wide. Good laptop spacebars are 5+ keys wide. All of them at least partially cover the M key to the right.)
2. Right Ctrl key isn't flush to the right edge of the main area to make room for the directional keys. Shortcut junkies who use right Ctrl will need some practice.
3. Esc key isn't flush to the top left and there are no spaces between the function keys on the top row.
4. 0 on the number pad is also half width to make room for the directional keys, so right thumb-ers beware.

title: Overall Great Trackball that's Improved with New Driver Software
text:
I've been holding off on this trackball for a long time, mostly due to the mixed reviews and expensive price.

Recently I decided to pull the trigger and am glad I did. The trackball is a pleasure to use and I have found it to be very accurate with a little tweaking. There was some squeaking from the ball when I first started to use it, but it didn't take long before that went away. The build quality overall feels very good and the tracking is smooth.

Many criticisms of this trackball from years ago is regarding the customization and the software. From my experience this has changed greatly over time as Kensington has greatly improved their software.

With their latest drivers and TrackballWorks (from their site) you can change the tracking settings, scrolling speed, button mapping, and more. The updated software addresses all these criticisms.

Unlike previous Kensington Trackballs there is no scroll wheel or scroll ring. Scrolling is performed by turning the ball clockwise or counterclockwise. You can also set a button to be the middle (3rd) mouse button for scrolling by holding the middle mouse button and moving the trackball to scroll in some applications. Some people may not like this, but I found that it works well for me.

As someone with signs of possible developing carpel tunnel I find this with a palm rest is a nice combination and change from a mouse and at least helps a bit. If you have trouble moving your wrists a lot you might find that this is more comfortable than a mouse. You still need to move your fingers to operate the ball, of course. As someone who's young (26) this is something I want to start addressing before it becomes a significant problem.

Sometimes you can find this trackball on sale. Even so, it can still be a bit expensive, even after being on the market for several years. If you like large trackballs or find mice uncomfortable it's worth trying however. Another alternative to this trackball is the Kensington Expert Mouse Trackball, which is similar but with a different body and a physical scroll ring.

I still mostly use a mouse for things like gaming, but for eight hours a day I'm on a computer at work and I'm using the Trackball for that. After using it for a few months I may write an update on my ongoing feelings.

title: Inexpensive, very functional, easy to use.
text:
This little camera is great. It does everything cameras costing 2 ~ 3 times as much will do, while being one of the least expensive out there. The fact it comes with a 4G MicroSD card included is what clinched my purchase.

The box came with a page of instructions on how to switch the language of the screen menu from ?Chinese? to English. If it weren't for that I might be less happy. It's only necessary to set it up once then just leave it alone. Still there are 4 buttons to be used in the correct sequence. Without English labeling it would have been a long frustrating nuisance, instead of a simple 2 minute deal.

I first used the suction cup mount with the idea that I would switch to the permanent one later, but so far the "temporary" suction mount is so nice that I haven't bothered to do the switch.

The camera automatically comes on when the car engine is started. Video is saved in approximately 2min consecutive clips until the SD is full, I didn't actually count how many clips that is but I'd guess around 10. Then it loops around saving the newest on top of the oldest. That means there is a recording of approximately the previous 20 minutes of your trip always available. Although it is divided up into 2 min clips. There is supposed to be a G-force sensor that would detect an accident and stop recording, so that video would be saved - not recorded over. I haven't tested that feature yet.
It doesn't instantly stop recording when the engine is turned off. There's about a 22 second delay before shutoff. During which it continues recording on it's own internal battery (that also keeps the time and date). Presumably so if there was a catasrophic situation where the cars electric power is cut, but there's there's still interesting stuff going on, this camera would catch at least the next 22 seconds of it.

It's quick simple and easy to pop the SD chip out and put it in the card reader of my computer when I want to view a playback of the video. There is a USB cable included with the unit, but I cannot imagine dismounting the entire camera and bringing it in to hook up to the computer instead of just the MicroSD.

I failed to notice at first that there is a switch underneath to select between higher and lower resolution recording modes. So for the first several days I was in the lower quality mode. It was nothing great, but I thought it was OK. When I did switch to the higher quality I didn't think it was that much super better. I assume people will understand that if they buy one of the least expensive cameras out there, they are not going to get the highest possible resolution quality. It's respectable and reasonable. You cannot read license plate numbers of cars speeding by in the other lane though. On the other hand, the 150degree wide viewing angle is one of the highest of any camera I saw. Without any obvious "fisheye" effect. You will record more of what's going on around your car, albeit in just average quality, than with any other camera.

The camera itself can be rotated to face either forward looking ahead through the windshield or back at the interior of the car. I can imagine why someone like a taxi driver might want to record what's happening inside the car, but I bought this to use as an accident camera facing ahead out at the other traffic. It seems to automatically orient "up" either way.
There are 8 infrared LEDs for low light video recording. They are adequare for illuminating the interior of the car. I couldn't image LEDs lighting up the road ahead of the car - and they don't. This is not a "nightvision" camera. It does a somewhat decent job of "low light" recording. It doesn't do no light. If your cellphone camera has video recording capability, then this is probably similar.

Even though I've had this camera for over a month I find myself still checking out the video on the screen while I'm driving. This is pretty silly since the screen is just displaying the same scene as looking straight ahead. It's distracting. There is the option of turning the screen off, and I should, but I haven't yet.

Overall I'm very happy with this camera. It has every feature I wanted and some I hadn't even thought of. The low price, good quality, ease of use, make it a great value.

title: Fantastic sound, great value!
text:
Bottom line: these cans are fantastic. Based on a review from The Wirecutter, I sprang for them, and for the past two months consecutively, give or take, I've worn them roughly thirteen to fourteen hours daily with virtually no fatigue. With a smaller, oval-shaped head, the fit is fantastic - snug but not clampingly painful. They arrived well-packaged and have held up swimmingly under dusty, but otherwise fairly standard, desk job conditions.

Sound-wise, of course, well worth every penny. Used with the analog-out of a modded HTC One M8 (no BoomSound or Clari-Fi enabled), the M4U 1s helped me rediscover nuances in Steve Davis's cymbal work on The Lynne Arriale Trio's "Home" album. Paired with a FiiO E17 DAC+amp (and/or an E12 amp) attached to a standard PC (the computer having fairly non-descript integrated "high-def audio" chips), these things really bring out Sean Reinert's and Sean Malone's amazing interplay on Cynic's most recent three releases, particularly on "Traced in Air." The M4U 1s make Photay's recent work sound as if you're right there, too. By themselves, the soundstage is more expansive, with clarity across bass, mids, and trebles without being overly boomy or sibilant.

As with many "step-up" headphones, you may realize that lossy compression (mp3 and so on) doesn't cut it if you really want to enjoy music, or heck, sounds. While the M4U 1s don't necessarily make you screech in horror at the noticeable distortion from source, you may find yourself reaching for CDs or DVDs (or their rips) as opposed to normal or even "extreme" streaming music.

In short, the M4U 1s are a superb value, and I eagerly anticipate many thousands of hours of sonic journeys with them.

title: Absolute rubbish. Avoid Asus Android tablets.
text:
I upgraded from a TF101 because I liked it so much. But I had rooted the TF101 and the ROM I used was speedy. The TF700 was fast and responsive until it started filling up, and three months out, it's so slow that it's turned into a svelte Amherst gray brick. When I do need to use the tablet, I have to wait about 10 minutes for the tablet to become usable. Whenever any app is updating in the background, the tablet is unusable. Whenever a background process is running (for instance, Gmail sync), the tablet is unusable. Whenever I type an email, the lag is so great that sometimes an entire sentence will appear several seconds after I typed it.

I'm still waiting for Asus to provide an official update to the TF700 with Android 4.3, but that hasn't happened and I've lost patience. To save on costs, Asus used the cheapest, slowest storage it could find on the market, which is a bottleneck for the rest of the otherwise top-of-the-line tablet (Tegra 3, bright HD LCD, premium finish, etc). Android 4.3 brings TRIM support. TRIM is a routine that runs in the background to track used blocks on your computer's storage, so the unused blocks can be rewritten efficiently. So I could root this device, void the warranty, and use a ROM that's much faster, or wait until Asus gets around to updating this tablet to a version of Android that's already 6 months old.

title: Defective unit?
text:
This little speaker has been frustrating me from day one. Since my experience is far worse than other Vine reviewers, I suspect my device itself is defective.

It looks very nice and is rather substantial. No worries about it tipping easily or getting blown over in the wind. And it's not too big to carry around in a pocket. One down-check: it does not include an AC adapter and comes with the shortest USB cable I have ever seen.

The speaker set up is straight forward. It pairs quickly with every Bluetooth-capable device I own with a verbal confirmation. Its sound quality is average at best. For its size, I expected something with more volume and clarity.

That's where my positive experience with this speaker ends, however. It randomly shuts itself off with no verbal indication of what's wrong. It will say "powering off" when it's idle too long or "ready to be paired" if it's awaiting a connection, but I get neither of these verbal cues. At first, I thought the problems might be due to a low battery. The LED is supposed to flash red when the battery is low, but I never saw it do this. In any event, it did not seem to be the source of the problem because it repeatedly shuts off within minutes of use after a full night's charge. This happens with all my devices so it's not an iOS or Android-related problem. I would test it with an aux cable if I had one, but that sort of defeats the whole purpose of a Bluetooth speaker.

If this speaker operated perfectly, I'd give it three stars. It's priced too high for the average experience it offers. Of course, that's also colored by my poor impression of its operation. I've contacted their customer service and have shipped the speaker back to them with the hopes I can have this issue resolved. Leaving the rating at 3 stars for now...

UPDATE 11/6 -- two months have now passed since returning the item. To their credit, I received a complimentary pair of their JAM Transit bluetooth earbuds for the inconvenience of returning my item. Unfortunately, I've heard nothing more from them. I've dropped my rating to 1 star. If this hadn't been a Vine freebie, I'd be seriously upset with their customer service at this point.

UPDATE 12/2 -- still no response from the company regarding the status of the speaker. In light of this, I cannot recommend any products from them and will not purchase from them in the future.

title: Absolutely love it!
text:
I've had the Marantz 6007 for about a month and absolutely love it. From the superb, compact and light design to the simple set-up, to the clean, crisp GUI (Graphical User Interface aka the menus), to the clear, warm sound, the Marantz 6007 has exceeded my expectations. $1,200 is a lot to spend on a receiver, and there are great options at lesser price points that are worth looking into. But I've found everything I wanted (and more) in the Marantz 6007.

The ease of set-up can't be overstated. Simply turn it on and it guides you through the connection of all your components and speakers. In all it took less than half an hour. This is my first "networked" receiver, and I never knew what I was missing. Along with the ability to update firmware (there have already been two since I purchased the unit), you get connectivity to Internet Radio, Pandora and Spotify among others (Spotify was a hugh selling point for me). Hopefully we'll get Netflilx and MLB.tv in the future...

The Apple App Store / Google Play remote app is a great bonus. I find myself using the app (on an iPhone) more often that I could have anticipated and haven't had any problems. The design and interface could be a little smoother, but you'll get used to it rather quickly. There's a handy info button to click on from the home screen that helps you understand all the options and how to customize the shortcuts. The app is especially nice for controlling volume from throughout the home and switching to networked apps. I most often use it to switch between Spotify playlists. Doing so with the unit's remote is a little cumbersome, especially when doing searches, as you're stuck with an old fashioned alphabet grid and you must select one character at a time. Whereas on the app, you have use of your phone's keyboard. Of course, the receiver also has Apple AirPlay, so you can stream music from your phone or iTunes library on your computer. It all works like a charm.

The unit does not have Wi-Fi, so you'll need to connect it to an ethernet cable to use AirPlay, networked options and the remote app (which itself still requires Wi-Fi to work, which I find strange, but I'm sure there's a technical explanation I'm not aware of!). My modem is on another floor, so I used a [[ASIN:B001AZUTCS Netgear 85Mbps Powerline Network Adapter Kit - XETB1001]]. If you follow the instrustions for setting up the adapter (e.g., you can't plug them into a power strip), you'll have no problems. I've never once lost connectivity with my Marantz 6007.

The sound on the Marantz is clean and warm. In fact, I almost find it a little too warm for the style of music I listen to (thrash and heavy metal). I prefer a little more punch. But the unit really shines on other styles of music and movies. I've been incredibly impressed with the sound on albums by the likes of Adele and Mumford & Sons. I'm also not using a subwoofer, so that may have something to do with the lack of punch on heavier music. And of course, there's numerous options to adjust the sound. I strongly suggest carefully reading through the Audyssey section (page 113) of the manual. The Audyssey setup, by the way, worked flawlessly. The measurments were accurate and the sound levels were considerably better balanced than on previous receivers I've used it on.

This is most noticible during TV programs. The Dynamic Volume for the most part solves the problem of sound variations between quiet and loud passages, without neutering or compressing the sound quality too much. And again, you can adjust the level of compression. With a baby on the way, the quality of this feature will be great for low-volume listening!

All in all, I enthusiastically rate the Marantz 6007 five stars. It's easy to use (dare I say it's idiot proof?!), but be sure to read through the manual (available on disc or download from the Marantz website as a PDF document) to best understand all the tweaks and options. It looks beautiful physically and has a great GUI. The AirPlay and networked options are incredibly convenient. As I sit upstairs writing this review, I'm using my iPhone to listen to various tracks via Spotify. It produces great sound, especially if you are used to lower priced receivers. And it's even somewhat future proof, with 3D and 4K playback ability and more HDMI inputs than you can shake a fist at. Highly recommended if you love music and movies and want to enjoy them at their fullest in your home.
