title: Great for school Average for travel
text:
Case Logic BEBP-115 Backpack

Pros:
High quality Nylon/Polyester
Lots of well placed pockets:
-Small *phone* pocket on top has nice felt interior
-Smugglers pocket *in bottom of back support* is a nice touch (used for airline tickets)
-Zippers on sides are great for things besides bottles but also keep bottles from moving
-- Mesh within side pockets help adjust to different sized bottles
Vanishing pocket in front is ideal for wallet, keys, etc
Handle on top and bottom (for storing in overhead compartment) seems very well made
Laptop and tablet pockets are well padded (NO problems with bottom padding)
Mesh pockets within other pockets are good for storing small things safely
Great for all types of electronics
Overall design is pleasing NOTE: blue accents on front of bag are little rubber strands
Back/lumbar padding is very generous
No problems with heating on back
Arm straps go all the way across the top and behind neck for added support
Chest strap is great addition
Main compartment could fit at least 3 large textbooks or several books, notebooks, folders
Small front pocket has a number of pockets for pens/pencils, notecards, etc. Even has pocket for individual pen (great for fountain pen or high end pen)
Velcro helps keep adjustment straps from dangling in front of you

Cons:
EDIT*** The shoulder straps (as some others have stated) are TOO WIDE. I'm a college male with fairly wide shoulders and while the bag has never slipped off my shoulders, the width gives it the feeling of outward movement. NOT RECOMMENDED FOR FEMALES WHO DO NOT HAVE BROAD SHOULDERS
Zippers could be better. Not bad, but not as good as Swissgear Synergy (best zippers I've ever felt)
- Only laptop pocket zipper is large, others are small
Over filled pockets will cut in to space of others. Clarify: If main pocket is bulging outward it will cut in to the space of the smaller pocket in front of it and make it hard to put pens or other peripheral in.
Not Great for travel:
Bag does not have much outward "give" and therefore not much space for clothing or other things
^^^see above about over filling pockets
Lots of pockets could have you searching for item for a while.
***Small "nitpicks"
- The individual pen/pencil holder does not have a cover over it so if bag is upside down it could slide out
- The vanishing pocket closes when zipped up so you have to make sure that you do in fact zip it all the way up (easier to zip all the way down) I believe they did this so nothing falls out if not zipped all the way up.

Additional information:
The bag is rather light, but since Case Logic's other bags are lighter and have the same pockets I'm going to refrain from calling it a Pro

Thoughts: It's odd that with features like a chest strap and lower front handle that this bag is not great for travel. It just doesn't have the interior size if you plan on taking a trip for few days and use it as a carry on. This bag is certainly more vertical than horizontal and it cuts down on the number of things you can fit in to it. That being said, it is ideal for school/college. With a great number of pockets for electronics, books, and pens/pencils I would definitely recommend it to students.

Overall 3.5/5 I will give it a 4 because I do not think a bag with such high quality materials should be rated at a 3 star

Advice: Buy if you are a student not if you plan to travel a lot. DO NOT PURCHASE IF FEMALE OR MALE WITH SMALL SHOULDERS.

Other bags to look in to:
SwissGear Synergy: Lots of pockets, loved by (Thousands) of users, brilliant zippers, pen pocket has cover -.-, great padding, slightly more space, laptop. Old bag so no tablet holder or lumbar compartment, slightly dated (though fine) appearance. You can't go wrong with this bag (If I needed another I would purchase this)
Case Logic RBP 115: Very similar to BEBP-115 but more space in front pocket (open instead of vanishing pocket, lighter, smaller footprint). Design could be unappealing for some. Probably has same size and zipper shortcomings as BEBP-115
Samsonite Tectonic: Can't say much about this bag because I haven't gotten much hands-on time with it, but people seem to enjoy it and it looks very nice. Samsonite, like Swiss gear and Case Logic is a top class company.

Hope this helped! Will update if there is anything to add or change. If this review helped, please answer "yes" to if this review was helpful. Also, feel free to comment if you have any questions

title: THE ULTIMATE BUDGET PORTRAIT LENS
text:
I love the 85mm focal length for portrairs in general, and feel that at least this much focal length is absolutely needed for "head shot" type portraits to avoid the perspective distortion that a shorter focal length will cause to facial features. In combination with the f1.8 aperture, you can create extremely shallow depth of field. This lens is also very sharp with lots of contrast wide open at f1.8 with no sherical aberration (haze) and minimal chromatic aberration, at a much lower level than lesser lenses.

If you're looking for that legendary portrait look that the Nikon 85mm 1.4 lenses gives us, but your on a budget, this gets you real close.

*EDIT* Just like nearly every G series prime, this is not a fast focusing lens. The only G series prime I've come across that focuses fast like the AFS pro zooms is the 50mm 1.8G.

title: Likely the Cheapest, Most Basic & Conservative Case Available
text:
This is probably one of the best an most conservative looking case for the least amount of money on the market.

Granted, it's shaped ugly and the colors do not match my house interior, but it provides enough air flow for my components and plenty of bays. The case also provides good/adequate wiring routing with places for pulling plastic wire ties through.

I choose to use the more wider wire ties (standard electrician ones from Home Depot) versus the very tiny wire ties the the case manufacturer provides. Using wires ties that are too small can slice through wire.

I enjoyed easily inserting the hard drive into the no-screw mounts. Same with the larger bays, no screws were needed for installing the cdrom/dvdrom.

Plenty of screws. Only other oversight, manufacturer should have given a spare one or two more no-tool required case screws in case a purchaser looses them.

Oh, and side cover no-tool screws, the two holes for securing each metal side appear not to line up well. Purchasers likely will need to apply pressure to the side of the case to get the screws to thread more easily. I also wire brushed some of the paint from the screw threads which slightly helped threading.

I don't like the red power/hdd lights. The red LED fan light will always be switched off. I would have preferred, at the least, blue or even grey lights. About the only time I need a case lit up would be on Christmas with Christmas lights, etc.

Plenty of ports and bays w/ ports on the front. Definitely a good ol' basic case like the old days, but can do without all the eye-candy and teeny-bopper features.

2012.11.03 - I have just installed a Gigabyte GA-Z77X-UP7 Extended ATX board into this case without seemingly any problems. The case's specs only state ATX sized boards, but this E-ATX board, which is only 1.5" wider then a standard ATX board and slightly less wider then E-ATX boards, seemingly fits. I'm not sure if there will be any issues.

2012.11.04 - Users having noise when plugging into the front jacks of this case should probably try disabling the "auto mute" within Alsa Mixer (alsamixer). The rear jack has no noise on the MIC jack. Seems if you want no problems with jacks, should probably install a front case panel with RCA phono or 1/4 inch phone connectors, or the three prong connectors for microphones.

2012.11.06 - It would appear the GA-Z77X-UP7 Extended ATX board, which has less width then a true E-ATX board, can fit quite well within this case. I've viewed the differences with the HAF X and the HAF 922, and the only difference appears to be the HAF X was released later, has >2" more height (between bottom of board and power supply), appears to have 1/4" less width between board and optical drive mounting, SSD inserts into the 3.5" drive bays, Dock-X which cannot be used for 3.5 face plate devices, and led lighting is on the front vs top of case. Everything else with the HAF X appears to be more nuisance for me. Oh, and the HAF X has optional wheels and the front covers can be detached from the front rather then reaching inside the case to release the plastic latches -- this is the reason for the funky front case design. My reasoning for sticking with the HAF 922, save my money for when a more conservative looking case is on the market. For now, everything currently fits and I can still lift the case as it's also 10 lbs. lighter then the HAF X.

2012.11.07 - I followed-up with the above ATX/EATX size difference and the non-stanadard size of the GA-Z77X-UP7 type boards currently on the market today. Although the person at Cooler Master fully acknowledged the size of the GA-Z77X-UP7 (less then EATX size), the person kept insisting the board would have problems fitting inside the case due to the motherboard's size, when in fact, the insides of the space within the two cases were identical except for the extended space at the bottom of the mounted board. Mounting plates were identical in size for the boards and the GA-Z77X-UP7 fit well. I also used a tape measure and realized that there might be an additional 1/4" more space within the 922 in between the right side of the board and the optical drive mounting case - after the board is mounted. Although I dislike the misleading, I enjoy Cooler Master's engineering and design for the ease of install & use features. I also think their still ugly cases, for which a girl would dislike having having such a case within a living room -- unless the living room were within the Death Star or Dark Maul's house. Also, the misleading information caused an increase in shipping costs to remote Fairbanks, Alaska, including shipping an additional case at my cost, for which wasn't needed and will now be returned. This also adds a slight increase in over head at the retail level, including the fact this item was originally shipped from the hurricane ravaged area Harrisburg PA which is ~100 miles in land of the ocean. Although the sales departments were oblivious to foreseeing this, it never pays to mislead or play games.

title: Excellent Case for Samsung ATIV 500t
text:
Like others reviewing this product, I was searching for a case for my Samsung ATIV 500t Smart PC with Windows 8. Found a cheap neoprene case from Target meant for 13.3" MacBooks to use for transportation until I found a suitable case for my needs. Discovered this case in late December 2012 and it was exactly what I was looking for - plus the price was right! Put in my order on Jan 3, 2013 and was part of the Jan 7 shipment of cases. Efficient shipping and delivery despite the backorder of everyone with 500t's purchasing the first "real" case for this device.

Put it on device yesterday (1/15) and was immediately happy with its form and function on the device. I have been using it enough now to see a couple problems with this case - one being the actual design of the case, the other being a problem when interacting with the device.

1) The standing functionality of this case for the tablet is exactly why I bought it. However, the lower angle setup - obtained by letting the 500t auto-rotate the screen 180-degrees from normal - isn't the best. I used it for typing but found that, due to the top becoming the bottom in this orientation (Start button at top of screen), my hands block out the light sensor and fool the sensor into thinking it's in a dark room and, therefore, to dim the screen. In bright locations with overhead lighting (such as a coffee shop), it can be difficult to read the screen when it does this. I solved it by just using the two-hand keyboard so my arm doesn't come close to covering the light sensor. Minor annoyance at worst, but something notable for anyone else purchasing this case and typing with it.

2) This case interacts with the device - something not stated anywhere I see. When the flap is closed on the face of the tablet, it appears to interact with a magnet embedded in the tablet and acts like when the screen on a laptop is closed and then puts it to sleep. An excellent feature resembling what the Microsoft Surface does! However, I am not able to fully use this functionality at this point in time. Upon closing the cover over the screen, the device sometimes gets "hung-up" on going into sleep mode and will not fully go to sleep nor wake - forcing me to force-shut it down with the power button. Major annoyance in this case. Looked through the event logger and kept finding an error associated with the "dptfpolicylpmservicehelper" which, upon further research, is a part of the low power mode (lpm) for the Intel Atom Clover Trail to manage power when under demanding circumstances (i.e. - running heavy programs or lots of programs at once). No other info seems to be available at this time, but some have noted the Dell XPS 12 tablet has similar problems with that component, so hopefully an update will come for that. Until then, I went into the power settings and changed the "What to do when the lid is closed" setting and changed it to "Do Nothing", which allows me to push the power button on the device to put it to sleep, then close the cover across it without any penalty. It does, however, allow it to wake up when the cover is pulled off, so it partially does its job. Since no one else is commenting about this problem, it could be how my tablet is interacting with the case, as I had major bugs right out of the box that have since been cleared up.

Otherwise, the build, appearance, setup and thought put into this case are exceptional! For an under-$20 case, this is well worth the price - even if you upgrade to a "better" one later. Cut-out for the S-pen, well-aligned cut-out for the back camera and flash, ability to access all ports and buttons on the device no problem, hand strap is fully functional and doesn't feel like it will give if whole unit is tipped side-to-side, and elastic strap to keep cover open or closed is a nice feature, especially to supplement the magnets (in closed configuration) to prevent premature opening. Front-facing camera is slightly blocked by a small part of case, but that can be compensated easily. Cover cannot be flipped around to cover the screen while the device is plugged in to the wall due to the charger extending beyond the device 1/2".

If you're on the fence about it - buy it! You'll thank yourself later for having a good-quality, professional-looking case that will protect your 500t Win8 tablet. I've only had it for a day so far and I'm more at ease when I carry it around to class or in the car.

title: Much More Comfortable Than Traditional Earbuds, And Blocks Sound
text:
As I've written in other reviews I have a noisy office, and there is no noise blocking ability to cubicle walls. Loud conversations are constant and when I have to concentrate to work some kind of headphone is a must. Most people in my office use the typical white iPod earbuds. Those kill my ears. Like, pain for days if I wear them for hours. Which I do, forty hours a week.

In my search for silence I purchased these six months ago. Although I did not use them all the time, they have gotten a good bit of use. The sound is amazing. And they are incredibly silent. At first they take a bit of getting used to just because they go far into the ear canal, but not as far as it sounds in the descriptions. They're not touching your brain or anything. But it's more than an earbud. For me, the external ear pain with an ear bud was bad, with these the internal pressure was only bad when I had a bad headache. After hours or days of use my ears would be sore. After a couple days there was no way I would put these in my ears because it was painful. But, I'm pretty sure they don't make these to be worn eight hours a day for five days in a row. I usually switch between external headphones and these even with the pain because the way they are able to keep noise out is wonderful.

Plus, to make it even more comfortable they come with a variety of different "tips" for the headphones. The conical ones shown in the pictures, then spongey kinds and little half circle ones. You're pretty much guaranteed to find the right fit. And they come in a little zippered pouch so you don't lose them.

I'm not going to pretend like these aren't expensive. They are. But when you really need silence and comfort these will do the trick. And if you just like sound quality you'll be pretty impressed as well.

title: The auto focus system is the best I've ever used (never shot with the 1DX)
text:
I've had the EOS 7D Mk II for about a week, and so far it's met every exception I had for it. The auto focus system is the best I've ever used (never shot with the 1DX). It is very responsive even in lower light. Shooting wildlife, it's hard to get a high rate of successful shots, but now I'm getting far more than I had with the original 7D or the 5D mk III. The 65-point cross type AF is perfect for wildlife and sports, and with the new Dual Pixel CMOS AF system, it's faster to boot.
Like the last couple of higher end Canons, the 7D Mk II is very customizable, with options for just about every button on the camera. The first thing I did is change my focusing button to "back focusing", because it works so much better than having the shutter release and the focusing on the same button.
As with other Canon higher ended cameras, the 7D Mk II is built with a lightweight magnesium alloy body that feels very solid and firm in your hands. I never had an issue with the original 7D body before, but the weather seals have been a problem, and the 7D Mk II is maybe the best weather sealed camera Canon offers right now. That's a huge plus for the rainy and snowy outings where you think "maybe I should just stay inside".
The low light performance has been excellent as well, though I've not done much work with the RAW files since Adobe hasn't released the codecs for the new Canon RAW files as of yet. Taking a picture of my cat at ISO 10,000 showed very light pixelation, which is great since anything over about ISO 800 with the older 7D became a worry.
Having the USB 3 and the dual card slots is also a huge plus over the original 7D. Now you can upload files something like 10x faster than with the USB 2, and you can shoot with both or either of the CF or SD cards, and have twice the storage.
The Kit version of this camera comes with the decent but limited 18-135mm IS STM lens. The STM is the new smoother quieter motor in the lens for movie-making that needs a smoother zoom option.
Last but not least, the Canon 7D Mk II comes with a new 20.2 megapixel CMOS that will allow up to as much as 51,200 ISO! That's pretty impressive, and although I haven't shot over 16,000 so far, the results have been very impressive. The flexibility to shoot with a much higher ISO is a huge part of why I bought this camera.
The Canon EOS 7DmkII has become the Wildlife and Sports photographers choice for cameras, with a new AF and 10FPS shooting, for the price, this camera will be very hard to beat.

title: Great buy
text: $10 for 3, prime shipping. This product is the best compromise between the very expensive branded screen protectors and the dirt cheap, just pay for shipping protectors. When reading reviews, keep in mind that air bubbles are caused by specks of dirt. Tiny hairs may cause bubbles at first but they go away after a day or two of use. The bubbles that don't go away are caused by specks of dirt. You have to clean well and even then you cannot expect perfection. This product is a good product, it's your own application that makes a difference. I have purchased enough screen protectors and never understood reviewers who say "there is a reason why these come in packs of 2,3,6 etc" I've always got them on satisfactorily on the first try, with replacements for later. Clean multiple times & use your old protector or tape to pick up stray specks of dirt and lint. I usually peel off the screen protector back completely, and while holding the edges only bend the screen protector and line up the holes for the button and the camera, then let go and smooth out. I've had people at the store do them for me and that's the way they have always done it. It's quick and minimizes the chances of getting dirt on your already clean screen. I'm sure paying more money will get you a fantastic screen protector that won't have bubbles even if there is dirt on your screen, but otherwise you can't find a better compromise than this. I usually stay clear of dirt cheap protectors because they're usually very thin and flimsy, scratch easier and are harder to apply resulting in more bubbles.

title: Do NOT attempt MoCA without it
text:
I thought I'd be smart and avoid buying the filter. After all, the filter must only be for chumps right? Wrong.

Right where the cable enters your house, but BEFORE it gets split anywhere, attach this filter (You can even connect it right onto the splitter). MoCA uses high frequency bandwidth to bounce their signals to each other across your entire house. The filter keeps them to just your house. Think of it as an electronic dam. If you want to get MoCA working in your house, adding the filter is your best bet.

title: 2012 Firmware upgrade causes Netflix to stop working
text:
We originally bought this player because we thought it would stream the internet wirelessly just like a laptop. Of course, if you've read about it, you will know that it uses "apps" that require "firmware" to work for specific sites.

We were originally disappointed to find that Amazon does not have an "app," and therefore we can't access Amazon to stream their content.

However, this player comes with a Netflix button and is supposed to stream Netflix - which it did, albeit clumsily. That is, until Tuesday, June 12, 2012 when they "upgraded the firmware." Now it no longer works, and according to Samsung's customer service, there is no pending upgrade to address the problem.

I spent two frustrating fourty-five-minute chat sessions where the CSRs had me do every diagnostic (I swear, I thought they were going to ask me to sacrifice a live chicken next) and then finally, when I'd reset every single bit of software and deleted and reinstalled Netflix, they told me it was a firmware issue (I had OPENED the chat asking if this was the case) and that there was currently no plan to address the issue.

It's possible that sometime in the future, Samsung will fix this app. However, if anything goes wrong, hope that you have several hours of your life you don't plan to use to offer their customer service department. They'll gladly waste that for you, even if they don't fix the issue.

title: Nothing better regardless of price. If you have no budget this is the one to get!
text:
I was in the market for a new router because I needed gigabit ethernet and my wndr3600 did not have that feature. Adding a gigabit ethernet switch solves the problem for my wired computers but limits wireless to wired transfers to 100mbit instead of the 300mbit wireless maximum. Therefore after plenty of research (lots and lots) I found my way to an ASUS RT-n56u, Netgear 3700, Netgear 3800, Netgear 4000 and even a Buffalo w/ ddwrt and a high end linksys.

With all those routers the big things to decide between was do I get one that can support 450 wireless, do I go for the one with DDWRT (very advanced and powerful firmware), or the one bye a trusted we dont play around kind of company ASUS.

After reading all those reviews I came to the 3800 because of 2 things:
1) 450 wireless adapters are uncommon and are not inside my macbook, my dv7, my ps3, xbox, iphone, or ipad. According to the reviews the 3800 had the absolute highest 300Mbit performance so going with a 450 capable unit would actually degrade my performance until 450 found its way into consumer devices.
2) This unit supports TIME MACHINE which made me very very happy (although after receiving it and learning of its 300GB limitation most of the happiness was gone)

So hear is my detailed review which is broken down into a few categories.

Feature set ***** 5 Stars - As far as features are concerned the only thing missing is 450mbit capability now that would be enough to loose half a star but because almost nothing comes with 450 and this thing will out perform other 450 routers while they are in 300 mode it isn't that big of a deal. Add in the fact that this thing has readyshare cloud (a cloudless feature) and the ability to support Time Machine backup in lion (although only up to 300GB) and that more than makes up for its lack of 450mbit wireless!

Performance ***** 5 Stars - As far as performance is concerned I am quite happy since the only thing that could be faster would be a 450mbit router but if wireless card isn't 450 capable then this router will actually out perform any 450 capable router on the market when they are in 300mbit mode. Since almost nothing comes built in with 450 I decided that it isn't even something important.

Ease of use **** 4 Stars - I am not a big believer in owners manuals. That said I am in the tech world and a lot of my time is spent answering questions that people should not be asking me. I believe people need to consult the manual then do a google search before calling technical support or asking a sales person how to do something. Therefore it is the software engineers and the project managers responsibility to ensure this doesn't happen. There should be something built in that makes it impossible for people to have any issues.

My 2 issues that knock 1 star off when added together.

1) When you plug your modem and computer in this thing should function immediately. If for any reason it wouldn't function a sticker should have been on the device warning you of anything that may stop you up. Netgear did a GREAT job on this router with those bits of information. Such as the default SSID and password which are unique not standard. Unfortunately when I plugged my modem and computer into the router the internet did NOT work immediately. What makes matters worse is entering 192.168.1.1 in the browser did not pull up the router even though ipconfig did show that to be the routers ip address. I had to plug my macbook in and open up its browser to find the router. So for some reason it did not like my PC at first. After my macbook talked to the router my PC could see the internet.

2) I plugged in a usb hard drive and although I really doubted it would work like magic I had my macbook look for a Time Machine. It did not find one which was no surprise. So into the router setting I go! I found nothing in settings that would explain my issue. No Time Machine checkbox, no link to explain the requirements of the time machine nothing NO HELP at all. I had to open the manual and turn to page 83 which explains that the drive must be HFS (but never says HFS) and it must be GUID or MBR. It also explains that you have a max of 300GB back up. This is actually very limited. I have a 500GB HD in my macbook, although it is not full because of the way Time Machine works a computer with just 200GB of data on it could easily end up with a larger than 300GB Time Machine backup. I honestly think that Netgear should work hard to resolve this issue and I also think they should highlight this limitation anywhere the feature is listed.

Unique Features *** 3 Stars - This router has 3 unique features. They are all mediocre at best. I wont bother explaining what the features do just what is wrong
1) Clear Channel - Only important if you are using 2.4GHz instead of 5GHz and you live in a congested area (apartments/condos). Even then advanced reviews have this feature pegged as a possible trouble maker and could even result in lost performance.
2) Readyshare cloud - This is NOT a cloud feature at all. Your files are in a HD plugged into your router a feature that most routers have. Most routers can even grant you access to these files remotely. The difference is instead of having to remember ip addresses that could change and which port to use this program acts as the middle man and makes it so all you need is a user name and password. It is kinda like using some 3rd party remote access program instead of the built in windows desktop sharing. They just make it easier and in case your ISP changes your IP address you wont loose the ability to connect. Do not let yourself think that this is in any way a replacement for true cloud programs that sync files across multiple computers. If netgear adds that ability then even though its still not cloud it will truly be an awesome and unique feature.
3) Time Machine - the need for you to consult the manual is one thing but the 300GB per computer limitation is a big problem when a computer with a mere 200GB of data on it could use up more than 300GB of Time Machine space.

My conclusion: Buy this router if it is in your price range. There honestly is not a better router. Now if you do not care about readyshare cloud (not really cloud based) or TIME MACHINE and price really matters to you then I would recommend you write down which features are most important to you and find a $60 router that has those features. You can get 80% of these features in a router for $60 it just depends on which 80%. But if you can afford $130 there is no better router regardless of the price. I would be willing to spend $200 on a router if that would have made it better but it would not have. One other thing though is if you have a Macbook with Lion or higher and you have over 200GB of data that needs to be backed up you may want to get an Apple router. If you have a Mac desktop computer then just plug an external in and don't even worry about a router.

title: Good for Basic Laptop Sound
text:
I bought this from one of those 'Daily Deal' websites that send out the daily email for bargain priced goods and services, not here at Amazon. The reason for the review is that a slip of paper came in the soundbar box asking to rate this product at Amazon, as per Vaas..."Help Us Build Our Brand".

I received the soundbar yesterday and immediately hooked it up...no directions included...to my laptop, which was pretty straight forward and didn't require a bunch of knowhow. The USB cord wraps around the unit for storage and it was a little tricky pulling the plug part out of it's cradle area. The tabs used to attach the speaker to the top of the screen are nicely padded and the center rear tab has a (flimsy) screw mechanism that once tightened a little, secures the soundbar to the top to avoid any falling. It's light enough that it puts no strain on the screen/lid, so it won't cause it to move in either direction. Once plugged in (Windows 7) it went through it's paces to install the drivers and was up and running within a minute or so. It turns out for me that the cord is too short as all 4 of my USB ports are along the front side of my HP Probook and the cord is taunt even with the soundbar slid to one side...this is a deal breaker for me as this creates an accident waiting to happen.

As for the sound reproduction, it's marginal at best...as another poster said...'very tinny'. I'm not looking for screen shaking bass, but a small inclusion of the lower octaves within the sound field would have been nice as there is absolutely none on this soundbar. We're talking an AM radio kind of sound...talk & speech are fine, but anything along the lines of music is hard to take. The amount of volume it produces is fantastic, you have to turn down the laptop's volume to about 20% to 25% to stop it from getting too loud...so from that standpoint it works great. That was my primary reason in buying a soundbar, to get an increase in volume that my laptop couldn't provide...and this fits the bill in that respect.

I was originally looking into the [[ASIN:B0043TB7OC Logitech Z205 Portable Computer Speaker - Black]] or the [[ASIN:B003VAK1I2 Logitech USB Laptop Speaker Z305]] but hesitated at both the price and the fact that they suffer from a USB plug failure rate that was too high for me. They are both superior in sound to the Vaas, but for the price and shortcomings, I'm not so sure. I paid $9.95 plus shipping and tax...so the Vaas Soundbar cost me about $16.00 and change...which in my opinion is about all it is worth, I wouldn't pay a penny more.

To wrap this up, if you only require a soundbar for mostly speech and not so much for music, this is a winner as long as you have your laptop's USB ports in the rear of your computer...not located on the front side area.

EDIT TO ADD: I downloaded a picture to the manufacturer's pictures section to show how I had to mount the soundbar so the USB cable would reach the ports on the side/front area of my laptop. Hope this helps.

UPDATE 12/6/2013: Well, it bit the dust almost a year to the day I received it. I tried plugging it into a few different USB ports and even tried it on two other laptops...DEAD! Can't say that I would recommend this product to anyone based on it's short lifespan.

title: Buy this
text:
This is the best camera you will own, and it is the cheapest camera you will own.

Compare :

I own

1. FujiFilm XPro-1 with the fixed 35mm 1.4 lens. Total cost (when I bought it) : $1800 camera body + $600 lens. (my favorite)
2. Nikon D7000 with fixed 50mm, fixed 35 mm, and 55-200mm zoom. Total cost (when I bought it) : $1000 camera body, $500 55mm, $150 35mm, $120 55-200mm. Extra battery, carrying case, etc.
3. iPhone 5. Total cost (when I bought it) : $300 one-time and contractually ~$75 a month.
4. GoPro Hero3 Black. Total cost (when I bought it) : $400. I purchased two additional batteries, color filters, and some accessories for mounting the camera.

What do I take with me all the places I like to go? The GoPro (and the iPhone but I mostly use the GoPro).

BUY THIS CAMERA!!!

It is the one and only camera that you can use for the most important shots in my life : my kid. I'm tired of shots from the sidelines where I get my kids in profile. They never stay still long enough to allow me to shoot them from the front. I'm either getting profile or chase-camera action shots. With the GoPro, I just mount it to the handlebars on her bike and let her do her thing, or I mount it on her helmet and get her perspective. There is an entire point of view that we can never capture with our $2000+ kits because we're not brave enough to hand the hardware over to our child (because it absolutely will get destroyed).

The GoPro is virtually indestructible. While I am quite certain that my daughter could find a way to destroy the camera were she so inclined, she is so busy destroying other things that the camera has so far survived unscathed. I've shot really fun videos at the water park both first perspective and third perspective, and I enjoy sharing these memories with my friends and family more than my Flickr account.

The GoPro tells the authentic story of your life. It shows things as they are, not as you frame them or enhance them. I'm all for photography as art (this is why I own the Fuji!) but the Fuji will never shoot my daughter as I want to remember her - funky, energetic, always in motion, and full of wonder.

I will buy more of these cameras with time. I can certainly stomach the cost of 3 @ $1200 to get all the points of view that I value which is still less than the body alone on the Fuji. It's worth it. Your memories are worth it. This is literally the cheapest and best camera you will ever own.

title: High-End Ultrabook Par Excellence
text:
I'm very happy with this machine. It has seen about two months service so far. On travel I use it essentially as I would a desktop replacement class laptop, but it weighs only three pounds and is very quiet even at high CPU load, provided you don't get the GPU engaged. The HDD/SSD combination suits my needs, so I don't need to consider an upgrade there. If you're frequently replacing large amounts of data in secondary memory as I do in my work, an HDD is a better choice. Three USB 3.0 ports are good and plenty, if you get yourself a Bluetooth mouse. Since I have a lot of eSATA external HDDs I got a Newertechnology eSATA adapter, and it works rock solid. I upgraded the OS to Windows Ultimate because I need the language support, and installed an 8GB Corsair memory upgrade to run the memory up to 10GB. Of course I updated drivers.

The display on this thing is absolutely to die for. If you run Win7 screen at 125% you find an acceptable balance between real estate and legibility. The keyboard and touch-pad seem fine to me, but then about the only gesture I ever use is "tap to click". The enclosure is much more handsome to my eye than an Air, open or closed.

Before I pulled the trigger I read a lot of review FUD about the two-piece enclosure and somewhat greater flex in the keyboard area. After getting it in my hands finally, the machine seems physically plenty solid and rigid to me. Yes, there is some display bleeding near the edges, visible only when the screen is active but run with a dead black image. I only ever see this when booting. The one issue I've got with the ASUS hardware/BIOS so far is that it seems to want a little extra fussing in order to recognize a bootable volume on a USB drive, when you boot with the "Escape" key held down. Moving the drive to a different port, or inserting the drive under Win 7 and doing "restart" instead of "shutdown" seems to help.

I never expect to take on a new machine without spending some time on OS configuration issues. That's a small chore given all the applications I need to load and configure for my work. If you pay attention to CPU load and do a little monitoring, you may find a couple of OS services you would like to disable. That done, I am more than happy with the performance, given being short of the full SSD treatment and having moved back from dual ported memory in order to bump memory size. The OS boots to the password prompt in 26 seconds. Yes, a full quad i7 as on Sony Vaio Z would be nice, but then I'd have to put up with much more noisy breathing.

This machine was last month named PC Magazine Editor's Choice for "High End Ultrabook." It will be interesting to see how long that sticks; the competition in this segment is fast and furious.

title: Great device for a bargain price
text:

Speed and power are on par with the Apple device (website browsing is actually a lot faster, thanks to amazon servers doing the heavy lifting), but since it is Android, you get a lot of the freedom and simplicity that comes with Linux based OS. I cannot stress this enough: no need for proprietary management software! You can just slap files on it, no need for crappy software to manage it, and you can view your folders and files with a simple free application. You can even see and get files from your network shares! It supports a number of audio and video formats, pity that there is no support for AVI. No big deal, also because no tablet supports them naively, and a simple converter will be easy to find.
Micro HDMI out makes this device a very handy portable video player, and again, thankfully, does not use proprietary cables (this means a $3 cable vs $39).
One drawback is that this device is not 100% Android, but has been modified by Amazon. Thus it does not have access to Google Play (the store). It has it's own store, that will have a good portion of the software on Google Play, but not all of it. Most of the time, alternative software is easy to find, yet it is still an annoyance. I also predict slower upgrade schedules for OS upgrades. Nothing to dock even half a star off.

Overall you are getting a BETTER tablet than the iPad at 1/2 the price.

E.g. this receiver might be a good option for an RV or cruising boat application, where your source power is DC but your application is more of a home theater audio system. You might want to connect a video audio source into the system, or you might have legacy CD players.

title: Dead On Arrival, but Fixable :)
text:
After using it for a few days I'm upping the rating on the ASUS MeMo Pad 7 to 4 stars.

The screen is clear and bright, 16G of storage is pretty good for a $79 tablet, and the sound is also pretty good for such small speakers (yes, there are two speakers which is a nice feature- most tablets only have one and pipe both stereo channels into the single speaker).

Note that this is NOT the "HD" model. The screen resolution is 1024x600, not the 12800x800 of the HD model. Frankly it looks fine to me and to be honest I doubt I'd notice the higher resolution. Both movies and videos look fine on the screen to me.

The *only* downside in my opinion is that it doesn't have a physical "Home" button the way most tablets do. The Back/Return, Home, and Menu/Recent buttons are all virtual (onscreen) and they move as the display rotates. Some people might like this but I'd like to have at least one actual physical button on the face of the tablet to wake it or display the lock screen.

Other than that, no complaints. It's a pretty decent deal for the money. I intend to use this solely as a music player connected via Bluetooth to a sound bar under my television, and for that it seems to work fine.

******************
Original Review:

title: Change of heart.....Welcome back!
text:
I had a previous model, UD5005, which I absolutely hated it. It was slow loading the discs, remote control did not appear to be taking charge of the player, frames freeze when watching movies, not impressive sounds, etc. While I do not claim to be an expert, I had a decent set-up with Pioneer Elite SC-55 with Martin Logan speakers so I know it is not the AV receiver or speaker issues. After few months, I switched to Oppo BDP-93 which was a huge step up from the Marantz. All the issues simply disappeared once I traded the player.
About a month ago, I moved and set-up a huge home theater (800 SQ FT) and I purchased a Marantz AV receiver, SR7007, to power up my 7.1 Martin Logan speakers including Descent-i sub, FX surrounds, Motif, Theos which made me "WOW"! The sound was amazingly clear that I REALLY felt like I was in the middle of movies or sitting in the front rows of concerts. I have been a Pioneer and Denon receiver guy but I always wanted to try a Marantz. Now, I am glad I finally had the courage to do so as I am in love with this receiver. While I was in love, I simply came across of reviews of the new UD5007 which surprisingly were mostly positive. I noticed the reviews mainly focused on the improvements made as if Marantz recognized that the previous model was a disaster. At this point, I was tempted to try the new model to see/feel the difference myself now that Marantz has entered my life again.
I pulled the trigger and ordered a UD5007. The player showed up within 3 days and I hurried plugging into the receiver I love. Before the player started the blu-ray disc I loaded, I was immediately impressed with how quickly it swallowed and loaded the menu on the display. I thought Oppo was fast and this new Marantz player was right up there with it, if not faster. Again, I am not an expert and I will not post the loading time in seconds and compare the video signals and resolutions. Instead, I will simply provide information for the typical users such as myself and share my opinions. I honestly could not tell much difference between the picture quality as both players are excellent. If I absolutely had to pick one, it would be Marantz as the picture appears to be just a little sharper to my eyes with the set-up I have. However, when it comes to the sound quality, big difference! Both movies and CDs sounded much clearer and crispier than before with Pioneer & Oppo. Pioneer & Oppo sound very warm but could not help to notice the studio like sound. Marantz AVR & UD5007 sound brighter with precision and dynamics. This may be because I now have Marantz receiver and universal player and they `sync' better??
Just like trying to figure out what is a good wine, I think a good universal player or receiver is something you enjoy watching or listening to. Having said that, I am more than satisfied with my set-up and the entertainment experience I get out of my new Marantz products with Martin Logan speakers.
Lastly, I have an Apple TV hooked up to the receiver so I will not use or comment on the networking or streaming capability piece but I strongly recommend the new model UD5007 for what this was intended, playing movies and music! I have a feeling that I will remain as a fan of Marantz for years to come.

title: Excellent camera and still comparable if not better than newer models
text:
I've owned this thing for 4 years or so now. Nikon has introduced a few models since then, but this thing is still just about perfect for the picture taking I do. Lots of lens choices, tons of features, ergonomics just fit my hands like I designed it for myself. I've looked at the newer stuff, and for the few things they've "improved" on, I still think this was and is the best fit for me. Only reason I could ever see moving it to second camera status is if I ever decide to go full frame. I'd love too, but tough to justify the price when this D90 does such a fine job even with the reduced sensor size.

Here's some points to consider if looking at one of these to buy. Its a 12.3 megapixel camera. Smallish by recent new cameras, but more than enough to print very nice pictures 11x14 or larger in some cases. If you are using it for 4x6, you will have excellent results. The camera does shoot HD video, but it is limited to the 720, it will not shoot 1080. In my experience, autofocus during video shoots leaves something to be desired. The camera, with the kit lens, 18-105, has very decent low light capabilities. Of course, the kit lens is slow, so a faster lens would improve low light capabilities. On a nice bright day, without using flash, the camera pops off 4.5 or 5 frames a second. I have used this camera a lot at the drag strip and have captured lots of great wheelie action using the continuious shooting. My daughter was also a polevaulter, and this feature allowed me to catch lots of great action shots as she went up and over the bar. I used it a few times, indoors, for high school basketball, with the 18-105 lens, it was slow and not so great. With a faster lens, excellent results indoors shooting action shots. The camera itself has lots of choices to select the type and heat range of the lighting you're shooting in, so great results are possible with incandesent, florescent, halogen, sunlight, moonlight, you name it, the camera can shoot in it.

There are quite a few in camera editing functions to correct, um, operator error. LOL. Camera shoots in both color and black and white. There are various settings which allow quit, low grade snapshots, fine picture quality, and up to RAW settings. RAW allows, actually demands, that you have computer capabilities to edit the photos. RAW prints cannot be processed at your local Wal-Mart. The detail possible and editing possible in RAW is unbelievable. Be forewarned tho, RAW eats up lots of storage on your SD cards. There is an option to shoot both fine and RAW at the same time, which allows easy printing of the fine, and the capability to edit and change appearances in the RAW format.

This camera has an internal focusing motor for the autofocus lens'. Nikon 3000 series does not have this feature. What does this mean? Not all lenses will autofocus on a 3000, where practically all autofocus lenses will function on the D90. There is also an auto/manual switch on the camera body which allows you to manually focus any lens attached to the camera if you desire more control than the autofocus feature allows. Speaking of lenses, the mounting design Nikon is using has been around since the late 70s. This means that some really nicely made Nikon lenses that you may have laying around from the 80s or 90s have a really good chance of working great on the D90. In the first part of my review, where I give my personal likings of the camera, I mention its a reduced sensor camera. This sorta works to your benefit. The reduced sensor has a multiplying effect on the lens rating. This is approximately 1.5 times. So, a 100mm lens on a D90 is equivalent to a 150mm lens on a full framed camera. 400mm is equal to 600mm, and so on.

The camera has a nice large screen on the back to select options in the cameras menu. You can also change to live view which allows the screen to function as the eye piece. The screen is stationary, it does not tilt, swivel, flip, etc. Using it in live view also slows down the reaction of the shutter a bit. On top of the camera is a small simple screen that shows many of your settings at a glance. Using the small screen and function buttons you can switch shot quality, ISO, check battery charge, number of shots taken and number remaining on card, F stop, flash, etc.

The camera also has two dials in very well placed positions. A front dial right below the shutter release, and a rear dial behind the shutter release. These dials do quite a few things, such as changing ISO, flash, and using both front and rear dials, you can change F stops and shutter speeds without pushing any other buttons first. So, for those desiring manual operation instead of auto, everything is very easy to change while looking through the eyepiece.

The camera has a pretty decent built in flash and the capability of adding external flash attachments.

In this review, I've only touched on a fraction of this cameras capabilities. I highly recommend this camera if you can get ahold of one new or used.

title: Works  with my iPhone 4s with a workaround
text:
I looked at several portable printers before I chose this one because it is the smallest printer that will produce satisfactory sized photos. The printer is about 4.5" x 3" x 1.25", or the size of a small book. Its not too heavy, but it does have a sizable charger (about 3.5" x 2" x1").
The POGO printer is smaller, but it is more for fun due to the small size of the photo stickers it prints. I travel and want to give instant prints on the fly as gifts. I had to jailbreak my iPhone (Apple Unlocker, takes 5 minutes), then installed a non-Apple application called AirBlueSharing. I am not promoting these but they worked very easily for me and you can find info on these online by others. Anyway, I was able to print using my iPhone via Bluetooth on my first try.
The Polaroid GL-10 worked very well, and I was able to go through about 4 ten packs of photos on one charge, which is really good in my opinion. The quality of the photos was very good using my iPhone, and more true to the photos on the phone than the ones I took with my Canon S100 digital camera (only USB with this camera) which I thought was a bit strange. The photos had some fuzziness around the edges when taken in low light, but were more crisp with good light. There is a tendency for white backgrounds in shadow to appear to have a slight magenta cast, but was not unpleasant nor distracting at all. All in all the printer performs as described, spitting out photos in under a minute. The prints are very
durable and come out dry. The cost per print is not bad, and a better deal if you get a ten pack of ten prints per pack (100 prints). I think its a nifty device and although
I was disappointed that it was not compatible with the iPhone right off the bat, the workaround was easy to do and cheap and did not affect my phone in any way, but please research any questions you have to satisfy yourself. I did not give it 5 stars because of the print quality, and the size of the photos, which I would prefer to be a little bit larger. Get an extra battery if you travel.

title: Exceeded expectations!
text:
I purchased this 32" LCD TV as a "slick deal" recently, which means I found it at an uncommonly low price, and purchased it on a whim.

Out of the box, I was pleased to learn that the picture quality was going to FAR exceed my expectations. I have discerning taste, and I can say with a clear conscience that the picture quality of this set is on par with what I've seen from Sony & Samsung. The black is black, the contrast is great, and the colors really pop. It is truly a stunning picture! And completely unexpected from a set of this price range (and brand name).

I read reviews that disparaged the sound quality before I received the TV - but I was pleased to learn upon setting it up that the sound quality was fine. It's average, mind you, but not terrible. I have it currently set up in a 14 x 23' carpeted & fully furnished family room and it sounds fine. I just wish it had an "analog audio-out" port so I could hook up one of my subwoofers to it.

Besides the picture quality, the HDTV antenna reception was an unexpected surprise. It's outstanding! I don't have an antenna connected to the TV, yet it pulls in every local channel that I get on my other LCD TV (that has a highly rated Leaf antenna connected to it)! In fact, this Toshiba TV provides BETTER reception than my other TV. None of the channels "come in and out." They just work, all the time, clear as day, in high def. Pretty impressive stuff! [In the spirit of full disclosure, my other LCD TV is a few years old and might not have a great tuner. So maybe all LCD TVs have great in-the-box reception these days. Take my feedback for what it's worth.]

All in all, I'm very impressed with this set from Toshiba. I never would have purchased one of their sets if I hadn't gotten such a good deal on it, but now I've opened my mind to their TVs. They certainly did a good job with this one! Particularly around the picture quality and over-the-air HDTV reception.

Quite impressive for this price range.

title: What could possibly be better?
text:
I don't know whethr or not I fit the typical mold of an audiophyle, but I am a blind music lover and musician, and I have a pretty discerning audio palette. I bought these speakers about fourteen months ago and then promptly moved into an apartment where I was unable to set them up. I considered returning them for a refund because of my inability to use them, but I realized that my living situation wasn't permanent, and I held onto my Polks and waited for my chance to use them.

Three weeks ago, following a long period of frustration, having moved finally into a place where I could set up my system, I dug the 6750's out of the box. And, my friends, it was well worth the wait!

When I purchased these speakers, I got them for just a hair under $200. I see that they're selling for $229 as I write this review. But if you ever see these speakers for $300 or less, do yourself a favor and buy them! I've never owned a set of $600 or $900 speakers, but I have heard speakers that sold for that much. And these Polks are every bit as great as those or better! The highs are crisp, the mids are clear and loud, and I cannot even come close to believing how deep and powerful the tiny eight-inch sub is. I have paired the system with a new Yamaha RXV371 receiver, and the setup was a no-brainer. With limited tweaking, the system in my living room sounds pretty much indistinguishable from the setup in most of the movie theaters I've frequented. The crossover for the sub works perfectly and the speakers do not distort at any volume that I can tolerate. There are some reviews on Amazon which mention that the speakers don't work particularly well for music reproduction. But, with all due respect to my fellow reviewers, this has not been my experience Of course, listening to music necessitates me to choose a different listening mode on my receiver, and I understand that not all receivers reproduce music well, but I do not have this problem.

Overall, I couldn't be happier with my system. I feel a little bit like a thief for having purchased the Polks so cheaply, but immersing myself in movies and music helps keep my mind off the guilt.

When my previous pair was stolen out of the break room at work, I went online to order another pair of the same model. Upon visiting the MEElec website, however, I saw this new model that caught my eye. I listen to a lot of drum and bass, dubstep, trap, and other electronic music. I love bass. One problem with the previous pair of earphones was that the bass wasn't punchy enough for my tastes, which is why this edm-inspired earphone caught my eye. The highs and mids were fantastic, they had a great amount of treble, and vocals were crisp and clear as if I was right in the studio with the artist. This pair of earphones was nowhere near that previous model. The bass is oversaturated, drowning out highs and mids, leaving them sounding muddled and stepped-on. Although the low-end sounded over-saturated, the bass still lacked the punch I was looking for. In fact, this pair seemed to have less punch in the bass than the balanced-armature earphones I had before. I feel like this was a waste of money and I wouldn't recommend them for the price. I actually upgraded to the $300 Westone 3's (which I got on sale on Amazon for $150.) They produce sound lightyears ahead of these earphones with a better all-around balance between highs, lows, and mids. It's been a long time since I used a pair of vanilla earphones that come with modern phones and iPods (the last time I used my iPod earphones was 2008 when they broke) so I couldn't accurately tell you how much of an upgrade these would be from any pair of stock earphones. title: Variation from one unit to another

*** ORIGINAL UNIT ***

I read the mixed reviews before purchasing, convinced that the complaints were the result of improper installation, and confident that I, an engineer, could follow directions and install it correctly. However, no matter what I did I couldn't get the mouse to power on.

I unpacked the components, plugged the base into my computer, placed the battery pack on the base and let it fully charge. I then installed the battery pack, being very careful to make sure it was snug and the locking tab fully engaged. No joy. The pack is so snug I had to pry it out with a tiny screwdriver (scraping the mouse). I've repeatedly removed and re-inserted the battery pack but am unable to get it to work. What a frustrating day!

*** REPLACEMENT UNIT ***

After finally giving up with my original unit, I concluded the unit must be defective and requested an exchange from Amazon. When the new unit arrived, I unpacked it, plugged the charger base into my computer, placed the batter pack on the charger, and waited for the light to stop blinking (I did this before going to bed, and in the morning it was fully charged). This unit slid right in to the mouse, no muss, no fuss, no screaming in frustration. So far, it works perfectly.

Conclusion: perhaps due to manufacturing issues (pure conjecture on my part), it seems that some units are defective and don't fit into the mouse properly and/or won't provide power to the mouse, while other units are fine.

*** UPDATE AFTER TWO MONTHS ***

The unit stopped working after two months. This has been extremely frustrating. I really wanted this product to work, and have spent a lot of time and effort on it.

When I got the TV on a Tuesday mid-day, I unpacked it, assembled it on its stand and plugged it in. The TV turned on immediately without me turning it on...when I looked at the screen there was a three to four inch-wide bar of solid color bands running from the top of the screen to the bottom just right of center. The rest of the screen to either side of the TV was a picture with the band running through it. Something was broken.

I called Sharp immediately and they started a claim. They sent me an email right away asking for a bunch of specific photos to take of the problem and send back to them so they could evaluate it. I was told on the phone that the photos would be reviewed within 1 to 2 business days. I took the photos right away and emailed them back to Sharp.

I didn't hear back from them, not even a "We got your email" response, by Thursday night so, wanting to make sure the photos got to Sharp, I resent my original email with a request for them to let me know that they had received it and expressing my disappointment that the TV was broken upon receipt. I didn't hear back from Sharp all day Friday while at work, so I called back on Friday afternoon to find out what the status of my claim was. I was told that they had received the email and were reviewing the photos but that they had not completed the review. The gentleman I spoke with (he said his name was George) said I should hear back from them by that afternoon - when I asked why I hadn't heard back from them within two business days, he explained that it was 1 to 3 business days, not 2. But he assured me that I would hear about the status of my claim very soon. Shortly after getting off the phone with him, I got an email from Sharp stating that my photos had been reviewed and that they would call me within 1 to 3 business days to let me know what was going on. Interestingly, on the following Monday morning (one day later) I got a response to the second email I had sent on Friday morning, but never did get a "we got your email" or "thanks for getting back to us" response.

On Wednesday of the following week, I finally got a call from Sharp. The lady I spoke (she said her name was Kim) with explained that Sharp had an offer for me: they were going to replace my TV because it couldn't be fixed based on what they saw in the photos I sent. But, Sharp didn't currently have this model of TV in stock and didn't know when they could actually send a new one because they had already run the production run of this model. I asked if it would be one day or two months, and she stated that it usually didn't take THAT long. I asked if Sharp couldn't get one from somewhere else, and Kim said no. I asked what my other option was and she said that I could return the TV through Amazon. She also explained though that there would be no cost for shipping the new TV, for the set up of that TV, or for the removal of the broken one that they had provided me. I said that was convenient for a TV I didn't know that would ever be sent since they had no possible way in the world to get one anywhere. Let's just say I was very frustrated that Sharp took so long to do anything about the broken TV, and then when Sharp finally did do something, it was to really an empty offer - sorry about that broken TV we gave you, deal with it. I have a feeling that had I taken their offer, they would eventually have contacted to let me know they were discontinuing that model and I would now be stuck with their busted TV or be upcharged to get Sharp's newest model. I told Kim that I would think about their "offer" and let them know what I decided.

After getting off the phone with Kim, I immediately contacted Amazon and explained what was going on. In retrospect, I should have done this the minute I realized the TV was broken. Amazon couldn't have been more helpful in arranging pickup of the old TV and refunding my money - I had bought the TV using a gift card, and the gentleman I spoke with (his name was Gabriel) was able to refund my money the next day so I could order a new TV right away without having to wait for Sharp's piece of junk to be returned. By the next Wednesday I had a new TV (not a Sharp) and on Thursday the shipper came and took the trash away.

Now as far as the TV itself went, the picture on the two halves of screen I could see was really nice, as was the menu. Set-up was a bit of a chore, but not terrible. Overall, I am sure I would have been very satisfied with that TV, had it worked, but it didn't, and that's when I foolishly decided to try to let the manufacturer, Sharp, take the responsibility to rectify their product's poor quality - "why punish Amazon when they didn't cause the issue", is what I thought. I work in manufacturing myself, and my company treats it customers like champions of the world, so as a customer of Sharp's I was quite distraught to be disregarded and generally treated as a nuisance by Sharp and it's associates. So, if you are thinking about buying this TV, or another Sharp model, keep in mind that there are many TV manufacturers out there. Sharp won't care about your frustration or disappointment if you get one of their products and it doesn't work right - or at least they won't express that they actually care and mean to do something about the problem they caused in a timely and efficient manner. I don't know that the other TV manufacturers would behave differently, but I don't know that they wouldn't, and I know how Sharp treated me. So, if you don't mind your hard earned dollars going to a company that doesn't care about you as a customer that keeps them in business or their responsibility to you, go ahead and order Sharp product. Or, if you do order a Sharp and it is defective, just return it through Amazon. Again, foolish of me not to right away, but I don't normally buy big ticket items online, and knowing how my company treats our customers, I figured Sharp would rectify the situation right away, not a week and a half later, and then not really at all. Oh, and don't expect anything for your inconvenience, frustration, disappointement, and lost time if you get a broken Sharp. Remember, they don't care about you.

title: For the price, a good deal
text:
First off, let's just get this out of the way. If you come to a Chromebook expecting a machine to run the latest games on or with expectations that it will do the same things as a $500 Windows laptop, you've come to the wrong place.

That said, if what you are looking for is a reasonably well-built lightweight machine that provides solid basic applications at a low cost, this is a great choice. Yes, it's just a machine that runs "just a web browser." But if you let that limit your view of what's possible, you're missing out.

Even inside Google's ecosystem lies enough power to provide most of your needs. A good solid word processor, a spreadsheet, a usable "forms" application for basic databases, and even a presentation graphics package. Throw in Google Mail and Picasa, and what else does a novice computer user need? Facebook, YouTube, and even some of the video services (although, because of its reliance on Microsoft Silverlight, sadly not Netflix) all run beautifully. It also does a fine job of playing local media stored on a thumb drive or even a small hard drive.

Even advanced users will find something to like about this Chromebook. It's super lightweight, all solid state, and the 6-hour battery life is perfect for a "second laptop" around the house or for the long excursions where carrying a full-function laptop is too much weight. Samsung's build quality is fantastic, especially for such a low-cost product. I'm a systems administrator, and it makes a perfect go-anywhere SSH and RDP terminal at a low-cost and light weight.

Chrome's "offline mode" does a superb job of letting you use Google Drive's features without needing a full-time net connection, so much of what makes this a usable machine doesn't need a tether to the network to work. As more and more applications are developed to support "offlining" (which is not just limited to Chromebooks) this will only improve.

No, it's not a replacement (yet) for a full-function computer for everybody. It is a great starter machine for a novice user, or a second machine for a more advanced user that's willing to accept that World of Warcraft isn't happening on this machine.

title: Not Just a Wafer-Thin Mint: This Drive's Got Lean Muscle
text:
My first desktop was an old-fashioned ATA job, in the days before "serial" came along and required its predecessor to be retroactively appended "parallel".

My second PC was the first I assembled, and to reflect the transition of the time it had both new SATA and the old PATA ports. Since then I have embraced many new acronyms: PCIe, SSD, BT, DDR3, USB 3.0. It's getting to the point motherboards are dropping Fire wire altogether, and the traditional mechanical hard drive is increasingly for data store rather than a primary system disk. I tested the [[ASIN:B006EKJCWM SanDisk Extreme 120 GB Solid State Drive SDSSDX-120G-G25]] as a dedicated gaming drive for Vine; now it is the C:\ of my secondary PC. My main work machine runs off a [[ASIN:B004W2JKZI Crucial m4 128GB Solid State Drive]] which at this time I have not reviewed.

Hybrids were an alternative I seriously considered to the higher cost of solid state gigabytes. And as it happens, Amazon Vine offered me the Seagate Laptop thin drive.

--Package--

Packing was a little precarious. The drive came sealed in an anti-static bag and nothing else--no clamshell, no box, no papers. Just the Amazon carton and some plastic bubble packs. It was free to slide around so the first thing I did was inspect it for damage.

At seven-millimeters versus ten millimeters, the drive is thinner than my SSDs, so that lived up to the name. As a platter drive though, it felt heavier in the hands. It has a shipping weight of 8 ounces, nearly double the solid state jobs. Despite the slapdash packaging, it was visually undamaged. Soon turned out to run fine as well.

Getting the drive into my tower was easy. My HDD cages all have cute lil' removable plastic trays with holes formed in the bottom just for 2.5-inch drives. If you don't have that, I've been told the [[ASIN:B002BH3Z8E SILVERSTONE SDP08 3.5 to 2 X 2.5-Inch Bay Converter]] might be the cure for what ails ya. If it was a solid state drive, you could also get away with just resting it on the floor of your case, or electrical taping it or something; I leave it up to you to decide whether this is feasible for a platter drive. Whatever the case, installing this drive is a case of BYOS--Bring Your Own Screws.

For first time Windows 7 set up, go into Disk Manager. Select the drive, get the Partition Wizard going, and the drive is recognized in a couple minutes. Done and done.

--Parameters--

I tested the Seagate hybrid drive in two rigs:

1) Formatted on a Custom Intel work machine: [[ASIN:B004EBUXI0 i5-2500 Quad-Core Processor]], Crucial M4 primary disk and [[ASIN:B005PBJF6O Intel Desktop Board DZ68BC]] motherboard, via the Marvell controllers.

2) Swapped into a Custom Intel play machine: [[ASIN:B007SZ0E1K Intel Core i5-3570K Quad-Core Processor 3.4 GHz 4 Core LGA 1155 - BX80637I53570K]], San Disk Extreme primary disk and [[ASIN:B007G51UV0 ASUS P8Z77-V PRO Intel Motherboard]], through the Intel controllers.

Both computers are Windows 7 systems. Neither is a laptop--I figure others will give you that experience, and so you will appreciate hearing how it worked in a PC. I did not overclock my processors or my RAM for these tests. I used the drive primarily to run Steam as well as several independently loaded games. Also used it to store game mods and patches, cheats and editors, and various readmes and walkthrough documents and videos. So a good mix of file and app types.

--Performance--

As other reviewers have noted, this drive uses a relatively slow 5400 RPM spindle and an 8 gig MLC NAND flash.

Per the need of the flash and the cache, programs need to boot a few times to get up to full speed. Once that happens they load as fast as or faster than the San Disk. Even when I was running it through the Marvell controllers on the DZ68BC board, which some folks complained about, I got good performance. Some of the heavyweights, like my copy of [[ASIN:B0065NP6NC Fallout: New Vegas]], are buggy enough out of the gate, and loaded down with gigabytes worth of mods, that save games move a little slow no matter what.

With the ASUS board I went straight for the Intel connectors. In this machine it is running a touch slower. However, the play PC only has 4 gigs of physical memory running at 1333 mhz, running off CPU video. I expect that when I add a discrete graphics card and a comfortable bump up to 8 GB of DDR3 at 1600 speed, the games will really fly.

--Capacity--

I have over sixty Steam games. Some are 10 gigabyte behemoths, and several have been inflated with gigabytes more of DLC and user mods. At 120 GB the SSDs just don't have it to hold them all. This is going to be a big decider: hybrids offer more storage for speeds just about as good.

Then again a conventional [[ASIN:B0036Q7MV0 Western Digital Caviar Black]], runnning 7200 RPM over SATA III, works plenty fine for Steam and boasts a full TB or more to store a bunch of photos and videos. Because my towers can hold up to six drives, I take advantage and tend to cap out on any one drive at a full terabyte to ensure I don't keep too many eggs in one basket.

The upshot? I prefer SSDs for running OS and most apps. The trick is to spill over to conventional HDDs to store all the photos, videos, and music tracks I produce. There is no way to share my productivity and my game apps on a single small solid state disk. Eventually the InDesign and CAD diagrams are going to join them. So if you need a one-disk compromise between the capacity and the speed, this hybrid could fit that niche. You can get this model in caps up to 1 TB.

--Swap `em Out--

Both machines are housed in [[ASIN:B005E983JW Corsair Carbide 500R Mid Towers]]. So I just pulled the drive tray out of one rig and stuck it in the other. The Intel-ASUS system picked it right up and automatically assigned a letter drive. Steam will have to authorize the new drive, and individual games will have to perform "first time set ups." Also, my older titles tend to store save games and user data in My Documents, so don't forget to copy those over! Many newer Steam games keep everything in the Steamapps folder.

Whether this swap will remain stable, or if I have to update this review with bad news, remains to be seen.

--Concern--

Seagate left a foul taste in my mouth ten years ago. Two Barracudas went bad on me under one year of purchase, six months apart. I jumped to Western Digital and never looked back. Crucial meanwhile, has become my go-to for solid state. I got to hand it to Seagate, though, so far this Thin Laptop hybrid is a smooth and flat little device. And if it rolls over and dies on me in less than three years, you'll hear about it in this review.

As it should be. Seagate is an industry leader who regularly scores firsts: the 5.25 inch drive in the 1980s, the 3+ terabyte drives in the 2010s. They got a rep to uphold.

So it's a good thing Seagate provides a website with a dedicated product and support page. Storage doesn't normally need drivers in a modern Windows system, and with modern boards you can flash controllers if necessary. There is no firmware update or any such thing for this model either at the time of this writing.

--Show 'Em The Money--

In the short trial period, across two slightly different operating environments this drive has performed as advertised: without a hitch, and without a lot of handicaps. Making it one of the few devices that get five full stars from me. I'm aware from other reviewers that this model moves a little slower than some of Seagates other hybrids, so if you chose to see it as four stars for that, I won't stop ya. At a current list price of eighty bucks, that tag sounds fine for 500 gigabytes of high speed storage. Just remember that for about the same cost you can get a full terabyte of straight HDD over SATA III and see plenty good enough performance for the compromise. The only question remaining is whether the Thin Laptop hybrid is gonna do it for your needs?

title: Works good with my HDTV for hooking to a Bluetooth headset
text:
I have a Panasonic VIERA TC-P42S30 1080p Plasma HDTV. Great HDTV but no easy way to hook it up to a Bluetooth headset. With these 2 items and a Toslink cable, you can do it for about $50.

• Etekcity Optical SPDIF Toslink Coaxial Digital to RCA L/R Analog Audio Converter with 3.5mm jack (http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B009X2JB8I)

• TaoTronics TT-BA01 Wireless Portable Bluetooth Stereo Music Transmitter for 3.5mm Audio Devices (http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B004B8GF7Y)

Connect a Digital Optical audio Toslink cable (http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B001TH7GSW) from the TV Digital Optical audio line out to the optical line in (SPDIF) on this digital to analog audio converter (http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B009X2JB8I). Then connect the 3.5mm plug of this Bluetooth transmitter (http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B004B8GF7Y) to the headphone output jack of the audio converter. Pair the Bluetooth transmitter to your Bluetooth headset and you are good to go. I am using the Kinivo BTH220 headset with no problems (http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B005LKB0IU).

title: Fine Match for iPad Air 2
text:
Fine Match for iPad Air 2

It seems odd to put a $9 case on an $830 tablet, but after having been through all sorts of different types and grades of cases for my old iPad 2, I decided to just get something with the features I know I want, as inexpensively as possible. The result -- this case -- is meeting or exceeding all my expectations.

I don't need ruggedness, but I do want to slip my iPad into my messenger bag without worrying about the other stuff in there banging up my tablet. This case is just the ticket for that.

I do spend a fair amount of time walking around with the iPad in one hand. A strap is a great help in that situation, making it less likely you'll drop the thing while reducing hand fatigue. The strap also facilitates using the stylus while standing, and the retaining loop means you'll have your stylus with you. Both great features.

The case creates a fine angle for watching videos or (something I do a lot) reading while eating at a table. All the holes for cameras and ports are in the right places, and the magnetic closure keeps the cover closed while putting the iPad to sleep.

It's surprisingly light in weight, helping to retain the weight advantage of the Air 2. Materials and workmanship are neither shoddy nor outstanding, but seem entirely adequate.

A fine case, and for the price, an incredible bargain.
