title: An in-depth review of a fantastic camera!
text:
To buy or not to buy in 2012?

MY QUALIFICATIONS:
I am a photographer, and have been for about 4 years now. I'm in between semi-pro and pro, and my main focus is wedding photography and engagements. I would say that about 90% of everything I shoot involves a person in some way, so please keep this in mind when reading my review. I am also a bit of a gear-head, in the sense that I love to stay current on knowing about the latest technologies. It is also important to know, however, that I do not necessarily believe that the latest and greatest advancements in photo tech are actually necessary, nor have I ever pre-ordered photography gear personally.

INTRO
I first used the 5D in 2010 (well after its release) when a friend lent me their camera for shooting a wedding. I shot my first weddings on a couple of rebels - a big mistake. At the time I didn't realize how important camera cache, AF speed and low-light performance all were in wedding photography and it was an experience I didn't want to repeat if I could help it. The 5D completely changed the way I shot, and in my biased opinion, helped me become a better photographer. The first wedding I shot on one was a dream! Just so you don't think that I was awed by the step up alone, I have shot with the 5D MkII, 5D MkIII, ID MkII, IDs MkII and the 7D since then.

BUILD QUALITY
Now as another reviewer has mentioned, Canon came under fire from some in regards to the build quality...I won't rehash what has already been said on this topic but allow me to express how much I enjoy the build quality of the 5D. It is not the same as the 1D series that's for sure (I also owned a 1Ds MkII Full Frame), however it beats the rebels and even the XXD series by a LONG shot. The camera feels very sturdy in the hand, and has a nice weight to it (no doubt due to the alloy body). I have owned two of these cameras, and borrowed one extensively (thanks Mike!) and overall have had very few issues with all three copies. One camera did suffer from the well-documented mirror issue (glue coming undone) however I had a backup camera with me, and Canon glued the mirror free of charge (including a CLA to boot)! For those of you with 5Ds, please be aware that this is STILL being done, even if your camera is out of warranty.

FEATURES
Now, this is perhaps the most controversial point in digital photography. Allow me to let you in on a little secret: camera companies want to make money more than they want to make cameras. Boom - I'll give you a minute to regather your exploded head. I jest, however at the same time I am dead serious. Even the noble photographic giants such as Canon and Nikon have to answer to shareholders. The way they stay on top? New features. Some of them are super handy, HD video for example (if you shoot it) or even Live View (which I hated at first). Many of them, are absolutely worthless. Who needs a camera that goes up to 160,000ISO? I have a rule to never shoot above 800ISO, and even then only in good lighting conditions! I say all this to say, don't get caught up in the gear games - you don't need a camera that was made in the last 6 months to make good pictures. Here is a short list of features, that make the 5D classic a contender in 2012:

- Full Frame. This is the main reason why most people buy this camera.
- 12.8 MP - enough to make great-looking poster size prints. Do you really need more?
- Extended ISO of 50-3200, more than you'll ever need.
- Large and bright viewfinder, with 97% coverage
- 17 RAW frames at 3FPS
- FANTASTIC image quality

SHOULD YOU GO NEWER?
There are a few reasons why you might want a newer camera. Now keep in mind, we are talking about a price jump of about $1000 for the 5D MkII (I'm ignoring APS-C cameras). Here are a few reasons why the jump might be worth it. If you find yourself nodding and pining for these features, then by all means go ahead. If, however, like me you don't think these are necessary for great pictures, move on!

- Video capabilities
- Larger LCDs with better resolutions
- Live View
- Faster FPS
- Slight increase in image quality
- Higher ISO, color bit rate and dynamic range

IMAGE QUALITY
I have to say that some of my best work has been done on the Canon 5D. Sure the 50D and 7D have newer sensors and processors, but when it comes down to it I can spot a shot from my 5D out of a batch of mixed files any day. Let's be honest for a second: image quality depends more on the glass you are using and the light available than your camera sensor. Sure, you will know if a picture was taken with an old Canon D60 (never heard of it? eBay has them for a hundred bucks), but overall the 5D keeps up with much never cameras. The full frame sensors allows for much nicer bokeh from closer up (google "full frame better bokeh" for a full explanation), something that is invaluable to a wedding photographer who doesn't get to control his or her environment.

OVERALL
I got my 5D in good used condition for almost the same price of an excellent used condition 50D (which my wife uses), but I rarely finding myself wanting to use the 50D. My wife gets some great shots and it is a fabulous camera, but having full frame really is that important to me. Will I upgrade to the 5D MkII/III? Of course I will. I do not believe, however, that it is worth a business loan. I have been using the 5Ds now for almost three years, and I will continue to do so until (a) they die, (b) I receive a surprise inheritance, or (c) Canon comes out with a full frame camera with new features I can't live without. If you are a serious photographer on a budget, don't let the manufacturing date scare you! The 5D is still a workhorse and I have met countless pro photographers that use them to this day. As long as my clients keep smiling in delight when they see their wedding pictures, I will continue to use this fine camera.

A TIP
There is only one grip on Amazon for this camera (BG-E4 equivalent) that is vastly over-priced. I found a Jenis grip on eBay for less than forty dollars. It ships from China, however it has given me no problems whatsoever, and is of the same quality as any other third-party grip I have used (and I have owned five different brands).

SUGGESTED ACCESSORIES
I have used or I own everything listed below, and have rated them at 4 stars or above:

[[ASIN:B001G9TYHE Remote Shutter Release Cord for Canon EOS 5D]] (I use this for astrophotography - excellent!)
[[ASIN:B003DWP29G 2 Pack of High Capacity Batteries For Canon EOS 5D]] (less durable, but single charge lasts just as long as OEM)
[[ASIN:B001JD4E68 Jenis Battery Grip for Canon 5D (Black)]] (as mentioned above, search for this elsewhere!)
[[ASIN:B000CSPOSI Canon Ee-D Focusing Screen for EOS 5D]] (essential for good composition!)

title: A Great Grab and Go Lens!
text:
Bought this lens for my girlfriends OM-D body as a "first lens". Wanted her to have something in the 24mm range--one of my all time favorite "standard" lenses from my old 35mm days--as well as something with a bit of reach. This lens fits the bill perfectly. It has a great, albeit "slow" 100mm portrait far end (f/6.3) but for grab and go work at auto ISO, it is fine.

The lens has motorized zoom (which I was not aware of) that can be easily overridden by pulling back on the zoom ring. Best of both worlds. You can also, then, place the lens in a special macro mode via switch. And it is a very powerful macro indeed. We're talking Geo. Washington on a dollar at a working distance around eight inches. Should be good for wildflowers I'd say. That's at 100mm by the way.

Picture quality is fine, especially in RAW as developed in Photoshop. Straight lines along the frame edge are generally very straight. Not a lot of any other noticeable distortions. Haven't had a chance to check chromatic aberrations (purple fringing, etc.). But nothing glaring (no pun intended) yet.

The smallish flash included with the OM-D body does not cast any noticeable shadow from this lens (yea!).

I bought this lens hoping for a factory box so I could take advantage of a rebate being offered (02/2013). However, this lens must have been salvaged from a kit or other Olympus deal because it came without a box, instructions, or warranty card. But, the low(er) cost more or less offsets what I would have (eventually, maybe) received from Olympus.

I am pleased.

title: 5 stars for the camera (so far) 5 stars for amazon's return service, and 1 star for the quality control of shipped items
text:
Update: Amazon's return/replacement service is great. Their quality control for items being shipped out did not catch the problems with the first camera I was sent.

I received a new (this time the camera really was new) camera within days of filing for the replacement/return. The new camera is new, and has no dust on the sensor. I believe the first camera I sent was used, in hindsight I recall there being no screen protector seal on the camera, and the date and other items were already programmed. The camera box was also missing the USB cable I received in the replacement box. I checked the number of shutter actuations with a free online program that reads this number from the exif data from an uploaded sooc photo. The first camera I received had over 300 pictures already taken on it. The replacement camera had not been used at all. I don't see the enormous amount of dust and fibers on the sensor that I saw on the original camera. Moral to the story, when you get a new camera, check to see that it is actually "new" a few shutter actuations is probably normal >100? still might be ok, but if there is visible wear to the camera, return it.

Yay! Can't wait to take some great pictures with this beautiful camera.

First Review:
This is the first camera that I've ever returned (my previous cameras have been the Panasonic DMC-FZ35 and the Nikon D7000, both excellent cameras that I have used for many many years: [...]).

This camera arrived to me with dust on the sensor. Just to be sure it was not the Rokinon 14mm lens I purchased, I took several test shots with another lens, the specs persisted. I then looked into the camera body itself and saw, dust, dust all over the sensor (it must be pretty bad when you can see the dust, and fine hairs, with your naked eye). My D7000, which has over 200,000 shots, and which has been taken out to the desert in wretched conditions, appears to have less dust inside it than this brand new camera.

I was so excited about this camera! :( My first full frame, with an impressive list of specs, and from the few test shots I made, the ISO 3200 shots looked better (less noisy, and retaining more detail) than shots made with ISO 1000 on my D7000.

I have returned the camera and have ordered a replacement D750, I'm hoping that perhaps the copy I was given from Amazon was lightly used and then returned, and that the light usage is the culprit for the dusty sensor (and it's not going be the D600 dust catastrophe all over again...you read about these things happening, but until you pay a large sum of money and have it happen to you, you don't realize how awful it feels to be on the receiving end of a defectively made piece of equipment that you've been saving and dreaming of for a very long time). I'll update this review after I receive the new copy.

title: The reason I hate it: 1) It only reads engine RPM from ...
text:
For those with 1XXX, 9XX and 8XX series units, this device is supposed to allow you to "use" NMEA 2000 data on the network. What were my expectations in buying this: 1) gather data from my other NMEA 2K devices on the network, 2) create a custom readout on my HB unit (similar to what's shown on pg. 35-37 in the installation guide), 3) being able to see navigational information on my remote gauge not associated with my console. All seems reasonable, right? You'd get this with Lowrance, Simrad, Furuno, Garmin, etc. The reason I hate it: 1) It only reads engine RPM from my network. Fuel flow (see page 36 in the installation manual) and all other data (fuel level, engine temp, etc) can not be selected. The HB rep said the manual is erroneous - can't be done. 2) the unit is one-way only. So, even though the HB obtains GPS lat-long, vessel heading, speed, etc - it DOES NOT output this information to the NMEA 2K network. In fact, when you go to the data box view, that information isn't included -even though the unit records the information internally!!!! Is that insane? So my bow gauge won't show depth, speed, heading, etc - all gathered by the HB unit! I have the latest firmware loaded (as of Jun14).
Do yourself a favor. If you have a newer HB unit, it presumably comes with NMEA 2K compatibility built in. If you have an older unit (like my 8XXc SI), you might as well start saving for a replacement - vice buying this garbage for $160. No Lowrance sensor or device is this expensive and they actually do something. HB needs to update their firmware to "Truly" support NMEA 2K on older units (as their numerous press releases imply). Take a look at a reputable marine electronics forum (hulltruth for instance). It's now apparent why no one appears to use HB sounders.

title: Depends On What You Need
text:
Let me start first by saying this was purchased for and installed in a 1976 Corvette. I suppose your results may vary depending on your vehicle, and the speakers and/or amps you pair it with. I have it paired with Polk 4 X 6 plate speakers in the dash, and Pioneer 3-way standalone cabinets in the rear. I am not using an amp (yet).

A Few Pros

-- Inexpensive compared to custom rebuilds and other vintage radios that can cost two or three times as much
-- Delivered quickly, worked as advertised with no glitches
-- Looks almost exactly as the stock 76 Corvette radio
-- Fit perfectly with no adjustments to the radio or to the car
-- Simple to operate
-- Radio reception is good (certainly better than the stock radio)
-- Power is adequate for my needs & the line-out jacks should provide for growth later. The USB input in the back is great and works well with the three phones & MP3 players I tested it with.

A Few Negatives / Suggestions

-- As mentioned by others, the clock function is worthless. If you need a clock function then this is not the unit for you. It only displays when you push a button and does not display when the unit is turned off.
-- The button used for the clock takes away from it being used as a 5th button for presets and in fact is easily confused as a preset. Why in the world they bothered is beyond me.
-- The knobs have a "cheap" feel although they look OK. It really wouldn't have cost the vendor any more to use a more universal shaft end to accommodate existing knobs (or just sell better knobs as an accessory). I will say that the shafts have a firm feel with good feedback.
-- The "vintage look" analog radio scale graphic is also useless and detracts from the overall visibility of the display. Basically, it looks good with the radio off - not so much with it on. An option to remove it would have been nice.

Summary - Would I buy it again?

Yes, I would buy it again. With my car the choices were to spend 3 - 4 times as much to convert my stock radio to modern technology, or modify (cut) my dash to fit a DIN-style unit. There is an adjustable shaft model from another vendor but the features were similar and the shaft adjustments looked like a pain. My goal was to be able to use an MP3 player 90% of the time, drive 4 speakers, and have a look that was not too far off from what the car came with. This unit accomplished that without chopping up an expensive dash piece and allows a new owner to put the original radio back if they want. Yes, it has some irritations but they are relatively minor and don't really detract from the basic functionality.

title: Monoprice products tend to be quite good -this item is an exception.
text:
Ordinarily, I find that Monoprice products are good - multiply that by how inexpensive they are, and I would say that makes Monoprice products quite good. They're not the very best, but their build quality is reliably good, they're functional, and they're CHEAP!
The semi-cheapness does show when one tries to attach the included sticky-foot. The bar can attach two ways. The foot has two little pegs that are meant to snap into the bottom of the bar. The spacing of these pegs is ever-so-slightly off, so that the two pieces will fit together, but will likely spring apart. The bar can also slide into the "c" shaped foot, and that seems to work. I have not actually mounted it this way, yet, so I can't say for sure how securely the bar is held.
But then there is a real exception to the "Monoprice products are good" rule. This item is heavy and the power switch inspires confidence, so the "build quality" portion of the rule appears to stand. And the item works, but only in a limited way. There is ALMOST NO off-axis functionality: my Wiimote must be on a line that is almost perpendicular to the bar in order for my Wii to "see" it. That is to say, I must be almost straight in front of the TV for this to work. (I must say that the range is good - I can be 15 or 20 feet away, as long as I am "straight" in front of the device.) I have not yet tried removing the plastic lenses from the front of the device, which one reviewer suggested would help. (He may not have been reviewing this item, but I might try it anyway.)
All in all, I must give this item a pass. If you ONLY want it for controlling your Wii (e.g. to select items from the menu), and you will be on-axis, this might be ok. If you want to play games that require it, or have any other reason for doing so, I would suggest you try a better light-bar.

title: Excellent no frills MP3 Player without display.
text:
MP3 Player module arrived with the Remote non-functional. Parts Express promptly replaced the player with a new player with a functioning remote and I did not have to return the non-functional player.

The MP3 FM player module has no display, and is supplied with a remote. The player module has a SD slot and a USB input. The player has an LED which blinks when the player is working. The player is supplied without a case, without a 5 Vdc power supply, without power switch, and without input and output connectors requiring that you supply these items and assemble the module into a usable MP3 player. The unit is supplied with a battery for the remote. The MP3 player remembers the track being played, and the volume setting. A connection diagram is supplied.

If you are not handy in building electronics equipment, I would give this unit a pass. If you realize this module will require some assembly and installation, and are handy in building electronics equipment you will be rewarded with excellent MP3 player performance.

I installed MP3 Module in Radio Shack plastic Box (2 X 2.5 X 5.0). I used screw on panel as the base. I Added rubber feet (Waxman Super Sliders Bumpers ½ inch 0 74523 02153 8) to the box. I added 12V input connector (Sunkee DC Power Jack, Screw Nut DIY 180 Degree X00017GVIL) and color coded (white/red) RCA input jacks (Radio Shack Gold plated, mount with nut). I used a Radio Shack Universal power adapter (1.5-12V dc) (273-1662) that I happened to have on hand, set to 4 Volts output. I used the type M output tip set so that the center conductor was positive.

The MP3 player has 5 equalization settings plus no equalization. With no equalization the player response is flat within 1.6 dB from 17 Hz to 20 kHz into a 23kOhm load (excellent). There is no signal clipping or digital saturation with the no-equalization setting even at maximum volume (excellent). There is no digitizing frequency on the output waveform (excellent). The digital volume control has 15 levels. The maximum output is approximately 1.8 Volts peak to peak into a 23kOhm load (0.64 V rms). Random noise is about 50 mV peak to peak (17.7 mV rms). No power supply noise was evident with a radio shack 4 Vdc power supply (excellent).

I consider the equalization setting s of this player as being incorrectly implemented and not of any particular usefulness. With a recording level of 0dB the equalization settings cause digital saturation. With a recording level of -6dB only one of the equalization settings causes digital saturation. Equalization setting 1 has no digital saturation at a recording level of -6dB with some attenuation of treble. Equalization setting 2 has no digital saturation at a recording level of -6dB with some boost of the treble. Equalization setting 3 has no digital saturation at a recording level of -6dB with some boost of the treble. Equalization setting 4 causes a midrange boost with digital saturation in the region of 1 KHz at a recording level of -6dB. Equalization setting 5 has no digital saturation at a recording level of -6dB with some boost of the midrange and treble. Therefore, I consider these settings basically not of any use since they do not accomplish a loudness setting or a normal room response setting. I recommend that the manufacturer revise the player to eliminate digital saturation at 0dB recording level at all settings, and incorporate a low volume loudness setting and a typical room response of a gradual increasing attenuation with increasing frequency. Another useful equalization setting is a midrange boost.

Since there is no display, you will need an oscilloscope to tell which equalization setting is in use.

The Remote on off button is non-functional. The remote mode button is non-functional. The mute, pause, next track, previous track, EQ, Volume up and Volume down keys are all functional. The remote has a fast forward function. The number pad can be used to select the track to be played.

Within the limitations above, the no frills MP3 player Module has excellent performance with no equalization and will require the addition of an amplifier to drive speakers and adjust the tone.

title: It works!  Thank you tech support!
text:
My husband wanted a Slingbox for his birthday -- complete with set up on his iPad. I wasn't thrilled with the Slingbox reviews so I decided to take a chance on this new product by Belkin. I am a soccer mom who is not intimidated by technology, but I do not have a tech background, and I hate to call tech support if I can avoid it. The @TV arrived today, and I immediately took it out of the box. Nice packaging, not too many wires, sleek box. It came with a quick start installation diagram that looked simple until I actually tried to connect all the wires. I don't really know my "video in" connections from my "video out" connections and nothing seemed to be working so I had to call tech support right off the bat. Drat. While I was waiting in the long Belkin queue, I downloaded the software to my PC so I could connect wirelessly. The software worked seamlessly.

I was eventually connected to my savior, Ron, in the Philippines. Thank you, Ron! He was incredibly patient, and stayed with me for nearly 2 (yes, 2!) hours while we tried a multitude of different combinations with the wires. We eventually diagnosed a faulty A/V wire. Luckily, my husband has lots of old wires in the drawers under the TV and I had a replacement. We plugged it in and it worked! I followed the rest of the online set up from my PC. I downloaded the free iPad App from iTunes, and I am now watching the Olympics wirelessly on my iPad in my bedroom. The features seem pretty cool. Anything I can do on the remote, I can now do on my iPad. It's a little slow changing channels and getting the program guide, but that is probably a factor of my crummy internet connection.

I was surprised that the iPhone app cost $12.99. I doubt I will watch TV on my phone so I am not downloading it yet. The TV on my iPad is not crystal clear, but again, that is probably my poor internet connection. I would certainly give Ron 5 stars, and the product truly does what it is supposed to do, but the faulty A/V wire, unclear set up diagram and the less than perfect picture will bring my review down to 4 stars. I will update my review when I take this baby on the road.

title: Great for DSLR Productions
text: I gave the product five starts because it works surprisingly well with DSLR's. However, when we compare it to other professional shotgun microphones, this one is decent. Many professional videographers use it because it is small, lightweight, and has great sound quality! Its noise reduction feature works very well. DSLR's normally have poor audio wiring inside. So when you purchase a mic like the NTG-2 or a high-end one like the NTG-8 along with an XLR to 3.5mm adapter, you get a lot of whitenoise. This mic is prepared for the poor wiring and uses a system that puts out the mono signal to both channels, making it stereo and getting rid of most whitenoise. To even further eliminate noise, you put the settings on High Pass Filter and +20dB. Then you go into your camera's audio settings and manually adjust the volume level to about 20-40%. (with a Canon T3i, that's 4 clicks up from the bottom). Be sure to purchase a wind muff, although there aren't many out there that will work too well, it will at least help. BE GENTLE WITH IT. I'm already having issues with mine. The area just above the hot shoe and just below the actual mount came loose and is getting dangerously close to breaking. To fix the problem, I have to use a boom pole. The battery is difficult to get in because of the stubborn lid. Luckily, if anything breaks, Rode offers a ten year warranty, so they've got you covered. One other small thing that bugged me is that the base doesn't pivot, so it's pretty annoying to get the right setup with a boom pole. To sum it all up, great mic for the price and task, buy a wind muff, High Pass and +20dB, 20-40% camera volume, BE GENTLE, doesn't pivot. Hope I helped and I hope that if this is the mic you choose, it will serve you well.

title: Finally, a weather radio I can live with
text:
I've been in the market for a home weather radio for a few years now (yes, a few years). It was actually a frustrating search as I couldn't find one that had all of the features I wanted without annoying issues. Midlands wouldn't shut off at EOM, Reecom had a back-to-back alert bug, Radio Shack models had reliability issues, and I even looked at a few others but they didn't have everything I wanted. Even this radio had a lot of problems when it was originally released, but I tracked it through all of the firmware updates until it finally seemed like it would work how I wanted it to. Thankfully, it has.
Overall, I absolutely LOVE this device. As a matter of fact, I was waiting for our first alert (besides the weekly test) to go off while we were home so I could hear it work before posting my review. We had a severe thunderstorm watch right as we were going to bed and it alerted us exactly how I expected. It does have a few drawbacks, but they are nothing that make me regret my purchase. Here are the pros and cons I found while I've had it:

Pros:
-You can set the date/time to use RDBS, which is a fancy way of saying it can sync the date/time from a local radio station if they transmit it. Mine has stayed synced with no issues since I've had it, so it's working great.
-It honors EOM. I almost asked for a Midland weather radio for Christmas as they seemed highly recommended online. Thankfully I found some reviews on Amazon that mentioned they do not honor the 3 burst EOM signal at the end of an alert and constantly go off for 5 minutes. That was a deal-breaker for me. This device works perfectly as right after the 3rd EOM burst, it shut off the radio. We could go back to sleep without having to get up to turn it off or be forced to listen to it for 5 minutes. The manual seems to indicate it works like the Midland, but it's incorrect as it shuts off after the EOM.
-It allows you to silence certain alerts. For instance, the weekly test is disabled, so it will receive the test and show it on the display, but won't do any audible alerts. I believe some alerts, like tornado warning, don't allow you to do this, but I feel that's excellent as events like those shouldn't allow you to accidentally disable them.
-It allows SAME codes, either single, or multiple, so you only get alerts for the counties/parishes you want. If you set multiple, you can even toggle them on and off in the menu instead of having to delete and add, if you want that type of control.
-It shows when the active alert will expire.
-It has 3 LEDs that light up for warning, watch and advisory. That's nice if you miss the broadcast, like if you're outside and you come in and see an LED you can know you have an active alert and what type it is.
-It has a weather button that you can press to listen to the weather channel you're using, which broadcasts current conditions and forecasts. I sometimes listen to this in the morning while getting dressed to get an idea of what the weather will be like today and for the week ahead. They even discuss the tropics during hurricane season, which being on the south coast is something I'm always monitoring. If you press the weather button again, it turns off.
-You can choose to have a siren alert, or voice alert, though the voice alert starts with a siren before the message is announced.
-The siren doesn't start off at full volume. Reviews of earlier versions of this radio indicated that in voice mode, there was no way to adjust the siren volume and it came on full blast. With this version, you can change the siren volume and it will affect the siren level that goes off before the voice alert, and it even does a "humane" version where it starts off low and increases in volume until reaching the volume you selected (Low, Middle, or High).
-It has the ability to add new alert codes in case new alerts are added to the system. I don't know if they'll ever add any new codes, but at least you have the option to add them.
-It has a history of expired alerts that you can scroll through.
-Display can be adjusted to turn off and you can adjust a timer for how long it stays on after a button press. This can be good if you use it in your bedroom and the light from the display is too much. I don't have it right next to my bed so I always leave the display on and it doesn't bother me.
-It comes with 2 alarms that are very customizable. Each allows you to wake up to a radio station or an alarm sound. You can set the time, the individual days of the week, and adjust the volume for the radio alarm and alarm sound (they both have their own volume setting). These both do the humane waking where they increase in volume to the volume you set.
-Sound quality is very good for a radio this size. You can even adjust the treble and bass, though I think it sounds fine with the defaults.
-It has a battery backup that uses 4 AA batteries. This is crucial since in severe weather, you want your weather radio to still work if the weather knocks out the power.

Cons:
-My main gripe is that it doesn't show the date/time of expired events while scrolling through them. The main reason why I would like this feature is because I wanted to use the weekly tests to verify that the radio is working correctly. Without the date/time of expired events, I can't easily see if the last alert I received was the weekly test for this week or weeks past. I have a workaround that relies on the fact that when you press the button to scroll through the alerts, if you do it again later it remembers the last one you were on. So I'll scroll down to expired alert # 3 for instance, and when I press the button to scroll later and it's on the same alert # 3, I know I haven't received a new one. If it resets me to #1, I know I had an alert since I last checked. I'm at least glad I discovered this so I can still use the weekly test to verify the radio is working, but it would be nice to know when those expired alerts happened.
-The display could be a con depending on where you have the radio as the angle is not adjustable and the viewing angle isn't that great. I'm not using this as my primary alarm clock, so it's not a big deal for me, but it's something to keep in mind if you want to be able to see the time while in bed.
-The menu exits after a little while of inactivity. This was annoying while trying to set up the radio since if you pause to figure out how you want to set something, it will frequently go back to the main screen and you'll have to browse back to the setting you want to change again. Once I had it programmed though, I rarely go through the menus except to change the alarm, so it hasn't bothered me since setup.
-The quick start manual is terrible. I usually read the manuals for electronics I buy, but the quick start is one I probably should have skipped. I find the main manual is much better to use when setting up. For instance, the quick start just says to select the channel of the weather radio you will use, with no mention of what channels map to what frequency. I found my local transmitter on the NOAA website and got the frequency, but I had no idea how this radio mapped the channels to the frequency. I found this information near the very end of the main manual, which IMO, is a terrible place to put it. That chart should have been in the beginning of the quick start so you could know what to enter.
-It does the humane volume increase while browsing for radio stations. The humane volume increase is great for alarm or weather alert mode, but is bizarre for channel surfing the radio.
-The description of "Defeat Siren" should be "Defeat Alert" since it controls if either of them do an audible alert.

Overall, the pros easily outweigh the cons. This is definitely the weather radio I've been waiting for and the one I would recommend to anybody looking to purchase one.

title: Slick, but I can't type on it
text:
This clever design promises to visually match the iPad 2, and serve as:
- a keyboard
- a case (even a smart case that automatically locks and unlocks the screen)
- a stand, in both portrait and landscape orientation

Unfortunately it doesn't work well for most of these tasks.

As a keyboard, it's a little too small, and the combination of key travel and spacing and overall flimsiness makes it almost impossible for me to type on quickly and accurately. I'm not exaggerating at all to say it's easier to use the onscreen keyboard, so what's the point of an external one? Among other problems, some keys (especially G and H) get stuck down under the frame around them; they don't generate spurious keystrokes when they do this but it sure feels weird.

If I type slowly and carefully, I can type accurately, but there's no point unless I can type faster and with more confidence than the onscreen keyboard, and that's not the case. Between small keys that are hard to hit, and inconsistent key travel so my fingers think I've pressed a key before it registers, I get tons of typos if I type at all fast, and even if I type slowly enough for accuracy, it doesn't feel good, and even when it does feel good it often doesn't understand me. And sometimes I'd see substantial lag between pressing a key and having it register onscreen.

As a case, it looks nice and doesn't expand the size of the iPad too much and it does protect the screen, and I could actually see myself carrying it around and using it as a case, if the keyboard worked better. It's not a bad case. But it's not all that easy to get the iPad in and out of the case, so for daily use I much prefer Apple's Smart Cover. (This case, like the Smart Cover, has magnets that tell the iPad when it should sleep because it's covered and when to wake up because you uncovered it. But it's hard enough to get this in and out of the case that you're likely to touch the screen and trigger unwanted actions while you're fumbling with it, so it's not really a win over having to lock and unlock it manually when you're ready.)

Finally, as a stand: in the horizontal (landscape) orientation it works surprisingly well. It's stable and holds the iPad at a nice angle on a desk, and better yet, in my lap. Again, if the keyboard actually worked for typing, I could see myself using it this way. However, in the vertical (portrait) orientation it doesn't work well at all; it's topheavy and the base doesn't stick out far enough to balance it, so it bounces as you type and will tip over at the slightest provocation. I can't believe they claim it was designed to work as a stand in portrait orientation.

In summary: nice size and nice match for the iPad, very portable, a decent case, a great stand for horizontal orientation, a horrible stand for vertical orientation, but not a good keyboard. I wanted to like it, but I can't recommend it.

title: Runs Incredibly Quietly and Cool.
text:
I began shopping for a new laptop for games about three months back. I settled initially on the MSI780DX because of its better video card. I had to return the MSI twice due to bad RAM. After a bit more research I bought this ASUSG74SX-DH73-3D and have been pretty happy.

PROS:

1) Incredibly Quiet - Even running Furmark, or a 3d game such as SWTOR, or Mass Effect, the fan never reaches anything more than barely audible. This is a stark contrast to the MSI780, which at max load would sound like a dustbuster hand vacuum.

2) Runs very Cool - I've been running Hardware Monitor and the Max CPU temp is 75C. The max GPU temp is 70C. This is with Prime95 and Furmark respectively.

3) Graphics are excellent - The Nvidia 560m is pretty nice for running SWTOR at max settings. I get framerates in the 30's to 70's depending on the situation. The 120 Hertz screen has a matte finish that is much easier on the eyes than the average reflective LCD. The 3D works fine for a large number of games. I don't like 3D so I don't use it all that much.

4) Stylish - The case is angular like an F117 and very subdued yet stylish. There are no garish lights. The matte finish is superb.

5) Storage - 2 750 Gigabyte hard drives should be adequate for almost anyone.

CONS:

1) The keyboard is not as good as the Steelseries that the MSI780 had. The keys are flat chicklet style and there are a couple of keys that if hit right on the edge will not register.

2) There is no NumLock key. For some insane reason, this gaming laptop replaced NumLock (which gamers use) with a dedicated hardwired calculator key.

3) The weight is substantial. The whole thing is about 10 pounds.

Overall I am pretty pleased. While the 560M is not as good as the 570M that the MSI sported, the much cooler temps, the quiet, and the most important thing - the lack of hardware faults, all make up for the slightly inferior graphics card.

title: Couldn't be happier
text:
I use this machine for electronic design. I write firmware, and do pretty intensive 3D cad.
The installed software contained essentially no bloatware, and the machine performs wonderfully.
At work, I have a Dell xeon workstation with their Nvidia Quadro, and I have pretty much given up using that machine since my laptop outperforms it significantly.

The keyboard feels great, even though I am used to the split keyboards like the Microsoft Natural keyboard.
The trackpad is as good as I ever expect a trackpad to be, but I usually use my space navigator and SteelSeries Sensei mouse. The five USB ports on the machine enable me to almost never need a hub.

I recently attended a training event where everyone had laptops. We needed to install and run a bunch of embedded systems software. It was kind of fun to be done with the install LONG before anyone else was. Let's face it, one reason you buy something like this is to inspire envy in your peers. Mission Accomplished. :)
This machine stands out in the crowd of black plastic slabs.

The power brick is, well... a Brick. I don't expect a machine like this to run from a wall-wart.
The power cable is long enough to find an outlet even in hotel rooms, where they tend to be rather inconveniently located.

The speakers and sound are wonderful, though I have to qualify that observation, I am 55 with the usual sorts of hearing issues at my age. Enjoy your hearing while you can, and take care of it! I'm listening to Lars Erstrand on the vibrophone at the moment, from an Opus-3 disc, and it sounds wonderful.

The screen certainly meets my needs, good contrast and sharp images.

The triple raid C drive is as fast as they say, HDTune reports 1500M.

I looked at many machines before choosing this one, and the deciding factor was raw performance. My desktop is a 4 GHz machine with 64G ram and Nvidia Titan card. This laptop isn't THAT powerful, but it definitely measures up to my needs. Mine is equipped with 32G ram and 3x128G SSD

I did install the Classic Shell which you can find on Sourceforge. I don't like the "metro" UI, and with 8.1 coming up it sounds like MS has heard that loud and clear from many users.

One tip I can pass on, the Pelican 1495 briefcase makes an excellent carry case, but if the laptop were 1/4 inch wider it wouldn't fit! I put the brick alongside the laptop and nestle the cables in twoard the case handle. The mouse, space nav, brick and cables all fit nicely but they don't leave much room for anything else. I didn't want a so-so case for this laptop. The MSI provided carry sleeve protects the case against rub marks while traveling.

Nitpicks: The fan control is pretty much all or nothing, and on full speed it is loud. Again, reasonable expectations help. Moving air causes noise. I am not displeased with this, just noting it. The thermal exhaust is significant when the machine is working hard.

Software used: Altium designer, Atmel AVR Studio 4 and 6, Mathcad, Solidworks 2013, Povray, MS Office, etc.

title: Dissapointing
text:
This book has been on my list for a while, I just had not gotten to it when over Christmas someone gave me the audio version. I blew through it over the last two days and, aferwards I was dissapointed. I decided to come here to find out if others had the same opinion. I am shocked to find the number of positive reviews. The only thing I can think of is people are coming here to rate Steve Jobs himself 5 stars, not the book.

This Biography is actually below average.

Many (read all) of the key points in Steve's life are quickly glossed over. Big life events and dramas end abruptly. The books says that Jobs made arrangements for Isaacson to have unfettered access to people to interview, and asked them to be candid. It does not feel that way. It is not feel like an exclusive behind the scenes look at his life. Many (way too many) quotes are taken from things jobs said live, in public, on a stage. Long quotes from his introduction of new products were included that were intended to inspire the reader about jobs' ability to dazzle people, the way people were inspired listening to Jobs at those announcements. In the context of a biography, these quotes do not work. There were stories from his life that the other did not bother getting Job's present opintion on. There were times when my stomach would literally twist at story drop offs. I wanted to reach through the page a push Isaacson aside and ask the obvious follow up question, or find out what happened on the next day, but the event would just be over.

The book is not smart. It is not well written or insightful. As others on here have said, the prose sounds like a early high school book report. At the end of listening to it, it felt like all I had was a timeline of events in my head about Steve, not a real sense of what it was like to be around him, work for him, etc.

Over and over Issaacson goes into way to much detail about how a product works and quickly goes over the design philosophy without mentioning anything about the people or dramas that took place that lead this amazing things into being. It is said over and over again that Jobs can be demanding, and difficult to work for. There are no Full Fledged, Complete, Fully Formed, Satisfying, Dramatic stories about this anywhere in the book. Not a single memorable, re-tellable, quintessential "Jobs" anecdote. Just small, barely mentioned tiffs.

He talks about Apple so much you forget the book is called Steve Jobs, you thinks its called Apple, Inc. Which would have been OK, but again, the story was not good. Instead it was "remember how awesome apple was, it has awesome commercials during the Super Bowl." He spend more time recounting every moment in the commercial than the story behind it.

The most infuriating part was the end. He spend a very, very long time debating the the difference in Apple's and Microsoft's business philosophy, which not only seemed out of place (i'll come back to this in a moment, with a vengeance) it was not well written or compelling. Many people have remarked on the number of times Isaacson says "reality distortion field" but its nothing compared to "full integrated" and "end-to-end user experience." Over and over he repeated these in his analysis without saying anything worthwhile or saying anything that was not already clear from the other parts of the book when the two were already compared.

However, aside from the inane repetition, it didn't belong there at the end. We had just seen the drama of Steve's last days at Apple and we are expecting to see his lasts days, when this debate appears unnecessarily. Lastly, because this book was published after Steve's passing, and Isaacson spent so much time recounting well known public involved events, you would think the worlds reaction to his death would be included. Its not

Isaacson is benefiting from the fact that its an "Official" biography and was published concurrent with Job's departure. Published at any other time, I cant imagine it was have garnered much attention. This work leaves so many holes and questions, it wont be last word on Jobs, and definitely wont be the best.

I bought this from the Microsoft on-line store as part of their signature series. They wouldn't allow my review on their site, so I'm putting one here.

I am a tech coordinator for a small school. I have bought dozens and dozens of computers for myself over the years, and hundreds for the school. This is one of the biggest disappointments I've had in a computer purchase.

First -- no DVD drive in the machine. I never noticed that in the tech specs, and would never have bought it if I did. Fortunately, I have an external Blu-Ray player.

Second -- the worse input devices I've ever used. The trackpad is terrible. If I leave the computer for a while, when I come back it takes about 5 seconds for it to start working again. Once it quit working for almost a full day. The keyboard has no numeric keypad, and the regular keys are HUGE, making it hard to touch type--the reach to the backspace key is impossible.

Third -- only 4 USB ports. One for the DVD, one for wireless keyboard/mouse, now I'm down to two. That's not enough!! To make matters worse, 3 of the 4 are at the back of the monitor stand, so whenever you need to switch those cables, you have to go to the back of the computer. The ports are at the bottom of the monitor stand, barely 1/2 inch above the desk. The bottom part of the stand is recessed inwards about 1/2 inch, so it is quite difficult to plug in a cable without careful examination you can't see the ports without dropping your head/eyes down to desk level. The one port that IS on the side is right next to the power switch. More than once I've accidentally turned the computer off when trying to plug a cable in to that side port.

Looking at the photos on-line of this computer, it seemed like a great design. In actual use, it's terrible.

The computer itself runs well, but nothing out of the ordinary considering it cost $1000. But plan on spending extra for a decent wireless keyboard/mouse and a USB hub before you have a useable system.

title: On board projector - now with external input!?!?
text:
I'm sure your first question is - IS THE PROJECTOR WORTH IT?

The projector is fun to play with and invariably impresses everyone who sees it. If you like having envious friends agog over your latest gadget, this is for you. Although it only puts out 13 ANSI lumens, it's ma much better option than huddling around a 3" screen. Even in a brightly lit room, it's a FAR better option than using the 3" screen. At 8" away (the closest it will focus) you get a VERY bright and sharp 5" (diagonal) image. At 24" away you get a bright 13" diagonal image - we've used the projector to show videos in hospital corridors, cafes, restaurants and even on car backseats (prior to this we had a HDR-PJ10 for about two years, which has 10 Lumens)

The closest Sony camcorder without the projector is the CX380. Comparing prices on Amazon, the difference is $150. For that price, you won't find a pico projector of any spec for that price. It simply won't be as compact and convenient as this. One nice upgrade from the PJ10 is that you can now use it with external HDMI input. Or should I say, you're supposed to be able to use it - I wanted to use MHL output from my phone but no luck. That would have been mind blowing.

The nice upgrade - smaller and much - this weighs 9.2 oz, a full 2.6 oz lighter than the 12.8 oz PJ10 Unfortunately, they also deleted the remote. It doesn't appear that any remote works for this iteration. Small sacrifice since I can't recall using the remote more than once or twice.

If you're looking for a pico projector, the 60 lumen 3M Roku projector is available for $220 and comes with a Roku streaming stick. The only problem is, with the charger and cables, you've easily tripled the junk to carry.

This is my first time typing anything using this, my new monitor stand. I'm embarrassed to say that it's actually helping me quite a bit. I imagined typing pages of screeds, making up for all of the negative reviews I've forgotten to write over the years. I cursed myself for buying it in the first place, then further cursed myself for arranging to return it, and then never bothering to send it back. Construction was an epic misery involving many different kinds of bolts, two different kinds of hex wrenches, and about forty-five minutes of my gripping the monitor between my chest and elbow while I struggled to tighten things lest the whole thing come crashing to the floor.

And now I am here, standing in front of this weird, giant object, having expended so much of my life-force in its creation--I actually find it harder to hate, feeling that I had a hand in bringing it into this world...

It looks absurd relative to my monitor's diminutive stature (17" is a mere periscope into the vast ocean that is computing--an expanse deserving of a far wider portal and no, no monitor stand no matter how robust can change this reality).

I would not recommend this to a friend.

title: Sturdy, easy to install
text:

I needed a 3-gang solution, but was unable to find one. Instead, I purchased a 3-gang decora switch plate and three of these. During assembly, I removed the 1-gang plates, installed them, then installed the 3-gang plate instead. They mounted very easily.

I only stuffed Cat6 and RG6 through them, so I can't attest to how they'd handle finished cables, but I can only imagine the bristles would help hide a lot. I stuffed 20 Cat6 (23 awg) through the first, 11 RG6 QS through the second, and 22 Cat6 (23 awg) through the third. There is still room for a few more Cat6 if you really wanted to pack them in.

I've included a picture that shows how I used this product to create a cable chase between the ceiling of my networking closet and my unfinished attic.

title: Not too bad!
text:
I am updating my review after having owned this product for almost 3 months now. I had previously given this product only 2 stars due to 2 reasons: First, I had to contact the manufacturer and have them send a replacement because the first tripod collar thumb screw was cross threaded and would not open, and it was a bit of a hassle but the manufacturer did end up sending me a replacement; and secondly, the replacement collar I received had a "gritty" feeling thumb screw, like it was not machined very well and there were lots of burrs on the threads of the thumb screw. I took care of this very quickly and easily by using a Dremel with a fine grit finishing abrasive buff wheel and just ran it over the threads two or three times very lightly. After that the thumb screw threaded in and out smoothly and locked securely.

In my last review also noted that the aluminum was very soft and there was a large gap in the collar when it was attached to the lens. After using this for a little while, the aluminum must have bent to the proper shape or something because there is no longer a gap and there is 100% contact around the lens...and in case you are wondering, I did not tighten it excessively onto my lens!

BUT after using this collar I feel it is very much worth it!! It holds the lens securely and fits great. I'm giving it 4 stars because of that horrible, gritty-feeling thumb screw that it came with...maybe I just had some bad luck and got one that slipped through quality control, but it was a very easy fix. I would recommend this product, definitely!

title: Infinity Primus P163BK a sleeper!
text:
I bought a pair of these to use with my short wave receivers. At 90db SPL, they are far more sensitive and have a better aural bandwidth, mainly at the low end, than the Realistic/Optimus metal cased speakers - or the dedicated communications receiver speakers - I had used. Oddly, at $85/ea delivered, they are cheaper, too! Sadly, I decided to try them... they worked great - but it just made me wonder how they'd sound in place of my old Polk Monitors in my office - and they became my new audio system's main speakers. The treble signals are better dispersed with the Infinitys standing on end than the Monitors, whose treble response did not disperse as close to the speaker as the Infinitys did and seemed to produce hot spots, which the Infinity did not produce. The Infinity's midrange is bright - not muddled or colored. The old Polk Monitors are perfect for my SW receivers, if a bit of aural overkill for most such listening.

The Infinity P163BK have had one other effect here - I now want them in my main surround sound system - replacing more Polk Monitors! Definitely 5 star - and a bargain.

Update 8/18/14: My move to a new home included a larger 'great room' - and another pair of P163's were needed for my larger HT. Sadly, at $105/ea then for the P163's, when the better P363's were briefly $107 - I went with the towers (WOW!). My new fronts had plenty of room on either side of the bookcases, opening up the bookshelves for more of my wife's 'stuff'. The P163's went back to my office. I hired a guy to run rear speaker wiring - and went to order another pair of P163's - and the P363's were at $107 - back-ordered a pair - then the P163's were $60/ea - I ordered a second pair, sitting them on DR chairs as speaker stands/pedestals. Then the second pair of P363's arrived - and went to the rear speaker position. The P163's went to the Lowe SW receivers, awaiting any further employment ('Communications' speakers for SW radios range from $60-$200 - and sound horrible!). I got a fifth P363 to replace my HT's twenty-year old Klipsch KV-2 center speaker - and removed the sub-woofer entirely. My HT is awesome, if I do say so myself. My office stereo is used more - some 3-channel 'surround' for viewing movies (Center channel is a recycled Polk Monitor - awaiting a back-ordered P153.). My 'system' includes a repurposed Sony BD hooked to the HDMI input of my 25" PC LCD HD monitor and a repurposed Yamaha 5.1 A/V receiver - and my first P163's - with a Polk 12" sub-woofer seldomly turned on. I have a new CD-player - an Onkyo C7030. I am trying to wear it out - and A/V receiver and the bare P163's. As a discerning audiophile - on a Pepsi Max diet/budget as opposed to beer, much less champagne, budget. The P163's are quite decent speakers - and improve with break-in. Sadly, they are all but gone now, with what's available a bit pricey.
Update 1/16/15: I replaced my office a/v receiver with a 50 Wpc TX-8020 stereo receiver by summer's end and my two P163's, after A-B-ing them for a few weeks, with my Christmas speakers - a pair of less efficient NTH SuperOne 2.1's. They have a clarity that is impressive.

[edited]

I can't help suspecting some folks are buying this and imagining it's going to grant them 'free' internet access. Let me say up front, it doesn't work that way. You have to subscribe to a service and have an account and password with a provider.

Having been using this for about a year, I've recently added another computer to my network. That meant re-hashing the settings in the modem again, attempting to get the wireless device recognized. It turns out the wireless adapter couldn't recognize the router because the router was configured to support only 'N' wifi, but the notebook adapter is a 150Mbps 'N' wifi, and couldn't connect without the router being reset to include backwards standards (wifi- a,b,g,n). So I didn't need to reset the modem at all. But I'm glad I took the time to explore the 'dynamic' settings, and the directional RIP standards. Everything connects faster now.

Using it for a gateway to my wireless LAN, it's connection once established is superior to the Westell 6100, we used for several years, which dropped the connection repeatedly on the wi-fi side, and was at best truculent about linking to Windows-7 on the wired connection.

That said, my former configuration of the wireless LAN certainly had errors in address, and protocol, from excessive reliance on the automated set up of the wireless router. After downloading and reading the PDF manual for this product, I was better informed about the relationship between the devices in my LAN.

Having saved printouts of the settings from the former configuration proved invaluable for determining addresses and balancing routing tables. Luck plus persistence and study has lent me success in setting up this connection. (It was necessary to make a service call previously to our ISP to enable dynamic address assignment. But this modem includes settings to alert the server machines to automate DNS, which the older modem didn't have.)

The software disc didn't apply to my configuration at all! It cannot set up a bridged connection automatically. And I might add, that it detects more than one service available through our phone cable. We can't use the direct connection it sets up because it's for only one computer. And it still requires our user-name and password.

It's a good piece of hardware, provided you'll read all it's manual settings and learn their terminology on the Google & the Wiki.

title: Excellent high powered microscope for hobby or college study
text:
This is NOT a toy. The majority of the body is metal, and solidly constructed. The threading on removable screw in components is very fine. The objective lenses included are top notch, and the microscope is capable of showing the nuclei and fine structures of eukaryotic cells. Prokaryotic, due to their small size, are hit or miss. I have personally identified and taken video of multiple species of amoeba and a few ciliates from my toilet. Vacuoles are normally visible in protozoa. A fantastic microscope.

***ONE HUGE DOWNSIDE***
The halogen bulb is hard to come by and has no options for upgrading. It is moreover a large producer of heat, gives a yellow light discoloring samples, and is most outstandingly UNDERPOWERED for anything past the second objective. You will NOT be able to see ANYTHING if you use this bulb. The microscope will be unusable if you attempt to use a darkfield condenser at ANY magnification. Phase contrast, though expensive and fantastic, is an insanely useless upgrade... unless---

***THE SOLUTION***
The microscope is wired internally such that the switch to turn it on is linked to the full power of the outlet the microscope is plugged into. There is no transformer until after the switch and the fuse. What this means is that you can cut specific wires to remove the halogen hardware, connect the wires to the contacts of a lamp socket, which can be adhered to the underside of the light aperture. At this point you can attach an LED flood light giving you more than enough light to use the highest objective in darkfield. Be aware however that this modification is tricky, will likely void your warranty, and will probably cause blindness if you aren't responsible with how you do your brightfield imaging. I am a tinker. If you are not, this microscope will never be worth even half of its power to you. The camera will be useless REGARDLESS of your magnification. Even at the best exposure your images will be black. Brown if you are lucky. That alone voids 300 dollars of the microscope value. The two objectives that will serve you on the halogen bulb will kill off another 200. You are left with a solid, finely crafted 600 dollar piece of quality lab equipment that can only perform worth 50 bucks. Your call

I modified it, and have no regrets

title: Good sound, bad housing design
text:
I am satisfied (just) with its sound, especially considering its size, but I might not recommend this to my friends.

1. Sound: (4.5/5)
Last night, I compared with some other old headphones/earphones I have, AKG K99 (over-the-ear), Sennheiser PXC 250 (on-ear, noise cancelling on), and Sennheiser CX-380 (in-ear-canal), which are in a similar price range (street price) roughly. I used Nexus 4 and an MP3 player as its sound source, because I guess most people use this for outdoor use. HK NI has pretty good mid and high, but when it comes to bass, there is no oomph, which can be expected naturally from its small-sized unit. If the included ear-tips can give you a perfect fit, you might feel a little bit differently. Overall, I felt its sound was quite similar to AKG K99's, well balanced across the entire frequency range with slight focus on upper-mid and high. This might be due to the fact that AKG got involved in its design. For me, AKG K99 was the best among them, PXC250 was a little bit better than HK NI, and CX380 was a lot worse than HK NI. Considering its small size, it provides quite descent sound, but if you are looking for bass-heavy headphones, HK NI is clearly not for you.

2. Design: (1/5)
I guess HK designers wanted to maintain an identity across the entire headphone line up. Rectangular design looks okay on its big brother BT or CL, but personally I think they should have used a different shape for in-ear headphone design. Rectangular ones simply do not fit into outer ear comfortably. It is not painful to wear HK NI, but not as comfortable as CX380. In addition, pushing the ear-tips in is okay, but removing them is quite uncomfortable because of its small, rectangular design. I usually use middle ear-tips, but with this one, I needed to use large ones in order to alleviate its uncomfortable fit. The wire is quite curly: even after around 10 days of use, it stays the same.

3. Three-button control: (4/5)
HK NI is for iPod/iPhone/iPad. So, only one button in the middle works correctly with Nexus 4: one short click for play/pause, one long click for Google now, two clicks for skip forward, and three clicks for skip backward. Google now works quite well with the microphone on the wire. I didn't test call connection or termination with this.

In short, HK NI gives you quite well balanced sound, but because of the not-so-ergonomic rectangular design, it is a little bit uncomfortable to wear.

title: Great promise - fait try - poor execution
text:
This is the only known MP3 player to incorporate an AM tuner. It and the FM tuner work quite well. The file system enables the serious music listener to arrange categories of music the way he likes--a real improvement over the way that the Sansa players function. So much for the good news.
The display is barely adequate and unworthy of this expensive piece. It is of low resolution and slow. It mangles non-English characters.
Many folders are not maintained in alpha-numeric order. The result is that instead of playing a classical piece in movement sequence of 1-2-3-4, it might play them 2-4-1-3. Clearly unacceptable.
The worst problem is that the CC Witness Plus can't digest certain pieces at all. Pieces that play on other devices will not only not play: they will cause the player to freeze. It's not surprising that C. Crane provides a reset button that can be pressed with a paperclip or sharp pencil. This is not a random occurrence; it occurs each time that an offending piece is attempted.
Though I am prepared to love this device for its features, I cannot abide its shortcomings. I shall take advantage of C. Crane's 60-day return policy.

title: Great monitor for amateurs and professionals.
text:
I bought this monitor a while back this year to go with my Sony HDR-CX560v camcorder. I was looking for a field monitor not only for recording footage at a better angle for a more professional touch, but also for reviewing footage instantly and getting to see a bigger and clearer image in detail. So far, this monitor has not disapointed with a high quality finish Sony always delivers, and supports full 1080P resolution for recording and playback. Very impressive for such a small monitor, hence the expensive price tag on this, but for all it can do, i'm very impressed by it.

It offers "Peaking" support for both DSLR and compatible Camcorder models(mostly a feature for DSLRs really), it features both 4:3 and 16:9 aspect ratios with variable viewing ratios if you want smaller viewing angles such as(4:3,90%,80% 16:9,90%,80%). It also features color temp control for 9300k, 7200k, and 6500k depending upon your settings to match the brightness and color ratio of whats displayed on the camcorders LCD screen. You can also zoom into scenes and objects on the monitor via the click wheel without having to manually zoom in from the camera.

It has a handy, folding hood shade that can be removed from the monitor that offers a view in bright sunlight. Much easier when the monitor has the shade on than looking at the LCD screen on the camera which can be washed out by sunlight and make you lose your shot. Place it onto a shooting grip and filming with the monitor is a dream when compared to viewing the LCD. It just feels more natural and you take out that struggle of dealing with shooting in bright sunlight.

It also has two interchangable screw mounts. One designed for DSLR docking slots, and one flat shoe mount for shooting grips or camera brackets. It comes with a small mini HDMI cable, has a headphone jack for audio monitoring, and does support a DC in port if your recording in a studio setting without having to rely on a battery.

Overall, I really like it. Its perfect for either photographers or videographers, DSRL's or Camcorder. If you want to add a little more stability and are going for a professional flaire, a monitor is a must. It really does change the dynamic of your filming when you have an increased view and closer detail of whats in front of you. Ive filmed a few things with it, and I pay much more attentions to what im doing rather than relying on the camcorder LCD, and sometimes I miss stuff that I wish I could have gone back and gotten into frame. The monitor definately takes care of that issue for me now. I really suggest it if you have the money, it is expensive since its pretty much a condensed HDTV monitor you can back away in your camera bag. But for all it can do, I have not regretted purchasing it.

text: I have always wanted a Leica because I have looked at sample images taken from Leica cameras and I have fallen in love with the way they appear. It is a tough obstacle to jump across having the Panasonic Lumix DMC-LX5 as an option as it is roughly half the cost of the Leica. Both cameras are comprised of the same inner parts, however the body on the Leica is very refined and simple and reflects a elegant style. The firmware on the Leica is improved over the Panasonic and produces sharper images. The camera is GREAT. However soon after the purchase, it did not seem like a "camera purchase", it instead felt that I joined a community for photography. You get a free download of the newest version of Adobe Lightroom and you become a member of the Leica Owners section. The photos, when shot in RAW, will provide all the materials you will need to edit them to art museum quality. The battery life is above sufficient. When shooting without the flash, in RAW, I was able to shoot around 500 photos. The controls are easy to get use to, and the menu will seem quirky to navigate at first but it easily sinks in.  I have a Canon 30D and the difference in picture quality is minimal. Overall This is a great camera and I would highly recommend it.

04/11/2013: After having these for a while now, I can safely say these are not worth the money. Don't get me wrong, the sound quality is great and they block out external sound really well BUT:

1. They are THE most delicate earbuds I have ever owned. It's not like I run with them or anything. Even just walking around with my iPod in my pocket, the plate of the volume control fell off within a month of purchasing it and I snapped it back on but then it still kept falling out. Thankfully I knew when they fell off so was able to find it on the ground and snap it on. Unfortunately, today, it fell off somewhere along the way to work and now I have ear buds that work but with no way to control the volume or answer / make calls.

Same with the ear buds that would come off the main ear phones from the simplest shake or just taking them out of my back pack and unwinding the chords.

2. They are not a good fit for people with big ear passages (this is after trying each and every ear bud that came with the box). The only way to really get them in your ear passage is to place it at the opening, lift your upper ear up a bit and softly push it in a fraction of an inch and then they stay put.

Just disappointing for I had high expectations for this product. Probably best to just find a cheaper one that, if it falls apart, I won't have to dish out $$ to replace them.

OLD REVIEW: Bought these a month ago thinking they were THE best ones to get. A month later, the sound quality is A-OK unless I really jam them up my ear which is not good. Also they do not block out outside sound as well as other headphones. And the headphones keep falling out my ear and the fit is not snug. I've tried all the different combinations that came with it to no avail. Maybe I just have Yoda ears...who knows. Just bummed that its not working out as I wanted. title: A Technical Specimen
text:
Sigma has done some amazing things recently for the market. Though it's far from the perfect lens, it has reasonably slapped all the major camera companies across lens market with their affordable, professional grade lenses.

Before I get into a wishlist for Sigma, here's what I love about the lens:

-Solid feel, and well balanced on magnesium alloyed camera bodies.
-Very sharp wide open.
-Insanely sharp stopped down, even competes with the Zeiss Otus at F4.
-Very little to no distortion.
-Well controlled chromatic aberration and little sagittal flaring.
-Smooth focus ring.
-Decent styling.
-Great microcontrast. But there is a downside to this. See below.
-Great bokeh at some distances.
-Nice hood with a rubberized ring that works very well and stores nicely flipped on the lens.

now for the things that can be improved, aka my wish list:
-Some weather sealing. A small rubber gasket near the mount will do, super easy, but not sure why they don't bother adding it.
-Use high-grade plastic instead of metal. Sure metal makes it feel more substantial and "pro" grade, but high-quality plastics feel just as great and cut down on the weight.
-The Bokeh is nice when the background is simple, and at certain focus distances, but it becomes extremely nervous and distracting when the background is not simple. I can't completely explain it without pictures, but because of the high contrast of the lens, the bokeh balls tend to be very prominent and have a sharp quality to them. Not good, but if you get the hang of where the bokeh works best, it's not a terrible thing.
-The lens cap feels cheap.
-The focus isn't consistent out of the box. If you're planning to buy this, get the USB dock. Everytime I microadjust the lens at one distance, it becomes a little off at another distance. Not fun to keep messing around with focus. But this will probably only bother pixel-peepers like me.

Well, overall, Sigma created a knockout lens. I would give it 4.5 stars, but I can't. I think besides the room for improvements, Sigma is definitely creating its own nitch in the market as the sharpest lens maker. I think their factories produce a lot of Zeiss lenses, which might explain their ability to do something like this. Might not be the perfect lens for everyone, but this will please pixel-peepers everywhere, assuming you don't have any focus issues.

Thanks for reading!

I bought two of these mice to replace the mice on both my main computer and a secondary computer, expecting the mouse to be the same as the one I had happily used for so long. title: Good value lens - comparison of Sony lenses
text:
SELP18105G: This lens is a good value for the features and cost. For $600, the lens has f-4 max aperture, standard OSS optical stabilization, 6x zoom (27-157mm 35mm equivalent), internal focusing (lens length remains constant for easier handling), power zoom (smoother focusing for videos and can be controlled by the free PlayMemories app), and good weight of 15.1oz (< 1 lb). Yes, there is mild chromatic aberration and distortion, but both of these can be compensated. The chromatic aberration is not always noticeable (depends on the scenery), and is virtually gone by reducing the aperture to f-5.0. The distortion only shows up in RAW images, and any decent photo editing software can correct it with one click.

SEL18200: This lens costs $250 more, but has 2x more zoom than the SELP18105G, but 1.3 higher f-stop at max zoom (smaller aperture, > 2x less light). Its about the same size as the SELP18105G, but weighs 18.5oz (3.4oz more). This lens does not have internal focusing or power zoom, but does have a relatively better stabilization that Sony dubbed Active OSS.

SEL18200le: This lens has the same featues as the SEL18200 lens, but costs $100 less because it only has the regular OSS, not the Active OSS. Due to that fact, it weighs in at 16.3oz and is 1cm shorter and 1cm smaller diameter than the SELP18105G. The issue with this lens is that critics noted it's basically a rebranded Tamron 18-200mm lens, so you are paying a premium just for the Sony name.

SELP18200: This lens is like combining the SELP18105 and SEL18200 lenses because it has the internal focusing and power zoom (indicated by the "P" in the model #), while providing 200mm zoom and Active OSS. See the above descriptions for benefits of these features. However, you are paying $1100 for this lens.

SEL55210: If you have the kit lens (SEL1650 or SEL1855) and are on a budget, then this lens is the best option for you since it's only $300. However, you will have to swap lenses whenever you cross the 50mm zoom boundary, which may cause dust to settle on your image sensor. Also, it does not have internal focusing or power zoom, but does have regular OSS.

SEL1670Z: This lens is Sony's premium lens with Carl Zeiss (indicated by the "Z" in the model #) AR-coated optics and f-4 max aperture, but costs $1000. But it has relatively weak zoom (24-105mm 35mm equivalent), and some reviews noted focusing issues. It has internal focusing and regular OSS, but no power zoom. For $1000, the lens should not have focusing problems, and the zoom needs to be stronger (at least 6x).

Comparing Sony's E-mount APS-C lenses, this lens (SELP18105G) is the best value for the price. I tested this lens on my Sony NEX-6 camera.

title: Cobra over Whistler - This Cobra Just Plain Works
text: I had bought and used Whistler XTR-130 for 3 weeks and started searching for another detector and came across this Cobra. Whistler had more false alerts than anything else, was not accurate, and failed more times than not alerting me until cops were sitting right next to me merely fifty feet away at 4-way stop signs. I want DETECTION, with the assumption being that I receive alerts BEFORE I see cops with my own eyes. That's the purpose of a detector in my book. Whistler failed, and would continue giving X band alerts even when I disabled it in City mode. The Cobra ESD7570 on the other hand is a far superior detector for a mere five bucks more, except for the LED display. The display is sorry, virtually invisible during the day and better, but not very brightly, visible at night, a definite design flaw that should've been corrected during manufacture. But I work and drive mostly at night, and have become familiar with the distinct sound of Ka alerts because it's been so accurate thus far, so it's not a deal breaker. The bright red Ka alert is acceptably visible during the day, which is my main concern around here. The Cobra thus far has good accuracy of detection, hardly a false alert to speak of, and alerting me of cops BEFORE I see them: up to more than a block away! Sufficient detection for me. I like the configurability, so that I can eliminate both X and K bands if need be. Cobra also saves your settings after you turn it off, unlike the Whistler. The VG2 and Spectre detections are pluses, with the latter being another advantage over the Whistler. My Cobra, while nothing too fancy, just plain works like a detector should, BEFORE you see the cops and giving you up to a half mile of reaction time. If not for the sorry LED display, it would get five stars. If you're looking for an inexpensive radar detector that lets your own eyes do the Ka detecting and will give you plenty of X band alerts, get the Whistler. If you want an inexpensive radar detector that uses its own laser eyes to detect Ka for you in plenty of time to spare, opt for the Cobra. Money well spent IMHO.
