title: Solved a Tough Indoor Reception Problem
text:
I live in a small apartment where "everyone has cable" so the landlord let the roof antenna die years ago, and refuses to allow anything hanging out a window. Legally, there's no "exclusive use area" for outside antennas. Furthermore, the building isn't wired for fiber optics and there are no south facing windows for a dish. Guess what -- the cable company knows all this, and jacks up the price accordingly.

Well, I got sick of playing monopoly with the cable company, and the 4221HD was my ticket to freedom! I did a great deal of research and came to the conclusion this antenna is just as good as the DB4e released recently to much fanfare. Unfortunately, range figures are very deceptive, and gain statistics are almost as bad. (There are two standard measures, dBd and dBi, and you can't find out which is being quoted without a lot of digging.)

On the subject of range, it's best to ignore the manufacturer's numbers. Go to tvfool dot com, put in your zip code, and get a signal analysis report. I get everything "in the green" with this antenna rock solid, and the signal has to burrow through the roof. Most of these stations -- including all the strongest channels -- are outside the 45 miles "range" quoted for this antenna.

The 4221HD is a little smaller than the DB4e with slightly narrower beam width, which makes it better for my indoor situation, where the signal bounces around like a meth addict.

For my installation, I left it right in the box it was shipped in. The box doesn't seem to affect reception at all. I cut the top half of the box off, exposing the top two bays as well as the balun, so the coax swings freely outside the box making it easy to twist the antenna round 180 degrees on a $6 lazy susan procured on eBay. I have the antenna as high as I can get it, in a corner where the roof is very shallow.

I also did two very simple hardware hacks described on a Canadian antenna site. I pulled off the 8 plastic squares covering the elements where they intersect, and I pulled out the balun so the flat metal strips are over a half inch from the boom.

I get a total of 27 stations, 20 of them rock solid 95% of the time. With subchannels, that adds up to over 50 separate channels with reliability greater than or equal to cable TV. However, I do need to rotate the antenna when I want local news from Milwaukee. (Small price to pay for freedom.)

I think antenna manufacturers need to reexamine their (ab)use of the English language and upgrade their marketing strategy. There is nothing magical about "indoor antennas" that makes them work better ... indoors! It's purely a marketing term to describe something small and aesthetically pleasing. This is not what the average consumer thinks when they hear claims such as "the SuperSignal XYZ is the most powerful indoor antenna you can get." Absolute nonsense. In many cases, a much better solution is an indoor installation of what is normally regarded as a small outdoor antenna. People can adapt. You will find a way to make it look pretty.

The big name antenna makers are double talking themselves out of happy customers while making the cable companies rich in the process.

It is not a slim case, but much less bulky than the kid style cases from companies like Fisher Price and far more protective. It is nice not to worry about handing babies and toddlers an ipad.

A few tips:
- Make sure the gasket in the connector stays in place. Our son started pulling it off so we put it down with a thin film of silicone.
- Keep the "o ring" clean and the glass underneath. We regularly clean the inside edge of the case to make sure junk doesn't migrate under the seal.

title: Good product but problem with Client mode.
text:
The product has great features, size, and price. Having a router PLUS wireless extender, bridge and client mode are the keys feature to me. And that's the reasons I purchase. Over the years, I have purchased many different routers, mostly Netgear and Linksys, but other brands as well. However, one thing that puzzle me is that "why doesn't the manufacturer make a bridge / client and extender all in one box? " This model is "golden" in terms of features and usefulness.

Additionally, I'd the facts that it uses standard micro-USB port to charge. It allows me to move it to higher location. TP-Link designed it right. Despite all these good features, I can only offer 3 stars for now, may be 4 stars max. There are 4 reasons why:

1.) Problem using Client Mode: the connection is not stable, it frequently "lose" connection. Even if it shows connected, there is no internet connection. I tested on a few different system and a few different router. it is the same. So, I am going to request exchange with Amazon to see if it solve the problem. Note: I only tested the product in router, bridge, and Client mode. I haven't tested the AP mode yet, as I have no need to so far.

2.) After each mode change, it requires reboot. That's ok, however, it requires longer time to re-initiate the connection. Sometimes, it doesn't even connect !! The time it needs to reconnect is around 3 to 5 min.

3.) I would prefer that it has an external switch that allows user to change mode, and not requiring a computer to connect to it,
then change mode. Additionally, there is no light or other indicator on the product to show which mode it is currently on now.

4.) The USB charging cable ... It is good that it has detachable, in the case it, one can repurchase a new one cheap and easily. However, it is too short. I hope the manufacture offer at least 4 feet .

I use this product for 2 areas. One is to make my Ethernet ready Laser printer to connect wirelessly. Two is allow other level of the house have better signal. .

title: Does the job, but a design flaw and a learning curve
text:
I purchased this a year ago and have used it for three main purposes: hunting/scouting, hiking and biking. I purchased the MotionX GPS software for $3 - it meets those needs. I don't need to do a lot of navigating, so I didn't get the turn-by-turn app. The free, downloadable maps are great. I live in a rural area so if I am going to a new place and plan ahead, I can get there with just the GPS app (no need for turn-by-turn directions). I also downloaded the Topo Maps app to download and use USGS maps. Between the two I can typically plot suitable hunting or hiking routes based on USFS and logging roads.

I have used this with good success after a learning curve.

1) I can't just throw this in my saddle pack, backpack or bird bag without some forethought. It must be pointing up and be unobstructed to get good, constant communication from a satellite. They warn you of this in the instructions, so just be aware that they aren't being overly conservative.

2) The power switch on the back can be switched off while bouncing in a pack or while taking it in and out of a pocket. I take some painter's tape and tape over it when carrying it in a pack. This is the design flaw. If the switch was recessed or had a cover that slid over it, that would solve the problem.

3) Be sure to put the iPod in sleep mode while recording a track to save power. It won't automatically go into sleep mode unless you do this.

4) Every once in a while I get a message "device not supported by iPod" or I simply can't get a signal. I just disconnect them, reboot the iPod, reconnect and all is well. Be aware that it can take up to a minute or two to get a signal depending on clarity of the satellite signal.

5) As mentioned by others, be sure to get the version verified compatible with 4g iPod touch. It comes with a little plastic insert to hold the thinner 4g iPod and works perfectly.

If you don't want to pay extra $$$$/month for a data package to use a smart phone (with GPS built in) but still want GPS - this is a great solution. I would recommend it.

***UPDATE Sept., 2012***

I recently purchased the [[ASIN:B003YGGFOW Arkon Handlebar Mount for Most Smartphones - Retail Packaging - Black]] to mount my iPod/GPS to my bike to solve problem 1 (orientation while on a bike) and mitigate problem 2 (getting switched off while in a pack/pocket). It holds the iPod quite securely so that it won't move around. I still recommend using tape over the switch, however. I have also used the iPod/GPS cradle in the case mounted on my bike with success. (The iPod did briefly overheat while sitting in the case in the sun when I took a break, however, so it isn't perfect.) I can easily access it while riding and it keeps the unit properly oriented for good satellite reception. I have used the iPod/GPS cradle in the case (without the handlebar mount) while hunting with great success - it adds a level of protection from the elements so I am comfortable taking it just about anywhere. I haven't dropped it yet (and am not about to try it) but the cushioning of the case feels adequate enough to buffer a fall from my hands. Not trying to sell anything, but the Arkon is a decent, inexpensive case that holds the iPod/GPS perfectly, adds a level of protection, matches the headphone port to the location of the cradle's headphone jack perfectly and allows access to the touch screen.

title: Great sound system!!!
text:
Pros:
- Easy set up
- Tons of inputs
- Fairly Priced
- Emulates surround sound very well
- Sound quality is sufficient for small-medium sized rooms

Cons:
- Glossy surface on sub-woofer scratches and blemishes easily
- Provided wiring feels cheap
- IR receiver is on front of sub-woofer

Summary:
I was looking for a good sound system to compliment the entertainment system in my room consisting of a:
- LG LK450 42"
- Cable box
- PS3
- XBOX 360
- PC

The speakers on the LG worked just fine, but the audiophile inside of me desired something more. Though 5.1 channel systems are a great, I currently own an old Bose 5.1 channel system in the main entertainment hall, setting them up can be tedious and honestly it would be overkill for my 12x12' sized room. A sound bar seemed like the perfect choice. Through much research via CNET reviews, amazon customer reviews, and product comparisons, I opted to choose the Sony HT-CT150. The main reason I bought this system compared to others was because of its array of inputs. My cable box, PS3, and XBOX 360 would be able to use the 3 HDMI inputs while my PC and PS3(movies) would use the optical inputs.

Set-up was a breeze. I bought some velcro at a nearby Lowes store and applied it to the underside of the speaker and the top of the tv. The speaker isn't very heavy so it was easy to lift up into position. The sub-woofer is decently sized but you MUST place it somewhere so that your remote can see the IR receiver. Those that want to hide their sub-woofer systems may shy away from this system unless they can come up with a clever way to do so. Connecting the wires is easy as well because they are properly labeled and colored; however, both the speaker wires and the optical cable that came in the box seem very cheap. There isn't much shielding if at all so for those of you that might be moving this system around a lot might want to consider getting better quality wires. Thankfully, there does not seem to be any interference once I tested the system out.

The speakers worked and I tested the system playing video games, watching some movies via netflix/youtube, and listening to music. After calibrating them to the specifications I liked, they all sounded great; however, to truly enjoy the power these speakers have to offer, you must test it with a device that supports DTS or Dolby Digital encoding. Once I popped in a blu-ray movie with DTS, I was blown away by the power of this system. The emulation of surround sound is done exceptionally well, it provided a good balance of highs mids and lows, and most of all, it shook up my room! I'm an avid fan of bringing down the house with powerful sound systems and this thing delivers! Keep in mind though that this set up was in a 12x12 sized room. This leads to a few don'ts:

- Don't expect anything more than spectacular in bigger sized rooms
- Don't expect the full experience of a 5.1 system
- Don't expect great sound out of the box, CALIBRATE IT TO YOUR ROOM!!! EVERY ROOM IS DIFFERENT!!!

Remember this and you should be able to determine if this sound system is right for you. Buy the product for what it's designed for and don't expect it to perform any better than that. Good job Sony!

title: Item stopped functioning 3 days after Amazon's return policy expired
text:
It was a pain to return it to Seagate, who only offer exchanges on damaged items. The item that was returned to me will not allow itself to be shared over a network. Honestly, I really wish I'd been able to return it through Amazon.

Judging from the Seagate website, the initial breakdown is a fairly common problem with this model and several others. The drive powers on and spins, but will not be seen by your computer. Some say that there *might* be a way to retrieve your data, but I wouldn't bet on it. The only way to get it replaced is to send it to Seagate. The S/N on the device generally does not match their records, so you will have to call/instant message Seagate support in order to do this. Then, Seagate sends a refurbished device back to you. That's right, you get the privilege of using someone else's returned drive.

I would hate to rate it any lower than 3/5 because Amazon's portion of the arrangement was spot on as usual.

title: Canon is keeping a defective camera on the market
text:
I recently order the Canon Powershot SX280 from Amazon with the intent of using it myself and then if I liked it to give one to my daughter as well. It was in response to my daughter asking for advice on her next camera. I already owned a Canon SX260 and was completely pleased with it, but wanted WiFi to be able to connect to my iPad and phone. When it came I charged it up and began to take pictures. All was well, but when I called my daughter about it, she immediately went on Amazon and read all of the reviews that had a one or two star rating. She called me back and said that she was concerned that so many of the reviews discussed a flaw in the battery monitoring system that caused the camera to shut down if it was used for video. I don't use video, so I had never tested that mode. When I switched to video, the SX280 began blinking the battery indicator in red. If I kept taking video or even switched to still mode the camera would turn off after a few seconds. It could be reset by powering on again, but if you again went to video mode it would repeat the cycle.

I then did a search on Google and found that this problem began being reported almost as soon as Canon put it on the market. A couple of months later they announced a new firmware load that was supposed to fix it. Apparently it did not. I read hundreds of customer complaints that their cameras just could not work if you used the video mode. I contacted Canon and asked them if they had a fix. Their reply was that I would have to send them the camera to evaluate the problem. Most of the customer complaints had said that when they sent their camera to Canon it would be returned with the exact same problem. I argued with Canon that they must have known about the defect considering the number of complaints, but they just ignored me and said that there was nothing they could do unless I sent them the camera.

Clearly the camera is defective. My guess is that it is a hardware issue and they cannot fix it with firmware upgrades. Why they would leave it on the market without fixing the camera circuitry is beyond me, but I suspect it is because if they admitted it was a hardware problem, or if they withdrew it from the market before the next model came out they might be subject to a recall situation.

I returned the camera to Amazon since it was only 6 days old.

text:

It does not have the options that some of the more popular radios have like a built in tuner or ports for more filters and there has been complaints about these short comings and ALINECO answered these with the dx-sr9t which has the ports for adding filters and a few more whips and jingles but it's price reflects that also. From what I've seen "which is not much" this radio does operate differently from the more popular radios and this frustrates a lot of the more experienced hams.
It was very frustrating and still is to set up a lot of the features cause the manual is not user friendly but the tech support for Alinco is very friendly and helpful. I had a heck of a time getting it configured for my straight key and the manual was no help for that, it showed the wiring and diagram's good but not the menu settings, that's where it gets really vague. I have yet to figure out the P-scan or program scan mode so I can set it to scan between two freq's of my choice. There is a clone/setup utility program for the pc and that is about the easiest way to set up the radio's features but it requires buying the usb/serial cable which I did. I still enjoy this radio and I would still recommend it to others as long as they are willing to deal with a bit of frustration/confusion at the beginning. 73 KG7FFU

title: Well balanced full sound, deep bass - it survived P90X but didn't survive pairing with 2 devices - recommended
text:
I've become a common evaluator of headphones for Amazon, having evaluated quite a few high quality over the ear headphones, in-the-ear bud-style products, and also lots of single-ear bluetooth earpieces. This is my first bluetooth wrap-around style headphone review. Overall I am impressed, but I have a few reservations.

COMFORT

Most important for this class of headphones is comfort and fit. These are behind the head style headphones that are designed to stay in even during strenuous activity. They come with 4 different ear bud silicone inserts, but I found the ones already installed worked just fine (there are 2 smaller options a 1 bigger one over the ones installed). The headphones form a nice seal inside the ears that doesn't feel too tight and stayed put. Behind the head, the headphones were a little large, but there is an additional adjustable band you can install that reduces the size quite well. Even on my larger head the headphones stayed put. The individual buds also pivoted to adjust to exact head shape.

How well did they stay put? I decided to do a Beach Body P90X Cardio workout including Yoga and they stayed put the entire time. Of course, they started to get a bit uncomfortable as I sweated, but it's to be expected. The point is that they did not move despite doing floor exercises and jumping jacks.

SOUND

Just as I would expect, they sound great and well balanced. Not too hard on the bass, not too hard on the treble. Hard rock for workouts, classical for relaxing - it all sounded great to me. Immersive sound while outside noises were completely blocked. I'd say my Audio Technica's or my Monster headphones with large pads are likely better sounding and fuller, but those are wired headphones with thick pads that are certainly not designed for workouts.

INTERFACE

The headphones arrived partially charged (a soothing voice told me they have 4 hours of charge). They were incredibly simple to use. I turned them on and had them paired with my iPhone in no time. The right ear features the power switch and volume control while the left ear has the multi-function button. The right ear also has the LED status light and a rubber-grommeted micro-USB port for charging. Thanks Motorola for using a standard charging port! The package includes a wall-wart micro-USB charger as well.

The place the interface suffers is in the multi-plexed switch. Push once to pause, twice to skip forward, three times to skip back. The instruction manual has a dozen phone features that can be activated, but you will need the manual to figure it out. It worked, but with so much space, couldn't we get more intuitive controls and a few more buttons?

BLUETOOTH RANGE

Unbelievably long. I use a Plantronics Legend with my phone and it will lose signal after a short distance. But with the S11-Flex HD, I can put my iPhone 4 in one corner of my house and walk to the other corner of the other floor and still get great sound. Truly impressive bluetooth range.

TELEPHONE CALLS

No problem here - I made a call and the microphone picked up my voice quite well. I was enjoying my music during a run and was able to easily take a call without missing a beat. Noise cancellation isn't great like a dedicated headset, but for switching to a phone call without removing the headset, it works very well.

BLUETOOTH FUNCTIONALITY

Sadly, here is where the headphones lose a star. First, I noticed that the volume switch on the headphones doesn't send a signal to the phone to change the volume (as my Plantronics devices do), but rather changes the volume of the headset. So if the phone volume is set low it can be impossible to get it turned up high enough using just the headset controls. Other bluetooth headphones I have owned send the signal to the phone to change the volume.

I was also disappointed that multipoint didn't work. My Plantronics Legend is paired to both my iPhone 4 and iPad 3, both running iOS 6.0.1. I routinely switch back and forth between them, so I know how it should work. The Motorola paired successfully to the iPhone 4, but when I tried to pair it to the iPad, the screen said pairing was "unsuccessful", but then it showed as connected in Settings. I had never seen that before. Sure enough, the audio prompts in the headset said it was connected to 2 devices, but the iPad never recognized it.

Switching the order, I deleted it from both devices, paired it to the iPad first and then the iPhone. The iPad then worked fine, but when I paired to the iPhone, I got the same "unsuccessful" message.

Sadly, I must report that at least for the iPhone/iPad, I could not get it to switch back and forth, even though the headset thinks it is paired to both.

CONCLUSION

Motorola has done a nice job with the form factor and audio quality here. The range is truly impressive, and the ability to keep up with the activity of P90X was truly impressive. These would be 5 star headphones, but the clunky multiplexed interface combined with the malfunctioning multipoint force me to detract a star. If you don't absolutely need multipoint, I recommend these headphones.

UPDATE September 2013:

When I wrote this review, I wasn't into running yet. I got into running about 8 months ago, and found this headset to be amazing for my runs. It stays put on my head and doesn't slip around. I love having it bluetooth-paired to my iPod Nano so I can listen to music while running. I do wish there was another switch to switch tracks though. The multifunction switch requires you to "double click" to skip a song, which isn't always easy while running. I also run with my iPhone and if someone calls, I am able to take the call with this headset, another nice feature.

I did want to note one thing. The bendy white plastic back of the headset started to develop cracks last month. I could still get it on my head, but it did not hold tight. A few other reviewers had the same issue. I called Motorola to complain, and they replaced the headset when I explained which part broke. It appears that this is a known issue with early models of the headset. The new one they sent looks a bit different - both control buttons are orange (on the old one, one was orange the other was black). I have had no issue with cracking since I got the new one.

A good accessory to consider as well is [[ASIN:B00B196IB4 Otterbox Motorola S11 Flex HD Headphone Case - Black]] to protect these headphones in a gym bag.

title: wow
text:
Needed to purchase an USB 3.0 card in order to get all of the speed possible out of my external hard drive.

This card is perfect for my needs. Three USB slots (only need one but you never know) with enough space between them to be able to put three cables in.
Installation was a breeze. Took the cover off the case, plugged the card into the available slot, plugged the power cable in (you really should use the power; a lot of USB devices require power), put the cover back on the case, rebooted the computer, installed the proper driver (TI in this case) off of the supplied CD, and voila, USB 3.0 transfer rates. Quick check of read/write access times with my external drive show the speed to be exactly as advertised.

Would highly recommend this product and this seller to anyone.... fast shipping, extremely well packaged (bubble envelope) and a product exactly as advertised that was easy to install. I couldn't ask for anything else.

title: Great with the 70-200 F/2.8, on IS II even better
text:
I got this to pair with my 70-200mm F/2.8 IS II since I needed a bit more reach, and didn't want to spring for a 300mm or 400mm lens.

I'm extremely happy with it, and have to say that on a high quality lens, like the 70-200/2.8 IS II, there is hardly any loss of functionality at all. Yes, you do lose two stops, but getting a 400mm F/5.6 is not bad at all, and the 4 stops of the IS on the IS II certainly helps a lot. And these days, with the ability to shoot high ISOs without much noise (such as on the 5D3), it's not an issue getting clear shots at 1/500s or faster during the day.

There is some SLIGHT image degradation, to be expected, but it is not noticeable at all unless you are seriously pixel peeping. Only at 100% crops would you be able to tell the difference, and the gain from the extra focal length far outweighs the slight loss in image quality.

You do also get slower autofocus, again, because of the reduced effective aperture size (less light passing through, so it's harder for your camera to detect focus). The 70-200/2.8 IS II has extremely quick autofocus to begin with, so the reduced speed is not too bad. On slower autofocus lenses (such as if you use this extender for macro work, like on the 180mm F/3.5L Macro), the autofocus is nearly downright impossible and you may just be better off using full time manual focus.

You also won't be able to use all the focus points that you're used to using, since you'll only be able to use the points that respond to f/5.6 or slower with a F/2.8 lens. On the 5D3, this means only the center rectangle of points (about 21 cross type points). The 1DS3 and 1DX give you a bit more focus point options at f/5.6. And on lower end cameras, you may be only able to use your center AF point.

On slower lenses, such as f/4 or slower, you may be limited to manual focus only. That's why I really only recommend using a 2x extender on an f/2.8 lens. On slower lenses, you're better off using a 1.4x extender.

The compact size and relatively light weight of the 2x extender makes it a must-bring any time I bring my 70-200 outdoors. Plus it gives me the flexibility of having either a 70-200/2.8 or a 140-400/5.6 at any time I want.

It's especially great to use for wildlife (especially birds and other animals) and sports, if you're shooting during the day. For anything more serious, or in lower light, you'll need to spring for a 300/2.8 or 400/2.8, which are prohibitively expensive unless you're using it regularly for your full time job.

title: Counterfeit chipset makes this item unusable
text:
First, a disclaimer. Multiple vendors sell this product, so it is not clear whether they all ship the exact same product. Although the seller who shipped this item to me was BestDealUSA, I believe this would apply to all the others (e.g., eForcity). I was lucky that they acted in a honorable manner and refunded my money promptly as soon as I notified them about the issue but you should beware. I hope this product will not be offered anymore (the vendor I used promised to investigate and stop carrying the product), here's why.

This RS232 to USB converter claims to be using the Prolific PL-2303 chipset - when inserted in the USB port, the "Device description" reads "Prolific USB-to-Serial Comm Port" and the hardware ID is "USB\VID_067B&PID_2303&REV_0300", which is the signature ID of the Prolific chipset. However, the device does not work (either with the included drivers or with the original drivers from the Prolific website). Furthermore, when visiting the Prolific website (I'm not allowed to provide a link, so you'll have to trust me) you see the following warning:

"Warning Notice:
Please be warned that counterfeit (fake) PL-2303HX (Chip Rev A) USB to Serial Controller ICs using Prolific's trademark logo, brandname, and device drivers, were being sold in the China market. Counterfeit IC products show exactly the same outside chip markings but generally are of poor quality and causes Windows driver compatibility issues (Yellow Mark Error Code 10). We issue this warning to all our customers and consumers to avoid confusion and false purchase."

That is exactly what I observed, both on Windows 7 x64 and Windows XP x86 systems. I am an engineer and I cannot fathom how someone would manufacture something like that and then try to sell it. I know many people (including me) are trying to save a buck by buying cheap electronics designed and made in China, but there is a limit to what can be tolerated.

The bottom line is, the device does not work, doesn't seem to have a chance of working, and thus, it is a complete waste of time to try and purchase it, and all vendors who carry this item should investigate and stop carrying it.

Pros
- Amazing zoom range
- Much cheaper than corresponding DSLR or ICL camera
- Good ergonomics
- Great screen
- Viewfinder

This lens is not for someone looking for great image quality, you just aren't going to get that with a sensor this size. It isn't for someone mainly shooting indoors without flash. It isn't for someone who wants a compact camera to carry around all the time.

Who it is for is someone who loves telephoto photography and doesn't want to invest thousands of dollars for a DSLR. title: Great Lens, user notes
text:
I have had this lens now for about 4 weeks. I use it for wild life photography in Rocky mountains.
I also use the Nikon 80-200, 80-400 and Sigma 50-500. This lens is as sharp as the 80-200 but with much better reach.
First and foremost the lens dose what Nikon claim it dose.

Here are some things to think about if your considering this lens.
This is a large and very heavy lens. and it gets heaver as the day goes by.
You can hand hold this lens because the VR II is vey effective, however for the best results you really need a good tripod and head. A Gimbal head would be best.
The VR II is very noisy and spooks the birds if you are close to them.

The lens comes with a way over done and large carrying case. It is almost like a back pack. It can be used to ship the lens and I am sure it would work fine. But it is too lager to be practical for every day use unless you work or use it out of your car.
There is a great deal of third party accessory for this lens, replacement foot, lens coat , protective case and hoods, etc. You will need some sort of practical protective case for filed use.

If you use this lens with Nikon's new cameras, D800, or D4, you will be rewarded with the ability to Auto focus at F8. This means you can use all Nikon AFS tele-convertors on this lens and be able to auto focus. This is a big deal since it gives you an 800mm F8 lens with auto focus if you use a Nikon TC-20E III tele-convertor.

I have used the TC-20E and TC-14E Both on the lens and have not notice Image degradation using RRS TC33 Tripods and Gimbal head. I am sure there is a bit of degradation but since I am no Moose Peterson I can't tell. Since all my images has some sort of degradation for other reasons than the use of Tele-convertors anyway. Your experience may vary.
The auto focus on the lens is faster than all the above lenses I mentioned, and stays fast even with the TC-20E.

One last word, Do not dismiss the size and weight issue. It is a real issue if you are going to cary this lens around all day hiking or sports shooting.
Traveling with this lens is also a challenge. You have to develop strategies around carrying this along with all other lenses and camera bodies through airports and deal with flight attendants who want you to check your bag with your all your gear and the $6000.00 lens in it.

I hope this help you, It is hard to justify spending the money on this lens but I have not regret it at all. Just wish I had done it sooner.

Update 4/10/2013:
Since I have used the lens for sometimes now, I thought I would share my experience:
As I mentioned in my original review I have been using the lens with TC14 and TC20. The images from TC20 at longer distances and wider f stops are much softer and more importantly, I experienced a lot of focusing issues not so much with speed as I am with accuracy, significant back focusing at longer distances (I am using D800). I have examined my technique and tested the combination at controlled environment, but no deference in performance, I also have a Nikon 300, 2.8. The TC20 performs much better with 300, 2.8.
So even though the TC20 is usable, I would not recommend using TC20 with this lens for moving subjects, like Birding or Sports shooting. Since I had issues with TC20, I purchased a TC17. I have to say that TC17 is not much better. On the other hand the TC14 has been a great combination and no issues at all.

title: It was a good try.
text:
So after playing with the DSC-QX10 I am returning it. I was really rooting for this to work. A few issues
1. Lag - Outdoors under sunlight, indoors, an area with too many access points, outside in the city. It lags where I cannot even take the picture I want because the opportunity is gone. It tries to adjust at the cost of not being able to function at a speed a normal point and shoot can.
2. Lack of flash - yes people still use this.
3. Barely fits the larger Note 3 phones.
4. Really? Wifi??? Sometimes if the phone is configured to connect to other pre-programmed wifi hotspot or access point, it will fight with the camera and disconnect leaving me with a "Internet not available disconnecting" message rendering my camera useless.
5. When wanting to browse the pictures on the device (from the phone) it self that didn't download to the phone, it is difficult and would disconnect before it would allow you to do it.
6. I need to disconnect the camera to post the picture directly to anything social media related. Since the phone is looking for internet and notices that the Sony camera doesn't have it, it will disconnect and then re-connect to your phone service to upload.
7. By the time I get the camera ready, the opportunity is gone.
8. Software that is in the camera's internal memory has nothing to do with the camera and is not compatible with the camera. Why was it included?

If this product line is to survive, I suggest to Sony, use Bluetooth. Needing to disconnect from the camera to connect to 4g/LTE to post a picture is ridiculous and takes up to a minute to perform. Also, put a flash in the darn thing. I am sure they know how to do that since they also made Sony RX II with its tiny flash. A few more functions such as being able to set how long exposure time is, and better aperture control would be nice. And last, make sure it can save the pictures to another folder on the phone, lets say, the DCIM folder on the SD card on the phone maybe where the gallery program can find it and not on the phone itself under the "Sony Memories" folder where gallery cannot find it. I was hoping that this was my point and shoot that I would carry and use everywhere. I am resigned to the fact that I will probably need to buy a point and shoot and look back at this and say "It was a good try" don't get me wrong, these take very good pictures under ideal circumstances (no wifi interference, not so much light, stationary and no need to post it right away), but it didn't hit my standards. Sorry Sony.

title: Adequate GPS functionality; decent mp3 playback; odd interface quirks...
text:
[[VIDEOID:259adaa05e4a4b6e0820a2c555dfdb79]] The Pyle PGSPW5 "navigation sporting unit" with a built-in .mp3 player is a device I really wanted to like. To its credit, it mostly performs adequately as a handheld GPS for leisure activities (but NOT for driving routes...which it doesn't claim to support) with an integrated digital music player.

What this product does well:
-provide GPS positions and retrieve/store locational data and altitude (in each of .gpx, .rte and .kml file formats)
-support non-extreme leisure activities such as geocaching, hiking and fishing.
-playback .mp3 and .mp4 audio. Sound quality (through headset only) was satisfactory; capacity limited to fixed 4GB internal memory.
-IPX7 rated for use in damp environments (but not immersion); this will be reduced when the access compartment is open to accommodate earbuds or the USB cable (for charging or data transfer).

Where this product is wide of the mark:
-Working in non-metric units. Imagine my surprise when I changed the preferences from metric to "imperial", and the GPS began rendering altitude in...yards. Really? This is a case where I can only ask: what were these developers thinking?
-Difficult to find (or recreate) user options. This unit arrived with more than 14000 miles indicated in its odometer display. Residue of its air travel from China perhaps? Worse than this was my utter inability to discover how to reset this essential element of information. The reset function was nowhere to be obviously found in any of the device settings/options. More surprises: it one point when I powered the device back on, the odometer was reading zero. Go figure.
-Miniscule type in the user guide (and none available online).
-Painfully slow battery recharging (plan on overnight).

If you bought this at the currently deeply discounted price (under one hundred dollars), you probably aren't too disappointed. But if I had spent the full list price on this, this product could have been hugely disappointing. I work with somebody who is a regular geocacher, and he is looking forward to having it join his geocaching took kit.

Note: This item was provided for review purposes.

title: Great Storage Unit - update 3/16/13
text:
I purchased this product to back up 3 of our laptops and 1 desktop. My computers consist of a Vista machine and Windows 7 32 bit and 64 bit machines and a Mac OS X Lion. I have had zero problems with the My Book Live 2TB unit. The only problems I ran into were IP address conflicts on my network, which was an easy fix, and my router had timed out on me for some reason preventing the first Mac OS X Lion back up to complete. Once the router problem was fixed I was able to back up all my computers to the My Book Live 2TB drive. Very very easy. I really have had zero issues with this unit.

I now, also, have the ability to access all of my files through this one drive on any of my computers, smart phones, iPad, and PS3 that are connected to my network. Very easy as well. It's great to have the ability to share our movies, pictures, and videos on our smart phones and PS3.

Overall I really like the storage drive.

UPDATE: 3/16/13:
Well I was happy with this product for about the first six months or so. I can no longer access the My Book Live 2TB drive directly. The menu, or screen, where one would log does not come up...ever. Backups have grown very slow, My Time Machine backups on my mac used to run well, now it never ever finished and the transfer speeds just keep getting slower and slower the longer the back up takes. It started to get so annoying that I just turned Time Machine off. I can still access the drive through a folder on my laptops and desktops but it is impossible to play with any of the settings as the menu for that screen has disappeared, as have the settings menus for the drive. This is preventing me from using the drive in the manner it was intended.

It is a very frustrating thing to not be able to access the menus of the My Book Live 2TB drive. Also, I no longer have the ability to share movies, pictures, and videos between PCs or smart phones using the drive. This really is a huge disappointment, especially when compared to how well it worked in the beginning.

After one year of use of this product I would not recommend it to anybody. Look somewhere else. DO NOT PURCHASE THE MY BOOK LIVE.

title: Slick and Smooth Application - and Bose Sound Quality!
text:
I ordered this system directly from Bose, but only after traveling to a Bose store to hear the unit.

Sound is very impressive (no surprise there). The ability to adjust the volume, song(s) playing and turn the unit on/off remotely is really neat. I don't use Apple devices, so this is all without Airplay.

Setup was pretty straightforward, although I had to do a factory reset of the unit once after the PC hosting my music collection wouldn't find the device. I finally decided this was caused by my PC being connected directly to my router via Ethernet. As soon as I disabled the Ethernet adapter and enabled WiFi, connect was successful. (Yeah, weird, I know.)

I also had to uninstall and then reinstall the desktop application after the application's icon wouldn't appear in my PCs system tray. This made it impossible to synchronize my music library.

The initial synchronization only showed limited playlists, albums and music files. Bose customer support pointed out the application's dependency on the local Window Media Player application. To this point, I hadn't used WMP - I used Media Monkey to organize and play music files. Once I let Windows Media Player update its music directory and database and synchronizing the Bose desktop application - all files appeared.

I'm looking forward to expanding my Bose Sound Touch equipment suite to get music streaming throughout the house.

This item is HIGHLY RECOMMENDED.

Edit 6/14/2014 - changing from 4 to 5 stars!

Since my last review, I've picked up a SoundTouch portable. Despite its small size, its sound actually challenges the output of the SoundTouch 20. It's battery life is terrific and the range of reception of its internal WiFi antenna is super - reaching all the way out to the back yard!

Bose's QA process with software updates is apparently getting better and the promise of new features, including supporting lossless formats, such as FLAC, has me pretty anxious to see this product line develop!

title: great still camera, but not fully usable as a video camera
text:
- As a still camera, this is a wonderful piece of equipment, and I have no complaints.

- As a video camera, the D7000 is a continuing source of frustration to me. Key issues are the following:

(1) The 20-minute recording limit is a major limitation. This should be increased to the capacity of the card, or at least to 60 minutes.

(2) The camera has several microphone sensitivity modes. One of these sets the level automatically, which would be very convenient if it worked. The problem with this mode is that the camera tends to set the sensitivity too high, producing saturation and distortion.

(3) When one uses the internal microphone, there is a fairly high level of noise from the auto-focus.

(4) When one uses a monaural external microphone, the camera should reproduce the input in both channels, but does not (one channel remains empty).

(5) When using an external microphone and a mixing board to reproduce the signal in both channels, there is intermittent electrical noise. (The volume of the noise is high enough to impact the intelligibility of spoken audio, i.e., this is not just an issue for music recordings). I don't hear the noise if I plug headphones directly into the mixing board, and that same output is being fed to the camera, so it's fairly clear that the noise is being generated by the camera itself.

To summarize, this is a great still camera, but not fully usable as a video camera.

title: Cool but needs a lot of work...
text:
This has been one of the coolest stereo's I have seen for a long time. When I first opened it up I was impressed with the build quality and how small the body of it was. I later realized that it does not mount up to any standard brackets due to its small size and had to modify my factory bracket to get it to sit the way I wanted it to. Another problem with it is the face of it is a lot larger than any car's standard DIN opening so it either has to stick out a lot or you have to cut things to make it fit. If it sticks out you will most likely have to use the sleeve for mounting which may not be an option for come cars and/or may require a dash kit. Hooking it up was easy and it sounds great. I bought a 32gb SD card for it but it did not work. I ended up using my old 32gb USB thumb drive instead which works fine. The line in functionality is awesome to have. I don't have any Apple products so I didn't try the iPod connector. Although this stereo has a lot of great features it also has it's downfalls. It is buggy, slow, sometimes crashes, and has intermittent issues with bluetooth connectivity.

Pros:
- Looks great
- Lots of great features
- Great noise cancellation/reduction
- Automatic volume control is awesome
- Bluetooth A2DP streaming works great
- Bluetooth network for internet streaming and maps is cool
- Easy to update

Cons:
- Size is not standard
- Crashes occasionally
- Freezes occasionally (then needs to be reset)
- Takes a while to start up (almost a minute after turning the key)
- Slugish UI
- Slugish when switching sources
- Does not remember previous source after being off
- Has intermittent bluetooth connectivity issues
- Maps App is pretty useless and is not the full Google Maps app
- Main menu/source items cannot be hidden if you don't use them
- Not all SD Cards work (it somehow makes the file system corrupt)
- No automatic dimmer (you have to set day/night mode manually)
- No shuffle folder option for USB drive

I would not recommend buying this stereo unless you are ready to pay for or do custom work to your car to get this installed and don't mind the things listed in the cons section. There are many other stereo's that offer the same features, are easier to install and have less issues. Parrot is coming out with a new 2Din stereo ([...]) with the same features as this one and more which will hopefully be a standard size. In my opinion it would be worth the wait if the new stereo has the cons fixed and is faster and more functional.

text:
I had a supplier use a much earlier model at a meeting and he demonstrated how it worked and how he could play meeting back (at accelerated speed) from his laptop and email a meeting to his partner who could also view them in the same way.

When I bought mine the descriptions did not make it clear that the PC based applications are gone. The fast playback is gone. Easy sharing is gone. You are bound to Evernote and its limitations or sending an image of the notes or having an audio of the meeting not connected to the images. Branding/watermarks are added to your notes by default and can be hard to get rid of. It was clear you need internet access to upload form the pen but not that you need fast internet access to make any useful use of the notes - and even then not so useful.

I wish they had been clearer about this in their promotional material at the time - it would have avoided so much disappointment.

Evernote is finicky about browsers etc - not just HTML5 but specific browsers - it is also far from intuitive. Then you end up with an to and throw between Evernote and Livescribe with support.

Because it is tied to an Evernote account I can't even sell it for $1. Wasted so much time trying to make it work.

title: Seems to overheat (Updated)
text:
Now, before I start this review I will say I've worked with entirely Intel processors so I could be doing something wrong.

I ordered this processor for a family member's build, they mostly just play internet games or minecraft (they're 7 and 9 years old) so I didn't want it to cost too much. I put everything together, turned the PC on and started setting it up. A while later I was curious on temps so I downloaded HWMonitor and noticed it was spiking to 70C. I took off the cooler (I ordered one instead of using stock) and cleaned/re-applied the paste. Did this a few times without luck, so I tried the stock. Same thing, I ordered a replacement just in case I got a bad one. It came today, it seemed better but after running for ~1 hour it started reaching 70-80C again. I have tried several ways of applying the paste and used two different coolers without luck. I did read posts saying it could be bad sensors, which is entirely possible as the PC runs fine but spikes under minimal load (30%).

In short, this processor runs great but seems to have overheating issues or I'm doing something wrong. In the future I will probably stick with Intel unless I can get this figured out.

Edit:
It seems it may not be the processors fault after all. Though I'm still not sure the direct cause, it could be due to a voltage issue or just inaccurate readings.

title: Compatible with Linux- has a great iPad app too
text:
I was looking for a Linux compatible all-in-one printer for wireless network printing. Brother is one of the few (if only) companies that consistently support Linux operating systems; therefore, I am very partial to Brother.
FYI, I am running Ubuntu 13.04, 64bit. First I manually set the printer to a static IP address (within the router's range), set the gateway, and subnet mask. Usually, after Ubuntu finds the printer, the drivers load automatically. Unfortunately, this did not occur as expected. I went to the Brother website and found .deb and .rpm files, but even after loading the .pdd file, it did not work. Finally, a FAQ section for the Linux drivers included an install file that I could run on the terminal. After downloading the file, I opened terminal and point to the script using the 'bash' command. So go to the folder, then type "bash brother_driver" The script prompted quite a bit of downloading and installing, but it worked perfectly.
Then the easy part, Brother has a wonderful iPad app that allows you to print and scan. After I installed the app, the app found the printer, scanned a document and emailed it.
Overall, yes, I would recommend this printer. I'm always going to be a Brother customer as long as they keep putting out drivers for Linux. Unlike other manufacturers, Brother is very helpful to customers; directions are detailed and help is available.

title: Works great with Printers and Desktops, anything with an Ethernet jack.
text:
We have had good success with the Asus EA-N66

It is a standalone wireless "client" that outputs Ethernet. So it, all by itself, creates the connection to the WiFi network, and lets any Ethernet device use it. We have used it with Printers and Desktops, but it would also work with an XBox or any Ethernet device. Note that this device does require power from a wall outlet, but you can also use a 100+ foot Cat5e Ethernet cord if you want to, so the placement location of this device is flexible. In fact, it can operate 3-in-1 "Access Point, Wi-Fi Bridge, and Range Extender Mode" and if you hook a network switch to it, multiple Ethernet clients can operate through it. It's all about flexibility, and I keep one on hand along with my set of Netgear Powerline Network Adapters "just in case" I need one for something.

It requires setup initially, as in you have to follow the directions in order to tell it what WiFi network to connect to. If you have compatible WiFi router you can just use the "push a button on each device and they automatically connect" method, which I found to work fine with an RT-N66U, but I still prefer to get in to the web page and do things myself.

The price point seems a bit high and has actually gone up since the EA-N66 first came out, so price may be a consideration for some, but it is also a dual band 2.4/5GHz 450+450 Mbps device using current 802.11n technology. No it's not 802.11ac but that's not yet a standard, and as far as I know today the only faster client adapters are USB and PCI Express which do not fill the Ethernet niche this device does.

There are no drivers required because the device you connect with Ethernet just sees a Network connection. So a Media player with an Ethernet port should work fine, the same as it would work plugged directly into your network switch. You do have to set up the device first. The worst possible setup is to have to plug it into a computer's Ethernet port with automatic IP (DHCP, the default of most computers), then open any browser, and go through the setup pages that appear in the browser. I personally do not recommend using the flat ribbon cable that comes with the EA-N66 as it is not "twisted" or Gigabit certified.

title: WOW
text:
I installed this HD in a 15 inch MacBook Pro (mid 2009). I was simply amazed at how much it has sped up the computer. The first time I booted from this HD I could notice the difference in speed. And from what I have read it will only get faster because of the SSD. Here are the steps I used to install this HD.
1. Buy this HD and an external enclosure. (I bought this one: Vantec NexStar TX 2.5-Inch SATA to USB 2.0)
2. Install the Seagate Momentus XT into the external enclosure.
3. Use the Disk Utility to format the HD to "Mac OS Extended (journaled)
4. Copy your internal HD to your new HD. I used Carbon Copy Cloner (<...>)
5. Once the Carbon Copy Cloner was done I tried to boot the computer from the Seagate Momentus XT while it was still in the external enclosure. Reboot the mac and hold the Option key to select the new HD. Booting from the external took a little bit of time. I imagine this is because of the limitations of the USB. If it boots then you should be good to go.
6. Shut down the MacBook and remove the old HD and install the new HD. Now you can put the old HD in the external enclosure to use for whatever.
7. Startup the macbook with the new HD installed.

When I did this everything was just as before. I didn't have to reinstall the OS or any of my app. Everything just worked like normal but faster. I did have to resign into my wifi network and DropBox wanted me to sign in again. But other than that it was a simple process. I couldn't be happier.

title: Not a proper Mac keyboard!
text:
I love my original IceKeys, but they're not fully compatible with OS X 10.7 and later. I was excited when I saw the IceKey2. Sadly, this is a WORSE keyboard under OS 10.7 and 10.8 than the original IceKey. I cannot recommend it to any user who is interested in using the Function keys.

The problem is that Macally HARDWIRED the Function keys. I have not been able to change their default assignments using either the Keyboard pref pane or Keyboard Maestro. If you want to assign anything to the keys, you must hit the Fn key (which unfortunately is at the opposite side of the keyboard to where it's located on Apple keyboards. This is a problem if you alternate between, say, a MacBook keyboard and a Macally keyboard, because you'll always need to remember where the Fn key is, and you'll also need to be sure to remember if you've programmed the Apple keyboard(s) via the Keyboard preferences.

There's another problem with Macally HARDWIRED function keys—they're just asking to be broken by future versions of OS X. All Apple needs to do is make a minor change to their default keyboard assignments, and the IceKey2 function key defaults are kaput.

The only thing positive I can say for this keyboard is that the feel is excellent. I think the IceKey action is one of the best available for Macs, and the keys feel great. If only Macally hadn't permanently programmed their own functions into the keys!

If all you want is a nice-feeling keyboard, the Macally is OK. But if you really want to USE the keyboard and make it work for you, look at other units.

Cutting to the chase - I'd get flicker on certain scenes during movie playback. Always the same scenes, at the exact same time - so it wasn't a fit issue. But the scenes played perfectly when I switched back to my old adapter and cable. Also - I found I wasn't able to play big (20 gig+) 3D rips, when the other cable could.

So . . . for most tablets and cameras this cable will work fine. I suspect this cable will be fine for the Tegra 2 tablets (Original Transformer, Galaxy Tab, Acer Iconia, etc.) since playback is generally limited to 720P. But if you play high quality video - it could be a problem - I don't know what the actual limitation is.

title: Can't beat the price
text:
For macro photography on a shoestring budget, you really can't beat these tubes. Beware of light leaks if you're using all of the tubes and a heavy lens (I've used them with my 70-200 f/4) because the torque can cause the tubes to bow a bit at the threads. Other than that, though, these work great.

Tip for stopping down with automatic lenses: connect your lens normally to your camera. Choose your aperture and then hold down the depth-of-field preview button. Disconnect the lens while still holding down the button, and your lens will now be stopped down and off of the camera so you can use it with these tubes (or reversed with a ring). The viewfinder will be crazy dark (especially if you go to f/16 or something) but you can use a flashlight or something to compose and focus if you're inside.

title: Terrible Picture Quality... Already boxed up and going back!
text:
I was excited to finally get a new Samsung TV that has all the latest tech. My family all have Samsung TVs, the original 65" series LED-LCDs and they are still running like champs. I wish I could have said the same for this one. When I first opened the box I noticed that the stand was as terrible as people made it out to be, I was wall mounting this TV so it wasn't a deal breaker for me. But if you don't wall mount this TV, be mindful of this.

Lets get to the reason why I am sending this TV back... the picture quality is horrendous. The TV is plagued with frame rate issues and horrendous lag. I was watching a BluRay (and before you ask it was Skyfall with most up to date software on both the TV and BluRay player) and whenever there was a lot of moving scenes it would get noticeably more choppy than normal and it would actually lag and look like it was skipping. I know for a fact that it isn't the BluRay disc because it did the exact same thing watching Netflix and Cable HD TV. I know the LED-LCDs aren't the best in regards to picture quality compared to a Plasma but this was terrible. It would randomly skip around looking like lag and it would get choppy for no reason.

I played around with almost every picture setting the TV has to offer and nothing helped. I would say that if this was a $800 TV I wouldn't be this upset, but for $2,000 you expect to get something that is top quality. I went to my local store where I usually buy my electronics and everyone there told me that ever since the ES line of Samsung TVs they have been rushing them out too quickly and its finally starting to show.

The Amigo microphone, in contrast, is unidirectional. It is also small and attractively styled. I just plugged it into a USB port on my computer and Windows installed the driver software automatically. I then had to go through the process of setting up a new microphone in the Dragon software. Unlike other times I've installed a new microphone, though, the setup process for this one was really fast and easy. title: Don't expect help from Logitech technical support for iPhone or iPad3
text:
I went the rounds with Logitech's technical support on this, because I read the review from "Nancy mother of guys," and from "The Savvy Shopper," each of whom said they use this with their iPhones. Nancy was specific that it was an iPhone 4S, which is what I have. I followed all the instructions, and the iPhone detected the keyboard but wouldn't pair with it. A co-worker has an iPad3, and we got the same error. I called technical support, and I was very direct and insistent with them, citing the reviews on Amazon. He said it only works with the iPad2. I made him talk to a supervisor, and he came back confirming that.

Well, not to be easily diverted, I went to the Logitech website, and in their product description for this keyboard, they say, "The keyboard pairs easily with iPad (and even iPhone or iPod touch) over Bluetooth wireless." So I called back to technical support. When I pressed this new tech and quoted their own website to him, he finally got down to the heart of the matter. Their technical support has been instructed that they will only SUPPORT connecting with the iPad or iPad2.

It turns out that I have a defective keyboard. I went to a nearby Verizon store and tried to connect with an iPad2 display model and got the same error. I like the keyboard. I like the feel, the size, the stand. So I'll give them two stars for that, but no more, because of a lousy experience with technical support. I guess I will send the keyboard back for a replacement.

I wish Logitech would get things together with their technical support to fully synchronize with the claims they make for this product on their website. They have a corporate policy that if you have an iPhone or iPad3, you won't get any help from technical support, even though their public statements are that it will work with those devices.

title: Good Value
text:
I wanted to get my feet wet with Astronomy and decided to get Binoculars first since I live in the city so there's little sense in buying a big telescope.

The first set of binoculars I got was Orion 7x50 Scenix. For about 100 bucks they were great. Crystal clear and everything. But in the back of my mind I kept wondering what if I had more magnification and a little more objective...so I bought these.

If I had never bought the Orions I would have given the Skymasters 5 stars. Lifetime no-fault warranty. Big objective lenses. 15x magnification. Light. Tripod adapter. These would have totally made me happy. However because I got the Orions I'm able to make a comparison and yeah the build quality of the Skymasters is a little wanting. The eyepieces move when you fold the eye cups down. There's a very slight optical imperfections with some objects that show up as sharp pinpoints with the Orions.

Not bad mind you. The price they can't be beat. With these on a really small cheap tripod I'm able to see Titan. Just barely but it's totally there. Can't see Saturns rings but I can tell there's something odd with its shape more than with the 7x Scenix.

So yeah thumbs up. For the price I doubt they can be beat. But not the end-all binoculars for stargazing. Also You'll want a tripod for these.

title: Excellent Portable Projector
text:
I cannot begin to praise this projector enough. There are so many little things done right on this guy especially when compared to other projectors around the same price point. It's clear to me that the designed at Epson have really put a lot of thought into this unit.

Setting up the projector was a breeze as I had going in minutes using the quick setup guide. In reality though, I didn't need the guide since setup was so straight forward -- the physical buttons on the unit and the remote are well labelled and supplemented with helpful icons, for example. Getting the picture displayed properly has been a chore with other projectors but this guy has a wonderful elevator level underneath that can easily be raised and lowered. The product also feels and looks like a quality product -- sturdy and solid with seemingly no cheap or flimsy plastic parts.

I could go into minute details here, but let's just get to the heart of the matter...

PROS
====
+ Gorgeous, bright picture
+ Remote included (and doesn't require perfect aim at the device to respond!)
+ Easy to use button and menus
+ Supports wireless LAN projection as well as VGA, HMDI, and USB
+ Integrated lens cover
+ Instant off -- no delayed cool down process
+ Excellent elevation lever on the bottom to get height just right
+ Carrying case included
+ Quiet fan
+ Free "Extra Care" service where Epson ships you a replacement unit if your unit malfunctions (often the next day!)
+ Tons of little features but done in a way that they don't overwhelm you if you aren't interested in them

CONS
====
+ Not quite what I would call 'ultracompact' as I've seen several units half this size
+ Menu could use a larger font (but it is still readable to me)
+ Slideshow mode doesn't offer option to play pictures in sub folders plus no pause supported although there is a manual slide slow
+ Built in speakers at max volume hard to hear clearly when more than 10 feet away

Despite the device being a little larger than expected, it still would fit inside a brief case or messenger bag. I'd gladly carry this device over the smaller projectors I've seen since the Epson does such a wonderful job and it is much easier to user the many of its competitors. Let's be clear here -- when you have a presentation to give, the last thing you need is stress from your projector so carrying an extra pound in weight is well worth it if it is this guy. Finally, I've only covered the tip of the iceberg. This project is loaded with all the features you expect and then some -- split screen mode, digital zoom, movable pointer overlay, etc. More importantly, the ability to find and use such features is easy but only if you want to access them. This projector is what I call an 'inviting' device in that people will be drawn towards it due to its simplicity instead of begging someone else to operate it.

title: An exercise in frustration
text:
I read many reviews on this product before purchasing, taking to heart the warnings that the JOTO Premium Screen Protector Film HD Ultra Clear could be difficult to install. Be warned, in my opinion these other reviewers are being exceptionally generous in their assessment of difficulty in installation -- the reality is much worse.

I've installed an number of different screen protectors on a number of different types of devices. So, when I read the reviews discussing the difficulty of installation, I have to admit that my ego got in the way, figuring I would not have the problems experienced by others.

The instructions for installation are printed on the rear panel of the package, just below the description of features -- the leading feature being "Anti-figferprint" (yes, this is as it appears on the package). This was the first warning flag. The instructions themselves appear pretty straightforward but fail to mention the purpose of one component -- a small sheet of translucent blue film adhered to a white sheet.

The instructions warn to clean the screen thoroughly. If you ignore my first recommendation and decide to take your chances with this product, then take this instruction to heart: exercise exceptional care in cleaning. The smallest particle of dust between the film an the screen results in a bubble. And you cant get these things out.

The instructions said clean thoroughly.

So I cleaned.

I cleaned thoroughly.

The installation of the first protective film sample included in the box resulted in three dust bubble and spots around the edge failing to adhere for no reason I could observe. I pulled off this first failure and decided to take another run at it.

I cleaned even more -- darn near becoming Amathophobic (yeah- I had to look that one up).
No Joy.

The problem is the film is statically charged and attracts dust, hair, etc.

I burned through all three of the protective films that come in the package in an effort to install at least one without blemish. All three included dust and edge bubbles. Most frustrating is that the last install turned out the worst.

Finally, for the record, the product may be "Anti-figferprint" (whatever that may mean) as stated on the package, but every touch of your finger WILL leave a print on the installed screen protector.

This laptop is definitely my daily driver and it still runs perfectly fine. However, I've been having a lot of trouble with some physical defects on this machine. The problem with the trackpad that I mentioned in an earlier review is still as present as ever and I've noticed that my spacebar key will not respond sometimes. Parts of the laptop are also falling off... I've lost a screw on the bottom and a couple cushion blocks on the surface of the laptop. Overall, however, since it still runs perfectly fine I've had no problem with it. However, I think toshiba should do a better job with manufacturing this laptop and making sure parts aren't falling off after less than a year.

----

I've been using this Chromebook for the past few days and have absolutely loved it. Everything is fast and the Chrome OS software doesn't limit any of the work that I usually do. I'm highly adjusted to working with the Cloud and Google Docs so this device was perfect for me. The keyboard and trackpad are also very good and responsive. So why the 3 stars? I've only put 3 days of use into this Chromebook and on Day 3 the trackpad has collapsed. I've spilled nothing on it and only put light use into it but the lower side of my trackpad seems to be digging lower than it should. Has this been a common hardware problem for anyone else using this device? The trackpad is still fully functional but the clicking rattles or is stiffer than usual.

Other than the trackpad defect (which I hope isn't a common problem shipped with every device), everything worked fine. I was thoroughly impressed with the software (speed, functionality, 1080p display) of the Toshiba Chromebook 2 HD.

title: One of the best keyboards I have used
text:
I am really sick of cheap rubber or just poorly made keyboards that break or have me slamming my hands into them just to make a few sentences appear... finally something has come along that is made not in rubber, cheaply, and is super responsive to my touch. The only true downside to this folio is that there is no latch to keep it closed, but you can work around that issue... and maybe Logitech will come out with a 2.0 version with a latch at a later time.

Overall I am very happy with this folio and keyboard but have broken down my pros and cons here for easy viewing:

Pros:
~Very durable keyboard- not cheap feeling and unresponsive to touch
~Overall folio weight and thickness (3/4" thickness) is not too much of a difference when I compare them to my heavy duty Belkin Cinema Folio Stand even with a keyboard
~No extra wires needed to charge keyboard
~Fast solar charging speed- it even charges in dim light for late at home office working
~Two viewing angles
~Open/close auto on/shutdown

Cons:
~No latch to close properly- BUT this can be fixed with some creative ideas. I was being a little lazy and took a jumbo rubber band (the really big and thick ones I use for arts and crafts) to hold it shut for now. But I have read in another review ways that you can get really creative to fix this issue
~No warning for when the battery is about to die
~Solar panel for charging located at the bottom- I feel that it should be at the top for when it is in use
~A little on the high price but you do get what you pay for- a keyboard and folio that is not cheaply made

title: Good for office work but not much else. Questionable support.
text:
IMPORTANT PLEASE READ:
As reported by The Register on August 12, 2015, Lenovo installed their Lenovo Service Engine into the computer's BIOS so it could not be removed, even with a complete wipe and reinstall of your hard drive. This piece of software has been found to be vulnerable to a buffer overflow attack that gives administrator-level privileges. In English, this means Lenovo sold you a computer that can be taken over by someone else. If you own this computer or any Lenovo computer manufactured between October 2014 and April 2015, please update your firmware to remove this vulnerability.

Notebooks go here: http://support.lenovo.com/nz/en/downloads/ds104370
Desktops go here: https://support.lenovo.com/nz/en/downloads/ds104373

Rating changed from three stars to one star.

My original review follows:

Yuck. Windows 8. I'll never get used to that Metro garbage and even though this computer comes with a touch screen, why would I want to mess it up with fingerprints? Speaking of the screen, it looks fine but it doesn't have a wide viewing angle and it reflects the light from lightbulbs and sunny windows. Even white walls reflect on to the screen. The true boot up time is 53 seconds (38 to boot, 15 after login). After I Win-D to get rid of the preinstalled Metro garbage, I take a look of what software came with the computer.

- Nitro Pro 8: An Adobe PDF viewer and Editor. Free trial only so I deleted it. Foxit Reader is better anyway, and free.
- Pokki - Supposedly a program that replaces the start menu but it doesn't work on this computer (nice job Lenovo)
- McAfee - Not only is this a terrible antivirus program, but it had a "critical update" that it forced me to install. It couldn't install the update and froze the computer until I restarted. Deleted. Get [[ASIN:B00EOAS4UA Bitdefender Internet Security 2014]] instead. Not only is it top ranked in detection but it lasts for two years.
- Cyberlink Power2Go 5 and PowerDVD 10 - Ancient CD and DVD reading and writing software, they're up to version 9 and 14, respectively.
- Maxthon 3 - Some browser I'm unfamiliar with so I removed it and installed Firefox

Most disturbing of all was the hardware scanner that comes with the computer. Don't get me wrong, I like the scanner because it scans each piece of hardware with short bursts of high performance requests to test the health of each component. The problem is my computer failed the test. When I called Lenovo at 1-877-4Lenovo and gave them my cryptic error message, they were surprisingly nonchalant of the results of their own scanner and told me to call them again when the computer breaks down. Not too helpful when your important data is lost, right? Let's just say I'm not keeping anything important on this computer.

Another problem I had was registering this computer with Lenovo. For some reason, I wasn't allowed to register until I downloaded something called the "Lenovo Dependency Package". Once that's downloaded I try to register a second time and it doesn't recognize the information I entered and it keeps asking me to register. This is going to be fun when I need to do a warranty claim.

The keyboard works alright and it comes with a standard 10-key. The trackpad, however is slid over to the left side of the computer. Great if you're a lefty but a bit unwieldy for a right handed person. You'll probably want a mouse. The graphics is Intel so forget about gaming and the max resolution is 1366x768 @ 60HZ. You can get away with casual titles like Bejeweled, Pogo, Angry Birds, and the like but look elsewhere if you like playing games.

The biggest issue I had while reviewing this computer is wondering trying to figure out why I would want it over a tablet. It has a large hard drive for storage so you may find it of use if you need to carry around a large number of files. Lenovo says it's 1TB however only 865GB is available due to the restoration software. Other than that I don't see why you wouldn't use a tablet instead.

If you do decide to get it, it should be plenty fast for Internet browsing and general office work. Just don't get it for gaming. And get plan on getting rid of a lot of useless software first. And be prepared for a lot of hassle when dealing with Lenovo's software.

title: Disregard the haters
text:
I just received my zenbook today in the mail and after just a few hours of fiddling, I can honestly say that I love this laptop. Don't listen to all these people who are complaining about the trackpad and the keyboard; asus has all but eliminated all the problems associated with the trackpad initially. I just switched from a macbook to this notebook, and find that the multigesture touchpad on this computer is just as competitive as the macbook's. Sure apple has had a few years headstart to work out the kinks, but asus is releasing updates FREQUENTLY in order to address any minute problems that you might encounter. Scrolling is smooth, the three finger gestures work like a charm; I honestly feel that this trackpad is more comfortable to use for extended periods of time than my macbook's was.

I can however see how some people might find the keyboard subpar. I am not one of them; I find switching from the macbook's chiclet style keyboard to this one to be a pretty seemless transition. I'm a pretty advanced typist (100+ wpm) and while the keys do not protrude like some laptop's keys do, I haven't found it to really be a problem thus far. However, this key style paired with the fact that it isn't lighted like the macbook air and the series 9 could pose a problem for more beginner typists who aren't comfortable looking at the screen while typing. As I just stated though, so far it hasn't been a problem and I imagine it to become less and less of a nuisance as I become more acclimated to the keyboard. It's simply a matter of getting used to it.

As far as aesthetics go, this computer can't be beat. From the minute you open the beautifully designed package and turn it on for the first time (which literally takes seconds by the way), you will know that you made the right choice. It looks very modernized and has a lot of brushed aluminum that simply stands out. Every friend I've shown it to thus far has been amazed by how great it looks.

Battery life seems phenomenal by the way, but that may be just because I'm coming from a laptop with a really mediocre battery. Either way, I anticipate getting at least 5+ hours from a single charge, browsing the internet while listening to music, etc. Just great.

PROS:

aesthetics
battery
trackpad
screen (really bright)
speed

cons:
keyboard (it really isn't that bad at all, just takes some adjusting to)
