title: Decent for money
text:
I will start by saying be careful of some of the reviews of this product. .I thought they looked a bit "canned" and when looking farther at the profiles of the users that posted them.. most of the good reviews only have 1 review making me think House of Marley is stacking the deck... That being said... here is my review.

I bought the headphones primarily for riding my motorcycle and wearing around on errands and such. I had purchased some Kilpsch si4 and some dre beats. The beats I was not impressed with at all for the money. The Klipsch had great sound but the cables were super thin so on the bike the wind would blow them everywhere. I preferred the flat cables of the Dre beats but the sound and the cost was a turnoff.

In came the House of Marley Zion... It is not a flat cable but it is thicker and covered in cloth so I thought it might be a good weight to prevent the wind.. I also read some decent 'independent' reviews by googling these headphones so I gave them a try. Once I got the correct earpiece size installed 'I usually always wear a large but was surprised that I needed the medium cones on these' I was happy with the sound.. It is a bit washed but it is bass heavy and what I want to listen to it works good... Oddly enough the feature I thought I would love the most I actually hate the most. The cloth cords.... OMG are they noisy.. When you walk with these things on be prepared to hear and FEEL a THUMP THUMP THUMP every time you take a step as the ipod controls bounce off your shirt and resonate through the cords. And if you turn your head from side to side or bend over be prepared for a nice noise that sounds like someone unzipped a zipper right next to your ear. This is from the braided cloth on the cord that sounds like a deep bass resonating zipper every time it passed over a surface... On the motorcycle the wind was still an issue with the cables blowing around considerably. And without a clip for my shirt as I had the the Klipsch headphones I had no way to keep the cable from flopping everywhere.

Pros.. Decent sound.. Good construction.. nice look.. nice price.

Cons... Unless you listen to music very LOUDLY.. be prepared to be annoyed by every step you take with a deep THUMP resonating through your ears.. You can avoid this by using the next larger size or smaller size earbuds that come with the headphones. You will not get a solid seal though then and you will lose about 70% of the base.

I may end up sending these back. Not sure yet. They seem more durable than the Klipsch but man I know there are some THUMP type noises with every pair of noise isolating buds I have had.. But these are pretty bad.

title: I'm no expert but for the price I'm super satisfied
text:
On my last car I replaced my stock stereo with an $800 kenwood, replaced all the speakers, got a sub and amp added in the runnk for close to $2000. The sound was a vast improvement but the stereo had too many features, was slow, and annoyed me more than it impressed me with the new functionality it had. to boot I couldn't control it on the steering wheel anymore...
So My new car is a 2014 Camry hybrid. I have the stock stereo with 6 speakers (2 6", 2 6X9, and 2 tweeters). Prior to buying this sub the sound was ok and the stereo sounded good at up to about 80-85% volume then got distorted. So I bought this along with a $10 wiring kit, and $10 channel converter to turn convert the signal from my rear speakers to a preamp signal for the amp (I reviewed these also in my review history if you are interested in them). The results were amazing. I adjusted my stereo turning the base all the way down, then adjusted the subs gain to make up the difference. Now I can turn my volume to 100% (which actually hurts my ears with some music) or run at 70% - 80% and hear loud clear bass, not available with hardly any stock or even upgraded stereos. I know with lots of $$$ that much better sound is possible but if you are looking for a huge increase in the quality of sound from your stock stereo this sub could sure be the answer. You will lose a lot of trunk space, and it will piss off the neighbors so please turn it down when getting close to home ;) Oh and wanted to add the type of music I have listened to. Hip hop, trance, soft rock, heavy metal, power metal and I will try lots more soon. Any issues I'll update.

title: Excellent for larger arms
text:
This is THE armband for anyone with larger arms. My biceps aren't massive by any means - 15.5 inches - but I tried on numerous armbands in several different stores and couldn't find any that fit comfortably without cutting off circulation. The XL size is the ONLY armband I've found that fit snugly but without cutting off circulation. The velcro band that holds your iPod/phone in the sleeve runs vertical so it holds your device much more securely than just a little tab of velcro that some others use. It's extremely elastic so it fits most accessories. All iPhones, including the 5, fit perfectly. I wasn't able to test it with a larger phone like the Galaxy S III but I'd be surprised if it didn't fit due to the elasticity. Also, the armband is extremely comfortable. I hardly notice I'm wearing it. Because your device is attached to a whole sleeve rather than just a strap, it never bounces around either.

The ONLY complaint I have about the product is the one many others have noticed - if you use it to run and sweat a lot, the sleeve becomes wet. In turn, so does the exterior of your iPod/phone. If the compartment was lined with rubber or something it would help to hold the item in place while also waterproofing but unfortunately that isn't the case. If you cut out a little sleeve for your device out of a ziplock bag and then put it in, the problem is solved. It's not the ideal solution, but for people with bigger arms, this is the only armband that can even fit so it's what I have to do. Again, unless you're sweating heavily it's a problem.

Overall, I'm extremely happy with my purchase and highly recommend it.

title: Good hub, but not UL listed, so beware.
text:
This is a good hub, and I don't have much to add to the other reviews -- except to note that it is not UL-listed. This doesn't necessarily mean it's dangerous, but it's not a good sign, since UL listing is almost ubiquitous for this kind of device, and is not difficult to get if your product is in fact safe.

EDIT 18-Jan-2012: I just got a personal response from the Plugable founder explaining that although the hub is not UL-listed, the power supply is:

"Unfortunately, UL listing is not inexpensive ($10-30K per test), so the amortized cost is much lower on a long-lived, high-volume product (like a power adapter, which won't change from year to year) .. vs the hub main unit, for which the technology turns over more quickly, and getting the UL listing would add at least $1-2 per unit. At $21.95 for the whole product, that's a big jump in customer cost, unfortunately."

I thought this was a reasonable clarification, and I really appreciate the personal response -- and the hub has been working like a champ since I bought it -- so I bumped this up another star.

title: With DD-WRT rock solid
text:
Out of the box the router had major issues, about every 2-3 days the router would lose it's setup and revert to factory default. This would leave network unencrypted, wireless devices unable to connect. It was a headache.
Two calls to TP-Link tech support were quick enough but they both said my issue was not possible and my unit defective. They wanted it returned.
After reading on line and doing research, I decided to risk voiding the warranty and install DD-WRT. Heck TP-Link advertises that their routers work with DD-WRT. The install was easy enough and now the router is rock solid. It has been running for over two months without a glitch, reboot, and any issues. With three 3rd party external antennas I get great coverage all over our large country home.
If you are looking for a router that will work straight out of the box and is easy to set up then keep shopping, this is not the router for you. The firmware stinks.
If you are a DIY person, like to hack equipment, are going to use DD-WRT anyways, or know a fair bit about computers then this is a great router. For the price this router works like a router 3 times more expensive. DD-WRT gives you complete control over the router. The network is very secure and tweaked just the way I like and need it. Just remember after you get this router, step one is install DD-WRT. Enjoy

title: Do *NOT* buy this for a stationary RV or mobile application!!! Read this FIRST!
text:
This thing works very well, my mistake was buying an inmotion dish for a stationary application. I assumed the only downside was cost was higher and there were no other tradeoffs, and if at some future point I wanted to use it inmotion, I wouldn't have to buy new equipment. The cost differential of stationary vs inmotion upfront purchase price was very small, vs cost of upgrading a stationary unit to inmotion, so I purchased an inmotion unit for my RV stationary application (mistake).

The difference between the stationary and inmotion dishes lies in the software algorithm used to run them:

An IN-MOTION dish goes through the following steps:
1. Boot up / home (reset) all motors to starting position (makes a loud noise for about 10 seconds)
2. Acquire GPS and satellite signals and lock on to primary satellite (no TV is available at this time)
3. Once satellite is locked, the dish will CONSTANTLY move (even if you are not) in tiny circles trying to find the best satellite signal since it assumes its in-motion and signals are constantly changing. It makes an awful vibrating noise while doing this, if you are in motion, it will do this indefinitely to remain locked onto satellite while in motion. TV is available during this mode.
4. If vehicle is not in motion for more than 10mins, the dish will go into a pre-stationary mode (TV viewing is interrupted during this time for about 30 seconds - 1 minute), where the vibrating noise stops and the dish moves slowly about once every 5 seconds to optimize the signal. This is an annoyance if you are watching TV about 10 minutes after power up, system will lose signal and interrupt viewing for 30seconds-1minute
5. After about 1 minute, it enters stationary mode (aka sleep mode), where the dish goes quiet and it will only move the dish if you change channels to a different satellite, or GPS speed exceeds 10mph. If GPS/vehicle speed exceeds 10mph, it will return to step3.

An STATIONARY dish goes through the following steps:
1. Boot up / home (reset) all motors to starting position (makes a loud noise for about 10 seconds)
2. Acquire GPS and satellite signals and lock on to primary satellite (no TV is available at this time)
3. The dish moves slowly about once every 5 seconds to optimize the signal this takes about 1 minute
4. The dish goes quiet and it will only move the dish if you change channels to a different satellite

So after a period of 10 minutes stationary, they will both behave the same, but the first 10 minutes of operation where the inmotion dish makes a lot of noise (vibrates on the roof on par with the air conditioner), where the stationary version would be ready in 1 minute.

There are a full row of dip switches under the dome to configure the unit which satellites to prefer, I wish they put one of them to put the dish in stationary mode.

There is also one other limitation of inmotion dishes, they only work in Western Arc or Hybrid arc modes, they do not support full eastern arc mode as the Stationary mission dish does. This is only a concern if you are in northeast US. It is because during the inmotion tracking/vibrating phase the 72degree and 77degree satellites are too close together in the sky, and the unit during the inmotion tracking will jump between the two satellites. The stationary dish has more precise positioning since its not constantly moving.

title: For the same reason it's easy to put on, it's easy to scratch
text:
In the past, most screen protectors I've used are rubbery in texture and usually made of silicon or something similar. The problem with these is that their softness leads to bubbles easily forming when you attach them and, the big problem, the protector peeling after a while as the friction from taking them in and out of your pockets (especially jeans pockets) moves edges of the flexible material.

When I saw this protector, I thought that they had finally solved that problem by using a more rigid material. Image those clear plastic windows they put in toy packaging--the ones that are rigid enough to keep their own shape. This material is closer to that than it is the rubbery silicone. It means that you can put it on a lot easier than you can the other kind of protector, especially since only the edges, not the part that goes over the screen itself, has adhesive. I was able to put two of these on in less than a minute total, and the material makes it nearly impossible for bubbles to form. I've only been using this a couple weeks, but no peeling so far (my older screen protectors would have shown signs of peeling at this point).

The drawback I discovered, however, to this rigid material is that it scratches VERY easily. There are already three prominent scratches on the protector. Now, I realize that the protector taking scratches is mainly the point of having one of these, but these don't strike me as stratches that would have formed on the gorilla glass. I've never scratched the screens on my old phones, even after I stopped using protectors. If the protector scratches this easily after just a couple weeks, I'm probably going to have to replace this every few months. It's not the cheapest of protectors, so I don't know if I'm going to be replacing this over and over again.

title: Sweet Storage
text:
I was given the opportunity to try out the Ready NAS 102. I currently have 3 internal hard drives and AT LEAST 3 external hard drives. I have never had the experience of using a NAS. In the past I have used the external hard drives as well as burning data to DVD and CD for storage and archiving. At the same time that I installed a Blu-Ray burner, I also received a NAS Storage device to test drive free from NETGEAR's Friends and Family program. It came with 2 Tb of storage, in the form of 2 Toshiba hard drives and was easy to install.

The setup was easy, following the instructions given. The added storage space was beneficial. In the past, searching for old reference documents or data was cumbersome, as I had to search and connect old external hard drives to search. Even more challenging was searching through binders of CDs or DVDs to find something. With the ReadyNAS, the search was greatly simplified. Transferring data is now very simple...as I just can just locate the data with my PC or one of my tablets and access it or transfer it over for portability.

The ReadyNAS has really made things simpler. It has also allowed me to allow other users to easily access select data through the network, something I have never been able to do since I normally shut my computer down when I am not using it. One of the many features is to limit access to certain folders. This has allowed me to keep private records and data secure so that only certain people can access these files.

I have limited experience with NAS and have really enjoyed using this device. Before this program, I never even considered using this. This definitely has broadened my knowledge of network usage. I am completely happy with the unit.

This is something I would definitely recommend to others. I have a lot of friends that also own external hard drives and will make sure to pass the information along.

There are many features I still need to learn, but so far, data transfer has been a breeze. I can't stress how this has really simplified a lot of things as well as freed up a lot of space on my internal hard drives.

title: A fine basic CD player
text:
For people in a hurry: I've had this TEAC CD-P1260 CD player for about 7 months, listening to it almost every day (or several hours a week), it sounds great and has worked flawlessly. The built-in headphone jack/amplifier works well. I am very pleased with the quality.

This TEAC P1260 is a basic CD player, meant to be installed as part of a stereo system for listening to music over speakers, though it's possible to use it all by itself by plugging headphones into the jack on the front. This player plays only commercial audio CDs, CD-R/RW copies of commercial CDs, and CD-R/RW discs with mp3 files. It will NOT play .wav files or anything else, and the manual says it may not play variable bit-rate mp3 files. I don't listen to mp3s because they sound crappy, so I can't confirm that. But a friend gave me a disc with .wav music files, and this TEAC CD player would not play it. Every other CD player in the house would, including an inexpensive boom box, so be aware that this P1260 is limited mainly to commercial audio CDs and copies of such CDs. I think that's what most people would use a CD player for anyway.

This is a quality item. It feels heavier to me than the 20-year-old CD players I own. The opening and closing of the drawer is quiet and dignified. The finish of the metal case is a matte black that doesn't look cheap. The display consists of white alphanumeric characters on a very soothing medium blue background. The buttons used for basic operation are arranged logically from left to right: open (close), play (pause), stop, skip back, skip forward. The labeling of the buttons is somewhat hard to see in dim light, a common problem with modern stereo equipment. There is another horizontal row of smaller buttons below the above for shuffle, repeat, program, and intro check (plays the first 10 seconds of each track) functions. I never used any of these functions. I also never used the remote, but I did note that the buttons are well spaced and also logically arranged. On the back are the tin-plated left and right RCA jacks for connecting the P1260 to an amplifier or stereo receiver; the necessary cable is included (about 1 meter long).

An outstanding feature of this low-priced CD player is the built-in headphone jack and amplifier with volume control. The jack is the large, 1/4 inch type, which means most headphones will require an adapter (decent headphones come with an adapter). Many audiophiles claim that a separate headphone amp is necessary for good listening, but I thought this built-in amp sounded just fine. It has enough power for even the most inefficient headphones in my collection. If the P1260 is connected to an amplifier, plugging headphones into the front jack will disconnect the RCA output jacks on the back.

The specifications given in the manual claim 8X oversampling, if you're interested, and the frequency response is 20-20kHz, within 2 dB. The frequency response could be a little tighter, but then it would cost a lot more.

Some credible reviews of this TEAC CD player have indicated reliability problems. As I said at the beginning, I have had mine for 7 months now, using it as much as most people would, maybe more, and I haven't had any problems (knock on wood!). In my experience, TEAC has always made quality audio equipment, so I really didn't expect to have problems. Maybe I have just been lucky so far. All I can report is my personal experience, which has been totally satisfactory. It sounds great, works great, looks great, and has the feel of a quality piece of audio equipment. I think it is a great buy for anyone looking for a no-frills, basic CD player.

text: I looked at (and physically tried) many iPad cases/covers for my "New iPad" (3rd gen). What I like about this one is that it fully encases the iPad, so it can't fall out when using it/photographing/video taping (in some unusual positions); the cover folds back to allow the iPad to be viewed/used at numerous different angles (for typing, viewing movies, etc.); and the case allows you to rotate the iPad to be used in vertical or horizontal format (believe me, you will WANT vertical as well as horizontal format). If I had to change one thing, I'd allow a little bit more room on the top, by the "on/off" button, since it's a little snug getting your finger in there. title: Do NOT trust your backups to it. What a piece of junk!
text:
I bought the GoFlex Pro and had high hopes that all my backup issues would be taken care of. The Memeo software that comes with it is easy to use and seemed comprehensive. No problem right? WRONG! UPDATE: I finally decided buckle down and figure out how to reset the router, and it was not easy and there are no clear directions on how to do it anywhere online. Basically, you have to go to the ASUS support site, down load the latest Utility and Firmware, extract the files, restart the router (with computer but without modem attached), go into your Local Area Connections and adjust the Internet Protocol Version 4 settings to locate the router, run the utility, load the firmware, reboot the router, adjust the Internet Protocol Version 4 settings again, attach the modem, and relocate the modem: EVERY TIME YOU HAVE A POWER OUTAGE.

Sometimes it worked as soon as it was powered up and several times it would take between 30 seconds and one minute for the sound to come on. Finally it stopped producing sound at all. But then the same issues reappeared. Finally it stopped producing any sound what so ever. I tried a different optical cable and an analog cable as well. All of the lights and controls appeared to be working, but no sound was coming out. I thought it might be a problem with the television, but when I moved the sound bar and bass amp to a different television it still failed to produce any sound. Fortunately I still had the receipt and was able to bring it back to where I purchased it (not Amazon). They were super cool about the refund ... almost too cool. When I asked if anyone else had returned a similar unit I learned that mine was not the first unsatisfactory experience with this item.

Original Review:
This unit is attached to a 40-inch LCD as a second television area and the room is not very large. It does what it is supposed to do at a price that is very affordable. The sound quality is a major improvement over the built-in TV speakers and with a little treble/bass adjustment the dialogue is quite clear. It can be a bit bass heavy, but you get used to it after a while. The bass amp is wired to the sound-bar, but there is ample cord to place it where it needs to go. Once it is in place I gathered and zipped-tied the excess wire to keep it safe. The one downside is to this unit is that the optical cable that comes in the box is of very poor quality. After setting it up the first thing you should do is replace the provided optical cable with a better one. The unit is also a little tall to be placed directly in front of the television as it may block the remote control sensors for the TV. This seems to be a common issue noted in the reviews of similar products. I removed the feet and attached it to the front of the television stand with a couple of well placed screws (instead of attaching it to the wall). Doing this also adjusted the front angle down slightly so that some of the sound bounces off the floor and blends a little better with the external bass amp. title: Best of breed pocket flash
text:
The olympus system is what makes this flash shine. I got this for free after rebate with the purchase of my OM-D.

It's fully TTL, has just enough power for 8 foot ceiling bounce, even with the kit zoom. To shut it off, you just flip it face down on the hot shoe. To save space, the hotshoe releases with a button linked to a locking pin. Just slide it in and it clicks into place. Push the release button, and slide it off. Simple. No more spinning wheels or flipping lock levers. This is how all flashes should attach and release.

The RC mode is what really seals the deal for me. It's Olympus' version of wireless flash control, ala Nikon CLS or Canon ETTL. Olympus's RC mode, especially on the OM-D, is FAR easier to use and to understand than the Canon ETTL equivalent. I was having a blast within seconds. (note to Olympus: make RC mode easier to get to in the camera menus) It is as automatic or as manual (down to third stops) as you want it to be. And unlike Canon's smallest wireless slave (220EX2), it can be assigned to A and B groups. Hook two of these to a macro rig, and you've got a sub $400 twin light rig.

Do be aware of the limitations of a small flash. It won't work much past 8 feet, and it's not going to power an umbrella or softbox as easily as a larger flash.

My only significant criticism is the paint job; it's very thin and scratches off VERY easily. If you're careful, that may not be an issue.

Overall, I highly recommend this flash, especially for portability obsessed Micro four thirds shooters.

title: Serious Defects in manufacturing
text:
I am not one to often write reviews on products, but this product deserves one.

I am a long time video/audiophile with a lot of experience with home theater. I have to say that these banana plugs have some serious defects. If you are using any kind of normal gauge wire (i.e. 16 AWG) you will find it VERY difficult to get these banana plugs to clamp down tight enough to hold the wire in place. I have tried from both the bottom and side, and every time the wire is easily pulled out of the connector. If you inspect them visually, when the center screw is fully tightened there is still an 1/8" of space inside the side hole that you can see through and this doesnt include the domed area inside the banana end which is probably at least another 1/8". The only way I have been able to get them to work is to remove the colored ring, which therefore allows you to screw the threaded connection a little further, but then you lose the benefit of being able to tell which wire is which. I have used several other types of banana plugs from cheap to expensive, and have never run into this issue before. It's almost as if whoever designed the plugs did not engineer them correctly. all 24 plugs share the same problem.

title: Smartshell Is Both Smart and a Shell!
text:
First, let me be clear I'm reviewing the smartshell case from Fintie. When I saw the number of negative reviews, I looked closer at those. It's obvious that being able to purchase different case models by clicking the appropriate model selection button, then buying that model, did one other thing. It dumped all the reviews for all those models into one review pool. So, if you start getting worried about the negatives, look at which model they're describing.

Now that we've gotten that out of the way, the smartshell is a plastic shell case. If you've ever used a shell case for a smartphone, you've got a mental image of thin, smooth plastic covering the back and sides of the phone, there's not much protection, and the device sets into the shell. That fits how the paperwhite fits into this case. And that's where the comparison ends. This Fintie case is notably thicker plastic, so there's more protection. There's an attached front cover (also plastic) to protect the screen.

Front and back are textured which makes the case look nicer than you'd expect and gives a good grip. Fintie claims this is the thinnest and lightest case for the paperwhite. If that's stretching the point, it's close to right. I'm not noticing a difference in weight and what little additional depth it adds actually makes the Kindle easier to hold. The cover is held closed by a magnet that doubles as a means of putting the Kindle in sleep mode. Both work well. The front cover can be folded back for one handed holding. The magnet doesn't accidentally put the paperwhite in sleep mode when the cover is folded back for reading.

If, for some reason, you need or want to remove the Kindle from the case, starting from the tab where the magnet seems to be the best way to do it. The bottom button and charging port are exposed for access. At $11.99 US, it's only slightly higher than many other cases, three times cheaper than "official" cases, and light years ahead in style and protection. If I got a second paperwhite, I'd also get another Fintie smartshell.

title: Impressive sound quality and comfort, but some minor drawbacks
text:
Reading many positive reviews from the head-fi.org, sound+image magazine, and digitaltrends.com had brought my attention to buy Yamaha EPH-100SL. I hoped that the sound of this earphone would overpower my favorite AKG-Q350, which I like for its treble, deep bass, loud, and cheap (50 bucks in Amazon!). I also believed that Yamaha, a company that makes musical instruments and electronics, should know sound quality better than other companies!

The package arrived on time and I was eager to try it right away. Then KAPOW!. My first comment when I first listened to the earphone. Clarty! even when I put "deep bass" equalizer on my iTouch. A clarity that I've missed in three of my IEM: Klipsch s4i, AKG Q350, V-Moda Vibrato. I hadn't "burned" the earphone and it's already sounded this good?? All the money I spent is invested into the earphone itself, for the sound quality, and not the pretty packaging and celebrity-endorsement (like Monster's deceiving products and false advertising).

However, I found some drawbacks from this earphone:

1. Not recommended for sport. It's not that it would fall off, but the sweat that sticks to the top of the "driver"(I'd say the speaker part) will cause the earphone to go off or stop functioning. But, I blew the speaker part with my mouth and thanks God it worked again. Yet it was the 1st day I tried the earphone too!

2. The eartip. Although the eartip is very comfortable to wear and I managed to listen for 2-3 hours, the tough part was to remove the tip, especially when trying out which size that fits perfectly to the ear. I had to pull it with nails and I was scared that I would tear off the tip when removing it from the earphone.

3. I wish they include a clipper in the package. I've gotten used to wear clips so that an earphone would not burden my ear so much. I believe that wearing clipper would prolong listening and increase comfortability. Yamaha came up with the "smart cable holder" but forgot the clipper? cmon!

4. It would be nice if there's a mic and controller so that I can switch songs quickly without taking my iTouch out from my pocket. But if they included the controller, it would be compatible only for Ipod...so this could be a dilemma.

But overall, the sound is too great that I forget all the drawback! I care the sound more than anything else! I would recommend this to anyone and hopefully Yamaha would release the one with in-line control :)

title: Used to Keep Video Server Alive - Customer Service Department Needs Repairing
text:
The best thing you can do for a computer system is give it clean power. This is the unit I decided on to do the trick when my APC unit failed. The replacement batteries for my older APC unit to run my server cost about the same as this unit. After doing research you will find that this unit is able to run with the newer computers that have switched over to the newer digital power supplies. This unit produces a clean and smooth sine wave output.
PROS:
- tons of menus on the front showing you draw on unit, battery condition, longevity of unit in the event of a power failure, and events recorded
- produces true sine wave
- can be programmed to shut down system
- I like the digital display showing real numbers as to how long the standby time would be based on the current load on the system
- much smaller than my huge APC model that produced the same output
- runs cool to the touch

CONS:
- haven't had any yet
- CUSTOMER SERVICE (Repair Department: See update below)

UPDATE 11/25/2014
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Used UPS while working on computer during power outage, UPS was on circuit to keep things clean. After a few hours this UPS started screaming. The voltage meter on the UPS showed me that that the generator was pumping out 130v instead of the acceptable range of 110-120v on the leg the computer system was on. I went to the generator and verified that yes, one of the output legs was too high. I moved the computer power feed to the other leg that was working correctly and the UPS was happy again.

Made me think that if I didn't have this UPS monitoring and filtering the power for my computer I could have fried some sensitive equipment. After the power failure was over we diagnosed the generator and found out that a diode in the generator's voltage regulator was failing.

This UPS warned me of a problem before damage resulted. It paid for itself that day.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
UPDATE 12-17-2015
CUSTOMER SERVICE NOT SO GOOD
- My DISPLAY BACKLIGHTING FAILED but otherwise the unit was still working fine. You could read the screen but only if the lights were off in the room.
I emailed customer service and asked if I could just swap out the plug-in display section of the unit. The employee I emailed (Cole Wa____k.) said this was possible. I called 12-16-15 to set up the part mailing and ended up speaking to another employee. This employee was not agreeable in allowing the swap. Instead he insisted that I mail the unit to them so they could swap out the display. After they got it, he said I'd get it back in about 3-4 weeks. Holy cow, this is a long time to be without protection. I asked for the employee's name and he gave a first name (Jeff), knowing corporations are large I asked for his last name too, he told me "I don't have a last name" and his tone started getting rude. All I wanted was his name so I could go back to the email contact and indicate who told me this was not possible anymore. The employee's response left a really bad taste in my mouth, especially since I have 11 UPS units, mostly from APC (with excellent customer support by-the-way), and now a few from CyberPower. When I call for support I don't expect to be treated rudely. Maybe I should go back and stick with APC for future needs.

Amazon helped me resolved this but surely CyberPower needs to fix their own repair department; especially WRT customer relations.

title: Can't beat it for the price!
text:
The tripod I received was not the Zeikos black & silver one in the picture... it is a Polaroid and it is all black. Much better in my opinion. Came with a durable Polaroid tripod bag and some lens cloths. Now on to the review!

The legs are a lightweight aluminum with plastic flip locks. Legs seem durable enough, but I'd be careful with the flip locks. Center crossbrace with hook for weight bag is a nice touch. Claims to have a 72" max height, but I'm 6'1" and the camcorder lens (Canon HF M41) at full height is a good 4-5" above my head, so I'd say it's more like 75".

Other nice touches:
- Circular bubble level at the top of the legs, and a second linear (tilt) bubble level beside the QR plate.
- Comes with 2 quick-release plates.
- QR plates mount into the tripod head front-to-rear and side-to-side to accommodate still or video cameras.
- Has self-leveling rubber feet.
- Tripod head flips up to the left for vertical shot framing.
- Pan/zoom/tilt lock down nice and tight.

The bad:
- Pan/zoom/tilt is NOT smooth at all, so don't expect to get good results when shooting video unless you lock it down.
- Plastic leg locks feel a bit flimsy. Time will tell how durable they are.
- QR plates feel like they might loosen up over time.

Conclusion:
I have a Manfrotto 055DXB w/701RC2 fluid head, so I know how a really GOOD tripod performs, and this ain't it. Having said that, I wasn't expecting Manfrotto performance for 1/10 the cost. I got this tripod to serve as a locked-down "B-cam" mount for weddings with enough height to shoot over the crowd, and I think it will serve very well in that capacity. Definitely worth 5 stars for the price, as long as you know what its strengths and weaknesses are.

title: Buyer Beware, Warranty worthless
text:
Buyer Beware! Panasonic will not honor their warranty!
I am very distressed that I am forced to post this complaint about Panasonic not honoring their explicit warranty on a Lumix DMC-TS3 "underwater" camera.
I am an experienced underwater photographer with three underwater cameras and 9 years experience. I have never had a case leakage or any damage to one of my cameras. I know how to care for expensive camera equipment at the beach and underwater.
I purchased a new Lumix DMC-TS3 "underwater and 6 foot drop proof" camera for my wife to use. She is also an experienced photographer and knows how to care for a camera. We liked the Lumix as an easy to use light weight simple point and shoot for shallow water snorkeling. One its first trip, only 6 weeks old, it failed after only 7 days of shallow snorkeling. It was never more than 6 feet underwater and at all times cared for exactly according to the manual. It was never dropped or otherwise damaged. I was sorry it failed so soon on its first trip but we did have our larger underwater cameras so I was not too concerned. I was sure Panasonic would replace or repair the camera and I would have been happy with that.
I returned the camera as instructed to Panasonic certain they would honor their warranty and advertising. I was shocked when they called and said the warranty was void because there was "condensation" inside the camera. I carefully explained that the camera was cared for exactly according to their manual and should be under warranty. I asked to speak to a supervisor and was told they would contact me in 3-4 working days. They never called or emailed me. I then called Panasonic warranty service two more times. Each time I got the same answer: the warranty was void and someone would call me but no one ever did. I am now left without a camera. I would never buy from Panasonic again and caution anyone else considering a purchase from them. If you do not care about a warranty and possible early camera failure then buy Panasonic, otherwise BEWARE PANASONIC. I have now found numerous other complaints on the web about the exact same treatment from Panasonic. This appears to be a corporate policy and not an isolated incident.

title: Put to the test, these babies never let me down
text:
My husband bought me these for Christmas because in my lab job, I have the ability to listen to music/podcasts/whatever for 8 hours straight virtually every day. I usually used the in-ear kind because they were less cumbersome (and I had to wear safety glasses all day, so the in-ears were more comfortable combined with those). But outside noise still came through the in-ears, and they often got snagged on things and ripped out of my ears. My husband thought I would like a change.

He was right, and I was more than impressed at his choice. Other over-the-ear types were just obnoxiously uncomfortable for all-day use. They gave me headaches - again, especially in combination with safety glasses. These, however, were nearly weightless and hugged my head where most headphones squeezed. I tend to need to adjust headphones to the smallest setting for my head size, being a smallish female, but that's annoying, too, to always be fiddling with/perfecting the band over the head. These have a wide, cushioned elastic headband that conforms to every head size (I know because all my work friends tried them on and confirmed it). That headband also made them stretch effortlessly over the arms of my safety glasses without adding additional pressure. Perfect! And the plastic outer frame bends so easily, and is so lightweight, that I never want to go back to any other material. They're so darn comfy.

As for sound, I won't lie, I don't have the highest standards. Not because I don't want to, but because I've so often had to settle for whatever phones I could afford or were the most convenient for my needs. Compared to my usual low-end pairs, these really impressed me. Not only was the sound itself very sharp, with solid bass, but the noise-canceling was amazing (sometimes to my managers' dismay!). If I needed to keep my hearing available, it was easy to pull one ear piece off and set it behind my ear while keeping the other comfortably on. I could do that for extended periods when needed and didn't find it to be a problem.

Finally, these were put through some abuse. With all-day, everyday use, the cord was snagged, the phones were dropped, shoved in drawers, stretched to the max, you name it. But they still look, and feel, brand new. Nothing warped or damaged them, which was a concern I had. The elastic band has also kept its elasticity despite being used on different-sized heads (these were loaned out regularly because everyone who tried them loved them). So if you need comfort, durability, and great sound, look no farther. Plus, the price when we got these was ridiculously low for the quality we got. I hope you enjoy them as much as I have!

The TV is heavy and once you install it on the base and tighten the 4 screws, it leans forward a bit from the top due to its weight i.e it is not completely straight vertically. This means that the steel bracket that the 4 screws go in has a faulty design. I guess it runs horizontally straight in the back instead of like a T shape to keep the upper TV from leaning forward. I might have a faulty set though. I placed a replacement order today and I'll update my stars review if the new TV is OK.

UPDATE 1/27/2014:
Second TV came today. It had few dents on the back near the upper bezel. I just documented it with CEVA and was hoping to get good consistent LED especially from the bottom edge since I don't really see the dent. Same problem, TV had non consistent lighting from the bottom like the 1st one. 3 spots now (at the bottom edge) instead of two in the first one. In addition, 2 others spots appeared on the top left. All appear as light grayish area of about 1"x1", some of this area is penetrated by thin bright ray in the middle of it breaking its grayish hue. You CANNOT SEE THESE unless you have a bright white, or off-white scenes. I'm very disappointed because I'm a Sony guy and still loyal till this moment. I fixed (a bit) the stand problem with my engineering background. Now it is not leaning forward that much like the first one but still not completely vertical on my water leveler. I got a price break because of the dent but to me, I'd rather pay full price with a perfect unit than accept a break and get a high blood pressure because I know there is something wrong with it everytime a bright scene comes. Not sure if I'll go for a third. I'll keep you posted.

UPDATE 2/17/2014
Third TV came today. It's the worst among all 3 TVs I got. Now these led edge blotches are everywhere, on bottom edge, top edge, and now some sides. I wished I had kept the first one since it had the least non-uniform edge lighting among the 3. I'm wondering how all these people, who rated this TV high, did not notice this mess with the edge lighting in bright scenes. This is garbage considering this a high tier TV. This is the end for me with Sony TVs.

title: Awesome value - an excellent grip for the price
text:
I used this battery grip with a rented Nikon D7100 for a weekend event shoot (over 2,000 photos taken with 2 camera bodies), and it held up very well. I have a similar off-brand battery grip for my own Nikon D7000, and this grip is built pretty much exactly the same.

Almost everything (besides the screw, wiring, and the connection between the battery holders and the grip itself) is plastic, and probably won't last years, but at this price, I'm not worried about that. The rubber grip feels just like the camera body's rubber, and looks almost identical to the Nikon pattern. From a foot away, I'd be surprised if anyone could tell a difference between this grip and the Nikon OEM grip.

The tripod screw that holds the grip to the body is able to be tightened as much as you want (the more the better, in some ways), though the little wheel you spin to tighten the screw is smaller than in the OEM grip and other off-brand grips I've used. It's not a big deal, but it makes your fingers feel slightly raw after tightening the grip snugly.

The shutter release button actually feels great on this grip--not spongy, not too sticky or solid--both half-pressing and fully depressing the button worked great throughout the weekend. The OK/rocker is a little more clumsy than the nice one on the back of the D7100, but it works. All other buttons and switches feel very slightly plasticky, but they also work without a problem, so I'm not complaining.

If you are going to use a vertical grip on your D7100 every day, instead of buying the expensive Nikon version of the grip, just buy a used D3 or something, and you'll have a 'built-in' vertical grip. The way I see it, I could buy two of these Neewer grips every year, and by the time I get a new camera body, I'll still be out ahead compared to buying just one Nikon grip. The difference between this and the Nikon is very slight, except when it comes to value :)

title: smokin' hot deal!
text:
Caught this on-sale for $60 ... took a chance and ordered two! ... shoulda ordered six!

I had checked the reviews first ... didn't see one bad one about the phone ... only the cell service ... which I had no intention of getting, anyhow!

My old .mp3 player (for my truck) was acting up, and I was looking to replace it! Didn't wanna pay $100+ for an iPod! The reviews on most everything else were spotty! So I figured I'd pick up a cheapo Android phone. Happened on the sale for these ... seemed like a no-brainer!

For whatever reason, it seems like the GPS on it is a secret?! It's there ... and works really well! Also, ya can save a map for offline use! ... so w/o cell service, or even wi-fi, ya can still use the GPS!

Not sure what the big deal is with "Muve" ... even the included 3gb microSD has it printed on there! ... not sure what the deal was, but it was only showing like 500mb free?! No matter, I dropped a 32gb in it!

I did have an issue using the stock music player ... it'd play my itunes .m4a's ok ... but not the .mp4's from my CD's?! I downloaded PowerAmp, and that works for both!

Everything else works flawlessly! ... wi-fi ... camera ... email ... browser ... calendar ... video ... GPS!

It even let me delete a few bloat apps! ... not "Muve", though!

UPDATE:

it's been a couple weeks, now ... PowerAmp was buggin' me ... I forget why ... but I installed (free) WinAmp ... had to create a "playlist" (all songs, one time) ... but it's got a nice widget ... it makes me hit the play button twice, to start playing ... but pause only once ... only issue I've had with it ... easy to say it's a WinAmp issue, but the fact remains, the stock music app don't work as it does on other such devices (see ".mp4"s, above)

as it usually sits in my truck, I noticed the battery would go down to less than half, after only one day ... I surmised it may be because it was either trying to connect to my (or work's) wi-fi, and/or the Cricket network ... even though I never activated the service, I still was showing a bar 'er two! ... as I rarely actually need/use wi-fi on it, I simply set it in airplane mode ... battery's lasting a good 5+ days, now! ... not so much a knock on the phone ... more on android ... it let's ya stop wi-fi ... but not cell service ... not without turning off wi-fi, too! ... it'd be nice if it let ya turn off cell service, only ... although, it could be, trying to connect to wi-fi, might still wear on the battery!

I'm guessing, without activating Cricket, I can't get an OTA android update?! I did find a custom ROM that looks purdy good ... but it requires a few hoops ... and with Gingerbread, I have everything I need, anyhow!

Oh, I almost forgot ... I've seen mine do it ... and I've heard from other owners, the same thing ... the phone'll reboot ... all by itself ... every now 'n then! ... it never did it while I was using it ... but every once in a while, I'd notice it was booting up, by itself! ... one theory was, it wasn't connecting to Cricket particularly well, and maybe somehow a reboot might help?! ... however, since I've been in airplane mode, it's not rebooted (on it's own), even once! ... perhaps there's some truth, to that theory?!

Again, every other bad review I had seen was regarding the Cricket service! ... if ya don't use that ... and probably keep it in airplane mode most of the time ... it's just like my old Galaxy S! ... well, except the 4 main button deallies are actually buttons, on this phone ... at first I didn't know how I felt about it ... after about 5min, I completely forgot about it ... 'til now! Anyhow, tactilely (sp?), they're nice buttons! ... even preferable!

If this ever gets back down near $60 again, I'll buy another two 'er three ... give 'em to the kids for stocking stuffers! Even at $90, it's very tempting!

title: Works great, great tool for expanding photo possibilities and is very fun.
text: Out of the box it was in perfect condition and was well packed and protected.  I got everything out to check all of the parts and then charged the batteries.  During that time I already had installed the apps on my phone and iPad for ground station but I did not have the DJI software on my computer, so I downloaded that from the DJI website.  I installed the driver and the software for the controller and the quadcopter.  I hooked the usb to the computer and copter and turned everything on and ran the checks, there was an update to the software too so installed that and then calibrated everything.  After testing controller through the software I took everything outside and even though the wind was blowing about 20 MPH, I lifted off the ground and flew around the front of the house and down the street, tried out the camera with stills and then finished off the flight with rolling video.  I only took it up to about 50 feet to avoid the hard gusts of wind we had but feel very confident on its ability.  After watching many many videos on these I am baffled that so many have been crashed.... It should be treated as a tool and not a toy and the chances of crashing are extremely reduced.  The FAA has a problem with these because they are not flown like an aircraft, if you were sitting in it you would not do the stupid things people do with them if it was their life at stake.  I am a pilot and took the small amount of time to "preflight" run software checks and calibrate everything so it would safe as I do when climbing into an old Cessna.  I suggest that people set up their own preflight plan and follow it every time.  The calibration of the compass before every flight takes less then 20 seconds so just do it every time you put in a new battery.  Side note, the kit I ordered said it came with a case and lanyard that was not included in what was delivered.

It has WAY more features than I will ever use since the original Garmin Fenix was intended for outdoor hiking/navigating/etc, but many features have came in handy while out and about. One nice feature is the ability to turn off features that you aren't currently using. This keeps the clutter out of your main screens.

As the watch has had more and more exposure to the market, Garmin has made some significant software improvements to the watch. One major improvement is data storing time. It only takes seconds now for what took minutes in the past after storing the data from a completed workout.

My only unknown at this point is on battery life. I compete at Ironman 140.6 mile triathlons, which is a very long day. Garmin claims 15 hours of battery life, so I am curious to see how that holds up in real world conditions. I have fairly small wrists (I am 5'3" and 125lbs), and I wear the watch all day, every day, with no problems so far. The watch band and pins seem very robust and have taken a good beating so far. Overall, so far, I am very happy with this watch.

title: Perfect TiVo Premiere Upgrade, easy and painless!
text:
Our TiVo Premiere has started having some problems the past few months: random reboots, lock ups, glitches in the recordings, etc. When it hung up while my wife was watching one of her favorite shows and finally responded a few minutes later in the recording, I started to consider that the hard drive may be failing. It just seemed like the box was trying to read part of the disk and having failures, eventually moved on to a part of the disk it could read. I did some research on how to check the hard drive from the diagnostics menu, and sure enough, the test had failures almost immediately.

After talking to TiVo about my options on getting the hard drive replaced ($350: $150 for a refurbished TiVo Premiere and $200 to transfer my Lifetime subscription) I decided to look into doing it myself. Do yourself a favor and search for "Ross Walker's Guide to Upgrading your TiVo" on the internet. Ross has captured, in exhaustive detail, the process of upgrading hard drives in most of the various TiVo models out there. Following his instructions was extremely easy and for the cost of a new drive and a couple of Torx screwdrivers, my TiVo Premiere continues to keep on working and now has triple the original recording capacity.

As with all of my hard drive reviews, I will update if and when the drive fails. However, so far, so good!

text:

It will not work right out of the box. Good thing i had an old Samsung Vibrant phone lying around the house. It was running Android 2.2 and it gave me the option to format this card, as soon as i popped it in. It only took 2 seconds to format and now works in all my Android devices. I popped this into my Android 3.0 tablet and it would NOT format the card, so i feel very fortunate to have my Samsung Vibrant handy. I really needed this extra memory for my HTC View tablet, so that i can add more movies on it. The tablet came with 32GB installed and now has over 90GB thanks to this little Sandisk guy. Apple is so stingy with memory and now my tablet has more memory than the most expensive iPad that's available. This card also functions great for turning a smartphone into an iPod Touch replacement. It was on sale for fifty bucks and so worth it. I don't recommend buying this if it cost more. SD cards can get extremely pricey. I only wish this came in 120GB.

**Also, i would not purchase this SD card from any other seller besides Amazon. I have had bad experiences from other sellers and their SD cards appeared to either be used or bootlegs because they did not come in proper Sandisk packaging**

**On a sad note, this SD card does NOT work on my Blackberry 9900 and i wish it did**

text: Given the price, one can't expect stupendous performance from this mic; and it is a sold performer. Using this mic, I always have to boost any audio that comes from the Zoom by at least 5db in post, if not more. Either that, or I have to turn the Zoom's levels up to 100, and that still doesn't get me into that -12/-7 sweet spot. This is my first shotgun mic, and I'm assuming more expensive mics might have slightly higher gain performance...but I dunno. As others have said, this mic's directional performance is very good, and does isolate other sounds that are not in its directional path. As a beginner's mic, its performance is satisfactory. It's better than nothing in most cases...but seems designed to be quickly outgrown by anyone whose skill level continues to develop. If I'm doing something wrong, and there is a way to wring more performance from this mic/recorder combo, please comment here.

title: Best headphones I've heard to date
text:
These headphones deserve all the praise they get.

I've tried all the ones in this price range, including the Sennheiser Momentums, and even the Sony MDR-1's.
These blow them both away, and of course, they sound tonnes better than Beats, which sound muffled and bloated in comparison.

First off, these have been considered as bass head cans. In my opinion, they are not.
They have detailed bass that can extend VERY far. They are only as bassy as a track needs. Never any more.
You may hear one song that goes very low, but then another will go even lower, and these headphones have no problem giving the power to you.
Detail throughout the range I should say is impressive, and I've heard a lot of details I've missed on previous sets.

They are amazing for all genres in my opinion, though they could be slightly better for rock/metal, but only because of the mids. They are slightly laid back, but you do get used to the sound, and never becomes a real issue. To improve the mids, you may be best opting for an amp, or do some slight tweaking in the EQ settings, but its not an issue to be honest.
I've listened to tonnes of other styles, including Acoustic, Classical, Trance, Ambient, DnB, Pop, etc, etc, and they perform flawlessly.

The sound stage is very wide. Almost to the point you hear stuff coming from the back of your head, and not just left/right. Very expansive in other words, and certainly the best I've heard in the price range.

Have a look online for some reviews where they list music samples they've tested the headphones with, and you will be guaranteed to be amazed with the quality.

If you have the money, give these a go!

title: Great value!!
text:
These speakers, while not attractive (and I believe much could be done in terms of design there), offer excellent sound for the price.
So here's the low-down:

Pros: quality--Altec has delivered a sturdy (enough--they aren't going in a construction zone) product that produces good sound.

price--$40.00 and under for a decent set of speakers for your pc is definitely affordable

Cons: bass control--you can alter the tone and volume (obviously) but not the bass level. In general, this would be more than nice to have. In fact, I think any speakers with an included subwoofer should allow you to have control over the level of the bass. Living in an apartment with neighbors both beside and below also makes this a feature that is more than useful and appreciated as I can only turn the volume up but so high with the speakers on because the bass can't get too loud.

set up--i'm not able to plug just the satellite speakers into my computer. Having the subwoofer is great, but I'd love the ability to choose whether or not I have it hooked up because of the aforementioned living arrangement issue.

power--others have pointed this out as well, and I agree: it is a serious draw-back. The power switch is on the back of the the subwoofer which is rather inconvenient.

stand--this isn't so much of a problem I think for people in general, I just personally think every subwoofer should come with an included but optional stand allowing for convenient free standing on the floor, and that, preferably, helps dampen bass transfer through the floor. Again, not important, but would be super awesome-sauce. (This subwoofer does have little feet built in, but they offer little clearance and if you are placing the speaker on a carpeted surface you may be concerned with overheating.)

Overall: I like this product and would totally buy it again, it was truly the best speaker set for the price range, and I definitely can't complain about the sound quality. I only gave it 3 stars because of the lack of bass control, power switch, and aesthetic design choice.

(Seriously Altec, that aesthetic caters to a rather niche market, these aren't designed or priced for a niche market overall, and you should consider not trying to showcase any aesthetic design {esp. when the product's solid} and stick with housing that is more simplistic and easily blendable or overlooked when sitting at a desk in someone's work space.)

So in this (?initial?) posting, let me tell you what shaped my decision between the 5D Mark III and the D800.

The Fred Miranda website did a direct comparison between the two and the D800 outperformed the 5D Mk III especially in the high contrast / dark area noise category. The Ken Rockwell review put the 5D Mk III on top. Site after site went back and forth, but the only review which gave pretty dramatic, objective material going against the Canon was the Fred Miranda review. But I had read about the High Dynamic Range features, the Auto Lighting Optimization features, and the Highlight Tone Priority features of the 5D Mark III and was convinced they could make moot the high contrast / dark area noise issue. And they DO. So far I cannot create worrisome noise in the shadows of a brightly lit object on what is a rare sunny day in January here where I live.

The FEEL of the camera is wonderful. Much like the feel of a 7D.

I could have bought a D800, and indeed I will likely pick one up eventually (unless Obama-care spanks me as much as I fear it will), but for now my Canon lens collection (including a 300 - 2.8 L and an 85 - 1.2 L II) will continue to be put to good use on this fine tool

title: Could be great with a better color wheel.
text:
I had high hopes for this projector coming from a 6 year old InFocus IN76 which was a great 720p projector until it recently died. So I started looking at new 1080p models and decided on the HD26 because of its excellent input lag for gaming and price point with features offered. It arrived and I was excited to start testing. The picture quality is good and bright after some tweaking with acceptable black levels, although I doubt it's anywhere near the claimed 25000:1. Then I booted up the XBOX 360 to play some games and really test the input lag. I'm happy to say there is absolutely no noticeable input lag, and that's great. Now here is the not so great part. I was seeing rainbows galore. Mostly when playing high contrast fast paced games. I thought I was not susceptible to the rainbow effect (RBE) since I had used a DLP projector for 6 years and never noticed them. So I began to dig deeper and found that this projector uses a 2x RGBCYW color wheel which will show more rainbow effect than say a 4x or 6x RGBRGB color wheel. Turns out my old InFocus had a 4x RGBRGB color wheel and that's why I never noticed the RBE.

Some people might be ok with this, or might not even see it at all (As you can see from the other reviews). There are claims that only 5% of people see the RBE, however, I showed quite a few people certain games on this unit and they all saw it. I would only see it on certain scenes when watching movies / TV so if that's all you plan on doing with this projector It's a great buy. But I mostly use a projector for gaming so this a deal breaker for me.

title: Small Package - Big Sound!
text:
I consider myself an amateur audiophile on a budget and have owned various equipment from Polk Audio, Harman Kardon, JBL, etc. I did a lot of research and compared many many models before deciding on the Flip 2 from JBL. I don't think it can be beat (no pun intended... Dre) based on size/weight ratio to sound output. THIS BABY GETS VERY LOUD!!!

In regard to audio quality, it has a surprisingly clean, very detailed (not too tinny) sound. You can actually feel the bass, just don't expect wall shaking, after all, this thing is only the size of a soda can. It can occasionally come across sounding a bit bright for my taste, but nothing a little tweak of an EQ can't fix.

As mentioned, I compared many models, including Bose, Ultimate Ears, Dre, etc. When it came time to buy, I was torn between the JBL Flip 2 and TDK Life on Record A33. Yep, the same TDK company that used to make blank cassette tapes (for those old enough to remember). I was shocked at the amount of bass and overall warmth that oozed out of the TDK. I actually preferred it over the Flip 2, but ultimately decided to go with JBL for these three reasons:

- Reputation: JBL has a superb reputation

- Price: The JBL price was 30% lower (Yes, I'm cheap)

- Weight: JBL weighs about 1/3 less

My only knock is the so-so battery life of about 5 hours per charge. However, I remind myself that it's pumping out an impressive 6 watts/channel. If battery life is that important, you can't go wrong with the JBL Charge.

Overall, I'm very pleased with my decision and highly recommend the Flip 2.

title: Mostly solved our signal problems
text:
I needed to do something to make our cell phones usable at home. We had signal, but not strong and just moving a couple of feet could result in a dropped call. I looked at cell phone boosters, but it looked like antenna placement was going to be too tricky to get the coverage I wanted. I tried every way I could think of to get Verizon to sell me a new 3G Network Extender for less than $250+tax, but I couldn't get them to budge. I was concerned about buying a "remanufactured" Network Extender, but the savings were too good to pass up.

I have had the unit set up for 5 days now and it seems to be mostly solving our problem. My biggest challenges have been related to the fact that no manual or warranty card (nor any paperwork of any kind, other than a packing slip) was included in the shipment. As reviewer "Tom" said below, even a remanufactured unit should come with a manual, shouldn't it? And, unlike "Tom", I was not able to get Amazon to give me anything for my trouble. Amazon would only offer to take the shipment back and give me a refund, which is not a very good way to solve the fact that I just wanted a manual and warranty card. They pointed the finger at ecom and ecom initially pointed the finger right back at Amazon. An ecom rep did call me today and give me a phone number for Samsung, but that still doesn't feel like it really solves my problem. So, buyer beware: You will need to find your own manual online in order to learn how to set the unit up. I went to verizonwireless.com/networkextender and looked through their setup help until I found a link to the manual ([...]). Also, I'm not sure what I'm going to do if I need to take advantage of the 90-day warranty, since I have absolutely no warranty information with the unit.

In setting the unit up, I faced a challenge in getting a GPS signal when the unit was placed where I needed to place it to get a good cell signal over most of my house. I had to put the unit down on my desk to be able to see enough sky to get a GPS signal. What I did was let the unit sit there until it acquired the GPS signal and then move it (without unplugging it) up into its final position. The GPS light is now flashing red, but the unit is working fine. If I ever lose power, I'll need to repeat these steps to get the GPS signal back.

The cell signal around our house was a little disappointing, given what I had read in other reviews. 5000 square feet is a circle of about a 40 foot radius. If I move 40 feet away in our house, I'm down to 0-1 bars. I called Verizon tech support to see if there was any way to increase the power of the Network Extender and they said they didn't think there was and that it normally covers a radius of about 30 feet. What this all means in my house is that I can't get the farthest reaches of the house without the Network Extender signal dropping out.

The Network Extender works very well where we spend most of our time in the living/dining rooms and kitchen (all within about 20-25 feet of the unit). We can now reliably use our phones and receive calls and texts at home. We don't use our phones for data, but I did some testing and it seemed to work fine.

title: Great for a while... but then...
text:
I bought this lens at my local camera store a little over a year ago. Right after I bought it, I noticed that I had quite a bit of glare when an exposed light bulb was in the shot. (I do real estate photography, and I typically shoot 2-4 houses a day) I went back to the camera store and got myself a new Hoya filter, which seemed to work quite well to get rid of the glare. As the year went on, I started to notice more and more CA (chromatic aberration) in my shots. I could actually see it getting worse and worse as time went on. Again, I work A LOT, so I can understand that the constant use and movement, in and out of the case, snapping on and off a tripod, might have an effect on the lens. But I could actually SEE things getting worse in my shots. It was almost as if one of the elements inside was shifting ever so slightly, which CAN be one of the causes of CA. I was also noticing that the front part of the lens seemed to be getting loose, and a bit wiggly. That didn't seem to affect the front element though, so I didn't worry about it too much. I have to say that the Push-Pull system for going from Auto-Focus to Manual stinks. Sometimes you have to turn the lens a little further to get it to pull back in, which takes it back out of focus. (If you don't know what I'm talking about, look at a Canon lens. There's a little switch that changes the lens from Auto-Focus to Manual. On this Tokina, you push the front focus ring OUT to go to Auto-Focus the lens, and then pull it back in to go to Manual.)

In the beginning of August, I updated my camera to the Canon T4i. This lens, which worked before, now wouldn't auto-focus properly. It would come close, but upon closer inspection of the photos, they would now be a bit off. I didn't think much of it because I very rarely ever use auto-focus, so I just ignored it.

THEN I started to get the Error01 message. Over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over. It was to the point where I couldn't work anymore. (Not to mention that the CA was outlandish and costing me so much post prod time!) I had to go back to my Canon 16-35mm (Which, at 10 years old, never gave me an issue. I only got the Tokina to go wider.) for a few shoots, simply because this lens wouldn't work. Yesterday I bought the Canon 10-22mm. I worked with it three times today, including a night shoot, and I couldn't be happier.

Something interesting that I read made me realize my mistake. It said, "Canon does NOT release it's specs to anyone, so any lens that you buy that's NOT a Canon has been reverse engineered. Buyer Beware." That's good advice I wish I'd heard before I bought this Tokina lens.

title: 10 Dives in Bali 0 - 62 ft
text:
I have used three cameras previously for underwater photography. All compact Canons with housings rated to 300 ft.

Just returned from a 6 day 10 dive safari in Bali. I used the Nikon 1 AW1 for all dives. Standard dive profile was to run along a line approximately 40 feet deep or shallower depending on the location of items of photographic interest. On one dive the item was Pygmy Seahorses that occurred at the 53 ft level so we took the risk and exceeded the 49 foot spec. The final photos show the shots were taken at 62 feet (as I understand it, the camera is not warranted against flooding, so its not like I could void the warranty). A note in this regard -- I saw the review from the guy whose camera flooded in spite of the fact he put extra lubricant on the seals etc. The camera was new out of the box and I had removed the lens once and put it back on immediately. I wanted to keep it as close to factory shipping specs as possible since I fully intended to push the depth limitations during the Bali trip. I did not put lubricant on the seals or mess with the camera in anyway except to change batteries and insert the memory card.

I have been a still photographer for more than 40 years using a range of high end cameras. I experimented with video briefly a few times over the years but did very little with the genre. The 1 AW1 converted me to video in one easy step. The camera is so light weight and easy to use (relatively speaking) that video was a logical next step. After a still photo is taken, a short video of the same subject becomes a logical extension of the process -- the camera makes this a very smooth and natural transition; since most of the shots were of coral reef animals, the opportunity to get animated video was too good to pass up.

The best and the worst things about the camera:

Best

1. Switching between video and still photos was as easy as pressing the appropriate button. No settings to change, no dials to rotate.
2. 1080p video with a preset underwater filter to reduce the blue. Excellent video quality-- the camera often seems to have better visibility (visual distance penetration through the water) than my underwater vision (my eyes are 20/20). I have killer video of two manta rays (at manta point -- somewhat murky water) that show them very nicely and much clearer than I saw them as I took the shots).
3. 14.2 photos in vivid color.
4. Pop up flash works well at short ranges normal for underwater photography (but of course only for still photography).
5. Zoom lens range is pretty effective for the distances normal to underwater photography.
6. Scuba filter setting -- USE IT.
7. Camera is so compact and well engineered it, at times, feels like an extension of your eyes (when they aren't awash in seawater) and makes photography/videography an extension of seeing.
8. The Bali dive master observed at one point that other divers using the GoPo would shoot a few seconds of video and run out of memory. I went to Bali with a 64 GB card in the camera and a second spare 64. After shooting for 10 dives and early 800 photos and videos, 20 GB remained on the original card. I never touched the second card.

Worst
1. Make sure you have a separate charged battery for each dive. Battery life is adequate but distinctly limited. Change batteries between each dive.
2. Hierarchical menus are well organized but contain a lot of information so it took me a bit of experimentation to find the scuba setting and other specific options of interest.
3. I would estimate that one third to two thirds of the time I found it difficult to impossible to see the photo subject clearly in the display screen. At least half the time I settled for centering the moving blur in the center of the view field. The most common reason for this was a combination of saltwater washing around in my mask (and in my eyes) and the fact that as bright as the display screen on the camera was, the intense tropical sun and great Bali water clarity rendered the display a bit too dark to see well. The standard camera limited angle of view was also a major factor. Keeping a moving fish lined up in the view finder, while maintaining neutral buoyancy is an art that worked well sometimes and not at all others. More than once I found my self vertical, head down in the water attempting to hold station on a group of tiny fish darting in and out of a coral head.
4. Because of the factors listed in 3 it would be good if the camera had motion control. However, the improvements offered by this feature would probably be limited since keeping a moving fish centered in the view finder often requires swinging the camera in a wide arc. The resulting video leaves much to be desired for a second or two until you can settle on the moving objects new track. I suspect the arc would not be smoothed by standard camera shake reduction technology.

I used the camera on a L shaped mount bar with one Sola 1200 underwater video light mounted to the bar on ball pivots and one
Sola 1200 light mounted to the back of my right hand.

Lights were a bit a a pain at times because it took 3 pushes up to set each at max illumination, and because the water clarity and tropical sun, overwhelmed the light put out by the units (recall I was usually at 40-45 feet or less). Deeper dives would have made the lights more useful but also exceed the camera spec. I would estimate the lights were only useful when shooting a relatively motionless subject (for example: clown fish in an anemone) within 2-10 feet.

The light mount bar was a great aid in positive camera handling. I suspect tracking a moving fish, with the camera only, might have made the camera seem a little too compact and the controls too close together. By holding the mount handle in my left hand and controlling the camera with my right (zoom and video/photo button) control was never an issue.

In summary
I have approximately 800 still and 1080p video segments. Nearly all are in focus and beautifully exposed. As you can probably tell I let the camera manage the focus and lighting, so I could concentrate on tracking the moving subject while maintaining neutral buoyancy. That was a full time job; sometimes, more than a full time job. Over the next few weeks I intend to put a best of video together and upload to UTube. Look for it with search string Bail, 10 dives, 0-62 feet.

title: Dark and Blotchy screen
text:
The screen on my first Kindle Paperwhite was terrible. It had a dark blue green hue with large areas of shadows and blotches and blobs of green and pink. The text did not render consistently as some looked bold and some letters looked washed out. I could not read on it because it was so bad. I got a replacement sent to me and at fist it was much better. But after a few days the screen has become shadowy and blotchy much like the first one did. It is slightly better, but not by much. Judging from all the negative posts I've seen on some forums, there are large numbers of the Kindle Paperwhite being returned due to screen defects. I think Amazon's quality control on the Kindle Paperwhite is really bad.

I will say that I've owned seven Kindles prior to the Kindle Paperwhite and this is the first time I've seen problems like this. Kindle Customer Service has been really nice, but too many units seem to be bad. I cannot recommend this product.

EDITED on October 18: I got a second replacement and unfortunately the screen on it was just as bad as the others. I returned all three units to Amazon and decided to wait until the next generation of Paperwhites is introduced. This first generation is obviously flawed. The firmware and design is really good, but the screen is virtually unusable.
