title: Don't buy, bad software.  It will NEVER FLY!
text:
What they don't make clear in the fancy color ads and all the videos of it supposedly flying around is that you are only buying the hardware, it doesn't come with any software to make it work so you have to depend on flaky unreliable shareware. They call it Open Sourced Software but that just means that it's written by other hobbyists in their basement and may or may not work. I have one that I've been trying to get working for weeks without any success. I've tried 3 of the most popular ground control programs, Qgroundcontrol that is recommended by Pixhawk on their website and both Mission Planner and APM Planner 2.0 that are available from 3D Robotics who sells the PX4 and none of them will work to program firmware on the board to make it work as a copter. The way it's supposed to work is that you install one of the versions of ground control programs on you PC or Mac then use that to upload software to the board to make it work and then configure it for the kind of craft you are going to be using it on. All 3 programs tend to crash, freeze or exit suddenly but if they keep running will display around 30-40 different kinds of errors when trying to upload software to the PX4. I did manage to get Mission Planner to configure the PX4 as a Plane once but when I try to set it up as a copter the program always crashes! I also tried 2 versions of APM Planner 2.0 for Ubuntu but they are no better than the Windows version! All the programs have forums and are on Github where you can post problems and issues but it doesn't help since they don't fix the issues except for QGC and it's being updated almost every day and is finally up to the point that it can upload firmware to the PX4 then connect to it and get flight data.
Update 2015: I'm reducing the rating to just one star since it's never been able to fly. It's been over a year now and so far NO versions of the crappy shareware programs like Qgroundcontrol have ever worked all the way through far enough to actually get to the point of trying to Arm the craft!

title: Great Product But Setup A Nightmare
text:
I was looking for a remote to tie all the electronic components of my entertainment system together. I thought this remote would be the answer to my prayers. I thought I would start simple and attempt to program the remote to control my LG TV and an AT&T U-Verse box. I thought it would be simple enough.

I grabbed the hardware, remote, and the IPad and started going through the directions. The free app downloaded just fine. However, on step 3, I found that IPad2, which I was using, was not supported. I shrugged and grabbed one of the kids’ IPod touch as it was not in the list of devices that would not work. I downloaded the app again and soon got a message that it would not work as the device was not on IOS 6. There was a link to set up the system via your PC that is on the same Wi-Fi network as the hub.

I was able to configure the hub portion of the system via my PC. I was required to create a Harmony account in the process, but that was fairly simple. I would then get a message telling me to visit myharmony.com to setup my remote. I went to the website and could find absolutely nothing on setting up my remote.

I gave up trying to set this thing up on the PC and started all over again with the wife’s iPad Mini. I downloaded the app again and found that it was able to connect to the hub. From there, it took me another 30 minutes of mindlessly wandering the app and hub to figure out how to configure the remote to work with the TV and the U-Verse box. I personally found trying to configure the remote the first time via the app was very unintuitive and was very frustrating.

On the flip side, once I got the remote configured, it works quite well. I do not have to point the remote at the “right angle” like I do with the U-Verse provided remote. The remote signal seems strong and seems to be able to communicate with the hub at almost any angle.

Once I was able to get the hub and remote configured, it worked quite well. However, at least for me, getting to the point where I could actually use the remote with a TV and a cable box was about 1.5 hours. I found this a bit excessive.

title: You're doing it wrong!!! -- This gizmo is an EXTREMELY HELPFUL TOOL at a fantastic price.
text:
Works great, and the results match other calibration tools in my home theater. Also assisted in calibrating a commercial live-audio installation. Audibly helped the commercial system and I could easily visualize the changes. I would advise you to use an averaging tool in making the measurement (AudioTool has this option) as instantaneous reading of pink noise is not the easiest to see what is happening. For the purpose of doing frequency calibration of a stereo system, seeing the average of pink noise results is more helpful, and then use instantaneous to dig out things you hear or see.

Who all those who blast this as: "This is a horrible microphone, my built in one is better" and the like, I'm sorry, but you have no idea what this microphone is for. You think this microphone is supposed to sound good, thinking that it has build built with "calibration". This is not a high-quality microphone (measurement-grade microphones don't come under $20, if even $200). This microphone has nothing fancy inside it. This is, however, a microphone what has been measured at a shiz-ton to frequencies to characterize the microphone's frequency response so you can have a reference point as to what you are measuring. Even if your reference is crappy, if you know what it is, you can make use out of it. What's the difference in amplitude between 4kHz and 30Hz on your iPhone/android's microphone??? You don't know. Even if one was measured for calibration offsets, do you really think every single unit will have the exact same response down to a dB? It MIGHT give you a ballpark... maybe.... if it's a full moon... wearing green??.

Sorry for turning this into a rant. I just hate seeing an awesomely useful tool for <$20 that does what a RANE calibration system does for $500+ get blasted as being a crappy product. A wrench does a pretty lousy job of spreading peanut butter on toast-- if you use a tool wrong, you will likely get bad results.

AudioTool app

title: I am extremely happy to report that everything works
text:
I recently bought a refurbished Dell OptiPlex 755 Mini-tower(largest case) - (Core 2 Duo - 3GHz) computer.

I figured I would just keep this new computer, and upgrade as I needed to in the future.

I found a refurbished power supply on Amazon for $69.99 shipped.

I figured I might get into some mild PC gaming, so the graphics card was next.
I did a lot of research, and asked lots of questions on computer forums.
I found the most powerful card that would work in my system, but unfortunately, it was a dual slot, and
my machine won't take a dual slot, and doesn't have much room on the inside for a long graphics card
either.
So, I figured I could put the graphics card on top of the machine and use this cable.

This cable says it's for pcie 2.0 and higher, but my system has a 1.0 version pcie slot.
I also had to get a 6-pin pcie, 12" extension power cable that attaches to my new power supply and the card.
I had seen a build where a guy used this cable because it was shielded. He had tried another brand and
had some type of electrical interference. That's why I chose the 3M brand.

Well, I am extremely happy to report that everything works. I could only find the graphics card I wanted as a refurbished one.
Also ordered from Amazon. I don't like buying used stuff, but my new system is all refurbished, and it works great.
I also had to twist this cable a half a turn in order to get my graphics card to lay with the fan up, so it
is a little pliable.
My application may seem weird to the average person, but It's the only way I could use a descent graphics card for gaming.

title: Honeywell 5815 - a worthy wireless sensor
text:
I purchased 2 of these for use with a Vista 20P [[ASIN:B003HF5KZK Ademco Vista 20p]] alarm system. The box included the sensor and the magnet. It took me a while to figure out how to program this into the Vista system, because the sensor has 4 loops. Each loop has to be programmed into a separate channel. Loop 2 is closed/secure, loop 4 is open/alarm. Loop 1 (closed) and loop 3 (open) are assigned to the external wired sensor. Yes, this wireless sensor has 2 contacts for wiring 1 or more additional magnetic wired sensors such as this [[ASIN:B000GUQKGW Ademco 945WH Honeywell 945WH Surface Mount Magnetic Contact w/ Leads]] in parallel. With one of these, in combination with a few cheap wired sensors you could protect a large window with multiple "doors" or multiple windows that are close by. This great feature is not mentioned anywhere on Amazon, but it is listed in the small pamphlet.

I have been arming the alarm every night, and so far the sensors have functioned properly. Battery life is estimated at 1-2 years, depending on use. When the alarm system is off the sensor only checks back with the Vista base every X minutes to conserve battery.

The sensor is small enough to fit and blend in with the white vinyl windows. I will post an update if there is a problem, but so far so good.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Update 1 November 2013

I added [[ASIN:B002MA8GKW Honeywell Ademco 5816WMWH White Door / Window Transmitter w/ Magnet]] to the alarm system to protect some doors. These sensors are bigger in size, but less in cost. I used them in 2 garage doors, so size was not a big deal. The original sensors continue working, same original battery from almost 2 years ago, and the system being armed every night. So far no issues.

HOW TO PROGRAM AN RF TRANSMITTER TO ADEMCO VISTA 20P

Enter programming mode: Enter Installer code (x-x-x-x) + 8 0 0.

Note1: Default installer code is 4-1-1-2 in case you don't know
Note2: Always exit programming using *99

Press [∗] + [Field Number] (for example, ∗56)

56 - Zone Programming - Use this menu mode to program zone information

Note: A display of "EE"or "Entry Error"means you have entered a nonexistent field. Simply re-enter [∗] plus a valid field number.

SET TO CONFIRM? If 1 (Yes) is entered, you will be prompted to confirm each transmitter after entering the serial and loop numbers (at the "XMIT TO CONFIRM"prompt later in this procedure).

Note: We recommend that you confirm the programming of every transmitter.

Zone Number for VISTA-20P:
wired zones 01-08 | wireless zones 09-48 | button zones 49-64

Enter Zn Num. Enter the zone number that you wish to program.

Summary Screen display appears. [∗] to continue

Zone Type (ZT) - (see table at right) - Each zone must be assigned to a zone type, which defines the way in which the system responds to faults in that zone. Enter the Zone Type code. See manual for more types

01 = Entry/exit #1 | 02 = Entry/exit #2 | 03 = Perimeter

Note:If 00 is entered, Delete Zone ? will be displayed.

Partition No. (P) - Enter the Partition number 1. [∗] to continue

Report Code (RC) - Leave default.. [∗] to continue

Hardwire Type - This prompt appears only for zone numbers 02-08. [∗] to continue

0 = EOL | 1 = NC (Normally Closed) | 2 = NO (Normally Open)

Response Time (RT) - This prompt appears only for hard-wired zones 01-08. [∗] to continue

Input Device type - This prompt is skipped for zones 1-8. Type is RF for all of the RF transmitters. [∗] to continue

Serial number Entry and Loop Number Entry - Used only when enrolling wireless transmitters.

a) Transmit two open/close sequences. If using a button-type transmitter, press and release the button twice, but wait about 4 seconds before pressing the button the second time.

b) manually enter the 7-digit serial number printed on the label of the transmitter.

Press the [✱] key -the cursor will move to the "L"position.

You can edit the loop number, if necessary. Loop 2 is closed/secure, loop 4 is open/alarm. Loop 1 (closed) and loop 3 (open) are assigned to the external wired sensor.

When the loop number is acceptable, press [✱]. Make sure the device and magnet loop is closed

XMIT TO CONFIRM PRESS ✱ TO SKIP - This prompt will only appear if you answered "Yes"at the first
prompt in this section.

Activate the loop input by separating the device from magnet or press button that corresponds to this zone.

Serial or Loop Numbers do not match after activating the transmitter. If a match is not obtained (i.e., summary display does not appear), press the [#] key twice and then enter (or transmit) the correct serial
number.

Summary Screen - Press [✱] to accept the zone information and continue

82 - Alpha Descriptor - Use this menu mode to assign descriptors to zones

Program Alpha ? Press 1 to continue.
Custom Words ? Press 0 to program standard alpha descriptors from the fixed vocabulary. The system will then automatically display the descriptor for zone 1.

Note: this is a "Summary mode,"and that no entries can be made. Entries can be made only when the display contains a flashing cursor, which signifies the "Entry mode."

Press [∗] to continue

enter [✱] plus the next zone number for which you wish to enter (or check) a descriptor. A summary display for that zone will appear. You must then press [✱] plus the same zone number again to gain access to the entry mode (flashing cursor) for that zone.

Press [#] plus the 3-digit number for the first word from the Alpha Vocabulary List.

Note: If you accidentally enter the wrong word, simply press [#] plus the correct 3-digit number for the word you want. Press [6] to accept the selected word and continue to the next word.

Enter the 3-digit number for the next word. Press [6] to accept the selected word and continue to the next word.

Enter the 3-digit number for the third word. Press [6] to accept the selected word and continue to the next word.

Example: The descriptor that we wish to enter for zone 99 is BACK DOOR. From the list, BACK = 013. You enter #013 then [6]. The next word is DOOR, whose number is "057.". Enter #057 then [6]. Press 8 to store the words in memory.

title: Not bad for the price
text:
A few years ago I bought 2 cheap monitors off a friend. One had a blown horn, the other was rattling and both were loaded with cheap poly woofers. I bought them for the cabs only. I recently wanted to build some close field monitors for our drummer during rehearsals only. The woofers were replaced with some older Peavey SP-12825 12" Scorpions I had in stock and ordered these PDS111 drivers to test if they would fit as a good horn choice which is a plastic 4" X 10" lens that really flares the mids freq's coming out. (Not a lot of room to work with. A large driver wont fit these cabs. I tried a 22A driver and it hit the top.) I re-worked the x-overs to bring it to a 1.5k point 10 ohm pad (I know they are rated at 2k but will never see high output). This pair will be run with a Peavey CS200 bridged (220 watts @ 4 ohm). I fired them up and they actually sound pretty good using a Shure SM58 studio matched mic and the music playback is also very nice. I know they are NOTHING like a JBL DT220ti or a Peavey RX14 but don't need to spend $ that for these monitors. I "burned" them for over an hour @ 50% amp and 40 db board out with MP3 playback insert. (around 50-60 watts nom. 92db and DDT compression on with near flat EQ with slight enhancements, >5db+ @ 63 to 128 & 4k to 10K and >5db cut @ 1K and 1.25K) So far so good. These are a surprisingly small lightweight driver and should work well where space is a premium. I recommend the PDS111 as a low priced driver for home music systems or low level practice sound. Just remember these are NOT PRO-GRADE tweeters and will NOT perform well in larger areas or high volume music playback conditions so please don't buy them for those purposes. We'll see how long they last!
UPDATE:
Been 5 years now. Used once or more per week and still kickin'. These little suckers really work!

title: 2nd Time is the Charm
text:
This is the first HD TV that I have ever purchased. I did quite a bit of shopping around and read many different product reviews before I made the decision that this TV was the one for me.

When my TV arrived at my doorstep, I was very excited to get it all hooked up. After I plugged it in, nothing happened, I tried everything. Finally after realizing that my new TV was not going to turn on I called Sony support. After 2 minutes of navigating through menus I finally get to talk to a real person.

The explain to me that my TV is broken, they are willing to send me a new one, along with a pre-paid shipping label. They ship it to me, (leave off the apartment number, have to get a call from Fed-Ex to find out what APT I live in) within a weeks time. Very excited this time and ready to put all of this behind me, only to find out that there is no pre-paid shipping label included. Thankfully the TV works this time, but no label to be seen.

title: Slim, Sexy, Clueless, and Edgy to Boot
text:
Published this on my blog and was asked to share here as well. The blog has the original images: http://blog.telaeris.com/?p=19541

This is one of those articles I hate to write. But I am sure I am not the first it has happened to - nor certainly will I be the last. But you get so attracted to the gorgeous lines and a smooth exterior that you throw caution and experience to the wind.

I am talking of course about my latest computer purchase which today I returned. I bought the Acer Aspire S7 - a machine with great specs: a fast I7 processor, 256GB SSD, full 1080P display, Gorilla glass touchscreen, and lightweight. These are what sold me on the machine and are the features I will most miss.

Having tested Windows 8 before, I knew the new touch interface wasn't for me. Hiding settings behind the odd corners and sides is not useful to those of us that want an intuitive interface. However with Start8, I was able to jump back to my comfortable desktop and have a fully functional start menu. First problem solved.

The next gotcha that hit me with this machine was strictly an issue from Microsoft's integration of Skype. I use Skype for both personal and business contacts and do not want to link my work e-mail into it, but Skype on Windows 8 forces you to link your digital IDs. Apparently lots of other people have had this issue too. And once you link accounts, there is no going back. I avoided this hassle by re-firing up my Trillian instant messenger account which supports Skype.

I could go on significantly about why I don't like the new Windows, but after paying $25 for these two pieces of shareware, I had dealt with the majority of my issues with the OS.

I was ultimately let down by the S7 in the one place that I didn't expect it...the hardware. Acer focused on making this machine beautiful, but they forgot about the human interface - the keyboard and track pad.

The keyboard in the S7 has the worst case of key bounce I have ever experienced. Over the course of a month, I could not make this machine avoid double typing keys. I tried different styles of typing, adjusted settings, all to no avail. Adding to my keyboard woes, Acer choose to eliminate the function key row, replacing it with a function key operating like the control key with the numbers. I found that I depend upon having function keys immediately available as shortcuts: F1 for help, F3 for searching, and lots more. These have become so ingrained into my habits, that holding an additional key to access their functionality was distracting. The odd thing was that the computer had plenty of space for a Function key row.

The next problem I encountered was the S7′s sharp lip on either side of the keyboard. With my over-sized hands, I would often find a cutting impression on my hands after using the computer for any period of time, which would make it very uncomfortable to work. Other laptops put this edge on the screen or eliminate it entirely.

The S7 also suffers from Apple-itis with its implementation of the "Uni-pad". As many good ideas as Steve Jobs had, eschewing buttons and specifically the right mouse button is just plain stupidity for the sake of meeting aesthetic goals. The beauty in buttons, both virtual and real, is that it is intuitively clear that they are meant to be pressed. Where, how, and with what number of fingers to touch the pad with to access context menus is about as unclear as it was to figure out how to close a program started from the Windows 8 Start Screen.

Owning the Acer S7 was like owning a gorgeous new sports car, only to find that the accelerator would sometime stick, the seat was uncomfortable, and you had no visibility. It obviously would not work in the long run, but from a street view, it certainly looked pretty.

Our blog is often about improving productivity. I hope my experiences with this product might allow others save time and to make informed decisions, both on Windows 8 and the Acer S7. My recommendation on these fronts follow:

1. If Acer fixes the issues with the keyboard, track pad and the sharp laptop edge, this will be a wonderful machine. I wanted to like this machine, but these flaws affected my day to day work so significantly, I had to return it.
2. If you use your computer for work at an office - you probably don't need a touchscreen.
3. The next Microsoft Windows is not far off. Wait for it. If you can't, shareware can fill the gaps quickly and cheaply.

title: Beautiful monitor
text:
This replaced a 19" Viewsonic from 2007 which I was very happy with but I wanted a larger one that could display two browser screens side by side that I could easily see from two feet away. This 24" Viewsonic does it perfectly. I run this on a Windows 8 computer and the picture is beautiful and flawless.

The monitor came well packaged, I took it out of the box, plugged in the VGA cable that was still attached to the computer from the old monitor, plugged in the power cord, adjusted the resolution to 1920x1080 and it was ready to use. No color, tint, contrast, or other adjustment was needed.

It came with a disk to install Viewsonic drivers and a Viewsonic monitor control app. It did not have the ones for Win 8 and I didn't bother to download the ones from their website because the drivers and control app that came with Win 8 worked fine for me. The computer is a Lenovo Intel I5 with the Intel Graphics and Media Control Panel app that handles the monitor adjustments just fine.

The monitor has built in speakers of OK quality but I don't use sound with this machine and would have been just as happy if there were no speakers.

The monitor is fully adjustable for tilt, height, pivot, and swivel. This was very important to me and many of the competitors' comparably priced units don't offer this. This monitor is exactly 22 inches wide and 17.75 inches high from the bottom of the base at the lowest height setting.

I also like the fact that it came with a three year warranty from Viewsonic.

I've had this monitor for three days now and am very happy with it and am glad that I didn't have to do any messing around to set it up.

02/04/13. I have these additional comments since my initial review. I have tried the adjustment buttons in the lower right front of the monitor and they all work properly. There is an input selector option to allow a switch between input on the VGA, DVI, or Displayport ports.

One minor item that is missing on this unit is the two cord keepers that my other two Viewsonics have. These are the keepers that bundle the cords and let them run down the back of the upright part of the stand. No big deal, but it would have been nice to have them included.

title: Capable camera, just need to get used to the UI
text:
My Panasonic G1 was showing its age and I was growing frustrated with its poor low-light performance and slow autofocus, plus I wanted a second body so I wouldn't have to switch lenses so often. I cross-shopped this against the Panasonic G3 and GH2; I recognize that the G3 is much less expensive (I could've almost gotten two bodies for the price of this one body + lens), and the GH2 is more comparable price-wise. When I played around with the G3 in a store, I discovered that I just didn't like how it felt, and I really missed the automatic EVF proximity sensor. I never did get an opportunity to actually hold a GH2, although I imagine I would have liked it a lot. At the end, what tipped the scales for me were:
- weatherproofing, since I take my camera on hikes, canoe trips, and mountain bike rides, sometimes under less-than-ideal conditions
- in-body image stabilization
- capability to add an external battery holder
- reportedly greater dynamic range
- weatherproof kit lens that goes wider than the Panasonic zooms (12mm-50mm)

After having used the OM-D for a few weeks, I can say that I'm happy with the purchase. The IBIS is the real deal, low light/high ISO performance has to be seen to be believed, and the autofocus is wicked fast. The capability and level of sophistication of this camera makes my old G1 look positively primitive. My only real complaint is that I wish the OM-D was a Panasonic, at least from a user interface perspective. I've spent two years shooting with one camera exclusively and I know how to get to all the controls and change all the settings that matter to me without thinking about it. Trying the Olympus for the first time, I knew the learning curve for this camera was going to be a steep one when I discovered that the Olympus zoom works opposite to the Panasonic zooms. I know that the UI on the OM-D is extremely configurable and I've done what I can to match the controls to what I'm used to, but I was only able to go so far. What I miss the most is the fact that the drive mode is not immediately available (on the G1 a lever quickly moves you from single exposure to burst to bracket to timer) and enabling exposure bracketing in particular is buried a couple of menu levels down. I also find it odd that not every button can be assigned to every function. Olympus has seen fit to limit which functions some buttons can take, and to make some buttons not customizable at all (D-pad up and left arrows, in particular). The touch screen menu is pretty comprehensive, but it still doesn't have the bracketing function, and because it's a capacitive screen and can't be operated while wearing gloves, I haven't gotten into the habit of using it. I also miss the fully-articulated LCD of the Panasonic cameras.

From an image quality and functionality point of view, the OM-D is exactly what I was looking for. Now all I have to do is get used to the UI...

title: I changed my mind
text:
I have been meaning to come back and edit this review for a long time.

What I said about the video capabilities of the camera still hold, but as a camera it is a great tool.

I started walking early every morning and at first I was taking my 2009 Canon SX1-is, but it was banging around hanging from my neck, so I took out the G-15. I bought a leather case for the camera and it was awkward to to get it off while out taking pictures, so I took it off and now the G-15 has been through heat and rain and cold and snow and has been dropped and bumped and covered in dust and it just keeps on ticking. And some beer has splashed on it too when taking pictures of bands.

On the coldest days of the recent winter the camera operated flawlessly and took some amazing shots. It is not great for action shots, but for low light sunrises and my bird watching, it is excellent. The fisheye lens feature is also great and it has a pretty robust bunch of settings for most imaginable shots.

The viewfinder is worthless, but the non-articulating screen is excellent and it has the great dual axis electronic level display.

The real star is the the camera's 28mm Wide-Angle 5x Optical Zoom lens with a focal length of 6.1-30.5mm (35mm film equivalent: 28-140mm) achieves f/1.8-f/2.8, it is amazingly versatile in every situation.

All this fits in your pocket, has awesome battery life and is incredibly durable. I just clean it regularly and think that next time I want a great video camera, I will get a video camera, but when I want a camera that can go anywhere and take great pictures, I grab the G-15.

[Wow, third Canon camera and this one is small and has great battery life, but the pictures aren't great and the HD video, which is why I bought this camera, is horrible because the picture is great, but the sound is rice krispies meets milk. Plus, less than 90 days return cost me -- if I had bought this camera at Best Buy or Wall Mart, they would, at minimun replace the camera to make sure I didn't get an expensive lemon for no extra cost. Amazon might lose a regular customer over this camera.]

title: ASUS T100
text:
I really shopped around before deciding on this laptop. My criteria were 1) quality, 2) speed and function, and 3) battery life and portability. I wish I could have found an 11 or 12 inch laptop with better than five hours of battery life, but on my budget of around $400, I couldn't find one... not a quality computer anyway. This is my third ASUS computer, and I have loved each one of them. I really feel that for the price, an ASUS gives you better quality than its competitors.

I'm middle aged and needing reading glasses, so this screen size is awfully small for me, but I felt it was offset by portability and that fantastic battery life. At first, I was really unhappy with the touchscreen: I had to hold onto the back of the computer in order to get enough leverage to press the screen with the stylus or a finger. This was really bothering me to the point of sending the computer back. It was actually starting to hurt my elbow! Solution: I downloaded "Perceptive Pixel Touch Driver" from the Microsoft Downloads Center. Instantly, the touchscreen became just as responsive as my iPad. Fantastic!! Thank you, whoever designed that driver.

The other issue that worried me was in regard to the keyboard dock. At first, it didn't work at all. Then I googled the problem and found that if you don't fully seat the tablet into the dock, it doesn't connect well. There should be two clear clicks. I think this problem was repeated with something more annoying: I got the keyboard working by pushing a bit on the tablet to make sure it was fully connected, but then every minute or so the computer would make an odd musical "doodle doodle" sound, shut down whatever I was working on, and pop up a dialog box regarding the D drive (this model has a 500 g dock, so the dock is actually D drive). I was ready to give up again, or gee, call customer assistance, but then I decided to try removing and re-attaching the tablet again. The problem seems to have disappeared. It seems that when you attach the tablet to the dock, you'd better press firmly and make sure it's fully seated.

Most of the difficulties I had with Windows 8.1, having come from Windows 7, were solved by using Google to find answers to my questions. Like, "how do I get rid of apps I don't want," or even "where are my apps?" "Where's Control Panel?"

This is one fun computer, now that I've worked out the kinks. I love this thing. I will keep buying ASUS in the future. If you need high portability but the ability to use Windows with its excellent programs-- like Microsoft Office, which is superior, despite criticism of the price, to all the other free word processors out there. Now I just have to find a good case for it because its kind of hard to hang onto, and the hinge bites into your legs when it's on your lap.

One last note: I've used this outdoors. It's not bad at all if you are in good shade. It's not an e-reader, and in my research I didn't find any computer that said it was great for outdoor viewing. And the screen is so small, you can use your head as shade! :D

title: Nice alarm clock, but two needed to be replaced within 17 months!
text:

Because the second unit lasted about 17 months, I reduced my rating from 4 back down to 2 stars. If anyone made an alarm clock with the features and styling of this alarm clock, I would buy it in a heart beat; Unit number three arrived shortly after the second one died.

In the latest version, the manufacturer took away the ability to set the alarm for individual days of the week. This is unfortunate, because I used this feature whenever I needed to get up at an unusual time or day for an appointment or travel.

If you can find an alarm clock that fits your needs from another manufacturer, buy it. Avoid Sangean if you can, their quality is questionable.

Update 1; I gave this alarm clock a second try, despite my original experience, and increased my rating from 2 to 4 stars.

I got around the battery backup issue by using a UPS just for the alarm clock (That is why I gave this great alarm clock just 4 out of 5 stars). The second unit did not have the spinning hands issue mentioned below, and has worked flawlessly since I purchased it about 6 month ago.

Hidden in the not-so-clear manual was a paragraph stating that every button on the top of this alarm clock acts as the snooze button. There is no individual button labeled "Snooze". A little odd, but I got used to it.

Original two star review; I thought I had found the Alarm Clock of my dreams; Atomic time sync, digital radio tuner (to lock onto weak stations or my hold station in bad weather), an alarm volume knob safely tucked out of reach (to avoid accidental muting), and nice styling.

I had three problems with the Sangean alarm clock; First, it does not have a battery power backup to hold the time for more than a few minutes. It took about 3 hours for the clock to sync for the first time in S.W. PA. Second, there is no snooze button and I could not find how to use the snooze in the manual! Third, at some point the analog clock went into a forward spin mode and just kept running.

The manual was nicely illustrated, but not very helpful. It was very short, NOT clear, and the sequence of buttons used to set the alarms is not intuitive (you set the days of the week while the minutes are flashing). Any questions you might have as to why things are happening will NOT be covered in this short manual. There is no trouble shooting section.

I had this first unit back in the box and ready to return to Amazon in less than 4 hours.

title: Solid Bag
text:
2016 UPDATE: This backpack was amazing! The only reason I no longer use it is because my dog chewed through one of the straps. It held up extremely well over the years (always packing it full with heavy books and binders) and I received numerous compliments. Nothing ever tore or looked compromised, including the hardware. Not the most comfortable with a heavy load but that was one con among many pros. I'll miss this backpack!

UPDATE: Over 1 year later the bag is still in great condition. No visible wear, tear or otherwise. Very very happy with this purchase! However, it can get a bit uncomfortable if worn for long periods of time.

Pros:

Very quick ship time. Received within 3 days of ordering.
Soft tan lining on the inside makes the bag seem high quality.
Easy snap buttons and good hardware (bigger zippers, sturdy clasps)
Roomy enough to hold 3-4 textbooks and a binder or two. Or a laptop (even larger ones) with a book or two.
Convenient pocket on the inside for holding pencils, cell phone, calculator, etc.

I really enjoy this bag! I had been searching for a rucksack style bag for quite some time and could not find one that met my school needs. When I found this one it was perfect! It is cute and has a unique rucksack style while still providing the functionality of a regular backpack. Essentially it IS a backpack with an extra flap and straps on top, and I really like that about it.

The hardware and snaps seem to be sturdy but time will tell if they hold up. I also like that I am able to pack quite a bit into it and it doesn't feel like it's going to rip or fall apart, and it has a cool pocket on the inside that makes it easy to access small bits and pieces. I don't wear it for a whole lot of time as I'm a part time college student, but it hasn't been uncomfortable to wear so far and has adjustable straps which is handy. I also really like that it seems to be a more saturated pink than you're lead to believe from the pictures. To me the pictures cast it as a baby pink color when in fact it's more of a light coral pink color, which is exactly what I was looking for.

Cons:

Has an odd smell from the inside lining.

So far in my use of this bag I haven't found much wrong with it. The only notable "weird" thing was an odd smell coming from the lining/inside of the bag when I first received it. If you leave the top open and let it air out it won't be a problem for more than a couple of days but it makes you wonder what that's all about.

All in all I really like this bag. It has the style, convenience, quality and functionality I was looking for. I would definitely recommend this and think it's a good price point for both high school and college students.

title: One of the better Miracast devices out there.
text:
I purchased this in the hopes that it would be able to stream the display for my Galaxy S3, Galaxy S4, and Surface Pro. I'm happy to say that it does all that, and very well.

Some competitors require a lot more setup in order to get the WiDi connection established. This device does away with all that, and just lets you connect with any device in range, with no effort whatsoever.

People who complain about latency: This is not a device that is supposed to replace an HDMI cable. It is a device for sharing media from your phone/tablet to your TV (think photos, videos, games), but it is NOT meant to replace your screen, or be instantaneous! Think of this device as a presentation tool - you should still use your phone, but others can see what you see on your phone's screen (with a 1/2 second delay).

One minor complaint I have is that the device does "stutter" occasionally, and I would imagine that it gets worse as you get farther away from the device (WiDi doesn't have a very long range, by my experience, it isn't like Wi-Fi where you will be able to use it throughout your house). This is something that probably affects all Miracast receivers, though, not just this device.

If you're looking for a wireless presentation solution for your Miracast-enabled phone/tablet, look no further.

title: Speed is not bad but not impressive
text:
I'm using the WD 1TB USB3 drive on a mid 2012 Macbook Air (11"). I have had no problem using it and obtaining high transfer speeds as other's have stated. I formatted it as Mac OS Extended (Journaled) and selected GUID as the partition scheme (under options... in disk utility).

The good:
I love the look of this drive. I didn't realize from the description that it comes with a USB 3 cable in the box - you should know the included cable is only about 15 inches but that's perfect for use with my laptop on my desk.
The price was very good but I try to avoid weighing the overall value of an item when reviewing it's merits as a device. So my opinion is based on my observation of the device for it's function not it's value.

The not so good:
My complaint is when copying a 5.09 GB file it is barely faster then my firewire 800 drive. Over firewire I can transfer at sustained transfer speeds of about 80 MB/s and bursts up to 84 MB/s. With this USB 3.0 drive it transfers at 84 MB/s sustained and bursts of 90 MB/s. Perhaps its a limitation associated with the 2.5" HDD but still I expected it to be closer to 100 MB/s. My basis for this expectation is what I get out of my old eSata drive on my four year old home built desktop with a 2.5" drive in a Rosewill enclosure from the same era.

I took a star for not being faster. With that said I'm happy with it and plan to keep it.

11/2/2012 Update:
I noticed something beneficial with this drive versus my old 3.5" external drive solution. Spin up time. I use the drive for my aperture library and it's spin up time is not even noticeable in everyday use as opposed to my old WD 7,200 RPM drive which took several seconds to spin up which was enough to be annoying at times.

title: UPDATED: Unbeatable Beats -- top road-warrior gear
text:
UPDATE: I purchased this headset on May 22, 2014. On Sept. 25, the right channel went out. On Oct. 11, I contacted BEATS and requested a replacement set. I will update this review when BEATS responds.

The sound is excellent, and the construction feels much more solid than the Bose or Sony noise-cancelling headsets. The battery life and noise-cancelling are better than my Sony set (I have never owned the Bose). I was expecting that level of quality, given Beats' reputation for great engineering. One big surprise, though, was how well they work making calls on my iPhone. The mike is sensitive, and several people have told me they couldn't tell I was using a headset on the call, including when I was calling from a noisy airport gate. The case is also excellent. It's solidly built and the headset folds into it very compactly, so I can carry it in my laptop case without it taking up much room. The volume control and play/pause/skip/ controls are built into one of two cables that come with the headset. I didn't find them very intuitive, but I got used to them quickly, and now they seem well designed. The only thing on my wishlist is that they would work without a battery when I don't need noise cancellation. I have to carry extra AA batteries to be sure I have sound on long trips. Two batteries can be carried in the case, however. I've had this headset for several months now, and I remain very impressed with it in every way.

title: Not compatible with Amazon Fire TV
text:
I purchased an Amazon Fire TV for use with this tv and it will do everything except stream videos. I can navigate the home screen menus and download apps, but it buffers and gives playback errors anytime you try to watch any video. I thought it was a faulty Fire TV so I was on the phone with tech support for an hour and got a replacement Fire TV shipped. It behaved the exact same way. I reset my wireless network and tried a wired connection, but still could not play videos. title: Don't be fooled by the small package
text:
First off, I would like to explain that this may be an ongoing review. I just bought this item last night, and being a person who understands electronics, I usually wait for my reviews. This time, I figured I would start the review, and then I can come back and edit. Therefore, you may see some updates or changes below.

Second, don't let my initial 4-star rating fool you. I was torn on how to rate this product for the value of what you pay, or vs. other speakers. I decided to put this up against much larger bluetooth speakers, and I think it speaks volumes that a $40 item is 4-stars compared to $150 bluetooth portable speakers.

I'm going to start with what most peopls call "cons", but I'm just going to note them as minor nuisances

-The cord is only about 6 inches long....BUT...its your standard android type charger. Since I'm a Samsung Galaxy boy, myself, I have a ton of these cables. It is currently charging with an old LG cable I found

-Some have mentioned a slight hum in the speaker. This is pretty common with most Bluetooth devices. This goes away when you start playing music. There have been some that said, "once you hear the hum, you always hear the hum". I purposely turned the music all the way down just to hear the hum. I listened to it at my desk for 5 minutes, and then played music again. I don't notice any hum, and I am TRYING to hear it. So, although there is, in fact, a hum, I'm not noticing it when in use.

-Its not a great bass machine, but again, is this really a con? Do people buy a prius to drag-race? Cannot really hold that against this machine, so again...that is why I said a "minor nuisance" (and that is a stretch)

-The power switch is on the bottom

-There is an extreeeeeemly loud series of beeps every time you turn it on. You know its coming, so you can try to shield it. Its still somewhat annoying, and not good for starting up in quiet places. There may be a way around this, I just haven not figured it out.

-The controls on the speaker itself are a little slow to respond, but honestly, who is going to use this? It is only a minor delay anyway. I just tested them to see what they were. I control everything from my phone.

I tried this thing out approximately 10 times in Bed Bath and Beyond. I kept messing with their display and was rather disappointed that I couldn not try my own music on their display. So, that kept me from trying it at first. Plus, I am always concerned that the display model is set up differently and it just won't sound as good at home in larger rooms...which takes me to my pros, and what I love about this (so far)

-The sound fills a room. Its not that massive BOSE sound, but its pretty close in how it fills a room. I listen to a lot of 90's acoustic rock and that stuff sounds incredible. Now, if you get to some of the newer club-rap type of music, there is not a lot of power, but it doesn't sound distorted either. Still sounds good, it just is not going to blow your hair back and rattle windows

-I had the phone about 15 feet away from the device and it played beautifully. What is funny is Pandora played clearer than my recorded music...here is why that is a pro. Because, I realized a lot of my recorded music is garbage from the internet and typically poor recordings, which leads me to believe that this device really picks out the clarity of songs. Much like a good set of headphones might actually make some of my bad recording actually sound bad because the headphones are so clear.

-The construction is very sturdy

- (pending a battery test)

- any standard charger that comes with most android phones can charge this.

-line in that will work with non-USB devices

-packaging is actually very nice. I will keep this for storage.

If you are skeptical about buying this, just buy it from a place that has easy returns. Thus far, I have no desire to return it. As far as performance goes, it is a solid 5-star product for the price. Again, I gave it four stars only because its slightly not as powerful as some bigger, more expensive speakers. I realize that may not be a fair assessment, but, again, I think it speaks more to the product that I give it 4 stars in comparing it to the larger portable Bluetooth speakers. I think the only way I would have a problem with this speaker in the future, is if for some reason performance decreases, or I find that the battery lasts a very short amount of time. I will update this, if needed, in the future. If you don't hear from me, that means its still doing well :)

title: Excellent Work/Gaming Computer
text:
Main usage of this product:
Animating/rendering in Maya 2014. Video editing. Gaming.

Pros:
1) Performance - With a nice sized SSD, dedicated GTX 870M with overclocking, seperate CPU and GPU dual rear-vented fans, and the i7 with plenty of memory, this machine is a beast. I've used it to animate and render in Autodesk Maya 2014 with no overheating or performance problems. Same goes for gaming. It runs any game in high/ultra setting that I throw at it with ease (ie, Skyrim, World of Warcraft, Farcry 3, just to name a few).
2) Cooling - This computer has the absolute best cooling I've ever seen in a laptop. The CPU and GPU have their own rear-blowing fan that does a great job at keeping it cool. It will get slightly warm after a few hours of use, but only if you're really testing out the hardware (ie, rendering in Maya, running Skyrim with mods in the highest possible setting), even then, it's the most heat efficient laptop I've used.
3) The list of pros could go on and on and on. Pretty much every aspect of this laptop feels great for a Game developer/video editor/gamer like myself.

Cons:
1) Battery Life - Let's admit it, you won't be buying this laptop for the battery efficiency.
2) Heavy - at 9.9 pounds, it's one hefty mobile computer.
3) Finding a backpack/computer case that fits it - At first, I bought a 17.3 inch case that didn't quite fit the dimensions. Make sure you find one that fits. (Dimensions ((WxHxD)) - 16.1 x 2.0 x 12.5" / 40.9 x 5.1 x 31.8 cm)
4) Windows 8.1 - Though I recently read that Microsoft is planning on releasing a patch in the future that will make this OS feel a bit more like Windows 7. This is good since the computer doesn't have a touch screen, and Windows 8.1 is pretty annoying.

Overall, I'd recommend this product to anyone that's looking for a powerful laptop that can easily support the high-spec demands of gamers, gaming development, and video editing professionals alike.

I would try to tuck the cord excess in my goggles or swim cap, but it would always end up falling down and usually make the earpiece come out of my ear mid-stroke. There is nothing more annoying than stopping half-way down the pool to put the thing back in your ear. Or the little ear pieces (made for different size ear canals) would come off in the pool. The over the ear part was also a nuisance because it was a bit bulky and would simply not stay close to my ear...I even tried (with no luck) to use my goggle strap to hold it down. And to make matters worse, once the things fell out of my ears and got water down in them, it would distort or muffle the sound...I would have to stop and kind of flick them to get the sound to return to normal.  Simply put these were more of a headache than anything. They might work better for someone else's ears, but the cord length would still be in the way. I recommend the speedo waterproof aqua beta brand instead!

title: Durable But Flawed
text:
The Belkin cover is durable and can stand some heavy usage. The cover is made from synthetic leather and lined with microfiber. The bungee belt wraps around the front cover to keep it closed. The iPad is held in the case with rubber claps that snap to each of the corners of the iPad making it a secure fit. The other plus side is the case is thin and light weight.

A few major downsides to the case is the magnetic locking feature built into the cover. When the cover is closed the rubber clasps on one edge of the iPad keeps the cover from making contact with the face of the iPad, causing the iPad to stay on. Another factor in this is the cover does not stretch to the corner pulling back away from the edge also causing the magnet to not trigger the lock function. So I just ended up turning the cover lock off in the settings.

The rolled cover keyboard setup is a hit or miss. I have had issues with the roll collapsing while typing.

The power button is also hard to access due to the rubber clamp that covers it.

So all in all the cover is nice but some of the key features are hindered due to bad design.

Pros:
- microfiber front cover
- bungee belt for keeping case closed
- tight fitting clasp on each corner to hold iPad secure.
- light weight / not bulky

Cons:
- magnetic lock/unlock cover
- keyboard roll position
- iPad power button access
- Cover doses not close properly

12) Nice on-screen display (OSD) for tweaking the system using the TV display - works through HDMI, unlike other receivers who use composite for OSD

Cons

The issues that others have with the trackpad really haven't cropped up with me. Sure, they might show their ugly little heads down the line, but for now, they are keeping a low profile.
The sound quality is impressive for the size and the price, and the wireless connectivity is perfect. The screen resolution works just fine for me, and so far, every program that I've installed has worked flawlessly.

text:
I've been using this "hybrid" drive for almost two months. I used it to replace a WD Scorpio WD2500BEVS (250GB 5400RPM) in my old Toshiba L305D-S5904 laptop with Windows Vista Home Premium 32bits. One month before the upgrade I returned the computer to factory conditions, to speed up it. The replacement was very easy using the Apricorn Upgrade Kit. All the cloning process took about 2.5 hours.
I did these measurements before and after the HDD replacement.
HDD | SSHD
Cold Boot 42s | 39s
Turn off 20s | 15s
Explorer 1s | 1s
Excel 2007 5s | 3s
Firefox 21 5s | 4s
Opera 12 9s | 6s
Window HDD index 5.2 | 5.9
My expectations about the new speed were higher than I got. Of course, now I have much more room because of the size of the new SSHD, but the speed increase is small. So I think, if I purchased a non Hybrid 1T Drive SATA III, I could save money without significative performance loss. Instead, if the new drive was a 7200RPM unit, I would be happier. If Seagate increases the solid state area size from 64MB to 4 or 8GB the drive will be worth of the "Hybrid" denomination and will give a real increase in performance..

I ordered this one form GeeClicks and actually got an "exact" clone, probably made by the original company.

I discovered not that GeeClicks now sells it as the;

2.7" 1080p Full Hd Car Video Recorder Dashcam G1W with G sensor Night Vision Motion Detection

by Geepro.

Here's a copy of my review on this item under the new listing.

It was labeled as the HD Black Box Car DVR 1080P that is listed on Amazon.com as the

Black Box Original Quality Real Full HD 1080P 1920x1080 H.264 G1W 2.7" LCD Car DVR Camera Recorder Dashboard Dashcam Black Box Video Recorder With G-sensor Night Vision Motion Detection Wide Degree 120° 4X Zoom.

Fortunately, I got an EXACT clone, NOT an inferior copy. It has the superior Novatek NT96650 processor.

The manual was a joke, but I quickly figured out how to use the dash cam.

Basically, the "M" or mode button enters the MENU and hitting the "M" or mode button twice enters the SETUP menu. The up and down arrows move up and down to the menu selections. The REC button enters the selection. Then, the up and down buttons allow selection again. Selection is again made with the REC button. It was quite intuitive.

The unit came with the video set for 50mhz "PAL," but is was easily reset to 60mhz NTSC for the US standard.

A little slip labeled "WARM TIPS" recommended a Kingston Class 10 card, but the SanDisk Class 4 that others have recommended works just fine.

Basically, this unit works perfectly to supplement my ABEO rear view mirror dash cam that I purchased on Amazon a year, ago. That camera has worked perfectly and blend into the windshield better than this one.

I mounted to on the rear window of the driver side of my Prius"v." to record the cars in back of me. It plugs in to the rear auxiliary power outlet and turns on and off with the power applied to the car, just like the front camera.

Fortunately, I got a exact clone of the Black Box G1W with the superior NT96650 processor.

title: Disappointment ranges from mild to extreme
text:
I've had the Kindle Fire for one month now and I feel experienced in it enough to write a review.

What I like: I like the screen size for movies, and books, and even comic books are readable in the full page view. I mostly enjoy this for comics, although Amazon's strangely quiet tiff with DC Comics and Comixology (DC is no longer available in the Comixology store app) is a real turn-off.

What I don't like: You can purchase a movie from Amazon and download it to watch offline. You would think that this improves the quality over streaming, depending upon your signal strength. In my experience, it has no beneficial effect, and in fact, oftentimes looks worse than streaming, even when I only have a couple of bars and am behind a closed door on the other side of the house from the router. The video quality is so bad at times that it is reminiscent of a twice recorded copy of a VHS tape from an 80s broadcast that's been uploaded to Youtube in the lowest quality setting. It is unwatchable at times. This is completely unacceptable for a movie I paid to rent and have only 24 hours to watch. Unlike some people, I don't have all day to watch movies. That's part of the reason the Fire appealed to me. I could have a movie on the go. But this makes it little worth the while or the cost.

What I like: The app store is serviceable enough, it's got a good selection and the apps work fairly well.

What I don't like: Some of the apps like Netflix, for example, are very unresponsive to the touch screen. I don't know whose fault this is, but it's a major annoyance. The Netflix app works flawlessly on my iPod, and one time when the picture quality and the syncing on the Fire rendered the movie unwatchable, I switched to my iPod and it worked beautifully. Again, don't know who to blame here, but the cards are stacking up against the Fire.

What I like: I love reading comics on the Fire. Even though the screen is a little small, the page looks great and vibrant and I have truly enjoyed reading comics on it. I should mention this is one of the prime reasons I got the Fire, so yay!

What I don't like: Again, the unavailability of DC comics at all on the Fire, except through their book store, and then it's only a limited number of exclusive trades. They are not available on Comixology and there is no DC app. Also, the guided view, which works so well on an iPod, is enlarged too much and becomes grainy. It doesn't need to fill the entire screen, it just has to be as big as a paper comic book. On the other hand, people have complained about Amazon's guided view which brings up a pop up magnification of a certain area, usually a word bubble, but I find that preferable to the other kind.

What I like: Its weight is about what you'd expect for a tablet, but the real draw is that you can hold it one hand--in portrait view.

What I don't like: In landscape view, it can be a little challenging to hold for say, two hours at a time. Unless you are resting the weight on your palm (looking down) you must hold it with two hands firmly if you are viewing from any other angle. Sure, it's a handheld, what do you expect, but the weight of it and lack of significant border space makes it hard to hold with one hand in landscape view. A minor annoyance. Perhaps a protective case could solve that problem.

What I like: You can view documents like pdfs simply by emailing them to a special address. It's really pretty nifty and now I'm able to read all these things that previously I could only read on my computer or had to actually print out and when you're talking about several hundred pages...

What I don't like: The formatting could be better. There is all this wasted space on the borders that could be used to increase the text size. Truthfully, unless you read it in landscape view, it's nearly impossible to read for an extended period. See above for problems on extended landscape viewing. Other than manually enlarging each page, there is no way to adjust the screen. No options toolbar whatsoever.

What I like: The web browser it okay and it's reasonably fast. It is flash capable, but...

What I don't like: Most videos on the web are not supported without some work around that's not even worth it. This is incredibly lame. Also, the support of flash (which Apple doesn't support) is really only meaningful as a bullet point. When you come down to it, things that work great on your PC just don't work at all on the Fire. Namely, Marvel Digital Comics, of which you can read over 10,000 on a flash capable device with a subscription. On the Fire, it just doesn't work at all even after enabling flash in the options. This was so unbelievably disappointing to me, I can't even begin to tell you.

Overall, I'm pretty disappointed with the Fire. My disappointments have ranged from mild to extreme. In all honesty, I would return it or sell it, except that it was a birthday gift from my wife. On the upside, I actually use it every day. Most of the time, it works pretty well, if you understand its limitations. Now I can read books at night while my wife sleeps next to me and don't have to have a light on, so for an insomniac like me, this greatly expands my nocturnal activities beyond merely watching movies.

One final note: the Youtube app lets you download videos to the Fire to watch offline. That's actually pretty sweet.

UPDATE: I figured out how to get the flash to work for reading Marvel digital comics. With a subscription I have read dozens upon dozens of comics on the Fire and really enjoyed the whole experience. It took a little tweaking, but this is not Amazon's fault, it's simply an interface issue with the comics reader on Marvel's website. But trust me, it does work and it looks great. The Fire has risen in my esteem since then and I use it all day long every day.

3. I eventually found an ASCII to HEX translator and tried to use the HEX version of the password to get the two devices talking to each other. This did the trick.
4. While I found it very odd that 10 other wireless devices (Macs, windows PCs, TVs, DVDs, iphones and ipads) on my network all hooked up to the Actiontec with the ASCII key, the Netgear required the Hex key to work.

Once solved, everything seems to be working very well.

title: A sturdy good value, but high 16x power I wanted has downside (& clouds judging brand-to-brand versus Nikon)
text:
I just received these Pentax XCF binoculars in 16x50 power so any dissatisfaction I have with the view through them mainly may be due to the very high power. I have a Nikon Action EX waterproof 12x50 binocular (which I like very much) that seems brighter and sharper across the field of view, but they cost nearly $100 more. That said, the bottom line is that for the price I paid, these XCF's are a bargain compared to the mass-market brands. I wish I had the 12x50 or 10x50 model to compare the Pentax brand more directly with other brands and particularly to judge, in general, between Pentax and Nikon. And I wonder how the distortion in a Nikon 16x lens compares with that I see in the Pentax.

Lens power aside, my XCF binocular was made in the Philippines so as of Aug. 2014, forget Made in Japan. The binoculars seem well constructed and sturdy...I see no problems with them in that regard. Strangely enough, I couldn't find mention of whether the binocular barrels are metal or plastic in reviews or specifications and STILL can't tell what they're made of. Usually metal feels cooler, but the rubber coating makes it hard to judge -- The barrels seem solid and I suspect they're metal. The XCF is more compact than my lower-power Nikon Actions. Some reviews complain about a stiff focus action...my focus wheel turns easily and focus is smooth and steady. Note that the XCF eyecups are simple "flip down" rather than fancier "twist-up". I missed that fact in the descriptions so it was a surprise. In fact the cheaper eyecup probably won't make much difference to me...at least they don't twist off as the other style can. AND what's with these "quality" brands including binocular cases (bags actually) without a shoulder strap...Neither my Pentax nor Nikon bag has a strap, or even D-rings for my own strap.

My advice is that unless one specifically wants 16x or higher power (as I did) then get a maximum of 10x50 or 12x50. Within a brand and model, the lower power will give a sharper and brighter image across the width of the lens, have a deeper zone that's in focus and will be easier to hold steady. AND if looking for 16x or higher power, then compare these to a higher quality lens before buying...I didn't do that, but then I've gotten superior utility and value for the price I paid. Finally, if one wants just ONE pleasing, work-horse binocular that's a keeper (rather than a collection like I've somehow amassed) then between brands, pay-up to get a 2nd-tier quality over a cheapo brand, or within a brand, pay-up to a next tier above the bottom tier model. Pentax and Nikon seem to be go-to mass-market brands a step ahead of the pack. I also like the rugged Bushnell H2O line, though that model comes with smaller 42mm max. lenses.

As I gain more experience with my Pentax XCF 16x50 binocular, I might bump my Star-rating up a star.

********** UPDATE 10/20/14
I recently bought a pair of Pentax PCF WP II (8x40) that I like very much. And I've used these 16x50 XCF's a bit more. I also got a pair of lower powered 10x50 XCF's that I'm NOT impressed with. After all that, I DEFINITELY would recommend upgrading to the Pentax PCF model for anyone who can afford the price bump. There's something just not-quite-as-good about the view through and feel of the XCF's.

title: Getting started with liquid cooling...a quiet and cost-effective start
text:
I just got this one from a Fry's Electronics store. Mostly, I was looking to reduce noise while making sure I have adequate cooling on my CPU. i would have been happy with an air cooler. However, this sucker delivers as a liquid CPU cooler.

In getting started with liquid cooling, the hottest part of your system is going to be the CPU. That said, there will be two reasons to get this cooler:

1) You're planning to overclock.
2) Your CPU cooling fan is making too much noise and driving you nuts.

I was holding out for a more elaborate liquid cooling kit, but #2 forced my hand.

With an adequate cooling system, liquid cooling works better than straight up air cooling because of chemistry and physics...water has a far greater heat capacity, that is, it takes more thermal energy to heat water than air. A liquid cooler sequesters all that heat in the liquid, and dumps the extra heat through a radiator, which is not only built to have high surface area to transfer heat to the air, but relocates that heat away from the components that can be damaged by it.

I cannot attest to reliability thus far, as I have recently installed it. However, performance-wise, it works better than my stock heatsink, and it's quiet. So quiet I don't even know my computer's on until I look at the case to see if the power's on.

Pros:
-Simple liquid cooling assembly. It's all put together, there's plenty of slack in the connections between the pump/waterblock and radiator. As long as your case has a 120mm fan vent, you should be able to fix this sucker in place.
-All in one kit, built and ready. If you're not a gearhead or techie geek, this is a one piece system. No liquid to measure or pour. All connections are made. The system is pre-filled. All you need is a philips-head screwdriver and enough adventure to unscrew the heatsink mount from your mainboard to put the new mounting brackets in place, and the kit includes brackets for all compatible CPU configurations.
-No special stuff, just simple physics. The contact surface (where the cooler meets the CPU) is copper. (Even comes pre-greased...unless you want to slap on your own thermal grease), it transfers heat to the water coolant. The coolant is sealed and contained in the cooling circuit.

Cons:
The instructions leave out key drawings. Namely, those which tell you which way to orient the retaining bracket (the gear-toothed hoop which holds the pump/waterblock to the CPU) to fit. I ended up putting in the mounting hardware the wrong way. Fortunately, all you need is some patience and a butter knife to ease the mounts out and fit them in the other way. This is the only reason why I dinged this product one star...this is supposed to be an easy kit, and not everyone has had the experience of assembling forty or fifty PC's over the course of decades.

Fear not, if you messed up, you can pry the screw mounts out, just push the tension clips in and nudge the other side out with a knife blade. It should pop free.

The mounting hardware consists of a retention ring (that's what holds the business end on the CPU) and the backplate (big square one for Intel, rectangular one for AMD). If you're using Intel, just line up the square backplate and see which holes center on the screws consistently.

Make sure the radiator fan follows case airflow. Usually, this means the radiator pulls dual duty, drawing air through the case and over the radiator. Fortunately Antec made this easy for newbies and amateurs. The fan has two arrows on it...one along the circumference to show the rotation of the fan...and the other shows the direction of airflow. Note which way the arrow's pointing, mount it so that the fan draws air out of the case through the radiator.

Final fitting is a little tricky, but here's some tips I found. When you thread the screws in that secure the retention ring to the mounting plate (these parts sandwich the mainboard, that's what holds it in place), only thread them on enough for them to grab. Then center the waterblock, turn it in place until it kinda feels right (you shouldn't have to squeeze in or force the coolant lines, this thing can mount at multiple angles), line up the teeth, then tighten it down.

Currently, I do hear a slight buzzing from the pump, but the system does perform, and it's WAY quieter than the older CPU air cooler. Additionally, the contact surface has some extra area that extends past the CPU, which I used to mount the thermistor for my fan controller so that it reads closer to the actual CPU temperature. At idle, it holds steady at 30C plus or minus 1 degree. The alarm is set below the high tolerance of 60C. The fan controller has the radiator fan running at 1020RPM, vs. the 2100-2400RPM of the stock fan.

This sucker should be built to last, and even if I have to sell it secondhand if I upgrade, I want to be able to say I'm selling a quality product with a long service life. I hope Antec makes my list of dependable products along with Intel, AMD, HP, Logitech, Thrustmaster, Apple, Asus, and MSI...products which I have had a positive track record over the years.

title: Great improvement, frustrating lens hood
text:
The MkI version of this lens has been my "workhorse" lens for years--usually my default lens-of-choice if I was headed out without a bagful of lenses. My biggest reservation of moving to the MkII was the filter size change from 77mm to 82mm, since I have a large collection of 77mm filters.

Yes, the MkII is noticeably sharper. But since there have been many detailed reviews on the optics of the MKII, I'll focus on the ergonomics of it.

The giant, deep round hood of the MkI has been replaced by a much shallower hood. Even though the MkII has a hood locking mechanism, it came off and hit the ground twice in my very first outing with the lens. I tried reversing the unlock button to the other side since I suspected it was bouncing into me and unlocking itself, but it still managed to fall off. Also the new shallower hood offers less scratch protection to the glass--I always liked how the glass of the MkI was protected deep inside that big hood and I managed to use it for years without the tiniest scratch. I'm more nervous about walking around with the lens cap off now.

A nice addition to the MkII is the focal length lock. I see two areas where this comes in handy: (1) after you set up a shot and screw on a neutral density lens you don't need to worry about messing up the focal length while screwing on the filter, and (2) it eliminates the issue I had with the MkI where I would point the lens straight up (on tripod) with a heavy filter on the end and the focal length would slowly dial itself from 24mm to around 30mm as gravity pulls the weight of the lens/filter down.

Overall, the MkII is like a sharper and speedier MkI that went on a diet and lost some weight and bulk. All I need now is new filters and some sort of jimmyrig to keep the hood affixed more securely.

title: The Screen Makes this Model a Winner!
text:
This is my 3rd Chromebook. The first, a Samsung 11.6". The 2nd, Toshiba's 13.3" from last year. And now this model and I must say this is by far the best Chromebook I've ever used. I won't go into a detailed review as Kenneth L. Rodina, M.D. and BKarno have written excellent and thorough reviews of this model. What makes this standout is the screen. It's Apple-like and I've been waiting for a Chromebook to have a good screen. It has brilliant color and resolution with a much wider viewing angle. Also, the sound it much improved with Skullcandy. I enjoy watching Nefliix on this device. The battery lasts 7 hours for me and that's streaming video from youtube with the screen at the second lowest brightness setting and the sound at the halfway mark. Last year's Toshiba had excellent battery life, too, but this model beats it by about 30 minutes. It took roughly 2 hours and 17 minutes to fully charge the battery. As for the screen, even with the brightness at the second lowest setting, it's plenty bright just like my Apple iPad. The power is just fine as I usually only have two tabs opened at the most. It streams Netflix, Amazon and youtube videos without problems. I like that this model is actually smaller and lighter than last year's model but has the same size screen. The keyboard is good as is the touchpad. I prefer to use a mouse and my bluetooth mouse links up just fine. The wireless connection now supports AC but my router is still at "N" so I can't really say how much better AC wireless is.

The only cons are that is still doesn't play Minecraft which my kids love. Skype doesn't work. Hangouts is fine but most of my friends use Skype. Microsoft is working on Skype to work inside the Chrome browser without a plugin but they say it will only be usable for Chrome under a windows computer. Microsoft owns both Minecraft and Skype so hopefully in the future they will make it usable on Chromebooks.

Lastly, I'm a Dish Network subscriber and use their sling media to watch TV on my computer and other devices. They just updated their plugin for the Chrome browser and it's excellent, but it won't work on my Chromebook.

All-in-all, this is, in my opinion, the best Chromebook out there and it's worth the extra $30 bucks for the superior screen and improved sound. In the future, I would like to see a 17.3" model, a touch screen once Chrome is optimized for it, a keyboard that lights up, and a small subwoofer under the hood to go with the good speakers.

title: Sound absolutely horrible
text:
I love CV floor speakers however I have to say I'm extremely disappointed in these bookshelf speakers. I returned them less than a week after purchase. Let me start off by saying that these speakers were hooked up to a brand new Denon receiver pushing 110 watts per channel. I am looking for speakers to replace by Bose 301's (current series, IV I think) and these are definitely not it. I've never been overly impressed with the Bose 301's however they sound decent and so far I haven't found anything better in that price point or less. I was hoping these would sound better however I was very, VERY wrong. Side by side using the same receiver, with the same audio... the Bose just blow these CVs out of the water.

The bass on these is shallow and muddled. I obviously wasn't expecting big boom from 5.25" speakers however I have a powered sub so I don't need the bookshelf speakers for bass. It's like they are trying to hard to do produce deep bass and the end result is just a hollow, sloppy, muddled sounding bass. It sounds like you put a cheap paper full range driver in a cardboard box. The bass is terrible, the mids are non-existent or just pure distortion and then you have tinnish sounding highs and that's it. No joke... everything else is missing.

There are many good reviews and I honestly can't figure out why how. These people are either fake or have LITERALLY nothing else to compare these speakers to. I am by no means an audiophile however I like to think I have a decent ear for good sound and these speakers miss the mark IN EVERY WAY. The only reason these even earn one star (besides the fact that it is the lowest rating) is because they technically "work". Not very well at all though.
