title: UPDATE - new firmware. have not fully investigated but many of the performance issues seem solved.
text:
Update-- 1/7/15 - New firmware has been released and although I have not explored it, it seems to address many of the issues I have mentioned. I am changing my review to a 3 temporarily and will probably move it to a 4 if all is fixed soon (I jsut wanted to update my review immediately as it seems they are trying)

Original below->
It's an amazing concept and I have gotten it to work.. On all of my macs, the software DOES NOT function properly a the time of this review. It's actually the worst piece of commercial software I have ever seen release publicly in years.

Not only does it not function properly, but it will actually MESS UP the rest of the operating system (until you unplug ). The only way I can even have the thing plugged in is if I use controllermate to disable all of the keys and remap them to different functioins - That part is easy - next I recommend you make a bash script to switch the keyboard layouts. The only thing I ever open the configurator for is to chop up image files for the keys - it's the one thing it doesn't get wrong.

Unless you have experience/the time to learn how to write your own software, this is not going to end well for mac users. I have not had time to try on any of my windows machines yet. If Lebedev is smart he will partner with controllermate like xKeys did.

Don't buy this, buy:
1) xKeys is great - it still requires work to add all your shortcuts and macros but it is an insanely reliable product -
2) razer has a keyboard (razer deathstalker lol) with about 10 of these keys with a touchscreen behind them - it's ~$200, has some pretty iffy reviews but if you JUST HAVE TO HAVE a keyboard with a screen in it, that's a much cheaper fix.
3) Get a smartphone app for it... I know I know - not nearly as 'cool' but it's a lot more practical and it's probably faster anyway. Get a cheapo tablet and make it your keybaord
4) clear rubber key cover for ipad - I forget the name of it but it exists... the action on the optimus keys is not impressive at all, it's actually unusable as a keyboard for anyone who types over 50 wpm as it seems to 'miss' some keystrokes (it's an old touchscreen with latency issues) - a rubber ipad cover is the way to go and get some cool custom keyboards in iOS
5) I have an ableton push - if you set it up as a controller you could do some pretty cool stuff with it and it's solid. It's for music but lots of possibilities (haha I also discovered making electronic music is a lot like coding.. sweet!)

Until I hacked the thing, it would bring all os rendering to a snails pace. The developer doesn't understand osx - and it's sad because they could literally hire someone for the price of one of these keyboards to fix it. If you decide to hack the thing, you can look up the optimus maximus - while there are no guides on fixing the popularis, it turns out it works pretty much the same way (except it doesn't have an individual screen in each key so not as cool, which is what just about everyone says).

Almost everyone else will be extremely disappointed if they purchase this at this point if they intend to use this with the current version of os x. I will definitely update my review as soon as I become aware of functioning software for the mac. I did try to contact them before I left this review but no luck. The product is also listed for up to $3000 less on Lebedev's Russian version of his website.

Anyway I'm sad to write a bad review because it devalues the thing I own but... I'd feel like a douchebag if I sold someone a $1500 keyboard that didn't work.

I contacted ttheir studio a few weeks ago asking for an explanation.. some help... told them I didn't even want a refund, but just please tell me how to fix the thing or send me the xcode files so I can fix it myself. No response yet - I understand that maybe they didn't get the email and those thigns do happen - but it doesn't change the way I feel about this product.

I have it working now and it's pretty nice, but it's not fit to be a consumer product - it's more in the category of something like oculus rift.

Pros:
-Nothing else comparable to it on the market
-Huge potential to reduce inefficiency in your workflow
-Draw whole layers onto the keyboard quickly via photoshop
-Activate/deactivate layers
-With the right configuration it looks amazing and is a true geek's gadget
-The casing is very solid and well designed combination of aluminum (I think, not positive) and clean plastic - the industrial design on that is spot-on (too bad it ends there)
-Makes an excellent shortcut keyboard as an addition to your existing keyboard

Cons:
-The packaged software DOES NOT WORK with the latest version of os x - even more troubling is it seems there might be comatibility issues with the firmware itself as this is more than a simple keyboard controller.
-NO linux compatibility out of the box
-The key action is pretty dismal - this is not something I would ever use to replace a typing keyboard. Let's put it this way - my personal version of hell would be having to use this every day as a primary keyboard - it would make you beg for rubber keycaps. If you have a mechanical keyboard it's not even in the same universe.
-There are not keys in each screen like some may believe (I knew this when buying so it was not anything that surprised me) - their other discontinued keyboard, the maximus, did have those. This is just keys with conductive silicone on top of a USB touchscreen. It serves it's purpose, but since the screen is so deep, the viewing angle greatly impacts how impressive this is. If you are directly above it, it's fine. If it's a foot in front of you, it's not so great.

God help you if the screen breaks somehow... I get the feeling that you might be on your own (probably very cheap but very annoying). In an interview at CES their flustered rep implied they would fix them but also didn't even know the resolution of this thing haha.

Fortunately anyone who buys this thing can probably afford the loss - even if it worked perfectly people think it's ridiculous... I would gladly pay twice the amount for something that wasn't complete crap as I am on the computer ~16-18 hours a day - one can only dream.

title: My windows 7 PC
text: I really have grown to like this PC.  I had windows programs that would not run on my '07 MacBook Pro and rather than get some software mash-up, I opted for this medium sized and powered PC.  The audio performance compared to the Mac is astounding and the ease of upgrade ability is refreshing - simple bottom door to RAM and HD.  The 15.6 LED screen is bright and easy on the battery life.  Again compared to the Mac it is physically bigger and I had to get a new bag but it does not get as hot when playing an intense game.  The fan is quieter and the plastic bottom does not transmit as much heat.  The Mac is more compact and nicer looking with its all metal finish but gets much hotter and noisier from the get go.  There are  more quality games for this Win 7 machine and I can play them at reasonable settings, thanks to the Nvidia GT 330M.  OSX is superior in my opinion but Win 7 is stable and able to easily run XP programs and with Google chrome's browser a breeze on the web.  Readyboost really works on this computer to give it more pep,esp w the  3.0 USB ports x2. CCleaner is a breeze to use to maintain things. Samsung really supports this PC with useful software and website to download the latest drivers, etc.  HDMI port is a great feature as is the built in SD card reader - battery life reasonable.  The keyboard is not back-lit like the Mac but the buttons work - for example the volume settings across different software.  The touch pad supports two finger scrolling which is easy to get used to.  I have a razer mouse Abyssus that is a perfect match for this computer - basic and beautifully functional.  Later I will give Win 8 a try but for now I am more than happy.

title: Bought it for $100, Amazon offering it for $80!! Nice!
text:
UPDATE: 1/7/2014: My middle-mouse button wasn't functioning around sometime in November, it wasn't registering my clicks, I was forced to use the side-button. Now into this year, the scrolling isn't working. I don't think it's a common problem, maybe I just have a defective batch..

I've noticed Amazon has listed this mouse for $80 when I bought it for $100! Might curve your choice of getting it even more.

My main reason for getting this one was because I wanted to replace my [[ASIN:B0007Z1M50 Logitech MX 518 High Performance Optical Gaming Mouse (Metal)]] I've had for nearly 5 years now and thought, "Wow, what an attractive mouse." The mouse is great but at such a steep price point it's difficult to determine if the price is worth the features it has to offer. It's great for FPS games but in terms of MOBAs/RPGs which require extremely long sessions, this mouse isn't as comfortable as the more ergonomic mice I've used around $40-60. My hand is in a claw position as I use it but I can't help but feel it would be better used if flat instead for this mouse in specific as it is quite long and would take up a greater portion compared to smaller mice. It's very easy to click down on when firing and the DPI switch helps from switching from sniping to CQB or even other games. It also comes with 5 5G weights which I've loaded all into the mouse making it slightly heavier (whereas others may prefer to toy around a bit more with it) and a mouse pad in a well-packaged box.

The software is easy to use and easily accessible on the Asus website. You are able to change up your profiles (what buttons do), change your dpi, change your lift height, double click speed, lines per scroll, etc. It's easy to use and quite handy.

What I like most about it is just how attractive it is and the unique design. The cord is braided, the mousewheel is rubberized for easier scrolling/grip, and the material is surprisingly more comfortable than I thought it'd be. It also came with a mouse pad! (Greatly needed for me)

What I disliked the most is how it isn't as comfortable as the [[ASIN:B005S0KHIC Logitech G9X Gaming Mouse Call of Duty: MW3 Edition (910-002764)]] and it tends to get dirtier faster. title: What a gem!  I love this thing!
text:
I read all the reviews and then bought one, and boy am I glad I did. Like most people writing these reviews, I'm using this device to control a Media Center PC driving my wall-mounted plasma TV. I'm running Win7 Home Premium on a Gateway mini-desktop PC in the bedroom closet on the other side of the wall from the TV, and there's no problem at all with range -- the wireless signals pass through the wall just fine. The green button to launch WMC is super handy, as are the D-Pad like transport controls (anybody who uses WMC knows, loves, and can't live without the "skip ahead 30 seconds" button) and the mute and volume controls in the upper right part of the device are also easy to find without looking.

One reviewer commented that tap-to-click should be enabled on touchpad, so you don't have to click the left mouse button, but I disagree. Too often when dragging the mouse cursor across the screen with a sensitive touchpad, you can accidentally drag some random thing and drop it some random place (especially when using the Windows Explorer file system), and Windows has no "undo" for this kind of inadvertent action. Without tap-to-click enabled on this keypad, you can drag with confidence until your mouse cursor is on the proper target and then click, right-click, or double-click what you intend to -- I see that as an advantage.

Also, other reviewers have complained that it takes many repeated swipes of the touchpad to move the mouse cursor across a big screen TV. Easy fix: Start > Control Panel > Hardware > Mouse > Pointer Options > Motion | Select a pointer speed. Make it "Fast" and shorter swipes on the touchpad move the mouse farther across the TV screen.

If I had one piece of advice for SMK to improve this delightful little gizmo, it would be to put raised rubber "nubs" on the Enter key and the Backspace key, because these are frequently used for navigating the WMC user interface. (Or have separate "Enter" and "Back" buttons like you find on a lot of Media Center remotes.) Excellent value for money in this just-right-sized device that fits in the drawer of my bedside table -- pick one up and you will be really happy that you did. (I've never written a review on Amazon before -- that's how much I like this thing.)

title: Good lens, but know what you are getting
text:
This lens is a "manual lens" and many folks today probably don't know what that means. I've been using SLR or DSLR cameras for almost 30 years, and the definition didn't fully register with me until I received this lens.

When you look through the viewfinder of an SLR/DSLR camera, you want to focus with the aperture completely open. This condition gives you the most light to see the subject and gives you the narrowest depth of field so that you can focus most precisely. Most lenses made in the last 30 years or so have been "automatic" in the sense that they keep the aperture completely open when you are looking through the viewfinder. When you press the shutter button, the aperture closes to whatever you have set (or whatever the camera's computer sets) just before the camera takes the image. For instance, if your lens has a maximum aperture of f3.5 and you are shooting at f8, then the lens is at f3.5 as you frame the picture. When you take the picture, the mirror that allows you to look through the camera's lens comes up to let light reach the sensor/film, the camera closes the aperture from the wide open f3.5 to the f8 that you've set, and then the camera opens the shutter. By the time the mirror drops again to let you see through the lens, the aperture is completely open again.

A manual lens works differently in that the camera can't close the aperture before taking the picture. To take a picture correctly, you generally need to focus with the aperture completely open and then close the aperture yourself by changing something on the lens. In the case of this lens, you'll need to turn a little ring to close the aperture. If your eyes are really good, you might be able to focus by keeping the aperture closed to whatever f-stop you use for shooting, but the ring tends to move as you change f-stop. To use this lens, you'll need to remember to close the aperture before taking every picture. Otherwise, you'll think that you are shooting at f16, but the picture will actually be exposed at f8. You could end up with some overexposed pictures.

If all of this adjusting sounds complicated, here's one bit of comfort. You'll probably want to do most of your photography with this lens at f8 which is the widest aperture opening. If you get used to shooting everything at f8, you may end up never really needing to close the aperture.

Not only can your camera not close the aperture, but also your camera's computer can't talk to the lens. You won't see anything in the viewfinder telling you where your aperture (f-stop) is set. Even many of us who claim to be "old school" have come to like seeing that information in the viewfinder display. You certainly can't use autofocus, and I couldn't get the little red "in-focus" lights to tell me whether I was in focus. This lens is not for someone who depends on the camera's computer to take pictures.

When we consider the cost of a modern camera lens, we need to consider all that we purchase in a modern lens. To begin, we purchase the lenses, and better glass means a higher cost. We purchase the metal tube and the mechanisms that hold the lenses and allow us to focus. Again, better quality mechanisms mean a higher cost. With most lenses, we are purchasing the electronics that allow our camera's computer to "talk to" the lens. With most lenses of the past 30 or so years, we are purchasing the "automatic" function that lets the camera close the aperture at the moment that we take the picture. The most important parts of getting a good picture are the quality of the glass and the mechanism. If the lens can't focus the image on the sensor/film, then we can't get good pictures. All of the automated stuff is just for convenience. With this lens, the manufacturer has spent nothing on convenience, but that means that everything that went into the lens is devoted to glass and mechanism. Neither is going to be as good as you'd get in a Canon L series lens, but if I'm going to use a $114 lens, I want everything that the manufacturer spends to go into glass and mechanism.

I've just received this lens and only taken a few pictures. Overall, they look pretty good for an inexpensive 500mm lens. Shooting with a long telephoto isn't easy anyway (particularly as I grow older). I shot in good light, and this lens is likely to be useless in bad light. However, when I have good light and a long distance to cover, I may get some very pleasing shots.

Purchasers need to consider a few things. First, this lens is very thin for its length. If you are driven by how your lens looks when attached to your camera, you need to be aware that this one will look a little funny. Secondly, this lens comes without a lens cap, without a filter, and without a back cap. I'd recommend purchasing a 67mm UV filter to protect the front of the lens, a 67mm lens cap, and a back cap that is made to receive Canon mounts. The lens is actually threaded at the back, and a mounting adapter is part of the package. You won't keep this lens on the camera all of the time, so you'll want to be able to keep the lens screwed onto the adapter and protected on the back with a cap. Most of us prefer to use a lens hood for most shooting. This lens doesn't have any kind of mount for modern lens hoods. I'd recommend buying a 67mm screw on lens hood. You'll need bright light to use this lens, and you won't want glare from nearby surfaces to cause reflections on the surface of your lens and filter. In the long run, I think you'll want at least a monopod to steady the lens when shooting. A very flimsy tripod is probably useless, but I doubt that the most expensive tripods are necessary.

I'll add to this review as I spend more time with this lens. I just wanted people to know what they are getting with this lens. If I had known these things, I'd have still purchased the lens. I just like having details explained.

title: No frills, value laptop
text:
Just bought this on Amazon a couple weeks ago. First impressions are lackluster - this laptop looks generic, devoid of any really refined style aesthetically. Simply, it looks cheap. I was disappointed that the screen was glossy - more reflection than my eyes care to deal with - matte would have been much better. One of the reviews I had read somewhere else online had mentioned a backlit keyboard, but alas, my unit sported no such thing. The description on Amazon.com listed four USB ports, but there were only three - two USB 2.0 and one USB 3.0. The headphone jack and the microphone jack are combined into one port, which I don't really care for. At the front of the unit there is an SD card reader that was not mentioned in the Amazon.com description. The HDD is on the slow side (5400rpm), but you will probaby not notice unless you are into alot of gaming.

On the good side, though the case is plastic it seems plenty solid enough. The keyboard is actually pretty good, I thought it had a nice feel to the keys when I type and is perfectly usable. The screen image (1600x900 pixels) is crisp and bright, and despite its glossiness still pleasant to view. The CPU is very fast, 6gb memory more than adequate for most media viewing, music and normal internet usage. The 0.3mp built in video camera works well if you like to SKYPE online. This system seems to play games decently well at lower settings, although serious gamers probably won't be very satisfied with its performance. The Bluray disc player is nice, and with the 17.3" screen this makes a nice movie player on the go. Computer runs quite cool, and the audio sound is ok, nothing to get too excited about. If you want to use it to watch movies, use the head phone jack or a set of good external speakers.

Best things about this laptop are the i5-3210 CPU and the Nvidia GeForce 610M discrete graphics card. The large 750gb HDD, though somewhat slow, will give most people more than enough storage, and 6gb memory make this laptop a decent value for the amount of money they are asking for it. Just wish it had more going for it in the style department, another USB port, and a matte screen. And the backlit keyboard would have been sweet!

title: Best all around lens in this focal length range and aperture
text:
I initially started looking at the Sigma 17-50 2.8 as an upgrade from my Nikon 18-55 VR kit lens. While I think the Nikon 18-55 VR is a great lens for the price, I wanted something with better resolution and a larger aperture for available light shots.

When looking at reviews, I also considered the Nikon 17-55 2.8 and the stabilized Tamron 17-50 2.8. At roughly twice the price and without stabilization, the Nikon was out. And, unfortunately, the stabilized version of the Tamron is optically inferior to the non-stabilized version of the Tamron. So, the Tamron was out. I'd summarize the reviews by saying that most felt that the Sigma was the best value for the money and, on average, optically as good as the Nikon and Tamron.

Per reviews and user comments, my concerns regarding the Sigma 17-50 2.8 were focus accuracy (mostly back focus) and soft corners. In as much, I did quite a bit of testing after I received it in order to insure I had a good copy. I found that focus accuracy was very good. Actually, I found it to be more accurate and consistent (at least under test conditions) than my Nikon 18-55 VR kit lens. And, while the corners are a bit soft wide open, they look pretty good by f/4. In fact, I found that when the lens is closed down a stop or two, the corners are actually sharper than those of my Nikon 18-55 VR kit lens. This is not something I expected.

Overall sharpness is quite good and is definitely a step up from the Nikon 18-55 VR kit lens. The build quality is wonderful. I do find the zoom ring to be a little bit too stiff, but not problematic (certainly better than having too much play or being too loose). The included lens case and lens hood are also very nice. Ignore the comments about the lens hood being too loose and falling off. Those folks aren't installing the lens hood onto the lens correctly. You need to continue to turn the lens hood until it snaps into place. It takes a bit of effort. However, once it snaps into place it cannot possibly loosen on its own!

While the lens comes with a standard one year US warranty, you will get an additional three years when you register it at the Sigma web site. So, assuming you register, you get a total of four years warranty in the US!

Overall I'm very pleased with the lens and feel that it's a great deal for $619. I will, however, be keeping my Nikon kit lens as it has better macro capabilities than the Sigma...

-Michael

title: Bionic Lapdock
text:
I love this thing, but there are a few things you should know before you buy it.
First it runs using your phone... so sometimes, especially if you have a lot of apps running in the background, it will lock up. Usually this only lasts a few seconds but once or twice i have had to close and reopen the lapdock. Which takes about 5 seconds and then im back up and running. If you dont know thats coming then you might be let down by the device, but for the most part I dont have the issue. (A rooted phone without crapware will probably preform better).
The next issue is the "full web browser" wont let you install various plug-ins because it too runs from the phone. Its really just a "webdock application" that runs when you plug in to the dock. So until you can install plug-ins in the embedded software on the phone I dont really see a work around for this issue, that aside, the browser works great. The only page that I couldnt load (and I tried to make it fail) was runescape. I dont play it, but if thats your game and you wanna play it here... you cant. not without updating the plug-in... which I couldnt do.

Now the positives: the keyboard makes texting awesome. you can post reviews like this one easily. youll forget you're even using your phone until you get a text or a phone call which pops up in the corner of the screen out of the way. The mousepad is okay and is easily turned on or off with a quick double tap in its corner. You can also plug in a standard USB mouse in to one of the two USB ports on the back. I havent tried many other USB devices as of yet, but I did try a USB hub that seemed to work (turning one of the USB ports in to three with memory card slots). The USB ports worked on the hub (so I had doubled my USB ports to four with it plugged in), but I regret to say I didnt try the memory card slots so I cant say if they worked or not. Perhaps my favorite thing about it is the size. I can slip it in to my folder and carry it with documents. Its a zip-up, standard paper sized folder. Its not going to fit in a paper folder but if you use one of the zip up folders, you should be able to do this too.

Oh it also charges your phone while its plugged in! (The lapdock has its own charging cable, similar to a typical laptop charging cable. Thus, it has its own battery life. I havent timed it, but its supposed to be around 10h. If I use it lightly it will last two or three days, but on a really boring day where I use it extensivly it will just last the day, but then my phones got a healthy charge left over to entertain me!)

Overall, this thing does what I want it to do (allows me to type up a story and set up excel docs easily along with a browser, keyboard and great screen) and I love it. It may not be for everyone, but as long as you expect the shortcomings of the device you'll love it too. Its when youre not expecting the minor problems that they become huge issues.

title: Five things you'll want to know about this tablet
text:
1. A mouse!
Ok, so I was amazed. Yes, with a Bluetooth mouse connected, an arrow icon actually appears on the screen and you can use it pretty much like any mouse on a conventional PC. I’m using the Microsoft Sculpt Touch mouse but any Bluetooth one will work. You can also connect a keyboard at the same time.

2. Limited amount of accessories and ridiculous prices thereof
Because of its newness, there are a limited number of accessories and cases for this tablet. Furthermore, I guess because companies like Zagg and Logitech believe you're willing to overpay for the tablet, they can charge you a premium for accessories. $129 for a keyboard/case? You must be kidding.

3. Amazon video/Flash player:
Streaming video from your Amazon account is hard. I was accustomed to using Amazon's streaming video app on the iPad to watch tv shows and movies I get from Amazon. There is no such app for Android devices. It can be done via the installation of an obscure “Dolphin” browser, an older version of Adobe Flash and then jimmying with settings to put it all together, but it's complicated especially with this tablet running KitKat. I was successful, but it took a while. I understand this is because of a disagreement between Google (Android's developer), Amazon and Adobe. This is very unlike Amazon and Google (but less so for Adobe) and I wish they would get over themselves and help their customers. BTW, there are no problems watching Netflix, YouTube or Hulu using their respective apps.

4. New Charging / sync connector on cord
The Note Pro uses a new Micro USB 3.0 connector. It's wider than the one that THE ENTIRE REST OF THE PLANET USES. You can use an old-style Micro USB charger, but it takes much longer to charge it than if you use the cord that comes with it. Also, there are no USB 3.0 car chargers (that I've been able to find, anyways)

5. Pricing and obsolescence
The "professional" reviews of this tablet are lukewarm- mostly revolving around the reviewer's opinion of its high price and "who would want a tablet with this large of a screen?" These reviews can slow sales and drive the price down. The price of this tablet may decline at a faster rate than usual. I took the recommendation of one of the reviewers. I purchased it without a contract.

Other thoughts:
I've been using this device intensively for a week now as a replacement for an aging iPad and hopefully a replacement for an infrequently used notebook. If you’re used to holding an iPad, this tablet will take some getting used to. Once you've had it for a few days, you won’t want to take your hands off of it. For me, it is a near-notebook replacement, especially if you add a keyboard and a mouse. The Hancom office software is shockingly close in appearance and functionality to Microsoft Office.

Although it's probably a function of the device's newness, many applications are designed for tablets with smaller screens. Some do not rotate, some do not fill the screen properly, etc.

This is the first widely available device running the "KitKat" version of Android. Expect some bugs. I spent a considerable amount of time installing apps, setting up email, etc. I found that the battery was draining quickly even with the unit off- like a drop from 80% to 50% in five hours with no use and the battery indicator said the source of the usage was the Android operating system. VZW's support determined that there was likely a software download that was running in background and "stuck" and that was draining the battery. The only way to fix the problem was to do a factory reset and re-install all the applications, redo the configuration, etc. After doing that, the battery life extended to what's been advertised- it lasts all day in frequent use and will clearly last for days with infrequent use before charging.

title: Works pretty well!
text:
This is my third Garmin GPS. Earlier I had used 1450LMT and 3790LMT. Here are my observations for those who may want to get more insights about this unit.

Pros:
1) The voice Command is pretty handy and works on most cases. If you end up with a scroll bar on any search page; the "UP" voice command may not always work. You may have to use the "BACK" or the "EXIT" command instead.
2) The volume on this unit is higher than the previous old ones that I had.
3) It has only one language (American-Jill) which speaks the name of the streets. Other options do not have this feature. Works pretty well!!
4) This is good for folks who have to make diversions while on road.
5) It shows up major restaurants, ATMs, gas stations, rail tracks, and rest areas while on the route. This is quite handy. Though the rest areas may not be always accessible on the direction of your route but it does pick up the nearby ones.

Cons:
1) At times it takes you through unpaved routes overlooking your route avoidance preferences. This has happened thrice to me.
2) The route it suggests is not always the best route. 3790LMT and 1450LMT shows up a better route when compared side by side.
3) This unit has a highly reflective glass which makes it very difficult to focus on sunny days especially for older folks. 3790LMT is the best as far as visibility and form factor goes.
4) Though I have the latest software update; I notice at times the unit hangs while you are connected to your phone.
5) The quality of Bluetooth connectivity is not great. Call quality is poor.
6) Find address by voice command feature would fail on 70% of the cases. Garmin needs to work on this I guess.

Overall while I am satisfied with this unit; I would say the 3790LMT is a unit which combines performance, consistency and value for money. It has a thinner form factor and has a very clear display rain or shine or and even at night times.
I personally feel 3590 LMT scores over 3790LMT only because of a better voice command feature. That's the key difference that I have so far noticed apart from displaying major landmarks viz. restaurants, gas stations on the route.

Hope it helps!!

title: Very buggy and not reliable over time
text:
I bought two of these Schlage outdoor wireless cameras for use with my Nexia Z-wave automation at home. The installation instructions are fair at best. While these are wireless cameras, you must follow a clunky process which entails using an Ethernet cable to your router. I finally got the cameras up and running and they worked very well. The night vision is superb (it almost looks like daylight).

After a few weeks of using them, one suddenly stopped working. The online troubleshooting is of zero help and simply tells you to reboot the device. Rebooting is burdensome process that entails un-mounting the camera and reconnecting it to an Ethernet cable to your router. You cannot reboot the devices wirelessly. After rebooting the first camera and then re-mounting it, a few days later the other camera suddenly stopped working. Again, I had to un-mount the camera and conduct the clunky rebooting process using the Ethernet cable and have it re-find my wireless network.

I've now repeated the above process three times on two entirely separate cameras. Based on this experience, I would not recommend this brand of camera to anyone due to the poor reliability. It makes me suspect that the other reviewers based their reviews on using these for a few days only--and not long term experience.

title: Do Not use Garmin vhf 100 with this product
text:
I bought a Tom Cat 255 boat with a Garmin 740 installed. The Coolest feature with a Garmin networked suite is that with a Garmin VHF 200 (but NOT VHF 100) + Garmin AIS 300 (class A) or Garmin AIS 600 (class B) you can touch the AIS target on the touchscreen plotter and direct dial the target bridge MMSI # . The Garmin AIS 300 is receive-only, the AIS 600 transmits your boat's info + receives others. For recreational cruisers, this is so much better than hailing 'the black and orange tug near SM 133' on VHF16. You see his name, SOG, direction, etc on the plotter when the AIS is networked to it...plus option to direct dial MMSI. I don't think any other marine electronics line offers this...a great idea that works in the real world on the boat. (Other suites you write down the MMSI from the plotter, program it into your VHF, and call it manually...takes 2 crew at cruise speeds). Again, the Garmin VHF 100 won't do this. It took me a lot of research to figure this out, hope to save you some time and quickly see the options in 100 words or less! Garmin has great info on building a 'plug and play' network. However, you do have to actually read the instructions and (gasp!) follow them to make it work.
Cheers!

title: Nice stand, poor instructions
text: This is a very nice TV stand.  Very well built.  Had to knock off one star in the rating because the instructions are poor.  Interestingly, the manual assigns part number references (1, 2, 3, etc) to all the pieces, however only  a couple of the parts were actually numbered.  Generally not an issue, but because of the tolerances, it does take extra time to figure it out.  Specifically, the supports for the bottom two shelves have to be in a certain position so that the guide/slit in the rear support is in the proper position for the bottom two glass shelves to slide into.  Also, the glass shelves can only go in one position.  The are three different widths, so it will take some playing around to get them in the proper position (i.e top, middle or bottom).  All-in-all not terrible, but it did cost about an extra 30 minutes in assembly time...which could have easily been avoided if they actually had numbers on the shelves and support bars, like the manual shows, but the number person must have run out of labels :)  Shopped around for a stand that was well built and could support our ~50 pound Onkyo amp (the bottom two shelves on this stand will support 66 pounds each, according to the manufacturer.  A lot of other similar stands we looked at did not have center supports under the tempered glass.  This stand surely does, and I am more confident that the tempered glass will not have any problems with the weights of our components because this has center supports under the glass shelves.

title: Perfect
text:
I bought my first Tivo in 1999 and still use it on a private cable system that has an analog channel tier. Very few consumer electronics devices last anywhere near that long. The new models seem to be every bit as sturdy as the originals and the software has had a lot of new features added over the last decade.

I started time shifting and skipping commercials back around 1989 using VCRs, then switched to Tivo when it came out. I haven't watched a commercial unwillingly in about a quarter of a century. Even if I had only watched an hour of network programming a day (a VERY conservative estimate), the practice has given me back nearly a full month of my life that would have otherwise been wasted sitting through stupid, unwanted advertising.

title: Awesome (but now replaced)
text:
This router is replacing a Linksys WRT-54GL and a WRT-54GC. Neither were providing the coverage needed at my new apartment. My setup has the wireless router and modem in the office. When I would try to access internet from the livingroom (2 rooms away) it would be noticeably laggy and slow. Even after setting up WDS on the WRT-54GL with another Wireless N router, it wasn't good enough. A big part of the problem was that my laptop picks up somewhere between 15 and 30 wireless networks at a time in my apartment building.

After setting up the RT-N66U, I have had no problems, and have no need for WDS. I have the entire apartment blanketed with both the 2.4ghz and 5.0ghz bands. I have my roommate use the 2.4ghz and I use the 5.0ghz connection. They both work very well. I love the interface for setting up the router, and everything involved with setup was a breeze.

Overall I would HIGHLY recommend this router to anyone looking for better coverage and performance.

EDIT 4/19/2015: It was great while it lasted, but my router up and died on Friday night. Must be a short somewhere in the router itself. While it was great while it lasted, the fact that it is barely a year outside the warranty and outright died has caused me to drop the review by a star. I have moved on to the RT-AC66U, hoping it lasts a bit longer than this one did.

title: Love This Cycling Computer, Not
text:
UPDATE AUGUST 1 2014
I just downgraded my review from 5 stars to 1 Star and Stongly encourage any purchaser considering this unit to look elsewhere. The Unit worked flawlessly for about a month BUT after 4 weeks the HRM strap stopped working so Timex sent me a new one and an $8 invoice for the replacement. 2 Days later I had the same problem many other reviewers had - The GPS Chip stopped working and so the unit would only work with a speed / cadence sensor - which meant it would record time speed and distance but it also meant it became useless for using with any tracking software like Strava, Ride With GPS, Connect, Map My Ride, etc ..... I have written to Timex 3 times but sadly have never received a response to my warranty claim - so now I just have a pretty but useless red & black box sitting on my shelf. I bought an Edge 510 on eBay and wish I would have just started that way. The Timex Customer Support is awful - This unit was in the end a temporary joy that turned into an exercise of frustration and wasted time and money. Don't Buy it. Our National Sports Retailer Mountain Equipment Coop (MEC) says thay had to stop carrying it because every unit they sold came back.
DON'T BUY ONE

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
After pouring through countless reviews of the Garmin 500, 510, 810, and this Timex Cycle Trainer and actually purchasing a 500, I returned the 500 and bought one of these and couldn't be happier.

The things I took into consideration included battery life, screen clarity in sun, features I would use and not use, ease of use, ease of set up, accuracy and the ability to upload data to the cloud so I could keep an historical record. I found that with the 510, 800 & 810, for me anyway, using the push buttons was easier that the touch screen.

First Impressions Out Of The Box
The Timex looks and feels great. The black and red case looks good and has a solid build quality and it FEELS like quality in the hand. That's a subjective thing to say, but i think you know what I mean; it just feels solid and the buttons are firm and responsive without being difficult to press. The battery has zero charge on it but it does charge up in about 4 hours, so you just need 4 hours of patience on the first use.

Mount and Mounting The Mount
While the Head Unit was charging, I went about the business of attaching the mount and a Garmin GSC10 Speed Cadence Sensor. When I first saw the mount I was disappointed first off because It requires zip ties to attach and secondly because it is taller that than the Garmin Mounts and my previous Sigma "Insert and Twist" mount. But now that its actually on my bike, I prefer it. connects solidly to the head unit with a confident "click". I have no fear about this thing coming loose and it slides out with a press of the release lever easily and I can reattach it with my eyes closed. I'm still not a big fan of zip ties so I attached the mount to my stem with GE All Purpose Silicone. The mount comes in 2 pieces: 1) a small rubber square with a curvature to fit your stem or bar and 2) the plastic mount mechanism. The rubber inserts into the the plastic and they are separate so that you can set the orientation as you wish - simple but clever. So, once determining my orientation, I put a bead of clear silicone on the inside edge of the mount and inserted the rubber. Then I put a generous bead of clear silicone on the curvature of the rubber and placed the entire mount unit exactly where I want it on my stem and now I have a permanent (but easy to remove) very clean fitment on my bike. The battery charged in about the same time for the silicone to cure. I followed a similar procedure to attach the Speed Cadence Sensor. I put a bead of silicone between the unit and the rubber (which is necessary because the adhesive used by Garmin won't hold the the rubber to the sensor in an impact) and between the rubber and the frame and it too is now solidly and neatly fixed to my bike.

ANT+ Sensors
The Timex ships with a heart rate sensor and it works and pairs flawlessly. As mentioned above I also bought the Garmin GSC 10 and I can tell you it paired up immediately with zero hassle and so far, 4 rides in, it still picks up speed cadence and heart on the first pedal stoke without any fiddling by me. I'm really impressed. For fun I took the Timex out for a ride on my second bike without sensors to check speed by GPS and it is very accurate and the GPS fix was quick.

The only question I had really was what about setting up a second bike with another GSC 10. Will it pick up the two independently? So I wrote to Timex Support as follows: " I guess part 2 of that question is this: If I pair the GPS unit to a second bike / ANT+ sensor, will I need to manually re-pair it to the first bike? Or will it automatically pick up each bike (as long as they are more than 30 feet apart). I was surprised to get the following answer less than half an hour later. I wasn't surprised by the answer, I was impressed by the speed of the answer: "It is supposed to pick up the new sensor without having to be specially paired, but like with most electronics, sometimes that doesn't work as well as it should. Try to see if it'll automatically detect the second sensor, but if it doesn't, the manual repairing shouldn't take more than 30 seconds." Based on my experience with the first bike, I'm confident it will pick up the second bike automatically.

The TIMEX Cycle Trainer does allow you to set up multiple bike profiles, but I can now tell that the ANT+ sensors wont tell the Timex which bike you're on, you'll need to manually switch bikes in the settings otherwise when switching bikes the TIMEX will just think you're on the same bike as before, even though it's connected to a different sensor. A little inconvenient but not a big deal and a firmware update should make it possible to associate a sensor to a bike profile. At present "Accessories" which the ANT+ Sensors are part of, are a category to themselves and not associated with bike profiles.

UPLOADING TO STRAVA / RIDEWITH GPS
This is really no problem. Training Peaks works fine but the other two options are prettier and have nice maps. This site will convert your Timex files easily [...] 's just a simple webpage, you don't need an account (infact there isn't even an option to create one) You just upload the timex file, convert it and download the converted file so you can import it into STRAVA or RIDE. I hope the creator of the converter site reads this so I can say thank you to him / her. There isn't even a contact or donate button - it just a benevolent service offered to us by a fellow cyclist. THANK YOU.

Customizing Screens
Simple Simple Simple with either the PC/Mac interface or on the unit itself

User Interface
4 Buttons works really well and is VERY Intuitive. I'm impressed.

Weight
On none of the reviews or even on the Timex Product Page could I find the weight. I can confidently say it is exactly 60 grams

The only downside I can see it that you cant create a route in any of the training sites and download them into the TIMEX (if there is a way, I haven't figured it out). It doesn't bother me. I couldn't do this with any previous cycle computer either and I didn't miss not having it. So for me the main purpose of the GPS is plotting ride data against geography which becomes meaningful after upload / historical review.

I love thing and am very happy with it. I'll post an update in a couple of months after I've had some regular and consistent interaction with it. But barring a defect found, I predict it will continue to be a very positive review. I hope this helps somebody. It answers some of the questions I couldn't find answers to. I'm not a pro rider but it gives me more info than I'll ever use but will cause me to train in a more intentional way than I would without it. I say buy with confidence.

title: but more like "Holy shamolie
text:
Update: What's it been? Three years? Yep, three years of constant daily use and being carried with me 10 hours a day and opened and closed a hundred times a day and being dropped once a week and finally the hinges broke. They didn't really "break" but the spring mechanism within them broke. It's still useable but if I have it on a table to use like a laptop it will flop all the way open now, rather than hold the ipad up at a nice angle.

Still......did I mention that I've been carrying this thing and using the absolute heck out of it for almost three year? That breaks down to about $2.70 a month for a really great keyboard and protective case. I can definitely live with that and I'm ordering another one.

I'll start by saying it's heavy. Not just heavy, but more like "Holy shamolie! Did I just strap a brick to my iPad Air?" heavy. Oh, and it's thick. Like five times the thickness of your iPad Air without a case.

OK, now that thats out of the way...... It is fantastic. They keys feel great and have the best feel of any iPad keyboard I've tried. The Logitech thin cover and the Sharkk keyboard feel like kids toys in comparison. These keys are solid, have a good feel, and don't make obnoxious clickety-clackety sounds like the competitors. I end up typing quite a bit at night so the backlighting is a real plus, although I do wish it had a simple white like my Macbook Pro. Still, the choices in color and the three dimming levels is a nice touch.

Did I mention that it's heavy? And thick?

For protection it feels like it is as good as it gets without being a truly "armored" case. It isn't waterproof. It doesn't offer any kid of screen protection unless it's in the closed position so while you can detach your iPad to use it as a traditional tablet, you'll lose any screen protection. I wish there was a way to use the Apple smart cover with this when you didn't have the keyboard attached.

Did I mention that it's heavy? And thick?

Overall, I like it. If you travel a lot with your iPad and still want a good feeling keyboard, this might be your ticket. Having been disappointed in the other keyboards I'd tried, I was considering buying the Apple keyboard bluetooth keyboard and origami stand. The problem is that it would make two more pieces to carry around and I'd need to always have a desk/table to type on. This takes care of it all with a good feeling keyboard and a rugged case all in one and it works great on your lap.

Did I mention that it's heavy? And thick?

Yes, I'd buy another one.

title: Great Ultra Small Transmitter
text:
I got the latest version of the Skyport transmitter so I would have a backup to my original Elinchrom Skyport kit. I have a total of four receivers Two are the original design and two are the latest. All of them work with either transmitter.

This unit works with any camera, digital, large format or medium format. They have an ultra low trigger voltage so they are safe for use with any camera. If the camera does not have a hot shoe, these come with extra cords to fit several different flash types. I am using these units with my Elinchrom, Broncolor and Norman flashes. IF you have a battery pack type flash, like the Norman 500's then you plug in one receiver into the battery pack, and all heads connected to the battery will fire. This way I can trigger four flashes with one transmitter and one receiver, eliminating the need to purchase slaves for each of the heads.

I have shot probably a couple thousand pics with no misfires, which to me is amazing. They are extremely light, weighing maybe an ounce or so but work well both indoors and even further outdoors. I walked approximately a half block up the street and still was able to fire the flash!

Price wise, they are priced below the cost of Pocket Wizards making it easy to afford backups just in case.

title: Really good cable but be sure that this is the one you want.
text:
This is excellent cable. Each conductor is 23AWG, which means it's very thick and it's solid copper. That means you are going to have no issues getting 1G or even 10G speeds on it. It's shielded so you can run it next to power cables if you need to. You can only terminate it with a shielded keystone jack made for it or a shielded patch panel. It's too thick for most Cat 6A RJ45 plugs. You cannot make patch panels out of this. The green/white, brown/white etc wires are all completely white so you have to be keep track when you wire this up to a jack. If you don't need the shielding get unshielded cable, it's easier to work with.

As long as you know what you are getting it's great cable. I wish cable matters sold some oversize RJ45 plugs that worked with this cable so I could use the leftover cable for patch cables.

Edit: I've found reasonably priced RJ45 plugs that can be used to terminate this wire so you can make patch cables or terminate it without having to use a patch panel. I had a lot of leftover cable and wanted to be able to use it for patch panels. The Platinum Tools Cat6A Shielded Jacks, Platinum Tools part number 106192C work. It's not easy to get the jack on right and you'll probably waste a few jacks with bad terminations before you get the hang of it but after wasting 4 jacks I've gotten about 30 on now and they work fine. The cable is really thick and not super flexible so it's not ideal for patch cables but still you can make them and they work great.

Do not get the Platinum Tools EZRJ45 jacks where the cable passes through the front of the jack. Those don't work.

title: So far, so good!
text:
[[VIDEOID:d76487d1f04bb25dc769ace51ed6db72]] My new AW100 replaced a Kodak Easyshare Sport C123 and a Canon SD400. The SD400 has been a great compact camera for the past 6+ years, but was getting long in the tooth esp since I bought a Windows 7 PC and couldn't get a driver (which created all kinds of issues with deleting subdirectories on the memory card). The Kodak went back within a couple days of use because a) it didn't have an optical zoom and I found I really missed that, and b) the pictures were too 'contrasty' where the highlights were blown out and the shadows all clipped to black. I guess for $80 the Kodak delivered its price-performance, but I only take pictures once and I want them to be good. I also have a Canon SLR but I don't take that fly fishing, backpacking, winter camping, nor to the beach.

I've only had the AW for about a week, but so far really enjoying it. The image quality is as good as any Canon point-shoot (my wife has a newer Canon SD). The menus are not quite as intuitive, and I had to spend a half day reading the 100 pg manual to really get a feel for how best to use this. Still, there are a lot of flexible options including control over ISO and shake, and it has some cool modes that the Canon's don't have such as shooting 8 or 10 consecutive pics and auto-saving the least blurry to the memory card. The 5x zoom is further augmented by a 5x digital zoom where the pixels are interpolated rather than cropping in. I haven't tried the digital zoom yet, but I think this will be superior if/when I need that extra close up.

I was also looking closely at the Panasonic Lumix but I chose the AW for superior video. I really like the stereo sound it captures, and the slow-motion video shots have already been a lot of fun. It allows you to record at 1/2 to 1/8 speed, or 2x speed, and you can even shift during the video shoot from normal speed to high or slow speed, and back. The other thing I liked about the AW over the Lumix is the 5cm macro. Have seen some stills on Youtube that looked pretty cool, and plan to try this out more now that I have a camera that can do it.

I probably won't take this scuba diving since it's only good to 33 feet, but that's about my range for snorkeling and I'm sure it'll come in handy next time I'm someplace I'd rather be. I'm also looking forward to shooting some underwater video of trout, and not having to wrap this in 3 ziplocks for a rainy day on the river (or just insurance against an unforeseen swimming opportunity). Video'ing a buddy fighting a fish, toggling to slow-motion during a reel-screaming run and jump -- yep I think this will be a fun toy.

Attaching a recent vid from the dog park, shot at 1/4 speed.

title: Beware of older lenses
text:
I was saving up for this macro for a long time. I chose it over the less expensive competitor lenses almost exclusively for its USM and inner focusing. I planned to use this lens mostly for taking pictures of insects, so the inner focusing is exceedingly important.

I bought a used version of this lens and was very disappointed. The lens was loud, terribly heavy, and much to my surprise, extended when it was focusing! I thought Canon was guilty of some grievously false advertising. It took some detective work from one of my friends to realize that Canon used to make a lens, also a 100mm f/2.8 macro, without USM or inner focusing. This, of course, was a very old lens, discontinued sometime in the early 1990s.

So, after returning that lens and getting an actual USM version, I am very pleased. The images are very sharp. The macro is a little difficult without IS, but I wasn't willing to save up and pay twice the price for the L series of this lens. Having to shoot with a higher shutter speed and ISO doesn't degrade the quality anywhere near enough for me to justify the extra cost. I read lots of negative reviews saying it is impossible to use this lens without a tripod, and that is simply not true. Even at 1:1 magnification, I can take clear, sharp images just holding it by hand.

There are only a few cons to this lens. The most obvious is how heavy it is (though not nearly as heavy as the non-USM version). On my Rebel XS, the weight difference was so great that it was difficult to hold the camera steady. On bulkier cameras, the shake is not a problem, but your hand might get tired after long periods of shooting. Also, in low light, the autofocus hunts, but it is nowhere near as bad as that on some of my cheaper lenses. Plus, this lens has full-time manual focus, so you can fine-tune the focus yourself.

In conclusion, this is a great macro lens if you want wonderful quality, but don't mind lacking the IS of the L lens. Images, both macro and regular telephoto, are crisp and sharp. The addition of USM and inner focusing make it worth buying this lens compared to competitor lenses. If you are buying this lens used, make sure to contact the seller and verify that it is the USM, inner-focusing model and not the old, clunky version.

title: Fantastic earbuds for travelling
text:
This is a great step up for those who like in-ear earbuds and need even less ambient background. I like the K391 NC because of the feature set: it's very compact for travel, it has a high quality microphone for chat/video calls, and the noise canceling makes a big difference on the airplane, and the price fit my budget.

The whole kit with cables fits nicely in a small bag that will fit nicely into a laptop bag pocket, and ultralight. Microphone quality is very good, and the mic/switch is at chin-height. On my Android phone (Galaxy Nexus) the call switch doubles as a pause button for my music player app. A nice surprise.

But one of the main reasons I got this was for noise cancelation, to make long flights more enjoyable and for that it works really well. Regular earbuds work pretty well due to the physical sound isolation, but I was very pleased when I turned on NC on the AKG because it lowered sound a lot. I used the headphones on two flights this week. On the first segment, a ~5 hour redeye flight, I was up at the front of the aircraft where it was quieter, where the ambient noise was more hiss (high frequency) than rumble/engine noise (low frequency). I'd guess it cuts down the noise by more than half. I left the headphones turned on but unplugged and the quiet helped me stay asleep on the plane.

The noise cancellation was even more noticeable on the return day flight. This time my seat was behind the wing and engine. The low frequency ambient noise was louder but even better, the NC cut out an even larger amount. Watching movies or listening to high dynamic range music is very pleasant.

I considered full over-ear headphones but I'd rather trade off whatever they might offer for a small size. I also considered the Bose in-ear NC headphones but stalled at the price.

I will probably keep taking a second pair of cheap earbuds for the gym when I travel. My experience with sweat, active electronics, active movement and flaky headphones is that expensive headphones don't belong at the gym.

And yes, sound quality is pretty good, too. The AKGs are definitely at the high end of all ear buds I've used.

title: Awesome h/w; Notably missing DNSMasq support for static dhcp hosts
text:
This is an all-around great router that replaced our 2-year-old NetGear WNDR3700 (which also runs DD-WRT). I bought it primarily for the vastly increased WiFi range talked about in reviews, and it did the trick, as we now get a signal in the furthest rooms, and our ChromeCast now shows 4/4 bars (through 3 walls and the TV) instead of 2/4 allowing it to finally stream 1080p from YouTube without a hiccup.

Biggest PROs of this router (all hardware):
1) #1 ranked router @ smallnetbuilder.com
2) AC WiFi support for new devices like the Galaxy Note 3 and Nexus 5.
3) Supports open DD-WRT firmware (turns a $200 router into a thousand-dollar router)

Biggest CON, BY FAR (in software), and the only reason I docked 1 star:
*) No DNSMasq support(!), which makes looking up static dhcp hosts impossible. e.g.: '$ ping laserjet' fails.

The latest Netgear firmware (V1.0.1.22 as of this review) thankfully supports static dhcp leases -- called an "Address Reservation Table" by Netgear -- which allows you to give devices on your LAN a static IP and hostname by MAC address. However, since Netgear isn't using DNSMasq, these hosts can't also be resolved by name on the LAN (192.168.1.1 nameserver), which makes their implementation only half-useful. If not for this glaring oversight I might've stuck with Netgear's stock firmware indefinitely, but it's crippling, and so I'm glad I have the option of flashing DD-WRT in order to get this functionality back, as well as hundreds of other features only seen in high-end routers, such as sshd, more vpn options, etc.

NetGear, if you're listening: please add dnsmasq support (instead of proxy to ISP only) in your next firmware update. This issue is also being talked about on your forums.

text:
I bought this for my 2007 Odyssey EX-L, which has no auxiliary connection of any kind. I had it professionally installed along with the BT35-HON by USA-Spec which I'll review later. All I can say about the installation is that one car stereo shop would not work with USA Spec products due to some bad experiences in the past and the shop that did the installation took nearly 4 hours and said they would not install them again. So if you're a DIY-er, be wary especially if you're installing both products like I did.

From my viewpoint, however, I LOVE this adapter! I connect my iPhone 4 and shut it in the slot below the climate controls and I have full control of my music from the factory head unit and steering wheel controls. You have a few options on how you want the radio preset buttons to behave. The mode mine is in assigns each preset to a sort category (All Songs - Playlists - Artists - Albums - Genre). There's also a mode which assigns the presets to the first 6 playlists on your device. You can also set it control from the device itself, but there's really no reason to since you really do have full control from the factory head unit without taking your eyes off the road.

For an example, if I want to randomly play through all my songs I push preset 2. If I want a specific artist, I push preset 4 and use the seek -/+ buttons to select the artist. Whichever sort order I'm in, the tuning knob changes the song. You can even turn random on or off from the head unit. I works almost exactly how I'd want it to if I could program it myself.

The only issue is, as far as I understand, that the channel -/+ buttons on the steering wheel behave different depending on your car. Some models will cycle through presets (like my Odyssey) and others will cycle through tracks. I would rather it do tracks. I'm going to see if that's something I can change.

Regarding sound quality, if your songs are CD-quality bit-rate, it sounds as good as your CDs. Regarding volume leveling, it doesn't seem to work as well as if you're listening to the device with headphones. Some songs can be louder than others. Not a big deal. Just turn the volume knob.

Overall, If you want iPod/iPhone integration that works with your Honda factory stereo, this is the adapter you want.

title: Very Nice Camera!
text:
I bought both the Nikon p510 camera and the Sony hx200v camera to see which I prefer. I took numerous pictures with both, but decided to keep the Nikon p510. Although both cameras took very nice pictures, I liked the way that people shots came out with the Nikon p510, especially indoors. The Nikon p510 seems to give a nice "matte" finish to skin shots and with a bit more color, whereas the Sony hx200v showed/emphasized more skin flaws. Also, indoor pics with the Sony were inconsistent - sometimes too yellow, and other times too white (overexposed). Although the Sony hx200v does have a "soft skin" setting, I felt it looked too unnatural (gave the skin too much of a porcelain doll finish). Also, the Nikon p510 seems to handle indoor pics better where there is a lot of backlight. Outdoor pics are nice with both cameras, but again I preferred the people pics with the Nikon p510 (the outdoor people pics taken with the Sony were more neutral toned). The only reason I give this review 4 stars is because the zoom can be a bit flaky when trying to focus with maximum zoom, in particular on small objects such as birds; sometimes it would focus right away, but a lot of times I had to keep adjusting the zoom before it decided to focus. Yet, I haven't had this problem with other types of pictures.

4/22/12 update: I think I found the solution to the problem I had with zooming on small objects. Pg 72 of the disc manual ("Using Focus Modes") talks about how to change focus modes. It seems that when I change the focus to "infinity", it focuses on the subject a lot quicker. I'm still going to play with this setting a bit more, but so far it seems to have helped. Also, after reading page 73 ("Available Focus Modes"), it looks like "manual focus" may also be helpful on zooming in on small objects. I will play with these settings for a while. If I find these settings consistently work, I will change my rating to 5 stars.

title: Suprisingly good quality
text:
All of these HDMI 2x1 "bi-Directional" switches seem to be the same model. The only difference appears to be the logo printed on the top. SO I bought the cheapest one, which was from Etekcity (they shipped it super fast by the way).

The switch is very small, but surprisingly heavy. I think it's good quality. It works perfectly as a "2 in, 1 out" switch. I have a laptop with an HDMI port that I use only for video streaming for an HDTV. I got tired of always plugging in the HDMI cable (and feared that the port would wear out) so I use this switch to toggle between my HDTV and the laptop's display. I actually only use 1 input on the switch (the laptop) and 1 output (the HDTV). So, 1 of the inputs on the switch is empty. That way I click the button on the switch to pick the display I want to use by switching between the laptop's input or the empty input (the empty input cuts signal between the laptop and the HDTV so the laptop's display works).

I really doubt that you will be able to use this switch as a "1 in 2 out" and watch 2 TVs simultaneously due to HDCP (copy protection) embedded in the HDMI signal. When you power on an HDTV and a video source (such as blu-ray player) the two units talk to each other and decide on the screen resolution (such as 720p or 1080p). Throw in another TV that is also trying to talk to the video source and the result is no signal at all! You need a proper "splitter" that will not let the 3rd device talk to the video source. If you want to watch 2 HDTVs at the same time, I recommend the "Cables Unlimited SWB-7852 2-Port HDMI Amplifier and Splitter with Power" that is sold on Amazon (I've had it since 2011 and it works great).

My only complaint is that the blue LEDs are super BRIGHT!

title: Good GPS, buggy update software.
text:
ORIGINAL REVIEW (was 1 star):

I just received the 3590LMT. I am returning it after running the update software and discovering that North American maps are not free.

The packaged instructions take you to a web site, which then has you download Garmin Express. Running Garmin Express with the device attached gives an opportunity to install free Full Europe maps, but North America map updates are only offered as extra cost purchases. And they are not cheap! $59.99 for just the lower 49 states.

The update software itself continues to be as klutzy as I have experienced with previous Garmin GPS's. The web site has you install Garmin Express, Garmin Express sends you back to the web for certain map update tasks, and the web page you are sent to just tells to install and manage maps with Garmin Express -- and endless loop.

UPDATED REVIEW: Before returning, I contacted Garmin tech support. They re-registered my unit, and the North American maps appeared for free download. So the issue appears not to have been with the unit itself, but rather with the Garmin Express software or the back-end systems that support it. So I have access to the free map updates.

Not perfect, but I am pleased with my choice.

Pros:
-- Very good voice control and recognizing spoken addresses. (See exception of places under Cons.)
-- Fast calculation.
-- Beautiful display.

Cons:
-- Display is less bright than my previous Garmin's.
-- The database of places (restaurants, etc.) is surprisingly limited. It does not recognize restaurants that have been open for years.
-- When you begin navigating from a parking lot or other location off the streets within the map database, the unit instructs you to go to "____" street. OK, that's fine, that is what Garmin's have always done. But what if you do not know the direction of that street? Drive to the purple route, right? Well, that may not work. When you start driving within the parking lot, you may quickly, perhaps immediately, lose sight of the purple intended route. I get to a street adjoining the parking lot. Do I turn left? Right? Where is my route?
-- "Recalculating" is gone. After often tiring of hearing that word, I thought it would be a good thing. Wrong! Now I have no alert that I missed a turn.
-- The Smartlink software requires a bluetooth link, but in operation it is sluggish, and the cell phone hands free functionality is not reliable with my Droid RAZR MAXX. Caveat: my cell phone has shown other signs of sluggishness of late. When this function works,(beam an address from Google Maps, Contacts, Calendar, etc.), it is wonderful.
-- Adding an intersection as a via point sometimes sends me on a long wandering side excursion.
-- As noted in the original review, the update software does not work reliably.
-- Garmin has limited tech support hours.

title: A nice TV with plenty of features (if you are lucky enough to receive one without defects).
text:
**Review for 55LM7600**
Yes, a nice TV. Great? Well, it could be, but there are some issues that LG will need to work on.

The Good:

Looks: LG really came up with a neat design where looks are concerned. The ultra thin bezel that surrounds the tv looks sharp. Others who have reviewed this TV have stated that the bezel is metal, but what I see is plastic. A nice durable stainless steel bezel would have been preferred, but LG decided not to go that route. The ribbon stand gives the TV a look that makes you think it's floating in air, another nice touch. Speaking of the stand, the stand is also plastic. Long term durability may be an issue, but so far so good. Again, something at the very least reinforced with metal would have been preferred since there is a rather large investment being held up by this engineered piece of plastic.

Picture Quality: There are pros, and cons. The pros are that the picture is beautiful. With a little tweaking colors are rich and vibrant (LG ships the TV with the picture tuned to the cool side, which at first made the picture appear a bit weak and a tad washed out). Black levels are not the best, but I have to say that to my eye they are completely satisfactory. While you may think that you are looking into a black hole while watching a plasma TV when screen goes dark, you won't get that reaction here. I don't feel that this is enough reason though to pass on this TV or to detract from it's rating. With the help of LED dimming on this TV, the black level is still very respectable.
Panel uniformity is very good, I have to admit that I had to order a replacement due to issues with the backlight bleeding through and causing the dreaded flashlight effect with the first TV that arrived (light carried around 7 inches out from the corners), but the second set resolved the issue with light colored corners and blacks that looked grey. There is still a small amount of light bleed at the top of the screen (about a ¼ inch band), but nothing that detracts from normal viewing. My experience has shown that to date there is no "perfect TV" on the market, with any new TV there seems to be some type of compromise. If flashlighting, blooming, edge bleeding, or blooming are going to be a huge issue for someone, my advice is to purchase a LCD TV with a standard florescent backlight, or direct LED backlight (plasma is another option, but the Panasonic ST30 I upgraded from suffered from burn in). Every LED edge lit LCD TV I have seen to date has shown these issues from one extent or another. You may not be able to see these issues in a brightly lit room or on the showroom floor of your local electronics retailer, but when you take it home and the lights dim, they will be waiting for you.

Motion Handling: With the fast response time of the panel used in this television, motion handling was super as far as any LCD TV is concerned. One thing that did concern me was that in researching the panel used in this TV, the panel refresh rate is not a true 240Hz but rather a 120Hz panel and a 240Hz effect achieved from "flashing" the back-light.

Viewing Angle: This TV features an IPS LCD panel and as far as viewing angles go, this type of panel will give you the second best viewing angle of all currently available TV's. Plasma and the soon to be available OLED are the only others to offer a better viewing angle. A conservative guess to my eye would be an off axis viewing angle of about 75 degrees before losing picture quality. Compared to the Samsung LED lit LCD I once owned this is nearly twice the off axis viewing angle I experienced before. If you decide to purchase any type of LCD TV I highly recommend making sure you look for a model with an IPS panel.

3D: Ok, I have to admit this feature is pretty cool. Before owning the LG we had a Panasonic plasma set that was also 3D capable, but with the price of the 3D glasses we never used it. LG not only offers passive 3D viewing, but they also include 6 pairs of glasses in the box. This is great because the glasses are light, comfortable, they don't require batteries, and the movie theatre glasses work just as well as those included. The 3D picture quality is outstanding with no cross talk, and amazing depth. Objects not only appear to jump off the screen at you, but they also appear to jump out in the distance through the screen and the wall behind it.

USB: If you happen to have media backed up on a hard drive and would like to view content on your TV, LG has you covered. The USB ports support external devices and all types of content including MP4 and MKV.

Cons:

Magic Wand remote: For normal TV use the magic wand remote is a bit of a pain to use. We quickly turned to a universal remote so that we can directly input channels and easily use features such as last channel. If you are using the web browser, the wand remote is easier to use, but we don't find much use for the built in browser.

Built in browser: The good news is that the built in browser supports flash, the bad news is that not all features on web pages seem to work. We enjoy using web services such as Crackle, and viewing past television programs on their respective networks websites. While the video does play, we have not found a way to enable full screen viewing. For this reason, we don't find ourselves using the web browsing feature much.

Flashlighting / Edge Bleeding: Here is where LG really loses points on an otherwise great product. The first set that was delivered had a terrible flashlight effect in the corners of the screen. So bad in fact that dark scenes would appear gray, and colors were a bit washed out. I understand that all LED edge lit TV's have this issue to some extent, but this was really bad. When you look at the price of these products, you expect more. The second set does show some bleeding along the top edge with small arches of light showing from where the LEDs are positioned around the edge, but this is really only seen in a completely dark room with the TV tuned to a channel with no signal. By doing this, you are looking at a black picture and the TV appears to disable the LED dimming. This is not however a real world scenario for viewing. During normal viewing there are times when the top ¼ inch of the screen shows a little edge bleed, but it's again in a completely dark room when it can be seen.

Dead Pixels: I was not expecting this. While watching one day on the second set that was delivered the screen changed to a commercial with a white background. There in front of me was a small black dot that upon further inspection turned out to be a dead pixel. Being that I had already exchanged one set for issues with flashlighting in the corners, the second set was returned and I called it quits with the LM7600 (as a side note, the meter on the TV showed only 136 hrs when the dead pixel appeared).

Menus: We have found the menus to be a bit difficult and not entirely intuitive to use. The manual is extremely poorly written and offers little to no help with navigating the features of the TV. Along with the difficulty in using the menus, we also find it awkward that the channels are not placed in numerical order, but instead are separated by channel type. What you end up with is a separate channel listing for digital, air, and cable channels. It would be nice if LG would have grouped all the channels together so that TV channel 2 is just one click away from digital 2-1 instead of having to flip through all the air or cable channels to get to the digital channels and vice versa (see magic wand remote).

Overall: If I had not experienced dying pixels on the second set, I would have gladly given a rating of four stars (subtracting one star for the flashlighting effect experienced by the first set). With the experience of having received two TV's that both had problems, and taking into consideration the price one will pay for the 55LM7600 I am forced to give a rating of one star to the LG 55LM7600. Maybe my expectations are unrealistic, but I expect value equal to the number of dollars I spend, and this experience really missed the mark.

*I feel it is important to add the model reviewed was the 55LM7600. Different sized versions may or may not perform the same way due to the inherent differences in manufacturing LCD panels.*
