title: Entry level price, features, and performance
text:
OUT OF THE BOX

Out of the box, there isn't much to say about the router itself. You've just got a router, power, network cable, and quick start guide. Although it's technically fully setup and ready to go when you plug it in. It's already got a unique access point name and password setup. There's even a physical switch that allows you to switch between Auto/Router/Bridge modes. Other than changing the default router password and other optional advanced settings, you almost don't even need to ever log into it's web interface.

Just connect everything as the diagram indicates, and it's pretty much ready to provide wireless and wired internet connectivity.

FEATURES & SETUP

The router has a pretty basic and easy to navigate web interface that allows you to make all of the changes you need. Which is also mobile friendly, should you prefer not using a PC. The AC 1200 doesn't have a lot of additional features. There's a guest mode, parental control, and that's about it.

To continue advanced setup or go with custom settings, you'll want to make sure it's in Router mode, regardless of your home setup. This is the default mode, such as when you have it connected to the modem directly. There is a nifty card on the bottom of the router which has the IP, password, and everything you need to jump in and start setting it up.

Which is exactly what I did to change the access point names, passwords, setup a static IP, and other less common "advanced" changes I do to make it work with my network. I've already got a separate server and router. All this thing needs to do is provide speedy WiFi. Otherwise functionality is completely the same.

This was all pretty straight forward, except I did run into my first issue when going into "Access Point" or "Bridge" mode, which is that it disable the ability to access the router's web interface. I updated the firmware, reset it, all no go. Per Buffalo tech support, the router defaults to a 192.168.11.100 IP address when going to Bridge mode. Unfortunately I still wasn't able to access it after troubleshooting, and there doesn't appear to be a way to change this functionality.

PERFORMANCE

I have 802.11ac and 802.11n devices in my two-story house, so I have plenty of devices to test the performance with. First, the router does actually have a gigabit WAN port so that you've got the potential for a lot of speed via your ISP or Local Network connection. This seems like a no-brainer to have with an AC router, but you'd be surprised. The other 4 LAN ports are only 100Mb. As for WiFi, the router is dual band, and is capable of handling both 2.4GHz and 5GHz as the same time.

For my initial test I used my Surface Pro 3 (Marvel Avastar Wireless-AC card) and a Dell XPS 11 (Intel 7260 WiFi card). Both devices seem to be maxing out right around 25MB/s file transfer speeds via my LAN connection with 5GHz on AC or N. 2.4GHz is naturally considerably slower, at around 10Mb/s or so.

It just doesn't seem to be capable of going faster than this. The router advertises speeds closer to 866Mb/s. In reality, you'd looking at roughly 40-50% of those speeds, in optimal conditions. And we're talking only a couple feet from the router itself. Also note the difference between bits and bytes (there are 8 bits in a Byte and b=bit / B=Byte). 25MB/s translates to 200Mb/s, which is a bit less than I'd expect for an AC router. Especially since my older 802.11n router could easily achieve those speeds.

PROS:

+ Easy Setup
+ Full gigabit WAN port
+ Important features are present
+ Small foot print
+ AC can still be faster for some WiFi cards

CONS:

- Less than expected AC wireless speeds
- Web interface not available in Bridge or AP mode
- LAN ports are only 100Mb
- No advanced features such as QoS and high power transmission

CONCLUSION:

Having an AC router will result in your AC capable devices likely performing better than they would with an 802.11n-only router. AC has better range and performance. I have since used other non-AC wireless cards transferring files over Wi-Fi with the Buffalo, and they're on par with what they did on my top-end D-Link 802.11n router. However, some newer AC wireless cards don't tend to do very well in non-AC environments. So there can be an improvement in performance, sometimes twice as fast.

However, if you really want the most AC can offer, I'd suggest spending a little more and going for the higher end models that can really move some bits. After all, if you're going to upgrade, you might as well do it right. But if you're just looking for a low cost current gen Access Point, and don't need a lot of features or super fast speeds, this one would get the job done.

title: If my retired Dad can configure AND put a password, anyone can!
text:
The best litmus test for ease of use of an electronic device is my parents.

To understand where I'm coming from, my parents didn't get their first cell phone until they were both in their retirement years. Then, for the longest time, I couldn't leave voicemail because they didn't know how to set it up the first time. After I set it up for them, it wasn't worth leaving voicemail because they didn't know how to check it! When the voicemail lady answers and tells you to press "One" my dad has to remove the phone from his ear, take off his glasses, hold the phone up and find and then press "One" and then by the time he puts it back up to his ear, he's missed what to do next or he's missed the entire voicemail or he can't hear anything. They also keep it turned off most of the time to "save electricity" but that's another story... "Mom/Dad! You don't need to keep turning it off! You don't need to save electricity!" "Son, we didn't raise you to waste electricity..."

So with that being said, you can't believe how shocked I was that my dad (I purchased this and had this direct shipped to him) was able to configure this AND put a WPA2 password for his WiFi network AND change the default administrator password as I had advised him to do. I was fully expecting to be on the phone for the next 3 hours walking him through this, but I didn't have to. Prior to him receiving it I had explained that unsecured networks with no passwords are bad and he needed to use a password and to choose WPA2 if prompted. Also I told him that the default password for Linksys and DLink routers are well known (ie. the default passwords are either "linksys" , username is admin and password is admin, etc) And anyone could log into his router and "mess things up" unless he changed the admin password to something besides default.

Anyways, it's been a number of months and I was recently down there for Thanksgiving and able to verify everything was secure and proper. Though I haven't personally seen Medialink's install/configuration program, it must be completely awesome in that my Dad of all people has all of this working great!

title: High Quality and Pocketable
text:
Finally, a competitor to the Sony RX100 series. I've been comparing the Canon G7X to my Sony RX100 for a couple of days. Here are some of my observations:

* Sony is slightly less thick and weighs a bit less. But both are definitely pocketable.
* Contrary to a review I read on Dpreview, the autofocus on the G7X is very fast...faster (more responsive) than the one on the RX100. I suspect Dpreview may have gotten a defective sample. But this one is lightning fast outdoors, and indoors. Even in fairly low light, the autofocus never hunted. It always snapped into focus instantly.
* shot to shot using JPEG is also very fast. I reeled off a dozen continuous shots with no slow down at all. Switch to RAW and the camera slows down considerably. It spends about 1 second to save the RAW file before letting you get another shot off.
* The G7X has an automatic lens cover which retracts when you turn it on, and closes when you turn the camera off.
*. The Dial around the lens can be customized for the feature you want. But not all features can be assigned the dial around the lens. But it lets you assign ISO, MR, WB, Zoom, DR Correction, Shadow Correct, Aspect Ratio and Custom. I left it on the Default which changes the feature depending on the shooting mode.
* You can also set the Ring Func button on the back. I set mine to metering more (Evaluative, Center, Spot). You can also assign a feature to the movie Record button. But I left mine on Record.
* At first glance Picture Quality appears fairly similar to the Sony RX100, which means it is excellent. (But see the update below of direct comparisons of same subject using JPEGs) At this level of picture quality there is little need to carry a DSLR. Thankfully, the G7X does not have the noise characteristic of the G1X Mark II (don't know what Canon was thinking of on that one).
* To my eyes the Canon lens is a bit sharper in the corners than the one on the Sony RX100. The Macro shot of the marigold shows off the sharpness.
* G7X has a nice touch screen. You can use it to point to the object you want to be in focus. It is very precise. You can also set it to take the picture when you touch the screen (again focusing on the point you touch). It is kind of fun, but I'm not used to taking pictures this way yet. Or, you can turn off the touch feature altogether.
*Annoyances: the wifi button is too easy to press even though it is recessed. So when putting the camera in my pocket or in a nifty case I have, it is too easy to accidentally turn on the camera by pressing the recessed wifi button. I haven't read the manual yet. So I need to check to see if it can be disabled. The Record button can also be turned on by accident. (But don't they all).

Overall a superb pocketable camera. I'll try to add to the review after I've used the camera more and read the manual.

Update October 31
==================
I did some extensive comparison JPEG shots between the Canon G7X and the Sony RX100. These were all taken on a cloudy day. I took shots at ISO 200, 400 and 800. In shot after shot the Sony was better exposed, showed more clarity and less noise. I was surprised at how much the difference is. You may get different results shooting RAW. But if you shoot JPEG, you are going to get better pictures shooting with the original RX100. I don't mean to take away from the excitement of the Canon G7X because it is an excellent camera. I'll try to post some comparison shots so you can see what I mean. Right now I can't find the "add photo" button.

title: Excellent Burner, But No LG Support For This "OEM" Version!
text:
This was the perfect and affordable Blu-Ray Burner [[ASIN:B007YWMCA8 LG Electronics 14x Internal BDXL Blu-Ray Burner Rewriter WH14NS40 - Bulk Drive - Black]] for my rebuilt PC via a MSI P-33 combo Motherboard and upgrade to Windows 7 Ultimate 64 bit (from Dell XPS 400 Win XP sp3 32 bit). I heeded the reviews about LG's lack of support for this particular "OEM" Burner (along with Window's!), and ensured I got Blu-Ray Burner software (Aiseesoft Blu-ray Ripper Ultimate) ahead of time.

The one thing I WASN'T ready for, was having to search for the latest WH14NS40 firmware, since NO software disc was included with the Burner, nor is it currently offered at the LG "Support" link for the Drive (only a pdf Manual is offered). But I was fortunate enough to find it at the "Firmwarehq" site after a 30 minute search, and the "txt" for the update states that it is for "Improved DVD-R Readability".

Also (IMPORTANT!!), I wasted hours trying to get Windows 7 to see the Drive and did exhaustive searching online for a solution, before learning that the Drive MUST be the "Master" Burner/Player Drive in the Motherboard's SATA chain (NO SATA cables included either with Burner either) in order for Windows to see it (had my Asus DVD-RW Drive hooked up first, beforehand).

So now it's up, running, and I'm HAPPY, since this was the final step in my upgrade.

text:
I will be short.
I purchased this item in February 2012. While it was working, the connections were stable, the range was acceptable(not great; about 25 meters), WiFi speeds were much less than advertised 300 MBps unless you were standing next to the unit.
It stopped working in October. I called Asus customer support. After several dropped calls, I finally got hold of them. They told me that they will not send me a replacement, but rather i have to ship it to them at my expense. They will either fix it or send another refurbished unit instead (no new units). After they received it, it took them about a week to ship back. They used FedEx ground, which took 9 days. The unit worked for only one month. I called them back (this time it took me two days to get through; constant dropped calls). Again the same answer - send back. It took them five days after FedEx showed they have received it to start the repair. Finally I received it back to discover that it was not repaired. It had the same problem. I called them back, and they confirmed that the technician assessed it working, and it wasn't repaired. After troubleshooting they were convinced that it is indeed broken. the operator told me that they will ship me a replacement unit while i ship this one back. the promised email with the instructions didn't arrive. Next day after 15 minute struggle with their phones, I got through. The agent told me that the previous agent was mistaken - they cannot send a replacement. He said that i will receive an email with the RMA and a faster return label. No emails again. I called them back and asked for the supervisor. This time they sent me a label. The item was delivered by FedEx in two days. After a week I tried to check the status of the RMA. Their system couldn't locate it. Called them again. The rep had to track the FedEx delivery to locate the item. It wasn't even picked up. He gave me a different RMA number and claimed that it will be repaired in 5 business days. A week passes. The RMA doesn't even show up in their system. Called them again; they couldn't find the RMA. The rep promised to find out and call back. That didn't happen. Called them after two days and asked for the supervisor. He found the unit, which was picked up for repair after 8 days after it was delivered, and it was still being "repaired". I received it in about 10 days - another refurbished router and the power adapter. You will not believe it; the adapter wasn't working. Good I had kept my original adapter. The router works however. This is a NIGHTMARE!!!
I will never, never, ever buy anything from Asus.
My suggestion - get other brands.

title: Everything I was hoping for and more.
text:
What I wanted (and got!): I primarily wanted a color-screen e-reader for books and magazines, with some extra capabilities for convenience and fun. I did not want a replacement for my laptop, nor did I expect to do a lot of web browsing, but I DID want apps and games.

Here's why I bought the Fire and not something else:

I had been wanting an e-reader for a long time when I bought the Kindle Fire. I did a lot of research and what it boiled down to is that the Fire had all the features I wanted, plus some advantages over the Nook, and at the price point I was looking for.

The ipad was out of my price range, so that one was eliminated first.

Next: I knew I wanted a color screen because I wanted to view magazines (ones with great photos like photography magazines and national geographic). So I narrowed it down to the Nook with the color screen and the Fire.

The Fire is $50 cheaper.

Also, I knew I was going to be buying Amazon content, so that was a point on the Fire's side.

The deciding factor was that Barnes & Noble put a limit on their Nooks for how much of its storage you can use for Non-B&N content. That really pissed me off. If I buy an electronic device, I expect that I can use it to store whatever I want. So although the Nook has 16GB of storage vs. the Fire's 8GB, B&N limits the 3rd party storage to 1GB. Thats right. You can only store 1GB worth of non-B&N stuff on your Nook.

Meanwhile I can tell you that now that I have my Fire, I have loaded it up with several magazine subscriptions (full color images) and over 500 books and a couple dozen apps, and I still have about 60% of my storage capacity left. I was initially worried that 8GB would not be enough for me, but that concern has since vanished.

To address the concern about the quirks of the fire:

1. The touch screen is not as good as an iPad...yes this is true...because its a third of the cost of an iPad. I still think it works well, and the fact that it is a little less sensitive than my iPhone screen doesn't bother me at all. Even when I am using the little boxes on my crossword app I still don't have any issues with the screen sensitivity. Its more of a "feeling" that you get (if you have ever had an iPhone or iPad), but I haven't found that it affects anything in a meaningful way. Like owning a fake Louis Vuitton handbag (if you are into that sort of thing), you wouldn't notice any difference if you had never had a real one, and if you HAVE had a real one, most of the differences are superficial anyway.

2. The Fire can not replace your computer. If you want something to replace your computer, then get something that can replace a computer! This is an E-reader with some tablet capabilities. That is exactly what I bought it for and that is exactly how I use it. If I was trying to replace my laptop with it then I probably wouldn't be so happy. Don't expect a burger to be a decent replacement for filet mignon. It may still be delicious, but its not going to satisfy your cravings for filet. If you want a filet, get a filet. The Fire is a great burger. (the filet in this metaphor is the iPad. :) )

3. It doesn't matter that the power button is on the bottom of the Fire because you can lock the screen in whatever position you want! I actually locked it in the vertical-upside down so when I read on my side in bed it doesn't try to switch to a horizontal view. The button location is a non-issue. I have never accidentally bumped it, and even if I did it doesn't even shut off the device, it just turns off the screen.

4. Speakers: I haven't even used them. In what situation would anyone watch something on a Fire without headphones? If you are at home you would watch your TV or your full size computer monitor, and if you are in public watching a movie or TV show and blaring the sound from the speakers instead of using headphones then FYI: You are being rude! Don't be that person that doesn't care about how you affect others. Keep your sound to yourself.

5. I have seen some comments that the quality on magazine images is not good. I guess I am sort of neutral on this point. It actually varies from magazine to magazine, so it MIGHT be the publisher's fault and not Amazon's. I don't know. But anyway, I think my magazines look nice on the Fire. On a couple of magazines the text is rather small so sometimes I have to zoom in to read the text. I don't mind though. However, the screen IS much smaller than a magazine page, and if you have trouble reading the text (especially if you want to view 2 pages in a horizontal format instead of 1 page in a vertical format) then you have to zoom in to read it, but the point is you CAN read it. This seems more a matter of effort than anything. Yes it would be awesome for teeny tiny text to be super clear, but how many of us could read text that size anyway? Also, if the magazines that don't look as good as others are due to the publisher's quality of image then the images are going to be difficult to view on ANY device, not just the Fire.

I just want to say that I feel like most of the complaints brought up by other reviewers were petty and had no real-world relevance; like they were very tech-saavy people who were getting WAY too picky about features that most people would never even think about. I'm not saying the reviews weren't valid or accurate, but I'm just not sure that reviewing the voltage of the Fire's charger is really anything that most people would care about. Hopefully these are helpful to most people:

My only 3 serious complaints:

1. The Fire only came with a charger, and not with a USB cable. I was actually a little mad about that. I know Amazon intends to make their profit off selling Amazon content to Fire users, and I can respect that. But I have several Amazon magazine subscriptions and other stuff I got from Amazon, and I don't have wifi in my house yet! The only way for me to get my AMAZON content from my laptop (on which I use my internet card, and that can't be used on my Fire) to my Fire is by using a cable seperately. So I had to go out and buy one. You're not encouraging Amazon purchases by making people go out and buy the cord that should have come with the Fire, you're just irritating them. Okay, rant over.

2. I agree with some others that the screen brightness could have more of a range of adjustability. I read in bed every day after my boyfriend has gone to sleep, and I wish it would dim lower than it does. Also, sometimes I read in a darkened living room when he is watching a movie but its one I'm not interested in, that is another occasion where it would be useful. But on the bright side at least it DOES have adjustable brightness. Amazon: maybe on the next generation we can get this option improved? I'd probably upgrade just for that feature.

3: The only time I really got annoyed when using my Fire was when I was on the Huffington Post app and wanted to view a slideshow of "Best Fashions of 2011" or some other brain candy like that, and it wouldn't work! The first time I accessed a slideshow in a webpage, it worked, then that one single slideshow has been stuck ever since! Now, I am going to calm myself down by listening to my own advice: don't expect the Fire to replace your PC. But if the Fire CAN read slideshows, then WHY is the same one stuck. No matter what slideshow I have clicked on in an app or webpage ever since that first one, the same first one shows up. That definitely needs to be fixed.

Summary time!

I am very very happy with my Fire. It is an awesome product and I think Amazon really hit the nail on the head with this one. I am definitely impressed that Amazon was able to make a product like this for $200. I would recommend it to anyone looking for a color e-reader, but NOT if: 1) you can afford an iPad; or 2) if you want a tablet that can replace your computer.

title: Awesome for old houses with old wiring
text:
Mostly everything is grounded these days. So old houses built in the 1950s with the 2 prong outlets all over the place need something to allow you to plug those devices in. Enter these adapters. Unscrew the screw holding the wall plate on and plug one of these in, then place the screw through the gold loop and tighten it back down. Any electricity traveling through the ground will go through the grounded screw (try and scrape the paint off of the back this screw so it makes a good contact.)

This is much less expensive than hiring an electrician or rewiring the outlets. I wouldn't recommend using these permanently, but they are great for when you are in a bind and need to plug something in.

title: Excellent Headset
text:
I have used this headset for just over a week now. I am very satisfied with them. I did a lot of research before making this purchase and I had a few things in mind when searching:
1. I wanted quality headphones that could handle music, movies, and games.
2. I wanted Active Noise Cancelling for use on an airplane or anywhere noisy.
3. I wanted a microphone for video chatting, gaming, or use with my cellphone.

I settled on these mostly because of the reviews. The sound quality is top notch. The headphones get remarkably loud for no amplification. Although this may be due to the fact that the headphones do an excellent job blocking outside noise. These sound amazing when listening to music. Obviously when compared to Bose or Beats or other brands that amplify music, you have to turn the volume up to achieve the same loudness. When you do, the sound quality is definitely on par. For gaming, there headphones do a decent job with surround sound, but this is also dependent on your sound card. If you are looking for true surround sound, you are better off with a USB headset with multiple drivers per ear.

The only caveat with these headphones is the noise cancelling (ANC). While it does a good job eliminating outside noise, it does so at the cost of the sound quality. The sound does flatten a bit. Most headphones make up for this with amplification and I am not sure why Asus left this out, but it is the one negative. Therefore, I will only use the ANC feature when necessary (on flights) and not regularly as I would with other headphones such as Audio Technica's or Beats.

title: Good looking mount, bad packaging & unforgiving install
text:
I replaced a fixed mount with this full motion mount to make it easier to watch TV in the kitchen and breakfast table. Let me say that once I got it installed, it is working as expected. Getting it to that point was a journey.

First, it came in shoddy packaging. The shipping box was ripped and the manufacturer's external packaging left something to be desired. Upon opening the boxes, I found screws rolling around loosely and felt the mount pieces were not secured well in the box.

If this is your first time to install a mount, the directions are worthless. A single sheet only provided a list of the parts and some arcane pictures of how to drill into studs. There were no verbiage or pictures on which screws to uses, how to use the spacers, or what to do if your studs are spaced farther than the mounting plate.

Yes, my house is from an era when building standards were not in place so the spacing between studs was closer 21 inches. The mounting plate does not span 21 inches. I think it was 18 or 19 inches...make a note to measure your stud spacing prior to buying or you will have to improvise.

Here is what I did to improvise. I have some left over plywood from some cabinets I built. I cut it down to span the stud gap and doubled up with two layers. I screwed the plywood into the studs then mounted the plate to the plywood. I was able to align the mount with one set of screws going into the studs. My TV is fairly light so I am pretty confident that this will hold well. Take into account the weight of your TV if you decide to go this route.

One last thing to note, there did not seem an easy way to separate out the articulating arm from the mounting base. It would have made installation way easier to separate the arms as the unit is heavy. I ended up extending the arms then resting it on my shoulders while I screwed the bolts in. Again, planning helps in this regard as i had measured and drilled the holes prior to placing the plywood on the wall.

in the end, what should have taken about 30 minutes to mount ended up taking about three hours. Plan ahead to make sure you have the right product for your situation and hopefully things will go smoother.

title: You just can't beat the price/performance of this lens
text:
When I first received the Canon EF 50mm f1.8 lens I thought I had been conned. It's very light, made of fairly cheap plastic and just felt like a toy rather than a proper camera lens but don't let the construction of the lens fool you.

Some people may be thinking I've got a zoom lens that does a lot more than just a fixed 55mm, so why would I want to spend money on this lens? In a word, aperture. Most zooms have apertures starting at around f4. This lens starts at f1.8. If you are not entirely sure what f stops, apertures etc. really mean, in non-technical terms, the lower the f stop number, the more light gets into the lens. The more light that gets into the lens the more control you have over shutter speed. In practical terms that means you are going to get far better pictures in low light, nightclubs, bars, at dusk etc. With a standard zoom lens, in low light, the shutter speed will have to decrease in order to let the proper amount of light in. With the lower shutter speed you are very prone to fuzzy images due to camera shake, or the target moving. With this lens, you can have a much higher shutter speed meaning these things are less likely to happen and you have sharp, clear pictures.

The canon 55 prime (a prime lens just means that it has a fixed focal length, not a zoom) is a joy to use. It produces sharp, clear pictures, so although the lens in cheap it doesn't appear that Canon skimped on the quality of the glass inside. Auto focus is fast however I'm not huge fan of the manual focus ring, it seems quite loose and turns to infinity but it does do its job. With the lens being so light you don't even notice the difference in weight on your camera, its as if it doesn't exist.

I tested this lens out on a Canon EOS 70D with wonderful results and for the price you just cannot beat it. The Canon EF 50mm f1.4 lens for example costs 3 times as much. Whether you are just getting started in photography or have been doing it for years, this is a must have lens. You just can't beat the price/performance.

The sensitivity of the tuner is truly amazing. AM & FM reception is great! I can even pick-up out-of-state FM stations that I never knew existed. Shortwave reception is very impressive using the long built-in extendable antenna. In fact is the best compact radio I've used for overall reception quality.
I usually use a larger desktop sized receiver with a long-wire antenna for shortwave reception, but this radio is great to take on the go.
This gem has so many great features such as the fine-tuning, lock-out switch (so you don't accidently turn on/off or change stations) and much more.
The sound quality is also excellent. In fact in my opinion, along with its twin, the Radio Shack 20-629, this is most impressive, best designed and overall the best portable multiband radio I've used in decades. This really is an impressive radio that performs as well or better than other more expensive portable multiband receivers.
You can't go wrong with the Sangean ATS 505P if you are looking for a great sounding multiband radio with outstanding sensitivity and reception. I would definitely recommend this radio to everyone.

title: Makes Old New
text:
Four months ago I received my Sony BD-CX960, a 400 disc blue ray mega changer, back from the Sony repair depot in Laredo, Texas. I sent it in for repair because after two years of moderate usage, several discs would not load. By the time I sent it in, the machine wouldn't recognize 35 our of 100 discs, all blu ray. After getting it back from Sony and setting it back up all discs loaded but after 10 hours of use, the discs would start dropping out again. First one then at last count 13. ENOUGH!!
Against Sony's specifications, I bought this lens cleaner and performed the cleaning once. Wait for the rep to finish talking then chapter up through six languages then it starts cleaning. At the end of the process all 13 discs were recognized again, just like brand new and after a month, still 5 X 5.
In appearance, the cleaning disc is well engineered and it is definitely worth the price. If you start experiencing playback issues with your blu ray player, I most assuredly recommend this Memorex Blu-Ray Lens Cleaner. It's too bad Sony apparently does not keep these in their tool kit.

title: From earbuds to these over-ears
text:
First let me say that I have never had a pair of over-ear headphones that were my own. I have only listened with some JVCs and Sony headphones that I have borrowed but I never liked the design of them. I felt that they hindered how well the song could be. And these headphones prove me right. I will also add that I used to listen to music with a pair of Sony earbuds. I will break up the review into the physical parts of the headphones (e.g. how it feels, its design) and how it sounds.

The Headphones:
The "TR _55LX" are pretty good for the price. The design specifically is very well done. The flexible material removes the need to adjust them to the listener's head. The cushion for the head not only flexible, but also comfortable. It feels like it isn't on your head. At least on top of your head. The ear parts are a little more intrusive, but I think that comes from me using earbuds. Despite that, the headphones go right over your ears and it is moderately comfortable. Although, under an extended period of time, your ears will be a little warm or irritated, but that might be expected.
The color (Black Bordeaux) and shape looks very modern and stylish. I particularly like that the ear pieces are ovals versus circles (Which the JVCs and Sony headphones I used had). I believe this adds to the its noise canceling quality. Which you can tell right away when you put them on. Everything is muffled but your music. The noise canceling isn't to such an extreme that you cannot hear anyone but they will definitely have to yell for you to hear.
The 4 ft (121.92 cm) "Tangle-Free" cord is a very nice touch too. The fact that it won't tangle as bad as my earbuds are a nice plus. Also, having the option to unplug at your ear is great. I never thought of how convenient that would be.

Sound Quality:
The quality of the sound is a bit spotty to me because sometimes it can sound good or just ok. It may be because I need to find MP3s that are higher quality.
When it's bad: the sound can buzz it bit if there is a lot going on the music. For example, "Karma" by Kamelot is stuck in mid tones and sometimes buzzes if the bass is too much and even "March of Mephisto" by the same band is a little wonky. The higher tones and lower tones are drowned out by the mid tones. The bass can be hit or miss; it will either sound like a satisfying Thump or will overbaring to the point of buzzing or scratchy. Additionally, I feel like the right ear is weaker than that left. At first I thought it was just my ears but I switched the ears so that the left ear sound would be in my right ear. The left ear is louder. I am unsure if this is on purpose or if it an error. Nevertheless it is more noticeable at lower volumes. It gives my right ear the feeling that it is underwater with the addition of noise canceling.
When it's good: it sounds GREAT! Everything that I mentioned above that would be bad mean nothing when it works. Typically, this is at higher volume levels. I don't mind this though.

Overall ( 3.5-4.0 Stars ):
These headphones are a great purchase for those who want a decent pair without spending +$100. Although if you want to have the studio quality headphones, buy a pair of those NOT these. Also, after hearing many kinds of music (anything from old rock and roll to new metal. Even some pop and trance music), these headphones are very focused around mid-tones. It is like someone left the equalizer in iTunes on a weird setting that only had bass (and mid-low tones) the priority.

I bought these at the discount price of $35.28 (about $45 w/ Shipping). At the price I paid for versus the listing price ($79.99) I believe this product is worth it, but only at discount, I wouldn't buy this at the full listed price. Maybe at $50-$60 at most. And if you can get it cheaper, then more power to you.

Again, if you want amazing quality headphones DO NOT BUY THESE!
BUT if you are looking for an adequate pair of head phones, purchase these at a discount.

Thank you for reading!

text: I love this computer.  I purchased the 29 inch screen and it is amazing.  I would have given 5 stars, but it comes with absolutely NO directions on setup.  There is a wireless mouse and keyboard that without directions how would you know how to set them up?  I searched the internet and found some answers, but had a hard time because my mouse didn't match the one on the Lenovo website and I couldn't find the dongle.  I have never had to call a manufacturer to set up a computer, but this time I did and he was wonderful, but they could save a lot of money by providing some directions.  The dongle is in the lid of the mouse and not inside the mouse - just in case anyone ends up looking for it like I did.  Once you find it you feel like a fool for not seeing it, but the pictures on the website direct you to inside the mouse and I was taking the lid off and setting it aside.  Then there are no directions on how to sync the mouse and the keyboard once you get the dongle in which is frustrating.  The keyboard is set up by pressing the F2,F3.F4 keys at the same time and taking the battery cover off and putting it back on without taking your fingers off the F keys - a red light on the keyboard will blink telling you it is working.  The mouse you have to push down on the left and right clickers as well as the scroll at the same time and turn the mouse switch on the back off and then back on.  A red light will blink letting you know it is synced.  A cursor will appear on the screen and you can begin.  It took me over an hour to get this information from Lenovo even though the gentlemen was spectacular and very patient.  I could have had this computer set up in 10 minutes if I had had an instruction booklet.  After all that, I am very pleased with the computer itself.  Hope this helps anyone else that experiences the frustration that I did.

title: So far it exceeds my expectations
text:
I just got the product, and so far I'm impressed. I'm a musician, and it looks like a perfect fit for recording gigs. Unlike the original user review, my product DID come with a user guide. It's minimal, but sufficient.

The product is small and seems sturdy, but lighter then I expected. People reviewing the release pictures of the product were worried about the microphones being easily damaged. The arms protecting the mics feel sturdy enough. I'm am concerned about wind however. The mics are exposed, and I don't see a great way to cover them with a wind shield, sense any wind shield could obstruct the camera view. Anyone who has recorded gigs outside knows that mics need a wind shield. We'll see. I plan to go to Guitar Center and see if they have anything usable. Worst case I'll hang a napkin around the mics.

The video looks great. It is a wide angle fixed lens, so you don't have to be far away at all in order to capture the state. If I had to estimate, it looks like the width of the image is double the distance. So if I go back 5 feet, I can capture a 10 foot state. There are no controls for zooming. And focus is also fixed. Anything from 3 inches away to infinity is in focus. I played around with it with very low lighting conditions, and the image looked better then I expected it to. The image didn't get grainy.

One thing I didn't know about the product before getting it, is it's ability to remotely monitor and operate through the use of the smart phone. I have an iPhone 5s. I downloaded the free app PlayMemories Mobile (from Sony) to my phone. With iPhone you connect your phone to the camera using the WIFI connection provided by the camera. If you have an Android, you can use NFC for an even easier setup. Once paired, the smartphone app displays a LIVE feed from the camera, and allows you to start and stop recording. This is perfect for being on stage, seeing that the camera view is good, and controlling recording sessions. It's a really good solution for live musicians. Others have talked about the fixed view screen on the camera being a huge issue because it is side mounted and fixed. The remote view capability on a smartphone is so much better then anything you could use with a screen being on the camera.

I've yet to use this at a gig. I'll post an update once I do. So far I think it's great!

UPDATE 12/23/2013

Here is a sample from when I first used the camera. As you can see it has a bit of a fish-eye effect. Because of it though, you can get much of the stage without being far away. I'm about 15 feet in front of the guitarist here. Also, the band isn't lit in any way. The camera did great in low light conditions. I'm happy with audio as well. The room was audibly bright. Brick walls and concrete floors. Still the audio sounds great for a live performance.

title: Great in theory, but . . . . . .
text:
I've been a big proponent of Denon products because lets face it, they know how to make a A/V receiver! However, I'm extremely disappointed with this product (S-5BD) and consequently, I'll be returning it to the retailer I purchased it from. The issue is this, I run my TV in another room and my components are located in another room. To do this, I use what is called a "Balun" to run CAT 5e lines between two Balun receivers that allow me to connect an HDMI cord from one receiver to my TV and the other HDMI to my receiver. Well, to do this, the Balun has to be powered to carry the signal, in this case, the distance of about 20 feet.

Well because the Balun has to be powered, this is sending just enough extra juice to the Denon S-5BD that it will trip the surge protector inside the unit and it won't turn on! So in order for me to get the unit to power on, I have to unplug the HDMI to the TV, power the unit on and then plug the HDMI back into the unit at a certain, precise point in the start-up so that it won't trip again.

Probably the most frustrating part of this whole thing is the fact that Denon insists on recruiting 3rd graders for their tech support team. I'm seriously not joking! I called Denon tech support 3 times people, count 'em 3 times and each time, with 3 different reps, their conclusion was to just return the unit for a new one. Well I returned this unit once and the replacement unit did the same exact thing. Nobody at Denon wanted to even take a sniff at what the problem might be and the candid response each time was, "Gee, that's weird it won't turn on, don't know what could be causing it."

Well it took the folks at ListenUp in Denver, CO to figure out the problem because Denon decided that they didn't want to. I didn't even have someone from tech support at ListenUp help me, it was a guy in their warehouse who took the time to try and figure out the problem with me.

Bottom line, Denon Receivers are fine, Denon DVD/Blu-Ray players are terrible and Denon customer service is like going to the dentist for a tooth extraction without novacaine. However, buy in confidence from ListenUp, they are the best!

title: I avoided projectors for years
text:
I avoided projectors for years.

They are loud, prone to shaking (if someone walks on the floor above, for example), have poor image quality, and are only good if your goal is "screen size above all else." This to me is like buying speakers based on their loudness rather than their sound quality.

Well, a friend had a beautiful custom house built which included a home theater room with a projector. In his case, he bought a Sony LCOS projector at 3x the price, but it shattered all my previous impressions of projectors:

- The image quality was fantastic -- far better than any LCD TV I have ever seen, and nearly the equal of Plasma
- I absolutely could not hear the projector unless I put my ear within half a meter.
- No image shake even during a large party.

I decided on a BenQ HT1075 after about 15 hours of research. So, what did I lose going with a MUCH cheaper projector?
- The image quality is still phenomenal. The contrast is not as good as the Sony, but surprisingly still better than ANY LCD TV I have ever seen.
- The BenQ has noticeable fan noise. It is not particularly annoying, but definitely audible. However, once a movie begins at any reasonable volume, the fan noise is impossible to notice even when straining to do so, except during silent scenes. As someone easily annoyed by fan noise, note that I did not find the fan unpleasant or distracting during such scenes.
- Unlike the Sony, pixels have a noticeable border around them, kind of a screen door look. However, this is not at all noticeable (even when trying) when sitting 9ft/3m away.
- The BenQ allows some adjustment (lens shift, zoom) but is very limited. Still, it was just fine for my room. That's what matters -- does it work in YOUR room?

I'll admit that the Sony is obviously the better projector, but I am very happy with my BenQ at 1/3 the cost.

For reference, I set up a 120" screen with the projector lens about 12ft away (the room is 13ft long).
The room is open and light does reach it through the stained glass on the front door windows, but the image contrast is still acceptable when in full brightness mode. In a dark room, you'll want to use eco mode.

Note that the projector does seem to forget some settings. It keeps forgetting that I have muted its speaker, and starts at volume 1.

title: Pretty fun
text:
Pros: Runs smooth (after installing a better OS), lots of free apps, fun to tinker with, fingerprint smudges are easily fixed with a screen protector, and same dual-core processor as other more expensive tablets.

Cons: Viewing angle (just like everyone else says), heavier than other tablets, not as much RAM as the other tablets with the same processor, the screen shows fingerprint smudges a bit too easily, and the touch screen isn't quite as sensitive as I like.

First of all, if you get this you should understand the viewing angles for this are limited. If you look straight-on it's good, but go lower and it isn't so great. You can move up a bit and it's acceptable... I wish it were the other way around, but I knew what I was getting into (when you set it on your lap you can't really sit up straight, you've gotta hunch over it or put your legs at an angle that makes the screen straight at your eyes). The viewing angle is a nuisance if you let kids play on it, like I let mine. It's hard for 2 kids to see the screen if they have it in their laps. If they prop it up and sit further back it's fine. I didn't really get it for the kids though, so not too upset about it.

Most games and apps I put on this work, but some didn't. A couple games would kind-of work and show big square blocks instead of the characters. I didn't put this in the "Cons" above because it wasn't a problem with most apps and shouldn't be a deciding factor for anyone to get this. If one app doesn't work, a lot of times you can find another app that does the same thing that does work.

Also, this has the same processor as a lot of other high-end tablets, but half the memory (512 mb, compared to 1 gb in more expensive), so I don't know if you can *really* put this in a class with the other tablets (or smartphones) that have the same processor. That said, this might be easier to overclock the CPU than the other tablets, which helps a bit. I recommend sticking around 1.2-1.3 ghz if you overclock, more isn't very noticeably faster and it'll run hotter; prolong the high speeds and I imagine the longevity of this device will go way down. 1.2-1.3 ghz doesn't cause an excess temperature increase.

This was a bit of a learning experience for me to do all the tinkering on this thing. I had to go to a site to download the original settings after I killed it, and had to install (and reinstall) that a few times. It was interesting to learn, since I really had no idea about that sort of thing beforehand. I'm a little bit of a computer nerd, but didn't have any experience with android devices. So not as big of a learning curve for me as it might be for someone who has no tech-experience whatsoever; that said, if you have no tech experience I don't really recommend this.

Anyway, after finding the android OS I liked (then deleting it because I put on too much too fast, then reinstalling it, rinse, repeat. Probably installed it 4 times before I decided it was the right OS for me) it ran smooth. Games work pretty well and scrolls through pics quickly. I really recommend you try out a lot of apps, pick the ones you like, then delete and reinstall the OS of your choice; just my opinion, but I think it runs smoother with less installed, even if the other programs don't run in the background. The touch screen sensitivity isn't the best, but good enough for me. If you get this order a screen protector with it. The smudges are ridiculous on the regular screen, and only a little extra for a screen protector. Screen protectors also doesn't scratch so easily, and if they do they're cheap to replace; the regular screen, not so much (if it is even replaceable).

So it was fun to tinker with, but at the time I'm writing this they have the Kindle Fire, which is smaller but runs as smoothly (in my opinion) and has much (much, much) better viewing angles, which makes up for the smaller size, in my humble opinion. Oh, and cheaper. If you can afford to buy something just to tinker with and learn about the technical side of an Android device, buy this. I probably spent 50 hours tinkering before I settled with an OS, and I could have spent a whole lot longer if I wanted to really experiment.

title: Combo Review of Wired 1R and Bluetooth 1RBT models
text:
MDR 1R: Henry Clay Would Like These Headphones ... ***** (Scroll down for 1RBT review.)

in other words, they are great compromisers! The MDR-1Rs are a successful fusion of the best traits of audiophile and consumer grade headphones. Both camps will find things to like about these phones, but both groups might grouse a bit about Sony's price point and relative lack of added "content" at that price point.

The 1Rs appear to be an evolution of the 50mm drivers originally used in the ZX 700/1000 headphones that were the top of the line about two years ago. The 1Rs use a smaller version of that liquid crystal polymer driver (now sized at 40mm) but also appear to have been tuned to give somewhat more bass. Compared to a ZX700 (the 50mm with plastic housing), the 1Rs have a bit more audible bass, so somewhat less pure accuracy, but the 1Rs also have a more forward presentation and a much wider soundstage, so they sound more realistic and lively than the somewhat detached and clinical ZX700s do. The 1Rs are immensely more accurate than the X10s, Sony's "Beats"- targeted celebrity bass cans, and also exceed that model in terms of comfort. However, at this writing, the X10s are also 33% less than the 1Rs and also appear more attractive and sturdy. But in terms of sound quality, the 1Rs are the best Sonys I have heard recently and indeed come close to being the best portable headphones I have heard.

The closed back 1Rs can be driven very well unamped by things like Ipads and Android phones, and can give more than adequate volume and high detail even when driven by such comparatively underpowered devices. The true virtue of the 1Rs is that they do most things well and nothing poorly. Unlike comparably priced models like the B&W P5 or ATH ESW9A, the 1R sounds very good with all genres - metal, pop, classical, jazz, electronic. The clarity and detail is roughly comparable to mid-priced home rig phones that need amps to sound good like the AKG K701 and Senn HD598. The bass as mentioned has some boosting going on, so fans of bass-focused musical types may well prefer the 1Rs over either the 701s or 598s. Yet at the same time, the bass does not run roughshod over the music as it does in something like the Beats or Sony X10s, so audiophiles who can live with a slight bass emphasis will be pleased in general.

The really commendable aspect of the 1Rs is the soundstage. The appearance of separation and layers in classical pieces is far more apparent in these phones then in the alleged "audiophile" closed back AKG K550s, at least when using the 550s with portable devices. When using my home rig with an amp, the K550s are more comparable, but for portable use and a more lively sound, the 1Rs are much superior.

Another great thing about the 1Rs is their comfort. The ZX700s had relatively shallow circumaural pads that put pressure on any ear lobes larger than those of Japanime characters, so long term comfort of that model was minimal for my somewhat larger than average ears. The 1Rs get the depth much better, so my ears do not touch the driver housing at all. The 1Rs are also very light, do not grip the head very hard, and very comfortable along the top band, so I can wear these cans for a few hours without having to take a break. Unlike the even pricier Senn Momentums, normal human ears can at least fit inside the cups, meaning most users will find the 1rs to be circumaural, which use was intended in the design.

The downside to this comfort is that the relatively loose grip gives only a medium level of closed headphone isolation. I find isolation from outside noise is better than say the Sony V6 or ATH ESW9, but nowhere near as good as the champs, the Senn 280s, ATH M50s, or Yamaha Pro 500s. However, the 1R will do for subway use in most cases (if you insist on playing the slow movements of piano sonatas, you may have the occasional washout).

Who else may not like the 1Rs? If you like stuff like rap or dubstep, you may want more bass. (The X10s are ready and able to meet your needs if so...) Even at that, many bass fans will be perfectly pleased with the 1R sound, especially given it's comfort.

What else is not to like here? Frankly, the price point seems about $50-$100 too much. The 1Rs are made entirely of plastic (sturdy attractive plastic, but plastic nonetheless) and when compared to the B&W P5s seem downright dowdy. The P5s sound worse in every way, but they look and feel snazzier. Another issue is the carrying case, really a pouch, which is the same synthetic canvas stuff used on many other headphones, Sonys and others. It's better than no carrying pouch at all (cough, AKG) or the usual pleather bag, but at this price point a nicer and / or sturdier pouch or even a hard case would reflect the pricing more. The 1Rs do not have a hinge in the arms (which makes them less creaky over the long term), so only the drivers rotate flat. In this large profile sort of storage situation, a hard case is useful (like that found in the cheaper Phiaton MS 400s). The detachable cables at least are nice, and the Apple remote on the shorter cable works well. In the minus column, the earpads cannot be replaced as they are permanently attached to the cups.

So we have an all-plastic body and wrap (high quality calendared protein leather, but still pleather nonetheless), non-replaceable ear pads, and a cheap carrying pouch; these are really the only problems in this model, and these are only an issue at the price point. A reduction in price solves these issues, and even at the current price point, the well-crafted compromises in accessible sound quality and accuracy, along with the commendably broad soundstage, and best in class comfort make these a great headphone.

Better sounding? In my collection, only the much more expensive Yamaha Pro 500s and Senn HD600 are superior, and both of those have other liabilities. (The Pro 500 is a lot less comfortable and the Senn 600 needs its own nuclear reactor to power it to good quality sound.)

Five stars for sound quality, versatility, comfort, and build quality. Take a star off if you are value conscious, like really thumpy bass, or despise plastic.

*************************************************************************************************************

MDR 1RBT: For Want of A Wire... Was The Kingdom Lost? ***

How badly do you need a Bluetooth headset? The reason why I ask is that the 1RBT sacrifices quite a few significant strengths of the 1R, all for the sake of its wireless feature set, and for roughly 133% of the 1R cost. If you want a good headphone and don't mind having a wire, stop reading now and go buy the 1R model.

Still here? OK, the good news is that as far as Bluetooth goes, the BT model Sony is at the top of its class. Bluetooth unfortunately has a few audio issues which no price point or brand is going to make go away. The music will always sound a bit more congested, will lack some subtle details, and will have a more limited dynamic range (i.e. less contrast between the loud and quiet parts of the recording.) But guess what? If you listen to Justin Bieber or The Killers, none of that matters. Most pop music is meant to sound congested (i.e. everything is centrally miked), has few fine details in the recording, and is recorded in a very limited dynamic audio range, i.e. eveything is loud. So any caveats about the 1RBT sounds in my review are meant for folks who listen to more complicated music, which suffers most in comparison to wired headphone models such as the 1R.

The 1RBT loses a lot of depth in the sound stage compared to the 1R. The soundstage still isn't dreadful, but it is roughly the same as say the ATH M50 or Senn HD25, which makes it comparable to other closed headphones. The sound signature is also changed dramatically with a lot more bass presence audible. Bass heads will be happy, audiophiles less so, as the pleasing compromise inherent in the wired 1R model is tossed out the window. Though the bass still does not actually ruin the music, there is more and more of a departure from what the recording is meant to sound like.

Other losses: comfort! The 1RBT is heavier than the 1R and the cup design is different so there is a little bit less space inside for the ears. My somewhat larger ears barely brushed against the driver grills, but this contact was enough to create a bit of an earlobe ache in anything more than 60-90 minutes of continuous listening. This is not an unreasonable standard, but compared to the light and comfy 1R, it feels like a bit of a loss.

Now the good news -- the 1RBT feature set is large and well-executed. Connection was easy and reliable with an Samsung Galaxy 3 phone, an Ipad, an IMac, and a touch Ipod. Setup was easy, and the NFC (touch linkage) functionality with the Galaxy phone also worked fine. Audio streaming was pretty coherent over home and business wifi networks, and in the street via ATT's LTE service. There would be the occasional hiccup lasting one second or less, but no complete failures or lengthy interruptions. This is pretty good for BT streaming, but of course a wired phone would be even better.

Audio quality is surprisingly good, once one accepts the smaller soundstage and deeper bass emphasis. Mids and highs are fine, the presentation is very forward and engaging, and most fine detail in the music comes forward. For instance, Mahler's 3rd Symphony by Chailly with the CGB was impressive and fun to listen to, and I did not feel that much was lacking. I felt less detail was being lost here than on say the Parrot Zik, and I also felt the balance between highs and mids was more accurate on the 1RBTs. The audio quality when streaming over the Samsung Galaxy 3 was best of all, better bass and fuller sound, but as the MDR1BTs do not support AptX, I am not certain as to why this should be so.

I am also pleased to report that unlike the several BT speakers I own, there is no "receiver hum" even at low volumes or with the signal paused, so the 1RBTs are very quiet phones with no interference noise caused by interplay of receiver and speaker magnet. The headphones include convenient and reliably functioning controls for answering calls, pausing, rewinding, and fast forwarding of song tracks. Phone call quality was decent, and the built in mic did a good job. Battery life matches Sony's 30 hour per charge claim. (The phones can be used in passive mode by connecting them to the source with an included wire. The wire goes into a single side of the BTs, but once inserted the wire props open a rubber flap that is normally sealed, so the rubber flap sticks out awkwardly. Sound quality is roughly the same in passive mode, but still nowhere near as good as in the wired 1R model.)

Isolation is mediocre, a bit worse than the ATH M50s, much worse than the Senn HD25 or Beyer 1350s. Roughly the same as the 1RS - i.e. barely adequate for subway use.Range seems to match the 10 meter range claimed by Sony, and can go through one - two walls with no breakup.

The carrying case is the exact same crappy burlap one offered with the 1Rs. At a 33% higher price point, this lame carrying bag is even more annoying. If you pay another $100 for the noise cancelling model of these phones, Sony finally gives you a hard shell case. (But check the reviews on sound quality of that model before buying, as most reviewers seem to be critical of that aspect of the NC model. A good carrying case is not the be all and end all!) The 1RBTs are also made of plastic and pleather, like the 1Rs, but unlike the 1Rs, you can at least replace the pads if they wear out. Other than that, the exact same component materials for a 33% higher price does not thrill the value oriented portions of the brain... Fortunately, like the 1Rs, build quality is excellent, so the plastic use is at least optimized and looks pretty nice aesthetically.

So what to make of these? If you are Albert Audiophile, you will not be listening to MP3s on a Bluetooth headset anyway, so some audio compromises are part of the whole BT experience. The 1RBTs seems to do a pretty good job of meeting the needs of non-audiophile users who just want a pretty decent sounding headset. As with the 1Rs, Sony's produces a sturdy and attractive product, though, also like the 1Rs, one made entirely of plastics.

The biggest issue to me is the losses seen from the 1R model: soundstage, balanced sound quality, and (to a smaller degree) comfort are all sacrificed in the transition. Wireless use is gained, so now you can cook or do laundry while listening to your tunes. Is this worth another roughly $100 and the loss of the other aspects? Well, you be the judge. If you absolutely need / want BT, this is IMO your best bet, but if you don't mind the wire, you can save some money with the 1Rs and also get better sound and comfort.

I rate these at 4 stars for decent objective sound quality, and best in class BT quality. Build quality, feature set, and ease of use impress. A star is deducted due to the significant lower value, and the fact that the cheaper wired version of these phones sounds so much better. If the sound was closer, and / or if Sony cut the price by a third, these would be 4 -5 stars. Three stars is my rating at this price point.

title: Competitive performance and price, but build quality and heat are a concern
text:
I always approach anything involving WD products positively because I think that their consumer-level drives (the WD Blue, Red and Black) are a terrific bang for the bung, and I've had great results with their reliability. So the fact that this device comes with two WD Red NAS 2TB drives is a positive.

The interface is fine, and the speed is pretty average for consumer-level NAS'es in this price range. I don't do elaborate testing, but I have a set of about 1TB of mixed data and the time to write that and then do updates allows me to get a pretty consistent idea of speeds.

What bothers me about these devices is that they are too plastic. They are supposed to be hot-swappable, but given the tabs you use to pull the drives out of the case, there's no way I'd do that with another drive still turning, as it's too easy to knock it about as the tabs can take a strong jank to get the drives out and I don't want to do that right next to a spinning drive.

However, the biggest problem for me is that they have no fans and depend on convection cooling, and I don't think that's good enough. I don't recall a competitor of theirs that doesn't have a fan and I've made a point of turning this (and other) devices off after running steadily for an hour and whereas drives in other units (including WD Reds, which I use often) are warm, while these are hot.

The problem for me is that price-wise you're not saving money with these: The disk-less version is usually about $190 on amazon and for that you can get the Synology DS213J, which has a great reputation, great reviews, and a nice quiet good-sized fan - and it seems more sturdily built.
Having said that, I've got another WD device like this and it hasn't failed yet, but then I've only had it online for about 8 months.

One thing I would mention: I would run this in "RAID 1" mode, which means that both drives are kept identical to each other: Updates are applied to both. This means that you only get 1 drive's worth of storage, but if one drive fails, you haven't lost your data. But that being the case, it makes far more sense (if you can swing the cost and need more than 2 TB of storage) to buy a unit with 3 or 4 TB drives, as the relative cost-per-gigabyte drops.

As for whether or not you're better off buying a unit with the drives already in it, or buying the unit and the drives separately, that varies with the weather: Right now, the prices are a wash, so you might as well get them with the unit, other times you save one way of the other.

All in all, I like this unit, but given the quality of the competition and the similarity in prices, I want a cooler-running unit. I am a vine reviewer and was given this unit to review. Would I buy it? No, I'd buy a Synology diskless and add WD drives. I've used D-Link in the past and thought they were fine too. I'd avoid Buffalo Technology like the plague - have had terrible problems with them, as have other people and their performance is sub-par. QNAP makes great stuff, but is way more expensive. (I should note that QNAP has a new 2-bay system that is under $200 diskless, but I know nothing about it. However, given that Synology has always been the one to beat in the consumer-priced space, I dunno....)

title: The best bang for buck video card at $250 price point
text:
Everyone once in a while one of those video cards come out that can overclock like mad and hit much above what it's supposed to..

At stock 7850 is actually pretty weak for a $250 card considering its next-gen. It's better than the somewhat cheaper geforce 560Ti but not by much. And it's slightly slower than 570. To make things worse it's not really much better than the previous gen Radeon 6950.

But the thing is amd has deliberately underclocked the 7850. That is because clock for clock the 7850 is only about 5% slower than the 7870. And the 7870 is a $300+ card. Surely, they couldn't allow the 7850 to have the higher 7870 clocks.

Here's the deal if you overclock this card it would pretty much lay to waste most video cards this side of the gtx580. And here's why:
1. 7850 scales VERY linearly with clock. That means if you overclock by 20% your real-world performance in games jumps by 20%.
2. 1050mhz (22% overclock) is pretty much guaranteed. There's not a single 7850 on the internet that couldn't do 1050 mhz.
3. I got one of the bad samples and ended up with a "bad" overclock of 1100 mhz 24/7 stable. Along with memory over clocks, i get 25-30% increase in frame rates compared to stock.
4. At those speeds the 7850 sails past the 570 and gives the 580 a run for its money. Its just unfair to compare it to the 560 Ti now.

A lot (but NOT all) of cards hit 1200 mhz. Beyond that the scaling is less linear. From 1200 mhz you'll only get a few fps for a huge increase in temps/power.

Simply put overclocked this really is the best video card at $250. If you don't you're throwing your money away. And there's no reason why you shouldn't.

If you're not overclocking you're missing out on 30% FREE performance. Please my friend, read up on overclocking and make the best of your money!

title: 3 Months In...
text:
I decided to use this system for a while before providing feedback. After about 3 months of 24/7 use, the system is performing well.

The Bad:
Out of the box, I discovered a dead cable for which I immediately contacted Swann customer service. They instructed me to simply email them with a copy of my invoice/receipt for the system (purchased through Amazon), with a description of the problem. After sending 3 different emails over the last several weeks, I've yet to receive a response. I have not yet called customer service back. Fortunately, I was able to source a quick replacement cable for little money through Amazon in the interim.

The picture quality is mediocre at best. The cameras are supposed to be full color, but they rarely display in color. 95% of the time the image is in grainy black and white regardless of lighting conditions (I've tried full natural light, partial natural light, total darkness, full synthetic light, and partial synthetic light). It doesn't seem to matter. The color adjustments through the DVR are of no use either.

The DVR interface is decent, though the remote control could be improved. Even with new batteries the remote doesn't seem to communicate with the DVR very well - I notice I have to press the buttons numerous times with greater than average pressure to get them to respond. The DVR is only about 6-7 ft. from my couch.

Aiming the cameras is difficult, as the setscrews intended to lock their position are laughable at best. I've had to reposition one of the cameras numerous times, and had to compromise on its position due to limitations in locking it into place where I want it - the set screws come loose and the camera moves. Also, the cameras have little shades that are supposed to slide back and forth to cover the lenses from direct light - they are extremely difficult to slide. I thought I was going to break one of the cameras just trying to move the shade about an inch.

The cables are fragile - I somehow damaged two of them while tacking them to the wall, though I have yet to determine where the damage occurred. I can't find any point where the cable insulation was compromised or kinked - they just stopped working.

I have not yet figured out how to get the motion feature to work so that the cameras only record when motion is detected. As of now, the system is recording 24/7.

I have not yet tried to setup the email feature to receive alert detection notifications. I'll add that to my review when/if I set that up and test it.

The Good:
The system was easy to set up, and required little effort to fine tune. The 65' cables are sufficiently long to cover my 3 story 1500 sq. ft. home with the DVR in a central location.

Networking was a little more involved than I anticipated, as I had to forward the ports for viewing over the internet and on my phone. Thankfully, a brief Google/YouTube search provided all the information I needed to assist with this. I had the system configured with two phones and 5 computers setup for remote viewing in just a couple of hours. The Android app is great, but only offers live viewing - there's no option that I can find for reviewing recordings on my phone (original HTC EVO 4G). The web application, however, does provide full functionality. The interface is easy and straightforward using a PC. The only drawback is that it is only supported in Internet Explorer, so you Firefox, Chrome, etc. users are out of luck unless you use IE to view your system.

The playback is good, with great options for indexing and searching.

Overall, this is a good entry-level system for the general user. The networking portion is not so easy, but with a little knowledge, some patience, and access to Google/YouTube it's not too bad. The cameras could be improved, but for the money, Swann delivers a good system for simple home/small business monitoring.

title: Simply the best low profile Intel cooler
text:
I've tested, written about and used many low profile coolers over the past couple of years building mini-ITX HTPC and office systems for clients including:

Silverstone NT07-1156
Gelid Slim Silence i-Plus
Titan DC-155A915Z/RPW

and this one is simply the best one out there under 37mm. First, the fan is the quietest among them all. Even the best still have a bit of a buzz but the Top Motor fan included on this one is smooth with no buzz. You have to put your ear within a foot of it with the top of the case open to hear anything. Second, the quality of this heatsink is the best. It's full copper and it comes with the thermal paste already applied. It's very heavy and easy to install with no backplate required. Third, and most important, it does a fantastic job keeping processors cool in these tiny little cases. I use it for builds in the Realan E-i5 (75mm high) and E-K3 (72mm tall) which are very small mini-ITX cases. For the E-K3, that the cooler uses the standard mounts is very important because the backplate on other coolers interferes with the VESA mount while the T459 does not interfere at all.

The only con is the way the fan is mounted. It's screwed into the heatsink from underneath meaning if it does fail and need to be changed, the heatsink will need to be removed.

For Intel builds in these mini-ITX cases I will use no other as long as these are available. I've found nothing quieter or better cooling in this size at this price. Perfect!

title: REVISED to 5 stars: Invellop product design: 5 stars...Invellop business practices: 1 star
text:
Revised (again!) on 4/15/12:
iPad 3 version arrived today and it works perfectly! This is the 1st case I've ever had (I've owned all three gens of iPad) that did ths piece of tech justice. Very highly reco this case.

----------------------------------
Revised on 3/16/12 @ 7:30 PM EST:

Haven't had this happen often - unfortunately - but this company actually surprised me. A couple of hours after my original post, I received an email from Invelop stating they had a true ipad3 compatible cover being released in 2 weeks and would ship to me as soon as available.

So, assuming the exchange for the new (fully iPad3 compatible) case goes well, I'm EXTREMELY happy with this case. As I said in my original review, the thing is gorgeous and offers a fair bit of protection with almost no bulk. It won't protect your case from a 4 foot drop onto concrete but for the day to day stuff, it's perfect and, again, it looks and feels great! Assuming the magnets on the new one they send work, I'll likely order a second in another color; they're that good and, at the price point, blow away every other case I've had for previous iPads.

-------------
ORIGINAL REVIEW:

First off: cover is gorgeous and exactly the feel and bulk I was looking for. No complaints on design at all - if you're buying this for an iPad 2.....

....which I didn't; I purchased it for the iPad3 that was arriving today. When I ordered the Invellop case 4 days ago, the description clearly stated that it was compatible with the new iPad. It's not: the magnets don't hold the cover closed and therefore do not activate the auto-on feature. A disclaimer has now been added by Invellop (some time over past 24-36 hours!) but it was fundamentally misleading to advertise this as an iPad 3 case.

Second issue with Invellop is misleading info regarding shipping cost; depending on where you look on their storefront, the cost for (expedited) shipping is anywhere from 4.99 to 8.99; I was charged the high end of that range and while $4 is a ridiculously insignificant amount to worry about in the context of an $800 electronics purchase, the misleading nature of the shipping policy is what is concerning.

I emailed the company to question both of these issues and received a prompt but surprisingly dismissive response; basically the message was, 'you should have waited until after you received your ipad3 before ordering a case'. Not sure how to even respond to that.

title: Beats Popular Brands for Globetrotters and Seasoned Travelers
text: I bought this power strip so that I could simultaneously charge my notebook, camera battery, iPad and Galaxy S5, without having to worry about power surges, particularly in developing countries.  There are two things I love about this power strip that I could not find in other popular products.  First, it is rated to be used for 100 volts (e.g., in North America) to 250 volts (e.g., in Southeast Asia).  Second, one USB is labeled for 2.4 amps (e.g, for tablet charging), and the other for 1.0 amps (e.g., for smartphone charging).  The similar popular items I've seen are only rated for approximately 110 volts, and can simultaneously charge an iPad and smartphone together, but very slowly.  I tested this power strip out on a 6-week holiday in Canada, followed by a business trip to Southeast Asia.  It performed exactly as expected.  I never even had to use my travel adapters for my mobile gadgets since I could plug the USB cables directly into the USB ports.  Of course, I  never blew the fuse, because the strip was intended for use in both 110 and 220 volt environments.  I highly recommend this for globetrotters and seasoned travelers who must have their gadgets functioning at all times.

I have read reviews for this amp and it was mentioned that a good processor was needed to hear its full potential, well now I have it. I love internet radio and have set my favorites, some stations audio is lesser than others but that is to be expected. I can play my itunes library through the AV 7701 but the only issue is my desktop is in another room and when I start play the volume is very loud on the AV. I believe there are setting I can make to control all of this from The AV.

Finally after all of this joy :) I'v yet to run Audyssey set-up. I guess I forgot, all that fuss about not having XT 32 Audyssey. I have yet to hear it, but I'm loving this Marantz AV 7701 unit.
Don't hesitate to step into the world of separate audio components you can't go wrong.

CC

Edit: 11/21/12 Finally ran Audyssey, here are the results:

I ran Audyssey twice last night with advice from you forum members and also refering to the Audyssey forum. Adjusted sub woofer volume from previous level of 12 o' clock (resulted in high negative trim -12db) to 3 o'clock (new result trim -8db). Ideally, final sub trim should be somewhere between -3.5db and +3.5db. So I lowered sub volume to about 5 o'clock ( about 2.0 on volume control) and the sub trim result is -2.5db which was good enough for me. I stored all of this, then went to manual speaker adjustmment and changed front speaker size to small and change crossover from 40 to 60hz.

The results are now fantastic. Listened to several CD's and I'm hearing more detail than ever. Vocals have a more natural tone and are smoother, I tested this by switching back and worth (Audyssey on/off). Listen to Parliament "Clones of Dr. Funk" cd, and I can clearly pick out one instrument and follow throughout the recording. Could have stayed up all night jammin Cd's with this new profound sound .
