title: Sturdy, Durable and Reliable
text:
My family and I like to travel a lot. In preparation for our Europe trip to 10 Euro countries in May 2013, I have another brand of adapter plug set but thought 1 set of adapter plug set is not enough for the electronic gadgets we are bringing so I have decided to buy another set. After extensive research, I have decided to purchase the Travel Smart by Conair M-500E Polarized Adapter Plug Set. After I received the product, I like what I saw and decided to purchase an additional adapter set so I have 3 sets total for our trip. The adapter plug is well built, elegant and does not look cheap.

The adapters have labels on them so you would know which adapter you need to use on a specific country. Here are the following adapters contained in the set:
Adapter 1 works on Great Britain, Ireland, Africa, Hong Kong, Singapore. (It has a metal third pin as ground)
Adapter 2 works on North America, South America, Japan, Caribbean
Adapter 3 works on Northern Europe
Adapter 4 works on Southern Europe, Middle East, Africa, Asia, Carribean
Adapter 5 works on Australia, New Zealand, Fiji, China

These adapters will work on 110V or 220V outlets but do they DO NOT convert voltage from 110V to 220V nor from 220V to 110V so if you are electronic gadgets work on 110V only then you may need to purchase voltage converter to 220V and vice-versa. I have tested these plug adapters in my laptop power adapter, DSLR battery chargers, rechargeable battery chargers, iphone/ipad chargers, kindle charger, other cellphone chargers with all of them have DUAL voltage (meaning these gadgets will work on both 110V and 220V outlets) and they all worked like a charm. The adapters fit perfectly on the outlets of the countries I have visited.

I will only mention the Euro countries that I have tested/used the adapters during our trip. The UK adapter worked like a charm in our London hotel. The Northern Europe adapter worked very well in France, Belgium, Germany, Austria. The Southern Europe adapter also worked well in Italy. Take note that the Northern Europe adapter and the Southern Europe adapter may look the same at first glance but they are different. I was unable to test these adapters with the other Euro countries we visited as we just went there for a sightseeing day trips but I believe these adapters will worked in the other Euro countries like Holland, Luxembourg, Czech Republic, Switzerland, etc.

I highly recommend this polarized adapter plug set!!!

title: Very, very nice!!
text:
I have two pairs of the "little brother" to these, the DV62si's, and like them a lot. These are even better!

These speakers are very Klipsch-like in their sound and performance, and that's a good thing being that I am a Klipsch fan (except for the price). I compared these to a pair of Klipsch B-3's, and these actually sound better. They have a similar sound, but minus the shrillness that some of the early Klipsch Synergy series had (I think they fixed that later on, my F-30's don't have that problem). Compared to the DV62s, these are much better balanced with less harshness from the tweeters.The bass response is slightly better than the DV62's as well. Interestingly; the FH's claim a higher sensitivity than the DV's (96 vs. 90). But the DV's play louder at a given wattage. Granted, I don't yet have near the break-in time on these as I do the DV's, so that might change. I will follow up after a month or so. These are more directional than the DV's as well, no doubt because of the horn loading.

IMO, these sound better than the comparable Klipsch Synergy speakers. Some compare them to the Klipsch Reference line; I was not able to do a side-by-side comparison, but I would expect them to fair well in such a contest.

Make no mistake, these are solidly audiophile grade speakers. I find them to be wonderfully balanced and accurate, and the imaging is excellent. There is none of the ear fatigue that is sometimes present with horn tweeters. They are bright, but pleasantly bright if that makes any sense. Forget the big name brands; there is nothing on the shelves of the big box stores that will better these, regardless of price. I have not heard a better sounding set of bookshelf speakers anywhere.

I strongly recommend these.

Good listening!

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

--Long Term Update--

I've had these for about 5 months now and I play them hard every weekend. They are in my workshop, and I drive them with a large PA amp. I am using 100-150 watts per channel on them and they have taken it in stride. It's clean power, mind you.

Put simply...these are some of the best sounding speakers I own! Extremely well balanced speakers with just the right amount of every frequency. I run them almost flat on the EQ, which is usually a sign of a balanced speaker. I do use a 12" powered sub along with them because I play them loud with lots of bass in my shop.

The cabinets are not the best looking that I've seen; but certainly not ugly. But the drivers are quite attractive with the cover off.

There are no speakers I know of at anywhere near the price that will touch them. They sound better than Klipsch Synergy speakers, and at less money. I have heard some compare them to the Klipsch Reference line, but I have not been able to test them personally. I suspect they would compare well though.

Regardless...these are solidly audiophile grade speakers. And for budget prices.

Buy them, you will be glad.

title: Good not Great-3.5 stars
text:
I won't get to technical since there are quite a few photo websites (try Photozone or DXO Mark) that have full reviews/testing on this lens.

I got the lens for use on a 2nd body, currently a refurb Canon T2i. The lens is not a top performer BUT it is certainly not priced in that range either. And this lens does produce very good images. To be honest, much better images than I expected for an extended zoom in this price range. The IS works well. The focusing is not a quick as some & at times it does search (see below*) but I would still rate its focus as better than average up to 200mm. And the optics do seem to be better than you would expect for a long zoom in this price range. Although again, beyond 200mm sharpness, etc. seem to fall off.

If you're not really happy with the typical extended zoom that Canon seems to be including in their kits now-a-days (the 55-250 mm or the 75-300 - w/ or w/o USM) AND you don't have the money or inclination to go with the 70-200mm L series- give this one a try. You won't drop a bundle and you'll get better results than with the bottom end lens. If you don't like it you can sell it on amazon or ebay and get most or all of your money back, as long as you shop around & you're careful what you pay for it, to use for a different lens.

*The lens sometime had difficulty focusing beyond 200mm & if the image was some distance off and/or did not stand out. If you run into this you can overcome this as long as you don't mind an extra step or two. Try focusing on something fairly similar but only about half the distance away. Once your camera & lens has pulled in & processed that info, then try focusing again the your actual subject. I know that sounds like a pain, and certainly won't work in a sports situation, but it does typically get you a better image when your camera processor & lens just can't pick up what you're after.

******
As an fyi, I've since sold this lens. I bought the Canon 70-200mm f/4L & ended up using that much more then this lens. Both the optics & focusing of the 70-200f4L are far superior. I recommend that lens over the 70-300mmis IF you do not need IS (I do a lot of shooting on a tripod now so I no longer use IS as much as I used to) & the extra 100mm isn't essential (ie. birding). Although, as I've indicated, I don't think the extra 100mm you pick up w/ the 70-300mm is really a sweet spot for the lens. You can pick up a refurbished Canon 70-200mm f/4L at Canon USA for about $400 if you wait for a good sale. The extra $50 is well worth it as long as you can do without the IS, etc.

Also, I owe a small apology to the Canon 55-250mm is. I picked up a refurb at Canon, on sale for about $120, & tested it w/ the T2i. It is DEFINITELY a cheap lens but it seems to do just as well as the 70-300mmis (again, only up to about 200mm). The optics and focusing seem incredibly similar. I don't use it very often but after spending only $120 for it, I don't think I'll be getting rid of it anytime soon. & it does give me peace of mind. When I'm forced to loan out my back up camera, this is one of the lens (along w/ the 18-55 kit lens) I loan out with it. So if you don't want spend 350-500 for the 70-300mmis or 400-500 for a refurb 70-200f4L, you may want to take a look @ the 55-250mmis jic. You can pick it up here or on Craigslist very reasonably.

The ptz feature of this camera is awesome and works great! However, while this camera says it is HD, the HD does not work over USB. Because it is only USB 2.0 and the camera does not compress the images well the USB bus can't handle the amount of data the camera is trying to send when you try to use high definition. This was especially the case when we were using Ustream. The frame rate would drop to 1 fps or less if we tried anything over 240p and if we tried to go up to 720p the USB bus would stop responding and give us errors. It's unfortunate that this camera does not work like the Logitech c920 as that camera will do high def over USB 2.0. I don't know how they manage it over USB 2.0, but it works (unlike this camera).

Now, when I called customer service they were very friendly and helpful even though they couldn't get the camera to work for me. title: Full modular joy but with one very annoying problem!
text: I really wanted to like this power supply but, as has been noted by several other reviewers it has fan noise problems. This is particularly unforgiveable since one of its marketing points is "Quiet 2-ball Bearing Fan for near-silent operation". However, that is not remotely accurate. The first one we bought had a constant ticking noise as well as high-pitched whine. The whine wasn't too bad but the ticking was far too noticeable and made it louder than every other fan in the PC - even when the 2 CPU and 2 GPU fans were running at full throttle. Even worse is the PSU fan runs all the time, even when the system is idle - something that other Gold certified power supplies don't do since the high efficiency means they produce very little residual heat. But if you have a PSU (like this one) with a noisy fan when the rest of the system is idling and relatively quiet, it is very obvious and very irritating. Amazon sent a replacement and that one was even worse. Between that and the several other reviews about this problem, it's clear EVGA is using a poor quality fan in the NEX650G - perhaps even the entire SuperNOVA lineup. If they would address these fan issues they'd have a real winner. It's fully modular with good quality cables - although oddly only 1 of the 4 VGA cables has double plugs for higher end GPUs. I really think 2 of the 4 should be that type. I appreciate the fact that EVGA makes an effort to respond to problems posted here and on other retail sites - although it is unknown if they actually go the extra mile when communicating outside the public eye. I also appreciate the free warranty extension offered when the product is registered; however, I believe that if they truly had their customer's best interests at heart they would simply make the longer warranty standard since, obviously, a lot of people either won't even be aware of the extension or will forget to register. Regardless, when/if EVGA releases a revision of this PSU with a MUCH better fan and thermal circuitry which leaves it off until actually needed, I'd be happy to recommend it. But, at this point, I would have to suggest going elsewhere unless you aren't bothered by it having a fan which I can honestly say is the noisiest I have ever heard in any PC power supply.

title: Quality with simplicity
text: The Yamaha A-S500 has restored my joy in listening. I started out building my own Dynakit stereo equipment in the '60s but had tried to "modernize" the last few years. Two different consumer-grade AV receivers had left me feeling frustrated listening to music. The digital conveniences were great (such as switching all the HDMI sources, etc.), but the audio sections were just plain anemic. The highs were missing in action and the lows had no guts (unless I used a good quality powered sub I have - and even then, there was a hole between the super-lows and the mid-bass). In addition, there were no loudness controls on either AV receiver, making low volume listening rather lackluster. I had even tried replacing my large, '70s vintage floor-standing speakers thinking that they might be aging or out of date. WRONG! All along, the problem was with the low-current power supplies and digital over-processing in the AV receivers. Swapping the A-S500 for the most recent AV receiver brought the excitement of hi-fi listening back into my living room. Even my (slightly) aging ears can hear the highs again and the lows will "tickle your innards." Clarity is back and I now remember what dynamic range is. The response throughout the frequency range is smooth without coloration. It's hard to explain how pleased I am with the A-S500.

title: Excellent headphones for the gym
text:
I am a casual audiophile and own a few pairs of high-end headphones, including Bose QC2s and a couple different variants of Monster's Turbine series. At the gym, however, I usually use less expensive models that fit more securely and are sweat resistant. I use headphones mainly while doing cardio on the treadmill or elliptical machines, and like many people, get annoyed by having the cord of the headphones bouncing around particularly while jogging. On the other hand, securing the cord too much means restricting where my ipod can be placed and how easy it is to access.

These headphones are a great solution. They fit securely, seem sweat resistant, and are lightweight and comfortable. Although there is still a short cord, it isn't nearly as objectionable as wired headphones and I barely notice it. The sound quality is advertised as "non-fatiguing" and, from what I can tell comparing them to my home headphones, what this means is a warm sound with extra bass and mid-range, and less high frequency detail. I certainly would not consider these audiophile-grade, but for the gym where I often need to crank the volume and portable audio gear can get rather harsh sounding, their sound tuning is appropriate and welcome.

I took one star off the review for a few minor shortcomings. The battery is small and I need to remember to charge them at least once every few gym visits -- they would be useless in situations where they are being used regularly for hours at a time. The quality on phone calls doesn't compare to a dedicated bluetooth headset with noise cancellation. Finally, like most in-ear headphones, the fit can be finicky and I had to experiment to find the right combination of ear tips and restraining clips that gave me a secure fit without going so deep and tight in the ear as to cause "booming" from footsteps on the treadmill (anyone who has run with ear buds probably knows what I am talking about).

I've only had them for a few weeks so I can't comment on long-term reliability, but otherwise I completely recommend these as great workout headphones.

title: Excellent pace, clarity, presence, balance
text:
Context: I've been a Sennheiser headphone audiophile since the release of the HD580s way back when. Have the HD650 as well, really a benchmark headphone. Have had excellent speakers my whole adult life, too. And am a musician. I know what music sounds like live.

I approached earbuds and iPhone lossy digital music with trepidation. My initial experiences were not encouraging, iPhone 3 era.

But now, fast-forward to 2013 and, I'm sold. Have Sennheiser's near-top IEMs, and they are fabulous. Started appreciating IEMs with Shure's E2s, which seemed the right price for iTunes music years ago. What they lacked in both the basses and highs, the sense of air you get with great headphones, they more than made up for in mid-range clarity and presence. Excellent for casual listening in an environment where I'm doing something else along with listening to music (which I rarely do, preferring complete focus).

I listen to everything, classical extensively, rap and electronic dance, country, music from around the world, you name it. I'm listening to Daft Punk's latest as I type this.

The SE315s are, well, just perfect. Not only is there a presence to the sound, the bass is TIGHT, which matters way more to me than sheer thump and volume. The transients, which are what I love hearing clearly the most, because they're where the life of a musical sound lives, are precise, and energetic, and free of distortion. This is what gives the SE315s that sense of being able to reveal things you haven't heard before.

No disrespect to the Sennheiser IEMs; they are very neutral as well, and I love 'em, but they're not as rugged as these, so I save them for special listening sessions.

At less than half the price of those, these are perfect all-rounders. I'm not sure I'd use them to master an album, but maybe that's just pretense on my part; the more I listen, the more I'm amazed.

The sign of a good IEM, and not just because of the isolation, is that you can turn the music DOWN and still hear everything.

In my experience, only these and the IE8s have accomplished this for earbuds. The top of the line Etymotics, as well.

But the SE315s are what I'll take with me everywhere. I look forward to many years of pleasure and reliability from them.

title: I love this camcorder
text:
The M500 is a steal for $350. It has the Canon HD CMOS Pro Image Sensor, the same sensor as the more expensive G10. The larger than average sensor means great low light performance. Set aperture priority and get ready for beautiful shallow depth of field on close ups with available light. The image stabilization is so smooth, it makes panning with my cheap tripod much better.

Super lightweight and small. 3.5 mm mic in, headphone out. If you don't feel like dealing with AVCHD, just use the MP4 setting. I like having the option since a free program like MPEG Streamclip can quickly convert MP4 to Apple Intermediate for use in FCP7. MP4 is limited to 30 minute files so use AVCHD for longer takes.

Good battery life but DO NOT record until the battery runs out. I accidentally did this and the file system on the SD card was corrupted, had to use file recovery software. This is probably the case with any SD card camcorder. It'd be nice if the software shut the camera down BEFORE it has zero power left.

I paid $500 early last year and felt it was worth the price. Now I want to buy another, it'd be great to have two for shooting live performances, which it does well due to the low light capabilities. Obviously it doesn't have the manual pro controls of a $1000 camcorder, but it's got the sensor and even the auto setting gives great results. For the price you can't go wrong.

title: Great sound but connecting to an amp's output requires more gear
text:
Short Version: The HD-DAC1 (DAC1) has great sound, cannot accept analog audio input from an amplifier without a level controller, and had trouble with the signals from one of my TVs, producing regular popping sounds reminiscent of a vinyl record with a scratch on it. (I place more blame on the TV.)

Long Version: I bought the DAC1 to replace two boxes in my best stereo/TV system, an Arcam rDAC-kw (rDAC) and a simple stereo receiver which only provided headphone functionality. My integrated amplifier is analog-only and does not have a headphone jack. When the DAC1 arrived, however, I tried it with my secondary stereo/TV system. Playing the cable box thru HDMI to the Samsung plasma TV (model PN51F5300B, purchased this August) and thru optical cable into the DAC1, I noticed regular popping sounds very similar to the sound from an old vinyl record with a scratch on it. Testing ruled out bad cables, long signal paths, and TV or cable box settings (please use plain PCM stereo, uncompressed). The DAC1 worked fine with the Sony TV in my best system; no pops. Conclusion: The DAC1 is intolerant of something in this particular Samsung TV's signal. This was confirmed when I used the rDAC in its place. The sound is pop-free. Score one for Arcam! This Samsung model has factory fresh software, is totally "dumb", cannot be connected to the internet, and Samsung refused to send me a USB stick with a software update. Since the rDAC works fine with it, I'm OK. Time will tell if other users see this problem. (Try a software update of the TV if you do.) Since I hear similar pops when I pause or fast forward my DVR, my hunch is that the circuits for signal drop out and reacquisition are somehow in play when processing the Samsung's signals.

The second issue is that the DAC1's analog input expects a low level input (from a smartphone or portable player), and the headphone output is distorted when connected with my amp's "Line Out". I bought a "remote level control" from an auto stereo store, two male-to-male RCA couplers, and an RCA to 3.5mm adapter plug to get this connection working. Total extra cost, $40. Other headphone amplifiers out there have much better connectivity with amps. This is a design flaw in my opinion. Valuable real estate on the back panel that could have been used for RCA inputs rigged to accept amplifier level input was instead used for a Marantz external remote control hookup. This connection can only be of value for die-hard Marantz groupies or Marantz corporate executives showing off the DAC1 to big-money stockholders at a cocktail party. The Marantz design engineers missed on this issue, (or got overruled by their bosses).

The sound from the DAC1 is wonderful. I prefer it to the rDAC as the DAC1 has slightly stronger bass. I prefer my Primare CD player's sound to having it's digital output played through the DAC1, but there is no shame in that. Average quality CD players and probably 90% of blu-ray players playing CDs will see greatly improved sound with the DAC1 doing the conversion to analog. Ripping CD's to a computer and playing that through the DAC1 might perform even better, but I will leave the DAC1's performance with computers for others to evaluate.

Bottom line. The great sound of the HD-DAC1 outweighs the connectivity design flaws and hopefully rare source signal quality intolerance issues described above. I am happy with this machine.

Again, none of this is documented, so you're on your own. Unless you want to solder headers on, the easiest way to add sensors may be to control it via serial or I2C with another microcontroller that has sensors.

If you just want to build non-interactive displays, the unit is great. Its real strength is the Raindowduino library. Not mucking about with figuring out the pin combinations for each pixel, just XY coordinates and 24bit color codes.

title: AF Not Accurate
text:
I used LensAlign and FocusTune to test this lens. The lens was mounted to an Arca-Swiss Z1G (giant) monoball and Gitzo 5000 series carbon-fiber legs, at a height of 42 inches. The ISO was 1600 and the shutter speed was 1/320. The lens-to-target distance was 26 feet and I used a shutter release. The camera body was a Nikon D4 that last week came back from Nikon NY after being adjusted for a back-focusing issue. For an overview of the lens AF performance, I took 4 shots at each micro-adjustment value from minus 20 to plus 20 in steps of 5 units. Based on the first tests and to look for the peak in the curve, I took 9 shots at each micro-adjustment value from plus 10 to plus 20 in steps of 2 units. Both curves go up from left to right, but do not come down. That is, there is no peak. This lens is focusing in front of the target by greater than 20 micro-adjustment units.
Why did Nikon ship such an expensive lens that is so far out of adjustment?
Can Nikon's Quality Control be this bad?

title: A Handy Device
text:
Quite a useful and versatile device. I ordered two, one to keep in the house and one to keep in my truck. The unit comes with four different connectors to attach to various devices. But, you really don't need them since most items are USB plugs nowadays. The device isn't going to power larger devices, but it IS handy for re-charging things using cell-phone style batteries, cameras which charge via USB, MP3 players, etc. In this mode, you can use re-chargeable and regular batteries in it. The instructions do say that it will recharge your device a little slower than the OEM charger that came with your device. This is the optimal setting they found without having the batteries over-heat.

Other than the above, you can charge AA and AAA re-chargeable batteries like a "normal" battery charger. With the one I'm keeping in my truck, I leave a set of 4 AA in a baggie. This gives me an emergency charger, and a set of re-chargeable AA batteries, that I can keep near no matter where I go. It charges 4 AA batteries in the same amount of time as my regular charger, and the push button switch makes it easy to go from charging the AA batteries to charging a device I plug it into.

I don't give it 5 stars because the instructions aren't especially clear, nor do they explain that there's a little "lever" over each pair of battery slots you must lift to seat the batteries in the device. Overall, though, this is worth the cost and will be handy to have around.

WARNING: If you're charging AA/AAA batteries with this device, rather than using them TO charge another device, then do NOT leave the batteries in this device too long after the light turns green (signifying their charge is complete). The AA/AAA batteries you just charged will begin to over-heat a LOT, bad enough it's like touching a hot pan when you try to remove the batteries.

Some reviewers say that you can build a better one on your own... Not quite.

I bought this to power small electronics in my new home in Africa. National Power is spotty where I'm at, leaving us with dark nights, etc. Also, I needed something portable to take to my office or to the rural villages if needed.

This battery has kept several low watt lamps going and all our small electronics, even a laptop. If you're smart about power management, you can make this thing really last on one charge. (Hint: use it to power your laptop when the laptop battery is at 100%, drawing only 10-13 watts/hour all day. Then use the laptop battery if/when the extreme is low. If you plug in a laptop's low/dead battery, it draws 65 watts/hr to charge it in 2-3 hours, but the heavy draw may trigger the extreme's battery safeguard when the extreme gets to about 20-40%.)

As for the build your own comment, the other reviewer was oversimplifying it. Just like any hobby/industry, there's the engineering types that swear they can do it better themselves. Maybe when the price was at $300, but now with it priced at $208, I don't think so. He left out quite a few components that I have come to view as necessary (AC input, etc)

Plus, that reviewer was missing one of the best features, the portability of this unit. The setup he talked about is not portable at all. This product is the equivalent of a laptop when that home made one is the equivalent of a desktop computer. Same performance, much different functionality and use.

If you're looking to turn your house solar, this may not be the best product. But if you're looking for small scale, portable, and VERY EASY TO USE, then Goal Zero is your best bet. Why? Because that is what they designed it for. Clearly. And at this price, its the best option in my mind.

title: Ideal for my needs
text:
This is the first LG product that I ever bought and I am quite impressed by the overall value it offers. For a selling price of $219 at COSTCO, this is a lower tier monitor because some of the high end ones sell at more than twice this amount. Despite the price tag, it delivers almost everything good models offer and more.

FUNCTIONALITY/ERGONOMICS:
I needed a monitor that could accommodate two windows at a very good resolution at the same time. I had a Dell 24 inch monitor, but it was not ideally suited for the job. Larger screen sizes come with height as well as width because of the traditional 16:9 aspect ratio. If you work long hours in front of a screen (which most people do these days) and are viewing two documents, it can give you neck/spondylitis issues if the monitor is at or higher than your eye level. Moving the neck up and down to view the entire document is not the best way to go about it. Ideally you should be looking 15 degrees or so below your eye level. The wider screen with 21:9 aspect ration layout lets you achieve that. You can open two windows at the same time that are easy to see and work with. Each window is 1280x1080 resolution- the highest you can get in this size. The screen only tilts to give you the best viewing angle. It does not move up and down. You will have to adjust your chair height if that is an issue. I found no need for this adjustment as long as your table height is correct for the chair. The monitor is only few inches above the table creating the perfect height level for me.

PICTURE/SOUND QUALITY:
This has a LED/IPS screen. Being LED, it is very thin and being IPS it has much better color accuracy and quality, as well as much wider viewing angle. Whether you can look down at it or across, there is no distortion in color or display. The screen is edge to edge with a very thin bezel at the bottom. You need to be EXTRA careful when opening the box and taking the screen out as you can damage the LED panel with the pressure from your finger or thumb. I have not compared this to other monitors in this class, but the overall picture quality is quite good. If you are using it for graphics design, this may not be for you. It also has built-in stereo speakers. The speaker quality is good, not great. If you want some real audio kick, you will need external speakers. It has outlets for both external speakers and headphones.

CONNECTIVITY:
It has plenty of input modes- HDMI (two) for connecting two laptops at the same time. It also has DVI-D and DP inputs with audio input for complete viewing and listening experience. No VGA, but that is not needed these days anyway. VGA output devices may not support this resolution anyway.

Overall, a great monitor for those who have a need to display two application windows at the same time. Single screen users may initially find this unnecessary waste of real estate and some money, but may end up finding this format more useful. After using this monitor for just few days, I like the idea of being able to see my desktop items while working on an application window. Highly recommend this product for the layout and format.

title: Price and Speed (D4)
text:
I'm being generous with a 4 star rating but I don't believe it deserves three stars either.

The good:
* It's compact and does what it claims to do.

The bad:
* It's expensive for something that should be built in to most cameras
* It doesn't support AGPS like most cell phones. This would help provide quicker position lock when the sky is obstructed
* The cable is a bit long for mounting on the hot shoe

Tips:
* If you use the adapter to locate the GP-1 on the camera strap, make sure you get a signal lock before moving around. The strap adapter isn't convenient but it give you back the use of the hot shoe.
* I find it helpful to wait for a signal lock before going about my shoot. Even if the GP-1 drops it's signal lock, you'll still get the position data
* If you don't get a lock, it sometimes helps to turn the camera off then back on and try again.

I've encountered odd behavior with this unit. While in India visiting the Taj Mahal, I could not get a lock despite having clear blue skies and no obstructions while out of doors. I stood still with the GP-1 mounted on the hot shoe but no matter what I did or how long I waited, I couldn't get a lock. The next day in another location I could get a lock almost immediately.

If the Nikon made a Bluetooth adapter that would use the AGPS from a smartphone, I would expect better performance at the expense of rapid battery drain from the cell phone.

Conclusion: The GP-1 is finicky and overpriced but it works. The unit is small and doesn't get in the way (unless you need the hot shoe). The cable is longer and most rigid than I would like. I feel like the GP-1 uses 10-15 year old technology and for the price, I would love to see more from Nikon. Don't expect this to get a rapid GPS signal like your cell phone that uses AGPS and you won't get a signal indoors, around tall buildings, or under a heavy tree canopy. I haven't encountered excessive batter drain with the GP-1 on the camera. The GP-1 seems to compromise in a lot of areas but at a premium price.

title: What an Amazing Piece of Technology!
text:
Samsung sure has changed my opinion of them with this TV. In other reviews of this product, Samsung apparently lost a fan or two, but they have a new one here. Based on some of the initial reviews I was sure skeptical about how this TV would perform. To pay a premium for a new technology that could potentially make some things worse, like adding blurring, fuzzy text, etc. is just completely unacceptable. After a very thorough and extensive review, I just don't see how those other reviews can be accurate. My personal experience with this TV is polar opposite. This TV makes everything better, and nothing worse.

I'll share what components I tested this TV with in a minute. First, let's get through some of the details. As others have noted, this TV is easy to put together and perform initial setup. The included stand is minimalist, involving three pieces and 8 total screws. You can have this put together in less than 5 minutes. You might need a hand taking the TV out of the box and putting it up on a mount or cabinet. The TV weighs 75lbs with its stand. Wish #1: I wish the TV could swivel on the stand, but it can't. Long term I will probably invest in an articulating wall mount.

Cabling it is also very simple. Just like any other TV except that the connectivity into the TV has been uncoupled from the TV itself, and lives in a separate box called the One Connect. All of your connections are made to the One Connect, which then attaches to the panel with a single 10 foot cable. This makes wall mounting the system a snap, and brings the connectivity closer to the devices for easy maintenance. I agree with another reviewer, this should be the new standard for TV's. Just awesome. Wish #2: I wish the power cord was longer than 5 feet. When I invest in the wall mount, I will probably have an electrician put an outlet behind where the TV mounts so power cord length is a non-issue.

The initial setup is guided by Samsung's very easy and intuitive user interface. You can easily be watching TV within 5 minutes of powering on. The TV comes with two remote controls. One is a standard remote control, and the other is more like the touch-pad on a laptop. Very modern, very smart. I was also able to successfully use U-verse guided remote control setup so that my U-verse remote controls the Samsung TV power, mute, volume, etc. I tried numerous U-verse codes, and none of them worked. The U-verse guided setup basically keeps guessing until it gets it right, and it finally set it up perfectly. Internet connectivity is also easy to set up. The TV supports both wireless and connected LAN. I happen to use powerline networking rather than wireless because I get better performance that way. I was actually able to stream UHD video samples from YouTube flawlessly. The TV allows you to customize the IP settings, choose DNS, Gateway, etc. I was able to setup OpenDNS and Google safe search so the TV Internet browser was much safer for our kids, which I like a lot.

So I mentioned earlier that I believe the TV makes everything better, and nothing worse. I tested the TV with the following components that I believe are typical of what most people will have:
1) U-verse DVR capable of outputting both 720p and 1080i via HDMI
2) 5 Year old Sharp Blu-ray player capable of outputting 1080p via HDMI
3) Wii U capable of outputting 1080p gaming via HDMI
4) Brand new "Samsung BD-F7500 4K Upscaling 3D Wi-Fi Blu-ray Disc Player" capable of outputting both 1080p and 4K via HDMI. I just bought this from Amazon for the sole purpose of testing an up-scaling 4K Blu-ray player with a 4K capable TV.

I tested each of the above components on my previous TV, which is a "LG Cinema Screen 55LM7600 55-Inch Cinema 3D 1080p 240Hz LED-LCD HDTV", -AND- this TV, the "Samsung UN55F9000 55-Inch 4K Ultra HD 120Hz 3D Smart LED TV". My LG TV currently retails for about $1500, but when I acquired it, it was a $2200 TV. I had both TV's, old and new, right next to each other on separate stands. Same Height, same size, same component inputs, etc.

Test #1 - U-verse everyday TV watching. This should be similar in quality to other cable and satellite providers. They may even have higher resolution, so your results could be even better. We watched more than 15 hours of various programming from our U-verse DVR, which is set to 1080i. The difference between this Samsung TV and our old LG TV was very noticeable. We watched animated content, sports, news, etc. In each case this TV always looked better than our old one, and it was unanimous across all 5 family members. We would play content from the DVR on the new TV, and then replay it 10 seconds later on the old one or vice versa. We even paused programs on one TV, and then switched over to view the paused program on other one. Again, this TV is superior in every case. Text is razor sharp and crystal clear. We couldn't find any motion blur at all, no matter how hard we tried. A golf ball in midflight on our old LG TV would actually have a second ball shadow in midair, and on this TV there was none. It's crystal clear. I dialed my U-verse receiver back to the default 720p, and it had a minor negative impact, most noticeable in fine details like text, grass, fabric, etc.

Test #2 - Regular 1080p Blu-ray output from a regular Blu-ray player. The Samsung UN55F9000 was superior in both regular non-Blu-ray DVD playback -AND- Blu-ray 1080p playback. I used animated content and nature content (Planet Earth). The Samsung really excels when a scene is dark and there are numerous subtle shades of black and grey. We used to have to close all of the shades in our media room when watching a dark movie like some of the Harry Potter or LOTR movies. The Samsung TV provides a much more clear and vibrant picture. Its handling of black is Plasma-like in quality. This is a vast improvement. We watched lots of content over and over again on both TV's, and the Samsung was the unanimous favorite.

Test #3 - Wii U (1080P Gaming). The Samsung UN55F9000 didn't significantly improve older Wii games from the 480p resolution days, but it didn't make them worse either. The few actual Wii U games we have that were designed for 1080P were greatly improved in terms of sharpness, color, and sound as well. One thing people forget about is that TV's make sound too. Some TV's make poor sound, and so then you go buy a sound bar or use a home theater system. This TV actually has very good sound. Good enough that I may neglect to hook up the sound bar we were using with our LG TV.

Test #4 - Up-scaling 4K Blu-ray Player. With reports from other reviewers that the TV struggled with blurring when up-scaling content, I thought a useful test would be to see if doing the up-scaling before it entered the TV would make a difference. My experience after comparing the two options is that there is no discernible difference between Up-scaling in the DVD player and sending 4K to the TV, or sending 1080p to the TV and letting it upscale to 4K. Both look really excellent. The TV recognizes Up-scaled content from the DVD player and reports it as such. A quick side-note on 3D, since this Blu-ray player is 3D capable. The 3D glasses that come with the Samsung UN55F9000 TV (model SSG-5100GB) are active, meaning they have a battery. They are very comfortable to wear. The TV comes with 4 of them, but extras are only $18 on Amazon. I already ordered another one since we are a family of 5. 3D performance is really excellent. The combination of the higher resolution and active 3D is a significant improvement over our other LG set. Historically we never really bought or rented much 3D content since we felt we had to sacrifice clarity for the 3D experience. That's not the case with this TV. You can have both 3D and clear at the same time. We will definitely rethink how we rent and buy movies going forward. Some of the newer DVD packs come with 3D, Blu-ray, and regular DVD media all in one, which is appealing.

So after all of this testing, I asked myself "Is the Samsung UN55F9000 really this good, or did my LG TV just suck?" To get a better idea of this, I took a field trip to Fry's Electronics to see a whole bunch of TV's up close. What I found was that the 4K UHD TV sets by both Samsung and Sony are superior to all of the regular 1080p TVs. It becomes really apparent when you are able to see the same content, at the same time, right next to each other. UHD TVs have much better resolution, better grey/black handling, and better fine grain detail. It's noticeable. Is it life changing? Probably not, but you can't say it's not a better picture, because it is. I found an LG TV similar to my old one, and I'm happy to say that it didn't suck. It wasn't quite as good as the Samsungs and Sonys, but it held its own with pretty much everything else on display. The 65" version of this Samsung 4K UHD TV that was on display had the best picture of every TV there. Even better than the UHD Sony. So don't be afraid that because your current TV is awesome, this one can't be better, because it is. (most likely) One additional note...if you are considering a very large LED panel for a home theater (70" and above), go see them first. They don't look very good in 1080p. Having 4K UHD will really help the large LED panels have the resolution they need for their large size.

So what are you paying for when you buy a TV like this?
1) A premium because you are an early adopter of new technology. At the time of this writing, the premium you are paying is about $500 vs. the 8000 series Samsung sets, which are comparable minus the UHD 4K aspect.
2) You are paying for and getting a better picture
3) You are paying for investment protection. 4K DVD players are coming out. The new XBOX One can output 4K. 4K movies are downloadable in some cases. It's just a matter of time before Blu-ray disks start showing up in 4K format.
4) The Smart TV functions. This TV is super smart, and it's all amazingly fast due to a quad-core processor. It is easily as fast as my wife's 1 year old laptop at web surfing, navigation, etc. My LG TV was a dog at this kind of thing.
5) Form. This is a truly beautiful piece of technology. It's sleek, almost minimalist in its looks.
6) This TV has a camera on top of it. Whaaaaaat? You can sit a family of 5 on the couch and do a Skype session with someone, and they will see your whole family sitting there, just as clear as day. Pretty awesome. No more gathering around the laptop and saying hi one at a time.

To sum it up, if you think you might be in the market for a TV like this, go check them out for yourself. The difference is pretty easy to see in a store. Stores have a way of making TVs look their absolute best, and so you wonder what it will look like when you get it home. That's why I tested all of these combinations of components...to hopefully give you a feel for that. Anyway, GREAT TV, couldn't be happier.

title: Ditch the smartphone apps
text:
I've only started running with a goal of running a marathon in Apr 2014. Since I want to take my training seriously I decided to get a proper GPS watch that I can use to track my progress. Having come from the cycling world, I was already familiar with Garmin as I have the Edge 510 and I tried using it for running but it was like using a fork to butter bread. As with most things, you get what you pay for. For the average runner, the 210 should do especially if an extra $100 is a big deal.

What I like about the FR220
- very light
- easy to operate (compared to the Edge 510 that I use for biking)
- auto pause (this was a big deal for me)
- Garmin connect (unable to use it with my current phone a Galaxy S3 mini) but it is not a big deal like cycling 55 miles away from starting point.
- vibrate alerts
- very light, I can barely feel it.
- accurate
- cadence (not sure how accurate it is as I don't have little experience in running)
- I can use it when travelling abroad (as opposed to smartphone).

What I don't like
- slower GPS signal locking. With the 510 it is instantaneous, even in the house. With the FR220 the wait is noticeable.
- the proprietary USB cable (Edge 510 has regular USB port).
- nothing else, really

What I would like to see
- More than 3 custom fields in 1 page like the Edge 510.
- Some people have mentioned virtual trainer, but I don't use this feature on the 510.

Having used Strava, Endomondo and Mapmyride apps with my smartphone, this GPS is worth the investment. You get much more and it has better accuracy. I still use my phone as a back-up but I normally delete the workouts. So right now, I just upload my workout in the 3 apps, when I'm done.

title: Works Great for Online Internet Meetings and Using With iPhone 5/5s
text:
I've been a long time Plantronics headset/phone user. I needed a lightweight headset to use with my laptop for online meetings/conference calls. I did not want to spend a lot of money as I was not too sure how many times I would be invited to online meetings.

When my headset arrived, I was impressed with the adapters that was included in the package.

For my online meetings, I connected the headset with the included USB adapter to my laptop. I was able to connect/access my AT&T Connect meeting. Once the meeting started, I noticed that the online meeting console was able to detect when I put my headset on mute and when it was live. Cool! The other folks in the meeting were able to hear me clearly just as I was able to hear them clearly as well.

I found the best use for this headset is with my iPhone 5/5s. I connect the headset with another included adapter/converter that connects to my iPhone. I'm now able to continue working while taking a call.

As previous reviewers have mentioned, the earpiece/headset has to be placed in and around the ear a certain way to fit comfortably. Once I figured out the placement, I found I could wear this for hours. I hardly notice the weight...it's that comfortable. I do have to clip the cable to my shirt/top neckline area in order for the cable not to pull or get tangled.

I have a tendency to walk around while talking on my iPhone. No problem. The cable is long enough that I can place my iPhone in my back pocket (jeans) and walk and talk and even take notes.

This is the best purchase I've made for a headset. The price is definitely a plus. I like the under the ear style as my ears are not sore after wearing/using this headset for a few hours. There's no pressure on top of my ear as I've encountered with other over the ear headsets I've tried.

If you don't mind having a wired headset, this is a great deal and it works great!

title: The Antidote To Bad TV Speakers
text:
Just hooked this up to our TV in the family room. I wanted something that did not involve having multiple speakers set up everywhere in the room and having to turn on an AVR and TV and deal with multiple remotes.etc..etc... The Klipsch 120 is just what the doctor ordered. It fits nicely under the TV. The sound is significantly better than the what our TV can produce. It can get very loud with out clipping or distortion. The instructions in the owners manual did not work for me. According to the instructions the lights on the 120 are suppose to flash and change colors indicating that you can move on to the next step in the process. My problem is that the lights flashed but the colors were not what the manual called for at any particular step. I was so so frustrated. This nonsense went on for 20 minutes. Then I tried it one more time and ignored the colors and just focused on the flashing of the lights. Victory!!!! My Verizon Fios remote works!!!

So here is what I did, I pressed the MUTE and the SOURCE buttons as called for in the instructions at the same time. As soon as the lights flashed, I pressed the MUTE button on the 120, as soon as the lights flashed, I pressed the MUTE on the Verizon remote 4X. The 120's lights stopped flashing and turned to GREEN. I repeated the same steps for the VOLUME. So from my foxhole, i more or less ignored the color of the lights and paid attention to how the lights were working i.e. flashing or solid. At no time did I need to use the remote that came with the TV.

title: Works well, could use more documentation.
text:
First thing: "auto-sensing" means that the Vcc on the cable is an INPUT -- you supply the power. This is unlike the fixed-voltage cables which will supply Vcc. So for example, you can't power an Arduino with this thing -- though it will work if the Arduino is powered by other means.

Second: DTR is not brought out, so for Arduino usage you'll have to manually reset the Arduino to program it.

These aren't "flaws" per se -- the cable does what it's supposed to -- but more like caveats to keep in mind.

On a positive note, it's a FTDI chip so you can use their excellent programming app to invert the Tx/Rx pins if you need to (as I did) as well as a bunch of other cool hacky stuff.

title: DirecTV charges $25 for this exact remote and it fixed my receiver
text:
I have an ancient model D12 DirecTV receiver that was starting to act up. I had to press the remote keys hard to make the receiver pay attention. Sometimes, the remote acted dead - the lights on the Mode switch wouldn't blink when the buttons were pressed - sometimes. The volume, however, directly controls the TV and it worked fine. Batteries were changed a couple of times.

In addition, the receiver acted like it was hanging. General weirdness.

I ordered this RC66 remote (exactly like the one that I already have) because the lights were not blinking on the old one. When I installed the two included batteries and tried it out, it worked fine with slight button push pressure. The receiver was still acting up so I just rebooted it - powered off/on. Now, everything is working fine.

The only thing I can figure, is that the old remote was stuttering and causing the receiver to get confused.

In any event, this remote works perfectly. You will want to search for the remote codes that your tv uses so that you can program the remote. The DirecTV site has the instructions for programming it.

Works fine. Price right. DirecTV charges $25 for this exact remote. You know that at this price, you really, really should have a spare - order two.

I gave it five stars even though the two included batteries failed after exactly two days.

title: I love it when things work right.
text:
I bought this cable to connect my 2011 MacBook Pro (with Thunderbolt) to a Toshiba HDTV. The cable is of good quality. It is inexpensive compared to other HDMI - MiniDisplayPort cables; at the Apple Store, the price for a similar item was $60! It appears sturdy and not cheap or flimsy, despite the low-end price. And it's nice and long, so I can hook up the cable, sit on the couch, type on my laptop's keyboard, and move stuff around on the TV.

It hooked up perfectly to the TV. Video sharing was immediate. The top and bottom of the screen were being cut off, so I could not see the menu bars. I had to go into my TV's menu and adjust the "Theater Settings" of the picture from "Natural" to "Native" to fix this. I have no idea what those terms mean, but I noticed no impact on my TV's picture after disconnecting the Mac, so I'm quite happy to leave it at this setting. (As an aside, why do the menu settings for A/V equipment always have such terrible U/I?)

Sound did not play through at first. I had to go into the Sound preference pane in System Preferences and choose my TV as the sound output device for HDMI. But once I did so, the sound played through to the TV as well. Perfect.

I have not tried this with a MacBook Pro that has a Mini DisplayPort (as opposed to Thunderbolt) connector. Apple says ([...]) that most models prior to 2010 will not output sound over the Mini DisplayPort. If you are buying this for use with one of those, then you may need a separate cable to run out from the headphone jack of your Mac to your TV.

Bottom line, it works amazingly well for the price. It took me perhaps 4 minutes tops to get everything to work just right.

title: Toyish plastic - made for a the $400 point-shoot crowd
text:
I sent it back and got the D7000 - wow what a difference. Thank you Amazon!

I'm disappointed at some of the reviewers boasting they feel they got a D800 at a D3200 price. This is STILL a D3200, and is meant for a very large, but very neophyte audience. Nikon knew there were millions looking for a DSLR for $500 - maybe so they could say they had one. Well here it is, and believe me you get what you pay for. If you believe the egos of the prior reviewers, you'll certainly be disappointed when you try take this camera out of the simple, picture-led guide mode.

True, this camera is very much entry-level, but it's REAL entry level. And the 24mp does not look like 24mp - unfortunately the way the computer processes the image it ends up looks more like 8mp. The images are hard to describe - it's like they're synthesized or over manipulated. Even the RAW seems compressed and lossy. I saw a side-side close up analysis/review of the image, and although it's 24mp, most of the pixels in, say, a 20 pixel radius are all the same! The camera doesn't have the power to distinguish the pixels for clarity like the higher end cameras. Point and shoots do this as a matter of course, then they brag they have "24mp" etc which may be misleading some into thinking "well 24mp is still 24mp". But it's not. Go do your online homework and look at the analysis photos from this camera. You'll see what I mean - and that pans out in real life. Just one step up, the D7000 is 10x the camera, and yields much brighter photos. It's sort of like an old round 50's style TV vs a new 90" hi res LED TV.

It's plastic case gives it a chintzy feel, it's VERY slow at shot acquisition (you will certainly wait a bit till it's figured out how to take the shot), autofocus is awful even with $3000 glass, metering is whacked, short battery life you name a bad trait and this camera has it. Oh - and don't get caught in the rain with it either.

However, it is lightweight. And to some that's quite important. Like a tourist that has to lug a his new SLR all over creation, when they're used to a little pocket camera. This camera is 1/2 the weight of any DSLR.

And it also has a real dumbed-down "guide" that takes about 30 seconds to setup a shot - so that whole sophomoric 7th-grade level guide thing is a bust. And the scene selector on top doesn't help at all either. In both my wife's, my 24 yr old son, my and my Mom's use, about 30/50 shots were blurred, mis-flashed, mis-exposed to WAY out of proportions etc. So why have 24mp for a camera that can't handle it?

The lens that it comes with (mandatory) is just more cheap plastic mess. If this camera was sold w/o the lens it would be in the $299 range. We put a $3k lens on this camera with little improvement - it still just can't cope. Don't fool yourself into thinking you're clever by purchasing a $4000 camera for $400. You've got a $400 camera.

But I wouldn't waste your time/money - get the D7000 and be done with it. If you're that hard up for $$ where you can't/won't shell out another $200 for the pro camera, then go back to a point and shoot

title: Too Large and Hurts to Wear for Long
text:
I'm a woman gamer and sought a gaming glove that would be a size to fit my small hands (size 6 glove). Unfortunately, this glove was still too large (designed more for a boy's hand).

The glove is also designed for Western European hands, and doesn't factor in the pinkie being shorter for Asians. The pinkie size for this glove was so large, I had almost an 3/4" of cloth above my finger tip (making it useless).

Other issue is the pure abrasiveness of the unlined glove and it's seams. It was scratchy and felt terrible (like rocks in a sock deal). I guess to keep some ventilation they parted with lining, but there needs to be something done about the seams that will rub against your fingers and not cause blisters. A gaming glove has to be comfortable to wear for hours at a time, even if this glove was broken in, the seams would still literally rub the wrong way.

It's a novel concept and a much needed one, but the application of this glove for it purpose still needs some QC. Not every gamer now is a guy, and gloves have to factor in anthropological differences.

Major suggestion: use more elastic open weave cloth and/or a sweat liner so the seams can't cause blisters (the glove out of the box is so stiff it's like it was starched, breaking it in can cause blisters...it was that stiff and the seams that abrasive).

title: True Hardware RAID and perfect for the price
text:
The market in RAID enclosures is saturated with underpriced (maybe overpriced to some) non-RAID junk and overpriced proprietary (meaning non-user modifiable here with respect to warranty), underperforming devices. I was worried at first that this device fell into the former given that it is expensive enough to be legit but I can't find any reviews of this device on any hardware site. The same is true of its manufacturer so I can only assume they don't have the marketing budget to provide free test units for the major web reviewers.
I have only had it running a few days now so I will update this later, but I wanted to get a review out to the web so that hopefully there will be more of these in stock on Amazon in the future or other sites.
The installation was the simplest I've seen, the drives are pressure fitted by the covers into the SATA slots, but this can be locked with provided keys to prevent busy hands that might try to remove drives.
I only had 4 x 3 TB so I turned it on without resetting RAID. My previous software RAID 10 showed up degraded from the last unit I tested.
I reset this with dip switches on the back and I had instant RAID 10 so it is truly hardware RAID. I tested copying my files over in batches: 1.81 T, 0.6 T, 100 G, 30-50G and the performance was consistently between 150-200 MB/s over USB 3.0 on my 2012 Mac Mini (The source is a fusion drive with Benchmarks of 400 MB/s Reads).
I will update this when I buy a 5th 3 TB drive and setup RAID 5 but I can wholeheartedly recommend this as a solid enclosure, with an internal PSU, great feel and from what I can tell produces good airflow for the drives with the internal fan. I say this because the free version of SMART on my mini does not support certain external devices.

title: The latest measurement fad - curiously missing some top companies
text:
If you love books on measurement and the latest trend or fad - this one is for you.
Like many before it - it attempts to reduce management to an equation, and really doesn't introduce anything new that hasn't been used before and overlooks a lot. Hand it to Bain to figure out a way to get more consulting fees from large clients who are detached from their customers. In looking over the companies listed (NPS Loyalty Forum on page 10), I noticed the absence of top customer satisfaction companies like Wegmans, Nordstrom, Panera - etc. Sure - they mention Apple - but it's the retail section - not corporate. Rest assured that Steve Jobs could have cared less about Net Promoter.
At any rate - the "Ultimate Question" they offer - I've seen that on surveys for many years. Curiously, they miss a big factor - that cross-tabulation with the amount that customer spends and their longevity is far more important that just the NPS value alone. As is pointed out by one of the other reviewers - never depend on just one metric.
A better measure of customer value is the 'frequent flier' types of programs - you can track the value of repeat customers and mine tremendous demographics. Not surprisingly, the 80/20 rule often applies - on both ends of the scale (meaning both good customers and toxic customers).
Another factor they don't seem to consider is that a customer may love you to death - and just not have the time or energy to promote you, or shallow loyalty which is switched to the next company who offers a rebate. Why should they promote you? Same goes for the malcontents. Anyone who has looked over any kind of review knows not to take the top cheerleading ones or the lowest snarky ones at face value. Look for the balanced reviews that address the values that are of concern to you.
Part of this measurement and 'management-by-equation' fad is the inability to successfully manage any aspect of business with a behavioral aspect - e.g., marketing (including customer satisfaction) sales, PR, HR, etc. Just look at the put-down of sales that is offered on the bottom of page 29 and sprinkled throughout the book. The authors clearly have never sold or carried quota, or had any professional sales training, or understand how sales professionals value repeat customers. Instead, they trot out old cliches to reinforce their "bad profits" premise. Bad profits really come from bad management (no mention if poster child AOL was a Bain client, of course) as does a misguided sales effort.
So NPS is worthwhile under the premise that something is better than nothing,(remember the classic work efficiency study at the turn of the century where they were measuring lighting levels - productivity went up with both increased lighting and also decreased lighting - what gives? Seems the workers just liked the attention) but NPS by no means the be-all, end-all that is presented. May help you get some budget dollars, though - gotta be trendy in the boardroom. Hey, remember Total Quality and Six Sigma?

title: Slim, Well Designed, Versatile Techno Gadget
text:
I bought one of these a couple weeks ago because our current vehicle (a Mazda 5) does not come with navigation and the vehicle we are contemplating purchasing can be ordered without it. I couldn't be more impressed. It attaches to the windshield easily; the magnetic connection between the windshield mount and device allows you to easily snap it off and hide it when you leave the car. When I first unpacked it, I spent 2 hours uploading the most-current software and maps (love that I get FREE lifetime updates). I spent about 2 hours reviewing the manual and looking at youtube videos on how it works. I even reprogrammed the main voice command introductory phrase and downloaded and am using the Garmin male employee's voice instead of the standard female voice, which annoyed me a bit.

I find the best way to use it when you know where you are going is to program the address at my desk and save it under the name of the location. Then, when you get in the car you can simply tell it to go there. For example, I programmed it for the Coachella Valley Preserve in 1000 Palms, then for the La Quinta resort where we were going to meet family from there and finally for the California Pizza Kitchen restaurant nearby. Each time I got in the car, I simply told it where to go and it plotted the route and took us there.

As they say in the instructions, the Nuvi does not replace common sense or specific knowledge. So, for example, at several points along the routes calculated by Nuvi I varied from the suggested route, as I knew a 'better way' to get there. No problem; Nuvi simply recalculates your route, without saying a word. Also, I usually look at Google Maps to see exactly where I'm going so that I'm not flying blind with only Nuvi to guide me. I'm an old map lover, so that may explain that.

The graphics on the device are brilliant, the voice command system works well and I really like the 'dashboard' which displays the speed limit on the road you are on, your speed, the direction you are traveling, your estimated arrival time, etc. Just brilliant.

I think you can still live without an automotive GPS system, but it certainly helps. This is a better device than many of the systems installed in vehicles and at a fraction of the usual price.

title: Definitely worth hearing
text:
I have audiophile tastes but not the budget. And frankly, my I have grown irritated with the audiophile market over the years, pushing $8000 cables, mpingo disks and the like. Nonetheless, a favorable review in Stereophile did bring this player to my attention. I purchased the player and its companion amp, the PM5004 at $750 for both. They replaced the feed from my laptop since my CD63SE bit the dust awhile back. Before the matching amp arrived I listened to the player with an old but well-regarded receiver. The player lacks SACD capability nor does it have a USB input like its $150 more expensive sibling, the CD6004. It does have a headphone jack, and a very nice feature whereby you can loop a musical passage. This is great if you are an amateur musician trying to figure out how to play a passage from the recording.

The unit is very sleek in black with blue lighting, matching the 5004 amplifier. The remote can also control the amplifier. The manual is good and there is an overall impression of good engineering and quality control. Marantz has gained some cachet since Ken Ishiwata took over as manager of product development.

The 5004 has a distinctive sound which is noticeably more dynamic, detailed, and transparent than I am used to hearing even in showrooms. The bass is powerful with plenty of pop on tympani and the like. On the negative side it can sound a little sharp-edged, though this might be the fault of the remastered CDs I have been playing rather than the player. I have been using old Dahlquist DQ12s which are fairly high-end 3-ways that go down pretty far in the bass. With these speakers I didn't sense any rolloff that was the CD player's fault. For the right purchaser the 5004 will be a great bargain. For the listener who prefers a warm, laid-back sort of sound I would not recommend it, though perhaps in combination with a NAD amp things would balance out. By using it with the PM5004 amp I am getting its full fury on old rock and loving it. My main question is whether I want SACD or USB capability enough to exercise my return privilege and get one of Marantz's more expensive models. If you are looking to put together a budget system with some high-end zip, the 5004 deserves a listen.

title: Great WAP for the price
text:
There are not enough review so this product online, but the few that do exist are very informative.

Firstly, it looks like smoke detector but is about 30% larger in every way. It could pass as a smoke detector if you disable the electric blue lights that come on when it is powered on (the UI can disable any or all of the 3 lights). Mounting it is as easy as mounting a smoke detector - assuming you already have Ethernet run to the ceiling location. I have several of these installed at various client locations and they are running nicely. Combine them with a great router that does QoS and VPN and I can check on the units and manage traffic remotely.

Be sure to buy a real PoE injector when you get this. The design of this unit assumes you will install it to a location that does not have power, so you need to power it from the switching closet.

So why not 5 stars? Engenius designed a great unit with very usable, stable firmware. However, they made a stupid mistake in not giving it a 1Gbps connection since Wireless N is supposed to offer 300Mbps WiFi speeds. This really doesn't make a difference for most internet speeds, but why would you design the bottleneck to be the wired network connection to the switch? Costs difference between Cat5e and Cat6 are negligible and most offices would require you to run a new Ethernet connection to the ceiling location, so what customer are you designing this for that would have a Cat5 cable already hanging from the ceiling in a centralized location good for wireless?

I see that Engenius release an EAP350 with gigabit. Can I trade in my EAP300?

title: GREAT Screen.  Good value.  Get it.  Get it now.
text:
If you are familiar with Chromebooks, you know that just about all of them provide good value, function about the same, and most have poor to mid-ling screens. Even ones with 1080P screens are still using older TN panels for the most part and have pretty below average looking screens. Don't be fooled with the other ones, none were very good until now.

Enter the Toshiba Chromebook 2. Its 1080P screen with its IPS panel is excellent. It is light years above any other Chromebook screen I have seen. I'm actually a bit surprised and quite pleased at just how good it is after reading the reviews of it. I wouldn't expect a $350 laptop (I got it for $299 on sale) to have this good a screen. Great colors, very bright, no issues with viewing angles. Outstanding. Full stop.

The rest of the Chromebook is nice as well. At 13.3 inches the keyboard has plenty of room for typing, has a great "chicklet" style keys that I love. They have decent travel and I can type very well on it. All the Chromebook keyboards have essentially the same layout - and it is an excellent one. It has a built in Search key where you can "OK Google" and use voice search.It has dedicated "overview" and "Fullscreen" buttons, and dedicated volume up.down brightness up/down keys. I can't tell you how valuable having those is in everyday use. Going back to a windows keyboard I am always wanting (having to "CTL or FN to get the same functionality). Great keyboard, well spaced with useful keys. Though, no CAPS LOCK key? EDIT : It turns out you can hit "alt + < search key>" to enable or disable CAPS LOCK. Loving this Chromebook :-)

Chrome OS operates about as expected, which is to say generally very well (if not spectacular). With 4GB of RAM I rarely have any issues with too many open tabs or other slowness. it is a great machine for web browsing, e-mail, using Hangouts for chats, video Hangouts, etc. The battery life is fine, though not spectacular. Lowering the brightness to about 50% gets you easily 8 to 10 hours. At full awesome brightness, perhaps 4 to 5 hours. No issues.

The Skullcandy speakers are pretty good for a Chromebook - though they are not great. I love Skullcandy earbuds and was pleased when I learned they were in the Chromebook 2.

The trackpad is very good. It is perfectly sensitive without being overly so for me. All that is adjustable in the settings of course. There is really nothing not to love that I have found so far.

For me, there is the Chromebook 2 and then there are all the other Chromebooks. The screen is that much better. Do yourself a favor and get it. You won't be sorry.

title: Surprise! These Magic Boxes Work
text: Being a Computer Technician I have to admit that I was skeptical. The concept of using the power lines in your home as your internet connection is an old concept, but with these babies, its a practical reality. My home has multiple computers and people using them, and all of them were demanding a solid connection to the internet. Unfortunately for me the home has a very large, and very old furnace system that tends to mess up wireless connections and weaken wireless signals. To the dread of some members of my household this means that it is an active dead zone for cell phones. As pleasing as that may be on family night (when we watch a movie together without cell phones going off) I was stuck with 2 choices: be lazy and string ugly, fat, gray Ethernet cables all over the house, or be my hard working technician self, and rout them through the walls/ceilings and setup Ethernet jacks in all bedrooms. Neither of these options appealed to me due to my busy work schedule, and I didn't want to lose a day off tearing the house walls apart. Fortunately after doing some research I found these. The trade-off seemed reasonable if they worked, and so I bought a pair to test them out. It became immediately apparent that these not only work well for the internet, but they are also very STABLE! I had the first family member using it stress test the thing by watching steaming movies, playing video games, and browsing/downloading content from the internet. To my delight the box handled it all with finesse! It was so simple to setup I kept thinking that this had to be some kind of modern witchcraft; literally all I had to do was plug them in and attach the Ethernet cables: All lights went green and the kid was on the internet! No Breaking into walls or stringing cables everywhere, these babies do exactly as advertise, and made all the stress of setting up a home network vanish. So I did the next logical thing: I bought another pair. Roughly $170 to get 3 family members on the internet, and all of them are running fine. I bought the first pair 2 months ago and have no problems yet, and I happily report that hasn't been any hiccups. Money well spent on these for my family in my opinion, and if you're like me and have a situation where a family member(s) is across the house from your router, and wireless is just not good enough, then look no further: This product is for you!

title: I wanted this to work.
text:
As others have noted, this package comes with everything you'll need to mount your projector on the ceiling. The mount can fit a variety of projectors (mine is a Optoma HD65)and the extension pole is useful to ensure the correct positioning of your image. The included instructions are straight-forward and cover both regular and concrete ceiling installation.

So why one star?

The bolts used to secure the mount to the ceiling are cheap. So cheap that they broke as I was screwing them into the ceiling. And I was screwing them in by hand. Before you ask, yes, I drilled in pilot holes (2 inches deep according to the instructions). The top of the bolts just broke off about a quarter inch from the top. The holes can be covered by spackle but my heart... it remains broken.

I cannot begin to describe how disappointed I am.

There are plenty of positive reviews for this product, so I know many others have found success where I have failed. But my experience can only truly be described with one star. A chain is only as strong as its weakest link, and the weak link here happens to be the part needed to secure the mount to the ceiling.

I'll probably try to find some replacement bolts at a hardware store if my heart ever recovers. In time, that recovery could lead me to update this review. Prospective buyers could consider getting some similar bolts before they begin. Don't let what happened to me happen to you.
