title: There is no aspect of this pen that is not deeply and horribly flawed. Their customer service to support this pen is a joke.
text:
I have four of these. I am a university professor, and I purchased them both as an instructional and a research tool. My comments here are based on issues that are common to all four pens that I own (two of which replaced pens that I previously purchased that did not work, so technically I've owned 6 of these). Nothing I say here can be written off as 'he must have received a lemon,' these are systemic and fundamental problems that you are highly likely to encounter. This pen is an utterly unreliable, poorly supported product that in no way works as advertised.

So, basically, don't get it. Don't assume the bad reviews are isolated, anomalous bad experiences that you probably won't have to deal with, because of 6 pens I've received, 4 of which I currently own, none of them has been anything short of a travesty. You'll lose recordings roughly 20% of the time, and the run-around you'll get from customer support is horrifying. I've heard good things about the Echo and the 3, but this pen is worse than useless; it's a liability. Here are some specific shortcomings:

Pen function:
The pen is able to consistently record writing and audio, and play back audio corresponding to writing when you tap the pen on the paper that was used during a recording. However, when offloading the files all four pens exported the static image of the paper without any motion or audio roughly one out of every five times, regardless of whether the pens were synced using a PC, Mac, or wifi. Essentially, in my experience with multiple pens over the course of a year and a half of use, you will be unable to offload correctly roughly 20% of your recordings

Evernote interface:
Most of the problems regarding Evernote working with the Sky have been fixed. However, if you share something with the Evernote share function, the person receiving the file will not receive a link to the dynamic recording, but to a static page with no audio or video functionality. To share the full recording you have to get to the recording online then pass around the link, which seems to imply that the recordings aren't actually that secure.

Customer support:
Livescribe customer support isn't equipped to deal with anything but the most rudimentary problems with this pen. Once you learn how to operate the pen correctly, you've basically surpassed their ability to troubleshoot. Almost every time I've lost data it has taken me over a week to have my problem addressed. I begin by trying to find the issue in their "knowledge" base articles, then do the live chat with a customer service representative. The customer service representative eventually realizes he or she is WAY out of his/her depth and says they'll open a ticket and have someone email me. The person emailing gives the condescending list of obvious stuff you've already tried, so you run all that stuff again to no effect. Eventually the technician or whomever it is starts trying things on their end, which occasionally works, but you've spent two weeks getting to this point already. The bulk of the time when they can't solve the problem they simply stop emailing, then when I send them a message to find out what the status is they either ignore the message, say it's an issue that will be fixed in a patch (spoiler alert, nothing ever really gets fixed in any patch), or say they're forwarding the problem on to some new person whose contact information I never receive, and who never gets back to me.

title: Great value for a very well built Samsung TV
text:
This TV is great. The picture is quite an improvement from my 7 year old Samsung LCD TV. Just beware you need to calibrate it to your preference. Calibration is super easy and you can find the setting recommenced by cnet on previous comments.

One important thing to note regarding the settings is to make sure you turn the eco mode off. If you do not, the TV will automatically adjust as lights comes on or dependent on any change in lighting in your room. Do not leave eco mode on or it will drive you crazy. I think Samsung has TV's set from the factory with it turned on for some reason. It really causes issues and frustrates people who are not so technically savvy to change or figure this out.

Anyway, overall this TV is a great value. The built in wifi works like a charm for me. If you want a better picture though, go with the 6400 model as it uses micro-dimming rather than edge light dimming. The 6400 model was about $300.00 more. If I had the chance again, I would have bought the 6400 because the difference in edge lit vs. micro-dimming really changes the picture.

UPDATE 11/25/14: After watching this TV for almost a month now, I see why some of the previous reviewers noticed the TV picture slowly dimming and brightening. This only happens when the TV picture is set on the "Standard" picture setting, which is the only setting that is an energy star mode. I've noticed this watching College Football games and it made me think my eyes were going bad. I would recommend changing your default factory picture setting from Standard mode to one of the other 3 modes(Dynamic, Natural or Movie) and calibrate your preferred settings on one of those 3 modes if your not concerned with saving energy. It really makes for a better viewing experience.

title: Works well, nice features, though somewhat expensive
text:
I had an old Series 2 analog Tivo that I had to replace. I did not have a service fee with the old system and didn't want one. So, I tried a Channel Master. It sort of worked, but they could not get it to work with my cable. Since the OTA signal is poor in the area, I have cable.

The Tivo worked with the cable after install of the M-Card. Comcast had some difficulty getting the settings right on the M-Card. But once it did, I've got everything I need in a DVR. I watch nearly all "broadcast TV." So, I would rather shift live TV, than get TV from various internet options. The two tuners are nearly always adequate to record what I want. The disk is reasonably large so if I fall behind, I can queue shows. I haven't found the internet apps particularly useful. Maybe the Youtube app if I unexpectedly find a lot of time on my hands.

The playback is very smooth - as good as original broadcast (not surprising for digital system). The FF & REW are much more responsive and easier to use than my neighbors' Verizon or Comcast systems. The SD stations look very good too.

The on screen guide is easy to use; setting up a season recording requires a lot of steps, but I'm not sure it can be simplified. I can eliminate the stations I don't watch from my guide making it easier to view what I care about. My Verizon and Comcast DVR neighbors can't do that and have to browse through hundreds of channels they will never watch.

The dilemma is the cost. However, my last Tivo last me 8 years. The payback period on "Lifetime Subscription" is just under three years. If this Tivo lasts me, what I think is a conservative 6 years, then this averages to under $7/month - less than nearly any other option for what I think is the highest quality DVR on the market. So, in the end, I think the Tivo is actually quite affordable even though there is a high initial outlay with the lifetime subscription.

Two design elements could easily be improved: (a) The coiled cord is far too springy: When moving a few feet from the telephone, the coils start to stretch and the headset is pulled away from the ear. Much better is simply to have an uncoiled cord. (b) The mute button switch is fiddly and stiff - it is made of smooth plastic and sits in a U-shaped channel. title: Multiple Uses, A Truly Worthwhile Hub...
text:
The [[ASIN:B00G537M7K Sabrent 2-Port Portable USB 2.0 Hub and 10/100/1000 Gigabit Ethernet LAN Network Adapter]] solves an often difficult problem, and does so with some really cool extras.

This hub is perfect for those who have a computer with a failed or faulty Ethernet port, or a computer that never had one at all (like some Ultrabooks). It's relatively easy to find USB Ethernet Network Adapters out there, however you often must give up one USB port on your computer to use them. With this adapter, you actually net gain one additional USB port, while allowing your computer to easily connect to a wired internet connection.

Performance wise, I was very impressed with this product. The USB ports on the hub functioned as expected and the wired internet connection through the Ethernet port on this hub performed at the specified transfer rate for the router I connected to.

What I most like about this hub is the portability factor. This is perfect for packing in a computer bag or brief case, especially for travel where Wi-Fi may not always be available. Designed in black, the hub is very stylish, and the smaller pigtail keeps the adapter with in arms reach at all times, but also keeps the unit from blocking nearby USB ports on the computer.

Generally, I'm very satisfied with the [[ASIN:B00G537M7K Sabrent 2-Port Portable USB 2.0 Hub and Gigabit Ethernet LAN Network Adapter]] . The unit functions as expected and delivers options few hubs on the market can today. After initial setup, which was very easy and painless, the hub is plug and play supported, meaning it's ready to go when you are. I think at the current price it's an amazing deal, and well worth the investment for anyone who travels, works from home, and anywhere in between.

Disclosure: I want you to know I received a sample product from the manufacturer for the purposes of providing this review. However, a review in exchange for the review sample was not promised. The views and opinions expressed in this review are my own, and in no way represent the views or opinions of the manufacturer or vendor.

title: High quality, works as designed, good instructions.
text:
TV mounts have become so inexpensive over the past several years that I had a bit of sticker shock when considering this item.

But I really wanted a mount that could move vertically, for my bathroom TV to have more comfortable options for both toilet and shower TV watching, and there are not many mounts that can accommodate that.

So I took the plunge, and am happy that I did. This is a very well constructed mount. It came with good instructions, all of the mounting hardware you would need for various TV sizes and wall materials, and it feels very sturdy when it's being adjusted.

Although you could install this with one person, two people really would be preferred. I found that I needed to hold it up to the wall (with the TV attached) before deciding the exact height that I wanted to place the mounting holes. And because it can articulate in so many ways and therefore won't "hold still" easily, that would have been very hard to do solo.

Because TV's have gotten so light, it seems that today's typical mounts are somewhat flimsy, because they no longer need to hold up 100+ lb plasma's. Even though this mount only supports up to 25 lbs, it feels like it has the same rugged quality that those older plasma type mounts used to have.

If you need the articulation features that this mount offers, I highly recommend it.

text:

2. EXTREMELY UNCOMFORTABLE. Did the developers even put the damn thing on before they sold it? After 5 minutes my ears start hurting. There's hardly any cushioning, and the earpiece is so shallow that it just smashes on your ear instead of giving some room between your ear and the headphone padding. I'm wearing them right now and they hurt. Literally the most uncomfortable headphone I've ever worn. I can't see how people are possibly hating on the beats yet saying this is better.

3. Mediocre bass and noise cancellation. I personally like overwhelming bass as I mostly listen to Hip-Hop and EDM, so that "Trunk Rattle" bass that the beats give you is something I LOVE. No where to be found on these. The sounds is clearer and more pronounced than my beats, but they don't HIT the way I like the 12s in my trunk to hit. Noise cancellation doesn't seem to make a difference.

4. Poorly constructed wire. I rarely wear these and already the wire is getting worn down to the point I have to fidget with it to play sound out both earpieces at the same time. Why not take notes from other companies and get a sideways connector since this happens to literally all headphone wires that don't have it? Not to mention it can't be replaced because it's specific to the headphone.

I highly doubt the designers put any thought into the durability or comfort of this products. Seems like they wanted to make a gimmicky "fancy" headphone with a sleek design so they could have a product on the headphone market to rip people off with. Would have sent this back but didn't want to disrespect the person who gifted these to me. The only good thing are the mids and highs that come out of it, but then again EVERY HEADPHONE CAN DO THAT. I'm not one to make blanket statements, but this is literally the worst pair of headphones I've ever had since those over-ear walkman headphones from the 90s, and even those were actually COMFORTABLE.

Sorry audiophiles but I'll be going back to my beats. If they constructed this headphone with half an inkling of comfort or durability in mind, I would say otherwise. These headphones are a joke and I'll never buy from this company again.

title: Great Mount for a 60" TV
text:
I mounted a 60" Sharp LED TV to this mount with no problems. I recieved it sooner than expected & it was 98% assembled out of the box. I followed the directions, took the time to do it right & it took about 20 minutes.

I always read the negative reviews first & I am baffled as to how people can have problems with this product. This mount is well made & I would recommend it to anyone that is concerned over the reviews stating it sags.

The mount can be easily installed by one person as I did below: You may need help to hang your tv on it once it is installed. I am laying this out because of the problems I read about in the other reviews.

1. Figure out where your studs are & drive a pin or finish nail on each side of it to be certain where the centers are. Make these small holes about 1/4" above where your mount holes will be drilled. These small holes will be covered by your mount.
2. Drill your first pilot hole into the center of the stud & run the first lag bolt & washer through the mount & get it near snug.
3. Extend the bracket so you can lean against it.
4. While leaning against the mount in a eyed up level position, lay your level on top of the wall bracket & get it level.
5. Pull your pencil from behind your ear & mark the second hole which is on the opposite side of your first hole.
6. Let it back down & drill the second hole in the center of the stud.
7. Move the mount back to the level position & install the lag bolt & washer.
8. Tighten the two lag bolts so they are just about crushing the mount into the wall.
8. You can now drill your bottom holes & install the lag bolts & washers. Make sure you are in the center of the studs.
10. Tighten & retighten all four lag bolts. If these are not tight, you will have problems with the TV sagging when the mount is extended. It is critical that the four lag bolt are tight against the mount. If you skip using the washers, you reduce the strength & stiffness of your mount.

Any fine tuning needed can be done on the 3 bolt swivel plate after the TV is on the mount.

The mounting bracket has holes so you can install mud rings & plates for your wiring. I will be installing a recessed power outlet on one side & a brush cover faceplate on the other for the signal cables on the other. The mounting bracket has wire chases so everything is neat & held to avoid crushing cables.

The only thing I will do to modify the mount is to drill a small hole in the upper portion of each pivot point to allow me to easily give each pivot a shot of WD-40 once in awhile. This should keep it operating smoothly & keep things from getting tweaked if it gets a little sticky from dust & oxidation.

title: Outstanding!!
text: These were great for a recent 14.5 hour flight overseas.  They drown out the airplane engine noise and other people with or without the music.  I really like that you can disconnect the cable and use the noise cancelling feature by itself.  Many higher priced models have a "hard-wired" cord that would get in the way if I were tired of listening to music and just wanted to sleep.  I will say that I tried running with them and heard a slight rattle in the right side.  It did not affect function, but it was bothersome to the point I would not try it again.  Overall this is minor because I really don't bother with music often while running.  I would use these while mowing the yard more often than running anyway.  I especially like the volume adjustment directly on the earpiece.  When the stewardess came by to ask me if I wanted food, I just turned down the volume, answered, then went right back to my movie/game/song with no interruptions and no need to remove the headphones or disturb my fellow passengers.  That sounds minor, but after sitting on a plane for so long that was a nice feature.  You can also listen to music just like a normal headset/headphones without the batteries or noise cancelling turned on.  With the noise cancelling on and music going, I could not hear a "dump truck driving through a nitroglycerin plant." - Uncle Lewis, Christmas Vacation, check it out :) Overall the quality of these is good and very much worth the price.  They are comfortable and the foam is soft.  The case and ability to fold down the ears on their side was a huge bonus while traveling and trying to keep my bag flat.  Again, many higher priced fail in this area because they either don't come with a case and/or the ears pieces do not move.  Have adjustable ear pieces should not be overlooked as it also allows a little more flexibility in comfort and head placement.  I put extra batteries, my iPhone charger, and another set of ear buds all inside the case along with the headphones, which made for easy access during flight.  I'm shocked that not every set of headphones comes with foldaway ear pieces, a case, volume control, and removable cable.  After having these I would never buy a set without all these features.

title: THE Best Compact Camera Around!
text:
I just purchased this camera thru Amazon. I REALLY REALLY needed a smaller compact camera to complement my other big and heavy DSLRs. I just want to say that this X10 i can take ANYWHERE. This is THE perfect compact camera for me, and i can take it and hide it under my coat without anybody even noticing it is there. Well, the camera is not tiny, but it sure feels like it, specially since it has that pretty wide range zoom lens. This is why i chose it over the X-E1 and the X-M1 coming out soon.

The built quality, design, performance, and image quality output are TOP NOTCH in this camera. I really don't know what the X20 has for double the price, but this X10 has everything i need. The low light performance is very very good indeed, considering it's small sensor size. Actually i read in many forums that the noise output from the X10 is not so good because of its small sensor, but all i can say is that many of those statements are just not true, because i have confirmed that. I have had many good ISO DSLRs and what i can say is that the ISO performance from the X10 can compete with some cameras with bigger sensors. Don't under estimate this little camera. I shot many photos in low light (in jpeg) and this thing outputs photos with very little noise, straight out of the camera. I am very impressed. I didn't even had it set to high ISO Priority mode, and if i PP the noise in LightRoom they would look even better. Pretty amazing indeed. Last time i had a point and shoot camera was around 8 years ago, and this X10 is a HUGE improvement from what we had back then.

I will say that this camera is not for a beginner. If you are going to buy this type of camera, you should know at least how certain functions work, such as ISO, Shutter and Aperture. Those are some of the simple and basic thing someone should already know, otherwise many of your pictures will come out very blurry and bad. And definitely you will HAVE to read the manual. This is a very high tech little camera.

I shopped around for a long long time. I looked at the famous Pentax MX-1 also, very very good camera also, but when i had the Pentax on my hand it just felt awkward and not normal. The X10 fits like a little glove, and it has a shoe for external flash already, which i will be using. The Fuji just has everything i wanted. I am extremely happy with my new X10. For it's current $349 price, i think this is one of THE best compact cameras out there.

The only thing i don't like is the very POOR battery life, but i read somewhere in flickr that Radio Shack sells a brand that lasts longer than this fuji battery that comes with the camera. I shot around 100 photos and the battery gave up. I did have the LCD on, since i am learning and playing with the camera a lot right now, but soon i will turn off the LCD and other recommended functions for longer batt life.

I still feel like giving this camera 5 stars.

title: Tiny Horn Loud Performance
text: The first thing I noticed about this horn was it's size. It's very small compared to the old stock one I had in my vehicle, which is nice because it was easier to install. This thing is also no slouch when it comes to sound; it's VERY LOUD for it's size. It comes with 2 wires looped on the back, one for it's soft chirp feature, and the other for the different tones. I ended up clipping the soft chirp loop because I thought it was too quiet, and who wants their alarm horn quiet anyway? The loop for the different tones also gives you additional sound options, but be aware that it's the processor in your alarm module that dictates what sounds are emitted, not the horn. However, this horn will produce slightly different tones, but they are still similar in sound to the stock sounds your alarm produces. For example, I have 2 vehicles with alarms, one with a stock alarm from the factory, and the other having a Viper aftermarket alarm. The Viper alarm normally produces the classic 6 tone sound you remember in the early 90's, which sounded like something out of Star Trek, but with this horn hooked up, it still had the 6 tones, but the actual sounds were different. This is because this horn has some kind of processor built into it, which explains the looped wires on the back. Now, with this horn hooked up to a factory 2 tone setup, it still produced 2 tones. So, while it has additional sound options, the duration and type of sound still depends on your alarm system. It's similar to a car stereo...the stereo produces the sound and the horn is just a speaker to hear it. Overall, a great addition to my stock alarm system, and extremely easy to hook up.

title: Good network player for Android devices
text:
I just got my Samsung SmartHub and thought I would share my experience with it. I had previously done my homework, so I went to the Samsung support page and reviewed the installation and firmware upgrade instructions, and I also prepared a few movie clips on a USB drive. Setup was very simple - I just followed the included instructions (which are the same as the ones online), although I did not use the CD. Instead, I just used IE and browsed to the IP address of the SmartHub (you can also browse to the name "smarthub"). The firmware was A00, so I upgraded it to the latest available. Once that was done, I changed the SSID, selected WPA2/AES, changed the password, then I changed the SAMBA password. Finally, I inserted my USB flash drive and disconnected the ethernet cable.

I connected my Nexus 7 to the SmartHub wifi network and fired up the Samsung Mobile Smart Hub app. It found the SmartHub immediately. After I registered the app and changed the SAMBA password, I went to the video player, found the clips, and played them back without any problems. After that I loaded a DVD and used the DVD player and had that working in a few minutes. I did get a message about the DVD region not matching, so I let it change whatever was needed. Finally, I switched to the music player and played back an MP3 file, which worked great.

Although this works for non-HD videos, I found that the Android Smart Hub app player can't handle any kind of HD content without stuttering. I'm pretty sure it's because the app can't take advantage of hardware acceleration, because I used BSPlayer (which does support hardware acceleration) and played back a couple of HD clips from the SmartHub without any problems at all. Another issue I discovered was my MP4 clips didn't work at all, but clips in a MKV container worked great. Again, this is a limitation of the player and not the device, because the MP4 clips play in BSPlayer.

Overall I'm happy with the performance of the SmartHub. The streaming works for DVD quality videos, which will be fine for me since this is going to be used by my kids during long trips. The Samsung app works well enough, and if my kids want to watch a HD movie, they can use BSPlayer instead. I hope that Samsung will update the app and add an option to use hardware acceleration at some point.

For $50, you just won't find a better portable media hub.

text:

As soon as I had it up I was pulling in some of the powerhouse stations 140 miles away to the southeast of me and weak college stations that I've never heard before to my direct south. It is very directional and this helps separate out stations that may be on the same or frequency but in different places. All this at only 15 feet off the ground and I live in a low spot. Being interested in picking up even more stations I will probably mount it higher.
Of course, your equipment and local terrain will play a role in how it performs at your home or office. As with all antennas, the higher you can get it the better.
This antenna is the perfect size and out performs FM antennas I've purchased in years past for the same price. Amazon and The Price Pros made finding and purchasing this antenna a most pleasant experience.

Hopped on this as soon as it came out for my Surface Pro 2. Worked great right out the box. Build quality is top notch, as expected from Plugable! I had already pre-installed the latest DisplayLink drivers as I also use a UD-3000 dock along with a USB3-HUB4AC1 while using the SP2 at work, so as you can tell, I'm a huge Plugable fan.

Right out the box it worked great! However, while using this hub with the SP2, you CANNOT spin up two external USB 3.0 HDD's, and Plugable does not include a way to provide external power to the hub. I even tried to get the most juice to the USB ports by unplugging the LAN cable and disabling the NIC in Device Manager, and also plugging the SP2 up to it's A/C adapter. However, it still would not spin the second drive up. Instead, I'll have to resort to a USB splitter cable with a USB AC>DC adapter in order to spin up the second drive.

YMMV, I'm sure the device the hub is plugged into is the determining factor on how many amps you will get out of the HUB, so this is probably more of a limitation with the Surface Pro 2 than it is with the hub.

title: A decent keyboard with a game breaking problem...
text:
So I purchased this Bluetooth Keyboard by Fosmon and I have to say it is OKAY.

Likes:

It is easy to connect with my PC, the design is nice, thin, and light-weight. A rechargeable battery that only takes about 2-2.5 hours to charge.

The Keys are not traditional spaced, but each of the keys are angled and right next to each other. The keyboard has a decent back-light (dedicated button is a plus). Their are four LED lights on indicating your connect to you device. Two battery indicator lights and a caps lock light.

Touch pad is nice and smooth as well and you can double tap on it as well.

Also there is a function that lets you navigated the keyboard as a remote/pointer as well as inverting the touch pad for a great feel.

Dis-likes:

There are a few things that have put me on the fence on truly enjoying this product and here is why.

The buttons are a bit small for me and you really have to press the button firmly for a proper response.

Although, you can double tap the touch pad you cannot pinch or pull which doesn't bother me. But what does there are no zoom-in or zoom-out keys for better viewing.(I connect my laptop to my HDTV half of the time) because of this I have to zoom in and out with the laptop touch pad (defeating the purpose of this remote for me)

As I mentioned before there are four LED lights (one indicating your btkb is connected) two lights are dedicated for the battery charging and a cap-lock. The problem is, I expected these lights to be indicators to let me know that I need to charge the keyboard (as mentioned in the instructions. Nope the battery lights are only active when you charging the device. It was annoying to have the keyboard cut in and out while I was typing and then completely die on me to realize it needed to be charged.

Now for the biggest problem that is potentially going to make me look for another bt-keyboard. When navigation with the keyboard (i.e. surfing the web, emails, etc...)
The mouse pad goes into standby-mode/cuts-out randomly and doesn't function until I hit a solid button. Mind you this is while I'm in mid-use of the keyboard.

This point is the main reason why I'm writing this review. The touch pad works fine then I would go to a website and after the site has loaded the mouse pad would stop working (after only seconds of waiting for the page to load) as well as random pointer movement when I was using the touch pad (moving the mouse pointer to the right and it slide (oddly slow) to the left randomly. This is frustrating and it made me turn of the keyboard and use my laptop kb instead.

I wish I could like this keyboard more. The problems for me are hard to overlook. I also have a SMK-Link wireless mini-touch pad with wireless dongle and I've never had a problem with the touch pad cutting in or out. I might be going to back to the SMK.

title: Solid Laptop for standard use.
text:
This is a solid little laptop. Let me start by saying, don't buy this for gaming, don't buy this if you don't know how to use/ don't want to learn how to use Windows 8. Aside from those two things I can't see why anyone would give this laptop a bad review. I'm studying computer science and I've been in college for the last 3 years. This laptop is better than any laptop I've owned over the last 3 years for school and for play. School wise it runs every program I need like a charm. No problem with Visual Studio whatsoever. Usually I have Visual Studio, Pandora, E-mail, and Word brought up all at the same time and even with all of that going this laptop runs strong and doesn't slow down at all. Great for all web browsing, streaming is great. I've streamed from Netflix, Youtube, and various anime sites with no problem. The fans run cool and are super super quiet. The keyboard is compact and has a logical layout that works well for me(an indicator light for caps lock would have been appreciated but is not included.) The touch pad works with no problem(though I still prefer using my usb mouse). It's super light and easy to carry around, that will be great for taking it on commutes to and from school. The design is durable, it looks professional and the design keeps it from getting smudged up or scratched. The battery holds up great compared to other laptops I've had in the past. I don't know the exact hours for battery life but I have noticed that even with heavy streaming I don't have to plug up as often as I have with various laptops in the past(including Acer which to me has the best battery life overall.) If you take care of it I feel this laptop will last a very long time. I'll update if anything goes wrong with it but so far it's running great. Overall it's a great inexpensive laptop 250 dollars and it does all I need.

It should be noted that this laptop DOES NOT have a single 500 gig hard drive, it has two hard drives one called OS with about 200 gig free and one called data with about 250 free. You have about 450 gig of usable space along with cloud storage given free from time to time from ASUS(when doing things like registering the laptop on ASUS site.) To me this isn't an issue because I use flash drives for all my school work and I have a few backup laptops. If you're using this as a primary computer and don't have any backups it may be a good idea to buy some cloud storage or flash drives for extra space if you need it.

-Update 1/28/16
After having this laptop for a little over a year I think a followup is in order. This laptop is still a beast, even after dragging it around from work, school, etc. I take it pretty much everywhere I go and to this day it still handles everything I need. Overall I'm still very happy with it. The laptop has taken 2 falls since I got it. One was about a 5ft drop onto concrete. I picked it up, turned it back on and have had no problems with it. The next was about a 3ft drop onto a rug (with hardwood under it). The laptop survived both falls without any damage (aside from aesthetics) the top of it is scratched but aside from that no other issues. My wife also bought this laptop after her old one died out and she has had no problems with hers either. The battery still holds up strong, I'm still not exactly sure how long it lasts but I can get through a whole school day without charging it.

I made the comment in the beginning not to get this for gaming. I still stand by that statement for the most part. I have run The Elder Scrolls Oblivion on it and it..... worked. I couldn't go past medium quality which to me looked almost as good as what it would on a PS3 or Xbox 360. I've also run Minecraft on it but I really don't recommend it. It's playable but it's not high quality by any means. I tried changing all kinds of settings to get it to look/run better but had no luck. The last game I played on it was Back to the Future (Telltale) which worked, but was very laggy. I still stand my ground that I wouldn't WANT to use this for gaming. It's more of the productivity styled laptop which is great for school and work.

title: Like a Calculator Watch but with more features.
text:
First off, my phone is the Sony Xperia Z3 Compact. If you have any additional questions, feel free to leave a comment.

Pro:
Has most if not all the features of Google Now. So if you already use that, this is an amazing addition. A lot of features are also available offline like scheduling and reminders.
Amazing screen. Visible even in bright daylight.
The wrist strap is pretty comfortable and adjustable like any regular watch.
4gb of memory on board for music storage.
Waterproof.
NFC to pair up. Takes up to no time to set up.
GPS navigation.
Bluetooth headset pairing is also easy through the prompts on screen.
Amazing battery life. Went 2 days with regular use like checking time and just screwing around with the settings and apps down to 50% battery.
Most notifications show up on the watch, as long as the app supports it.
Reliable voice to text software.
Has vibration for notifications as well as for step by step navigation.

Con:
Wrist strap is a dust and debris magnet. Dust stick to it like glue. But you can just wash them off with running water.
You definitely need a screen protector. The face does not seem durable at all and does look like it'll scratch easily. I use Skinomi® TechSkin from Amazon.
Seems to disconnect at the most inopportune time. Like while I'm trying to send texts while driving. Also, it's a small screen on your wrist, so proof reading your texts while driving on this is kinda hard.
When you listen to your music from the watch via bluetooth, you can't use the bluetooth headset to talk with the phone because they aren't connected together. But if you listen to the music on your phone via bluetooth, you can control the volume and skip back and forth the tracks using the watch and answer or deny calls using the watch.
No speaker, so you can't talk to your wrist like the Sony SmartBand Talk.
As of now, the LifeLog app doesn't do much of anything with the SmartWatch 3. Also does not track sleep.

Other thoughts:
Goes great with a $.99 app called Facer that allows you to customize the watch face yourself. It comes with a very easy to use interface to make customized watch faces or you can go to their website to download one from other users. Also, even though you can include alarms on the watch, I wouldn't rely on it unless you're a light sleeper, because the vibration isn't all that strong. Just enough for you to notice while you're awake and not make any noise.

Edit 1/7/15:
Right now, there aren't really many fitness apps that track useful information outside from jogging, walking, or running. If that's all you do, then you have a bunch of apps to choose from, but if you're like me and use the gym and use stationary machines, you're not gonna get the most out of this watch. I'm still having connection issues every now and then when I try to send texts via the watch along with other features that require the phone.

Compared to a $13 Casio CA53W Calculator Watch you can get on Amazon, it's like a more advanced and sexier version, but not as simple to use and very expensive. If you really want something to pair up with your phone as well as be a very great stand alone device, get this watch. If you just want an awesome watch that can do more than keep time, buy this: [[ASIN:B000GB1R7S Casio Men's CA53W Calculator Watch]]

I mean the picture is good either way but when you compare the both of them it is such a difference. This feature should be on every camera and in my opinion was worth everything i paid for it due to the quality of pictures. I will update as I go along and give this rating a 4 star until i work through some more testing.
As far as video I am still doing some filming with 1080i AVCHD and so far so good.

title: Excellent Sound For A Ridiculously Low Price
text:
UPDATE: 3/4/18 My overall impressions of the APA150 remain the same. A great value for your audio dollar.

This is especially true when using a pair of APA150's in bridged mode which triples the power per channel into an 8 ohm speaker
load - from 50 watts per channel to 150 watts per channel. The best improvement going from one stereo APA150
to a pair of APA 150 monoblocks is in regard to separation and sound staging. Two APA150s are better than one, sound
wise.

In mono mode, these amplifiers also offer a greater sense of control and perform effortlessly with the speakers that
I'm using - vintage pairs of Linn Audio Kan I's and KEF Reference Series 101's; both of which are fairly inefficient (the Linn Kan I is 83DB@1watt and the KEF Reference Series 101 is 81DB@1watt). The APA150s perform quite well when compared to my Quicksilver MiniMite tube monoblocks and Antique Sound Lab Wave 25 tube monoblocks. The APA150's don't have quite the transparency of these amplifiers, however, they are a fraction of the cost and because of the additional power offer better bass response.

If you want to try tube amplification yet don't want to spend the money on an expensive tube setup,
you can add an inexpensive tube line stage preamplifier to the APA150 to get the best of both sonic worlds; the warmth
of tubes and the power and dynamics of solid state.

The FX Audio TU-01 tube line stage ranks as one of the great bargains in affordable audio for about $35 - including a power supply and shipping. The *Little Dot II MK II is also an excellent choice at about $140 shipped. Both of these are available for sale on E-bay as well as Amazon, so you'd be wise to shop around for the best price. Especially on E-bay, where there are several merchants selling these preamplifiers. The same is true for the Dayton Audio APA150.

* I recently purchased both the FX Audio TU-01 and the Little Dot II MK II, and remain quite impressed with the sound quality
of these two little gems. They are also surprisingly well constructed for the price.

The Little Dot II MK II is also a very impressive little dedicated headphone amplifier. For $139.99 delivered, I can't think
of a better value for the money.

Of course, you'll need a good quality pair of audio interconnects in order to interface one of these preamplifiers with the APA150 (or APA150 mono amp combo). There are quality interconnects and speaker wire to be found at affordable prices on both Amazon and E-bay. Mediabridge comes to mind here.

However, if you want to step up to the next level I highly recommend a company on E-bay that sells all types of interconnects and speaker wire which are custom made for the buyer. Because of this the turnaround time can take a week or two, however, these cables are really outstanding for the money and as well made as any audio cable I have ever seen. The name of the company is Amplifier Surgery. I should state that I have nothing to do with this company. I have purchased some cables from them over the past few years and have found them to be of extremely good quality.

All cables are manufactured in house by this company and the product is both very well made and quite good sounding.

As with the APA150 and the Little Dot and the FX preamp's, the Amplifier Surgery cables are highly recommended!

Earlier...

UPDATE: 12/3/17 - Recently purchased another APA150 so that I can use it with the one I already have
as a pair of monoblock amplifiers. I'll be adding an active tube preamplifier for a bit more warmth.

The APA150 is 50 watts per channel into an 8 ohm speaker load when used in stereo mode. When used as a monoblock
amplifier, the APA150 triples in power to 150 watts per channel.

The APA150 continues to impress me with its sound quality, solid construction and price. It's an
excellent value whether it's used on its own or with an active preamplifier.

UPDATE: 7/8/17 - I have had my APA150 for about three and a
half years now and for the most part it
has been a terrific little amplifier. It sounds surprisingly good using it with my Sony Pro Walkman
cassette deck and Pro Walkman CD player; as well as with the streaming audio from my Dell notebook.

I purchased mine on sale back in the Winter of 2013/14 along with a Mediabridge interconnect (these are
fantastic interconnects for the money - nice sounding and very well made - as is the company's speaker
wire). With the exception of the sensing feature which has since
stopped working properly (when left in
the on position the APA 150 senses when an audio signal is being fed to its input jacks and goes from
standby to on mode) the APA has been working flawlessly.

The sensing feature is nice because it keeps the amplifier standby mode ( a pre-warmed up state as opposed to have to turn the amplifier on from a cold state) However, this feature has been a reliability issue with my amplifier.

Other than this caveat, the APA 150 is a terrific little 50 watt per channel amplifier (50 wpc into 8 ohms) that plays surprisingly loud in a decent sized studio.

Highly recommended! Especially at the $125 (including shipping no sales tax) that I paid for it.

Earlier: Winter 2013/14

I recently took delivery of this amplifier and remain amazed at how it can be produced so inexpensively.

First off, this is a well constructed amplifier with gold plated 5 way binding posts and a separate power cord, rather than a captive mains.

Moreover, aside from the fact that the top pair of binding posts is mounted a bit too close to the bottom pair, the APA150 is well laid out.

Furthermore, given the inclusion of a subwoofer control, stereo/mono switch, and a switch which (when in the on position) takes the amplifier from standby mode to active mode when an audio signal is fed into the input jacks of the APA150, this amplifier really does represent an excellent value.

The APA150 was on sale at PartsExpress.com for $125, including shipping. So I purchased one.

As for sonics, the APA 150 sounds a bit compressed when you first turn it on, however, after a few hours of warm up its sound improves noticeably.

While not the last word in definition or sound staging, the APA150 still manages to faithfully honor the music.

Which is to say that it's musical and involving to listen to. At 50 wpc into 8 ohms, it's also more than powerful enough for my 1980s' Linn Kan I series bookshelf monitors, which rated at 85 DB @ 1 watt, are not particularly efficient speakers.

However, in spite of this the Kans sound quite good when paired with the Dayton APA150. Moreover, for under $500 for both the speakers and APA 150, this system offers sound quality that compares favorably with systems costing three to four times as much.

Given that my main system these days is comprised of my Dell Inspiron netbook as a source component, the APA150, and my Linn Kans, I have also considered purchasing a D/A converter to use with my headphones, as well as to interface the Dell with the input jacks on the Dayton APA150.

However, thus far I have found the sound card in the Inspiron to be more than just listenable. It actually sounds quite good, when the APA150 is connected to my Apple I-music software through the Inspiron's headphone jack.

As such, I don't know whether or not it's worth spending an extra C-note or perhaps even as much as $300 or so (retail price for a Meridian Explorer D/A converter) on a mini D/A converter. I am still amazed at just how good this system sounds when the APA150 is fed by the headphone jack on the Inspiron.

I've heard that certain computer manufacturers use better quality sound cards than other companies do, so perhaps this is why the Inspiron sounds as good as it does.

As for the APA150, this is a great little amplifier for a computer system, or even an affordable home hi-fi system. It's compact, well constructed, and very pleasant sounding. Moreover, given its ridiculously low price, the APA150 goes to show just how overpriced so much of the mid-fi market is. And how insanely over priced so much of the high end audio market is.

If the APA150 turns out to be a durable amp that lasts five or more years, it will be an even better value.

I will update how this amplifier stands up over the next year.

Thus far, highly recommended!

title: Solid laptop, windows 8 works well.
text:
This thing is a huge step up over the previous Acer's that my brother and father have owned. The processor is sufficiently quick for my needs (student), and the size is great. Screen resolution is nice, and the bright colors of the new OS pop a little more with this display than the old acers (I'm doing a side by side comparison). I could carry it easily in one hand while walking to class. The biggest drawback is battery life, but I'll look into upgrading the battery if it starts to bug me. Boot time is blazing on this thing, especially if you only close the screen instead of powering down every time you're not using it. The laptop takes only 2 seconds to come out of hibernation after clicking the power button. The added spacing and indentation between the keys makes the keyboard much more functional than on previous acers, and the touchscreen is easy to use. On that note, I have absolutely no idea how all the buffoons out there can go around claiming that W8 is confusing or tricky. Within 10 minutes of using the new OS for the first time, I was having few difficulties and could move a little faster than I used to on W7. Obviously the biggest advantages to the touchscreen and new functionality come with the apps designed for those features (as opposed to legacy apps), but that should go without saying.

Now, without further ado, I will solve the million dollar "I can't live without my start button" issue in three easy steps:
1. From ANY, I repeat, ANY app or screen in the desktop view: Swipe in from any side of the screen (corner touch with mouse) and click start, or just click the mouse in bottom left corner.
2. Swipe up from the bottom while in "metro" aka start view.
3. Click "All Apps". BAM! You have the all program menu, just like in the good old days.

And now a few observations about that process:
1. The steps above took me a comparable amount of time to what it would take to pull up the programs menu in W7, but Win8 is actually the quicker option if I began from an app in metro view and didn't need step 1.
2. The new "All apps" menu is much easier to use than the old "All programs" scroll bar. If I pinch the screen to zoom out, it pulls up an alphabet that I can use to pick apps by their first letter should I ever have problems finding one. There is also the same search button that pops up in w7 after clicking start.
3. It took me all of five minutes to figure these things out, and I've never even touched a Win8 PC before.
4. There is probably a quicker way to do that, but I haven't gotten around to watching the tutorial on windows 8 yet.

Point is, if you can handle a smartphone, Win8 (and this pc) should be a piece of cake for you.

After searching the internet, I found this product and the fact it was sold on Amazon made me comfortable in buying it. The seller (Tech Gears 4 Me) was very quick to ship this and I received within 3 business days of ordering.

After I received it, I plugged it the 4 pin end into the fan and the 5 pin end into the motherboard and it worked exactly as it should. Fan immediately started being controlled by the motherboard and running at a much lower speed.

This is a great, inexpensive solution for anyone who wants to change out the stock fan on their Dell.

title: Good, but not Great
text:
I bought this router almost entirely because of all the 5-star reviews, and I want to provide a bit of balance.

It's a good, solid, consumer-grade router... But some of the features are a little lack-luster.

The guest wireless, for example, doesn't work nearly as well as it could. There's no option to run a DHCP/DNS server for just the guest network - it's either on, or off, for the entire device. This means that since I've got DHCP and DNS running on a separate server on my LAN, I'm unable to segregate the guest network from my LAN traffic. What this means is that the guest network is just a different SSID for my main network - it isn't actually restricting traffic in any useful way.

QoS is similarly unimpressive. I'm unable to limit a specific host or network in any meaningful way. I cannot, for example, limit my guest network to just 5mbps.

It's still a pretty good router. It's got a good, strong wireless signal. Good range. And it'll certainly handle more traffic than some $50 Wal-Mart special.

title: Great sound, no fluff, bells or whistles.
text:
An excellent sound machine for individuals who consider themselves audiophiles, who crave the portability and elegance of a music player but are sick of flat touch screens and the mediocre music reproduction that usually plagues most modern portable music playing apparatuses.

You feed it music files and charge the battery through a direct, simple USB connection to any computer. File transfer is basically drag-and-drop. You may create folders instead of playlists (it does not have them). There is no wifi, GPS tracking or large touch screens to this contraption. You navigate files and volume control via physical buttons - a great feature slowly disappearing from current devices. The D to A converter and excellent pre-amp built in allow for playing almost any music file on earth, and allow for excellent sound reproduction even with high-resistance professional headphones.

The only annoying aspect of this thing has to do with the VERY SLOW charge time using the USB. Some will not like not having playlists - but as I have mentioned you may use folders created on the computer and dragged and dropped into the machine's memory - it will play your files by folder.

To sum things up: if you want to listen to music and enjoy hi-fi quality and you don't really need the bells and whistles of modern portable devices - this one is definitely for you!!

title: Cheap Lens And It Shows In Almost Every Aspect
text:
I received this lens as part of a GF5 kit. Before purchasing the kit I was aware of its reputation of not being a stellar lens and yet I have still been disappointed. For several years I managed a professional photography store and tested many kit zoom lens. The Panasonic 14-42mm is one of the weakest performing kit lenses I've shot and it comes as no surprise to me that Panasonic is replacing the 14-42mm kit lens for their 2013 cameras.

Like many kit lenses to keep costs down the lens barrel is made of plastic. While it makes for a lightweight lens, it also feels very cheap. The lens mount is also made of plastic instead of metal. Having a metal mount does help the durability of the lens. I used to have the Nikon 18-105mm lens which has a plastic mount. One time between shots I set the camera on the ground. While arranging some stuff for the next picture, I accidentally kicked the camera (not very hard) and broke the plastic lens mount. The repair cost on the lens was around $90.

As others have noted the zoom on the 14-42mm is very choppy. I've had the lens for about 2 months and the zoom has loosened up a bit but it is still too choppy for shooting videos.

The image quality from the lens varies by focal length. At 14mm the images have good center sharpness but the edges and corners are blurry. The bottom left corner is particularly bad with this lens on both my GF5 and G5. Even stopping down to f/8 which is usually lenses sweet spot for edge to edge sharpness barely helps to improve the sharpness of the edges and corners at 14mm. The best focal lengths for image quality from this lens comes between 20-25mm. At these focal lengths I get good results wide open and stopped down to f/8. At 42mm the images are soft. On the GF5 because of the lower megapixel capability (12MP) it is barely noticeable. But on the G5 which is 16MP the images shot at 42mm are clearly soft, much softer than the images shot at 25mm.

The one shining aspect of this lens is its AF. The AF is fast and silent which makes it ideal for videos. It's just too bad the zoom is so choppy.

If you are thinking of purchasing this lens for a GF3 or GF5 be aware that the lens blocks the flash coverage at focal lengths from 14-25mm. At 14mm it is quite bad, casting a shadow from about middle of the frame on down to the lower corners.

title: Amazing speed for a niche audience
text:
10,000 RPM drives never quite caught on in the consumer market. They came close with the earliest Velociraptor drives, which offered world class speeds, albeit at a higher price and smaller capacity than mainstream drives. SSDs eventually took over the faster though costlier and smaller niche. Yet the VelociRaptor still survives. Will it thrive?

Well at 50% or so faster than the [[ASIN:B006W3ZXJC My Book Thunderbolt Duo 6 TB dual-drive storage - WDBUPB0060JSL-NESN]] there is compelling speed, though most users would rather have the added capacity and lower cost. For those of you editing HD video on a Macbook (Pro) and in need of more space (a common need), well this may be the answer. You get speed that can only be matched by SSDs (at a relatively large capacity) and larger RAID arrays (not exactly portable). If you need this kind of speed and the other solutions are not a good fit, well then keep reading.

As a ready to go solution, you can simply plug it in your Thunderbolt port (it can daisy chain on to another device), and it's ready to go (Mac formatted HFS+) in RAID-0 striped array complete with a Thunderbolt cable. It can be used with Time Machine, but that's not really the best use of this device. Nor is it without compromises, even beyond what's already been addressed. It's kinda loud and runs hot (most RAID setups will). In short if you're doing anything that doesn't require maximum hard drive performance, there are way better options.

Pros
* Great for HD video editing
* Fastest solution of it's kind (2 drives adding up to 2tb)
* Included cable ($50 value)
* Daisy chain capable

Cons
* Pricey
* Hot and loud
* Thunderbolt only
* Better solutions for most users

title: Lots of features, good looking shots
text:
INTRODUCTION & OVERVIEW:
For a pocket camera, there's a lot to love about the Cybershot DSC-W730. This is a great pocket camera that I can take anywhere because of its small size. I'm not a photo professional, so I think it takes decent photos and movies. However, there are some trade-offs. The camera has an entirely plastic body. This makes it lightweight but it also gives it a cheap feel. The LCD screen is smaller than my other cameras because of the overall small size (only 3" diagonal) but it's adequate.

The battery charges directly in the camera, so I don't think having a spare battery is a viable option. The battery charges one of two ways: via the mini-USB cable plugged into the power adapter and into the wall, or via the mini-USB cable plugged into a computer USB slot.

I like that there's a built-in instruction guide in the camera, so if I'm away from home I can still check how to use a feature if I forget.

While this camera is intuitive to use, transferring images to my PC was not. I expected to connect it to my PC and find it as a drive (like with every other camera I've used) but the DSC-W730 will not show up under File Explore by default. It required me to download and install the SONY "Play Memories" software for transfer of my photos and videos.

I love the Panorama mode! Set the camera to this and it automatically takes five shots in a sweep, all adjusted exposure etc, and stitches them right on the camera for remarkably cool panorama shot.

There are some photo effects, like those you might normally apply via additional software on your PC, that you can apply directly on the camera as you take the shot. I particularly like the Partial Color effect. It takes a b&w shot with the color of my choice highlighted. EG: a red rose, only the rose would be red and the background would be b&w. This makes for some truly striking imagery. Can be applied to stills, movies, or panoramas.

IN THE BOX:
* Sony DCS-W730 camera
* Wrist strap
* Sony NP-BN lithium ion battery
* Proprietary Mini-USB cable
* Power charging adapter
* User's Guide
NOTE: The camera does not come with any sort of flash card included, not even a tiny one. You'll need to supply your own

STILL IMAGE MODES:
* Easy
* Intelligent Auto - Exposure adjustment with automatic settings
* Program - Auto exposure with adjustable settings
* Picture Effect - shoot images with different effects applied. Toy (toy camera look, you can change the color hue: normal, cool, warm, green, magenta), Pop (pop and colorful scenes), Partial Color (b&w shots with one extracted color: red, green, blue, yellow), Soft High-Key (warm fresh shots emphasizing bright areas)
* Scene Selection - select best scene mode for environment and shoot (Soft Skin, Soft Snap, Landscape, Night Portrait, Night Scene, High Sensitivity, Gourmet, Pet, Beach, Snow, Fireworks)
* Smile Detection (three sensitivities)
* Face detection
* Continuous shooting mode
* Red Eye reduction

IMAGE SIZES:
* 4:3 (16Mb) for prints up to13"x19"
* 4:3 (10Mb) for prints up to 11"x17"
* 4:3 (5Mb) for prints up to 8"x10"
* 4:3 (VGA) smaller size for email
* 16:9 (12Mb) 11"x17" for viewing on HDTVs
* 16:9 (2Mb) for viewing on HDTVs

SWEEP PANORAMA MODES:
* Sweep mode
* Picture effects: Pop (pop and colorful scenes), Partial Color (b&w shot with one extracted color: red, green, blue, yellow), Soft High-Key (warm fresh shots emphasizing bright areas)

PANORAMA IMAGE SIZE:
* Standard
* Wide
* 360 degrees

MOVIE MODES:
* Auto
* Movie steady mode (two modes: Standard or Active)
* Auto white balance (or selectable to Daylight, Cloudy, Fluorescent 1, Fluorescent 2, Fluorescent 3, Incandescent, One Push, or set it yourself)
* Picture effects: Toy (toy camera look, you can change the color hue: normal, cool, warm, green, magenta), Pop (pop and colorful scenes), Partial Color (b&w movies with one extracted color: red, green, blue, yellow), Soft High-Key (warm fresh shots emphasizing bright areas)

MOVIE IMAGE SIZES:
* 720 Fine 1280x720
* 720 Standard 1280x720
* VGA for web uploads

IN CONCLUSION:
For a small pocket camera, I think the DSC-W730 does a terrific job with point and click photos. There are enough features to keep me amused, but my basic use will be for stills, movies, and the occasional panorama and I will probably be shooting in "Intelligent Auto" mode for all of these because I think the camera does a great job with the automatic settings. I would recommend this camera to my friends and family, although I would first point out that the transfer of photos to a PC requires the download of the SONY software. Otherwise 4-better-than-average stars from me.

title: The perfect go-bag!
text:
This is my favorite go-to camera/travel day bag, and holds everything I need for around town trips. It looks like a regular bag, not a camera bag, and in tourist areas, keeping your camera stealth can really help with thieves. For those who don't want to carry a camera, the camera padding compartment is removable, allowing you to use it as a regular day bag.

The main compartment is well-padded, with an adjustable divider, and nicely holds my Nikon D3200 with a 18-140mm lens. It won't comfortably hold large full-frame dslr's with large lenses, but the smaller consumer level dslr's and any size point and shoot, will fit nicely with room for a accessories, sunglasses and a wallet. The camera compartment easily comes out if you don't need it.

A pocket on the outside front of the main compartment will hold a small book, pens, papers, or various other personal items, and includes a sturdy piece of grosgrain ribbon with a grommet, for attaching a carabiner or quick-release set of keys.

A pocket on the exterior flap, has a zipper that appears to be waterproof, (I was in one downpour, and the contents remained dry), and this pocket will hold a cell phone, notepad, and other small personal items.

A smaller back pocket (with what appears to be another waterproof zipper) will hold a few small items such as plane tickets, passport, or papers.

The best part of this bag, is that just outside of the main interior compartment is a dedicated, padded iPad/tablet sleeve. This feature alone makes the bag worth the price.

title: Good non-wiring camera with one horrible flaw...
text:
Very small and discrete and easy to hide away. The setup is simple and quick. I think the image quality is fine. This is a small, battery operated security camera, not a camcorder. The quality is about as good as one can reasonably expect. It’s good enough to identify who walks into range and that’s what matters. Of course this depends on how far away you put it from the target area. Mine is about six feet away. The battery life is decent. Depending on the settings the battery will last about two months, maybe three.

Two bad things about the VueZone:

1. It’s completely worthless in low light unless you also purchase the relatively large IR accessory. The IR accessory completely negates the discreteness of the camera. If you expect to get night use out of it, you’re better off making sure your porch light is bright enough.

2. The optional outdoor shell is nice and fairly solid; but the screws that come with it are so shallow it wouldn’t take much for someone to snap it off and run away with it. Hopefully it’d record a good video before that happened.

COMPLETELY UNACCEPTABLE :

You can’t review motion events as they’re occurring. This means that you have to wait until the camera stops recording, uploads to the website and then wait for the website to place it in your library and make it available for viewing. The purpose of a security camera is to immediately know who’s snooping around your house. Is it the mailman making a delivery or is someone getting ready to break into your house? You’ll waste precious time waiting for VueZone. That’s insane! I was going to purchase additional units, but this problem alone makes me wonder if I should look for a better solution from another company.

title: Servicable, Not Perfect!
text:
We MacBook Air users tend to be those who appreciate cutting-edge engineering with statement type cosmetics. It is kind of ironic, to begin with, that many of us want to cover up this electronic thing of beauty. There lies the "fly-in-the ointment" as many of us want to shield our Airs from the ravages of use. I guess we are going to have to make some compromises and that is exactly what, I feel, the Knopa keyboard cover is. It isn't close to perfect, but it is very functional. The functionality takes a bit of getting use to. First, I thought the cover was downright ugly on the Air (I still do). Add to that I didn't feel it melted as I expected around the keys as there were tiny air gaps that just never really seem to go away. The feel, thus air gaps and all, takes a bit of getting use to. It does degrade the keyboard experience tactilly almost as much as visually. But, and here's why it is staying on my Air: it works. Yes, you get use to it both in fit and function and it gives you peace of mind that you are protecting your machine. It is easy as pie on or off so that is good.

While I'd like to see if there are better alternatives out there this is about the cheapest insurance policy for keeping debris and wear off your keyboard ever. After a period of aclimation it seems less intrusive if still far from perfect. If you want your keys protected you can't seriously go wrong if you try this since the investment is slight. As such I recommend it with the caveats mentioned and the knowledge that there may be much better out there I am not personally aware of.

Pros: It is handsome, sturdy, lightweight and does what it's supposed to do - holds your K-Fire 8.9. It does the following: turns the tablet off and on as you close and open the cover; holds the tablet securely; provides 2 positions to view the tablet in; and provide back and front protection. The exterior is attractive, better looking than the photo conveys, with a suede-like texture.
FYI: This cover will provide basic protect from contact damage, like scratches, etc. It won't provide impact protection. The Fire is held in place by 4 strong elastic pieces, so the tablet could fall out if it is dropped. Most likely that wouldn't happen, but that possibility should be noted. Also, there is no place to hold a stylus. However, if you have a stylus that had an attachment to plug the headphones hole, you can store a stylus that way. The stylus will be held inside the cover via the plug, and lay along the spine.
A significant issue, already noted by another reviewer: this cover really does smell!! Strong chemical smell. Of course, every molecule of the cover is synthetic, so a smell isn't unexpected. I will leave the cover open (without the Fire inside) and hope that the smell fades away.
As for the price - with a 30% discount offered through the Amazon Local program, I paid $30 for this cover, tax & shipping included. That is a fair price. the original price of $40 is TOO MUCH, in my opinion. An appropriate price would be $20 to $25 plus shipping and tax.

title: I was skeptical until I got some; too bad Polk does not make a good center to match
text:
After lots of research, I think that these might be the best stereo speakers you can get for the money. Great midrange, soundstage and detail.

Previously, I had been conned by mail order speakers and on line reviews. I bought Aperion 633T speakers at $1000 a pair. A couple of on line articles claimed that they were better than any $2000 speakers you could buy in the stores. That is simply not true. These $1500 per pair speakers completely blow away the mail order speakers. There is just no comparison. (Althought the Aperion speakers are much better looking)

The RTi A9 is a minor tweak of the earlier RTi12 speakers. The cabinets have had curves added. But, more importantly, the sound has been tweaked a little to remove some the brightness that some complained about on the RTi12.

You do need power to run these speakers, but you don't have to go over board. I am using a 140 watt per channel Pioneer Elite and have these speakers in a large room. It is sufficient. If you have a receiver with extra channels you aren't using, you can bi-amp the speakers.

I don't think these speakers are that great in the looks department. They are huge, black boxes with some curves added. They are black painted oak veneer. To me, they look like a homemade plywood box spray painted black (sort of like the speaker enclosure my dad made 40 years ago). One of Polk's selling point is the real wood enclosure, but I think many black vinyl enclosures look better. The cherry is much nicer, but still not the nicest cherry enclosure when compared to the competitors like Aperion (which are gorgeous).

Unfortunately, Polk does not make a center channel speaker that equals the performance of these towers. The center channel speaker, is the CSi A6. It is a two way speaker, using two 6-1/2" midranges and the same tweater as the towers. I don't think it has the depth, range or clarity to match the towers.

title: Cheap, UNSAFE product! NOT GENUINE Lenovo adapter! NOT WORTH YOUR TIME OR MONEY
text:
I ordered this ac adapter, because my original one broke and I needed a replacement for my Lenovo ThinkPad L420. Well when the adapter arrived in the mail, it didn't work. It was packaged in a small box, with only one thin layer of bubble wrap around it. There was nothing else inside except the adapter. Not ever an order receipt. I contacted the seller through Amazon and they told me that sometimes the adapters get damaged in shipping, and they would send me a replacement. (Maybe if they packaged it better, it wouldn't haven't gotten damaged in the first place.) I also asked them if, maybe the problem was that I ordered the wrong adapter, but they assured me the one I ordered was compatible with my laptop.

When I received the second adapter, it also came poorly packaged. This time, in a padded envelope with again, just one layer of bubble wrap around it, without any other paperwork. It seemed to work at first, but within a day of use the power supply got extremely hot! The plastic casing on the side started to warp a bit from the heat! This can't be safe!

I should also note that both of the adapters they sent me (the broken one and the replacement), had a slightly off color yellow connector that didn't match my laptop. The two adapters didn't even match each other in color. I have very high doubts that this adapter is a genuine Lenovo product like the company claims!

title: HDMI switching perfection!  Very satisfied with this product.
text:
Recently I was in the market for an 8 port HDMI switch. Unfortunately there are not many options out there to choose from and I wasn't interested in cascading switches or spending 10-20 times the money for a 8x8 HDMI matrix switch instead. To make matters worse, of the 8 port HDMI switches I did find none of them offered customer reviews anywhere online that I could find, so naturally I was a bit hesitant to purchase the IOGEAR Avior GHSW8181 8-Port HDMI Switch. I ended up going with this switch, because I was already familiar with the IOGEAR brand name and it met all the requirements I was looking for. Thankfully I could not have made a better choice. Figured it was about time someone online posted a review of this product so here goes.

I'll first note that the pictures of the IOGEAR Avior GHSW8181 8-Port HDMI Switch I had found online don't do this product justice. I was immediately impressed with the looks of this switch once receiving it as well as the build quality which is excellent. There is nothing about this switch that looks or feels cheap. The LED indicators on the front of the unit are also very tastefully done. They are sufficiently bright enough to clearly see which inputs are active and which one is currently selected without at the same time being annoying in any way, i.e. they don't light up like a Christmas tree blinding you or annoyingly blink. The particular HDMI cables I'm using with the switch are also firmly held in place per the inputs on the back of the switch which I was happy to see.

I was also looking specifically for an HDMI switch that if offered, allowed for any auto-detection feature to be disabled. In my case I want my remote control solution to always determine which input the switch should be set to. I never want the switch to change inputs automatically based on which ports are active or become active. Well I'm happy to say that this switch works as advertised per the ability to disable the auto-detection feature by sending it the appropriate RS-232 command. Works like a charm as do all of the other RS-232 commands.

As far as the actual HDMI switching goes, so far this switch has been nothing short of perfection. I purchased this HDMI switch for use with 6 Sony BDP-CX7000ES Blu-ray changers I recently added to my setup. I'm running various length HDMI cables (3-5 feet runs) from each changer to the HDMI switch, then from the HDMI switch to my Onkyo TX-NR818 Home Theater Receiver using a Monoprice 60ft Slim Series High Speed HDMI® Cable w/ RedMere® Technology. The signal then continues on from my Onkyo receiver to my Samsung PN58B860 Plasma Display. Haven't had as much as a hiccup after a month of heavy use. The HDMI switching has been spot on each and every time. Perfectly consistent. No sync issues of any kind. Takes all of a second or two for my receiver and display to sync up with the signal which remains stable 100% of the time. Most importantly, the picture and sound quality have been perfect just as if I was running each of the Blu-ray changers to my receiver separately. I don't watch 3D Blu-ray content so I can't speak to that, but I am sending 1080p 24hz video and lossless audio from the switch and again, no issues. Highly recommended.
____________________________

IMPORTANT UPDATE (3/28/2018)

You'll want to read the below if you're having trouble getting this switch to not change inputs automatically when a source device connected to another port is powered on. The "Power On Detection" feature is not used for that purpose. Thankfully there are commands available for this per the ATEN version of this switch. I've confirmed the ATEN serial commands work with the IOGEAR version of the switch as well. See the below taken from the IOGEAR manual.

Power On Detection - if one of the HDMI source devices is powered off or unplugged, the switch will automatically switch to the next active port. The Power On Detection feature is turned on by default.

Note that the above feature is not intended to enable/disable automatic switching when a new source device is powered on. The above feature is actually the "Go To" feature as documented in the manual for the ATEN version of the switch. See below.

swmode goto off [Enter] // Disable Go To (default)
swmode goto on [Enter] // Switch to next port with a powered on source device when the current input source device is powered off.

To actually prevent automatic switching when a new source device is powered on you'll need to send the switch the Switch Mode "default" command (swmode default\r). Additional Switch Mode commands provided below as well.

swmode next [Enter] // Switch priority is placed on the next port that has a new source device connected to it. (default)
swmode default [Enter] // The switch behaves normally without automatic switching.
swmode ixx auto [Enter] // Places priority on a selected port so that when a source is connected to the said port it's selected automatically and can't be changed until the source is unplugged or auto switching mode is disabled with the default comment.

The ATEN manual also documents the commands for turning on and off the output port. Again, more commands not included in the IOGEAR manual.

sw on [Enter] // Turn on the output port.
sw off [Enter] // Turn off the output port

And now some backstory...
I own two of the IOGEAR switches now. I purchased the first one back in 2013. At that time I was under the mistaken impression that turning off the "Power On Detection" feature would prevent any and all automatic switching. It wasn't until I purchased a second one of these switches here recently that I realized the "Power On Detection" feature wasn't what I thought it was. The reason it took me this long to realize it was due to the first switch I purchased having been set to the Switch Mode "default" out the box. (swmode default\r) There's simply no other explanation as for the past 4 plus years automatic switching has never taken place when a new source device has been powered on.

With the second switch I just purchased the Switch Mode was definitely set to "next" (swmode next\r). Noticed immediately that automatic switching was still taking place after having sent the "Power On Detection - Off" command (pod off\r). That's when I took a second look at the manual realizing the "Power On Detection" feature wasn't what I thought it was. I then performed a few searches online stumbling on to the ATEN version of the switch. Looked over the ATEN manual hitting pay dirt! Added the missing serial commands to my trusty Pronto Professional TSU9600 remote, then testing to confirm. The rest is history. Gotta love it!
