title: As essential as my workstation
text:
I was looking for portable external drive options but couldn't find anything that was trustable. Based on the reviews from a wide range of external drive products, most of the problems/complaints stem either from useless or poorly implemented aspects of the external enclosures, power management, worthless software preinstalled, or bad hard drive manufacturing (of course). I stumbled upon the cavalry and had a major light bulb above the head moment. Once you find a family of dependable hard drives (Seagate Momentus and Western Digital Scorpios get good ratings and have been working well for me), just eliminate the "middleware" completely, assuming this (the cavalry) can do the job.

Getting this was probably one of the best purchasing decisions I've made this year. With USB 3.0 access speeds this works great as an external drive - actually two externals if you use both ports. I never have done it this way since I'm always afraid of what would happen if pressing the DB/Clone button with two live drives in the slots (and I'm the personality type that would eventually be tempted enough to find out). I've run it all day long and haven't had significant heat buildup on the drive itself. Running virtual machines and MSSQL databases through this as a "native" drive has been seamless with no notable performance costs. Rather than having piles of external drives (each with their own AC bricks and dated enclosure design hang-ups) this supplies a much more efficient long term solution. There are plenty of external enclosure options out there if at some point you need a bare drive to go portable, so you've got the best of both worlds with this.

BUT THEN comes the best part - as a complete image copier this thing will have paid for itself the first time you backup an OS/Application drive. I always do regular data backups, but the process of effectively backing up the OS and the application installation base is a whole different matter. I'm in software development and have a good 20 GB of baseline application installations (everything from MSSQL server, Visual studio, Eclipse with piles of extended libraries, MySQL, Tomcat, etc...) plus at least another 20 GB of additional installations and more virtual machine installations then I can count. If I had a primary drive failure it would take upwards of an entire week of full time attention to start with an empty hard drive and get it up to a point where I would be functioning at my job again. This little device eliminates this rebuild issue completely. I have a Dell Precision workstation that allows me to remove the primary drive with relative ease. After getting the workstation home I bought an identical second hard drive of the same type and size. Once a month I take out the OS/App drive and use the cavalry to clone it to the second drive. A 750 GB drive takes somewhere around 2.5 hours to complete and since it's a sector-by-sector clone it makes a clean OS installation on any drive (preformatted or not) of equivalent or greater size and eliminates problems with large virtual hard disks that would be painful if not impossible to backup otherwise. I cycle the backups (the last live drive is the next backup drive so each one gets used for a month and is then archived) and the first startup in the replacement drive is almost completely seamless - windows 7 recognizes the new OS drive as new equipment and asks for a second restart and then it's back to work. The older OS drive is safely stowed away in a box, the new clone OS/App drive is working its shift, and I'm sleeping much better at night knowing a hard drive failure will only put me back for as long as it takes to put in the backup drive and turn the computer back on. I went overboard and bought a third hard drive and cloned the base OS without any other installations so I've got a clean copy with no additional software clutter. Once a month I run windows update on it to keep it up to date so I have a pristine start point to build out a completely different baseline installation. My workstation is now INVINCIBLE. It's a three headed beast that can quickly keep coming back from the dead no matter what swarm of viruses, bad software installations or spilled red bulls get thrown at it...

Also, if you do have a hard drive with suspect problems this gadget doesn't even need to be connected to a computer to work as emergency backup. Just pop in the suspect drive and replacement drive, turn on the cavalry and click the DB button. Come back in a few hours and when the indicator has stopped blinking you're done. Couldn't be easier.

After six months of use as an external drive host and monthly backups (OS + Data drives totaling 1.25 TB which takes under 4 hours to complete) this continues to work as expected without complaints. I can't recommend it highly enough. I'll never buy a case-locked external drive again and it's nice to know I can recycle older laptop/workstation drives (both 2.5" and 3.5" variations) *and* I have an autonomous disk cloner all in one package. Good job Calvary.

title: Keyboard of the God's
text:
This is by far the best keyboard that I have ever touch in my life.

EDIT 2/19/2022: Purchased in 9/2012, nearly 10 later It has been replaced with a 75% RGB linear switch keyboard for most gaming application and night time use but this full sized filco keyboard still sees near daily use. Its a freaking tank, literally, so its a pain to travel with it but I have. I used to take it back and forth to my office when I was a grad student , you get used to the weight but the size makes it hard to stick it into a full backpack safely.
This thing has seen a lot of abuse and keeps trucking. Recently spilt ginger ale on it. Some switches got sticky but have worked themselves out to being fine again. The "space bar" is more rattly that a baby rattle after experiencing better stabalizers imo. Hopefully newer models have better ones now. Im planning on desoldering and swapping worn and used switches with new ones, fixing the spacebar rattle
and lube it up in the future.
The keycaps have shined and are lettering slightly faded especially on more frequently used keys but in all honesty arent as bad as other keys this old and used. I have worn through the original "WASD" keys and the ones from the add on pack that are blue and red from gaming over the years. I plan on swapping out for all new key set soon as a 10 year refresh.

----END EDIT----
Pros: The feeling is meaty and full. You know that you press keys and even if you mistype (It still happens sometimes but infact a lot less than any other keyboard I have had.

The keys are spaced out a little more but not a lot so you have to get used to it. Instead this seperation I feel is a more natural feel. I dont have finger strain from typing ever.

It is super fun to type. I have brought this keyboard with me to places just so I could type on it. I love it that much.

Keys are easily removed to allow a thorough cleaning of the keyboard and for custimazation. I also bought the wasd key pack as I game and there are a whole list of after market keys to allow you to custamize your set up.

The cherry switches have yet to fail me. In time I can update this if anything happens but if all goes according to plan they will last a long time.

The sound that the keys make is magic to the ears. This is my humble opinion but I feel that it is an important aspect of typing. If i am typing a lot then I do not wish to hear a bunch or dud or bad sounding keys.

The cherry brown switches are not super loud as they are the middle ground.

Perfect for gamers, some may say get a different color switch, but I recommend that if you are going to be doing any typing beyond gaming get the brown switches.

The keyboard feels solid. Being a 4lb keyboard with a steel backplate would do this. I feel that I got all my money's worth in construction.

Solid, thick and well made cord with a velcro strap that isnt a cheap add on. I frequently use this strap to change the length of the cord so it is not hanging over desks or getting in the way of other things.

Cons:
It is a little heavy (about 4lb) so if you are frequently traveling than this might not be the keyboard for you.

I dont think this is a con but other might. There is NO added features( except for the standard windows key). No volume control, no backlight, no screen, macros, nothing. But what you pay for is a solid board that will never fail and bring pleasure to your typing. Filco has outdone themselves by sticking to japanese tradition, doing one thing and doing it perfect. (the light from my screen is enough to light the keys during low light operation.

It may be a little pricy. at about 150 this is an investment for the long haul, but it can go the distance. If your looking for a consistant gaming board this is it, if your looking for a keyboard because you program or type lots of documents this is it. But if you are a casual internet browser or do not consistantly use a keyboard for long periods of time (I am a college student in science so I am always typing reports and doing essays as well as programming.) then I suggest finding a cheaper keyboard.

All in all I do and have recommend this keyboard to many of my friends and allowed them to use it. They all love it and nearly had to fight one of them to get it back. Also A recommendation of mine is to the the key remover as it can be a pain in the butt to remove some of the keys at first if you have never done this ( On a mechanical keyboard). It will make cleaning very easy. I clean my board about once a month to keep dust and other particals that have migrated their way into my keyboard.

I do not know how Filco is as a company for customer service. Being a japanese company and with a product that is as polished as this then I would assume that IF there was an issue with your keyboard they would fix it. Just might be a little tough communicating. But this is just a guess.
Final verdict: BUY IT NOW!!!!!!!!

title: Crystal Clear - As  Good as any 6.5' Speaker Made
text:
I have always been into quality sound components and equipment from the day of 4 and 8 track stereo, I guess I just gave away my age... Make no mistake, I've been a rock and blues musician for 35 years and love good music played loud and proud. And Clean and Clear. The local car stereo shop is a Rockford dealer and they had never seen or sold these. Probably because few could afford them, I couldn't find a single review anywhere when I purchased prior to the one review posted on July 17...so I purchased these on a hunch that at a discount of 70% of the list price of $1699 (I paid $514), how bad can they be?

Well these did not disappoint. I had a set of Focal Polyglass 6.5's in my previous truck and they were very good, but these far exceed them IMO. This is one of the better purchases I have made in car audio...I have them a few weeks now and they are as good as anything I've ever heard. I did a lot of research before selecting the T562's, I looked at all the top competing brands - JL Audio, Focal etc..I have a 2013 Toyota Tacoma Access Cab, the head unit is a Pioneer AVH-X4500BT. When choosing this level of quality for your sound system, you won't be happy unless the other components of your setup are well matched. Choose a quality amp that has enough power to drive the speakers. I use a separate amp just for the sub... In my system the T562's are driven by Rockford Power T400-2 400 watt Stereo Amp with a 10" Rockford Sub Box behind the passenger seat driven by a Rockford Punch P300-2 300-Watt Stereo Amp. I used 80 mil GTMAT on the entire interior so that also helps the real sound of the speakers come through and dampens vibrations. I think it's important to note that there a lot of personal preference when it comes to what sounds good, and choice will depend on the type of music your into. When you get to this level of top of the line speaker quality it's going to be good as long as the rest of your system is on par with the speakers. My head unit has an 8 band EQ and this helps shape the sound to your personal preferences.

Bottom line...these are fantastic speakers at a great price that will probably make any music sound great, make sure you get the rest of your setup right (good Amp, Sub etc) to bring out the quality...

The solar panel is well placed and comes with a micro usb end. The battery pack that comes with the backpack is very well made. It surprised me it has a matte black finish. It comes with a zip pouch that has adapters for iPhone Samsung phones Nokia and others;also,comes with a usb wall charger to plug in the battery to charge at home. I will try to give a future update on this product when I have spent more time with it. So far I am impressed with the quality of this backpack.

Update: I decided to buy another battery pack I used the Intocircuit Power Castle Series PC11200 11200mAh Heavy Duty, but it wouldn't take a charge from the solar panel. So I returned it to get a Maxboost Pulse 10000mAh which will take power from the solar panel plus it came with a flashlight that comes in handy. What I do is charge one battery packs at night and let the author battery pack charge using solar panel. This worked well for me hiking and camping in the woods. I also use this backpack for school there is some complaints one being the backpack is a little top heavy from the solar panel in the front so some times it will tip forward if you don't have something solid in the laptop pocket. The color of the backpack bugs me i wish it was solid black cause the two tone color makes me think my backpacks open when its on my back. It's not a big problem just something that bugs me. Also wish this backpack had a bigger side pocket to fit a water bottle. All in all I am still happy with this backpack.

title: Braided, short, inexpensive, full-featured
text:
This cable will work well with anything that supports HDMI, being built to comply with the current HDMI 1.4 standard.

- You may consider this product if you have TWO devices that support HDMI 1.4 such as TVs and Blu-ray players. For these, the cable will carry through HD images and Ethernet data therefore eliminating the need for one dedicated Ethernet cable and one Ethernet port.
- You may also consider this cable if you currently need an extra HDMI cable but you are planning to to replace your existing equipment with some HDMI 1.4 ready hardware such as a 3D Blu-ray player.
- You may also consider this if you need an HDMI cable plain and simple because it will work with anything that requires HDMI.
- You should definitely consider this cable if you prefer 'braided' cables.

If you consider taking advantage of the Ethernet support, keep in mind that BOTH connected devices need to support the HDMI 1.4 standard for this cable to make a difference and that it is NOT possible to upgrade any existing equipment (TV, Blu-ray player) to support HDMI 1.4. This being said, I would not buy an HDMI cable today unless it was v1.4 given that the price difference is insignificant or non-existent.

HOW GOOD IS IT?
On my equipment, this worked as well as any other HDMI wire. It replaced an older HDMI v1.3 wire at the back of my entertainment center and, nothing unexpected happened. The picture on my TV was as beautiful as before.

Briefly, this cable:

- Behaves as a HDMI 1.3x 'high speed' or 'category 2' cable.
- As a 'high speed' HDMI 1.4 cable, it supports video resolutions of 1080p and can go as high as 4K.
- The 'data channel' (Ethernet support) works only with HDMI 1.4 ready equipment.
- The 'audio return channel' is another feature supported by HDMI 1.4 ready equipment only. It will allow for audio to be sent 'back' from, let's say a TV to the HDMI 1.4 compliant receiver, therefore eliminating the need for a dedicated audio cable.
- It should support all the HDMI 1.4 extra color palettes because those are implemented by the HDMI 1.4 compliant connected equipment.

A 5-star rating should be fair for this cable because it is fully HDMI 1.4/1.3x and the price is right.

END OF REVIEW

______________________________________________________

What follows is the byproduct of me attempting to clarify 'HDMI 1.4' for myself and understanding this specific product's features. I thought I'd share.

WHAT'S IN A NAME? (understanding this cable's features)

- HDMI 1.4 is a HDMI standard adopted in 2009, backward compatible with HDMI 1.3. This cable should work with your existing equipment.
- HIGH SPEED indicates that this cable supports resolutions of 1080p or higher and 3D video (unlike the HDMI 1.4 STANDARD cables which, believe it or not, are limited to 720p/1080i - why? nobody knows).
- ETHERNET means that this cable supports a full-duplex 100 Mb/sec Ethernet connection - if you have 2 HDMI 1.4 ready devices and they both need an network connection, this cable will carry through the Ethernet datastream to the second device, therefore saving you the need for one extra Ethernet cable.
- Audio Return Channel would save you the need of a dedicated audio cable between 2 HDMI 1.4 compliant devices.
- This cable supports the full set of 3D features found in the new TVs.

THE HDMI 1.4x DIFFERENCE

HDMI 1.4 allows for the following new features:

- Ethernet Channel - allows for the 2 connected devices to communicate with each other and share one network connection.
- Audio Return Channel - eliminates the need of a second cable if you want to send audio from your TV back to your receiver.
- 3D - It's supported by HDMI 1.3x but HDMI 1.4a specifically supports all the currently agreed-upon industry standards
- 4K resolution - good to have it but there is nothing on today's market that would take advantage of this
- Expanded support for new color spaces - by supporting sYCC601, AdobeRGB, and AdobeYCC601 it better aligns your display with the color spaces supported by digital cameras.
- Type D connector - the 'Micro' connector is to be used by small, portable devices with supported resolutions of up to 1080p.

The HDMI Consortium defines 4 broad types of HDMI 1.4 cables:

* Standard HDMI Cable
* High Speed HDMI Cable
* Standard HDMI Cable with Ethernet
* High Speed HDMI Cable with Ethernet

Of the above, only the 'High Speed HDMI Cable with Ethernet' makes sense and is emerging as the common HDMI 1.4 cable standard.

'Standard' cables are limited to lower-resolution displays up to (approx. 720p or 1080i) and I am not aware of such products on the market. High Speed cables support higher-resolution display (e.g. 1080p). They can deliver all video content currently defined for the HDMI standard (i.e. more than two 1080p/60 video streams, including 3D). HDMI cables with Ethernet are capable of sending 100/mbps over the HDMI Ethernet Channel. Since it is not likely that many HDMI 1.4 'standard' cables will be made or sold, I suspect that the crippled 'standard' type exists only to allow for calling the cables that support 1080p 'high speed' which sounds good and high-end.

title: Great soundbar with some quirks
text:
Overall I love it but it can be found cheaper. I have had this on my wish list since it was released, at 1200$ it is incredibly over priced and does not perform up to the cost. I have waited and it has came down in price gradually, but I came across a large retailer discounting it at 499$ and jumped on it. Unboxing it I will say it is well packed but there is and incredible amount of wasted space since the box has to fit the largest piece the sub the bar takes up the other 5% I'm surprised they don't separate them and save shipping. Mounting was Easy enough it's fairly light and I was able to get it on the wall in a 1/2 hour, the only problem was the mounting holes are about 12inches apart so most people won't get both screws into a stud just one. When they released this samsung stated it was more for larger TVs with a few more features over their HW-F750, I have a 60 inch and the soundbar is about 5 inches short on both sides so I do wish it was slightly longer for larger TVs. Install took 5 mins, I do have a Samsung tv that is soundshare (Bluetooth sound) compatible, I just had to switch the TV to search for it and it connected on its own. I love this feature as I didn't want to see any wires and due to a stud between my TV wiring and the input for the soundbar I didn't want anymore holes in my wall. Sound: I will say it didn't sound that great out of the box, but after a few days it has gotten way better (I don't know if its the vacuum tubes needing to break in or what) I also calibrated the whole setup using the included microphone and on board setup which helped a lot. The subwoofer is probably the the let down as it basically relays all the sound, so basically you hear everything instead of just the lows. I will say I am no audiophile but I do have higher end head phones and IEMs and know what something of this price should sound like.

Pros: Good sound with calibration and breakin, great looking, high build quality, packed with features, easy to setup,
Cons: Bar needs to be longer, High priced, 4 lights in the middle for power and volume are on all the time and are distracting in low light, sub relays all sound through instead of just lows.

Overall I would only recommend buying this at a lower price, at the price I bought it at I am very happy with the performance and features.

The hardware settings and drivers might be set to run this OS but it maxes out the Memory and CPU usage pretty much constantly. Opened the task manager to keep an eye on what makes it max out and opening this window alone (nothing else running) brought it up to 99% CPU usage and jumped between 70-80% Memory usage. I will be upgrading the Ram as soon as I get paid and getting a new OS as soon as humanly possible. It won't run Netflix, Youtube videos glitch and don't load, even the simplest Gif image files run worse than my 2 year old smartphone. I had a 2007 Dell made Alienware that ran better than this thing. Also had a 2005... TWO THOUSAND FIVE(!!!!) IBM Thinkpad with 2gb Ram and an 80gb hard drive that would run videos better and didn't max out so easily. Got stuck on updates and had to wait for it to revert, it was stuck on update "32 of 60" for over an hour and froze. The craftsmanship is exactly what you would expect; plastic and light, keys are weird and the set up is hard to get used to at first but the number pad addition is cool, I need that for work so that part is okay by me for sure. But if you need this thing for ANYTHING important or work related right off the bat don't even think about buying this thing unless you have some Ram laying around and are really good with swapping out operating systems and updating drivers manually and all of that headache. Basically this computer would (and hopefully will be) be good for some upgrades, which are reportedly easy to do, and will run Ubuntu or some other way less demanding OS better than Windows -hate-. Also, disk drive is odd at times, it works fine and video replay is actually pretty good when watching a movie etc but it sometimes just doesn't recognize the disk and I can't really figure out how to fix that issue. Sidenote; the noted problems with the wireless card, actually haven't had any issues with that at all it recognized our Wifi with no issues and if I had passwords at work it picks up signal from 10+ routers and there's only 5-6 in our building so that's cool. Hopefully this helps someone else, like I said I think it has potential with some work and a little money but as is... I wouldn't give this thing to a 12 year old for Christmas because it won't even run the simple things like Flash games without clocking out pretty hard. (No offense to any 12 year olds out there looking at this, you're better than this laptop. It's a compliment)

title: DUNU's Flagship Triple Driver
text:
I have been a DUNU fan for a couple of years so when I read they had a triple driver hybrid IEM in their lineup I was anxious to get my hands on a pair. My first pair of DUNU earphones was DN-12 Trident that I still consider DUNU's best budget earphones.
My second pair of DUNU earphones was the modestly priced DN-13 Crius which uses a single balanced armature driver. The DN-13 Crius may be a bit light in bass but offers remarkably clear mids and highs. The DN-13 is great for many types of music just the way it's tuned but I find I need to give it a little help with bass by boosting lower bass response with an equalizer.

So on to the DN-1000 which uses a dynamic driver plus 2 balanced armature drivers. The cost at the time of this review is around $200 plus shipping. I paid a total of $220. I could not find a US seller that had them in stock so I had to order from China and wait 4 weeks for delivery. The DN-1000 produces very clear mids and highs from the balanced armature drivers and manages to pull off clean deep bass response from it's dynamic divers. It produces plenty of lower bass without drowning out the mids. It does sound better than the DN-12 or the DN-13 but that is expected with earphones costing many times as much.
At $200 plus shipping cost I don't consider it to be quite the bargain the DN-12 is which can be found for around $30. It does however give excellent sound and is priced lower than many if not all other triple driver hybrid IEMs.
I do not know what the metal is that DUNU uses for the bodies on the DN-1000. It may be titanium as on the DN-12. It is certainly a heavier metal than aluminum. The weight can make them uncomfortable for extended wear if worn cord down. I wear them with the strain reliefs up and the cords over my ears to help with the weight and eliminate noise transmitted by the cords.
Like the DN-12 models I own they stick out of my head enough to cause discomfort if my ear lays against my pillow while wearing them. For that reason I do not wear these in bed opting for the non in-ear types or a pair of Panasonic RPHJE355A for listening to music in bed.

NOTE.... If you expect to get decent sound and bass response from this or virtually any other in-ear type earphone it is crucial that the tips fit tightly on the nozzle of the earphone and fit your ear canal tightly enough to create a good seal. Leakage at either place will produce poor overall sound and very little bass response. I know most people reading this already know how important fit and seal is so this is not aimed at you. I do feel that this is not emphasized enough. I believe poor fit and / or seal is often the problem when some reviewers mention weak bass and poor sound quality when reviewing earphones that do indeed have good sound and bass response.

title: EXCELLENT sound quality and features.
text:
This is an AWESOME voice recorder. I've been using this now for several years of lectures and I would buy it again in a heartbeat.

Get this. period.

Ok. where to start? this picks up the lecture voice clearly in rooms of different types (labs, lecture halls, small rooms, large rooms, etc). the sound quality is excellent. you can set many features on this (might be a bit daunting to set up at first, but play with it and it will become clear quickly what setting you need for it to be optimized for your needs). I think the different setting options is why it is so good in so many different acoustic settings. you can set it to record the whole group in a conference, a single person dictation, or to emphasize a particular person in a group when everyone else is yakking away out of sequence. it can focus on what you want and not have major distortion or be overwhelmed by say, a low background noise of an air conditioner vent or equipment nearby or have group conversation muddle out what's being said. Olympus knows their stuff here and did this right. I have mine set to get the instructor clearly (male or female, both sound clear and loud) but I can also hear questions from the back of the room with certain settings. simply amazing.

the battery life is great. I record for about 6 hours a day and then play back while driving or studying. the battery is good for at least 3 or 4 days, but I do my best to keep it charged because the information is critical, so I prob could go longer on it but I don't. you can use the internal memory, but I just bought a micro sd card and it holds weeks of lectures at least (I don't think ive ever filled it up actually, but its nice to know I won't). every few days I just plug it n via the micro usb to usb cable to my laptop, and download the files to the Olympus software. I have mine set for mp3 format, but you can do wav and a few others if you want. it has a setting so you can just plug it in via usb (to a laptop or wall usb outlet thingy) to charge or have it charge while you file transfer. the rechargeable battery does last a long time, but you can also swap it out for a standard battery if you forgot to charge it and it ran out. no biggie.

playback is great. I can have many different levels of speed adjustment to hear lecture playbacks quickly but still be understandable. I haven't used the podcast feature, no idea on that one. its got stereo recording (you can set to mono) and playback, and is fully compatible with external microphones and mp3 player type earbuds. I sometimes playback on the speaker, but usually listen via headset or run it through my car speakers while driving via the headphone out port.

the folders, file names, etc are very customizable which is great, so I can quickly access whichever folder or lecture and keep my files stored in that section.

I really got this for the sound quality. it is exceptional. the clarity is amazing. I've shown friends with hearing issues or attention/memory issues this and they get one themselves and agree its just a great tool to have so if they miss part of a lecture its all within easy playback. I've even burned cds for people who miss class or put the file on a flashdrive so they can hear the lecture they missed, and they are amazed at the sound quality of it. ***this puts other voice recorders to shame!*** they all say' wow! mine doesn't sound like that. I can barely hear mine when I play it. I can actually hear and understand what they're saying on yours.' point is, its worth the money to get something that actually works and works extremely well.

not sure what else to say. just if you get this you won't go wrong. oh, I know, when I first got this as a test for it I turned it on in one corner of a room and talked at normal voice and walked around and left the room and went into other rooms across a house and could STILL hear my own voice clearly. I figured I would just find where it cut out---but it clearly picked up the sound everywhere I went. that is amazing.

if you've got one and you're having any trouble at all I would say take a look at the settings because it gives you a lot of options - but it also has a lot of 'preset settings' to make it easy for you to just pick one or another if you don't want to figure out what you need. then you can go back and fine tune that preset to bring out say, the speakers voice, or the group speaking or block out low level vibration noise that may be drowning out other sounds or whatever. so you have a lot of control, but they also help you use them and take advantage of them even if all the options are too much to figure out (presets, use the presets, and then tweak them a bit if you want to).

this is the higher end model (an older version now) and I also have a lower end model as a backup (I left this once in a lecture hall n didn't get it back for a few days). the lower end models don't have as many features. this has the absolute best sound quality also. the other model I have has the usb port that you slide in and out of the unit to plug it in, and after using both I have to say I really prefer just plugging in a usb cable, tho they both work fine.

title: No Buyer's Remorse here!!
text:
My trusty oll' 8-year-old Dell XPS 410, running Windows XP, finally gave out just two weeks after XP went EOL (Coincidence, or...? :) ). It was a hard failure, so I was dead in the water- I needed to get back up and running, so I didn't really have time to shop around (I traditionally look for bargains at the Dell outlet). So I googled around, saw this on The Big River, and liked the specss- the quickest quad core in its family, decent RAM, lots of USB ports, DVD/CD, and memory card ports. So I took the plunge and ordered it, expecting to be kicking myself a week later. But not so!

This machine and OS is VERY fast. Yes, I salvaged my SSD drives from my 410 and installed one as the new boot drive here, but this thing FLIES! I should have made the switch long before my hand was forced. Can't imagine how much time and frustration I could have saved. On the 410, I constantly had to restart Firefox because it would flake out. Now, I open oodles of taps on Chrome (I made that switch too) and nary a hitch. It's like a new world out there!

PROS: FAST! #1: Lots of USB ports (including some USB 3.0. #2:: Dual monitor ports out of the box. #3:Handy card readers. #4: Decent memory for Win7x64 (although I will upgrade to 16GB sometime soon). #5: Smaller and lighter than my 410. #6: It's not Windows 8. :)

CONS: #1: Really a huge step backward in case design. The 410 was no-tool box- open it up and remove/replace components in seconds. This one requires a screwdriver as well as some moxie to get things lined up to button it back up. And the drive bays are very different, too. I had to jump through some hoops to get the SSD into the carrier (and I'm still not sure it's right). I had to order a drive bay adapter for the second SSD- I haven't installed it yet, but I'm expecting a tricky time getting that one in there, too. They shoulda stuck with the old style drive bays, but I guess these are cheaper to manufacture. #2: With SSDs so cheap now (nearing 50 bucks for a 64GB; under a hundred sometimes for 128GB) there's no reason that most mid-to-high end systems shouldn't come standard with an SSD as a boot device. I'm somewhat tech savvy, so I was able to use the proper tools and procedures to swap my boot device to an SSD, but it's probably too much for your average Joe to handle. And the difference between a spinning disk and SSD is so pronounced that it's pretty much a no-brainer. #3: Not nearly as much bloatware as I would expect from Dell. Sure, some useless things that you might want to remove, but not the desktop-cluttering conglomerate of stuff like I'd seen in the past.

Sure, there are other cheaper systems out there. But while not a 'gaming' system per se, this is just about as good a box as you're gonna get for your money if you're someone impatient like me who wants a rather snappy system.

title: Oustanding overall value, only a few minor issues
text:
Up front, I'm very pleased with this set. This is my second Samsung Smart TV, the other being the 2013 UN32EH5300 (another 32" model). This TV is definitely sharper and more responsive. I've found no reason to be disappointed with it, and would recommend it over the older model. The one feature that really shines is Smart View, which allows me to mirror what I'm watching on my tablet.

Setup was easy, by simply plugging it in it came on and started in setup mode. As soon as I connected it to my home network, it searched for and found a firmware update and installed it. The TV supports wired as well as 2.4GHz and 5GHz WIFI. Adding the cable channels came next and went without a hitch as well. Finally I added my Amazon Prime, again with no issues. The only downside was that this model did not support the TWC Cable Viewer, allowing me to watch all of my HD digital subscription channels without a cable box *** 24 Aug 2014 Update: The ROM was recently updated and the TV now supports TWC TV App ***

The picture is bright and clean, the blacks are black, and darker colors/areas in the image are not muggy. The sound is fine for me, but I'm no audiophile like some of the other reviewers seem to be. After watching a couple of hours of cable, I streamed an episode of a show via Amazon prime and followed up by streaming a video off of my NAS (with built in Media Server), I didn't have any (TV related) issues with either streaming source. My network was stable the whole time, so I didn't experience any brief drops that required the TV to recover the video stream.

Overall, I'm very pleased with this TV. My only issues are stylistic differences between the remote and the Smart TV interface on this TV and my older UN32EH5300. These issues are very minor, and not worth pulling a star for.

*** 24 Aug 2014 Update: To date, my TV has received three ROM updates. ROM updates are easy. Updates automatically download when available, a discreet message will appear along the upper edge of the screen when ready to run asking you to restart the TV. Hit OK and the TV turns off and back on with the newest update installed ... takes no more than 10 seconds.

title: Piece of junk
text:
The Panasonic Lumix camera takes really amazing shots underwater, takes HD movies, which are also pretty swell, and it's pretty easy to operate. The manufacturers want you to replace the seals on the underwater cameras each year, but Panasonic wanted 160 bucks to replace them, and since we only paid 249 for the camera, it seemed excessive to me. Knowing that this camera would last one season as well, I decided to purchase an underwater housing. After a lot of research, I bought the Ikelite housing.

It has been a MAJOR disappointment. If I had to rate it out of ten, I'd give it a 1. It looks to me to be a case designed for another camera, that they jury rigged to fit this camera. Let's start with the positives. The button to turn on the camera is easily depressed and does a good job of turning the camera off and on. OK, that's it for the positives! Seriously - the rest of the case is a complete joke. The "knob" to zoom the lens, is on the front of the housing, making it impossible to do with one hand. It sticks and will continue to zoom the camera until it is completely zoomed, and then you can't take a picture, until you release the toggle. That's a real pain!

Taking a picture is also a two-handed affair. Normally, to take a picture on ANY camera in the universe, you push a button down. Not on this housing - it is a stupid rocker, that you must twist! What that means is that you can't dive down, put the camera in front of you, and press the button. Nope, you have to use one hand to hold the housing, then use your other hand to twist the rocker to get the picture. That motion of twisting the rocker, leads to many shots being slightly blurry. This is easily the stupidest thing I've ever seen!

The button to turn on the video mode, is not right over the video button on the camera, so they put a cheap plastic plug on the plunger, with a little bump on the edge of a circle of plastic, and it may or may not turn on the video. Mostly it does not. Because the button easily twists, the movie mode will last only a few times, sometimes as few as once, before the cheap plastic plug twists, and the movie mode simply can't be turned on.

The cluster of buttons for the special functions, flash, macro, etc are too close together to be of any use underwater. Only two of the five actually work, even out of the water! You can change the flash mode, and that's it.

Ikelite should be ashamed of themselves for this terrible piece of crap. I would never buy another thing from Ikelite. This is a ripoff of the highest order.

title: Excellent sound, superior quality
text:
I got these as a gift and I've been using them steadily for nearly three months and have nothing but praise for the product.

These earphones are well-designed for even my thick-fingered paws, and have excellent sound reproduction. I wear them while at the gym on an elliptical trainer and what I like about these earphones is, no matter device what I bring with me, I can count on the sound reproduction from these earphones to be excellent. If I bring my Kindle and watch a movie while grinding through my routine, the experience may not be the same as being in a theater but the sound nearly is. (One of my favorite films is *The Avengers* and I've picked up several nuances wearing these headphones that I missed when I saw the film in the theater.)

Or, if I'm using my smarter-than-me phone, I can field calls from my spouse while listening to its FM stations or to my modest library of audiobooks and MP3s. The cord has a toggle to answer the phone.

At my community center, there is a USB plugin on the elliptical trainers for users' devices, and thousands of plugs have been jammed into and jerked out of the earphone jack. Yet when I plugged in these earphones, the music from my jump drive (I have a thumb drive with my "workout music" that includes warmup, working out, and cool down tunes) came through beautifully. I still sweated liked a maniac, but managed to keep pace with the music.

These headphones come with a bigger manual than my first cell phone. Instructions are written in accessible English and the handy carrying case is useful and not a gimmicky add on. There is also a volume control on the cord that I use, but which I consider the weakest feature of this fine product.

I also like the fact that this headset cord can be shortened -- there's a sturdy plug about 18 or 20 inches from the headphone-Y. My set also came with a sturdy armband so you have your device on you while walking, lifting or workng out. By unhooking the Y, you shorten the amount of cord you're lugging around. But when I'm on the elliptical I need that extra length and plug the cord back togehter. For me, this is a very convenient feature.

I am very impressed. This is a quality product is well worth the price.

text:
I got these headphones based on Sennheiser's sterling reputation for good sound, as well as the good reviews on the internet and the removable/exchangeable headphone cord.

Comparing these phones to the Audio Technica ATH-M50 and the Grado SR-80i, I have to say that I am a bit disappointed with the sound. The ATH-M50 in particular seems to have much clearer, prominent, and revealing high frequency reproduction. It was like taking a veil off the music. I discovered this when I was listening to a guitar track in which I had to hear a low-level, detailed palm muting aspect of a rhythm track. I could barely hear it with these phones, but it came in clear with the Audio Technicas. Granted, those headphones might also sound etched and bright to others, but I just found them to be revealing and detailed without overwhelming the bass and midrange. The AT's sound more like a neutral studio headphone should. Even the Grados seemed to have a more detailed high end, as well as a neutral midrange without overwhelming the bass. These 'phones sounded muffled in direct comparison.

title: Frustrating web browsing experience
text:
I didn't buy my Tablet 7 from Amazon but thought I'd leave a review anyway. It's a fairly well made item and does a reasonable job of Skype, playing YouTube videos and showing pictures to friends, but web browsing can be absolutely maddening.

The first problem isn't with the device itself but with the web browsers. Most websites are so full of advertising links it's nearly impossible to scroll downward without inadvertently opening a link and going to another website. If developers would create a browser with permanently visible scroll bars down the side and across the bottom, it would eliminate this problem.

The second problem is with the device - the multi-touch zoom feature is way too sensitive. As I'm scrolling through web pages, nearly half of all downward swipes will zoom the screen in as if I'm using two fingers. I'm constantly having to zoom back out. I bought a stylus to see if it would help but it's actually worse! There seems to be no way to turn multi-touch off, or reduce the sensitivity.

I'd like to love this product but so far it's just been a frustrating experience.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
10/24/2013 Update:

I've had this tablet now for four months and I thought I should update my original review. Although the comments above are still valid, I have a few kinder words for it after a few months use. It's a nice Kindle reader - you can increase / decrease the backlighting and the app features work well on the Slate. I've used it to Skype quite a bit and it does a descent job. My son said I appeared a bit grainy at his end, but the ease of use balances that out (fast and easy connections). As a camera, the images aren't great quality, but it's a tablet! The three camera settings (still, video, and panoramic) are easy to switch between and there's practically no lag time - and the panoramic mode is rather fun. The battery life is Ok - unless you have Bluetooth turned on (which burns through a charge rather quickly).

Overall, it's a well made device and with patience you can find the right apps that work well with it.

title: First impressions from a photo enthusiast
text:
I am not a professional and can't speak to all the technical specs on this lens. I'm writing primarly for people who own the Canon Rebel T3i (or similar cameras) and just want to take more professional-looking pictures because you love photography and want to capture cool moments, do some creative stuff, travel, and share your pics with friends and family. After all, we're not working for National Geographic. We take pictures because we like taking pictures. It's that simple.

This is my third prime lens. I already own the Canon EF 85mm f/1.8 (a fantastic telephoto portrait lens) and the Canon 50mm f/1.4 (my funnest lens). So why did I buy this lens? I wanted a moderate wide angle prime lens that could also function as a normal lens and even do great close-ups. Folks, this is it! I'll try not to gush, but this lens comes out of the box crying, "Use me!" It feels professional, solid, well-built, and it is super easy to use. This lens never gets in the way taking great shots, which is another way of saying, you never have to fight with it. Screw it on your T3i and start firing away--indoor low light, outdoor, close-ups, groups shots, the whole deal. It is fast becoming the most creative lens I own, even competing with the venerable 50mm f/1.4.

Speaking of fast, holy cow, I can hardly hear it focus, it is so quiet. And it's the fastest focusing lens I own. Plus, the f/1.8 means you can shoot without a flash almost in the dark!

There have been some negative reviews of this lens, as there are for every lens. But I decided I would have to use this lens in order to appreciate it. I'm glad I did. It's becoming my favorite.

UPDATE 6/10/12: Recently I've been doing some twilight cityscape photos for practice. It's a new type of photography for me. This lens is very impressive and it's the one I'm using now for nighttime shots as I get better at it. The time lapse shots of car lights seem to be turning out quite good, and the pics are nice and sharp.

title: Surprisingly good
text:
The video head for my main tripod for broadcast work cost over 5,000 USD. But coupled with its carbon fiber legs, it's a bit of a monster - needing an extra person just to move it around. It handles a full size HDCAM camera with a 1000mm lens the size of a volkswagon.
But in recent years cameras have gotten smaller and lighter - and better. A Canon C300 doesn't need anything like as big a tripod and with some of our film shoots now using only these smaller cameras, we needed a lightweight tripod.

Reviews can be a mixed blessing - research into a lightweight system left me more confused than anything - the new Ace systems looked good - but I already had a set of good fiber legs with a 75mm bowl and the Ace doesn't come as a head-only option. I'm no fan of Libec or Vinten, having used some of their systems in the past and the Miller options were just too expensive to be justified for the occasional, small camera only C300 shoots.
Manfrotto has gotten better over the years - but the 503HDV head we had lying around is just lousy. Which left the 504 - though many reviews I found were pretty damning.
But Amazon has a good returns policy so if it really was as bad as reviewed elsewhere then at least I could send it back.

The 504 is pretty solid - heavier than some alternatives - but that tends to be a good thing when you want support. The controls are easy and positive (unlike some systems where they're mushy and you find yourself over tightening just to be sure of a lock).
With a C300 and 70-200 lens the head is more than good enough to provide smooth and stable moves, no vibration, no stickiness in the pans. It handles everything with ease - anyone who has used a camera on a video head barely able to support it knows how nervous that can make a day's filming. The 504 has no issues with the C300.

Couple of niggling things about it...
The locking 'handle' that secures it to the bowl is horrible - very poor design - way too long, too narrow. I much prefer a short wide fixing as used on the top end Sachtlers. Also the screw thread is about 3 times too long - takes an age to fix the damn thing. Though this is probably essential because of the long handle design - a shorter thread would be at risk from the leverage inherent in the handle length.
The counter balance system was on the highest position for the C300 which surprised me - would have hoped for a bit more play since the C300 is not that heavy and way below the max weight for the head. I suspect it wouldn't handle a fully rigged F3 or similar with cages, external power and recorder.

Other aspects which I thought would be a downfall, actually were non issues - it really isn't heavy (go use a Ronford for a while if you think it is) and there is no backlash in panning.

Coupled with the Miller Solo carbon fiber legs it is a very nice, cheap system...able to handle its task with ease and tough enough to last a while. And so lightweight it can be carried around on just one finger. After years of tripods weighing a minimum of 20 pounds, that's a nice change.

title: Great for reading in bed
text:
The Paperwhite is my third Kindle. I also have the "second generation" keyboard version and the Fire, and I use them for different things. I love Kindles, and I love Amazon but the Paperwhite is the first Kindle since the Fire that I have felt like I just "had to have."

I really like the Paperwhite. I plan to use it 95% of the time for reading in bed, so it will have a pretty much permanent place on my night table. One of my main reasons for purchasing the Fire was the lighted screen, because I have never met a book light I could stand. Although the Fire is okay for reading in the dark, I can never really get the light to a level that is comfortable. The Paperwhite works perfectly for this (I'm sure it's the difference between backlighting - the Fire - and front lighting - the Paperwhite.) There is some unevenness to the Paperwhite's screen when the light is turned up high, but nothing that makes it a deal breaker for me.

I was happy to see that the light can be turned off for daylight reading. Some early reviews and comments I've read had me thinking the light had to be on all the time, i.e., could only be turned down to "1" but not completely off. That is not true. Reading in daylight, with the light off, the screen looks pretty much like my Kindle 2. The resolution is perhaps a bit crisper but I can't honestly say I notice much of a difference there.

I love how lightweight the Paperwhite is; it's noticeably lighter than my Kindle 2 and, of course, MUCH lighter than the Fire. I don't love the fact that it's so much smaller, which might sound odd, but that fact coupled with the combination of a touch screen and relatively small bezel make it a bit more difficult to hold. Again, not a deal breaker...just noticeable (and the reason I give it four stars instead of five. I'd give it 4.5 if that were possible.)

Finally, this isn't a comment on the device itself but I continue to laugh at the complaints about special offers. I don't understand why this is such a big deal. First of all, for $20 paid ANY time (either at purchase or later on) they can be eliminated. (And, I don't view this as an "extra" $20; I view the $119 cost vs. $139 as a discount for allowing Amazon to send me special offers.) Second, they do not interfere with the reading experience AT ALL; once you open the book and start reading they are nowhere to be found. Third, some of them are actually good deals that I appreciate receiving. Not everyone feels that way, of course, but for heavens sake just pay the $20 and they will go away. I really don't understand why some people find them so intrusive, but Amazon does offer the option to not participate...so get over it!

Bottom line: this is a great addition to my Kindle family and I will definitely be keeping it.

title: Cannot build for this price!!! (edited from 5 star)
text:
After about a three weeks of searching for a computer i stumbled upon this one. I was a little worried about Amazon's lack of details about this computer and was worried that i would receive a computer with just the processor memory and video cards. I was very happy to see a full (Nice looking) pc in front of me! The AMD FX 8150 eight core processor is the best you can get nowadays and for the system to come with dual Radeon HD 6850 in crossfire makes this an absolute steal at this price. There is an almost obnoxious amount of USB 2.0 ports as well as (2) USB 3.0 ports (which was never stated in the description) HDMI outs, new SATA interface, memory expandable up to 32gb, four different fans cooling the system, and THe ever so useful USB Charge ports (charges items plugged in while computer is 'off') The installed windows 7 64-bit OS works like it should and i have had no problems with the computer so far after about two weeks of fairly heavy use. I have tested out the dual HD6850 cards by pushing GTA IV with the latest graphical mods available with the game never dropping below 30FPS. Trainz Sim 12 which is a pretty heavy memory program ran without a hiccup. Modern Warefare 2 ran on maxed out settings without any problems at all. Mass Effect with a bunch of graphic mods ran without fail as well.
The bottom line is that i took the specs to two different computer builders in my area and was quoted $300-$600 more than i paid for it here and they were only going to throw in 8gb of memory.
Another interesting note is that i went to ibuypower.com's website and built a custom pc with the exact specs this had, and was quoted $1,450
$1,200 is a steal for this computer, get it before Amazon realizes they have it priced to low.

EDIT:
i am getting some radom BSOD that happen for no reason, it seems to happen more when watching videos. has not happened while gaming. ibuypower's customer service is really top notch, they are more than helpful in the situation. Brought it down from 5 stars becasue for $1,300 there shouldnt be any BSOD. i would buy this computer all over again however and still feel that this was a good deal.

title: Great for navigation, other features lacking
text:
Overview: If you are like me you probably are starting to realize that your smartphone isn't quite the navigation road warrior you thought it was. You've probably lost 3G coverage and had no maps. You might have gotten lost. And probably the last in a long line of navigational mishaps that make you confront your problem ... calling people you normally avoid to ask, "Hey, are you near a computer? Can you pull up Google Maps and tell me how to get to...".

If you're still reading my review then I guess the answer to one or more of these question is "Yes". My initial apprehension about buying a new GPS unit goes back to my previous GPS, a Mio unit. The first unit cost nearly $300, had bad routes, points of interests such as restaurants no longer existed, and the much needed map updates cost nearly as much as the device. However, I couldn't have been more wrong when I started looking at the new GPS offerings. Many units can be had for under $100 and even units like this one are surprisingly affordable given the features like Bluetooth, lifetime updates, and so on.

I chose Garmin primarily due to peer recommendations along with their use of Navteq maps. A quick overview Navteq is based in the US and Tele Atlas in Europe. As you might guess (and my previous GPS that used Tele Atlas showed) maps from Navteq tend to be more accurate here than Tele Atlas tho the tables would be turned in Europe.

Likes:

As mentioned earlier, the maps are very good on this unit. After purchasing the unit I installed the map update and it included details like the newly completed roads/overpasses in my area. I can't say the same about my old unit. The free map updates are nice but my understanding is "lifetime" means the useful product lifetime of the device (so some number of years) and not as long as you own the device. That is probably OK because after some number of years you will probably want a better/newer unit.

Voice recognition is handy. There is no training involved and it is pretty easy to use. You can customize a phrase to begin accepting commands, by default "voice command". You then have a list of options which you can say (you can even say "up" and "down" to scroll through options). You will typically have a reasonable range of commands you can say to make the voice command word as well. For example if you looked up a restaurant you could pick the number in the list (if there are multiple results) or say the name of the one you want if the result only showed up once in the list. You can start navigation by saying "yes" or "navigate".

If you have a bluetooth-enabled phone you can pair your GPS with the phone and dial numbers or look up people from your phone's directory. The speaker volume is lower than I would prefer but not terrible.

For the most part, the places I've asked to get navigation to have been available by default. For specific places I wanted to be sure are there I look them up on Google Maps and upload them to the Garmin. This is pretty easy to do and Garmin has instructions on their site.

The dashboard configuration is really nice. You can choose what information is displayed on the screen based on your preference. This can be elevation, direction, current speed, time to destination, distance to destination, etc.

The posted speed is a nice feature but I find in some places it is not accurate. My old GPS would let you set an audible warning if your speed exceeded the posted speed by an adjustable amount which this unit doesn't have. If you go over the speed (even by 1mph) it will turn the current speed font color to red. It doesn't alert me but I might have that turned off since several spots on my commute home have the wrong posted speed.

Lane guide shows you what the lane layout is at major intersections on a highway. It seems to be fairly accurate but I haven't really been anywhere that had confused lane configurations that I needed help with.

Because of the traffic, current speed / traffic speed, and Bluetooth I find leaving the GPS on is useful even when I'm not navigating.

Neutral:

Traffic. It works in Dallas and several other major cities but doesn't work in rural areas. It seems to work ok but I've had some false reports like an overturned vehicle where there wasn't one. It also tends to mark parts of a road as being congested instead of the entire route. My morning commute has about 3-4 spots where traffic slows down so the GPS beeps and offers me alternate routes at each junction. In fairness, I have seen the GPS recommend the same route to me 90% of the time and then some days it suggests another route which ends up being quicker. Normally, it seems to be due to an existing accident or existing road congestion.

Free voices, dashboards, and icons. There are really novelties but nice they are free. For example you can get Sesame Street voices, Star Wards voices, and icons from cars, trucks, and SUVs to obscure items like a Tie Fighter or Rubber Duck. They are fairly easy to load on the device. The problem with voices however is that you lose the "speak street name" functionality. Obviously, it would be difficult and expensive to have a voice actor say every street name where the default voice is a synthesized voice with some algorithms to make sure the names are pronounced correctly.

There are a reasonable amount of things that can be customized but it would be nice if there were profiles. For example, most of the time I want to use multiple passenger lanes, avoid unpaved roads, take the fastest route, and don't care about tolls. However, sometimes none of these might apply. There are also options to map details, voices, dashboards, etc. Most of the time my settings are fine but if I go skiing I might want to show elevation (normally I don't), might allow taking unpaved roads, etc.

There are games/apps available which might add some value to some but I've never used them.

Dislikes:

Not specific to this unit but alleys and parking lots prove problematic. If you enter an alley you will be asked to navigate to the nearest road before navigation can continue. More annoying is if your destination is in a shopping center navigation ends on the street nearest the location. One example, I was going to a restaurant and it told me to go up to the next intersection and take a right. It wasn't aware there was a shopping center entrance on the road I was on that led directly to the restaurant.

There was an option to use HOV lanes but it either doesn't stay defaulted to On or I'm not choosing that as a route. I normally have my daughter in the car with me so I can make use of the dedicated lane for multi-passenger vehicles. Unfortunately, my nav will tell me to "keep right" at HOV entrances and exits and also doesn't account for special entrances and exits for HOV which requires route recalculations. Likewise, I get traffic alerts and alternate route suggestions that don't apply.

Traffic is free but ad supported so you get little banner ads on the GPS screen sometimes.

Final thoughts:

If you don't care about Bluetooth or traffic you can go for a cheaper model with lifetime maps. For the price this GPS performs well and is easy to use.

title: Jury's still out.
text:
BLAZING speed across the USB 3.0 connection. I didn't monitor it closely, but at one point saw my transfer rate pegged at 125MBps. Pretty sweet compared to the USB 2.0 range of 4.5-5.5MBps using this same hardware.

Firm physical connection of the power cord between USB ports? Yup. Hardware jostling or accidental pulling of hanging cords? Nope--I was elsewhere in the room doing other stuff.

Sometimes it would run a few minutes without problem, but sometimes would disconnect and reconnect every few seconds. My 130GB of data should have moved in less than 30 minutes, but I spent hour after un-waning hour rechecking physical connections or futzing with the cords or restarting power supplies or giving it a rest in case it had gotten too hot, or whatever.

The Seagate rep seems pretty responsible about addressing all these negative reviews here in the jungle of amazon, but the fact that there are SO MANY bad reviews across a pretty wide variety of issues kind of leaves a stink in the air even after the garbage has been taken out. IF I can get this thing humming, might I bump my rating to 3 stars instead of 2? Perhaps. If I can't transform it into a Steady Eddie, I'll probably come back and drop my rating to a 1. But for sure if I owned Seagate stock, right now I'd be in "sell" mode on that investment.

title: Excellent upgrade from 5.1
text:
Let me start out by saying this will be a limited review addressing only a few of this receivers features. I use a Plasma TV, blu-ray player, HD DVR, and Roku streaming device in my set-up.

Sooo, I purchased this receiver for just one reason. To finally obtain REAL 7.1 and enjoy the benefits of uncompressed audio in my home theatre. Basically, I bought a brand new receiver just to get HDMI inputs. The reason this is a limited review is because I own no Apple products, I don't have Sirius radio, I don't need bluetooth, I don't use Zone 2 output, and I use hard wired (RJ-45) internet connect (I have enough wireless gear already) so I won't be able to tell you if the wireless dongle ($150??) works well. I have NOTHING connected (input or output) to Composite video, component video, nor do I use the analog stereo jacks. CNET claims that Pioneers streaming is geared toward Apple and they don't offer much else but if you have Apple or Roku you can just use those devices to stream internet content (such as Pandora) and the 1021 has Home Media Group which streams internet radio and all of the music on your PC.

So my review is really about set-up, functionality, reliability (I have read 50 or 60 of the reviews out here), audio/video quality, glitchiness (firmware issues, rebooting, HDMI weirdness), whether or not this 9.1 thing with the front height speakers is going to float my boat, and anything else that seems relevant to point out.

Set-up: Out of the box, I hooked up all 10 speakers (7.1 plus both "front height" channels). Then performed the MCACC speaker setup. That took some time and while most people rave about this feature, I have mixed reviews. The speaker distances were not totally accurate, some of the volume levels needed tweaking, and it misidentified my speaker sizes robbing much of the base from my 18" sub. I manually fixed that by changing all speakers to small and additionally changing the sub-woofer setting from yes to plus which routes additional bass from the Left Right and Center channels to the sub. Huge improvement, now the bass rocks out.

Before I was able to complete the MCACC setup, the receiver "froze" several times before releasing the menu to me. Annoying, especially since that was the first thing I did (first impressions) but it settled down and behaved normally after a couple of power on/off cycles.

There is a note on Pioneers website telling you to upgrade the firmware but it is a little dated. My unit is brand new and firmware ends in 073 while the website update ends in 031. I called Pioneer support (very friendly and helpful BTW) and he said I was fine and that newer units ship with the latest firmware.

AV nav software a little glitchy and really useless if you have ANY electronics/install/setup experience. Took long time to install on Windows 7 and really does not offer much at all and is absolutely not required to use any feature of the unit.

I run HDMI only and I suspect most peoples problems center around using old analog stuff and thinking somehow video conversion will save them. It won't, just buy a 1080p TV and run it all thru HDMI and leave video conversion off. The chip is not top shelf and any newer HD television has a comparable scaler built in, and you don't want to process the signal twice. Switching between inputs takes a second or two but that is to be expected because of the HDCP handshake. Also, the picture gets weird color spikes while switching but only for a split second. Picture quality excellent. A word about HDMI pass-through: If you want to see/hear the source on your TV with the receiver off, it is a pain. 1021's HDMI control must be on (default factory setting), your device (blu-ray, cable company DVR, etc) must have it enabled through its menu and most DVR's don't have that function (I am pretty sure of this). Also, your TV must have it enabled and then you better hope all three devices agree to it. It would be easier to run separate component video/analog stereo cables from each device into your TV (if it has enough inputs) and watch High Definition TV/Movies with audio THAT way if you really want to bypass the receiver (late at night so the wife does not go ballistic on you).

Internet Radio and HMG: Songs on your computer stream uninterrupted and your TV displays time elapsed/remaining, song title, artist, album title, album art (if applicable), file type, genre, and bit rate. Internet radio is cool and streams smoothly and continuously, I love it! Titles scroll across the receivers display but if you want to navigate, it is best to leave the TV on. You could just pick a station and play it for hours with the TV off and not fiddle with it if you don't want to risk burn in (I have a plasma).

USB input: It recognizes and plays off any flash drive from 256mb to 32gb, also plays my Sony Walkman mp3 player S Series. The interface is minimal and song navigation is tedious (if you have 2,408 songs, then it just lists them alphabetically). Clearly, they expect you to use an iPad. It is fast and works well but they need better software for non-Apple folks.

Audio: I am impressed with the audio performance of this unit. Movie dialogue is clear at low volume, the sound stage/presence across the front is excellent, far superior to my previous setup. The addition of the front height channel speakers and maybe the MCACC setup have brought out everything in the sound tracks. The music also streams through the 9.1 set up and even mp3 files which are notoriously weak/exposed on quality hi fi audio systems, sound great. The signal is distributed throughout and I can achieve high volumes with deep bass and excellent high end. That was WAY more than I had expected from the music side of performance.

In closing, even though I am not utilizing a good portion of this receivers abilities, I still am pleased with the upgrade from 5.1 and am searching Netflix for DTS 7.1 movie titles so I can enjoy the uncompressed audio playback that this receiver delivers!

I will add to this review if I try any additional features or notice any problems with the 1021. Also, I bought elsewhere and Amazon was $50 bucks cheaper...pays to look here first!!!!!!!!!!

title: Avoid the Chromebook! - 6 month's experience and I totally regret my purchase.
text:
If you think tech support is frustrating with Windows, wait until you deal with Samsung, HP (for the cloud printer) and Google.

The concept is great but this is NOT ready for the public. The limits are maddening and it is very buggy!

I have spent more than 4 1/2 hours today on a recurring issue: The sound won't play through the speakers when I re-open the unit. It is a known issue and discussed on the web but no one has a solution. As with most tech support solutions, Samsung wants me to do a hard re-set, which requires a 4gb flash drive that is set up from a 'windows, linux or mac' computer. Great! And the comments online say that this won't solve this issue! Samsung wants me to return the Chromebook and I'm out of luck for the time without a computer. THE ISSUE IS STILL NOT RESOLVED.

There are so many bugs - the pages crash constantly and the videos are slow and jerky. Printing is a NIGHTMARE! I have spent hours on the phone with HP and I can't get this problems resolved. The print options with Chromebook are severely limited (you can't even choose the number of copies) and the windows don't display properly. Cloud printing is easy with my old Windows XP laptop, But when I try to print the same document with the Chromebook, the printer starts flashing and demands to be shut down. Other times, it says that the document was printed but nothing happens. Google blames HP, HP blames Google. NO RESOLUTION! And good luck getting someone from Google on the phone...

There are so many other nuisances and bugs you'll discover as you use it. When typing in the web page or Google search, the pages show as loaded but nothing happens.
