title: Wanted to Love These but Bluetooth + Cellular Not There Yet
text:
I've been looking for a headset to replace a wired Plantronics headset I had for use with my landline but for which the cord wore out over time so that sound had crackling. No good for business calls (coaching calls). After doing a lot of research and reading all of the wonderful reviews here, I ordered these. I returned them for 2 reasons: #1 clients could not hear / understand me. #2 They were wearing a hole in the top of my head. More below.

PROS
These are incredibly feature rich and easy to operate. This was my first relatively high end headset and I operated it right out of the box, no issues. Connected to my IPhone 4S fine, although sometimes lost the connection on incoming calls. Easy answer when the connection stayed, easy hangup, easy mute, easy to turn on noise cancelling. Also very easy to listen to music and that connection stayed consistently.

CONS
My #1 reason for getting this headset was to be able to hold clear, high quality coaching calls. It did not work for this. Although I could hear people decently, people on the other end of my call said they could not hear me. I think the problem is bluetooth combined with cellular technology, rather than this particular headset. There is a cell tower about 2 blocks up the street, and when I use the IPhone regularly or on speaker I have an excellent connection. But for some reason when using this headset the sound deteriorated greatly.

The second large con for me is the shear weight of the headset. After wearing this for an hour the crown of my head felt like a hole had been rubbed into it. These are heavy, and no matter how I adjusted the length of the headset band, they still sat heavy on my head.

I ended up going with the wired Bose QC25 after testing them out in-store against the bluetooth Bose headset. I made test calls on both in store. I was told sound from the wireless bluetooth headset sounded as if I were in a tunnel. I was told the sound from the wired QC25 was acceptable. I've been using the Bose QC25 for about 2 weeks now, and clients report sound quality is good, often indistinguishable from a landline. I'm keeping them.

title: Decent enough Mac Bluetooth mouse
text:
The iHome Bluetooth Mouse is a decent enough clone of the Apple Magic Mouse for half the price. However, I didn't love the mouse but it did work great.

The setup was simple - what's weird is that when you press the battery release button, one giant piece of plastic comes off that covers the side of the mouse completely. A little weird, but it worked. The pairing with my Macbook Air (running 10.8.2) was quick and painless.

Once up and running, the mouse tracked well and moved nicely without feeling jumpy on the screen. It took a few seconds to wake up the mouse when resuming from sleep, which was slower than other BT mice I've used. I've used the Magic Mouse and yet never did anything with the surface and gestures and am more comfortable with the scroll wheel.

My major gripe is with the size of the mouse. Yes, I know, it's supposed to be small, but when you have larger hands, the mouse feels frail and working with my laptop for more than 30 minutes feels a bit awkward when I'm used to larger mice on the desktop. I wouldn't get something like this for a desktop or if I had planned on spending long hours working. However, for laptop users, this mouse would be great.

Overall, the iHome Bluetooth Mac Mouse is a good buy when compared to the Magic Mouse. There is something to be said about the aesthetics of the Magic Mouse, but at double the cost and then some, the iHome clone will do the same job and just as well. 4 stars.

title: Simply a great value - Low cost, very quiet and easy to install.
text:
Every now and then I encounter a product that removes any buyer's remorse. This is one such product. I was seeking an inexpensive CPU cooling solution for a secondary computer that was still using the stock AMD cooling fan. Since this system is not our primary use computer I couldn't justify spending a lot of money just to replace the louder stock heat sink and fan. I was not concerned about lowering CPU temperatures, just making the system quieter while not hurting the cooling of the computer. This fan and heat sink work perfectly with that goal in mind - at least on the modest AMD Athlon 64 X2 4200+ processor on which it was installed. My experience based on this hardware was:

- Extremely quiet operation compared to stock AMD heat sink/fan
- 2-degree celsuis lower CPU temperature than stock cooling solution
- Extremely simple installation on AM2 socket (loosen two screws, attach clips to stock mounting bracket on system board and tighten screws)

The larger fan and lower operating speed no doubt are the biggest reasons this cooler is so much quieter than the stock fan - it runs about 1500 rpm slower than the stock CPU fan after the system has been on for over 30 minutes. Regardeless of the reason, it has satisfied my primary goal - quiet cooling at a low cost.

Overall this CPU cooler is just an excellent value.

title: Worth it despite what you might think.
text: This stuff is simply the best you can buy. Don't be confused by the 18k vs 24k that is just the different tube sizes. Dropped my temps by another 3° C compared to my cooler master stuff.  Which really surprised me because I wasn't expecting to see more than maybe 1° C of difference. Yet low and behold it's making a pretty big difference. I used it on my CPU when I switched to a new water cooling block. After seeing the difference I decided to try it out on my GPU's. I have two MSI twin frozer 580's in SLI and was surprised to see in Afterburner that my top card is down 5° C normally (it's covered by the second card mind you)  the second card which is only part covered by my Physx card is 7 to 9° cooler than normal. Pretty nice improvement overall. SO yes is it more expensive than say some Artic Silver 5 yes. Is it worth the expense to see a few degrees in drops of temps? Well that depends on you really. Most of the time I would say no but here's the thing. Every degree matters when it comes to the life and longevity of your hardware. Add to the fact you get a bunch of paste in this tube enough to last you a very long time.  So for me as an enthusiast I would say yes. For the average consumer it might take a little talking into sure but it will be worth your time and money no matter what.

pretty much anything that writes data to /sdcard, which are ALL the apps and games out there... will have to be squeezed into the 5GB available space in the SGT2.... Update (Dec 1st, 2012): After rejecting my RMA, Monster returned the headphones to me without the piece that fell off. Thus, I can't even have them repaired myself. Customer service continues to be completely unresponsive.

Update (Dec 8th, 2012). Customer service finally responded indicating that they didn't honor the warranty because the base was completely separated from the earbud. title: My Living Room Tablet
text:
I got the Sony Tablet S just before Mother's Day, when they had $50 off deal plus a free docking station. I down loaded the Ice Cream Sandwich operating system immediately, and these comments are based on the ICS. I am very pleased with Tablet S: it is now my "Living Room Tablet."

Pros:
-Fast boot time
-Handy charging/docking station allows selected apps to run while "sleeping" tab is in dock
-Acts as remote control for home theater
-Easy to handle
-Full size SD card slot
-Wi-Fi works well
-Responsive touch, good looking video
Cons:
-No HDMI port
-Needs special cable for USB hookup
-Media "throwing" seems flaky

Many of the adverse reviews I have seen on the Sony S seem to have been answered, things like Wi-Fi performance, crashes, battery life, etc. I still working my way through this thing, but it seems sound. I haven't got my Bluetooth headset to work with the tablet, but what else is new.

For the remote control app, I used the simple set-up technique and quickly got the tablet working with my TV, AVR, blu-ray player, and DVR. Volume control punch-down would be the only addition I could ask for. Strangely, the Sony HD radio is not supported, although you can manually copy button presses to add such components.

I have a Logitech "Revue" running Google TV. The Google TV control system marches to its own beat, but I installed an app called "Able Remote." It does a fine job of controlling Google TV. "Throwing" media to the Google TV from the tablet was a problem, but I installed an app called "AVIA" which took care of that problem.

The lack of HDMI support is disappointing in the living room. Hulu and such run well on the tablet: it would be nice to be able to feed that to the tv.

The charging/docking system is a must, in my opinion. The tablet slides easily into the dock. When the tablet is docked, I usually run a program called "Cassandra," which displays time, temperature, and news. Nice use of the tablet when its not being actively used.

"Angry Birds" and "Pinball Heroes" run great, videos look very nice, the cameras work: what else is there to say?

Some users (myself included) had trouble getting this thing to work. Before you fire off a one-star review, here are a few troubleshooting tips I wished I'd known first:

Older versions of the software don't work with some of the newer bike computers. If your docking station came with an older version of the Data Center software, update it to the newest version through the SigmaSport.com website (it's a free update).

I had trouble entering my CD code into the website to sign up for the update. You have to enter it in ALL CAPS and include the dashes.

If the drivers for the docking station didn't load when you installed the software you might have to do it manually. That also happened to me, and I found the instructions on Sigma's website. The instructions are for Windows Vista, but if you're using a different version of Windows you can figure out what to do from there.

text:
The 60D is the second camera I have used a battery grip on. The first was the Canon T2i and the inexpensive grip that I bought worked fine. When I got the 60D, I immediately bought another inexpensive grip for it. Looked good, fit good, recognized the batteries, and worked fine at first. But then even newly charged batteries would be completely discharged in a couple of days. I assumed there must be something wrong with the camera and made arrangements to send it back. Fortunately, however, before doing so I decided to make some tests. I also did research on the internet and discovered this was a common problem with knockoff battery grips. I then checked the comments of users for all the knockoffs sold by Amazon and found that for each one or two purchasers reported having a problem exactly like what I was experiencing.

Also during my internet research I found reports from testers not connected with Canon that said that the only battery grip never having this problem was the Cannon grip.

Yes, the odds were good that had I bought another knockoff that it would have worked fine, but I did not want to take that chance.

It is also true that since you get more than 1000 shots with the battery for the 60D that you could easily do without the second battery. But I like the grip because it balances the camera very nicely with my zoom lens, and also makes it easier for me to hold.

So I bought the Canon grip and the problem that was so troubling to me is a thing of the past. The peace of mind I now have is worth the extra money I paid to get the genuine Canon grip.

title: Cannot beat the features and quality for the money!!!
text:
So to start this off review i just want to say this receiver for the money is untouchable. Sure there are much better receivers out there. But i really had a hard time justifying spending the extra money for the same features. Basically when i was looking to purchase this receiver i compared it to three other receivers:

1.) Pioneer VSX921K
2.) Yamaha RX-V667
3.) Onkyo HT RC360

So basically when comparing these to the Sony, the first thing that was an easy choice was the price. When i purchased the receiver it was $245.99. All the others all above $300.00. So this was the biggest thing that made me want to buy it. Second was features. Basically all the receivers have the same features give or take some unique ones that are unique to that brand. The next thing was this is a 7.2 receiver. The site says 7.1, but it does have an extra sub out which makes it 7.2. Next was the 3D capabilities, not that i will ever use it, but I might you never know. Lastly the power was something that was a huge selling point. Now i know people say you will never get those true power numbers, and most people say they are meaningless but its nice to know you are getting a lot of power if its ever needed.

There are three things that bothered me about this receiver

1.) Auto calibration. Its a cool feature, that has potential, but isn't very accurate. I have my theatre in a small room, and when it did the audio test to calibrate the system it was really crazy off. I did a test run with the auto calibration with a Movie, and it sent the reviver in protection mode within 20 sec of use. I called Sony support, and talked to someone in India who spoke horrible english, an dafter talking to him he suggested that i manually adjust the speaker settings, he also asked me how my speakers were set up and it they were matching. I said yes, but said for my center channel I use two smaller speakers and tie them together into one. He said that this was causing the receiver to go into protection mode because of an irregular current traveling through the speaker. He suggested i use only one speaker. It did the trick, i ordered the BIC America FH6-LCR center channel speaker (which BTW is soo freaking awesome!!!!!) and it has been perfect ever since. But getting back to the auto calibration tool it doesn't work well at all. I had to spend 20 min setting up the speakers so that way everything worked smoothly, without over loading the system. Coming from a 5.1 surround sound system to a 7.2 system the system demands are very different.

2.) I really dont like is the remote. Its huge, and bulky. Programming it is a nightmare, I ended up giving up.

3.) Lastly, and this really isn't something that is a deal breaker, but just annoying for me. The screen on the receiver is always on. When the receiver is off it says: "Stand by" and when i sleep i like my room pitch black. Like i said not a deal breaker, but people who are light sensitive its really annoying.

So basically it really comes down to what you like. The things I mentioned are just minnor annoyances. The key features that this receiver has for the money is unreal. The economy sucks, times are hard, I dont have a lot of money to blow on expensive stuff. So by saving $100 - 150.00 for a receiver that has the same features as a higher end receiver. You do the math. Save your self some money, this receiver rocks.

I suggest you find a movie that has 7.1 DTS-HD surround to hear the real potential of this receiver. I recently bought Cars 2, and it has 7.1 DTS-HD, and DAMN is all i can say. I heard noises, that i have never heard before, and the sound was immersive and clean. Its amazing! Enjoy!

Another movie that is an audio delight when played on this receiver was Master and Commander. I have heard a lot of surround sound in my day, but WOW!!! You feel like you are there at the battles, yo uhear every creek, and noise. If you close you eyes you feel like you are right there!

Enjoy!

title: Warning, the Garmin Nuvi2370 will cost you more!
text:
I bought the Nuvi2370 through Amazon for use in US and Europe. However when I received it I found that the current maps had not been installed in the device and that I had to download them myself. However when I tried to do this (through the Garmin site) I was told that there was not enough memory in the device and that I should add a MicroSD card. That costs $15.

Thus your product description was misleading by omitting to say that the customer would have to spend more money to make the device current.

Garmin customer service, which cannot be accessed by phone unless you have a lot of free time, responded to an e-mail saying "Not always will you need a Micro SD card for more Memory. However in cases like yours your unit has 2 maps on the unit and may need more room. If you look at the smaller print in this link it does say you may need a SD card to update a unit."

So, these are the ingredients of a deception. First, they sell the device with outdated maps (no warning). Since the unit comes (as advertised) with US and European maps, they knew that the update would not fit in the internal memory. So, instead of equipping the device with the necessary extra memory, they keep quiet and let the customer figure it out. Finally, when one complains they tell you should have looked at the smaller print in their web site.

title: Not impressed
text:
Some background:

I currently have cable TV (Cox), cable internet, and have had Dish in the past. My bill isn't outrageous compared to what a lot of people I know pay, but regardless, I think it is too much. So I want to "cut the cord" for TV. However, I'm not willing to do without a DVR. I'll cover that in another review (if Amazon decides to sell the product, Simple TV)

First step - establish good TV reception. I'm in southwest Omaha, and , according to TV Fool, I should be able to get about 12 primary (think the ".1") channels with an indoor or attic mount antenna, and several more for outdoor.

I connected the Sky HDTV to my bedroom TV (a new RCA 32" LCD) with unimpressive results. The antenna was indoors for the test, so I moved it around and rescanned several times, but still wasn't able to receive even all of the channels labeled that an internal antenna should get. I moved to the living room and retested on my 5 year old Samsung plasma. Slightly better results (the TV probably has a better tuner), and then moved the antenna out to the deck to continue testing with different locations and pointing different ways. I was able to pull in all of the channels labeled for indoor antennas and the next level up, but nothing more, and several of those "easy" to get channels were very weak. This isn't at all what I expect from an antenna priced where it is (currently $170) and with the reputation of the Leaf I expected considerably more.

The antenna itself is very nice looking, leaves won't get caught in it if mounted outdoors, it is also nice and small. The included antenna preamplifier is a little junky, the "power" supply (a micro USB cord) fits in the amp either direction, not very high quality. Interestingly, I did try without the amp and got pretty much nothing, so apparently it was working. Actually, I got more channels with JUST the amp plugged and no antenna than I did with just the antenna!

I will say - the 1 star review isn't because this item didn't work at all, it is because it didn't work very well (and didn't live anywhere near up to its 60 mile range - I was unable to get channels starting in the high 30 mile range) and due to the price of comparables.

Last, I did decide to try a much lower cost, much more reviewed solution, the RCA ANT751R and it's amplifier. Both of these are about $70 from Amazon today. Wow - these work very well. I get MORE channels than I did with the Sky HDTV, and it is must lower cost. No, it isn't as pretty, and no, they didn't include ANY cables in their boxes like Mohu did, but more channels, cheaper, and higher quality channels...? Easy choice.

title: Once you get it to work, it performs as it's suppose too
text:
I purchased this as a gift after reading the reviews on it. This is going to be connected to a Samsung Blu-ray player and setup in Client Mode. I was asked to setup the unit and after spending 4 hours of trying to setup the unit in Client Mode I fired off an email to customer support and they told me all I had to do was reset the unit and it would work.

So after resetting the unit for the (4th) fourth time it finally connected to my wireless network using WPA and I was able to connect to the internet.

I know some of you may be wondering why it took 4 hours to troubleshoot and get the unit to connect in Client Mode so I will list some of the steps I took so hopefully somewhere down the road I'll save someone some time should they decide to use this unit in Client mode.

After un-boxing the unit and connecting it my laptop running Windows 8 I turned off my wireless and configured my local area connection per the instructions from the cd rom and website. (IP: 192.168.0.15 and subnet mask of 255.255.255.0).

I logged into the unit via I.E. I started with the quick setup. I chose the Client Mode option and I clicked save next I clicked on Survey and chose my SSID. Then I chose the wireless security and input my security key. Next I rebooted the unit and waited for it to come up. When the unit did come up it showed no internet connection. So I ran the diagnostics from the System Tools link and I could not ping anything outside ([...] [...] etc..) nor could I ping the unit itself.

Next I did a factory reset of the unit and it rebooted. I ran thought the above steps to setup Client Mode and received the same results.

I reset the unit via the pin hole reset button and this time I tried a manual setup of the unit. I clicked on Working Mode and chose Client Mode. I clicked Save and was brought to the next screen where it asked me do a survey and choose my SSID which I did and entered my security type and key. I clicked on save and rebooted only to have the same results.

At this point I turned the wireless back on my laptop and did some Google searches to see if I could find more info on setting this unit up in Client Mode. My searches did not turn up any answers so I went to the support forum on the TP-Link website and I discovered a new firmware ver. for the unit. I downloaded and upgraded the firmware on the unit and then proceeded through the same steps above with the same results of not being able to connect to the internet.

Other steps that I tried were to add the Network address of the wireless network to the units Network settings this had no effect. So on the 3rd reset of the unit I decide I had spent way too much time trying to get this unit connected in Client Mode so I filled out a Customer Support form on the TP-Link website and I received an email response suggesting I reset the unit and it worked.

So that's my story.

title: Loudest Cord on Earth Hurts Rating of Kickass Headphones
text:
First things first - excellent (5-star) sound, made even more excellent by the (5-star) price. I'm used to constantly replacing really crappy earbuds ($15 and under), because they always seem to break at the plug. The clarity was eye-opening -- I heard things I'd never heard before, even on albums I've been listening to for over a decade. The materials have a quality feel, and I was excited at the prospect of a more durable woven cord.

There are several complaints about bass not being powerful enough. For starters, if you're really looking at lots of thumping bass, there's really only so far earbuds with that itty-bitty 10mm driver can go. I had to play around with the settings on my Sansa to adjust from my old-hat $12 jobbies, but soon found a good mix. At first I wasn't getting any bass either, until I found a good position that engaged the noise reduction and really "locked" the earbuds into my ear canal. All was well, for a brief moment.

If you do have the earbuds "locked" into your ear canals for noise reduction, DO NOT MOVE. AT ALL. That fabric cord -- which should be named "the Serpent of Cacophony" -- will drown out nearly anything with its incessant SWEEP SWOOP SWEEP SWOOP SWEEP SWOOP as it rubs against, well, anything. It's worst when the cord rubs against another fabric -- you know, whatever your shirt, pants, or jacket are made of.

They must have woven this thing using corduroy pants, or material leftover from those compostable "Sun Chips" bags that crinkled at over 90dB. I'm all for recycling, but this renders the phones far less usable for me. I read the reviews mentioning the microphonics; I'm a commuter and I knew the risks, but I honestly didn't think that the issue could be this disruptive.

Tiny little lumberjacks inside the Serpent, drunkenly sawing logs roughly in time with the most reserved of your movements. Walking, sitting, breathing deep, reaching into your pocket, turning your head, riding a bus... unavoidable little things like this will result in a SWOOP SWEEP SWOOP funneled directly into your brain, right when you wanted to hear that great trombone harmony. The only way to hear anything over it is to turn the music up to the point where your ears bleed from the midrange soaring. Anyone who *didn't* mention any problem with this must have the Serpent of Cacophony completely taped down or wrapped up in cottonballs or something -- any tips on how to alleviate this would be greatly appreciated.

I thought the fabric cord was going to be a Godsend. It isn't. I thought it would tangle less. It doesn't; if anything, it seems to contort itself into a knotted old phone cord more easily than cheapo rubber. It doesn't even come with a right-angle plug -- I bet a right-angle plug would ease plug strain without requiring the use of Sun Chip bags. Even the $3 headphones have that nailed down!

I bought these upmarket (for me) 'phones with the express purpose of longevity, and the audio quality has me hoping I can find a way to circumvent this ridiculous cord issue so I can keep them. I'd love to buy RHA again -- their audio engineers have worked some magic -- but the Serpent of Cacophony needs to be refined or replaced.

I have had a kindle keyboard since it came out. I lost mine when the new ones came out and still bought it. So why 2 stars? I'll tell you.

Screen
5 stars. Love it. A little slow to refresh but it looks so good I could read it all night (and I do).

Hardware
5 stars. Awesome battery life. Small. Light. Feels good in hand. Buttons are small, but I shouldn't be using them too much...or so I thought...

Software
Negative 1 million stars. Whoever designed it has a doodoo for brains. Keep in mind you have to use mininbuttons to do anything. There is no effort to minimize their use. The menu system is counterintuitive. The control system for menus is complicated and there is little information on the screens. Lots of options you use once are listed first, but the ones you need are listed later (more button pushing). Amazon also really wants you to buy their books. How can I tell? Because it is so obviously transparent. They only save settings and metadata for their own books on the cloud. You can only save collection lists for Amazon books. The Kindle comes with no sync software to keep copies of your books or transfer new books on the computer. You only option is the Cloud and Amazon books. You can't even upload books (which are text files, not like it should be a big deal). You pretty much have to use Calibre if you want to get your money's worth out if the Kindle.

Also, on a device that holds 1000s of books, and in a culture that birthed librarians, you would think organizing would be a killer app to build in. But no. Allow me to rant. I have 600 books on Calibre, BTW.

1. Categorizing: Does Amazon let you organize your books in any way OTHER than by title, author, or collection (with recently read first, ensuring an ever shifting list). NO. Why? Why not by genre? Why no metadata search? Why no desktop software to add metadata? I am boggled.

2. Making collections: oh yes, I love adding books into collections with a 6 step process when I include going back to where I was, with a screen that refreshes once per second, not to mention typing the names of 25 collections on a tiny keyboard, anytime I want to reorganize my library. Why no desktop management software like itunes?!!?! I am stymied.

3. Do people know every book in their library? Do they remember every detail? What about the books they bought to read months later? I guess Amazons beta testers can, because there is absolutely no way to read a synopsis of your books (or "the back" of paper books). Amazon doesn't even include them, so I have to write them myself in Calibre. Lazy publishers/Amazon. For completeness...why? I am befuddled. Which brings me to my next complaints...

4.No, I do not like seeing my library as a list. If I can't read a summary, then I at least need to see the cover to trigger a memory. Is there anyway to scroll through, with cover thumbnails? No. Did publishers redo the covers a little so they wouldn't be all one color? No. Did anyone proofread major, popular works to make sure there were no spelling mistakes or font incompatibilities (it is a book after all)? No. Its like they want ebooks to die. I understand, I guess.

I love my Kindle, I really do. I just hate Amazons software. I don't want to read a lightbulb. But if I cant' t actually USE my kindle because I can't find or organize my books, then why the hell did I buy it? I might well ust get an ipad and be able to manage my library a lot better on itunes in addition to watching movies and stuff.

I need an e-ink screen. Sure, I could get a Fire...but why? I have used a Fire, it is a POS and it is not e-ink (the kindles major selling point). If you need e-ink and long battery life, get a KK. Anything else, save the $$ and get an iPad. Apparently the new one has a screen that gets a lot dimmer.

I will just have to suffer with kindle keyboard...or likely, move back to paper books.

title: This is the best all around portable speaker for its size!
text:
I first bought the JBL Flip at Best Buy for listening to music at my office. The Flip's sound is fantastic, but in thinking long-term, I did not like that the battery only lasted roughly 4 hours on low volume. The last day I was able to return the Flip per the receipt, I saw the Charge at Best Buy. I wanted to weigh the factors of whether it would be worth the extra $50 to buy the charge, and in my opinion, it definitely is worth it.
1. You get 10-12 hours of battery life(can bring camping/beach/hotel), versus 4 hours on a good day with the Flip.
2. You can charge your cell phone from the Charge device by plugging it into one end(USB), while you're playing it, or even if you're not playing it.
3. It has excellent sound. I actually like the sound a LITTLE bit better on the Flip, but considering all you can do with a speaker that will last 10-12 hours vs 4 hours, and have a way to charge your phone as well, plus a bit better bass that doesn't distort, I exchanged my Flip for the Charge, after using the flip for 2 weeks, and have ZERO regrets, as this is one sweet device.
I did not like the smallest Jambox whatsoever, compared to either JBL devices. The larger Jambox is a different story, but that story costs $300 and not fair to compare on size/sound/price.

A new must-have for camping/beach/hotel stays!

title: So much better than my Axis camera. Mac users read this.
text:
[[VIDEOID:mo3BN2SH2BAJR6V]]I purchased this camera with some anxiety since I am a Mac user and I was concerned about being able to set it up. And indeed it did require a Windows environment to do the initial set-up. Running Windows 7 in Parallels I was able to discover the camera and change the IP address to be compatible with my network using the included SADP software. I was immediately struck by the high quality of the video on this camera. It is dramatically superior to the Axis 207MW that I had been using (mounted Indoor pointed through a window since it is not an outdoor camera). I have not had experience with infra-red cameras before and I am very impressed by the image quality in near total darkness. I am using it powered by PoE with the TP-Link TL-POE150S. It becomes even more complicated than that- I am also using a TP-Link Powerline adaptor (TL-PA4010) to extend my connection from my router without having to run 200 feet of Cat 5 cable the full length of my house. Much to my relief this is working without a problem.

The camera weighs more than I expected. This is because of its high quality construction.I am very likely to purchase another one of these very reasonably priced cameras.

The only problem I've had is that I am unable to view the camera video through my Mac browsers. I have to use either Firefox or Safari browser in a Windows environment to see the video in a browser. But this has not been a major problem since I use the camera in conjunction with SecuritySpy Software which handles the camera well. With SecuritySpy I can set up motion detection, video recordings, email notification, uploads to ftp servers, etc. So Windows is not so important once the camera has been initially set-up. And the live video can easily be viewed on my iPhone or iPad with the free app available at the App Store.

Take a look at the short movie I created from a motion actuated recording from my camera on my front porch. I think it gives you a good idea of the high quality video image.

title: Simple and effective.
text: This is a great little problem solver for when you have a TV with just a single cable box or disc player as the source and you want to keep the source hidden away.  In my case I was wall mounting a flatscreen and I had a DirecTV Genie mini DVR attached to the back of the TV for a nice clean installation.  All I had to do was attach the IR receiver of this repeater system on the front of the TV in the corner right next to the IR receiver for the TV using the double sided adhesive included.  Then I attached the IR transmitter to the DirecTV Genie mini DVR IR receiver on the back of the TV.  I plugged in the USB connector to a port on the TV (I could have also used the one on the DVR) and zip tied the cables neatly.  There is no programming or setup involved because the repeater simply "repeats" the signal received from your remote to the device that is hidden away.  While in most cases you will want to power this system using one of the many USB ports found on all electronics these days, but it is nice that they also include an AC power adapter for additional flexibility.

title: Love and hate
text:
We love the Freetime feature! Coming from an IPad, it took sometime getting used to the Kindle swiping and not having a home button to go to. Since this is more of a parent controlled tablet, there is initial set-up to be done. I love that the apps they can see is geared towards their age. My kids were so excited to get a couple of app choices without having to "pay" for them. I've set up two profiles for my daughter (3) and son (6), they have since ignored the ipad and fought over the kindle.

Pros:
- Different profiles for everyone.
- ability to control apps that the kids can see. We can really download any app from the Kindle store and decide if we want our kids to have access.
- The limited time feature. I've set it to first read 30 minutes of books before playing any games or videos. I've noticed that my son is loving books more and is very excited to read new books every night.
- 2 year warranty

Cons:
- Coming from Ipad it does take a little getting used to but my son loves the swiping of books and apps. He said it's easier to find vs the ipad.
- It took me a while to figure out how to make the home screen appear but tapping in the middle of the screen did the trick (while reading books, have not tested videos and apps)

Switching profiles is easy, just press the power button, tap the profile icon and it should let you select the available profile.

My daughter has been begging me to buy her one too but she has to make do with our old Ipad, I'm not spending anymore $$$.

*** Update 11/4/2014

Okay we have the tablet for more than 2 weeks now, everything has been going well until we run out of storage. It was frustrating to us as we have a lot of apps to install. Not only that, there are times that I would approve an app and it would not finish downloading at all in the child's profile. It will forever have that orange/yellow status. It works fine on my profile but not on my child's profile! I added a new profile for 2nd child and whatever app I try to approve it just doesn't come up in her profile.

I wanted to love this, I do but the 4 gb usable storage is just not cutting it for us plus there are still a lot of bugs to be fixed for this tablet. I am downgrading this to 2 stars. I instead bought a refurbished kindle fire 3rd gen with 32g, will install freetime and buy a kid proof case. That should do it for the space issue.

title: A great mid-tier bass and treble-centric headphone for those without powerful amps.
text:
Before I start, I just wanna mention that I have owned TWO of the DT990/600ohms, and one DT990 Pro 250ohm.

The 32ohm tends to get dismissed as being inferior to the higher ohm variants due mostly to the simple notion that higher ohm = better quality.

That's partially true, but not completely.

The DT990 32ohm sounds almost EXACTLY like the 600ohm, give or take some refinement here and there.

That being said, people are making the mistake of buying the 250ohm and 600ohm, and pairing them up with portable amps, or even straight into their devices thinking that just because they are loud enough, they are driven properly. That can't be further from the truth. With the less than stellar equipment, the 32ohm headphone WILL sound better, because they do not require a lot of power in comparison to the others.

The 32ohm sounds very crisp, with deep, punchy bass. The DT990 treble is still a thing (meaning that it can be screechy... which is something all DT990s share), but not much more of a difference than the others. The mids are still recessed in comparison to the lows and highs, but they are still very clean and clear. This is a headphone for those of us that like bass and treble, no doubt.

If you're not looking into spending money on a big desktop amp, and want something that can sound good unamped (and better with a portable amp), the 32ohm will not disappoint. Even when directly compared to the higher ohm variants of powerful equipment, the 32ohm sounds very close to the others, like 95% the same.

title: It may be your disk...
text:
I bought two of these to house two known-good disk drives that I had pulled out of another machine. Unfortunately no combination worked at all...my Windows 7 machines would not recognize either drive, no matter how I interchanged them. I called PUREX and a technician just kept telling me it was the fault of my disk drives and that I had to call the manufacturer (Western Digital and Seagate). He was right, but not much help. I didn't want to wait in another telephone queue, so I pulled up Windows Disk Manager (Control Panel / Administrative Tools / Storage / Disk Management) and was able to recreate partitions and format the drives just fine. I should have done that in the first place. It turns out that my disks had come from a RAID machine and were not recognizable as ordinary NTFS disks by Windows. Both enclosures have been performing really well at full speed on my high-speed USB 3.0 ports.

The product comes with three kinds of screws and you have to be careful to use the right type of screw in the right place. A phillips screwdriver is also included!

I hope that helps somebody.

title: Great compact headphones for work!
text:
I was looking for a set of on-ear headphones for use at work. I am in an office where I was trying to accomplish three things:

-I needed headphones that didn't make me look like I was unavailable or not working... so no over ear huge headphones
-I wanted premium headphones that had great sound
-I wanted headphones that blocked out most outside sounds, but not all (and work great on airplanes)

I looked around for a few weeks and sampled over a dozen models. These headphones fit the bill perfectly... and were the only ones that did.

These headphones have a very broad frequency response and are fairly even in intensity across frequencies. Unlike some other headphones (Beats, I'm looking at you!) these headphones give a nice strong bass response without being out of context. This makes these headphones very versatile. I can use them for Netflix, spoken word audio, and music and they work great on them all. This is very important to me because I may be using these headphones for music one minute and listening to a web-based training class the next. It's also nice that these headphones have a built in microphone for quick calls that come in while listening to music. They also come with a nice case. I can't speak highly enough about these headphones and I strongly recommend them.

One recommendation, the cord these come with is a little short for work so I suggest you buy a headphone cable extension cord... it helps when plugging into the laptop.

First things first, yes, you will eat up rolls of 35mm quickly with this camera. One 360 degree photo burns through about 4 standard frames of 35mm. Second, get yourself a Digitaliza 35mm mask. Trust me, your standard masks that came with the scanner aren't going to capture the sprocket holes that this camera exposes. Speaking of scanners, make sure it's a backlit type. Standard flatbed won't usually scan film anyway. I'm personally using a Canoscan 9000F and it does the job. However, and this can be pretty important. Make sure to upgrade your scanner software. The OEM probably won't know how to deal with sprocket holes in the scan. Mine didn't. I had to upgrade VueScan and I've heard SilverFast also does the trick.
Yes, it might seem like a lot to go through, in addition to now having to work with film but if you're really interested in something different, it'll definitely be worth the extra effort.
BTW, learn to use the Polar Coordinates effect with your scans.

title: Easy replacement for Comcast - No call needed
text:
If you're looking for a modem to save you $8 a month with Comcast (they just raised my rental rate), you just found it. It will pay for itself in 7-8 months, and is 3x as powerful as the fastest service speed Comcast offers in my area (50MB up/10MB down). I had no change in speed after switching, but had a relatively new Comcast rental modem.

The main reason for this review is to let you know that I had NONE of the trouble some people mentioned here setting up with Comcast. I did NOT have to call them, I just plugged the modem in and plugged it into my computer. Opened up a web browser (Chrome) and followed the form that popped up. I just needed the account # and phone # of my account. I didn't need the MAC address of the router, it filled in automatically. The whole setup was painless and took 10 minutes.

Three things to note before you buy:
1 - This modem supports 150MB/s, and there is a newer version (SB6141) that supports 300MB/s. For 99.9% of you at this time, that does not matter because your internet isn't that fast anyway. This modem is capable of speeds 3x as fast as the fastest service I can get, but the 6141 is technically more "future proof". This version is less expensive, and isn't white.

2 - This is NOT a telephony modem. If your modem doubles as a phone line in the same box, this modem cannot do that for you.

3 - There is not a wireless router built into this modem (no WiFi). You need a separate wireless router with it, and it's better that you do that anyway.

Long story short, if you hate Comcast as much as I do, give Amazon your money instead and buy this modem.

***EDIT 2/6/14: I got my hands on a 6141 (the newer version of this modem) and gave it a shot. For some reason, the speeds were inconsistent and slower than this modem with Comcast. Perhaps I got a dud, but the 6121 consistently performed better with no unexpected difficulty.

title: Great on UHF, not so great on VHF
text:
I did a lot of research on indoor TV antennas. This one was the highest rated.
At one point it picked up 50 stations, great, except all of them were the upper channels.
22-70. There's not a lot I want to watch up there.
I want the broadcast VHF, you know, NBC, ABC, FOX, CBS.
I wanted to watch football when the game is on locally.
I'm 16 miles from the transmitter according to the charts.
I can't get any of those reliably. Maybe if I move it around, it works for a couple hours,
then it breaks up. My living room is on the wrong side of the house, away from the antennas.
The problem is my (Samsung) TV doesn't allow you to "add channels". You have to search again.
I'd love if it had a "signal strength" meter, like my Sharp Aquos, but no. It will be hunt and peck.

The design and workmanship is top notch. Even the cable is nicely finished. The amplifier is powered by my
USB port on the TV so I don't need to plug it in (ac)

Sunday, I'll try it again or compare with my huge and awkward Terk rabbit ears.

UPDATE:
Well, I held the antenna in my hand and tried several locations. Here's the problem.
Your body makes a difference. The best signal was when I stood in the LR holding the antenna over my head like the statue of liberty.
Obviously, that wasn't a solution, so I tried on the wall, but good spots broke up when I walked away.
Also, make sure you don't touch the metal connector because that will make your body part of the antenna. (It gets better)
Nothing was perfect for all channels, but oddly, the best compromise was placing the antenna flat on top of a lamp in the corner.
That's where it remains today. I watched Fox football and later NBC Sunday night without touching the antenna.
Now, Mohu has jacked up the price by $6. Jeez, this thing is getting too expensive, I need another for the bedroom TV now.
Maybe I'll try the Amazon for half the cost. I tried Wal*Mart's $10 rabbit ears in the bedroom, and they sucked. No VHF.
With modern TV's you can't tune to a channel and play with the rabbit ears. You won't see the channel unless it's decent enough to
scan in. So moving the antenna requires another scan.

title: Be careful with this drive and software
text:
Note: Dec 2013 Update follows the initial review
===============================================================
I bought the 3 TB drive to back up my Dell XPS 15 750MB hard drive as well as to store my ever increasing inventory of video files. It seamed like a great price for $149

The hard drive came with Seagate software called Dashboard for backing up user document files. It was easy and worked well. It created a backup of my document directory and gave me the option for having both added or changed files updated at a time of my choosing.

What happened next was more of a Microsoft issue than Seagate. When trying to use Windows 7 backup to create a disc image on the Seagate, it kept failing halfway through giving me error messages. This happened to me before on other large external hard drives over 2TB, so I thought I would fix it by partitioning the drive into a 750GB and 2.25TB drives. I then tried to back it up on the 750GB partition but had the same problem. It took me 2 hours to figure out Windows 7 backup will not work with these hard drive because of the way the sectors are sized. I did however find a free Seagate program called Seagate Disc Wizard that you can download for free at Seagate's website that will create a disc image backup without this issue.

Pros
- Seagate Dashboard is great for backing up and recovering individual user files and Disc Wizard for creating disc images in case of system failure
- Its quiet
- Its fast. Created a 320GB disc image in about 45 min.
- Runs cool after 1 hour of continuous backup
- Great pricing
- There are 5 lights on the front that illuminate sequentially as the hard drive fills up

Cons
- Will not work with Windows 7 image backup utility (cant create backup image of your hard drive using Windows 7)
- No stand so if you stand it upright it can easily tip over
- There is an activity light on the front that is supposed to tell you when the unit is in use, but it only flashes from full brightness to 75% brightness (instead of going fully out) so its hard to tell when the hard drive is in use when viewed from over 2 feet away.

-----------------------------------------
IMPORTANT Dec 14 2013 Update.

Not so happy anymore. Just went through hell and back with this hard drive. The summary? My Dell laptop internal hard drive crashed. I needed to rely on my mirror image which was created on this Seagate 3T external hard drive. The hard drive worked but the software (neither Seagates Disc Wizard nor Dashboard) worked. Bottom line, buy this as a hardware backup only if your going to use third party software for backup (like Acronis) as Seagates software doesnt work, and Windows 7 will not recognize any backup files on a hard drive >1T (Windows 8 may have fixed this problem).
---------------------------
The details? I will only add that I booted from the Seagate boot disk (when reinstalling a disk image, the only way to get the computer to recognize this Seagate external hard drive is with the Seagate (or Acronis) boot disk, ... the computer WONT RECOGNIZE THIS SEAGATE EXTERNAL HARD DRIVE IF USING WINDOWS 7 AS A BOOT DISK!), then tried to re-image the new hard drive that Dell installed (it was still under warranty) with my tib file (image backup) that was created using Seagates disk wizard on this hard drive, the recovery (or "Recovering Partition" as Seagate calls it) would take 3 hours to reach 99% completion, and then in the last 20-30 sec, always finish with a big red "X" with the message "Recovery Operation Failed", No explanation. No error code...no anything. I then ran Windows 7 repair off the Windows boot disc and it said my new hard drive: Partition table is corrupt. Error code = 0x490

I tried reinstalling the tib image and repairing the new hard drive using the windows boot disk several times and wanted to pull the hair out of my head as, unless you have the CD disc's for all the programs installed on your computer, a disk image is the only way to recover your PROGRAMS (not user files). I called Seagate text support and they said my tib file must be corrupt, even though it consistently checked out as valid backup when scanned by Disc Wizard (ie, the Seagate tech didnt know what they were talking about as you will see). After countless hours I realized Seagate licenses a "lite" version of Acronis backup software that they re-title "Disk Wizard" or "Dashboard" that is really not up to the job. The problem was Seagate's version of the software was deleting the partition and, once I bought and created an Acronis boot disc, I used it to undelete the partition and voila, my hard drive had been re-imaged on the new drive all along, Seagates software just couldnt "see" it. Seagates software was deleting the partition and making it "appear" as though the image hadnt been installed and the partition table was corrupt! And if I listed to the Seagate tech "expert", I would have deleted the tib file and lost most of my programs.

Then I tried to reinstall my user files that were backed up using Dashboard (as the tib image was about a month older than my Dashboard user files backup), but Seagates Dashboard didnt recognize the latest backup version of my files, only the version that was 6 months older. So I had to manually go into the hundreds of backup directories to recover my latest user files (which took hours).

Bottom line, the HARDWARE was fine, but dont plan on using Windows 7 or Seagate's software if you are planning on using this for a disk image or user file backup. If your not using it for disk imaging, or not using Dashboard to backup user files, its fine. Changing this from 4 stars to 3

title: Fantastic Sound BUT One serious design flaw you can easily fix
text:
These speakers are fantastic, especially at this price point. My review has two parts--one about the sound and one about a pretty amazing design flaw that is easily fixed. I highly recommend these speakers. They are an incredible value. However, if you get a pair, see my comments below on the design flaw.

Sound and Quality

A little background about me. I've been into stereos and good sound my whole life. I was introduced to high quality equipment by my father over 45 years ago, and have always had excellent equipment. I've had many amplifiers and a good number of speakers over the years, and I've listened to a lot of different equipment in showrooms and hifi stores. My bias is that I am after what sounds great to me, not what costs a fortune or what is in vogue with audiophiles (my view is that some of them really do know their stuff and some do not and are just paying a fortune for stuff that sounds no better than things costing far less).

I mention my own tendencies because these speakers really do sound fantastic for this price point. The build quality is amazing, and they look good, too. You cannot really tell from the pictures, but they are not large. They are towers, for sure, but they take up a modest amount of space which is excellent unless you have a lot of room. They put out a lot of sound for their size. I use them in a medium size family room in a finished basement. I am using them with my favorite (now quite old) amplifier/receiver of the many amplifiers I have had had over the years (an Onkyo TX-840). I use these speakers in a stereo--not surround or theatre setup--setting. This particular model of Onkyo has a sound I like better than anything I've ever owned, and I have long thought they sounded particularly good with Polk speakers, which is why I wanted to try the TSi-300s. And I am really happy I got these

These Polks have a warm, full sound. The highs and mids are clear and I can more readily pick out things like locations of instruments (e.g., cymbals and such) than with the Infinities they are replacing. The sound is not harsh but it is very clear (not mushy). What I was not prepared for was just how good the low end is for this size speaker. While there are plenty of reviewers who note these need a subwoofer because the bottom is not the strong suit, I frankly think that is only the case if you are looking for a rattling low end for movie sound tracks. For music (and most movies), what these TSi-300s can do on the bottom without a sub is pretty surprising to me (it's excellent). I have two very good quality subwoofers from Polk. I forget but I think they are each rated at 250 watts or so, and Polk is very conservative in their ratings (as an example, see how happy people are with the Polk sub PSW10 here on Amazon. That's not a model I have, but unless you have a very large room, I bet it's a fantastic unit for the price).

Back to the bottom. I tried these TSi-300s with and without one of my subwoofers. I found that, for music (including music with a lot of bass in the mix), I did not like the sound any better with the sub than without it. The TSi-300s perform amazingly well on the low end for their size--much better than I expected. If, however, you want to use these speakers for a home theatre, or even with just a left-right set up that includes a lot of movie watching where you want to feel your body shake, then you'd want a sub with them. Ditto if you have a large room and love hip-hop or club-like dance music, you probably would want a sub. But even at that, I would not assume you would want or need the sub. I am genuinely surprised at just how excellent these perform on the bottom--really delighted in fact.

As you can see from the reviews here at Amazon, people who have purchased these are very happy with them. If you'd like to check out some external reviews, here's one that put me over the top for trying these TSi-300s. Search for: TSi-300s review Ralf Neels. That will get you there. He does a very nice review, and what he says matches my sense of these speakers very well (though, he has better ears than me to discern a slight lack in the mid-bass region). Note that he says you could not get better sound at twice the price. I agree completely with him except that I'd say you'd not find better sound at several times the price (except, I think at double the price, the TSi500s would likely sound even better). But for what else is out there, you could pay a lot more to get sound as good as this (as long as you like this type of sound signature, which I'd call crisp, distinct, yet on the warm/smooth side).

Okay, so what's not to like. Here is the design problem, and it's real and serious but easily fixed. I will write to Polk about this in a few days.

Design Problem

After I had these for a few days, and was enjoying the sound a lot, I occasionally noticed a sort of little fizzt or fuzz sound whiz by, especially in a particular register on the higher end. I thought my left speaker had a tweeter problem. I listened to various things trying to pick up just what was wrong. Then I tried tightening down my connections more, and realized that one might not have been a little loose. The problem seemed to go away and I was happy. Then it came back after a few days. Importantly, I truly think many people would not hear this little bit of a problem, and it was intermittent, so it was really bugging me as I was trying to figure out why this would be happening.

Finally, I had decided there was just something wrong with the left speaker and I was going to take it back (maybe the set, because I'd already spent hours trying to figure this out and was frustrated). As I was disconnecting the left speaker, I noticed something about the metal strip that connects the posts for the bi-amping feature. It was loose even though the wire nuts were tightened down all the way.

What's bi-amping? A speaker that can do bi-amping allows you to run a separate amplifier for the high end of the speaker and the low end, so it gives you two sets of posts to connect the wires (one for the highs and one for the lows). Now, honestly, why Polk would build this function into a speaker at this price point mystifies me. Only really hard core audiophiles are going to be interested, and they are not buying Polk speakers in this price range--trust me on that. Here's why this matters to you if you get a pair. You are likely not interested in bi-amping. Here's where the metal strip that was lose on mine, comes in. The metal strip connects the two negative posts together and the two positive posts together so that when you connect your speaker wires to one set of posts, the others are connected too (so you get both the high and the low end).

The problem is the design. Once the speaker wires are in the holes, and the nuts on the posts are tightened down on wires as tight as at least I could make them, the little metal strips were still not locked into place. I could not on my speakers) tighten the nuts down far enough to actually solidly clamp those little strips in place. They were slightly loose after connecting the speaker wires, and that means the connection from one set of posts to the other was not solid. Hence, after hours of fiddling around, I realized only as I was disconnecting these speakers to return them why the high end on the one side was sometimes a little tiny bit fritzy.

If you get these and do not want this problem, you can solve it in one of several ways. After you connect speaker wires, try wiggling the little brass colored metal strips (you'll see--it's obvious what I mean once you see them; or see the two pictures I posted). If you can wiggle them, you need to solve this problem. The way I solved it was to cut four very short wires, and connect each set of plus and minus posts (red and black) on each speaker, along with, of course, reconnecting the wires from the amplifier to one set of the posts on each speaker. Essentially, I created a better connection between the high and low end of the speakers than Polk supplied, given the bi-amping design. Another solution would be to connect to the speakers using banana plugs. This would solve the problem because if you tighten down the nuts on the connection posts all the way, without any speaker wires needing to go through the posts, the metal strips are held down solidly and make good contact. Again, if you cannot picture this, trust me, it will be obvious once you have the speakers.

I highly recommend these speakers. Just check carefully if those metal strips have any looseness at all once you connect your amplifier, and solve that problem if it exists.

title: Versatile lens, best alpha mount superzoom by a hair
text:
Purchased the Amazon Warehouse Deals version in Used - Very Good condition. The lens was like new, couldn't spot a single sign of use. Came in all original packaging with all parts. Very different then my experiences with other outlets used equipment. I am glad I went for the Amazon purchase over the online camera store I was looking at that had a used version at the time. Very happy with my AWD experience.

As for the lens, it is very versatile, and the convenience of a single lens for 18-250 comes at a price (photos are a little soft throughout the range compared to shorter zooms and primes). However, I think this lens is the best of any of the superzooms on an alpha with a good auto focus motor. The a55 has a great motor, and the AF is fast. The benefit of this Sony lens compared to the Tamron 18-250, the Sigma 18-250, or even the Tamron 18-270 PZD is in the accuracy of the AF. I used the Tamron 18-250, which many people say is the same lens optically, and it was accurate with focus far less often than this Sony even in the limited testing I have done with my new lens. I would still like to try the Tamron PZD, but I doubt it will be much different. What pushes the Sony over the edge is the available lens profiles to correct distortion in many software packages.

One pleasant surprise is the relatively close shortest focal distance. Close-up shots at the tele end are certainly macro like. Not sure what the ratio is, but it is better than I expected.

The 18-250 is better than the kit 18-55 is almost every way. It is brighter at their shared apertures (beyond 18mm) and it is just as sharp or sharper wide open. The kit auto-focus is a touch faster overall, and the kit lens is much smaller and lighter. Keeping the kit lens is a no-brainer though; at this point they are worth barely $50 used.

This lens replaces the Sony 16-105 for me, and I can't see any reason to stay with that lens unless the extra 2mm are very important. There is certainly a difference on the wide-end between the two. 2mm makes a big difference in FOV. However across their shared focal lengths the 18-250 has wider apertures and is much sharper in the 50-75mm range and somewhat sharper at 100mm. Further, the autofocus is better and faster in low light (still hunts compared to my 50mm f1.8, but its not hard to get used to as long as you have a slow moving subject).

So far, I am very happy with the lens, and I expect it will get a ton of use.

title: bought one for me and one for my wife's car
text:
The only think I don't like is that it wiggles out over time, but every RV adapter I've ever had does that. Very aggravating. Besides that it's performance is awesome.

Words to the wise:
1) make sure the volume is all the way up to 30
2) play around with the output volume of your phone ... I found that if I exceeded 80% the quality of the music went down - especially for the bass. Crank it to as high can go without distortion and then always use that level for the best quality.
3) sometimes it depends on where the phone is located in reference to the device.
4) if you detune it for a second then tune it back it will clear up the noise.
5) if you can't connect or loose connection turn it off (button on the RV plug) then back on.
6) sometimes just changing the FM requency a tiny bit like 93.4 to 93.6 makes all the difference.
7) for me the auto-tune feature that finds an empty channel for you is completely worthless, you're better off just moving it around.
8) don't be surprised if the clearest signal is on an FM frequency that is already being used by a radio station.
9) if you have 2 of them (one for each car), make sure that when you connect with your phone change the name of the connection that your phone has listed to something that makes sense (example: TruckBT, CarBT), otherwise you'll get frustrated when you think it isn't connecting, when it's connecting to the other vehicle (or trying to)

title: All It Took Was 15 Minutes
text:
Let me first say that I am in no way an audiophile, producer, mixer, or anything of the sort. I love music and I enjoy listening to several genres, but I am just that; a casual listener. About six months ago I bought a pair of Beats Studio (2013 black/red) and thought they were a great pair of headphones. They were moderately comfortable until after two hours of continuous use, produced generous bass, and could generate fairly crisp highs. Originally the Beats Studio headphones were a solid choice for $300 until I decided to look for something better. Near the end of September, I started to dig around on audiophile forums and popular review websites on various different headphones; Audio-Technica ATH-M50, Beats Pro, Sennheiser Momentum, V-Moda M-100, AKG K545, and Bose QC 25 to name a few. The range of price varied quite a bit, where the ATH-M50s got as low as $130 here at Amazon and the Beats Pro were nearing $450 for select colors. But I concluded that price wasn't a determining factor for a new pair of cans; it was all about quality at this point. After reviewing both positive and somewhat negative reviews on several headphones, the V-Moda M-100s came out as my first candidate. I could sit here and type on about the impressive process in which these headphones went under in their production, but instead allow me to tell you about my personal experiences with these cans.

All it took was a 15 minute test drive at a local Microsoft store. One of their employees grabbed a pair off the shelf, and after getting the headphones out of the box, I was left alone with the music on my phone and the matte black M-100s. Believe me when I say my expectations were high; the moment I got the first track to play, I was shell shocked. Lows, mids, and highs were outstandingly precise. Punchy, natural bass; solid, tight mids; clean, powerful highs. Every expectation was blown out of proportion and the ridiculous amount of detail produced an entirely new perspective to each and every song. In the 15 minutes of test driving the profound V-Moda headphones, a grin progressively grew on my face from beginning to end. I left the store in excessive excitement knowing I had found what I was looking for...and more. That night the V-Moda M-100s were ordered from Amazon.

Two weeks later I feel compelled to write about my experience. Straight out of the box these sounded fantastic. Just like the test drive, except this pair was now mine. The build quality is to brag about, the design is stunningly eye-catching, and the fact that V-Moda offers custom plates makes these all-the-more personal. At first wear I found discomfort around my ears after a few hours, but surprisingly enough, the discomfort went away the more I wore them.
All-in-all, the V-Moda M-100s are the best headphones I have ever come across. V-Moda has managed to not only break, but shatter all of my expectations and I am thrilled to be one of their customers. And as I said before I am no audiophile and thus I probably can't describe sound quality as sophisticated as an expert could, but I can tell you that as outstanding as everything is with these headphones, the sound quality continues to impress. Every listen they seem to sound better and better; making me fall in love even harder.

title: Just what I was looking for...
text:
This review is for the axion 7" Portable LCD TV, model AXN-8706. I've been wanting to get another little portable tv to replace the RCA/Radio Shack analog 3" TFT handheld TV (model 16-3062) that no longer works since everything switched over to digital channels. This 7" portable seems to fit the bill. I'm happy with it.

The television was easy to setup and program in all the local stations. The picture is pretty decent, even given that the screen resolution is only 480x234. I've been watching the Olympics on it and haven't had too many issues with reading text on the screen.

Ok, some information on the television:
1) The TV came with a small remote, which is around 3.25" x 2" and maybe 3/8" thick. It has one of those mylar keypads, with the raised bubble buttons - which is pretty standard for inexpensive electronics like this.

2) The screen resolution for this tv is 480x234, which in my opinion is a really low resolution screen. But all of the other 7" digital tvs I looked at have that same screen resloution. It's low, but in tv mode you still get a pretty decent picture. In slideshow mode, viewing photos off a thumb drive or SD memory card, the pictures are pretty low-rez and very blurry. I really don't suggest using this as a substitute for a photoframe. I've got a pretty cheap photoframe which has a much higher screen resolution and the pictures on it look a heck of a lot better.

3) When I first started looking around for another portable tv, I narrowed my choice down to this one and the RCA 7" TV, model RTV 86073. The reason I picked the axion over the RCA was that this axion model came equipped with both a usb port and a SD memory card slot - and that the unit could play MP4 videos. I've tested both a USB drive and several SD cards and both work great. The one and only complaint I have is that the SD card slot does not go that deep into the unit - so you have about ½ the SD card sticking out the side of the unit. No big deal really though. MP4 movies work fine with this unit. It's important to get the right balance of image resolution and compression for smooth playback with devices like this. I tried a number of configurations, and the one that seems to work the best is the one for an Apple iPod Touch. That matches the screen resolution and playback capability of the TV the best in my opinion. I don't plan on watching a whole lot of videos on this, but it's nice to know that I can if I want.

4) Battery life - I've played the tv for a bit more than 2 hours on battery, after first charging the unit over night. When the battery starts to lose it's charge, you will get a blinking red battery icon in the lower right-hand side of the screen.

5) Antenna - the antenna that come with the unit is pretty small, about 5" tall. It has a magnetic base that allows you to stick it to any metal surface (right now I have it stuck to the ceiling a/c vent). It has about 6 or 7 feet of cable and has an F-connector that plugs into the jack on the side of the unit. The f-connector is the smooth, non-thread kind. You can pretty much use any standard antenna that has a connector like that - the thread kind will not work.

text:
Before I explain why I love this product so much, let me confess that I'm not really using this Sonos component like the Sonos folks would probably prefer. The Sonos product line is a "system" and most buyers probably buy Sonos speakers in addition to the Connect module, but I have an existing wireless speak system in my home, through which I piped various sources of music and radio, such as music from my [[ASIN:B00192VWVY Aluratek AIRMM01F Internet Radio Alarm Clock with built-in WiFi (Black)]] and my [[ASIN:B001FA1O0O Apple iPod touch 8GB (4th Generation) - Black - Current Version]].

I connected the Connect via an Ethernet cord directly to my router. I also connected to the Connect an [[ASIN:B008ALA2RC Airport Express Base Station]].

Now that the Sonos connect is up and running, I will never need to use the Aluratek Internet Radio or the iPod with my home speaker system, ever. The Sonos Connect is absolutely amazing.

Here is why I love it so much:

- It really is as easy as they say to get things connected. While nerds like me like a challenge and do enjoy figuring out how to make a poorly designed product work better, sometimes its nice to just have the product do what it was supposed to do in the first place. It took me about 5 minutes after I installed the software to get the system working.

- Puts all of my "sources," including my iTunes library, and other sources, such as Sirius and Audible, plus my favorite radio stations from around the world, together, in one unified system.

- Free "controllers." The controllers are how you tell the Sonos system what to play, how loud to play it, etc. You can put the controller on any of your computers. The iPad application is amazing. The app is free and it is a dream to use. I wish all apps were designed so well.

I can't comment on the quality of the "sound" since I am using non-Sonos speakers, but there is absolutely never any technical problems, such as lags or such. I am tempted to get a Sonos speaker to see what I'm missing, but I'm afraid if I buy one I won't be able to stop at just 1.

In sum, this is a product that does what it says it does. Now, if I could only figure out how to make it portable and take it with me away from my home...

title: Logitech has outdone itself
text:

Pros:
- 40 ft distance from phone before it started losing connection
- Sound is amazing
- Sound is amazing at high levels
- Isn't easily drowned from outside noises
- Bass sounds like bass, not like its from a hip-hop junkie's car stereo which only has a single 24" sub and doesn't know what a tweeter is.
- I can hear mids again
--My Favorite--
- Build Quality - Built like a D*** ROCK. Looks pretty good too

Currently there seems to be a massive boom in BT enabled, portable speakers. So much so that everyone is releasing a new product every quarter. Very hard to keep up with this and its hard to find something you want as it seems Bose/JamBox/Beats are drowning out other products through advertising. I live around a bunch of people who like to hang outside, most of them using BT speakers and all of them using at least one of the big ones listed above. The big Bose outside sounded weak, the JamBox was muddied and the Beats was overly eq'd for bass. I decided to give this one a shot since everyone on here seemed to really love it and to top it off it was cheaper. The ability to be loud outside was a big driving factor, if not I'd use one of the smaller ones for inside purposes. I also wanted something with a handle, which is much more ergonomic and practical then making a thinner box that's easy to pick up from the corner. Handles >>>> Corners

I am very happy with my purchase, from the music quality to the grippy underside, to the build quality it has makes it one really good purchase. Remember the UE symbol is the front side.

title: Does not count laps properly
text:
My wife bought for me this Garmin Swim watch at Amazon as a present. I am returning it after having tried it for three swimming sessions.
The problem with it is that it does not count the laps properly: sometimes misses one and sometimes increases the count by two, very erratically.
I found myself paying more attention to the watch than to my swimming (I am sure the other swimmers may have found amusing how I tried to get a missed lap counted by shaking frantically my hand!)

Another thing that you may want to know is that to see and graph your data you do have to create an online account. The only thing that is installed in your machine is the driver for the USB transceiver that wirelessly retrieves the data from the watch.

I do not like either what the manual says about "avoid operating the watch's buttons under the water". So, what happens if the watch has a leak? Are they going to blame you for using it in the water?

Finally, Linux users be aware that only Windows and Mac are supported. The driver for the USB transceiver does not work neither with Wine nor with WindowsXP running in VirtualBox.

title: Works but some things to be aware of.
text:
Purpose: to control my ATT DVR in the LR from the BR while extending the HDMI from the DVR to the TV in the BR.

In addition to the Cat5 or 6 cables, you will need to purchase mud rings rated for low voltage cabling to mount the plates on the wall. I installed and connected these wall plates with Cat5 cables inside the wall that separates my living room and bedroom. I live in a manufactured home and once I cut the openings in the walls, the first thing I noticed is that my walls are only 3". The cables plug into the wall plate perpendicular to the wall which caused them to bend against the adjacent wall once I mounted the plates. This may not be as much of a concern with the usual 3.5" wall.

Result: Operates as advertised. I am able to control the BR TV and LR DVR by one ATT remote, and still use the original ATT remote to control the LR TV and DVR. Finding the "eye" on my DVR required using a flashlight at different angles before I was successful. Apparently attaching the emitter bulb to the DVR eye does not prevent the LR remote from signaling the DVR as it normally does. On occasion one press of the BR remote button does not activate the function, (i.e. volume, channel, etc.) but after the second press, all buttons activate fine thereafter.

One reviewer mentioned not being able to use an HDMI splitter, however I'm using a powered 1X2 switcher, not a splitter, with no problem. There is an "equalizer adjustment" on the receiver plate in the event of sparkling or flickering tv images. I left it where it was when I received it (7, lowest) and the picture is fine. I'm very pleased with the look and operation. I can only guess that problems noted by other reviewers - such as taking a long time to turn components on or screens going black - could be due to improper installation.

So I'm posting this with the info as the title. I really think the seller ought to provide more specs on this unit, so you can know *before* you order it.

All it has in the way of video output is the old fashioned kind, and an optical kind that I don't even know if my TV supports. It does come with a cable, but it's too short for my location, so I will have to purchase a longer one.

I'm thrilled that I can now play discs from pretty much anywhere, but I'm annoyed that I did not have sufficient info about this unit before I bought it - I might have spent more and gotten HDMI output, had I known.
