title: I Don't Understand Why These Are Not More Popular - Love It!
text:
I've been using this for just a little over a month now. This is the first time I've tried using a pen mouse, and I have to say I really love it. For me, it is really the best way to control the cursor. It definitely is more ergonomic than a standard mouse and i've noticed alot less wrist pain since I've started using it. Perhaps more importantly, the portability of this mouse is fantastic, I take this into meeting in my pocket and pull it out as needed. I use the mouse at work for probably 6-7 hours a day. At that level of use I got about 3 weeks out of the first AAA battery. I can't say enough good things about this device and highly recommend it.

I will say that using this format of mouse is a little bit of its own skill and there is a little bit of a learning curve. In particular as other reviewers have mentioned, the right click button takes some time to get the right technique. Since the tip doesn't create resistance pressing sideways for the right click function will move the mouse. I have adapted by allowing my middle finger to rest lightly on the surface as I move the mouse, applying more pressure to the finger when I right or left click to create resistance to prevent the mouse from moving. Resting your fingers on the surface also helps with the other technique issue, which is maintaining a consistent angle in the hand. The responsiveness of the mouse is very consistent, but using it at significantly different angles will affect its sensitivity. Resting at least one finger on the surface helps to maintain a more consistent angel and allows you to use your fingers to give more precision when necessary. It might sound like a bit of a hassle, but it becomes second nature very quickly and I have found in less than a month, I have more speed and control than I did using a standard mouse. The best way to think about the technique is to approach the grip thinking of the device as a standard mouse that happens to be shaped like a pen rather than as a pen which happens to function as a mouse.

The last learning curve issue deals with the fact that it is more cumbersome to put down and pick up the pen mouse, to get around this I actually continue to hold the pen mouse in my hand while typing, sort of tucking it under my hand with my thumb, never really moving my thumb out of position. Doing it this way allows me to actually switch between typing and mousing very quickly, at least as quickly as transitioning from mouse to keyboard, and possibly faster, since my mouse is always where my hand is rather than having to move my hand to where the mouse is. Like I said it only took about a week to pretty much nail this down, and its not so much a detractor as just a difference you should be aware of.

Unfortunately, these havn't become very popular yet so it seems that there are no well know companies are designing and manufacturing these devices. As a result the design isn't quite as refined as it could be, although its still great. In general the materials have a cheap feel to them. I've been using this pretty heavily and havnt been afraid of knocking it around abit, and its held together great but the finish on this doesn't proclaim quality. Also, the available colors and trims available on these could use some work and contribute to the "cheap" look. Perhaps the biggest bummer is that there is no storage for the dongle inside the pen. In reality, I'm not moving between computers alot so this is no big deal but it would be a nice touch. One last thing with regard to the scroll wheel, the scroll wheel works perfectly. However this devices just uses standard drivers, and the calibration of the scroll wheel sensitivity was a little goofy. title: KVARs don't work for residential houses but....
text:
If you search the internet, you will find that these KVAR units are capacitors that will improve the power factor if you have inductive loads (e.g. motors for AC, pumps, etc). However your utility company does not charge you a penalty for a poor power factor. Only commercial/industrial sites will be charged for poor power factors and these units are typically installed in those units. When I contacted the company with these facts, they agreed with me. "You should not purchase this unit to improve your power factor and you will not see any savings based on power factor improvement." Surprised by the admission, I asked them how this unit could possibly save money on a residential unit. They indicated that the savings could only be realized if you install the unit at the motor/load and only if the motor/load is at least 20 feet from your electrical panel. You never want to install this unit at your electrical panel since there are no savings there.

A capacitor in parallel with an inductive load will supply any instanteous demand by the motor and not require current to travel over the > 20 foot resistive distance to the panel. The savings is the heat dissipated over the 20 feet from the panel to the motor for the instant demand of the motor. Some savings, but not the dramatic savings being claimed. Most people are not told this and they install at their panel with no savings being realized. I have no objective data myself on these claims but in theory there may be some savings.

title: Remove battery and it goes brain dead
text:
For me -- taking pictures of non-mobile, inanimate objects -- the camera does what I want. The pictures come out sharp, and I have no complaints there. Others have issues with the slow turn around time between photos. I agree that this is *not* a good camera for sporting events or taking pictures of the kids (when you want to take a bunch of pictures quickly so that you can select the best one later).

Personally, I selected the S9300 specifically for the GPS feature.

I have two gripes against the camera:

1. If you remove the battery, the settings -- at least whether to include GPS location information -- gets reset back to the factory default. I missed the GPS information on a number of shots due to this "feature."

2. My camera doesn't charge very well through the USB -- meaning that I have to remove the battery and put it in the external charger. Which brings me back to issue #1.

If I had known all the limitations of this camera before I bought, I probably still would have, but I would have started with a completely different set of procedures. I would have started out with a spare battery and the car recharger to ensure that I always had a fresh battery. I also would go through all the menu options each time after changing the battery to ensure they were set the way that I wanted them.

This camera does not inspire loyalty to Nikon. If another camera comes out with similar features and price point -- but doesn't go brain dead every time you replace the battery -- I'll go with it instead.

title: Excellent compact camcorder case
text:
The Case Logic Compact Camcorder Case is, as its name suggests, a compact case that is well suited to smaller full camcorders, as well as portable and pocket camcorders. I have been using it with a Canon Vixia HF R20, which measures about 4.5"L x 2.75"D x 2"H. The inner pocket accommodates this device snugly. It might handle a camcorder slightly longer in any measurement (~.25"-.5"), but will not likely fit anything much longer than the stated dimensions.

The design surprised me somewhat. When I first unzipped the zipper, which unzips one side of the case, the side pivots outward by the bottom seam. Two elastic straps prevent the side from flopping out completely. The side that pivots out has a formed pocket, into which the camcorder fits. This pocket is where the padding for the camcorder is located. There is an inner pocket to this formed pocket, where you can easily keep a spare (if slim) battery, extra SD cards, etc. The formed pocket is lined with a soft mesh fabric, which is breathable and soft enough not to mar or scratch your camcorder. There is a little bit of room at the very bottom of the case, which may accommodate a thicker battery if yours does not work well in the inner side pocket, perhaps a USB cable, and even a charger if it is no larger than 1" in height and with a 5" x 2.5" footprint. The user's manual might fit in the bottom too, or up against the side opposite the one that opens.

The zipper is heavy duty and is the standard 2-zipper (with zipper pulls) type of opening. A detachable shoulder strap is provided, as well as an integrated belt loop (side opposite from the one that zips open) and carrying handle. The ends of the handle are what the shoulder strap attaches to, so when the shoulder strap is used, the handle pulls tight to the top of the case. Pretty cool design. The 2 sides of the outer shell are a textured black rubberized material, and the center portion is black nylon. A black toned Case Logic logo is located on the side that opens.

In use, I found the Compact Camcorder Case to be well made, of high quality materials, and durable. It was easy to access my camcorder, and the camcorder was well protected while in the case.

Here are some specific Pros and Cons:

Pros:

Quality materials: soft lining, formed sides, rugged zippers all speak to the good quality of the materials used in the case.

Protective design: the rugged, formed sides offer good protection for the contents, especially when the bag might bounce or bang around as you are sightseeing, or get squeezed into larger luggage. The stiffness of the sides helps disperse any pressure applied to the case from other objects.

Compact: this is not the case for carrying every accessory ever invented for your camcorder, not for large camcorders. It is compact for those occasions when you want good protection with minimal space usage.

Understated: black all around, except the pocket lining on the inside, which is a turquoise blue. No bright logos that scream: EXPENSIVE CAMCORDER INSIDE!!! Many travel sites advise using understated designs such as this to not attract thieves while traveling.

Handle pulls tight to the case when shoulder strap is used: this is a pretty cool feature that makes the case a little less "grabbable" by someone that shouldn't be grabbing your stuff.

Good value: the case is not expensive and being a smart design and made of durable materials, provides a good value.

Great warranty: Case Logic usually provides a generous warranty on their products, and this one is no exception. Twenty-five years. That's a statement about their confidence in their products, right there.

Cons:

Can't find any.

Bottom Line:

If you need a compact, well-made, low-key case for a small camcorder, then I recommend this one. Case Logic has been making cases for a long time, and they really do come up with designs that are smart and logical, and are backed by long warranties.

title: Wonderful TV
text:
I recently purchased the SONY KDL-40W600B TV and BDP-S3200 Blu-Ray player. I'm very happy with both and give them both five stars.

The TV assembles very easily, with a bent metal stand that is simple and not wobbly.

The feature set is very impressive for both devices. The remote for each device has buttons that control the essential features of the other device.

Immediately after turning the system on and logging both devices onto my home Wi-Fi, both devices looked for updates and installed them.

TV picture quality is wonderful.

I was surprised by a few things, however.

One surprise: Judging by the specs for the two devices, the streaming capabilities seemed to be identical. I assumed that they would have very similar user interfaces for the streaming features, maybe to the point of being a little redundant. But in fact, the interfaces for the streaming features are very different.

One big difference is that Amazon Prime works on the BDP-S3200 Blu-Ray player, but not on the KDL-40W600B TV. I assume that at some point SONY will issue an update that activates the Amazon Prime app on the TV. But for now, I'm very glad that I have the Blu-Ray player to access Amazon Prime.

Another big difference is that the BDP-S3200 Blu-ray player has a web browser, while the KDL-40W600B TV does not. This sounds like a big deal, but in fact the web browser on the Blu-ray player is so clunky that I don't care to use it. I am not surprised by that: sometimes it seems like all the reviews that I have read of streaming TVs either (a) complain that they have no browser or (b) complain although they do have a browser, it is useless. (One really needs good apps to access online content, and the KDL-40W600b has lots and lots of apps. For instance, I have been amazed at how well the YouTube app works.)

Another big difference in the interfaces for the two devices is in the way that they access the media files on my networked home computer. The Blu-Ray player displays the folder tree structure, making it easy to navigate to the files that I want. The TV displays the folders in a big matrix, making it very difficult to find folders.

But that difference is moot, really. The truth is that neither device is very handy for browsing the media files on my home computer, and the truth is that it doesn't matter. The reason it does not matter is that it is extremely easy to browse the media files using a computer, and then just play the media to the TV. That is, I commonly use Windows Media player on a laptop in my kitchen to browse through my music collection that is stored on a computer in my office. The browsing is very fast. When I find the album that I want to play, I just tell Windows Media Player to play it to the SONY TV. The TV turns on automatically, and the sound comes out through the nice self-powered Boston Acoustics speaker system that I have attached to the TV.

Another surprise: There is a significant difference in ergonomics of the remotes. The remote for the blu-ray player has four large arrow buttons around a center select button. It is very easy to use those arrow buttons, even in the dark. The remote for the TV is a little annoying because the four arrow buttons are not so large, and they are surrounded by an outer ring of buttons that have other functions related to the smart features. Sitting in the dark with my big thumbs, it is easy to press one of the outer buttons when I meant to press an arrow key. This sends the TV off to someplace that I didn't want to go, which is a nuisance. FAIL.

But regardless of the little gripes that I have about some details of the streaming features or the remotes, the big conclusion is that I really love both these devices and would highly recommend them both.

I look forward to adding a SONY home theater receiver to my system in coming months, so that I can use my larger Hi-Fi speakers.

title: Great Camera, Poor HP Support
text:
I bought this to be a "happy-snapper" to keep at my holiday home. It turned out to be a much better camera than that, and I now carry it with me all the time. Both the optics and software are as good, or maybe better than my many times more expensive Canon DSLRs.

Other reviewers complained about the crowd of buttons and switches on the right hand side of the top and back of the camera. It's true that it takes a while learning how to hold the camera without unintentionally changing modes or even turning it off, but eventually even the congenitally clumsy like myself can learn the way.

Only one thing keeps this from being a 5-star: even after downloading and reading the complete User's Manual from Hewlett Packard, I still had problems downloading pictures directly from the camera (i.e. downloading with the SD card installed in the camera, rather than popping out the SD card and downloading it directly). This section of the manual is skimpy and contains a couple of other obvious errors, so I concluded that the problem was not with the camera but the procedure.

I contacted HP Technical Support by email, and received an automated response promising an answer in 24 hours. After a week with no further reply, I contacted the retailer who gave me a telephone number for HP technical support. I called that number and, after the usual long hold got an operator who gave me a different phone number to call. I called that number and, after a maze of robo-support options, reached another operator who told me that "We don't support that camera!".

It is a good camera, I got it for a good price from this vendor, and both they and Amazon have treated me well over the years, so I'm going to keep it. But, if it ever goes wrong, I won't be expecting too much help from the manufacturer.

title: The box works great except it seems to not work with soundbar's
text:
I received my Fire TV a couple of days ago and the install and setup went smooth and was very simple.

When the box started up it walks you through setting up your network and required an update which took a few min to do.
It plays a start up video for the first time which is annoying because there is no skip for the video. Power cycle just restarts the video and if you do a factory reset you have to watch it all over again.
It already had all my Prime account info loaded so it connected directly with Amazon which made it nice to see the prime movies without having to register the box or do a setup.

I like the prime display that shows in the upper left hand corner what is on Prime and what is not. It makes it easy to see what I get with my service for free unlike my other player I have to look into each movie to see what is Prime.

One major problem is that it appears that the Fire TV will not work with a sound bar. This is a big let down since 3 of my TV's have sound bars and this box will not work with any of them. I called support and their resolution was to plug it directly into my TV which did work but it didn't solve the problem.

I was able to get it working with my sound bar by using the optical cable connection from the Fire TV to my sound bar and connecting the HDMI directly to my TV and it works as expected. This poses a problem because it requires me to change the TV input anytime I want to watch the Fire TV.

I am now on the fence if I should buy any more of these. If you are okay with using your TV sound or using the optical connection to your sound bar and HDMI into your TV then I would recommend this box. If you don't want to go through all that then look at the Roku 3.

title: Excellent Replacement in the Front Doors of a 96 Ford Explorer EXT (not rear).
text:
These speakers are a true 6x8, not a 5x7 with with frame mounting for a 6x8 application.

Love the fact that they had a factory installed gasket on the back side of the frame for proper sealing.

Very, very beefy speaker from top to bottom, heavy (large) magnet and had no issues with the tweeter mounting configuration rubbing or pressing against the door panel grill. (like others has said, but in other vehicles)

THEY WILL NOT FIT IN THE REAR DOORS OF A 96 EXPLORER EXT. (speaker depth is the issue, more than 1/4" of clearance issues, so wanting to obtain a factory appearance, I decided NOT to build spacer plates which would have created a press on the oem door panel grill) I went with the Rockford P1683 in the rear doors - fit perfect without modification of any kind.

I am running these T1682 in the front doors and the P1683 in the rear doors, paralleled on channels 1 and 2 of a Precision Power PC450 amplifier - which is around 75 watts per channel under a 2 ohm load.

They are handling the power just fine with some fine tuning of the head unit and the active high pass crossover that the PC450 has.

I am very happy.

I was really excited to buy this product. The ads on TV and on the Amazon site show a clearly superior product. It is BEYOND annoying to see the LED lights at the bottom of the screen. Only in pure daylight is the screen truly paper white. In any other kind of lighting or if you try to read in bed, the dark shadows at the bottom of the screen (and they are very DISTINCT) make this product less than the promised ad - and name implies: Paper White.

If you dig deeper on Amazon's site and follow the links that explain the screen further you are taken to a page that shows these shadows and the suggestion is made that you do not see them as much if you do not use the Paper White with the light at its brightest in a dark room. The whole purpose for me to buy it was to read in bed - and not have my husband kept awake by a light. The ad above shows you being able to do that - and it shows an evenly lit screen. If you look at their examples on the links to explain the screen you can clearly see that this is an issue - they try to explain it away by saying it is not in the area where type is.

I called Amazon and they gladly sent me another one and then said that all of them were not the same and some were actually worse in this regard! They sent me another and they were right - it was worse. They offered to send me another and I said, "no thank you". I would rather wait until they solved this problem in version three or four than settle for this.

title: Awesome!
text:
I love these large, commercial power bars, and this one is my favorite so far. I also own a generic one I got at home depot, and one from a company called Prime that I picked up at Orchard Supply Hardware, but this [[ASIN:B000051174 Tripp Lite PS4816 16-Outlet Power Strip 15-Amp, 15-Foot Cord]] is by far the coolest.

1) Tons of outlets. 16 on a single strip! I'm a huge computer nerd, running a full tower, three displays, five gazillion external drives & various and sundry accessories.

2) More organized cords! Endlessly chaining traditional power strips together is both tiresome and unsightly. This keeps everything on a single strip.

3) Mountable. I see from other reviewers that some don't receive mounting hardware, but I did and it works great. I screwed mine into the underside of my desk surface, and it really helps to hide the clutter and makes it easier to clean the floor.

4) Very tight sockets. This is actually an advantage. Since my strip is mounted under the surface of the desk, power cords, bricks, etc., some of them quite heavy, are all dangling from the bar. The tight fit of the sockets holds them lock-solid.

5) Well constructed. It feels like a quality piece of hardware. The power switch is inside a flip-cap that prevents you from accidentally bumping it off. The cord is heavy - feeling more like a quality power tool than a regular extension cord.

There's only one thing I would change. I wish the individual sockets were rotated 90°. It would be a bit non-standard, but the advantage would be that most power bricks would stick out to the side rather than block the adjacent socket. (If you get a strip with fewer sockets, you'd probably have enough space between each that it wouldn't matter so much.)

I paired this strip with a product from Ikea called "signum," and it keeps all my cables tucked tightly under the rear surface of my desk, with nothing dangling on the floor or down the wall.

This setup works so well, I got a second one for my girlfriend and she's out posting pictures of it all over the web.

title: It works!
text:
As a Ham Radio operator...I build my own antennas...including my own TV antennas. Even though I had been using flat HDTV antennas I've built out of cardboard and aluminum foil and worked when I lived less than 10 miles from the towers on the other side of town...I was not able to get hardly any channels to feed my TV and TV tuners. Even tried two soda cans screwed to a 75-300 ohm balun which gave me a signal which was unstable at the best and totally unwatchable at the worst.

With the new TV season coming up...wanted to try something better than what I have tried. Was originally going to purchase the Mohu model just like this...but the reviews mentioned this one was just like it...only cheaper...so I bought it. When I hooked it to my distribution amp and fed it to my two dual TV tuners and my TV...there were only three stations I could not pick up. Was even able to pick up signals I never knew about...even when I was living less than 10 miles from the towers. Even tvfool.com and the NAB site said I couldn't list all of the channels I am picking up with this antenna. I believe the second site listed 3-5 channels total...IF I had an outside antenna.

With it hanging upside down in the window behind the blinds on the second floor in my bedroom...due to living in an HOA...was able to pick up 27 of the 30 channels available. Was it worth the cost...OH YEAH!

title: MSP19U - Great Alternative to the Expensive Wacom Cintiq!
text:
As a digital artist, I have been drooling over the Wacom Cintiqs, but could never afford the high price tag. Until recently, there didn't seem to be any alternatives, either. Then a friend told me about the Yiynova interactive pen tablets and I had to check them out. I recently purchased the MSP19U and I couldn't be happier! The monitor's colors are great and the pen works fluidly in applications like Photoshop. I even have tested it with 3D sculpting in programs like ZBrush and modo! I noticed no visible lag and no jitters. Drawing digitally has never been more natural (or more fun)! I can highly recommend this product to anyone looking to create art digitally!

The Panda City, the distributor for the United States, is great to work with, too. They have responded promptly to my emails and answered any questions I have asked. A great product and great support at a reasonable price? Who could ask for me?

If you have used a Cintiq, there are a few things to note about the MSP19U: It does not have customizable buttons on the actual display like the Cintiq does. The stand does not detach or rotate (like the stand on the previous Cintiq did), but since canvas rotation is a keyboard shortcut in Photoshop, this was a non-issue for me. Also, the Yiynova pen does not have an eraser end. This is a feature I never used when I was using a Cintiq, so it's a non-issue for me as well.

The screen resolution is odd: 1444 x 900, but I don't notice when painting using the MSP19U. It looks great, works great, and so I am very happy with my purchase.

title: AWESOME LAPTOP
text: I have used the Toshiba Qosmio x775 3dv80 for 6 months already and I have to say its one of the best laptops I have used. While I could have bought a simpler and less exempsive laptop, the toshiba qosmio was worth every dollar. Not only are the graphics amazing, but so is the sound! I often blast the speakers to its maximum and its incredible how lound and crisp the sound is. Also, the speed of the computer is something to also note. It starts up relatively fast and using photoshop and lightroom with it is a breeze. However before buying this laptop you should now that this is a desktop replacement, so I would not buy it if you are looking for a thin and long lasting battery in your laptop. The computer itself weighs around 7 pounds but its charger is the size of a brick! If you are carrying it in a backpack or a bag it should weigh around 10 pounds (HORRIBLE FOR YOUR BACK). But however, this computer has the power of a desktop but its in a more portable form. Also you should know that this laptop must be placed on a solid surface. While you think that this multimedia laptop will tackle all of its task, you are correct, however the computer is at its max power and it releases really hot air through its vents on the side. Also the brick charger which I had mentioned before gets just as hot, so be careful and leave it somewhere safe. Once I was watching a blue-ray movie with my dad and I started to feel the hot air on my lap. I highly recommend leaving it on your desk or table. Also, be extremely careful when you are charging the laptop. The charger which you connect on the side of the laptop, doesn't stay in very well, so if someone happened to walk by and you had removed your battery for some reason, the computer will shut off right there. This has happened to me around 12 times already, the charger/plug is a true pain, this is something to note about all qosmio x775 laptops! Also you should know that the webcam is very poor. If you were looking to take lots of pictures with your laptop for some reason, I would not purchases this laptop. Although you would think that Toshiba will put a full hd camera for their two webcams, the pictures come out very grayish and very pixelish. Recording videos is the same thing, the image quality is poor but the microphone is actually impecable so at least you will be able to hear what you record. In additon you should not get this laptop if you are looking for a long battery life, since you barely get 2.5 hours on the lowest setting! Besides all the negatives I have listed, this machine is actually amazing. You should classify it as a desktop replacement not a portable video-gaming laptop!

title: Good Receiver for the Price
text:
I have purchase Onkyo TX-NR509 2 months ago and I am satisfied with its overall performance.

Pros:
- I did not like how Audyssey set up the system but I have manually adjusted the settings and the movies and the music sounds good. Receiver's manual is great to explain how to set up the system.
- The internet features are great. I usually listen to Pandora, last.fm and slacker radio on the internet. Even better is the vtuner radio. With this, I can listen to any radio from any part of the world if they have a stream over the internet. Having access to BBC radios over the receiver is great.
- I like the Onkyo remote. I can control my TV, XBox and blu-ray player with the remote, it eliminated the need for a universal remote for me.
- The android remote app is very useful to do basic tasks conveniently such as changing the center speaker level, bass level or browsing through internet radios. It also lets you to stream music from your android device to the receiver (airplay without a fancy name).
- It plays lossless audio (flac) and sounds great.

Cons: (Perhaps these are mostly due to the fact that this is a basic, entry level receiver)
- I wish there was custom equalizers in the system. It only allows you to change bass and treble manually. You need to use Audyssey Dynamic EQ (whatever they give you with that). So, most configuration is on speaker levels.
- I rarely see flickering issues with XBox 360. (I should add a few notes here before blaming the receiver: I power 130 w @ 6 ohm speakers with this, so I think it runs a bit hot and I only see that problem when I play games for long times. I did not try to change the HDMI cable yet to see if it will solve the problem. I've never seen this problem with the blu-ray player though).
- I use the Onkyo wifi dongle for the internet connection. It has only one usb port and it is occupied by the dongle. When I need to hook up a usb drive, I lose the internet connection (I don't have an ethernet connection near the receiver). Although the wifi is stable for the internet radios and for streaming mp3 files, it has troubles streaming larger size files (such as flac). It constantly keeps pausing and buffering if you stream flac files over DLNA.
- The UI of the receiver on TV is a basic and if there is some moving element on its UI, you will see static white lines on your screen. Not a major problem but annoying. I switch to a static page while listening to internet radio to eliminate this problem.

I would have rated it 3.5/5, so I am making it a 4/5.

title: Good for some things
text:
This keyboard case, according to the box, is made of water-repellent materials and and is "amazingly" thin and light. I'm in no hurry to test the water-repelling capabilities of the case and am inclined to take their word for that. I suppose that it's reasonably thin and light, but after buying a shiny new iPad Air, it's a bit sad to put it inside a case that makes it feel pretty much like my old first-gen iPad. The good news is that it's quite easy to remove the case, so I can get the "air" feeling back when I want to. Here's some more information about my experience with this keyboard case, starting with some good points which are followed by some not-so-good points.

Good:

The case holds the iPad Air securely with clips on the top edge of the iPad and magnets on the bottom edge. I know someone who has another kind of Logitech case that simply has a slot to hold the iPad. On that other case, the iPad has fallen out several times while he was holding it in his lap on a bus. With this case, the iPad is not likely to fall unless the whole case falls with it.

It's quite easy to put the iPad in the case and take it out again. The way you put the iPad in is to wedge it in between two corners. It takes a few seconds to put it in or take it out. If I want to use the iPad without the keyboard for a few minutes, say five minutes or less, I would just fold the keyboard around and out of the way, but if I'm going to use it without the keyboard for five minutes or more I would remove it from the case.

Not so good:

The keyboard takes some getting used to. The caps lock key is combined with the A key and the tab key is combined with the Q key, so you have to press the function key first if you want to use caps lock or tab. Because there aren't a separate keys for caps lock and tab, I find myself putting my left hand too far to the right, which is more annoying than having to press the function key to use caps lock or tab. Also, the left shift key is smaller than usual, which also throws off my typing sometimes.

Another annoyance for me is the fact that the control key is to the right of the space key rather than to the left. Perhaps Emacs users are the only people in the world who use the control key on a regular basis, but they do, and I doubt that there is any large group of people that use a function key as a routine part of typing. If they would have swapped the control key and the function key it would have made me and other Emacs users happy without making anyone unhappy.

Neither here nor there (yet):

The documentation says that the battery can last up to three months but should be charged once a month. I haven't the chance to test that.

There are a number of iOS-specific function keys, like a Home key, pause, play, and volume keys, and so on. I suppose those are useful, but I haven't found much reason for using them. I'm good with using the usual buttons or controls on the touch screen.

Summary

As cases go, it protects the screen without being too bulky. The fabric has a reasonably nice feel to it.

The bottom line is that although this keyboard has full-sized keys, it is not a full keyboard like my Apple Bluetooth keyboard or my friend's keyboard (which is also a Logitech keyboard). It won't work for me to use to connect to a server via ssh and edit files. On the other hand, for typing notes, email messages, calendar items, and Google Plus posts, it works well.

title: Good Case
text:
I have all manner of tablet devices. Ipad 4th generation, iPad mini, Samsung Galaxy Note 10.1, Kindle HD 8.9, iPhone 5, etc. I am a snob regarding cases. I will personally go through 2-3 cases before I find one that fits my needs and style. For the iPad mini, there are not many options yet. While the Belkin case leaves some things to be desired, it works well for my personal situation.

I work primarily on flat serfaces. I take notes a lot in various meetings, nd I use it to teach (I am a Youth Pastor). It still allows the ipad to fit comfortably in my hand but gives me fast access to a keyboard when needed. I was not looking for the same level of use as I get from my ZaggKeys for the iPad 4 where I might be typing for an hour +. I wanted a case that makes it convenient to type and didn't add a lot of bulk. I was as concerned with overall protection, but I did want a good quality product.

The keys, and surrounding plastic do rub up against the screen when closed. I have a screen cover on my iPad so this is no concern to me. It might be for you, though. When the keyboard is in use, you need to fold down the flap that covers the back of the iPad itselv and fold a piece under so it creates a way for the ipad to stand up and be angled. This setup is great on paper, but if you need to touch the screen a lot, you will see that there is a lot of "wiggle." This doesn't bother me, but I also don't mind holding the ipad with one hand while I tap with the other, then go back to typing. You do not want to put this on a very slipery surface as the mechanics that hold up the ipad at an angle require some resistance on the table or it will simply slide out from the weight of the iPad.

Like I said. For my purposes it works good. It's merely a way to have easier access to typing when I need it. Most of my time is spent holding and tapping right on the screen. If you need to do a LOT of typing, this may not be for your. The keyboard itself is a bit small but I have already gotten used to it and I have big hands.

title: Serious protection for your ASUS tablet
text:

Once you apply it to your tablet the look and feel are dramatically different. The mesh on the back looks like body armor, I got several questions from friends when they saw it.

I am also posting some pictures of the precision of the cut. This fits like a glove for the tablet. I purchased a similar product for my wife's iPad and it did NOT have this type of precision cut. If you own this tablet and carry it around with you, I highly recommend the MilitaryShield cover.

A couple of tips for those new to putting on these types of protectors.

Don't do both on a single night. The front screen needs the solution (it is a wet application). Getting that solution under the back will prevent it from sticking. So I recommend you do the screen protector one night before going to bed. The screen needs to dry before you can really use (on my device the touch screen was really confused with that water under the sheet).

When applying the back start on one side. Look at their YouTube videos for good techniques. I also use a hair dryer on the corners and edges. You put the hair dryer on low and lay it on a cabinet. Then I take the device and apply gentle pressure while the hair dryer is blowing on that same surface. Do this 15-20 seconds at a time on each side and you are done.

text:
Having the best phone (as of the date of this review) on the best network (love or hate Verizon, no one can deny that the coverage is just there when and where you need it) with an unlimited data plan means that productivity will always be had with this device. Coming from the Note 2 (which I had for a couple of months before I sold it to someone coming from a HTC Thunderbolt...suffice it to say he loves life too), the FULL HD (1920x1080--1080p on this device!!), improved S-Pen, improved S-Voice (it's cute, but I would rather use Google Voice Search), what isn't there to love about this phone.

Yes, there are people who will cry about the size. To those I say, the market is dictating that cell phone makers go big, or go home. I have big hands, and I can tell you that it feels good to have something in my hand(s) that won't feel like it'll break. Cell phone quality is excellent, the build is more sturdier than the Note 2 (there were people crying about a loose home button, but that wasn't in mine. I buy that defects could happen, but those are exceptions, not rules in regard to the Note 3.) My phone is currently awaiting a wallet case that experienced problems, but right now is housed in a Ventev case (which I reviewed) and a Spigen Ultra Crystal screen protector (full screen and I'll review that too, but BUY IT!! Really protects the phone!!!) Surfing the web, reading e-mail, streaming music from Google Play on High and no cache (because I got unlimited data... :D), the phone does it all with such speed.

But the best part I love that beats the Note 2 hands down?! Battery Life!!! I have had this thing for a week and so far, the battery last a good day and half to 2 days before I even see a low percent. I have not used the MicroUSB 3.0 cable that came with the Note 3, because honestly, the million and one USB chargers with 2.0 cable do a great job charging my phone. All I would have done was open up yet one more USB cable, so I have left that in the box.

Bottom line, buy this phone!! It is the best phone on the market AND it will be well over a year before this phone becomes "old" Full HD, MicroUSB 3.0, 3 GB of RAM, 32 GB internal space (coupled with the 32GB I stuck in there from my Droid Charge...) and much, much more. I could have written a more technical review, but you want to know how my experience is overall, and I'm telling you...I have never been so happy to early adopt a device. I hardly EVER do it, but I am glad I did. You will too!!

title: A good but flawed attempt from Belkin
text:
I'm the "Tech Daddy" on the Huffington Post, and I really wanted to like this device -- really! I'd been tracking it since it was first announced a little less than 2 years ago. At one time I chalked it up to vaporware, as the release date kept changing. But finally it was here and I couldn't wait to order it.

After all that anticipation, I'm sorry to say the device is is less than stellar, for the following reasons:

1. YOU CANNOT BOOT FROM IT -- nowhere online or in any print materials does Belkin mention this. Even on their own website they don't bring it up! BTW, there is no manual for the device; only an FAQ, and it's pretty paltry. Anyway, I had backed up a client's Mac to their new USB 3 external drive, and I used the Dock to connect that drive as their MacBook Pro doesn't have USB 3 ports. But it DOES have Thunderbolt! Using the Dock, the backup speeds were very impressive, indeed. HOWEVER ... I found that I could not boot from that drive, or any connected device, because they weren't recognized at startup. Bad Belkin!

2. THE ESATA PORT IS GONE -- originally the device as described by Belkin was going to have an eSata port. But when I unboxed the product, there was none to be found. I since learned that Belkin revised the device TWICE since its original announcement, and decided to drop the eSata port. That was one of the main reasons I wanted it: to use the eSata ports on my external drives. I did manage a workaround, though: I got a $30 eSata to USB3 cable and did it that way.

3. USB3 SPEED IS LIMITED TO 2.5GB/S -- the promise of unleashing full 5GB/S USB3 speed will have to wait for another day. For whatever reason, Belkin very quietly, and in small print, says 2.5GB/S is the maximum using the Dock. Really?

4. YOU MUST USE OS X 10.8.4 FOR THE DOCK TO FUNCTION ON A MAC -- not a huge problem, except when I tried to backup my client's drive from their Mac running OS X 10.7.5. The idea was to back it up, then completely reformat the machine for a new user. Instead I had to waste 20 minutes updating the system to 10.8.4 before I could start the backup. I *think* I still saved time overall, but not that much.

As for what some others have complained about -- flaky behavior or devices disappearing off the desktop -- I didn't see any of that. However, the caveats I just listed are enough for me to send it back and wait for Sonnet's even MORE expensive, but also WAY more juicy Echo 15 with 15 -- count 'em -- 15 ports! The Echo 15 will not only feature bootability and eSata, but a built-in DVD or Blu-Ray drive AND a traditional or SSD drive as well. For what I'm looking for, that'll be a lot better I'm sure.

title: Dialog enhancer technology is fantastic, but have realistic expectations
text:
I disdain speaker wires. Those awful, winding things that end up seemingly everywhere. I likewise loathe the space rugs and makeshift solutions to hide the darn things as to eliminate the eyesore that my quest for surround sound unleashed.

Due to said angry sentiments, I ended up a SoundMatters devotee, an outstanding virtual surround sound system from a company that backed its products up x1000. It's good that they did, as I went through multiple units due to power board and/or speaker failures. Almost like clockwork and every 6 months, I was sending in my semi-expensive SoundMatters device back to the Company for a repair or paid upgrade.

SoundMatters outpriced me and eventually transitioned their business model. I eventually ended up with a decent Sharp Soundbar, inputs limited to RCA cables. I've got no beef with this ridiculously affordable soundbar, but - in exception to better upper range clarity - it was only a small improvement over Sony Bravia TV speaker range.

My friends, the ZVOX 555 brings the joy back. Build quality (huzzah for real wood!) on these are fantastic, price point awesome (even more so for the refurb, direct from manufacturer units = $100 less and look brand new), low profile sneaky classy. It's not that my Vizio speakers were 'bad,' they simply didn't discern sound type. To be frank, it literally took the money back guarantee to take the ZVOX plunge since there wasn't a glaring sound issue to address.

Clearly I was suffering from sound-based, Stockholm Syndrome, because - whew - the ZVOX is a master at separating distinct sound elements. Even on lower volumes, the dialog enhancer is a wunderkind at bringing crisp audio elements across a room and beyond. I was missing tons of audio on sports and movie programming, I discovered. The technology is so good, that hearing sports play-by-play is a breeze even in the next room, while cooking and fans whirring.

With this being said, the ZVOX 550 doesn't even pretend to offer virtual surround sound. There's no ear gymnastics - ala the Bose Wave Radio - of tricking one into thinking the audio surrounds them. This unit does one thing...and does it well: bring out individualistic sound elements in brilliant fashion, housed in an affordable, well built package. Thus, if you're looking for something more substantial in immersion, the ZVOX 550 is unfortunately not the path to travel.

Energy wise - and mirroring soundbars - the ZVOX 550 drops into standby mode when not in use. It awakens from slumber with a simple volume button press and/or manual power on. Related and worth noting, a learning remote [[ASIN:B001KC08A4 URC WR7 Universal Remote Control for up to 7 A/V Components with 4 Favorite Channel Buttons]] is a nice accompaniment to this device. ZVOX codes are hard to come by, but easily remedied with manual learning functions.

title: Pricey, but Excellent Quality and Worthwhile for Amazon.com Support

The reason I chose an Amazon case over all 3rd party cases is their unbelievable support team. Two years ago when I had a kindle keyboard, my $35 Amazon case was recalled. I pre-ordered the persimmon colored case the day it came out. Several weeks later, my estimated shipping date was pushed back by two weeks. After live chatting Amazon, they casually upgraded me to 1 day shipping - and the case ended up being shipped on its original date!

PROS:
Auto wake-up feature is fantastic. The screen lights-up upon opening the case, greeting you in preparation for your reading. This makes it so you don't have to use the slightly-awkward positioned power button.
Form fit is great. Unlike Kindle Keyboard Cases, this case is manufactured perfectly without the use of hinges. No worries of the kindle potentially falling out.
Sylish - I personally love the real leather and inside cloth-like look of the case. The persimmon color is bright but not gaudy.
There are no distractions - such as straps holding the kindle in place.

CONS:
Price. I personally think that $30 would've been a much more fair price, seeing as how all of the third-party cases are in the $10-25 range. That being said, you'll never have to buy another paperwhite case.
Although it may seem difficult to remove the Kindle from its case, just follow the advice in the comment section below. It works wonders :)

OVERALL:
The auto-wakeup feature and tight fit of the kindle far outweigh the cons of having a high price and not being able to easily remove the e-reader. Amazon.com support is just too good to pass up.

title: Incredible sound and an overload of accessories
text:
When I first received the box for the Logitech UE 900 Noise-Isolating Headphones, I thought I must have been sent the wrong item due to the size and weight of the package. The packaging immediately lets you know you've got a high quality item, a step up from my last pair, UE700.

As you can tell from the product page, you get a lot of options with these headphones!
Two sets of cables: one for normal use (black) and one with a mic, phone/audio controls and a clip (blue). The earbuds themselves are interchangeable which is something I'd never seen before. And to be honest, I'm always a little worried one of them will fall off when I'm not paying attention, but that's why you have...

A very solid carrying case with pegs for a spare pair of ear cushions and a ¼-inch adapter jack (also something new to me for this type of product)

An airplane adapter which is supposed to reduce the sudden volume change from onboard announcements (can't wait to try this!)

I'd never had bendable over-the-ear headphones before so this took some getting used to. But it's definitely worth the effort to get them in the correct shape over your ear so they give the best sound possible. Because the cables are bendable, you can also wear them normally without putting them over your ear but you can lose some sound quality and they don't stay in as well.

Another thing that took some getting used to was the texture of the audio cable. It's sort of braided and initially had a rough feel to it because I'm more accustomed to regular, smooth cables. But that's really a minor thing.

Overall, if you're looking for an amazing pair of over the ear headphones that you can adjust to your comfort, I can't imagine there's anything better out there.

title: Nikon quality control lags, thank you Amazon for accepting returns!
text: I was very excited about this lens and I wanted to complement my  Nikon and Tamron lens selection with this wide angle to telephoto lens. For $1,000 invested in this lens I was happy with the general quality of photos though  the sharpness of portrait photos at maximum aperture f3.5 70mm zoom is inferior to the Tamron 24-70 f2.8 at 70mm . Also heavy vignetting in all corners.  Then as I was enlarging a photo to frame a detail, I noticed three spots on the photos upper left corner. I then reviewed all my photos taken with other lenses and did not see the spots. I removed the lenses and photographed a white sheet of paper to see if camera had spots on sensor: no spots. I then re-attached this lens and photographed a white sheet of paper: voila! at 33% magnification you could pick three clear spots up!  So definitely a lens problem. I understand that we all have our bad days and Nikon probably does too. I would forgive spots escaping detection on mass produced APC cameras which are cheaper by half for comparable FX focal length. But when the cost of a lens is $1,000 or higher as for this item, Nikon should have a better quality control system. Amazon is fabulous as always in allowing return no problems. I have requested same lens and will update this post after I receive the new one and test it.

title: Nice camera but it leaked
text:
We got this camera just prior to a trip to Hawaii. The camera is about typical for ease of use, and we got some good photos from it. The video quality was better than expected, particularly the "anti shake". It was very impressive video for a small camera!

The issue was when we took it snorkeling. We followed the instructions, and also did a test in fresh water in the sink and it did fine. So, we took it on a boat trip to a snorkeling site. It was in the water for about an hour, mostly just surface snorkeling, but a few surface dives down to about 10 ft depth. The camera was rated to 40 ft depth, so I figured that 10 ft should be fine.

Well, it wasn't. We got it back to shore, rinsed it in fresh water, allowed it to drain and dry, then opened it. It was wet inside the door. The next day it was not working. So, we returned it to Amazon for a refund (which was processed immediately with no problems).

The good news is that the photos and video from the snorkeling survived just fine, and we got some really good video of a sea turtle. If you do get this camera, note that it has a "beach and snorkeling" mode, and an "underwater" mode. The main difference is the color balance. Even if you are just snorkeling on the surface, try the "underwater" mode. We much preferred the color in those images.

Other people have posted similar leaking problems here, and if you look at other, similar cameras, they all seem to have some problems. Maybe they should all be called "splashproof" or something!

Anyway, I give the camera a low score because it leaked, but not a single star, because it did a good job while it did work!

text:

But these headphones are ridiculously quiet (wired) and even worse so when connected through Bluetooth. When I have them wired and cranked all the way up, I feel like they are only half as loud as they should be. Bluetooth on them is practically pointless. They are so quiet that I started wondering if there may be something wrong with them, but after reading through a few other reviews this seems to be the norm.
After having listened to these, I would only be willing to pay in the $100-$125 range. For the amount spent on these, you could get a lower end version of Beats or Bose (my father has a pair of older Bose headphones that go over the ear but don't completely cover them and they sound much better). Being the type of person I am, I figured these may have been a better deal since they aren't one of the bigger fads out there right now but I was wrong.

I am a commuter in a busy metropolitan area and so any cover I have needs to make it through day to day travel, and packing in and out of my back pack or hand bag. Be careful if you pop it in your purse, back pack or brief case. Anything can slide in and scratch your screen. The flimsiness of the spine is also a concern. By the end of the month, it seems like it was twisting around a bit. This spine is made of a different material than the back and front covers. I think it's just heavier plastic and easily breaks with too much handling. Since I commute and take this Kindle everywhere, it started looking a little loose. SO, it will remain my emergency cover if the other more sturdy cover has to be replaced. It has its usefulness. None are really worth more than say 7 or 8 bucks, which is what they cost to make probably. title: Missed the photos of a lifetime
text:
I purchased the Nikon V1, plus the 30-110mm lens, and flash two months before a trip out of the country. As I knew that I would be hiking now and then, I wanted something smaller and lighter than my DSLR, but not a point and shoot. The first month and a half of pictures taken before the vacation were beautiful and clearly in focus - even fast moving children and pets. I was thrilled. I've used Canon cameras for 35 years and the difference was amazing. However, after shooting a children's musical performance (not video, but still) for about half an hour, I noticed the camera was heating up and feeling very hot in my hands. It was determined that the battery was NOT one of the recalled ones and that my camera was fine. Returning it to Nikon would have taken too long, as now my trip was two weeks away.
I took it on the trip (with some fear) and after viewing the nearly 1,800 photos, I realized that I have missed many photos of a lifetime. Three-fourths of the photos are out-of-focus. Although it was cool weather, the camera continued to heat up and I once got a message on the screen that the camera's "internal temperature was too high and the camera would shut off momentarily." After waiting a few minutes and missing some fabulous pictures, it came back on. I have tried many different exposures, focus settings, auto-focus, etc. and have determined that no matter what the setting, as soon as the camera starts to heat up, the pictures will be out of focus. I am returning it to Nikon. Maybe I have a lemon, but after spending $1,600 on the camera, lenses, flash, filters, and mount-adapter, I am clearly disappointed. I could have taken better pictures with my iPhone!

[[VIDEOID:68ced429ab125c20c622d86d2c5ea272]] Optically, this lens is considered identical to [[ASIN:B002IKLJVE its predecessor]], so read those reviews to learn about image quality. The only real difference is that this new version uses more metal and less plastic, which makes it a bit smaller but heavier (it's still very light). And it's available in silver.

The video review is shot through this lens. It doesn't have much except a demonstration of focus speed and noise, and a few sample photographs (Amazon never published the photo I uploaded, maybe because it wasn't a photo of the product).

There were basically only two complaints ever made about [[ASIN:B002IKLJVE the previous model]]: (1) focusing was noisy and slow, and (2) noise banding in the shadows on Olympus bodies. I can't speak to the second because I only have a Panasonic body (G6). As for the first, I can only say that focusing is definitely louder and slower than my kit lens (the new version of the 14-42mm zoom), but I probably wouldn't have even noticed the noise if I wasn't specifically looking for it. It seems pretty quiet to me, a relative beginner. Recording video using the built-in microphones on the G6, there is a tiny bit of noise captured, but I barely notice it (I'll demonstrate in a video review). I would use a separate audio recorder if I was going for maximum quality anyway.

Panasonic's official but unstated position seems to be that this lens doesn't need a hood. Panasonic doesn't make one that fits on it, nor is there any way to attach one aside from the filter threads. I went ahead and got a cheap screw-in one, but so far I haven't been able to tell the difference.

title: if you are gamer or if you need high compute power, this is it!
text:
This machine is a true powerhouse: it comes with the 3.6GHz i7-4790 processor (near the absolute top of the line for Intel processors), 16GB of DDR3-RAM, and a 2TB hard disk (7200 RPM SATA), on-board gigabit ethernet, 10 USB ports (4 USB2.0 and 6 USB3.0 ports), an HDMI port, a muti-card reader, plus the usual DVI and VGA outputs, as well as audio outputs. It even includes wireless b/g/n card (which is very nice, but I don't need it). This is a machine for gamers and for those who need serious compute power.

Two of the USB2.0 ports are in the back. Use those for your keyboard and mouse, which are low speed devices. There is a convenient accessory tray at the top with two more USB2.0 ports, one of which can be used to charge your smart phone. Connect your high speed external hard drives to the USB3.0 ports in the back for better speed, but you also have two front ones for convenience for temporary connections. There is a dedicated display port in the back too, but I personally prefer to use HDMI. The computer comes with four unused expansion slots for PCIe cards. If you are a gamer, and if you want to add a very high power graphics card (or two) you have room for it.

When I started up the machine everything worked immediately. The set up was easy and straightforward. It immediately detected all other computers and printers on my home network without prompting. Then I installed a few programs I need, including disk partitioning software. (The Windows 8.1.1 comes with its own disk partitioning software, but it does not deal with Linux partitions.) Most PC users do not need disk partitioning, but I do because this will soon become a triple-boot machine with Windows and with two different flavors of Linux. Even if you do not care about booting other operating systems, you may still want to partition your disk into at least two pieces so that your data and the Windows system software will reside on different partitions. Doing so makes system upgrades and recoveries and restore points much easier to deal with. If you don't know what disk partitions are, don't even try this. But if you know what you are doing, then I highly recommend it on a high-powered machine like this one.

You can tell that I am absolutely tickled pink with my new machine. Isn't there any negatives at all? Unfortunately yes, but they are not related to the machine itself, but to the OS. Windows 8.1.1 is a smart-phone and tablet operating system. But Windows 8.x is not appropriate for high-powered machines in my opinion. If all you want is to read e-mail, surf the web, check the weather, and watch videos, a tablet will be more than sufficient. You don't need to buy a powerhouse like this one. If so, Windows 8.1.1 is really great. In this case, however, Dell should have offered a Windows-7 downgrade, which would have made this machine even more attractive. Both Dell and HP occasionally offer Windows-7 downgrades on their very high-end machines, but unfortunately not on this one. (I guess they are under pressure from Microsoft to migrate everybody to Windows-8, or else ...) There are ways to make Windows-8 look and act like Windows-7, but they go about 70% to 80% of the way, not 100%. (Microsoft will claim that Windows-8 can do everything Windows-7 can do, and I am sure they are correct, but finding every little thing one needs is made extremely difficult under Windows-8.)

Despite the lack of Windows-7 downgrade, I will rate this machine 5-stars. It is that good!

title: For what it is and the price paid, it is outstanding.
text:
I need to start this review with the caveat that I bought this item during a Black Friday sale so my purchase price was approximately half of the listed price. With that perspective, this tablet has exceeded all of my expectations. I have since seen the item listed for $89 and at this price it remains a very good deal. I also own an ASUS Transformer TF300T so I am familiar with both the Android OS and a high-end Android tablet.

PROS:

The 754TPC is surprisingly fast for a single core processor. When Google Play is installing or updating software, then you will notice a response lag, but if you are working with one program, the tablet is adequately fast. For most games, Audible, Kingsoft Office, Netflix, and Kindle apps, I did not experience any performance issues. The battery time seems above average for a device of this size. Starting with a full charge, I can play backgammon and/or UNO all day and have 60% battery life remaining. I have watched two Netflix movies with perhaps 48% battery remaining. The device has a micro-SD slot and I have successfully used a 32GB Class 10 card in it. It has a micro-USB slot for charging and connecting it to computers. The WIFI works extremely well for me, I have yet to have the device drop a connection. The device came with Google Play and the King Kong store. Most people reading this review are familiar with Google Play. King Kong is a list of software that is listed by category. It seems to have a good selection, but I have not tried any.

CONS:

After a month of continuous usage, I have discovered only four cons. For three of the cons, I am unwilling to deduct a star because of the low purchase price. The device does not have bluetooth capability. For me, this means that I cannot connect the tablet to my other devices to share files or play games; no big loss. I also do not like that the a/c charger tablet connector is a cylinder type, which means that the charger will require more research effort on my part in order to replace it. However, I can charge the device using a standard micro-USB cable. The most noticeable con is the font display resolution. You can change the font size in the Settings, but for some reason the fonts are not as clear as I would expect. For this reason, I deducted a star. The last con is that while iVIEW has published a firmware update, I was unable to download and run the installation program. There may be developer ROMs available, but the device currently meets all of my needs so I will leave it as it is.

In conclusion, I am extremely happy with this device.

title: Excellent Ballhead for D7000
text:
I was looking for a ball head that would support a moderately heavy camera rig without sagging. I had purchased a Dolica tripod and ball head from Amazon when I first got into photography. It constantly sagged and eventually broke. This head replaces that one, though I'm currently using it on that tripod. Though the tripod is not particularly solid itself, this head has made a huge difference in usability for tripod shots. I have a Nikon D7000 with battery grip attached to it, and have tested this head with a Sigma 17-50 2.8 as well as a Sigma 70-200 2.8 and the Sigma 70-200 2.8 combined with a 2.0 teleconverter (which makes it a big, long lens). With the big lens, I attach the quick release plate to the lens collar, with the smaller lens, the plate is attached to the tripod socket of the battery grip. In my usage, I haven't seen the head sag at all once I have it tightened down.

As for features, the adjustable friction control is wonderful. It allows you to control the amount of friction that is on the head when it isn't locked down. This make it so that you can put just enough friction on the ball so that it will hold still while you lock it the rest of the way down. When using the big lens combos, I can add a little more friction to make it move without flopping around, and with the smaller lens combo, I can make it move a little easier. In both cases, properly adjusting the friction knob allows for more precise alignment of the head.

I like the locking knob too. It's big enough that I can grab it and tighten it down easily. The knob can also pull out and be readjusted so that it is always in the right position for your hand.

The quick release plate is suprisingly nifty. I wasn't sure what I would think of it, but it actually works really well. First and foremost, it holds very tightly. No movement whatsoever. But, it also latches onto the head very easily. With the latching mechanism locked open, just dropping the camera and plate onto the head causes the lock to engage. It makes it easy to put the camera on the head with just one hand.

I have to say that given my limited experience with ball heads, this is far and away the best I've ever used. I've never used a Really Right Stuff ball head, so I can't compare, but I can say that this one works really well for my uses at about a fourth of the price. The next step for me is a tripod that is sturdier, but this ball head made a far bigger difference than I would have imagined. If you're looking for a good, solid head that won't break the bank, I definitely think this one fits the bill!

title: You've never had this much fun with 7 inches!
text:
When I first ordered this tablet for my son, I thought, "It's going to be too small for him to
be able to play his games on! I mean, he's going from a 32 inch tv, to a 7 inch gizmo!" ,but it was the only thing he asked for,and for $79, I couldn't beat the price...and if it meant I wouldn't have to keep giving up the laptop,so he could watch origami videos on youtube,I was willing to give it a try!
So,it arrived before the estimated time,as usual! (Thank you,Amazon!) I opened it up and said, "Oh,come here honey..
look at how cute it is." My wife comes in the room and immediately says, "SEND IT BACK...there is no way that little thing is going to keep our son entertained!" I told her I would,but it would have to wait until Monday. In the meantime,I went to Google Play and installed a bunch of free games and tried them out. AngryBirdsStarWars, excellent response time from this little device. And aiming is much easier than using the mouse on the laptop! She's caught me playing a few times and reminded me that,"it's going back Mondaaaay",in that voice that means,do or die...well,just as I was getting ready to uninstall all of the games and pack it up this morning, I noticed a game on GooglePlay...Air Hockey Glow...I knew this may be my shot to save our son's Christmas! She and I have had epic air hockey matches in the past and if this game was any good at all,she couldn't resist! I installed it and tried it out first. AWESOME! The glow is impressive! Bright colors! You use your finger to move the puck and since the monitor is only 7 inches,you can play anywhere! So,I made my plan of attack!
" Oh,sweety...where are you?", I yelled down the hall. She came into the room,hands on hips,ready to yell at me,when she saw that sweet glow from that little screen and instead of screaming at me for bothering her again,she asked,"is that air hockey?". "Why,It most certainly is",I said. "How do you play?",she asked,while drying her hands on the towel hanging on her shoulder. "I'm not really sure...I just found it and installed it a second ago..would you like to try it out with me?",I asked (Look,I couldn't tell her the truth and let her know,I had a leg up.I know as long as she's losing,she'll keep playing and our son has a better chance of getting his Christmas present. If that puts me on the naughty list,so be it! :) She said,"Sure,but only one game;That kitchen isn't going to clean its self!". So,30 minutes later we're having a blast. We're tied at 3 games apiece,and I defy anyone to tell me this is any less exciting than any game 7 in World Series history! I mean,the stare down at the beginning of the game was worth $79! I told her I would never tell anyone who won game 7,so I won't...ok,it was me! Longer story,slightly shorter...our son gets his tablet and she wants one after Christmas,(and an immediate rematch) because our thoughtful family members always get us Amazon gift cards!

title: Great sound, WAY too expensive, NOT user friendly
text:
We bought this as an accessory along with the Sennheiser RS 180 transmitter/headphone set.
[[ASIN:B002TLT10S Sennheiser RS 180 Digital Wireless Headphone System]]

PROS: Outstanding sound quality, 1800 sq ft home, two stories, can get sound anywhere in the place including the remote garage. We got this model specifically because I am nearly deaf in one ear so can adjust volume independently R/L. Also, we can both preset our volumes and use the volume control on the component receiver as needed with no further need to adjust headphone volumes. Over some 20 years, we have had several other wired and wireless headphones. Both sound and wearer comfort with these is noticeably better than any we've had before. A freaking expensive product, but since the sound and comfort is so much better than what we've had before, we can live with the expense.

CONS: As another reviewer said, connecting headsets with the transmitter is a pain in the neck ... and other places as well. We can always get both to connect, but IF one is already in use for more than a few minutes (my wife watches "her" shows, then I join later to watch "our" shows), the second headset refuses to connect UNLESS we turn everything off, then turn all back on while standing within three feet of the transmitter. Whoever designed the connection system on this product deserves to be fired without bonuses. But, despite the frustration, we have always been able to connect ... eventually.

Summary: The system, when connected, is a solid five. The connection procedure gets a one only because we can connect.

UPDATE 12 April 3013.
Bought a second transmitter/headphone set with another supplemental headphone for the upstairs TV. The supplemental headphone would not pair. I contacted Sennheiser Support by phone AFTER I tried every possible method to pair several times. The agent was ... less than competent ... could not seem to understand repeated "We already tried that several times." Waste of time. Contacted Amazon and they replaced it at no charge. The replacement also would not pair no matter what we tried. It is being returned for refund. I would NEVER have bought this system if I could have found anything else that had good left/right balance controls to accommodate my hearing loss.

After having used this system for several months, there are additional CONS: The controls on the headset are buttons on the right-ear side, all are adjacent and - literally - impossible to adjust with the headset on. So, not only is the "pairing" procedure a pain, any adjustments to volume and balance have to be made by taking the headset off, hoping the adjustment is correctly done, and putting the headset on again. More often than not, this has to be repeated (because broadcasters can't seem to be consistent with their volume settings, adjustment is occasionally needed).

The summary is, Sennheiser has put stylish design ahead of function and ease of use. I've reduced the rating from four starts to two.

title: Very Easy Phone-to-Car Hookup for Music and Calls
text:
Since my Mazda3 does not have Bluetooth support built-in to it, this Kinivo device was the next best thing for me to hook up my Android phone wirelessly over Bluetooth to my car's AUX 3.5mm input, and then to playback music/podcasts and take calls over it. Other than the power connection to my phone (as needed), it stays completely wire-free, and eliminates the pain of trying to conceal/route an audio cable to where my phone is mounted on the dash.
On the negative side, it does attempt to mess with the original audio levels a bit, has no apparent noise reduction, has a very small audio lag, and a limited cable length. Still, for the $35 price tag and the simplicity of the design, it does very well and the negatives are not enough of a problem for me to knock off a full star for. I'd give it a 4.5 if possible. Truthfully I was a bit leery of this no-name-brand at first, but it looks like they make a good product. Details below.

Requirements:
1) This BTC450 is an AUX-based unit, which means your car's stereo must have a 3.5mm female input jack on the front faceplate, in the glovebox, in the armrest, ... somewhere. Most cars started having them either by default or as an option since the mid 2000s. My 2007 model has one inside the armrest.
2) The unit has a single 3 foot cord coming off the circular microphone/control, that then splits into two cords of 1 foot each for the power and audio. So you must have a cigarette lighter plug within 2 feet of the AUX input, and a clean/flat place to mount the mic/control puck within 3 feet of the split. You could get an extension for the audio cable if need be, but the power port can't be further than 4 feet away from the puck (3ft + 1ft) since the power cable is not-removable.
3) Bluetooth support on your phone or MP3 player. It needs to be v2.1 compatible, which is somewhat standard for phones in the past couple years.
4) I highly recommend getting a "ground loop isolator" like this one, [[ASIN:B001EAQTRI PAC Ground Loop Isolator]], to go in-line between the unit and your car's AUX. At least in the case of my last two cars, I've had problems with a nasty buzz noise when hooking up any type of audio device that is also powered by the car.

Initial syncing was dead simple due to the bluetooth 2.1 support: press the center puck button to "advertise it" to other devices, choose it for pairing on your phone, and you're done. No PIN or software needed.

Auto-Connect! A big plus for me is the fact that it powers off when the car is turned off (no forgetting), it auto-powers-on and connects to my phone within seconds of ignition (no pushing a sync button), and it stays on the entire time even when there is no audio (no power-saving). This is not the case with the battery-based MotorMouth & Belkin units which don't react to power loss/gain. No batteries in the Kinivo means it is not portable, but then again if it's always in the car and always plugged in, I don't see the sense in having a battery anyway. When the car is turned off, the phone detects the loss of connection and pauses the music while it attempts to reconnect - finally giving up and pausing until you say otherwise. The cigarette lighter adapter for power is smaller than most, so it's nicely unobtrusive. Now your mileage may vary if your car does not power down the cigarette lighter plug when the car is turned off. Most do, but if yours does not, you run the risk of draining your battery.

Microphone quality is actually quite good. My voice was clear and distinct when used with my voice recorder app. People I called could hear me even when the microphone was 90 degrees to my right, as opposed to right in front of me. However when road noise and A/C noise came on, it was picked up as well. There appears to be no intelligence to filter or deal with that noise. This was not a deal-breaker for me because I could still be understood and didn't need to repeat myself. It was just not as clear and was more difficult for the caller to hear.

Sound quality was surprisingly good. I used a good-quality, thick 3.5mm stereo audio cable as the "standard" while switching back-and-forth to compare. The Kinivo seemed to increase the stereo separation a bit, making the music more enveloping and clearer. The volume was higher than what was received on the cable (setting "10" instead of "16"), which theoretically means a cleaner signal and less need for amplification. A bit of a negative: the bass level was noticeably enhanced, such that I had to use my car's equalizer to take it down to "-2". Some may like the bass - I don't. The unit advertises support for Bluetooth A2DP (Advanced Audio Distribution Profile) for high quality stereo audio transmission with a minimum bitrate of 345 Kbit/sec. I admit I'm not a die-hard audiophile, but I know low bit-rates and bad encoders when I hear them. In this case there was no discernible drop in the audio quality itself on my mid-range car speakers in a quiet environment. The connection was solid with no audio dropouts after testing it during several hours of driving to/from work. When a call comes in, it pauses the music, and resumes when done.

The puck controls were intuitive and compatible with my Galaxy Note 2. There are two buttons on the edge for track skip/previous, and the center button starts/plays/pauses music. It brought up the Google Music app automatically and picked the current playlist. The microphone is in a small opening on one side of the puck. In the bluetooth settings for the phone, I could choose whether to enable it for phone calls, for media, or for both. Very convenient if you don't want both. The puck comes with a sticky pad to adhere it to some place in your car. I did not test it, since I had no need. I let it sit in a groove in the center console.

There was a small audio delay when adjusting playback from the phone. For example, when "pause" is pressed, the audio would continue for a split second and then stop. Not enough to be a problem, but not the immediate response you would get with a hard-wire.

I finally settled on buying this unit, but the other big-name competition I choose from were:

[[ASIN:B004CLYJ2I Belkin Bluetooth Car Hands-Free Kit, US Version]]
[[ASIN:B0036ORN2U Scosche motorMOUTH Plug and Play Bluetooth Handsfree and Streaming Audio Car Kit]]
[[ASIN:B004KPLS7K Griffin Technology BlueTrip AUX]]

I skipped these others due to complaints about the lack of auto-connect on power-on and audio quality issues.
