title: Excellent experience; it appears that newer software addresses concerns posted in "older" reviews
text:
I've read a bunch of reviews on Amazon regarding this mouse, and I've discovered a rather critical flaw in their review system: people are complaining a bit about the lack of swipe configurability and the lack of control of scrolling. It's obvious to me that they were not using the latest software that, by default, I downloaded and installed for the mouse. All of the top reviews' negative complaints have been addressed, IMHO, by the software but are still listed as if they were existing issues on the front review page for the mouse.

The make-or-break deal for me with touch mice is that the mouse had to support thumb gestures for forward/back movement; I use that action a lot and didn't want to sacrifice it. This mouse appeared to be the only mouse that supported thumb gestures.

My take? I like it. A lot. So much that I bought a second one to replace my home mouse.

The "wow!" factor for me was the scroll-ability of the mouse. With a few simple changes to the software to adjust scrolling acceleration, sensitivity, and speed, I have far more control over scrolling around a document than I had with a mouse wheel: With a wheel, I was often spinning and spinning to move "down" a lengthy document. With the settings tweaked to my liking, I can quickly navigate to any position of the document with a short (and precise) finger-swipe. I work with so many large files at work that being able to zip around a large chunk of code is a great boon to me.

If scrolling is a "single finger swipe", the mouse also has several other gestures, all fully reconfigurable: Two finger swipe up/down/left/right, and a three-finger up/down swipe. I've left the two-finger up/down swipe to the default "maximize / minimize windows", but changed the two-finger left/right swipe from "Snap window to left/right screen" to the "End" and "Home" keys for quicker document navigation. The three-finger up/down gestures were defaulted to something like "hide all apps" and "show all apps as tiny windows so you can choose which one to bring to the foreground". I've replaced them with "Control-W (close tab)" and "Alt+F4 (close app)".

The thumb gesture works pretty well, ya flick your thumb to the left and right on the mouse and it does it's job. this was the hardest gesture for me to "learn" as I was "trained" to do a side-click where my thumb button once was.

The software also allows one to create gestures on an app-by-app basis; I'll be doing this with my coding editor to set up heavily used functions to specific gestures.

Another "liberating" thing I've found myself doing is scrolling with any finger on the mouse; it doesn't "care" if your finger is positioned in the middle of the mouse or not; I've adapted to scrolling with my pointer finger instead of my third because I have finer motor control over it than my middle finger.

The only negative experience that I've had is training myself to keep my hand still on top of the mouse; I've often scrolled around a document without wanting to just because I've never had to be aware of finger movements on top of the mouse's surface. The mouse is doing exactly what it's supposed to; it just took me a little while to not have any accidental scrolling.

title: Extension Cable for OBD-II Bluetooth Devices
text:
It works.

The plugs themselves are of good build quality and strength. The cable is flexible but also appears well made and strong. In most vehicles, the 1 meter length is more than adequate.

Using this extension cable enables you to attach/detach an inexpensive bluetooth device like the Elm327 to your vehicle's OBD port so that you can read error codes or monitor engine sensors.

There are two main advantages to using cables like this one:

The ports built into many vehicles are somewhat delicate and usually found under the dashboard console. Your legs can inadvertently bump these devices when they stick out, potentially damaging the port itself. Often cheaply made, these ports are expensive to replace.

The Elm327 and other devices remain at least partially "active" even when your vehicle is parked with the engine off. This drains some battery power and some users have had problems with that. Constantly plugging and unplugging the device to prevent battery drain poses similar risks of damaging the port.

[[ASIN:B0076KBPNI Yongtek Bluetooth Diagnostic Scanner Wireless]]

Using this extension cable, you can plug/unplug OBD-II scan devices like the Elm327 without that risk. You don't have to crawl underneath the dashboard each time to connect/disconnect the device. You simply attach/detach it each time from the extended end of the cable.

The right-angle plug shown above is what connects to your vehicle. This makes it easy to route the cable using velcro or other fasteners in such a way as to prevent your feet from contact with the cable or bluetooth device.

We successfully use these cables on two vehicles. With our electric LEAF, we can monitor battery health and my real state-of-charge. We can accurately gauge if my battery's overall charge is declining due to weather or age. The android LEAF Spy app is used for this.

When we want to monitor our Mini-Cooper S, we just move the Elm327 to that vehicle and plug it into the end of the cable. Android App Torque or Torque Pro can monitor many different engine sensors and track "Engine Light" error codes.

We are pleased with these cables because of build quality, flexibility of the cable itself, length and price.

title: Why no noise-cancelling when bluetooth is off?
text:
I can see the complaints about ear comfort. The pads press down on the ear structures and seem a bit uncomfortable even when you first put them on. Then it becomes more irritating the longer you wear them. And for comparison, a friend was over with a Sony noise-cancelling model but no bluetooth. The ear pad design was very different. The padding more or less surrounds the ear and is much more comfortable - there is a much more narrow rim of foam as opposed to this model with a wad of foam pressing on the ear.

But even more odd, at least, in my opinion, you cannot use the noise cancelling function alone. If you terminate the bluetooth connection and just want QUIET and noise cancelling, say to read a book on an airplane, the noise-cancelling automatically turns off after a short set period of time. What, to save battery power? I want noise-cancelling when I want it and not just when listening to an audio signal whether music or video. I guess you can keep the bluetooth connection and not listen to anything but that sucks down the battery of the cell phone or tablet or whatever.

I have to be honest, I did not purchase these for a superb audiophile experience but to hide hums and buzzes and noise on a plane or when the air conditioner or fan are too noisy. So I'm not really rating those features so much as utility and comfort.

I am pretty certain they are going back.

title: Just Installed This Last Night
text:
I was a bit apprehensive about doing this install, even though my technical and mechanical skills are very high, mostly because I lack patience for small, meticulous work like this. But I manned up and jumped right in last night. After quickly skimming a YouTube video for items in the device to watch out for during replacement, I began. I'm not going to go over the technical aspects so much as there are literally dozens of awesome tutorials out there.

My digitizer was very shattered...on a scale of 1 - 10 (1 being a crack and 10 being completely blown out all over the place) mine was about a 7. Many tutorials are going to tell you to take your time, be patient and carefully pull your broken screen off with a bunch of tools...this is good advice. I got a small flat head and a hairdryer and carefully, but quickly chiseled out the screen. I probably wasn't nearly as careful as they tell you to be because I broke a lot of glass and created many new shards, but was careful to brush them aside while working. These glass shards are VERY small and sharp. Please be careful not to lose any otherwise you may find them in your hands and/or feet later on down the road. After about an hour of pulling the border glass off in various sized chunks, I was able to pull the remaining portion of the screen off with ease.

Once the old screen was off I cleaned out the remaining shards and glue and place the new ditizer back in. I then checked the functionality of the new digitizer, the wifi, the volume, the lock and the power buttons before putting everything back together. This is my biggest recommendation... CHECK ALL BUTTON AND DEVICE FUNCTIONALITY BEFORE SCREWING THE LCD BACK IN AND GLUING / STICKING THE NEW DIGITIZER IN PLACE! If you get everything back in place and then find out you did break you volume buttons, or put the digitizer cables in upside-down, you're going to be hating life when you realize you have to do everything all over again. But this time you have to do it without breaking the digitizer.

Moral of the story, my device is working perfectly. The digitizer I got was excellent quality, no dead spots found, it's the correct size, crystal clear, looks and feels like the original and for a fraction of the cost of the OEM digitizer replacement. I really have no idea why anyone would complain about this product...unless they worked on the Apple "genius" bar and are losing massive amounts of money because people are realizing they don't need to pay astronomical amounts of money for repairs to their locked down / proprietary / non universal products that break when a butterfly touches them. Noooooooooo, that couldn't be the case.

Update: It's been a year and a half since I did this replacement. The replacement screen and digitizer is still working strong even after a few more drops and two and three year olds playing with it. Don't know if the screens going out now are the same as I received, but the one I got was cheap and very durable.

Certainly if you are looking for pristine recordings of quiet atmospheres, you'll be wanting to look for something else as this microphone is not up to that task. Compared to the in-built microphone on the GoPro, it's a vast improvement...but really that isn't saying much given just how terrible the GoPro's mic actually is.

title: Great Replacement For The Nexus 7
text:
This is my third Android Tablet. I have had two of the Nexus 7; Version 1 and Version 2. Both were excellent in both build quality and performance. The NVIDIA Tablet is better than the Nexus in 3 major ways: 1) Bigger and brighter screen 2) better speakers and 3) more port options (HDMI and SD-card). The Android OS functions exactly as you would expect on this tablet, and all of my previous apps and settings transferred over from my Nexus 7 tablet to this one without a hitch through my Google Account.
I like they way they marked the power cord and the power connector with a Green marker. It makes it easier to find and insert the USB power connector in the right orientation.
I like the width of the bezel when in landscape - there is enough room to hold it without affecting the screen.
So why 4 stars? The on/off and volume buttons are hard to use. I wish they protruded just a little further and were a little easier to feel and to push. I actually wish they were more like the buttons on my wife's iPad Mini.
Then there is the Autorotate problem, which NVIDIA has acknowledged on their support site and the moderator there says "We are aware of this problem and are working on it." Or words to that effect. Autorotate works fine for a while, but then after the tablet sleeps, autorotate doesn't always work on wakeup. When it quits working I do a Restart and it always works again. This really is annoying and it is inconsistent about which way it locks up, sometimes in landscape and sometimes in portrait. But no amount of shaking or spinning will correct it. The only thing that works is reboot. I do hope NVIDIA fixes this.
As far as build goes, mine is perfect. But note the comments from other users about cracks in the corners.
I cannot comment on the controller. I bought it but sent it back unused when I read on the NVIDIA site it would not connect to other devices.
I guess I should have read that first. I am not going to use this tablet for gaming anyway. I wanted it for the Android tablet features. I have a Gaming PC with a 27" monitor so I have trouble doing games on a tablet.
Bottom line: I really like this tablet and overall it is a great improvement over my last two Nexus 7s. At 299 the price is right. I agree with a previous comment that said do not pay more than that. Wait for Amazon to get more at 299 (with Prime), or go to Best Buy.

title: Full of cons masquerading as pros
text:
So I received my tablet after fighting in BestBuy. Here I brought home the tablet I thought was best on the market and believe me it is NOT!

Pros: Fast CPU, everything running fast and very smooth. Finishing touch on the tablet is high class, the feel is perfect. Asus 4.1 is not the latest version of Android but it is very very close! Flash is also a big pro, compared to the TF300 at least. Triumph over Nexus 10 and 7 thanks to its supporting MicroSD card so you can easily upgrade your storage with affordable price, the ease of transferring your files, and you don't have to put yourself on the cloud like you have to with the iPad. So MicroSD is probably the biggest pro. One more pro over the Samsung competitors is that you have the option to turn the tablet into a netbook with physical keyboard and extra battery life!

Cons: I didn't think it would be a con, but the aluminum back cover is a con! Extremely easy to be scratched doesn't help. And the charging port is also aluminum. And the aluminum "bar" is extremely easy to be bent! I charged my tablet while it was on the shelf with the wire hanging and a day later I found that "bar" in a V shape! (Should have known better and buy extra warranty at this point!" After a few time of bending and try to bend it back, the port is completely broken! Won't charge anymore and I saw my tablet die after its battery ran out. Then while I was trying to contact Asus for repairing. Two day later, I pull out the tablet after leaving it lying on the floor and I found a crack between the camera hole and the flash light. Either something happened that cracked it without me knowing, or I suspect the aluminum part shrink due to the cold weather, much faster than the carbon fiber part on top thus corrupting the top part. The reason I think this is after I pulled it out, I found the aluminum back extremely cold while the carbon part only slightly cold.
Anyway, the tablet is a bust for me. If you decide to buy the damn thing, make sure you buy extra warranty. But you might want to wait for the next generation of tablet. Asus has disappointed me big time! I will just put it on eBay to see if I can get any money back.

title: One Computer to Bind Them All
text:
I've had my Surface Pro since the end of February, and at last I feel confident about an overall report on what it means to a businessman who's a bit of a "road warrior". Kudos to Microsoft on a brilliant, innovative design, and a really solid, well-built product as well. I have dropped mine once or twice (onto carpet), and while I don't recommend this, it did not even "reboot". While my fingers are not as small or nimble as they were 20 years ago and my eyesight not quite as good, this computer works . . . and I sometimes think if I'd only had this thing when I was 20. . .

My overall impression is this is the greatest portable computer or laptop I've ever owned -- as revolutionary in its own way as the original "green screen" COMPAQ "luggable" was at forty-something pounds--granted the Surface Pro will not produce the body-building effect that a race through an airport with a COMPAQ could. It performs as well as my 3 years-old HP ENVY-17 (Windows score 5.6), and weighs in about 1/5th of the weight. The Smartglass interface to my Xbox adds a lot of enjoyment to entertainment such as "Game of Thrones" and some movies that can make use of the functionality, and it's nice to be able to play some light Xbox games (Solitaire, Mahjong) when I need a mindless time-killer. The Xbox Music interface to "my music" playlists, etc., is very enjoyable and does not add any overhead to the storage space. I wish it had a phone built in -- because I like to carry my computer with me all of the time, and why have to carry TWO devices that are largely redundant. Better camera OR no camera would have been fine with me.

While I have colleagues who have very successfully used the Apple IPad in its various incarnations, those notepads (or the Windows Surface RT) are not a computer! They can run apps but not the software that they use in their offices -- almost inevitably Microsoft Office. I can not only run Microsoft Office 2013, but I can run Adobe Acrobat Pro as well as Clio, the law-office management tool I use, as well as all of the other small programs that keep me productive. I can run most of them simultaneously. If I have Wi-Fi access as I usually do in court, I have access to all my forms, notes, and client documents. Incidentally, after my experience with the Gorilla glass on my Kindle HD, I decided NOT to add a plastic screen protector to the Surface Pro, because the extra protection seems redundant and has slightly interfered with the touch displays of my phones and my Kindles. When you look at the price-performance-weight tradeoffs, all in all, I am amazed with the outstanding job Microsoft did putting this together. Price especially, when you consider you are getting a real computer, becomes reasonable. In my viewpoint, if you could plug it HDMI into a big monitor, it would be a desktop replacement for most people, when docked with a "big keyboard". A big "touchscreen" monitor would be the very best.

BOOT-TIME IS AMAZING
My Windows 7 HP ENVY (that is a desktop replacement) boots in about 4 minutes from a cold start. That seems like forever when you are trying to get something done urgently -- it trips the legendary "critical need detector". The Surface Pro books in less than 15 seconds -- actually more like less than ten. I spend more time with the password (those no-longer-quite-so-nimble fingers) than it does booting -- this is AMAZING.

INPUT.
The Surface Pro has great flexibility of input. The touch screen is brilliant and perfectly sensitive to fingers while ignoring my casual palm resting on it. However, I have large (fat) fingers and sometimes it is difficult to select just the item I want in regular view. No problem! Just use your fingers to enlarge the screen and select away. I have the Microsoft Touch Cover I find very useful for light typing such as URLs and passwords, and which attaches by a bit of "magnetic magic" while putting the machine to sleep (and protecting the glass) if you are on the go. The Cover's touchpad is unacceptable, so I either use the stylus or the very fine Microsoft Wedge Mouse as the "fine" pointing device. With the included stylus, I can take handwritten notes in Office OneNote in Court, or I can use the built-in onscreen stylus keyboard which even recognizes my cursive scrawl while walking, which astounds me. Finally, I use a Logitech H800 Bluetooth headset for voice recognition and dictation, and find very good functionality in Windows 8, on its on, without additional special dictation software. Training and practice are important. While in a VERY quiet environment, you can use voice-control with the built-in Microphone, you will definitely want a Bluetooth headset.

NETWORKING
Wi-Fi connectivity and speed is fine. If you are using big documents OR streaming video on a balky network, use a Ethernet-USB3 adapter but ONLY on your secure private networks, unless you add additional software security.

BATTERY LIFE
While it was a big fear when I bought the Surface Pro, I tend to get about 3-4 hours of use, depending on how actively I am using Wi-Fi to access the internet and that's good for me almost all the time. I did run it to empty once on purpose at about 3.4 hours. It would not suffice during a trial, but there is almost always an AC plug in a courtroom -- just a question of how accessible to counsel's tables in some of the older courtrooms I've used. I have run the device all the way down on purpose at about 4 hours, but the charger is so lightweight, it's hard for me to understand why one would be bothered by the charge. (Even booths in many restaurants have AC plugs these days!)

CAMERAS
Cameras are useful in making a video-record of client interviews, using Skype for video calls and not much else. They take poor quality photos -- about what I get (and see) from most cell phones.

VIDEO
Whether surfing the internet or looking at movies, HD Video quality is first rate. It is a mystery to me why Microsft uses a VGA adapter in the Surface Pro while using the far more advanced HDMI that they do on the Surface RT. While I can and frequently do connect it to my big Samsung monitor, the display is not nearly as good as DVI or HDMI input. I guess one can make the argument that VGA is the lowest common denominator for external displays such as projectors. While the VGA adapter is not in and of itself heavy, it gets that way when you attach it to a heavy, pretty-much-obsolete VGA cable. The video does get a bit "eccentric" when you plug into an "outboard" monitor, by which I mean the touchscreen on the Surface Pro becomes balky or non-responsive -- or maybe that's the inherent limitation of VGA. You can work around the two-monitor problem by just using a mouse and keyboard combination. Nonetheless, if I was putting a bug into Microsoft's ear for the "Surface Pro II", I'd say make this a top priority, and sell this with a dock as a desktop replacement.

SOUND.
Sound from the built-in speakers is okay, but not nearly as amazing as my Kindle Fire HD. (Real kudos, Amazon!) Video makes up for most of that shortcoming in movies. HD is "true HD". Loudness of the built-in speakers is satisfactory for a personal experience in a quiet space, but headphones are a must for High Quality music, special effects in movies, and in most gaming. External speakers sound pretty good through the headphone jack, and I listen to Audible audio-books and music with my fine Sennheiser headphones. If I really want to be finicky, the audio output is not what I get on my "hand-built" PC using a super-separate video card -- my point is overall you can enjoy music via headphones -- by the speakers, not so much, but it's okay for background in the office. Of course, it's great to be able to stay in touch with my assistant from just about anywhere.

PROCESSING
64 bit processing does everything (with the exception of video-intensive games) that I've thrown at it, including minor video and photo processing. This is a real computer, and you are not going to choke it down with the largest of spreadsheets. I know some people have reported heat problems (and who am I to doubt them), but I have had absolutely no problem, even in HD Streaming video or playing some relatively simple games. I find myself occasionally with several documents in Word and Acrobat Pro, Outlook, Internet Explorer, and a couple of other things going (maybe background music), and I do not notice any lag or any stuttering in the music.

STORAGE
With everything I need to be productive (and a good bit of entertainment -- Kindle, Netflix, Window Media Center, Skydrive, Dropbox, etc. to boot), I still have about 70 GB left out of the nominal 128GB. While I originally had some misgivings about a lack of storage space, they were wrong. I did acquire (and encrypt) a 32GB SDX card to backup the OS and Drive to, and it works well. Backup (to me) does not seem as simple as it did in Windows 7, and I downloaded the Windows 7 disk imaging software from the Microsoft Store.

SECURITY
As near as I can tell, Windows Defender (as I think it's called) is perfectly adequate protection so far, and I am required by Texas law to keep client data on encrypted devices, so I use BitLocker (that's built into Windows 8) on the main drive and on the externals too (there's a convenient "automatic" decrypt feature that lets you into them automatically when they are connected to your Windows 8 computer). The "picture password" is a great feature of Windows 8 in my opinion. I rotate pictures and touchscreen gestures frequently. I tried installing the latest version of Norton's suite, but it actually interfered with me being able to access my own "secure" networks. I'm sure I could have fixed it with tech support, but I was grumpy about it and ditched it.

WINDOWS 8.
I came to Windows 8 from two powerful Windows 7 computers, and my experience and satisfaction with that OS were high. Yet now that I am becoming more aware of Windows 8's refinements (and overcoming the frustration with some things being "moved around") I really think it's a great improvement to computing. I'm using SkyDrive and Office 2013, and that is really helpful for personal things -- it's very satisfying to see all of my software pretty much synched and pretty much without paying attention. It is a great surprise that Outlook (in the cloud) really does synch.

APPS
Microsoft has (and is getting a lot more) useful Apps, but there is an "app-gap" compared to the Ipad. Among things it needs are a good shopping and grocery management program that effectively uses the camera as a scanner to read packaging. The Kindle App is special -- reading two pages at once has become a great way to read, but I still prefer the lighter weight of the Kindle HD for reading in bed. (I like its sound better too.)

PROBLEMS I HAVEN'T NOTICED -- HEAT. I've tried everything except playing games that would drive the video into some sort of overload, and I cannot make any part of the Surface "noticeably warmer than background" to my touch.

WHAT IT NEEDS IMO:
A good DC charger to work in your car (people who work out of their cars for longer than four hours at a time might have a real problem with power).
A telephone "dongle" so I can ditch my cell phone.

THE ROAD WARRIOR's SURFACE KIT (at about 5 lbs + bag)
(1) The Surface Pro with the Touch Cover or the Type Cover for "light" typing and a little extra protection for that beautiful screen.
(2) Microsoft Wedge Mouse
(3) Microsoft Wedge Keyboard (a bit small for my hands, but very nice touch.
(4) Extra charger, USB3 cable and extension cable, and 4-port USB3 Hub).
(5) USB3-to-Ethernet adapter (for when speed is everything).
(6) 1 TB or larger external hard-drive. (I have a ruggedized one that is really quite amazing)
(7) Surface Pro VGA adaptor -- you really won't like it, but it's the only way you can hook up a big monitor to it, and it (with the VGA cable) will be one of the heaviest things in your kit.
(8) Bluetooth headset -- for Skype or voice control and dictation.

BELOW THE SURFACE -- something to hook to a cell-phone network and a good portable scanner. I have a Scansnap S1300 that works every well with it.

I'm still looking for the one perfect bag "to bind them all". I have found one that is leather (and looks like something a lawyer should take to court) -- key thing is it only has to have room for a few legal folders (mostly for show) and this thing. And of course, I have found a Maxpedition bag that holds and protects everything really well, but looks like I'm ready to parachute into a 3d world country -- just nothing that hits the sweet spot in between. Any suggestions in response to this review are welcome.

REVISED 4/29/2013 - a helpful commenter has pointed out that the Apple video display adapter is compatible which would make other digital-display formats available. I've found a super protective sleeve for about $60 from sfbags.com that provides stand-alone convenience with real protection. Do NOT leave the computer "ON" rather than asleep and forget it in a protective sleeve, as it will get quite hot over time.

title: Purchase, return, and repeat.
text: Nice display and handy quick-mount feature, but I had a persistent problem where the depth would periodically "freeze up" and flash, as if the transducer was out of the water, then re-acquire.  Unfortunately this could last up to 20-30 seconds and by the time you got your depth reading back you were often in the wrong place (it was very aggravating). This happened just occasionally, while motoring or even while drifting with the motor off. No interference with the transducer, no turbulence, etc.  Thought it was a fluke so I exchanged if for another. Within minutes the new one did the same. Perhaps it was something about my boat (simple 14 ft aluminum fishing boat) or my installation, but the Humminbird 596c HD that I replaced it with has been flawless. I'd stay away from this one and stick with a company that has many more years in the sonar industry under it's belt.

Well it does not like HDMI link set up on my Sony TV which turns on/off my Yamaha AV receiver.  It turns everything on OK, but refuses to turn the AV receiver off.  Customer service was very knowledgeable and had me turn off the HDMI link on my Sony TV.  That pretty much solved the problem, but now my alternate (wife's) remote doesn't work properly. With all the customizations and programming ability of this device, it does not allow for this fairly common issue. They could not program the power on/off button sequence to change. I also had several times where the mute came on for no apparent reason on startup of watching TV activity.  The last issue I had was an occasional synching problem where one device did not respond when an activity was chosen.  This put everything out of synch. ie TV on, AV off Repeated toggling yeilded TV off, AV on etc requiring manual override.  Not the end of the world and common to other remotes.  But unless I get a second Harmony, for my wife (or myself) the HDMI problem is non functional for my setup. A nice device with a few flaws.  Mine is going back.  Too bad...

title: Setup takes a bit of work, but the results are worth it!
text:
inReach SE delivers as promised and I'm happy with the performance and usability. I previously used a SPOT Messenger so I'm familiar with the concepts behind this device and that helped get me past some initial issues. It is apparent that Delorme didn't make all their internal deadlines before releasing this device as a few edges are still a bit rough. For example, there are two web sites to use in setting up inReach SE (Explore and Enterprise). Both are similar, but not identical, in features and you need to work with both to get set up correctly. Another example is that you can't (yet) synch your Explore page with your device, but that feature is promised soon. One "gotcha" that wasn't spelled out clearly in the documentation (to me anyway) is the MapShare setup requirements. If you set up all the parameters correctly, you still don't see any users (you!) on the MapShare page at the web address provided. What you do see is a message telling you that all users are filtered out and to change your filter settings. The trick to this is that you have to send at least one MapShare message or track point from your inReach SE before it will list you as a user. Not hard to do -- but you have to know you need to do it. I got that tip on my second call to tech support and I don't recall seeing it in the setup pages or documentation.

I did have to update the firmware before setting up, but that exercise went smoothly following the instructions provided.

I haven't tested it from the wilderness, but theoretically if it works from my house it should work anywhere. Take your time on the setup and it all comes together nicely.
It does what it says it will do and it appears to do it well, so I rated it 5 stars.

title: Trial And Error
text:
As a professional student who commutes via foot, my bag is used daily and consistently holds
1) laptop
2) 1 notebook of notes, 1.5inch
3) one review book
4) refillable bottle
5) assorted pens, flash drives, etc

In terms of storage capacity - this backpack has been WONDERFUL. So many compartments and each of them perfectly sized. Everything has its specific place, which makes it so much easier to retrieve objects - rather than say, having only one big pocket and fishing through it for all my things.

In terms of quality of construction - this backpack has been absolutely DREADFUL. Within 2 months the straps began to fray; 1 month afterwards, the shoulder padding has completely worn and the strap has now compressed itself into a painful tourniquet that digs itself into my shoulder. I had attempted to delay the bag's disintegration, by reducing the load placed on the bag, however, the bag itself bears a significant weight. Likewise, the inner pockets have torn holes at their corners, so that any small object placed into them will soon find themselves "drained" out of their inner pocket and deposited into the larger pocket or some unknown fold within the layers of the backpack.

SwissGear has become notorious for horrible straps. While the bag itself is well thought out - what good is a backpack that can not be carried on your back? The bag is a good buy, if you don't mind re-attaching new straps for yourself - however, a fine quality shoulder strap may cost you 30-50% cost of the bag.

Unfortunately, I am still looking for a good backpack company myself - that can balance both functionality and professionalism. I may soon try a Kelty brand backpack.

title: Great Image Quality for a reasonable price.
text:
Just, first, a little background. Photography is my hobby not my profession. I have had several cameras over the years from a Canon T1i, to a Sony A55, to a Sony A77, to a Sony A7. I have just replaced the A7 with an A7r. I first bought the A7 thinking that the A7r was terrible at focusing. I was able to try a A7r at the CES show. I found that the focusing was really not an issue. So I sold my A7 and got the A7r.

FOCUSING - Focusing is really not a issue with me. I have used the A7r for a month now. It focuses quickly in almost all lighting conditions. The only time that it does not focus well is in pitch black rooms, but then there is nothing to take a picture off. I took pictures of the interiors of homes with no flash and had no problems focusing. I have taken pictures of fast action sports. This camera is a little slow for that purpose, but you can prefocus on a spot and wait for the action. This works great. I had a hard time focusing on birds in flight (BIF) but did manage to get a few good shots (manual focus to infinity and capture the bird.)

LIGHT LEAKS - I do not normally take long exposures with my lens cap on, so this has not been an issue with me.

BATTERY LIFE - This is a weakness. I have just bought several more batteries and carry them with me. I have also bought a external charger. I like the internal charger; this way I can charge two batteries at a time. I normally drain 1 1/2 batteries during a day of heavy shooting.

LENS - There are not many full frame e-mount lenses available. If you buy the appropriate metabones adapter, just about any lens will work. I have a TAMRON 18-200 lens (to get image stabilization, sony has disabled this with their e-mount lens). I get 15 mega-pixel images. This is plenty resolution for me. I also have the Zeiss 24-70 lens to use for high quality work. And boy the detail really overwhelms me. Since there is no anti aliasing filter the sharpness is great in the center of the frame. Images are slightly soft at the corners but I like that. It brings the viewer focus towards the center of the frame.

SUMMARY - There is no perfect camera in all respects. The Sony A7r is the closest that I have found. It has excellent image quality for a great price (full frame comparisons). I would highly recommend this camera to photography enthusiasts. If you are a pro then I think that one for the Canikon cameras in the $5,000.00 price range may be a better fit. I would recommend the A7r over the A7. I have had both. The A7r image quality is significantly better.

Happy shooting !!!

title: Couldn't have ended better!
text:
I just finished the trilogy and WOW. Reading books 1 & 2 I just could not put it down, I had it on my mind all of the events transpiring and what will happened next. The ending was perfect and I felt completely content in my heart and happy for them. I laughed, cried a little, blushed at times, cheered for them and even learned from them. Christian and Ana weathered the storm and I could not have imagined a better ending. Heck, he even cries a little! The Epilogue was even better. The bonus chapters brought us into Christian's mind and we can see from the very beginning as much as he tried, he never truly saw Ana as another sub. I honestly don't want more, it's perfect that way it is and they are at peace with their lives and that makes me completely satisfied with this trilogy. I have NEVER said that about a book before because I have never become emotionally attached to characters like this. We learn that unconditional love can be tried and tested and in the end, it will win. We see a very dark soul become free and embrace the fact his wife genuinely loves him, Fifty Shades and all.
When it was all said and done --I missed so much what we had in the beginning. It reminded me that relationships are hard, but if I want to be happy... really happy... then it takes work. I learned to feel more comfortable in my sensuality, to not be afraid to ask for what I want and need from him. Life is so hard and if we can find our way back to even a little bit of the jealousy, the great sex, and being so into each other we can't stand it then maybe, just maybe, we won't end up on the down side of the statistics.

text:
My grandfather once told me that all cheeses were made in the same factory so it doesn't matter which cheddar, for example, you purchase. This isn't literally true, of course, but the point he was trying to make is that something that costs more isn't always better than a cheaper version of the same thing. With his voice in mind I purchased both the Polaroid [[ASIN:B009DMJWDC Polaroid Canon EOS Macro Extension Tube Set For Extreme Close Up Photography]] AND the [[ASIN:B0000DZ5OE Canon EF 12 II Extension Tube For EOS Digital Cameras]] and put them to the test to see which was the greater value. Here are my findings:

1. I'm happy that I bought both.

2. They decidedly do not represent different price points of the same thing. The fact that I originally thought they did only reflects my growing, yet still weak, expertise in the paraphernalia of macro photography.

3. The Polaroid tube is made up of 7mm, 14mm, and 28mm lengths that can be used individually or in any combination.

4. The Polaroid tube is just that...a tube, and supports no electronic connection between camera body and lens. In my book this is absolutely fine as long as what you are photographing is not moving and you have the time to make the necessary positional, exposure, and lighting corrections. Photographing jewelry in a static and controlled environment would be a good example.

5. The Canon tube, more like a thick ring actually (The [[ASIN:B0000U1N38 Canon EF 25 II Extension Tube for EOS Digital Cameras]] is a bit more tube-like.) is of a single fixed 12mm length and supports complete connectivity between camera and lens so that exposure and focusing are done as seamlessly with the EF 12 as without. This is a huge benefit if what you are trying to photograph is in a changing environment or moving. Macro photos of insects comes to mind. Yes, I actually did this while building lesson plans for my Biology class.

So, while my experiment to determine relative value was a bit misguided, I did end up with two devices I use frequently and would be unhappy to part with. As I said, they are not 'of a kind' and have separate yet strong appeal. If the Canon tube is a cheese it would be a fine Brillat-Savarin while the Polaroid isn't a cheese at all, but a really nice set of pliers.

title: Great little fish finder
text:
Have had this for about a week and took it out a couple of times.
As other reviewers have commented, it works quite well. After messing with it, I can't imagine fishing without one. Knowing where the fish are and are not is invaluable. Of course it can't tell if they're biting !

A few observations to add to the already good reviews of this product:

1) The RF45 "rubber ducky" unit that you cast into the water is smaller than I expected, but that's good. It is light and casts well.
2) The display you wear on your wrist is a somewhat large, and thick, watch. This is fine. The resolution was good enough to see what needs to be seen, and lack of greyscale does not seem to compromise the utility.
3) The user manual is very well written, but as you might expect for something with few buttons, it takes some study to understand what you've bought. The operation of the watch-unit took a while to learn initially, but is straighforward after you use it a couple times. (It has defaults, so you can probably just use it if you don't want to study the manual...)
4) The RF45 rubber-ducky seems faily durable. I actually dropped mine on the concrete and it bounced and survived. But I don't recommend repeating this experiment.
5) The display unit I got had a bit of a manufacturing quality-control issue. All the pixels were quite dark, requiring me to find the part of the manual that explains how to adjust the LCD contrast. After setting it on the lowest setting (1, rather than the default of 5) it seems to work fine - but I wish I could adjust it even lower.
6) While not needed, "programming" the RF45 rubber-ducky (if you want to switch channels, turn on the light, etc) is a bit cumbersome, and can't be done without the manual. Moreover, I have to wonder if some reviews that said the thing stopped working might have been because the RF45 got "reprogrammed" to channel B without the user knowing it? (You wet your finger and tap two or 3 times, etc to program which sounds like a recipe for trouble with random wetting events that could happen at some point as folks handle the unit)
7) The wrist unit claims to run for 40 hours on the battery, so having extra batteries is probably a good idea (it includes an extra one in the package - but I bought 5 more for about 6 dollars)
8) The RF45 rubber-ducky has a non-replaceable battery. It claims to run for 500 hours, but you should probably be careful how you store it when not in use to make sure it doesn't run down the battery (keep it dry, etc). I bought an extra to have as a backup (for about 25 bucks). Shelf-life claims to be 3 years.

So - how does it work? In a word - GREAT. No complaints. It has been great fun measuring the lake-bottom depth and contour and the alarm is pretty cool when fish swim by.

The wireless sender worked well when I cast it from the pier (range was fine for the wireless), but it did lose the signal once when I was trolling it behind my inflatable boat. BUT - this is a difficult situation for the wireless system to handle as the RF45 antenna was partly/mostly submerged due to the boat movement and my wrist was only about a foot off the water. As long as your wrist is not close to the water, it seems to be fine.

Bottom line - get one and try it !

title: Excellent binoculars and a great value
text:
I was looking for a pair of binoculars that would be light enough and compact enough for me to take along on walks and runs and do some birding on the side. Until recently I've been using a cheap pair of 8x21 that were certainly very light and compact but were terrible in the quality department. When I looked for a higher quality replacement of the same size I found that the price points were widely separated - it seemed like I could get cheap ones for about $20 or really expensive ones from Leica and others costing hundreds of $. That's when I decided to purchase a 10x25 - the extra power and low light performance could be had for a reasonably small sacrifice in weight.

I've found the Bushnell Legend Ultra HD 10x25s to be very satisfactory. On the plus side, they're compact, light bright and very sharp in the centre (about 30% of the diameter). There's no noticable chromatic aberration in that region. Outside of that however, CA is just about noticable when observing small birds against a bright sky. Not enough to be a big distraction but certainly noticable, particularly if you're looking for it. This isn't really much of a problem because if I do see a bird in the outer regions, I'll move to center it in my FOV for further observations. I wouldn't actually try to observe a bird off center.

Focusing is smooth and the eyecups are quite comfortable. Eye relief is also good. The hinges are just a tad stiffer than they need to be. For some strange reason, I had to set the right diopter a little off-center (not at the 0 mark) even though for a couple other binoculars, I set it at the 0 mark.

The neck strap that comes with the binocs is useless. The center portion is a stiff imitation leather strap in a very mismatched light tan color. The ends are black nylon straps. The stiffness of the center portion make the strap uncomfortable. I tried them and took them off. I usually just carry them in the pocket (which they fill!) of my running shorts or in the palm of my hand.

Overall a satisfactory purchase.

title: Excellent for the price; great telephoto
text:
I bought this camera specifically to take hiking in Utah in areas with ancient Native American (Ancestral Puebloan/Anasazi) cliff dwellings, some of which can only be seen at a distance. Its telephoto lens is what most attracted me to it.

One reviewer, an accomplished photographer, determined that it was hard to get quality prints with this camera. Simplifying his recommendations a little, when he used the "P" [Program] setting and "raw" picture quality (resulting in unprocessed image data, which he would process later), and an ISO of 64 (preferably) or 100, he got his best photos. His assessment of the "fine" picture quality setting was that it was not that fine, hence he went for "raw." He also used "exposure compensation" to adjust brightness. Because of his review, when I was in Utah, I often took photos with the "Auto" setting (which defaults to the "standard" picture quality - although apparently I had it set to "fine" most of the time without realizing it) as well as the "P" setting so I could compare them later. Because I don't trust myself with processing image data, when I used "P", I selected "Fine" for the picture quality rather than "raw." At first, I tried to select 64 or 100 ISO, but I did not always have enough light to do that, and/or I needed a tripod (which I didn't have) to allow for a slower shutter speed without blurring, so I ended up letting the camera chose the ISO, which was not as low as the reviewer recommended. I did not fool with the exposure compensation. I used 14 megapixels for the best quality prints (menu button>capture>picture size>14MP).

Most of the time (not always), pictures taken in Auto had a little richer (better) color than those taken in "P." Sometimes (infrequently) Auto would distort the color, making tan sandstone more pinkish. When I printed my pictures at home (Canon iP3600 printer, Canon software program - from Amazon), and I made 8" x 10" prints of both Auto and "P" pictures, to the naked eye, both types of prints were comparable and very good quality. Even using a magnifier, I could not notice a difference in them. I could not say one type of prints was better than the other. In the end, I was very pleased with the picture quality of all of my pictures, and I don't think the average person would have any problem with them as 8" x 10"s. Perhaps if larger prints were made, I had used all of the photographer/reviewer's recommendations, or I had a discerning eye of a professional photographer, a difference in quality would be apparent??? (You would want a low ISO, and to uses a tripod, for quality large prints.)

When taking distance shots, with trees, etc., in the foreground, the auto focus was a problem. It tended to focus on the closer object(s) rather than the distant subject that I wanted to be in focus. (I did not get into using manual focus, but doing so might have solved this problem.)

Because of concerns raised by reviewers about camera movement when the telephoto is extended, I took one reviewer's advice and got a monopod, and a "ball head" for shifting the camera's angle easily. A problem I found was that the ball head was apparently made for tripods with different size threads and would not screw onto the monopod. I tried a second "ball head" as well as a different monopod and had the same result. (On Amazon, for a few dollars you can buy a 1/4" to 3/8" converter which might have solved my problem.) Finally I bought a Canon monopod that came with a ball head attached (Canon Monopod 500 through Amazon), which worked well. In the "field," however, while the monopod kept the camera steadier than were I just standing and holding the camera, with higher magnification, there was still camera movement, especially with a little wind. What I really needed was a tripod (with a ball head). I found that if I was able to sit down, with my feet on the ground and knees up, and my elbows on my knees, I could hold the camera pretty steady - not as steady as would be the case with a tripod, but steadier than with the monopod. Whenever possible, this is what I did for distance shots, and it was sufficient. It was rare that any of my many distance shots were a little blurred (including ones taken with the monopod).

I used rechargeable batteries, both the Kodak ones that came with the camera and another brand that also made a 15 min. charger, which I purchased. The 15 min. charger seemed to work better, in terms of how long the battery lasted between charges, than the charger that came with the camera. A set of batteries lasted one day (taking a lot of pictures - 150+) to three days. I like that I can use regular AA batteries (or rechargeable batteries) so I don't have to worry about a not being able to use the camera once a special (non standard) rechargeable battery goes dead.

This camera is amazing in low light situations when not using the flash. I like that it is easy to turn the flash on or off. I also like that the camera takes SD or SDHC memory cards and does not just rely on internal memory. (I tend to use a 4GB SDHC card, which works well. I have read that it can take a little longer for the camera to function with cards with a high GB capacity but I do not know how true that is or what GB is ideal for camera functioning. It will take up to a 32 GB card.) I appreciate that one can easily switch from the electronic view finder to LCD screen and that the LCD screen is pretty large (3"). (I usually used the viewfinder when taking pictures.) I was relieved that all or almost all of what I saw in the viewfinder/LCD screen seemed to appear on the printed photo, in other words little or nothing was lost on the edges. It is also easy to review pictures and to delete ones you don't want.

Since the camera is a little slower in functioning than some other cameras, it might not be the best for action photos. (One professional review described it as having a 3.6 sec. shot-to-shot time.)

For far away and close up shots, the lens is remarkable. Sometimes stopping the telephoto where you want it would be challenging (it moves through its range pretty quickly) but this was not a significant problem.

Opening and closing the little door for the batteries can be a little hard, but I don't consider that a big deal. Using the silver button shutter release when taking vertical shots was a little difficult, and its use made it harder to keep the camera steady. When you are about to turn the camera on, remove the lens cover first, otherwise it will have to warn you the lens cover is on and it takes longer to turn the camera on.

Overall, this is a very good camera that is lightweight for its size and relatively inexpensive. If you want a camera with an amazing telephoto, and very adequate picture quality for the non-professional, this one is a very good choice.

title: What the Viewer MFR doesn't tell you about the product
text:
I just purchased and installed this viewer 12/2012. The product construction is all plastic including the lens and then painted to look like brass. In a hot climate and with the door facing south this viewer may not last long. Only time will tell.

A small portion of the gold paint had already rubbed off in shipping. The installation instructions are too generic. For a solid core wood door simply follow the installation guidelines for this product with the following exceptions which apply to all doors. Drill a small pilot hole as a guide for the larger pilot bit that acts as a guide for the 1 3/4" hole saw. Make sure that this pilot hole is placed such that the 1 3/4" hole saw will (if possible) encompass (remove) the old viewer hole. Before installing the new viewer it is important to thoroughly clean and remove all debris from inside the 1 3/4" hole otherwise the lens will be contaminated.

If the door is a hollow core door (usually filled with foam or other insulating material) and covered with thinly clad metal, fiberglass or PVC then read on. Separately drilling the pilot hole for your 1 3/4 inch hole saw will allow you to determine what type of door materials you are working with. It is important to understand that neither a fiberglass nor a PVC clad door has sufficient material strength to allow the 1 3/4 hole saw's pilot bit to properly guide (restrain) the pilot bit and saw blade while using a power drill. The saw and pilot bit will wobble and dance around on the surface of the door. What I recommend is to use another separate drill bit to drill the final pilot hole. Next, with the hole saw's pilot bit inserted into the pilot hole, turn the hole saw by hand while applying pressure. This will take a little time but eventually you will cut the proper size hole without incurring any door damage.

title: Worth the Wait
text:
I purchased this processor to replace an old Q9965 I'd had in my LGA 775 build for years. I've got to say I am completely satisfied with the purchase.

This processor is fast, like blazingly fast. I do alot of gaming and animation and this thing just crushes whatever I throw at it. I'd really get my monies worth if I did video editing or used more threading intesive programs, but part of the reason I got the i7 over the i5 of comparable quality is just because I wont buy another processor for a few years and I figured why not, maybe in the future I will use more threading intensive applications. Took my Windows Experience Index up to 7.8 out of 7.9 .

I waited for a while to upgrade to the Core i series of processors and really wanted the Ivy Bridge so I ended up waiting an extra few months to snag this thing. Can't say that I regret purchasing over the Sandy Bridge, performance increase comparatively is negligable though. About 3-6% better performance out of the Ivy Bridge. The Ivy Bridge also runs hotter than Sandy Bridge, but even with the stock fan it stays cool enough under load.

Integrated graphics (especially with a Z77 chipset motherboard) are a pretty neat feature, however I do not utilize it as I'm running with a 470 gtx. The really nice thing about this processor is that it has native support for USB 3.0, SATA III, and PCI Express 3.0 right out of the gate. Making it relatively future proof for at least the next few years (granted your motherboard has support). So when I do get that new graphics card I dont have to worry about compatibilty issues :)

I would highly recommend purchasing this processor if you're looking for a new Ivy Bridge. I would not however recommend upgrading from a Sandy Bridge for this, as the difference in performance is minimal at best. No need to speed another $350 on a cpu that does what your old one does except 4% better. But if you're still stuck 2 or 3 generations back as I was, this makes a world of difference, you wont be sorry.

title: High Price, High Performance
text:
I've written an extensive review of this lens on my website, complete with photographic and video examples. I'll share some of the finer points of this lens here, but for the full review, just google this lens and matthew durr photography.

So, making this review quick and concise: what does this lens do well on a NEX-7?
-Extremely high cross-frame sharpness
-Negligible chromatic aberrations, both in- and out-of-focus
-Stellar build quality
-Smooth bokeh up close
-Superb rubberized focus ring (it's fly-by-wire focusing though)

What holds the Touit 32mm back
-Bokeh gets a little busy as focus distance increases
-Multiple flare reflections
-Noticeable barrel distortion for a prime lens
-Expensive at $900

This lens can be a tough one to recommend to just anyone with a NEX (or Fuji camera, for that matter) considering its price. Compared to its most obvious competition, the Sony 35mm f/1.8 OSS at half the price, the Zeiss doesn't present a very high value. In some ways, like distortion and bokeh, the Sony actually performs better. In terms of pure photographic potential, the Zeiss is superior. But for anyone who wants to go handheld at night, or record handheld video often, the optical stabilization in the Sony makes it a marginally better lens. Both the Sony 35mm and Zeiss 32mm are great lenses, with different attributes to each.

title: It's a 22 pin card
text: The picture depicts the card as shipped with 22 pins (11 before and 11 after the key notch)  For more information about PCI standards check out the PCI express wiki at en.wikipedia.org  The 4 pins exceeding the physical PCI Express x1 specification will require to install it in a longer slot (i.e. Asus Sabertooth Z87 PCIe 2.0 slots are physically limited to 18 pins) The controller chipset is a Marvell 9230, the 18 pin version (SI-PEX40064) of this card uses the Marvel 9215 controller. title: Yellow tint needs to be addressed by Dell
text:
I am just getting ready to return the third sample of this monitor that has a YELLOW TINT issue. My original order was for two P2414H monitors to use side by side on a Mac Pro. One of the monitors from my original shipment has a beautiful crisp, clear, and color accurate display. The other monitor from the same delivery had a very annoying yellowish tint that affected all colors displayed on the screen and cannot be corrected by calibration. I returned the defective one for a replacement and received another monitor with the yellow tint problem. I have one sample of a correctly functioning monitor so I know that Dell is capable of manufacturing an excellent product. I've tried to get Amazon to contact Dell to get the issue resolved. So far, all Amazon will do is continue to replace the monitors that I return or provide a refund.

The experience has been extremely frustrating. I recommend not purchasing the P2414H until Dell acknowledges the problem, recalls the defective units, and FIXES the root cause. All of the units are Rev A00 (including the one that does not exhibit the problem). They were manufactured in July 2013.

title: 7720 - For RV use - Not bad if you can accept GPS Quirks
text:
I'll write this backwards:
1) I only tried this locally in a pickup truck, not had the chance to try For Real on the road with an RV.
2) I returned my 7720 to Amazon within the 30 days, and got a refund less $7 shipping, very straightforward online procedure.
3) The $7 loss was well worth it after I got a 7715 on Ebay for about $90 less! More of that later!
4) Basic Appraisal and warning to Beginners: (a) I'm a beginner to GPS and am having to get used to GPS quirks. Example: to leave my workplace I can just turn left onto the main street. GPS tells me to go straight on, then drive 'around the block' to get back onto the main street! Why? But a friend's older Garmin says the same thing! So it's a general GPS quirk, not just Rand McNally. Same applies to my main route home: I take a more-direct backroad (which is still fine for trucks/RV's) but I cannot get the GPS to take that route! It's 1st choice is actually a dangerous, narrow windy route miles away, up through hills - when there's actually another better route. (and yes I DID try different settings: shortest route, quickest route, CAR not RV, etc!). So the point is, I'm not sure it can be trusted to give the 'best' route. My worry is: if I take a trip in an area I don't know, how many extra miles will this GPS be taking me? Friend's attitude is: use an atlas, and the GPS only mainly as a Get-Me-Out-Of-Here tool, where at least any longer route is still preferable to being lost for hours!
I've been reading reviews of this 7720 compared to previous versions (eg 7710). I can assure you screen is bright and clear. It doesn't nag when Re-Calculating (which it mostly does fairly quickly) when you take a different route to what it expected. Nice large screen (now the problem where to mount it!). But I keep forgetting how to get from one function to another - one main complaint about this GPS. I wish there was a clearer better (more logical) way. There might be some quirks in there too - things I wish it did, but doesn't. I spent 45 mins trying to 'teach it' my favoured route home, by AVOIDing some routes it kept trying to use, and setting VIA's for the route I wanted, but had to give up when after about 5-6 'correction steps' it would just ignore everything I told it and go back to its first suggestion: and each time my forgetting how to jump back and forth between screens/functions to set them up!
I know Garmmin users prefer Garmins, and they might well have better menus etc. But must admit, from reading reviews on this GPS vs the Garmin equivalent, I didn't see many people saying they 'HATE this and MUCH prefer the Garmin'... Leading me to believe this is just as good as the - more expensive - Garmin, that they both have their own problems and quirks. So I decided not to 'buy and try' a Garmin! People say this Rand has useful campsite info, which I like the sound of, though the few campsites I tried 'at random' had not-much info. Maybe because I was only trying smaller cheaper ones?! Need to check it out For Real on the road. (Garmin-lover friend tried this and said 'it gives TOO much info'!)
5) Now - the 7715. Not many people realise Rand brought out a 7715 and just sold them in Walmart. Not sure if they are still there. It's almost identical, it does also have the video input like the 7720, but doesn't have 'predictive traffic' (so what?) nor access to Rand's own trip photos and videos (so what?) - and it's CHEAPER! Go hunt for them, there must be some somewhere! I got one.

title: Very good GPS
text:
I have resisted buying a gps or laser rangefinder for many years. I had no use for a clumsy device that I would surely lose. Not to mention the time and effort to use it. Then I read about a gps device called "I am Caddie." It sounded great. It was small, light and clipped to the visor of my golf hat. All I had to do was push a button and it would tell me the distance to the center of the green. On the way to buy "I am Caddie" I ran across the Golf Buddy and bought it instead. I am glad that I did.

The main reason I chose Golf Buddy was the display. I didn't have to push a button. The distance was always on display. I had the choice to remove my hat and read the distance, or push the button and hear the distance. The same button would toggle between center, front and back of green. The distance is accurate and quickly displayed. You can walk toward the green and see the distance change. The battery lasts more than 36 holes per charge and it seems like every course is already in Golf Buddy. There is nothing to download.

There is one flaw. The Golf Buddy automatically recognizes the tee that you are on and automatically gives you the distance to that hole. If you hook or slice your shot onto or near another tee, the Golf Buddy will change holes. This can be an inconvience. But, as long as you do not stray onto another tee, you could play an entire round without ever touching the Golf Buddy. One final note, I can't tell that I am wearing the Golf Buddy on my hat.

Easy to navigate.

I wish that it would allow two aps of any type to run at once: I can play solitaire (or another simple game) while listening to an audio book, but cannot have a video running while playing solitaire. I wish the silk browser were a bit quicker to load.

But the beautiful interface and lightweight, functional design have me absolutely convinced I made the best choice out of the options available.

Worth your money!

Highly recommend.

title: Poor materials, superb display
text:
So after weeks of watching, I went ahead and bought two of these monitors for 265 when a resaler (Triplenet pricing) was having a sale. First impressions were good, the monitors had a simplistic, utilitarian design I especially liked and the stands seemed solid (I'm using a monitor stand so I can't comment on those). Upon installation I was blown away by the display quality and viewing angles. The rumors are really true about these monitors; even though it's only a 78% gamut display, you won't know the difference unless you are a professional who relies on color accuracy. The display will blow you away if you are coming from a TN panel. I spent the afternoon looking at photos, admiring the quality of the color reproduction. It's actually much similar to getting a new pair of glasses. Also I'd like to add that the input lag is minimal and I was able to play FPS games with no ill effect.

However, a month into the purchase I noticed a small plastic plate in the rear had popped out. I had to use a knife to lift the plastic to pop it back in. It hasn't set properly and still pops out slightly. Now, I don't know if this was a defect or a shipping problem, but it is an issue that I believe has to do with the cheap plastic construction used on the monitor. On a related note, the (Amazing) panel feels cheaply constructed on a physical level. When you push in the panel, it has way too much play, going a few millimeters past its point. Now I know these seem like trivial, superficial problems, but I expected much more from such a highly regarded monitor that costs about $280 average (at the time).

Overall, I'm happy with the monitor, but just beware of what it really is before you dive in. An entry-level monitor with cheap materials with a great display. The construction is really just a minor gripe, and monitor does its job well, so I'm giving this 4 stars.

Pros:
Great colors and viewing angle (The 178 degree viewing angle makes portrait orientation a possibility)
Intuitive menu makes for easy, quick adjustments
USB hub is very useful
Comes with most cables, but not DisplayPort
Clean, modern design

Cons:
Flimsy construction, a lot of play in the display
Cheap materials used
Anti glare causes some discoloration at certain angles (very, very minimal)

EDIT: Just noticed the damaged/defected monitor also has a yellowish tint compared to the other one. I never really noticed until now, dropping a star for that. For me, the color wasn't such a big issue, but for many others, it might be huge. Again, take this monitor for what it is: an upgrade for the average consumer, not for professional creatives who rely on color accuracy.

Update from 9/13/2014: Got a chance to use the stand, and I can certainly say that this monitor is rugged where it matters, although there is some shaking if you are typing really hard. But, for 99% of the time, you won't even notice it. Aside from the stand, everything is working as it should, and I've had no problems except for this tiny bright dot that only shows when there is a white background. Not a huge issue but it's there... so I stand by my original rating of 3 stars. The value is there, but Dell's QA could use some work.

As an 80 Plus Platinum certified PSU the efficiency is top notch, and it provides more than enough power for any reasonable build. GIven the extreme efficiency and build quality this is a PSU that you can carry with you to future builds, so the price isn't a problem. title: I shoot with a D5100 and I really liked the heft of the lens/camera combination
text: My first test trial with this lens was early morning about 30 minutes after sunrise. I have to admit I am very impressed with the lens. I am not a professional and have never used "professional" grade glass however I do have enough experience (and common sense!) to know if a piece of equipment is junk or not. This is not junk. The lens itself is "dense" when holding it, meaning it does not feel light or cheap. That alone does not mean it is quality but it is a first impression. I shoot with a D5100 and I really liked the heft of the lens/camera combination. I shot about 40 frames mostly at either 11mm or 16mm, ISO 100 and my aperture set at F4. As I was using aperture priority my shutter speed varied from 1/30th to 1/80th while shooting a variety of different subjects. The park I was at contains a small lake separated by a foot bridge and several trees with differing shades of green leaves. With the sun shining down from just over the tops of the trees there was a nice light with contrast and reflections in the water. The lens focused accurately without hesitation. I never felt like the lens was hunting ( I was using center point auto-focus as suggested by a review I had read for this lens). After a preliminary review of the raw files it is my opinion that Tokina has solved the chromatic aberration problem they have been notoriously known for along with edge to edge sharpness. I know that it will take more than 40 images to make a final determination of how good this lens however so far, based on this early test I feel this lens is a winner. I have several air shows I will be attending in the coming months with will afford multiple opportunities to put the lens through its paces.

title: Poor Quality Control=A Ruined Christmas
text:
After reading reviews for this product on multiple websites, my wife and I settled on this microscope for our 6 year-old son, a budding doctor and scientist. Amazon was great as usual, with the microscope arriving in great condition and in time for Christmas.

After opening it we encountered one minor and one major issue. First, although the instruction manual is lengthy, it mentions absolutely nothing about the ocular lens. As it has been mentioned on other sites, if you're not careful taking it out of the box, it will come apart. We poured through the instruction booklet but found nothing about this critical part of the microscope. After some online sleuthing, we were able to piece it back together. This was not a huge deal but could have been addressed somewhere in the manual.

The major issue we had was the battery compartment construction. When it was put together, one of the battery connectors was not installed properly, leaving the end with the spring (the - connection) at almost a 45 degree angle. Clearly a build flaw, what's most disconcerting is that there is an inspection/QC sticker less than two inches from the error. So, long story short, no microscope on Christmas.

Thames and Kosmos must do a better job of inspecting their products before letting them out the door.

title: A fantastic keyboard!
text:
Logitech has always been a trustworthy company in the past and this keyboard is no exception. It's extremely light, very thin, the keys have good response while not being loud, the USB receiver has a very low profile so I can keep it attached to my laptop without worrying about it catching on things. It comes with a bigger USB dongle attachment for the receiver for desktop use, as well as a soft cloth for cleaning the two solar panels on the keyboard itself. I play a fair number of computer games and have had zero trouble with response time while gaming.

When they say you don't need direct sunlight to charge it, they're not kidding. In a reasonable well-lit room I can earn a positive charge even at night. I've never 'run out' of battery yet.

The only negative I can think of is if you're transporting the keyboard it could be easy for the top panel to become scuffed or scratched. I keep pretty good care of mine so I can't speak to how it would affect the solar panels. Individuals arguing that the surface collects fingerprints easily -- yes, it does, but even on the solar panels it doesn't affect the performance. If you're very concerned about appearances it's a simple matter to use the cloth to keep it clean.

I have never used a wireless keyboard before because of battery concerns. A device that charges itself is a huge plus -- I'd love to see them figure out a way to have a self-charging wireless mouse next!!

This keyboard works natively in Linux. For Windows users it also has a 'Solar App' that will tell you battery percentage AND how much of a charge you're pulling in from ambient or direct light. (A 60-watt lightbulb nearby was sufficient to generate positive charge in the middle of the night.)

text:

I watch YouTube Videos and movies with my Virgin Mobile hotspot; it is an excellent e-reader and the accessories that come with it make it an affordable bargain. Certainly there are better tablets but for the price and for what it does it is a sensible purchase. For those who care little about status symbols or are honest about their budgets, this will work for you. Just purchase a 32gb sdhc card, Office pro and you are in business. Enjoy.

3-24-12 I wanted to update my comments on the Cruz for the haters out there! I have been able to download 4 additional browsers and many news and mag apps that should be checked out. A great browser is QQ, which runs on cloud; Dolphin, Maxthon, Skyfire and MSN mobile are also good. Overdrive Media console is a good app for downloading library books for reading.

The Amazon app store is getting better, offering more apps, as well as Get Jar apps. There are plenty of productivity apps for those of us who are not game players. This reader/tablet does well for those of us who are budget conscious (the working poor) and recognize that an IPad cost more than a mortgage payment! So that was a no brainer to bypass it. I got my Cruz at Walmart.

It is sufficient.

4-29-12

I have continued to evaluate this product as I seem to be enjoying it quite a bit. I continue to add apps thru the Amazon Marketplace and many of the games based the old Simon are great. There is Lost Jungle, Mahjong and quite a few reader apps which I use for all the free ebooks out there. What I am pleasantly surprised about is the email app that came with it. I downloaded Hotmail and Yahoo email apps for my personal emails. I utilze the on board email app for my business emails and calendar which is a boon for this android.

I have learned a little patience as it is not as quick on the net as some of the 3.0 and higher droids but it is no problem. I find myself using only the QQ and Skyfire Browsers now. I keep my device functioning well by cleaning out the cache weekly.

I brought my tablet from Walmart for 80.00. It is still the best bargain available. Enjoy the discovery.

title: Stunning Picture Quality, 3D is Amazing
text:
I am blown away by the quality of the picture. 2D HDTV viewing is phenomenal. Coming from a Sony 55" NX720 (no slouch in PQ department either) I can say that the this set BEATS the Sony hands down. The build quality is excellent, and I like the design of the base. Where this HDTV really shines for me is 3D viewing! Having dealt with Active 3D technology from Sony for the past 1.5 years, I can definitively state that Passive 3D is BETTER for me. With Active the crosstalk was horrendous. The glasses were heavy, had to be charged, and gave me headaches due to the active shudder flashing. Plus, the crosstalk was present across the top of the screen, rendering 1/3rd of the picture blurry. This sucked for games and for watching ESPN 3D where the score text is kept. I've already watched Avengers 3D and Tron Legacy 3D on this LG and it's a brand new experience. I can actually enjoy the movie now. Everything is in focus and comfortable to watch. My wife and kids now WANT to watch 3D again! 2D viewing is a very pleasant experience, the best I've seen. The clarity is amazing.

The TV interface is very well organized, and quick. The remote is easy to use (if you've used a Wii then you can use this) but I setup my Logitech Harmony remote so I don't really use the "magic" remote anymore. In short, I am very pleased with this LG set (my first LG!), the WAF is off the charts, and my kids love watching 3D again.

title: One of the finest in a long time
text:
Having cut my teeth in electronics and especially being enthralled with radio, I have over the few decades owned many different brands of radio, even the odd Sony, as well as antiques. The two aspects of radio I enjoy are the fact that it works, that is, one can receive information from distances through thin air, and being able to receive stations from far distances. So sensitivity is key to my selecting a radio.

The Sony ICF38 I acquired was done sight unseen, used, and for a good price. I never heard of it nor even wanted to buy a modern AM-FM radio since most are digital and are not the best of performers, especially in the AM band. And the sound quality (I am also a designer and builder of hi-end audio equipment) is usually less than acceptable.

The Sony ICF38 has many of them beat. Sensitivity and selectivity, the ability to separate stations close together, and nice musical sound is beyond what I expected from such a low priced radio. It is so sensitive it rivals an old Zenith transistor radio I have that uses what is called TRF tuning. I pick up stations far away so clearly that it is astonishing. FM is also very sensitive. So sensitive that one need not extend the antenna at all to receive most local stations clearly. To do so actually will overdrive the FM section. So only extend the antenna if one is in a fringe area. I believe the complaints from others about the FM reception is due to that fact.

As an engineer and electronics experimenter, I did take mine apart and align it for optimum performance. And this radio sure did not benefit as much as you'd think, as out of the box it performs remarkably well.

All in all for an analog AM-FM radio, and the good price, one can not go wrong.
