title: Better than you probably think.
text:
Pleasantly surprised! After a home robbery where the thieves stole our beloved Samsung plasma tv, we were put in the position of shopping for a replacement. Honestly, I was quite spoiled by having a plasma originally - many of the LCD and LED HDtvs we shopped simply looked sub-par in the black levels and overly bright with the whites. Of course, I know from experience you can't just go by what they look like on the shelf in the retail store, you need to get that thing at home and tweak the settings before ultimately deciding. I should also admit that I'm kinda cheap, I'll pay for quality but I can handle a little less than perfect if I'm going to save a decent amount.

I stumbled across this tv during a Cyber Monday sale and couldn't beat the price. Not super sure how much I'd like it once I got it or how long it would last, I optioned for a reasonably priced 3 year warranty.

I set it up last night and have to say I was QUITE impressed with the picture quality right out of the box. However, my wife and I were both freaking out at the way everything looked 'too fake' and soap opera-ish. Messing with the image settings and going to 'advanced' settings at the bottom, you can turn off the motion sync, which I would highly recommend. It might be ok for sports or something, but why else would anyone use that?

The blacks aren't as rich and detailed as my old plasma and the bright whites are still blinding when watching at night, but the color and crispness of the image is really really good. We're sitting about 8-9 feet from the tv and anything bigger would almost be too big. It's a great size.

Pros? 3 HDMI ports! One of the HDMI ports is MHL ready, so you can run mobile content directly from a smartphone (with a connector) or with the roku stick, without the need to plug them into the power sockets. It's Big. The stand that it sits on is SOLID. I'm not going to freak out if my cat goes slithering around it. The remote is not bad, has 'favorites' option which allows you to hide channels and set your favorite channels.

Cons? Now digital audio out, only optical audio - not really a negative, but I already digital audio cables so I was a little bummed. No audio delay option, which comes in really handy when running audio to 2 different sources. Depending on the input, I have to either turn off tv audio or my surround sound system because of the slight delay which can be really annoying. Blacks can be a little muddy for really dark scenes, especially when viewed in a dark room, but that's common with most LED / LCD tvs today. Remote can be a little sensitive - you have to directly aim it to the bottom left of the screen for it to work, but that's really a minor complaint.

title: BlueAnt t2 "A big steps down"
text:
Had the t1 for two years and finally beat it up, loved the quality of the t1 but was really excited when the t2 was announced as the new upgrade. When the t2 came I immediately linked it, which is so easy with blueant. Grabbed the over the ear mount and stuck it in my ear.

T2 assessment.

Because of the design of the over-the-ear mount it presses against the back of your ear which I instantly thought might be a problem of extended use. In addition to pressing against your ear it has a counter effect of pulling the ear bud out of the canal. What that does is leave you with a bad seal in the ear resulting in a "tinny" sound and even weak sound.

T2 use.

Besides being uncomfortable I had a huge problem with "staying connected." Now, by this I don't mean it would go from synced to un-synced, I mean it was going in and out of perfect continuity. What i mean by that is when I was talking to someone they said I was breaking up, going in and out. Also, I like to use my phone with media, so while listening to music it would skip in and out like the bt was out of range even though the phone and t2 was fully charged and the phone was in my pocket.

T2 Conclusion. The sound quality, or sound filtering may or may not be improved to the other side of the conversation, but the most important aspect of a Bluetooth device was lacking. When a bt is uncomfortable and does not stay constantly linked, then it is not practical. It did eventually hurt my ear because of the mount and never gave a continues, uninterrupted connection, therefore it is on its way back to the store. I opted to buy the t1 again and probably won't look back.

title: Pointless waste of time
text:
I guess I should have paid attention to all the negative reviews. It seems that they were right on the money. I will be returning the unit ASAP.

- Setting up

The unit itself seems a little cheaply made. The front door does not fit well, and insists on detaching constantly. Inserting the drives is fairly easy, although I did have some trouble with an older SATA drive, which seems to be a few fractions of a millimeter off spec.

- USB 2.0

I populated the enclosure with two pre-formatted drives and two unpartitioned drives. The unit stared up without any problems, and the two formatted drives mounted automatically. The other two drives were visible in the drive manager, and initializing them was quite simple. I successfully copied about 40GB from one drive to another.

- USB 3.0

I attached the unit to a USB 3.0 port (that I had previously verified as working). The blue LEDs on the front of the unit flickered for quite a long time, following which I received a message from Windows stating that a drive needed to be formatted. This was repeated for all four drives, and the entire sequence was repeated three times while the device tried to initialize. On the fourth time around, the drives mounted correctly.

I was able to browse all of the drives with Explorer. However, as soon as I attempted to copy any data to the unit, all four drives immediately dismounted and I had to power cycle the device to get them to mount once more. I tried the test one more time, with precisely the same results.

- SATA

I connected the device to a SATA port. Only drive 0 mounted. This was expected, as the motherboard that I was using did not support a SATA port multiplier.

I moved the SATA cable to a SATA adapter that did offer a port multiplier. This time, all four drives mounted. I started a copy test once more. The drives dismounted after a few minutes. Nothing I did would make the copy stable.

- Conclusion

The device does not work. Period. What's more, these issues have been known for some time now, but the manufacturers appear to be uninterested in correcting the problem.

Simply put, unless you intend to use the enclosure as a USB 2.0 external drive, it simply will not work. Don't bother with it. You can't fix it, and it absolutely, 100% will fail.

title: Fixed network setup issue!
text:
I thought I'd post a quick review to share how I fixed the network issues (not being able to connect the scale to the wifi network during the initial setup) in case anyone else has a similar issue. As has been mentioned on several reviews, the scale only works with 802.11 "B" networks... it won't work on 802.11 "N" wireless networks. Since my wifi router handles all bands (A/B/G/N) simultaneously I thought it wouldn't be a problem. Well, when I went to set it up, I could never get my PC to recognize my scale... it kept telling me to remove the batteries, wait 10 seconds, and then try again. No luck any time I did this. I was trying this from a PC connected to my network using an 802.11 "N" adapter. So then I thought, what if I tried setting it up from a pc that was using a "B" adapter (so that both the PC and the scale were on the same band)? I booted up an old netbook, connected to my network using its internal 802.11 "B" adapter, and presto - scale showed up when I went through the setup steps. So, it seems you might have to make sure you are using the same band wireless if you are setting up from a PC connected to your network via WIFI (at least for me). Otherwise, perhaps try from a PC that is connected to the router via ethernet. Just thought I'd share my fix to what seems to be a common problem.

Now that its setup - I love the scale. Works very well, and syncs quickly to my fitbit.com account.

title: Meets expectations; used daily.
text:
Received as a birthday gift around the holidays and I have used it every day ever since.

I am a bit of a techno-phile. I've been using computers since the days of parachute pants and the mullet. I have both Windows and Linux computers and have fully embraced the Android OS. I still cannot bring myself to spend the money required to own Apple products, so I cannot and will not compare this to an iPad.

What a handy device it really is! It's wifi ready, has a headphone jack, a mini-HDMI output, and it can be charged with either a supplied A/C charger or a micro-USB charger. Its 7” screen size keeps the whole thing manageable but much bigger than a phone screen. I think it’s an excellent balance of size and convenience. My wife can keep it in her pocketbook without feeling weighted down or feeling like it has taken over her bag. If I had to, I could keep it in the front pocket of a pair of slacks (not jeans, though).

Even a newbie Android user should be able to figure out how to use this tablet. Follow the instructions to fully charge the batteries before using without the plug. But I started working on it right away with the device plugged in. The Settings screen is accessible through the bottom of the screen and the apps list button on the home screen. Through Settings you can get to the wifi settings where you log in to your local network. I was on the internet in less than a couple of minutes. After a quick download through the Play store, all my favorite apps including IMDB, Accuweather, Firefox and more were immediately available. It also loaded my favorite games including 7 Little Words, Angry Birds and Texas Hold’em. To add a recent picture I took as my wallpaper, I loaded QuickPic to organize my pictures and Tonido to access all my favorite files from my home computer.

I asked for this tablet as a gift to provide two tasks, both of which it handles very well.

The first is to give me internet access - mostly IMDB - while I'm watching TV with the Queen. The wife and I love to watch TV and movies and we are always wondering where we've seen that actor/actress before. It works very well for just about any online access you will need. I’ve even used it in the kitchen to try a new recipe for banana bread.

The other task was to have an easily portable tablet available for when the Queen and I are running errands or on a road trip. I've installed the 'hot-spot' option on my cell phone so when we're out and about, we can easily log into the internet via wifi while driving or shopping. Our previous tools for that were either our cell phones (not as easy to see) or our laptops (too big and clunky for the car). This tablet provides the perfect balance.

Some downsides to the Y88 are the battery life and the availability of apps. My favorite weather app is WeatherBug which is not available for this tablet. Not sure if it’s the tablet or WeatherBug that’s at fault here, but I found a reasonable solution with Accuweather. There were a few other apps that I looked into loading and they were not available, but I’ve also found viable workarounds. The battery issue is not unusual for tablets, so no major complaint here. I’ve dug up some eBay sourced micro-USB chargers from around the house and have plugged them in where I sit with my tablet around the house and just operate ‘wired’ as necessary. Not that big a deal. We do the same in the car until we need to go wireless. Simple.

Overall, this tablet met all my expectations. Hope it does the same for you!

title: Very slow and unintuitive controls
text:
First of all it is a decent radio. Has great sound out, screen is nice, and plays MP3s off the DVD drive or the USB port. Pandora controls for my Galaxy Nexus over Bluetooth. Has an adapter for Apple products, but no microUSB for Android\windows phones. Haven't tried to plug in the phone to the USB, but according to manual Android only compatible over Bluetooth. Has a remote, that I will have to get used to because of the unintuitive controls on the front of the radio.

The Biggest cons:
1. Very slow Mp3 startup. From car turn on to start playing a file off either the USB Drive or DVD it takes 45seconds. My factory stereo was within five seconds (CD with mp3s in folders).
2. The unintuitive GUI. The most important controls for the stereo are on the right side. The least used features on the left. Next, Previous, Play/Pause, all on the right away from the driver. Change folder is on the left side (I always seem to push this button instead of the next song button).
3. Would have really liked more buttons, especially a next, previous and play/pause button. Not a fan of touch screen in a car, but I like the large screen that shows mp3 file data.

A couple minor cons:
1. No cover for faceplate.
2. The stupid brake cable...easy to disable by grounding the wire (no need to buy one of those cables, just ground it to the chassis or the ground wire for your stereo).
3. Those that use a standard Metra/Scoshe install kit, be aware that this stereo is too large to fit it over the back end. Just remove the stereo's face, trim plate, and mounting cage and slide it from the front and it will fit. It will not fit over the back end of the stereo without trimming the mounting kit.
4. Limited to 250 folder and 5000 files. I had no problem with the 5000 file limit, but I have all my artists broken down by album. It's not 250 folders per level, but 250 total folders.

I still haven't used the phone connected by BT, so unsure if that works as expected. I have no interest in Sat Radio or any of the apps. Would be nice to have my phone's screen imaged onto the front of the deck (especially for Navigation), but I won't take any points off for that.

Edit (June 2014): I was able to get the boot time down to 15 seconds. Instead of having a folder for each album, I now have a folder for each artist. I also used another flash drive (so the old one could be the culprit).
I also found another CON: You can not have randomize songs and stay in a folder. It's either or. So, you can have it mix one folder, and as soon as it's gone through all the songs it will move to the next folder. Or you can have it stay in that one folder, but it won't mix your songs instead playing in Alphabetic order. So, for me the random folder is good enough, but once it has played the last song I have to press folder back and mix folder again.

text:
The sound quality is amazing however the Apple Air barely allows you to stream music any farther than 35 or 40 feet without skipping. I am using Time Warner cable Internet which is pinging at 18ms with a download speed of 15mbs and an upload speed of 2mbs. I am running a Netgear R6300 which is one of the fastest routers around. My modem is of equal quality.

The set up was not difficult and takes about 5 plus minutes.

My complaint is the lousy streaming capabilities not the excellent sound quality. If this system would have had a workable Airplay capability I would have rated it 5 stars. When you pay $867 the Airplay system should work.

Update 12/23/12; We just received Apple TV as a gift and connected it to a plasma TV which is about 4 feet further away than the spot we had the B&W A7 set up. If you recall the B&W would not stream to this location without skipping or long interruptions. The Apple TV is able to stream both music and video perfectly with no skipping or interruptions to this location. This demonstrates and proves to some extent that the B&W A7 has issues with its Air Play.

Update 12/30/12: To further prove my point that the B&W A7 has poor music streaming abilities on 12/28/12 we set up a newly purchased Samsung DA E750 in the same exact location as we previously had the B&W A7. We used the same router and network setup that we used with the B&W A7. The only difference is that the Samsung DA E750 streams music flawlessly without skipping or interruptions using Airplay. In conclusion, despite having excellent audio quality the B&W A7 has poor music streaming qualities using Airplay.

title: Decent but there are better out there for less
text:
Upgrading from a OCZ Vertex 3 256 GB Drive to this Samsung 840.
The Samsung is a little slower in Seq Read speeds about 498 MB/s vs the OCZ 529 MB/s. Seq writes are much lower around 317 MB/s vs OCZ 492 MB/s.
Random Reads are much better at around 66.5K IOPS vs the OCZ which is at 46.3K IOPS (quite a bit below the 840 series published specs of up to 98,000).
However, Random writes are much less than the OCZ Vertex 3, Which has around 74.3K IOPS where the 840 has around 22.8K IOPS. Which is significantly below the "up to" 70,000 makes me wonder if I got a crappy drive. Poor QA? They do test these things right??

The drive comes with a tuning appilcation "Samsung SSD Magician". This is for tuning the drive and running performance tests. Pretty neat but when I went to the "Disk Clone" function. It told me I need to install Symantec Ghost 15. It give me a link to the Samsung download site where I was able to download and install Ghost. However, there was no valid code to activate Ghost that came with my drive. I checked the back of my CD lable but the code that was there was "Invalid" and I had to end up hunting a 3rd party application to copy my data over or buy it from Symantec. I found this very irritating since the box says it has data migration software. But then again nothing said it would work ;)

Over all it is almost twice the size at 500 GB, Over twice the price and it also seemed to have at least twice the agrivation.

If I had a do over button, I would stick with OCZ Agility drives.

Note - All speed tests were done with the included Samsung SSD Magician application that is included with the drive.

Meanwhile, I have tried to use the T650 without going through this fake driver update. No response at all from the cursor on my screen. I'm using a PC running Windows 7. If I ever get this thing to work, I will come back and update this review.

As for the physical device itself, it is larger than the touchpad in my laptop. It has enough weight to it that it won't flop around on my desk (like an earlier (smaller, lightweight) external touchpad did). When I first removed it from the box and placed it on my desk, I tried running my fingers over the top. When my fingers are totally dry, they move over the surface just fine. But if my fingertips are even a little bit moist, they stick more than glide. So I don't know yet how well this will work over the course of a full day of using this device.

UPDATE: I tried going to the download website (URL provided in documentation). I downloaded and installed the suggested software. But as part of this process, it requires plugging in the receiver, which triggers the request to register, which then takes you to the SALES website for software that will keep your drivers up-to-date. And my touchpad still will not work. UGH!

I may try using the touchpad with my computer at home to see if I get better results. But for now, I am very disappointed.

SECOND UPDATE: plugged the receiver into my laptop at home. Device driver installed automatically, without any problems. Both work and home laptops are running Windows 7. HOWEVER, home computer was purchased new with Windows 7 already installed. Work computer had different version of Windows when purchased, but was recently updated to Windows 7. Perhaps the difference in installing the driver is due more to the different computer manufacturers? One Dell, the other HP. At any rate, I had purchased with the intent to use at work, so I am still disappointed that the driver won't install or is not available. But other than that, it is working fine. Now I need to learn the various gestures that are available.

title: Nice Little external box for SATA II / USB 3
text:
The box takes a SATA II (3gps) drive and connects it to a USB 3 port. It sheds heat quickly. Two screws hold in one end cap to the aluminum box. You remove the end cap to insert the drive, taking care when tightening not to strip the aluminum channels that hold the screws. Longer screws with more threads would make it less likely that one would strip the channels but they seem long enough as it is if you use an appropriately sized screw driver and don't go nuts torquing in the screws, you'll be alright.

Two shorter, flat head screws hold the drive to the curcuit board/end cap. You might find it hard to get moth screws lined up. Don't tighten them both unitl both oare threaded in most of the way -- this will make for easier alignment. The hard drive slides onto the SATA connectors snaugly against the curicut board - this is a good thing as it helps keep the connection from wiggling and deteriorating -- take you time and use a little care getting the drive onto the connector.

Don't believe the USB 3 speeds printed on the box; your SATA II drive will never work that fast. USB 3 transfer rates exceed SATA II, so you'll get all you can in terms of speed for your SATA II drive but the SATA II will limit what you can get from the USB 3. If you can forgive this one small market deception, which the whole hard drive industry exploits, then you can enjoy getting the most from your SATA II drive. Note that SATA II is often called SATA 3 Gbps to make it sound like SATA III. SATA II transfers at up to 3 Gbps and SATA III at up to 6. If you can forgive them this one other common market deception, which the whole hard drive industry exploits (seems the industry can't quite tell the truth about disk sizes or speeds ;) ), you can enjoy your SATA II drive performing well with this box.

There's no shock cushioning built into the box, so you don't want to bang it around lest you harm the drive. Most boxes have a rigid attachment at the electrical connector, which tends to defeat any shock absorption anyway. The box itself seems to be reasonably rugged. I didn't do any quantitative stress tests, but bouncing it around the shop didn't cause any functional degradation the box.

If you've been using a USB 2 box, putting your SATA II drive in this box will you very noticeable improvement. If your backup operation, say, used to take an hour or so, it'll probably only take 1-15 minutes now.

I think the sales blurb says it takes up to 500GB drives. Actually, it takes any 2.5" drive up to 9.5 mm tall, so it can take, e.g., The Western Digital Black 750GB 2.5" drive. However, 1,000 GB (1 Terabyte) and larger drives still tend to exceed the 9.5mm height and won't fit. Although this will likely change soon as technology advances.

You will feel the box warm up if you do prolonged read/writes to the drive. This is normal -- the aluminum box is absorbing heat form the hard drive and radiating it to the room air -- plastic boxes tend to hold in the heat. I've used these for 100GB backups (you could call it a prolonged write operation, and the drive didn't not get anywhere near manufacturer's maximum operating specs.

title: One of the best GPSr's I have ever owned
text:
I have owned quite a few handheld GPSr's over the past 15 years. In total, about 20 units, 15 of which were Garmin's. I use them primarily for hiking and geocaching, and generally prefer durable, stand-alone GPSr's over a smartphone app.

That said, I am quite impressed by the 62s. My previous unit was an Oregon 300 and I just recently traded it in for this one since I was not happy with the touchscreen. The 62s is a very solid device, with sturdy buttons, ample memory for maps, user-replaceable batteries (AAs), and a super sharp screen which is easy to see in daylight. The menus are laid out very well, and are intuitive enough for beginner users. This is one area Garmin has really improved over the years - adding the right shortcuts on screens where there weren't any on past models. The unit is also fully integrated with geocaching GPX files, so you can view caches, log attempts, view hints, and customize to your heart's content.

The 62s comes with a high sensitivity receiver which not only finds your position quickly, but also maintains your position even when the sky is significantly blocked (e.g. thick forest, high walled canyons, etc.) By the time it has booted up, it will be ready to go (cold starts may take up to a minute though). Very impressive, especially when compared to the older Garmins from the early 2000s (i.e. original etrex). Track logging is accurate, and compass and altimeter features work very well for the price point. I do wish the compass needle updated faster as it did on the older models. Currently, it swings slowly, which makes it a bit more difficult when closing in on a geocache since you can overcorrect your target more easily.

Overall, I am quite impressed with the 62s. It is the type of GPS I would be happy owning for the long-run. Very solid and durable design. I would highly recommend it to any geocaching and/or hiking enthusiast!

+Solid design
+Robust menu system
+Geocaching features well integrated
+Good battery life
+Takes standard AA batteries!
+Fits well in the hand
+Strong antenna

After mounting a more modern and more powerful deck, they sounded great for a 4" speaker. The new deck only has 20 watts/channel, and naturally the THD is much lower than the old one. For those who bash these in the reviews, you have to understand your application and what will give you the best performance. If you need a 4" speaker for your application, these are the speakers you want. Period.

title: Once fully updated this Tablet rocks!
text:
Ok, most of us that are tech inclined know this tablet has had a rough start. Lots of glitches, some claimed factory defects and the dock has been a disaster. However, to ASUS's credit these things are slowly but surely being sorted out. I myself came close to returning the tablet for a brightness issue where it would slowly change in increments up and down even though auto brightness and power saver were turned off. Asus employees could not help me find a solution thru email and live chat online. However, there is a fix for this issue. When you go to the update section on the tablet for the first time it will go and get an update to bring the tablet up to version 4.3 android. However, for those of us that did that in November or early December we didn't get the final update. For that I had to go to the Asus website and in the support section download the newest update which is build number 10.26.1.18. If you have that you are all set(previous update was 10.26.1.7). If not, download the appropriate region file for you and unzip the file. It's very important that you get the correct region which you will know from Settings/About/Software/Build number on your Tablet. After unzipped you will find another zipped folder. Leave this one zipped and put it on a blank microsd card(2GB or larger in size). To be safe, back up all important info you have created on the tablet and charge your tablet fully(Updates sometimes go horribly wrong unfortunately so do this at your own risk). Then, load the card into the tablet while it's on and it should recognize there is an update now there. Follow the instructions and update. For me this has fixed my issue completely. I have been using the tablet heavily for a couple days now with no incremental dimming glitches. If this all sounds confusing find a friend that knows how to update electronics to help you. I just thought I'd share this since i have had the hardest time finding any answers.

As for the tablet performance. It runs really smoothly with a clean version of android. Also, the screen clarity is just amazing at 1600. Some have said it's not as bright as the Samsung Note 2014 which I havn't personaly had the time to check out in stores but the Asus Tf701t has plenty of brightness for me especially when set to outdoor mode. I just keep it on full brightness without outdoor mode as I only use it indoors. When Amazon figures out the dock situation i will get one of those as a few websites have said asus had defects on the models from October and before. November on are supposedly fixed. I personaly find the keyboard dock to be a much better accessory than a pen. Plus this tablet is almost $200 less than the Samsung. Don't get me wrong the Samsung tablets are beautiful pieces of tech but all the bells and whistles were not needed by me. Got the TF701T on sale for $400 which it has been sticking pretty close to lately. The only gripe I have with this tablet is the lack of stereo speakers. There is no reason to have only one speaker anymore when you are talking about a high end tablet like this one. I'll just use headphones :-)

title: Maybe you'll love it but it turned out that it's not what I was looking for
text:
I'm a corporate video producer at a small company. I'm not a professor of filmmaking or anything but I know my way around a camera.

My theory was that even though I'm used to using higher-end HD camcordesr at work (Panasonic AF-100 or Canon 5D, for example), I'd want a more basic camcorder for home use. My primary criteria going into my purchasing research: something HD, something I can quickly get out & turn on to record my family, acceptable image quality, and no autofocus motor sounds. My old camcorder was a Canon F20, an SD camcorder that has some pretty bad autofocus motor sounds. My wife hated that, and it wasn't exactly my favorite thing either. I also didn't think I would need to spend a ton of money, so this camcorder looked good. It's been awhile since I owned a Sony. I didn't want to spend money on a Sony projector camcorder because I didn't think I'd ever use the projector.

I was disappointed to find that this camcorder's mic picks up some of the autofocus motor sounds. Certainly not as bad as my old SD camcorder! But bad enough that I noticed it without trying too hard, so I returned it. The image quality also wasn't what I wanted either, looked too grainy for me. I decided I'd have to increase my budget and get something else. After a bunch of research (looking all the way up at the Canon G30 and some other expensive comparable Sony), I bought a Panasonic X920 on Amazon. I've had it for over a month now and I'm happy with it.

So, to summarize: my two complaints with this camera were the autofocus noises and the picture quality. If those were better, I'd likely still have this camera. The built-in USB cable is a great feature. full 1080p 60fps is cool too.

title: Great Z77 board
text:
This is my 5th ASUS board. While I considered other brands, I decided to spend a few extra bucks for the peace of mind of knowing this thing was going to work without hassle. Once again, ASUS didn't let me down. Put in my i7-3770k and everything started up with no problems. UEFI BIOS was pretty cool - nice to be able to use a mouse! The starting BIOS menu had everything needed to get things up and running quickly, with all the fun stuff just a click away in the "Advanced" menu. This was a nice improvement on previous BIOSes - having all the critical items in one place and not have having to dig through all the detailed settings from the start. Haven't really played around with (but am looking forward to) overclocking yet, nor have I played around with the hybrid GPU, thermal radar, and various other software utilites yet, so I can't really comment on that aspect of the board.

Positives:
- UEFI BIOS - easy to get started. Worked out of the box with no update needed.
- Thermal armor looks pretty sweet. Yeah looks aren't really a factor in most mobo purchasing decisions, but hey - its a bonus.
- My kids love being able to charge their devices even while the machine is powered down - nice touch.
- Q-connector much easier than plugging in every little connector one at a time.
- All the standard Intel chipset goodness is there - 6Gb/s SATA, plenty of USB 3.0/2.0 connections, Intel LAN controller, etc.

A few notes for those considering getting this board:
(hard to call these negatives, as they probably won't be a factor for many)
- For those with big CPU heatsinks (Scythe Mugen 2 is what I'm using), you may not be able to use memory sticks with big heat sinks. I used Corsair "Low Profile" memory and it fit just fine, but memory with fins/etc sticking out would have had me choosing between a new heatsink, new memory, or limiting myself to 2 slots.
- For those who want a perfectly silent system, you might consider removing the thermal armor and the fans needed to keep the air moving underneath. This is the closest thing I have to a complaint, definitely not enough to take a full star off, but the fans for the "thermal armor" are now the only audible part of my system. Its not loud (my laptop is a lot louder), but barely audible. It may be possible to tune the fan speed down a bit, but like i said, I haven't played around with that quite yet.

EDIT: I have now adjusted fans via the supplied software - noise is now a non-issue.

If you want the capability to do so, the SL1000 gets you there the most affordably. It offers a larger, 3 inch 920K dot tilting LCD, a 920K EVF as well: a better treatment than several more expensive cameras in this class. Consider the [[ASIN:B00BEHRQB4 Sony DSC-HX300/B 20 MP Digital Camera with 50x Optical Image Stabilized Zoom and 3-Inch LCD (Black)]] (about $400 at the time of this writing) that lacks RAW, and in general isn't as competent a camera, despite its comparatively high price.

If the end use is standard prints, the internet, along with 8 x 10s from time to time, you'll be happy. Give it plenty of light, try to shoot at lower ISOs, you'll be more than happy. It is no secret that more pictures are taken every day with cellphones than with any other device. It is also no secret that sales of the smaller point and shoot cameras have plummeted, but long zoom cameras have been in demand. The SL1000 does everything that your smartphone cannot, and that's a good thing.

There are a *lot* of choices out there, but not at $250. You can also spend $360 [[ASIN:B00CDIK48U Sony DSC-HX50V/B 20.4MP Digital Camera with 3-Inch LCD Screen (Black)]] and more on pocket cameras, and more. You can spend a lot more on bridge-class cameras as well. The "Ultimate Compact Camera," according to some, is the [[ASIN:B00ATM1MVA Fujifilm X100S 16 MP Digital Camera with 2.8-Inch LCD (Silver)]]. It is about $1300, though, with no optical zoom at all.

Just two years ago, no bridge camera with a 1200mm zoom was even available. And, whether we like it or not, two years from now there are going to be several more options that some will call significant. That's why the SL1000 makes sense. Anyone would call it a generally very good camera if you didn't know what brand it was. For $250, though, it is a screamingly good, outstandingly superb camera. It isn't necessarily the best bridge camera, it isn't, but it is the best for the least dollars. If you are willing to spend more, yes . . . the SX-50 Canon, the Fuji FinePix HS50EXR are all quite worthy of your consideration, as are the Fuji X-S1 and the Panasonic FZ-200. For the money, though, at this price point . . . the SL1000 is a lot of bang for the buck.

You'll probably want to drop twenty bucks for [[ASIN:B00AZOIG9I Pack Of 2 NP-85 Batteries And Charger Kit For FujiFilm FinePix SL240 SL260 SL280 SL300 SL305 SL1000 Digital Camera + More!!]] and [[ASIN:B003VNKNEQ Transcend 16GB Class 10 SDHC Flash Memory Card (TS16GSDHC10E)]] to get up and running. The 350 shot battery life is good, compared to the Nikon P520's 200 shots for example, but use outdoors in cooler weather nerfs that a bit, and even a small amount of video can run the battery down quickly.

It is a far better-featured camera than expected, with the EVF and LCD quickly putting the more expensive Canon SX-50 and Panasonic FZ-70 units both to shame. Scoring 2,773 lines per picture height via Imatest, it is one of the sharpest len arrays ever put on a bridge camera. Nor can most bridge class cameras match the 1080p60 video capability of this economical powerhouse. It should surprise very few that this camera likes a lot of light, and if you are going to spend a lot of time at the 1000mm - 1200mm area, a good tripod is your friend. I won't suggest that this is my favorite wildlife / outdoors camera, the [[ASIN:B008MB6ZX0 Panasonic Lumix DMC-FZ200 12.1 MP Digital Camera with CMOS Sensor and 24x Optical Zoom - Black]] is, a far better camera for my purposes with commensurately higher price tag to go along with it.

The SL1000 delivers solidly on its intended target: a huge zoom range for not huge dollars.

title: Good Idea, Poor Design and Execution
text:
After having a disappointing result with the [[ASIN:B004QK7HI8 Paper Thin Leaf Indoor HDTV Antenna]], I started looking around for a better antenna that was amplified and had better VHF reception. This antenna seemed to be the best bet based on all the reviews for it, and other ones that pointed to it, but that wasn't the case. I'll give it credit for being a simple design - only three big parts to assemble without tools: the base, the antenna, and the amplifier.

Now onto the actual performance of the antenna. On the box, Terk boasts, "Perfect antenna for local HDTV reception (channels 2-69) up to 45 miles from broadcast tower", which was ideal for me, as all of the local antennas are within a 15-mile radius from my place. When I hooked it up, it worked a whole lot better than the Leaf Antenna did, but it still failed to pick up some of the VHF stations.

Because of the lack of VHF reception, this meant I had to mess with the dipoles, which brings me to the "Poor Design and Exception" part of my title. The amplifier is part of the plug itself and has a short permanent coax cable to hook into the TV, and a permanently affixed cable to the antenna itself, which you would then connect into the amp. All of which greatly limited where you could put the antenna. Additionally, as you can see from the pictures, the antenna has an extremely small base which works fine with the antenna when mounted, but the permanent coax cable comes out the bottom of the base with the option of routing it to the front or rear, but the cable protrudes just a little below the base itself, which makes it a little wobbly. Now going back to the dipoles - they not only look silly when fully extended and trying to get the best reception, they don't seem to work, and they also help to destabilize the base as well.

It would help if they made the base a little bit wider, and gave the option of using your own longer coax cable, than to be chained to the permanently affixed ones. I gave it 3 stars because it ended up doing well, better than the leaf antenna, but docked a star for not pulling the VHF stations (despite all the different angles I put the dipoles at and rooms I put the antenna in), and docked another one for the poor design. The one antenna that I did end up going with that actually was able to snag the VHF signals was the [[ASIN:B001DFZ5II Winegard SS-3000 Amplified Indoor UHF/VHF Antenna]], as it was a simple and straight forward design, and picked up all of the local stations (though it is a little directionally dependent).

Oh and before anyone asks, yes, I did rescan each and every time I tried a new location.

title: Product Listed With Incorrect Description -- does NOT have a dimmer
text:
I ordered 2 of the [[ASIN:B001U61G10 Emerson CKS1702 SmartSet Alarm Clock Radio]] SPECIFICALLY because it was (and still is, as of the writing of this review) listed with the following description, "The clock radio features a large, easy-to-read LED display with dimmer control so it is easy on your eyes in the dark."

So, in short, the clock worked OK -- for the 5 minutes I had it plugged in. But, no dimmer control = return for refund, and my search continues.

title: Excellent for Power Outages & Camping!
text:
I bought my Coleman MicroPacker Compact Battery Lantern a few years ago mainly because of common power outages where I was living. Like many things, there are both good qualities and bad qualities of this lantern. However, there are more good things about this lantern than there are bad. Really, the only negative things I have to say about this lantern is that it is a bit small, given its name, but also doesn't have a mode where it can make a spotlight like many similar lanterns are capable of doing. Although, this lantern has an excellent battery life, is sufficiently bright enough for a small room, like a bedroom or 4-person sized tent if you're a camper. This lamp is also very portable and features a nice little hanging hook on top of it, ideal for tents.

I've noticed in several other lanterns similar to this one that they have some way of making them turn into a spotlight. This particular lantern lacks that sometimes handy feature. You have to keep in mind, though, that this is indeed a lantern and not really made for lighting things for distance but rather for area. On the same token, this is a smaller lantern and doesn't adequately light a very big area. It will sufficiently light a bedroom or bathroom during a power outage or what have you, or a small to medium-sized tent for the camper, but I wouldn't use this lantern to light more than that unless you have several of them.

These two negative aspects I mentioned above are outweighed by the great qualities about this lantern. Probably the best thing about this lamp is its battery life. The lantern uses two bright pure white light LEDs for illumination. As you're probably aware, LEDs take very little power in comparison with traditional incandescent light bulbs, giving this lantern far greater battery life than those. Also, you don't have to worry about replacing the bulbs themselves with a lantern like this as LEDs will last a very long time. I've yet to personally see an LED "burnout" and I use LEDs on all my flashlights whenever and wherever I can.

Given this lantern's namesake, it is rather small. But being smaller than the average lantern means that it's very portable. Believe it or not, I actually used to use kerosene lamps to light my house during power outages before I got smart and switched to lanterns. I liked the kerosene lanterns because they were surprisingly bright and would easily light a large sized room sufficiently, like a living room or kitchen. The portability gave me the option to go from room to room with my Coleman lantern, plus I didn't have to worry about a hot flame or even accidentally dropping the lantern which would be a disaster with a kerosene lamp!

This lamp was an impulse purchase for me in a local department store one time, but I felt safe in buying it mainly because it's made from a trusted company like Coleman who specialize in items such as this. I'd recommend this lantern greatly for tent campers as it's ideal for that, especially with the little hook at the top. There are usually places at the top center of small and medium sized tents for hanging lanterns such as this which is probably what Coleman had in mind for it when they designed it. Like I said, this is a great backup source of illumination as well during a power outage. Something that you can keep around the house and it'll be there when you need it.

title: Terrible
text: Ok So I did a lot of research into this type of camera stabilizer.  Being that Lensse makes several models I was careful to read up on their products and specifically the technical aspects of weight and balance. Both My HD cameras are not heavy at all. That is the specific reason I chose this specific model. I have a nice flip knock off that takes pretty good HD video for what it is, I also have a cannon power shot 3500 IS that I really enjoy using for video. Now I realize neither camera is pro quality and both are basically point and shoot material, I also realize for the price this stabilizer might be lacking in some areas. The design is pretty common. There are many weak points to this design mainly the materials used which in IMO are trash. The Gimbel is somewhat ok the design is not perfect but for the price its really not any different than a lot of other similar models. The biggest issue is its flimsy. The main bar is covered in rubber and is no where near solid enough.  the weights included are all the same you get 3. They have off set holes that allow you to swivel them to counter balance for offset. This is where things fail. While I can balance my camera it leans to one side. The weights do not extend far enough to counter the tilting of the entire assembly. If you add additional weight your only asking for trouble. It comes close to being straight but then its bottom heavy and and it sways. No matter how well you balance it, its a pendulum. Even with my other camera which did balance perfectly for this thing, it sways and swings like a pendulum clock for infinity. Again, i was VERY careful to choose this model based on the weight of my camera's in KG, ounces and pounds. This met all the criteria described by Lensse. Bottom line, It does not work. While using these devices is an art in itself and takes a LOT of practice the product has to start out designed well. This one is not. Its a cheap knock off. You can view videos all you want but honestly the entire Merlin design is flawed if you ask me. Its going to sway it going to take hours to balance and its not for light camera's. I know there are tons of videos on DYI merlin type devices, again don't waste your time. They all shake they all sway and they all are flawed. Now if your not really into doing a professional shoot I suppose  you an build one or buy one of the other knock offs but don't expect much. title: The Little Keyfob that Cried Wolf (but is still somewhat useful)
text:
I bought this for someone who tends to misplace either her keys or her phone on a regular basis. In THEORY, this is a great product -- so long as you have either the key fob OR the phone, you can find the other one. However, this product doesn't work as it should. There are really two different use cases for this product and I'll address both below. This review ASSUMES that you know how to connect a Bluetooth device to your phone and that you remember to charge the key fob every 4 or 5 days.

Use Case 1) You have EITHER your keys OR your phone and need to find the one you don't have. This feature works just fine. If you hit the button on the key fob, your phone will sound off. If you use the app to find the key fob, the key fob will sound off. The key fob's alarm isn't particularly loud. It's loud enough to locate them if you tend to just set them down somewhere, but if your keys are in the pocket of the jeans at the bottom of the clothes hamper then you're probably out of luck.

Use Case 2) You tend to leave either your keys or your phone behind and want an alert when you wander too far away. This feature sends so many "false alarms" that it's safe to say that it isn't effective. The product has no way of measuring distance -- all it does is alert whenever the Bluetooth connection between the key fob and the phone is lost. The manufacturer never implies anything different, so this isn't their fault -- it does exactly what it was designed to do. The problem is that "Bluetooth connection dropped" is not the same as "More than 30 or so feet away." As anyone who's ever used a Bluetooth accessory knows, there are plenty of other reasons a Bluetooth connection can drop. This results in a LOT of false alarms -- so many that you become accustomed to them and start to assume that they're all false alarms. That completely defeats the purpose. Worse yet, while the key fob just beeps, your phone plays whatever ringtone or song you choose to use as the "alarm." (So don't pick a song unless you want all of your friends to know you like it.)

The phone app DOES have some nifty extra features: It's location aware and you can choose to e-mail, Twitter, or Facebook alerts if you want. If you do, then a link to the "last known location" of your keys will get e-mailed to you or posted to Twitter or Facebook. Keep in mind that a) This is not really the last known location of your keys ... it's where you were when the Bluetooth connection dropped (see above), and b) I have no idea why you'd want to advertise to the world where you lose your keys (or phone) -- especially given the number of false alarms.

HOWEVER, so long as you know the limitations, you can still get good use out of this thing. As I said, the false alarms are annoying and defeat the purpose ... so shut them off. Yep, you read that right ... shut OFF the alarm on the phone. Here's the step-by-step procedure for making this thing work in what I'll call "stealth mode."

1) In the app settings, shut OFF the phone's proximity alarm. (Leave the other alarm turned on.)
2) Turn ON e-mail alerts.
3) In your e-mail program, create a "rule" or "filter" to send all of those e-mails you're going to get to their own folder so they don't bother you until you need them. (Alternately, you could use a different e-mail address for this purpose.)
DONE

If you do this, you will still be able to push the button on the key fob to find your phone or use the app to make the key fob beep. Also, the key fob will beep when Bluetooth disconnects, but your annoying phone alarm won't go off all the time. If you ever DO misplace your keys, just look at the last e-mail you got from the device. It'll get you close, then just make the keys beep. This will even work to find your phone provided you have some other way to get to your e-mail.

So there's the deal... If you go into your purchase knowing that THIS is what you're paying for, you should be fine. I found mine clearanced at a local store, so it was worth it to me.

text: I replaced the old paper cone speakers in my '98 Suburban with these. They were quite inexpensive, so I didn't expect a whole lot. But I was pleasantly surprised by the quality of sound. The 3 way system really brings out the mid range and treble. I would recommend these speakers.

title: wonderful looks and sound
text:
I use these with a push-pull tube amp for music. They need to be a foot or more away from a wall, and completely isolated from any furniture or shelves. There is an audible hump somewhere around 140hz and this is unbearable if augmented by stands or shelves. I actually have to EQ it out. The good news is that is the only flaw, and once tuned out, these are magical. The soundstage is broad and deep. The bass is quick and accurate down to 80. Roll-off below that just begs for a fast subwoofer to take over. I mated these to an SVS PB10-NSD and it is lightning-quick, and I had to tune the phase by about -50 deg or so until it matched the MLs, and gave me that bottomless, uniform bass I love so much.

I have a dedicated AV room and I placed these on wood/marble stands between my home theatre fronts and center speakers to get them to ear level. I have gotten into the habit of showing off my "wall of sound" to friends, when I only have the MLs and the sub playing. After a few tracks, I ask them how they like the center channel speaker, and they'll comment that it sounds fantastic. I then ask them to get up close to it and listen, and there is a visible shock/surprise on people's faces when they hear absolutely no sound coming from the center channel. When they figure out that only the "dinky" MLs are playing, they cannot believe it and usually walk over to one or the other of the fronts of the HT system just to make sure. Then they sit down and listen awhile more and point to various spots in the room from which sounds seem to be coming.

The treble is non-fatiguing in the same way that ultra high-end silk dome tweeters are, but with another degree of clarity. Voices sound like people in the room. Mid-bass has that magical intangible "I'll know it when I hear it" experience.

You cannot go wrong here.

title: Great fit, simple application!
text:
As with any product like this, the most important thing is to TAKE YOUR TIME. Make sure you clean the camera screen well - you don't want to see any particles, dust, or nose grease on it before you apply this.

The peel-off order is clearly labeled 1-2. When applying, the best place to do it is in a steamy bathroom (i.e., after a shower) to minimize dust in the air. I peel off about 1/2 of the #1 side (sticky side), keeping it face down so dust doesn't land on it, and line up the uncovered end with the camera's screen. No need to press it down, it should adhere cleanly and quickly. Slowly remove the rest of the #1 peel-off, and watch for bubbles before laying it down completely. If you have any bubbles due to dust, carefully lift the protector and use a piece of scotch tape to remove the dust from the sticky side of the protector - don't use your finger! After it's adhered to the screen, gently pull off the #2 film, being careful not to lift the entire protector off the screen. Press out any air bubbles with your thumb by "sweeping" them to the edges, and you're done!

The fit of the protector is very precise - there is MAYBE 0.5-1mm at one end of the screen that isn't covered - to me, that's an excellent fit.

Obviously, it's not going to protect the screen from a heavy impact, but it seems sturdy enough to avoid scratches from normal use. And you get 3 of them!

Would recommend!

title: It DOES work for CenturyLink(previously known as Qwest) 12mbps dsl and linksys WRT54GL Router.
text:
Just set this up in Tucson Arizona for CenturyLink 12mbps speed and I used the same settings some people described here:

PPPoE
VPI=0
VCI=32
Mode=MMODE
QoS=UBR
all others default

The problem I had was that I first was given the wrong username and password and the first Centurylink lady told me that this modem only supported up to a 7mbs speed and said it was necessary I got another modem.I think it was my mistake for the username because I was spelling it Quest instead of Qwest.I then called Actiontec support and they verifed this to be wrong and confirmed to me that this modem supports up to 20mbps speeds.

I also noticed that I had to disconnect from the wireless network to be able to access the 192.168.0.1
modem setup page. That is the number you would place on an internet browser(just like a website address) to access the modem set up page.

Everything is running normal so far no disconnections and much better than my 8-10 month old Qwest Zyxel Q100 modem that was getting disconnected almost every 5 minutes at times.Keep in mind I have only had this modem running for about 5 hours but I will definitely update this review if it fails me later on. This works for CenturyLink just fine as long as you make sure you get your username and password correctly which is case sensitive so keep that in mind.

The Actiontec tech told me that if one gets a solid red light on the internet light on the modem that this usually signifies one has the wrong username and password.So if that happens make sure you call CenturyLink again to confirm your username and password. I have this connected to a Linksys WRT54GL Router and it works just fine AFTER The initial setup via ethernet cable connected to my laptop.Dont set up your modem with a router connected to the modem.Only after u get a green internet light you can connect router and according to the actiontec technician its required to power cycle or unplug your router's power cable to get it to work properly after it is connected to the modem.

With my setup of this modem and the Linksys Router, Xbox Live ran just fine based on an initial test I did with playing Black ops.As I said i'll update if issues arrive.

Based on my experience the Actiontec Technical support was much more prepared than CenturyLink so if you have any issues they should walk you through the setup process if you need it.Actiontec tech even asked me for the Centurylink's contact number and we did a conference call with them to get the username and password so he went beyond my expectations.Unlike CenturyLink lady that just lied to me or had false information. The next Centurylink lady was much better though so it really depends who you get.

The only reason I'm knocking down a star is because I had a dropped Skype call and it was an issue on my side so not so sure how much the modem has to do with that issue but skype did tell me something was wrong with my connection. Got it for about $50 on a retail store so if you can wait you can save by getting it online.

Update November 1 2012:

Considering the fact that I went through about 4 new modems I found out that the modems I was using were not the problem but Century Link was the real problem. Although initially the Actiontec modem worked great I started having problems about a week after and I also tried new modems recommended and sent by Centurylink free of charge because I told them I wanted to cancel my internet service with them. I gave up on CenturyLink and switched to Cox Cable internet and what a difference! no disconnections and reliable connection speeds. Cable internet speeds can vary but not too much variation and best of all no more random disconnections!!!

title: Runs PERFECTLY!...but you need to know how to setup a router
text:
A couple weeks later and, this is working like a champ! You do need to know how to setup a router correctly, though, meaning if you have no prior experience setting up a router, you should get help setting up. Don't bother running the software that comes on the CD, it'll just crap everything up; just open your browser and enter the IP address of the router (192.169.0.1) and do your setup that way.

Depending on your devices, you might have to play with some settings a bit to get everything to work, but these are mostly in the encryption types. If you choose WPA Personal, select WPA or WPA2 for the encryption type and, you should be good to go. Also, don't forget to secure your wireless network and set a new administrator password for the router. I use the DIR-665 on the 5GHz frequency for 802.11n only and--this covers my MacBooks, iPads and wireless printer. I have a Linksys router slaved to this one running on 2.5GHz for 802.11g only as a separate wireless network for our BlackBerrys, wireless internet for our TV. I always have had my Xbox and PS3 hardwired to the router so, I don't have to worry about that. I have found that for the 802.11n only setting, you do have to make sure the UPnP box is checked, but this should be checked by default.

If you're a Mac user like me, you can't use the SharePort utility from D-links site...this is for PC's only. You have to download SX Virtual Link instead...this is the version of SharePort software for Mac. You can download it here:

[...]

Just select the Mac version from the table, download and install. I have all my iTunes libraries and photos on an external hard drive connected to my DIR-665. SX Virtual Link runs iTunes through the router like a champ!...I always have good connections and the speed is just like you're plugged into the hard drive on your Mac, totally easy to use and flawless. This is the only work around I've needed to do to get all the functionality out of this router with my Mac, everything else is straightforward.

Also, when I checked my NAT status on Xbox, it was already open; I checked this on MW2, MW3, and Reach just to be sure and, all games reported I have an open NAT. Nice not to have to go in to this router and enter all the data to forward the required ports.

title: Great TV for the price
text:
I got this TV on a whim. I'd been wanting to get a large screen TV for probably the past 10 years but never had the money. I saw the price and couldn't pass it up. I haven't been disappointed. It has a great picture, bright colors, extremely clear sound, and easy controls. Originally, I figured if it was a dud, it wasn't much more for it than a smaller TV. I'm notorious for buying TVs that don't live up to expectations, but this isn't one of them.

It's actually pretty light for the size. The hold-back is that it's bulky. It takes two people to move it, but I wouldn't do it any other way. I would get a pretty large stand or one that's made for it. Make sure it's stable. It's pretty easy to tip, and that'd be an expensive mistake.

I'm not technologically literate. I fumble and know a little, but I'm by no means an expert at electronic connections. This was pretty easy to set up. I had a little trouble trying to set it up with cable not through a cable box. I had the box on another TV at the time. After I moved the box to it, there wasn't a problem. I'm sure it was me and not the TV, though.

We got a surround sound system to go with the TV. Despite the good sound that the TV has, we wanted more power and output. The TV has a little trouble recognizing the receiver or the receiver has a little trouble sending info to the TV. I don't know if it's me, the receiver, or the TV. It just takes a little time for everything to begin communicating. I've been dealing with it, but I'm going to start troubleshooting it and see if I can figure out how everything will turn on at the same time rather than taking a few minutes for everything to recognize each other. Recently, we got a DVR from the cable company. When connected directly to the TV, it takes a few seconds to connect and works fine. When connected through the receiver, it takes 30 minutes for everything to begin working. So, I'm thinking the receiver is the problem.

We can connect the laptop to the TV. It, again, takes a few minutes to recognize the laptop resolution (when connected directly to the TV), but Mitsubishi put a notice in the manual informing the purchaser that it won't work with certain resolutions. It takes time, but it works.

Overall, this is a fantastic TV. It's not as slim, but that's okay. It's not heavy, and it works well. Definitely worth the purchase. I expect to have this TV for a long time to come.

title: Nice receiver with plenty of power output
text: I just put together my own budget audio system after plenty of research on multiple speaker systems. I already own a 5.1 home theater surround sound but wanted a 2.1 audiophile system to listen to music, watch movies, and play video games. I opted for the Sony STRDH130 as I've had good experience with Sony receivers before, with my other audio system being connected to a Sony receiver. I was able to turn this into a 2.1 system by using a Polk Audio PSW10 subwoofer that allows you to hook up this receiver to it, and then output the audio from the subwoofer to the two speakers, which are Pioneer SP-BS21-LR. Install took approximately 1 hour including cutting and preparing my own 16 gauge speaker wire that I purchased along with the receiver. The AUX port on the back of the receiver is great for hooking up an MP3 player/smartphone directly or hooking it into an Airport Express which allows you to stream music wirelessly to this receiver. I left all of the settings on the receiver at the default as I controlled the equalizer directly on my MP3 player wirelessly over Airplay. Total cost for this system including the 50ft of 16 gauge speaker wire cost approx. $245 give or take a few dollars. The sub was $80, the pioneers were $40 for the pair (on sale), and the receiver was $118. This is much much better than a soundbar and subwoofer setup. The sound is very deep, rich, and warm with great high notes. I uploaded a picture of my complete setup under the user pictures for this product. I highly recommend this alternative if you're not looking to break the bank.

title: Impressive performance based on size and price
text:
I built a small Bluetooth boom box based on this little powerhouse, using five pairs of small, low wattage speakers of varying impedance. The speakers were used... pulled from various devices that I was throwing out, such as obsolete mobile device docks, clock radios, and mini stereo systems. I e-mailed the company and got confirmation that this amplifier is stable down to at least 2 ohms, and wired the speakers to take full advantage of this.

The results were incredible and far beyond what I expected from such a physically small (and fairly inexpensive) amplifier. At very high volumes, I get zero distortion and unbelievable volume, with no hiss during quiet or silent segments of music. Even after hours of playing this thing loud it doesn't get very hot. I am so impressed with the performance of this amplifier I call it the "magic box". The big, clear sound and tiny size defy much of what I've learned in my experience in the audio industry.

Be warned, however, that unfortunately the Bluetooth reception leaves much to be desired. The range is very limited from what I've experienced. It seems like 8 to 10 feet is the max range to get an uninterrupted signal from my iPhone or iPad. Any further, and I get some intermittent cut-off in the music. It is very sensitive to line of sight, even at closer ranges. I have found that simply changing the angle or direction that the iPhone is facing in some instances can cause a brief moment of silence.

One more gripe, just a slight annoyance, is the loud BEEP emitted once your device has been successfully connected to the amplifier. It's loud and unpleasant, and I think they could have made it a little more subtle.

You might ask, then, why 5 stars? I feel like the audio performance eclipses these minor inconveniences, and overall this unit turned out to be way more than what I expected at this price.

title: Product description and Instructions are misleading
text:
The product description is misleading. It says "Install the pre-loaded NTFS driver for Mac, and use the drive interchangeably between PC and Mac computers without reformatting the drive." This implies that the needed driver that would enable users to drag and drop files between Mac and PC is in the installation file that comes with the hard drive. During installation it even asks if the hard drive will be used Mac and PC or Mac only. You'd think choosing the Mac and PC option would install that needed driver to make it read/write on Mac, but it does not. All it does is install the Dashboard software that uploads/downloads your social media content. The instructions were unhelpful, and the support page for Mac even says "Install the included software which has a special driver that will allow the NTFS partition to be read and written under MacOS" with a Note that says "If the driver is not installed, then the drive will be read-only under MacOS." THIS IS FALSE! The software DOES NOT include the special driver and the hard drive will still be read-only. You have to go to the Downloads section of the Seagate website and install the file "NTFS Driver for Mac OS." This additional VITAL step is not mentioned anywhere in the instructions, the product description, the box, or on that support page for Mac. Something just told me to check the Downloads section of the website, and I saw the driver file there, tried it and it worked, ending the hours of headache and frustration.

So if you purchased, or plan to purchase this hard drive so you can save files from both your Mac and Windows computers, I'm letting you know (because Seagate doesn't) that you need to go to the Downloads section of their website and install the NTFS Driver for Mac OS for it work on your Mac.

title: Good basic TT
text:
This little thing has everything you need to begin the foray into serious vinyl listening. Don't think that means it's audiophile quality, it's not, but it is better than all those Crosely USB/faux vintage things. Pros would be it's (barely) S-shaped tonearm, removable headshell and cartridge, tone arm counterweight, strobe timing light and pitch adjust. Cons would be that the stock cartridge is pretty bad at tracking. Setting this table up I got pretty bad sibilant distortion in the FIRST track unless I had the tracking force dialed up much higher than I would like for the record's sake. Along with that, this table does not come with any of the specs needed for true audiophile tuning. It does not give overhang adjustment, optimum cartridge weight or optimum tracking force for the stock cartridge. My girlfriend uses this table for casual listening, she doesn't spend near as much time with her records as I do so these mystery settings probably don't affect her much but they surely bothered me when I was setting it up.

Right out of the box it definitely needs a cartridge; at the very least so you can have some idea as to what to set the vertical tracking force at. Overall the unit functions well, puts out good sound with or without the internal pre-amp on. The thing is a bit flimsy. Very plasticky and the "shock absorbing" feet are a bit too loose and seem to be more "shock causing" than anything. If you want an alright table that gives you better control than the trendy "all-in-one" systems this is a good place to start. If you want an audiophile turntable turn away now.

I would buy this table again for a friend who is a light listener but I wouldn't buy it for myself.

I'm hoping Sony releases the HX60V in the US. It's currently only available outside the US. That will combine more manual functions with better video quality. At least that is my hope.

title: Lots of problems at first, but once figured out I'm happy with my purchase.
text:
I do a lot of boondocking (dry camping in my RV) in places far away from cities and towns. I am also Canadian and spend half the year in the states. Because of my unique situation I was searching for a device I could use both in Canada and the States without having to buy two separate ones. This one seemed to be the answer to my problems. The price was right so I ordered it, it came within 3 days.

Right when I took it out of the package and charged it I knew something wasn't right with the device. Even though it had been charging for hours, as soon as I unplugged it it would turn off immediately. I figured that maybe it would work better once I had the sim card in so started working on that.

Turns out getting just a sim card and plan from a wireless company is NOT easy when you don't want to buy the device from them too. I tried at least 4 different wireless companies in the states who refused to give me just the sim card. Finally I had to go with AT&T even though their prices for data were higher than most companies. I figured I could do it over the phone, which a representative told me would be no problem, but it turns out it was a problem. I ended up having to drive 2 hours to the nearest AT&T store to get the sim card in person. Wasn't very happy about that since I was driving in a 32 foot motorhome.

Finally I had the sim card and the Novatel device, but even when the device was charging it wouldn't turn on for longer than a minute or two before it shut down. I contacted the company and they were great, they immediately shipped me a new one which came in another 3 days.

FINALLY with the NEW Novatel device AND the AT&T simcard I was able to get online! I have been using it for a little over a month now and am still happy with my purchase. It has worked in about 95% of the places I have tried it.

The battery still doesn't last long, but since I have solar panels it's no problem for me to charge it regularly. It was stressful to get everything set up, but once I did it was worth it. If I had gone through AT&T to buy this device it would have cost me $200 and wouldn't be unlocked. Well worth the price in my opinion. Just make sure you look into getting the sim card before you buy it to make sure it's possible.

title: Great concept with much untapped potential
text:
I have been using Escort Live for over a month now and am very happy with the product.
I have not experienced any build quality issues that others have stated so maybe that was just a bad batch?
There are a few minor bugs in the android version of the software but I've been in touch with Escort to report them and from what I've been told the developers are working on a new release.

Pros: (or things I like about Escort Live)
-It gives you the ability to update the firmware of your detector without sending it back in to Escort.
-It basically allows you to have a concealed display for your detector. This is very nice for those living in areas where detectors are illegal. The detector itself can be hidden and the display viewed on the smartphone.
-It allows for GPS based locking out of false alerts. This is great for those that want the performance of the M3 antenna (Redline, STi-Magnum, STi-R/STi-R+, 9500CI) but don't want to pay over $1000 for the remote units with GPS, 9500CI or STi-R+.
-Last but not least, the sharing of alerts.

Cons:
-There are a few bugs in the software.
-You have to open the app on your phone every time you drive if you want to use Live. (I admit I'm lazy and at times don't feel like doing this)
-We are in the early stages of Escort Live deployment so some areas won't see heavy Escort Live use.

Personally the first three Pros were enough to get me interested in Escort Live regardless of the amount of people using it at the time; however, around 80% of the time I open the application there is at least one Live Ka alert somewhere on the map. The amount of people using Live in your area will obviously vary depending on where you live; I believe Escort is going to be coming out with a trial version of just the app so people can check and see how many other people are using it in their area before they buy.

I used to use trapster, but I've switched over to Live because trapster was plagued with too many falses. When I see an alert on Live I know it came from someone running an RD who actually picked up the cops radar, not someone who saw a cop getting McDoanlds and decided to report it anyway. I know that Escort has quite a bit invested in Live so I'm confident that the app itself will be refined and improved over time.

Suggestions:
1. Make a widget for the android version so that Live can run in the background and seamlessly connect without intervention from the user.
2. Allow the Live Cloud as a whole to learn over time. For example, if live Ka alerts get repeatedly reported in a general area, mark that area as a speed trap.

title: Easy to setup, but so-so performance
text:
I've been looking for some small monitoring cameras that I can leave at my vacation home when it's unattended, and the Dropcam seemed like one of the better options. It's small, easy to power and requires no PC or appliance, instead recording video to a cloud service provided by the vendor.

On the positive side, this is one of the easier products of its type to install and configure. You connect the cable to your PC, a configuration program starts, you enter your WiFi information and you're done. Really simple, and I'm sure just about anyone can succeed here - no technical skills needed.

There's also a mobile app that gives you live view for free, and if you're willing to pay for it, there's a cloud-based DVR that records your video. The device comes with a two-week trial for the cloud DVR service, so you can get a sense of whether it's worth the money.

Image quality is good in bright light - less good in dim or high contrast (that is, mix of bright and dim). It may be HD in the sense that it's 720p, but the video stream is so compressed, there's quite a bit of pixelation and muddiness, to the extent that you sometimes can't even tell who you are looking at from ten feet away. Motion is also somewhat jerky and the images tend to be somewhat blurry if there's lots of motion.

Still, this is a great device for, say, baby monitoring or keeping track of when the kids get home. There are a few limitations, however.

For one, you can't program in multiple WiFi networks, so if you're like me and you have multiple SSIDs where you want to use the device, you need to plug it into a PC to reconfigure and time you move between networks.

Second, the device stand is fairly large and cumbersome given the size of the camera. Yes, you can remove the camera itself and find a way to mount it without the stand - but with the stand (as pictured in the product description), it's a bit too large to be unobtrusive. For example, although I have wide windowsills, the base of the camera is a bit too wide to sit on one of them.

Also, the camera itself is not weather sealed and so it's pretty useless for outdoor monitoring. You really can't, for example, park it looking outside a window - the night vision simply reflects off the glass, giving you glare instead of clear outdoor pictures. It's very much an indoor only solution.

I have mixed thoughts about the cloud recording approach you get with Dropcam. While the live viewing is free and easy to use from a mobile device, recording is expensive and error-prone, and you're locked into the Dropcam service. I suppose I'd pay $99/year for it if it worked reliably, but I'm not so sure this is the case. Although it advertises it keeps the last seven days of video online, my experience is that you get way less than 50% coverage within that seven day period.

The cloud recording approach Dropcam uses is also dependent on lots of bandwidth. I have Verizon FiOS 50mb service - generally screams, but I still couldn't get reliable cloud recording with this device. When I go back and look at the recorded video stream, there are too many "No recording available" segments. As other reviewers mention, you will definitely need to be careful if you're on an Internet plan that limits your monthly usage. Plus, it's hard for me to imagine getting good results with multiple cameras on a single network.

Unlike some other cameras that support various network and device standards, there's no way to simply run some PoE network cables to these devices and control them with your own choice of software. You're pretty much locked in to the vendor's apps and network services.

There's also flaws in the motion detection software.

Another vendor I tried was able to sent me an alert exactly as motion was detected - I could see the person triggering the event, and I really wouldn't have to search through the video stream to figure out what was going on.

Not so with the Dropcam. In the first few weeks I owned it, I've had perhaps 100 motion alerts, and exactly zero have depicted the actual person or object triggering the alert. In most cases, because of the holes in the recording, it's rare to find the cause of the alert by reviewing the video stream online. I find this to be very frustrating: you get an alert that the camera detected motion, but you're not able to see what the camera saw.

Bottom line is that the Dropcam offers great packaging, simple setup and a good solution for live viewing an indoor object, so long as you have lots of bandwidth. If this is what you're looking for, then it's worth a try.
