title: Great phone, has good call quality, and more features and processing grunt than you know what to do with...
text:
UPDATED 11/12/2013

I know I may not appear a "Verified Buyer", but I purchased this phone through our primary's Amazon account. I most certainly do own this device. With that out of the way, here are my thoughts after a week of ownership. Also, if you have questions, go ahead and ask. I'll answer them as time allows - I know what it is like to plop down 250 bucks on something and not know that ONE thing you just can't find out about it anywhere. Anyways, on to my impressions.

First of all, I did not have this phone prior to the update that was issued to fix call quality. I cannot say for certain the update fixed it, as I never experienced the problem, but what I can tell you is that while I've used it (I immediately installed the update when I got the phone), all the calls I've made have been crystal clear both on my end and on the the callers end. So if that was a worry for you, I would say you can cross that off the list now.

Let's quickly talk about who this phone isn't for. Go ahead and skip this section if you are a tech head like me and already poured over tech specs and sheets well before it released. This phone is, unquestionably, huge. It is able to be HELD with one hand, but it's usefulness one handed is somewhat limited. I'm a 6'0 tall guy, slightly above average sized hands. I use Thumb Keyboard as my replacement for stock, and I cannot easily reach the left hand side of the keyboard. It can be done, but it requires some finagling in the hand (that incidentally has it resting precariously on the tips of my fingers near the center of the back of the device). Using the "one handed operation" setting within Thumb Keyboard (or stock for that matter) squashes it to to the side and one handed typing can be accomplished easier that way. But there are plenty of buttons still out of reach. Any keys on the top, for example the Search button on the top of the Play Store, is impossible to reach with your thumb one-handed. You also can't easily reach the capacitive menu button (located to the left of the home button) while operating one handed. The latter two are obnoxious to say the least. So long as you plan to use it mostly with two hands - hold it in one and touch with the other) - usability is perfectly fine.

Given that, I can't recommend this phone to anyone who truly wants a phone that can be fully operated one handed. The absolute tips of the scale in terms of one handed operation that I can recommend would be the HTC One (that is what the other two people on my plan got - also great phones) with their 4.7 inch screens. The Note 3 also hase has an incredible amount of power. It will crunch through anything you throw at it, but it is rather overkill at the moment. If you want a future proof level set of internals, this phone certainly fits the bill. But if you are basically going to take phone calls, do some texting, emailing, web browsing and casual gaming, this will be overkill. You can easily get away with the HTC One (or phones of its ilk) with it's previous gen Snapdragon 600 processor.

I'll keep the rhetoric to a minimum and get down to brass tacks afterwards. You've probably read a million reviews on this phone already trying to determine if you'll pull the trigger so you don't need me to wax poetical. This phone, aside from it's still somewhat underwhelming construction (it's not cheap, just not HTC One typed premium), is nearly perfect in every other category. The screen is fantastic - I leave mine set to about 35% brightness and that seems to be the sweet spot for me between readability and power-usage. The ear-piece speaker is pretty good, though not great. Same can be said for the external loudspeaker, but at least it is in fact loud (you can even press a button on the upper right hand side of the stock dialer for "Extra Volume"). I don't care for it's placement though. It's not ideal for directionality, but it is also placed in such a way that my hand covers it when I hold the phone in landscape orientation for gaming and video watching. That is one of the only knocks I have against it actually.

Going back to its internals - its Snapdragon 800 processor, Adreno 330 GPU and 3 gigabytes of RAM are all incredibly powerful top tier components. It's basically overkill. I noticed while playing games that the phone would get hot - borderline excessively so - after 5 plus minutes of gaming. That was true of games ranging from Plants vs Zombies 2 to Modern Combat 4. I decided to enable "Power Saving Mode - CPU Power Saving" - something I basically never do on anything ever. I want it to perform above and beyond. But I can say that this phone doesn't see any ill effects from enabling this in day to day performance, or in gaming. I do gather it only limits the CPU clock and not the GPU clock, but it saves you a bit of energy AND keeps the phone cool even after fairly decent length gaming sessions. The framerate on PvZ2, Modern Combat 4, NOVA 3 and others all remained consistently high. In fact, I ran the Epic Citadel benchmark with settings on "Ultra High Quality" and "100% Rendering Resolution Percentage" and got 54-55 FPS whether I left the CPU Power Mode checked or unchecked. So given that, until I find a task that needs it, I'll be keeping this "power saving" feature on - I'd suggest you probably do the same.

One handed operation is also aided by the fact that you can dig into the Settings menu, under the Controls tab and find One-handed Operation. Here you can enable "use for all screens" which will allow you to use a quick left to right swipe gesture from the edge of the screen to minimize the window down to a fraction of the screen. I use this the few times I want to reach the top-most corners of the screen one handed (or the menu button, as virtual keys for the main buttons also show up in this windowed mode).

I would also suggest grabbing "Folder Organizer" by Fabio Collini. It allows you to group things into folders where you can change the layout to be a list with icons and text (a scrollable list that you can select individual items across a row encompassing nearly the width of the screen making one handed selection very easy). It has other benefits, I've been using it for ages. Makes changing individual app shortcut icons very easy as well.

I've found battery life on this device to be well under what I've read in professional reviews. They struggle to kill the battery in a 24 hour period. With a 3200 milliamp battery in this beast, I'd imagine it should be. And still, I find myself looking at the battery stats and seeing 3 hours of screen time and 12 hours of up time with around 20% battery remaining fairly regularly. How power users stretch the Note 3 to have over 24 hours (and some cases closer to 36-48 hours) is beyond me. I turn off features I don't need, keep the brightness down, keep my wireless radios in check - all for naught. It will definitely get you through a work day, but if you are going to be away from an outlet for 12+ hours, I'd be a bit antsy if I've done any medium to heavy usage that day. In standby mode, you'll get plenty of life out of the battery though. I do wonder if there were some ill effects to battery life after the update to address call quality - the discrepancy in battery life seems a bit too drastic and stark in comparison.

The S-pen is nice, I will certainly use it, but I wouldn't let it sway you if it was going to dissuade you from getting another phone/phablet. Clearly if you need finite control in certain applications for work or what have you, the stylus on this thing cannot be beat. It does do handwriting quite well and it's pin point precision allows for very fine drawing - not pencil/pen level, but very good nonetheless. I'll also take this opportunity to touch on the "pen-window" functionality. It's limited app selection makes it less appealing in practice than it sounds in theory. I like to use it to have quick access to a Google Hangouts chat window, or maybe a web browser. This also goes for the "mutli-screen" mode. The fact only a fraction of your apps will support either makes this really killer multitasking feature fairly useless. Until they give us access to all our apps via these methods (already done via custom ROMs so it's clearly possible, just restricted by Samsung), it's largely gimmicky. Useful sometimes, but you'll more than likely end up in my shoes - using it because it's there when you get the phone and then never using it again. It's just that limited.

One other thing to note is the expandable SD storage is good for files and such, but don't expect to be moving apps over to it. I have a ton of games and other apps that command large file sizes. If you try to use "move to SD card", you'll be able to...but the kicker is that the SD card in this device is actually an emulated one - it simply sees your internal storage as the SD card. You cannot move items to the external SD card, which is a bummer to me. I still have a ton of apps, and you get around 25 gigs for app storage, so it's not like you are limited. But it is a con I didn't anticipate, and imagine others may find this restriction a bit too limiting for their needs.

In any event, there are my kind of rambling thoughts on the phone. As I continue to use the phone, I will probably come back and add to the review and update or correct my opinions as I have more time under my belt with this juggernaut. Hope there were some useful bits in there - and your fears about voice quality have been assuaged. Again, feel free to ask questions.

title: It a good value
text:
I got my Chromebook several days ago. I've worked with it for a few hours and am keeping it.

Pros

- Great value for the price
- Super light
- Easy to import favorites
- From what little I've done with Google app.s, they seem to be reasonable
- It does save and apply the passwords I'd like to save, e.g., my email passwords and a few other who-cares-if-I-lose them sites
- Starts up in just a few seconds
- Decent speaker for the price
- A decent amount of background options
- Works with a mouse

Cons

- Wi-Fi is really, really slow. I've run several speed tests at speakeasy.net against my Windows laptop and the Chromebook is woefully slower, so any video at all stops and starts a lot Update: When I place the Chromebook next to my router, it runs great. 15' and 1 wall away, it's bad. It must be the Wi-Fi antenna.
- The base documentation is negligible. I had to use help a lot to figure how to change settings. For example, how to reset the clock to Central time isn't at all easy to find
- Since there's no offline app.s, I had to buy a cloud password manager for my financial web passwords at $1 a month. I know, not a lot but it's more than free
- The keyboard isn't very tactile. It feels cheap
- Despite having a cursor speed control for a mouse, it doesn't seem to affect the speed so it takes a lot of mouse movement to get the cursor across a screen
- Printing may be a hassle, but I don't see myself ever needing to print anything from it anyway

Like I say, I haven't used it a lot yet but it's a keeper so far. This Chromebook will never be a workhorse laptop, but is fine for surfing.

title: Awesome performance for low price --on par with my Luxman!
text:
Well, my Luxman R115 finally died. The R115 was a VERY high end receiver made in the early-mid '80's (some of their amps cost today around $10,000 and Luxman is comparable to MacIntosh while Harman Kardon is generally more comparable to Pioneer, etc.). Let me also say this is my first Harman Kardon unit, and I grew up with an audiophile father who was a superb electrical engineer. We had Bose 901's way back in the late '70's or early '80's and those were driven using MacIntosh gear, so I'm no foreigner to quality sound (though not a true audiophile myself).

First let me say I thought I'd be taking a downgrade. I was pretty sure of it. That old Luxman still has a following and they still sell for $250 and up. Not many heavily used stereos from the '80's can say that. But I can't afford a NEW Luxman right now, and I needed something to drive my Bose series V 901's that sounded decent and refused to purchase used audio gear that old and sight and sound unseen/heard. No point in having 901's and a crappy receiver or amp.

Well, I was pleasantly surprised. Not only did the HK3490 pretty much match the Luxman in sound quality, it actually comes through somewhat clearer. Now many of you would say, "yeah, no crap, it is 30 years newer!", but had you experience the Luxman and the 901's together you'd have pretty high expectations regardless of the date of manufacture. I suppose the biggest difference between the old Luxman and the new HK3490 is that the Luxman has a good deal more power. This isn't so much of a drawback as the HK drives them fine with more power than I really need, but it is worth mentioning as these 901's can take one hell of a beating. You won't blow a pair with just a home receiver.

But the most important thing to mention is that the HK doesn't seem to prefer highs or lows at full power, it seems to deliver the sound across the range as you'd expect a quality stereo to do. The Luxman was that way too, but in its final days it seemed to prefer lows more than highs. I hate to admit it, but this HK3490 may even surpass a new R115 or R117 could you find one. You may expect that though given the HK3490 IS 30 years newer, BUT bear in mind it uses the same old analog technology.

The 3490 essentially connects using the same high quality connections in the back as the Luxman and has basically the same kinds of "old school" stereo connections with the nice addition of optical outputs as well.

As for controls, the HK3490 is infinitely easier to use, as in user friendly. Gone are some of the archaic nonsensical controls that many of the audiophile analog gear from the past had, instead relying on newer technology, I assume, to integrate this into the circuitry itself.

All in all, I'd say the HK3490 is a GREAT deal, both in quality and price, and for those that are missing that great Luxman sound and can't shell out the $5000 or whatever it would take to replace it with a new model, this may be for you.

Note this isn't a home theatre device and doesn't support any kind of surround sound save "Dolby Virtual Surround" which is supposed to make recordings coded in surround sound just a bit better. I haven't tried that yet, most of my CD's are classical recordings and many are remastered from original '50's and '60's recordings. But I must admit that Beethoven's 9th sounds better when driven loud, vs. the Luxman, just due to the non-preference for the lows.

If you need an analog device or a just a good audio receiver for that fine turntable and don't want to break the bank, the $330-$350 or whatever we paid for it is actually a steal. VERY satisfied. Because if it was lacking, these Bose 901's would certainly uncover it.

For the price and quality, I'd say it is worth having this for your music alone, say you use 901's or some other high end speakers for two channel stereo, and reserve your decent 5.1 or 7.1 or whatever for movies and the like, because I'm pretty sure you'd need to shell out quite a bit more for one of those just to get similar quality sound from your music were you to use it in a dual role. It would also make a great setup, for say a bedroom, if you already have a killer HT setup in the living room or den for instance.

For the price, I'm not so sure it has much competition. Very satisfied, and I'd have expected to have paid a good deal more for the same quality. Obviously the fact it is based on old technology keeps the price down (but consider tube amps --old tech there that STILL doesn't have competition!) Great job Harman Kardon!

At the moment, I also use this setup to monitor the television output which has this computer, the cable, PS3 and Blu-ray, and it sound pretty damn good and sometimes the sound, without surround, is so clear and precise it sounds like it is in the room with you (but 901's kind of have that effect as it is --next best thing to surround if you ask me). Good enough to fool a pair of bird dogs with superb hearing as well.

I could go on I guess as I'm obviously quite satisfied, but you get the point. Again, for the price you won't be disappointed for an analog receiver.

title: Was on the edge at first, but now....
text:
Absolutely love my Xbox One. I was a bit hesitant at first because I have an amazing computer that can blow this graphically out of the water. However, upon reading about all of the multimedia functions of the XB1 (ESPN channel, Netflix, Amazon Video, Hulu, watching my TV through it, connecting Windows Media player from my computer to and also being able to stream movies from my computer, plus numerous other apps on the XB1) I finally bought one at Gamestop because I wanted to trade in my Wii U. I have not looked back! I bought the one without the Kinect and now have a kinect being shipped to me that I bought on Ebay for $50 ($7 S&H). I went about a month without having a Kinect and was torn because of some mixed reviews, but in the end decided to grab it.
It had been a long time since I owned any Xbox, as I had a PS3 and loved it. I switched over once again because of the multimedia functions. Some people are complaining about the XB1 not doing 1080p, but with an update that Microsoft put out it now does support full 1080p. On top of trading in my Wii U for this, I was also able to sell my Blu Ray player since the XB1 comes with a very fast Blu Ray reader (just gotta download the free app). I would highly recommend getting the Energize rechargable battery pack for the controller, though I have heard that the two AA batteries last much longer than most people expected. Xbox Live Gold is also great as you get 2+ free games a month, plus often times decent discounts on other games, plus discounts on Xbox Video movies (just picked up several box office hits today for $8.99 apiece in full HD), and sometimes free TV shows.
Another common thing said against the XB1 and for the PS4 is that the PS4 is more powerful. Well, if it is, its by so little it hardly matters. Game developers have discovered that if they disable Kinect functionality that they get an extra 10% power, which makes up the difference the PS4 had. The PS4 is no doubt a great gaming machine and has some multimedia functions itself, but its not nearly as good at multimedia as the XB1.
Overall, if you are on the edge I would recommend buying the XB1. It would be hard to be disappointed with it
(please note that if you buy it, the first update that occurs if connected to the internet does take a bit, and if it seems to freeze just hold the power button for 6 seconds or so and it'll turn off then you turn it back on. Only a few XB1's are effected by it but its worth knowing)

title: Very good monitor and yes, it is tiltable!
text:
I've known about Viewsonic for a number of years but never had the need for one. When ordering a new computer I suddenly had a need for a monitor and checked out all the reviews. This one looked to be good for my needs and the price was certainly right.

The monitor is a good one and it literally worked fine right out of the box. I never even used the set-up disc. Clear, crisp, fast, etc. I'm not a gamer or a graphic artist so it meets my needs just fine.

In the reviews I read that the monitor does not have an adjustable tilt and, since I found this hard to believe, I ordered it anyway. At first blush, when you assemble the monitor on its stand, it does not tilt. Further, the factory setting is absolutely unacceptable unless you were planning to sit it on a bunch of phone books. The factory setting for tilt is absolutely vertical. No tilt at all. for me to be comfortable, I'd have to raise it about 8 to 10 inches above the desk. Looking at the back, where the stand connector attaches to the back of the monitor It appeared to have some tilt capability. If you unscrew the plastic stand attachment from the back with the two screws that are deep in recesses and pull off the plastic attachment, there is a nut (I think it was 8mm) and if you loosen that, you will find that it does indeed swivel (tilt). I set it for the tilt I wanted, tightened it back up and it's just the way I want it. I suppose that if you left the nut slightly loose, you would be able to tilt it up and down for multiple users but I just tightened mine pretty snug and, since the tilt is fine for me, it doesn't need further adjustment. Took a couple of minutes for some trial and error and it's fine now.

This adjustment might not be for the user who isn't comfortable taking the covers off things and doesn't have the right tools - a small Phillips head screwdriver and some metric wrenches - but it's a quick fix and makes this monitor a great deal.

Bob

title: Wrong plastic for this design
text:
I purchased this cover after thoroughly reading all the reviews, and I really liked this cover as a more affordable alternative to the Kindle brand hard cover--I liked the color and texture of the leather, it is very slim and not bulky, and the weight and feel of it with my Kindle Paperwhite inside was just right.

As reported by one other reviewer, when I received my cover I also found a tiny bit of dried adhesive stuck to the front of the snap closure tab, but I just used a little bit of Goo Gone on a cotton swab, which removed it just fine and did not harm the leather finish.
I also found the magnet of the tab closure to be not that strong, but since the Kindle fits so tightly in the cover, the closure is more decorative than anything else (and I suspect they may hesitate to use a super-strong magnet, which could possibly have adverse effects on the electronics of the Kindle).

There was just one really serious drawback to this cover: the moment I snapped my Kindle into the cover, stress cracks appeared in the top corners of the interior plastic. Maybe these cracks would never have developed into an actual breakage, as reported by one other reviewer (though cracks do tend to propagate over time, so it seems likely that eventually they would have) but it didn't give me a good feeling, and I know I would have been looking at them and worrying about it all the time, so I decided to send the cover back (though removing my Kindle from it was a challenge).

Because I preferred to have the hard cover style versus a folio style cover, I went ahead and paid the astronomical price of $40 for the Kindle brand cover, and now I see what the main difference is between the Kindle and August covers: the August cover uses a harder, more brittle type of plastic, and the Kindle cover uses a rubberized, more flexible type of plastic, which is more forgiving of the stress of snapping the Kindle into it.

It is unfortunate because I liked the August cover in every other way, and would have kept it if not for this design flaw (which is probably part of the reason it is so much cheaper than the Kindle brand cover.)

August makes some very nice looking and reasonably priced leather folio style covers (these are generally more padded, and the Kindle slides into a sort of pocket to hold it inside the cover), and if I had been really unable or unwilling to pay $40 for the Kindle brand hard cover, I probably would have purchased one of those instead.

title: Works well, most software supports it, easy enough to use, not much else to say.
text:
It's an inexpensive way to get into Z-Wave home automation, and I think it's one of the cheaper ones out there (if not the cheapest). It works well enough for what it is and it's easy to pair items to it. I have mine on an old laptop. I haven't had an issue pairing any of my devices to it - Door/Window sensors, a Schlage lock, and a wireless siren.

Ignore the complaints that it doesn't come with software. That's not a knock on the device. If you think you're going to spend $40 and get a whole home automation setup minus the devices then look at something more expensive. The benefit of this is you can try lots of different software; you're not limited to a single application. You can use InControl, HomeSeer, OpenRemote, to name a few. All of them work with the Z-Stick, which is why I went with it over a VeraLite - I wanted to find the software that would do what I wanted to do. Too many complaints in the Vera forums regarding the software that I went with this instead.

Keep in mind much of the software out there is going to be fairly expensive, but most if not all allow a try-before-you-buy option. You'll at least be able to determine what works and doesn't work for you. If you decide to go with a full solution (Controller+Software) then you aren't out very much.

title: Doesn't work as advertised with Google Nexus 10
text:

I found no indication of this in other reviews, and there is no obvious support for the Nexus 10. Have searched for about an hour now on the net, starting with Logitech support/forums, then to a general search. Ran across a Google Play app called "Logitech Keyboard Config App" for the Galaxy tabs, but when I downloaded it and opened it, got a message that my tablet wasn't supported (yes, a Nexus isn't a Galaxy, but they're both Samsung and at least one "Google" user said it worked in the app reviews).

Will contact Logitech support more directly, but the company should already have info out. This is a problem that's close to a year old as far as I can tell.

The keyboard itself is comfortable and works far better for me than any built-in keyboard I've tried on several tablet keyboard/cover combinations. title: The Best USB Cable Available On Amazon For Under A Benjamin...
text:
A few years ago, when I was a beginner in computer audio, Pangea Audio 24AWG solid silver USB cable was one of the first aftermarket USB cables that I bought. There were 02 factors that determined my purchase decision. 1: I had particularly enjoyed Pangea Audio’s budget AC 14SE power cords and HD-24PCe HDMI cables and 2: The 24AWG 'solid pure silver' simply tricked me into buying one.

At that time, I was using the Pangea Audio USB cable with a portable setup. The Pangea Audio USB cable was definitely an improvement over the stock USB cables that I had with me but it came with a price; the Pangea Audio USB cable was just too stiff as their HDMI cables, it lacked the flexibility that I desired for my portable setup. After a few months of careful use, the plastic sheathing at the bottom of the Type B connector, of the Pangea Audio USB cable started cracking up. I do not expect this for this price!

I then tried the WireWorld Starlight 7 USB cable. For the same price as the Pangea Audio USB cable, the WireWorld Starlight is more flexible, well-engineered and better-built USB cable. It also sounds much more detailed and transparent than the Pangea Audio USB cable, despite the fact that it uses 'silver plated' copper conductors. An expensive audiophile lesson there. For those strictly wanting to shop from Amazon, the WireWorld Starlight USB cable offers the best value for money performance currently for under a Benjamin (USD 100).

Since then, I have had the chance to try a few USB cables under the USD 100 mark and I have to say that USB cables do make a difference but at the same time, I’m hesitant to go past the USD 100 mark. Especially when you get decent computer audio performance from portable DAC/Amp that costs USD 200 these days. Spending too much money on USB cables defies logic. At least for me, as I’m someone who is always on the lookout for good audio for affordable money.

Of all the USB cables that I’ve tried, over the years, the dual-headed USB cable is clearly superior by design and is ideal for computer audio. These cables have the power and data cables in separate cables and that is what gives them a performance edge over conventional USB cables. This also makes them more expensive than conventional USB cables. The dual-headed USB cable can be used with an external battery especially when using a DAC that works off an external 5v power supply. It offers better fidelity than most conventional USB cables can achieve by design.

Dual-headed USB cables are all the rage now amongst computer audiophiles. As much as I wanted to try them, the steep prices just kept me away. In my search for an affordable dual-headed USB cable, I recently came across an lesser known cable brand by the name of Audiocadabra. I first spotted them in an audio classifieds website in the UK. I ordered their dual-headed handcrafted Optimus USB cable, directly from their website, which cost a mere USD 89 with free shipping to the US.

The first time I plugged in the Audiocadabra Optimus dual-headed USB cable it sounded very detailed. I gave them a good 200hrs of burn-in, just like what Audiocadabra suggests on their website, before I started some serious listening. Post burn-in, they do mellow down a lot and now sounds way more detailed and transparent than the Pangea Audio Solid Silver USB cable, more blacker and tactile than the WireWorld Starlight USB cable.

The improvements I heard with Audiocadabra dual-headed Optimus cable over the WireWorld Starlight is most notable in the midrange. I felt like I have moved a few rows ahead in the venue and the background noise feels like it has dropped a notch or two. The presentation is more holographic. The attack and decay of instruments sounds believable and feels good to listen to. And surprisingly it has all the details without feeling clinical at all.

My observation is purely based on listening to the above USB cables with my favourite Sennheiser HD650 cans with a selection of DACs that I have collected over the years. Sometimes keeping an open mind leads you to unexpected surprises. Though Audiocadabra was an unfamiliar company to me, their customer service and prompt responses are commendable. I’m sure I will be trying Audiocadabra’s other handcrafted cables with confidence in the future.

I now have the Audiocadabra Optimus dual-headed USB cable in use with my main computer system. They are my new reference USB cable. The WireWorld Starlight is currently being used as my mobile USB cable that travels in my laptop bag. The Pangea Audio has now found a temporary resting place, in my loft, with other cables in a large brown card-board box. I think I’ll soon list it on Audiogon to fund some new purchases before X’mas this year.

title: Cheaper than buying the drive by itself
text:
I ordered one of these specifically for the actual UJ-220 Blu-Ray drive itself to replace the DVD/CD drive in my Lenovo E420 laptop with Windows 7 Professional. This drive does NOT come with any software to play Blu-Ray movies so you will have to purchase that separate. This external USB Blu-Ray drive is really just a laptop optical disc drive inside an external enclosure. Opening this drive will void the warranty.

-For the tech savvy, you can do the same at your own risk:
To easily swap the drives, just make sure you have the same style slim drive in your current notebook/laptop and that it is actually removable. You can find out this info by looking for the service manual on your Laptop/Notebook manufacturer's website and comparing the pictures to that of a UJ-220, Google it. Take your time, this whole process took me 20-30 minutes but I've replaced laptop disc drives before.

To get the drive out of the enclosure there are 2 screws on the back side where the USB connectors are. 1 is visible, the other is under a tiny white warranty sticker. Unscrew both Phillips screws, then easily pop the top off and you can access the drive and the enclosure adapter and unplug the drive from it. If you do not unscrew both before removing the top you will break 2 small black clips on the enclosure.

Follow these easy instructions to pull out your current disc drive if you have a Lenovo e420 laptop: http://support.lenovo.com/en_US/product-and-parts/detail.page?&DocID=PD015066

Eject the drive tray and power off your laptop. Then remove the battery from your laptop, unscrew the bottom cover where your memory resides and look for a single screw right in the middle area on the side where the disc drive is and unscrew it. At that point you should be able to pop the drive out with very little effort. If you are careful you can easily swap the face plates on the drive in the laptop and the one on this external drive. Make sure to move the little black hook on the back of the drive that was in the laptop over to this one. You should be able to put the new one in and screw the 1 screw back in place and have it look exactly like it did before except now you will have a Blu-Ray drive.

You can put the face that came with the external drive on your old laptop optical disc drive. Then you can attach the drive to the USB connectors and fit it right back into the external enclosure and still have a working USB DVD/CD drive to use if you ever need it. Take your time and organize your screws as you remove them so you can remember which goes where since there are a couple that are different sizes. Take your time, if you are in a rush wait until you have nothing better to do in the afternoon. Rushing will not help you swap the drives right and being forceful can and will break some of the plastic clips on these parts. Do this at your own risk!

title: A Great Black Friday Week Buy!
text:
Disclaimer: The 5 star rating is for picture quality.

I upgraded to this TV because my plasma (which was only 5 years old) was starting to go bad. An issue came up that would have required replacing the plasma panel, which cannot be purchased anymore (the panel would have cost $300 anyway). I came from a 50" Samsung PN50C450 (720p) so this TV's display blows my old one out of the water.

I'll start off by saying I bought this as a Black Friday week special. This series TV is really more the mid-range, but the 6500 series did not offer much more in terms of picture quality. The upgrade processor makes the Smart TV functions in that one a little more responsive, but I use other devices mainly for any "connected" uses. Having those built into the TV is fine but I will probably stay with my previous behavior.

Out of the box, this TV is nice but I feel a few adjustments need to be made. By default, Clear Motion is turned on. If you want your picture to have the Soap Opera effect and look weird, leave it on. This is software in the TV that speeds up the refresh rate. I have yet to watch football or hockey on it yet, but I will check those out to see if it maybe those programs are worth having the setting on for. For everything else (including video games), your best bet is to turn it off. It makes the picture look unnatural.

Any time you go into a store and look at a TV, the TVs you see are ALWAYS calibrated to make some displays look better than others. This is because retailers at times will want to move more of one model than another. If you do your research, you can find a few sites that reviewed this model and can give you the "right" calibration settings. I found that RTINGS gave spot on calibration settings.

title: Great Product, Go Buy One!
text:
I just bought a Surface Pro as my first tablet. I have been holding off from entering the tablet market, because up until now, all tablets have basically been big cell phones. They run the same operating systems as my phone (iOS or Android). Why would I need a second cell phone, with a big screen, that can't make phone calls?

However, you cannot compare the Surface with all previous tablets. It is a new product - think of it as an Ultrabook in a tablet form factor. It is just as good as any of the ultrabook laptops out there, but its small, light, and easy to carry around.

I love having a full computer, running windows 8, and being able to do anything I could do on a traditional laptop. The device works great, its fast, and it can handle whatever you throw at it. Obviously, the lack of discrete graphics card makes gaming a bit sub-par, but that's not the purpose of this kind of device.

I bought the type-cover keyboard, and while the spacing takes a little getting used to, it works great and is very responsive. I hear complaints about the trackpad, but I'm not seeing the issue. I agree it is a little too small, but it works very well for me.

The stylus also is very well coordinated with the computer - the screen very precisely tracks where you are pointing.

I also purchased the wedge mouse, which i love. Between the mouse and the keyboard, I can have a traditional laptop when I want one, or i can remove the keyboard, and have a tablet when I want that instead. The versatility of the device is amazing.

The only downside is the battery life could be better, but I don't fault Microsoft for that. The space constraints of the device do not allow for a massive lap-top size battery to power laptop quality components under the hood. Running an i5-3317 processor takes more juice than the little cell-phone processors found in most tablets. I'm sure with future iterations, they will figure out ways to expand the battery life.

Overall, if you're looking for a device that can be both a laptop and a tablet, this is the winner. And compared buying the latest ultrabook, the price is fairly competitive.

title: Great monitor -- IF it doesn't have a persistent high-pitched tone and you don't get caught in the ninth circle of Asus support
text:
#donotbuyASUS

This monitor is beautiful. Very good colors, very easy to set up and use. Lived up to the reviews.

Until ONE MONTH LATER, when the high-pitched tone started.

At first, it was for just 5 minutes or so, right after the monitor went idle. And then it was whenever the monitor wasn't in active use. Yes, all the time. The only way to make it stop was to unplug it. Thankfully, it didn't make the sound when I was using it. But still.

By then, I had gotten rid of the original packaging. So I turned to Asus and the warranty repair.

And so began the odyssey.

I sent the monitor in ($140 for shipping supplies and shipping), and after about 3 weeks, they sent it back, repaired.

With a chunk taken out of the screen, in the middle. Grrr.

Today is March 17. I sent in photos of the damage on February 6. The guy who got the photos didn't put them in the file. The photos weren't in the right place in the file. They needed to do a "stock check," which apparently takes weeks because they have so much unsold stock. They found the item. No, they didn't. Yes, they did -- or maybe a different (better!) monitor. A supervisor called saying the case was being expedited. He promised to send me his contact info. He did not.

Twelve days ago, they claimed to have located a replacement, and they sent me a FedEx label so I could send them the damaged monitor. As per instructions, I called to tell them the tracking number, proving it was in the system. Oops, the guy put the number in the wrong place in the file. Oh, yes, there it is. They promised a new monitor within a couple of days. Yeah, right.

I have been on hold now for 25 minutes, eagerly waiting to make contact so I can find out the next plot twist in this saga.

Each person I have talked to has been perfectly nice. But the system as a whole is the Keystone Kops Do Tech Support. Luckily, this monitor is for home use and I have my work laptop.

[My laptop is a Lenovo Yoga whose battery flat out died after 1 year. Took the Geek Squad 5 weeks to figure out a replacement battery. Had to buy another laptop to tide me over. An Asus (now, I shudder). But that's another story.]

Update:
March 17 still. I was actually on hold for 1 hour and 10 minutes. They said they are contacting the corporate office to see what the hold-up is. I got the guy's email address and he said I could follow up with him directly. We'll see how this goes. The last guy gave me his email address and never responded.

Update:
March 18. Emailed to follow up. Never heard back.

Update:
March 20. Swore for the first time talking to an Asus rep (and apologized). Escalated to a supervisor. I was told the monitor was located and needed to be tested, and it probably would be sent to me in 48 hours. I don't believe them, but there's nothing I can do. Got the supervisor's email address. Not holding my breath.

Update:
March 26. Unbelievable. THE LONG-PROMISED MONITOR ARRIVED!!! Good thing I was home, because I had to sign for it. They could have gained so much goodwill if they had told me it was on its way, with a tracking number.

No high-pitched sound (so far).

title: Still trying to get a unit that will work for more than a few weeks.
text:
I originally purchased a DualAV GPSX251 in August 2011 and the Navigon USA App. I am happy with Navigon, but a few months after using the GPS, it would no longer charge my 3d generation iPod when plugged into my car in GPS mode. So I sent it back for a replacement. The replacement worked well for a few months and then I started having difficulty getting an initial position. If I fiddled with the switch I could get it to connect. Then it quit. I sent it in under warranty for the second time and got my new unit around Feb 15. It worked great for two days. Then started taking forever to initialize again. Today, Feb 21, I can't get it to work at all. I'm following the directions. The location services icon just blinks on and off every 10 seconds and never seems to connect. The Dual test app can't connect either.

I was wanting to use Navigon NZ next week when I go to New Zealand, but I guess I'm out of luck. I think I just have a large battery brick now. I wish it worked.

I'd buy a different GPS receiver if I were you.

title: Worst Keyboard Ever
text:
This is quite literally the worst keyboard that I've ever seen. The main problem is that the keys stick and they don't punch easily, making it very difficult to type. I grew up with mechanical keyboards and can type quite fast. This keyboard slows me down considerably, because I'm constantly having to punch keys twice and this usually requires erasing keys punched afterward, first. I don't know if I have a defective keyboard or if other people just don't type as fast, but I've never used a keyboard this bad in my life.

The mouse is also horrible. I've always preferred Logitech mice, because the quality was better. I had my last Logitech wireless mouse for 10 years before it quit working. The problem with this one is that the scroll functionality with the wheel button never worked and this causes the page to jump all over the place. Trying to navigate any lengthy page using the mouse is miserable, because you're constantly moving around several pages on accident and having to find your way back.

I would NEVER use this set for real work, because it would cause all sorts of potentially costly problems. But I have used it for some time on my home computer and it never gets any better. I simply haven't taken the time to replace it, yet, but I'll be buying a new Microsoft desktop combo to do that very soon. It's sad, because I've always preferred Logitech products and never minded spending more money for them, but this product is totally unacceptable and leaves me to believe that Logitech has really gone downhill recently. I've owned several dozen keyboards in my lifetime and rarely will I only give a product a single star, but this one deserves it.

title: Not at all well suited for HTPC use
text: I've read a few other reviews that suggest this drive is noisy.  It indeed is, and this is why.  When you insert a CD, DVD, or BRD, the drive spins up to max speed and stays there no matter how slowly the data is actually read.  While playing media this drive just whizzes away at full speed instead of slowing down to a quiet speed that better matches the 1x speed data is actually being consumed at.  Furthermore the drive makes rather loud clicking, buzzing, and beeping noises during seeks.  All in all, it might be OK in a laptop (and indeed the drive seems to perform fine except for noise), but in an HTPC or other application where quietness is priority, this is not the drive you want.  Unfortunately there are not many alternatives for a BRD burner at this time.  The options open up a bit if a BRD ROM/DVD Burner combo drive is acceptable and considerably if BRD is not a requirement at all.

title: it is hard to not recommend it. Having worked as a professional photographer for ...
text:
I haven't used it much yet, but I can say that for $200, it is hard to not recommend it. Having worked as a professional photographer for several years, and having owned both pocket-sized and SLR-like digitals, I would say that the following are the important points to consider when making a camera purchase:

1. Price (duh). If you don't want to spend $800 or more for a real camera (or at least something close to one), the next option is an SLR-like model (again - this one was only $200 - a big plus).

2. SLR-Like vs. Pocket-Sized. To be honest, considering the capabilities of most phones nowadays, I don't undestand why they even still make pocket-sized cameras. (Although there are some that are sort of a cross between a pocket-sized & SLR-like that have a lot of zoom and give you a bit of something to hold onto). (And personally, I consider having something to hold onto to be a big plus).

3. Zoom. With 34x optical zoom, its a no-brainer. That's more zoom than you could get out of a 400mm lens with a doubler! (Try lugging one of those around). It also has image stabilization (a necessity for a long zoom shot).

4. Pixels/Picture Quality. As some of you know, more pixels does not necessarily equate to a better picture. I have an old 5 meg Olympus which has a 7 meg interpolated mode which still takes as good or better pics than anything I have seen since. (But it is as slow as Christmas). As far as I know, the quality & clarity is the pics from this camera are comparable to other 16 meg cameras on the market, but I would still keep it in the highest quality (least compressed/interpolated) mode.

5. Auto Focus Speed. This is a BIG PLUS with this camera and a crucial factor which none of the mfgs. include in their specs. The primary reason that we wanted a new camera is because my wife and I were fed up with trying to take pictures of our little girl with a camera that would almost always never focus quickly enough to get the shot. If you read the specs regarding "continuous shooting" you will see that it will shoot ~6.7 fps (max ~5 frames) in Continuous High mode. That doesn't actually tell you how fast it will focus, but is the only means of comparison that most mfgs. provide. Also, one camera review/testing site rates the "shutter lag" when in autofocus at 2/10 to 4/10 of a sec. I don't think there is anything else out there in the same price range that comes close.

6. Batteries. It seemed odd that Nikon would have gone with AA's rather than the usual proprietary lithium, but I have decided that it might come in handy sometime to be able to just put in some new AA's rather than having to recharge. (And you can always use rechargeable AA's if you want).

7. Focus Point. I discovered that you can go into the menu and select different focus points just like a real camera! (Despite having a face detection mode [which, if it is like other cameras, you will never use because it will increase the focus time], if you shoot a lot of portraits, it is a big plus to be able to quickly focus on the eyes/face & then take the shot without having to bring the camera down). Unfortunately, there doesn't seem to be any way to tell the camera to keep the point that you selected. (You have to go into the menu & reset it each time you turn the camera off).

8. AWB (Auto White Balance). I had looked at a review which compared this camera to others in the same class, which included sample pics taken in different lighting conditions. I was thus very disappointed to discover that it pretty much sucks in getting the white balance right when shooting indoors. (A BIG MINUS, but probably not much worse than the competition).

9. User Interface. The number & placement of dedicated function buttons is pretty much the same as most digital cameras nowadays. However, they are placed so close to the edge (under the "heel" of your thumb when you hold the camera) that I keep inadvertently pressing one or more of them. Maybe in the next model they will put a bit of a lip or ridge there to help prevent that?

10. Viewfinder/View Screen. The fact that the view screen can be extended & rotated allows you to stand and look down at it (thus allowing you to get a lower camera angle). That is actually a big plus for those who are aware of such things and often find themselves shooting from a kneeling position. However, the absence of a viewfinder is a BIG MINUS in my opinion. If you read some of the other reviews, you will see that people complain about trying to use the screen in bright sunlight. You must in effect resort to shooting blindly and hoping that you manage to get a couple of good shots. That is true for most digital cameras, and unless you already have a thousand pics on your card, it doesn't really matter if you take a hundred pics & keep only one. Still, if Nikon had only included a viewfinder, they could have had a camera that without question would have been a real winner.

title: Saved my (extremely rainy) trip pictures and protected my camera.

title: Quick, Easy, and nice quality...
text:
I gave the dropcam 5 stars. I'll do my best to review after owning for a full week and tinkering around with these really cool devices.

PROS:
*daylight or in light - the cameras offer incredible quality - HD quality yes @ close range.
*a lot of great features that are built in such as motion detection, that you can toggle what device you want to send the alerts too
*i downloaded software for use on my android, my iPad, and my MacAir - all were very easy to use and pretty straightforward.
*hands down one of the easiest to assemble and get up and running of an electronic device or any mechanical device that i've ever purchased. basically 3 or 4 components comprise each camera system - take out of the box pop the camera into the holder, plug the usb cord into your camera then the other end into your PC and the device basically walks you through an auto-installation - this does not get any simpler than this.
*the lag time between what's happening and what you see on the camera is pretty short - i realize a lot of that has to do with the wifi speed, but i've been impressed with this.
*the talk feature is non-static sounding so it sounds nice - actually having a decent conversation between your android, iPad or Mac is totally possible! this is really cool.
*enabling and disabling the blue status light is a plus for me - my kids don't know that the camera is on - they have assumed now since we've had this a week, that once the blue light is on the camera is on...oh how not true.

CONS:
*night vision mode - objects directly in front to about 5-10' out are pretty recognizeable no where near HD quality though obviously. after that objects are sketchy.
*not auto-panning - you have to do all of this manual - which means you set it in place and the one upside to this is that it does have a wide field of view... but you can't rotate the camera to monitor an object.
*the back of the camera can get very very hot when you have it on and it's got wifi connection. you really (in my opinion) have to watch keeping the rear-end of the camera near or touching anything due to it being very hot.
*the one software feature i guess you could call it that i'm not real fond of is the actual zoom feature and how you have to choose the section you want to zoom in on instead of being able to pan the camera to the area you specifically want centered.

The con's are minimal and most people wouldn't even notice them - the camera for $149 is a steal - excellent value, and really really a great little product. I'm very pleased.

title: ... invest in the Tivo systems or wait for something better / cheaper to come along
text:
If you are on the fence about whether to invest in the Tivo systems or wait for something better / cheaper to come along, I highly suggest that you wait. Read on for why.

Short version

I was pretty let down by several aspects of the Tivo including functionality, ease of use, and customer support. The only reason people buy this and rate it highly is because of how bad cable company DVRs, customer support, and costs are. Tivo is only slight notch above them. If you are looking for a cablecard product with high quality, fully functional, mature product with good customer service like other consumer electronic products from Apple, Roku, etc., you'll have to keep waiting. Based on my horrible experience, I give this product only two stars for being only slightly better than other horrible offerings from the cable companies

Long version

* The install nightmare that was all Tivo's fault.

I had read mixed stories about the difficulty of first getting the cable card working with the Tivo which requires some support from the cable company. So I did hours of reading about the different problems so that I'd be fully prepared for the cable company install. 10 hours later of dealing with cable company installers, phone support, picking up new cable cards, etc., I was still without working cable. I finally decided to buy two more Tivo Roamio units in case mine was bad. Sure enough, my original unit was bad.

There were no diagnostics on the Tivo that indicated any problems. There was no mention of the unit possibly being bad from the Tivo Customer supported. And obviously, their quality control/testing at their factory is non-existent.

Afterwards, I called customer support to complain and to see what they were willing to do to make it right. Keep in mind that they had full records of my support calls trying to get my unit installed. I basically asked for a few months of free service since they'd wasted many hours of my life. The girl on the phone offered NOTHING, zilch, zero. I then asked to speak with her supervisor. He also refused to offer me a few months of free service but finally conceded to offered to let me buy a lifetime subscription at the discounted return customer's price. I reluctantly bought it given the lack of another quality choice for a cable box.

About 90 days after using the second Tivo, it died. I called them and they shipped my a replacement. It was then I found out that they only have a 90-day unlimited warranty, not one year!!! If your device dies after 90-days, you have to pay a substantial fee for them to send you another unit, and the other unit you get is a refurb, not a new unit!!! Wow. Luckily, I was able to get it replaced under the 90-day unlimited warranty period. Name any quality consumer electronics product that does not have at least a full one year replacement policy.

After I got my replacement refurb unit, I hooked it up, called Tivo (who also showed by Tivo mini account on the account). First, they are so technologically backwards, they were unable to transfer my scheduled program recordings to the new unit. Second, the Tivo Mini would not connect/sync with my replacement Roamio. I had to call several times. I was first told it takes 48 to 72 hours for it to sync. Why? That makes no sense. Second, it did not sync up in that time frame.

On the Tivo mini, I had problems with the Netflix App loging several times that required my to reset the Tivo Mini back to factory settings and set up everything again (not a quick process).

* Functionality

As a smart TV device, it's the worst possible device I've seen on the market. It has the standard Netflix, Pandora, and Spotify apps, thought he Spotify app is a very minimal featured version that's nothing close to the functionality of other smart tv devices or on Android/iOS. The Amazon Instant Video app lacks Amazon Prime Video support. You can only watch content you purchase. Rhapsody is the only App it has. That's it, like 5 or 6 apps. There is an Opera TV store but this appears to be an after thought. It doesn't have anything you'd want (like HBO Go, etc.) and is klunky to get to and use. It's bascially an after thought and something that allows them to claim they have an app store on their marketing materials.

Seeing how you will need at least one other smart TV device connected to your TV or receiver input, now you want to swtich between these device. Unfortunately, the Tivo Roamio lacks a technology called HDMI-CEC which can allow whatever device you are using to automatically be switched to by the TV or receiver. Roku and other quality devices all have this feature.

I purchased the aftermarket RF remote which is programmable for controlling TV and receivers to a limited degree (as I found out). There is a power button that can be used for power on or power off but not both (no toggle capability). WTF? You can program another button, such as Mute, to perform that role but then you lose your mute functionality. Really bad design.

Watching DVR'd content has a very frustrating a quirk. If you touch the remote and bring any menus up, the content you are watching is display in a small window in the top right corner. But there is no intuitive method to force it to go full screen again. Your left having to go back through your recordings, find the content you are watching, and click resume. Not the worst thing in the world but just an example of lack of polish and intelligence with this product.

Lastly, if there is a show you want to record the upcoming season, if the show is over 2 or 3 weeks away from starting, Tivo is unable to set a season pass (what they call they recording of all new episodes). You can only do this once the show is near to starting. How stupid is that? They could easily look back at previous programming data, to grab information about the last season to help them automatically set up a season pass for the next season, whenever it arrives. They have some other lame functionality to record anything with keywords in it that you can enter, but that will just end up recording a bunch of junk that you don't care about.

Their online web interface is a mess, like something from the mid 2000s.

* Conclusion

I had one of the first or second Tivo devices back in the early 2000s. It was a technological wonder for its time. Fast forward over a decade later and I'm sad how bad a once innovative company and product has become. It seems they simply try to do the least amount possible that keep them just ahead of the cable companies and their instrinsic problems that come with lack of competition. The only reason this product sells is because companies that design and sell quality products have avoided the Cablecard mess and bet (incorrectly) on IPTV coming to fruition. We are left with a very expensive (particularly with the service costs), poorly implemented product with bad quality control and customer service.

title: Skeptical because of some reviews, but satisfied.
text:
I was really skeptical in purchasing this Mono Class D Amp because of some reviews saying that when you turn up the gain, the amp will automatically shut off; but given the price point and 300 watt RMS @ 4Ohms and 500 watt RMS at 2Ohms, I figure it was worth a shot to try out and if all else fails, you could always return it defective on Amazon.

I hooked up this amp using 8Guage Wire and it works fine after some adjustments. I am pushing a 10" low profile woofer rated at 200 watts RMS and 800 watts max, and it does the job just fine; almost sounds like I have a 12" woofer. I turned on the LPF (low pass filter) on my head unit, and set the cross over at 100Hz; set the bass boost to 18db and it sounds near perfect. Being on a budget and for the price, I am satisfied.

My setup:
-Pioneer AVIC-5000NEX Head Unit
- Kenwood KAC-5001PS Amplifier
- Pioneer TS-SWX251 Low-Profile Sub-woofer

If this did not work out, my alternative amplifier would of been an Alpine Monoblock MRV-M500. It has generally the same specifications and has excellent reviews, but costs a little more. So really depends on how much you're willing to spend and whether you want to take a chance on this because I don't know if there was a bad bunch of these amps because of some of the reviews, seems hit or miss.

I say as long as you match the RMS output with your subwoofer RMS or go above that, I think you should be fine. You never want to use an amp that has a significantly lower RMS output for sub-woofers that have much higher RMS inputs; this will overheat the amp and make it work harder and shut it down into protection mode. Hope this general rule of thumb helps. Always look at RMS values instead of peak/max values as these are what really matter.

title: Usable IF You Have a Newer Higher Power Burner
text: OK, here is the scoop with these discs.  If you have an older model burner you will start getting significant errors starting around 18 Gig of data. The issue seems to be these discs have a high burn threshold.  If you record a movie the first 2/3 of the movie is fine. As you get further along (further out towards the edge of the disc) the data will start to become significantly corrupted. As you get further out from the center, the velocity significantly increases and each bit the burner tries to burn covers much more area than when you are near the hub.  This effectively dilutes and spreads the laser's burn power over a greater area. Normally you can slow the burn speed to improve reliability but even 1X and slower didn't help much with my 2009 model burner.  I upgraded to a newer 12x LITEON unit which has newer much more powerful lasers. So far I have had good luck and no failures through the whole disc on the ones I have burn so far.  I burn at 2X and don't push my luck.  I never had any issues with the 6X Verbatim discs I burned with the older burner, so I think it's fair to say that these are cheap because they have issues.  Issues which I feel can be remedied with a newer high speed(high power) burner and slowing down the speed to 2X.

title: Nothing like what I expected from Sennheiser
text:
I purchased a pair of Sennheiser HD 202 II Professional Headphones a few years ago and was completely blown away. I am an avid music fan of all genres, but by no means an audiophile. The baffling of outside noise, the comfort of the ear pads which were large enough to cover my "Spock" ears really sold me. I had never owned a pair of headphones worth saving, but these were amazing--the sound was rich and authentic and the headset light and comfortable. Unfortunately the cord eventually wore out and I could only hear out of the left side so I threw them away just past the warranty expiration.

I was sold on Sennheiser so I bought a pair of Sennheiser CX 300B MK II Precision Enhanced Bass Earbuds to replace them. These, these are hands down the greatest ear buds ever made. Beats Dr. Dre (I borrowed a pair, nice but not as good with the Bass). Light, (I travel constantly so that is a plus). They dampen noise to near silence (great in the plane or crowded area). Easy mobility (for running or hiking). I will buy them again and after this, go write a nice little review for them.

However, I wanted to replicate my listening experience with Sennheiser over-the-ear phones so went a step up and bought the Sennheiser HD 429 Headphones. I was so excited I watched a youtube video review of them before deciding to buy them. Got them in the midst of a snowstorm and set up a nice evening of listening to music.

Headphones--clunky and heavy.
Sound--muddy

I listened to every genre I owned. The sound reproduction was muddy (messed with my eq) and I found the only songs I enjoyed were the acoustic sets. The sound was clear, but not defined like on my Sennheiser CX 300s.

I've given these earphones several days and many hours and I just find them uncomfortable and the sound not defined or crisp. I find the baffling appalling--my wife can hear everything even with the volume set low.

Again, I'm not an expert here and just an average guy who doesn't like to spend hard earned money on products that don't deliver. Sennheiser I still love you--so no hard feelings. Love the buds!

I just want to say...it works as of Jan. 15, 2014. At first I was extremely reluctant because I read reviews stating that the tablet does not work for windows 8. Well, I have windows 8.1 and it is working perfectly fine for me. I just followed the instructions that other people put in their reviews and the tablet worked right when I plugged it in. If you want to hear how I did it I'll write it out, although I think plenty of other reviews clearly stated how to install the Huion H610 pro tablet.

Here is how I installed the tablet for Windows 8.1:

1) DO NOT PLUG IN THE TABLET.
2) Make sure you don't have any other tablet drivers installed (like Wacom). Uninstall all of them and then RESTART the computer.
3) Install the Huion H610 pro driver. I got an installation CD, but you can also go to the Huion website ([...]) and download the driver too. Open Setup, click OK to everything. When the driver is finished installing RESTART the computer. Check to see if the driver is installed in Programs in the Control Panel.
4) Plug in the tablet and the tablet icon should pop up in the lower right corner.

Done.

Really, it probably took me 20 minutes, and the pressure and the buttons are working just fine for me on Windows 8.1. Photoshop CS6 and Paint Tool Sai works just fine with this tablet as well.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
New review March 5, 2014

First, I apologize for not leaving a proper product review. I just wanted to let other people know that it does work for Windows 8.1 when I first got it so they can try it out too.

Anyways, now I got the chance to really try things out, and it's pretty good.

Pros:

I like it for the price and size, and it is definitely more precise than my old small Wacom. Also, I'm one of the lucky people that found the installation process easy and fast (for windows 8.1 at least). The product is sturdy and the overall design of the tablet is nice. The surface seems like it won't get scratched as easily (but I always put a protective plastic layer on my tablets, so I'm not sure). The product comes with replaceable nibs and the little circular metal clip that helps pull the nib out of the pen. The buttons and shortcut keys are nifty and neat, but personally I never use them. The pen lasts a long time without recharge (I used it for several days without charging it).

Cons:

It is hard to reach the higher pressures and you have to push down really hard to get to the desired line weight. I'm hoping that Huion will fix this somehow maybe through a driver update if they can. The biggest problem I have with the tablet is the pen. I hate the pen. I don't like how the nib seems to have a spring in it. If it is suppose to stimulate a real pencil or pen it shouldn't have the spring. I used it for about a month now and I just can't get use to it. I also don't like the feel of the pen. It just doesn't have the right weight or grip to feel comfortable, but it is sort of what you expect from a tablet with this price. The pen does not have a eraser, but that does not bother me since I never use it anyways. Sometimes the pressure glitches out while I'm drawing and leaves a nice fat streak. It goes back to normal later, but I prefer if it didn't happen at all. Also, the pressure won't work properly if you open the program first and then plug in the tablet. This might be more of an issue with the program though. All you have to do is close the program and reopen the program with the tablet already plugged in.

In short, sometimes the tablet works fine and I like it, other times...I just don't like the overall feel of it and it bothers me.

I know it sounds like a lot of cons, but it's a decent tablet for those with a budget. It is an upgrade from a Wacom Bamboo tablet; however,the Huion H610 Pro is not as good as a Wacom Intuos Pro and if you do have the money definitely go for the Wacom Intuos Pro instead. (I have tried both tablets and Wacom Intuos Pro is definitely better). However this is still an excellent tablet for all your digital projects and you can't beat the size and price.

If Huion fixed the pressure sensitivity and some of the glitches than this tablet would be 5 stars. I'll give it a 4, though personally it is closer to a 3.5 because I really dislike the pen, but it might not be an issue with everyone.

text:
I had high hopes for this alarm clock, but it failed me on a few keys aspects.

First off, you cannot set the volume of the radio when using it as the alarm. It is EXTREMELY loud. I do not like to be startled awake, and that it is exactly what it does. If it let me set the volume instead of it being preset, then I would still be using it.

Secondly, when the radio is playing it does not show what time it is...it just displays what station is playing and never goes back to time until you turn the radio off. Most stations announce often enough what I am listening to that I don't need the constant reminder displayed on the screen.

Lastly, the screen is bright and does not have a setting to adjust that. I feel like I am in a horror movie when I wake up to my room cast in an eerie green glow.

With that said, there are positives. The display is clear and easy to read. I really didn't think the clock and alarms were that hard to set. The radio works really well and even gets a station I like that is hard to get. You can choose either standard 12-hour clock or military style 24 hour clock display...I still just use the 12-hour display, but thought that it was a neat feature.

If you are a sound-sleeper and have a hard time waking up then this alarm clock is right for you because you won't be able to accidentally have it at a quite volume. If you don't like to be scared when the alarm go off and have other people a few rooms away say that they could hear your alarm, then you should pass on this.

Hope this helps!

title: understand the tradeoffs
text:
This unit gives you sine wave output with no frills at an attractive price.

Be aware of the limitations of this new model at its price point. This is not a desktop product, so don't expect extras like ethernet or coax surge protection. It is less capable than some other APC UPSs with equivalent VA ratings; for example, the SMC1000 is rated for 600 watts, vs. 700 for the SMT1000. It has a 2-year warranty, rather than the 3 year warranty carried by most recent APC products.

Most importantly, this unit uses the new "Microlink" protocol, and does not have an expansion slot for adding a UPSLink interface. This means it will never be possible to fully interact with this unit using open source software, such as NUT or apcupsd; you can only get the most basic information out of it, such as line power up or down. Neither NUT nor apcupsd will be able to query it for load, output voltage, recent events, or many other things.

If these limitations don't concern you, it's a good value, and is the lowest-priced APC UPS with sine wave output. It's perfect for protecting the availability of a small server.

I noted that another reviewer complained of noise, but mine is nearly silent except when operating on backup power.
