title: There Is A Lot To LIke; It's A Keeper
text:
April 21/14 addition:

1. The default color setting is FinepixCOLOR: Std (for standard). If you think a little more saturation will help your photos, open the menu, scroll down to FinepixCOLOR, click on it, then choose "Chrome" from the list. This will increase the saturation, but not to an excessive degree. It is good to have this option since tastes differ.

2. If you expect to be using this camera in wet weather, take a look at the Lowepro Nova 140AW camera bag. It is a good size for this camera, even with a lens hood on, but more important, it is well protected from the rain. Lowepro is known for making good camera cases, and generally they come with a rain cover, but what sets this camera apart is that you can open the case when the cover is on. The small pockets on front of the flap and on the sides of the case are covered, the the main compartment, where the camera is kept, can be opened and closed with ease.

Original:

The Finepix S1 is not my first camera. I am an advanced intermediate and have owned a number of them. In addition to the S1, my present cameras are a Canon 60d dslr, a Canon SX280, my travel and walk around camera, a Canon camcorder, and now the S1.

I know that regardless of what else a camera does the most important is taking good photos. The S1 meets that test, so far I am very satisfied with the clarity and quality of the photos. The S1 is a keeper.

For the past couple of days I have been "playing" with the S1, experimenting with many of its offerings. I would like to share some of my findings and impression in this review.

Zoom: All I can say is wow! I can think of many times in the past when I would have loved to have this camera in my hands. I took the Finepix S1, the Canon 60d with a 70-300 mm lens, and the Canon SX280 point and shoot with a 20X lens to the harbor to photograph a boat at anchor quite a long way out. It was not even close. The Faststone image viewer that I use reported that the focal length of the shot with the 60d was 70mm (this is not the 35mm equivalent, which would be a higher number); the focal length of the little SX280 was 90mm; and the focal length of the S1 was 215mm. A huge difference, and it was obvious when you compared the photos.

Normally I rely only on optical zoom, but for this test I turned on the digital zoom available on the S1. It is said this almost doubles the default 50X to 100X, and I could see that in the photos. With the 50X the boat was close, with digital zoom turned on, it looked like I could step on the deck.

All the photos from the 3 cameras were clear and usable, but the S1 100X photos with the digital zoom turned on were not as sharp as the others. I can spruce them up in post processing, but out of the camera the photos at S1 50X were noticeably sharper.

To get a close up of the distant boat equal to the S1 zoomed to 50X with the much more expensive 60d with 70-300mm lens would require a lens of enormous length and cost, and so heavy it would have to always to be supported by a tripod.

It should also be mentioned that the S1 makes it easy to zoom out when you are shooting. There is a lever around the shutter button that you operate with your right hand, this is common on many cameras, but on the S1 there is also a lever on the other side that can easily be operated by your left hand. This makes it possible to keep the shutter half-way down to focus with your right hand while you zoom out or in with your left hand. This is a very nice feature. It also works very well when shooting video.

Image Stabilization: I was impressed with how clear and sharp the photos were even though I was not braced when I took the photos. The S1 compensated very well for my shakiness. That is good for the confidence when using the camera.

Vari-angle LCD: The S1 uses 920K dots, which gives you a very clear view in good color of what you are shooting, if your preference is to focus using the screen. Most companies use a lower resolution display to help keep the cost down.

It is important to know that for shooting "P", "S", "A", and "M" the menu (image size) gives you the option of 4 aspect ratios: 4:3 (default), 16:9, 3:2 and 1:1. 4:3 and 16:9 are the most commonly used. If you choose 16:9, what you see on the screen will be different than what you see if you choose 4:3. The scene if you choose 16:9 is less high in relation to width than 4:3, so what you see on the screen has a black bar at top and bottom to fill the space left by the reduction in height. The image you see if you choose 4:3 fills the screen. The black that you see with 16:9 does not appear in the image you upload/print. If the black bar bothers you, this feature will be considered by you as a negative. But I like it because I can see exactly what I will get when I upload/print the photo. (Think of it as something like what happens when you anchor the left side of a piece of stretchy material and pull on the ride side. As the material stretches, it gets narrower. Same amount of material, but it looks wider and narrower.)

(If the sun seems too bright to use the LCD monitor, you can use the viewfinder. However, the S1 does have a setting for the LCD monitor for bright, sunny days, but that should be used only on days that it is really needed because it uses a lot of battery juice.)

Viewfinder: My preference is the viewfinder; the SX280 is the only photo camera I have owned that did not have a view finder, so I have seen a lot of them. I can say with certainty that the viewfinder of the S1, which also uses 920K dots, is the best I have used both in terms of the area covered and the clarity and brightness of the scene to be photographed. One negative is that color you see in the viewfinder is somewhat washed out (this is not true of the LCD monitor), but that is not how the photos will look. For some, another negative is the the scene seen through the viewfinder does completely fill the window in the same way that it does the LCD monitor. There is a wide black line around the window like a frame. This does not bother me, but it does some.

Panorama: You turn this on from the mode dial. I have done panoramas before, but never so easily. Up to now I always had to take overlapping photos then stitch them together with software. S1, however, does the work for you. The defaults are 120 degrees swinging camera to the right, but you can change them to swing to the left and/or 160 or 180 degrees if you prefer. To make the panorama, press the shutter, then immediately lift your finger, and while holding the camera in place turn your body in the indicated direction. Both on the screen and in the viewfinder you will see a white line move across the screen. When it gets to the end, it will stop automatically. If you press the shutter while this line is moving, you will end the panorama and nothing will be recorded So press, but do not hold down the shutter button. You can experiment with speed of moving your body, just don't go too slow.

(You are better able to keep the camera level if you rotate your body than if you try to rotate the camera.)

When I checked the panoramas on the Faststone photo viewer I found they were of good quality, but they were "thinner" so to speak than what I was seeing in the view finder. For example, when making a panorama of the condominium where I live, I could see the sky in the viewfinder. However, the photo had part of the roof of the 3-story buildings cut off. Taking another, I pointed the camera a little higher and ended up with the view I wanted.

But I soon found that you don't have to wait to know if you got the panorama you wanted. When the white line has crossed the screen, the result shows briefly on the LCD monitor or in the view finder, so you can tell right away whether a retake is needed.

You also have the option of making panoramas in the traditional way: take overlapping photos and stitch them together with a software program like Canon's PhotoStitch. With my other cameras, this was my only option.

Advanced Mode: Another option on the mode dial, besides all the the usual and panorama, is what they call "advanced" but is actually good for all users. Choose it and you are offered several options include "pro low-light", which is good for shooting in low light; "natural, where 2 photos are taken of the same thing, one with flash and one without; "zoom bracketing", where 3 shots are taken, 1 regular and 2 that are cropped to different degrees, giving you 3 options to choose from; and HDR where 3 photos are taken at different exposures and put together by the camera so that you get a photo that shows the whole range of exposure.

All of these options work well and I'm sure I will use them all on occasion.

Continuous Shooting (sometimes called burst mode): You activate this by pressing a button on the top of the camera. There are 3 options, high, medium and low, which can be read as very fast, a little less fast, and the slowest of the 3. Whichever you chose, you will get about 9 shots while you press the shutter button. High will give you 9 shots at about 10 fps, medium gives 9 shots at about 5 fps, and low is 9 shots at 3 fps. It is important to know this so you can chose the setting best for you at the time. If you are shooting a sports event and certain you can anticipate the crucial moment, then use "high" to get 9 shots of that moment to choose from. If less certain, then chose medium or low because the 9 shots will be spread over more seconds.

Which ever you choose, it takes about 4 seconds for the camera to clear so you can shoot another burst.

Exposure Compensation: With other cameras, I have tended to rely on post processing to make corrections in the exposure. This worked well with the dslr cameras because I was shooting RAW. With point and shoot cameras shooting .jpeg, it was not as satisfactory. But I didn't use the exposure compensation on those cameras because it seemed like too much work and took too much time to open the menus, scroll to find exposure compensation and make the change needed to photograph a very bright, very dark, or high contrast subject. The S1 makes it easy. Press the exposure compensation button on the top of the camera, the exposure compensation indicator will appear at the bottom of the monitor or viewfinder. Then while looking at the lcd monitor or through the viewfinder, use your thumb to rotate the dial between the movie button and the mode dial. As you rotate the dial, a yellow dot will move over the indicator, either increasing or reducing exposure, and you can see the scene or subject getting lighter or darker. When it looks right, take the photo, which when uploaded to your computer or printer will look just like it did on the screen when you took the shot. To check this out, I photographed scenes and subjects with no compensation, then photographed the same scenes and subjects after dialing in some compensation. In every case, the compensated photo was better and looked just like I expected from seeing it on the monitor before taking the shot. It is so easy to do, there really is no excuse for not making a correction before pressing the shutter button if it looks like the photo will be too dark or too light. To illustrate, I have uploaded before compensation and after compensation images so you can see what a difference a little compensation makes. In this case only +0.67. Look in the gallery.

AE Bkt (Exposure Bracketing): Another way to manage exposure compensation that some may prefer is AE Bkt, one of the options that becomes available when you press the button for continuous shooting. Press the button and you get 5 options: Continuous shooting high, medium, low, best frame capture, and AE Bkt. Using the "selector button" on the back of the camera scroll to AE Bkt and press "Ok". When you take your shot, the camera will take 3 images: 0 exposure compensation, +0.33 and -0.33. At your leisure, you can pick the one you think is best. If you think more compensation might be needed, press the exposure compensation button and follow the instruction above to chose 0.67 or 1.0, either plus or minus. Then when you take your shot the camera will follow your instructions when taking the 3 photos, for example 0 compensation, +0.67 and -0>67. +0.33/-0.33 is the default setting, however, if you expect to be mostly using 0.67 or 1.00 exposure compensation, you can change the default setting.

Camera Body: According to Fujifilm, it is safe to use this camera in the rain or dusty conditions because 70 areas of the body have been sealed. This sets the S1 apart from the other bridge cameras and is especially important to me because my son and I are booked on a cruise to Alaska the first week in June and they say there is a lot of wet weather there. I will update this review when I get back and report if I got all the shots and video that I wanted even though it meant shooting in the rain,

But the weather resistance is not the only thing that impresses me about the S1 body. It looks like a serious mid-range dslr yet is aesthetically pleasing with molded curves and rubberized matt black finish. In your hand it feels sold, like it would withstand a few knocks, but fits comfortably with a nice molded indentation for your middle finger and a rubberized patch on the back for your thumb. Also, the dials and buttons are well placed and easy to use. Once you get acquainted with them, which takes some practice as well as trial and error, you will be able make many adjustments with little difficulty as the need arises.

All in all, this is a very nice camera. It takes good photos and video; looks professional; has a lot of shooting options for photos and video, such as filters, panorama, HDR, red-eye removal, up to 10 face-detection, and interval shooting; built in WiFi; a very long zoom; and sealing that enables shooting on bad-weather days.

In the box is an abbreviated manual that gives setup instructions, but there is a full user manual on the CD. I highly recommend that you download it. The user manual is good, but you will still need to play around with camera to make full use of many of the options. More than a little of what I have told you above was not in the manual, but discovered through use of the camera.

title: I'm a converted "Bose Basher"!  Please listen to the system in your own home before you judge!
text:
I've had this system for about a week now and I'm really, really enjoying it! I'm starting to believe Bose is really the King of Sound Engineering. If you're looking for an unobtrusive system that has audiophile quality sound I would highly recommend this system.

I consider myself a sound nerd and I enjoy listening to and comparing any and all sound systems available on the market today. I've owned a Cerwin Vega system with LS-12's, Energy Take Classic 5.1 system, and my most recent system is a Definitive Technology system consisting of 3 Mythos Eights for L,C,R channels, two Gem XL's for surrounds and TWO Supercube II subwoofers. At this time I've already taken down my Def Tech set and replaced them with this one! When I first hooked up the Bose system I left my Def Techs up on the walls and set the Jewel Cube Speakers on my entertainment center and found a reasonable place to temporarily place the surrounds for testing. My initial reaction upon my first listen was they sound very similar if not crisper and wider sound dispersion than my mythos eights! The wider dispersion is likely achieved with Bose's direct/reflecting technology. During a lot of songs I would have had a hard time deciding which speaker was playing and the Jewel Cubes had the inferior placement on my Entertainment center. I'd be able to tell off axis easier because the jewel's sound terrific quite a bit off axis where the Mythos would loose sound quality. The whole room becomes a big sweet spot with the Bose. The only other way you'd get the nice wide dispersion with other speakers would likely be with bipolar speakers which have rear firing drivers that reflect off the back walls.

The Jewel Cubes seem to produce such an amazing clarity on a wide variety of tones that just cannot be matched. The Bose speakers really do defy the laws of physics because of how teeny tiny they are yet they sound like large, wide dispersion tower bipolar speakers. The M.S.R.P on my Def tech speaker system that I compared them to alone was over $4000 but I was able to achieve them for around $2500 on sale when the new models started coming out. I had the def techs hooked up to a Pioneer VSX-9040txh receiver which I reviewed awhile back. I also reviewed the Mythos Eights. I think I MIGHT possibly be able to achieve SLIGHTLY better sound than the Bose with my Def Techs if I bought a top of the line receiver to hook them up to but I don't even want to bother trying. So with the Pioneer receiver which was made in 2009 or 2010 I actually prefer the sound of the Bose Jewel Cubes over the def techs. I also don't know if I'd be able to create the ultra wide dispersion because they lack the reflected sound of the Bose.

The acoustimass module at first didn't seem to compete at all with the TWO supercubes II's when I had the module facing forward. I've now turned it sideways facing a corner about 2 feet away from the corner like I saw at the Bose demo store I just visited and it really improved the bass output significantly. It could be that it calibrated better this way with the adaptiq. I tried running a bass sweep on it and I don't notice any gap that all the Bose Bashers seem to bring up in all of their posts. I did a test at 25 hz with no sound coming out. 30 hz the module starts making some decent bass. 35 hz sounds even more powerful. The supercubes could produce bass down to around 25 hz so I'm missing about 5 hz of the ultra Low Frequency Effects. After setting up the module sideways it can suprisingly fill the relatively large room with an open side into the dining room/kitchen with bass similar to having two subs with almost unnoticeable peaks and dips across all listening areas. I also get better upper bass frequencies with the acoustimass module than the supercubes. Tones around 100 hz I couldn't seem to get pronounced sound with my deftech supercube's with many, many different setting changes with the receiver and the subs. The acoustimass module seems to belt out all the bass relatively evenly from about 35 hz to somewhere around 200+ hz when the Jewel's kick in.

I would also like to mention that on the Bose console we ended up turning OFF the Audio Compression setting for each source which is defaulted to "Enhance Dialogue". Be sure to change it to OFF for each source. To me the voices sounded a bit muffled at times and actually harder to hear voices with it turned on. With it turned off voices sound very clear and still loud and actually easier to understand.

The V35 really has me now thinking that I have the perfectly calibrated system that I've been dreaming of. My def tech system always came close but somehow disappointed me in small yet noticeable ways which became annoying after spending so much on it and adjusting settings for years. The Bose system also plays louder than 99% of people would ever need and I've detected no audible distortion so far with the loud volumes I've tested it at. The speakers are much more elegant looking than any other system I've had due to their tiny almost invisible size. Our livingroom looks like a livingroom now and not a speaker demo room yet I feel like I'm at a top notch theater. All types of music is pure bliss to listen to on this system. Highly recommended so far. I'll update if my opinion changes.

-Update 6/9/2014-

So I've had this system for about 4 months now and I still couldn't be more satisfied. No problems with it whatsoever. I love having one high quality universal remote now as well. Saves space by having less remotes, a smaller, sleeker receiver and tiny speakers. Since I wrote this review I've added a Bose UTS-20B stand for my Jewel center channel which really looks sharp and it raises the speaker about 7 or 8 inches off my shelf which seems to compliment the sound quality as well. If you don't want to mess with installing these speakers in the wall with the Bose UB-20B and you have a shelf to set them on you would be totally happy buying three UTS-20B for your Right, Center and Left speakers. You can also buy the Bose UFS-20B if you'd like to place your front speakers on the floor which are basically the same thing just much taller. Thank you Bose!

title: Hard time picking between the PSW505 and F12? Let me help, I own both
text:
Let me make myself clear before I begin. I love Polk, I originally was going to make my system all Polk however, as any half decent audiophile knows, one company simply does not make the best of everything. I have [[ASIN:B00631YX62 Polk Audio Monitor70 Series II Floorstanding Loudspeaker (Black) Each]] as fronts [[ASIN:B0018QROM2 Polk Audio CS10 Center Channel Speaker (Single, Black)]] and [[ASIN:B00012F7CI BIC America Venturi DV84 2-Way Tower Speaker, Black (Single)]] rears. I own the Polk PSW505 and have been using it on my main surround system for the past 7 months

I wasn't content at all with my Polk PSW505 as you can see in my over 1000 word review of the PSW505 on Amazon, so I saved up money to try the F12 and planned to send it back after testing it out. Honestly, I didn't want the f12 to sound better than my Polk. I tried to tell myself the no name Bic f12 could not compete with the Polk PSW505, that sub is practically God of home subwoofers on Amazon. As the current owner of both, I would advise you to buy this f12 and never look back.

My main issue with the PSW505 was port noise. When my Polk sub hit below 30 hertz it sounded just awful and unless you just watch Teletubbies, Dora the explorer, and Sesame Street your sub will be forced to hit below 30 hertz. This becomes very important if you are watching blu rays with Dolby True HD or DTS HD Master Audio. This sub can punch, roll, and roar much beyond its $200 price tag. With my Polk PSW505 it struggled to hit some lows in Dark Knight among other Blu rays as well as music with heavy bass. That is not the case with the F12 not only will it hit these low notes, but it will shake the room while maintaining clarity.

I have seen quite a few negative reviews on the build quality of this Bic F12 I would agree and disagree. I have disassembled the Polk 505 multiple times so I am more than aware of its build quality, but have not yet taken apart the Bic. I believe the PSW505 has a better exterior finish than the F12, bic clearly did not spend as much on the cabinet. Bic spent its money on the driver and amplifier, which far surpass the Polks driver in quality. I would know this because Polk has sent me two PSW505 drivers(the actual 12 inch speaker) and they somehow even sound muddy and distort when not inside the cabinet. The F12 has a very nice metallic looking driver and it does outperform the PSW505

I know its difficult to believe that this f12 sub will outperform the tried and true 505 but it really does. Don't stray away from the Bic just because it isn't a big brand. Polks subs have a premium to them because of the brand. With this Bic all your paying for the sub. For example Klipsch, Energy, and def techs are great well-known subs but they have a markup because of the name. In contrast HSU, Outlaw, Epik, and SVS are not household names but they will destroy the big names in performance without the markup.

Don't let the brand scare you! Bic customers are some of the happiest in home audio. If you have any questions about the differences between these 2 sub-woofers please leave a comment and I will be happy to respond.

title: Works very well, but not a major upgrade over the AV 200 line.
text:
I live in a two story home built in 2005 that I purchased in 2009 from the original owners. One would have thought that the dumbf#$@! who built my subdivision would have included Cat5 cabling in the walls as a standard feature of the early 21st century, but they would be mistaken. Upon moving in, I purchased some excellent Netgear AV-200 Powerline products so that I could use the standard electrical cabling in my walls to pass information as well. I had my dual band wireless router upstairs and ran a cable out to an AV-200 Ultra Adapter at the nearby socket, and then to the four port Entertainment hub at a socket downstairs. I had great results and usually passed around 9 Mbps thru the electrical lines (which is fine, because I could stream a 3D high definition movie from Vudu for example, but I could not pass something like DTS Master Audio (which requires up to 24 Mbps since it is lossless) or Dolby TrueHD (which requires 18 Mbps)). In late 2011, I changed out my AV-200 equipment for the more expensive and supposedly faster AV-500 stuff. At best, I am currently getting about 11.8 Mbps thru the electrical lines, and more commonly, I am able to pass about 9.8 Mbps of data. Therefore, I have two rankings for the latest Netgear Powerline stuff:

In comparison to spotty wireless hotspots spread throughout a house - Five stars. The Netgear Powerline stuff really does work, and work well. Very glad I purchased it and it solves my problem in a neat, tidy and fast manner.

In comparison to the older Netgear Powerline AV-200 line of equipment - Two stars. Not much reason to upgrade to the faster AV-500 line of equipment, and if I remember some of my classwork from grad school, this is due to signal processing and electrical engineering limitations inherent in most electrical cabling setups used in home construction when passing a modulated digital signal along with the standard 60 hertz alternating current (the Claude Shannon entropy content on the line can only be made so small). If you already own the older AV-200 stuff, dont bother spending more. If not, then try the AV-500 stuff, but the increase is marginal.

title: Great card for conquering 1080p over 60FPS, or beginning to take 4k seriously 30FPS or higher.
text:
I recently got a 144hz gaming monitor so I could remove v-sync from my games. This cured screen tearing issues I was having with a lot games I played including lousy ports of Ubisoft titles like Assassin's creed. I also game with a Mini ITX build so I knew what SLI wasn't in my future.

This card really fit the ticket. It replaced a rather loud and toasty Radeon 7950, and helped push up frame rates by 50% - 75% in newer titles. Dragon Age Inquisition ran noticeably smoother, and Shadows of Mordor seemed worlds better with a more stable framerate of 60fps or higher. Wolfenstein: The New Order seems to run well over 60 FPS and with reductions in blurring, my reaction time has been so good Nazi Germany has no idea what hit them.

The card crushes titles a year old or more, and with the high refresh rate of the monitor, the responsiveness of controls has been a joy. Sonic Generations runs well over 60FPS and the actual responsiveness of my setup makes the game seem much more enjoyable than the console counterparts. With the reduction in motion blur, high response rate and high FPS, it's been a treat.

This is my first Nvidia card and i've noticed a few things.

1. It runs quieter and cooler than my Radeon 7950. But that's to be expected given how new the 970 is. Nvidia touted the cooler technology as well.

2. The bundled software seems cleaner and easier to use. Geforce experience settings are nice and helpful for properly tweaking game options for my card. The actual driver options are clean and simple to use. ATI's were bloated and cumbersome.

3. I can play games in full screen now. Not windowed mode, which caused micro stuttering on every single ATI card I ever owned. The 4800, the 6800 and the 9500 series cards all had it.

4. It's more expensive than ATI. But the above 3 notes should begin to explain why.
.

This is a great card. That's all I can really say. It really makes consoles like the PS4 look very dated just over a year into their release. The 7950 I had already was beefier than anything Sony or Microsoft put out, Nvidia just takes it to a whole new level. Gamers of all stripes owe it to themselves to explore the quality of PC gaming, and this is a great card to take the plunge with.

Here's the issues I came across:

(1) The headset hook doesn't adjust very well, it's designed to hook into the stem in a horseshoe groove. I was afraid the Bluetooth would fall off if I adjusted it too much.

(2) The sound quality is unreliable. People said they could hear me fine on the other end, but I heard some intermittent static like Saran Wrap being crumpled into a ball.

(3) When powering up, it takes this headset an average of 8-10 seconds to pair to my phone, even if they're right on top of each other. By comparison, my hands-free speakerphone takes about 5 seconds to pair up.

(4) When I first started using this headset, I could connect with Youtube, but after about 2 weeks, I got the error message "BT headset is not supported this audio type". It doesn't work at all with Youtube anymore.

(5) This is my biggest gripe - the Command Button is unbelievably sensitive. Since this headset doesn't fit comfortably into my ear, I occasionally have to move it during calls to hear people. If I barely touch the Command button, the next thing I hear is "Call Terminated".

I figured a 2nd-generation Bluetooth wouldn't have this many issues, but I was wrong.

I wouldn't recommend this product, not for this asking price.

I was pleasantly surprised with the results from this camera. Compared to the 630 it's a far superior device. The 630 could take good photos in daylight outdoors but struggled otherwise. The 310 does really well in all lighting conditions that I've tried so far. It's so good that we've even started taking only it when we go out, and leaving the DSLR at home.

The optical zoom range on this camera is really great. This was a real plus for me. It's really nice to not rely on digital zoom just to get close to a subject. I don't use the digital zoom much at all.

With a camera this fast, make sure you get a good card. I spent money to get a 32GB Sandisk 45MB/sec card, and am glad that I did. I've never once had to wait for something to be stored. This camera can generate a lot of data when shooting in some of the high-speed and hi-res video modes, so you want a card that can handle it.

Battery life is good (I've managed 200 photos without seeing the low battery warning) but I'd still recommend a second battery if you want to use it all day long without turning it off after each photo to save battery.

Very strongly recommend this camera. I'm delighted with it, and so far have not found a feature or aspect of the camera that I'm not happy with.

title: Great little voice recorder. Excellent value for the money.
text:
I attend a lot of investment related seminars. I need a voice recorder for seminar recording purpose. Besides the requirement of good voice recording quality, I have following additional mandatory requirements:
(1) the capability of downloading the recorded voices into PC for archiving,
(2) the recorded files must be in a format that can be listened, edited by main-stream software tools. I do not want files in proprietary formats. And I don't want to install any vendor provided special software.

This RCA VR532R digital voice recorder meets all my requirements.

Pro:
a) Low cost. I haven't been able to find another one that is cheaper.
b) Great Portability: The recorder size is small. It's easy to carry around.
c) Nice voice recording quality. I can not say it has the best voice recording quality to record life music performance. But for recording conversation from seminars, it's good.
d) The recorded voice files can be easily copied and past to PC, without the need of installing any additional software. All I need is just the window explorer.
e) It has 3 recording quality modes. By selecting the HQ (high quality) recording mode, it saves files in WAV format. The WV format is one of the main-stream audio formats. Virtually all main-stream software tools takes this format. And it is one of the native format that window supports (without the need of installing additional software).

The package comes with RCA's own software CD. But I don't bother to install any software from the included CD.

Some people complain about the placement of the included USB. I don't know why, and I don't see anything wrong about how the USB connector is placed.

Some people complain that the device is still draining battery when it is in OFF mode. The recorder need power to drive it's internal clock. So, it can put correct date/time to index the recorded files. If you don't care about the correct date/time setting, you can just remove the battery when you don't use it.

All in all, this voice recorder fits my need well and I am very happy with the price. Great Value.

title: Suitable Tent
text:
I have never worked with this type of light box before, so I have no way of judging it against the pros and cons of other light boxes. However, this one seems suitable, as I mentioned in the title.

It is not too hard to set up, despite the illegible instruction flyer that comes with it. It does not pop open: instead it consists of three white panels and one black panel that unfold and stick together with Velcro. It is not too hard to understand.

I believe that the lights are 5000 Kelvin, which in my mind constitutes a good light quality. They certainly improve the lighting inside the tent, though I have not tested them with my camera yet. The lights do not have extenders to move the height up and down, though they do have swivels between the stem of the tripod and the light itself so that you can adjust the angle of the lighting. When set up, they are 10 inches high. They come with instructions that warn that the lights can get hot and that you must not leave them burning continuously for over an hour. In fact, the lights do become too hot to handle if you leave them on for more than a few minutes, but there is an on/off switch on the back of the light that makes it very easy to turn them off between photos. The one thing that really bothers me about the lights is that no one mentions anywhere that you really need a top boom light to shoot light onto your work from overhead. I have an office light that seems to work, but I use a custom white balance on my camera to compensate for light from various sources.

The tripod is inadequate for my DSLR. The tripod that ships with this set is quite lightweight, although sturdy for what it is. It has a ball head on top, and will probably support point-and-shoot and small camcorders quite well. I was going to use a tabletop tripod of some kind, but I was not impressed with the selection, and discovered that I can use the full-sized tripod that I bought for my camera, placed at the edge of the table that I set the light tent up on.

That leaves us the backdrops. The backdrops are made of sheet material that crease easily, and of course they come out of the box well creased. They can be ironed with little trouble. Here's how you do it: first of all you need the following

One ironing board
One iron
One Lint roller
One wet sponge

The sole of the iron should be clean. Inspect it by sliding it on the ironing board and seeing if it glides or if it sticks. If it sticks, please clean it. You'll need a [[ASIN:B0006V875S Rowenta ZD100 Non-Toxic Soleplate Cleaner Kit]] to get the goop off. After you have done that, use the lint roller to clean your ironing board.

It is important to set the temperature on your iron to the lowest setting for polyester and silk. Make sure that the steam setting is off. You will be using temperatures that are too low for steam, and if the steam setting is on, it will drip water all over the piece you are ironing. Let it warm up for a while. While you are doing that, lay out your first backdrop with the flocked side down. Use the wet sponge to dampen the wrinkled areas. When you think that the iron is warm, go to work on flattening the wrinkled areas. It doesn't hurt to stretch the backdrop a bit while you are ironing it. If you work at it for while, and the iron is not working, edge the temperature up in the direction toward cotton, but do not set it at cotton or above. Find a temperature that works on the wrinkles. If the iron starts to stick, the temperature is too high, and you must set the temperature down a bit, and possibly reclean your iron sole. You may have to iron the wrinkles two or three times, but that is okay. When you have worked the wrinkles out of your backdrop, flip it over and use the lint roller to remove any bits that contrast with the backdrop. Lay it out flat to cool and dry. Repeat with the other backdrops. They should go easier because you have found the right iron setting.

Bear in mind that these backdrops will wrinkle again very easily. Try to find a place where you can store them laying flat. I hung my backdrops using a skirt hanger, and hung them in my closet. If you are a sewer, you can go to the fabric store and pick out a nice piece of velveteen and sew some Velcro along the top. That will probably take care of the creasing problem. I think that that is what I will do.

I picked this set because it came with lights and because it was inexpensive. You get what you pay for, and I believe that this set is a good deal for what it is.

title: Very good sound for the price, and a perfect fit with a Smith Variant helmet
text:
I've tried a to ski a few times with my in-ear buds in place, and always found the experience uncomfortable and a little nerve-wracking... the earpads press in on the buds, the rub of the cord was transmitted into the buds, wind noise was high, and the lack of audible feedback (the sound of my edges on the snow, and more importantly, the sounds around me) really bugged me. I had hesitated for a long time to upgrade to in-helmet sound, but decided to give the Direct Connect Skull Candy audio for Smith Helmets (actually bought four pairs for the entire family).

The installation is a snap (even in my wife's non-Smith helmet, which had similar pockets in the ear pads), with a short pigtail emerging from the left earpad, and a double-male-ended connector to go from the helmet to your device.

Pros: Sound quality is very good, with typical Skull Candy bass bias. Wind noise isn't too much of an issue (and I was skiing fast on a very windy day) thanks to the placement inside the earpads. A good amount of ambient sound still makes it past the drop-in speakers, so you don't feel completely cut off, as long as you're not running the volume too loud. And, in the end, it's really nice just to have your favorite music playing while you do your favorite things. Adds to the pleasure in subtle ways.

Cons: The connector cord "breaks away" very easily if you catch it. For that matter, the fact that you *have* a connector cord dangling between your jacket and your helmet is kind of annoying (gong to look into a Bluetooth transceiver that can be plugged into the Skull Candy speakers instead). And... to be fair... listening to tunes while skiing with family and friends is a bit anti-social... even with moderate volumes, regular conversation is a bit dampened.

Overall, a good buy, good sound, decent design (ignoring the connector cable), and great service by the Amazon vendor who fulfilled my order.

title: Great if you modify the install instructions
text: The official DishNetwork "Installation Instructions" 2452207 in general are very good except I found I could not make it work if I made the initial tuning for 72  Also, they show three wires coming off the LNB, however, you do not need to run three wires from the LNB to your receiver, only one --- but they do not tell you that, nor the fact that it makes no difference which LNB port you use to attach your one wire. Second, they tell you to use a peaking meter and do a set up for satellite 72 -----  well I don't have a peaking meter and no matter how I tried, even though I got a strong signal on 72, when I then did the "Check Switch" step I never was able to get a signal for 77 and 61.5 (even after multiple tries --- and with my one wire attached to the 72 port on the LNB). But when I did my initial setup for 61.5 (with my one wire on that 61.5 LNB port -and- with aluminum foil over the 72 & 77 heads of the LNB); then when I removed the aluminum foil and did the "Check Switch" step, both 72 and 77 also came in strongly. However, in my case whereas the tables for my zip code said to use 183 degrees for 72, I found I needed to use 186 degrees for the 61.5 setup ---- I agree that setup for skew is not critical ---- after fine tuning elevation and azimuth, then adjusting skew by even huge amounts (like 15-20 degrees) made no difference in signal strength.

text:
I ordered this case for three features: the case, the hand strap, and the stand.

The case is just okay. I would prefer something ultra slim like the Moko Slim-Fit for the Kindle Fire (http://www.amazon.com/MoKo-Slim-fit-Amazon-Kindle-Tablet-Black/dp/B008J7EU9I/ref=sr_1_cc_1?s=aps&ie=UTF8&qid=1361906091&sr=1-1-catcorr&keywords=moko+slim-fit+kindle+fire) or the Apple Smart Cover for the iPad (http://www.amazon.com/Apple-iPad-Leather-Smart-Cover/dp/B004QKM5MG/ref=sr_1_cc_3?s=aps&ie=UTF8&qid=1361906191&sr=1-3-catcorr&keywords=ipad+smart+cover). But I couldn't find anything like that that offered the other two features, so I settled on this one.

As a stand, it is next to useless. The rubber "feet" promptly slide away until it bumps up against the nearest stable object or collapses, whichever comes first. You can prop it up if you have something on the surface to brace the back of the stand against, and if you get it at just the right angle, and you're careful not to nudge the table or allow a stiff breeze to come through.

The hand strap is useful. I assume that people who are complaining about the awkward angle have larger hands. My hands are not dainty by any means, but I'm able to slide my fingers in up to the last knuckles and still hold it diagonally. This is both stable and comfortable. In most situations though, the advantages over holding the kindle case-free are negligible. The exception is when reading lying down in bed or any other odd angle.

It looks nice enough. However, adding more than 2x the bulk is both less aesthetically appealing and less functional--I can't slip it easily into a pocket of my purse as I can without a case.

Features I do like: the corner tab mount (as opposed to the cut-out pocket found on other cases), the vertical flip opening, and the elastic band to close.

In summary: An okay protective case if you don't mind the bulk, but not worth the price.

title: Great motherboard, if it works
text:
After just two weeks of use, the ethernet port on my first board suddenly stopped working. I ordered a replacement and Amazon of course shipped it quickly. I have the new board in now and my system was working great for another 3 months. Just yesterday the ethernet port on the second board died. It was working the night before but when I turned the computer on in the morning it didn't work. The computer wasn't moved or anything overnight, just powered off. So I decided to purchase a PCIe gigabit card instead of dealing with warranty repairs from Asus. I'm knocking off a star for quality control issues. I hope the rest of the motherboard lasts...

In any case my new system is screaming fast! Here are my specs:

- Intel i5 4570S
- 8GB G.Skill 1866MHZ CL8
- Nvidia GTX 650 Ti
- Samsung 840 Pro SSD (running Ubuntu 13.04 64-bit)
- Some Apple SSD pulled from a friend's Macbook (running Windows 7 64-bit)
- 2 older HDDs for storage
- ASUS 24B3ST optical drive
- Silverstone ST50F-P power supply

Just a note in case you're upgrading instead of buying all new stuff: I was planning on keeping my case and my old optical drive since it was working, but failed to notice that this board doesn't have any IDE connectors on it. Thus, I wound up having to buy a SATA optical drive. Too bad because my old drive still functions just fine...

Here are some random comments and thoughts:

- BIOS is very easy to use. I had to drop into BIOS to increase RAM speed from the standard 1600MHz to 1866MHz. I also changed the order of the drives for how they boot, and changed the graphics settings to use the PCI-E output only. If you're using the integrated graphics from your CPU then it will dedicate a small portion of your memory (I think it was 64MB) to the graphics chip. I didn't want this so I set graphics to PCI-E only. I'm not overclocking the CPU at all but the menus to do so all seem very easy and intuitive.

- Everything works great out of the box with Ubuntu 13.04 (it's a 3.8 kernel which has support for lots of the latest stuff). Just install and you're ready to go. In Windows 7 there were many things that didn't work because the drivers weren't installed (USB3, LAN, etc.). You could insert the CD when running through the Windows installer and load the drivers into memory that way so that everything works after first boot. I opted to download the drivers from the ASUS website rather than using the ones on the provided CD (to make sure I had the latest versions). All devices seem to be working now in Windows 7.

- I had some problems with Windows 7, though I don't think they are specific to this board. The first time I tried to generate my WEI score I got a BSOD and the system kept rebooting. It would never let me login and I couldn't even repair it. I just had to completely reinstall. Reading up online it seems like it may have been a driver issue, but I didn't have much installed at that point other than the nvidia drivers, 7zip, and notepad++. Weird. Also had to disconnect all of the other drives in order for Windows to properly install SP1. Why? I don't know. I got a code 800F0A12 when I tried installing SP1 and after a quick search I found someone saying that Windows must be the "first" drive or else it won't install. It's not the first drive because my Linux SSD is. Once I disconnected the other 3 drives and booted into Windows it installed SP1 just fine. Then I connected the other drives back up and it still boots fine. I didn't even need to run update-grub.

- Benchmarks are fantastic!! WEI score of 7.5 in Windows 7 pro (64-bit). I ran the free version of Geekbench (limited to 32-bit tests only) and got 9989 in Windows 7 and a whopping 12914 under Ubuntu 13.04. Yep -- 30% faster under Linux using the exact same hardware (ok the SSDs are different). Yet another reason that Linux owns.

- Games all run smooth as butter. I haven't tested any Windows games yet (I only have a few that are only supported on Windows) but tested several Steam games on Linux. Serious Sam 3 was probably my most taxing game on my old setup and now at 1920x1080 it is liquid smooth at 50-60 FPS (CPU setting was Ultra, and the two memory settings were High). TF2 never drops below 150FPS on all of the highest settings at 1920x1080. Trine2 looks incredible at highest settings. You get the point.

- My system seriously boots up in like 5 seconds now. Programs launch/open almost instantly. If you don't have a SATA3 SSD yet, then GET ONE!

title: Outstanding with one minor gripe
text:
I bought the MB-D10 for my D700. Although the grip was originally designed for the D300, when put on the D700 it doesn't look all that bad. Of course that will be subjective but to me I like how it looks.

The build quality of the battery grip is awesome. The rubber is exactly the same that is on the D700 body. To me, the grip on the battery is a little bit deeper than the grip that is on the D700 body and I must admit gripping the battery feels more natural than gripping the body. Go figure.

The command and sub-command dials on the grip feel just like the ones on the D700 body. The sub-command dial is a bit more recessed in on the grip though. The shutter release seems just a tiny bit different than what's on the body. The shutter on the body gives a bit more resistance when you press the button all the way down. IMO, the shutter on the grip is NOT overly sensitive. It just doesn't feel as tight compared to what's on the body but it is still very, very good.

The battery grip will add weight and size to the D700 but the positive to this is that it counter balances the weight when you have a heavy lens attached to the body. For example, my 24-70mm attached to the body without the grip is a bit front heavy, but with the grip on, the balance is perfect.

My only gripe with the battery grip, and the reason for a 4 star rating instead of a 5, is that the control pad on the grip is way too small and very stiff. It's extremely difficult to move that around to select a focus point or to cycle through your photos.

Overall, I highly recommend the battery grip.

title: Renewed Confidence in Livescribe - Repurchased
text:
As a long time user of Pulse and Echo, I find this to be a great new platform for the pen. It clearly does as advertised. The only reason for the 3 stars is that I feel the pen is and feels a bit on the low end side. The materials and build are not high quality, like the Pulse and Echo and the rattling of the ink cartridge brings that low end factor down even more. There is no grip so my finger sometimes slides down the pen barrel a little when writing. The barrel should have had some texture, not the smudge attracting plastic it has now. I do like the fact that we no longer need a cap, the cartridge retracts and it has a clip for your shirt pocket. It would be nice to have the ability to clear the pen's memory down the road (not too concerned now). All in all, it's okay, I will continue to use it. The Monverde refills I purchased work quite well.

Update: 12/11 - I requested a return authorization with Livescribe (since I bought directly from them). I just cannot deal with the cheap feel of the pen and the rattling noise. On the good side, I kept my Echo and even though there is a small crack in the barrel, LS will replace the barrel free as it has been a known issue. The barrel I am talking about is the front piece where the ink refill is inserted. I will wait for the next iteration of the LS3 if one comes along and is built better. Meanwhile, my Echo will (and has) serve me well.

Update: 5/5/2015 - Many moons later. I work with a company who is so secure, I am not allowed to access the USB ports for the company provided laptop. So I re-purchased this pen years later and come to think of it, I'm speechless. I'm without speech. The pen allows me to record notes on my iPhone. Since I cannot plug the Echo in my company laptop, I cannot install the Echo desktop to search notes. No longer an issue with Livescribe 3 Smartpen. Now I have my notes, portable, and searchable on my iPhone. Additionally, has anyone noticed that the pen actually feels better made than before. It does not feel cheap anymore! The ink cartridge no longer rattles, and the overall build quality has improved vastly. Maybe it's me. Maybe Livescribe is using a new facility to manufacture this pen? Who knows. Also love the fact that I can use a PIN to protect the pen in case it's lost which encrypts the Bluetooth! Bottom line, is that I am happy and will continue to use it. There are 2 issues however that I would like fixed. One is the date handler on the iPhone Livescribe 3 IOS 8 app. It says March xx, 2019 (where xx is a number from 1 to 31). I usually write the date in my notes anyway however this would be great when fixed. Also, in the Livescribe 3 IOS 8 app when searching your notes the app is not highlighting the search results like the Echo desktop. It would be easier to locate the notes you are searching for by a yellow highlight on each match. Livescribe, I have renewed confidence in you, please hear us out and fix this. Thank you.

title: Finding Nemo looks AMAZING!
text: At first I thought, like some other reviewers, my Samsung TV wasn't working. I went online and found a short checklist to make sure everything was set-up properly. 1) was the TV plugged in? 2) After plugging in the TV did I press the power button? 3) Was it connected to my media player or computer? 4) Make sure all the cables were securely fastened. It could be one or any of these reasons that the TV wasn't displaying anything. For me it was all of them. It's been years since I bought a new TV and I guess I just kinda assumed the technology was good enough so that no set-up was required. That and it said plug and play. The plug part is VERY important! If you at plug the TV into a power outlet you can at least get what they call "snow" to show up on the screen. Don't stop there! This TV can do so much more!! I plugged a cable into my blu-ray player and then into the hole in the TV that fit the other end of the cable.  Nothing happened at first but my friend who is a technology whiz told me I had to press the source button on the remote. Oh man! Still nothing. I was starting to get a little frustrated because I didn't just want to look at snow, a burning fire over some logs would have been much more appealing than the pre-loaded snow video.  A couple weeks later my tech buddy just happened to stop over (I hate when people come by unannounced especially dealers).  He noticed that the remote felt light and asked to see the TV's packaging. He pulled out two small cylinders that were in a tight plastic wrapping and put them into a "secret" compartment in the remote control and pressed the source button. WOW!!! the snow switched to my favorite movie, Finding Nemo. The same movie I had wanted to watch when I fired up my blu-ray player many days before.  It's a brilliant movie about a small orange fish that was born with a horribly deformed small fin on one side of his little body. This fish is raised by an over-protective father fish that doesn't let Nemo experience the ocean like the other fish can. I don't blame the father fish though, because of what happens in the beginning of the film. I won't spoil it but a barracuda eats all of Nemo's brothers and sisters. The wife fish uses this as a clever way to cover up her escape from the boring father fish who thinks she is dead too. In the end little Nemo finally experiences a great adventure, overcoming many of life's obstacles (sharks and what not) in the process.  Anyway, it's a great film and I highly recommend it, thats why I'm giving this TV 5 stars!

title: Beautiful, and fatally flawed.
text:
Overall Summary
----------------------
I bought the UE9000 directly from Logitech during a Black Friday sale, and I got them at a steep discount ($1XY).

I've owned them for about six months now, and I waited to give a full objective review. The reason I am so torn about the UE9000s is the painful discrepancy between the insane sound quality, beautiful aesthetics, and the *horrid* ergonomics. It's like a Audi R8, but with metal spikes for seats.

The leather padding on headband is inadequate for the weight of the headset. My head starts hurting (not ears) after wearing them for more than an hour. I'm a person with a big head, and a high pain threshold who enjoys wearing headphones all day. The fact that these actually hurt is a *massive failure* in my mind, and a disappointment, really.

I've had a pair of hacked Sennheiser HD555's as my primary drivers which I've used for about three years, due to comfort. The plush foam and weight distribution makes them perfect in that sense. You can wear those things all day and forget that they're on your head (not a joke- has happened).

Onto the sound quality/bluetooth functionality/information you wish every product came with:

Sound Quality
-----------------
Bass: Best in the wireless class, bar none. (10/10)
Mids: Excellent. (9/10)
Highs: Phenomenal. (10/10)
A2DP Bluetooth: Excellent/minor buffering every 5-10 min (9/10)
APT-X Bluetooth: Lossless/Wired Equivalent (10/10)

If I were rating these on sound quality alone, they'd be a 10/10.

Sound Modes/Profiles
---------------------------
The UE9000 has three modes that I don't believe they talk about adequately:

1. Passive (No Power, Wired, NC OFF): Directly connected via wire, all power is driven by the hardware of whatever device you are using. They sound quite good, comparable to any other expensive pair of headphones, but not in the 4XY range. More like 1XY-2XY.

2. Active (Powered, Wired, AMP ON, EQ ON, NC OFF): Obviously, there is a built in equalizer profile and amplifier in these headphones, as the volume jumps dramatically, and the soundstage is significantly modified. Bass is absolutely excellent in this mode, even at the highest possible volumes, there is no distortion. It may be "too overbearing" for some, particularly those who enjoy very flat-line looking EQs. You can keep this mode off. (I primarily listen to Industrial Metal, so this is a non-issue.)

3. Active Always On (Powered, Bluetooth, AMP ON, EQ ON, NC ON): In Bluetooth mode, the active profile is automatically enabled; which in my opinion is what you want it to be set on while using it with mobile devices *anyway* for the built-in amplifier; however noise canceling is also enabled. Again, some people prefer a more "neutral" sound, and the lack of a passive bluetooth mode might detract from their experience.

About the "Hiss": There is an audible hiss that occurs when there's nothing playing while the headphones are in an active profile. If you're used to amplifiers, you'll be familiar with this sound. Once you begin playing music, there's a signal to gain, and the hiss disappears completely.

Bluetooth Compatibility
-----------------------------
Horrid. The Bluetooth Driver Stack that the hardware uses identifies itself as a "phone", that is, it refuses to pair with anything that doesn't support BOTH microphone audio in, and stereo out .

This basically nixes the cheap transmitter/bluetooth dongle market, such as the Avantee Saturn (which has APT-X), and other generic devices.

However, most "smart devices" which can enable the Voice profile will pair with the UE9000 - Android phones, PCs, etc; and you can manually disable the microphone in bluetooth settings thereafter.

Microphone/Call Quality
-------------------------
Unfortunately, A2DP doesn't have enough bandwidth to support both stereo stream out, and microphone aux in. This does all sorts of wonders to the stream as you could imagine, making the audio input sound like garbage (think of in-car bluetooth phones).

For all intents and purposes, the microphone on the UE9000s should be used ONLY for noise-canceling, as it just flat out sucks for every other purpose.

The actual hardware microphone is quite good - I've managed to listen to the pure microphone aux in on a forced feedback loop, and it sounds transparent.

For the social aspect - with the headphones in active mode, you *really* don't want to be walking around and essentially screaming your conversation in public anyway. It's much more civil to slump the headphones down on your neck and answer the phone normally.

Conclusion
--------------
Beautiful, black, silver, and blue. Fatally flawed. Absolutely amazing for the one hour you can stand it. (6/10)

title: Don't know why the other reviews are so harsh, but...
text:
Alright, first of all, two qualifications: normally, I do not buy products rated under 4 stars on Amazon. Secondly, I am a lead systems engineer (but also worked for a long period at a high end retail tech company that rhymes with chapel, so I believe in the balance of functionality vs. simplicity that people need to be happy). Now that that's out of the way, I am a bit dumbfounded by the harsh reviews of this product. I am willing to admit that this product is a software-based product and that can change over time. However, knowing that going into the purchase, that can also be an advantage or a disadvantage. In my case, it's both, but let me explain further in a minute. Finally, there are a lot of universal remote products out there, but here's why I decided to go with the Logitech Harmony Link after searching all over and reading up the universal remote roundup listed here: http://www.amazon.com/Universal-Remote-iPhone-iPad-iPod/lm/R2LI1P9SJKHZWE/ref=cm_lm_byauthor_full

Decisions:

+Software vs. Hardware:
-If software based (i.e. adding software onto a smartphone or other device): Add-on accessory vs no add-on accessory
-If hardware based (i.e. physical button remote): touchscreen button remotes had to be compact and portable with a variety of physical buttons, not just a giant touchscreen device.

+Price:
-To save up and wait or to go with a less expensive product and hope it does everything I want.

Conclusions:

This may not be the way for everyone to go through their process, but here is how I came down to my decision...

1) I knew I did not want a dongle to have to plug into a smartphone to use for remote capabilities because that's just one more thing to keep track of and won't stay in the device permanently, so that sliced the list in half.
2) I knew I did not want a touchscreen, because they are expensive and I have an iPhone and iPad, 2 touch-screens already, so that ruled out the "touchpad" based remotes.
3) It needs to be expandable, to work behind closed cabinets and control things like a bluetooth-based PS3, and control less common devices like my B&W Panorama sound bar.
4) Preferably, could more than one remote control the system so you don't pass the remote around?
5) There are 2 reasons for a universal remote... 1) something that controls everything and 2) Something that you can keep track of and won't fumble around for asking "where's the remote."

Finally, with all that said, I asked myself "what product will solve all five of these issues in one sweep?"

So, I came down to two products, oddly enough, made by the same company... the Logitech Harmony 900 physical remote, if I were to go hardware based, and the Logitech Harmony Link, if I were to go software based.

To make the decision easier, the Logitech Harmony 900 is $349 and the Harmony Link is $99. The Harmony Link has as PS3 add-on adapter for $49 and can extra IR blasters for accessibility to other devices, or, and RF adapter for behind cabinets. For the complete system if you were to max it out, you're still under $300, with no extra remote to fumble with, and you can even add more remotes to the system just by installing the software onto smartphones (so you can use unused iPod touches or your kids' smartphone). Plus, the software can be easily updated to add additional capabilities or interface enhancements. If I were to pick the Logitech Harmony 900, I'm at least at $349 and I have only 1 remote that I have to pass around, keep track of, and if I wanted a second remote, it's another $349.

Now, just by the nature of the fact that most people always have their smartphone ON them, why not solve the first problem of trying to always find the remote with everyone having a remote that always stays on them, because it's on their smartphone? Done.
No dongles? Done.
Expandable? Done.
Wide array of accessories that are compatible? Done.
Easy set-up? Done.
Relatively inexpensive and multi-person expandable? Done.

Pretty simple decision at that point.

After initial setup on the computer, it works like a charm. Here's what it is NOT:

-A physical button remote replacement (it's software based)
-A virtual touchscreen version of your physical remotes (it has its own interface)
-A quick action device (can't just pick up and click, have to launch the app, but reconnects to device in less than a second)
-A standalone device that doesn't rely on other services (needs wi-fi to operate)
-Another device to charge/replace batteries (just charge your phone as you would)

To conclude, the Logitech Harmony Link is probably the best product for a software based solution, and if I were not to use the software-based solution, due to popularity of the Logitech products leading to the vast array of device compatibility, I would probably go with the Logitech Harmony 900 remote instead. Until I decide differently, the Logitech Harmony Link offers a flexible solution that allows me to use my iPhone, iPad, and other Android based smartphones to control my set of devices, quite easily. The software is easy to set up, works well, the IR transmitter is reliable, and you don't need any additional dongles. Just plug the IR transmitter into an outlet anywhere in the room, or behind a cabinet with the devices themselves. So, back to my original statement, I don't really know what all the fuss is about; this is a pretty great product.

text:

The best mode is center-weighted metering, almost no misfire. For spot and matrix metering, it only fires correctly 1 out of 4 frames. When I tried highlight-weighted metering (only available on D810 and D750), it was lost at all. You can see the flash is firing but not synced with shutters at all. I can even noticed it fires between two continuous shots. That is ridiculous. For a $400 flash, how can it not work for the simplest task? Although my main purpose is to use them remotely, I still need it on camera as commander unit and do some fill flash. This kind of bad performance broke the deal immediately. Return and refund!

Before I pack it for return I also tested it remotely. The optical remote sensor is right in front of SU800. Still missed a lot. Even I set it to manual mode, it has 1 off-synced shot out of 5. For remote TTL, in 7 continuous shots, it missed 4, correctly fired 2, and totally overwhelmed 1. I cannot imagine what will happen if I use it for work, it will be a nightmare.

I guess this flash may work with D4/D4s/Df better, because those famous pros supported by Phottix are using them. But obviously Phottix is not paying enough attention on D810.

title: Stunning - Detailed - Rivals the Competition
text:
My review will be solely based upon the audio. While I am extremely impressed by the video, I am using a 8-year old Sony 60" LCD and frankly, don't feel that is a good enough reference unit to comment on the video. I'm looking at upgrading to a plasma soon and will edit this review when I do.

I'd give this player 25 stars if that was an option.

I have lived with this unit for a few weeks now and blown away.

My system: Thiel 3.5 Speakers, Counter Point 3000 Preamp, Counterpoint 220 Amp, Theta Digital Processor Gen 3.

Approximately 20-years ago I spent close to $4,000 on the Theta Digital Processor because I grew up in the 50's/60's on good sound systems from the start, used to vinyl and natural detailed sound. The D/A converters 20-years ago were terrible. I can't listen to generic digital units or compressed music formats like MP3. They just sound terrible.

I went from the analogue outputs of the OPPO to the analogue inputs of my preamp and bypassed the Theta. Frankly, I didn't know what to expect, but what I've heard is far beyond my wildest expectations.

My audio & video collection is vast, SACD, HDCD, regular CD, DVD, etc. I listen to every thing from Folk to Opera. I've been playing guitar since I was a child and know sound.

No matter what I throw at this player, the resulting sound is nothing short of breath-taking. There aren't enough superlatives to adequately describe my satisfaction. The sound staging, detail, accuracy, tonal quality, every thing that makes sound, sound good, is provided in spades by this player. The fact it can decode so much is a huge plus, not to mention the build quality.

In the end, if "sound" is vital to you, get this player; don't even hesitate. OPPO has a 30-day return policy if you need to hear it for yourself first. Take advantage of it, but if you send it back, I'd be amazed. It is so obvious this player was built by folks who not only understand what they are doing, but do what they do out of pure love and passion for quality sound. Bravo !!!!!!

UPDATE: July 23, 2013 - Still love the player for reasons given, however, I find the limitation of 720p for NetFlix streaming a real let down and with no update to improve this have removed a start. There is no excuse for this given the overall quality of the player.

title: Very nice system!
text:
I ordered this plus Corsair 8GB, Intel i5 2400, and Asus DVD drive. It all arrived even a bit early (but see below about the memory). It is a beautiful-looking box, and everything works very nicely and it is extremely quiet!

I have not had any chance to check performance or the Windows Experience Index, but it FEELS fast. I'm running Ubuntu Linux 12.04.

Just a few items that contributed to 4-* rather than 5-*

1) The screws that came with it are not the right size to match up with either the DVD or the HDD that I had. It needs a smaller size (which I luckily had)

2) The heat sink compound is pretty think and hard to spread evenly. Maybe it all is these days, but that is different from anything I have used earlier. Having only done this a few times it made me a bit nervous that I was getting good thermal contact.

3) The documentation consists of only a single sheet of mostly pictures and diagrams. The enclosed CD/DVD had a manual (in different languages) but it was exactly the same sheet, not a more detailed text. Without anything more than pictures it was a bit more nerve-wracking to put the CPU in. In particular, there were three things that the diagram seemed to say I should remove (mylar cover of CPU socket, mylar cover on the ICE thermal connector, and something else on the socket). Unfortunately I could not really tell what was what from the diagram and I could only find 1 thing to remove. It turns out that there was one additional cover but it was in the accesories box and not actually on the socket where it was supposed to be.

A couple additional cautions (which don't contribute to lowering the rating, but I wish I had known).

1) The HDD space is for a 3.5" drive, not a 2". I was installing a disk from a laptop, and it works but does not physically fit well. I suspect it will not be a good thing to use forever since there is not much thermal contact with the case.

2) One of the SATA cables was pre-installed and threaded to the back of the case. That was a bit mysterious until I realized that it actually was in a good position to plug into the DVD drive, and having it threaded through the case keeps it out of the way.

3) The Amazon catalog page suggested "other who ordered this also got..." an Asus DVD drive, which seems fine, but also Corsair memory from a Marketplace vendor. I did not notice that it was not fulfilled by Amazon, until after I ordered it the expected delivery time was a week out rather than the normal Prime 2-day. I was pretty annoyed about this! I finally ordered the same memory from Amazon directly; it was not only less expensive but arrived in 2 days. (The marketplace version has not arrived yet and they refused to cancel it!). So use caution! Prime eligible no longer means it will be there in 2 days! (I'll review the actual items and or the vendor separately).

September 1, 2012:

Another couple of cautions:

1) There is a very weird BIOS setting called EuP "Energy using Product" (well duh!). It is apparently a quick way to set up some energy saving functions, and when it is on, Wake On LAN can not be enabled. If disable EuP, you can enable WOL. Would be nice if it were a bit clearer what this particular function is for. The text for it says "Enable EuP function". Thanks.

2) This particular CPU (the I5 2400) does not support hyperthreads. This is not Shuttle's fault; I should have checked the Intel web site more carefully. I looked to be sure it supported multiple cores and virtualization accelerations, but did not even notice the hyperthreads. Not a big deal for me, just a surprise.

Oct 10, 2012:

One thing that I never mentioned, and pretty small: The 'suspend' function works well, but there is no indication from the outside whether the system is off or in suspend. Usually systems flash the power light when it is suspended. I thought there might be a BIOS setting, but I could not find one.

title: 2 Different TV's with the same problem of turning off
text: This was my fourth LG TV and I really wanted to like this.  I have three other LG TV's in the following sizes, 32", 47" and 55".  This is the 2013 year model and my other TV's were from 2011 and 2012.  When the TV arrived I unpacked the boxed and noticed a 4" x 4" bracket that was not listed in the manual.  After looking at it again, I noticed that it was a Joey mounting bracket from DishNetwork's Hopper system!!!  Now how did that get in there?  It was even wrapped in the white foam like the rest of the TV.  After looking closer at the box, there was two rows of tape on the top of the box sealing it closed.  I hooked up the TV and it powered on for about 4 seconds and then turned off.  After 1/2 of trying to get the TV to stay on, I called LG's support and they were of no help.  After changing to a different power cord, the TV would stay on for 4 minutes and then turn off for 15 seconds and then back on.  The next morning I tried it again and it would not stay on for more than 4 minutes without turning off.  My final thoughts were that this must have been returned and somehow reshipped out.  So I had this TV returned and a replacement sent.  The next TV did the same thing!!  Agh! I decided to move this TV to another room with a different Sat Receiver and HDMI cable just to make sure there wasn't a problem in that room.  The results were the same.  8-(.  I hooked up my old TV and it is working great, so it is not a power or Sat problem.  The 30 day support from Amazon was refreshing!!  No over seas support and they were located in Oregon.  The tech went through the usual fixes for this type of problem and it looks like another defective TV.  Thumbs up to Amazon and their return process, but thumbs down for this model so far.  I did notice that this model is stripped down in that it will not play video through the USB port like two of my other LG TVs.  It looks like the newer models will not play video unless it is a higher end version unlike last years models.  8-(  What's up with this LG????  I will most likely check out the Samsung version of this TV now.  On a side note, when I could get this TV to power on, the picture looked much better than the Vizio 26" model it was replacing, but the Vizio got the last laugh as lest it would stay on! <G>

The sound quality of this player is great. I know that it's possible to find something better, but, considering the price and the size of this thing, this sound quality is simply amazing. I tried this player with several headphones (Sennheiser HD600, Sennheiser HD280, Klipsch X10). I prefer the sound of Klipsch X10 - perhaps, because of their slightly rolled-off high frequencies. I mostly listen to classical music (piano, violin, violin concertos, symphonies, etc.) I find that the player (together with Klipsch X10 headphones) produces very good sound:

1) It is very detailed. Nuances of musical performance and concert hall reverberation tails are rendered beautifully.

2) Instrument timbres are realistic (in good recordings, see #4).

3). It is pleasant and possible to listen for a long time.

4). It is neutral - both regarding the timbres and emotions. What I mean is that the player does not seem to introduce emotions to the music that are not present in the original recordings. One can clearly hear that some performances are very musical and exciting while other performances are less emotional and some are... well... borderline boring. The same applies to instrument timbres. All recordings sound better on this player compared to my iPod Classic or a cell phone, but only good recordings sound very much better.

The most significant glitch of this player that I experienced is the following: sometimes it skips approx. the last 2 seconds in an mp3 file. This problem does not seems to appear at all with flac and wav files though. This may be already fixed in the latest firmware but I haven't had time to test it yet. There was also a minor glitch in one of the menus that only appeared a couple of times.

I would highly recommend this player to those who listen to music performed on acoustic instruments and appreciate high quality sound. I'm quite happy with electronic music on this player too, but the advantages are less noticeable for this genre. I'm very impressed.

title: Great Value, Does Have Quirks

The touchpad is okay, but I've found it to be very very touchy so far, sometimes it even likes to move without your finger actually touching it. I usually disable the touch-to-click functionality (Fn-F8), as it usually creates for me more issues than it solves.

That's also where it should be mentioned that some of the features around this are not well documented. You can control the sensitivity of the touchpad with Fn-Space, and it's "kind of" mentioned on the box, but it's not really documented. You'd also think based off of the pictures that Fn-F8 turns off the touchpad altogether, but in actuality it just disables tap-to-click. I wish there were at least some basic instructions with it. I know this is very straight-forward, it's a keyboard and touchpad, but something would be nice.

Those quirks aren't enough for me to say this isn't worth it. It's well priced, well sized, and once you get used to it, a very versatile device.
