title: great for diy point-of-sale pc
text:
i bought this mini desktop pc with the intention of using it solely for the base of a diy point-of-sale setup at my bar. i don't need a pc with a super-fast processor or GoBs of memory. it just needs to be reliable, modern, and most of all, small. this fits the bill perfectly!

i'm not a huge fan of w8, but there are workarounds for that. the touchscreen monitor i bought ([[ASIN:B00FE8MLY6 found here]]) is a perfect compliment for this system, as it provides a couple extra USB ports on the monitor and uses HDMI input for the video. this tower (i'm not sure if you can call this pc a tower, as it's actually quite small for a desktop) hides perfectly behind the monitor. the keyboard has the island-style keys, which makes it thinner and easier to tuck away. the mouse is a standard optical.

overall, this is a very basic unit, and offers few frills beyond hdmi and usb3.0. that's exactly what i wanted, so for my setup, it was perfect! i could have easily spent $2500+ on a pre-packaged pos system. this pc, along with the monitor i mentioned earlier, a heavy-duty cash drawer, and a thermal receipt printer, cost me under $700. that's an insane amount of savings! i definitely recommend this inexpensive pc for anyone looking to build out their own pos system.

**update 12/2/14**
since this review has been voted as fairly helpful by all of you, i thought it would be worthwhile to offer an update. it's been about four months since i first wrote this review. everything seems to be going very well with the pos, for the most part. the only issue i've witnessed is that the pc requires a reboot at least once a week to avoid poor performance. it tends to freeze up when coming out of screensaver if you don't reboot with that frequency. it's worthwhile to follow a regular boot schedule anyways, because there are windows updates pushed out almost weekly, and many of them require a restart to take effect.

other than that, the pc has given me virtually no troubles at all. there was one time where the touch monitor didn't re-connect after coming out of snooze, but i think that's a problem with the monitor itself. i'm less than pleased with the monitor for several reasons, and would actually recommend avoiding it and spending a few extra dollars on something designed for pos use. i understand this goes against my earlier recommendation, but that's what sometimes happens after you live with a person long enough to learn their weaknesses ;)

i'm still convinced that this is probably the best pc for the money when it comes to building a pos on your own. and for the price, it's surely not going to hurt your wallet to give it a try.

**update 3/31/14**
the hdmi port on the back of the pc has stopped working. i'm not sure if an employee banged the cable around and broke the port loose from the main board, or if this is symptomatic of a larger issue with lower-quality components used to make a discount pc. everything else seems to still be in working order, and i was able to run a vga cable to the monitor to restore the display. i'm not knocking off a star until i have a chance to crack open the pc housing and get a look at the backside of the port, to possibly determine the cause of its failure.

Fire it up, direct a browser to 192.168.8.1 and the login screen tells me the WAN cable is not connected. Oh, but it is. Tried a second cable, no change. Connected that cable directly from the cable modem to the computer and internet access is fine. Reconnect the cable modem to the router WAN input and same thing - tells me the WAN cable is not connected. Called Medialink after 5PM EST, they were very nice, got back to me in less than an hour. They agreed it sounded like the router is defective. Wanted me to send it back to them with up to a 5 business day turnaround.

title: Unit defective.  Poor support from E-Prance.  Even worse support from Amazon.
text:
The unit arrived and installed fine. It seemed to be working OK and I checked after a few days to verify my driving time was being recorded. It appeared that it was. I checked again after a few more weeks, and found several alarming things:
1) The unit would stop recording between 30-60 seconds! I'm not talking about the screen going off because of the screensaver feature. I mean the DVR would exit the RECORD mode and go into STANDBY mode for no reason. Sometimes it would start recording again for another 30-60 seconds, and other times it wouldn't. So, if I took a 2 hour car ride, I might have 8 minutes of captured video to show for it. Also, I did not set the DVR to record in these short segments. I had it set to record in ten minute blocks.
2) The unit lost track of the date and time. It would default back to 1/1/2013. So, when I would try to view a particular day's driving, I would have no idea which file to view.
3) I tried to return the unit to Amazon, but, since I'd had the unit for over 30 days, they refused to accept a return.
4) I contacted E-Prince tech support and wasted several days exchanging e-mails with Nancy. She was no help and said I needed to try again for a return from Amazon. E-Prince would do nothing for me.
5) I re-contacted Amazon and begged for a return. They finally agreed and gave me an RMA. But, when they processed the RMA, they took out a $12 "Restocking Fee" What? I was never told this when I had the rep on the phone. And - Amazon is going to put back a defective product into stock?

I'm sure that I had a bad unit, and I see lots of other people are happy with their purchase. Unfortunately, I wasn't one of the lucky ones. You should be warned that this product essentially has a 30-day warranty and that's it. Amazon sold me a defective product and is charging me $12 for the experience.

title: Decent Action Camera, With Some Issues.
text:
Compared to the Hero 2 I have this camera has some advantages.
First among them is battery life. This is a drastic improvement over my Hero2, even with the battery backpak. It is also a bit smaller and lighter. The lens is a bit of an improvement in areas like near object sharpness. The new video modes for HD don't really impress me as the frame rate drops to get them. I find the color to be superior to the Hero2, it's quite a bit more vivid, without looking fake. It's also far superior to the Hero2 in low-light shooting. WiFi is an "upgrade" of sorts from the Hero2. It isn't a simple setup and it drains the battery quickly and doesn't have a very long range. The close stills are as good as my HTC phone, not as good as my iPhone 5. Sound capture was very good, I found it clearer than the Hero2.

The major con for me is that objects about 8-10 feet away are blurred. I find this unacceptable for action video as the background is as important to me as the foreground. The still shots suffer from this as would be expected.

The camera is constructed every bit as solid as the Hero2. I would still expect to use bacpak batteries for longer shoots.

Also, all my shooting was done on fast, high quality class 10 SD cards. Don't cheap out here or you will definitely be unsatisfied with the video!

Overall, it's a decent camera for the price, the blurring of slighlty distant objects may not bother others as it does me, so I can't not recommend it based on that. The near objects are very crisp. However, if the budget allows, I would look at the Hero3+ Black Edition and compare.

title: Compact and adaptable
text:
This little "convertible" isn't much bigger than some CB microphones. I'm particularly pleased with the three modes of power; AA batteries, NiMH rechargeables, or 12v vehicle. The mobile vehicle adapter includes both a plug-in cigarette lighter power point and a coax connector for an external antenna. I use the Midland 18-2442 magnetic mount (it will tune to SWR of about 1.5 on channels 1 and 40) to significantly increase the range to several miles, depending on conditions. As a mobile radio, it works pretty well given that it's a one (small) size fits all type of unit. But what I really got this for was to use it as a handheld walkie-talkie. And that's where it truly shines. The provided rubber duckie antenna is nice and short, but it severely limits your transmit range. Use it if you don't need to talk more than a couple hundred yards. I mounted the Cobra HA TA telescoping whip antenna and got a tremendous increase in performance. Battery life is pretty good. The rechargeables will last all day with reasonable usage. Plug it into the charger overnight and you're ready for the next day. The weather alert is a nice feature, too.

All in all, a very useful small radio that really comes to life when connected to a decent antenna. Recommended for those who need a versatile CB for automobile and handheld applications.

title: Excellent for the Amateur Photographer
text:
When I was looking to purchase this model from Amazon's sister (step-son, whatever) site, woot, I read the reviews here and found most were written by those who know what they're talking about when it comes to cameras. That's all well and good and their opinions were valuable, but let's be honest, I'm a mom of three under the age of five who rarely ventures out of "Auto" mode when it comes to photography. I don't know camera technicalities and I don't have time to learn them right now (though I look forward to the day when I can). I just need a camera that will photograph my kids and, yet, still give me quality images.

I found what I was looking for with this camera. The images are sharp and, while it sometimes takes a little longer than I'd like to focus, it still works quicker than my previous point-and-shoot (which often took a full 5-10 seconds to focus and still came out blurry - that doesn't hack it with active kids). Best of all, I used this baby yesterday while attending the birth of a friend, which means, of course, the hospital lighting was less-than-ideal (aka VERY dim) and the photos came out beautifully! There was no grainy texture, no washed out faces. And the zoom worked well enough that I was able to grab close shots of baby without having to stick the camera (and its flash) right in his face.

Thus, from a complete amateur's point-of-view, this camera is worth its salt. The panoramic, which I've tried a few times, works great and looks stunning. Macro shots of birthday flowers look professional.

My only complaint is how long it takes to view photos. Another reviewer mentioned having to have the camera on to review photos in playback, and this is true (and slightly annoying but not too bad), but what frustrates me is that it takes a full ten-seconds between pushing the play-back button and the images coming up - and if you don't think that sounds like too long, count it out, it's longer than you think and frustrating when you want to check quickly if you got the shot). Clearly, however, this minor flaw is not enough for me to ding the camera even one full star.

I love this little guy and I wouldn't trade it.

title: Review: Chrome OS for power users
text:
Warning: Holistic, long review incoming.

UPDATE: This is a review that describes much of the *potential* usage of this device. Getting the *most* from this "thin-client" requires a certain level of knowledge about Linux, or a certain tenacity for learning. However, because the web is becoming so powerful, you may not need to know anything more than your Google password to get your money's worth from this device. If, however, you want to "kick it up a notch", or just learn a little about what the web really is and where it's headed, read on!

-----------------
Short vocabulary primer:
"native software" : Traditional software (like Microsoft Office) that runs on a specific platform (like MS Windows or Mac OS) and provides high-level functionality to users, usually available offline.
"webapp" : Web Application. A website using modern programming technologies to provide high-quality software to the end-user, usually intended to replace a native software equivalent. Examples include Gmail, Google Docs (to replace MS Office), Google Calendar (to replace MS Outlook), Angry Birds, and countless others in the Chrome Web Store.
"X11" : A Linux program responsible for the display and basic management of windows on your screen in just about any Linux computer, including this Chromebook. Also ships by default with Mac OS X!
"ssh" : "Secure SHell". A fast, secure way of accessing the command-line of another computer (a "server") through the computer you're sitting at (a "client"). Provides lots of powerful tools for client-server communication and data transfer.
"X11-forwarding" : A way of telling X11 to send data through SSH. This allows you to run windowed (not just terminal) applications on a remote computer while displaying the resulting windows, buttons, text, etc. on the computer you're sitting in front of - i.e. this Chromebook.
"chroot" : "CHange ROOT". This is an advanced feature. A way of hot-swapping Unix-based operating systems WITHOUT rebooting your computer. This provides a way to run a traditional operating system and native software alongside Chrome OS, greatly enhancing its offline capabilities. Easy to set up thanks to project "crouton" by dnschneid, available on GitHub (can't link it in a review, sorry!), which provides a simple hotkey for changing operating systems on-the-fly!
-----------------

TL;DR: Contrary to what other reviewers would lead you to believe, Chrome OS offers thin-client capabilities beyond that of simple web browsing due to the advanced state of modern web and networking technologies. Use this device as a gateway to your other machines using remote protocols like SSH and FTP, and you'll get much more use out of it -- and a little Linux knowledge will go a long way!

Many other reviewers have talked about the hardware, the software, the ups-and-downs of the Samsung $250 Chromebook. I'm not going to talk about that -- much. Instead, this review will be half discussion, half "how-to". As far as the hardware goes: suffice to say the device has a decent screen, good touchpad, GREAT keyboard, and is silent, efficient, and affordable. This design philosophy of efficiency and minimalism extends into the software of this machine. With modern computers and even portable devices getting ever-larger, more powerful, and more power-hungry, this choice of design can be a little off-putting. Here's why the Chromebook, and the underlying Chrome OS, has a vital place among your other devices because of this unusual design choice.

(NB: The jaw-dropping Chromebook Pixel was released recently, which flies in the face of the minimalist design of the software shared by these two devices. In my opinion, it's a giant step in the wrong direction, and this $250 device is superior in design in almost every way. Here's why.)

I couldn't find any reviews that discussed what this device is really capable of, so I thought I'd post my own thoughts. People tend to emphasize how little a Chromebook can do - what you lose when you make the switch. That's not at all what I see when I look at a Chromebook. But first, some background: I consider myself a "power user", and I'm writing to people who want to get the most from this device like I do. I'm experienced with Linux, I subscribe to basically every Google service, and I love getting a little command-line action (to taste). I've installed and used Arch Linux several times on various computers, and I've developed a taste for the brand of minimalism presented by lightweight Linux like Arch and Chrome OS. That said, I was initially underwhelmed when I got my Chromebook; it really seems like "just a browser" at first glance, just as most other reviewers would have you believe. Believe me, it has much more to offer. In truth, there's a whole Linux system under Chrome OS that's capable of much more, and it doesn't take much effort to bring it out.

Please note that my usage of this device is by no means typical, but it exposes areas of Chrome OS's potential that are left untapped by the average user. My work as a student involves lots of web searches, document composition using Google Docs, computer program development and compiling using an editor and gcc, data processing and graphing using Google Sheets and GNUPlot, document processing using LaTeX, and VPN access to my university's network. The Chromebook handles even my most advanced use-cases beautifully, thanks in large part to web applications and technologies outside the Chrome OS itself -- and here's how.

The ultimate power-user option is to simply dual-boot with a "real" Linux distro - for example, Ubuntu ARM. I've shied away from this option because of hardware compatibility concerns, battery life issues, and space limitations; the same argument can be made against a "chroot" environment, which is another solid power-user option. I do, generally, want to use this device for the web, so sticking with Chrome OS is a logical choice - besides, performance in Chrome OS is second-to-none, as this device truly does boot in the advertised 7 seconds. What's more, I really do enjoy the clean, minimalistic feel of Chrome OS: no desktop icons, no (visible) complex folder structures, no micromanaging files or bookmarks between devices, no bloatware, no fuss. It's great!

UPDATE: chroot'ing into a traditional OS works beautifully and is very easy to set up using a project called "crouton" by dnschneid on GitHub. Well worth a look!

But within the first ten minutes of using the device, I found that I wanted it to be more than "just a browser," and that's when something clicked. Instead of thinking about this device as a browser, I now call it a "thin client". It's a gateway to the internet and to your other machines. This is by no means a primary computer for someone like me, but it can be used as an interface to a primary computer. This crucial concept can be implemented in many ways, but my primary use-case has been with SSH, or "secure shell". With a little creative port-forwarding, I set up an SSH server to run on both my home server (running Debian) and my desktop (running Ubuntu), each accessible from the internet on its own port. While opening a port to the internet is generally inadvisable, securing the SSH connection with a password or (preferably) a private key provides a sufficient barrier to the outside world, in my opinion. Forwarding another port allowed me to wake or even boot my desktop over the internet using Wake-on-LAN technology, so I don't have to worry about leaving it on all the time and the amount of electricity being sucked down by its mammoth 750W PSU.

With an SSH server running on my desktop and server, it was then a simple matter of pressing CTRL+ALT+T on the Chromebook, typing "shell" at the prompt, and using a simple bash alias to initiate the SSH session. Once I'm connected, I have full access to my desktop's considerable horsepower or my server's vast storage from anywhere in the world using my new Chromebook - a light, power-efficient, sleek, and easy-to-replace interface to my other devices. While most of my work technically happens on my desktop, it no longer has to happen at my desktop. I've found that I can get serious work done on my desktop using my Chromebook from the living room, on campus, or anywhere with WiFi. Remote-accessing my primary computer has afforded me a new degree of freedom with where I work without changing how I work.

There are limitations to this approach, namely the difficulty of using graphical applications over the network; X11 forwarding over SSH has issues with the redrawing mechanism of Chrome OS's Aura window manager, resulting in orphaned remote windows that are only visible when they are being redrawn. Despite this, I've found that terminal access to my machines is more than enough for writing programs using vim, compiling using gcc (with my desktop's full horsepower), copying files to/from my server or desktop using scp ("secure copy"), and running/debugging my programs remotely. Familiarity and comfort at the command-line allows me to perform these tasks smoothly over a nearly lag-free SSH connection instead of resorting to slower, more graphically-intense, and ultimately less-elegant options like VNC, RDP, or Chrome Remote Desktop.

Of course, the thin-client concept extends to more than just a server-client relationship with your own hardware. Web apps are becoming more advanced as web technologies continue to develop rapidly. For me, a shining example of this evolution is a small website called ShareLaTeX. ShareLaTeX is a free or subscription-based service that allows you to compose in the document-programming language LaTeX using only a modern browser, complete with syntax-highlighting, error-checking, and code completion. You can store all of your document's assets on their servers, access them from anywhere, and compile your document into a PDF or DVI using the server-side compiler. You can even view your source code and the output PDF side-by-side in their well-designed web interface. Additionally, ShareLaTeX provides a "Google Docs"-style collaboration feature that allows you to compose documents with several other users. (But, this isn't a ShareLaTeX review, so let's move on.)

Even if you don't use or care about LaTeX, it's important to take stock of what this means for the web as a whole. It comes down to this: processor-heavy tasks like compiling programs are being offloaded to a server, while the (lightweight) interface can be presented on something much less beefy. It's this brand of duality that tech companies like Google, Apple, Microsoft, Sony, and countless smaller companies like ShareLaTeX are pushing as the future of the web. As a prospective Chromebook user, this should put a big smile on your face, and here's why:

Web-based software, and the software to which you can interface on your own devices, will just keep getting better and better. The web simply will not go "out of date" for the foreseeable future, meaning that it's nigh-impossible for your Chromebook to go out-of-date, no matter how processor-intensive the software of the future becomes. Bolstering this is the fact that Google regularly releases updates for Chrome OS every six weeks, and to date even the venerable Cr-48 (the very first Chromebook) runs the latest version, meaning our considerably more powerful Samsung Chromebook will be supported on the software side for a very, very long time.

In conclusion, the Samsung Chromebook and its unique Chrome OS embodies a paradigm shift in mobile computing that can be difficult to grasp for the average user. I urge you to think of this computer as a "thin client", an interface to the web and to your own devices. Web and network technologies like SSH, FTP, and HTML5 allow you to access resources far surpassing those on-board this device -- whether those resources are your own, or those offered by one of an increasing number of web services. Chrome OS serves as a gateway to those resources and services, therefore its relevance as a platform must be evaluated in terms of the quality of said resources and services. Knowledge, then, becomes critical: knowledge of the command line, desktop software that can run via command line (like GNU Octave and GNUPlot), and web services relevant to your own work will allow you to use the web and your Chromebook in exciting, productive new ways. Thanks for reading, and I hope you've learned something from this review!

title: This plate fits the Sony VCT-R630 RM tripod
text:
I bought this (Giottos 6E01) to replace a cracked/abused plate on a used Sony VCT-R630 RM tripod that fell into my hands in a "package deal". Original plates for this discontinued tripod are long gone, and I couldn't find a recommended replacement online. I went from published dimensions to try this one and it fits pretty darn well.

It is a little "snug" going in, and the locking lever only swings closed about 1/2 of the way - a little further to snug it up tight (with the original, the lever swings 80% closed under spring pressure, and locks tightly when gently pressed all the way closed).

It seems to be made of plastic and rubber, but appears stoutly built. It has a flip-up finger tab on the base of the screw, allowing "no-tool" installation onto the camera.

I also tried the Giottos MH 620 plate and it fits well too (maybe just a little less snug, but very similar). The 6E01 is very close to the form factor of the original plate (broader/longer top of almost exactly the same shape), while the MH 620 (which has a cast metal body) has a small top covered with a rubber pad. The MH 620 has much less contact area to the bottom of the camera - though you'll find that this doesn't matter much due to the slight flexibility of the the 6E01.

Due to the way the VCT-R630 RM tripod accepts the quick-release plate, you might (might, I say) have trouble with these plates attached to some large cameras (the plate kind of slips in tipped, under an angled guide on one side of the "receiver" hole). If so, a small amount of trimming would fix that - which would be easier on the 6E01, since it seems to be plastic, not metal. (You could probably get away with a little judicious trimming on the tripod side as an alternative, if this is an issue.)

title: Great design, but file compression may be an issue for photographers
text:
I bought this drive for storage of JPG landscape photos on long road trips where cloud storage and computer access would not be available. The plan was first to put the photos on my iPad for editing, then upload them to the drive as a backup.

The Media Drive is a beautifully designed product, and it worked very well with both an iPad Air and iPhone 5C. The companion Sandisk iOS app makes it easy to browse photos on both devices, and uploading photos to the drive via its wireless connection is easy and relatively fast. When connected to my Mac with a USB cable, the drive appears on my desktop, making it easy to transfer and manage files.

There is only one (unchangeable) default destination folder on the drive for uploaded photos, but it also accepts an SD card, with its own default destination folder. The Sandisk app lets you choose whether photos go to the drive or the card. This makes it easy to use it as backup for both myself and my wife, without getting our photos mixed up. I had no problem using a 32GB SD card for this.

So far, so good. Unfortunately, it turns out that the drive automatically reduces each photo to 2048 pixels wide when they are uploaded to it. This may have been intended to maximize the number of photos the drive can store, but it does cause a loss of resolution and image quality. There is no way to turn off this compression.

Sandisk tech support confirms that this is a "known issue" and their development team is "working on it". Let's hope that a future firmware update will let the drive maintain the original file sizes and quality. As it stands, though, photographers should be aware of this issue when considering the product.

title: GTX 970 Assassin Edition
text:
Asus should probably rename the card to 970 assassin edition, because of its non existent non footprint.

Other reviews have covered the pros, but i can't help but to emphasis on how silent this card is running. Noise don't really bother me until i got the R9 290, since then i got noise phobia, so i become very picky in terms of fans DB for my next card.

The card handles everything with good fps, and play moderate demanding titles like dota 2, fifa 15 etc without the need of fan spinning, 0db means u won't any fan noise at all (not considering other components from your system).

I tested COH 2 which is known to be graphic intensive, it does spin up the fan and max temp reach 70C at most, fan speed around 50%. But at that point the fan is still not audible at all. I tried to adjust it to 70-100 region and enclosed in a good case it is still not audible. I am so amazed that i forced myself to purposely pick up the noise because i find the fan performance hard to believe.

Granted, you can hear the fan if you put your ear next to the fan (1 feet distance), but anything more than that the fans is nearly non existent (in a good way).

One more thing, my ambient temp is around 30C, and usually i need to turn on AC when gaming, but this time even when i forget to turn on the AC i won't realize it until i actually saw the AC unit, not because of the hot temp. the power saving may cut ur bill by a little but not having AC to drive down room temp definitely will cut down ur electric bill.

Anyway, it idles at 45C for the 0db fan feature so if it bothers you, spin it up with MSI afterburner (asus tweak is so buggy).
I noticed that my games looks washed out than usual. I decided to play around with NV control panel, and when i slide the digital vibrance +1 it restores all the contrasts and gamut etc.

I found out that it is a HDMI bug so the solution is to tweak it with a registry to send full RGB signal. If you ever noticed your desktop color looks faded with this card on HDMI do try the fix

If you are deciding btw gbyte, asus and MSI my advise is to go with this 1 for the superior fan performance, although MSI also feature the silent fans it is not as good, and if you are willing to scarifies a few FPS diff for a less noise you can’t go wrong with this card.

title: Please Read Before Making Your Purchase. Samsung outsources the panels on certain models.
text:
Please read if you're interested in buying this television. Samsung is known to outsource their panels on certain sizes of their LED line-up. The last thing I want is for you to spent $1,000 on a LED with a poor panel. If you're interested in either the H6350 or the H6400, please avoid the 50 inch and 65 inch models. These models outsource their panels to AU Electronics. I would recomment the 55 inch, or the 48 inch models, as they feature Samsung panels. If you are looking to get a 60 inch, just know that Sharp manufactures the panels in Samsung's 60 inch 6350 and 6400. It is still a great panel, but not a Samsung panel (And isn't that why you're paying the extra money for a Samsung?).

Things to look for when buying your television. There is a sticker on the box of the TV with a code that starts with either T, U, W, A, M, or H

T, U, W = Samsung Panel (6350, 6400 = 32 inch, 40 inch, 48 inch, 55 inch)
A, M = AU Electonics, Mei (6350, 6400 = 50 inch, 65 inch) AVOID this panel
H = Sharp (6350, 6400 = 60 inch)

Ironically, all the 5500 models (low end Samsungs) offer Samsung panels

title: All that I ask and more
text:
I had been dying to try a Wake-Up light because I'm always fully awake feeling well rested, bounding delightedly out of bed long before my alarm goes off in the Summer when my bedroom is flooded with sunlight and birdsong in the Summer. (It's practically an annoying Disney movie in my bedroom while I'm trying to sleep in the Summer months.) In the winter I turn into a hibernating bear and often end up snoozing my alarm and crawling groggy and grumpy from my bed.

The Philips HF3510 Wake-Up Light is a great size (rather large actually without taking up TOO much room on my bedside table) that gradually floods the room with natural-seeming light (it looks like a little glowing sun). There are quite a few buttons and you'll definitely have to read through the instructions before you're first go but nothing too complicated and some nice options.

The light isn't going to just snap on at full intensity the second you set your alarm to; be prepared for a very gradual lightening that gently sends natural signals to your body that it's time to wake up. There are noise/radio settings as well if you need that to do the trick; there are 3 "natural" sounds and an FM radio. Still, don't expect to really be able to "snooze" this alarm unless you want a 9 minute nap.

A nice feature is the reverse "sleep" option that will start out bright and gradually dim till you fall asleep (you can adjust this to a slow, hour-long sunset in your room).

I'd definitely recommend a Wake-Up light for anyone, but I especially loved the aesthetic design of the Philips HF3510; since it's something I have to look at every day this is important. It does all that I ask it to and a bit extra!

title: Excellent 70 inch TV
text:
1)Picture quality (PQ): Overall, the PQ is quite impressive, especially for a mid tier 70 inch TV. PQ for any TV is impacted on the video source, but if you have a good quality video source from your cable or direct TV provider, you will not be disappointed. Blue ray PQ is outstanding. For watching sports, I recommend turning off MotionFlow. MotionFlow creates that "soap opera-effect". It may be good for movies (subjective), but causes blurring of rapid moving objects such as a hockey puck.

3)Screen uniformity: No issues with blotches or light leakage that I can tell. I'm not an extreme videophille, so perhaps I just don't notice them.

4)3D: Initially I was not a big fan of 3D TV, but Sony's incorporation of passive 3D technology creates an experience that is much more enjoyable for me. The glasses are comfortable. Even simulated 2D to 3D is pretty decent on this TV.

5)Video games: I'm a casual gamer and I have had no issues that I have observed so far. This TV has been rated great for video games, see below

http://www.displaylag.com/introducing-2013s-best-hdtvs-for-gaming-part-1/

6)Screen reflectiveness: My room has a lot of open windows. Luckily this TV has a "semi matte" screen, which helps reduce reflections. I was initially interested in the Sharp or Vizio 70 inch, which are full matte screens. But, I felt the PQ was somewhat diminished because of the full matte screens. I still enjoy watching Samsung TVs, but the highly reflective screens were not an option for me.

7)Placement of TV: I am using the stand that accompanied the TV. It's not the best looking stand, just adequate, I wish it was black. I've read on other forums the stand caused their Sony R550A to lean back a bit. I haven't had any noticeable issues, but be aware of this.

8)Viewing angles: As with most LED TVs, PQ is less optimal at increased viewing angles, and this holds true for this TV. I didn't notice increased viewing angles being better than other LED TVs of similar size on PQ.

9)Price: I think the price of this TV is very competitive with the other 70 inch smart 3D TVs. I've heard great comments for both the Vizio and Sharp, but this Sony TV fit my needs a bit better.

In summary, a great mid tier 70 inch LED TV that I am very happy with.

title: OK product but NOT at $70 price - flimsy and broke twice in first 24 hours of use
text:
*** EDIT/UPDATE from 2 to 3 stars because they have excellent customer service. I contacted Sealife about my issues and they said this was not normal and paid to ship me a brand new one - replaced for free with no questions asked ***

I did a lot of research before buying a monopod for my GoPro Hero 3+ and decided not to buy the dozens of similar monopods out there priced at $20 because they had poor reviews being too cheap and easily breaking; so I opted to spend the full $70 to get this "higher quality" monopod. Unfortunately, this was not worth the extra $50, and seemed to be just a cheap and breakable as the rest.

I purchased this solely for a 3 day trip on the Great Barrier Reef. On my second dive (of 11), the screw at the bottom of the monopod completely stripped (as has been complained about several times on this review forum before) and left the pole completely detached from wrist strap in the middle of my dive. This should be a fairly easy fix, but I was out in the middle of the ocean without a spare screw, so I jerry-rigged it and tied the washer to the top of the pole where you can adjust the angle of your camera.

While this fix was not ideal and made it almost impossible to use the monopod properly, it at least gave me some reassurance that I would not lose my camera. The next day, the screw that handles the adjuster completely broke off as well; so now, not only do I have nothing to tie my wrist strap to, but I cannot adjust the angle of the camera (e.g. flip it from selfie to flat to POV). I had to do the majority of my dives freely holding onto the monopod with no strap, and did not have the ability to adjust the camera angle (because the adjuster had broken off). Given that your hands are at a premium (to use your regulator, BCD, check your compass, air pressure, depth, etc.) this is not ideal, if I took my hand off the pole for one second my camera would be lost forever. All of this occured within the span of 24 hours of me opening this product.

All that being said, besides the flimsy safety strap feature and the cheap screws, the actual product is great. You can extend it to get great shots from far away and contract it into your travel bag. You can flip the camera to get selfies, rotate it flat to use like a normal camera, or flip it all the way to get a POV extended from several feet away (until the adjuster breaks like mine).

BOTTOM LINE: just go buy a $20 monopod and save yourself $50. I've learned they all do the same thing with no real difference in quality or sturdiness.

title: For shoppers who can't decide  if they should pull the trigger
text:
There are a lot of Amazon reviews that make this lamp look like a piece of junk, designed to hoodwink consumers. Here are a few honest words to help shoppers out.

When it comes to a replacement lamp, there are two choices:
a) the genuine epson lamp, at $300 from Epson, or about $250 from a handful of authorized sellers such as Adorama and B&H.
b) an aftermarket lamp from Amazon and other online retailers, some of whom specialize in projector lamps, with prices ranging from $37 to $200

Because of the huge range of prices, and some scathing negative reviews, it's hard to know what to make of it all.

Regarding the genuine lamp - Amazon doesn't sell it, which is surprising. You can buy from Epson at full price, or a few other retailers, but it's hard to know whether it's an OEM product, if they don't say so explicitly. They might list the Epson model-number, or show the name "Epson" but how can you be sure? And when it turns up in a brown box, how do you even know it was made by Epson.

Some vendors say it uses a 'genuine osram' lamp, and that this is the same manufacturer that Epson used, and that the only difference was the plastic housing. I didn't see "Osram" anywhere on my (now deceased) Epson OEM lamp, and the manufacturer refers to it as E-TORL (Epson Twin Optics Reflection Lamp)

I have seen this product offered by vendors, whose web-site name suggests that they specialize in projector lamps (lampexperts, projectorlamps, etc.) who sell the AFTERMARKET lamp, but try to disguise the fact, because they are trying to sell it for $200. (still a good discount from the OEM lamp) - One vendor published questions from consumers with questions like "is this OEM" or "is it made by the same company that made the project"? Their answers try to disguise the fact that it's not made by Epson, saying that the lamp was made by the same company Epson used (Osram) with a "compatible" housing. These "wizards-of-oz" are trying to fool consumers.

I believe you have two true choices:
1. be a smart shopper and buy from Amazon at $37, or
2. be a cautious consumer, and buy from Epson at $300.

The latter is not a bad choice! With Epson, you know it will work to spec, and you'll be looked-after. The aftermarket product might have problems as you already know, but given the huge gap, it has to be worth a try, right? At that price, you can afford two, and keep one as a backup (or return within 30 days once you're totally satisfied)

I chose THIS LAMP. It arrived fast with Prime (thanks Amazon!! you rock) in a brown box with foam padding. No instructions, but clear instructions are in the Epson user guide. It's a user-replacable part, and it's super-easy. I put a screwdriver in the slot to release the door, removed two screws. The old one popped out, and the new one went right in. The bulb sits in a slightly different position, so i had to adjust the focus (for the first time in over 3 years). That is all. The whole process took less than 5 minutes, and I never had to take the projector down from its ceiling mount.

The image was the same brightness as before, maybe slightly dimmer, but i heard it will get brighter during the break-in period of 10 or 20 hours. I am super-stoked I got a great lamp for a great price! Woo hoo!

Now regarding those negative reviews: don't believe everything you read on Amazon! Seriously. Some reviewers have an agenda. They might have a business that sells them for $200, and they are trying to scare consumers. This happens more than you would think. Other reviewers had a genuine issue, maybe it was a bad part, maybe they made an honest mistake, or maybe they were careless. Don't worry, you're covered by the seller's warranty, and even your credit card company will refund you if the seller gives you a hard time.

So make a stand. BUY THIS LAMP. Don't buy from those ripoff merchants who sell for $191, because you think $37 is somehow too good to be true.

title: Audiophile's Opinion: Effective and Versatile
text:
While this product seems expensive as an add-on to do what an iOS device (iPad, Pod, Phone, etc.) already does, it's practically free when compared to high-end audio investment cost. Using it as a headphone amp, all you do is plug the Lightning end of your iOS device's cable into the device and the USB end into the iDo. Then plug your headphones into the iDo and voila. Other reviewers have already said that this device greatly improves typical iOS-device sound, and it does. I confess that I'm comparing it to the iPhone 5's audio output, and the iPhone 5's audio is a significant step down in sound quality from earlier iPhones and iPods, probably because it is so small and lightweight. But there's nothing wrong with the iPhone 5's digital signal, and that's what the iDo uses. I'd say the iDo will take you 75 percent of the way from iPhone 5 sound to what you'd get from an audiophile rig costing 10 times a much and taking up 20 times as much space. That's a good deal. If you're an audiophile (audiofool?) or if you happen to have a home theater receiver, you have options that may produce even better sound.

The iDo is especially good as a headphone amp, but you can do more with it. It has RCA line-level jacks on the back that respond to the volume control. You can connect it to a boom box or set of computer speakers or whatever. if you're a 'phile, you can input it either to your preamp for switching or directly to power amp(s) if you have separates and don't need the switching. A more important option is to use the coaxial digital output. If you're a 'phile who has a separate digital-to-analog converter (DAC), you can do it that way. If you have a home theater rig, you probably have the ability to connect the digital output to your home theater receiver. If you have an expensive receiver, its built in DACs are probably better than what's in the iDo. Whether or not that's true, your home theater receiver is the gateway to your home theater speakers. No question that this is how 90 percent of digital-output users will do it. Understand that when you use the coaxial output, you are bypassing the iDo's built-in DAC and analog amplification entirely. Get a coaxial digital cable if you decide to do this. If you have an old composite or component video cable, that will do in a pinch.

If you have a home theater receiver with a USB input or bluetooth, you may be able to play your cell phone directly through the receiver. If that's your objective, check those options first.

I tried using the digital output going directly into a high-end DAC, and it sounded superb, as you'd expect. Going this route, I have a true, high-end music server in my iPhone 5 (I have 1000 songs from ripped CDs using Apple lossless compression on my iPhone.) The message is that it produces a clean digital signal. If you have any home theater receiver, this is a way to use the iDo, even though, in that mode, all it is probably doing is routing the digital signal to the coax output. (I'm guessing that there's no processing involved -- there may be.)

One technical aside: the volume control, which affects the line-out as well as the headphone output, is analog instead of digital. It is digitally controlled, but the actual volume reduction uses analog components. This is a good thing. Reducing volume digitally into standard DACs can produce very bad sound.

So what am I saying? The iDo is an outstanding headphone amp. It can serve as a DAC plus a preamp. It can produce a coaxial digital signal. So it can be just an add-on to your iPhone to upgrade the headphone sound, or it can turn your iOS device into an outstanding music server for a home theater or even a high-end audio rig (if the rig has DAC capability).

To me it's gratifying to see other reviewers praising a product whose sole function in most applications is sound quality improvement. It's a sign that in an age of synthetic sound, people still hear differences in quality, and people still care enough to go out of their way to get better sound. I'm tempted to buy another iDo so I can have one at work and one at home -- actually, I could use two at home. It's a great product that exceeds expectation.

***Update*** If you're primarily interested in using the digital output, check the NuForce website for a cheaper option.

title: great for copying photos from my camera to my Android phone
text:
I use this card for copying JPEG photos from my camera to my Android smartphone. This allows me to email photos immediately in the field via my phone's data connection, without having to plug the card in to my laptop and search for a WiFi hotspot. This is great for journalists, travelers, or just heavy Facebook or Instagram users. Yes, you could use your phone's camera, but a dedicated camera takes way better photos, especially in low light conditions or zooming in or macro closeups. Copying a photo from my camera to my phone takes about 3 seconds.

Setting up the connection between the Eye-Fi card and your phone does require some semi-complicated configuration work involving both your PC and your phone, so make sure you figure it out well ahead of time. The process is not documented with the instruction manual or in the PC app, but you can find it on the Eye-Fi web site. You only need to do this setup once.

Aside from the one-time setup issues, another issue is that this card needs lots of power. I figure I need 3 times as much camera battery power when using this card compared to a regular memory card. My camera can normally take about 300 photos on one battery charge. With this card copying all my photos to my phone via WiFi, I only get about 100 photos per battery charge, so bring lots of spare batteries.

This card also burns your cell phone battery. I use my smartphone for lots of things, so hard to measure the impact of the EyeFi, but I can easily burn through almost 2 smartphone batteries while using this card (for 200 photos), while I can usually last a full day on just one battery when I'm not using this card. Think twice about using this card if you do not have spare batteries for your phone.

I only copy JPEG photos to my phone with this card. I set my camera to shoot JPEG+RAW, but this Eye-Fi only transfers the JPEGs. That's fine with me since the RAW files are huge and would take forever to copy and my phone's RAW-to-JPEG conversion probably is not as good as the camera's. RAW files have more detail for printing, but I can always copy the RAW files to my PC using the old card reader.

I would give this card 5 stars if not for the battery issue, and also the price is kind of expensive if you're not using it all the time in the field.

title: may do some fancy things but won't do the basics
text:
I wanted an mp3 player with a) enough capacity to hold the several hundred CDs I had finally ripped to disk, b) Blue tooth, and c) radio. After scouring the reviews and specifications over the web this appeared to be the only one that matched what I wanted.

Downloading was neither easy nor straightforward. You can't just plug in the USB and drag and drop; you first have to download a rather clunky app from Apple which immediately angered me by insisting that every time I connect the iPod it would back everything up either onto my tablet or onto Apple's servers. I don't want it doing either of these things but as far as I can tell this cannot be disabled.

Then, once I'd downloaded my music to the iPod I discovered that you can't list your albums by artist and you can't even list your albums by title. If a CD has tracks by different artists then it won't register as an album - each track is listed separately (I have since discovered that you can fix this by editing the info for each track manually - pathetic - after the first 100 or so tracks it gets really tedious.). Also it insists on taking up half the screen with pictures of album covers, which may be ok for some people but you can't disable it so you can only list 4 items per screen. If you have a bunch of compilation albums and each one takes up 6 screens then it gets pretty messy and really tedious to scroll through.

If you want to play more than one item you must make a playlist. Not a problem until you find that you can't add an album to the playlist; you can't even open an album and 'select all' tracks, you have to select each track individually. You have a 4 hour drive ahead and want to set it to play 6 albums? Have fun selecting the 90 tracks one at a time manually.

Finally, I assumed that 'radio' meant radio. It doesn't. It means access to a limited amount of streamed content from Apple and only when you have a wi-fi connection. I live in the country and hardly ever have access to wi-fi when not at home.

.... Three days later.... it got worse!!!! When I plugged the iPod back into my tablet to recharge, it erased all 4000+ songs! I don't store any music etc. on my tablet (that's what the iPod is for!) so when I plugged it in it decided that 'sync' meant delete anything that wasn't on the tablet. I spent an hour reinstalling everything and cannot find an option to disable this misfeature. I tried picking the option 'sync only highlighted songs/folders' and it said if I did that it would delete everything off the iPod. Apparently I'm not going to be able to download anything more to it because it will delete everything else.

Being a teacher I thought I'd ask the students since they know these things inside out. Everything I asked them they said "No, you can't do that, it's an apple"

Apple users may be used to crippled products that only allow you to do what Apple has decided you can do. I come from the world of open source software, shareware, etc. so for me this is the most disappointing piece of junk electronics I have ever bought. My first and last Apple product.

title: King of the Android Tablets.
text:
I've tried and reviewed several android tablets over the years on Amazon. Most of the tablets I have had a chance to use actually were adequate for the money, especially if you were looking primarily for a "toy" or something to play an occasional game of angry birds, check email, or do some casual web browsing.

The Nexus 7 however is in a different league. It is perfectly capable of being a primary means of doing most day to day activities on the web, social media, email and entertainment. The quad core 1 ghz processor is lightening fast and multi-tasks smoothly. Graphics are very clean and smooth. Battery life is very good, especially if you keep wifi and location services turned off when not needed.

I use it often as an E-reader when I want to read in lighting that isn't enough for my Sony reader. Most low end tablets that I have tried in the past were not sharp enough to use in this manner for any length of time without eye fatigue from the low res background and text, but I can read comfortably for hours on the nexus.

I have used it on Netflix and downloaded movies with no problems at all. One of the more demanding apps I have run on it is an RC helicopter simulator, and it ran just as smoothly as it does on my PC. I'm not a big gamer, so I have not tried it on any heavy duty games, but I feel confident it would perform well.

There are a few things to be aware of with this tablet though.

The unit has no external storage directly...in other words no SD or Micro SD slot. That being the case for the extra $50 I would go with the 16GB unit and not the 8 unless you do not care to store much on your tablet. The 8 GB unit will only give you around 6GB of free storage. There is now a program available for about $3.00 however that will allow you to use a usb stick as external storage and to play back media without having to put it on the tablet. The program, called Nexus Media Importer does not require you to root your tablet. You also have to have a cable for this but these are available for $1 - $5 on Amazon.com. Be careful here though as many of the cheapie ones ship from overseas, and quality could be questionable as well. I would spend the extra four bucks and get a domestically shipped one from a known manufacturer. It is a micro-usb to female usb adapter.

One other minor annoyance is that for some reason, ASUS / Google chose to lock certain functions of the tablet in Portrait mode. This also is easily fixed with an external program available for a very reasonable cost called "Rotate". Once run and configured the tablet will automatically switch from portrait to landscape mode when you turn it over. I think this program is also around two or three dollars on google play. Keep in mind that currently you get a $25 credit for downloads with the purchase of the tablet, so you have no out of pocket expense for the software.

Apparently there were some quality control issues on the early runs of the tablet. Several problems were possible. There was a problem with the screen not being mounted properly and appearing to be too high on one side or the other. There was also a problem with the screen losing touch sensitivity on one side after extended or demanding use like a game that used the quad core processor heavily.
There was also an issue with the screws inside the tablet not being tightened properly causing a creak or other noise when the tablet was handled. There is a fix for this on the internet but you need to be aware that it could void your warranty if you accidentally leave any signs that the tablet has been opened. Search Youtube for detailed videos on how to do this procedure. There also have been reported issues with the built in microphone and / or speakers not functioning properly.

I personally had to return the first 16 GB that I purchased to Walmart for a refund as it was the last one they had at the time I bought it. It had the screen sensitivity problem mentioned above. I then went to the local Office Depot, which had several 8 and 16 GB models in stock. I explained the potential problems to the sales person and asked if I could try the unit before I purchased it to avoid a potential return, and she agreed. The first one she brought out was an 8 GB, Serial number beginning with C60...the video display on it was totally defective...it appeared very washed out. She then brought me another one, a 16GB model, serial number beginning with C70, (the same serial series btw, as the one I had already returned to Walmart).

This one appeared to work perfectly with no physical defects showing. Once I got it home and had used it a couple of days I noticed a little noise when I put pressure on certain areas so I removed the back and tightened all the screws around the edge of the frame slightly. Again, do this at your own risk, and be sure not to over-tighten them...just snug them up...these are tiny screws and can probably be stripped very easily. There are several detailed videos on exactly how to remove the back cover available on Youtube...by all means watch one before attempting it yourself.

I believe that the manufacturer has been made aware of these problems and probably taken steps to correct them in more recently manufactured units. If I had the option I would avoid C60 serial number units unless you are absolutely certain you can return the unit if it proves to be defective. I would advise buying one locally if at all possible in preference to ordering it as it will probably be much easier to get it replaced if necessary.

Overall, once I found a good one and downloaded the software mentioned above, I am absolutely thrilled with the tablet. I think it was worth the effort I put into it.

title: Don't buy: bad touchscreen technology
text:
The Polaroid S7 Android tablet was very attractive at $90 from Kohls, so I bought two. That was a bit foolish.

First off, I liked the fact that it would charge through the USB, unlike the AGPtek [[ASIN:B009C30WBS AGPtek 7 inch Android 4.0 Capacitive Touch Screen Tablet PC (Wi-Fi G-sensor, 800*480, 1GHz, 512MB DDR3, 8GB built-in Capacity with Expandable Micro SD Card Slot, Front Camera, Support 3G 3D 1080P HD Flash 11.1 & Multi-language)]], my first Android tablet. Similarly, the LCD looks nice, and felt good in the hands. At least, however, the AGPtek worked.

_BAD_TOUCHSCREEN_
The first thing I noticed was that it seemed to have problems with touch. I thought it was the protective sheet over the face. Not so. It worked inconsistently even after removal (bad idea, see below). This was particularly noticeable and irritating when using the virtual keyboard; rotating the device around so that it flipped helped, but imagine trying to text while rotating it... hardly considered useful. I wanted to determine the cause, and being that I work with alpha touchscreen hardware, I believed that there were "dead zones" in the digitizer. There were, but not in a way I expected.

I wrote a simple app that marked the places where I tapped the screen. Tapping left a pattern that indicated a flawed touchscreen design. _The digitizer blocks out the screen in near 1cm grid_ from edge to edge! This means that many of the keys on the virtual keyboard cannot be clicked. After tapping (I tested both devices), there was a clear, *wide* grid. I verified the app on my Android cellphone and found no problem.

All in all, that was a significant showstopper for Android which relies on a good touchscreen. (It's a pity I can't post screen snapshots of what I discovered. They are surprising. Can anyone think of a way...?)

_NO_GOOGLE_STORE_
The device lacks Google Store App. Their website states that they're not certified and that:

"Our tablets are not licenced with GooglePlay store as of yet. However, we find that the Google Android market caters mainly to smart phones. Polaroid Tablet users can download apps by downloading the Amazon App Store application or by loading .apk files directly onto the device using the preloaded 'Apk Installer' or 'Download Manager' (depending on your model number) which will be located in your tablet's app menu. Polaroid Tablets are pre-installed with a homescreen widget titled 'Download App Stores'. From here you can download a variety of App Stores which you can download apps from."

What chutzpah! All the great apps found on Google Play are, according to this citation, "cater[ed] mainly to smart phones." Hmmm... sounds like they're not committed to getting licensed.

There are many videos on how to install the Google Play Store, but all of the ones I found require access through the developer's debug interface. All the drivers I tried failed to be recognized by Eclipse and ADB. I sent several emails to their support, and their only response to date has been "Tell us why."

Bottom line: all the apps I bought on play.google.com are unavailable /and/ unlikely to be available any time soon.

_WEAK_GLASS_
Simply, it took little time to get the glass scratched. I never had that problem before with other touch screens; so, if you intend to keep it, I recommend *not* removing the protective sheet.

_FLAKY_DEVICE_
One of the tablets began to "flake out." We're trying to resurrect it now.

<<<UPDATE>>>
_DANGEROUS RECHARGE_
When recharging, the device turns itself back on! This means that the device will be running and if you're in your car (like we were driving back from a long trip), the device will overheat! It got hot enough that touching it was painful.

title: Amazing Piece of Equipment - Objective Review
text:
I have been shooting with my 6D now for over three years. I know a lot of people out there gripe that it has only 11 focus points, or that only the center point is actually cross type, but this camera is not meant for shooting fast action sports. Sure, you can shoot fast action objects, just make sure you use the center point, and manually track your subjects. Personally, I use my body for landscapes, cityscapes, and some portraits of my kids. For fast action sports, and other items like that, I use my 7D Mark II.

PROS:
1.) Battery Life - Excellent! I can get almost 1,000 photos on one single charge. Come to think of it, I never really counted how many shots I can get on a single charge; however, I have never needed to take 1,000 images in a single day. I have gone on several one-week vacations, and only charged the batteries before I left. It has a great power saving mode, and saves batteries after the set duration of inactivity.
2.) Weight - It's a bit heavier than the Rebel series bodies, but much lighter and smaller than the 5D series of full frames, and definitely more compact than the 1D series of full frames.
3.) WiFi - I don't use it much, but when I do, it's amazing. I use my iPhone 6S Plus as a remote, a live preview screen, and I can even do a quick edit of a RAW file on my iPad on the go if I need to. The Canon EOS app is really solid.
4.) Image Quality - Needless to say, it's amazing. I use all Canon L glass, which makes it even more amazing. As a side note, if you want superior image quality, and a quick prime, please check out the Sigma ART series lenses. I also have their 50 1.4 and 24 1.4, and these lenses shine on the 6D. They rarely leave my camera.
5.) ISO - Excellent! I will push the ISO up to 6400 without even thinking about it. I keep the Auto ISO up to that amount, because I'm so confident that I won't miss a shot when I use Auto ISO mode

CONS:
1.) GPS - Good, but man it's a battery drainer....
2.) SD Card - Only one SD card slot, but not a deal breaker.
3.) Focus Points - As stated, if you aren't shooting a pro sports game or something really fast, you won't miss it.

You know, that's about all the cons! There really aren't that many. I have also attached some of my work with this camera.

title: Don't trust positive reviews that are older than one year!
text:
I needed a bunch of Micro SD readers in September 2012. I tried a few (about 5) different models before choosing the one to use en mass. This one turned out to be my pick due to its superior design and quality of manufacturing, in spite of its higher cost. (I particularly liked the small button used to push the card out of the reader.)

Over the course of one year, about half of the readers stopped working. The cards were unreadable when used inside of those failed readers, and fine when used in some other way. While I was annoyed by these failures, I still liked the convenience of this model, so I decided to buy a few more of the same.

When the new shipment came in October 2013, I was greatly disappointed by the obvious change in manufacturing quality. Most of the readers in the latest batch were unusable. Typically the cards were not readable in them at all. Sometimes they would work, but often the shape was so deformed that they needed to be forced into a USB slot. In that case, they would often disintegrate when pulled out! It seems that while the design of this product is still the best, the manufacturing quality has fallen below the level when it can be useful.

I don't know if the following information is relevant, but the readers in the old "good" batch were black, and the new "bad" ones are white. In addition, the circuit boards are actually not the same in the two batches, although they look exactly the same on the outside.

title: Shatter-proof and water-proof! No more is needed!
text:
I got this for my boys for their visit to Grandma's last summer. My oldest is 11, and he's constantly wanting to take pictures. He's very artistic and loves photography. Unfortunately, he's at the age of the "butter-fingers"--he drops everything! And his brothers are not much further down the totem pole--actually, they're still little more than cavemen at times. After much deliberation and watching of YouTube demonstrations and reviews (Panasonic Lumix ranked well on all), we chose the Panasonic Lumix because it is shatter-proof and water-proof, and, more importantly, is more affordable compared with other models.

So, here we are nearly six months later...I have personally witnessed this poor camera dropped several times on our tile floor from about 4 feet. It looks great and still operates like new, and there's no telling what the boys have put it through when I am not around! It has taken nearly 2,000 photos and countless videos--(yes, it was a little hard having to go through 1,000 shots, each with a full commentary of just that one week at Grandma's, but the experience was wonderful for the guys). Despite the lack of skill of the photographers, most of the pictures turned out very well. They were mostly clear and not blurry. My sons took lots of pictures inside caves and museums, which have remarkably turned out well with the low light. Of course, since the photographers are under the age of 11, there are quite a few pictures in which the subject is not known and has to be thoroughly explained (e.g., "Mom, can't you see that really cool pebble in the grass?" and "I took a picture of the sky because that cloud looked like a jellyfish!")

I have not yet tested its waterproof capabilities. Apparently, there are some simple steps to lock down the camera before submerging it. However, it has been subjected to a couple of minor spills with not problems. This has definitely been a good buy for us since now the kids leave my more expensive camera alone. It can also be a backup camera for the family since it performs quite well anyway.

title: Extremely happy with TV; Nervous about warranty/Firmware update
text:
*************UPDATE 1/5/12*****************
SW Version pre firmware update: V8-0RSC801-LF1V041
SW Version post firmware update: V8-0RSC801-LF1V041

After performing firmware update today the SW Version did not change (as listed in Menu>Setup>System Information)

*************REVIEW 1/4/12*****************
Before Christmas I woke up to an Amazon gold box deal for this TV for $260. My stomach tensed with excitement that I may be able to actually afford my first LCD TV. After an hour of model/brand research I clicked back to Amazon to purchase and it was sold out. Damn me and my lack of impulsiveness. On Christmas day, however, when this TV was back in stock and listed for $300 I decided not to pass on this again, even at $40 more, and ordered TV 12/25/11.

TV arrived 12/28/11, setup was extremely easy: 4 screws in glass base, cable/sat channel scan (took about 8 minutes for scan), plug Xbox in via hdmi and cable in via coax and BOOM, up and running with my first HDTV. My jaw dropped when I tuned to the HD weather channel! Let me say again this is my first hdtv so I have no means of comparison but to a standard def Sanyo CRT, so I am no connoisseur, but 7 days later I am still in awe. Put in Enslaved Xbox 360 game and an audible "Whoooa!" was my first reaction to seeing a game in 1080p.

Read the instruction manual cover to cover, tweaking settings as best I could, turning off the auto lighting and backlight functions, setting up a Personal picture setting to go along with the preset modes, adding 10 channels to the 'favorites' button on the remote. The remote is decent, but I do have a difficult time finding the circular +/- channel and +/- volume buttons in the dark as there are 2 circular buttons above the + volume + channel that, although slightly smaller, don't 'feel' much different. The 8-watt speakers work well for me as my living room is small and I'm only 11 feet from the TV. That said, I plan on buying [[ASIN:B0027VT6V4 Cyber Acoustics Subwoofer Satellite System (CA-3602)]] 2.1 speakers to connect to the R/L audio out next month to enhance sound.

My current concern is 'to update firmware or not to update firmware?'. Right now I have not updated, although I did go ahead and put the update on a FAT formatted flash drive. Do I update and risk the TV going black as some have stated in these reviews and requiring a return to Amazon, or do I just leave well enough alone since I have no problems with the TV auto-powering on or changing volume? Other reviews indicate successful firmware update. I am so torn, but if i'm going to try it I need to do it within the 30 day return window. Gah! I will update with result if I get brave and try it.

The scariest thing about this TV is the reviews i've read about the TLC customer service nightmares. I have decided that on day 29 of my Amazon purchase I will definitely be buying a 3 year warranty from Square Trade for peace of mind.

Pros:
-Best deal on hdtv I found
-Beautiful HD picture
-Tons of inputs including 3xHDMI
-Input Skip to hide inputs you don't use, Channel Skip to hide unwanted channels (you heard me home shopping channels)
-Setup menu is extremely easy to use
-Glass stand is sturdy and attractive (subjective of course)
-Silver strip accent goes well with my black and silver entertainment center (subjective)
-I can walk almost all the way to the side of the Tv and still see the image clearly
-Samsung LCD panel
-remote makes it extremely easy to adjust aspect ratio and access 10 favorite channels and just feels good on button press

Cons:
-Firmware update hassle
-No optical audio out
-Possible sketchy TLC customer service/warranty
-Subpar remote design on the +/- channel & volume in my opinion (still make mistakes with those in the dark d/t similar feeling buttons above)
-SD channels look very 'blah'
-Light bleed in top left/right corners when screen is solid black; NOT noticeable at all when image on screen
-I have to switch between picture settings (Eco/Sports/Cinematic/Vibrant/Natural/Personal) often for tv shows/sports/movies/xbox games. Being that this is my first hdtv maybe this is normal, although I still haven't found a great setting for very dark movies after trying to adjust Personal picture mode for this purpose.
-With my PS2 plugged in via RCA, each time I make a selection on a DVD (play, skip forward, etc) there is an annoying 'pop' sound from the speakers. This does not occur on xbox via hdmi.
-If you turn off an input and take too long to decide what you want to do/watch next, the TV will power off after a few minutes (it does warn you first). This could just as easily go in the Pro's category for some.

TLDR: Love the TV, love the price, nervous about TLC warranty/customer svc, nervous about doing firmware update. Would definitely recommend this to friends with the stipulation that they purchase a Square Trade warranty.

title: Works great! Suggest watching the related Youtube video to avoid programming mistakes
text:
After I experienced my neighbor's remote access keypad for their garage door (not this brand), I had to get one. I have a 1994-circa Genie G2500 screw-drive type opener with 12 DIP switches. Genie sells a remote keypad but it only works with units with "intellicode" capability. Saw this on Amazon, but because I wasn't convinced it would work, I purchased it from a local big box home improvement store to simplify a return if needed.

Instructions are pretty clear with regard to identifying the opener (Genie with 2-position DIP switch is a Type 2 unit). I used the instruction sheet to select a 4-digit PIN, the DIP switch type (13 in my case), and the DIP switch sequence (found on the drive unit or on the hand held remote control). There may be some confusion when translating the switches ON/OFF pattern to 1s and 2s (for ON and OFF, respectively). Perhaps not intuitive at first glance, but take it slow and you'll get it.

Once you've got the "program" written down, just follow the instructions on how to enter them into the KLIK2U.

Here's a Gotcha (at least it was for me): according to the instructions, you start the programming by pressing the * and # keys simultaneously until the keypad stops flashing. You then continued the process of entering the PIN, ID type, and DIP switch sequence by pressing each, followed by the # key. I did this, but I mistakenly waited after each step for the keypad to stop flashing (i.e., go dim). Unbeknownst to me, the unit was "timing out" and subsequent information was not recognized.

I went through the steps a couple of more times without success, until it occurred to me that the data entry should be done BEFORE the keypad timed out. In hindsight, I was over-thinking the instructions, and only mention it in case some one else makes the same wrong assumption. Also in hindsight, if you review the Youtube video, you'll not go wrong.

Once I entered everything correctly, the KLIK2U operated perfectly.

As mentioned in several comments, the sliding door tends to stick and pop off once you've pushed/pulled hard enough to get it moving. Agree that a flip up door is preferable. I suppose someone unfamiliar with the unit may have difficulty figuring out how to open it. The upside is that there is less chance moisture or bugs will get inside. Also, I see some complaints about there not being an "enter" button, or alpha-numeric keys, not accommodating more than one door, no temp code option, etc. None are deal breakers for me, but they may be for you so decide accordingly.

text:

One thing I knew I wanted to do was add a sub to the factory stereo. At First I thought about going with a pre-made bass set up like the Infinity Basslink or a Bazooka. After some research I decided I would spend a bit more and get something I would really be happy with. Keep in mind this review is designed more for someone who has experience with doing an install of this type, your own results may vary.

After setting my budget, 400$, I decided I wanted to go either with dual 10s or a single 12. I decided I would be better off with the single 12 to help save on trunk space. Since this is a review is for the Sub I concentrate there as best I can. I was looking for 2 things; 1. A Dual Voice Coil (DVC) Sub that could run at 2 ohms 2. A Name that had a good reputation. Anyone who has done any car audio work knows you can tell a lot about a sub by its weight and the size of the magnet on the unit. Since you can't actually feel the weight when shopping online you have to go off of specs and look, in combination with reviews. Since this Sub had less reviews I was taking a bit of a chance there but I felt like it was warranted in this case.

I am running this sub with a Rockford Fosgate Prime R500 amp and the sub is in an Atrend E12Sv B Box Series 12-Inch Single Vented Subwoofer Enclosure. I get a very clean sound and a solid punch with no distortion at all. The amp has a lot of features that help the set up as well. Once I have a chance to spec out the amp I expect the sound to continue to improve, but even just straight into the car it sounds great.

title: Powerful studio monitor!!
text:
Use: I use this in a "bedroom" setup and also use these at house parties and small venues.

I bought a pair of these after owning the Numark NPM5s for about two years and must say what a difference these make! These monitors are three times more powerful than the NPM5s. They are a lot more heavier and are made to withstand some serious "on the road" wear and use. Unlike the NPM5s which only require one power plug, the NPM100s both require their own power source.

There is a cool looking blue light that illuminates when the speaker is turned on. It's located on the back of the unit next to the power switch. This blue LED light is so bright that I use it as a ambient light when its dark. These monitors come with mounting points for speaker stands and can be mounted several different ways. The monitor can be placed in the upright position like in the photo, or placed in the landscape position on it's side. When placed in this position, the speakers are facing up at a pretty good angle.

The overall appearance and construction of these monitors is great. After owning the NPM5s, it is clear that the NPM100s are built to withstand some serious knocking around. Each NPM100 is about 17lbs and will not rattle or move around where ever it is placed. The NPM5s would sometimes rattle away and move around when played at high volumes, the NPM100s are solid performers! There is a gain knob on the back of each monitor that can be adjusted from 0 to 10 to tweak your sound. Unlike the NPM5s which have a gain treble and bass, the NPM100s do not. They are primarily powered monitors so any EQ adjustments will need to be made by the mixer or interface being used.

After about 20 minutes of use, the monitors became very warm, but there is a heat sink on the back of each monitor to help cool the amp and speaker system. There is also a clip light that will blink RED when the monitor is breaching it's peak performance of 200W. Although it would be hard to clip with these speakers due to their compact powerful performance, it's good to have a warning that you are about to blow the unit!

PROS:

Great sound reproduction, these monitors are LOUD!
Tough construction, built to last
Powerful enough to be used at a small bar or club
Great for house parties
XLR, RCA, and 1/4 inputs

CONS:

The neighbors will not like your new monitors!
No indented handle or grip to pick-up and move around the unit
Power cord could be a little longer

In conclusion, if your on the market for a pair of serious monitors for either home use (I feel sorry for your neighbors) or at small to average size bar or outdoor event, look no further. These monitors will perform every time and for the price, you can't go wrong! I highly recommend these monitors!

Be advised that some sellers on amazon may stock these that came from another country. On the box these came in, there was a label advising which country and volt requirement there were to be used in. Make sure you don't purchase some for a foreign country as the power plugs will be different!
