title: Here is what I have done with the Fire HD 32 after 3 days
text:
Before I describe what I have done with the Fire HD 32 in 3 days, a little about my techie level.

Retired, 65 plus, set up one desktop and two laptops on wifi using Century Link Prism router, including Epson Workforce 845 printer wireless. Kindle DX owner 3 years.

OK, here goes:

After opening the box, I played with the Fire for a few minutes. Very intuitive. The battery level on the pull down "More":"Device" screen was around 35% so I decided to charge it using my 3-year old Kindle DX charger/cord. That is when I discovered the old cord was defective because when I wiggled it, the "charging" indicator would go off and on - mostly off. And my DX, after being plugged into that same cord for 4 days prior, was nearly dead. So I plugged the USB cable that came with the HD into the charger and viola! - charging nirvana.

During the first few minutes after turning on the Fire it took a minute or two to download updated software automatically.

First, wifi setup. It found my router immediately. I punched my 7 digit code into the very responsive keyboard and within roughly 4 seconds I was connected.

It took me less than 2 minutes to link both my gmail and yahoo mail accounts to the email program that came with the Fire. Access to both sets of emails on one device is more than I discovered to do with my desktop - and it set itself up automatically and instantly. All contacts that I had on yahoo also were visible and revisable on the Fire.

Next was my calendar. I already had my Outlook calender on my desktop linked to a Google calendar. That combination worked flawlessly. Connecting the Fire calendar app with my Google calendar took most of 15 seconds.

All of my previously downloaded books and cloud music were immediately available on the Fire once I intuitively followed a simple step.

The real fun part was downloading and experimenting with several "free", several $0.99, and a couple of $1.99 programs. The ones I've downloaded so far and really appreciate are:

*The Free Dictionary
*Calculator Plus
*Scanner Radio Pro (listen to public safety and public service radios around the nation/world)
*Photo Editor Plus (I quickly learned it is possible to use the Fire as a decent low res camera. This program isn't necessary, but helps clean up images you take with the Fire or download from other sources.
*WiFi Analyzer (very cool real time graphs and wifi data)
*Zillow (show details of real estate around the nation)
*MapQuest (I wasn't sure Fire did maps and satellite images. But this program works great.)
*eWeatherHD - An excellent, impressive weather program for anywhere in the world. Very detailed information.
*Weather Live - Scroll to any selected City; beautiful interactive background indicating conditions; more basic data than eWeatherHD
*TrackIt Deluxe (a hurricane/topical storm tracking program with great satellite images any time of year)
*CIA World Factbook
*Pandora
*TuneIn Radio Pro (select from hundreds/thousands of worldwide radio stations from a variety of categories of programming.)
*A variety of other specific, single purpose radio programming apps.

...and finally, so far, (I sprung for the 13 bucks) PrinterShare Premium to print web pages and notes I create (easy set up and reliable use).

The Kindle Fire HD32 exceeded my expectations. I expect to use this device for most of my laptop and desktop tasks except extended typing.

By the way, I don't notice the ads. And the "Customers also bought" suggestions are appreciated and useful.

A solid 5 stars!

title: A great Android tablet and iPad Retina alternative
text:
The ASUS MeMo Pad 10 FHD is a fantastic Android tablet for those who want something similar to the iPad with Retina display but running Android instead. The screen isn't quite as bright as the latest iPad with the brightness turned all the way up (so it might be very difficult to see the screen under direct sunlight) and the screen on my ASUS MeMo Pad 10 FHD needed to be adjusted using the included app that lets you increase the color saturation. However, this IPS display has GREAT viewing angles and has essentially the same image quality as the iPad.

The Memo Pad FHD also has a microSD card slot so you can add additional storage to your tablet ... something the iPad and most alternative Android tablets don't have.

The performance of the Intel processor and graphics are "class leading" but I never had any problems or significant lag when viewing websites, video, playing games, running productivity apps for work or editing photos on this tablet.

I will say that the tablet is a little bigger than some other 10-inch tablets (like the iPad) because of the screen ratio so it barely fits inside some "universal" tablet cases designed for 10-inch tablets.

I found that the battery life varies dramatically depending on the apps you're running. I get 8 to 10 hours of battery life with this tablet when I'm mostly just browsing websites and watching a couple of short video clips on YouTube. If I play a bunch of games that have to connect with servers (because they're multiplayer games) then the battery life might only be 4+ hours before I get the alert message that I need to plug in the charger.

In short, I would highly recommend this tablet to anyone who is looking for an Android tablet with a great screen and good features. It's not an iPad ... but some people consider that to be a good thing.

title: So beautiful, but major flaw makes dangerous to use
text:
Every G 1/4 port stripped/shredded due to soft material.

This product looks so beautiful and high quality: aluminum backplate, aluminum circular rings to mount the tube, real glass, frosted center cylinder with rubber grommet to easily mount an LED, good port spacing, nickel-plated plugs. But the manufacturer cheaped-out on the most critical part of the entire design -- the end caps and port holes. While mounted to aluminum rings, the caps/port holes are actually made of soft plastic or acetal. They shred as you thread in any kind of fitting. I tried all 3 ports very gently, carefully trying to start the threading straight on each with different G 1/4" fittings, but the outer thread immediately collapses and from there no matter how much time you invest, nothing will thread straight or tight. Additional context: I have other acetal in my current loop as well as past loops, none have shredded like this one. Also, all my fittings are XSPC brand G 1/4.

I would gladly pay another $20 to have better materials rather than the most critical part being a cheap plastic. (Also note that some online reviews describe the ends as aluminum; what they mean is the rings holding the end caps to the backplate are aluminum. The product description on Amazon accurately describes the caps as acetal.) At the very least, the holes should be drilled slightly smaller allowing you to self-tap your own fittings. With this design, even if you manage to get your 2-3 fittings installed perfectly the first time, what happens when you have to change a fitting? Currently requesting a return on mine but unsure what to do as I have already designed a compact system around this unit's dimensions and screw spacing, and love everything else about the unit except this glaring materials flaw.

**UPDATE**
Purchased a 2nd one of these from another retailer to test. Please see uploaded pictures -- exact same behavior on the 2nd reservoir. All three holes shredded while threaded with XSPC-branded compression fittings. Note that not only are the threads collapsing/shredding into pieces, but the fitting is actually cutting into the hole and enlarging it (this may be difficult to see in my photos, however it was easy to see the difference in hole size on the ports I had not yet threaded all the way down). I left all the fittings threaded on the 2nd reservoir and did some pressure testing with a kitchen hose... didn't leak, so set it up in my system and slowly filled up the loop. The system has been running for a few weeks now without any leaks from the reservoir. The problems are 1) the shredded material easily could have gotten into my loop, 2) every fitting threaded slightly crooked, 3) I am afraid to ever undo these fittings to change their arrangement, swap fittings, clean, or whatever because the fitting removed so much material and likely would not tighten down again. One-time use only and will remain a worry to me, would change if hadn't designed a custom case around this reservoir...

One unrelated, significant annoyance pointing to a design that needs revision...... During filling, the fill port CONSTANTLY creates a "bubble" over the fill port. Meaning, a layer of water sits over the top of the internal frosted light tube, filling the gap between the frosted tube cap and the opening into the reservoir below. I believe this is a form of water surface tension (Wikipedia the phenomenon). It indicates the product was not designed with enough space between the fill port opening and the top of the light tube to prevent water from forming a thin layer of skin/surface cohesion. The practical result is that no matter how quickly or slowly I poured, whether I poured carefully from a straight container, used a fat funnel, or even poured through a straw angled between the top of the light tube and the fill port opening, the water would repeatedly form a "skin" of water, blocking any additional water and repeatedly causing spills into my case (of course I had wrapped everything up with towels before starting to fill). It was very difficult to break this skin/bubble to be able to pour again; most often, I had to get a towel and dab out the water bubble. I would take off another star as this made it take about 1.5hrs to do a single fill-up, tediously dripping, blotting, dripping, blotting... Too bad I already rated it 1 star for the materials issue.

title: Best of the convertable Windows 8 laptop tablets, 2nd gen model with much improved battery life, highly recommended
text:
This is one of a new breed of convertible laptops created to take advantage of the Windows 8 paradigm, which allows use as both as tablet and a laptop. While this category is expected to grow, right now, there are essentially only a modest number of entrants, and only two that could be reasonably be called innovative: The Dell XPS 12 (this one), and the Lenovo Yoga 13. The Dell and Lenovo sport similar power specs (cpu, memory, hard drive, battery life), but the Dell has a much higher resolution, better, screen. In my opinion, the Dell takes that competition handily.

This is actually the second generation of the XPS 12, which replaces the earlier model which was released last year ([[ASIN:B004GAR91S Dell XPS 12 12.5-Inch Convertible 2-in-1 Touchscreen Ultrabook]]). The new version is almost identical to the older version in all physical terms, with the primary difference being that it's slightly lighter (about 3 ounces lighter). Under the hood, there is one very significant difference: This new model uses Intel's latest "Haswell" line of processes. These processors are APPRECIABLY more energy efficient than the previous generation processors ("Ivy Bridge") that were used in the previous iteration of the XPS12. This means that run time on a full battery charge has increased from around 5 hours to around 8 hours. (!!!!) That single change--to run time on a full charge--addresses what many considered to be one of the major downsides of the previous generation XPS 12. (Note: The two processor lines, Haswell and Ivy Bridge, are pretty close to indistinguishable in terms of performance, with the Haswell just ever-so-slightly better [PassMark scores of 3380 and 3278 for the Haswell and Ivy Bridge, respectively, with higher being better]).

Now, focusing on the XPS 12 as a total package: This is a terrific piece of hardware, with a lot of pros, and only a few significant cons.

Summarizing,

Pros:

Beautiful super high resolution 1920x1080 12.5" screen
Very high build quality
Terrific innovative screen that rotates in the frame to go from laptop/keyboard to tablet configuration
Very responsive with even the base configuration of an Intel I5 processor and 4Gb memory
Incredibly fast boot time (10-15 seconds)
Very good keyboard
Responsive touchscreen which operates in both laptop and tablet modes
Fast SSD drive in all configurations
Decent webcam (1.3mp)
Light, portable charging cable.
Bluetooth, Wireless N (5 + 2.4Ghz)
Backlit keys on keyboard
Battery life is 8+ hours (New for this version!)

Eh:

Weight is 3.2 pounds, which isn't heavy, but isn't super light for a 12.5" laptop. A bit heavy feeling in tablet mode
Speakers are predictably mediocre for a small laptop
Base configuration has only a 128Gb mSata SSD hard drive. However, the hard drive IS user replaceable.

Cons:

No HDMI or VGA port. Only a graphics mini displayport, which means you will need to carry a mini displayport -> HDMI or VGA adapter if you want to use this for business or with a TV/external monitor.
Memory is soldiered to motherboard and is not upgradeable. Fortunately, even the base configuration 4Gb of memory is more than sufficient.
Only two USB ports (both USB 3.0, however)
Battery is not easily user swapped/replacable
No built in media card reader. If you want to the SD card from your camera, you'll need to carry an external reader.
No GPS
No wired Ethernet port. If you want wired Ethernet, you'll need to buy a USB-to-Ethernet adapter. (You have wireless Ethernet, of course).

Of the cons, the worst, in my opinion, is the fact that the battery is not easily swapped/replaced. While the 8+ hour run time is very respectable, one can expect battery life to diminish over time, and I am not looking forward to dealing with that eventuality. Also, I like to carry a spare battery to swap out for long trips. That's not possible here.

Having struggled with various underpowered Android based tablets, including the Asus TF301/keyboard dock, I can say that using the XPS 12 in tablet mode is like a huge weight has been lifted. The XPS 12 screams when surfing the web, which is something I can't say about any Android (or Mac) tablet I've used--and I've used a lot of them.

People have complained about the lack of apps in the Windows 8 app store--and it's true that the Windows 8 app store is pretty anemic compared to Andoid or Mac. But some of the most important apps are there (Skype, Netflix, etc.) and it's still growing. There are enough to make using the tablet mode acceptable now...and the responsiveness provided by the Intel I5 processor makes it a pleasure to use.

There are a few configuration options available for the XPS 12, all related to the processor (a few speeds of I5 and I7), memory (4Gb or 8Gb) and hard drive size (128Gb or 256Gb or 512Gb). My recommendation: Any of the available processor speeds will be more than acceptable and the difference between the I5 and I7 processors for almost any user will be negligible. Similarly, most users will not need the 8Gb of memory. Windows 8 runs perfectly fine on 4Gb of memory. Unless you plan on running memory hog processes (advanced video editing, certain scientific apps, etc.) you won't need the extra memory. If you do need the extra memory, however, you need to order the laptop with 8Gb installed from the factory, as the memory is not user-upgradeable (it's soldiered to the motherboard...grrr...) A larger hard drive than the 128Gb SSD that comes installed on the base model is definitely a nice feature. But the hard drive IS user replaceable, and the incremental cost of getting the 256Gb mSata SSD from Dell is more than it would be to buy that 256Gb mSata SSD on the aftermarket and clone your 128Gb drive onto it. (You will also wind up with a spare 128Gb drive that way). Unless you are scared of the idea of hard drive cloning/migration, I'd recommend that path. Please note that this laptop uses the mSata configuration hard drive, rather than a full sized SSD to save space. mSata drives tend to be a bit more expensive than standard SSD drives.

Overall, this is a terrific laptop, and buying the least expensive configuration version is, for most, the recommended route. In addition, the newer generation processor used for this updated version of the XPS 12 had addressed one of the major limitations of the earlier version, bumping the battery life to over eight hours.

title: Excellent solution for a 17" MacBook Pro
text:
I did a lot of research and review reading before choosing this cooling pad for my 17" MacBook Pro which runs very hot when charging a battery & when using Photoshop CS6 for intensive design work and also when client computers are connected to it for repair of those units (running TechTool, DiskWarrior, etc.). Recently the OEM battery ended up splitting apart -- now that could be from heat OR defect or both -- and I didn't want to have the same issue with the replacement battery which is brand new (non-Apple) and not cheap. The pad is JUST big enough to hold the 17" MacBook. It made a huge difference within minutes of being used with the laptop charging a battery and displaying a movie! The top surface near the screen would normally get very hot when a battery was being charged especially, but within minutes of the cool pad being in use, the surface is barely lukewarm. The bottom of the laptop which gets very hot during battery charging and intensive use was/is many degrees cooler.

PROS:
* Very open design allowing for maximum air flow from all sides.
* Sturdy metal grill over the whole top surface (probably aluminum, though it feels a bit rigid for it to be pure aluminum).
* Excellent air flow! More than I expected, actually.
* VERY quiet (21dBA according to manufacturer specs.)!! The typical laptop cooling laptop fans (for both Macs. & PCs) are far louder and, in the case of my MacBook Pro, would completely drown out any noise coming from this cooling pad (when running at full speed). Definite bonus to have the cooling pad running with very little noise!
* Very sturdy and quite big rubber feet on the bottom ensure that slipping on surfaces isn't likely. With the added weight of a laptop sitting on the cooling pad, I don't see how it would move even if cords are accidentally yanked.
* Speaking of cords, the channel underneath the unit for the USB cord is very well designed and effectively keeps excess cord length out of the way.
* Nice long USB cord so the unit can be plugged into any available USB port on any laptop -- be it on the sides or the back.
* Pass through feature on the plug is very handy for laptops with limited USB ports available. Since the plug is a bit "chunky" some may not like to deal with it on the sides of their laptops -- especially Mac. users -- so I'll note that the cooling pad DOES work just as effectively when plugged into a USB hub. This is where the additional cord length would come in handy as well. I didn't try it with a USB power unit plugged into a wall outlet, so I can't say if that would work -- though I can't see why it wouldn't.
* Flip down feet on the back bottom surface allows for tilting of the laptop. Handy because the cool pad does raise the computer up about 2". The angling "feet" would also serve to increase airflow even more.
* Stays on even when the laptop is put into "sleep" mode -- at least with Macs. it does. Some of that will be dependent on laptop make and model.... Many PC laptops cut power to USB ports when in "sleep" or "suspend" mode.

CONS:
* Minor --- do wish the product came in at least a silver/aluminum finish.
* Minor to Moderate --- would be nice if the unit had an optional power adapter connection for those who don't want the unit to drain power from a laptop running on battery power. Also, as noted above in the pros section, some laptops cut power to USB ports when in "sleep" or "suspend" mode and all do so when the computer is turned off. This is a con because those computers are still capable of charging batteries and, thereby, heating up. Macs. especially get very warm while charging batteries. So, how big a con this is depends on your individual computer's functions.
* Moderate --- the pass through connector could & should be much smaller. It sticks out quite a bit and I can see how someone could damage the USB port by hitting the connector accidentally. This risk is only magnified when another USB device is piggy-backed onto the already big connector. This is also where a power adapter would come in handy so users wouldn't have to plug it into their USB ports, thereby eliminating the risk of damage. The plug itself if well constructed and quite sturdy, but, because it IS so tough, the ports could easily sustain damage from accidental impact.

NOTE:
The cooling pad has a raised center grill directly above the fan. I note this only because I'm not sure there isn't a laptop out there somewhere which doesn't have "feet" to keep it slightly raised above the surface it rests on. If your laptop doesn't have "feet" you may have some difficulty resting it with any stability on this cooling pad.

CONCLUSION:
All in all, I'm very happy with this cooling pad and would definitely purchase it again. As an Apple tech. support provider, I'll also be recommending this cooling pad to my clients! If you have an Apple laptop that you use for more than just surfing the web and word processing, this cooling pad is an indispensable tool to extend the life of your computer's hardware. You don't need fancy LED lights, etc., which just draw more power.... A cooling fan just needs to cool a laptop efficiently & effectively... That's what this unit does and does it well!

title: Worth the upgrade over Sound Blaster Z or Zx
text:
You can read my other review on the Sound Blaster Z and see that I was pretty disappointed with it. I had the following problems:

- First of all, there was some red dust from the package caked all over the card and in the contacts and everything which can't be good... They could have at least put it in an anti-static bag.

(The ZxR package had no red dust!)

- There is a crackling/static/hissing noise which seems to be caused by the RAM from my video card as it only happens when more complex graphics appear like in video games or while viewing large pictures or flash objects. I tried pretty much every suggestion such as disabling my onboard audio in the BIOS, reloading drivers, updating drivers, cleaning off the contacts on the card and reinserting it, underclocking the memory on my graphics card, etc. The problem is, I can't move the sound card to any other spot and the metal shield has large openings so there is still plenty of room for EMI to seep through and cause that noise. I wish they would have just covered the whole card in that shielding. I am considering trying to add my own shielding around it to hopefully solve this super annoying noise which didn't ever happen with my onboard sound.

(The ZxR has no distortion despite being in the same spot as the Z - clearly it has better shielding!)

- The red LED light is bright and annoying since I have my computer on my desk and it has a window. You cannot disable it. I put something in front of my case to block out the light though.

(The ZxR has no annoying LED light!)

- The headphone/speaker mode switching doesn't seem to work properly which was a big reason I bought this card. Now to be fair, it may have something to do with my graphics card HDMI controls interfering with it but even so, I was hoping the Sound Blaster would override that so I could simply click one button to switch. Sometimes it even messes up so much that I have to restart.

(This seemed to work better but I found a workaround for it either way so no biggie.)

- The volume leveling is a mess. Some applications are very loud while others are not. So I constantly have to adjust my volume and occasionally get my ears blown out. With the Windows (8) controls, anything over "30" is too loud. Although I'm glad you can always get sufficient volume, it's still too loud at "1" sometimes so it's not well matched/balanced in that regard and thus yet another annoyance.

(With the ZxR, the external volume adjuster allows me to fine tune the level of audio so I am able to get it much quieter than before!)

- There is a little bit of lag and some distortion which cuts out/off your voice when you turn on some of the CrystalVoice enhancements such as noise reduction, smart volume, and echo cancellation which is too bad so it's not worth using them.

(With the ZxR, others have said I sound much clearer than before so the mic is definitely better!)

- Lastly, it doesn't actually sound that great. I kid you not, my phone (with headphones plugged in it) actually sounds better with most things. It just doesn't sound well balanced no matter how much I mess with the equalizer or SBX settings. I mean, it's not terrible - I have found some settings which do give it more punch overall than the onboard Realtek audio did but that's not saying too much. Now it could be that these headphones are not ideal for this card. They are high quality studio monitoring headphones which generally make things sound really good but maybe they just aren't a good match for this card. I also compared it to my old my old X-Fi card (PCI on Windows XP) and I think it sounded a little better than this new one and it didn't have any of these problems. I'm not sure but the point is it's probably not worth upgrading if you're coming from an X-Fi.

(The ZxR also seems to sound a little better than the Z. I wouldn't say there is a huge difference but it does at least sound better than my older X-Fi now.)

I'd like to add one more comment about the Z that I had. I did not mention this in my original review because I thought that it may have something to do with my motherboard or chassis but the card would not fit properly in the board. It was a little off centered and it drove me mad trying to fully get it seated in there. It just wouldn't properly line up and even wore some of my contacts down trying to fit it in there. With the new ZxR, it fit in the slot and chassis perfectly the very first time - so it was the card's fault after all.

So in summary, the Sound Blaster Z is a junky sound card while the ZxR is a great sound card. I was very hesitant spending the extra money and was about to give up on Creative all together but decided to give them one last try and am very glad I did. This card is well worth the money in my opinion and I hope it continues to work well for me in the years to come.

title: Made for RSX, 2002 and up, w/ Bose stereo
text:
Like the other reviewers said, this harness made the installation easy.
Unfortunately, this was not my first wiring harness. I got the "straight" wire (no RCA plug) at first, when I hooked it up to the Pioneer CD player. it took along time figuring out which wire goes where. Back then, I did not realize that my 2006 RSX Type S, w/Bose has two amplifiers, one for the four speakers output, and the other for the SUB. Hooking it directly to the stereo's speaker output created a somewhat irritating white noise; noticeable when muted (power on, volume 0). That setup did give me a powerful sound; it was loud even just at 23 out of 62 volume setting. My main issue was the white noise.
I have also tried it without the Bose amp. I had to rig the "Bose amp plug" so I can use the existing speaker wires. It worked, with just the Pioneer stereo, but the sound was a little "bright and hollowed" I reconsidered and decided to live with the white noise and use the Bose amp to get the more powerful sound.
When I saw this harness few days ago, I wanted to try it; hoping to improve my audio quality, or at least, minimize the clutter of wires in the back of the stereo.
Well, it definitely decreased the wiring clutter. With the 8 speaker wires turned into two fat wires, I only have to connect the other 4 wires complete the job.
The sound is less powerful - now, I have to turn it up to 45 to get to (unbearable) loud (out of 62 max). However, the sound did get cleaner. When muted, there is blissful silence, with no white noise, or any noise. I can tweak the treble on the equalizer a little higher and deeper bass to get more sound.
I am happy with the purchase since I like the Bose amps. I am a little disappointed to bypass the Pioneer stereo 50 watt / 22 RMS per channel internal amp. Well, at the end, this is the best sound setup out of the ones I tried.
I also replaced all the speakers with Kenwood 3-way, kept the original tweeters and the sub. The Kenwood sounds much better than Bose speakers, highs, lows and great detail. Bose speakers are good for those listeners that prefers "warmth" over "detail."

title: ScreenDim saved the kindle fire HD
text:
I have owned the second generation kindle and this is my first kindle fire. I have been using this for close to 3 months now and my review is below:

Size (4 stars):
* The size is good for me to read books and watch videos.
* Since I read more books than watch videos I might have preferred the apples iPad dimensions probably better (little more wider). However it is also much costlier than the fire.

Screen (3 stars):
* Screen is very good and crisp.
* Sometimes I feel I pressed a link but it will actually press the one below - so not very accurate to touch. This is sometimes annoying.
* It is really bright to read at night when the lights are turned off - even when the brightness settings is set to the lowest. This was the biggest deal breaker for me. However the screen dim app saved the kindle and I did not send it back. That is the best app for the kindle for my usage.

Power button (3 stars):
* The power button is placed in the top of the kindle almost very hard to find without looking at it.

Software (1 star):
* The software is just horrible. They have heavily customized android as many know. It has crashed on me close to 10 times in the last 3 months. The whole device will suddenly become unresponsive and it will automatically restart after 2 to 3 minutes.
* I was looking forward to use the silk browser after I saw the amazon demo. It was easily the worst browser so far. It crashes almost all the time. I am now using the dolphin browser which is decent.
* Many people complain about the carousel (homepage) but I think I got used to it now.
* Accessing amazon's content is awesome - they have done that very well. It is easy to access videos, books, etc. I believe this was the primary purpose for the kindle when amazon built it probably. This is excellent.
* Email app - It is not good and I dont use it. The push notifications of gmail did not work for me but I did not care to check it since my phone has a much better app than fighting with this.

Apps (3 stars):
* Apps are very limited to the kindle as many know. I knew this before I bought it so this is ok.
* I installed the 1mobile app and that gave me access to almost all the android apps. Many dont work as expected like chrome browser, firefox, etc. However dolphin browser, dropbox and some other apps works. I had to get the apk file of 1mobile and install it - I think they call this process sideloading.

Will I recommend it or buy it again:
It will be a NO. The software provided is so limited to use for anything else apart from browsing amazon content that paying $249 (I got this in a deal) seems high. If I had known these issues before I would have probably went for the iPad mini or a prev generation iPad by paying a little extra. If the only reason you buy is to access amazon content (which I think many wont) this will be an excellent choice. If not, it is better to shell out the little extra to get the iOS tables or android tablets.

title: Focusing issues...
text:
I have to agree with the previous 1 star reviewer, and he is spot on. And before you numbskulls tell me that I should read before I buy... I did! Let me quote directly from Steiner's own website specifically for this model:

"Steiner's individual eyepiece focus makes for comfortable viewing. Simple to adjust and easy to use, even with one hand. If both eyes are of the same diopter strength, simply set both of the adjusting rings on the eyecups to "0" and you will see clearly from 20 yards to infinity. If not, adjust both oculars individually for razor sharp images. Once adjusted, everything will be sharp and clear from approx 20 yards to infinity for varying distances."

Did you read that? Once adjusted EVERYTHING will be sharp and clear from 20 yards to infinity. This is completely false and not true. As the previous reviewer stated, you can focus on one spot, then look about another 50 yards further, and it's out of focus. You have to keep refocusing everywhere you look. Perhaps I got a bad pair? In fairness, I emailed Steiner directly about 2 weeks ago asking if this was normal and they never responded to me.

As far as the quality, these are amazing. The rubber body armor felt bullet proof. The Prisms were flawless and once focused, the images were spectacularly 3D. I didn't think the weight was all that bad. For these qualities I gave it 2 stars instead of 1.

In the end, the binos didn't live up to Steiner's own product description and use from their website nor contacting me back regarding my concerns. I returned them back to Amazon for a refund.

title: Great for Lync, Skype, etc. not so much for music
text:
Comfort:
OK. Leather ear pads and foam could be softer. Not nearly as comfortable as Bose OE's for example. You can bend/form the mic boom to fit your face. Just barely enough length to fit over my head; could actually use another 1/2 inch extension on both sides.

Voice:
Great. Good noise canceling microphone. Auto-answer sensor works well; it somehow "knows" when you put it on your head and will automatically answer an incoming Lync call.

Music:
Don't expect to be wow'ed by it's range. Frequency response on the upper high and bottom low end is lacking a great deal. I thought it had some sort of auto-equalization to adapt itself to music vs. voice.. but maybe this isn't working. For example, a pair of 25 year old Radio Shack "Pro 25" OE headphones are much better sounding at full spectrum.

Overall, good for what you probably bought it for. Just don't expect too much out of the earphone fidelity on full-spectrum audio.

title: Purchase at your own risk, especially if you like nonexistent support
text:
Update to original review:

I have 2 of these, remote viewing is unavailable regardless of the quality of your connection, support is unavailable, just online knowledge base which is useless. Both NVRs went through an "update" of some sort and now neither will record over the previous recordings. I am currently using a couple of old laptops with 2tb hard drives as recording devices. One of these systems is less than 6 months old. I went thru 7-8 cameras with the original system before replacing the cheap cat 5 cables with Cat 6e cables. The second system I went with the better cables from the onset and no issues what so ever with the cameras failing. I am shopping for a replacement system and it sure won't be a Zmodo.

I was skeptical of this system, reviews were all over the place, but in the end, it is actually a very good system.

You get plenty of cable for a average sized house, actually, I could have used 1 25ft and 3 50ft cables and still had plenty. The system is plug and play, install the camera, route the cable and plug it in. You will have to play with the image settings and get a good balance between night and day images.

Tools/Things you will need to make the install easy:

Fish-tape
Small straight edge
Tape measure
Short piece of braided nylon twine
Holesaw set
1/4" hollow punch
1/4" drill bit
Cordless drill
Extended #2 Phillips driver bit
3/4" wood spade
3/16" flat rubber for dust seals
Drywall screws
Drywall anchors
Cable guides
Hammer
5 blank Outlet covers(4 for cameras and 1 for entry into the house near the NVR)

I chose to route my cables thru the eaves of the house into the attic, it keeps the plugs out of the weather and out of the way of tampering. I used blank outlet covers and used a hole saw to cut a 1 3/16" hole in the center, then cut a 1 1/2" hole in the eave to route the cable. I bought a rubber mudflap that was 3/16" thick for a dust seal, trim the rubber to fit under the outlet cover, then made a small 3/16" hole with a hollow punch, then slit the rubber from the hole to the edge, slip the cable into the hole, place the rubber between the outlet cover and eave and use drywall screws to install the cover. I also used plastic cable guides to route the cables up against the rafters to protect them. I also used an old desktop flat screen monitor for my monitor. I chose to mount it on a flat screen mount behind the clothes rack in the laundry room, I can pull it out and do what I need to do, then push it back out of the way. I also used a wireless mouse and put the NVR unit on a battery backup. It keeps the entire system functional even if the power is out for extended periods.

I will update this later after it has been installed for a while.

title: Wireless Speakers - Good Price, Fair Product
text: Based on other reviews, I was expecting a little better sound quality (fidelity and frequency range) out of these wireless speakers. Even though it is easy to set up, and allows the speakers to be powered via batteries or via the AC/DC power adapters, the signal quality and signal range was just good to fair, especially if the base station and speakers are separated by more than 50 feet and there is a wall in-between. The sound momentarily cuts in-and-out when someone walks near the speakers, and the frequency range is both limited on the low and high ends of the spectrum. Although the volume on each speaker is adjustable, there is no way to adjust the tone. The base station has a switch that allows it to transmit on one of two frequencies, but I've noticed that both frequencies result in the same sound quality. If I press the "auto-tune" buttons on the speakers, the sound quality improves momentarily, but eventually the sound degrades, briefly cuts in-and-out, and sometimes a small amount of static occurs. Overall, the sound quality reminds me of an old 2.4 GHz wireless telephone that I threw out years ago.

title: Simple. Sturdy. Perfect.
text:
The Logitech N315 Portable Lapdesk is one of the best purchases I have made off Amazon recently. It gets daily use and is one of the few things I own that I cannot complain a bit about, because it is simply perfect. I view this lapdesk as one of my everyday necessities.

The top is an anti-slip material that firmly grips your laptop or netbook. It feels safe to carry my laptop on it when I move from room to room, and I don't have to worry about it slipping off if I shift my sitting position. The top WILL attract some dirt, hair and fur over time, but it easily washes off. Simple maintenance.

The bottom is plastic but has two long strips of a gripping material which helps it stay on your lap and serves as little feet to cushion when you set it down on a hard surface.

The mousepad easily slides in and out. It is the perfect size and has a surprisingly sturdy feel. The edges have a slight rise to help keep your mouse from sliding off when you are shifting in your seat.

The entire lapdesk is incredibly thin and lightweight. Despite this, it feels very solid. It's the perfect size for my 15.6" Asus laptop and easily slips into the laptop's neoprene carrying case for travel.

It separates my body heat from the laptop's heat, which helps keep my lap and the computer cooler. It may not have a built-in fan to increase the laptop's cooling ability, but I have not found that to be a problem since I typically have a fan running in the room at all times.

The lapdesk also works well as a writing desk if you are using a notebook or even writing on thick cards. You can't write well on it if you are using just one or two sheets of copy paper, as the surface is a little soft and has tiny dimples all over it. title: Best replacement available for your stock cooler
text:
I dont want to kindle any arguments, but the criticism from many of the bad reviews is not the fault of the heatsink. This isn't something that will drop your temperatures if you're previous heatsink was correctly installed. It doesn't advertise itself as a cooling "upgrade" in that sense to begin with.

It is at best wishful thinking that any $15 heat sink to properly cool a high-end cpu under a high load (or even normal use which still pushes it enough that you're using all those cores and the high clock speed).

What you get for your money is a fan with better build quality+quality thermal paste compared to a sock cooler. You can rest assured that when its installed, it isn't going to get loose or break/wear out its mounting materials.

You also get a huge reduction in noise. This thing is flat out silent. When I put it at full speed in bios, even putting my ear on the case over it did nothing more than go up enough decibles to be detectable with the noise of any given component drowning it out.

For some of the worst AMD stock coolers, it is a performance upgrade. Thats not why its a steal for under $20 though. It performs phenominally better than your basic heat sink in some areas and isn't inferior in other areas. If you are buying an aftermarket heatsink because you want lower temps and/or increased ability to push a cpu to the limit without getting hot, spend another $15 and get a coolmaster!

This is for the people who think the cost of a CPU merits spending a bit more to get a higher quality heat-sink, or judge the price worth it to mitigate the sounds of a tower, or want some peace of mind that they won't need to open their case to solve inadequate placement or less sturdy heat sinks.

So for what this product is, 5 stars hands down. It only disapoints if you buy it with unrealistic expectations.

text: These are worse than useless.  They work well enough at first to raise your hopes but they break connection maybe once every 10 hours or so (absolutely no pattern I could discern). title: Comparing Pure Sine Wave UPS for Home/Office from APC and Cyberpower
text:
This review is for: CyberPower CP850PFCLCD 510W UPS

OVERVIEW:
-----------

The home and small office UPS models we'll compare are:

- APC: SMT750, SMT1000
- APC: SMC1000, SMC1500
- CyberPower: CP850PFCLCD, CP1000PFCLCD, CP1350PFCLCD
- CyberPower: PR750LCD, PR1000LCD, PR1500LCD

These all:

(A) KEEP ELECTRICITY GOING DURING A BLACKOUT and give a computer TIME TO SAFELY AUTO-SHUTDOWN.

(B) Produce a PURE SINE WAVE to work with power supplies with Active PFC, like those on most Apple Macs, lots of newer windows PCs, etc.

(C) Cost in the low hundreds, so we avoid server room type features like zero transfer time, external batteries, etc.

We'll compare:
- How long things run during a blackout (RUNTIME)
- The WATTS they handle
- NOISE
- OUTLET COUNT and how many have battery power

We'll also compare:
- AVR CAPABILITY including BOOST and TRIM (explained later)
- RECHARGE TIME
- Size, cord length, other

Okay, let's get started, I'm looking for two that are quiet, can shutdown Window PCs and Macs safely, have good runtime, and some other things.

- Here are some REAL WORLD TESTED COMPUTER RUNTIMES measured from blackout start TO START OF COMPUTER HIBERNATION (configured to hibernate close to battery running out). These times depend on UPS battery charge measurement capability and hibernate timing flexibility, not just battery size.

100W TEST:

All loads measured directly and externally (not with their UPS internal meters and to avoid UPS efficiency differences). Batteries first get 10 hour charge for tests.

- Consider choosing a UPS with claimed runtime at least 50% MORE THAN YOU THINK YOU NEED.

- These UPS will shut-off WELL BEFORE THEY REACH 0% battery, often at 9%-20% full. This way when the electricity returns they come back on without needing manual restart.

- Slightly lowered the runtime of 100W for the SMT1000 for readability.

(3)
NOISE:
-------

APC SMT750/SMT1000:

These have NO FAN (APC models with 1400VA+ and those with external batteries have fans). I only hear a SMT750 MAKE NOISE WHEN ON BATTERY POWER (ex: blackout), they make a fairly QUIET HUMMING like an aquarium pump, tested at 100W, 200W, 300W, and 400W. I measured 38dB (APC says 41dB max), in a quiet room you can hear it, but it's not loud nor annoying. You can configure for no alert beeps, too.

It would FORCE THE UPS TO MAKE NOISE if you plug something in that FLICKERS, like a lamp that flickers just a little at a lower dimmer setting.

APC SMC1000:

Has NO FAN. Likely same noise profile as SMT1000 (above). APC notes 41db (same as SMT1000).

APC SMC1500:

Has fan (APC estimates 45dB max) which runs when:
- The battery charges
- The unit supplies battery power
- The temperature hits 104F
- The load is over 75% of unit wattage capability (675W+).

CYBERPOWER PR750LCD/PR1000LCD/PR1500LCD:

I hear a PR750LCD MAKE NOISE ONLY WHEN ON BATTERY POWER, only 39-41dB up close. The humming noise is like a quiet aquarium pump, can be heard in a quiet room but isn't annoying. It has a fan, though I have not heard it run at 100W, 200W, 300W, or 400W loads on a PR750LCD.

The PR1500LCD fan though CAN clearly be heard I'm told (on battery power). I'm told it's only as loud as a "quiet conversation". I don't know about the PR1000LCD.

You can configure for no alert beeps (APPLY ENABLE and then APPLY DISABLE on the Config page).

It would FORCE THE UPS TO MAKE NOISE at 44dB or so at 1' if you plug something in that FLICKERS, like a lamp that flickers a bit at a low dimmer setting.

CYBERPOWER CP850PFCLCD/CP1000PFCLCD/CP1350PFCLCD:

These have a small fan in them. When the fan runs, which I HEAR ONLY WHEN ON BATTERY POWER on a CP850PFCLCD, it has a quiet but audible, higher pitch sound. I measured 39dB at 1' at 100W, 200W, 300W, and 400W loads, so it's fairly quiet. You can configure for no alert beeps, too.

(4)
ABILITY TO SHUTDOWN
COMPUTERS SAFELY:
-----------------------

These models can all shutdown Windows PCs and Apple Macs (OS version dependent) safely during power issues (most Linux flavors, too). Except for PCs or OS that predate Hibernate, of course. More on the Apple Mac graceful shutdown in the Apple section later.

> WHAT IS HIBERNATE:

To SAVE THINGS JUST AS THEY WERE before a blackout (not just shutdown) these UPS models can put a Windows PC into HIBERNATE. On Apple Macs this is called SAFE SLEEP (OSX 10.4+). The computers know how to do this, the UPS just tells them to.

For some UPS's we must configure the hibernate option (vs. shutdown), for others it's the default.

HIBERNATE doesn't "save" an open document, but rather freezes it in time so upon starting the computer everything is just as it was before.

> HIBERNATE vs. SHUTDOWN:

If you tell it to SHUTDOWN gracefully WITHOUT HIBERNATE mode, the computer will often ask users to save their work (ex: word docs) and then it will shutdown often too quickly for anyone to save it. Thus hibernate is often chosen.

Of these, only the CyberPower PRxxxLCD allows the OPTION of TRULY SAVING open application files (ex: word docs) while it does a SHUTDOWN on the computer. Most folks, however, want the choice whether to save the file in its present state or not after hibernation, but there it is if you need it.

> WINDOWS - IS HIBERNATE SAME AS SLEEP?:

No. HIBERNATE saves the RAM to hard drive and shuts the computer down. This was invented for laptops to save battery and be less at risk of the hard drive writing while being jostled. SLEEP doesn't shut things down, it just saves energy and restarts faster than hibernate.

> SMART CARDS:

APC SMT and CyberPower PR models can have "SMART CARDS" plugged in to allow the graceful shutdown of multiple computers on the network even if the computers aren't plugged into the UPS. As noted in the Apple section below, older versions of SMT software allowed this for Apple Macs, but no longer.

(5)
APPLE COMPUTERS (MACS/OSX):
-------------------------------

Setting an Apple Mac to allow a UPS to shutdown safely is different below OSX 10.6 vs. 10.6+. The directions for this is in an APC doc (it works for CyberPower, too), "How to configure native shutdown on Macintosh OS X .." (avail online or from support).

With Apple Macs the user configures the Apple OSX's Energy Saver shutdown options (System Preferences) to allow a UPS signal to the Mac (via USB) to shut the computer down safely. The USB must be connected from the UPS to the Mac for the UPS preferences option to show. Some OSX versions MAY HAVE A BUG that don't allow the shutdown preferences to save after a computer restart, be sure to test. I know it works in 10.6.8.

There is no APC or CyberPower software now to load on Apple Macs for DISPLAYING OR CONFIGURING UPS settings. You could do so from UPS display buttons (more so with SMT and PRxxxLCD) or from a Windows PC and then switch the USB connection back to the Apple Mac. You could even get a super cheap used Windows laptop just for that purpose.

> APC:

Can UPS shutdown 1 Apple Mac? - YES
Can UPS shutdown 2+ Apple Macs over Network? (w/network card) - NOT ANY MORE
Can Apple Mac be used to view or configure UPS? - NO

If you add a NETWORK CARD to an APC SMT model there USED TO BE software to load on Apple Macs to allow the UPS to safely shutdown many Apple Macs over the network, however it's just Windows and Linux now. APC support didn't know if this will return for Macs nor for what OSX versions it used to work for.

> CYBERPOWER:

Can my UPS shutdown 1 Apple Mac? - YES
Can my UPS shutdown 2+ Apple Macs over Network? - NO
Can Apple Mac be used to view or configure UPS? - NO

A PR model with a NETWORK CARD can safely shutdown lots of computers over the network. However, it never did for Apple computers.

(6)
AVR AND CONTROL OF VOLTAGE
LEVELS FOR BATTERY KICK-IN:
------------------------------

All these models have AVR (Automatic Voltage Regulation).

With AVR, WITHOUT USING THE BATTERY, when voltage drops into a low range (brownout) the voltage steps up (boost) by either a fixed amount or a percentage. When the voltage rises into a high range way above 120V (overload) AVR steps the voltage down (trim).

If the voltage drops even below the low AVR range (ex: under 82V-106V), or rises even above the high AVR range (ex: over 127V-144V), the unit TRANSFERS to battery power (120V). Those voltage levels (default or user set) where AVR or regular AC power stops and the battery kicks in are TRANSFER POINTS.

Some models ONLY HAVE AVR BOOST (no trim), like APC SMC and Cyberpower CPxxxPFCLCD models. APC SMT and Cyberpower PR models have both AVR boost and trim.

Here is a comparative summary:

APC
A - SMT750
B - SMT1000
C - SMC1000
D - SMC1500
CyberPower
E - CP850PFCLCD
F - CP1000PFCLCD
G - CP1350PFCLCD
H - PR750LCD
I - PR1000LCD
J - PR1500LCD

A/B:
AVR boost: Yes
AVR trim: Yes
You can set transfer point from utility/online to AVR Boost: 97V-106V (default 106V)
You can set transfer point from utility/online to AVR Trim: 127V-136V (default 127V)

C/D:
AVR boost: Yes
AVR trim: No
You can set voltage transfer points INDIRECTLY through the sensitivity setting.
The transfer point from AVR Boost to battery is always 95V, I'm told.
SENSITIVITY
Low_ - Transfer point from utility/online to AVR Boost is 97V, to battery high is 136V
Med_ - Transfer point from utility/online to AVR Boost is 103V, to battery high is 130V
High - Transfer point from utility/online to AVR Boost is 106V, to battery high is 127V (default)

E/F/G:
AVR boost: Yes
AVR trim: No
You can set transfer point from utility/online to AVR Boost: 97V-106V (default 102V)
You can set transfer point from utility/online to Battery: 127V-136V (default 131V)

H/I/J:
AVR boost: Yes
AVR trim: Yes
You can only set lowest/highest voltage (before AVR kicks in) with the SENSITIVITY (low/med/high) setting.
It only looks like you can also select the voltages directly, however it is a confirmed bug, just ignore.

(7)
"SENSITIVITY" SETTINGS:
-------------------------

The sensitivity setting means something different for each model family.

> APC SMTxxx ("POWER QUALITY SENSITIVITY"):

- NORMAL (Default)
*2ms-4ms Transfer time

- REDUCED
*6ms-8ms Transfer time

- LOW
*8ms-10ms Transfer time

TRANSFER TIME is the time taken to switch to battery power. APC says longer transfer times are better for noisy electrical environments like lower power quality home generators. This can reduce the switching to battery and lengthen battery life in that circumstance.

> APC SMCxxx ("POWER QUALITY SENSITIVITY"):

- NORMAL (Default)
*2ms-4ms Transfer time
*Sets low transfer point from online/utility to AVR Boost at 106V
*Sets high transfer point from online/utility to battery at 127V

- REDUCED
*6ms-8ms Transfer time
*Sets low transfer point from online/utility to AVR Boost at 103V
*Sets high transfer point from online/utility to battery at 130V

- LOW
*8ms-10ms Transfer time
*Sets low transfer point from online/utility to AVR Boost at 97V
*Sets high transfer point from online/utility to battery at 136V

> CYBERPOWER CPxxxPFCLCD ("INPUT VOLTAGE SENSITIVITY"):

- HIGH (CyberPower Recommended if quality power source)
*Sets battery transfer points to 88V/136V

- MEDIUM (Default)
*Sets battery transfer points to 88V/139V (DEFAULT).

- LOW
*Sets battery transfer points to 78V/144V. Best setting if the power is from a low quality power source like many home generators. Support noted their OL (online) models work even better with generators.

Support says transfer time is ALMOST ALWAYS AROUND 4ms, so sensitivity setting has no affect on transfer time (unlike the APC models).

> CYBERPOWER PRxxxLCD ("DETECTED SENSITIVITY"):

- HIGH
*Sets AVR low/high transfer points to 88V/136V into a tighter range to use AVR less and battery more, resulting in more stable power but more battery use.

- MEDIUM
*Sets AVR transfer points to 88V/139V (Default).

- LOW
*Sets AVR transfer points to 78V/142V to use AVR more and battery less, reducing battery use if input voltage ranges that much.

Support says transfer time is ALMOST ALWAYS AROUND 4ms, so sensitivity setting has no affect on transfer time (unlike the APC models).

(8)
SURGE PROTECTION
AND EMI/RFI INTERFERENCE
REDUCTION:
---------------------------

All these models have UL1449 3rd Edition Listedsurge protection. They were tested with powerful surges and survived still operational.

- CLAMPING VOLTAGE:

This is the maximum voltage allowed through to the equipment, the lower the better of course. During the period power is not allowed through due to clamping, the UPS is supplying power. Note that there is debate which is a more useful measure for surge suppression, clamping voltage or let-through voltage (technically not the same).

You might ask of what use is clamping voltage for a UPS, after all for example 330V clamping voltage is much higher than any voltage level the UPS switches to AVR or battery. Clamping voltage is an extra layer of protection for a UPS due to the power and speed of many transient surges.

CyberPower - 330V CLAMPING VOLTAGE
APC - 330V CLAMPING VOLTAGE

- SACRIFICIAL?:

CyberPower and APC - All these models are sacrificial for big surges (per support), bigger than the UL1449 test surges, of course. The button on the back is the classic circuit breaker OVERLOAD PROTECTION like all good modern certified surge protectors have (they strongly recommend 12A max, they often trip on 15A). This helps prevent fires, but does not make a unit non-sacrificial per se.

- JOULES:

I've included the values here and will let the user decide if it is important, just know that it is a matter of controversy. Many engineers conclude that standards bodies feel that Joules is an inferior, misleading measure by which to compare a units suppression capability.

CyberPower - These are rated 1030 Joules
APC - These are rated 455-540 Joules

- EMI/RFI NOISE/INTERFERENCE REDUCTION:

This is more than just helpful to audio and media hardware. This can greatly help lower let through voltage from surges more than MOVs do alone in the 50kHz-150kHZ range according to a well considered Eaton white paper.

CyberPower - Their models here have EMI/RFI NOISE ATTENUATION max of 48dB in the 150kHz to 100MHz range.
APC - Don't have APC numbers for this.

- ETHERNET AND COAX/CABLE
SURGE PROTECTION:

Only the CyberPower CPxxxPFCLCD models have these built-in, too.

If using the SMC/SMT or PR models one needs separate surge protection for ethernet and/or coax/cable. Dedicated Coax/Cable and/or Ethernet surge protection and a little patch cabling to make it work is easy to find online.

The Ethernet surge protection is for 10/100 Base-T Ethernet, NOT GIGABIT Ethernet (1000 Base-T).

- ISOLATED OUTLETS:

None of these models have isolated outlets (i.e., like Isobars, Furman PST-8D, etc.).

- DISPLAYING SITE WIRING ISSUES:

An example of a site wiring issue is if electrical ground is missing in an old home, thus the unit surge protection is inactive. They all report this, the APC SMT's and CyberPower PRxxxLCD's report this actively on displays and the CPxxxPFCLCD's do so with a LED bulb on the back.

- CAN I PLUG-IN SURGE PROTECTOR
BEFORE OR AFTER UPS?:

The manufacturers said technically yes and said many clients do, but they don't recommend it. Some reasons manufacturers recommend against it include:

(a) UL1449 surge protection certification is for plugging the unit right into a wall outlet.
(b) Can cause UPS to misjudge actual wattage going through, possibly causing overload.
(c) Should be using PDU's instead for efficient power distribution.
(d) Surge protectors in-line with each other can actually increase total tolerance for surges, reducing effectiveness.
(e) User loses equipment protection coverage, among other reasons because determining liability becomes difficult.

PDUs plugged into an APC UPS that aren't APC made won't void the UPS warranty I'm told but can void the equipment protection guarantee.

WHICH IS EASIEST TO USE:
---------------------------

The CyberPower CPxxxPFCLCD models are the most CONSUMER-FRIENDLY and the EASIEST TO USE and manage we review here. For example:

- The included GUI software is super user-friendly.
- The easiest to move around, like a super heavy book.

The very USER-FRIENDLY GUI (Powerpanel Personal Edition - PPPE) included has more limited, more selective configuration and monitoring capabilities.

> SOME OF PPPE'S CONS:

- It DOES EVENT LOGGING COUNTS WELL for different time periods and displays time of the last event. However, unlike the other models it has NO EVENT LOGGING (not even event start and stop times)**.

- No ALERT EMAILING/texting (The APC's and the PR's do) with included PPPE software**.

- It requires the RUNTIME LEFT on the UPS before computer shutdown to be AT LEAST 5 MINUTES. Some users prefer more control over runtime IF THEY HAVE A FAST SHUTDOWN (ex: Put OS on solid state drive).

- It does NOT have LOGGING OF POWER INFO, which tracks power values like frequency, voltage, load, etc. The SMC/SMT and PRxxxLCD models do.

**Note: We can download the PowerPanel Business Edition to get the EMAILING/texting alert or event logging ability on a CPxxxPFCLCD. However, PPBE is less attuned to the needs of a novice and there are compatibility issues, though if these features are critical to you, you can make it work.

"ADAPTIVE SINEWAVE"
DOCUMENTATION MISUNDERSTANDING
FOR THE CPxxxPFCLCD MODELS:
------------------------------------

The CPxxxPFCLCD models output a PURE SINE WAVE and CyberPower states they always have. However, they still have web and paper documentation that use THEIR OLD MARKETING TERM "Adaptive Sinewave" which mistakenly suggests it produces a modified sine wave. Also a 2010 article by a respected website said this was a modified sinewave, however CyberPower says this isn't so and never was.

WHAT ABOUT
CYBERPOWER PP MODELS?:
--------------------------

The PP models work just fine, however they don't have some features expected by the market today and are being PHASED OUT, and essentially absorbed by the long-running PR model line.

SOME THINGS NOT TO PLUG
INTO A UPS OR ON THE SAME
WALL BRANCH CIRCUIT AS ONE:
------------------------------

Hook these up to a separate surge suppressor and preferably to an outlet on another branch circuit (i.e., different circuit box circuit breaker).

- Laserwriter
- Paper shredder
- Copier
- Space heater
- Sump pump
- Dehumidifier
- Most big electrical needy machines

UPS SHUTDOWN AFTER COMPUTER HIBERNATION:
-----------------------------------------------

> Why Shutdown UPS?

There are benefits to auto-shutting down a UPS after it shuts down a PC. By not running a battery way down the UPS can restart without manual help when power returns, battery life improves, and recharge time lessens. Also, a UPS needs to restart in order for a Windows PC to be automatically rebooted after it was shutdown if you wanted that (and if the computer allows it).

> The Scenario

The power returns from a blackout and you want to get back to work, so you start up the computer and while it is starting up or you are starting to work the UPS goes down crashing the computer! (and turning off anything else plugged into it).

What happened? In most user or default configurations the UPS goes down 2-8 minutes or so after the command to shutdown the PC goes out. With some UPS models the UPS will then STILL GO DOWN at a set time after the computer hibernates EVEN IF THE POWER RETURNS.

> Solution

Test if your model does this. If so, find time before UPS shuts down after PC hibernates and TRAIN USERS NOT TO RESTART COMPUTER JUST AFTER BLACKOUT ENDS but instead for that time and to check display for time before UPS shutdown report.

LINE INTERACTIVE vs. DOUBLE CONVERSION
TOPOLOGIES:
------------------------------------------

LINE INTERACTIVE:

These models all have a line interactive topology, this means they go from AC power to battery and back at specific voltages. There is a short transfer time usually 2-8 milliseconds depending on model. Let's now look at the next level up ...

DOUBLE CONVERSION "ONLINE":

- Can TOLERATE greater input fluctuations without impacting output
- ZERO TRANSFER TIME to battery since output runs continuously

- Significantly MORE EXPENSIVE
- Often much NOISIER
- Few % less efficient with electricity

Examples:
- APC Smart-UPS Online model RT 1500VA:
[[ASIN:B004LNNNWY APC SMART-UPS RT 1500VA (120V) - E77654]]
- CyberPower OL Smart App Online model OL1000RTXL2U:
[[ASIN:B00A6AYV8Q CyberPower Smart App Online OL1000RTXL2U - UPS - 900 Watt - 1000 VA (OL1000RTXL3U) -]]

HOW TO REBOOT COMPUTER AFTER BLACKOUT:
---------------------------------------------

APC UPS models have an option to bring a Windows PC back up after the blackout ends (assuming the UPS shut it down), and it's an easy configuration option. However, 2 prerequisites are:

- The PC motherboard bios needs hibernate to be enabled
- The UPS needs to have been shutdown (put to sleep is more accurate, it is still "on" if plugged in)

SOME GREEN
QUESTIONS ANSWERED:
-----------------------

WHEN NOTHING PLUGGED INTO UPS:

(a) When not recharging, they all use between 4W-9W.

(b) When recharging, the CyberPower ones use 4W-8W.

(c) When recharging, the APC models use 15W-17W for most of the recharge period. Note that the APC models recharge in up to 3 hours vs. the CyberPower ones taking up to 8 hours.

(d) These UPS models use 1W-3W more when on than when shut-off.

SUGGESTION:
-------------

Given all the UPS units made, comments on Amazon and other sites can't statistically represent a large enough sampling to tell us how likely we are to get a lemon. However comments can give us a great idea WHAT TO TEST FOR just after we get them so we can more quickly check if we have a lemon so we can get an easy exchange.

Some things to test for:
- Is battery recharge under load much slower than claimed
- Runtime with intended load
- Noise under load
- Set up and execute a PC hibernate or other safe shutdown
- Review temperature in logs (APC only)

TO THE MANUFACTURERS:
-------------------------

If you find inaccuracies, please note them in comments and I'll modify accordingly.

title: Simply an awesome bang-for-the-buck home theater!
text:
I've owned this system for about 6 months now, use it every day to watch TV. I purchased it when I moved into a townhouse, where my former Philips Sonowave just wasn't cutting it. The Sonowave was good for a bedroom setting but was WAY underpowered for the townhouse setting.

It's my first Home Theater and it's simply awesome for what you pay for. I use it to watch digital cable, play PS3 games, movies from a blu-ray player, movies from my computer, movies from a network drive, streaming movies and videos, YouTube... it all sounds great. It's perfect for a townhouse.

- The bass is surprisingly quite powerful for a basic system, though the pwoer settings may be a bit too strong
- A lot of configurable settings (ie. Treble/Bass/Subwoofer levels, all separate speaker levels (ie.center channel), pre-defined audio settings for different types of Music... etc)
- Wish the Remote was illuminated
- A lot of inputs (esp. HDMI)
- No 3.5mm input
- The iPhone detection and usability is not that great... the usability of the built in iPhone functions need to be less restrictive. You are unable to control your music via your iPhone once it is synced up to the receiver, you need to use the Receiver's interface -- which is pretty cumbersome.
- Subwoofer is a tad too light and it's a down-firing subwoofer, so on occasion when listening to something with alot of powerful bass, the subwoofer tends to move on its own a few inches here or there. On one occasion it moved a foot away after a movie. [Sitting on laminate flooring]. This can be corrected with some stickies on the feet for grip or setting something on top of the subwoofer -- shouldn't be a problem on carpet.

The iPhone interface and the moving Subwoofer are the reasons I only gave it 4/5 stars, otherwise it would be 5/5.

Although this system sounds great, don't expect super-rich audiophile-level deep bass and clear treble audio; But for sub-$300, I'm not sure you can do any better!

title: Great sound and functionality at a great price
text:
I have been using the Creative WP-350 headset for a month now. Overall it has been a good experience. Paired easily out of the box w/ my Nexus phone. Pros and cons below:

Pros:
* Sound quality (both in and out) is great both for phone and music usage.
* Mic was extremely sensitive in picking up my voice. (All usage was indoors.)
* The feel of the ear pieces on the ears is just right -- not too tight, not too lose. (No you can NOT run with this headset on!)
* Music play / pause / stop is easy to control from the headset.

Cons:
* The box was rather hard to open. The manual went flying out when I finally got the box opened!
* You have to spend 10 minutes to read the manual before you use any advanced features of the headset like call switching, putting a call on hold, etc. (The manual is thick, but it has instructions in 20 languages, so it takes <10 minutes to read one language!)
* A lot of high use features (mute / unmute for example) were not obvious. (BTW, mute / unmute feature takes a little practice to use. The two buttons that need to be pressed together to use this feature are on a curved surface and are hard to press together simultaneously.)
* The phone / pause / play buttons are printed on the plastic. A little bit more tactile feedback on the buttons would help locating them.
* The promised voice recognition-based dialing did not work very well. Not sure if this is the phone's problem or the headset's problem. (Ultimately the phone's voice recognition software is used.)
* It is a very feature rich product. Different things happen on 1 / 2 / 3 second press and hold of the phone button. Invariably when I was trying to reject a call, I landed up switching the headset off.
* It will take a good amount of practice to learn all the features and get the timings of the "hold the button" right.

Despite my numerically larger number of cons, I like the product and it has become part of my daily use.

title: Super thin, Sharp looking, performs well
text:
For the price I paid for this monitor ($139) this was a fantastic buy. 23" is bigger than expected, the picture is great, the monitor is super thin, and there's not detectable lag or ghosting. Both arrived without any dead pixels and I haven't had an issue since.

My only minor gripe is that the dynamic contrast is highly noticeable. This results in some darker than I would like games and movies, and it's visible when the monitor decides the scene is bright enough to adjust to a brighter setting. Kind of like flicking on a light switch.

Additionally, the stands have a small footprint which results in a lot of wobbling whenever anything bumps the desk.

In retrospect I wish I had bought something with VESA mounting holes, but that did not factor into my rating here.

Gave it a shot and was very pleased. Of course I can't compare them side by side, OEM to this one, but it seems to perform just as good as new. For my application this speaker was a great choice. One negative though, the terminals are not marked for polarity. I did this replacement late at night and I was already settled down in my shorts so I had to get dressed, out to the garage for some wire, hook up the speaker to a AA battery and bump it to find the polarity. Would it have hurt them guys to have put a red dot on one of the terminals? Really.

title: Lightning fast and easy to use
text:
Got the enclosure to consolidate several external hard drives that all their own enclosures. Many of the enclosures external drives come with have minimal ventilation and tend to run hot which probably isn't helpful for their lifespans.

Besides being able to consolidate 4 drives (I noticed they had an 8 bay enclosure after I got mine), I really wanted to get something faster than USB 2.0 which was running painfully slow when moving large files around. Since my computer only has USB 2.0 ports built in, I had to get a USB 3.0 card. I figured I would get one with enough ports, so I ended up with the Uspeed PCI-E to USB 3.0 4-Ports Express Card Adapter With 4-Pin Power Connector.

After installing the Uspeed card and loading the drivers, I connected the ProBox and started moving drives into it. I ended up moving two 750GB drives, one 2TB drive and one 1.5TB drive, all Seagate Barracuda 7200 drives.

My computer is a Dual Core 3.0Ghz with Windows 7 Ultimate 64, 4GB of ram, Intel Motherboard and the main drive is a 300GB WD VelociRaptor running at 10.000 RPM.

I started moving some files around and the speed increase was phenomenal. I didn't test before and after numbers, but I noticed large files were taking a fraction of the time when moved from drive to drive, and from the main HD to the USB drives and back.

The enclosure is tastefully designed, but it is smaller than I thought it would be. I have never been a huge fan of the Blue LED craze that appears to have taken over every electronic device since they tend to be annoyingly bright. The fan settings, bus and connection indicators are not obscenely bright, but the drive status LED's make it look like a Rave club after it gets dark.
Since the drive is in my office, they don't bother me, but I could see someone with a desk in his bedroom looking for some tape to dim them down.

The power connector on the side is an odd design, I feel like a more logical place would be on the back, but its more quirky than a design flaw.

I was planing on using the eSATA port initially, but I don't believe that my built in eSATA controller supports Port Multiplier, so I figured it would be easier to just go to USB 3.0. According to my research, the speed difference between eSATA and USB 3.0 is supposed to negligible. Testing reports appear to give neither one an edge, with different file sizes favoring one or the other.

Some people have reported some fan noise, mine has been whisper quiet from day one so I have not had any fan noise issues. If it becomes an issue, the manual rather helpfully suggests replacing the fan with a 12V ball bearing 80mm x 20mm fan and it appears to be relatively straightforward task, and they are widely available.

The enclosure does appear to have 3 different sleep modes, it either turns off with your computer when the SYNC arrow is Blue, or it goes into Sleep mode if it is Amber. You can turn the sync mode off, then the enclosure stays on unless you manually turn it off when you power down your computer. If you leave it in Blue, you have to manually turn the enclosure on after you power on your computer (helpful if you rarely use the drives except for backups or occasional storage). If you leave it in Amber, it goes to sleep and wakes up with your computer.

Overall, the enclosure has met or exceeded my expectations.

Conclusion: Fast, sleek and quiet. My only regret if I had one would be I probably should have gotten the 8 bay model, since I still have a few more hard drives I like to move over. I guess the bright side is two 4 bay enclosures are less expensive than one 8 bay enclosure, and the two won't stick out quite as much as the larger one, since they 8 bay one is probably close to the size of a computer mini-tower.

UPDATE: As of March 2014, my enclosure is still working like a champ connected to my USB 3.0 card. I have taken drives in and out to rotate and upgrade sizes, it is always full with 750GB to 2TB in size. Some people have reported USB 3.0 issues, I have yet to see any in fairly regular use.

Strictly a thumbs down on both these fronts.
