title: Perfect bag for street shooting and travel
text:
I compared the CityWalker 10 and 20 bags side-by-side and decided that the CityWalker 20 was larger than I needed. I already have 10 other bags (mostly by Domke and LowePro) and wanted a bag that was just large enough to carry a restricted amount of gear for a full day of street photography and travel without shoulder fatigue. The CityWalker 10 is perfect for my needs. In fact, the description for this bag does not do it justice by stating that is suitable for a DSLR with normal zoom, another small lens, and a flash. My typical photo kit consists of a a lot more gear than that, including:

- Sony A7R with battery pack attached and a FE 24-70mm F4 zoom with hood attached in shooting position - this fits in the center lens compartment with the zoom pointed down.
- Sony FE 70-200mm F4 zoom with hood reversed. This is a large lens, and when shooting I can place the zoom in the bag with the hood in shooting position - the bag top flap can still be fastened.
- Sony FE 55mm F1.8 placed in the center compartment under the camera body/normal zoom.
- Sony HVL-F43M flash placed between the padded lens compartment and the exterior nylon bag.
- Tripod foot for the 70-200 zoom - this fits under the flash between the lens compartment and the exterior bag.
- I intend to add the Sony FE 16-35mm F4 zoom to this kit. This lens is not available but by its specifications should easily fit in the third padded lens compartment.
- The various pockets have room for a 6" phone, an iPad, extra batteries and miscellaneous accessories. If I fill everything nook and cranny of the bag it becomes heavier than I care to carry for an all-day walking outing. Yet for airline travel and other transport needs, it will do the job when I need to carry everything in one bag.

I tried a Think Tank Retrospect 10 bag and found it to be nearly twice as heavy (empty) while having less capacity and a stiffer shape that made it hard to expand for additional gear.

As noted before, this bag is the perfect compromise for my needs. Key features that make it stand out from other bags:

- It is lightweight but still durable. It may not have the rugged character of a Domke bag after extended use, but I expect it to wear well and retain its shape.
- The interior padded compartment is removable and easily configured for various combinations of body and lenses.
- The zippers appear to be above average, and the velcro fasteners throughout the bag are well placed.
- The padded compartment along the front of bag will hold an iPad or other electronics. My Surface Pro 3 with 11" screen will even fit.
- The padded/non-slip should pad is the best design I've yet used.
- There are several interior, zipped compartments for smaller items.
- The elastic exterior compartments at either end of the bag are suitable for a water bottle or other small items.
- The quiet velcro silencers for the bag top flap is a great concept when you need to be discreet.
- A document pocket on the back of the bag is convenient and large enough to hold a magazine. I find this pocket is a good place to put my cell phone.
- The bag comes with a compact rain cover that should provide good protection. I haven't had a need to use it; however, the rain cover is a bit of a nuisance to attach.

I plan to update this review after more extended usage. At this time it is my preferred bag for my prime photo kit.

title: Great Normal Zoom for DX Cameras
text:
I purchased the Sigma 17-50 f/2.8 lens from a local dealer a little over three months ago and absolutely love it. I previously had a Tamron 28-75 f/2.8 lens that was my first foray into the "professional" lens category (that is lenses with a fixed 2.8 aperture throughout the zoom range). While I loved the 2.8 ability of the Tamron, I found it to be a little like the high ISO range of my cameras--there if I needed it in a pinch, but better to avoid it for maximum image quality. As I used other quality lenses, I discovered that the Tamron just didn't hold up to the others. It was just too soft at 2.8. With that said, the primary reason I went for the Sigma was that I missed the wide angle with a lens that only went to 28mm. There's a huge difference between 17mm and 28mm. Not as much between 50mm and 75mm.

IMAGE QUALITY:
I shot the Sigma lens on my camera (a Nikon D7000) before purchasing because I wanted to ensure I got one that had good sharpness and also good, accurate focusing. My lens does both. I was amazed when I shot this lens wide open at 2.8. The center of the lens was still very sharp (I haven't really paid attention to much beyond the center, as my focus point is usually near the center). I have no qualms about sharpness when using this lens at 2.8. The focusing of the lens has also been spot on for me. It focuses very quickly and accurately in most any light I have thrown at it. It also seems to do just fine in continuous focus mode. My wife actually grabbed my camera to take a couple of pictures of me with the kids and just used the last setting I had, which was Aperture Priority at f/2.8 in continuous AF. Even in the hands of my wife (who doesn't know the ins and outs of my camera), the lens nailed focus and was perfectly sharp. On my Tamron lens, these photos would have been out of focus, soft, or both. The only downside to this lens in the focusing department has been that the focus ring spins during focusing, so you need to keep your fingers off of it. It also doesn't allow instant manual focus override by turning the focus ring either. You need to flip a switch to move to manual focus. These are minor things in my mind though.

OPTICAL STABILIZATION:
I wasn't sure that the OS feature was terribly necessary on a normal zoom like this, but I thought it would be nice to have regardless, as it should allow me to shoot things that don't move at pretty low shutter speeds. I tested it out and I was able to get comparably sharp shots right around 3 stops slower than I could hand-holding without OS. I was pretty pleased with this outcome, as it meant I could shoot at lower ISOs or f-stops if needed. The OS does take a second to kick in (as does any such system), but is effective and the effect can be seen even through the viewfinder. I find it essentially silent. I can't hear it with my eye to the camera, though I can hear it with my ear to the lens. For practical purposes, I consider it to be silent.

BUILD QUALITY:
I don't have much to say about the build quality other than it seems like a very solid lens to me. My Tamron lens felt cheap in my hands, the Sigma does not. Most of my other Sigma lenses have felt solid too, so I wasn't too worried. It doesn't move where it shouldn't, and moves smoothly in the places where it should. I had heard early reports of the lens hood not staying on this lens, but mine snaps on securely and hasn't come loose at all when I'm using it. I have seen some flare with this lens (even with the hood on), but it has been in some flare-prone situations (strong light directly into the lens). I don't think it's a huge deal, but I do keep my hood on in cases where flare might be a problem.

Overall, I'm thrilled with this lens. I was debating between getting a used Nikon 17-55 f/2.8 or this lens brand new. Even new, this lens was quite a bit cheaper than the Nikon, and while I'm sure the Nikon lens is of excellent quality, I believe the Sigma is too. Apart from the few minor niggles I mentioned above, I have absolutely no complaints about this lens--I love it!

title: Amazing sound, amazing features, and easy to use for the whole family.
text:
<Appearance/Quality:>
This is a solid piece of equipment with some significant weight to it. I like the simple clean look - two knobs, power button, and display screen. The rest of the buttons and front connectors are hidden behind a flip down panel. The first one I bought had some issue with the auto-protection kicking in and shutting down the receiver. I did some troubleshooting and it seems this is a feature to protect the receiver from short circuits. So I rechecked and reattached all my wiring. Still didn't fix the problem. I exchanged the receiver and the new one works great. I guess the initial one must have been defective. The new unit is working flawlessly and has brought new life to my old speaker set-up.

<Features:>
Wow. I absolutely love all the features this receiver has. This receiver can be set up as a 9.2 system, but only with 7 channels amplified. I have it set up as a 7.1 with two extra speakers on zone 2 so that I can listen while I'm outside on the BBQ and the family is inside watching TV. Network integration (via ethernet connection) is great, although it doesn't have WiFi. However, once you've got it connected to your network, you can control it wirelessly from any network device, like your phone, tablet, or laptop. Also, for Apple users it's got Airplay (which my wife absolutely loves to use.) The phone/tablet app is a little laggy, but still super cool. I love that it has built in Spotify, Pandora, Internet Radio, and SiriusXM and these are all controlable through the app. Although, I haven't used the Sirius, I have used the rest and they work great. I love being able to control what's playing from my cell phone without having the TV on. While the app is free, I do wish it was a bit more user friendly and fine-tuned.
The Audessy XT32 is absolutely amazing and fairly easy to do (although it takes a bit of time). It vastly improves the sound quality. I even tried matching different brands of speakers and they sound much better together after running Audessy than if I run them directly without any calibration (I still recommend having the same brand and series of speakers though to match the timber.)
I won't go over the rest of the features, because they are listed in the item description and generally self-explanatory. This receiver will handle pretty much any time of modern technology with a few exceptions: if you want a unit what has WiFi, Bluetooth, and does Dolby Atmos, you should consider the AVR-x4100.

<Installation/Ease of use>
Setup is a breeze if you connect it to your TV and follow the onscreen instructions. I won't describe what types of inputs/outputs it has (that information is readily available), but for people using older technology (i.e. s-video, digital audio, rca, component, etc.) this receiver is still compatible with most older technology as well. The layout on the back looks like most any receiver and I found it to be better laid out than my old Sony receiver.
In a matter of minutes I was able to show both my wife and my sister in law how to use a lot of the features on this receiver, and neither one of them is particularly technically inclined. They regularly use Pandora, internet radio, and the Airplay feature of the receiver (in addition to regular TV and BluRay use.)

<Overall Impression>
I absolutely love this receiver. However, at it's price, I wouldn't recommend it to everybody. If you can live with 2 zones (instead of 3), a less effective version of Audessy, and 105 watts/channel I'd consider the much cheaper x3000. However, for the money, you won't find the type of features on the x4000 on other receivers in the same price range.

The cameras that come with this system are 420 lines and unless the individual is fairly close it would be hard to indentify the person.

Aposonic has some other cameras and I may purchase a higher res camera to use like for our entry way.

All in all this camera system is very good. Does not feel or look like low quality and customer service has always been very helpful and right there when you needed to speak with them and they spoke ENGLISH which was a plus as you could understand them.

title: Pretty good, not great
text:
I have some criticisms that probably shouldn't affect the score. Those are these: 1, why is it when I buy a mid priced home theater 3D blu ray system from a leading brand can it not come with an HDMI cord? Would've have been nice to be able to set everything up right out of the box. But I asked around and apparently none of them do, so I digress. Also, this system has ipod/iphone integration. Which is super cool. But I own a Samsung Galaxy. Would have been cool if there was some integration for that, too, considering its the same brand...... But....I digress.

Now, to the stuff that matters. The Samsung Home blu ray player has an excellent stereo sound, great for listening to music. While it doesn't come with an AUX cord, there is an input for AUX in the back for hooking up your mp3 player or non-apple smartphone. The cords are very cheap and can be found at any major retailer. Music sounds fantastic, and it goes much louder than I could play in my apartment.

The 5.1 also sounds very good for live music dvd's in 5.1. Not quite fantastic, but really good sound.

What DOESN'T sound very good is the dialogue in movies. I've noticed this at other people's houses with other cheaper systems before, but was hoping that I was paying enough money that it wouldn't be a problem on this one. CHeap 5.1's are way worse, but this isn't as much better as I was hoping for. Dialogue in movies coming through the central speaker does not sound very good. It isn't just a volume issue, which can be dealt with in the setup. Its a sound quality issue. Not sure if its that the central speaker lacks range, or if there is something else at play. There's a slight buzz sound when people talk and the sound lacks distinction and clarity. For all I know, it could be the fault of the people coding blu-rays. Not sure. But I watched a couple differnt blu ray movies, and the dialogue sound quality was fairly poor regardless, which is in stark contrast coming out of the central speaker compared to the rest of the sounds coming from everywhere else, which sound fantastic.

Overall, its a fairly nice player for a good price. Music through the stereo sounds great, and music dvds through the 5.1 also sound really good. But I got this in part to watch movies, and movies contain dialogue, and the dialogue just doesn't sound very good. I shouldn't have expected too much more than what it offers consider it really isn't that pricey. The netflix integration is cool. Built in wi-fi is a plus. If a friend asked me if I thought this player should be purchased, I'd say yes but get the higher price point. The cool thing about samsung is they certainly don't limit you on price point options.

title: Best protector I've ever used for ANY device
text:
Having used screen protectors on my smartphones, I purchased this based on the reviews and expecting the usual plastic screen with sticky side, etc. I was surprised (and initially concerned) to open the package and find what appeared to be a relatively thick plastic screen and a liquid solution specifically used to apply the screen! This seemed a lot more involved than my previous protector screens and I was a little worried that this would be more complicated, and hence, easier for me to screw up.

After reading the instructions thoroughly, and then two more times, I felt confident enough to give it a shot. Considering the price, if I messed up royally it wouldn't be like I'd lost a huge investment.

5 minutes later, and I was amazed at how awesome this protector looked and functioned. I have never had a protector screen go on without ANY dust/bubbles trapped under the screen (maybe just me?). I applied a ton of the liquid solution they included and did notice some trapped liquid under the screen but the little tool they provide (quality plastic, not cardboard) did an amazing job of pushing it out.

At first, I was a little concerned because I did notice some marks from where I removed the sticky screen from the paper but then placed it back on (which happens I think if you peel some off and then it goes back as you try to apply just 'SOME' of the screen to the tablet) but it was only noticeable at certain angles in the sunlight. And it ended up disappearing anyways as the instructions said those things would.

I've now been using it for about 2 weeks and have not seen a single scuff or mark on it. It definitely feels and performs like military grade material. I wish they made a matte/non-glare version but this will be more than enough for now.

My ONLY complaint, and not bad enough to take any points off, is that the screen may possibly perform TOO well in some respects. I've noticed that, while playing games that have dual-analog controllers displayed on screen, the controllers seem to respond slower, as if my movements are somewhat buffered or padded too much. I've only noticed this on 1 particular game (Monster Shooter) and I was not able to test this before the screen protector so I'm not even positive it is the protector and not simply the tablet or the game. BUT, if you play a lot of those types of games, try and see if you notice any degradation in this aspect. But again, for me, even if this is caused by the protector, it's a small price to pay for such an awesomely clear/strong product!

title: A step down for Creative's Zen Series
text:
This is my very first review on Amazon, and I wish I could be more forgiving. I have been a customer of Creative's Zen Series MP3 players for about 7 years, starting with the Zen V, then the Zen Mozaic, and finally with the Zen X-Fi3. I thought the move to touchscreen would be a welcome added feature that previous iterations of Zens did not have. After using it for about 2 weeks, I would rather use my Zen Mozaic over my new X-Fi3. I will break it down into a simple list of pros and cons for you:

Pros:
1. Relatively inexpensive, compared with certain other digital audio players on the market.
2. Bright and vivid screen is easy to see.
3. Micro SD card slot is a welcome addition, alllowing you to have plenty of extra space for other media.
4. Bluetooth has been added with this series...things are always better with Bluetooth!
5. Creative kept the external speaker which was added with the Zen Mozaic, which although the sound is what you'd expect from a tiny external speaker, is still cool.
6. X-Fi feature is a nice touch which allows you to equalize your music to the type you like

Cons:
1. The player, when first turned on, takes a while to boot up, and then when it does, if you have a Micro SD card in it, the player reads the information on the card as well, which takes several more seconds.
2. Navigating the Music menus for a certain album or artist is now a pain. The Zen Mozaic had a nice alphabet scroll menu on the right side of the screen for quickly locating the album or artist you want. The X-Fi3 does not have this handy feature. When I am on the treadmill at the gym, I do not want to spend 2 minutes scrolling through 400 artist names trying to get to the R's to play my Rage Against the Machine songs.
3. Navigation of music menus is further hampered by how slowly the Zen responds to my touch. If I select music, then albums, it takes several seconds to pull up my albums, and when I select an album, it takes a further few seconds to pull up the available music in that album.

Hopefully, a firmware update can fix some of these issues. At the end of the day, it's still (overall) a nice addition to the Zen series of players. Does it outshine the Zen Mozaic? A debate can be made for both sides on that one. My recommendation? If you are just looking for a nice media player for listening to music at the office or at home, get it. However, if you are looking for something to use while at the gym working out, go with the Zen Mozaic. It allows you to find and play music seamlessly. Or go with a different player altogether.

title: I Want to Like It, But Costly and Time Consuming Mistake
text:
Top points for the premium materials on the front panel and for being about the only non-budget case in these dimensions. For its size, cable management is good. The big fan cools the drives very well and brings a lot of air into the case. CPU cooler and GPU supports are clever. Rubber feet are excellent. But there are so many frustrating issues that ruin it:

* The front fan is noisy. This is a deal breaker for me. Low speed setting is loud, high speed setting is "ready for take off". If you like lots of airflow and the sounds to prove it, then this is the case for you. Not sure if there is any way to make it quiet, not being a PWM fan means you can't use modern motherboards to control it. On the low setting it needs almost full voltage to start it so simple voltage reduction is out of the question. Because of its odd 180mm size, replacement options are very limited. The only real option seems to be one of Silverstone's other non-PWM fans that will run down to 7v, then some kind of fan control. A bunch of extra money for something that should have been right in the first place.

* The top power supply intake seems pointless. If you put the power supply fan-up with an open-cooler GPU, there is only a small exhaust from the top of the case. With the power supply fan down temperatures were good.

* The case structure is very floppy. The panels pull it mostly into shape, right down to the last thumb screw. Yuck. The steel is not very thick, but maybe thick enough for a case this small *if* the panels weren't holding the shape together.

* The padded drive mounts are silly. You can't tighten down the screws properly without distorting the cage. Be very careful or you'll pop the welds. I was being careful, but apparently not enough. I don't understand why they didn't just use grommets like everyone else.

* The paint is very soft. The front panel materials may look great, marked paint does not. I was so careful during the build, then while turning it around to take a photo of the bad panel fit for Silverstone support, the unplugged video cable brushed the case and took off a chunk of paint. What wasn't clear in the other mentions of damaged paint I read is that you don't get scratched black paint - the black flakes completely off and you see through to gray. It is very noticeable.

* The front audio connectors are junk. You have to push so hard to seat the connector that the whole PC slides across the table.

* This is the most fiddly, time consuming case I have ever worked in. It is not because it is tight, getting your hands in there is actually fairly easy. There are just too many parts to remove and so many screws. Having so many different kinds of screws is a pain too. I misplaced one of the 3mm countersunk screws for a while, was not fun.

* As others have mentioned, quality control is fairly ordinary. My case's factory assembly was very sloppy, including one of the side panel hooks crushed resulting in a bowed panel.

Update: After just a few hours of running time the panels have started to rattle during drive access. This is a modest build, stock Intel cooler, decent Nvidia graphics card with reference cooler, one hard drive and no DVD. I can't figure out how the average ratings for this case are so high - outside of the main front panel aluminum, the build quality and quality control of this case is terrible - thin, soft steel, badly fitting parts. Everything I would expect from a case 1/4 the cost of this one. Yuck, yuck, yuck.

Update 2: I contacted Silverstone support about some of the issues I've had with this case. I wanted to know whether things like side panel rattle or the 1/8" gaps in panel fit were expected, correctable, or, that I had received a defective case and should return it. Responses were slow, extremely evasive and not helpful. But I did glean that with a WD Black drive you will "feel or hear those vibration and noise easily than other series (as blue or green)", which was curious to hear given I said I had a WD Blue drive. I can't imagine what to expect with 4 drive bays populated. Also, the issue of crushed side panel hooks seems to be known to them, since they suggested I check for that. With apparently no further suggestions, they have stopped responding all together.

title: device works well but online ordering and Customer service not so much
text:
We ordered the original Magic Jack in Jan of 2011 without any problems and it arrived quickly and was installed in a matter of minutes no problem.

Since it had to be plugged into my desktop computer the only time I encountered any problems were when someone was surfing the net on my computer at the same time as taking a phone call. There were some reverb, echoes and skipping so it made it hard to have a conversation, but only when my computer and phone were being used a the same time. When others used laptops I didn't seem to notice problems.

We love the device so much so that we decided that when our 1 year was up we would purchase the newest Magic Jack Plus so that i would no longer need to leave my computer on 24/7 in order to receive or make phone calls.

In Late Dec. of 2011 I attempted to order the new Magic Jack Plus via an email that would allow me to get the new Magic Jack Plus at a half price for a limited 48 hour purchase time. I was looking forward to getting the new device especially at this great price.
However at the end of my attempt to order via the net, following all the directions including entering my credit card number, I was still uncertain if the order went through properly since I got a pop up stating there was some kind of error. When I pushed retry it told me that I could be charged a second time if I pushed retry so I called the company to make sure the order was complete. After a long wait the lady told me that she was unable to see if the order was processed and that I would have to wait a couple of days or weeks to see if I would get a confirmation email or if the bill showed up on my credit card. She assured me that the sale price would remain available even if I waited. So I relucktanly hung up the phone. Note: Since I made the call I was given a Chat ID number at this time Dec. 2011, the same day I attempted to puchase the new Magic Jack Plus.

I waited till late Jan.2012 before attempting to contact the company again since I had still not received any confirmation email nor had I received my new Magic Jack Plus device in the mail.
I gave them the 1st chat number that I received in Dec. at this time as well so that they would be able to see what took place then. However The customer service person gave me a new chat number as a reference so all my information could be retrieved for reference.

I was on the phone and the internet customer service for nearly 4 hours getting the run around.I repeatadly explained to them that I attempted to order the Magic Jack Plus in Dec.2011 and that I even had the customer ID chat number from the extensive chat. But apparently the chat numbers are of no use. They refused to allow me to purchase the magic jack plus at the sale price and only told me that I would have to get online to reorder the magic jack plus at the reg. price.
So discouraged and frustrated I went back online to reorder the magic jack plus and once again the order faild even though I put in everything including my credit card number.

Today Feb. 15, 2012 I found an email stating that I was being charged for a renewal of my old magic. SO, I got back on the phone and explained everything all over again to the customer service person only to be told that she showed no such purchase was made via the net. And if I wanted to purchase the Magic Jack Plus I would have to go to Radio Shack to purchase it. I told her I didn't want to pay for the renewal of $29 for my old magic jack AND purchase a new Magic Jack Plus. She told me that I would have to cancel my renewal now. So I did just that.

While the original Magic Jack device works great, the customer service via the net AND/OR the phone have alot to be desired.

Maybe with any luck someone from the company will see this and find a way to fix all the problems so nobody else has to have such an ordeal.

I have since ordered a new Magic Jack Plus using an 800 number I found in a flyer, and I used my cell phone to make the order. NOW we will see if this will work. OMG!!!!

Unfortunatly I did NOT get the half price sale price nor did I get the free shipping that I would have gotten had the 1st and 2nd attempt went through, but maybe with any luck and the use of an 800 number, (that of which is totally different then the other numbers I called previously), I will get the New Magic Jack Plus in 5 to 10 business days.
Wish me luck. :)

Glutton for punishment. lol

Please note: This device was NOT purchased via Amazon.com and all of the problems encountered where directly with and from the Magic Jack Company Customer Service alone, and that we have no problems with nor have we ever had any problems with Amazon.com.

title: Flex on the Roll
text:
This crane / jib is well built and an excellent value, especially if you compare it to other pro ones that cost way more.
Adds so much production value to the shots. I even use it on some regular hand held shots to help hold steady.
However, my one only biggest complaint is the flex on the mounting bracket where you attach the camera.
There is considerable flex after mounting a DSLR rig to it. In airplane terms: it rolls clockwise. In other words it tilts to the right, since it hangs to the right of the main arm. So the camera, when facing forward, looking down the length of the arm, is always off level and tilted to the right.
I have tried bending and flexing it back, but it always relaxes back after mounting equipment to it.
The simple solution was to level the tripod that the crane is mounted, to compensate for the slight angle, but alas, as soon as you swing and pan in either direction, the angle is worse in one way or the other.
The obvious solution would be to mount an adjustable head on the bracket, which is what I've done. However, now I need to buy another tripod head so I can do the quick release thing from crane to tripod without having to unscrew everything back and forth every time I switch between supports.
There really shouldn't be any flex there at all. Aside from that, a good product.

title: Loud but without much bass
text:
The construction of the Eagle Tech ET-AR604H-BR is solid; nothing feels cheap. The speakers are approximately the size you'd expect to find on a boombox (portable detachable stereo), but without the box/receiver. Since the ET-AR604H-BR has its own built-in amp, you can plug devices directly into it--such as an iPod, smartphone, or other .mp3 player.

You can also plug the speakers into your home entertainment center. Such as to a TV, DVD player, or gaming console.

Due to the size, I found the speakers a little awkward to find a place for. Too small to sit on the ground, but too big to fit onto my TV stand.

The manufacturer claims "Punchy Bass," but I'm not feeling it. In fact, even with the bass maxed and volume turned all the way up, it struggles to push out a strong low frequency. This makes sense since the speakers are only 5" around and the boxes not large enough to develop any sort of deep acoustics, but all the same I was disappointed in the lack of decent bass.

Another item the manufacturer claims is crankability. That they got right. What I mean by crankability is the aptitude of the ET-AR604H-BR for being loud. With the volume cranked to max, the speakers hold their sound without faltering. I was impressed with this because I've owned many a speaker that rattles or washes out under such conditions. In this case, the sound traveled well across my entire house (good for wild parties! That is, if I ever had wild parties . . . :-/)

The key to these speakers is finding the right usage for them. Using them inside my house for watching movies is a disappointment; explosions are flat. But put them with a backyard theater setup and they'd be excellent; no deep rumbles to disturb the neighbors, but loud enough for everyone watching to hear what's going on.

Also, if space is an issue and you want loud, or if you want portability, give the ET-AR604H-BR a look (like small, obnoxious dogs, they have a lot of bark for the bite). If space isn't an issue and you don't plan on transporting your system, then I suggest sticking with a traditional setup for fuller range of sound.

text:

The tripod is sturdy and telescoping legs are secure and well made. The mount feels very well made, though the clutches feel a tad cheap, they still lock and unlock very easily.

I did have an issue with the EZ finder finder scope. It would not light up, and contained no batteries. It was useless, and was very difficult to find objects without it. No collimation was needed, as the mirrors came aligned very nicely out of the box. It did include instructions on how to collimate and included a collimation cap.

This will be a great scope for years to come, my son looks forward to clear nights to look at the stars!!

On a dark overcast day, I find the high ISO setting  I have to use to get an adequate shutter speed (I shoot in AV mode) to handle the action borderline acceptable.

title: Fantastic little radio!
text:
Great little dynamo/battery radio all around. It has AM/FM/WX bands and they all work better than almost any other radio I own. The volume can get pretty high--at least 75-80dB measured from a distance of a couple inches from the speaker. The speaker does not have the greatest sound quality, but I've heard much worse too. The tuning knob has a satisfying soft click with each incremental movement. It doesn't come with an AC adaptor, but a lot of common 6 volt AC adaptors will work as long as they're positive-polarity and the plug fits. I used a cord from a Delphi Roady2 XM radio. I've also cranked the dynamo (before charging it on AC power). I haven't tried regular batteries in it, but I may never have to, given how long this radio holds a charge.

I live almost exactly halfway between Milwaukee and Chicago, and while it might seem like I'd have all sorts of choices for radio listening because of two major metro radio markets, the truth is that it can be tricky to pick up stations here. Chicago and Milwaukee are each at least 40-50 miles away, depending on the exact location of the transmitters, so neither market comes in exceptionally clear without a great antenna (same problem here for over-the-air HDTV). Even my Midland weather alert radio has trouble picking up the 2 or 3 local weather frequencies. This little bugger picks up all of them VERY clearly; one of them sounds like it's broadcasting a mile away on this RadioShack radio, whereas the same weather station sounds like it's 30 miles from here on the Midland. FM is pretty exceptional as well, often getting stations in clearly that other much higher-priced receivers can't get.

For those listeners in the same area (far northern Lake County IL), a couple such difficult-to-receive stations from Chicago are 98.7 WFMT, 96.3 WBBM, 100.3 WILV, 94.7 WLS and 93.9 WLIT. Although I don't listen to all of those stations, I sometimes use them to aim antennas because they tend to be harder to get. From Milwaukee, some I have trouble getting on more expensive receivers are 94.5 WLWK, 95.7 WRIT, 97.3 WRNW, 99.1 WMYX and 102.1 WLUM.

For you DXers, where this radio really shines is on the AM band (most DXers wouldn't use an emergency dynamo-powered radio for that purpose, but this one is pretty good at it). For years growing up in central Indiana, I could easily receive two major NYC stations at night--770 WABC and 880 WCBS. However, after moving much closer to Chicago, I haven't been able to receive those two stations even at night because there are local stations right next door on the tuning dial: 780 WBBM and 890 WLS. This radio picks them up. I was able to clearly receive 650 WSM from Nashville TN, 700 WLW from Cincinnati OH and 750 WSB from Atlanta GA without even trying too hard. It's much easier to pick up lower power local AM stations during the daytime with this radio because the frequency separation is that good. I haven't experienced any bleedover from stronger stations.

The handy USB port on the back will charge my power-hungry Samsung Galaxy S4 (albeit not completely). You're probably not going to charge a smartphone's battery more than a few percent unless you want to turn the crank on this thing for hours, but it will do nicely in a pinch. I don't have an iPhone, so I don't know whether it will charge those--they seem to be pickier about the minimum amount of current required to charge. And forget about charging an iPad or tablet. I measured a stable 4.98-5.02 volts and 0.26-0.35 amps. I don't know how long the charge in the built-in rechargeable battery would last, but I wouldn't be surprised to get 5-10% of a charge to my Galaxy S4 out of it.

The flashlight isn't the brightest--I measured a fairly dim 2500-3000 lux at a distance of about 1-2 inches from the bulb, perhaps about the brightness of an LED night light. If you take this radio camping (as it has a great weather band and the USB charger), the light should be enough to see the path from your tent to wherever you have to go to do your business. The handle is great too--makes it easy to aim the flashlight and/or hang it from a tree branch--you're only limited by your own creativity.

I really must say that I'm impressed with the quality of this radio, especially for the price. No, I didn't buy it here on Amazon, but rather on a leading auction site. Sometimes the price is about the same, but at 11-14 clams, it's a great bargain. It might be worth double that to someone who appreciates an all-in-one radio/USB charger/flashlight or something that gets great reception during a power outage. Highly recommended!

title: Outstanding!
text:
3/28/13 Update:

1 - Unit still working well BUT still no Miracast!!! Very, very annoying, especially since Apple TV has been doing this kind of function for a long time.

2 - Downloaded Aquamail Pro to get around built in Asus/Android emailer deficiency. (Not being able to easily select account on outgoing email - This capability looks like it was deliberately disabled by Asus or Android.) Aquamail works very well.

3 - The unit is in constant use when traveling and as a couchpad. We still love it.
>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>

Im an electrical engineer and mid level geek who loves new technology.

I use an Ipad 2 regularly (Ipad 1 earlier), and this is every bit as good. I compared it to an Ipad 3 in the store, and I could not see any major differences, except price. After a charge, I turned my new TF700 on, found the Wi-Fi screen and quickly set up my system. I was asked if I wanted to download Flash. I said yes, and it installed within a minute or so. So far so good.

I played with some of the more obvious features and all worked well. I copied some music from my PC onto a micro SD card, plugged it into the tablet, and it was detected and useable immediately. I grew so confident that I then set up my 3 mailboxes (2 ISP and 1 Gmail). The email front end is very nice, since it permits incoming mail to be displayed from individual accounts, or as one combined view. On outgoing mail, (even via my ISP), it picked up and used my Gmail contact list. That encouraged me to combine several email contact lists, including my wife's, into one master contact list on Gmail. (Gmail tools for doing this are easy to use.) Then, even the ISP mail can use the master contact list. It also found the apps I had downloaded from Android Market (now renamed) onto my Android phone, and downloaded those to the tablet as well. I downloaded Skype and was video conferencing in minutes. Wow! I was getting more pleased by the minute.

Then, since the tablet was delivered with Android Ice Cream Sandwich (4.0.3), I checked to download the expected Jelly Bean (4.1.1) update. Nothing there. I tried that for 4 more days, also posting questions on the ASUS site and Amazon BB. Everyone else seemed to be getting JB within a few hours of trying. Why was my Infinity a wallflower? Then finally, after 5 days of hitting the "check for updates button", a large download arrived. Hooray, I had Android 4.1.1! Frankly, I could not tell much difference, but this was definitely not a scientific test. I wish the ASUS FAQ had said that it could take several days before the download of the update might happen. That would have prevented a lot of anxiety. My guess is that they are rationing capacity on their download servers.

I also bought an ASUS USB adapter; a very small device that adapts the TF700's multiport to accept a USB device. Wanting to experiment, I plugged a 16 GB cheap generic USB stick from my car into the adapter, and within about 15 minutes had copied about 8.7 GB of my music from the stick to the tablet's internal 32 GB memory. I clicked on the music player icon on the screen (it's the orange headphone icon, third from the bottom right on the picture), and immediately got to play choices from my almost 3000 pieces of (mp3 and wma) music. The tablet allows me to sort the music in many ways - actually its better in displaying - sorting music choices than the (Clarion/Bose) system in my car. I also tried other media experiments including YouTube, emails with video attachments, and streaming PBS shows. All have worked well. So has the superb amazing Google voice recognition.

I bought this unit because I wanted a large high end tablet to use as a "couch-pad" and to replace
My old Acer 8.9" XP netbook for email when I travel. I wanted the unit to include a GPS, have the ability to easily do file transfers from memory sticks and cards, and not break the bank. (If possible, I also did not want to be dependent on the Apple universe, but my Ipad 1 and 2 experiences were so positive that I was willing to relax that restriction, if needed.) So far the TF700 fills the bill perfectly, at lower than Ipad cost.

BUT, there is one key thing this unit does not do. It does not wirelessly mirror its screen to my TV like Apple Airplay/Apple TV and Intel WI-Di do. (I recently saw a great demo of this at our local computer club.) That is a big shortfall that I know is being worked on via methods such as Miracast. I tested a temporary solution via a 15' cheap HDMI cable to my TV, and the TF700 performed perfectly - streaming a PBS Upstairs Downstairs to my 65" screen. I'm really hoping that the Android industry gets its act together quickly to provide wireless streaming like an ipad with Apple TV!

Except for that, thus far, the TF700 has done everything I have asked it to do, perfectly. It has the solid build and feel of a Lexus. It is definitely an outstanding product, especially at this price!

This is happening at a time range anywhere from every 2 to 20 minutes. The only way to reconnect is to unplug the wireless piece from the tablet and replug it and it comes back on. But it is very annoying to repeat this.

I have read about interference of 2.4 GHz devices. I have 2.4GHz Logitech keyboard and Mouse and a wireless router. In order to do a test I have turned off the wireless of my router and connected my laptop directly with Ethernet cable. I also unplugged the Logitech Keyboard and mouse, and started to use the laptop's keyboard and mouse pad. This was just to test if the tablet wireless signal was affected by these devices. title: Perfection for a 3-layer PET protector. Excellent cut and fit. Care put into the packaging. Far best of three I had tried.
text:
These protectors are similar to most other 3-layer PET screen protectors, but are manufactured perfectly in the ways that matter.
Pros:
CUT. The top has three cutouts that align 100% perfectly with the screen. You have a perfect guide as to whether your application is in the right place.
FIT. The fit is perfect because the sides bend down over the screen perfectly...there is no lip waiting to get caught on the edge of a case or to get pulled loose on a cloth.
BONUS STUFF. The package contains some bonuses that help: A large wiping cloth, a sticker to take off dust while applying, and a rubber scraper. The big cloth is a bonus. The sticker was more effective than my usual standby of scotch tape.

Con:
I think it would have been easier to apply if the peeling would have originated from the sensor cutout side. As it is, you peel and stick from the bottom and there is no room for slop when it comes to the sensors up top. It makes fiddling with the position awkward because the whole protector is unpeeled (i.e., gathering dust) at that time. It could have been avoided by putting the peel tape on the top instead of the bottom.
Nevertheless, it was not a significantly more difficult application than any other one and the perfection needed in the position was worthwhile to create the excellent fit.

Note: I use a Poetic Borderline bumper case and there is no interference between the case and the protector...no edge bubbling or scraping between them.

The feel and look are such that I cannot tell the difference between this and the screen without a protector at all.

I have only used 3-layer PET screen protectors (on about 8 different phones across my whole family). I've never had a problem with them until I got the Nexus 5.
-One set I got from ebay wasn't even close to spec (the sensor cutouts were in very incorrect positions).
-Another set I got from ebay (extremeguards) worked well except the top did not adhere correctly (leaving bubbles near the top sensors).

The Anker protector is perfect. This will be the one that I keep on for good. Save yourself the time and get the best right now.

UPDATE: 3 months later and I am still on the same screen protector. It still looks great. The only bummer is that this exact same one isn't sold for the other phones I have in the family. Granted, I'm easy on my phones, but this is amazing...it still looks like new.

Note: I was supplied a sample for test and evaluation. However, my review is fair and honest. Really. I wouldn't hold back if the product were bad.

text:
You are probably familiar with the negative aspects of this camera already: the focus is still on the slow side, even after the firmware update to version 2.02. However, at current prices, this is a ridiculously easy recommendation. The picture quality produced by the full-size APS-C sensor is *so much* better than even high-end digicams, with rich skin tones and blurry backgrounds that are simply not possible with the smaller sensors in those cameras. And with the 22mm f/2.0 prime lens (my recommendation due to its utility in flashless indoor photography), it actually still fits into a large pocket.

Think of it this way: the 22mm lens retails for around $200 anyway, so during the best sales, you are essentially getting the camera body for $100. At some later date, you can pick up the successor to the EOS-M, which will have superior focusing, and is rumored to come with an improved zoom lens. At that point you will have two quality lenses, and a backup body, probably for under $1000. And you can play with this imperfect but enjoyable gem in the meantime.

title: Pogoplug: A plug without an outlet
text:
The Pogoplug series 4 is an internet device that will connect to the Pogoplug website to upload items from various external hard drives. The only requirement is that the connection cable must plug into a USB drive. There are 2 USB ports for external hard drives.

Setup is fairly straight-forward. Plug in. Connect Ethernet cable from a router. Connect external hard drives. Sign up a Pogoplug account.

However, that is where the ease ends. It will ONLY categorize the external hard drive contents. It is able to recognize your current computer's inner hard drive and is able to upload 5 GB worth of data into your Pogoplug.

After 5 GB, it requires a monthly subscription. So, after buying a $100 device, you wouldn't think there would be a monthly subscription. If Pogoplug is able to upload 5GB - why not more? It is merely another avenue to create revenue.

At this point, Pogoplug has required a $100 investment whereas Dropbox or SugarSync allows similar data storage services and prices without the initial hardware investment. Disappointing to say the least. It should also be noted that the external hard drive contents ARE NOT uploaded to an external source (ie a cloud). It is merely a "link" to the contents. This means if your home internet goes down - then your files are inaccessible AND if you do have Internet you must wait until the file is UPLOADED and THEN YOU MUST DOWNLOAD IT. (A worthless concept as well).

Finally, of course, if the Pogoplug website ever is removed (and let's be honest, many products come and go in this space), your Pogoplug is left completely useless.

Move along, people. Nothing to see here.

title: Amazon released the Kraken.
text:
First off I'm a tech junkie and own a Roku, Chromecast, Boxee and Apple TV. I gave up cable 3 years ago and haven't looked back. Instead I have put my trust into streaming devices. At heart I'm a hardcore gamer and when I heard about the Amazon Fire TV I got extremely excited. I've read various reviews from various popular blogs that really didn't seem to answer any questions that I had about the device before purchasing it. So, I felt compelled to write a small review about what YOU need to know about the Amazon Fire TV.

The Fire TV is a sexy little device that looks good in the living room. It's small and will fit in any entertainment center. After hooking up the device your greeted with a short tutorial. What I really disliked about Roku, Boxee, and Apple TV is when you navigate through Apps such as Hulu or Netflix it gets very sluggish. You don't have that issue with the Fire TV. With the speedy hardware it makes navigating through Hulu or Netflix is a breeze. Talking about apps, Amazon really hit a home-run with it's app library. I was delighted to see some of the apps that I use on my phone in the starting line-up. Also, if your a mobile gamer you won't be disappointed as Amazon actually some awesome hit's ready to go. Now, one of the main selling points of the Boxee was it's ability to play a lot of the popular video formats. After finding out that Plex was available for the Fire TV I jump aboard. Now I have the best of both worlds, a fast device and also a device that is capable of streaming popular video formats. Now, what's special about the Fire TV is Amazon's Prime membership. Should you opt in? Well, it's up to you. I'm a Prime member and enjoy the line-up that Amazon currently has, also Amazon is working hard to bring more movies to their line-up as well. It's certainly a lot better than Netflix, and I'm a Netflix customer. And last, the Voice Search is totally awesome. At first I thought it was gimmick but after using it I can't go to any other streaming device. This thing makes typing a thing of the past. The Voice Search is very powerful I would say it's on par with Siri. Yes, I said it.

So is it worth the purchase? YES!

Pros:

1.) Great App lineup
2.) Device looks great in the living room ;-)
3.) Netflix & Hulu aren't sluggish.
4.) ASAP Technology is AWESOME.
5.) Voice Search is AWESOME once you try it your hooked.
6.) Listening to Pandora while playing games.

Cons:
1.) Interface is cluttered. Need to be able to configure the inteface.
2.) The game controller isn't comfortable. A pro controller needs to be offered.
3.) Controller support needs to be offered.
4.) Needs more network options, proxy, ports etc;
5.) Needs more memory for apps. This is the type of device that will turn you into an app junkie.

title: Exactly what I needed at half of what I was prepared to pay.
text:
Lately all the photo magazines have been touting the 18-250 mm zoom that Sigma just released, so this lettle gem of 18-200 mm has run its course of reviews and benchmark tests as well as the glossy full-page ads that Sigma has been buying in the monthlies. I used telefoto lenses when digital was starting to replace film, and I worked/played with a Minolta 300mm zoom. Image quality was ok, but the very reason you buy a telefoto is to aim quickly and shoot. I can't do that with a 300mm. I was in China with this grenade launcher and I saw a blue hawk soar over my head, grabbed the Minolta and tried to find the bird in my viewfinder, but I really needed a spotter scope. I caught a full shot the exotic soaring beauty in the corner of the print.

Problems like this all but disappear with a moderate telefoto designed as brilliantly as the 18-200 Sigma. I use it with a Canon mount on my Rebel T1i. One needs to spend some time with it playing and shooting in the neighborhood to become used to it, but the learning curve demands very little time and effort, and the reward of the first few shots will keep you motivated. Quality is excellent, response to the camera body (white balance, exposure adjustments etc.) is in perfect synch. There were some complaints about "creep" in reviews of the 18-250mm, but 1)that goes with the telefoto territory and 2) the 18-200 has shown very little of that. Besides, you simply turn the sleeve counterclockwise and lock it in one swift movement--who can complain?

So far I have no negatives to report on this fine little enhancement. The Canon body has all the gizmos I need. Now if I could get my computer to work I could print some of these shots that certainly look like prizewinners in the little screen on the back.

Thomas Barran, Brooklyn

title: Doesn't fully work. Garmin support horrible!
text:
I received my 665 and spent a few hours doing a very neat installation on my bike. I got the XM working easily, just like it had withmy 376C this was replacing. I was excited to have the phone capabilities. My iPhone 4S paired right up, but when I place a call I can hear the person on the other end, but they couldn't hear me. I called Garmin support and held for quite some time and then got someone to help me. They walked me through some things to try, and had me hook the unit up to the computer to make sure it was up to date, and it was. After trying everything he suggested it was still doing the exact same thing, so I called and held and held again. This time when the support rep had me hook it up to the computer and open a folder he said my unit was missing files that could only be installed at the factory. He told me to send my unit and all accessories back. I explained that many of the accessories were already installed and that it was a few hour install. He said it didn't matter. I complained and he said he would talk with a supervisor. After hold for quite a while he came back and gave me a return number and said they would mail a new unit after they received mine, but then he had trouble inputting it into the computer. Turns out the 665 has been discontinued and they could only replace it with a refurbished unit! Oh well, I wanted one that at least worked, so I mailed mine off and waited for over a week for the refurbished unit to get to me. Hooked it to the computer to make sure it was all all up to date and put it in the cradle on the bike. It does the exact same thing! I am extremely unhappy.

I have searched online and there seems to be a fair number of folks with various intercom systems that have the exact same problem. Garmin told me the iPhone 4S is 100% compatible with the Zumo 665. Now I have wasted almost two weeks, and I have a refurbished unit when I paid for a new one, and it still doesn't work properly. Not at all a happy camper. I will contact the amazon seller and see if they can help at all.

UPDATE 6/10/2014: The Zumo 665 has continued to disappoint. I have wasted hours on the phone with Garmin tech support. The device frequently shuts down randomly. The screen will freeze and not change. The screen calibration goes haywire. In order to plan routes with Garmin Basecamp I have to hook my 665 to the computer. Express won't allow me to download the maps to my PC, even after a couple of hours spent with tech support to try to remedy it. The help file for Basecamp doesn't always work. In a 450 mile ride the device turned itself off ten times, and the screen froze a half dozen times and I had to restart the device. No amount of resets seems to cure the problem. I have read they are sensitive to errors on sd cards, so I have tried it without a card installed and it doesn't make a difference. The seller Dealboss offered nothing, no help at all. Will never purchase anything through them again. I continue to be extremely disappointed with the Zumo 665 as well as the associated Garmin software.

title: This must be a practical joke!
text:
At first glance, this Bluetooth headset by BlueAnt looks to be professionally made, and packaged. It looks expensive, and like a quality headset. But looks, as is made clear in my experience with this headset, can definitely be deceiving.

First off, comfort and sensible design: I couldn't get this thing to properly seat in my ear canal because of the way the ear hook attaches to the headset. Unlike my Samsung Bluetooth headset, where the channel for the ear hook allows it full rotation without snapping off of the headset, this BlueAnt headset's ear hook channel does not go completely around the speaker stem, and is fixed in one position. Try to move it from that position, and the hook unseats itself from the headset, allowing the headset to easily fall out of your ear (in fact, you'd be hard-pressed to get the daggone thing to stay IN your ear at any point, from my experience, but most DEFINITELY at THAT one). The ear cushions themselves all either seem too big - especially with that nonsensical half rubber band built into the side (the presence of which is never explained) - or too small; I never encountered a comfortable, Goldilocks-esque "just right". And, for the cushions that don't have that rubber band, there's only large, and small. No medium came in my package, and no, it didn't drop down in the packaging when I removed the headset; it just isn't there.

But, okay, it's a Bluetooth headset, and should have quality sound and audio, right? WRONG! I was holding my phone in my hand, no more than a foot from the headset, and it didn't matter whether I was on a call (where my callers complained I sounded ridiculously tinny and hollow, to the point where my voice was distorted enough that trying to carry on a conversation with this thing on was well nigh impossible), or trying to listen to music. Even in simply listening to my music collection on my phone, the sound dropped out every second and a half, as it had also done on my calls. No, it wasn't the quality of the Mp3s. There were no scratches that caused that skipping, it was just the ineptitude of this headset.

Overall, I'm just disgusted with the quality of this headset. I've owned my fair share of Bluetooth headsets in my time, and this has really, truly, got to be the worst one that I've ever attempted to use. I seriously can't think of a worse one. BlueAnt shouldn't even be giving these away, because the sheer ridiculousness of their poor quality would be enough that nobody would get any use out of them to make the setup of it worthwhile. The features it offers sound great, but what do those count for when the entire function of the thing - to transmit sound - is such a colossal failure? Unfathomably bad! And at seventy bucks, too? They must be off their rockers!

Jabra has always served me well when it came to in-ear and Bluetooth headsets. If you're interested in a new Bluetooth headset, I'd suggest you go with one of theirs, instead. Don't even bother with this thing. SO not worth the money!!!

title: Good Sound Quality in a Great Package
text:
Note: This is an adaptation of my review of the [[ASIN:B005KFONIU Bose SoundLink Wireless Mobile Speaker - Nylon]], which is also an excellent option, as noted below.

I recently purchased several bluetooth speakers to test in my bedroom and office in hopes that I would like one enough to keep. Before I get into the details, I'll cut to the chase and let you know that I decided to keep the Big Jambox over the Bose SoundLink. While the Bose puts out a truly impressive amount of sound from such a small, portable package, the sound quality is not as good as the Big Jambox at low to normal volume levels.

The products I tested were the Bose SoundLink Wireless, Jawbone Jambox, Jawbone Big Jambox, and Logitech Wireless Boombox. Without getting into too much detail about other products, I found that the two best speakers for filling a medium to large room with music were the Bose SoundLink and Big Jambox, which isn't a surprise given the that these are the two most expensive speakers of the bunch, both priced at $299. Ultimately, though, I felt that the Big Jambox sounded and looked better (for my taste), so I returned the Bose and Logitech Wireless Boombox (I also kept the little Jambox for my office, which doesn't sound nearly as good as the bigger speakers, but makes for a great ultra-portable speaker for half the price ($150)).

My biggest problem with the sound of the Bose Soundlink is that there's far too much bass at low to normal volume levels. This is a problem for me because the bass clouds the rest of the music -- vocals become difficult to hear and the treble is nearly non-existent. The Bose sounds muddy and veiled under these circumstances, especially in small rooms. And to be clear, I'm a big fan of bass. I hate speakers that have no bass because the music I listen to (jazz, pop, hip hop, electronic) really benefit from bass. In contrast, the Big Jambox has a much better balance of bass, midrange, and treble at low to normal volume levels, providing a clearer overall sound.*

However, this is only an issue when the volume on the Bose is lower. As you turn the volume up, the bass becomes less pronounced, as if the other frequencies get louder but the bass stays at the same level. It sounds much much better when the volume is cranked up. In fact, I would say the Bose sounds significantly better than the Big Jambox at high volumes -- at their loudest settings, the Bose projects a bigger, richer sound than the Big Jambox, which can sound a bit shrill and boxed in at its higher settings. The "better" speaker ultimately comes down to how loud you listen to music.

This isn't to say that the Big Jambox sounds bad at high volumes. Frankly, I don't think anyone relying on a small wireless speaker is expecting perfection. The Big Jambox can still fill a very large room with an impressive amount of sound, and I find that it tends to distort less at higher volumes than the Bose. Not to mention the Big Jambox comes in a fantastic package. The speaker in white is extremely attractive, well built, has a long battery life, syncs easily with multiple devices, and has a great speakerphone option. Ultimately, I preferred the sound of the Big Jambox for my use and decided to keep that speaker. If you're more of a party-level listener, though, you would be wise to choose differently.

*One issue I've had with the Big Jambox is that, unlike the Bose, the Big Jambox emits a static "hissing" sound that is audible in a quiet room. If you listen to music at low volume or sit near the speaker, this sound will be very obvious (and possibly quite annoying). The Bose has no hiss sound whatsoever. I'm hoping this is an issue Jawbone can fix with a firmware update, as they did with the little Jambox, but it's not much of an issue for me since I listen at normal volumes and never sit near the speaker.

title: I love this TV
text:
Pros:
Bright, vivid picture quality.
Handles fast moving picture better than comparable models.
3D is amazing.
Large Screen size for the money
Good sound for a flat panel.

Cons:
"Flashlighting"
Viewing Angle issues
Glossy Screen

I'm not afraid to say that I got an absolute steal on this TV. Through price matching I got it at a storefront for $1750 INCLUDING a 3d blu-ray player and 2 pairs of Sharp's Active 3D glasses. I originally went into the store to see the Samsung UN60D6400 in person, but was quickly turned off by how poorly it handled the football game being played by the store. Motion blur all over the place. Both of the TVs next to it (Samsung Un60d7000 and the Sharp LC60le835u) handled it considerably better, with a noticeable edge actually going to the sharp. In fact, I didn't notice any of that pixelated look at all, even with the poor feed that stores display their units on. Factor in the price difference, and it became a no-brainer that the Sharp was the TV for me.

I did not purchase this TV specifically for the 3D capabilities, but since I got the deal that I got I picked up The Lion King 3D bluray and I am completely blown away by its ability. One complaint that I've read all over the internet is that the 3D cheapens and darkens the image on the screen. This TV, even directly out of the box, has a much brighter display- so the dimming caused by the 3D makes it on par about with what most TVs look like in standard mode. I love how bright and vibrant the TV looks, even directly out of the box. It even handles the blacks extremely well. I've become a 3D fan, simply because of how well this TV displays those images. Also, most flat panels produce VERY poor sound quality. You can actually get away with just using the factory speakers on this TV and it even provides a little 'punch' to the movies. I highly recommend getting a surround sound system if you are investing this kind of money into a TV, but you will do alright with just the regular speakers.

I wish I could give this TV a 5-star, because I adore it, and I would have bought the same deal over again 100 times out of 100; however I do want to make sure people are aware of a couple issues. Whenever I first put in a blu-ray, there is definite "flashlight" effect where certain spots of the TV with no image show brighter than other spots of the tv. I will qualify that by saying that I have watched some dark movies and paused on the blackest scenes possible, and when it is actually displaying an image I can't find even a trace of the flashlighting, it only seems to be when the movie is loading. I am sure some people will be turned off by the bright spots on the load screen. Also, the viewing angle of this TV definitely has a little bit of an issue. That doesn't at ALL mean that if you are sitting on the extreme sides you won't see a picture, it just means that the picture looks better sitting directly in front of it than it does from extreme angles. Even standing right along side you can still SEE a picture (not that you'd ever watch from that angle anyway), but the further out to the sides you get from the tv, the colors wash out slightly. Again, to me this is nitpicking, because the way my room is laid out, no seats will suffer from any loss of Picture Quality. If you are planning on putting the TV in a bright room, this TV has a Plasma-like gloss to the display and can definitely pick up more reflection than most LEDs do. As long as you are putting it in a room without excess light, that shouldn't be a problem.

Overall I'd give this TV a 90/100, only docking some points for flashlight effects and viewing angle. I really wish I could give this 4.5 stars, but Amazon does not give that option. I am a little leary of putting a 5-star review on it because of just a few small issues, so 4 stars it is. Still a VERY HIGHLY recommended purchase.

title: Good for content you don't access often. First backup - long & painful. Cannot expect more with 800Mhz CPU & 250 MB RAM.
text:
WD My Book 2TB is a very good storage for music, pictures and videos which you don't access too often.

Pros

- Excellent out of the box experience. Connect the power and the network cable, and the drive shows up immediately on windows 7
- Comes with basic file shares. Easy to understand and populate with contents, as a first time user.
- Nice web user interface.
- Smooth usage after the first time backup / file transfer
- Excellent wd2go and wd photos iOS applications.

Cons

- The first session of transferring files is going to be painful. The speed is extremely slow on WiFi ( ~3 to 5 mbps ) and ~12 mbps wired. This is with a decent Cisco Linksys N900 router !
- The unit has a 800MHz CPU ( my unit has the APM82181 cpu ) and just 250 MB RAM. This, in addition to the disk drivers probably explains the slow speed. Many would blame the routers for speed, but that is not the right bottleneck.
- Considering the speed, probably not good for auto-backup.
- Copying files across shares does not do an internal copy. It seems to download everything to the device from where copy was initiated. And then it uploads the content back to the destination folder. Not sure why !!!

Some useful tips
- As a novice user, its better to have the drive wired to the router, for large file transfers.
- For better access control, get familiar to the users and shares. Create multiple users with their private shares. Then provide them access to the other shares rather that putting everything in the public shares. This way, sharing contents with family and friends is much more controlled.
- [ A bit risky but rewarding tip ]
If you are comfortable with Linux shell, open ssh access with [...]
Now copying files across the shares is a breeze !!
And the possibilities to manage the device are endless. You can customize it the way you want.

title: Takes Some Experimentation
text:
The Sto-Fen flash diffuser is a quality product. It's substantial in construction and fits the SB-400 snugly. This isn't going to fall off and be lost. The diffuser is large enough to allow the flash head to rotate throughout its entire range, but the diffuser must be removed to allow adjustment. The instructions provided are meager but adequate, and Sto-Fen's website has more information.

So how does it work? That's where the experimentation comes in. The diffuser certainly changes the quality of the flash. Used for interior shots, the effect is to soften the light while reducing its range. I found that spot metering gave me a brighter exposure in my application. The other effect of the diffuser was a slight color cast. The recommended settings bounce the diffused flash, and that can result in some unexpected coloring. Shooting the flash straight on through the diffuser avoided this result. With or without the diffuser, the camera is still using a direct light source. There's less harshness in the flash, but shadowing remains. A diffuser is not a substitute for more sophisticated lighting.

That said, I find the diffuser to be a useful addition to my camera kit. Using it effectively takes an investment in time. I have to experiment and see how it works in my environment. It's not something I would use all the time, but the cost is modest, and I'm glad I have it in hand.

title: Technology to come. . .
text:
A little background: I've been a film user probably forever. Only 7 years ago I decided to go digital with a Canon EOS30D and never looked back. I'm in no way a "pro" by definition, but I do know what I want to do and what "tools" to achieve them with. Fast forward to the NEX-7. What a piece of technology! First things first: This is not a camera you want to "upgrade" to if you come from a point-n-shoot background or basic DSLR's. Smaller, compact and radical menu designs will quickly frustrate even the most seasoned pro DSLR users. But if you take the time to learn about it, just like how you would learn going from film to digital, it is a VERY powerful camera. With respect to other reviewers on this site the Tri-Nav system IS highly "customizable" [Gary L. Friedman covers this in his NEX-7 ebook].

I had rented it from our local camera shop [with the kit 18-55mm] to try it out. At first I was totally unimpressed and brought it back. The clerk offered me the Zeiss F1.8 to try with the NEX-7. What a night & day difference! YES! to take advantage of the Sony sensor you NEED quality glass to compliment it. So I bought the body only and purchased the Zeiss F1.8 & a Tamron Zoom lens [for traveling]. My passion for photography is ignited again and I'm excited to build a system about the NEX. Yes, there are limitations right now because there are not a lot of accessories and lenses for the NEX system. Sony has always been slow in that regard. But, I also purchased an adaptor to use my older Canon lenses [unfortunately, manual F-stop and focus] and am able to get those shots I so desire. OK, so pros & cons for me:

PROS
1) Compact body LOADED with features.
2) Electronic View Finder [EVF] is a big game changer enabling me to "see" what the sensor sees.
3) Tilt-screen lets me get those overhead shots or low to the ground POV scenes that I like for street photography.
4) With fast SD cards I can get action shots in RAW at about 4 to 7fps depending on the scene. I get 10 to 12fps with JPG.
5) "Peeking" focus assist helps with the telephoto shots
6) FAST startup and responsive controls. You hardly ever miss any shots you want to take.
7) LIVE VIEW mode is maintained through continuous shooting up to about 5fps
8) All the data overlays on the live view screen helps set up shots.
9) Low light shots are/at equal to the DSLR 'cousins'.
10) and, of course, the Image Quality is the best! [with good glass!]. Pixel peepers may even find it hard to fault the images.

CONS
1) There is no way at this time [firmware?] to save different shoot settings like the way DSLRs cans save 2 or 3 settings. So unless you are in iA mode you have to think about every shot you do. This is one reason why point-n-shoot upgraders WILL get frustrated with this camera.
2) Auto ISO is only limited to 1600 max.
3) Auto Bracketing is limited [+/- 0.7 is not a lot to work with]
*note firmware 1.01 now adds ev +3 or -3 with 3 shots auto.
4) Battery life sucks so I have auto off feature ON and I carry a spare battery. With the fast startup I won't miss much.
5) The hot-shoe is Sony proprietary so unless you have an adaptor it uses only Sony flashes and accessories.
6) Pop-up flash will cast shadows on zoom lenses
7) Not many good E-Lenses. . . YET!
8) In low light the EV is VERY grainy. Hard to compose shots. Switching to the Live View glows on your face too much.
9) Sometimes it takes time for the NEX to track in low light. [Uses Contrast AF. Wish it was Phase like the Sony DSLRs]

[FYI if you want to see what I use this with you are free to take a look at some of my pics: [...]]

Movie Mode: I admit I have not used this feature a lot since I am mostly a stills photographer. But it works well enough. I did not take many movies with it, but I was impressed at the high-quality, the autofocusing, and the overall ease.

Overall this is an amazing piece of technology coming from a film background. It does take some getting used to handling and using. I took the time to learn and found this easy to setup. Not as easy as it's bigger DSLR cousins, but easy enough for what it does. Sony has got a winner with the NEX. Can't wait to see what else is coming!
