title: Great earbuds w/ a mic for listening to EDM while running.
text:
V-Moda Bass Freq Metal 3-Button Apple (Nero) Review

First off, I am really picky when it comes to ear buds. I was born with horrible designed ear canals that often hurt when it comes to using ear buds for longer than twenty minutes. At home I have a pair of Sony MDR-V6s[[ASIN:B00001WRSJ Sony MDR-V6 Monitor Series Headphones with CCAW Voice Coil]] and Audio Technica ATH-M30s, so I've listened to "good" headphones but I am definitely not an audiophile, maybe a novice if applicable.

OK, so I needed a new pair of ear buds. Originally I have used MEElectronics Sport-Fi M6 for a year. They worked very well, very good at noise isolation, when I clapped my hands some sound would be heard still. I liked how those ear buds were supported by my ear. But I accidentally ripped one of the wires to the ear bud during summer of 2013 so I was left with the ear buds from the Samsung Galaxy S4. Those were alot worse, hurt my ears, and now I am somewhat glad that one of my dogs ate the ear buds.

After running once with the ATH-M30s, I knew I looked incredibly silly, so after a payday I wanted a new pair of ear buds. I wanted to get something louder than the Sport-Fi M6, preferably with bass. I did not know what I was looking for, I looked at the Sennheiser CX300 & 280 as I do like their PXC 250 alot. Also looked at JLabs, some JVCs, & Sonys too. It took me awhile to browse, I really wanted to try those twist to fit Sennheisers as one reviewer said they worked very well. Before I bit the bullet, I saw some V-Modas variations, because their Crossfades are rated very well. After a few looking around, I found these in my favorite Electronics color, black. Had to get them. So I bought them and I was very surprised that Amazon shipped them to me on Sunday (bought it late Friday night).

Build Quality:
Opened them up, they come with three different ear buds and a little soft fabric bag to hold them. V-Moda is printed on the bag with their "-v-" symbol but it seems it would wear over time. Cute stuff, but I needed to know how well they played. The 3.5MM jack is interesting because its not a plain straight one or right angle, rather its kinda like a broken wishbone, pistol or half of a peace symbol without the outer circle. THAT might be a bother to some users, it is different from what I'm used to but it doesn't apply to my Galaxy S4 with the running armband or Otterbox Defender case. I am not sure if these are waterproof and I won't take that chance. For the ear bud wires the main cord is decently sized, not super thick but very flexible. I had gotten the 3 button one and I am sure it will take time to remember the placement of the buttons. When the wire splits to the ear buds it gets definitely thinner and the cylinder piece that holds it seems plasticy, but looks very nice still. Now I don't think this wire will be very sturdy, but the Sport-Fi M6 had a reinforced wire that ripped easily when I gave it a good tug underneath heavy blankets. The actual ear buds are made of metal or a nice metalic plastic. It looks very nice with the small grooves, definitely well built.

The Sound:
So I plugged it in, played some AFX, I immediately felt the bass I was searching for. Like driving a car with a decent sound system, I felt the bass but only in my ears. I was immediately in love with the sound. They isolate sound very well, better than the M6. So that night I listened to more EDM and classical. They work very very good, I have gotten tired of the piercing sound the MDR-V6s give out on some of the vocals, but those are monitor headphones and aren't necessarily for everyday listening (still great never the less). You can hear the musicians hand movement very well when it comes to the strings. When it comes to the EDM there isn't much distortion in there and when it comes to bass heavy songs, the ear buds don't distort too much when it comes to the big booms, they can still produce sounds. I am sure if I had spent $50 I would of gotten less distortion but, well 30 dollars seemed like a good deal, plus I wasn't sure if it had a mic for phone calling. I am very happy with the sound I do get, Hard Rock will sound fine with these as well.

While running:
I was immediately in love with these, but I knew I had to run with em. My ears do get uncomfortable, but they seem to be better then the M6 by a lot. I would just move them a bit when I would be bothered. As I said they isolate sound very well, which means they don't let any sound leak through. So I put them on and started to run. I had forgotten to snap on the attachment that pinches clothings so the cord doesn't bounce around. I grabbed the cord and threw it behind my head over my shoulder, it worked very well. A reviewer made a comment upon how it crackles when the jack is moved. From the running it does move a bit, so a little bit of wiggling it around and it stopped conflicting with my shirt. But the crackle sound was very small from what I was used to. Today just happened to be a cool day so I didn't sweat that much but the ear buds stay well in place in my ear canals and they don't bug me much as the wire doesn't touch the side of my face. It was a very fun run, the sound I wanted felt very good. I did get uncomfortable while wearing them yes, but that is my ears fault. Compared to the M6 I would often adjust them because they would somewhat loosed while running, these however stayed in place well.

The drawback:
There is a drawback on these but it isn't something that really bothered me. I had gotten the 3 button model but when it comes to using it on my S4 w/ AOKP rom, the only button that works is the Pause/Play button. The volume buttons do not work for my media, but I don't see it as a big deal because my phone is in reach. I do not believe it works as a volume controller for a laptop either. I am not sure if it needs extra software for android or how well it works for iPhone, but it is not a hassle for me. title: Very cool radio with a few problems.
text:
Overall, I have to say that this is a fantastic radio. It sounds great, the bluetooth phone mode is flawless and the visuals are the best I've ever seen on any radio (and I've had a lot of them). The HD radio gets great reception and I love the way it sorts music when you play it through the USB stick. There's definitely plenty of features to keep you busy. The people that left a bad review because it wasn't compatible with their phone is just silly. Do some research first!

Now there are a couple bugs I found with this radio.

The "visualizer mode" has a lot of lag on this model and takes sometimes 10 - 30 seconds to load. This isn't a problem on the lower model XAV602BT. This isn't a deal breaker, just a bit annoying.

The main problem is as of right now, this radio will not work with the Sony XA-NV300T navigation module. It seems to have a software problem. When it temporarily loses GPS reception, the radio doesn't know what to do so it just reboots the navigation module which takes 20 seconds or more. This happens every 1 - 10 minutes so as of right now it's not usable. I have the XAV602BT with the same XA-NV300T module in my other car and it works perfect. I tried swapping GPS modules and even got a 2nd XAV712HD radio and it has the exact same problem. The Sony technical support is just short of useless. I feel I'd get more help if I talked to a robot then a person that knows absolutely nothing about the problem that just looks up the answer on their PC with the conclusion that "it's broken". Sorry, it's not broken. That doesn't explain why 2 of them with 2 different nav modules have the exact same problem. It's a software problem. If you look at the recent firmware updates, version 1.20 says "fixes GPS recovery XAV602BT only". Hopefully this same update will happen for this radio in the near future because I'd hate to get rid of it.

But if you don't need the navigation module because you use the GPS on your phone then this radio will work great for you!

title: Dont spend the premium expecting a quality system
text:
At the time that I purchased this system (april 2012) it had an almost 800 dollar price tag from amazon. I assumed paying more meant I would get higher quality cameras and more importantly higher quality software. Having previously owned an SVAT 4 camera setup which was less than half as much it left much to desire in a security setup. I will start with the pros of this system.

Pros
- It supports audio monitoring
- They have an android app (albeit buggy)
- The video quality is decent enough to make out a face if the cameras are positioned properly

Cons
- The finish on the cameras is awful. They started oxidizing/fading and turning gold in the Arizona sun 2 WEEKS after install
- The screws that come with it are trash (the heads literally snap right off under low torque)
- Forget about getting the mobile/web browser app to work if you have an app (details below)
I work in IT/Networking for a living and am very technically savvy. I attempted to use multiple routers with every possible setting (UPNP/Firewall/DMZ/flashing different firmware/static routing/e.t.c.)I eventually gave in and connected a switch behind the cable modem + paid a monthly premium for a second IP address for the DVR and moblie viewing still was not functioning. When I called their technical support (outsourced to india) I spoke to a representative about the situation who kept stating "sir you have to forward the correct ports in your router" I had to argue with her that that was irrelevant because the DVR was not behind a router and the interface was connected directly to the ISPs WAN. After 15 minutes of arguing I requested to speak with a higher tier of support. I was transferred to a supervisor who was polite and said he would email me instructions to update the firmware on the DVR to see if that solved the issue. I never received the email even though I verbally confirmed my email address (Yes I checked my spam filter). I had to call back again and request the link to download new firmware. This time I received the email so I had to run out to the store to buy a usb flash drive. The firmware update went smoothly (yay! one thing went right) and after trying a few different ports I was able to get mobile view working on both the web browser and android.
- One of the cameras died after 6 months
- The web viewer does not work with windows 8 no matter what browser/security settings you try

With its current amazon price (just over 500) I can say you get what you pay for. If you are looking at a quality setup then look elsewhere.

title: Excellent, but you need preparation, patience,and some luck
text:
First time I bought it I tried to apply it on the screen of my macbook pro and was not successful. I had read the reviews and had opened the shower tub to keep the room as dust-free as it gets. I laid the laptop flat down (the screen down on top of a soft piece of cloth) and after cleaning the screen carefully I peeled of the 1st cover and started the application. Problem is that although I thought I had it perfectly aligned (on the sides: along the long parts of the screen), in fact it was not (we are talking about fractions of mm). As a result once I was 3/4 finished it was touching the long side edge and could not sit firmly on the screen letting air coming in.. I peeled it off, but then I was already upset, completely inpatient, did it wrong and just threw it away.

I bought it again, and did all the same steps, did the work in the shower room, with the tub open until the mirror went foggy, then I closed the tup, cleaned the screen with the microfiber piece of cloth, and started very carefully: Peeled off only 3-4 cm of cover #1, applied it so that it touches the short side of the screen but kept almost 0.5mm from the 2 long sides. Then continued slowly. I aligned it perfectly and kept going , while using the little carton (vertically from top to bottom) to remove any air-bubbles (in fact I did not get more than 4-5 along the way, just make sure screen is perfectly clean) as I progressed. Once I progressed, I released 3-5cm of the cover#1 and kept going the same way. I finished in 5-7 minutes, and It fit perfectly my laptop, without even 1 bubble, or without even a molecule of dust or anything. Perfect all because of (1) the 'tub' hint , (2) because I cleaned the screen perfectly before, and (3) because I aligned it perfectly at the beginning. It cost me twice, but I don't regret it as I hate screen marks and scratches which inevitably come. Love it.

title: GREAT combination of control and easy of use
text:
I've been enjoying photography for nearly 40 years, and if there's one lesson I've learned in that time, it's that most folks would do better to spend LESS money on a camera and more on learning how to take better pictures. Time after time, I see people toting around expensive cameras loaded with features they don't know how to use, ignoring fundamental photographic principles, all based on the assumption that the high cost of their camera will compensate for what they don't know. Well, it won't. Save money and buy a camera like this one and spend the rest of your photography budget on some good introductory classes and LOTS of time in the field practicing.

Panasonic burst on the scene a few years ago with a line of cameras that deliver great performance at a great price AND provide wonderful feedback to the shooter before and after the shot is taken. Controls are intuitive, zoom range is amazing and overall quality is certainly suitable for enthusiastic amateurs or even professionals who don't need to print large format images. It's light to carry and hold and offers all the features you need for true creative control. In a year's worth of shooting, I only miss having a true digital SLR about 1/2 of 1% of the time ... not enough to justify unless you have more money floating around than you know what to do with. I've shot with SLR's for a long, long time, but this camera made me all but forget about them.

title: As good as a cabled mouse
text:
My wife needed a new mouse on her pc, and we agreed to try a wireless mouse instead of a wired one. She and I have only used wired mice before, and had never tried a wireless one. For the price, the Microsoft Wireless Mobile Mouse 4000 is as good as any wired mouse I have used.

Installation was automatic...Windows 7 and Vista both recognized it immediately, installed the appropriate drivers, and a minute later, it was fully functional.

The only downside, is that the USB nano transceiver has a very short range, and the signal is easily blocked by metal PC cases or other things in the way. I installed it in a spare USB port in the back of desktop pc. It worked OK, BUT performance was herky jerky, and not even close to what I could tolerate. I then installed the USB nano transceiver in a USB hub that I have on top of desktop case, about 36" line of site from the mouse, and voila! Perfect performance.

I then made a few tweaks of the acceleration and speed, and it now performs exactly like the wired mouse I have used for years.

I then installed another one on my wife's Vista desktop, but this time placed it in one of her USB ports on the front panel of her PC. Again, after some automatic driver installation, within a minute hers was working perfectly as well.

There are probably lots of other wireless mice that you can spend 3-4 times as much on, and sure, they may have longer range, longer battery life, etc. But for the price, the assured Microsoft compatibility, and with none of the bloated "mouse software" that is so common with other brands, this is the mouse to buy. Recommend it highly.

title: Defective and ill-conceived

Two days after the vacation started, the camera failed utterly:  every picture turned out black, although the viewfinder looked great and the focus seemed to be working.  I attempted some phone troubleshooting and it looks like the shutter was working fine, but the image sensor was completely blown.  This camera was securely packed, not jostled, not mistreated at all - it's just a failure.  While troubleshooting I searched the Internet and found that this happens a LOT.  Either the shutter or the image sensor fails and the only option is to send the camera in for repairs that last for weeks:  not really an option when you're camping across the country.  Nikon states that they are "not responsible for lost photo ops" but they really should be responsible for product quality, and they should replace every defective unit by overnight mail if need be.  I will be getting this unit fixed at their expense and then maybe foist it upon an unsuspecting charity before running out to buy another brand.  Nikon has lost a customer with this piece of junk.

title: Nice concept, works to an extent but not aesthetically pleasing solution
text:
I bought a small snoop insert for a small Timbuk 2 classic messenger bag

I can’t fault the quality of the snoop insert.
The camera snoop insert itself is a great concept
But the integration of it with the messenger bag that it’s supposed to pair with is not.

Here’s why. After inserting the snoop insert to the bag and making sure it fits snugly with no gap at the bottom or side.
The fitting is great. That’s not the issue. The issue is when you start putting your DSLR in.
It has space for an APS-C sized DSLR with zoom lens (mine’s a 18-250mm) a full size flash and maybe a video cam or another lens.
My way to placed the DSLR is vertically in. that is the lens is touching the bottom of the bag and the viewfinder and LCD facing you when you look top down

When you zip it up it closed perfectly. When you try to close the messenger bag’s flap, it also secure firmly but unsightly.
That’s because the flap is too short and the inner Velcro/zipped compartment area is visible.

You have to rearrange your gear (e.g. place the DLSR sideways) sacrificing room to reduce the height so that you can squeeze the top part and the flap can cover it fully without exposing the Velcro area.
Another way is to change out a zoom lens with a kit lens or other shorter lens. The height of your flash even when folded may hinder the complete cover of the bag.

Yes, it’s functional but not aesthetically pleasing. In fact purposed built camera messenger bag caters to this bulge and lengthen the cover (speaking from my experience with Crumplers).

So if you are planning to get this so that you can also make use of your existing messenger bag as a camera bag as well.
Stop and consider if you do not mind the cover only comes down half the bag.

title: There are many much better headphones for the price. Do not even consider these.
text:
I wanted to spend about $30-40 on a pair of headphones so I bought four high rated pairs and compared them: Panasonic HTF-600, Sennheiser HD 419, JVC HARX700, and Monoprice 108323. I burned them all in for about 30 hours.

The Sennheisers were absolutely the worse of the bunch. The only pro was they were comfortable and the lightest of the bunch. The velvet padding felt nice and didn't get hot. Other than that, the other three were worlds away in terms of build quality and sound quality. The HD419s felt like a cheap toy that would break any second. The wire is about as thick as fishing line. An the sound - horrible. Muddly, muffled, and quiet. They have no treble at all. They do have some bass, but not as much as the panasonics or monoprice.

Over all I ranked them from best to worst: panasonic, monoprice, JVC, sennheiser. These headphones just are not competitive for the price. I thought that since the high end sennheisers are very good that their low end might be good as well, but this is not the case. These are cheapo headphones meant to be sold in best buy to people who recognize the name but don't actually care about quality.

title: Slate vs. mini
text:
As an owner of an iPad 2, iPad mini, Samsung Galaxy S5 and Amazon Kindle Keyboard, I was excited to have a chance to test out this Beats Special Edition Slate.

The device I have that is the most comparable to the Slate is the iPad mini, and so my review focuses on comparing the advantages and disadvantages that each one offers.

Beyond obvious hardware differences such as the Slate's 7" screen vs. mini's wider 7.9" one, I found the Slate to be thicker than the mini. And even though the screen is smaller, the Slate weighs more at 11.4 ounces whereas the mini is at 10.9 ounces. But ultimately, the weight difference is slight, and one of the reasons for the thickness of the Slate is the removable stylus, which I found to be more useful than I had expected -- especially when clicking on small hyperlinks in the browser.

Another reason for the thickness is the Slate's front stereo speakers. These are much better than the mini's speakers that are seated at the bottom edge. Because the Slate has the dual front speakers, it works much better for watching movies, listening to music, and viewing videos on YouTube. The sound is louder and easier to make out than on the mini. However, don't expect much bass. The speakers, while more advanced, are still a bit tinny. If you want to rock out with the quality that Beats is known for, you are best attaching a pair of Beats headphones (obviously, these are not included).

Another advantage I found with the Slate over the mini is the ability to have multiple profiles. I was able to create a profile on the Slate for myself, my wife, and my daughter. This way, I can log into all my web and app accounts without having anyone else going into them. For instance, I can log into Facebook under my profile and my wife can under hers. Also, I can password protect my profile should I not want anyone else having access to it. Apple's way of thinking is that everyone in the household should have their own tablet, thus there is no need for profiles. However, financial considerations aside, it's nice taking only one table on a car trip and simply sharing it.

The ability to add inexpensive external memory into the Slate is a great advantage too. With Apple, you have to pay quite a bit to get a memory intensive tablet. We're talking hundreds more. But with the Slate, you can simply toss in a Micro SD for much less. This is a more cost effective way to store videos and music.

I have yet to try it out, but the Slate has a Mirco-HDMI hookup that you can connect to a TV (the cable is not provided). The mini does not have an HDMI port. I can see this being a nice feature if you want to stream video content between the two devices, but keep in mind you can do this without cables depending on the TV's capabilities (for instance, you can stream wirelessly through several apps if you have a Chromecast plugged in).

Now, here are some of the things I didn't like about the Slate over the mini. For instance, the battery life on the Slate claims 9-hours. The mini 10-hours. But in reality, there's more than a one hour difference between the two. I've found that I can keep my iPad going for a good week without charging, whereas the Slate only a few days. Part of this is due to the difference between how Android and OSX uses and manages memory (and standby time). And depending on what you do with the device, the battery drains quicker (eg: videos on a bright screen drains quicker than a book on a dimm screen). I mainly use my tablets for checking email, surfing, and reading with the occasional Netflix watching. And between the mini and the Slate, I get a much longer reading life out of the mini (I have both screen brightnesses down low).

Along with this is the annoying grayware/crapware installed on the Slate. A good majority of it is not removable. Meaning, you can't get rid of it. Not unless you root the device, which voids the warranty and messes with future software updates. So you are stuck with junk like Box, edjing, and Evernote.You are also stuck with Beats music, which comes with a 14-day trial (It's $9.99 a month for a 1-user license after that ($14.99 for family plan)). Don't want to pay? You don't have to, but you are stuck with the app cluttering your device.

Another issue I came across on the Slate was a really loud clicking noise that sounded every time I typed a key. Even though I turned all of the sounds off, it still clicked to my ear's dismay. You'd think this was something you could turn off under the sound menu, right? Nope. After doing a fair amount of digging, I found it under: Settings > Language & input > Keyboard & Input Methods. Then, click on the settings icon under "Google Keyboard." Uncheck "Sound on keypress." Why they don't make turning that off easier, I'll never know.

The Slate and the mini have a different home button too. On the mini, there's a physical button at the bottom of the device. On the Slate, the button is only accessible on the screen. Meaning, it isn't instantly available -- at least, it isn't always one click away. Depending on the app, the home button may or may not disappear. Of course, you can typically get it back by swiping upward from the bottom part of the screen, but I personally prefer a physical button for quickly and easy access. I'm getting more used to having it on the screen now, but I still prefer it on the device itself.

Finally, I want to mention my biggest annoyance with the Slate over the mini. On the screen itself there are around 40 horizontal lines from top to bottom (in portrait position). They are evenly spaced like lines on notepaper. Granted, they are hard to see. It took me a day or two before I noticed them. In a dark room you can't see them at all, but if a lamp shines directly on the screen or sunlight gleams through a window, they will appear. I don't understand what these lines are or why they are necessary, but they are there regardless of what app or window you are in. It's part of the hardware, so they are unremovable. That said, the average user might not notice them or even care, but to more picky users like me, I find my annoyance level rising every time I see them.

Between the Slate and the mini, I lean towards the mini. But in reality, the Slate has much to offer too. They are both very nice devices and can perform the same general operations. If you want to watch lots of movies and listen to music, the Slate has the advantage over sound. It is also the way to go if having multiple user profiles is important to you. Otherwise, I think the iPad mini is a better overall device with its longer battery life and better screen.

as I had originally thought. Ordered the Compucessory Power Duster from
Amazon at a less expensive price than the Dust Off ones and I am very pleased with the product (The Compucessory) one, NOT the Dust-Off.

I've deleted two stars because in thinking about it, NO can of compressed air should be difficult to use and these are; they are difficult to press to spray, and the top mechanism itself is not as it should be, just a simple press and spray. It's almost like these cans are what was once called "seconds" or rejects or whatever the terminology these days is when merchandise cannot be sold in the average retail store because of some defect.

I live in New York City where the hardware stores charge anywhere from $8.00 to $10.00 per can for compressed air. And that's all it is, compressed air, so brands never really entered the picture until I ordered these and had a very difficult time with the top mechanism on the can. Usually you just snap off the plastic tab at the top, place the straw provided in its place and presto, you're ready to go.

However, these cans of Dust-Off, were difficult to maneuver because of the way the top spray mechanism is placed. I've been using compressed air for 40 years, and have never, ever had to think twice about it. The Dust-Off cans, in my opinion, turned a simple task into something more complicated and time consuming and that just shouldn't be... The spray mechanism is hard to use and I also felt like the amount of compressed air per can seemed to get used up more rapidly than they should have, and since I am not even slightly double jointed (if there is such a thing as being "slightly"), I wouldn't order these again unless they were one third of the price and even then I'd have to think about it.

For first-time users, PLEASE DO NOT SHAKE THE CAN of any compressed gas... Just flip off the top plastic tab, put the straw in the designated hole and spray. When the can starts getting cold, stop for a while and let it warm up a bit before using it again. This is true with any compressed gas spray. You have to get accustomed to how much pressure to use and to use short spurts. Once you've acquired this simple skill, compressed gas should be so easy to use you don't have to think about it.

The Dust-Off brand just was difficult and different from what I'm used to in terms of pressing down to use it; I found it awkward to manipulate, which made an extremely easy task, more time consuming than it should be. I guess I was surprised because I had never experienced any difficulty with compressed air before, no matter what the task was at hand. I also felt that the amount of air in each can seemed to get used up quicker than they should have and I went through the four cans rather rapidly, so this made me question whether or not I had been sent the original Dust-Off brand or some kind of imitation. I'm convinced that the design of the top mechanism is defective.

After so many years of using compressed air, from photography to computers, and all sorts of different ways, I had to question why I was having difficulty using this particular product. Something was amiss, the design of the top mechanism, the pressure required for use, the rapidity in which the air was used up in each can. When you use a product for so long, when something is different, you notice it right away.

The air pressure is as it should be, but it usually is, and doesn't warrant any extra stars because this is the way a can of compressed air should work. Try another brand. The Dust-Off air pressure isn't any different than the Compucessory brand, nor should it be in any other brand. Compressed gas (or air) are all the same. Order the one I mention or any other brand, but don't waste your money on this one. Compressed gas dusters (or whatever fancy name they're giving pressurized air these days) are all the same by any other name. So why order a product that wastes both your time and money? The price may be attractive, but in this case you are not even getting what you paid for.

title: Hooray for a great lefty mouse at a decent price

As soon as I realized that I had to press the little button on the inside to make it lefty friendly--DUH--it was very intuitive and comfortable to use. The scroll button I feel should be higher on the mouse--I have to angle my hand down a bit to use my index finger to scroll. However, I'm sure it will soon become second nature to use my third finger to scroll.

I love that the DXT comes in a size for small hands, and I actually like it better than my Evoluent, which is definitely a lot bulkier. Sure it's way more pricey than a normal mouse, but if you're having wrist problems this may save your life. I am so elated that I bought this thing. There are a lot of ergo mice options out there, but this one comes at a decent price compared to others, with a great, compact and comfortable design.

I took one star off because once in a while for some reason, if I try to click on something with the mouse, it just won't "stick" on my computer and actually select the item I want. I have to click the tiny button on the button to the "Red" setting and slow the mouse down to select the item. After tooling around with that for a while, the mouse seems to work as normal again.

PS: If you are having trouble with the "reaction time" of the mouse in general, make sure to press the aforementioned tiny button on the bottom of the mouse to specify Slow, Medium, or Fast.

title: For those who don't believe any hype quickly
text:
Pros:

1) Inexpensive without letting go of quality sound and construction

2) Thicker rubberized leather-like muffs to cover the drivers, unlike some leading brands putting flimsy thin layer that tears into little pieces over time.

3) Holds up reasonably well in the gym, given you quickly wipe it clean after the workout as sweat would eventually start deteriorating the muffs.

4) More than satisfying sound reproduction quality for most listeners. Remember that crappy music (both quality and content wise) will sound crappy all the time. But that theory apart, there is just enough bass but it doesn't rule your world like Beats and doesn't get annoying. It has a good thump. The extreme highs can be a bit better but they are absolutely fine the way they are. The mid frequencies (vocals) are admirable.

Cons:

1) The button placement could be a bit better, perhaps on top of the cans, but some people may prefer pressing the buttons with their thumbs but I didn't like it.

2) The cans could be a little bit bigger so they sit around my (rather big) ears, but small to medium ears will fit in just fine and it will be a lot more comfortable for them. The comfort for me is fine, but I felt the need within a couple of hours to take them off for a minute or two and wear them again. Again, smaller ears won't have to do this in my opinion.

3) Mini-USB charger port. It is sturdier I agree, but it is just not common anymore. I have many micro-USB cables but just this one mini-USB charger cable that came with it (which is very well constructed and long).

4) Slight sound leakage at higher volumes in very quiet environments.

I was surprised by this headphones, and it is a keeper.

title: Defective product, shoddy customer service
text:
I loved this computer when I first bought it: high capacity, sleek design, smooth keyboard action, superior speaker sound quality, essentially everything I had looked for in a computer. Plus, for a small additional cost, we were able to add the touchscreen feature that my wife wanted. We really loved it until a few weeks ago, when we discovered that the right side hinge was pulling out of place. After attempting to call Toshiba a few times about the problem and being left on ever-lasting hold, only to give up after 20-30 minutes each time, I noticed that now the cover was separating slightly from the screen, wedged apart by the loose hinge creating upward pressure on the lid. Now I persevered in contacting Toshiba, and actually did get through to a representative on several occasions, each time explaining patiently to a good-natured but profoundly unhelpful customer service representative that the computer had not been dropped, bumped or damaged in any way, that the hinge had simply worked its way loose in the course of normal opening and closing of the cover. After emailing photographs - twice, for the first email apparently never reached Toshiba- I was finally told by a manager that Toshiba considered the problem to be "physical damage" to the computer, and not a "mechanical" defect covered by the manufacturer's warrantee. The best solution offered was to take the computer to a nearby service center where I could pay to have the computer repaired. I was flabbergasted.

I have purchased at least a dozen Toshiba products over the years, and some have lasted longer than others, but this is the first that failed in any way when it was still , for all intents and purposes, brand new. Some research on the internet reveals that spontaneously broken plastic hinges are a common problem with this line of laptops, and I have not read a single account in which Toshiba gladly or even willingly took responsibility for the failure of their product to stand up to normal wear and tear from everyday use. Furthermore, each time I have spoken with Toshiba I have been promised a call back within 24 to 48 hours, and despite being told "don't worry, we will take care of the problem" at the end of each conversation, not one of my six or seven phone calls has to this day been returned. Each time I have had to call Toshiba back and explain the problem all over again in some kind of Groundhog Day recurring bad dream.

When I spend $750 to purchase a brand new computer, I expect a well-known company to stand by its product and honor its warrantee, its contract with the purchaser. Toshiba apparently doesn't see things that way, and would rather put the screws to a customer by insinuating that I was somehow responsible for damaging the computer, event though they were entirely unwilling to look at it to see that there is not a single mark or scratch anywhere near the computer, and clearly aware that the hinges on these computers are frequently defective. Do NOT buy this computer. It may work nicely for a week, a month, maybe two or three, but you will always have to worry about the hinges suddenly failing without warning, knowing that Toshiba will give you the run around when you ask them to stand by their product and honor their warrantee. Better to buy yourself a Dell ( far more reliable customer service), a Lenovo (far more sturdy construction), anything other than a Toshiba. If you do after you read this, you can't say that I didn't warn you.

title: Superlative Sound, but Issues With Comfort, Quality & Customer Service
text:
The HP50 is the finest sounding portable headphone I have heard, and comes close to being a portable Sennheiser HD600, which is high praise indeed. The HP 50 give amazing levels of clarity, resolution, and dynamic impact, and is also reasonably neutral, with maybe a slight boost in the mid-bass area. You are definitely getting highly accurate sound reproduction here at the core level, though the "RoomFeel" technology modifies things a bit, especially in terms of transient response (esp. drums). The Room Feel acoustical theory apparently mutes transient response a bit to avoid listener fatigue. This works for me - when I listen to metal for lengthy sessions, the HP50 works a lot better than say the Yamaha Pro 500 or ATH M50, but the accuracy of the response is somewhat compromised, which may alienate purists.

However, there is an issue with poorly recorded / mastered albums with significant drum presence; these will sound very lifeless on the HP50s - e.g. Pantera, Down both sounded very mediocre on the HP50s, even though both groups sounded just fine on other headphones. Classical and jazz bring out the best in the HP50s and the transient response feels more natural and full there, which is probably due to the mastering quality. I don't want to get rock and metal fans worried for the most part - well mastered stuff like Muse and Tool sound excellent, but it's the sludgier / lo-fi side of rock that sounds a bit washed out on the HP50s. (This was an issue with the HD600s also, so I think the comparison is very accurate!)

Besides the Room Feel response modification issue that may affect some recordings, the HP50s have two other issues. First, the headband design assumes the listener has a square head, and there is a inward sloping section right in the middle part of the headband that causes me significant pain right in the middle of the band. I have no idea why they designed the phones that way, maybe to maintain constant tension on the earcups to maintain a good seal, but whatever the design intent was, these are among the least comfortable designs I own, being outdone only by the Yamaha Pro 500s in long term discomfort capability. The pressure on the ears is fine, but that wedge in the middle of your scalp starts to hurt after about an hour. You can move the band around a bit on your head, and / or take a 5 minute rest and you can then keep on listening for another 45-60 minutes. I have indeed listened to the HP50s for hours without needing to go to the ER or take Tylenol, but I needed a lot of micro-adjustments and a few rest periods of several minutes in order to get through the marathon. The HP50s sound good and unique enough to endure a bit of pain, and depending on your head shape and size (I wear a size L hat) you may be just fine.

Second issue, and the biggest liability, is build quality / warranty. In my first month of ownership, the Ipod 3 button cable shorted and needed to be replaced. (No trauma involved, just a few days of crackling, and then no sound from it at all.) The company took about a month to get the replacement cable to me, and it involved a lot of emails and use of the rather non-intuitive customer service interface on the NAD site. I had to hunt around to find a way to contact NAD on their site, then had to establish a user ID and account to contact them, and then had to submit a question through the website to get service. Then the company required me to provide proof of purchase from an authorized dealer before they would send me the $5 cable for free, and then they forgot to send it out for a few weeks, and claimed I had failed to provide my address, though I did that in the initial contact. I re-provided my address and eventually got the cable.

Though this is not anywhere near as bad as say AKG customer service (think 3 or 4 months of waiting...) it also does not compare well with B&W, at the same price point. My P5s had the same issue shortly after purchase, and B&W sent me a replacement cable overnight after a single 2 minute phone call to a number on their website and with no proof of purchase needed. If you're selling a $300 pair of headphones, you ought to maybe be a tad friendlier to your customers IMO.

Then things got worse. After 5 months of ownership, the wiring between the two drivers failed, and now I only get sound from one side or the other of the phones. (You can plug the cable into either side; whichever side I have the cable plugged into works and the other side is silent.) I contacted NAD and was told the company does not do its own warranty service but instead I must return the phones to the original point of purchase, and the authorized dealer will replace them. (Note this replacement will only be done by an authorized dealer; if you buy from an unauthorized dealer, even at list price, I would think you might have a problem...)

The dealer was great and provided quick and efficient service, but I had to pay to ship the HP50s to them, which will cost maybe $20 or so, and will of course involve me standing in line at the UPS store or Post Office. Again, though this is not the worst problem ever in life, it is irritating to have to pay for warranty service for a $300 pair of headphones. Also, the point of failure here is one that I have never seen happen on anything other than a $25 pair of Philips cheapies I had owned 10 years ago. If this was some exotic technology that failed, like a new type of planar driver or some such, I might be more accepting of the issue, but wiring from one driver to another? Come on guys, get the simple stuff right for three hundred bills!

It seems frankly, that NAD is a tiny company that does not have its act together in terms of manufacturing high quality headphones or supporting them. Not sure how they are in terms of their other electronic devices, but Sennheiser produces higher quality headphones and supports them better. If only the HP50 did not sound as good as it does, I would just write NAD off. But the impressive sound quality of the HP50s, along with their unique and enjoyable Room Feel signature gives me the patience to reluctantly jump through a few more hoops here than I would for lesser sounding headphones. But you may not be as patient as me, especially if you think a luxury headphone price point should also give you world class build quality and customer service.

So takeaway points:

1) Buy from an authorized dealer; be 100% certain the dealer is authorized, check the NAD website.
2) Be prepared for some discomfort during use, especially if you have a big head.
3) Expect the worse in terms of build quality, and be prepared for a somewhat onerous customer service experience if problems do develop.

As I said, I think the HP50s are worth all this trouble, but if they break again, that's all for me, and I will update the review if and when that happens.

title: So far the PL-89s have been fine. My issue has to do with the complete ...
text:
So far the PL-89s have been fine. My issue has to do with the complete lack of service/warranty available from BIC/Acoustech.

I bought TWO PL89s and TWO PL200 subwoofers. They looked and sounded great. Then I heard crackling coming from the left side. The PL200 subs were wired in series with each of my Acoustech PL89 tower speakers. One of the PL89s had stopped working. I assumed it must be something in the PL200 subwoofer crossover that was causing the problem. SO I wired directly to the PL89, buypassing the PL200 and its crossover and the PL89 worked fine. If I wire to the sub, it works, but the PL89s don't. Simple right? I've had both subs and the towers for less than 6 months. So here comes the good part.

I call the Acoustec BIC America at 877.558.4242. A recorded message of a woman's voice plays telling me to select 2 to get warranty/technical support. I do, and the very same person answers the phone. She tells me she doesn't know anything technical and tells me to call Sean at 480.489.4536. So I do and I get nothing but a VM, day after day after day. When I again call back to the number listed in my instruction booklet I get the same woman as before, who now takes an attitude with me because her "tech guy" must not be available, or whatever. This has gone on for days and as of today I have moved both Acoustech PL200 subs to the garage and will be buying new subwoofers from a different manufacturer. It will be a company with local sales, service, and warranty facilities where I live. I live in the small burg of Las Vegas. I am writing the Acoustechs PL200s off as a total loss and holding my breath on the PL89s. There is NO WARRANTY. There is NO SERVICE. You can't even buy replacement parts from Acoustech BIC.

I can't believe I spent so much money for Acoustech gear and the warranty/service is non existent. Buy this stuff only if service and warranty isn't important to you.

title: Great System; Some Setup Suggestions
text:
I highly recommend the Panasonic SC-HTB550 Stereo System. Even though I have a couple of suggestions, I still give it five stars.

I wanted a system to bring all my devices together and one I could control with my TV remote. I have an 18-month old Panasonic TV with Viera Link. I read several reviews before settling on this unit. One reviewer said the stereo volume bar no longer shows up on his Panasonic TV but I was pleasantly surprised to see the volume bar display a stereo volume setting on my TV screen. I was also pleasantly surprised to find other devices hooked into my TV (one through an HDMI port and another with RCA cables) play back through the Stereo System. I don't believe the playback coming through the RCA cables is in HD but it is a gaming system so it sounds fair enough. I connected my Apple TV using an HDMI port on my TV and HD movies streaming through Netflix sound great.

I am using the vertical (upright) configuration and I would make this recommendation to anyone who chooses this setup: attach the front ornaments to the speaker stands BEFORE attaching them to the speakers. The instructions state to attach the ornaments to the speakers, insert the speaker cables, and then attach the base to the ornaments. I had difficulty trying to balance the speaker base properly against the ornament whilst attempting to thread a screw down an angled hole and screw it into the base. It was much easier to attach the base to the ornament first, thread the speaker wire, and then slip the ornament into the speaker and fix it in place. That is just my recommendation.

The instructions to get the Viera Link set up between the TV and the receiver were not really wonderful. The instructions provided with the Theater System are cursory in my opinion. I referred back to my TV manual for guidance but it was not much help. I'm honestly not sure exactly what steps I used to get the TV and the Stereo System to synch up or I would write them here for others to follow. I kept tweaking my setup on the TV and all of a sudden, the TV recognized the Home Theater System. I would suggest reading your TV manual carefully if you plan to use the Viera Link and be prepared to do a bit of trial and error. I hope it will synch up on the first attempt for you - and perhaps it will - but don't get frustrated if it doesn't. Keep trying different settings.

The product sounds great. The subwoofer links up wirelessly to the unit. The system looks very nice. As other reviewers have mentioned it is no audiophile-level system but I would personally be hard pressed to go back to watching TV listening to the sound coming through TV speakers unless I absolutely had to.

These turntables are rock solid, have great features for mixing and scratching, and look great. They don't look like 1200s, but they have a sleek. I find Stanton and Vestax turntables to look toy-like. The Numark TTXs don't.

After all the use I've put these TTXs through, one takes ever-so-slightly longer to spin up than the other. It's hardly noticeable, I just happen to be an engineer and a scratch DJ, so I am very observant of these things.

If you are looking for a new (or first) pair of decks - do yourself a favor and buy these. They cannot be beat for the price, and they are competitive (if not the best) with any top-tier DJ turntable.

The 3D features are fair, but not spectacular (not a big fan of Tridef), although the monitor itself, without any third party 3d software will work fairly good at producing some level of depth when the 3D feature is on (some adjustments need to be done to achieve good results). title: I'm delighted!
text:
I got my hands on my GoPro Hero 3 Black as quickly as I could after it was announced, and I'm delighted with the camera and the video and images it produces. This camera makes big improvements over the Hero 2--it's smaller, faster, lighter, more sensitive in low light and has more resolution and output options. This is my third generation GoPro, it's hard to believe the advances GoPro has made since my first Hero HD.

This camera has been redesigned. It's design is tighter, sleeker and sexier than the Hero2, and the rubberized texture of the body feels good in your hands. The camera body is black on 5 sides (and silver on the front). The Hero 3 Black is lighter than the 2, but it feels more solidly constructed. I haven't tested the claims of splash resistance of the new design ;).

GoPro cameras are made to go anywhere...or at least anywhere I have been, and they have mounts and cases that protect the camera itself and let you capture video places you'd never think of taking a conventional camera. I've taken my GoPros snowboarding, sailing, hiking, camping, to burningman, on camping trips, cliff jumping, and strapped it to my head, my wrist, my chest, to the roof of the car, to a kayak and its paddles, and to a dog.

Before GoPro, I never had a camera that I could just "set and forget" and come up with consistently excellent results. The Hero 3 Black has a better, flatter wide angle, fixed focus lens. With it, subjects are always in focus. The image stabilization is magic. There is none of the motion-sickness-inducing jitter that you get when you strap a normal video camera to a car or boat.

There are just a couple of minor drawbacks: the housings are redesigned, so previous generation housings won't work with the Hero 3. The mounts (chesties, head, wrist, etc.) work fine with the new housings. My older LCD backpack works with the new camera, and the battery backpack does too.

I know that you can't future-proof everything that you shoot today, but I want to record the highest quality source material so that when I come back to it later, I'll be able to get the most out of it. The extra prostyle features of the Hero 3 Black made the decision for me. The GoPro Hero 3 White and Silver models are similar to the Black edition, with a pared-down set of features. They are solid alternatives that will do just fine, and and at the same time keep you in the latest technology.

This is a brand new product that was introduced in the fall of 2012. Since this is just December, I haven't seen big discounts from MSRP of $399.99. This price is competitive with cameras by other manufacturers, and given its performance, I think it's a good value for money.

title: Awesome backpack to grow into...and it carries a tripod!!!
text:
After much research - including multiple visits to brick & mortar camera shops for first-hand handling of MANY camera backpacks - I finally pulled the trigger and selected this Lowepro Fastpack 350 over several competitors, including different models and sizes in the Lowepro line.

I used this bag for the first time over the past week of July 4, 2012 while in California visiting family and must say I am SO happy with my choice!!

The top pocket is large enough to carry multiple items I would normally carry in a separate backpack, including sandals, a shirt, ipod, cell, snacks and several other things. The bottom half has enough pockets to hold my Canon T3i, two lenses, multiple batteries w/charger, filters, remote controls, HD connector and extra SD cards. The back pocket holds a large laptop that is next on my 'wish' list...for now, it was PERFECT for holding several magazines for me and my family.

PLUS, there's a side a can holder that's tough and can constrict with the pull of a clamp...which made it perfect for holding my 40" tripod. I used a climbers clasp to connect the backpack's top loop to the carrying arm of the tripod bag. Not once did the tripod fall out, dislodge or feel unbalanced. Bought the climber's clasp for $1.00.

The best part was being able to carry-on the backpack with tripod attached and still be able to shove it under the seat in front of me enough to not have the hostess hassle me about putting it in the overhead bin.

When taking pictures, the side access for the camera and lenses was GREAT!! Not having to take the backpack off to access those items made me feel like I could concentrate on my scene and the camera settings while on the fly...so much more efficient and fun than the old way: put the bag down, open the compartments, pull the camera out, take pictures while worrying about my bag that wasn't on my shoulder. The bag is big enough that I know I won't outgrow it. In fact, I'm about to start researching a new zoom lens which will fit nicely, thank you.

The shoulder straps are really comfortable and have micro-adjustments to make them fit perfectly, along with the chest strap which is also adjustable.

When you sit the bag down, it doesn't topple over even with a tripod in the side/can pocket. This bag is well-made and rugged and you feel your gear will remain protected.

Finally, there was something very positive about the peace of mind I felt while we were walking in heavy, almost chaotic, tourist traffic at Venice Beach, CA. The flap covering the camera compartment and the zipper configuration made it tough for a thief to steal my camera gear. The Lowepro logos are unobtrusive enough that this backpack didn't cause thieves to single me out for my costly gear.

This camera backpack merits serious consideration by anyone who likes to take pictures and cares about protecting and accessing their gear while travelling.

That peace of mind and the ease of use of this camera backpack enabled me to focus on whether to snap shots of the colors and scenes that unfolded in front of me instead of worrying about the intent of thieves around me...I am officially donating my old camera bag to charity.

title: Once at the head of the pack, now not so much
text:
In my search for a portable Bluetooth speaker system, I finally decided to stop taking reviewers' advice and instead go listen myself...so I headed down to my local big box retailer. I spent about an hour in the aisle performing comparisons using my phone and the same set of songs for each system. I tested using Bluetooth and, when possible, the 3.5mm connector. Thus, while the setting may not have been a fair representation of someone's home, the relative comparison between units seemed valid.

The result - while the original JamBox set the initial bar in the portable Bluetooth speaker system market, it has since been left behind by many other models near its price. I found that almost every other option in this price range (or a bit above) destroyed this system.

Its bigger brother, the Big JamBox, has far more bass and sounds much less like a small portable monaural speaker. That said, the sound is still a bit thin compared to some of the other options. It's also quite a bit larger than the original JamBox...and significantly more expensive.

In a size not much larger than the original JamBox and at the same price, the Jabra Solemate delivers far more bass, which is not surprising given its weight (implying larger speaker magnets). That said, it is still a bit thin at some levels and not super pleasing at low levels....but it is still more pleasing than the JamBox...and its street price is often lower.

Priced a bit higher, the UE Boom is an amazing speaker given its size. It can also can be paired up with second unit for either stereo or distributed sound. This system is perhaps the first system to which I listened that did not seem to say "yeah, it's portable and sounds that way."

And shocker of shockers, Bose (often overrated) really delivered with the SoundLink Mini. REALLY delivered...for $199. The sound profile may actually be a bit too bassy for some, but this thing provides room-filling sound and is generally pleasing to listen to at all volume levels. I'm sure audiophiles would disagree, but audiophiles probably shouldn't be reading reviews of Bluetooth speakers. ;)

There are also many other options in this price range and form factor, but I won't go through them all. Hopefully you get the idea - you can do far better in late 2013 than the original JamBox...and there is no way that it is worth $150 in light of the price and performance of other competing systems. Heck, I have seen the Solemate at $110 as recently as this week.

BTW, I cannot figure out why the black version of the JamBox is currently listing for $185 on Amazon. That elevated price has got to be some sort of recent anomaly. I suggest that if you have decided on the JamBox, don't even consider buying it at that price. It has been available for $120 new.

cheers,
Scuba

It's not perfect and lacks the magnetic hinge that kept the iPad connected to the keyboard of the Logitech, but it's made of aluminum that is stiffer than the Logitech and doesn't creak when you hold it and it's only $19.95. I used 2 of these lights on a shoot yesterday as hair lights. There was enough light with good throw. The color/temp with the orange tung filter was still a bit greenish. I fixed it by taping the pink filter and some gels to warm it up to a flattering color (a great investment for strobe and now these led lights is the GamColor 4"x5" gel swatch book with hundreds of colors including diffusion gels and fabrics). I'm going to add a velcro strip to the lights and to the gels I used so that I can quickly swap filters next time.

I found the need for gobo's on these because the beam is wider than you might think. Yesturday I opted to dim it down and angle them away because of the spill. Again, the velcro I think will help to add flags on the sides of the unit (like my strobist gobos). I might try to rig up something like the Arri Broadcaster Intensifier which is a mirrored box that extends beyond the unit like a snoot and amplifies the beam. I didn't find a strange multishadow effect I've heard about with leds, but I had 2 layers of plastic diffusion.

The build quality is better than I anticipated after all the grumbling in the reviews. It's a <$40 unit, it's not going to be more than plastic. But it's not super cheapo. I didn't use the hot shoe because I was pleased to find that there are tripod or lighting screw holes in the bottom of the shoe that are metal. So I attached my lights using the screw and skipped the hotshoe all together. I also didnt rely on the built in elbow joint to angle the light, I tightened that down and left it. Instead I used my umbrella holder on my light stand to do the angling of the units (along with a nifty T shaped accessory that helped me mount both lights on one stand, I could have 2 more on it too)

I found that leaving the AA batteries in overnight seemed to drain them, not sure if the off switch really turns it off. So I'm pulling the batteries out for storage (another reviewer said that their batteries started leaking in the unit so there might be issues with this).

Overall, I'm please.

title: WARING!!! Do not try to wash your Kindle Reader!!
text:
Imagine my horror when I was removing a large fuzzy blanket from my washer and looked inside the machine and saw my Kindle just laying there at the bottom. Not moving, just laying there looking clean as a whistle. It was a gift for Mother''s Day from my son and daughter in law and I loved using it. I removed it and knew at first glance it was probably "doa". I pushed the on slide and for about two seconds it sputtered and then died. OMG!!! I had some wonderful books saved up to read. I had special books saved in the archives to read again. I kept looking at my very lifeless Kindle.....pleading with it to just go on long enough for me to finish the book I was half way through. Alas, it chocked and died in my hands. I panicked and called Kindle for some help. Of course after two years it was no longer under warranty. The voice at the other end of the phone tried to comfort me. She explained there were several Kindle's on holiday special and to my great relief she informed me that as soon as I had a new one in hand and registered they could restore all the books I had ordered. I would be able to access the ones I had saved in archives to read again someday. She assured me I would not lose anything I had on my now deceased Kindle. Since I could not face more than 3 days without it, I immediately placed my order. That was Friday and on Tuesday my new Kindle arrived. I did know it was not the same as my old pal....this one is a little smaller and the keyboard comes on screen with the push of a button instead of always
being on front like a typewriter. I like the new feature much more. I registered my Kindle and with the push of the key on the computer.....WOW!!! Up came the welcome, calling me by name and telling me I was using Kindle 2. I guess it will serve as a reminder forever to shake out the blankets before I wash them. title: Orion StarMax 90mm TableTop Maksutov-Cassegrain Telescope
text:
I have a 12" Meade LX200-ACF, but it is not something I can travel with, so naturally the Orion StarMax 90mm Mak-Cass seemed like a good choice as it is a very portable Cassegrain. It turns out that this telescope is an excellent choice for any portable scope. I am very impressed with Orion's optics, and the sturdiness of this scope. I do not use it with the table top mount, but instead purchased a Vista Explorer 60-Inch Lightweight Tripod from Amazon and mounted it onto the tripod, and it works incredibly well.

The long focal lenght on this telescope give it some real magnification, which allows for a more serious survey of the night sky. The images are very crisp, and 90mm of aperature, though not much, is much better than the many 60, 70 and 80mm refractors that are also marketed as travel scopes.

I recommend this telescope to anyone that is looking for a good travel or "grab and go" telescope, as well as to anyone looking for their first telescope.

title: Best performing and best value I found in a wireless speaker with multiple inputs
text: To open, I am a bit surprised to be writing this review.  I am a long-time "audiophile" and I expected to be extolling the virtues of the Martin Logan Crescendo over this speaker.  I bought my first Martin Logan speakers in the early 90's and figured the Crescendo would blow the JBL L8 out of the water on sound quality, but for a stiff price premium (plus, overall the Crescendo probably looks a little more stylish). But, that was not to be.  I have posted a review of the Crescendo (three stars) as well, which you can read if like me you were trying to decide between the two.  This unit does not have the midrange purity and transparency of the Martin Logan, so many audiophiles would stop right there.  However, this unit is more fun, works better for its intended application (at least the application I intended which was as a guest room speaker that guests could easily use to stream background music, etc.)  The JBL has better bass (some people complain of excess bass which I don't hear but the app you can download to control this speaker includes some tone controls so you can tweak that aspect of the sound if you so desire), a much more open treble if not quite as "pure" as the Martin Logan and a much more dynamic and punchy sound.  Everyone who has listened to both speakers in my house describes the JBL as better for its intended use, which is not, after all, critical listening to reference recordings.  Certainly my kids (adults) will prefer this speaker since some of what they listen to is hip-hop and modern R and B.  It is also much more intuitive to use than the Martin Logan which was a big deal for me since, again, it is going into a guest bedroom.  Finally, it is $300 dollars less.  The bottom line is that in this relatively small category, which is wireless speakers that sound pretty good with multiple types of inputs (so in my case the Bowers and Wilkins A7 need not apply given its lack of Bluetooth) this is the best I have found all factors taken into account.  I am actually kind of blown away for what this product offers for $600.  It is a far better sounding and more flexible solution for whole house audio than things like in-ceiling speaker wired to some kind of dock (and far less money than that) and far more flexible than say the Sonos system due to its multiple inputs.  It also handles high resolution music files up to 24/96 which the Sonos, for example, doesn't.  This is an excellent product.  Bottom line, I kept the JBL L8 and returned the Crescendo.  Well done JBL, this is a mature, modern, wireless product.

title: Beware! May ruin your tablet!
text:
I feel obliged to write a review after my horrible experience with this product to warn fellow customers.
I bought this for my brand new LG G Pad 8.3. In terms of shipping, packaging, etc. everything was ok, as it usually is with Amazon. Before applying the screen protector, I read the included instructions, and also watched the recommended video on Youtube. While applying, I followed every instruction to the letter, down to the tiniest detail.
Following application, I waited for 24 hours before turning on my tablet, as recommended. Immediately upon turning on, my tablet's screen started acting up. It kept registering touches although I really wasn't touching it. I thought it might be due to some residual application fluid between the screen protector and the screen, and waited for another 6 hours before trying it again. By this time, my screen has been completely ruined. Large areas of the screen were completely unresponsive to touch, and other areas seemed to be registering touches spontaneously, causing it to go completely haywire. I removed the screen protector, in the hope that things would resolve, but unfortunately, my screen had been permanently damaged.
I contacted the seller (iTech Accessory), and after exchanging e-mails back and forth for a week (during which time iTech apparently also contacted the manufacturer ArmorSuit), all they could offer me was to pick one of 2 options:
#1- a $20 gift card, or
#2- a new screen protector.
I am not sure what this was meant to achieve, since I was obviously not going to accept either of these ridiculous attempts at appeasement. My tablet cost me $350, and a $20 gift card contributes next to nothing towards buying a new one. A new screen protector is worthless for me, as I do not have a working tablet to apply it on. (Even if I did, I would rather have no protector than to undergo this harrowing experience again).
Upon contacting Amazon, they clearly told me that all they could do was to issue a refund for the faulty screen protector, but could not help me in any other way.
So, now I am left with a completely ruined tablet. I strongly discourage fellow customers from buying this screen protector for their LG G Pad, and would recommend going without a screen protector than to go with this option.

title: A Decent Windows-format Keyboard that can be used on a Mac
text:
- Comparing to the Apple Keyboard:

The keyboard is about 1/2 cm wider (width) and 1 cm shorter (depth due to the lack of battery) in comparison to Apple's wireless keyboard. The keys are sturdy and has a flat feel. However, the texture of the keys are rough in comparison to the smooth keys from Apple.

The quality of the keyboard is basically plastic as most have said previously. However, when you compare the weight, it's pretty much the same (if you ignore the fact that batteries generally tend to add extra weight).

- Overall Product Review:

Out of the box, I noticed some of the keys look lopsided. They seemed like it was put on in a hurry. However, paying the price I did ($16) in comparison to a normal keyboard ($30+), it was to be expected.

This is a decent backup (with Windows/Mac features) especially in the age of wireless keyboards. The keys are flat exactly like laptop and the iconic Apple keyboards in comparison to other USB ones where the raised keys usually feel rather bulky.

When comparing to wireless keyboards, the product is pretty compact and due to the USB feature, no charging is necessary. One of my pet peeves about wireless keyboards is the fact that charging is required and most modern keyboards lack even one mini-USB/USB port for backup charges. In this day and age, I prefer accessibility to technology rather than how far my keyboard can be from my computer. I'm not Superman with amazing eyesight, I don't need to be a mile away. As a writer and computer programmer, I do prefer being able to spend hours at my computer typing. If I run out of battery, it defeats the whole purpose of having a keyboard especially for a desktop.

One feature I like is the Caps Lock, Num Lock, and Scroll Lock buttons lighting up at the top right corner to indicate what state it is in.

The keystroke response is decent. I type over 80 words per minute, there seems to be random lags in response which depending on the person might be an annoyance. However, this isn't an overly valid complaint because no matter what type of keyboard you get (Apple, Dell, Logitech, Microsoft), you will never match up to a mechanical keyboard in terms of fast response times. If you want fast response times, you should look to buy a mechanical keyboard.

----------
Additional Information
----------

- Windows 7 Setup:

No setup required. Once you connect the USB port, you should automatically be able to start typing with the keyboard.

- Mac OS 10.9.4 Setup:

When you start up your Mac Operating System, the Keyboard Setup Assistant should automatically detect the un-identified keyboard. Default set up is the "ANSI (United States and Others)" setting which is described as the "Standard 101-key or 102-key keyboard and some other keyboards".

Your Mac commands should be the same. Alt-key should be the Alt/Option-key and Windows-key should be the Command-key, it's just swapped for the Windows Operating System format.

I tested the Fn key with the Mac calculator and you can use both the regular 1-0 number keys or put your finger on the Fn-key and use the blue number pad available.

Downside is the lack of the Eject-key where it is needed to execute some commands (like putting your computer to sleep) but there should always be alternative non-shortcut ways in doing this. The keyboard also doesn't have default display lighting, volume, and multimedia keys which may need to be done manually or set up in the System Preferences > Keyboard > Shortcuts section.

title: Very snappy! Why spend more?
text:
Edit: Kingston has recently did something shady. Turns out they replaced the original NAND controller in this product from the superior synchronous NAND to the inferior asynchronous NAND. My unit contains the original synchronous NAND but newer ones will not match the performance, therefore I will drop this from 5 to 4 stars.

When I began choosing parts for a brand new build I knew I wanted to go with an SSD. Hard drives are the primary bottlenecks in everyday performance nowadays considering spacious memory and powerful CPU's are quite affordable. This may not be Kingston's top of the line model but I doubt anyone would really notice a difference.

Boot times in Windows 7 are blazing and when I do make it to the desktop there is no "pop in" effect. The whole desktop complete with startup programs in the tray are all instantly finished loading and ready to go. My computer is able to go from powered off to browsing the web in 35 seconds! Not too shabby.

The physical size was interesting. it actually included an optional adapter to make it fat enough to fit into standard laptop hard drive compartments. Hard to imagine such capacity and speed in so small of a package!

Make sure your motherboard bios is set to use AHCI with this drive to increase performance. My motherboard actually defaulted to IDE with this drive when I installed Windows. I had to go back and go do some minor registry editing to be able to make windows use it in AHCI mode after the fact. It was totally worth it though; I managed to get a windows experience index score of 7.9 for hard drive transfer speeds, the highest score you can achieve! (In comparison, I had a 7.8 before switching to AHCI mode)

I highly recommend this drive to the average user. I'm certainly happy with the speeds although there are most definitely faster (and more expensive!) options available.

title: Great product, better than others because of the price
text:
I've been looking at A2DP Bluetooth devices for some time now. I recently hopped back on the health wagon again, and was looking for something I could use while running or riding my bike. Items I was looking at:

Motorola S10-HD Bluetooth Headphones
Sony WM600 Bluetooth Adapter
Jabra Clipper Bluetooth Adapter
Samsung HS3000 Bluetooth Adapter

I picked up the Motorola S10-HD at Costco due to their flexible return policy. I figured if I didn't like it, I'd just return it. Pairing the device was easy, but I didn't like the interference the wraparound headset caused with my prescription eyeglasses. Audio wise the bass was pleasant, but the treble was weak in clarity, along with some latency when I changed the track or changed the volume (which was to be expected). So I returned the headset and looked at what clip on options on Amazon I could use.

I had been eying the Sony WM600 for almost a year, given that it was small and had good reviews, aside from the touch control implementation (which almost all reviewers were very vocal about even if they liked the unit otherwise). Looking at newer options, the Jabra Clipper looked like a good option since it was weather compliant, but I was disassuaded by the multi-use button control.

The HS3000 popped up while looking at the Clipper, and after reading the reviews, the one aspect that caught my attention was a glowing review about the APT-X support. I hadn't heard of this, but interested in the (future) opportunity for better audio quality and near zero latency, I took the plunge and gave the HS3000 a shot. At $30, I figured even if I hated it I could still use it as a backup device. I would just have to wait in hopes that some OEM would release a mobile phone that supported APT-X.

Got the device, charged it fully, and gave it a spin on my Motorola Droid RAZR. Pairing was quick, but I would expect that from any modern Bluetooth device. Listening to the audio, it was like night and day from the Motorola S10-HD. With crisp audio and robust bass, I felt like I was listening to my headphones directly in the jack. Then I put on a H264 native video on my phone, and I could only detect the most micro amounts of latency (less than a quarter of a second). Wow, I thought, if this is just the normal bluetooth connection, what will APT-X be like? Well, I looked up a supported APTX list online, and turns out the Motorola RAZR is one of the first mobile devices to support this standard. Newer 2012 devices like the Samsung Galaxy SIII and the HTC One series also support this codec.

I've been using the device for several days now, and here's my takeaway:

Tested with: Motorola Droid RAZR, Sony MDR-V700 monitor headphones, Apple iPhone/iPod Touch earphones

Build Quality: Inexpensive plastic build - nice texture, but doesn't feel "solid". Not the cheapest I've seen, but probably not a unit you want to drop.
Battery Life: Absolutely fantastic.
Audio Quality & Paring: Great!
Interface: The buttons are very responsive. I've been able to use all buttons by feel, as there are only three on one side, and four on the other. However, even when reading the manual, I had a hard time figuring out how to get a read on the remaining battery level. I think you have to un-pair the connected device in order to get the read out. Everything else has been extreamly straightforward otherwise.
Concerns: I'm a little concerned about how well the power switch and USB power port will hold up in the long run. As a result, I'm very gentle with these two items whenever I use them. The bundled headphones are not good.

The clip attached fine to my t-shirts, but I didn't like the headphones hitting my neck. I attached the HS3000 to a laynard and it's worked great. My wife can hear me perfectly even with this device resting on my torso and me being a bit of a mumbler (which has always been a problem for Bluetooth devices in the past). In the event I'm active during stormy weather I'm planning on putting the lanyard on the inside of my shirt (away from the elements).

Ultimately I would strongly recommend this device on the following grounds:
- Very good price (at $30-$35)
- APT-X is fantastic if you have the proper support from your device, the bluetooth works fine even if it doesn't (just expect a little latency)
- No single multi-button interface since each key has its place
- Sounds great on the headphones of your choosing (and choice is king)
