title: Serious documentation, feature and firmware issues
text:
I purchased this router to upgrade my home network based on excellent user reviews. My own home network situation includes VoIP, and since my family does a lot of video streaming, QoS is a necessary feature to ensure our phone connections don't stutter. My previous router, a D-Link DIR-655, served us ably for a long time until it started showing signs of age. So I got this one, set it up, and ensured it was running the latest official Asus firmware (3.0.0.3.178, downloaded 23 August 2012).

But: The new Asus router's QoS standard settings do not prioritize VoIP! Amazing. In fact, it's as if Asus has never heard of VoIP, and their documentation is barely comprehensible (and incorrect) on the topic of QoS in general. There is no VoIP-related setting to select in the QoS setup panel; you must manually specify the ports your VoIP provider uses. The documentation is no help, as it is maddeningly bad: for example, the router's online documentation contains such pearls of wisdom as "There are two kinds of packek, web packets(use HTTP at 80 port) and P2P packets(use other port) which want to go to the WAN" --see for yourself, that's a direct quote, typos and all, from [...] --the page you are directed to when you click the "QoS FAQ" link in the router's setup page. Two kinds of packek? Web and P2P? What nonsense is this?

Worse, enabling the QoS brought the throughput of the router to its knees. Various online speed tests showed my download throughput plummeted from the 20Mbps typical of my ISP to 0.2Mbps after enabling the QoS, and latencies went from typically less than 4msec to 40-50msec. Unfortunately, disabling QoS didn't fix the problem. Rebooting the router turned out to be the cure. As in: the thing must be rebooted EVERY time I attempt to modify the QoS settings. The behavior is very repeatable, and the QoS engine in this router causes serious throughput reduction even after rebooting and even with just a single entry to prioritize my VoIP traffic.

On the plus side, the built-in PPTP VPN server works very well and is easy to set up (although Asus' free dynamic DNS service is not documented at all: there is no sign-up, just type in a unique name and you're done).

There are enough positive reviews of this router that I'm not quite to the point of giving up on it quite yet. I hope to find some combination of settings that might work for me and be stable. But the crappy documentation and reboot-hungry firmware are not encouraging. I'd say there's an 80% chance that I'll be returning this for another D-Link.

UPDATE: I gave up on this unit. The firmware is just too terrible. Back it goes.

Could someone please convince me to keep the MBA and use it for grad school? If this thing had a better resolution screen with a matte coating I'd be raving about it.

title: Not All That
text:
Through an ordering mishap, I ended up buying BOTH an ASUS VS248H-P LED backlit/LCD display -and- a Viewsonic VX2453mh LED backlit/LCD display. If you are not aware, these two models are head-to-head competitors.

I have a Early to Mid 2011 MBP (depending on which incidental Appstore utility will not install because it doesn't support this recent a model). I use a Kanex iAdapt MDPHDMIV2 HDMI V2 - Mini DisplayPort to HDMI Adapter to adapt the Thunderbolt port on the MBP to HDMI out.

Basically, the Viewsonic VX2453mh is plain better, even though it is a refurbished unit, and the ASUS display is brand spanking new.

The ASUS display has beaucoup more video controls, and they are sorely needed. The Viewsonic has far fewer possible adjustments, apparently b/c they are not needed.

My criteria: how closely can the external display mimic the OUTSTANDING on-board display included with my MBP, whose maximum resolution is 1440X900.

The Viewsonic was fairly close right out of the non-factory box. It required very little adjustment to reproduce several multi-color website pages open in windows on both the on-board display and the external display. Within five minutes, I was able to adjust the Viewsonic such that while quickly shifting my visual focus from display to display, I could barely tell any difference in shading, contrast, color saturation, brightness, subtle gradient color shading reproduction, and so forth. It was frankly, an amazing experience, and I did not expect it was even possible.

The ASUS on the other hand is a dog in this regard, and after several tries over several days, has finally yielded an acceptably close facsimile of the on-board display - and only "acceptable". Just close enough that I don't want to go to the trouble of sending it back. I have relegated this display to the office, for use opening email, spreadsheets docs and such. Diss-appointing.

Had I known I would have bought TWO refurbished Viewsonic displays.

Either I have a less than stellar example of the ASUS display, or the other folks reviewing it here are not accustomed to any real level of display excellence. You will have to decide.

title: Nice looking in real life
text:
The bracket that holds the thermometer is made of metal. The thermometer itself is made of plastic. The housing and the top and the bottom too. However, the top and bottom of the thermometer look to be made of metal - it is very convincing. To the point I had to tap on it to make sure it wasn't metal.

You can pivot the arms to adjust the angle and then also spin the thermometer itself to get it positioned perfectly. You need to be looking straight at it to read it - reading it from the side is not going to work. But if you are facing it correctly the column of mercury is thick enough that it is easy to read. I have mine mounted on a screened in porch about 2.5 feet from the glass door onto the porch and I can easily read it from inside. It seems to be pretty accurate.

The downsides? It comes with very cheap screws which are probably not even galvanized. So I replaced the screws with two brass screws and used those to mount it. I would expect the screws would rust in a year or two if you don't get better ones to mount it.

I imagine it will last a good while in the protected location of my screened in porch. But I'd be worried about the fake metal finish not holding up somewhere where it is more exposed to both weather and direct sunlight. You should mount this thermometer (or any thermometer) in the shade and away from where it will get a lot of direct exposure to the weather.

I am knocking off one star for not making clear that the whole thing isn't made of metal - and for the cheap screws. But it looks very nice in person and so I am basically satisfied.

I called customer service which went to a call center in India. Not to much problems just some problems understanding the person. I have now sent it to warranty $43 dollars shipping. Warranty goes to:

Hyper Microsystems
100 Lakeview Parkway
Vernon, IL 60061

So when considering whether to buy this TV factor in about 40 to 50 bucks and see if you can get a better and more reliable TV. Maybe more if you factor in hassle and down time.

There's a few arcade style games, etc. No "must haves" that motivated me to spend those free 1000 coins that come for free with the game controller.

With more apps and games available and more free content FROM AMAZON or a working "other viewing options" feature that included Netflix would bump it up a star.

I don't hate the device at all. It's just not that ... exciting. I'm going to play around with it, but I suspect I'll be giving it away to the next friend who expresses interest. I'll stick with the Mac Mini which I still think is one of your best options as a cord cutter (IMHO).

title: Has worked fine for over a month of testing
text:
We've left this on for over a month now without issues to test a firewall appliance and it just stayed luke warm and never got too hot to touch.

There's a switch in the back where you can select the input voltage, either 110V or 220V. We've only used it in the US at 110V input and 220V output in the front. Please note that this is quite a bit heavier than travel transformers that are popular for temporary use.

However, this transformer does not change the Hz from 50 to 60 or vice versa. In Europe, it's only 50 Hz, so this transformer can only take down the voltage to 110V but does not increase the cycles to 60 Hz. Likewise in the US, this transformer does not reduce the cycles to 50 Hz. This mainly affects devices that rely on timing such as clocks and the speed of motors.

FYI...many devices like your cell phone/camera charger, laptops, and shavers are already 100-240V 50/60 Hz and usable worldwide with the appropriate $2 adapter plug. Just carefully check the label.

title: O.k., but you can probably do a little better for the price
text:
I got this DVD player a cheap replacement for my old one. I mainly wanted something to use for playing DVDs I get from rental places, because I do not like putting those heavily used (scratched and full of greasy finger prints) DVDs in my nice Blu-Ray player. If you are using a cathode ray television, then this progressive scan DVD player will be fine. It has component video output, and for audio there is a coaxial output if you have a decent sound system. If you are using an HD television, then you will probably want to spend the extra dollars for an up-converting DVD player that has HDMI output. The device is a little cheap feeling, but I wasn't expecting much for the price.

Also, another reason that I keep around a cheap DVD player is because I have a lot of import DVDs from England, Japan, and China. The drawback with this device is that Sony players make it very difficult/impossible to jailbreak the region blocking programs. I purchased and equivalent player from CyberHome** (progressive scan, component video, coaxial audio) for less money, and it was very easy to recode that device to play DVDs from all regions. If you're one of the few who also watch world-wide cinema, then you'll want to get a different player for that purpose.

(**unfortunately, I don't believe that these players are still being made.)

title: Decent, but very lacking
text:
I ordered this even with bad reviews that were posted here just because even if a product is good, the person them-self may be defective. And now some of those reviews I validated by my own personal experience. Usually I'm a big fan of Asus with items ranging from laptops all the way to video cards, but this item is going into my waste of time storage box.

Requirements:

I needed a extender to boost my 5ghz signal. Currently I have a usb adaptor that worked pretty well with 1 bar in my office space on the other side of the house from the router. Only problem was that it would lose signal from time to time and I would have move my laptop to regain the signal and then move it back to my desk where it would work for awhile. Then I'd have to repeat the cycle when the signal was lost again. I bought a more powerful router to try to boost the output, but due to the materials the house has incorporated into it (3 concrete load bearing walls,) not much of a difference was made. So I saw this and figured that it may be the answer I needed. Problem was it wasn't. I gave this a little under a month to prove it's stuff, but I could of written the review 3 days after I received it due to no real change.

Pro's:
Easy to setup
Nice looks
Strong signal and better the decent range when extending

Cons:
Setup is too easy with presets installed and very little tweaks available unless you have the time to browse forums or are heavily IT trained (which I am.) In order to set up, you need to move the computer and extender to within range of the router (or move the router to within range of the extender) in order to receive the SSD signal. There is no manually entering the information for networks not in range unless you are tech savvy or have time to cruise the forums.

Cord is too short unless you want to place real low. It may be a slight problem for some people, but for me I wanted this pretty much out of sight. But the cord is barely long enough to reach from a floor-based power strip to the top of my desk. Many times that I've installed extenders for others or at work, I usually have at least 5' of power lead to work with. This one has a power lead just under 3' including the power connection itself. As I said, not a problem for some people, but it limits placement of the extender.

Reliability is not something this is known for by me. I had to reset this thing (hard and soft) more times then I even want to count.

Multi-use is nice for an extender, but it didn't really take with this. After a couple of weeks of resetting, I moved this to a direct connect to the Ethernet port on my computer and use it as an adapter. I received less signal according to this with more drops then my thumb sized 5ghz. And dropping down to the 2.4ghz didn't offer any improvement as well. On my D-link thumb sized adapter, I received 1-2 bars 5ghz and 4 bars 2.4ghz. On this, I received 0-1 bar 5ghz and 2-3 bar 2.4ghz. So I received less signal even though I had more options to move the Asus around to try to catch better signal. On using it as a router, it was pretty decent with good speed when connected to other devices, but the drops requiring a reboot of the router in order to get reconnected was very annoying.

So my view on this is mixed. If you want it for light use and not for long periods of time, then this may be for you. Hardware.. This product WORKS great if you have the network and hardware able to run it. Do not expect this to work if your using an old dual core windows vista pc. My friend was able to successfully run the same setup on a i3 standard desktop that is 2 years old and has a single hard drive. If you AMD from 2004 is able to run this call me I will send you a cookie. (I suspect people buying this are experienced / educated users)

Network: USE WIRED... If you complain that this does not work and your using wireless connection to your extenders cry me a river I have no sympathy for you. With a 1G multiple switch wired home network (100mbs will be able to handle most activities) with 6 active extenders all on HD channels this is just a small blip on the network consumption chart. Now I have used wireless in one room in my house (as a test) and it did function ~properly (wireless N or better needed) I did notice a slight lag with the remote over wireless but it was minimal at best (I can tell the difference between 30ms and 60ms ping when I game)

Summary: This product is a serious device for power users. It works amazingly well and is a way to save some $$ from renting DVR/Cable boxes. I have set custom channel maps (make ESPN channel 1, FOX channel 2,... etc) / deleted channels / set recordings / commercial removal for dvr shows. Average Joe who understands how networks / windows media center works should be able to get this running with a couple Xbox extenders in an hr.

title: Extremely Slow Transfer Rates -- But There is a solution.  Read here.
text:
Note: This is a review for folks using MacOSX who are experiencing extremely slow transfer rates to a WD MyBook Live 3TB NAS
Note: My MacBook Pro to WD transfer speed to the MyBook Live went from sustained 5Kbps to a sustained 40-50Mbps as a result of the following
Note: Don't actually type in the quotes below when entering unix commands

I don't use Time Machine for backups, but did want to transfer about 350GB worth of music files from a MacBook Pro to my new 3T WD MyBook Live. Dragging the files from the laptop to the shared drive is a comedy of errors. I averaged about 5 Kbps (YES, Kb, not KB, Mb or MB) with brief 5-10 second bursts of 5-9MBps that would occur every 3 to 5 minutes. So, this is what I did:

1) DISABLING MEDIACRAWLER ON THE WD LIVE DEVICE

I Took Kenneth Krutsch's advice and disabled Mediacrawler

1a) First enable SSH --> Go to your MyBook in a browser --> "http://192.168.1.11/UI/ssh" (you may have a different IP address -- I'm using DHCP) --> Click "Enable SSH" and write down the username and password you need.

1b) THIS NEXT SECTION IS ALL IN THE OSX TERMINAL. Kill the mediacrawlerd process --> SSH to your MyBook Live using the Terminal app that comes with Mac OSX. Go to launchpad and type in Terminal in the search box. Then in the terminal window type "ssh username:192.168.1.11" --> then enter your password. (remember: you wrote down both the username and password above) --> then type "cd .." to get to the root directory --> then type "cd /usr/mediacrawler" to get to the directory with mediacrawlered in it. --> then make it so it won't run by itself --> type: "chmod -x mediacrawlerd" --> then find the mediacrawlered process ID by typing "ps ux" --> look for mediacrawlered in this list, and the PID is in the second column from the left. Kill the mediacrawlered process once and for all by typing "Kill -9 [the PID]" <-- don't type the brackets

2) TRANSFERRING FILES

I took others' advice and decided to use RSYNC, a command that you also access via the OSX Terminal, to transfer files, instead of using the finder to drag files from my drive to the WD NAS.

2a) Decide which files you want to transfer -- I chose /Users/[YOUR MAC OSX USERNAME]/Music/iTunes/* --> A star at the end signifies that you want to copy over everything in that directory

2b) Decide where on the WD NAS you want to transfer the files. I chose "Shared Music", which on my NAS, is at /nfs/Public/Shared Music/.

2c) Set up the rsync process in a new Mac OS X Terminal window:

rsync -vauxhizP -delete /Users/[YOUR MAC OSX USERNAME]/Music/iTunes/* '[Your SSH Username]@192.168.1.11:/nfs/Public/Shared\ Music/'

hit enter, enter your password when asked.

And that did it.

Now I'm showing sustained 5 MB/s transfers.

Thank you, Western Digital, for NOT ONLY simultaneously wasting 3 days of my life cobbling this duct tape solution together, BUT ALSO for letting me Geek out on this! I can't shake the feeling that you owe me.

title: Solid Performer vs. Dell Venue 8 Pro
text:
The Lenovo is a good tablet and should suffice for users of previous Windows tablets and those familiar with Windows 8.1

Brief review and comparison vs. the Dell Venue 8 pro:

Processor/Memory:

The Dell has the 3740D and utilizes single channel memory -- 2GB max
The Lenovo has the 3740 and utilizes dual channel memory -- 4GB max (but the Lenovo does not allow for a memory upgrade)
A look at the System Performance file shows a 6.4 memory for the Dell and 7.1 for the Lenovo.
The other performance scores are virtually identical.
So theoretically, the Lenovo should be a bit more snappy but I haven't really noticed it yet in "real world" use.

Physical:
Under similar loads the Dell's back gets a bit warmer than the Lenovo's. The Lenovo has never become *hot*, so far.

The Dell *feels* nicer and more solid, the Lenovo makes a few creaking noises if flexed even a little.

The Dell's buttons certainly feel better with a good tactile response, the Lenovo's feel "mushy".

Screen:

The Lenovo screen can be made the brightest, but the Dell screen can be made the darkest and looks better in a low light environment. The Dell seems to reproduce colors better at the widest angles while the Lenovo washes out (both are still, IPS though). The Dell has warmer screen temperature, the Lenovo is a bit on the cool side (partially explains the perception of brighter but the backlight is a contributor also).

Sound:

I'm still evaluating the sound, Dell has released an update for both firmware and screen.

Misc:

Haven't tried the Dell active pen, no one locally has it. A Targus aluminum barreled capacitive stylus works pretty good. Both have good handwriting recognition.

The Dell has the more feature-ladden BIOS while the Lenovo's is fairly simple. The Dell also has a nice hardware diagnostic menu/program as well.

The Lenovo camera allows for panoramic shots the Dell does not (same Windows app version)

The Lenovo has GPS the Dell does not.

I had to return my first Lenovo as the SD card slot was broken and wouldn't hold the sdcard. The second Lenovo was fine.

Impression:

The Lenovo is a fine, if not extraordinarily well-built tablet. Snappy performance.

title: Definitely a hidden gem of a phone
text:
I'll start by saying I have an iPhone 5. I love it but some things are better on Android. I had purchased a Galaxy S4 and to my surprise, I actually didn't care for it. It was HUGE (though it had a super nice 5" full HD screen) and the screen was not as responsive during text messaging as my previous Galaxy phones were. That latter problem was driving me crazy and it didn't matter which keyboard I tried or which app I was using. And I've had ALL the Galaxy S phones - the original, the S II, the S III, and then the S4.

Enter the Galaxy Express. I decided I didn't want to spend a fortune. The Galaxy Express was the best combination of price and features - the Snapdragon S4 Plus CPU in this phone is no slouch. It also runs the latest Android which is another plus. This phone also has the newest 4G LTE, which I was not going to compromise on. The older (but still fast) 4G "HSPA+" network is fine but LTE is the future, so I wouldn't buy a phone without it if I'm spending a few hundred bucks.

I LOVE the Galaxy Express! I'm picky as hell but for the price and feature set, I think Samsung/AT&T got it right. The screen is not super ultra HD but it's crisp and clear. The camera isn't 13 MP (it's 5 MP) but the pictures are clear and are more than enough for Facebook, Instagram, and emailing. The touch screen is very responsive, Android runs smooth, and battery life surprisingly great for a smartphone. I charge it every other day. I need to charge my iPhone at least once a day, if not twice!

Pros:
- Price
- 4G LTE
- Snapdragon S4 Plus CPU w/ 1GB RAM
- Super AMOLED Plus screen
- Battery life

Cons:
- It's not bleeding edge (but it's bargain priced, a worthy trade off!)

All in all, very pleased. I find it a little insane that phones without a contract these days exceed the price of my Sony Vaio laptop! Seriously? This little gem of a phone has a great price tag and the performance to back it up. I LOVE 4G LTE. Everything loads so quickly but be careful not to burn through your data allowance - use WiFi when you're at home!

title: Nice TV, HORRIBLE mounting system and false advertising!
text:
Let me start by saying this TV has a nice picture and a great price and if your not wall mounting this TV then don't hesitate to buy it.

However if you do plan to wall mount your new TV, DO NOT BUY THIS MODEL! First off it is advertised at 200 x 200 VESA mount, this is a lie! Look up the manual online and it will tell you the mount is 266mm x 275mm! So then you think, well as long as i just get a tilt mount with 2 vertical 'hook' brackets for the back then it shouldn't be an issue, WRONG! The back of the TV has a raised section in the middle where the computer board and TV inputs are located, so majority of the TV is .5" thick, but then in the middle of the back there is a raised section that is about 1" - 1.5" thicker than the rest of the TV. There are inputs on the side and bottom of this raised section. The mounting holes are on the skinny part of the tv, RIGHT NEXT TO THE RAISED SECTION! so you have absolutely no way to get a mounting bracket up against the holes, and even if you could you would be blocking inputs, including the power input! Then you think, well most mounts come with spacers so you should be able to use those, NOPE! this raised area is so much higher that 2 different mounts spacers were not thick enough. So in order to get this mounted I had to go to the hardware store and get PVC pipe to use as spacers, and longer screws to hold the brackets. I ended up getting the thing mounted, but it took a trip to the hardware store and allot of messing around.

title: The water bladder compartment can hold a laptop!
text:
I bought this bag 2.5 years ago and continue to be very happy with it. It's very lightweight and it has that rare combination of a side-access camera compartment on one side, and a water bottle pouch on the other. I was waiting for that for a LONG TIME. I use it for weekend jaunts, travelling, hiking and camping. It's been an incredibly versatile bag and I use it even for those times when the only camera gear I'm packing is a single point-and-shoot. The interesting thing about this bag is that it is not advertised or marketed as having a computer compartment, but its water bladder slot actually works quite well for carrying a laptop. Sure, it doesn't provide the same protection since it's not padded, but it still works very well, as long as your laptop is on the small side. I've used it with my 13" Macbook Air and Thinkpad X220. And of course, tablets fit in it without any problem at all.

The bag's compact size also lets it fit easily under airplane seats and on amusement park rides.

Camera Compartment:
I shoot with a micro four-thirds camera system and its camera compartment has enough room for a body, several lenses, a flash, and other odds and ends (I put 2 or 3 lenses in the same pouch...if this bothers you, you can always add padding between them using dividers from other camera bags or come up with your own system, such as using lens pouches). When flying to a destination, I overstuff this compartment with additional items such as FRS radios, battery chargers, etc.

Water Bladder Compartment:
When flying to a destination, I use the water bladder slot to carry an AC power bar, chargers and cables, and a tablet or laptop (13" Macbook Air, Thinkpad X220, or iPad). At the destination I use the slot for spare clothes or to carry a tablet.
It's also very useful for carrying large books. For hiking or camping, I put clothing items in it, such as a silicon nylon tarp, waterproof socks, or a rain shell. Or if I'm going on a long hike in hot weather, I'll use it for my water bladder.

Main Compartment:
When travelling to a destination, I load this compartment with a spare change of clothes, in case my luggage gets lost. When out and about, I usually put food in this compartment.
When travelling, the zippered pocket is used for any important documents (passport, etc), SIM cards, and any other small, important items such as my house keys.
I also keep a couple of organizer pouches in this compartment, one of which is always attached to the clip that comes out of the zippered pocket. One pouch contains camera stuff (spare batteries, SD cards, remote control cord, etc). The other contains miscellaneous small items such as ear plugs, head phones, head phone splitter jack, AA batteries.
Because the camera compartment doesn't occupy the full width of the bag, it is possible to insert something all the way down to the bottom of the bag. I've put a thin, travel tripod in the bag that way, when the side pocket was already occupied by a water bottle.
The draw string closure has enough material that you can load the bag with enough stuff that it exceeds the height of the (ie: it looks like you have a grey duffel bag sticking out the top). This is a handy feature for those times when you need to carry extra food, clothing or other gear. I have used this ability a lot.

Top Flap Pocket:
Frequently accessed items are stored here, such as my wallet, sunglasses, car keys, lip balm, floss, phone, etc.

Side Pocket:
Usually used for a water bottle, other times I've used it as a temporary place to stow a camera lens or binoculars. And sometimes I use it to carry a tripod.

Rear Slot Pocket:
I usually stuff a rain shell in there, or a travel towel. My thin fleece lined jacket that I usually wear doesn't fit in there very well.

Under the Top Flap:
I'll usually store my jacket across the top of the pack and under the top flap. The bag has bottom straps where I could attach my jacket but I don't like the idea of my jacket being on the ground when I put the bag down.

Waist Belt Pockets:
I don't really use them. I've used them once or twice to carry lens caps or polarizer filters but I usually have the straps done up so tight that it's not really convenient to put anything bulky in them. And to be perfectly honest, I often forget that the pockets even exist.

Rain Cover:
Besides using it for weather protection, I also use it when in dusty environments.

title: Compared to the Nikon 10-24, this lens is the clear winner (if you don't need the range.)
text:
I first used a DX wide angle years ago at my old job - the Nikon 12-24 f/4. Loved that lens, even at 12mm f/4.

So last summer when I was shopping for a DX WA of my own, the Nikon 10-24 3.5-4.5 seemed like a no brainer. I figured I would use it mostly wide open at 10mm, so the slightly larger aperture and wider end seemed like a step up. However, after using it for a while I was never really happy with the sharpness of the images my copy delivered. It was good but not great (I use WA's to feature a subject prominently in the frame, not for landscapes, so I like to shoot close to wide open if possible.)

I didn't have access to the Nikon 12-24 f/4 anymore to compare to, but after discovering the Tokina 11-16 f/2.8, I decided to look into the Tokina 11-16 as a possible replacement.

After almost a year and a lot of research, I decided to go for a Tokina 11-16. Since I still had the 10-24, I did tripod comparisons with a remote shutter, comparing the lenses at 11mm f/3.5, 11mm f/5.6, 11mm f/8, 16mm f/4, 16mm f/5.6, 16mm f/8 from exactly the same position, without moving the tripod.

In every shot comparison the Tokina images at 100% were obviously sharper than the Nikon images - just as I suspected, and as my research suggested. Wonderful! Now, I may have received a great copy of the Tokina, and had a not-so-great copy of the Nikon. But in my real-world tests using the Nikon previously, I never thought the sharpness was "bad" - just not amazing. And I always wondered if starting at f/2.8 meant a sharper f/8 when I got there. The answer for me is: it does. This Tokina's sharpness is great! As a bonus, I get f/2.8 throughout the limited range if I need it.

So, in summary...

TOKINA 11-16 PROS:

- Sharp. Sharper than the Nikon 10-24 between 11-16mm and f/4-8.
- Fast. Option of using f/2.8 throughout the range.
- Solid. This lens feels pro grade and the Nikon feels plasticky.
- Price! Remarkably, this lens is currently $200 less expensive brand new then the Nikon 10-24 is, brand new.

TOKINA 11-16 CONS:

- Range. Less range than the 10-24. Sometimes being able to go to 24mm was handy and meant I wouldn't need to swap lenses.

TOKINA 11-16 NEUTRAL:

- Color/Contrast. Color overall seems better delivered on the Nikon. Although to be fair, I didn't test for this (i.e. used AWB in all shots.) Contrast seems to be about the same as the Nikon.

As a final note, I was concerned that the Auto Distortion Control menu option on my Nikon DSLR would be greyed out with the Tokina 11-16 as it is with my old discontinued Tokina 50-135. But the answer is, it is not! The camera recognizes the lens for Auto Distortion Control. Meaning I can get straight lines SOOC just like I did with the Nikon lens. Very convenient if you're like me and try to get as much right as possible in the camera to avoid post processing.

title: Fantastic Resolution, love the compact body
text:
I am a long time Canon person with 6 Canon mount lenses and a Canon 5D Mk III. I bought the Sony A7R because I wanted to try the higher resolution that has long been available for Nikon 800E users but not for Canon fans. I bought the A7R with the Metabones Canon EF adapter but also the Sony/Zeiss 35MM F2.8 and the Sony/Zeiss 24-70mmm F4.0.

I am still getting used to the a7R and where all the buttons are located. Right off the bat, you have to love the size and lightweight of the body. I think that the a7R and 2 lenses and flash would weigh the same as the Canon 5D and 1 lens. I have also owned Leica equipment and the a7R reminded me of how easy it is to just have the camera around since it is smaller and lighter. The programmable buttons are great and I think after set up the camera can do everything I would like. I feel confident that when I take a picture it will turn out well.

I also like the options for wireless controlling the camera from the iPhone app or small wireless remote control. I have also gotten a small Sony flash.

OK, downsides. The major complaint is the shutter which is a little loud and has a lot of moving parts. Normally with the 35mm, I just snapped away. However, I can think of many situations where you might wish it was quieter. Second, not a real complaint but my adapting to the Sony is the electronic viewfinder and how quickly it goes to sleep to save power. You have to push down on the shutter button to get it to wake up. Which leads me to No. 3 - power consumption. The camera does consume its battery relatively quickly. I have gotten the grip accessory which lets you insert two batteries. A good thing to get and it actually makes the camera easier to hold.

With the 35mm F2.8, the Sony focuses quickly and the pictures are very sharp - excellent - from F4.0 onwards. The 35mm really shows off the high resolution of the Sony 36.4 MP and you can pixel peek all day long. You can read some of the reviews of the 35mm and you know that this lens is one of the best available at any price. This is a great lens to leave on the camera all the time. It is very compact and the combination A7R and 35mm is a great combination for traveling or walking about. It gives you the portability of a small snapshot camera but the resolution of the most professional large body device. I just got the Sony 24-70mm F4.0 so I cannot comment.

On adapting Canon mount lenses, I have tried the A7R with the Canon 24-70 F2.8 L II - the new one - with the Metabones adapter. My major issue is that the focusing took a long time with some hunting. I guess I should be amazed that it worked at all! The auto exposure worked fine and the Canon lens really showed its great resolution at all focal lengths. I don't think this is the combination for street shooting but it would work for some carefully composed pictures. The Canon 24-70 on the Canon 5D III is works beautifully so I think the fault is the hybrid mixing of two systems. I also used the A7R with several Zeiss Canon mount lenses I have - the 21mm and the 18mm - and they worked fine and are very sharp. In this case, the focusing is manual.

My conclusion is that native Sony/Zeiss lenses work great and focus quickly. Canon mount lenses do not focus as quickly but it is a cheap price to pay to be able to use your Canon lenses on the Sony system when you want.

The bottom line for me is that I really enjoy the a7R. It is small and compact and is the kind of camera that you will carry on that next trip to Asia or Europe - or to see the kids play. The light weight and size make it easy to throw in a briefcase or camera bag. Finally, with the Metabones adapter, you can use your other lenses and see if they are up to 36 MP. I am happy I bought the a7R and I am still finding out its many features. Fun!

title: Perfect for my action camera (sort of)
text:
So I have a Polaroid XS100 action camera and I wanted this extender/monopod to use with it for more stable shots underwater and also to take on hikes and things like that. Before I get into the bad thing about using it for that, I will start with the good things..

This thing is small and light and perfect to throw in your pack or stick in a pocket and go. The length, in my opinion, is perfect because it allows the shaft to still be fairly thick at the top which gives it a more solid overall feel. The wrist strap is going to come in handy at times and the grip feels nice in the hand. Overall the head on it is nicely designed and is likely accommodating for several different cameras. The built in swivel/tilt head is very convenient as many monopods I looked at required an additional purchase for that.

Now for the bad...

On my Polaroid XS100, it comes from the factory as waterproof so there is a nice case around it and o-rings where they need to be which makes the camera slightly bigger compared to what a non-waterproof case may be. With that said, the threads on the XSP2 are too short to safely secure the camera to the extender. I was able to get about 1/2 a thread into the camera and luckily tested it out to ensure stability but the camera fell off seconds after. The problem is because of the case around the camera, the threads don't start immediately at the edge of it and are recessed slightly into the hole. After looking at other camera accessories locally in B&M stores seeing if I could find some sort of extension, I realized the screw on the extender is seemingly short compared to just about everything else I saw. Typically I would say this is a negative about the camera instead of the extender and that's how I viewed it until I went looking around. I would assume it may be by design and makes you use their accessories for your Go-Pro and such but it is annoying none the less.

With that said, it is nice to have friends who work in a machine shop. I was able to have him make a longer screw with the same design that fit perfectly into the factory housing. It is completely metal so it is more sturdy than the XShot one anyway. Those who don't have a friend who works in a machine shop may not be able to accommodate certain cameras and this may be why there is a steep rise of these used from Amazon Warehouse.

So overall I love the size, length, weight, and design but the screw could be one or two threads longer and would not have been a problem for me but it is what it is. Maybe as the action camera market grows they will address this or maybe I got a runt and nobody else has had this problem.

text:

After reading all the reviews, I was still hesitant about pulling the trigger on these headphones. After breaking my TripleFi-10's, I needed a replacement while trying to find audiologists to make ear molds for a reshelling. I could have bought a semi-decent replacement in the $30-50 range, or 4 earphones in the $10 range, returning the ones I did not like. I also have the Monoprice 8320 for workouts.

These blow everything else out of the water. They were good without the Comply foam tips, but sound unbelievable for $8.99 with the tips. title: SHIPPING issues review - Amazon failed 3rd times the charm
text:
This review is regarding solely shipping and customer service issues with Amazon, for the Kindle Paperwhite. I say this so as not to receive unhelpful remarks about the product itself (which I have yet to even enjoy) - but to educate potential Amazon buyers of getting their Kindle Paperwhite through Amazon. Seriously - buyers beware.

1st Kindle Paperwhite: Received as Christmas present from husband. Paperwhite was in it's sleek black box, packaged with another Kindle and various books in a typical Amazon cardboard box. Opened Paperwhite item to discover scratch on lower left hand screen. Amazon insisted on registering item before Return process - due to 'holiday shipping issues' replacement would not be overnight.

2nd Kindle Paperwhite: 12/31/2013 - (photo on item page) Opened typical Amazon cardboard box to discover a Kindle Paperwhite and it's cord floating at the bottom of the box between 3 bubble inserts. NO black box...... Was it refurbished? Why was it out of the black box sliding around the bottom of cardboard? Called Amazon - was assured it was a brand new Kindle Paperwhite. Which begs the question: Why is it out of it's secure black box then?? They have no clue. Amazon admitted shipping idiocy and processed another return for replacement. Oh - BTW I was reminded at this point that my husband's purchase date of 12/10 still stands as the 30 day warranty marker - since the 1st Kindle had been registered before return process (at THEIR suggestion) Nice catch huh?

3rd Kindle Paperwhite: 1/3/2014 - (photo on item page) Kindle Paperwhite Black box with USPS label slapped on the side sitting on my damp front door step. No Amazon cardboard box or safe packaging...... Just a Kindle screaming "steal me, please." WOW. Called Amazon, and the shipping Customer Service manager assured me that that is how ALL KINDLES are being shipped. Hmmmm, funny as that's not how the first or second one was. I asked the manager to explain to me the difference between this nonsense and having an XBox 360 container, plain as day sitting on a doorstep with a UPS label on it?......... crickets.....The manager seemed frustrated with me and said she "could not guarantee how the 4th replacement would be packaged or shipped..... but I have 5 more business days until my warranty for a 'non-refurbished' replacement is up." How is this even fair?

So I asked..... can I purchase a Kindle Paperwhite with ads at my local Best Buy and just call Amazon to pay for the ads to be removed? She said 'Yes.' So my final response was - then send me a return label & refund my husband immediately, as Amazon cannot intelligently package anything valuable to save their soul.

*Final slap in the face: My in-law had his Amazon purchased Paperwhite returned for replacement on 12/26 as well due to dead pixels on his screen. He still has not received his replacement due to Amazon choosing Fed-Ex as his delivery method, and Fed-Ex refusing to deliver to his PO Box - which is all he has. Classy :)

title: Absolutely awesome little thing!
text:
I have recently replaced my iPhone 4S with an iPhone 5, and since then have been suffering from lack of interface support with all of my charging/speaker docks. I have an expensive JBL speaker dock and a couple of other fairly portable ones with great sound quality... and now I cannot use them without an adapter, and the phone does not fit in them with the case... major pain in the behind.

We were at a party at friends' house and he was using a tiny bluetooth lousy, horrible sound little speaker that annoyed me to tears because I have very sensitive hearing and I cannot stand bad sound quality, so I started looking on Amazon on my phone for better alternatives that evening. When we got home I researched several of these speakers, and at the end decided that due to my previously great experience with JBL products, and the combination of size/price and features, this speaker is a good choice.

I received it a few days ago and boy am I surprised. First of all I was sure it was going to be much larger, so the size was originally a suspicious surprise as I expected less than ideal sound quality with this size, but when I took it out of the box and paired it with my phone in 10 seconds, and started playing some tracks that I usually use to test out sound systems - and I was very pleasantly surprised.

Since then I have been playing music on this thing for like 18 hours a day. I put it on the mantle in the living room and it fills up the room beautifully, I did not even reach the full volume setting and the sound quality is absolutely superb.

The battery lasted about 7 hours of playback today until I charged it - it did not even die, I just plugged it in eventually.

I am very very happy with this purchase, I am one of those people who despite being a technology freak, takes some time to adopt new technologies due to quality concerns. I did not believe that bluetooth connection could produce such high quality sound, and I am very happy to find out that I was mistaken.

The only thing that is a bit annoying, is that I forget it is my phone which is producing the audio, and if I cover it or put it under my arm when I am carrying the baby around, the sound will jump and stop because of the bluetooth, but that is the phone and not the speaker.

All in all, definitely 5 stars. Very good value for the money and so easy to operate with my MacBook Air, iPhone, and iPad.

title: Serial ports are becoming a thing of the past. Very few if any new computers have them. USB  to RS-232 ...
text: Serial ports are quickly becoming a thing of the past. Finding a computer that comes with serial ports nowadays, is next to imposable.  They are called legacy devices and there is little support for them. I bought this plugable usb adapter to use with / on my old (Amateur Radio) terminal node controller - TNC. The serial connector on the back of the TNC is a DB-25 female. I couldn't find this rs-232 serial adapter (prolific chipset) with a DB25 male plug / connector. So I ordered a gender changer that has - a db9 female on one end and a db25 (pins) male on the other. The gender changer plugs right into the db-25 female on the back of the TNC and the two male screw lugs fit and tighten up on the back of the TNC. Then the Plugable serial adapter plugs onto the gender changer and the 2 screw pins tighten up to the gender changer. After I was done, it was all connected up with nice tight connections. My TNC is an old pk-232-mbx. There is probably other serial adapters out there that would work, but I have faith in the latest prolific chipset and Plugable devices.

title: Fantastic Device with a not so fantastic companion app.
text:
I finally installed this Receiver after having to build a custom double din dashboard support for my car (the single din support was broken by a thief and I had no way to hold a receiver there)...

First I have to say that I really like this concept, it is something I've been dreaming about with the smartphone revolution... and it makes a lot of sense today.

Now, what most people need to know, things to consider (not really issues, but definitely something to improve upon):

1- There really should be some sort of D-pad, or 4 directions arrows, or at the very least, left/right arrows (for skipping songs, changing stations, etc). The dependancy on the Remote Control is TOO big on this device... Specially when App Remote does not fully control the receiver.... which brings me to the next point

2- App Remote is whitin itself a great idea to improve the usability of many receivers, but it should include a lot more functionality... 2.1- such as Remote Control mode (to substitute your RC in case of being lost)
2.2- It should be able to manage Favorite Stations inside Tuner mode (just place "1,2,3,4,5,6" buttons somewhere on the interface)
2.3- It should be able to hide unwanted or unused apps such as USB, SMS, etc
2.4- It should be able to re-arrange the icons, not only alphabetically...
2.5- It should be able to move with up/down arrows of the RC instead of only left/right...

3- The USB port is able to provide a "standard" and "high" charging mode (you can change it in settings while the receiver is off)... But in spite that setting, Android phones will recognize it as USB charging (aka computer) instead of AC charging... I managed to fool it by isolating the 2 middle contacts of the short USB cable with a small stripe of electric tape.... But even when my phone recognized it as AC Charging, the high temperature I get during the day, and the fact that my phone screen is always on (and with brightness at 85%) the phone charge extremely slowly, sometimes it stops charging and sometimes it even discharges while plugged. For those of you with newer Xperias, hopefully the magnetic pin provides better charging. I will try to get the Z3 Compact in the future.

4- Bluetooth Calling only comes through the Front Speakers of your car, so if you only have 2 speakers, you might want to plug those to the corresponding front speakers cable. I made the mistake of pluging them in the back and I get no sound from calls... So instead of changing connection I will get small front speakers so I can fully take advante of my system.

5- The Voice controlled app sucks. Just like that... I think it is riskier to try and use it and get failed attempts, making you mad while driving, than simply touch your phone and get it over with. I am not encouraging anyone to break your local law or get distracted, good drivers know their limitaitons and in my case I limit my interaction with my phone/receiver to only do it while at a Stop Light, Traffic, etc not moving. (While moving I keep the RC in my hand and operate without taking the eyes off the road)

In conclusion... this Receiver is a fantastic idea and I am glad I got it, it might not be for everyone, and mostly aimed to people who knows how to take advantage of its phones. It is definitely better with Xperia devices, but you can use it with almost any other phone (iOS, Android).

I would rate the Receiver 4.5 stars, but I have to remove half star because of App Remote limitations... I am willing to ignore the receiver's flaws when Sony improve App Remote, since it is literally the face of my car stereo.

title: Optics are not aligned product is not usable -
text:
After reading the glowing reviews on this product I was very disappointed to discover that the product is of very poor quality. In my case I did not discover this until after the return window had closed so I'm left with a set of non usable binoculars.

These binoculars were bought as a christmas gift to my wife. I used them just briefly and found that they were hard to focus, but I didn't get a chance to investigate fully at the time. My wife complained that these binoculars were too powerful and she was having trouble with them. I didn't listen, unfortunately.

So this weekend I had 20 minutes to investigate the cause of the difficulty in focusing with these binoculars. I started out by closing one eye and using the center wheel to focus on a distant object, I then opened my other eye and used the combiner focus to merge the two eyes (standard binocular focusing technique). No joy. I was perplexed, this always worked. I then focused on a distant horizon with one eye open, then switching to the opposite eye open. The horizon jumped up about 2 degrees. I finally figured out why these binoculars were difficult to focus, they couldn't be focused with both eyes open!!!

If you buy these check them by looking way out at the horizon and make sure you can focus out there. If you can't return them, I wish I did.

I guess I can break them into two rather small telescopes, since you can't use these as binoculars.

title: Amazing little device
text:
After a lot of research and comparison shopping here on Amazon.com, I ended up going with the 3M Streaming Projector w/Roku. The day I got the package, I quickly opened it, and did my normal routine of setting up my new electronic device without reading the owner's manual. For me this is a true test of a products "Apple'esqness", meaning how intuitive is the device, do I need to stop what I'm doing and pick up the manual and read and follow step by step instructions? For this device it was a resounding No. I was able to take it out of the box, attach my new "Cable Matters Gold Plated Mini DisplayPort to HDMI Cable" to my Macbook Pro and I was watching videos within a couple mins.

The initial picture was blurry so I used the scroll wheel focus adjustment and was able to bring it into reasonable focus quickly. The picture wasn't perfect but it wasn't bad at all. So after watching some music videos I decided to test out the Roku stick. The Roku stick is not something to pass by as just something included with this projector, non of the other projectors in this class had anything like it and to add a Roku box you will spend another $80-$100.

The Roku stick took some setting up. You have to go to their website, set up an account (which was painless), get your projector connected to the internet, and then go through the login process. Once this is completed the Roku stick worked great and I was logged into my Netflixs account and was watching movies in no time. Outstanding little addition to this portable projector.

The speaker on the projector is small, so you cannot realistically expect it to push out great sound. But, if you don't have external speakers to hook up to, or you need to go completely wireless, you can run this projector on battery and use the internal speaker and still enjoy a flick.

I marked this projector down one star because of the focus scroll wheel. It seems to have some play in it, meaning you start scrolling and nothing happens for a short distance and then it suddenly start focusing. You have to play with it for a while going back and forth to finally get the picture within reasonable focus. One thing to note though, your image is only as good as your source. So if you are watching a subpar video it will look even worse on this projector. If you have a good quality picture it will spit it out in 720p and look pretty darn good.

I ran this in my family room with a lot of light coming in and had it around 60" on a portable screen. The brightness was high enough for me to enjoy what I was watching. In a dark room it looks very, very good. The reviewers here who badmouth projectors, especially small ones like this, because the picture is washed out in anything but a dark room doesn't know a thing about projectors. Unless you spend a great deal of money, you are not going to get a picture like you do from a TV, and no projector is going to look good in a lit room than a TV at any price range.

So overall this is a great device that when you consider the savings here on Amazon.com along with the Roku stick it's a bargain that I highly recommend.

title: Decent for the price... pros and cons...
text:
Much has already been written about this model already, so I'll just give my pro and con list for the most part, based on my experience. While I do stock photography and use a DSLR for that, I wanted a more casual camera for around the house, and I'm not lofty in my expectations. I know what you should (and should not) expect for a price (and from Fuji, based on past Fuji camera experience).

Pro List:

1) Manual Zoom ring gives the "feel" of a DSLR w/manual focusing available.
2) Ability to use filters on lens.
3) Good hand grip and handling overall. Can use in full auto or lots of manual controls.
4) Non-proprietary AA batteries make it handy when traveling. I suggest "eneloop" rechargeable brand.
5) Overall good image quality (for a non-pro camera level) once you learn how to leave the full auto and adjust settings.
6) Tilt LCD.
7) Hot shoe for external flash (if you feel the need for it).
8) Very fast focusing under most conditions.

Con List:

1) Electronic eye viewfinder is very low res and very small.
2) Battery compartment door shifts when gripping camera a bit (irritating).
3) Image stabilization is sensor shift type - not lens type, so not as effective (and nearly worthless at 700mm full zoom).
4) Image quality is only best when you use the priority modes (7 megapixel resolution give or take) as opposed to full resolution mode.
5) Blows highlights easily unless you use the highlight priority mode.
6) No printed instruction book - can be hard to learn to use all manual items for those who might not be tech heads.

I would recommend this camera if you get it under $300 via Amazon or Costco who is also offering it for this price, and as long as you realize that while it LOOKS like a digital SLR, it is NOT a digital SLR. If you completely rely on the camera's full auto mode, then the image quality is "ok". If you take the time to read the CD manual and make some more manual adjustments to the settings outside of auto mode, then I bump up the image quality to "good". Using the camera at it's full 16mp resolution produces the poorest results. Once you get a couple of priority mode settings down and reduce the photos to a smaller size in-camera at around 7 megapixels, then images improve a good deal; of course, this means in order to get the best from this camera, you're sacrificing pixels - and you're paying essentially for a 7 megapixel camera instead of a 16 megapixel camera. Being able to use AA batteries is a plus for travelers.

My largest complaint is the type of image stabilization (IS) that is used in this camera, where the sensor itself is "shifted" instead of the lens having a stabilizing mechanism inside of it. Sensor shift IS is not as effective, and as a result, I found that when using this camera at full 30X zoom, I rarely get usable photos - even in bright sunny conditions and even when allowing the camera to up the sensitivity automatically to up to 400iso. Backing it off to around 500mm (per the guide that's printed on the lens barrel) fixes this for the most part, and the images are once again sharp, though this means it's not truly a 30X camera if you can't really use the zoom fully without a tripod. Not a great choice for bird and wildlife watchers if you expect the full zoom out of it to work perfectly, then.

Overall grade based on the level of camera it is, who it's aimed at, and price = B-

title: Pay a little more for the HF3520 if you must have a sunrise simulator
text:
The Philips HF3510/60 light is a useful way to wake up that misses on several fronts. It provides a sunrise simulation that will wake most people up. It unfortunately doesn't do much else well, either as an alarm clock, radio, or seasonal light. 3 stars, and if you're going to spend this kind of money on a wakeup light you're probably better off spending a little more on the [[ASIN:B0093162RM Philips HF3520]] instead.

Much of this review is similar to that of the HF3520; the two boxes are largely identical except for 2 features. The first is that this has 3 alarm sounds instead of 5, which is largely irrelevant since if this is used correctly, you'll wake up to the sunrise instead.

The second is far more relevant. The problem with the sunrise feature on this model is that it is both inflexible and far more jarring. The HF3520 offers a sunrise starting at red, progressing through orange and yellow to white. The color progression is unique among sunrise simulators and really quite neat; unless exhausted, I tend to wake up somewhere between red to orange most mornings and so set the timer for its short duration of 20 minutes. In contrast, the HF3510 has one light color - yellow - and a fixed 30 minute sunrise. You can certainly decrease the maximum intensity of the yellow light, but there's a definite difference between slowly being roused by the equivalent of a gentle candle versus a dimmed lightbulb that starts shining 30 minutes before the time set on the alarm clock.

This proves important as the new Philips wakeup lights do anything well except for sunrise simulation. The alarm clock is ok, but as other reviewers have pointed out the buttons are far, far too small - you risk knocking it off your night stand trying to push them, and setting the alarm and using snooze aren't particularly intuitive. The sounds on the alarm clock aren't graduated, nor are there many of them; in general, something like the alarm on the [[ASIN:B008I20LJ2 Zeo]] provides a much more pleasant audio wake up.

It's also disappointing that there's no AM radio or 2.5mm headphone jack to allow external devices. For more audio options than the weak FM radio, Philips clearly wants consumers to purchase the more expensive [[ASIN:B0093162SQ HF3550]], with the presumption that they own an Iphone 4 or below to pipe in audio. It's theoretically possible to buy a third-party FM modulator for a workaround, but that's an awful lot of effort to put in to achieve the same functionality in an expensive device that most cheap $20 alarm clocks provide out of the box.

Most importantly, even at full intensity the 300 lux light is enough to wake up most people but is far too weak to provide the recommended light dosage for morning exposure. Putting this side-by-side with the older 10000 lux [[ASIN:B0018804AY Britelite 6]] is like comparing the sun to a candle. Even the little [[ASIN:B001I45XL8 GoLite]] puts out far more powerful lux than this. As such, it really isn't useful for anything more than just waking you up, and that's a shame.

That's why while both models are somewhat overpriced, this is even more relatively overpriced than its big brother, since the major benefit of a sunrise simulator is diminished by how this version is stripped down. You're better off just paying a little more for the HF3520 instead. 3 stars.

text:
Unlike many other reviewers who are using the iPico to watch movies, I am using it for artistic purposes and am a bit disappointed. The problem is that when projecting landscape images from my photo album the aspect ratio is distorted and the images appear wide, circles turn to ovals, thin people look fat. Not very flattering.

Furthermore, I contacted their support department and got absolutely no response. No 'got your email' email. No follow up. No 'use our chat person'. This is unacceptable for a consumer product and I'm just happy that I am not having serious problems with it - or I'd feel pretty stuck.

It's a very cool little projector that does a fine job at a limited number of things. Just wish I'd known about it's image distortion problems before picking one up.

Update: I did hear back from General Imaging several days later. While they were courteous and well informed, there is no work around to the image distortion problem. There is another app - iResizer for iphone - that will allow you to distort your images to compensate for the elongation that the iPico will do. title: NVIDIA has put together an amazing board here
text:

With hardware that is many times more powerful than the RasberryPi and other small/low power SoC mini PC's, this has the performance and expand-ability to handle a wide variety of uses. I hope though strong sales the price will be able to come down (due to manufacturing efficiency and the accessories market will pick up.

Uses for these boards range from a 2nd desktop, network router (with a 2nd Ethernet port coming off the pcie slot and maybe a USB wifi adapter), or a file server, and perhaps the largest potential: an extremely efficient HTPC to play media on your TV.

The existing arm boards are too slow for many functions and too expensive for what they offer. Now we just need this to come down in price a little bit and include a case & power brick and they will be flying off the shelf.

But be aware, this board currently only supports Ubuntu OS (no support for Windows on ARM or Android) although again if this becomes popular we may see other options open up.

title: Trouble with HDMI Cable
text:
To start off with, I would like to have given the Kindle Fire HD 5 stars, but
for the problem I encountered connecting it to my Sony Bravia HDTV.

The issue is that Amazon does not say anything about the type of Micro-HDMI
cable to use. I assumed that the one that I had purchased a year ago for my
Android phone would work. It did not...

After talking with customer support (they were very responsive, but not helpful),
I thought I would try buying an expensive cable at Staples. This one did not work
either. Amazon then sent me a new Kindle.

I decided to check out cables listed on Amazon, read the reviews, and found one
that people said they found worked. I purchased it quickly and tried it
on my original Fire HD. It worked!!! I returned the replacement Kindle.

The moral of the story is: Not all Micro-HDMI cables are created equally :(

This one does work:
Mediabridge Flex Series - High Speed Micro-HDMI to HDMI Cable with Ethernet (6 Feet)

I hope Amamzon support and their documentation will be updated to prevent
future customers from having this problem.

Happy now, but frustrated.

P.S. This cable does not cost that much. It would help if Amazon included
it in their Kindle package.
P.S.S. After getting this to work via direct connect to my TV, I tried connecting
through my Yamaha 6.1 Amp with HDMI switching... works great.

title: Lots of Desktop Space w/ Semi-Open Firmware
text:
Works great as a developer monitor too bad it's just 30Hz. I know most people mention the service menu accessed by 0000 but I found there is also an engineering menu by pressing 2947. I was trying to disable the boot animation so I could reduce the startup time but the option doesn't seem to work.

I looked through the firmware image and it's a MIPS process inside running the 2.6.34 kernel and even has some RealTek usb wireless drivers included. If you could find a way to configure networking on the wireless interface you could use telnet which is enabled. It also has an httpd server included but it doesn't do anything useful. The init scripts claim it's a RealTek Linux distribution.

I didn't try to modify boot images or the menu but it should be possible with little work. I just didn't want to attempt it without a way to reflash the image and unbrick it. I'm wondering where the UART is at which I guess might be able to unbrick it if just the menu was broken.

title: Very good, with caveats
text:
I purchased this for the purpose of mounting a Toshiba Thrive to my tripod for use as a controller and focusing monitor for my HD DSLR video rig. Since this is not made specifically for this use, I had to convert it to a flat mount by cutting off the right angled piece of the bracket with a Dremel tool, and then drilling four holes through which I run two u-bolts to fasten the assembly to my tripod upright.

The biggest issue, as I see it, is that the gooseneck is not centered in the tablet mounting frame, and the frame cannot be sufficiently tightened to the gooseneck to keep it from seeking the lowest point when you mount a largish tablet to it. What this means, specifically, is that my 10" Thrive did not rest at a proper horizontal orientation when mounted - rather, it spun such that it was oriented diagonally and was useless to me. I had to fix this by spot welding the mounting bracket to the tripod. This is obviously not something I would recommend to most users of this mount, but it worked just fine for my use.

That said, this is an extremely sturdy mount now that I have welded the bracket to the gooseneck to prevent it from rotating, and the gooseneck itself will hold virtually any position you can force it into.

This product is a bit of a paradox, but with the proper modifications, works exactly as I need it to.

title: Horrible photos in incandescent or bright lighting!
text:
I had an old dinosaur of a Sony that took 1280 by 640 photos, max quality. It weighed a ton and was a solid 1/2 cubic foot block of dead weight (or so it seemed). So it was HIGH time to upgrade. So seeing the wonderful reviews on this camera, and being happy with my previous one in spite of it being outdated, I happily ordered this one!

Boy, what a PAIN this one was. We have incandescent lighting and no matter how many "auto" settings I tried, I couldn't get the pictures to come out without them having a yellowish tint to them. On top of it, since we have a large family, the pictures were consistently ruined by one kid or another moving and making a big blurry area. It was terrible! So I did research and changed some settings on the camera so that the shutter speed and other settings were better. I changed the White Balance to get rid of the yellow tinge (FINALLY!!). Still, it was very much a pain to have to constantly reset the white balance before I took any pictures. Some of the pictures were still blurry, but it was ACCEPTABLE, barely. Then I brought it to my new daughter's baptism and I got NOT ONE good picture because of the light coming through the windows. I am SO frustrated. I would have used my DINOSAUR camera if I would have known that this brand new, almost $200 dollar camera COULD NOT TAKE BETTER PHOTOS!!!! What good is a camera if you have to be messing around with settings before each one? Who has time to be messing with this before your child's special event, in the Church, etc??? I am FLABBERGASTED by all the 5 star reviews on this thing!

So to continue the saga, I brought the camera to Best Buy to pick out a new one... and to see if I had a lemon. Lo a behold the camera was acting fine THERE, under their fluorescent light... but was still a bit on the blurry side and the colors weren't quite right. Picked out a new Nikon Coolpix S9100 that took excellent pictures in the store, brought that home, and it's PERFECT. You point it at your kids, it takes a picture perfectly. You then point it out the window at the bright light and it adjusts and comes out perfect. Voila! A camera that works!

Oddly enough, I went to Sam's Club later that day after Best Buy and guess which camera I saw there? This Sony one! And guess what it did as soon as I tested THAT one in the store? Yup, blurry picture and glare coming from the door of Sam's. How in the WORLD did this camera get such good reviews??!!! Needless to say I'm returning it even though I'm past the 30 day window and probably won't get my full refund back. Adios, piece of junk! Pretty pitiful that you can't even take as solid pictures as a Sony from 10 years ago (that one takes 3.5" floppy disc too, just to show you how old it is! LOL)

I was not disappointed. This is a very nice scanner and a good value if (repeat, if) you are patient and understand the limitations of the radio and the manual. If you want a be-all-to-end-all scanner, then spend $400-$500. This $100 unit will not suit you. Based upon my limited use so far I have found that the sensitivity is good and adjacent channel rejection is good. The functions are clearly marked and the display is clear and easily read. The speaker is terrible (normal for smaller radios) and you should purchase an after market speaker. The included accessories (antennas, DC power options, etc.) are good. An external antenna (AntennaCraft ST-2 for instance) is a good idea.
Given the price I would say:
Appearance - 5 (Nice smaller unit)
Features - 4
Sensitivity / Rejection - 4 (This is based upon limited use so far and is subject to later revision)
Ease of Use - 3 (Needs better manual. Programming is a pain, but worth it.)
Overall - 4

title: Simplicity is a good thing...
text:
There's not much to say about this product except that it does EXACTLY what its intended to do and it does it well.

I was looking for a way to store SD cards that was space conscious, simple, and secure. I found just that. Many of the products out there for SD card storage offer nice storage, but too often either take up too much room, or are hard to gets cards in and out of. (Big fingers make it that much worse)

This case when folded in half still takes up a surprisingly small amount of space, and if the intent is something thin, then simply unfold it and it's barely more than 1/4" thick. Folded, it slides easily into a pocket.

My other most common complaint is the ease of getting your cards in and out. Thin vinyl sleeves are great, but offer little in the way of protection and can be "fiddly" sliding cards in and out. It seems like every card I want, doesn't want to slide out of the sleeve, and the ones I don't want, fall out on their own. This case offers hard shell protection, and when you open ONE compartment, you get one card - easy in, easy out. I don't see it as a negative, but the compartments are big enough that the cards do "rattle around" slightly when stored - I cured this by simply sticking a small sticky felt pad (very thin) in the bottom of each compartment. This did two things, stopped the cards from moving in the case at all, and offered a bit of shock absorption for the cards... can't hurt. :)

As a photographer, the content of my SD Cards is valuable and this case makes sense... inexpensive, protective, easily stored/carried, and easy card access.

I left the rating at 5 stars based on how well this item is working for me today - if that changes, I will amend my review.

Along those lines, I can't address the durability of the plastic over time and how temperature may play a role, but...
it's doing exactly what I need and I plan on getting at least one more.

title: Helpful Hints to Get the VT60 Be Even Better
text:
I have to agree with all the superlatives mentioned by other reviewers of this product. A couple of things that took some research to find, but I think will help make this Plasma TV even better, are the following:

#1) Instead of paying a professional calibrator to calibrate the TV, here's a link to settings that you can do yourself, and have the best picture quality ever!
[...]

This will REALLY help you get the best viewing experience, and prevent you from experiencing that fake-looking "soap-opera" look when watching movies, tv, etc.

#2) This TV also comes pre-loaded with ad banners. It's actually easy to turn off, so here are the instructions:

Menu > Setup > Display customization > Smart VIERA Banner >

#3) I've connected a laptop to my Plasma Panasonic VT60 using HDMI cable, and in order to get better audio, I had bought [[ASIN:B00GNHPFRW Bose® Companion® 3 Series II Multimedia Speaker System]]s (I actually got them from Costco, since they were about $50 cheaper). I connected the Bose speakers to my laptop (I am not sure how to connect them directly to my new Plasma TV), but I was having trouble with the audio. Every time I played something on my laptop (and since it was connected to my Plasma, I would be able to see everything on the Plasma), the audio was NOT coming from the Bose speakers, but from the Plasma TV's speakers. I realize that HDMI cables carry both video AND audio, but I wanted to have the audio come to my Bose speakers, NOT my Panasonic Plasma TV speakers (Bose sounds soooooo much better). I realized all I had to do was fix a setting on my HP laptop, not my TV. I needed to go to the settings on my laptop under Control Panel > Sound > then choose "Speakers and Headphones" as the DEFAULT, and that fixed all my problems.

As I navigate & learn more about my new TV, I will update my post to reflect helpful hints.

title: Worldwide adapter except Switzerland; takes 2-prong plugs only (incl US polarized plugs).
text:
This is the most compact and lightweight travel adapter for 2-prong N. American plugs (Type A). Unlike many budget (and non-budget) Universal adapters this particular one takes N. American polarized 2-prong plugs commonly found in shavers, hairdryers and other bathroom appliances - the type where one flat prong is a bit bigger than the other flat prong.

This adapter does not take nor adapt to the Swiss, grounded plug where the middle earth-pin is round, and the plugs are 3 in a row. In fact, most multi-country travel adapters do not fit the Swiss plugs because they are so different.

The build quality is ok at best probably due to its light weight. Adjusting the prongs feels a bit fiddly and fragile at the beginning, but is secure once adjusted. As long as the receiving outlet is not too tight, then this does what it's designed to do. It has so far survived over 40 trips in the past 2 years to countries all over Asia and Europe.

This travel adapter is rated to 6A and not the usual 13A that most Universal Adapters are. As in most travel adapters, the middle pin is plastic and does not provide grounding.

Recommended as a lightweight backup travel adapter for use in N. America, UK, Europe (except Switzerland), Australia and parts of Asia.

Use in UK/Ireland:
Several other reviewers have said that this adapter does not fit into the sockets in the UK & Ireland. This is just simply a misunderstanding where the assumption was that the UK & Ireland are in Europe and so the user configures this adapter to fit a Continental-European socket. The correct format/configuration for this adapter is to follow the instructions for Hong Kong/India (former British colonies) to be used for the UK & Ireland. Additionally, there is a safety feature built into the new British-style sockets where one must push the top pin into the slot to open the slots for the 2 bottom pins. To conclude, this works in the UK, but you must follow the directions for Hong Kong/India.
