title: Graphics editing on a budget
text:
What's special about this LG IPS231P monitor is its e-IPS technology and yet the price is still the same as the conventional TN type monitors.

It's awful to edit photos on a a conventional TN based monitor. The color and contrast shift when my head moves a couple inches from right to left, and I could never be sure what the image really looks like. It's especially worse when viewing a photo on a larger screen, since the corners look darker and warmer than the middle of the screen. IPS type monitor can fix this viewing angle problem, but I couldn't afford the cost that usually runs double to triple the conventional TN monitor price. That's why I had been using the old humongous CRT monitor that took up half of my desk. Everybody laughed when they saw that beast.

Within the last year, several makers started producing cheaper IPS monitors, using e-IPS, with the "e" probably stands for "economy". This monitor has the same advantage as true IPS, meaning the color and contrast don't shift depending on viewing angle. The cheap price comes with a couple of set backs, compared to true IPS:

1. The wide angle isn't as wide as true IPS. But it's still much better than TN. I can see a huge difference between the TN monitor at my office and the IPS231P monitor in this test: [...] (replace the underscore with the dot to see the page)

2. The color depth isn't true 8-bit. It's actually 6-bit that's extended to 8-bit. While I can see all the color shades here www_lagom_nl/lcd-test/contrast.php, the gradient test www_lagom_nl/lcd-test/gradient.php shows some minor banding.

If you're looking for vibrant colors, this monitor isn't it. Vibrant color is not the same as true colors. Look around and you'll see that true colors in the real world are actually more subdued. The problem with using an artificially vibrant monitor is that your photos look worse when you print them out or when other people view them on their screens.

One overhyped feature is the colors. While the colors are accurate, a good quality TN monitor will be just as accurate. Some newer TN monitors actually do better. The real advantage over the TN monitor is that the colors remain accurate when viewing angle changes, and stays accurate from one edge of the screen to the other. The IPS231P only covers the sRGB color space, not the extended AdobeRGB color space. This is why professional graphics editors should look for true IPS monitors. Being an armature graphics editor, sRGB is good enough for me, mostly because everything else in my workflow use sRGB, like printers, cameras, editors and browsers.

The pixel response time is slower than TN monitors, but in practice it doesn't matter much. Tests show that it's more like 15ms lag rather than the 5ms in the specification. However, during action and sport movies, I could not see any ghosting even if I tried to look for it. Only hard-core gamers need to worry about this.

Another thing that doesn't matter much, and yet attracted most of the complaints is the light leaks in the corners due to the new LED lighting. The leaks are very faint, and only visible when the entire screen is completely black.

While lacking HDMI port, this monitor supports HDCP encryption via its DVI port, so that you can still watch blu-ray on your computer. There's a cheap DVI to HDMI converter that you can buy if necessary.

You should also look at these competing models: Asus ML239H, NEC EA232WMi, Dell U2312HM. They have about the same graphics quality, with differences mainly in the features. The Dell and Asus have better pixel response time and have HDMI port, but the Dell is more expensive, and the Asus doesn't have adjustable height. The NEC adds 4 USB ports and costs more.

The bottom line is that this monitor is much better than the conventional TN type, but can't match true high-end IPS type. The affordable price compared to true IPS type is what makes it attractive.

-- Update May 22nd 2012 --

I understand now why people think the color from this monitor is more vibrant. It's because of the deeper black. It makes colors look more saturated and also increases the contrast. In other words, cheaper TN-type monitors don't have enough black, which make darker colors look pale.

The built-in speakers sound worse than those on my laptop. It makes movies hard to understand. Only good enough for software beeps and dings. If you watch movies or hear music from your computer at all, you'll need real speakers.

I measured power usage with a Kill-A-Watt device. The monitor only consumes 20 watts on the lowest brightness (which is still a little too bright for my dark room).

title: Can't perform THE most basic function.
text:
I originally wrote a much more generous review for this product. In concept it was exactly what I was looking for and seemed to be the exact device for some specialized needs.

That all changed however ... shortly after opening the box. BOTH times.

Long story short it doesn't connect to the internet. Read the other reviews around here. It's obviously a MAJOR issue yet the company holds their hands over their ears while loudly projecting "LA LA LA LA". At first I spent 45 minutes in a chat, deleting a driver, doing a factory reset, and downloading a new networking driver from the site.

Day 2, we came to the conclusion that immediately after rebooting, it was back to the beginning with the device not connecting to the internet all over again. Time for an RMA.

I waited a WEEK for the RMA label I was told would be coming by U.S. Mail. I finally called and had to pester the rep on the phone until he would e-mail the label so I could print it off. That e-mail also NEVER arrived. I ended up going to the FedEx store and spending nearly 45 minutes getting the defective unit shipped off using the FedEx store's rep to find this return authorization and printing off the label.

10 days later I have the unit back and now it not only doesn't get online for the apps through the Start screen (just like before) but now not even IE on the desktop will browse! NO internet connectivity AT ALL.

Bear in mind this is a house where at one time or another 4 different laptops, a destop computer, a wireless printer, three smart phones, and two e-readers have all connected to the router and surfed online flawlessly ... but NOT THIS ASUS!

And just to be sure it wasn't only the network here, I took it to two airports and a local bread restaurant ... this device would not connect and browse on any of these WiFi connections.

On the last hour-plus phone call, the rep was actually taking me through the EXACT SAME ROUTINE as the very first chat. This time I'm sure it was going to go better because ... ummm I don't know WHY. It was absolutely brain-dead process rather than actual trouble shooting. The rep didn't even know that Win 8 had a startup wizard which retrieved settings! Not exactly helpful or knowledgeable assistance. He refused to escalate the call, hung up after I held for his supervisor over 15 minutes.

All totaled, 3 chat sessions, 4 phone calls later and a trip to the FedEx store in a blizzard, (easily better than 4 hours of my time) wasted. This unit is in a box and headed back to Amazon.

Save yourself the frustration, pay more, get something that works. Your time is too valuable to burn on this good idea which went horribly wrong somewhere in the implementation.

This experience with ASUS is not at all a motivator to make me consider another of their products. I have NEVER had so much trouble right out of the box with any piece of hardware ... nor have I ever encountered a less competent staff "supporting" a product.

title: Pleasantly Surprised
text:
Upgraded from Phenom II 965 Processor.

System:
FX 6300 Processor
Asrock Extreme4 970 Board
Corsair Vengeance DDR3 1600MHz
OCZ 600 Watt PSU 80+ Bronze
AMD Radeon 7870XT Graphics Processor

I read reviews claiming this was a nice upgrade from phenom II's, I sort of doubted them, but was interested in this six core when I saw it dip to the price of 109 USD.

Differences from Phenom II 965:

The Phenom II 965 had a weaker memory controller than this FX series processor, I am very pleased to see my options increased for overclocking my ram if I so choose. The Phenom II 965 supported a max memory speed of 1600MHz, whereas in my bios the FX 6300 potentially allows me to clock my ram at speeds up to 2133MHz, not that my ram is good enough for that sort of overclock.

The processor itself idles around the same temps as Phenom II 965 did, but runs much cooler under full load. Several Websites also tell me that the fx 6300 is more energy efficient, since I have no way of measuring power usage, I'm just going to take their word for it.

I ran some benchmarks and it performs as advertised, all six cores stable at stock speeds in prime95 tests.

Outperforms Phenom II in single threaded benchmarks by a bit, it also outperforms in multi threaded, but that isn't exactly a fair comparison with the two extra cores.

In games it seems to outperform the Phenom II by several FPS. I noticed a bit of an improvement in Planetside 2 and Minecraft in particular. Fraps Benchmarks confirmed this.

Overall It's a good processor, and it fits my needs. The two extra cores are a bit pointless for my uses, but it was a 5 dollar difference between this and the Fx 4300, and they may prove useful, so I don't mind having them. Best of all, I didn't need to buy a new motherboard to install it.

title: Exceptional sound, good comfort, great mobility , echo during tv
text:
Volume - excellent, maximum setting is very uncomfortable

Bass - excellent.

Clarity - excellent - meets Sennheiser reputation.

Overall sound quality - surprising and extraordinary -- almost as good as my Sennheiser 580's (which are wired).

User friendliness - setup is intuitive.

Signal - excellent, was able to walk full extent of home with zero loss of signal.

Bluetooth - nope. The choice here was between your entertainment center/some fixed location vs your iphone/laptop, and the choice was clearly made for home entertainment situations. Another choice was between the superior "Kleer" audio transmission and the inferior bluetooth signal, and considerations that favored audiophile needs won out.

Interference - no conflict with wifi or other signals, as some are reporting.

Comfort - excellent, but people with large ears may have a problem right away. Otherwise these are soft and extremely lightweight.

Aesthetics - large and goofy, though nowhere near as ridiculous as the Pioneer SE-DRS3000C. These clearly favor function over form.

Privacy - none. If your intent is to prevent the world from knowing you listen to Justin Bieber or Katy Perry, then these headphones will not keep your shameful secret.

Sound isolation - these aren't isolation headphones.

Controls - if you've read more than five reviews then you already know the controls weren't designed to be used blindly. It would be nice at times to be able to adjust the volume without taking them off, so I'll play around with putting on tape so my fingers can feel out the controls better. Edit: Solution for the controls issue: glue a couple objects to the volume buttons after you are certain you approve of the other features of the headphones. I used those little rubber thingies you can get in most hardware stores, and now I can feel the volume buttons (and the power button in between them) with no problem.

With tv - this is the unit's single greatest point against it. What people are reporting about the echo is true, so unless your tv has a special syncing option you won't be able to watch this with your headphones on while other people watch without them. The only real alternative is to buy extra headphones (the unit can support up to four) and have the whole family wearing them, though people who don't need them will probably resent this pretty quickly. This single design mishap is costing the headphones a full star, but in light of the headphones greatest strengths (sound quality and signal strength) I'll be keeping them anyway because the primary motive for buying them was for work, and not for the entertainment center.

Solution for the problem many people are reporting regarding the signal cutting out at low volumes: Max out the volume on your primary source (in my case my laptop computer) and control the volume from the headphones. This eliminates the cutout and, oddly enough, a high pitch whine (don't ask me why).

title: not a good choice if you have tremors and/or repetitive stress injuries
text:
Admission: I've used Macs exclusively since 1993, so my PC knowledge is limited to machines I've used at various jobs and had IT people fix for me. This review won't be so much about tech stuff (which is well covered elsewhere) as the physical experience of using this computer.

As a Windows rookie, I kind of hoped ordering something in my price range with a fair number of reviews and at least a 4-star average would just work out and I wouldn't have to think about it anymore. It did not.

I had read the reviews saying the speakers were on the bottom, but then there were comments saying they weren't and I thought maybe people were confused or there were a few lemons. I bought the red i3 version and the speakers were absolutely definitely on the bottom. It sounded rather good when I tilted it to lie on its screen, and if you can think of any reason anybody would ever want to do that, do let me know.

I have moderate hand/arm tremors and multiple chronic/recurring RSIs (carpal tunnel and cubital tunnel syndromes, tendinitis). The size and weight of the machine triggered the hell out of the RSIs - it's been 3 days and a whole bunch of Vicodin and I'm still in a tremendous amount of pain. I had read that the touchpad was extremely sensitive, but figured I could simply adjust that (I'm on frequent bedrest and mostly use laptops in my actual lap so external mice aren't a great option). The thing was, due to the tremors, it took me a full hour of the cursor jumping all over the place and literally dozens of unintended windows popping open to even be able to get to the control panel to make that change. I figured I could minimize using it if I mostly stuck with keyboard commands but the keyboard was so large I had to hold my hand in an extremely awkward position to do that.

If you're a strong, healthy, non-shaky person, that last paragraph is probably useless to you - but if you share any of my conditions and aren't currently in a financial position to drop a grand on a compact, reliable laptop, you may want to explore the wonderful world of netbooks.

title: Third Time is a Charm for USB
text: SUMMARY: It's an average unit at an average price with a 5 yr warranty and free tech support and looks cool with non-smelly velvet texture from a great company - one of my favorites - recommended.  DETAILS: Busy lives mean you have less time to wait around for data to move!  USB-3 ("super-speed USB", or SS-USB) has arrived with the new electronics standard advertising (potentially) 10x the maximum speed of USB-2 (5000 Mbps vs. 480 Mbps).  It's rare to see that full speed yet (initial USB-3 products were about 2x USB-2), but developers continue to squeeze more speed from their products. The Samsung Story 2TB USB-3 external hard disk drive on a fully-capable USB-3 PC port hits 6x the USB-2 maximum (hard drive to hard drive, transfering a 6GB DVD movie in one minute, a CD in 6 seconds, or 100MB per second).  So how does this new Kingston USB-3 capable (USB-2 compatible) memory stick rate?  After reformatting mine to NTFS, pretty much as advertised at the Kingston web site:  USB 3.0: 70MB/s read, 30MB/s write and USB 2.0: 30MB/s read, 25MB/s write.  Most "cheap" $5 USB-2 sticks are lucky to reach the Windows ReadyBoost minimum speed of 5MB per second, with many far slower.  This is Kingston's new "mid-range" offering and, like hard drives, is priced accordingly based on speed and size (pay more, get more). The rubbery coating provides drop protection and it does not smell bad like some cheap rubber products (thanks!).  It has a velvet-like texture - very unique - and looks nice and makes a good conversation piece.  It has an activity LED near the lanyard hole, comes with lanyard, and the cap fits snuggly on the front and back (a bit less snug with lanyard). At 16GB, it provides a mid-range size and performance for a mid-range price, and the backward compatability allows users to nearly max-out their USB-2 now and go faster if they upgrade later to USB-3 ports on their computers.  Want cheaper: try Kingston's DataTraveler G3 as a decent product at ~ 5MB/sec (at $5 each for 4GB, cheap enough to give away if necessary, available in packs of 4).  Want the fastest: try Kingston's NEW DataTraveler HyperX 3 - it reads at 200MB/sec near the max. USB-3 limit, and gets quite warm when you push extended large data transfers, but cools via its expopsed metal skin.  Any can support encryption with free tools like TrueCrypt.  We'll consider Intel's Thunderbolt when it becomes widely available.  :-)

title: Fraudulent Rebate Denials - Beware
text:
Let me start by saying that I am pleased with the quality and performance of the monitor itself. My issue is not with Asus products, rather the company with whom they contract their rebates - 4MyRebate.com. In April 2013, I purchased this monitor as well as an Asus motherboard as part of a new computer build. The same month (and well before the deadline) I mailed two Asus rebates (one for the motherboard, another for the monitor in the amounts of $15 and $10 respectively) to the Asus/4myrebate.com rebate center. These were mailed separately to avoid any confusion and I made copies of all the forms/invoices/barcodes before mailing. For nearly two months, the tracking system at Asus/4myrebate.com showed they hadn't received either submission. Then, on June 16, 2013, the following update was logged:

6/14/2013 3:38:42 AM Claim Declined - Signed Rebate Form is missing- Copy of Receipt/Invoice or Packing List is missing- Original UPC/Serial Number Barcode Label is missing- No proof of purchase- Barcode label is missing- Reseller is not eligible for this offer- No proof of purchase date in documentation

With the exception of the time logged, the updates were identical for both of my rebates. As I stated, I have copies of all the forms and barcodes -- and know for a FACT that all of the claimed "missing" items were included and the reseller (Amazon and Newegg) eligible. Clearly, as this occurred with both my submissions and has occurred to many other consumers as well, 4myrebate.com is engaged in fraudulent activity with the denial of valid rebates and needs to be investigated at minimum. I've read that only between 40-60% of rebates are ever redeemed -- well, with scams like this, no wonder that figure is so low. So if, like me, you are buying this monitor (or other products utilizing 4MyRebate.com) because of the supposed rebate, please beware of this activity. And if you too are scammed out of your money, let others know. It may seem like a small amount, but this company profits by denying these en masse and assuming no one will take the time to speak up.

Added note -- I purchased a video card from NVIDIA one month later and submitted that rebate form to a different processing company. That rebate has already been processed and mailed as I write this.

title: great value
text:
i've had this tv for a month now and am very impressed. once i shut off the 'smooth motion' it got rid of the 'soap opera' effect in the picture, and now looks fantastic. good sound for a hdtv, but if you want thumping bass, use an external system. the menu and settings are easy, although i'd like to see a quicker way to change picture modes (movie,sports,etc). the internet apps are nice, and the tv has very good wireless reception, full bars and >15mbps from across the house in another room (over 50ft). it's nice for internet radio (pandora, tune-in, etc) and streaming movies works sweet, full HDX. the usb ports work great for flash drives but unfortunately not hard drives, not sure why they did that. but i can play lots of different video formats from a usb drive, not everything, but 90%. it also has DLNA, which works sweet for streaming muusic/pictures/video from my pc/laptop (setup using windows media player) or my android phone.

EDIT: one thing about media playback - it's not as nice as some others (samsung for one) in that you have limited fast forwarding/rewinding options. could be an annoyance in getting back to the same spot way into a movie, but it's minor issue (IMO).

as far as putting the stand on, i didn't need instructions to put the 1 screw in, and had no problems at all. not sure why anyone would under-rate a tv because they couldn't figure out how to put the stand on, but oh well :/

it does take about 30 seconds to turn on/boot up, so that takes getting used to, but not surprising as it is a smart tv with networking.

EDIT: what i originally wrote here about some 'motion blur' was actually pixalation/blocking effect, not from the tv, but from the source picture quality (comcast cable, and others, use compression which lowers picture quality). This does not occur on the tv from a high quality source (blue-ray, vudu hdx stream, etc).

overall a very good tv at a great price.

title: Worth the price,  a Quality photo & camcorder in one package, with the backing of Sony's technology.
text:
In a nutshell: This is a VERY nice camera AND video camera..yes it is expensive, but SONY technology has brought many innovations that really bring a "bang for the buck" on this camera. If you don't have an SLR or video camera, and want to get a very nice "all in one" camera you won't do wrong by getting this camera.

Ok.. more details.. I use a Canon EOS Rebel T2i, that when I bought it through Amazon it came with both the standard lens and a zoom 55-250mm lens. I love my camera and basically I am "used" to it.

When I opened this up, I noticed right away it is MUCH more compact, it has a nice weight to it and very balanced.
I added some pictures to show you how it comes. You get the body, a 18-55mm lens ( pretty standard, nice..) a lens hood, strap,
battery with wire free charger and CD's. No case, no memory card. I added some pictures of it in the product details (above)

Ok.. What I LOVE .. it is easy to use.. charge up the battery up and start taking pictures..
Other Pro's:
1) It has ELEVEN filters... so you can get really "artsy" easily, with no outside software ( Photoshop, Corel etc...)
2) VERY easy and reliable video.. this I knew would be a home run.. I have a SONY video cam, so I knew this would be a seamless no brainer.
3) Battery Life.. for a tiny battery.. this sucker really holds a charge! I have not tested the battery life on video, but so far it really holds a nice charge taking photos.
4) Lens Quality.. the included lens (18-55mm) is nice, capable, distortion free and a good basic lens.

***** MAJOR PLUS *****
5) NON-SONY lens adapter available!
.. although I have not tried it, there IS an adapter (optional) that you can use your Canon, Nikon, Olympus etc..lenses on it..
This is a MAJOR PLUS... Lenses are expensive.. several hundred dollars a pop at least! It is NICE to be able to use these on this camera! Again I have several Canon Lenses, and have not tried it with this camera, I am wondering if he auto-stabilize works with this camera - but I DO like the idea very much!

6 & 7 ) "Intelligent Auto Focus (..and iAUTO mode)"
these "Pre-focus as you compose the shot, further reducing focusing time to a bare minimum."
.. in other words.. makes it a "point and shoot camera.." ( a high end one!) It is nice to just take a picture without worrying about speeds, exposures etc.. and a VERY nice picture which leads me to:

8) A Whopping 24.3 Mega Pixels! I mean.. that is HUGE.. actually it is enormous!
So what is the big deal? Well the big deal is Yes..if you are taking normal pics of the kids and the pets you don't "need this"..
The big deal is that if you take a picture in this ultra high meg range, and you notice something you like that is smaller,
you can zoom and crop and play with that section of the image *without* magnifying the image.

For example I took a picture of a hawk.. it was very high up.. I took it in full resolution, then brought it to Photoshop, and was able to crop the hawk by itself, and it was still over 3000 x 3000 pixels and crystal clear.

9) "Auto tracking" as perfected with their video cameras, you can lock onto a subject and the camera will stay focused on the subject.. great for kids & pets

10) Compact! I can't believe they squeezed all this power into such a tiny package.

11) A well made and printed manual, many camera ( and other things) come with CD or a link to the manual, the manual that comes with it, goes over everything in easy to use instructions.

12) The "Tru-Finder OLED electronic viewfinder" It is incredibly sharp and detailed. The 3" screen tilts and really fights glare very well .. but it leads me into the Cons:

The Cons:
1) No "real" viewfinder I like to look though the camera itself, not at a screen.. (This is just a personal preference.)

2) Again this is nitpicking.. nothing to do with the camera, just an observation this is a fairly expensive camera it should of included:
2a) A carrying case
2b) A Memory card or stick.. come on SONY throw in a 4 gig card or stick!
2c) No Zoom lens? (again I bought the Canon 2TI with the 15-55mm lens AND a 55-250mm lens for about 980 bucks)

Maybe include a 30%-40% off coupon for one accessory ( case, Lens, memory lens etc..) with the purchase of the camera?

Again this is only nitpicking.. this is a really great camera!

In a nutshell, this camera really does crank out stunning pictures, has a massive array of "special affects" built into it,
and also shoots the best video I have seen on something that is a "camera" first.

Throw in the fact that you can attach your other brand lenses to this.. and you know what?
SONY may just have a real contender in the market here!

Will it replace Canon. Nikon etc.. as a "go to" DSLR? I don't know, however I do know I could point & shoot this cam straight out of the box. I know there is sticker shock with the price, but if you don't have a quality camera and a quality video cam, this WILL do the job of *both* in my opinion, and therefore justify the price.

I use this as a "go-to camera" when I just don't know what I am going to shoot, say at a party .. what am I going to take? pictures? videos? Bring this and I can do a quality job with both!

Jim

title: Easy Plug & Play, fast, and secure alternative to WiFi networking.
text:
Using power outlets to connect to or expand a home/office network is simple and convenient. This newer version of Netgear's Powerline AV 200 "Nano" adapter kit (XAVB2101) piqued my interest because I've used the [[ASIN:B0036R9YA6 NETGEAR Powerline AV 200 "Ultra" Adapter Kit (XAVB2001)]] since August 2010.

Likes:
>All Netgear Powerline adapters are backwards compatible with older models.
>Connect to all devices with Ethernet connections (those without built-in Wi-Fi capability).
>Very simple installation for the Nano (just like the Ultra) : Plug one Ethernet cable into a network modem or router, plug the other end into a Powerline AV 200 adapter that's plugged into an electrical outlet. DON'T plug the adapter into a surge protector or power strip outlet; signal will be degraded or it won't work at all.

Plug another Powerline adapter into another outlet (in the same building) wherever you choose. Connect via Ethernet cable to your computer, Xbox360, PS3, Blu-Ray player, TiVo, Slingbox, DVR, or broadband capable Smart TV, etc. Voilà, home network connection and the Internet.

No software installation, no setups, and no configurations necessary. A Resource CD is included if you want to bother with it.

Three lights: Power, Powerline (indicates network connectivity and signal strength), and Ethernet (broadband traffic). Green lights mean optimal conditions for all three.
>Easy to expand home network without the shortcomings of WiFi network (interference with other wireless devices using the same 2.4Ghz frequency, security concerns even with WPA, degradation of signals due to range or obstructions, etc.)
>Nano is more compact (approx. 2"x2.5"x1.25") than the old Ultra (approx. 2.5"x3.25"x1.5") but when plugged into the lower outlet (of the typical 2-outlet wall plate), both Nano and Ultra still keep the upper outlet accessible for other devices.
>So far all of my Powerline adapters at various locations (upstairs/downstairs) around the house have >80 Mbps link rates. No problems when streaming or downloading online movies and videos in HD.
>The Nano and Ultra adapters only have one Ethernet port each but I simply use a [[ASIN:B00006B9HO NETGEAR FS608 8-Port Fast Ethernet Switch]] so multiple devices can connect to the internet using just one Powerline adapter.
>Energy saver feature: auto shut-down when idle.
>There's even a security feature for folks in dorm rooms or apartments with shared wiring. Push the security button on one adapter after lights are green and then press the security button on the other adapter within two minutes. Press the factory reset button to return to default setting. It's questionable how far the range of one's home network extends using the Powerline adapters but I still use the Security feature in my single family house as a precautionary measure.

Dislikes:
>The strength of power outlet link rates will be highly dependent upon the quality of electrical wiring in the office/home, the range from router to adapter, and other electrical devices/appliances interference. The Powerline adapters may not work optimally with all outlets.
>At $82.80 (at time of review) for a kit with two Powerline adapters, the costs can quickly add up when setting up a Powerline network in many rooms.

Bottom Line:
Other than the more compact size of the Nano, everything functions the same as the old Ultra. Compared to my 2.4Ghz wireless router where I have to change channels on a regular basis (too many 2.4Ghz wireless phones and routers everywhere), this Powerline connection is far more stable and secure using the Security feature. Connecting or expanding one's network is quick and painless. Enjoy!

*** Update Oct. 23, 2013. Price for this Powerline kit has dropped to an affordable $48.95.***

title: Finally the tablet I was waiting for.
text:
I wanted a tablet that had a 10.1" screen, could play HD .mkv movies, was able to play the latest android games and came with a digitizer pen so I could take notes during my lectures and annotate on my class e-book. Almost a year ago I bought the Lenovo Thinkpad tablet and while the hardware was very good quality, the software was the let down, also the tegra 2 cpu just couldnt handle the HD mkv movies. I eventually sold it as I was rarely using it. When I saw the specs of the Galaxy Note 10.1 it looked like the answer to my tablet needs.

The tablet's pros:
- very fast performing general operations eg. opening apps & navagating around the O/S
- able to play the HD .mkv movies (it can even stream them from my server), which the tegra 2 cpus struggled with
- very good at multitasking using the including multitasking apps
- excellent at note taking using both the built in s-note app and Quill
- long battery life (only had to charge it once or so a week)
- nice loud stereo speakers

Cons:
- no HD screen; although the screen isn't bad, given the price of the tablet and how this is a flagship model it should have come with a higher resolution screen like its competitors from Asus and Apple
- build quality; again while not bad, it just doesnt feel like a $500US tablet with all the plastic.
- design of the pen and placement in the tablet; the pen is a little too slim and short and it is very easy to put it in wrong in the tablet slot.

If you are looking to upgrade your last gen tablet or even purchase one for the first time, the Note 10.1 is a good place to start.

title: Love my lynx, but hate this buggy keyboard
text:
I bought a [[ASIN:B009AEPJ8U Lenovo IdeaPad K3 Lynx 11.6-Inch 64 GB Tablet]], and despite some bad reviews I got the [[ASIN:B00AWAVSJA Lenovo IdeaTab Lynx K3011 Keyboard Dock]] dock to go along with it. BIG mistake! I can echo the comments of the previous reviewer, and so many of the reviews to be found on other sites, that this keyboard dock has several problems.

1. It randomly drops keystrokes. This is not good when you're busily typing an email, and inexcusable given that it's effectively a USB keyboard. I've tried a bluetooth keyboard with this computer and had no problems at all.

2. The touchpad is a little too "touchy." The slightest, tiniest graze of a finger will leave you typing your last name in your password field (or whatever).

3. Getting the computer to release takes a hard pull and a hard, deep push on the release button. I've nearly sent the whole thing flying across the room when it unexpectedly didn't let go.

4. Lenovo's solution to supporting this whisper-thin tablet was to completely envelop it in plastic where it docks with the keyboard. It's functional, but ugly and it's so thick that it prevents the keyboard-tablet combo from fitting into an 11" case.

There are four nice things about this keyboard/dock that others have noted, but they don't outweigh the problems.

1. The addition of full-sized USB ports is awesome.
2. The "short term" battery is nice, though hardly necessary for a power-sipper like the Lynx
3. The support for the Lynx, while bulky, certainly holds the screen upright and secure, unlike any other tablet keyboards out there.
4. The deep, clicky, mechanical keys are nice to type on. They give nice mechanical feedback, which makes the dropped keystrokes all the more annoying.

In short, this feels like a rushed engineering job. Buy a Lynx, but get a nice bluetooth keyboard to go with it rather than this lemon.

title: Samsung vs ASUS vs Amazon
text:
Whilst scanning Amazon for a USB CD/DVD writer, I spotted an ASUS unit -a well established and highly reputable brand- and the price and review ratings were good, so I bought it. Upon receiving the drive and copying some files off a CD to a solid state hard drive (SSD) it seemed the drive was a bit pokey on the transfer rate. So I ordered two other USB writers from Amazon; this Samsung unit and an Amazon Basics unit. After timing the transfer rate on all three drives, as well as measuring the transfer rate on my four year old HP DV6 laptop for reference, I realized that the ASUS was not so pokey after all... but I also stumbled on the fact the Samsung unit was three times faster than any of the other drives, including my laptop! All told I think the Samsung is a better deal. Here is a mini-review:

Drive models tested:
ASUS External Slim 8X DVD-RW Writer ([[ASIN:B006HUMYCO ASUS External Slim 8X DVD-RW Stylish Cut Design Optical Drive SDRW-08D2S-U/BLK/G/AS]])
Samsung USB 2.0 Ultra Portable External DVD Writer ([[ASIN:B00DBV28TG Samsung USB 2.0 Ultra Portable External DVD Writer Model SE-218CB/RSBS]])
AmazonBasics USB 2.0 8x DVD Writer ([[ASIN:B003M0NT1M AmazonBasics USB 2.0 8x DVD Writer External Optical Drive (Black)]])

Speed Tests:
Transfer Rate (copy 266MB file from CDROM to SSD) Windows 8.1
ASUS drive.............1.25MB/s avg (3 minutes 18 seconds)
Samsung drive..........3.0MB/s avg (1 minutes 35 seconds)
Amazon Basics drive....1.10MB/s avg (3 minutes 25 seconds)
HP laptop..............1.2MB/s avg (3 minutes 20 seconds)

Included Software:
ASUS drive............A couple of power management utilities, and a link to a firmware upgrade procedure that did not work.
Samsung drive.........Nero Express Essentials v12 (media management utilities, backup utilities, media player*, firmware updater)
Amazon Basics drive...Cyberlink Media Suite v10 (media management utilities, no media player)

* requires $5 upgrade to play MPEG media such as DVD movies

I did not run any burning benchmarks, mainly because I was short of blank media at the time. But the ASUS and the Amazon Basics units would have to have some remarkably better burn speeds over the Samsung to beat it out, given that I read from CD/DVD media far more often that I write to it. The Samsung also has the best bundled software. It actually comes with a media player, albeit a crippled one that requires an update to play DVD movies encoded with the popular MPEG-2 compression codec. To be fair, a royalty is paid to the MPEG mafia for each unit of player software that includes the MPEG codec (the word is that Windows 8 doesn't include a media player for MPEG movies because Microsoft no longer wanted to pay a $2 license fee to distribute the codecs in a world increasingly moving to streaming media).

title: Onyx Plus makes SiriusXM better!
text:
This unit is what makes Sirius work for me. My wife has the "built-in" Sirius unit by the manufacturer. It operates just like a radio. No frills.

I have this aftermarket unit, and I'm blown away. The unit records all 10 of your presets (or maybe 20?) so that when you switch channels, it plays from the beginning of the song. Unlike FM or the "built-in Sirius radio" in my other car where you are just listening in real-time. This feature is handy for mulitple reasons. It is nice to hear everything from the beginning, just as if I was using an MP3 player and was just fast-forwarding to the next song. Instead I'm just switching stations and listening from the beginning.

Added bonus? If you are driving through a tunnel, it is likely you'll have some buffer of audio to listen to while sitting in traffic with no line-of-sight to the satellite.

Another great feature? Song and artist alert! Nearly any song by Electric Light Orchestra can put me in a good mood. Yet, I don't always want to listen in on 70s on 7 or Classic Vinyl. I set the artist alert and any time ELO comes on, I hit one button on the unit and it just tunes right to that station.

And what is even better? The artist alert works across stations outside of my presets. Apparently the unit scans the entire SiriusXM bandwidth and captures the Artist/Song information and checks it against my alerts.

The only con of the system is that I installed it myself. Which isn't really a fault of the unit. I could have paid a professional to run the wiring. But even someone that was not comfortable with installing it, it took about 20-30 minutes. I just managed to run the cabling along the footboards/carpet of the car and affixed it with some tape. 6 months later, it is holding up fine.

title: Great comfort and sound, let down by cheap cable and low volume
text:
I stumbled across these new Philips Uptowns after trawling through many pages of over-the-ear headphones. After reading the many positive Amazon Vine reviews, I decided to take a chance and get a pair for myself to try out.

These headphones look and feel great. They're not too heavy, and the memory-foam padding provides a comfortable seal over the ears. They sound great too, and have a clear soundstage, bright treble, decent mids and, in my opinion, just the right amount of bass. It's not as low, rumbly, and overpowering as with the Dre Beats, but it is brought forward just enough to give a nice overall sound profile.

However, where these headphones fall apart is the cable and volume control. While being a good design, the flat cable feels cheap, especially so for a $100+ pair of headphones. The volume control also is worryingly cheap quality plastic, and doesn't even control volume on the device, which controllers on Klipsch and Monster / Dre headphones do.

Speaking of volume, these headphones are extremely quiet. I have to crank the sound really high on all devices I've used this thing with: my ipod, my phone, my computer, and even my bass amplifier. Don't expect to be blasting sound out of these things. Sound isolation is good, but then again volume is fairly low.

All in all these sound, feel, and look great, but are let down by cheap cable/volume controls and low sound output, which is something I didn't expect from a pair of headphones at this price point.

08/30/2013 Edit: Added a star since the price is now around $75. Also now play these through a [[ASIN:B0070UFMOW Fiio E17 USB DAC Headphone Amplifier]] and the volume issue is much improved.

title: Not Cat 5e Cable!
text:
I bought this cable to run in the walls of my house so that I could have a connection in my living room to the router in the office. I cut off the the end of the cable to attach it to the wall jack, and of course I see two things wrong.

1.) The wires are not twisted. Cat5e cable is supposed to contain 4 pairs of twisted wires. Since they're not twisted, the cable might suffer at high speeds. Buyer beware.
2.) The colors are not correct. Cat 5e cable has distinct colors (white/orange and orange, for example, would be twisted together). All of the colors in this cable are solid, so it's impossible to determine how you would wire this at the jack.

I would not purchase this cable. Despite the price, it's very cheap and incorrectly made.

title: Doesn't hold a candle to the SRSX5 -  "RADIO" sound versus "STEREO SPEAKER" sound
text:
I saw this at Costco today, and was excited. Beside being a techie, in general, I'm always open to an ever-smaller footprint bluetooth speaker. I use it in my kitchen, streaming from my Galaxy Note 3, as well as my iPad. But sometimes I take it with me in my car, so I'm open to a smaller speaker.

I have bought four iterations of Sony bluetooth speakers: the SRS BTX 300, the SRS BTX 500. the SRSX5, and now the SRSX3.

Here's my take:

SRS BTX 500 - Love this. GREAT SOUND. I still own it, but have installed it in my friend's apartment for when we're making dinner on the patio/ grill. Big, rich sound - but the negative is the SIZE and WEIGHT. But GREAT speaker.

SRS BTX 300 - Nix. I had bought this to test against the 500, and it was vastly inferior.

SRSX5 - LOVE this speaker. This is one I am using at home, with my phone and iPad. But again, I saw the new smaller one at Costco, and gave it a shot.

SRSX3 - NIX NIX NIX. I am triple-nixing because this is a new item, and people will be persuaded by the positive reviews here. But I have played the 3 and the 5 side by side, while on battery, playing '40s music, broadway, Disco, and talk, to get a sense of the sound. The best way for me to compare the 3 and the 5 is to say that the 3 struck me immediately as sounding like a radio. A bit tinny treble, and okay bass. It was, like, okay, but not great. And each time I switched back to the 5, I went, "AH," that's better. The 5 has a richer sound, so even the treble, like a clarinet or speaking voice, has a touch of bass in it to deepen and enrich the sound. And when I switched back to the 3, I again heard that tinny thinner sound, minus the grounding bass within the treble. I was reminded of table model radios when I was a kid.

Bottom line: SRSX3 versus SRSX5 - No comparision, in my book. The 5 is richer and fuller, with an ample bass and rich treble. The 3 is tinny - it's okay for an inexpensive portable bluetooth speaker - around $100 or less - but if you're envisioning an AMAZING sound, go with the SRSX5. It's superb, ALMOST as good as the SRSBTX500, which is really big to be truly compact.

Try the SRSX5 - and skip the SRSX3.

title: Rarely leave without it now.
text:
I'm an undergrad in college and am pretty audiophilic, as I listen to music while studying, walking to classes, and really whenever I can. I've gone through countless ear-buds and a few headphones, and this product just tops everything I've ever had. I listen to everything from classical to punk, metal, acoustic, rock, blues, rap and on. These headphones handle them all splendidly.

The quality is great, it's a very full sound, not too bass heavy, and all the highs and mids come out well. I actually heard very minute parts of songs that I've never heard through my earbuds. I mainly use these in bluetooth mode and it's pretty indistinguishable from it's wired sound, which makes the experience even more awesome! Plus the battery last forever (16-20 hours) so I just charge it whenever I sleep every few days or so (keep in mind I use these extensively every day). And if the day ever comes when the battery dies, I can just use the wire!

The build is sturdy, it would definitely take some effort to break, unlike the other few headphones I've had. The padding is very comfortable too. I do have small ears so they fit nicely over my ears and serve a dual purpose as my ear muffs when it's cold out. I do hear people with bigger ears may get uncomfortable wearing these because they don't fit completely over. For me, they do eliminate some outside noise, which is fantastic, considering they are not noise canceling.

They paired real easy to all my devices and I was happy to find out that iDevices have a little battery meter in the status bar that shows the headphone's battery when paired! The microphone is alright, I've had better, but it gets the job done. I can get pretty far from these with no loss of signal. When I go down floor and to other rooms, only then does it start to get a little choppy. The controls are nice, just typical V-up, V-down, Power, next, previous, and play/pause buttons. The little manual that comes with it basically explains everything you need to know about it's bluetooth use, no complaints about its interface.

Obviously these are not super high quality headphones though, but I got them on sale for under 100 and amazon tends to have this item on sale and if you combo that with a gift card, this item is a steal. So if you are a student, or someone not wanting to spend too much and getting the biggest bang, wait for this item to go under 100, and it's an amazing deal! Still a pretty good deal at it's retail price, but I'm a student and if it's not on sale it's not for me XD. Anyway, just buy these lol.

title: My Gaming/Editing Rig Loves This Card
text:
[...]
MSRP 349.99 (at the time of this review) The card started at around $400-429.99 at launch, I believe.
Check for rebates, They generally have a $20 MIR listed on the EVGA site and Amazon is pretty good about including them as well.

---------------------------------------------------------
--- Why I bought a new card
---------------------------------------------------------

I pretty much bought this card to get more out of my Battlefield 4 gaming experience. I played the Beta with my old HD 6850 and constantly felt that I was at a disadvantage because I was only getting about 30-50 frames in 3 Flag Domination. Conquest was much worse.

I picked up a 120hz BenQ monitor and this card can easily push out 60+ frames to feed the monitor. I'd say it averages about 70-110 with a mixture of Ultra/High/Medium settings. I'm not sure because my CPU (AMD 1090T Black 3.2ghz, stock and OC'd up to 3.8) is a bottleneck at the moment. I'm splitting my editing and gaming rig into two machines soon and will be putting a AMD FX-8350 4.0Ghz (OC on this chip is insane) into an Asus Sabertooth 990FX Motherboard so that bottleneck should be gone. I'm pretty sure with some settings tweaking I should be able to get some smooth 120hz gameplay.

I'm starting a gaming channel on YouTube and utilize Adobe Photoshop, Premiere and After Effects. These and many other cards have started to utilize GPU-acceleration for rendering and previews. The CUDA-cores on this card are 5th in the NVIDIA (not considering Quadro cards since they are for workstations) to only the 690, 780, 780 ti and Titan. Editing videos has been much less of a pain with this card.

---------------------------------------------------------
--- Special Offers (At the time of my purchase - Nov 2013)
---------------------------------------------------------

I received my 3 Free game codes (Splinter Cell Blacklist, Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag, and Batman: Arkham Origins) promptly and have no problem getting them setup. I don't like that I had to install Ubisoft's software to install SC and AC. It would have been nice and easier if it was through steam but EVGA and even NVIDIA can't do much about that. The card runs all three games great at high settings.

I didn't utilize the $100 off of the NVIDIA Shield. It looks like a cool device but not something I need at the moment.

---------------------------------------------------------
--- Important Specs and Performance
---------------------------------------------------------

ACX (Active cooling xtreme). The card is hefty and feels like a high quality product especially compared to my old card. That heft comes from the internal reinforcement/heat spreading plate, the heat pipes and 2 large heat sinks (1 over the VRAM and the other directly over the GK104 Kepler chip. It runs pretty cool out of the box. The cooling seems much better than the reference cards from what I've noticed and read. I didn't realize it until turned everything up to Ultra in BF4 but I hadn't heard the fan at all over the sound of my case fans and mechnical HDDs. It only became audible when the card became very very stressed (BF4 - max settings with 2 adjacent 1080p monitors [not in surround). Very very quiet.

The SC means it has a factory Overclock and runs at higher Base clock and Boost Clock speeds. This is further tweakable with EVGAs Precision X software for anyone interested in a higher OC. Reading reviews from sights such as Anandtech on OC performance this card performs better than pretty much every other non-reference card from every other manufacturer. I'm not a huge overclocker but that potential offers an extra 5-10% increase over the factory OC that could add some extra longevity to the card.

The card Supports 4 concurrent displays out of the box which is great. I believe it can support 3 monitors of the same size and resolution in both normal and 3D surround (multimonitor immersive gaming). 3D requires an NVIDIA 3D Vision ready monitor. I haven't tried this but it's nice to know it's there if I pick up a title that offers a better experience in 3D (I haven't yet. I use the 120hz purely for smoother FPS experiences). If I upgrade to another card (I'll most likely stick with EVGA) and plop this into my editing rig. Having 3 monitors for Adobe Premiere is AMAZING and great for video production workflow amonst everything else.

I haven't utilized the Double Bios yet as I haven't OC'd the card. It seems like a nice feature to have if you like pushing the limits of the card to get maximum performance.

I've heard a lot of people talking about PCI Express 3.0. This card supports it but very few AMD chipsets seem to support it (FM2/+). A decent amount of Intel 1150/1155 socket Mobos seem to have it. However, unless your picking up 3 of these to run in SLI (which it can support) the extra bandwidth won't be of much use right now.

The 2GB of GDDR5 RAM and standard right now and more than adequate for most uses right now. EVGA and other manufacturers have some 3GB versions of the 770 and other cards out right now but I've only seen a few people mention the increase being very helpful (Games like Elder's Scrolls and 4 display workstations seem to benefit from more ram). In the future having more RAM could be very useful as new titles will likely make it necessary.

I'm pretty sure this utilizes the reference PCB design. Other manufacturers and possibly other makes of this card from EVGA have redesigned PCBs to provided better power that is often needed for higher quality parts. That said, the components on the PCB look very high quality and the board doesn't seem to suffer from it at all

-------------------
---NVIDIA'isms
-------------------

All of the anti-aliasing and such capabilities are pretty standard among all of the Kepler architecture cards so you can ignore them if trying to decide between this and say the 680. I'm pretty sure AMD have their own proprietary version of these technologies also.

What is nice is the capabilities of NVIDIA GeForce Experience and more specifically Shadow Play. Look these up if you haven't heard of them. But quickly, with SP you can record gameplay straight from the card to your hard drive with little to no performance hit such as you might see with FRAPS or other programs. This is because of an onboard H.264 encoding ship on NVIDIA Kepler cards (600 and up I believe). It's great for someone like myself who wants to start sharing their gaming experience on YouTube. They've also introducing steaming capabilities using Twitch which also opens up some new possibilities for those who might not have done so previously because the performance decrease and cost of building a streaming rig.

------------
---Looks
------------

I really like the look of EVGA's cards. They don't seem over designed like something you'd see in the Bat Cave, but have a more elegant style with simple Black/Gold/Silver color schemes. I've had windowed cases and besides on something like a test-bench all you are ever going to see is the side of the heat shroud and the PCB (unless you have a backplate which I do wish was included with this card). I'm hoping they saved money on a simpler design and spent it on more reliable parts and R&D. Base on the OC speeds I've seen for this card I'm guessing they have.

------------
---Conclusion
------------
I got everything I expected from this card and more. I bought it on an Amazon Lighting deal for $329.99 which was much lower than anywhere else I saw online at the time.

I'd rate this card as a Med to High tier card. There are a lot of SKUS for EVGA 770 so make sure you check to make sure people are talking about the same card in reviews and such EVGA 770s include lower to higher Price, Clock speeds and RAM. I wanted to spend less than $400 on my GPU and knew that the more I saved, the more I could put into other components such as a 120hz monitor, 250GB SSD, CPU, Mobo, etc.

I own multiple systems including my gaming/editing rig, and HTPC and media server. I run AMD on all of their backwards compatibility so I can hand down parts between machines. That said, I could have waited and saved for another month and picked up a higher performing card (780 for instance). Instead I picked a card that offered what I would need for at least the next 8 months or so knowing I can upgrade and put this card into my soon to be split off editing rig.

Picking a component like this is all about doing your research, figuring out your budget, figuring out exactly what you need and how long it needs to last (this is the difficult part for me) and then finding a product that fits in that sweet spot.

EVGA is a brand I've heard a lot of good things about from sites and people I trusted, and this card fit all the criteria I mentioned above. Every month you spend saving or waiting for a better deal is time your getting the gaming experience you want. There will be a ton of new cards coming out in the next year (funny how CES is in Jan right!?!) and prices will drop and I'll probably see this card's price go down here and otherwise. But I'm enjoying my experience right now and don't feel like I'll be losing out.

This was a big purchase for me so I thought I'd leave a big review. Good luck with your choice.

title: Defective Trackpad
text:
[[VIDEOID:53ee958d33ffc4762076199c20c9d08b]] Let me first start by saying that I have owned 3 ASUS laptops before this one, and I have loved them all. They were all netbooks, and I have no problem trading a little speed for battery life. Each ASUS I've owned has outperformed what I expected from its specs and has been a solid, reliable workstation for me.

With this laptop, however, there seems to be a manufacturing problem related to the power supply. When the power cord is plugged in, the trackpad becomes jumpy and unresponsive. It seems as though some electromagnetic radiation from the power supply causes a disturbance in the trackpad's capacitive sensing. Generally, the trackpad is responsive, and the multitouch functions are perfectly acceptable, but when the computer is plugged in, the trackpad is basically unusable, as shown in the video. I did a little more debugging in attempt to find the origin of the problem. I found that if I place my hand just to the right of the trackpad on the case, it works nearly as well as when the computer is unplugged. This confirms for me that the power supply is somehow creating some sort of electromagnetic disturbance that is getting conducted to the trackpad.

Furthermore, this issue has been persistent in two computers. I sent my original purchase back for an exchange thinking that it was just a fluke defect or something (after a quick search, I didn't find anyone else complaining about this exact issue), but when the new computer arrived, it had the same problem.

Most people probably won't care (or maybe not even notice). You can just use the touch screen or a mouse when it's plugged in, or you can just make sure your palm is touching the laptop case. However, this issue makes me wonder what else might be receiving this electromagnetic disturbance. I suspect that some components may wear down faster due to this, but it could also be fine in the end. Either way, this lack of quality control seems to be a huge oversight to me, and is enough for me to not one to own one at all.

Another issue worth mentioning is the WiFi. Generally it's fine, but it experiences a sizable lag on occasion and will intermittently drop the signal.

I really wanted to like this computer. It is small, lightweight, and has a solid feel as well as a great set of specs. It turns on quick, and aside from the issues above, it works like a champ. It is too bad that the trackpad issue is a deal breaker for me.

title: The Kindle Fire and Breast Cancer
text:
I just want to say that as a woman undergoing treatment for breast cancer (currently doing radiation therapy), I would be lost without my Kindle Fire. On days when I am feeling energetic, I read - often the cheesey novels I can get at a great discount or even free (and which are about as much as my brain can handle). On days when I am not doing as well, solitaire or other simple games keep me entertained. Waiting for appointments, or even in the evenings when I am too tired to do anything else, it keeps me going. And I can send messages or read Facebook to get some encouragement when I need it, especially when I can't use my cell phone.

There are many other patients I see with their Kindles at the hospital. Really, if you know someone who has been diagnosed, why not think about getting them a Kindle? They will appreciate it more than almost anything else you could do for them.

Addendum: I want to add a big thank you to those who have responded with good wishes. I am lucky - they caught my cancer early, and I have really amazing doctors (I work at a large university with a remarkable medical research center). I sincerely appreciate your comments!-L.

title: Pretty decent buuuuut
text:
OVERALL:

Sound 8.5/10 Very good soundstage for such a price and a tremendous bass to boost.

Design 9/10 This is subjective to the individual but I liked the design a lot.

Durability 8/10 Sturdy light aluminum enables these to take a bit of a beating.

Comfort 6.5/10 Nothing great, but you won't notice them unless you think about it.

The good:

-One of the best contenders for an IEM for this price; money well spent.

-Sound quality: Great highs. The sound signature of these is like a V. You can really hear the highs with these more-so than I had anticipated. The mids are decent as well, though for $70, despite being nothing to scold at, it's nothing to really praise, either. Detailed bass. The bass isn't like the V-Moda IEMs or iBeats I've owned before. The bass is punchy and actually allows you to hear the mids and highs a lot better, though some of it still bleeds out into the mid range, but nothing I can really complain about for how immersive yet accurate the bass is.

-Build quality: It's very light-weight despite being pretty darn durable. I dropped a textbook on them and no damage whatsoever was done. The cord is also nice; smooth rubber makes it resistant to getting tangled all the time.

-Design: I really liked the 9mm design. It was originally what attracted my attention. I got the black ones and they're a nice metallic dull color.

The bad:

-In the details it was supposed to come with 3 sets of red eartips and 3 sets of black. The case included only the black ones. This is just a small annoyance. The eartips go in your ear and will never be seen by you or anyone else while you're using them so it doesn't really matter what color they are since the material and size are the same. I'm not going to hold them accountable; this is more for letting others know the updated specifications of the item.

-Bass may be a little overpowering for genres that are not already bass-oriented. To fix this, you can just mess with your EQ settings a bit and it'll be fine.

Nothing extraordinary:

-Comfort: It fits well enough, better than conventional earbuds by far, but that's to be expected from any pair of earbuds $50+.

-Mic: I hope you didn't buy these for the mic. I sure didn't. But I went ahead and tried the audio on it anyway. It's mediocre at best and annoying to use at worst. I would just use it as a pause and play button. (I plugged it into an iPhone and pushing the button toggled the music on and off)

title: Auto-off feature annoys, can't be changed
text:
So, I purchased these to use at work with my recent-model iMac to play music without bothering coworkers. The problem that annoys me is that the transmitter station only transmits to the headphones when it "senses" sound coming from the computer. This means that even in the middle of a piece of classical music, when the instruments fall silent, the very faint hiss behind the recording cuts out. When they begin playing again, the hiss returns. This is even true for the millisecond delays between phrases when an announcer speaks. I can easily tune out and ignore the slight hiss behind recordings when it is constant, but when it is cutting in and out throughout the piece of music or monologue, it's very irritating. To be honest, it's irritating enough that I'm not willing to pay north of 300 bucks for these otherwise great headphones.

I'm returning them and picking up another pair of the PX 100 wired headphones that have done well for me at home for several years at a fraction of the price.

title: Does exactly what I want! - when it wants to. :(
text:
I recently setup a DLNA server wirelessly connected to my home network. I was watching content from the sever using my xbox 360 but my girlfriend was annoyed by how many menus needed to be navigated and having to use a game controller. So for awhile I used a HTPC but it was old and didn't work very well. After doing some research I found that the WD TV Live Hub did everything I needed. Supported DLNA, played shared network media including music and movies. Netflix and other online video service capable. Small form factor that supports HDMI and best of all, a little remote for navigation.

Received the unit and hook up/setup were easy. Had it going in 15 minutes. The unit immediately detected a firmware update that I let proceed. After a few resets I was at the main menu. I then navigated each options menu setting my preferences accordingly along with network connectivity. The Live Hub immediately saw my DLNA server without issue.

I've played multiple file types successfully including mkv, mp4, avi, etc. Image quality is great. Sound is also good even though I'm using the TV as the audio processor with an optical output to a 5.1 surround sound system. The netflix navigation takes a bit of getting used to as it is different than the xbox or webpage interface.

I have not placed any media on the internal HD yet as all of my media is on my DLNA server. But knowing that if I run out of room the space is there is great.

I recommend this to anyone who doesn't use cable and uses netflix, hulu, etc plus wanting to play local media off a DLNA server.

***Update***

After using this for almost a year, I have found that WD's support of the product isn't that great. The unit has received 3 updates but none have resolved freezing issues and random no sound issues. Frequently when opening an application like Netflix, the application will hang or the whole unit will lock up. If I do get something to play, there will be no sound. That will require me to either exit Netflix and open a local file to play and then go back to Netflix, or power cycle the unit. Also, navigating the on screen menu's is painfully slow. Youtube being one of the most frustrating and poorly written applications, Netflix being almost just as bad. Honestly, there are better alternatives out there now.

It is also partly rigid to allow the adapter to be pointed in whatever direction you might need.

When I purchased this, the adapter was offered with a mail in rebate. I've never had an issue in the past with mail in rebates with other companies, but Asus has been a different story. In order to receive a rebate, you need a signed rebate form (provided by them), a copy of receipt/invoice or Packing List, and the original UPC. I sent the signed rebate form, the email receipt/order confirmation from Amazon, and the original UPC. But apparently the email from Amazon isn't good enough for them, which is not clear at all from the rebate form. So if you want to get the rebate, make sure you go back onto your account on Amazon, go your orders and click the Invoice button and print that off or else your rebate will be denied and you'll have to go through this whole process again to re-submit. I spoke with a rep on the phone who said the email I provided is just an order confirmation and does not qualify as a receipt. Seems a lot like they're just mincing words, and definitely has not left a great impression with me. Hopefully if I have to deal with customer service again, in the event any issues arise with my adapter, they won't be this difficult to deal with.

title: Handy, retains sharpness, minimal colour cast, but ...
text:
NOTE: This was initially a four-star review. I've posted a note at the end of this review to explain why I have changed the Hoya's rating to two stars.

Neutral density filters reduce the amount of light reaching a camera's lens, and this can be useful in two situations. The first is when a photographer wishes to shoot at a wide aperture to blur the background of a shot in bright sunlight. The second situation is when a photographer wishes to lengthen his exposure times for creative purposes such as blurring the movement of water.

The Hoya Variable Density 3-400 consists of two polarising filters mounted on top of each other which block varying amounts of light depending on the degree to which the front one is rotated.

This ability to vary the strength of the filter is useful because it saves a photographer from having to carry several filters of different strengths. It also allows him or her to briefly reduce the filtering effect in order to focus before increasing the strength of the filter to take the shot (some cameras are unable to focus through strong ND filters).

The Hoya 3-400 officially blocks between 1.5 and 9 stops of light. However, I have been able to block between 9 and 10 stops of light without incurring negative effects (notably an x-shaped pattern which occurs with most variable ND filters when they are pushed past their official limits).

The Hoya has several advantages over other variable ND filters.

Firstly, it is cheap. This might seem an odd statement when you are forking out $100 or more for a couple of pieces of glass, but some competing variable NDs (notably the Singh Ray offering) can cost more than $300.

Secondly, images retain their sharpness when shot through this filter, which is certainly not the case with no-name variable ND filters.

Thirdly, the filter rarely imparts a colour-cast, and when it does it is quite easily corrected. In comparison, my top-quality B+W 10-stop filter produces a much stronger colour-cast despite only blocking less than a stop more light.

There are, however, some negatives.

The filter does not have any of the fancy coatings used these days to reduce flare and allow for easier cleaning.

The build-quality of the filter is good, but not nearly as good as my 58mm B+W Kaesemann polariser. The B+W's two brass filter rings glide very smoothly over each other, whereas the Hoya's two aluminium rings are firm, then loose then firm again as they are rotated.

The biggest problem with this filter, however, is the is the fact that it lacks a front thread.

I typically store my filters by the common method of screwing them into a "stack" and fixing metal caps to each end of the stack. To my annoyance, I discovered that the Hoya does not have filter threads on the front! This means that it is impossible to protect it with a metal stack cap, or even with a common lens cap.

Presumably, Hoya left off the front theads in order to keep the filter as narrow as possible and guard against vignetting. Frankly, I would rather put up with a touch of vignetting in order to be able to store the filter safely in a compact way.

In short, I recommend this filter. With caveats.

UPDATE:

I returned this filter. Why? Because this review was based on my experiences shooting at normal to telephoto focal lengths. When I tried shooting landscapes at a wide focal length (24mm full-frame equivalent) I was only able to get about 4 stops out of the filter before the "x" pattern kicked in.

Since I expected to use the filter mostly with wide-angle lenses in future, I returned it while I still could.

I have reverted to using fixed-ND filters.

title: The Price Seems High... Until You Use It!
text:
I've always wanted whole house, zoned audio. I have the necessary skills and knowledge to install it and have actually designed it about 3 times! But I'm lazy and have never put any of those designs to use. So I've been looking at Sonos for about 3 years as an alternative. Finally, I ordered a Play:1 to use as a "portable around the house" speaker and this Connect to hook up to my AVR in my media room. I received the Play:1 first, so I followed the wireless setup instructions and was connected in just a few minutes. I immediately fell in love. The sound from such a small device is great. Even though it's small, it has good weight to it, so it doesn't feel cheap either. It's great for casual listening, background listening in small to medium rooms.

I'm not familiar with the older versions of the Android app, but I have zero problems with this one. Of course, every app could be "better" if you wish you could do something that it can't or in a different way that it does (like the way you get to the EQ settings, for example), but I think it works great overall. I had a small complaint about it not supporting multiple accounts of one service, but they recently added that capability. Some hate it and think of it as a security hole, but I love the fact that I can tell visitors who want to listen to just download the app and get on my wifi. It's created a wonderful social listening environment. No one has to ask me to play something. They can just play whatever they want and we all hear the music we want.

Once I received my Connect, I connected it to my AVR in my media closet where I also have a network switch. I was afraid that it would not automatically transition from streaming over my normal wifi network to using it's own, so I had planned on factory resetting the Play:1 and starting over. But instead, I just went ahead and plugged an Ethernet cable into it, connected it to my AVR, and plugged in the power and it "just worked" after the normal simple setup of a new device. I figured out how to verify, and found out it was now using the Sonos wifi to reach the Play:1 instead of my normal wifi. Great!

Nothing else much to say about it that hasn't been said, but I definitely recommend the Connect!

I am now designing a new whole house system with various Sonos components. It's against my normal preference of building non-proprietary systems, but I have to say that I like the way they've done this one. That and based on the fact that they've been doing this for a long time, I have enough confidence that Sonos will be supporting this for a good amount of time in the future. Let's hope I'm right!

As far as the price, it seems high. But when I used it for the first time instead of my other methods of getting music from my phone to my AVR, it was instantly worth it! I would buy a lot more Sonos products right now if they were less espensive. But the thing is that I am still going to buy them, it will just take longer. Bottom line, they priced it at a point to keep customers buying over the long term instead of just buying everything right now and nothing else in the future. I can't be mad at them for that.

title: Love what it can do but not perfect
text:
I'm really enjoying it's strengths such as stunningly vivid daylight shots and excellent low light quality. I have a Canon T2i and find the sharpness to be on a par with that. Very nice to have that in a such a compact package. The video quality is very close to my Panasonic tm700 which shoots 1080/60p and is absolutely amazingly lifelike. The tm700 has a better stabalizer, not much, and focuses faster, again minor but noticeable. There are effects in fully auto mode that I love. Great fun and simple to apply. The scenes are also very quick and useful for special conditions.

Here's what I don't like. I was taking a video of a friend and noticed that the skin tone was over saturated with red. It looked like a sunburn. This was in an office with artificial lighting. I've also noticed it at home or anywhere there's not a particularly bright light source. The other seeming defect is that I've noticed spots in the frame when the background, also indoors, is tan/orange/yellow. The first time I noticed it the iso was 3200. The same shot with 800 iso had no trace of the spots. The spots appeared several times more at iso 3200 in the exact same location in the frame and changing between 18-55 kit lens and f2.8/16 didn't effect the outcome. I also noticed the same exact spots when is happened to use iso 100 and 1 second shutter speed. Examples can be found on Flickr if you search for tags nex-5n spots. This could be just my camera, I don't know of course. I've just noticed it. It's not dust.

I will post any updates. I've not yet contacted Sony customer service but will.

as of 3/20/2012
I've upgraded the firmware to 1.01, verified it, and retaken some shots of tan walls to see if spots persisted and they do. They're very faint though. This is still a superb camera and I don't hesitate to use it in any lighting situation. Five stars if for perfect though so that stays but disappointed is overstating it.

Thanks for the response on the firmware update. I feel better having done that. The spots still quite possibly could be removed with a thorough cleaning. I used the setup cleaning mode to no effect and I've only used it in pristine condition and for only a month so we'll see.

as of 3/30/2012
I purchased a cleaning kit for the sensor and was able after 20 or so passes with the various pads and wipes to remove all the spots. It's a bit unnerving because you think, at least a novice like myself, that too hard and you'll destroy the filter or sensor, not enough and it'll never be perfect. I do not for the life of me know how such indelible stains, not dust, got on there. I only changed lenses indoors. I'll continue to monitor it and see if this mirrorless type of camera just attracts debris more readily.

Other than that it's been a great camera. The images and video are stunning.

as of 4/1/2012
New spots have appeared on the sensor. They show up noticeably on sky blue background. I change lenses infrequently and only indoors so every few days cleaning is not an option. I can't return the camera but I will return the 18-200 lens. Just not worth it given the delicate and dangerous job of cleaning the sensor.

as of 4/5/2012
Amazon kindly sent me a replacement for which I'm grateful as I was beyond the 30 day window. I unboxed it, attached a lens and tried the 2 settings (iso 3200 on a light background and then 1 second exposure on blue sky) that revealed the sensor spots I've had an issue with and similar spots appeared on this camera too. Right out of the box. As far as I can see I'm the only one complaining and I still gravitate to this camera every day. Love the images and the size. There are no visible spots or dust under iso 3200 and faster than 1 second. I can live with that.

title: Good protection, but very thick and bad viewing angles.
text:
Well, I have to say I am pretty disappointed in this cover. I used a coupon for it so I don't want to return it and pay even more for a different case. $55? For a CASE? Jeez. So my first problem with this case....the price. The leather quality is good, but it's simply not worth that. Unfortunately with a new product you are limited on cases for a while.

Biggest problem: the viewing angles. Even at the widest angle, I find it barely tolerable to watch movies, or anything really, on the Fire. My biggest use for a standing case is on an airplane or at a table, where the screen is fairly close to my body. I wish the case tilted more to give a better angle. It is ok in portrait view, but in landscape? Forget about it. I have a case on my Motorola Xoom that allows a much better viewing angle and it much more comfortable to watch things on.

Second problem: It's thick. VERY thick, and heavy. It nearly doubles the weight of the Fire. Yes, it does seem like it will protect very well, but the cover is just a little too padded for me. I feel like I have a giant first-gen device in my bag instead of a svelte new Kindle Fire HD.

Third problem: The ports/the magnet for auto screen off. When in the default position, the ports to charge it are covered up but the case so it must be open to charge. "But WAIT!" you are thinking. "Read the other reviews!" you are saying. "The case turns around! The holster turns 180 degrees!" Yes, it does turn around so you can access the ports, and that's awesome. But there is a HUGE, HUGE problem (gaping hole, Marware!) The magnets in the case are only oriented to work for auto on/off when the Fire is turned in the default "correct" position! So I have to constantly turn my Fire around and around, or choose what is more important....charging or auto on/off.

Marware, I did not pay $55 for this case with the expectation of it being anything other than perfect. Such a gaping hole in something so simple (adding magnets to two positions so auto on/off works all the time) is a huge oversight. The poor viewing angle is a part of the design, and so is the weight of the cover. It's obviously not the right one for me. But is there anything better? The Amazon case is a bit strange and doesn't sit up well for viewing. The Otterbox case is insanely expensive and heavy. The Marware MicroShell is nice and thin, but only has one viewing angle and no auto/on off. The Belkin and Crown cases have an ugly bezel cover. The only one with any potential is the Marware Vibe. I may order that one to try it out, but then I will be disappointed to lose the revolving feature.

Too bad, Marware. An expensive case that still doesn't hit the mark. I'm disappointed I wasted a coupon on this.
