title: A Fun Toy With A Few Flaws
text:
This is my first android device and I was considering purchasing a tablet for quite a few months now. I was considering an Apple iPad 2, but I really did not need a desktop replacement. Also, I could not justify $500 (I'm a grad student, I'm poor!) I just wanted a tablet for simple things; such as reading, surfing the net, e-mail, chat, and movies. Therefore, I did not need a very fancy device, hence the reason why I chose to purchase the Kindle Fire.

The Pros:

1- The device looks great; it certainly does not look cheap.

2- The screen is very vivid and crisp

3- It is simple to navigate

4- the speaker system is good, but it is better with headphones.

5- Tons of books, films, and TV programs to choose from. As a student, I get 6 months free of Amazon Prime and only pay $39/yr. I'm definitely taking advantage of it!

The Cons:

1- Web browsing is a bit slow

2- Sometimes, buttons are unresponsive and I have to press them twice, sometimes three times, for them to become responsive. It's a bit annoying, but not a big deal.

3- The brightness setting is still too bright even when it is dimmed all the way. This is a con for me because I have very sensitive eyes. However, I discovered an app that fixed this problem.

4- For a 7" tablet, it is still a bit heavy. I personally cannot hold it for a long period of time in my hand while reading. My wrist becomes a bit strained.

5- You cannot customize the home screen (you can only do this by rooting your device)

The cons are minor for me and really like this tablet as it suits my needs. If you're looking for a simple tablet for simple things, this is it. A lot of people are comparing this to the iPad 2, which is complete nonsense in every sense of the word because the iPad will come out the winner. Of course the iPad 2 has a lot more features, it's a desktop replacement, people. You cannot compare any $500 tablet with a $200 one.

I highly recommend this product and would have given it 5 stars if there were no cons. Amazon has always been reliable for me and they have made a great new device for a great price. Get yours today! Thanks Amazon!

title: 5 year update: still great Flexible External Drive System
text:
Update: i’ve now been using this external drive for five years, and it still performs like a champ. I never did get additional drives to add to it because the originals are still working great and I don’t need more space.

I've had this drive for two weeks now, working with it heavily as I transfer files off of a 2009 Mac Pro. The most important advantage to me is that this drive is bootable with my MacBook Pro (Early 2011, 16GB, 2.7 GHz Intel Core i7). That is, using Carbon Copy Cloner I can produce a disk which can then be then be booted from using the thunderbolt cable that comes with this drive. The only time I had problems was when I attempted to boot from an older system (I think it was 10.6), but then I did some software upgrades (one of which was a thunderbolt upgrade) as well as updating that older system to 10.8 and then all went well. I do notice that its a little sluggish when running from the external drive, however. The drives that go into the slots are very well-built, and operate without an extra power supply (just the usb), and whisper quiet. I purchased an additional 1TB drive from Amazon, last week for one hundred fifty, probably decreased amount because G-Technology has just release a 500GB SSD drive for this system. This is a great sign because it means G-Technology will continue supporting this expandable system for the future. Once the price of those SSD drives decreases (the 500GB SSD is a ridiculous five hundred right now) I will be getting those too. Right now I'm using it in JBOD mode, but if I choose, I can put this in 2 different RAID configurations (for safety or extreme speed), if I want to in the future. The fact that this has 2 Thunderbolt ports in the back is a huge advantage as it allows other disks or Displays to daisy chain off that one thunderbolt port on my MacBook Pro. It's really well designed: I don't even have to have the disk on to use the external Display at the end of the thunderbolt chain. The unit is quite small, great looking, and so quiet I haven't heard it yet (I'm very sensitive to noisy fans on computers). The only negative is the LEDs flashing on the drives in a dark room -- when will manufacturers get over their fascination with these overly bright annoying lights? Obviously they are cheap to add to electronics because they are everywhere. Unless you like having your darkened room turned into a disco, get some tape and carefully cover those lights (use as little as possible because the glue from the tape will leave a residue as it gets hot over time and melts onto the disk exterior). The problem is finding tape that lets the right amount of light through so you don't lose that advantage. I can only conclude design engineers never turn lights off in their homes or are disco fanatics.

title: Lenovo y510p Review
text:
My interest in writing this review is that it will be helpful information for others who are looking for a gaming laptop that is configurable, and powerful. My primary purpose for purchasing this laptop was to have a mobile gaming console that I could work on away from my desk.

This computer fits that need perfectly.

Pros: Powerful, fast, easy to upgrade.
Cons: Design is faulty in a few areas.

I purchased the model that has two graphics cards, on is in the ultrabay. Exhaustive research confirms that this additional graphics card makes this perform on par with highest performing mobile graphics cards. This plays all of my games on Utra including the Titanfall Beta.

The i7 is wonderfully fast.

The Hdd is 5400 rpm. I upgraded this to an SSD. The additional SSD hard drive that is advertised (on some model variants) is not a separate hard drive, it is a cache on the 7400 rpm HDD and if you replace the original hard drive it will not function. Having replaced the standard HDD with an SSD this computer is the fastest computer I have owned. It boots to the login screen in under a second in Windows 8.1.

The top of the laptop is aluminum which is very sturdy but shows prints. The bottom half is plastic and there is an edge around the keyboard that is sharp on the bottom of my wrists as I type. The red back-lit keyboard is nice eye candy, but it is a little out of place in conference style professional environments.

Bottom Line: Powerhouse computer. The dual graphics card performs remarkably well. With an SSD upgrade it is incredibly snappy. Minor design complaints don't stop this computer from being the best computer I have ever owned.

title: 5 separate problems within 1 week
text:
First off, let me say that I'm a professional software engineer and I have worked in networking departments in the past. I'm not an expert, but I do like to think that I have deep knowledge about networking. I've been using this router for about a week, with their latest firmware (Version 1.0.3.68_1.1.31), and I've noticed 5 separate issues.

1. Two devices, my laptop and my phone, were both assigned the same IP address, both using DHCP. Releasing and renewing my laptop IP fixed this, but it was pretty scary that it happened after only 2 days.
2. Both of my chromecast devices quit working at the same time. Rebooting the router fixed them both immediately.
3. I tried to set up my printer using WPS. After trying about 10 times in different ways, I finally gave up and used a USB cable to configure my printer.
4. After a few days of successfully using uPNP for port forwarding, it was no longer working. Setting up manual port forwarding fixed this.
5. After a few days of successfully using port forwarding, port forwarding quit working. Rebooting the router fixed it immediately.

I'll accept that maybe not all 5 issues are the router's fault. Maybe the WPS on my printer is just broken. But I thoroughly investigated every other issue before resorting to rebooting the router. I have no other explanation other than the router is just unstable in several different ways. If you search, you can find lots of people with broken Nighthawk r7000 routers waiting for their new firmware update. I thought they would have fixed everything by now, but I guess not.

If you want a router that you can just set up and forget about, this is not it. To me, that makes it useless.

title: Awesome Tablet
text:
I bought this tablet for my daughter's birthday and she is turning 7. I haven't seen her reaction yet, but I have enjoyed simply setting it up for her. I can't judge the screen resolution since I left the plastic wrap on it during setup. I have had multiple Android phones and tablets (including Kindle) over the years as well as an iPad 2 and 3. My pharmacy students all have iPad Minis so I've got a pretty decent basis for comparison. My primary comparison will be to my beloved (and expensive) ASUS Slider.

This tablet is sharp looking, tough and light weight. It has a perfect form factor for a child. As a 10" tablet user, I viewed the Nexus 7 initially as a toy but was very mistaken. It's at least twice as "snappy" as my Slider and pops up a surprisingly large and useful keyboard. Everything from cold boot, WiFi, app performance and screen response are faster than anything I've seen including my iPad 3. Setup was made easier due to NFC with my Galaxy Nexus phone.

One complaint I have is that the micro USB has difficult insertion likely due to the HDMI combo. For this reason I found a cheap Qi wireless charger online so that my daughter can easily keep the tablet charged. If you only want to pay $20 for Qi, you have to get it from deep inside mainland China (via Newegg) so it takes a while.

Another complaint that I have is that the tablet is very Google ID centric. With an age limit of 13, this makes it virtually impossible to set up an Android device for a child. I found very little guidance online for this dilemma which is very surprising.

Comparisons to the iPad mini are inevitable, but the Nexus 7 has technology and functionality beyond the current mini and iOS 6. Reviewers are incorrect when they state the 7 comes with Android 4.3. It does a very quick, forced upgrade once you give it a WiFi connection, however. Speed comparisons will likely be misleading in reviews. The processor is, of course, much more powerful than the Apple competition, but needs to be due to Google's nearly disastrous decision to rely on sluggish and flaky Java.

Overall, this is a fantastic tablet and second to none in my opinion. It has every feature you would expect from a tablet and more. Bluetooth LE is going to become very important and I already am using speed/cadence and HR with my iPhone 4s. There will be many more devices coming to market since a coin battery can power them for months.

Bottom line? You get a very feature packed and fast tablet for the price of a reader. The decision is a no brainer.

title: It's just OK
text:
This review is for the Case Logic LAPS-114 14-Inch computer sleeve. It is intended for my Lenovo Edge E420 notebook.

Amazon combines reviews of this sleeve with reviews for similar products having different dimensions. This is a bad idea. Finding relevant information is tedious. For all their size and might, Amazon should look at how retailers like New Egg present customer's reviews -- their presentation is far more helpful.

I wouldn't normally bother leaving a rating of three stars or less; implying a mediocre product. This product deserves more.

The quality is excellent. The padding is great. However, I'm not convinced the exterior material is tough enough to resist snags. Most laptop sleeves use this material, so maybe it's tougher than I think. It feels good on the hand.

I looked at local stores hoping to examine a Case Logic sleeve like this one. No luck. I didn't like any of the few sleeves I saw locally. On Amazon, they show a different Case Logic product marked as 14.1 inches. I should have bought that sleeve instead of this one.

This sleeve is too small to quickly or comfortably insert and remove my computer. I need a slightly-larger sleeve and a longer zipper. I'm being picky. The sleeve may stretch out a bit over time -- I doubt it. My Edge E420 is one of Lenovo's less-expensive computers. It has no metal frame; i.e.: more plastic. It may be correspondingly larger than a high-end model. Some people may feel this sleeve fits perfectly. I say it's too snug.

I'm sticking with this sleeve for now. It fits adequately. I give the LAPS-114 just three stars because it's too snug for my Lenovo Edge E420 computer.

Update: I purchased a Case Logic PLS-14 14.1 inch sleeve (different retailer) to replace this one. The new sleeve fits better. It has more room for my E420.

The PLS-14 sleeve works better in day-to-day use. But it has thinner padding than the previous LAPS-114. I prefer the materials of the LAPS-114. The LAPS-114 is better for keeping my laptop within luggage or a backpack. So I'm keeping both sleeves. Ridiculous, I know. Hope this helps.

title: Great speakers for a couple hundred bucks
text:
Buying stereo speakers sight-unseen is probably one of the riskiest things you can do. But rest assured, if you snag these, you won't go wrong. What I'm going to say here will probably sound like a contradiction, because I'm arguing here that it's okay to buy these sight unseen. The quality of stereo speakers is such a subjective thing -- describing sound quality with words is like singing about food. But I guess you could say I took a listen so you don't have to, and I could hear the difference.

I was contemplating the purchase of a pair of Pioneer SP-FS51 speakers -- a pretty popular model that seems to get excellent reviews from just about everyone. I really don't want to say much about pricing, because that changes from day to day and getting into precise figures isn't fair to anyone. But let me just say that on this particular day, when I found myself thinking it was time finally to get new speakers, the regular prices online for the Pioneers and the sale price in a big local electronics chain store were roughly the same. If I could have found the Pioneers cheaper online, I probably would have bought the Pioneers sight unseen. I am so glad I didn't.

Since there really wasn't a price difference, I decided to visit the store. When the salesman powered on the switching device so I could give them a listen, the knob was switched to the Onkyo SKF4800s, and we heard them for a few seconds -- then he switched to the Pioneers, OMG, the difference was enormous. The Pioneers sounded like a kitchen-table radio by comparison. "Switch back to those Onkyos," I said. It wasn't my imagination. We switched back and forth a few times. Maybe the Pioneers needed a subwoofer to round out the sound. That could have been part of it. The Onkyos don't need one. The midranges on the Onkyos also seemed much clearer, and no subwoofer would make a difference there. The Onkyos delivered precisely the kind of crisply defined sound I expect from a modern speaker. The volume from the Onkyos was also quite a bit louder than the Pioneers, even though the salesman made no adjustment to the volume control.

Even the salesman had to admit there was a big difference in the definition of the sound from the two speakers. "You expect that, though," he said. "The list price is higher for the Onkyos." This is true; they are not the same price point, but it's not that big of a difference -- the price difference is just a little more than a tank of gas these days.

I think it is useful for me to compare the Pioneers with the Onkyos here because I notice many shoppers have been posting messages in online forums in which they appear to be considering a choice between these two models. All things being even, the Pioneers are probably going to be a bit cheaper, maybe by $50-$80, depending on whether there is a sale. But you know what? The sound is so much clearer and sharper that it's worth spending the extra money. Of course I sucked in my breath and went for the Onkyos. Once I heard 'em, no way could I be satisfied with the Pioneers.

I'm not one of those snooty hi-fi folks who spends a lot of time listening to speakers in the nosebleed price range, so I can't tell you how these compare with the really high-end stuff. I've been listening to regular-guy stereo equipment for the last 30 years. Sometimes I've heard really good speakers in my friends' homes and have been forced to concede that theirs sound better than mine. But what do you expect when they're spending $500 or $1000, and I'm listening to speakers my dad bought in 1966? Or speakers that were considered sorta above-average in 1988? Until now, the kind of speakers you could get for a couple hundred bucks, which is all I'm willing to spend, really weren't that much of an improvement on the kind of stuff I had been using. And the speakers that cost about $500 sounded so much better that it was hard to see a good reason to buy anything. I would only be disappointed.

But the Onkyos? Oh my gosh. They're a couple hundred bucks. These are sooo much better than what I've been using. So much better than any speakers I've ever owned. The sound seems as crisp and as sharp as my friends' $500-and-up speakers. The only reason I give four stars instead of five is that I am sure there are better speakers out there costing ooodles of money. Certainly I didn't listen to absolutely everything on the market, either -- it would have been nice to give the Polks a listen, even though I know we're talking more like $300 for those. But jeez, I have never in all my years heard speakers like these around $200.

title: EP-3 with this lens and VF-2 = Sweet Set-Up
text:
I am an advanced amateur. Grew up using rangefinders, then SLRs, and always prime (legacy) glass. Not a fan of zooms for a number of reasons. I like to pick the right lens when shooting (that's part of the art of photography), primes are much faster than zooms so less light is required, they have a shallower depth of field, and they are lighter. For the same $$$ a fixed focal length prime lens will beat any zoom

For above reasons I purchased the E-P3 with Oly 17mm f/2.8 lens, rather than the kit zoom. It's a great lens! It really is a pancake lens, flat enough that the camera with lens fits into a jacket pocket. This makes a great set-up for street photography. The 17mm is equivalent to a 34mm lens on a full sized DSLR, a wide angle lens, but not too wide for everyday use. I've had a lot of fun shooting with this lens. It is my grab the camera and go lens.

My next lens will be the Oly 45mm. Another prime glass. Like I said, I prefer to change a lens than to use a zoom. So, am I happy with the 17mm? Absolutely! It is well made and fits my E-P3 perfectly. I have no reservations recommending this lens to anyone who enjoys the art of photography!

title: Very disappointing, but a no cost solutions found; returning it
text:
3 minute setup? - hardly. How about an hour and a half and a really bad mood?

I plugged this thing in and selected range extender which is what I bought it for. The first difficulty was that I had to enter my router's long and complicated password in one of these microscopic "keyboards" that infest everything and keep me off most internet apps in the first place. That took about four tries and 10 minutes. Then the extender found a network of my router. Oh, good! -- well, no. My router has two networks, at 2.4 and 5 giga whatsits. The extender found the one that the router was not using. That took about 45 minutes of frustration to figure out. Why should this be? I suppose Almond was too busy working on their "3 minute setup" slogan and their 18-word instruction manual to impart some information that might actually be useful to users. I couldn't get the extender to even detect the active network, let alone use it. However my Kindle which is what I bought the extender for in the first place saw them all so I told the Kindle to do the heavy lifting to get something to work.

So, finally I actually extended my router's range by a few feet; however the 2.4 Ghz network lost the signal more frequently than the previous unextended 5 Ghz network at slightly lesser range, and on the second day it got much worse at acquiring and holding the signal. This got more and more frustrating, so I tried a Kim Komando trick that I didn't think would actually work; I cobbled and riveted together some scrap aluminum in my garage to form a shield around my router's three antenna and pointed the rig in the direction that I wanted the signal's range to increase. Voila, it worked to the tune of about 35 or 40 feet which was enough in my case. Cost, zero - so the Almond Extender is going back tomorrow.

Looking back on this fiasco, I suppose some of the blame is on me because I took the advertising at face value and did not bother to research routers and networks and bands and extenders and Ghz and limitations and on an on... But I shouldn't have to. Computing shouldn't be a sweat act anymore.

title: bubbly...
text:
I originally ordered this item, and after after applying all three of the screen protectors that it came with, wrote a less than favorable review. The original protectors came in a clear plastic jacket with absolutely no guidance as to how to apply the protectors. My experience resulted in a huge number of bubbles under the protectors, which simply could not be coaxed out.
The supplier read my review, and immediately sent me a replacement. The replacement came in a much more professional plastic jacket, with instructions. However, the basic problem is not solved. The instructions more clearly describe the general application, as the protector has both a layer under and over it to be removed. However, unless there is some trick to applying the protector, I still ended up with lots of bubbles. For the most part the bubbles are invisible, as they really dont show up when the screen is brightly lit. However, with darker media, they become fairly obvious. The protector is quite thin, and doesnt reduce the screen light by much. And, of course, the screen is protected. But, the bubbles just dont go away. So, if your primary interest is screen protection and low cost, this is a good product. If you dont want bubbles, you probably either need a course on how to apply the protector, or find an alternative.

I bought this keyboard to pair with my Kindle Fire 7" HD. As soon as I got it out of the box, I had it connected to my kindle within minutes. There was a slight delay with the keys... letters would show up maybe 1-2 seconds after I'd typed them. Most importantly, many letters would repeat over and over, anywhere from 3-20 times as if I was holding a key down. Okay, that's annoying!

Then experimentally, I paired the keyboard with my iPhone4. That was also a simple process. There was NO delay, and NO repeated letters! It pairs beautifully with my iPhone, better than with the Kindle Fire.

Unfortunately as soon as I tried to pair the keyboard back with my Kindle Fire HD, it will NOT work! Believe me, my husband and I have troubleshooted, and tried every scenario possible. The Kindle recognizes the keyboard, states that it is in fact connected, but clearly is not. We thought that if we could "forget this device" like the iPhone has an option for, maybe we could start from scratch and re-pair the keyboard to the Kindle that it would work, but there is no option for that. My husband's career is in technology and even worked the Bluetooth phenomenon behind the scenes, and he says that this is likely a bug within the Kindle Fire itself, because the keyboard continues to pair with our iPhones effortlessly.

I just wondered if anyone else has experienced this as well? I see others complain of choppy connections too. This SHOULD be easily fixed by connecting the Kindle to a computer and downloading the latest updates and software... as long as the engineers behind Kindle KNOW of these bugs and have fixed them or not. I plan on calling customer service tomorrow to see what they can do for me. I will update when I can.

title: Huge beautiful screen - no sacrifice performance
text:
Selection of computer or latop (if your lap will hold the size and weight of this thing) is a very subjective matter. To me this is more of an all-in-one desktop than a laptop as it is more than twice the size of a (Asus) Chromebook and almost three times the size of my Sony Vaio laptop. I'll preface this review by saying that I have an Asus Chromebook that is a great product, so my expectations were high.

The rest are less (but still somewhat) subjective statements:

PROs:
- big beautiful screen. Can be opened with one hand, but begs for two hands so as not to over torque the hinge on the other side with the leverage from this huge screen
- intel i7 and NVIDIA GeForce GTX860M are comparable to any similarly equipped desktop or all in one. ABSOLUTELY no performance sacrifice here
- dual USB ports on BOTH SIDES which is very convenient for allowing you to select which side to plug in USB devices
- BluRay/DVD player is on theft side. I find it awkward that it is on the opposite side of the power cord requiring access to both sides instead of just one ...
- Windows 8.1 installed. For good or bad, this isn't a review of Windows 8.1
- minimal packaging which is a plus
- backlit keyboard is easy to use in the dark

CONs:
- BluRay software included DOES NOT PLAY BLURAY DISCS. Acer's included software out of the box SAYS it will not play BluRay or DVD movies out of the box and requires downloading a DIFFERENT PROGRAM CyberLink PowerDVD (NOT AN UPGRADE) to play movies. Its worse than that even. It requires you to then uninstall Cyberlink PowerMediaPlayer which comes pre-installed (why did Asus bother installing this then).I think it is unacceptable to sell a unit like this without a working DVD + BluRay player. If you spend the $$ on a BluRay drive, I assume you want this function packaged in
- Comes with installed with McAfee -- which itself is a virus because it is almost impossible to remove (I tried). It wants to re-install itself
- Comes pre-installed with gobs of Acer cloud and other apps which are mostly advertisements or enticements to use Acer services, software, etc. I can see how they are trying to be helpful, but really, it just creates more work to have to remove all of the tiles, software, etc.
- Comes littered with tiles (programs) on the Win 8 desktop which are marketplaces to buy stuff. You'd think this was a retail kiosk turn-key system, not a "personal" computer. Took me almost an hour to remove most of the tiles and uninstall most of this software
- No backup CD's or DVDs included
- Ethernet jack has a partial flip down opening on the clip side of the RJ-45. (a) this does not cover the Ethernet port to protect it from dust/dirt when not in use and (b) I am 100% confident this will break. I really have no idea why Asus would design this to be less reliable by INTRODUCING A MOVING PART TO AN ETHERNET CONNECTION. Seriously, I have a laptop that weighs under 3lbs and is like 1/2 the thickness of this monster and it has a normal Ethernet port, there is just no reason to do this.
- backlit keyboard contributes to burning through battery faster
- stickers are on crooked, sad to see on a brand new item and shows lack of care in manufacturing
- "Black Edition" printing on touch pad -- ridiculous marketing. OHH -- LOOK this is a "special laptop" because it is black. Seriously ? What a waste. They'd be better off lowering the price by 1cent and removing the "Black Edition" marketing

Summary
If you're seriously considering purchasing a system like this it is because you need the performance of a local processor, BluRay/DVD, etc. Here, you are not making any performance sacrifice compared to a desktop or all in one. As a "portable" solution, I personally find it huge and could never travel with something this large, nor could I think of a reason other than gaming or video editing that would really require a monster machine like this. But if either of those or a similar demand drives you to a CPU/graphics performance solution (rather than lower cost, lighter weight, or convenience), than this is the pickup and go box for you.

title: Watch out for flexing joints...
text:
I'm a tall guy (6'3") and bought this monopod (my first) based on length and quality.

The good news -- it certainly is tall! At my height a 65" monopod would probably be sufficient. The extra height is nice, but unnecessary in most circumstances.

Now onto the Gitzo quality. I own a Series 3 tripod and it is expensive and solid. Rock solid. Not going anywhere. So I had high expectations for this monopod, particularly at this price point.

While the machining and fit and finish are top-notch, I noticed significant flex in the lower section of the monopod. On inspection, I saw both the thin 16mm-diameter lower section flexing, but also somewhat of a hinging movement in the two lower leg joints. This flexing resolved somewhat when not using the lower-most section, but what good is a tall monopod if it can't be tall?

Long story short, I ended up returning this monopod and going with a ROCK SOLID Sirui at about half the price, the same weight, and greater load capacity.

Maybe my unit of the 3551 was flawed -- who knows -- but who really has time to go back and forth and back and forth in search of the perfect sample, particularly when other brands are in the market with competitive products at significantly lower price points.

I'll keep my Gitzo tripod for now, after years of faithful service, but were I doing it over, I would certainly give Sirui tripods a real shot as well...

title: Much better than expected
text:
Bought this on a whim, on the way to the zoo. Was frustrated on a prior trip with a 70-200 and a 300 (both Canon L series). Wanted more reach.

Took a bunch of shots, hand-held, even at 500mm and was astonished at how sharp they were - even ones where I wasn't really trying that hard. Put it on a monopod, too, and was able to get some shots that would have just been frustrating with a shorter lens.

I have 6 Canon "L" lenses. I sold my only other Sigma (20mm) and had become an "L" snob. This lens makes me willing to consider other Sigma lenses. Makes me want to buy some, actually.

The biggest drawback of this lens is the weight - it is a BEAST. I can't carry it and anything else other than my camera. It's that heavy. I actually bought a baby stroller to put it in for the next zoo trip so that we can take more gear. I bought an RRS collar plate for it, and a RRS monopod tilt-head to see if it's easier to handle on the next trip. I am a small woman and this lens is going to require some strength-building to use for longer periods - even though my shooting arm is already pretty strong from using the 70-200 2.8L II on a gripped FF.

I love this lens so much I've been driving Texas back country roads looking for things to shoot - goats, horses, longhorns. Anything with fur, just to marvel at the detail captured.

I am not a "pro" sports or wildlife photog, so can't say how it compares with the $6k+ options out there.

title: Works great!
text:
I needed to get better wireless coverage in my 2nd floor bonus room, as my wireless router is on the first floor on the other side of my house. I originally looked into a wireless extender/repeater for upstairs when I noticed these powerline adapters (one with Wireless). I figured I can have the best of both worlds by hardwiring my blu-ray player and having great wireless coverage too.

This product worked perfectly. I was skeptical about using the electrical wiring, but I'm sold now. It was very easy to set these up...it basically creates another wireless network to connect to, and you can set a password to keep it secure (I used the same password as my wireless router). I plugged the wireless adapter into the electrical outlet behind my blu-ray player & tv in the bonus room. I tried both wireless and wired with my blu-ray, and the streaming apps worked great either way. The wired connection is a little faster, so I'm using it. The kit came with the ethernet cables for each adapter. Now I can use my laptop, kindle, etc wirelessly in that room and get solid streaming through the wired connection on the blu-ray.

For a little more than the cost of a wireless repeater or the standard powerline adapter kits, you can get both worlds with this. I recommend it.

title: You can do better for the price
text: As the title of my review states, there are better values out there. These headphones put a lot of pressure on the top of your head, are heavy, and just flat out not very comfortable to wear. I also never really liked how vocals sounded through these; I felt they weren't very accurately reproduced. I would recommend the Panasonic RPHT360 which cost less, are more comfortable, sound much clearer with equal if not better bass (to me), and are more durable. Yes, the replaceable cord seems like a good idea but my pair and my friend's pair (who also bought these) both started rattling on one side at medium low volumes and only got worse as you turned them up. A replaceable cord isn't going to fix a defect inside the cup, which I took apart to see what could be causing the rattle but never figured it out. Yes, I know about Monoprice's awesome return policy... but it was past 30 days for a refund and to send these back to exchange them will cost you at least $5. I already preferred the sound of my Panasonics so I didn't bother. My friend sent his back but said the second pair "never sounded as good" which I thought is interesting to know since he is not an audiophile or anything but could recognize a difference in quality between two pairs. Although these are hyped up quite a bit on the Headfi website, I really wanted to like these "rebranded Kicker HP541 headphones" or also known as "Audio Technica m50 killers" but they sadly just didn't cut it for me.

title: Great hardware...
text:
I really enjoy playing tablet video games with the Nyko controller. The Nyko controller is VERY nice including the texture of the plastic controller, the shape of the controller in your hands, the layout (much like xbox 360) and the sturdy build. This controller feels like it will last for a long time and looks great.

Out of the box I charged the gamepad (via USB charger) and downloaded a bunch of games. Once charged I used the Nyko launcher and was able to play all the games they had pre-sets for including (Cordy, Samurai II, Sonic CD, Trial Xtreme 2, Meganoid and GTA III). Without using the Nyko launcher I was able to play several games with native gamepad ability including (ShadowGun, Zombie Driver, Gunman Clive, TriaX2 and Edge). Playing ShadowGun (and a couple of others) makes your android tablet feel like a game console, very cool!

The only cons I have with this is the software which can be fixed by updates (crossing my fingers). The first issue is the Nyko launcher only has 6 game presets prebuilt in it. I have tried to add other games but none of the games I have added see inputs from the controller. I know I am adding the games to the launcher correctly but I guess it is only going to work on a few games out there. This is one place Nyko could really help itself and its customers (build more game profiles). The second large con is that the games that work with the launcher require you to pair the Nyko controller through the launcher. The other games that have native support for gamepads (listed above) require you to pair the Nyko controller through the tablet bluetooth settings not the launcher (they do not work vice versa). This isn't a problem if you're only playing one game a day but when playing several in a row or showing it to friends it is extremely cumbersome.

One last comment (if Nyko reads this). A simple forum on their web page that says what games work and what games don't would be a huge help. I have been searching all over for games to try...

Again, great system, just needs software updates to fix the cons.

**UPDATE 02/26/2013**
Ok, I am finding that I can run any App that works with HW (hardware input). The Nyko controller can emulate not only a controller but a keyboard too. Today I installed Snes9x EX+, MAME4droid and MAME4droid Reloaded and all three work GREAT! Nothing better than playing an old arcade favorite with this great feeling controller in your hand. Note, it took a few hours of messing around with the Nyko launcher and the emulator to get these to work perfectly.

**UPDATE 03/03/2013**
I have just uploaded a bunch of photos, screenshots and captions to help illustrate what I talked about above. Hope it is useful.

**UPDATE 11/11/2013**
I just read someone said this would not work on Android 4.x. That is not true. I have ran this on my Galaxy Tablet with Android OS version 4.1, 4.2 and now just tested with 4.3.

The Nyko Android software has been updated a lot since my original post. I haven't messed with it much but it appears to be have addressed the pairing issue I complained about AND they have a "Compatible games list" in the application now!!!!

**UPDATE 11/27/2013**
I just paired the Nyko Playpad with my Windows 8.1 tablet. I am able to play the Windows game Pac-Man DX in Mouse mode with no problem and was able to play MAME games in playpad mode. I am not sure how many other games work but it was neat to see it work on Windows.

Also, I purchased a second remote to use in two player MAME games but I can't seem to get the second Nyko Playpad to go into two player mode. There is clearly a light on the back which says 1 and 2 but when pairing them up, the light on both controllers always go to 1. I wrote Nyko twice with no reply.

**UPDATE 01/18/2015
I just used this with the Amazon Fire Stick and it worked great. Another note, this unit is coming up on two years old and the batteries are still doing great and it works just fine with my latest tablet Samsung Galaxy Note 2014/KitKat 4.4.2.

title: LG customer support quote "If you spent $900 on them like you did on your iPhone 6 Plus we would replace them immediately"
text:
I would put up a blank star if I could.

I purchased these from the local AT&T store. They were pretty good for the beginning. I liked the wireless feature, they sounded "decent" as long as you used the right sized earbud and created a tight seal in your ear canal. All was grand at first.

After about two weeks I noticed the the Pause/Play button quit working. At first I figured it was just a software issue so I deleted the device from my iPhone and repaired it. It worked for a brief amount of time but I had to do that process about 3 more times in the next couple of weeks. It got really old after a while having to do that so I just ignored it for a while.

Well, I then decided I would do it again and get it working. Only this time, it didn't start working again. This may sound petty, but it's a real pain in the rear to have to take your phone out all of the time to pause or play the music.

I went back down to the AT&T store and asked if they had anyone come in with the same issues. The guy at the counter had the same headset and said his were doing it to and that I had to call LG and they would send me a new pair. That wasn't a good sign, but I was content with the idea of them sending me a new pair. Oh how I was wrong.

When you call LG, you get "JR" in the Philippines who is just overjoyed to help you in your dire situation. He gladly will give you the address so that you can 1) Find a box 2) Remind you that you better have that receipt to prove that you are under warranty (even though the headphones haven't been out long enough to be out of warranty) 3) Pay to ship the box to LG 4) And chance that they might not replace with a new pair but attempt to repair yours.

After I got of the phone with LG I got pretty mad. I didn't see how this was all my problem since I paid so much for these and they crapped out so fast. I can see why they don't want to send you a new pair and want you to go through the hassle of shipping and paying for it yourself. They are banking that you won't do it. title: The perfect charger that is perfect for camping or long car rides.
text:
USB charged devices have been very popular in the last decade, but what do you do when you are camping in the wild, miles from a power source? You can’t, unless you have the PortaPow 4x AA/AAA USB Battery Charger and Power Bank.

▶ Package Contents
• Battery Pack
• Charger Cable
• 3 x Connectors: Micro USB, Mini USB, Apple 'Wide' (30 Pin)
• User Guide

▶ Accessories
This device comes with a 20.5 inch charger cable. What is unique about this cable is that it is a USB to USB or connector to attach an Apple 30 pin, Mini USB, or Micro USB connector. The USB to USB connector is used to charge any AA or AAA rechargeable battery, which is very unique that you can charge batteries by USB. The three different connectors are used to connect a wide variety of mobile devices, and is a very nice feature, despite the $14.99 price tag. The only accessory that could make this more perfect is a carrying bag to carry everything together.

▶ Specifications
• Power Input: 800mA / 5V
• Power Output: 500mA / 5V
• Certifications: CE and RoHS Compliant
• Charging Protection: Timer, Over Current, reverse polarity, defective and non-rechargeable battery detection
• Guarantee: 1 Year

▶ Hardware
The battery pack is very small and light (4.6 x 3 x 1 inches; 4.2 oz). You can safely assume the product weight would increase when batteries are attached to the device. This device has a hard plastic body, with a transparent red slider and outline, and a white non-transparent top and bottom. I can imagine this device being durable and able to take a beating from bumps and scrapes, but wouldn’t advise to drop this product. The slider also acts as a cover for the batteries, has the PortaPow name, logo, and model name “4x AA USB Rechargeable Battery,” and is able to slide approximately 2 inches, allowing batteries to be installed without any fitting issues. Under the slider is place for AA or AAA batteries, with a flap to clip down the positive terminal for AAA batteries (clip up for AA batteries), and a spring-like metal connector for the negative terminal. Do note that AAA batteries may be loose for the spring on the negative terminal, which means you may need to use needle nose pliers or a knife to lift the spring up to an optiminal position. Also on the top face is a 1.5 inch black button with three LEDs inside.

LED Statuses:
Red LED: Charging batteries
Green LED: Finished charging batteries
Blue LED: Ready to output power

The LED statuses are very nice for a budget friendly device. On the top has the USB port for charging rechargeable batteries or charging mobile devices, and on the back has four screws and the specifications, which are listed above. I overall like the concept and design of this device, but wish AAA batteries fit better.

▶ Setup
Setup for this device is fairly simple. If you want to charge the rechargeable batteries, simply plug the USB into the appropriate port, and the other USB into a computer, or for best results, a 2.1A USB wall charger. The time to charge your rechargeable batteries will depend on the manufacturer, capacity of the batteries, and whether it is lithium ion, nickel-metal hydride, or nickel cadmium. You will know your batteries are fully charged when the LED goes from RED to GREEN.

▶ Testing
It is difficult to accurately test the efficiency of this charger, as it depends highly on the type of battery and manufacturer, however, I can test the current and voltage output for different devices to give you a good idea that this charger can output. For my test, I attached 4 disposable AA and AAA batteries for brand name and off-brand. Each item was tested twice per device using my Centech USB Meter.

Nexus 7 68% Charged
4x AAA Rayovac (1.5V Alkaline):
Current: 0.53A
Voltage: 4.94V
Peak Current: 0.54A
Minimum Voltage (to power device): 4.82V

4x AA Utilitech (1.5V Alkaline):
Current: 0.96A
Voltage: 4.84V
Peak Current: 0.84A
Minimum Voltage (to power device): 4.67V

Jackery Giant 2/3 LEDs
4x AAA Rayovac (1.5V Alkaline):
Current: 0.69A
Voltage: 4.40V
Peak Current: 0.73A
Minimum Voltage (to power device): 4.3V

4x AA Utilitech (1.5V Alkaline):
Current: 0.68A
Voltage: 4.95V
Peak Current: 0.69A
Minimum Voltage (to power device): 4.83V

RAVPower 6000mA 3/4 LEDs
4x AAA Rayovac (1.5V Alkaline):
Current: 0.67A
Voltage: 4.77V
Peak Current: 0.67A
Minimum Voltage (to power device): 4.66V

4x AA Utilitech (1.5V Alkaline):
Current: 0.64A
Voltage: 4.97V
Peak Current: 0.64A
Minimum Voltage (to power device): 4.96V

As you can see, my mobile device tested better for the AA batteries than AAA, but the external batteries seemed to produce better results for AAA than AA. Also, even though the output is rated at 800mA, I received a rating close to 1000mA with my AA batteries. As you can see from these tests, the battery manufacturer and type will determine different outputs for different devices. I am overall satisfied by these results.

▶ Final Thoughts
I see the best situation to use this device is when you are away from a power source for an extended period of time, such as a road trip or camping trip, where you will see several convenient stores but not a power source. I think the fact that you can charge rechargeable batteries is a good added feature, but I see this used more with disposable batteries. Because of the budget friendly price tag, versatility, concept, and build of the device, I give this product a 5 star rating. I would recommend this to individuals who are in these unique situations, or want to gift this to their loved ones as a stocking stuffer.

Pros:
+ The perfect stocking stuffer for under $20.
+ Ability to charge your mobile device, or rechargeable batteries, without the need for an external power outlet.
+ Includes several accessories for most Android and older Apple devices.
+ LED indicator for charging batteries or ready to output power.

Cons:
- Negative terminal spring may not be tight enough for AAA batteries, which means you may need to lift the spring with needle-nose pliers or a knife.

I was provided a sample in exchange for a thorough and honest review.

title: well made questionalbe as to usefulness
text:
Pros:
Very well made:
1.Strong quality fabric
2. heavy duty zippers with pulls
3. rubber material on bottom to help with wear and tear
4. Shoulder belt made from strong but softer material so it doesn't cut into your body - padded area for shoulder
5. Nice padding for camera I thought the bag itself was heavy - it weighs 1.8 lbs!
6. Densely woven fabric is water resistant, although it doesn't say so. I sprayed the back of it with the kitchen faucet spray feature - excess water beaded up and rolled off - the fabric did absorb some water but was dry within 5 minutes.
7. Side pockets hold an average size water bottle
8. Multipe pockets: flap pocket semi functional. Zip compartment with pockets under the flap most functional for wallet/keys/phone etc. Small zip pocket in main body maybe for keys? It's a shallow pocket on 2" deep so not quite sure what I'd put in there other than keys.
9. comfortable to wear across body - if somewhat heavy - with my camera/wallet/keys/phone/ipad/flash/full water bottle - it was 7.8 lbs
10. handle on top to carry is nice option
11. ipad with leather cover actually fits into the ipad pocket! the ipad pocket is lightly padded for additional protection
12. separate, padded, removable "pouch" for camera, with drawstring closure and handles. Nice for easy removal if you alternate using as a purse or a camera bag
13. If used as a purse, it's more functional, holding ipad, book, make up bag, plenty of room in the pockets under the flap for wallet, phone, etc. Space available in flap pocket if you want to put your phone there

Cons:
Design flaws:
1. the outer flap has a curved zipper pocket which is unusable if you use this as a camera bag. I could only unzip it a couple inches and barely get 2 fingers in.
2. the snaps on the outer flap were VERY difficult for me to close, I could not do so when wearing the bag, I had to put the bag on the counter and use force
3. The heavy duty zipper for the main compartment is long and the ends extend into the stretch pockets on the sides, so if you do put a water bottle in this portion will extend a few inches in front or in back of the water bottle.
4. Suggested use for side pockets was water bottle and umbrella - both do fit nicely but the umbrella extends above the top of the bag which was awkward as it kept hitting my body.
5. my panasonic camera fit into the smaller camera bag, but there was absolutely no room for additional lens as shown in the picture. I could barely squeeze the flash in. My Panasonic is about 5.25" across the back, the camera bag was approx 7" across with the camera in it so you can see there is no room for additional lens. Your camera may be smaller. There is a smaller pocket in the camera 'pouch' for an extra battery.
6. As you know, once you begin filling up all the pockets provided, the pockets become less functional as space is used. For instance IF you used the flap pocket, it's difficult to fill the pocket space under the flap. IF you have your camera in the bag, only the slimmest items will fit into the pockets under the flap and the flap pocket is useless

I would use this bag for work, I felt it was more functional. It could be a purse/briefcase and is not oversized. The bag balances well across body and would be comfortable while waiting for train or bus. I felt the bag was secure, so it would be difficult to rip off your ipad or phone (as opposed to many bags I have seen which gape open) I found it less functional as a camera bag, I would use it only for short photography sessions when I wouldn't want to change lenses etc. I also have a cannon camera backpack, which I think is more functional when I'm planning to be out for most of the day, there's plenty of room for ipad, water, wallets etc.
Oddly, that bag when fully loaded including additional lens AND camera weighed 9 lbs..

title: Charge me up!
text:
To install this, I unscrewed the battery cap on my relatively recent Apple Wireless Keyboard (2 AA battery version), took the batteries out, and replaced them with the supplied battery and cap. Took about two minutes, and was easy to do. I don't have a trackpad, so I can't comment on that, though it is supposed to work with that as well.

I plugged mine into a spare Apple USB "cube" charger because I use my keyboard on a desk without a computer (I use it with my iPads). This worked fine, and as long as the battery cap is sitting in the charger, it will charge. It is wireless, but the base is touching the cap, so it isn't like it will just charge being nearby.

The fit and finish on this product is first-rate, and matches the keyboard exactly, or at least so closely it won't bother you. It looks and feels like a piece of Apple equipment, which is great.

For me, I do wonder if it is necessary. That's because the Apple rechargeable batteries I was using before last a really long time, so it wasn't that big a deal to swap them out when needed. The Mobee device does add a bit of bulk, which isn't as good for travel. Still, by leaving it in the charger, I know it is always fully charged and ready to go, so that is a pretty big advantage. Also, not everyone has good rechargeables, so if you are using disposable batteries for your keyboard, this is a terrific alternative.

Overall, I'd say it isn't a necessary purchase, but is fun to have, works well, and looks good.

Sean P. Logue, 2012

title: Good value!  Met all my expectations...
text:
I purchased the RS120 headphone/charger system and a second pair of [[ASIN:B000EBPJCO Sennheiser HDR120 Supplemental HiFi Wireless Headphones]] (without a charger) for my wife and I to use in our bedroom so that we could watch a little TV without waking our sleeping toddler across the hall. We've had them for about two weeks now and have used them on numerous occasions. They work very well. Sound quality is fine. These are not audiophile Sennheisers, they're not priced as if they were. They are not intended for critical listening, or for reproducing 7.1 theater sound systems. They are simple stereo wireless headphones.

Our bedroom TV is wall mounted (using this [[ASIN:B001OCY3RY VideoSecu Low Profile TV Wall Mount]]) and I have all the cables routed inside the wall including the audio cable that connects to the headphone base. The base itself is located in the room next to our bedroom (my office). Since the headphones use RF (instead of IR) the signal goes right through the wall. RF interference has not been a problem either (the house is saturated with wireless signals and the base is located in a room with two or three computers that are running all the time).

Range is good. I haven't tested the limit of the range, but the headphones work everywhere in the house (meaning we can walk downstairs to the kitchen while still listening to the TV).

Setup was very simple. Plug the base in, connect the audio cable to the TV. Charge the headphones. Turn them on. Tune them and you have audio.

Things the be aware of:

1. The base has a 3.5mm (standard mini headphone size) stereo input jack and comes with an stereo RCA-to-3.5mm converter and a fairly long stereo RCA cable (long enough for my needs by far). Your TV needs to have analog audio outputs. The base does NOT have digital audio inputs. The outputs on your TV will be fixed level, or variable-level (or user selectable). Our Vizio TV has selectable outputs and I selected fixed-level. This means that the headphones are used to control the volume instead of the TV remote. For us, this works well as we can each independently adjust the volume without affecting the other listener. (The downside? The mute button on the TV remote does nothing).

2. I have two headphones, but the charging station can only charge one at a time. This isn't a problem. You just need to be aware that you can only fit one at a time on the charger and manage your charging so you don't end up with a dead battery when you need them.

3. I'm still on my first charge cycle and we've used the headphones for at least 5 hours over the last two weeks. So far no sign of running them out.

4. The headphones use standard AAA NiMH batteries (provided). I'm considering buying a few more just so I have a few charged ready-to-go batteries around in case I do ever forget to charge the headphones (and our baby monitor uses the same).

5. I did not mount my base on the wall (it just sits on my desk), but it does have a single keyhole mount slot. I don't think it would look very good stuck on the wall, but if needed, it'll work.

6. This is the only drawback I've found so far, but at this price point I didn't really consider this a negative: The headphones are not the type that go over your ears. The lay flat on the ear. There is no surround. Some people might find this uncomfortable during a long listening session. When I first put them on, my initial reaction was: "these are not going to be comfortable". But after using them for a while now, they really are not too bad. The comfort isn't great, but not bad either. The other trait with the lack of a surround is that they do not isolate sound. You can hear other noises in the room (good for us, we can here the baby monitor), but you can also hear the other person's headphones if they are listening at a loud level (and your trying to read a book, or sleep). Again, only a problem if the other person is cranking it up. This hasn't been a problem for us. I've never heard my wife's headphones while I read or sleep.

So I give these 5 stars because they met my expectations in every way. I was not expecting high-end audio, but I was expecting easy setup and decent sound quality for a reasonable price. And that's what I got.

Even very good motherboards make a lot of compromises when it comes to sound. Internal DA converters are mediocre at best so using an external anologue amp (even a good one) will get you more volume but the sound will suffer even more for having been amped. The Answer is an external DAC (Digital Audio Converter) combined with a head amp. Alas there are quite a few out there. The problem is finding something reasonably priced and stil be an improvement in sound quality as well as be able to deliver lots of volume. After wading through scores of reviews here and other places I found that the Topping TP30 consistanly had extremely good reviews with almost no negatives. The unit is substantial and weighty for its size and not at all flimsy or cheap in construction. Plug it in and it installs seamlessly! Its Truly plug and play, windows does not even install drivers for it. It essentialy deactivates your sound card and takes it place (While plugged in and turned on). OK So how does it sound? Well your milage may vary......however I could not beleive how much crisper and more detailed the sound was. This was true across the board. I tried listening to low bit rate Mp3 (128) to very high bit rate (320), Also to Flacc and refference quality Wav files. The types of Music range from Classical to Jazz to Blues and Progressive Rock. Its a very pleasurable experience to pick up nuances and details in music that you are already very familiar with. If your an Audiophile and you have good source material on your computer and a decent set of headphones this little device should bring a big smile to your face. It did for me. title: Your best bet if you need to add sata 3 to your motherboard - but read this for important info
text:
Disclaimer: I understand how "finicky" this area of computer parts can be...meaning solid state drive controller cards. A lot of people report issues for one thing or another, so I cannot say what will and will not work for other people.

First off, I was a PRIME candidate for having to add sata 3 to my motherboard. I have an EVGA p55 FTW 200 motherboard (AWESOME motherboard) but it came out JUST before sata 3 was the standard. So this and the p55 classified are pretty much the best motherboards made without sata 3 or usb 3.0. So for people like us, it is VERY worth adding in a card like this when upgrading to a ssd (which is a must now, especially with the ssd's coming out now and the prices.)

So here is the info that you NEED TO KNOW...

DO NOT USE THIS CARD IN A PCI EXPRESS X1 SLOT!!!! (I should say "as long as you can help it") I know it is a x1 card, but I can not see recommending this to someone if they have no choice but to put it in a x1 slot. At first I was skeptical that moving it from the x1 to the x16 would make all that big of a difference, since it still just a x1 card. Wrong. The chip on this card can handle MUCH faster speeds than what the 250mbps x1 pipeline can. You will still technically be bottlenecked down to the pci express x4 or x16 (whichever you use) speed of 5gbps instead of true sata 3 6gbps, but you will HARDLY notice the difference, and never come close to saturating even 5gbps. The only time you will notice the numbers is during benchmarks.

And yes....pci express is maxed out at 5gbps, just in case you didn't know. Again, this should NOT be a deal breaker, just something people should know about these cards.

I had installed this in the x1 slot, hooking up a Corsair Force gt 64gb SSD to it. Before setting up a new windows 7, I wanted to make sure to have the card set up, so I went to rosewill's website and got the newest drivers for the card. After a restart everything fired right up, and the hard drive was found and everything seemed to be fine. I made sure to turn on AHCI in my bios.

Windows 7 installed fine, and I already noticed ENORMOUS performance gains in installs, boot time, seek time, etc. I made sure to turn on trim support as well (you can find out how to do this and AHCI with a 2 second google search)

Installed in the x1 slot, I was seeing VERY slow speeds with the force gt. Rated at about 555/495, I was expecting to see at least 350/300....nope....i didn't realize the x1 slot would bottleneck so badly. I'm talking speeds as low as 200/150. Marginally faster than my 150/100 speeds of my wd caviar blacks mechanical hard drives. I then did some reading, and thought that maybe it was because I was using a sata 2 cable. Got a sata 3 cable. No difference in speed. So i switched it to a x16 slot (i have 3 x16 on this board)....voila! speeds of about 375/325 now. Sure, it's not as fast as the rated speeds, but trust me i am THRILLED with these speeds. Performance-wise you would never tell the difference, and I am just happy I got sata 3 working so easily for so cheap. - NOTE - I would still highly recommend using a sata 3 cable. As long as you can buy them cheap, might as well go with sata 3. They are slightly better conductors and a bit thicker, but are mostly a marketing gimmick. Still, doesn't hurt.

So why market a x1 card as a x1 sata 3 controller when at x1 speeds it is completely bottlenecked? Well, I don't quite understand why these companies aren't at least recommending in the product description that you should use at least pci express x4, but I can understand making a x1 card like this. It is TINY, and is completely compatible with x4 or x16 slots.

So this is by far the best option that people in my situation have. PERIOD. revo drives and the like (pci express ssd's) are getting a little bit cheaper, but I would still have to recommend for now at least, getting this card and buying a $100 ssd. You will not get the 6gbps, but you will still see a 200% increase in performance.

Also the product came super fast, and I have always liked rosewill, they seem pretty legit. Seems like anyone that may have had any issues with their products, they are very quick to reply and do their best to help, this is why I went with this card. I have heard so much about problems with sandforce and marvell (force gt) so I was worried I'd have some conflicts, but I could not be happier with how everything is running. Not a single issue yet.

corsair h50 cooler
4 gigs g.skill 2133mhz
corsair 750w psu
3x caviar black 750gig hd's
1x corsair force gt 64gb ssd

title: Perfect for Bodyboarders!
text:
If you YouTube search "IBA GoPro Highlights" you'll see that all the riders use this chest strap but turn it around backwards so that the camera is resting on your lower back. That way when you're riding a wave the camera captures a sick over the shoulder almost half-body shot of your ride.

I tested this in BIG surf. 8' - 10' Hawaiian waves, which any rider will tell you... They have some serious power. Enough to slam you to the reef, drown you, etc. Now, one addition I made to this chest harness is:

I bought a steel fishing liter. You can buy this at most tackle shops. It's steel fishing line about 12" long. They use it for catching big ocean fish that would bite the line off, like sharks. You take your 12" of line, cut it down to like 2-4", then thread one part through the harness mount, and one part around the gopro.

Essentially you're making a steel leash. Since I had it on my back I wanted to have the mental reassurance that if it did pop off - It would stay attached to the harness.

I also have the Backdoor Floaty attached to my GoPro as well, the big orange foam float. With the steel liter, and the orange float, you can feel pretty safe on any size surf. Any bodyboarder that has a gopro, should buy this! The only thing it doesn't work for is drop-knee riding. You can flip it around to your chest like it supposed to be worn, but it's too hard to paddle with the camera smashing against your board. For drop knee riders, I would recommend the Australian 50mm Pole mount, or the head strap mount.

Lastly, whichever mount I use, I ALWAYS have a steel liter around it. I've had it pop off my surfboard mount many times (i surf too), and I've had it pop off my 50mm pole mount. Hopefully this long-winded review will help you in making your next purchase.

title: Great travel camera
text:
First off, this camera is the best point and shoot I've ever owned. The versatility and the built in features/modes allow you to capture any situation you come across. To date I have travelled through the Galapagos, Ecuador and Peru and Florida with this camera. I've never had a single problem with the toughness of this camera. I originally bought a small case to toss it in but after using it for awhile I wasn't worried about it getting messed up throwing it in a pouch of my back pack. There are some things I'd like to be better, but they might be a limitation to all these types of cameras though. I outlined them in pros and cons.

Pros:

Great quality pictures
- I have a Fujifilm HS30EXR as well that I used travelling. It's a lot more convient to carry this around. The Fuji has better results in the end but the TS4 compares really well. In an age where 90% of photos are just going to be resized and emailed or posted on Facebook this camera is way more than good enough on quality.

Great features
- Lots of modes that are easily accessed. The more comfortable you get the faster you'll get at switching modes too. I left it in the iA mode most of the time but picking a specific mode can make a difference and is worth the effort.

Size
- It's not as small as others but it feels substantial and you can get a good grip on it, which I think is better. I've used a fuji that was more streamlined and it was a little too small. I'd be nervous to use it n water. That was not a problem here. I could fit in the front pocket of my jeans, it'd be better in a cargo pocket though.

Toughness
- I've gone snorkeling twice a day for a week, had sand rubbed all over it, dropped it, submerged it over the side of a boat while going down the amazon to see how the pictures would turn out. It survived it all easily. Really is a great and tough camera.

Battery life
- Battery life is great. I wish I could say how many shots I got before I recharged it. I never use flash and the battery would last two days for me on average. Probably took about a 50-100 pictures a day and left the camera on to get a GPS lock and have it ready for a photo. The battery was never fully drained. I took it on a four day hike where I only had one battery the last day it almost died because I was taking a lot of video.

GPS and altimeter etc
- Maybe it's kind of a gimmick but I think it is really cool to see exactly where you were. In a worst case scenario the built in compass could probably help you out of a bind as well.

Lanyard
- The included lanyard is probably pretty standard but it was a good diameter and feel. I say this because I cinched it down to make sure it never got away from me when swimming and I never had any irritation and all the salt water never discolored it or wore it down.

Dedicated video button is convenient.

Cons:

Foggy lens
- I have a quite a few pictures that were ruined by fog in the lens. Nothing you can really do about it when it happens and I think it'd be really difficult to fix after the fact. It definitely ruined a couple picture I really wanted to turn out. I think this is a hazard of this type of camera, not really the TS4 itself.

GPS lock
-Perfectly clear skies and it had to of taken well over five minutes. My Garmin watch doesn't take that long on cloudy days. Sometimes it would get a fix really quick and scroll the name of the location and country right away. I think this is a con because when I pull a point and shoot out of my camera I want to take a picture and have it work right away with an accurate GPS tag.

Panorama Problems
-I was in these massive sand dunes in Peru and wanted to take a panorama of the view. I tried at least 10-15 times to take a panorama changing sweep directions and widths and views hoping the camera would capture one. Always got error messages along the lines of go faster or slower or keep levelt. Keep in mind I've been using this camera for awhile at this point and had taken many panoramas. I'm not sure if it was the lack of contrast from sand dune to sand dune but I never got the picture.

Underwater warning
-It shows up every time. I get it, I read the instructions, I acknowledged them. Now I'll still have to do it every time I turn on the camera.

I have used three other brands of tough cameras, Fuji, Pentax and Casio, this one is by far the best in picture quality and features/ease of use. I think you just have to accept the cons if you want this type of camera. I debated giving this four/five stars because five stars really should mean it is perfect. I ended up giving it five stars because this really is the best tough camera you can get right now.

title: Powerful Specs in a Gorgeous and Affordable Package.
text:
Pros
+ Bang for your buck--you get a fairly powerful machine with great features for not lot of money.
+ Gorgeous design--this thing is beautiful to look at on or off (all my friends want one).
+ Fast--performs well and boots up very quickly; the instant-on feature is awesome.
+ Portable--while large, this thing is very light. The power brick is compact, too.
+ Glass screen is not only very pretty, but makes the touch-interface a joy to use.

Nitpicks
- Let's all agree that Windows 8 is a tragedy.
- Mechanical HDD--while they're cheap and you're given a lot of hdd space, they're fragile and always precarious in notebooks.
- Low resolution screen--hey, they had to cut back somewhere to make this so affordable, but nothing I'm not used to (coming from a Asus UL50VT, which has the same resolution). Still, the colors are vibrant.
- Touchpad mouse is disobedient. It works, but sometimes it's not very responsive--especially the smart gestures.
- Subpar keyboard--it's functional, but there's flex and the travel distance is too shallow.
- Stretches the boundary on "ultrabook."
- Shameful battery life.

Let's be clear, for the amount you're paying, you're getting an absolutely gorgeous laptop that packs a punch for very little money--which is why I jumped on this as soon as I learned about it. I see this machine as the successor to the absolutely awesome UL50VT, which was a great machine for the price. I am glad to see that Asus has continued the tradition of offering powerful, feature-rich machines for the fiscally conscientious.

This machine is able to keep up with me as a multitasking "poweruser" (I'll watch movies and open about thirty tabs in Chrome while I write stuff in Word). The 6GB of ram really goes far in offering smooth performance. The i5 processor is fairly beefy, too, and is able to handle just about everything I threw at it without complaint. While this machine has no dedicated graphics card, do not let that fool you; I was genuinely shocked (and happy) that I could run Starcraft II: Heart of the Swarm well on "medium" settings.

The glass screen is both gorgeous and makes the touch screen a joy to use. The colors are surprisingly vibrant, and it's actually hard to tell sometimes that the screen is not 1080p, but for a 15.6" screen, the resolution is still quite low--though, I am used to this because my old UL50VT had the same issue. Also, the speakers are actually pretty decent thanks to the SonicMaster technology they employ.

The notebook is also very light, which makes it very easy to transport. However, its size does stretch the boundaries of what an "ultrabook" is. While easy to transport for its weight, its large size is a little unwieldy for what I'd consider a truly "go-and-compute-anywhere" experience. As well, the battery life is actually shockingly bad. I could squeeze 9 hours of battery life from the UL50VT, whereas this thing gets a little over 4 and a half hours at best, which feels like a step back. This also hinders portability in that you don't get terribly long to use it off the cord. At least, however, the power brick is small and highly portable--though I wish it were a tad longer. Ultimately, this machine is a lot more portable than the UL50VT that I had.

My one true disappointment is the keyboard, which as I mentioned above, has a far too shallow travel distance. Typing on this machine, therefore, is functional (my wpm has not been affected) but far from a pleasant experience--something about it just feels off.

Bottom line, this is just a great machine that can't be beat for the price. Other notebook computers with similar specs cost a lot more than this. Couple great performance with beautiful design, and you get an affordable ultrabook that's frankly hard to beat. Sure, there are drawbacks here and there, but for what you are paying, you won't be disappointed.

title: Vanguard PH-123v vs Manfrotto 701HD vs Manfrotto 502
text:
First, the Manfrotto and Vanguard plates are interchangeable. - All of my Manfrotto plates fit on the Vanguard (including the larger one you get on the 502). Conversely the Vanguard plate fits on my Manfrotto heads.

I got the Vanguard PH-123v because I needed a compact fluid head to replace my Manfrotto 701HD.
A little history:
Bought the Manfrotto 701HD. Didn't hate it, but didn't like it compared to higher end heads.
Added the Manfrotto 502 to the collection. Love it but it's huge (especially when compared to the Vanguard and the 701).
Bought the Vanguard, used it for a short time now.

Comparison -
Size:
Vanguard & 701HD - Excellent - They are pretty much the same size. They are both small and very portable.
Manfrotto 503 - Sucks - It is considerably bigger and I usually have to travel with it disconnected from the legs because it does not fit my tripod bags.
All of the handle the DSLRs and midsize video cameras I use. I imagine the 503 would have no problem with a larger video camera, but that's not what it's made for. Also the 503 is the best when I use portable cranes because it is so solid.

Build quality:
All of them are excellent where it counts. Vanguard handle feels a little cheap (but who cares).

Tilt (moving the head up and down):
Vanguard - Good - On the left side is the tension knob. It works as expected. On the right side there is an option to turn on and off the tension. If it's on the tilt speed is still what you set it at and the head will stay where you left it if you take you off the handle. If it is off then the head will TRY to retune to center. This option doesn't really work very well. Overall though the tilt is smooth and predictable. Wish there was more play in the tension. Also there is a little audible drag noise when you go up and down. Since I never use onboard audio it doesn't matter to me, but thought you should know. It might go away after a few hundred tilts.
701HD - Good - One adjustment of the left for tension. I find that I sometimes get a jerk in the shot if I unlock it during shooting.
503 - Excellent - Lock is on the right and the drag tension is on the left. You can set the speed of tilt to exactly what you want and lock it down in a sec.

Pan (moving the head left and right):
Vanguard - Ok - There is one knob that adjusts the pan. The easiest tension level is still pretty tight.
701HD - Terrible - There is one knob that adjusts the pan which essentially does nothing at all. The easiest tension level is very tight. (This is the reason I was replacing it to begin with.)
503 - Excellent - There is a locking knob in the front and a tension ring all the way around. This is by far the best pan I have ever used at this price point. The ring should be set before you make the shot but it's still usable if you're shooting a live event.

In all the Vanguard is better than the Manfrotto 701HD and smaller than the 502, so it's been upgraded to travel status.
-----
Update - Sorry, I just downgraded this from a 4 star to a 1 star, purely for durability.
Just officially broke the Vanguard PH-123v. It separated (in my tripod bag) at the fluid head! For the record, fluid from the fluid head is the stickiest substance in the world. Washed my hands three times and I'm still sticking to the keys as I write this.

If I could add pics (editing the original review) I would love to show you where this head broke, because it sucks!!
