title: Excellent headset
text:
I bought this as a replacement headset for a Sony that I have used for a couple of years. The Sony failed only because the microphone "pod" on the wire came apart and shorted the wires. This Samsung has the advantage of using any standard headphones so there is less to break. I haven't found anything I don't like about this unit after several months of using it. It was easy to pair with my phone (Samsung Galaxy Nexus running JellyBean) and with my Windows 7 laptop. The sound is good for phone calls and for listening to music; not stereophile good, but good for general listening. The range is about the same as the other two BT headsets I have used, not great, but I can roam anywhere in my apartment. This unit I like because I can plug my home stereo into the BT headset, then roam around the house with my phone or laptop playing music or a movie without any cords, and control the sound from wherever I am. Other reviewers have noted issues with the number and placement of buttons, and I see the issues, but they aren't really any big deal to me. I won't go back over them other than to say that I don't have a big problem with any of them.

In my usual usage of a standard headset, I grabbed an old badge lanyard from work and clipped the receiver unit on. Then I used the short headphones that came with it and attached them with little velcro strips (cut from a cord keeper) so that I can wear the lanyard and have the headset in front where the microphone needs to be. This keeps me from having to find a way to clip the headset to my clothes; not always easy to find a good spot. So, those headphones are pretty much dedicated to the lanyard but I can use the headset for other things with another set of headphones if I want. I feel these give me the best of several different ways of using the bluetooth stereo.

title: 92-inch is absolutely monstrous.
text:
[[VIDEOID:mo1K1GSLK896VDC]]I just bought the 92" from Aarons. It was right around the same price as it is on Amazon, just a few hundred more. They carried the TV into my house and set it up for me. Be warned: The TV is extremely heavy. It took 4 men to carry it off of their truck and into my house. It's easy to set up and the remote is really easy to figure out. Another warning: you need to sit at least ten feet away from the television so that the picture isn't blurry. It also needs to be on a stand because it doesn't have a wall mount. Another warning: it needs to lean against the wall because it's kind of tippy if it's not well supported. However, I left my dog alone with it in the bedroom for a few hours while I ran to the store. He loves to climb on things and jump up on them whenever possible. The TV was still standing just fine. If you go to the Aarons website and type in "TV Console", click on '72" TV Console'. That's the one that we got with our television. I'm not sure exactly how much it costs and I can't find it on Amazon. It hangs over a little bit on each side by about 6 inches. With this stand, it's approximately six feet tall. My wife is 5' 2" and when she stretches her arm up flatfoot, she barely reaches the top of it. Without the stand, it's about four and half feet tall. It's also pretty wide; about 8 feet. The television is a little over two feet wide, so when you're planning out the space of ten feet, make sure you take that into consideration. It is a lot of money for a television and I wouldn't recommend buying it if you need to move anytime soon. Before you choose to buy a television that large, make sure that there's plenty of room to put it.

ONE MORE THING I RECENTLY FOUND OUT!!! Make sure you view the Mitsubishi website. On there, they have a list of authorized dealers. Amazon is an authorized dealer, however some of their resellers are not. On the website it states:

"DON'T BE FOOLED! While Amazon is an authorized online retailer of Mitsubishi products, many resellers who sell on the Amazon marketplace are not. When purchasing, it is important to note where the product is being "shipped from and sold by," which is stated clearly in the header for each product on Amazon.com."

Why does this matter? If you're not using an authorized dealer, there isn't a warranty with it. It's better to pay a few hundred more to have your TV under warranty. To find out if the place you're looking at buying your TV is authorized to sell it to you, type "Mitsubishi TV" into Google. The website will be "mitsubishi-tv dot com" You'll want to make sure the little hyphen is there. Click on the website. On the left hand side, navigate to "Retail Locator". When you click on that, you can either type in your zip code or click the gray box that says "See Online Retailers" on the right hand side. If you scroll down on the page that comes up for online retailers, they also show common unauthorized dealers, including ones from Amazon and eBay.

UPDATE!!!
Glad we bought the TV at Aarons. About a month ago, our stand broke. We called them and they came and replaced it with a new one for free. Our first one was wood, with beautiful doors, but the weight of the TV caused it to bow and the doors no longer closed.
Today, 3/19/2013, the sound from our PS3 stopped working. I checked our Wii and the sound on that worked fine, but that uses AV cords. I checked the sound using a headset connected to the PS3 and that worked fine. I checked my XBox 360, and the sound on that, which is also HDMI, doesn't work either. Called someone and they'll be here on Thursday, 3/21/2013, to take a look.

I recorded the game using my Samsung Galaxy S3 cell phone. The colors look a lot better than they seem in the video. title: I should have bought this from the start!
text:
Does the Sonos Playbar even need another 5-star review? Probably not, but here I am writing one at 1 a.m. because I am so happy with it. When I was looking at options, I was shooting for the $500 price range, so I bought a Polk Magnifi soundbar. After having problems with two of those in a row, I coughed up the extra money and bought the Sonos. I hadn't seriously considered the Sonos before because 1) I thought I'd have to invest another $700 for the subwoofer to get halfway decent sound, 2) I wasn't blown away by the in-store demo, and 3) I thought it would be a hassle to set up. After my frustrating experience with Polk, I just bought the Sonos based on Amazon reviews. It will take me months before I'll be able to fork over $700 for the subwoofer, but I couldn't believe how amazing it sounds without it. Whatever they're doing on the in-store demo, they should rethink it (or maybe it's just the large space in the store) because it doesn't do it justice. The dialogue is the clearest I have heard (and there's an enhance mode and a night mode in the app). When I listened to iTunes (through my Apple TV) through it for the first time, I actually started to get emotional, I was so thrilled to finally end up with something that didn't feel like a compromise. It makes me want to buy more speakers for surround (first) and then a sub--not because it doesn't already sound amazing, but because I'm excited at the thought that it can get even better. I wish I had bought this in the first place, but I'm glad I ended up with it. What I would have wanted to know about this back when I was first looking is:
1. It has the most user-friendly (like Apple-style easy) set-up you can imagine for something so hi-tech
2. Movie dialogue sounds more clear and crisp on this than on anything I've heard (as good as any higher-priced Bose)
3. You can expand the system over time
4. You definitely do not need the subwoofer to great a full range of great sound (not that I won't get one when I can afford it)
5. The Sonos customer service is very responsive. Dish remotes have some strange quirks that I haven't yet worked out, but Sonos was great about getting me a case number to work through it (within 24 hours). I use my iPhone or iPad to control the soundbar, but it can learn your remote as well.
6. If you don't want to mount it on the wall, and if you don't have space for it in front of your tv (my shelf isn't deep enough), you can buy a shelf (I bought the TG Manufacturing Ltd CSB-3205-ECO Center Stage Soundbar Speaker TV Mount 30-90) that sits on the top of your tv and the Sonos can be safely perched on it.
7. There seem to be loads of music streaming options and the sound is actually good enough that you will use it for music, not just movies.

title: Best Bluetooth Ever
text:
I am writing this review while listening to the Samsung HS3000 Stereo Clip on Headsets and my MacBook Pro. The audio is impressive, even with the included short-cable ear buds. Anyone who has tried to use Bluetooth audio on a MacBook knows the frustrations and aggravations of this arrangement. For those who haven't MacBooks are notorious for Bluetooth performance issues.

This device uses the ATP-X codec to transfer audio at a higher quality, which is supported by Mac OS X Lion. The improvement over the older SBC of the standard Bluetooth profile is tremendous. I am using the headset while using an Apple Bluetooth Keyboard and a Bluetooth Magic Mouse. Audio is perfect with no skips, drops or artifacts. It works better and sounds better than my Motorola S9s, Plantronics 590s, or Plantronics 855s. I like those products quite well but it's not a fair comparison since the tech in the Samsung is newer.

Many reviews have commented on the size of the buttons and yes, while they are small, they are also positioned so if you are careful, it is not a problem to use the volume up/down or the play/stop/pause and track advance and rewind features. It's true they could have placed the buttons on the top surface perhaps but industrial design or electrical layout consideration won out.

On my recent flight, I streamed audio from this clip to Bose Quiet Comfort 2 headphones and it was perfect. Many folks who travel like noise cancelling headphones but until now it was a corded option only. Now you can use your favorite headphones or ear buds and still get the convenience of wireless streaming audio. The AVRCP features (play/stop/pause/ff/rew/vol) work perfectly with my iPhone, iPad and MacBook. I'm really not an Apple bigot, it works with my Windows 7 machine as well. Only the MacBook as the ATP-X codec but the audio sounds good and performs well on the other devices.

I would recommend this to anyone who wants Bluetooth and has despaired of getting decent wireless audio (especially from a MacBook).

Pros
* Use your favorite earbuds/headphones
* Battery life is as advertised
* Phenomenal audio with OS X Lion (APT-X compatible) Macs
* Remote functions work as advertised
* Phone functionality is not as good as best-in-class phone-only devices but adequate
* Inexpensive for functionality

Cons
* Small buttons take some getting use to - forget it if you have tater-tot fingers
* APT-X support is not universal on all devices so if you're a diehard, you'll still need to buy a stand-alone APT-X adapter. It still works with standard SBC in Bluetooth A2DP so you haven't lost anything.

title: What a bargain and there is no hum or any noise
text:
I had to come back this review and put a note in about hum: There is no design flaw. Everyone does not have hum. Mine is 100% as dead quiet as can be. Hum can be caused by several things and is easy to eliminate. 1- a bad tube will usually cause static, but hum is possible. 2- a ground loop with the rest of your system which is eliminated by using a cheater plug on 1 or many of your components. 3- Using poorly shielded, unshielded, or not using self shielding cables (Kimber are self shielding). 4- running your phono interconnects too close to other components or power cords. 5- not grounding the phono part of your system 6- using a MM cartridge (most are very prone to hum yet a high output MC cartridge which gets set up exactly like a MM cartridge, cost about the same and virtually never has a hum problem. You may have one or many of these problems. Look at this stuff before blaming any phono pre-amp.

I have used one of these as a phono preamp for about 3 years. Of course I put in better tubes. Now, first off, this takes a high end moving coil just fine and even takes a medium output moving coil fine if your per-amp has several gain settings, like the Rogue, or you don't need to play loudly, or if you just turn it's volume all the way up. So I am using a medium output Ortophon MC cartridge and really like the sound.

Recently I decided to replace my $3000 pre-amp with this as a regular pre-amp. It was an experiment. I changed to some better power chords and put in GE 5 Star 12AU7 tubes (inexpensive tube at about $25 each). I have to say, while the soundstage might have decreased just a little, the sound is beautifully sweet, musical, and clear. I like using my better stereo pre-amp more, but this is still quite respectable for non-analog components.

This unit is truly an exceptional bargain. There are better for $3000+, but I am not sure there are any for less then that.

By the way, yes the front turntable connectors mean you need longer wires if you want the front facing you, but it is a small price to pay and frankly doesn't bother me at all.

title: Comes loaded with crappy W8 and died after installing W7
text:
1. It's not a real SSD. The 24GB of SSD is used to cache data - the operating system is installed on the regular slow 5400rpm harddrive.
2. This laptop comes with Windows 8 and loaded with bloatware. Right off the bat, I was using almost 2.5 GB / 4 GB of RAM just to run the OS. After removing numerous bloatware programs, I was still using up 2/4 GB of RAM. Windows 8 is a resource hog and the interface is terrible.
3. I tried to install Windows 7 on the SSD...now my entire system is bricked. It can't boot into windows at all - it crashes into a blue screen when I try to boot normally or try a system repair with the windows disc. Then it briefly had sporadic problems with constantly restarting into bios (it couldn't even get past the bios), which I eventually solved by booting into a saved version of BIOS. But now my laptop is still bricked and can't launch the OS and can't even install a new OS. Piece of crap!
4. When it was working, the fan started spinning up very fast for no reason (HW monitor said CPU temps were a cool 45'C), and the fans are quite loud.

***Update, I just found out why this computer is a piece of crap...it's because of Windows 8. Apparently all windows 8 laptops are required by Microsoft to have BIOS that locks the computer into ONLY being able to use windows 8. If you try to install windows 7 or another OS, the BIOS will basically kill your computer and prevent it from working properly. Windows 8 is a piece of junk and the new restrictive features means I will be staying far far away from any laptop with W8.

***Update #2, apparently there is a way to install non-W8 OS on a W8 hardwared computer...but it involves jumping through a series of hoops. You need to turn off UEFI and secure boot to install Windows 7, and even then it doesn't allow you to duel boot into W8 (making the W8 OEM you just bought with the computer worthless). Furthermore, sometimes even this doesn't work, and the BIOS is hardware locked to only use Windows 8, thus forcing you to download a program to force-flash an older BIOS onto the motherboard. All this headache just to use a non-craptastic OS.

title: Good
text:
I'd start off by saying this is a great price for studio lighting and the best deal I've found. I'm extremely happy with these for the price.

THINGS TO KNOW:

These come with all the necessary parts to build your two soft boxes, on two light stands with the 4 bulbs in each light set up. The only output adjustments are two light switches on the back of each unit allowing you to turn on and off 2 of the 4 bulbs. These bulbs are the smaller ones measuring about 4 and 1/2 inches in length and 2 inches thick. There is an adjustment knob on the back of each unit tilted "fuse" but I can't figure out if that has any function at all and there are no instructions on it. They are powered by standard wall sockets with a standard cord running from each unit. The build quality on all of these is moderate. It's not cheap but it's not professional either.

The locks for size adjustment on the light stands aren't standard clip locks but twist locks. These light set ups are made for a studio set up and not for taking on the road. They are a hassle and a half to set up and it takes very long to break them down.

Don't be deceived by the carrying bag you see in the picture. It's extremely cheap and doesn't have any compartments for storing any of the light or soft box parts. There are zero dividers inside, it literally is just a cheap black bag. You basically have to keep all the packing material and boxes that they come in and re-pack the bulbs and parts every time you put it away.

For the price and for my usage I can't complain at all. I'm very happy with the light output and the price. It hasn't' given me any problems yet and I don't for see it ever giving me problems.

On another note, for those curious, this 3.0 flash is considerably larger and more boxy than the equivalent Transcent 2.0 version. title: Great Basic Composite A-V Cable
text: Needed this for a revised home A-V set-up that included a VCR (remember those?). The original cable that came with the unit was only 3 feet long, and I needed one to reach a new wall-mounted TV. The item is perfect for this application, at an excellent price point: it is cheaper than anything at the shack, depot, and some other online A-V specialty dealers. This is a perfectly acceptable cable if you are ever going to require a simple composite video and L+R audio connection again. The cable seems well made; the video wire (yellow tip) is thicker than the red and white audio wires.  My only quibble is the proximity to the end of the cable of the split (where the 3 wires branch off), ~6". It's fine on the back of a VCR where the jacks are right next to each other; not so good on the back of the TV where the jacks are farther apart. Not a major problem though.

title: Looks like a joke, works like a magician
text:
A flat, laminated piece of (cardboard?) does not inspire confidence when it comes to tuning in a TV transmission. Shockingly, the leaf delivers on its dubious promise, and then some. This is my second antenna/amp setup of this type, the first being a [[ASIN:B0063705PE Winegard Company FL-5000 FlatWave HDTV Indoor Digital Flat Antenna - Made in USA]], that upon installation in our bedroom immediately brought in 3 Kentucky PBS stations not previously tune-able with our old antenna, on top of the 3 stations more locally broadcast. When we paired the Winegard with the [[ASIN:B00AW48DS0 Mohu Jolt HDTV Antenna Amplifier]], we were able to tune 3 more stations from the Ion Network that previously had been available only intermittently, and only when the master bedroom door was open, and when the antenna was extended and tilted "just so".

That Winegard would have been a Mohu, only at that time, the (now superseded) generation of Mohu Leaf featured a fairly short coax cable, that users reported having to augment with a longer extension cable, often, in order to optimally position the antenna. I don't know if this newer unit with its Clean Peak filter technology is all that superior to the old Phemt amplifier on the [[ASIN:B006GQIIEM Leaf Plus Amplified Indoor HDTV Antenna]], but it works every bit as well in our kitchen as the Winegard/Jolt combo does in our bedroom, and maybe even edges the Winegard out by a bit. I say "maybe" because this antenna is positioned very close to a Northern facing window, where it would have taken a good 20 feet of coax to achieve the same in the room with the Winegard. What was gained by the window-close positioning was an (inconsistent) lock on 3 stations, each better than 60 miles away from our Lexington location, in Cincinnati and Louisville. However, the bedroom unit benefits from being oriented to more reliably pick up signals coming from a Southern/southeastern direction, and that's the drawback of any antenna of this style - limited directional reception. You start by knowing where your transmission towers are, and work from there.

Another nice thing about the Leaf Ultimate is that the generous (16') coax cable included can be unscrewed from the flat antenna. This wasn't possible with the Winegard when we bought it, and from the photos on the product page for the LeafPlus, it would appear that this modification is fairly new. (Please feel free to comment if I am wrong, here.)

I don't think you can go wrong with either brand, and I welcome the improvements that are, apparently, being spurred by competition between Winegard and Mohu.

Worked great "out of the box" and setup is easy peasy. I'll miss our old Terk [[ASIN:B0007MXZB2 Terk HDTVa Indoor Amplified High-Definition Antenna for Off-Air HDTV Reception]], if only for it's `30s movie ray gun looks (this is the second time it's been replaced by a wall hugging antenna), but we are well on our way now to being a rabbit-ears free home!

title: Last remaining issues of the 7990 series are diminishing
text:
I used one of these in a burn-in rig for about 2 weeks. The card was actually $1000 at the time, but since the price is now ~650, it deserves those 2 stars back.

Pros: Decently cool for a dual-GPU card. You might need an AC unit on the same floor just to be safe though.
OpenCL performance is outstanding.
Gaming performance for the price is great, but see "stutter" in cons.
Overall value is awesome, card isn't gargantuanly huge.

Cons: Hotter than a single GPU card.
Uses more power than a single GPU card.
Extra memory often goes unused.
Old games sometimes can't fully utilize the second GPU (DirectX 9 or older)
Stutter is sufficiently noticeable in SOME games. Other game handle it fine and don't show any at all. I guess it's how the developers built the games. Anyways, AMD is fixing stuttering with the upcoming catalyst drivers. I installed the beta of it and saw a noticeable improvement in even the worst of the stuttering games.

Buy this if: You were about to buy a 7970 and have ~$100 to spare.
You want the best card for $600
You want to save $400 over a Titan

Don't buy this if: You play older games that could stutter
You are waiting for the next generation of cards. This is GCN 1.0 from early 2012. September or October will deliver a new batch.
Your power supply is below the bare minimum of 800W or so.

The one problem with this cover that prevents a five-star rating from me is that when holding the Kindle while reading, the cover has sharp edges that dig into my fingers. If that doesn't happen, though, then I will just have to use the cover as a prop, and remove it completely for holding the Kindle with my hands while reading.

title: This one seems like a keeper
text:
I've tried the Eye-Fi and the Transcend Wifi Cards and each have had issues for me.

The Eye-Fi card is just too inflexible for me in what you can and can't do with the files on it. Once you transfer a file somewhere once, you can't send it anywhere else from the card. Come on Eye-Fi.

The Transcend was nice but it's wireless range in my SL1 was abysmal and was about 5 feet. To transfer something from the camera to my PC, I had to put the camera right next to the router, otherwise it would fail to transfer anything. Plus the browser interface was extremely clunky.

The EZ-Share, on the otherhand has nice wireless range, even in my SL1 and has an ok Android app(could use some refinement and additional options) that does the job transfering things from my camera to the phone, or just viewing the pictures on the card.

The one shortcoming is it does NOT integrate with my home network. It will only act as a wireless access point that you can connect to. However, EZ Share offers a PC application that you can run on you Laptop or Home PC(if it has wireless). You can then have your Laptop or PC connect to the card and the PC application(or you can also use your browser) will see the card and you can transfer the photos over using the PC app. You can also set the card to auto transfer, when the app sees the card.

I'd like to see additonal options on the PC app too, something that auto creates a new directory, based on the date, like the Eye-Fi software does.

It also has a switch on the card to turn the wireless on and off, which is nice if you know you aren't going to use the wireless. HOWEVER, with that switch being so small, I can see it being fragile. I can see the switch wearing out if you use it too much. So I am going to see how the card and my battery does if I just leave it on all the time.

I wish Amazon would add a prime option for the 32GB version of this card.

Pros,
Good wireless Range
Descent Android App
Bonus PC application as well
With the PC app, you can connect to the card and transfer things to your PC(can also use browser , but it isn't as flexible)

Cons
Cannot connect to a router, only works as access point
Android App can use some refinement
On/Off switch seems like it can wear out easy

title: Kindle Fire HD 8.9" Leather Case: Stylish, sturdy and very thin
text:
Right up front, I like this case, and suspect that others will feel the same way once they get it into their hands. That was not my initial impression when I received it here, but after a few weeks of using it, found it to exceed my somewhat picky expectations.

The [[ASIN:B00825BZUY Amazon Kindle Fire HD 8.9" Standing Leather Case]] in Onyx Black is an attractive case, and outer cover is genuine leather, not the faux leather with the chemical smell that we've encountered with some of these. It's thin enough to make one wonder how sturdy it could be, yet someone took the time to engineer this one the right way, as the form-fitted interior shell holds a Kindle Fire HD 8.9" device perfectly; just snap it in and you're good to go.

But first here are the subjective likes and dislikes on this case, then the observations as an owner.

Likes:

+ The case is thin; slips into a briefcase or messenger bag easily
+ Protective shell; all sides and corners are protected
+ Functional; has three different viewing angles.
+ Automatic sleep &wake lid; turns device on/off, even when rotated 180 degrees
+ Snap-in mounting system; holds the Kindle Fire HD 8.9" securely
+ Ports: easy access to charging and HDMI ports while inside case, even closed
+ Integrated magnetic closure; keeps the Kindle Fire closed when you desire
+ Cover offers good protection for the screen; easy to clean
+ Durable leather case; lined with soft microfiber interior

Dislikes:

- A hand strap would help for reading use when commuting on public transportation

Observations:

Once installed, the integrated interior plastic shell enclosure on this case not only holds the Kindle Fire HD 8.9" tablets securely without the flimsy little elastic straps found in some cases, it allows the device to snaps into place and doesn't mar the surface, as I've found in previous models from other companies. The power switch, the HDMI and USB Micro-B charging port and headphone jack are not obstructed, as we find with some other cases that are not certified as "Made for Kindle" accessories.

But how does it compare with the [[ASIN:B009X01C64 Marware Revolve Portrait and Landscape Standing Case for Kindle Fire HD 8.9"]], which I have been using until I received this one?

The easiest way to explain this is that they are different cases and have different uses and functions, yet each is a high-quality product. Both will only fit the Kindle Fire HD 8.9" series, so if you have a different Kindle model, these are not for you. The Marware Revolve lives up to its name by offering 180° rotation for full port access while inside case, but it's counterpoint is that it's thick. The Amazon Standing Leather Case doesn't revolve, but it's very thin, and excellent for travel and packing the Kindle Fire HD 8.9" into places where space may be a premium.

That being said, these are both high quality cases, and where I may be inclined to use the Marware case when not in transit for a week or two, the Amazon product is a first-class case for those whose lifestyle is mobile, and where space may be at a premium.

Summary:

The [[ASIN:B00825BZUY Amazon Kindle Fire HD 8.9" Standing Leather Case]] is conspicuous in in terms of sturdiness, quality of construction, simplicity, pure functionality and the fact that it's so thin. The mounting system is quite secure, which offers protection to the device from all sides and corners. Stylish, sturdy and very thin, this one is highly recommended to users of the Kindle Fire HD 8.9" series.

2/21/2013

title: Top Quality Hardware, Excellent Customer Service, but not compatible with some PC motherboards
text:
When I saw this USB 3.0 adapter card on Amazon I was excited. It looked like a solidly constructed card at a reasonable price. The projected shipping date was approx. one week, but it was delivered it within 36 hours! It came very well packaged and with very clear step-by-step installation instruction and the USB 3.0 driver software on a CD. The installation of the card was very easy, and it fit perfectly into the available PCI express slot of my PC.

At the end, as per the included instructions, I installed the driver software, and that's where the problems started. My PC is a relatively new HP desktop with Windows 7 Professional and its tech specs clearly indicated that it was designed and constructed to receive USB 3.0 cards. There was no indication anywhere that I was limited to a now discontinued and hard to obtain specific HP USB 3.0 card (at more than twice the price of the Satechi card) to accomplish this task. At this point, I'm clearly more disappointed in HP than I am in Satechi or Amazon, although Satechi's software might have a small role in the problem too.

One way or another, it was a huge waste of time with no positive outcome for anybody but Satechi was "exemplary" in providing me with a top-quality hardware at a very reasonable price, shipping it very fast, and expediting the item's return smoothly and very professionally when it was necessary to do so.

I would not hesitate to purchase from Satechi or Amazon again.

The unit works well, but does have a little wind noise issue outdoor that is easily solved with a foam wind screen over the mics. I bought a shoe mount adapter and place the unit on top of one of the cameras.

This unit is about 1 second long per hour when trying to sync it to the video cameras.. The issue is easily resolved by syncing at the beginning and end of each hour-long segment and shrinking the audio track to match the video track sync points.

You'll also want to adjust the input level as to not overdrive the recorder. I use MP3 256, and it works great!

I've also used the unit when recording lectures and stage shows where wired or wireless mics were not usable.Again, create a sync point at the beginning and end of each clip...even if just a single hand-clap.

If I lost this unit somehow, I'd buy another!

title: It grows on you
text:
I bought this laptop to replace a five-year old Gateway. I was looking for a larger display and the blu-ray drive was appealing, as was the 8GB of RAM and I7 processor. However, this machine has a serious flaw that HP has been unable to correct. The cursor jumps around randomly when you are typing. For instance, it's happened two dozen times already as I type this review. It will jump several lines up or down or just go back several words. It will also just randomly highlight lines of text, which causes them to vanish as soon as you type another letter. Despite hours with HP tech support, they have been unable to correct the problem. An online search reveals that this is a problem endemic to HP laptops. The only way I can correct it is to disable the track pad and use a mouse. Yet I could never use a mouse when traveing, for instance, because this laptop takes up all the space on an airline tray table. There's no room to use a mouse. I'm returning this and getting a Mac Book. I'd give it zero stars, if I could (it took me five tries just to type this last sentence). One more thing, despite the advertised 10 1/2 hour battery life, the best I've gotten is five hours and that's just word processing (or trying to use Word, I should say). A major fail for HP.

Status update:
After more time with HP Tech support, the problem has still not been resolved. We've removed and reinstalled the track pad drivers and reduced the sensitivity of the pointer and palm detector. However, as long as I make absolutely ZERO contact with the case, I can type successfully. If my palms rest anywhere within ten inches of the track pad, the pointer starts jumping around. I'll give HP tech support good marks, because they're always available and they've been trying their best to solve the problem. It's also nice to speak with someone who speaks English as a native language. The display is terrific and blu-rays look great, so in effect I've paid a thousand dollars for a blu-ray player. I'm adding a star because of the responsive tech support and all the other features that work well, everything but the hypersensitive track pad. I'm still leaning toward returning it for a refund but I'm going to give HP a bit longer to try to solve the problem. Stay tuned.

March 28 Update:

On the verge of returning this machine, I decided to give it one last lengthy test. I took it on a two-week road trip, which covered over 6000 miles,and included plane travel and two days on the Empire Builder from Chicago to Seattle. I truly wrung out this machine. I've pretty much solved the jumping cursor problem by never resting my hands on the case. It's tiresome and annoying, which is why the max I can rate this is four stars. Actually, I can rest my left palm on the computer with no problem. It's only the right side of the case that seems to cause the problem. I've tried netbooks and an IPad to get my work done when I travel. The keyboards on netbooks are just too small and the IPad . . . well, it's a fun gadget for some things and a great picture viewer, but for the heavy duty word processing, spread sheets, data bases, and the like that I need, it falls far short. And I like my Kindle far better for a book reader. But I digress. During my trip I was working on research projects, designs, contracts and proposals. I was also watching blu ray movies, editing photos and videos, and making data discs backups. This machine did everything with flying colors (mostly). I've managed to get the battery life up to eight and a half hours, which included watching two movies, and four hours of heavy duty power point work. I love the power of this processor and the ample RAM. Graphics are terrific. I'm carrying it around in a TSA-friendly (an oxymoron, if there ever was one) Mobile Edge 17.3 back pack. Yep, this laptop is big and heavy, but the Mobile Edge fits nicely on my roll-aboard,so that's pretty much a non-issue. It took me a long time to like this product but I'm satisfied now. The only thing that keeps me from giving it five stars is the wonky track pad. At least I've raised my rating from the original one-star I gave it.

title: Purchased 3 so Far, Great as a Larger Netbook
text:
I think the big thing people have to realize about netbooks is that they will never be speed or power demons. They are not a replacement for a desktop or a full size laptop. I have several customers that had 10" Asus or Dell netbooks and they served them well, but it was time to upgrade. I think the difference I like with this model is an addition to an 11.6" screen (about 20% bigger than a 10" screen), it also has a Pentium dual core processor and 4GB of RAM, so you gain some of that horsepower you lose with the standard Atom processor in most netbooks.

PROS:

* Larger screen than older traditional netbooks gives you a higher resolution view and task windows are no longer cutoff on the top or bottom
* Pentium vs. Atom processor makes a huge difference. I'll give up some battery for the extra processing power.
* 4GB of RAM. Most netbooks came with 1 or 2GB of RAM at most and aren't upgradeable. 4GB is about a minimum I spec for computer anymore, so this is a nice bonus for a netbook.
* Weighs only about 3 pounds and is very thin. It may be a bit bigger than my old 10" netbook, but not that much and it is much thinner and lighter. I'll take that trade as well.
* Windows 7 64-bit - Can take full advantage of all 4GB
* 500GB hard drive - nice to have tons of storage. I doubt many will use that much drive space unless you were downloading movies to take on the road. Thinking about upgrading mine to an SSD drive to see if that helps with battery and speed, but it may not be justified when I have less than $400 in these. Unless I really needed that extra bit of battery life or that marginal amount of speed, it's probably not worth the time and cost to upgrade. I would have spent $1000 and gotten a Ultrabook, which is in a different class of laptop.
* Come with Office 2010 Starter. Enough for most people on the road or as a secondary computer. So, the price includes a basic Office suite and it is your choice to upgrade or not.

CONS:

* Yes, battery is not as good as my old netbook, which could run several days using it off and on and still have several hours of battery left. I might get 4-5 hours on a charge using it continously, but I still get a full day or two out of it using it off and on as I visit customers. I think if I can get through a normal full day and still have a charge left, then it doesn't really matter. I tend to charge both of them each night anyway. So, not really a con to me, but just throwing it out there of you are a hard core user and need a full days use. I think there is some offset with the additional speead I gain over my old one, so it also doesn't have to run as long to accomplish the same tasks.

I think the 11.6" screen is a great improvement to netbooks. It gives me more real estate to work with and is still small enough to throw in a netbook sleeve and carry into an office with my portfolio. I like the Pentium processor over the Atom and having a full 4GB of RAM. The nice thing about netbooks is you have a choice. I purchased the same Acer with an Atom processor for another customer so they can have something when they go out of town on the weekends and he is just as happy. Not a power user, doesn't care, but liked to have the extra battery so he doesn't have to carry his charger with him. If you don't have a need to spend $600+ on a decent full size laptop, then I think this is the ticket. Small, fast, enough battery to get you through the day and you can't beat the price.

title: Better than the Jambox
text:
Picked this up yesterday and was able to pair it up very easily via bluetooth. I was also able to switch between the Jambox and the flip very easily with no real delay. The look and feel of the JBL flips are fantastic. It has a grill mesh that makes the product feel sturdy and not cheap at all. The flip comes in white and black. But I don't think the whites are available yet.

Features:
Auxiliary input on the back with a power adapter port. There's a volume rocker on the side with the power button and an answer/end button. There's no USB port like the Jambox. So the only way for you to power the device is if you plug it into the wall outlet. It takes about 3 hours to fully charge the unit. You will get about 5 hours of music on this unit depending on how loud you have the volume set to. I love the fact that the speakers project upward when laid flat. Unlike the Jambox, where the speakers are projected on a flat plane. If you are listening to the Jambox while seated, it will not project the sound directly at you and you lose some of the luster. I had to actually hold the Jambox about a foot from me to really take advantage of the sound. Whereas the JBL seats tilted, the sound projects alot better and you get the full sound of the song being played. The JBL can also be stood up as it has rubber grips on the end so that it won't move when music is playing.

Sound:
The highs are clear and crisp. The mids can sound like it's coming out of a can sometimes. But after a while, your ears will adjust and it will not be a problem. The bass is not as deep as what I would like, but it's decent enough where it isn't the star. The one thing that I was really impressed about was the volume capacity. It can go twice as high as the Jambox. Even at it's peak volume, you will hear little to no distortion. This was very surprising as the Jambox had a hard time handling music at high volumes. You can hear the distortion from the highs and lows. One thing I failed to mention is that the Jambox will start to move when playing music with bass in it. It actually fell off the shelf at one point.

Cons:
As mentioned above, there's no USB port to charge or update the unit like the Jambox. I haven't had it long enough to try out the built in speaker phone. No battery indicator whether it be on the iPhone or on the device. I guess when the power button turns red means it's running low.

title: Does the job.
text:
I bought this camera because I am planning to take a backpacking trip to New Zealand in a couple of months, and wanted something that could take a bit of a beating while I'm out there. When I am kayaking, I want to be able to take a camera out with me. I am also about to go parasailing, so I got the camera now so that I could test it out on the water.

I had originally planned on taking a very expensive DSLR to NZ, but was convinced otherwise because it is extremely heavy for a backpacker, and I would also probably eventually end up breaking it. Instead of breaking a very expensive camera, I bought this camera, for $100, at this link:
http://www.amazon.com/Coleman-Waterproof-Digital-Floating-Accessory/dp/B004WSLZ5U/ref=sr_1_5?ie=UTF8&qid=1342658199&sr=8-5&keywords=coleman+digital+camera
Even though I bought the camera in a kit instead of from this page, I thought I should write the review here because the camera seems to be taking quite a beating from reviews of people who probably didn't understand the camera.
First of all, this camera is NOT a camera for people who are serious photographers looking for high quality shots. You don't buy a camera for $100 and expect it to take professional photos. It's pretty simple. If you are looking for something like that, you might want to up your budget for a camera by about $1,000.00. I knew that when I bought it. That said, there are a few things you need to expect if you buy this. First of all, there IS a delay between the time you press the button for a photo, and the time it takes the photo. This isn't a particularly big issue for me. Also, the image quality isn't the best, but it does the job I wanted it to do. Another note is that photo quality is generally better outdoors than indoors. However, I was able to get decent shots.

When I turned on the camera, I was surprised to realize that it actually has a menu that lets you change the ISO, exposure,IMAGE QUALITY, white balance, and it also has several types of flash that you can use, which greatly change the quality of the photo. Many people have complained about poor photo quality, but if they would just take the time to change some settings, they would get a much better photo.

I saw one complaint on the reviews about how hard it was to shut the door to the battery pack. It isn't difficult. If you try to just shut the door, it will not do it easily. However, there is a lever on the door- all you have to do is hold it back, and the door shuts easily. It might be a little tricky the first time to break it in, but I didn't have any issues. I might also add, I am a girl who is not very strong.Personally, I would rather have a sturdy door than one that opens easily and exposes the battery and memory card to water.

Another complaint was that the microphone flooded. Here's a trick- use the plug. Problem solved.

I used this camera in water and it was fine. If you are expecting excellent photos in the water, DON'T USE IT IN MURKY WATER. If you get icky photos because of it, it's not the camera's fault. It's your own dang fault because you took a photo of murky water. If you want crystal clear photos, get a water purifier.

One reviewer commented that you couldn't get sound unless you plugged in a microphone. Not true. YOU DO NOT NEED TO PLUG IN A MICROPHONE. If you take the plug off the microphone, you WILL record sound. You will not hear it though until you load the video onto your computer. Why? Because its STUPID to put a speaker on a camera that is supposed to go underwater.

One other complaint from a reviewer was this: "The "extra" battery that came with the kit doesn't fit the camera properly. It is a generic battery that pops out every time you try to charge the thing." -Jessica
How about turning the battery, Jessica? If you put the battery in the wrong way, it WILL pop out. It's to let you know that the battery is in wrong. I put it in wrong at first, but then I turned it around and guess what? It stayed in. EPIPHANY.

All in all, this camera does what I want it to. I didn't expect professional photographs- it's a cheap camera. I will certainly miss my DSLR while I am in NZ, but it wouldn't stand a chance. This Coleman camera IS rugged. I also liked the blue color that I got. It was pretty. Except for the one, maybe two, reviews I saw about the camera having a defect, most of the reviews I saw were simple things that people could have figured out, had they simply taken the time to learn about the camera.

title: Bluetooth isn't as loud as FM
text:
First of all, I want to clarify which model of this device I am actually reviewing. This is a review for the iHome Bluetooth Wireless Rechargable Boombox with FM Radio, model iBT4GC. As far as I can tell, this model differs from models iBT4GE and iBT4UC in only one way, and this is a direct quote from Amazon's own product description: "The iBT4 also has FM radio a line-in jack as well as a line-out jack fo Model Number: iBT4GC". (Sorry about the mildly strange wording there. I simply copied and pasted the text from Amazon's product description onto this review.)
Anyway, let's get on with the product review... Purchased one of these from a local retailer about a week ago. When using the FM radio feature, the sound quality was amazing and the max volume was very loud and almost distortion-free. However, when I paired it up via Bluetooth to a Samsung Galaxy Tab 2 10" tablet (which was very easy and quick to do, by the way), the max volume from the Bluetooth boombox was very low, and the sound quality dropped a lot. It sounded very muffled. Got the same result when I paired it up with a third-generation iPod Touch.
Also tried plugging the Galaxy Tab 2 and the iPod Touch up to the boombox using the boombox's included aux-in patch cord. Again, the max volume was very low, and the sound quality dropped precipitously compared to the sound of the FM radio.
Ended up returning the iBT4GC boombox to the local retailer for a refund the next day...

It also came with a nice external flash accessory but the on-board flash was just fine for most chores. We wished it had just a wee bit more wide-angle (maybe down to 15-16mm instead of the 17mm now).

Cons were that it could not stand up on a table with the zoom lens, it really is a two-handed camera, and the wink-shot didn't work at all (lol). Also, not many lens using the new smaller Samsung lens design - I see this being a major hurdle for Mini users. Lenses make the systems popular!

I see this cam as a really cute point-and-shoot with MUCH better image quality in a tiny thin package. For $500, I can't see a lot of competition, but if you spend this much perhaps one would consider systems such as the QM1 ($600 and even smaller than the Mini, if that is possible), the A6000 ($700 for a killer E-mount system), and now the amazing Sony RX1000 III ($800). For the extra $300, the RX100 also has a "we-fie" flip up screen mode, a real (!) EVF, 1.8-2.8 lens, and loads of features. All being said, I did enjoy my time with the Nx Mini.

title: Buy the Fuji 3D W3 instead!
text: As just a camera, this can't compare favorably in any way with most hundred-dollar point and shoots.  It's okay, but just barely.  But as a 3D camera it has two serious shortcomings: 1.Whereas when in 2D mode it's a reasonably adjustable camera: it has various modes, and manual overrides, which allow a reasonable amount of control. But when in 3D mode, it becomes a totally auto camera with no manual adjustments possible. 2. Much more significant: the lenses are only one and a quarter inches apart.  Average adult human eyes are two and a half inches apart, which is where stereo cameras have traditionally placed the lenses. The result of this in the pictures taken by this camera is Stereo Lite: the 3D effect is very diminished.  It's hard to imagine why anyone would make a 3D camera with the lenses so close together.  Get the Fuji 3D W3 - it has some shortcomings too, but it's MUCH better than this Panasonic, and is also currently being remaindered at very low prices - Amazon has it for under $190, and Newegg is (at this moment anyway) selling refurbished ones for $125. title: Great buy
text:
I travel a fair amount and have been researching options for mobile computing. Netbooks and ultraportables are still on my list. But before that, I wanted to try out the iPad + keyboard option since I always have my iPad with me anyway. I've been shopping for a keyboard for my iPad 2 for quite some time. The folio models seemed too bulky when closed and were somewhat flimsy when open (and not sitting directly on a tabletop/desk). I have an Apple keyboard that I use at home but it's not convenient for travel. The Logitech Ultrathin Keyboard Cover seemed like a great option. I had a chance to test drive it this week while attending a conference.

Pros:
-The magnet that holds the iPad in landscape mode for typing is sufficiently strong. You can pick up the keyboard/iPad combo comfortably without worrying it is going to fall. Useful when moving from table to table, etc.
-Since the keyboard is rigid, you can easily type with it sitting on your lap. Because of the small form factor, you have to keep your legs pretty close together but it's manageable.
-Keys are smaller but well spaced and have good travel and tactile feedback. Keys are a bit loud but not so much that it's obnoxious. I was able to type nearly as fast as I can on a full size keyboard.
-Arrow keys, Fn keys (particularly the ones for manipulating text like cut/copy/paste) and the "Home" key are very helpful when typing on the iPad.
-Looks sharp. When closed, it might easily be mistaken for a Macbook Air.
-When not typing, it makes a great stand to read, watch videos, etc. (It can also support the iPad in portrait orientation, but without any magnet holding it in place.)
-Easy to install/remove. Because of the magnet, it's very easy to remove when you just want the iPad without a keyboard (e.g. to hold in your hand when reading). No straps or velcro like some of the folio models.

Cons:
-It's marginally useful as a cover. The spine magnet is not as strong as it should be. It attaches like a smartcover but should have a stronger magnet because the keyboard carries more weight than just a cover. When pulling it out of my bag, oftentimes the keyboard had separated from the iPad. With the "cover" askew inside my bag, the iPad screen is vulnerable to scratching. Probably best to keep the entire contraption in a protective sleeve.
-The delete key (which actually functions as a backspace key) is small. Found myself often hitting the nearby "=" key often. Just takes some getting used to.
-The keyboard doesn't fold over out of the way like a smartcover does. If you want to pick up and hold the iPad, you must remove the keyboard entirely.
-Autocorrect doesn't work on the iPad when using a bluetooth keyboard. So you have to remember to capitalize words, type periods, etc. Not really Logitech's fault however.
-The on/off switch and bluetooth button are right next to each other. Makes it harder to manipulate the on/off switch with confidence without looking at it.

Bluetooth sync was easy as expected. I used the keyboard to type notes during conference workshops on tabletops or on my lap. I also used it in the hotel room, in the lobby, etc. on various surfaces for email and web surfing. Worked equally well everywhere I tried it. It's a super form factor for typing on an airplane tray table (or your lap) but technically... you're not allowed to use bluetooth devices on airplanes.

Bottomline:
The pros far outweigh the cons. Solid purchase. So far I am very happy with the keyboard and it performs well. I would recommend it.

title: Represent Yourself

2.) Make sure you rub your decal across BEFORE you peel it off for sticking. This will help make sure that your entire decal comes off when you do peel it.
3.) Peel decal off slowly, making sure every piece (yes, all pieces are separate) comes off the backing with the clear adhesive tape.
4.) Square up decal and carefully place on surface. YOU GET ONE CHANCE! DON'T MESS THIS UP! :)
5.) Rub across the surface of the decal, making sure to give each individual piece attention.
6.) Peel off clear adhesive slowly to make sure the decal is completely left behind.

7.) Admire your achievement and celebrate with a showing of your favorite Ghibli film AND EAT ICE CREAM!

title: Let's do a little math...
text:
I find it extremely hilarious that people are claiming to be computer literate, but complaining that the hard drive only shows 293 gigabytes (GB) after installed. So let's have a lesson. Hard drive manufacturers advertise 1 GB as 1,000,000,000 bytes. All manufacturers do this, and this is correct. Computer operating systems (OS), including the OS running on the Xbox 360, see a GB in terms of binary (2^30 bytes, or 1,073,741,824 bytes). This is also correct.

1,000,000,000 bytes = 1 GB reported by the manufacturer
1,073,741,824 bytes = 1 GB formatted by the OS

The OS sees 320,000,000,000 bytes on the hard drive (the manufacturer didn't lie), and reports it in terms of binary GB. The math is as follows: (320,000,000,000 bytes)/(1,073,741,824 bytes PER OS formatted GB). The result is approximately 298 OS formatted GB. Microsoft has firmware, OS, games, and other info on the hard drive built in, which takes up about 5 GB. This is why the Xbox reports a new drive as 293 GB.

The drive works, and works well. It is a snap to install, and there are no initialization steps to take. It just works. Don't rate something low because you're not intelligent enough to know how operating systems report GB.

title: Perfect size Camera Bag
text:
What I wanted in a camera bag: (1) good protection; (2) not overly large or bulky; and (3) not blah black. The Domke Small Shoulder and Belt Bag exceeded these expectations. As a note, I have a Canon PowerShot SX40 HS.

1) Protection: the bag is nicely padded around the exterior. The bottom of the bag is sturdy, and won't bend, and therefore, won't allow anything to damage your camera. There are 2 removable dividers to keep your camera separated and secure from any accessories. The bag is made of tough canvas and is water-resistant. The shoulder strap has double non-grip strips to keep it securely on your shoulder. And the ring and clip attaching the shoulder strap to the bag seem nearly unbreakable. The front flap is secured by 2" tall velcro - in other words, it isn't opening by itself. Excellent protection.

2) My camera is on the smaller side (better than a point & shoot, but not a professional camera). It doesn't have a removable lens, so I didn't need an overly large bag. This bag was perfect. There is ample room for the camera, the battery wall charger and the cables in the main compartment. I can easily fit the camera in multiple ways. Plus there are two front pockets for easy access to additional memory cards. I actually have room to add a small wallet.

3) It's not only black. Every other bag I looked at only came in black. What is it about black and camera bags? Black just screams "this is a camera bag." Not exactly low profile. The color I bought is called sand. I call it "safari khaki" because it sounds more exotic. And while it does have the ridged shape of a camera bag, it could be mistaken just for a regular shoulder bag. It also comes in "jungle" olive green.

The other thing I really like is you can use the strap on your shoulder or thread it through belt loop to wear on your waist. Perfect if you need to climb something and have your hands free.

It is a bit on the pricey side, but camera bags are not where you want to skimp, especially if you have a nice camera. If you have a point-n-shoot you bought at Walmart, then maybe this isn't the bag for you. But if you've invested a bit more in a camera, I definitely recommend the Domke 700-51D F-5XA Small Shoulder and Belt Bag.

title: Great sounds, good looks for a great price
text:
I ordered these speakers sight unseen from Amazon, based on user reviews. I had these speakers delivered to my disabled brother in NH, so I flew out from Colorado (with a sub woofer in tow) and setup his new surround sound. I was replacing components for him as well so the setup for me took about 3 hours.

Boxing: The folks at Fluance are serious about protecting their speakers in shipment, all of them were double boxed and they also floated in foam inserts within the boxes. A note of caution, the two floor standing speakers come in one BIG box that's a little unweilding and heavy, you need two people to get it to the room your going to set it up in.

Setup: This is your normal setup for a surround system. Their speaker wire connectors are the industry standard red and black with an ample receiving hole for a serious gauge monster cable. Because of my brothers room configuration we had to place the floor speakers in the back of his room, more about that later.

Look/Finish: We really liked the oak look of the speakers, it lends a modern look to my brothers entertainment room. There was no damage to the corners of the speakers from shipping, they were in great condition. The two floor standing speakers come with 4ea screw-in type levelers/isolaters that screw into the bottom of the speaker. These were particularly handy as I could get each speaker level on an old New England wooden floor.

Sound: So we spent a good part of the afternoon setting up, went out to dinner, then came back and watched War of the Worlds (Tom Cruise version). I was truly amazed at the sound quality of these speakers. At one point during the movie, my sister who was also in attendance, turned around to me and said she'd never heard surround speaks sound so good. The crispness of the cataclysmic events that occur during this movie was incredible, absolutely no distortion even at high volume. This brings me back to the unusual configuration we had to go with for the surround system. We'd put the large speakers in the back of the room in the corners and the center and what were supposed to be the surround speakers I'd ended placing within an in-wall entertainment/bookshelf setup where the TV was. Even the surround speakers acting as the primary L/R speakers sounded great.

For the money I'd say you can't go wrong with this setup. I'm very pleased with the system that I purchased for my brother, and he's been calling me daily to let me know what songs he's listened to and how good it sounds!

title: Confusing, and Expensive for a 1-time use
text:
First, the confusing parts. In order to control what gets transferred to your new PC, you have to go through every User folder and every other folder in order to not transfer over such things as application settings. But even after you take the great pains to go through this, you will still be, perhaps horrifically, surprised to find that either you missed something or it transferred them anyway. I started this a couple of times, unsure that I wouldn't make a mistake in the selection process. I clicked the Save button, but it didn't seem to save anything.

It gives you categories of content, like Video and Music and such. I thought, "How handy is that!" But it doesn't say whether it's going to aggregate the content it finds or put them in comparable (if not the same, mapped) locations. And if you wanted to move, say, only music, you'd still have to deselect all the other options ... carefully.

Another part of the confusion is: when transferring application settings, what exactly is going to happen? For instance, I had Office 2003 installed on my Vista machine, and 2011 on my Win7 machine. There is no indication about what would happen or if anything would happen. Will it overwrite my registration keys? It leaves unknown the answers to too many questions.

Finally, in the confusing department is the main screen that shows you three things that are being scanned. The two computers and the shared stuff. It doesn't tell you why its scanning your new computer --- and the UI leads one to suspect that the transfer can happen in two directions? Or maybe it might tell you if you're overwriting something with the same name? Unanswered scary questions.

Then there is its use-span. According to the Help department, the cable cannot be used for any other purpose. I had hoped that it might be a useful USB-USB Bridge cable. Nope. So if you don't have need to move your files more than once or continually, this is a one-pop shot...for $15 (or $39).

I think that the value of this transfer cable is very specifically targeted. That's not a bad thing; but it makes it hard for non-geeks to appreciate without questions, worry, and fears.

title: Nice Small Camera, Small-Minded Manufacturer
text:
THE GOOD: The NEX 3N is said to be the world's smallest camera based on the APS-C sensor, which is the second-largest sensor (about 16mm by 24mm) commonly found in mass-market cameras. The result is fine photo quality in a small package, with good high-ISO performance. Moreover, the 16-50mm e-mount kit lens is optically decent, and retracts to semi-pancake dimensions when the camera is off. So you get true DSLR-like performance in a box that approaches pocket size -- and is indeed pocket-ish size when paired with one of Sony's true pancake lenses, such as the new and nice and very expensive 20mm e-mount.

THE BAD: The 3N handles slowly thanks to so many functions and settings being based in menus rather than in manual controls; a settings-control wheel that's small, jumpy and hard to handle; slowish focusing, and the 16-50mm kit lens, which telescopes at a leisurely rate. Worse, the 3N lacks some of the settings that we take for granted today in any capable camera, such as the ability to customize the parameters of the auto-ISO function or even to control the volume of the focusing beep.

THE UGLY: In a fit of the Cheaps and/or the Dumbs, Sony decided not to include a battery charger with this camera. Apparently, they've made the same annoying move with the NEX 6, which is the $1,000 big brother of the 3N. But that's OK, says Sony, because owners can charge the battery inside the camera -- using a tiny cable that the company did include in the kit. (I haven't encountered this very bad in-camera-charging idea since I bought a Canon G1 in 2001.) Sure, Sony, this is just what I want to do on my vacation: sit in a hotel room watching my camera charge my spare battery. Of course, a Sony website will happily sell you the company's very own (and very good) NEX-class charger for $55 plus tax (at other websites it costs more like $40, if you can find it). I would much have preferred a higher 3N kit price -- with the furshlugginer charger included.

I wanted to love this thing--but it terrible in its current form and I'm sending it back on the same day I got it. :-(

title: DOA ... update: Makes static noise now ...
text:
My grandmother lives in a retirement home and her loud TV was bothering neighbors. I installed the TV Ears 2.3 system and she absolutely loved it. I mean, she reeeeeally loved it. I assumed that with daily use, the battery pack would go out at some point. Well, after a few years, it died.
This review is for the battery pack I ordered to replace the dead one. First, I was disappointed in the price. Then, to add to it, from the look of the reviews, it was a) a crapshoot whether it would perform even close to how it did prior and b) if it happened to not work, getting any sort of relief from the manufacturer would be difficult. I usually would not have taken the risk, but my grandmother would not allow me to install a corded system in place of the TV ears. I had to the TV Ears it working again. So, I installed the pack and it didn't work at all - nothing - no charge lights or anything. I have not contacted TV Ears yet, but the outlook is not good when considering other experiences. I will update this as I deal with the manufacturer.
UPDATE: I removed the battery pack - let me mention here that the battery pack is held on with two tiny philips screws that are not only tiny but would prefer to strip than screw ... okay, that sounds really bad. I reinstalled it and tried to get it screwed on tighter, but walked a very fine line with a stripped screw being one slip away. Upon turning them on, again I heard nothing. Then, I squeezed the battery pack section against the headphones and heard static followed by silence. By squeezing it I was able to replicate this but got nothing better than static. I just saw that Costco has the set for sale again - I could just get her another set ... she is 91 after all.

title: Not as good as I'd hoped...
text:
I received my new Kindle PW today and have spent a couple of hours with it so far. I will update this review after I spend a few weeks with the device. Note that my star rating is for the current device as a whole, but most of my review is relative to the previous generation Kindle.

I'm upgrading from the [[ASIN:B0051QVESA previous generation, non-touch kindle]], which I've had from Day-One and have been using in the [[ASIN:B004SD1ZPY official lighted leather cover]]. Prior to that, I had a second-generation Kindle...

Upon unpacking the device, I was a little bit disappointed to learn that it's actually slightly larger than my other Kindle; the difference is not huge, but it's noticeable to me. I s'pose they had to make room for the LED lighting and the touch hardware (it's my understanding that the older Kindle Touch is even larger yet).

I'm REALLY disappointed that the page-turn buttons have been removed. I'd become accustomed to reading with the Kindle in my left hand with my thumb resting gently on the Next-Page button. An almost imperceptible press of the thumb is all it took to move to the next page; half of the time I wasn't even really aware of pressing the button! Now I have to reach over the "Previous-Page" portion of the screen in order to touch the "Next Page" portion of the screen. Admittedly, it's not THAT big of a movement, but those buttons were perfect and they were built into the size bezel of the Kindle, so they took up no space. Kindle Touch users probably just roll their eyes about this since they never had the page-turn buttons to begin with but to me, the lack of physical buttons is... Irritating. I've already accidentally turned pages several times through incidental contact with the screen. Grrr.

I'm having mixed feelings about the LED lighting and since that's really the only significant new feature for this generation, that means I've having mixed feelings about the device as a whole. In low to medium (good) ambient lighting, it makes a definite difference. With the ambient lighting right at the point where you'd start thinking about putting an extra light on the previous Kindle, the Paperwhite (with the LED lighting turned up about halfway) lives up to it's name - the background looks white and the contrast is noticeably improved over the previous generation Kindle (with no extra lighting). However, as the ambient light level starts to get lower, the background takes on more of a blue-ish hue and that's even more apparent when you increase the level of the LED lighting. I'd looks odd, but I'm hoping that it's something I'll adjust to over time.

At the brighter LED settings, there's very obvious shadowing on the bottom quarter of the screen; this becomes much more apparent as the ambient lighting gets lower. The technical side of my brain tells me that I shouldn't be surprised that 4 evenly spaced LEDs are causing some visible "artifacts". I got suckered and bought Amazon's marketing hype, tho! Technically, the screen illumination IS much more even than what's achieved with the previous Kindle inside the official illuminated case. The LEDs create this strange, almost checkerboard shadow pattern, though and combined with the odd blue hue to the display, I'm finding it to be a bit distracting. Time will tell if this is something that I can get used to...

With the LED lighting turned all the way down (effectively off), the contrast ratio of the Kindle Paperwhite is near indistinguishable from the previous generation. Comparing them side-by-side in a decently lit room, nobody here can decisively say that one has better contrast than the other. The fonts on the Paperwhite definitely look nicer and do seem to benefit from the higher resolution, tho.

The smallest margin setting is still pretty large - it leaves a 1/4" screen border around the text. That's almost what... 25% of the screen that's unused? I can see the need for having SOME margin in order to keep the text separated from the black bezel, but c'mon Amazon, give us some options to reduce the margins smaller than 1/4"; that much wasted space is just silly!

Ultimately, I think I'll be able to adjust to everything that I've "griped" about but I'm definitely not getting rid of my other Kindle just yet...

title: Google BEFORE You Buy !
text:
UPDATE: March 31, 2014

An alert reader of my original review (original review and link to reader's comment, below), wrote that he did a net-search for the 'cutting-out' problem I had described with this headset, the subject of the original reveiw.
In his search the reader found no mention. So I searched again to verify.

The reader/'commenter' is right.
Apparently, the cut-out problem is frequent with the h900- MY MISTAKE- but only seldom mentioned [for example, in Amazon Reviews, Great Britain] for the unit being reviewed here, the h800.

The problem with my unit- potentially anyone's problem so still something of which to be aware- possibly, is interference. Potential interference is a noted concern that may cause the unit to cut out- potential interference from almost anything that also transmits: your router, your cell, your other wireless perfipherals.

What muddies the picture is that I bought two of these h800 headsets: one never had a problem, the other cuts out every time i make a call. Listening is fine, it is Skype speaking that cuts the unit in/out as often as every 10 seconds [it beeps off and on again- including with completely recharged battery]- as mentioned in original review. Whether the cause is interference, a defect with design as originally considered, or a defect in my single unit only, my rating remains the same-
Don't Buy.

I bought two. One works, the other does not. Judging by the number of high reviews here, my own bad luck in receiving a defective unit seems the most likely explanation. But with warnings on the net about interference and after my experience with one bad unit out of two bought, then had I to do over for myself, I'd look for a different headset, an headset that delivered same function but without any asterisks.

[The unit i bought that does work would have earned a high rating, had I not bought the second which acted as described in original review]

To sum, my best advice- from my experience- remains as in orginal review.

ORIGINAL REVIEW:
Save Your Money !
I bought this headset once, liked it.
Liked it so much I tossed an equally expensive older, bulkier headset and ordered another h800 headset.

I wanted two of these- one for travel, one for desk.
The second pair never worked.
Cuts in/out constantly- every 3 seconds.
I kept thinking the battery/charging had a problem since my first one worked [works] flawlessly- so I used my first set all the time till finally got around to checking into this second one further.

I searched the net:
Check for yourself before buying.
A 3 minute search revealed that this is a common fault. The set turns itself on/off several times a minute, making headset conversation impossible.
Another 70$ into the trash.
So: one out of two works.
Are you willing to gamble 70$ on 50% odds?

Again, don't take my word. Google "logitech Headset cuts out" or some such phrase-
google BEFORE you buy.

If you buy one of these and it works, you will like it.
If your luck is not that good, either stay away or return it before Amazon's window of open return expireses.
[I assumed my second set would work since the first one worked so well, so never investigated till Amazon's window plus about one day had gone by.]
Better yet- buy a different headset- there are lots out there. Some may even be reliable.

title: Touchpad Improperly Glued
text:
My tablet had a problem with the touchpad and I was not able to use the right side of the touchpad. The touchpad was pasted into the groove at a crooked angle so that part of the touchpad was laying over the edge of the recessed area that holds the touchpad.

UPDATE: I got the touchpad to seat itself within the recessed area so that the lip was not over the edge. This maybe a freak happening but I was using the touchpad on a bunched up towel...yes, a bunched up cloth towel... so there was no stability or hardness. In other words, my computer was sitting on a spongy and giving surface. (Towel must be bunched up, not laying flat) No it was not easy to use and I had to balance the computer with my fingers to type. While using the computer on a bunched up towel, I noticed the touchpad was more giving on the right side and I continued to touch the right side until the touchpad seated itself properly into the groove! Now I can use the right side of the touchpad sans towel.

So if any of you have an improperly seated touchpad, try the towel trick. You may have hold the edge of the computer for just a little stability but it worked...for me.

title: Reason to Buy Tecsun PL-660 over Sangen ATS-909X
text:
I was torn between the Tecsun PL-660 and the Sangen ATS-909X, which is almost twice the price. The Tecsun is more sensitive with the whip antenna and is generally more portable, while the Sangen is larger with a great looking display. They both have certain features that the other lacks. For example the PL-660 has the air band and bfo for easier SSB tuning, while the ATS-909x has RDS on FM and communicates more information on its display to the listener.

The major shortcoming on the ATS-909x is the number of memory presets available. Although the total sounds large at 406 presets there are only 18 for AM and 27 for FM, which is totally insufficient. In comparison, the PL-660 has 2000 memory presets available and more importantly the first memory page alone (P0) has 800 memory presets with 100 for AM and 100 for FM. Given the fact that on a random night I was able to scan 52 AM stations and 63 FM stations into the memory of the PL-660, it is mystifying why the memory presets on the ATS-909x are so inadequate.
