title: EXTREMELY HAPPY!
text:
One word, AWESOME! After reading the reviews for this mount I was a little skeptical. But after purchasing a Cheetah flat mount 6 months ago, I figured I would give it a try. If I didn't like it, or if parts were missing I could return it. Well, this is one customer who will not be returning this mount. If you're like me, you read the reviews, gather all the information you can and make an educated purchase. The reviews for this item were so scattered, I felt compelled to write one myself.

Quite a few of the reviews complained about the lack of "words" on the instructions. Let me be the first to tell you, there are words. They tell you what parts/tools are needed and what basic knowledge you need to install this mount. For example: "Ensure bracket is in the center of the wood stud." Pretty basic knowledge right? But honestly that's all you need to know to install one of these. You will not get a novel giving you EVERY step you need to take to get this thing up on your wall. If that is what you need, call a friend, or hire someone to do it for you. Anyone with a working knowledge of gravity and the capability to use a cordless drill/screw driver can install one of these. All the parts were there and because I was mounting a 32" Samsung LCD there were even extra parts. I didn't need to use the extender plates intended for use with larger TVs, nor did I need all the mounting screws that were included. Since this fits 100 x 100, 200 x 200, 300 x 300 and 400 x 400 mounting methods, I have at least 12 screws sitting unused. Mounting took me a total of 30 minutes. I could have done this as a one man job, but I recruited my wife to hold the level while I screwed the mounting plate into the center of the stud. The swivel is awesome and the 15° optional tilt is simply icing on the cake.

My TV is now mounted and swiveled into the corner above my dresser. Perfect angle and degree of tilt to watch TV in bed without putting an extra pillow under your head to get the right viewing angle. Less neck kinks and complaints from my wife that my knees are in the way, make this customer a happy man.

title: Headphones-Charger Melted Together!
text:
First – sorry for the long story.
Second – sorry to all those who wrote “don’t buy this” reviews…I should have listened.
Third – to everyone who wrote about how terrible Motorola support was…it was even worse than that!
A quick review of how these headphones worked (when they were working). They paired very well with both my iPhone 5 and an Android tablet…occasional Bluetooth drops, but chalked those up to the tablet. The sound wasn’t great, but it was good enough. They were comfortable enough to get me through a 90-minute aerobic/weights workout, and charged very quickly. They would occasionally not turn on, or just shut off with no reason, but I always managed to get it to work OK.
I took great care of these, wiping them off after every use, and treating them very carefully. However, after about 3 months, the LED light that glows red->yellow->green when charging would only work sometimes, but I figured as long as it kept charging I was OK with it. Strangely enough, the same LED worked fine in blue mode when pairing with the iPhone/tablet.
9/17/2014 – I left the headphones charging overnight (as I’ve done often before), but when I picked them up the next morning they were hot. So hot in fact that the plastic around the end of the micro-USB charge plug had melted, and the plug-in place on the headphones had burned brownish-black. I pulled them apart, and some melted plastic pulled away, kind of like melted mozzarella cheese. I haven’t tried turning on the headphones to see if they still work, but it’s obvious I’ll never be charging these again!

Went to the Motorola customer support site, and requested an online chat. After over 24 minutes of waiting to get to number 1 in the queue, my window message switched to:
Status: Canceled
There are no agents available to chat with you right now. Please try again later.

I tried again…this time getting the message:
You are currently number 1 in the queue. You should be connected to an agent in about 14:25. The average amount of time a customer has to wait is 14:25.
After exactly 14:25, the message updated to say:
You are currently number 1 in the queue. We apologize for the delay. We will assign you to an agent as soon as one is available. The average amount of time a customer has to wait is 14:25.
After waiting another 15 or so minutes, I “left” the non-conversation and tried starting over, getting:
You are currently number 38 in the queue. You should be connected to an agent in about 22:11. The average amount of time a customer has to wait is 22:13.
While waiting for the online chat, I decided to call the support number (800-734-5870). After answering a few automated questions to get to the right type of device, I got put on hold with some horrible warbling repeating-every-23-seconds classical music, and then every 30 seconds a nice lady would come on and tell me how all of their representatives are busy and how important my call is to them, and please hold, as my call will be answered in the order received, or soon, alternately. After just short of 13 minutes on hold, the music went silent for a few seconds, and then they disconnected me.
I was still waiting for the chat window, but again, after the 22:11, I got the same message:
Status: Canceled
There are no agents available to chat with you right now. Please try again later.

Why in the world would you “count down” from 38 in the queue to 1, and only then tell a customer there are NO AGENTS AVAILABLE TO CHAT???? So the 37 people before me got to chat with someone? Or did they get the same treatment?
I finally ended up sending an email. I gave a quick recap of the problem and asked if it was possible to get a replacement. I received a response email saying:
Your question has been received. You should expect a response from us within 24 hours.
No word, no response, no answering chat, no answering phones, nothing! I’ve always had a fondness for Motorola – probably from some of the phone technology from years past – but I had no idea how far they’d fallen. Whatever fondness I had for them has completely evaporated – this is certainly not the Motorola of yesteryear.

title: Good for pros and intermediates
text:
This camera can be used by pros, gifted amateurs and intermediates alike. It is fine for beginners who are serious about becoming good photographers. Beginners who are looking for a P&S with interchangeable lenses will be unhappy, because you need to know something -- not alot -- about photo basics that go beyond pointing and shooting.
One of its great attractions is that if all you want is a high-quality, low cost SLR, you can have it by buying the base model at a fantastic price with the kit lens (an unbelievable $260 for astonishing technology). Basically, this option provides you with an upscale P&S at an unbelievable price.
If you are serious about becoming a decent photographer, you don't work with LCD displays -- you want a viewfinder, which will cost an additional $250. So the camera now costs $510.
The quality of pix with the 14-42 kit lens is okay, but not in the same league as what I get with my Nikon D7000 or my unbelievably sharp Fuji X100. If you want really clear shots that win awards in photo contests, then you must pay an additional $500 bucks for a Panasonic Lumix pancake lens -- 20mm, with an impressive f1.7 aperture. (Note: 20mm with 4/3 = 40mm with standard 35mm cameras) You have now reached the $1,000 range, and have a decent, light weight camera that might win you a prize or two in photo contests. Important note: If what you want is a walk around camera, get the fixed lens Fuji X100 for $1,200. The crispness of its photos would impress Ansel Adams.
If you are going to shoot tigers and such at a distance, then you need to spend another $300 for a 40mm-150mm telephoto lens (equivalent to 80mm-300mm in the 35mm world). Your now $1,300 camera can get decent results with this lens. Personally, if I want good telephoto shots, I will lug my larger Nikon D7000 to get crystal clear shots of the lion taking down the zebra at 500 meters. Telephoto shots on the E-PL1 may win you a prize if you get a unique shot, but they won't give you the clarity you get with larger CMOS cameras.
The big secret with the E-PL1, for those who want near professional level performance, is the 9mm-18mm wide angle lens ($500-$600). Wow! Great results: 90% of what I get with my Nikon D-7000 with a wide angle lens. In looking at reviews of this camera, I haven't see comments of this great capability. Check out newspaper photos and advertising photos: most are wide angle. That's what the pros use. The tiny Olympus with a 9mm-18mm lens can give you fantastic, crystal clear wide angle photos.
Here's the configuration I suggest for the prospective E-PL1 buyer. Buy the standard camera (with kit lens) for $260. Pay an additional $250 for the viewfinder. Spend $500 for the Lumix high-performing, 20mm f1.7 lens. Finally, buy the wide angle 9mm-18mm lens for $500-$600. Total cost: $1,600 for an extremely light weight camera system that will get you great photos.
But, if all you want is an SLR upgrade to your P&S, spring for the measley $260 for the basic camera, which gives you a great camera that you may want to upgrade, as you develop your photo shooting skills.

title: Very Easy Setup ...
text: I'm rating this player 5 stars but reserve the right to come back later if things go sour.  I offer that caveat because I just bought and set up my new player yesterday and I really don't want to vouch for long-term performance yet, for obvious reasons.  I bought this one after hassling with a Samsung for hours and hours over a period of about three days.  The Samsung just would not play Blu-ray discs.  I updated the firmware and repeatedly checked for another update - there was none.  I spent a lot of time, too much, on duckduckgo and even google, trying to figure out the problem.  Along those lines, you may want to do some research before you consider getting a Samsung, especially if you want to play Blu-ray discs.  Lots of problems to be found in the search engines.  But, maybe I just got unlucky with Samsung.  And, maybe I just got lucky with this Sony.  All of these players have their problems.  No wonder.  None of us is willing to pay $1,000 for one of these things so the manufacturers don't make many at that price and quality level.  Therefore, we must accept the consequence, which is: many of them just won't work ... to wit: my experience with Samsung.  Now, this Sony got less than its share of cursing on the internet reviews and comments and it seemed likely that it might do the one thing I want it to do:  play Blu-ray discs.  Setup instructions were intelligible and clear and concise.  You don't have to read a book to get the thing started.  I don't want the thing to become my hobby; I just want it to play discs.  Basically, you plug the thing in and hook up an HDMI cable (which is NOT included) and the device takes it from there.  Connecting wirelessly to the internet, surprisingly (after my hair pulling experience with the Samsung) went very smoothly, too.  Sony has lots of apps and the usual Netflix, etc.  Throughput seems to be pretty fast on my average speed home WiFi.  I mostly use the internet connection on my disc players just to keep the firmware updated conveniently.  (I've got another box that I use for all the Netflix/internet stuff.)  My wife likes the fact that the thing is nice and small; she doesn't need to make a fashion statement with the darned TV boxes.  I like the facts that: 1) It was extremely easy to set the thing up and get it running; and, 2) IT ACTUALLY PLAYS BLU-RAY DISCS!  If I note problems later, after I've had the thing for a while, I'll let you know.  Good luck!

title: Perfect if you know how to apply it
text:
These are good quality screen protectors. Made of film like material. Smudging and glare is only barely worse than the unprotected screen, so no complaints from me.

If you apply it well, you won't see bubbles. Instructions are on the package. Tips:
. Dust is the #1 cause for bubbles. Bubbles without dust in it can be squeezed out, but with dust, it's impossible. Make sure you clean surface thoroughly and avoid dusty places. The film itself attracts dust like a magnet because of static electricity.
. Before you peel off the cover layer, put it on the screen and see how it fits.
. Apply on the long edge first. That way you won't get alignment problem.
. The cut out is for the front camera on top, not the Galaxy logo at the bottom.
. If you make a mistake, use 2 pieces of scotch tape to lift it out and re-apply.

title: Great sound, but too painful to wear
text:
Update 1/1/2015: I gave the K701s a three-star rating because they are so extremely uncomfortable. Since posting my original review, I have modified my K701s. I bought a piece of foam weather stripping at the hardware store (about 3/8 inch thick) and super-glued a piece on the underside of the headband. I can now wear my K701s for several hours. Dear AKG, please redesign the headband of the K701s to provide more padding.

The Short Review:

Pros:
The K701 headphones by AKG may be the best sounding headphones in the 1 to 500 dollar price range if: (1) they are used with a headphone amplifier or high-end audio card; and (2) they are substantially broken in (aka, burned in).

Cons:
(1) Major con: These headphones are so torturously uncomfortable I can wear them for only 40 minutes without feeling an intolerable pain at the top of my head. (See Road Warrior's review of this product.) If you wear your headphones for less than one hour per day, then maybe this "con" won't be a big issue for you.
(2) Minor con: The K701s require a substantial break-in period (at least 500 hours). A lot of folks don't think headphone performance changes with use; honestly, these K701s sounded much, much better after 1000 hours of use (I left them playing continuously for six weeks).
(3) Major, minor, or no con (depending on your personal tastes): The K701s are "bass light" compared to other headphones. Some folks defend the K701s by calling them "neutral"; well, I know what a live bass guitar sounds like, and the K701s cannot reproduce the sounds of a live bass guitar.

Some Technical Facts:
- The K701 headphones have an impedance of 62 ohms at 1000 Hz. Therefore, they are NOT the best choice for direct connection to an iPod or computer. For an iPod or computer, you would probably be happier with headphones that have an impedance of 32 ohms or less.
- These are full-sized "semi-open" headphones. That means that folks around you will hear them. If you want to keep your listening experience private, then you should considering buying headphones with a "closed" acoustic seal.

Sound Quality
With a headphone amplifier:
- After 1000 hours of break-in: 5.0 stars (considering the price)
- After 500 hours of break-in: 4.5 stars
- Out of the box: 3.0 stars

With iPod or computer (after break-in), no amplifier: 3.5 stars

Comfort: 1.0 star (painful to wear after about 40 minutes)

The Wordy Review:

I am NOT an audiophile; however, I do have a nice headphone amplifier with matching digital-to-analog converter (DAC) and external power supply. I listen mostly to rock, classical (orchestral), and guitar music of all styles. With a headphone amplifier, I have used the K701s to listen to CDs, LPs, iPod (lossless and 320 kb/s files), and movies and television (Blu-ray player, streaming services, and cable TV). I have also used the K701s with an iPod (unamplified), laptop computer, and a desktop computer equipped with a 300 ohm sound card. My conclusion: You really need a headphone amplifier with the K701s. If you are looking for headphones to use with an iPod or laptop computer forget the K701s and shop around for 32 ohm (or less) headphones instead.

The AKG K701 headphones may be the best sounding headphones for the price. In fact, the K701s sound even better than some headphones costing twice as much. Tragically, all of the folks I know who own the K701s say the same thing: They sound great, but they are way too uncomfortable. I rarely use these headphones anymore simply because they are painful to wear.

After a long break-in period, the K701s sound amazing. I own headphones that sound better, but those headphones cost substantially more. Although "bass light," the K701s are mostly "neutral"; the K701s sound great with symphonic music. I have read some folks believe the treble is over-emphasized. For rock 'n' roll, some folks might long for more bass (my other headphones more accurately reproduce low frequencies, such as the low end of the piano or an electric bass). I am very pleased with the high accuracy of the K701s; however; if it's on the original recording, you'll hear it; you'll even hear annoying tape hiss (almost all music originally recorded in the 1950s, 1960, and 1970s has tape hiss).

These headphones require a substantial burn-in period. I would recommend that you give them at least a 300 hour "burn in" before you use them (i.e., don't pass judgment on them until they have been played for at least 300 hours). Directly out of the box, the K701s do not impress. Upon receipt, I hooked mine up to a headphone amplifier for approximately three weeks (operating 24 hour per day). During this period, I checked the sound at least once per day. After a 500 hour burn-in, they were certainly acceptable (4.5 stars); after another 500 hours of burn-in (six weeks total), they reached their 5-star performance level. Before burn-in, my Sennheiser HD-650 headphones sounded much, much better than the K701s; after the 1000 hour burn-in, the K701s sound at least as good as the HD-650s, maybe even a slight bit better for orchestral music.

In spite of their awesome sound, the K701s are so hideously uncomfortable I rarely use them. I cannot wear them for more than one hour a day (without pain in the top of my head). In contrast, I can (and do) comfortably wear my Sennheiser HD-650 headphones for hours on end. I have read that some unhappy K701 users have found clever ways to pad the headphone band. I did not want to bother with such foolishness, so I banished the sadistically uncomfortable K701s to a closet shelf. My [[ASIN:B00018MSNI Sennheiser HD 650 Headphones]] and [[ASIN:B00890YNBK Beyerdynamic T90 New Tesla Audiophile High End Headphone]] are much more comfortable.

I have performed comparison tests with the K701s using original CDs, "lossless" digital files, and MP3 files at various bitrates. Your 128 kb/s files will sound terrible with the K701s; this is not the fault of the headphones, they are just faithfully playing the source material. For iPod or computer, you'll definitely want to use "lossless" or 320 kb/s encoding.

The K701s have a permanently attached cable. This means that the normal user cannot easily upgrade or replace the cables. The "stock" cable is pretty good; so this may not be a big issue.

The Benefits of a Headphone Amplifier:

You really need a headphone amplifier for the AKG K701 headphones. No kidding, it makes a huge difference. Luckily, lots and lots of folks are now manufacturing them; you have lots of choices in a very wide price range (100 to 2000 dollars). The K701s sound relatively anemic when directly connected to an iPod or a computer; but they sound awe-inspiring when connected to a decent headphone amplifier. Quite simply, an iPod or computer (or even the "Phones" jack on your receiver) doesn't have sufficient power to drive these headphones to their full glory. Also, if you are listening to music stored on your PC, you might consider getting a nice digital-to-analog converter (DAC). A good DAC makes a big difference in sound quality.

The Miracle of Crossfeed:

Beside power, another reason to get a headphone amp is get a "crossfeed" circuit. If you don't know what crossfeed is, perform a little web research. My headphone amp has a crossfeed circuit: it makes a huge difference. In brief, when a recording is produced, the engineer balances the left and right channels with the assumption that playback will be through a two-loudspeaker system, not through headphones. When listening to speakers, your left ear will hear a portion of the sound from the right speaker, and your right ear will hear a portion of the sound from the left speaker. In this way, your brain can properly place the instruments and vocals right to left as well as front to back (i.e., the brain creates the illusion of a "soundstage"). This effect is missing if you listen to music or computer games using headphones connected to a source that does not have crossfeed. Now, some folks don't care about soundstage; some music is recorded without an intentional soundstage; for some types of music, a soundstage is meaningless (e.g., a lot of club music). However, if soundstage is important to you, get a headphone amplifier that has a crossfeed circuit. By the way, open headphones (like the K701s) have better soundstage than closed headphones, but even then you'll never hear the proper soundstage without an effective crossfeed circuit.

Summary:

I think the K701s are the best sounding headphones in their price range (although a little weak in the base). Tragically, the K701s are so painfully uncomfortable to wear I do not use them and cannot recommend them. I feel a little upset that I wasted my money on them.

title: Very impressed.
text: I was very skeptical about this...not because of the product but because of the reliability and worry whether it may ruin the records ( I am very new to this vinyl stuff). Watched reviews and how to use in YouTube and pulled a trigger. As illustrated in the manual (detail enough), I poured the distilled water, added three cap full of the agent (4oz bottle), submerged my record, spin clockwise and counterclock wise, and wipe out the excess liquid. Then, wow...........the statics and noise of the record were dramatically reduced. After cleaning about 20 records or so, here are my conclusion. If you have a record(s) with minor dirt, fingerprints, and whatever, it will clean them up pretty good. If you have a records with some serious dirt, it won't cure it. Some of my records are older than my age (30+) years and those are beloved by my father (meaning heavily used and he, as far as I remember, never really deep cleaned them other than dusting off prior to play them). When I cleaned them through this Spin-Clean, the noise level was reduced but it doesn't clean them deep enough. However, some of newer stuff with less damaged records, it does a remarkable job. When I say "damage", it means dirty not scratched broker chipped. It won't cure them. It simply clean them (not deep enough but enough to remove statics and dusts). Now my test session is over, I am planning to clean some of my REAL stuff. And one more thing is that be patient and gentle when you clean yours with this. Also, recommend to run a couple of test cleaning with whatever records that you really don't care if it is damaged. I feel like it gets broken in after two or three records are cleaned.

title: Nighthawk-X8
text:
Keyboard's great...

Mechanical Keys
Cherry Browns. Keys actually feel lighter than the Filco Ninja that I have for the office (this is for home/gaming). If you're not familiar with Cherry keys, browns are tactile action - you feel a little "bump" when you push the key down and it registers. This is similar to Cherry Blues which are tactile feedback - you feel AND hear a "click" (sounds like a mouse click). So, browns are quieter, but you'll still get that clack-clack-clack when and if you bottom out the keys (push them down all the way). With these though, you could learn to touch-type - you only tap the key just enough to register the keypress - and it'd be practically silent.

Design
I like the matte keyboard over the glossy surface of the Blackwidow Ultimate that I had. Backlighting for the keys is very well centered. 5 modes of lighting: Breathing, Maximum (3), Medium (2), Minimum (1), Off. If you have a G700, the casing for this looks like its keyboard brother - a tool for battle. Cable is offset a 3/4s to the right which kind of bothers me (desktop on left and I'm right-handed), but that's personal preference and I just have to move stuff around my desk. There aren't any logos of the company visibly on the keyboard (unlike the CoolerMaster one). Font doesn't seem to be custom (unlike the Razer font which looks pretty awesome). Very... what's the word... humble(?) for a keyboard of its class.

Features
Two USB 2.0s, microphone, and audio jack on the keyboard (like the Blackwidow Ultimate). Braided cable to computer. Gold-plated USB for durability. Comes with a wrist pad (I know, I know, pictures speak a thousand words). There are macros, but I haven't downloaded or installed the software. Take note - the scroll-lock light has been replaced for "G" mode, which is macro-recording mode.

But I'm returning it
Was a gift for someone. Took it out to test it and make sure it was 100% (not Das, Filco, Steelseries, or Razer - don't know the company). Played a couple games of Starcraft 2, which took a little getting used to (I have a Blackwidow Ultimate at home). And it was great. I have to say, I was liking it very much. Having the backlight on breathe created this sort of atmosphere for the game, too. Played with lights off and lighting was perfect - the keys are NOT clear, so the lights don't blind you. Everything was going alright. Then, I had some work to do in Excel. Pressed the num-lock key by instinct and started typing. Made a mistake somewhere and I thought I pressed the num-lock again, so I looked down to check and the light was off. So I pushed it again and it was still off. "Hm, that's weird." Tried caps-lock, scroll-lock, and num-lock again and again and determined that the num-lock light was just out (this is also how I found that the scroll-lock indicator is actually for "G" mode, too). I mean, it's a small thing, right? $150 for a backlit Cherry brown, not a tenkeyless, either. But that num-lock light is a function of the keyboard which should work with or without backlighting. So, just a fluke for me, but that knocks a star off because I'm not getting shipping back, going to have to pay for shipping to return, and along with that, I'm also paying in time waiting. Sent in a return request yesterday (got the keyboard yesterday) and will update review with customer service. Ordered a Blackwidow Stealth Ultimate as a back-up, but really wish this was 100% first time though. Probably just going to return it if the Stealth comes before return goes through.

title: I've used a number of them during the past few years.
text:
My hobby during the past 12 years of retirement has been breathing life back into older computers (335 to date) and giving them free to disadvantaged kids and their families. In that more and more school systems are coming to rely on the internet, WI FI has become nearly a necessity on computers used by those students. Of late I have needed a reliable, inexpensive dongle with good scabbing range because most of the computers I rework never had that capability. The different versions of the NETGEAR WG111 that have been offered over those years have proven to be exactly what I needed. I have never had a problem with any of the ones I have personally kept and used and have yet to receive a complaint about any of the ones I have given away.

The CD that comes with it has managed to make any brand computer WI FI capable that I have installed it in. Also, the generous length cable supplied with the NETGEAR WG111 allows one to "seek" the best signal spot---like back in the Rabbit Ears era of TV. Using a parabolic reflector with the cable and dongle really helps boost the signal for whatever brand of router happens to be in the mix. I found that a dish of about 16 inch dia. with about a 4 inch depth allows the focal point to occur at about the line across the dish opening; so it's simple to run a piece of tape across the middle of the opening and stick the dongle to it in the middle. The best reflector I've found so far is the curved lid from a cooking Wak. A simple way to find the focal point of your reflector dish is: F = Dia squared over 16 times C. F is focal point. Dia. is the distance across the middle of dish opening, and C is the distance at the center of the opening down to the bottom of the inside center of the curved "dish"----aka parabolic reflector.

I have absolutely no connection to or with NETGEAR----only my intention to give credit where credit is due. I wish you the same good results that I have experienced.

title: After 6 months of light use (87 hours according HWinfo) SSD dies after 2 hours being active
text:
After 6 months of light use (87 hours according to HWinfo) SSD causes windows to crash after 2 hours. I was unluckily one of the people that got stuck with an Asynchronous chip which is what Kingston changed to to keep the SSD cheap. Anyways, over time I lived with it because I had put it into an old laptop that needed the boost and this was on sale back in February so it hadn't bothered me that my speeds were pretty bad (SATA 2 Read 180 MB/s and Write 90 MB/s) but over time I noticed that certain programs like photoshop, lightroom, and even Chrome and Mozilla had become much slower in the last month or so.

Then, about 2 nights ago when I was on YouTube all of a sudden the laptop just instantly died, straight to a black screen. I booted it backup and ran Western Digital Diagnostics and after 50 seconds of it not scanning any sectors it again went straight to a black screen. Just to make sure it was the Kingston drive I had popped in the 6 year old WD Scorpio Black and formatted it with Windows 7 Pro just like on the SSD it worked great the last week or so and even felt quicker!

Conclusion: I believe I got stuck with a particularly bad drive but, I will never get another Kingston until they switch back to Synchronous chips vs Asynchronous and I advise anyone looking for a cheap SSD to go for the new Crucial MX100 256GB for 115$ or a Samsung 840 EVO 250GB which has unbelievable performance for only 130$ and SanDisks 256GB Ultra Plus SSD for 110$.

title: More Than Just a Reader
text:
I've had my Kindle Fire for about 4 months now, and I have to say it is probably the most handy tech device I've ever owned. The screen resolution is bright and clear. There is ample storage to save books, apps, and any other content your heart desires (although having external storage capabilities such as SD would be a huge plus). The WiFi function is easy to use and quick to engage. Another thing I wish for on this device is external volume controls (rather than having to change it via the on-screen menu). The battery life is very good too.

I've done everything on this device, from surfing the web, to reading books, to playing games, to watching TV shows and movies, to using both POP and Exchange Server e-mail accounts (paid app required for using Exchange server e-mail). I have a whole host of apps from the Amazon Kindle store, which has a great selection of apps for just about any interest or need, many of which are free or extremely low-priced. Kindle books, on average, are less expensive than their printed counterparts, and there is an enormous selection from which to choose. I also uploaded some personal and professional reference documents (Adobe PDF), so I can refer to them on the go, rather than having to lug around (for example) my community CC&R's, software or process user guides, company policies, industry periodicals, etc.

One thing I really love to do with my Kindle Fire is set it up in front of my toddler neice and either play Angry Birds (she only likes the intro, with the music) or let her play Kids Doodle, a drawing app I downloaded for free. I've also downloaded a couple of childrens' picture books, which she really enjoys, and somehow she instinctively knew how to turn the page! Be sure to always have a good supply of pre-moistened lense wipes if you're going to let a child play with your Kindle Fire!

Another favorite use of my Kindle Fire is for bible study. Serious bible students know that it's vital to have a commentary, dictionary and handbook in order to get the most out of their studies. To carry all of these printed books would require a catalog case on wheels. Not so with the Kindle Fire!! All of these large volumes fit easily onto the internal storage.

Since the Kindle Fire is so portable, it's easy to pull out and use when you encounter any sort of delay (traffic, long line, etc.) and catch up on your reading, check the news, goof around on Facebook, or play a game. I've never had a very good reading habit, but have gotten noticeably better now that I have the handy Kindle Fire. The Kindle Fire fits nicely into my purse as well.

In short, there's far more to this device than meets the eye. If you don't have the money to shell out on an iPad or similar overpriced tablet, this is a perfectly good alternative.

I installed this modem after a hellish experience with Comcast Xfinity order and installation. I knew it would be bad but: Just why is it that the cable companies have had horrible customer experience for *decades* now? They could all learn a lot from Apple...
Anyhow, this modem is fine. Strangely, I still experience slowdowns, delays, and other network stalls I don't ever get with Fios 12/2, and with Xfinity, the speed is 25/3! (I ordered 12/2 but, they upped the speed just when I got the order for my type of plan.)
There is ONE major flaw with the modem design. The Link light on the front blinks CONSTANTLY. This is fine if your modem is in the basement or a closet but, I think most people have it on or near a desk, home office, or bedroom. It is incredibly annoying and totally un-needed. To show data, Motorola only needs to show the light solid (not blinking)as long as data is detected every 30 or so seconds and/or make it smart and know that, if it has been detecting for a few minutes, it can stop blinking and just be solid. This would be fine for troubleshooting, which is all it is for anyhow!
The blinking Link light gets a negative 5 stars!

title: Same Classic Garmin HRM Spikes - UPDATED to 4 Stars
text:
A couple of years back I was using the Forerunner 110 model, and became increasingly frustrated at the inaccurate heart rate spikes. It was always the same: The first 5 minutes of the run would show some crazy HR number, until I guess enough sweat built up to create a sufficient contact to render an accurate reading. For the last 8 months, I've used a Polar HRM and paired it with my iPhone using Endomondo. For $60, I hate a HRM that worked as soon as I put it on, without any spikes!

I took a chance on the Garmin 620 because I like a lot of the features, and figured, "Hey, if Polar can make a HRM that picks up the heart beat right away, then surely Garmin has figured it out by now." WRONG! Just got the 620, and my first run was a carbon copy of my experience with the 110. The first 5 minutes had my HR at an absurd 183, until it suddenly started working and showed me in the 140s to 160s for remainder of run (I will attach a photo of the graph separately). (NOTE: See update - Spikes issue seems to be resolved)

Other negatives:

1) Advertised as a "high-resolution color display." Is this a joke? It's black and white, with some screens that have horribly muted colors.

2) Too many divided sections on each display. Very hard to read. Still trying to find a way to create a custom page with a single read out that is larger. Again, will adjuster rating if that feature is available and I just haven't found it.

3) Somewhat convoluted and not the best user interface. I do like the ability to tap the screen to switch.

There are some things I really like about the 620. If the HRM worked properly, I like how it auto-pairs with the watch. I also notice the 620 quickly finds satellites.

I am going to give this a couple of more runs, and some additional research, but unless I can remedy these issues, this is going back.

----UPDATE----

I have now had about 5 straight workouts without the spikes being an issue. I use conductor gel, which seems to help quite a bit. I still believe the bluetooth HRMs are better, but using gel is not a big deal. Additionally, there are features of this watch that I am finding very useful and impressive. I've done quite a few runs at this point, and really like the information I get from this product. The recovery time feature has been very useful, and is helping me not to OVER train. I also like the recovery check after the first few minutes. But what I found really impressive was when I did my first gym workout yesterday on an elliptical. Personally, I like the elliptical over the treadmill when in the gym, because all the running I do outside is tough enough on the joints. The new accelerometer in the 620 is supposed to eliminate the need for a foot pod on the treadmill, but I could find nothing about whether it worked for an elliptical machine. It does work, and very well I might add! This was really a surprise, but the distance was almost dead on with the machine.

As for the display and interface, I stand by my comments that you should not expect what you might think a high-res display to be. I can live with that, but that's why I can't do a full five stars. As for the interface, it's not so bad once you get used to it.

Conclusion: I am really coming around to this watch, and I would recommend it.

title: Confused by the strap...
text:
I purchased this case to use with the BaoFeng UV82 radio. The radio fits in the case nicely, however the display is not visible while in the case. I have an external speaker/mic that connects to the radio, and this case does not interfere with it.

What puzzles me is the neck/waist strap. It has three ends that each have a clip on the end, and the case has clips on the top and D-rings on the bottom. Usually, the clips would attach to the D-rings, but in this case (no pun intended), the radio would hang upside down if you clipped only onto the D-rings. It is confusing just trying to figure out what the intent of the designer was.

What I like about the case is that there are several ways to use it: attached to a belt, clipped to almost anything, or hanging by the strap (with the caveats mentioned above). For the price, it seems fairly well made, and I would recommend it for anyone looking for an inexpensive radio holster.

What I don't like is the confusing strap.

I also wish there were a way to view the display while the radio is in the holster, but this probably doesn't really matter much, since it will mostly be used on a belt in my case. This isn't really the fault of the holster, but more of a statement of the design of the radio.

Overall, I'm very pleased with this radio holster/case.

title: modern design and all of the great reviews this antenna has
text: After installing this antenna in my attic and re-scanning my TV, I was able to receive only ONE of the 9 broadcast TV stations available in my metropolitan area.  I tried re-orienting the antenna all thru 360 degrees and back again, re-scanning dozens of times, but it simply would not work.  I even tried replacing the whole down-link cable with a brand new 25 foot length of RG-6 cable, but that did not help either. Finally, I had to re-connect the TV back to the 30-year old yagi antenna (also in my attic) in order to restore 6 of the 9 the stations in my area. With the new, modern design and all of the great reviews this antenna has, I was hoping to receive more channels with it, not less.  Perhaps I just got a bad one - but this is very disappointing because my HOA rules won't allow me to mount an antenna on my roof top. An expensive lesson.

title: Okay Bluetooth Device, Half A$$ Software!
text:
I bought this product from another website. I actually bought 2, one for my desktop and one for my laptop. I first installed the device on my desktop using the software provided from Trendnet's website and all went well. No popups asking for registration or data limits imposed.

A couple of weeks later, I installed the second device on my laptop. The install went well and I was able to connect to my bluetooth speaker with no problem. A few minutes later the connection drops and a popup comes in stating that I may have been victim to counterfeiting and that the serial no or whatever has been duplicated. I follow the link to the software mfg website and they have this page setup to clear confusion it seems alot of people are having with the software and its counterfeit protection scheme which causes this popup to appear. Well it says to download version 8 and all you will have to do is enter the device's serial no. Well that version is not being offered but their latest version 10 is which cost $28...BS!!! I know I didn't use the one I installed on the desktop because the one I installed on the laptop was still sealed in it's packaging!

So after reading a review here from someone else who had the same issue, I uninstalled the product's software, restarted the machine, plugged in the bluetooth adapter and Windows automatically searched, found, and installed the proper software. A reboot later and all is well (so far, I will keep you updated).

Also know that the adapter fits VERY tight in the USB slot. Take care when installing and removing from the USB slot.

title: tough camera
text:
I bought this camera for a trip to Hawaii mostly because of its price. There aren't too many options out there for water proof cameras that take 1080p video and has large LCD viewfinders, all for under $180.

The battery life is excellent. During my 7 day trip, it never ran out on me during the middle of the day and I took plenty of pictures and videos.

I went snorkeling and kayaking on 3 separate occasions and took the camera down maybe 6 ft under water, banged it on corrals a few times by accident, left some scratches on both the plastic and metal exterior, but there were no leak or moisture inside the lens, LCD, or the battery compartment. At the end of the day I just soak and rinse the camera in tap water as instructed in the manual.

The picture quality isn't great, some of the pictures actually look no better than pictures I took with my cellphone. But I kind was expecting it so it wasn't too big a let down.

It also lacks manual adjustment to things like shutter speed, exposure time, or white balance. But it does provide quite a lot automatic moods, ranging from panorama mode where you can specify field of view and just scan the scenery on the fly (useful), to several underwater video mode (decent), to taking self portrait of 2+ people based on proximity of faces using face recognition (funny but doesn't work well).

Minus 1 star for the unspectacular picture quality and lack of manual settings, 4 stars for the toughness and the price.

Edit: changing my review from a 4 star to 2 star. After not using it for 2 years, I dusted it off in hope of selling it. Upon turning it on, I found the LCD screen has several black bars running down the middle. Prior to putting it away I exercised all the precautions including soaking it in fresh water to get all the salt out and cleaning it. Then, just recently I took another look at it, ready to take it to e-recycling, and noticed the battery has become bloated. I paid around $150 for the camera, I suppose it's OK for a week long trip since it has better image quality than a disposable, but I wished I had paid more for a higher quality action camera like the GoPro, which I image I could get more use out of today.

title: NETGEAR Wireless Router - N900 Dual Band Gigabit
text:
Hello - I live in a 2400 square foot house. We have our wireless router downstairs and our laptops are on the main level 1 flight up. We had SEVERAL problems with our old router and we would have to go down and reset it continuously. We finally convinced Comcast to send over their best and brightest technician who did a once over our entire setup. He helped us realize it wasn't our cable internet but more likely our router. He recommended we get a 40-50 dollar NETGEAR at Walmart.

I'm the type of guy that likes to buy something 1x and have it last for as long as possible. So I'm willing to spend a little more for a great piece of equipment that will last for 4-6-10 years. This router was just north of $160 US dollars. But I must tell you, this router is awesome. Looking down at my connection speed upstairs with MS Outlook for work, Firefox running 5 browsers, and my 2nd laptop connected too, I still have 65MB. I often range from 125mb-175mb. Something important many people don't realize is that anything thing with a motor will degrade your wireless signal. So if your spouse turns on the microwave, a vacuum cleaner, your dryer, dish washer, just about anything it will immediately decrease your signal 20-50mb. Because this router has such a high frequency, even when my wife turns on a piece of equipment or I am doing heavy use for work, I never drop below 40-50mb. I hope this helps, I strongly recommend this n900.

title: Best native E-mount lens for Sony NEX
text:
I was kind of skeptical that this lens wouldn't be that significantly better than Sony 18-55mm f3.5-5.6 kit lens for the Sony NEX system. However, after trying out the lens, it's probably the best native lens for the system. It's almost glued onto my Sony NEX 5N most of the time. It's quite sharp though you need to stop down a little a bit maybe around f2.2 from images to start getting pretty sharp. It lacks that 3D super micro-contrast look you might get from using an adapted Contax G 45mm f2.0 but it's still quite good.

From actually using the lens, this lens is superior at short to mid-range distances but doesn't do as well as infinity. Rendering is quite fantastic. It also focuses pretty close probably at around 6 inches. The manual focus ring on this lens is mechanically best I've tried for native NEX lenses with very smooth action.

The only negatives for lens is that it's rather expensive for the price. For the price, I expected it to have a faster aperture of f1.4. I would also preferred that it had OSS or a type of image stabilization even though that's usually not necessary for wide angle lenses.

title: low price = low voltage
text:
When I checked the voltages of these 10 Maxell batteries on my digital multimeter, 4 displayed 1.479v or less, 2 displayed between 1.492v and 1.496v, 1 displayed 1.520v, and 3 displayed between 1.584v and 1.586v. Pretty bad when more than 66% of the batteries fail to meet the 1.5v voltage show on the package. Can't even blame it on an expiration date, since there was none anywhere on the packaging.

I also sent this information to the seller (Best Price Mirror, Blue Jay, CA) as well, and I will update this review with any response and/or action they provide.

Update: 10/5/13 - I received an exceptionally prompt reply to my inquiry stating "We feel badly they do not seem to within specs as we purchase them twice monthly from Maxell". Although it was not entirely clear who was responding - Best Price Mirror or Amazon Marketplace - they also issued a refund, and noted that they are forwarding the information to Maxell. title: Works well, but Big in Size
text: The perils of buying non-Apple 8-pin Lightning cables are well documented.  I took a chance on one of these (no reviews yet) because they are "Apple Certified" and less than half the price ($12 vs. $29) of a genuine Apple 6ft/2m cable.  The cable arrived in a high quality plastic case and appears to be a robust construction.  When compared to the 3ft/1m cable that came with my iPad Air, the cable is larger in diameter (4mm vs. 3mm) and the molded "shell" of the 8-pin connector is also bigger in size (W-12mm, L-14mm, T-5mm).  The bigger plug has not been an issue with the cases on both my iPad Air and iPhone 5S, but you should carefully measure to ensure that the larger plug is not going to be a fit issue.  Overall, a very nice cable at a great price point.

Never the less the weight feels good I've carried it on my shoulder for 2 hour long walk/photo sessions, and not only was it not an issue but the foam padding was a nice extra.

The main joint at the top between the lets and head is treated aluminum not plastic so it's got some strength where it needs it. I've used a track rail on this to do a lot of macro photography, and it was incredibly stable even for HDR shots. As a hobbyist and not a pro I can't appreciate the value here for just under $100, I can't find another Tripod as well built and load bearing as this. The head has 3 removable handles and pivots in XYZ axis, you'll have to eye ball accuracy but it's still fantastic to have that versatility.

I highly recommend for anyone wanting something that's incredible value and quality for the price. If you have a $500+ camera with a $1-200 lens please invest in a good Tripod, not only will this provide stability and security for you equipment but extend your photograph range as well.

title: Excellent! -- Say goodbye to cheap external HDDs!
text:
Given that hard drive failures cause endless hassles and wasted time and that ready-made external hard drive units are built using cheapo (failure-prone) hard-drives, I decided to go the route of building my own using this enclosure. I purchased a 2TB Western Digital Black Caviar drive (these drives still have a 5-year warranty!).
Assembling the drive was a 5-minute job. It took longer to take it out of the package than to pop the hard drive into the enclosure and have it ready to run. As other reviewers pointed out, the drive retaining clip is flimsy plastic, but so long as you don't drop this thing, it should last fine.
The USB 3 connection is blazing fast. Cooling is excellent. The fans are audible, but very quiet. Using a freeware app which permits reading information from the drive (including current temperature), I verified that it runs just as cool as my internal hard drives, and this despite the fact that my internal hard drives sit behind an 8-inch diameter cooling fan at the front of a very well ventilated case. One reservation I have about this unit is that the cooling fans are always on, even when the hard drive powers down, leading to more rapid dust accumulation in the unit, more frequent cleaning being required, and I would presume, more rapid component wear. Since the enclosure does possess a large and easy to use power switch (on the back of the unit, however), I simply turn it off when not in use, as I only occasionally use it for backing up new files resulting from video editing.
In response to a common concern about hard drives in external enclosures -- yes, the drive does automatically power down after having been idle. I never measured how long it takes to automatically power down, but seems like about half an hour. I don't know if this is a built-in function of the enclosure or whether this is controlled by Windows 7, but it does work, so this enclosure need not leave you with a hard drive unnecessarily running 24/7.
Would have given this nifty little device a 5-star rating, save for the issues of delicate construction and cooling fans being always on. Am planning on purchasing another one of these units without hesitation.

It works great with my Win7.5 phone - I just push the big button and it activates my voice command. It works better over BT than it does by regular microphone - it rarely misinterprets my voice commands with the headset. I don't have to unlock my phone first to do voice dialing, though I do have to unlock it to do the voice search. One thing I don't like about Win 7.5 is how easy it is to accidently hang up or press the speaker phone while holding it to my ear, so the headset makes phone calls less frustrating.

The multipoint probably works fine with two actual phones. I could get the headset to pair to my computer over basic stuff, but the comptuer doesn't have the drivers I need to make it work as a headset for phone calls. Not the headset's fault, but I could have bought a less expensive headset for just my phone. And the stereo feature is interesting, but I don't listen to music on my phone all that much, mostly just podcasts and those are fine in mono.

It's comfortable enough. Easy to switch the earpiece to either side. attractive enough.

With all that I would have given it a 4, but Samsung lost another star for the failure of its documentation. Yeah, I'm one of those people who actually read the manuals. This one sucked. So small I needed a magnifying glass. So confusing I had to infer a lot to get things the way I wanted them. And they didn't post a copy on line, which I consider 100% necessary because I don't hang onto the things.

I like it well enough to keep using it. But I'd buy one with more basic features next time.

title: This is a REAL computer - favorite tablet yet!
text:
My wife has an iPad (3rd generation) and I have an ASUS TF300 Android tablet. Both are great devices, but are completely limited as tablet devices (which is good for ease of use, but that comes with constraints). For a brand new computer illiterate person, an Apple product is a great way to go. But for those of us who have been using Windows for the last 20 years, you may have been wishing there was a device that has the best of all worlds. This is it.

I was hesitant to dive into the Surface tablet when that came out, because it did not have a normal version of Windows. I'm still a Windows XP holdout on my home machines (desktop and laptops). But this Dell Venue Pro tablet has a TRUE version of Windows 8.1 With a quick swipe (or button press) you have the traditional blank slate of a traditional Windows desktop, right down to the trashcan. You can install any Windows software (that runs on 8.1) on this device. So far it has been able to run anything I throw at it with ease.

I love the Google Chrome browser, so my first download was Google Chrome. It took about 2 minutes to download and install it. There were no screwball "app stores" to deal with; I just directly downloaded the regular desktop browser version and installed it. The beauty of this tablet is that it CAN run "apps" (that you download the same way you would on a phone), but you can run all of the normal Windows programs you would normally have to run on a desktop machine. The touch controls take a few minutes to learn, but works quite well (even using browsers designed for normal desktop use).

The product comes with Microsoft Office (Excel, Word, and PowerPoint). These aren't some lousy stripped down "tablet lite" versions. They are the real deal just like you would run on your desktop. There isn't an expiration date or trial period or a bait and switch (no Microsoft Works here); honestly, this thing is truly running MS Office, and with ease! The only gripe I have is that you had to enter the product key from the packaging that came with the tablet, so it wasn't pre-configured, but not a big deal. That is an incredible value, especially depending on how you plan to use this device. Otherwise, the initial setup was a breeze. Right off the bat there was a preinstalled Kindle app, and after one click (and entering my username and password) my entire Kindle library was availabe. Very nice.

Performance is incredibly snappy. Response for all screen or button presses is instant. Loads faster than my year old Asus tablet (which I love, but it just isn't snappy at all). The 32GB size does not have much extra space (only about 10GB free from the get-go). But it has an expansion port for micro SD cards, so for not much money you can have plenty of expansion (already ordered by 64GB card). The unit is well made overall. The screen is incredibly sharp (I can't imagine needing a higher resolution; at some point it just becomes a number that is meaningless, much like the megapixel rating on a camera).

The device has the Miracast technology. For about $25 I bought an HDMI wireless plug/dongle (like a thumb drive) that will display the image from the tablet on my TV. So throw in a cheap Bluetooth mouse and keyboard, and you have a full featured computer on your hands. Or you can use it to watch and stream movies on a big TV. The possibilities are endless.

This is more machine than many users would ever use, so I still advise many friends and family members to pick up a Kindle Fire or an iPad. But for the money if you are looking for a tablet that can truly behave like a PC, then give this little guy a try. HIGHLY recommended!!!

title: This lens is all about quality and bokeh
text:
There are already so many reviews about this lens, and the technical deets about the lens itself. I'll stick to the main draws.

Bokeh:

Yes, it achieves incredible bokeh at f/1.4. The DOF is very shallow at that f-stop, and you can get that buttery-smooth bokeh you desire. In addish, it has a more "rounded" out-of-focus detail than its competitors. It's aesthetically pleasing for sure.

Build quality:

Bottom line is most 50mm primes suck in build quality. They look like something that only an amateur would use. This lens is well built, durable, and hefty. The 77mm glass is oversized, that is a benefit as most aberrations occur at the outer part of the aspherical glass lens, this one eliminates those aberrations by being oversized.

Focus:

It's a fast prime, with the auto-focus there are rarely any errors. It focuses quickly and accurately.

That aspherical lens:

77mm is large for a 50mm f/1.4, as such you get to purchase a rather large and heavy duty 77mm filter for it, it's hefty, durable, and adds a great deal to that new 50mm f/1.4 lens.

How I'm using it:

This lens is a lens suitable for both a Full-frame camera, and a crop sensor camera. I'm using it on a crop sensor camera, 1.6 to be exact. That renders this lens as a 80mm lens. I considered getting an 85mm as they seem to be all the rage at this point, but that's for a full-frame, 80mm seems to be the best alternative for a crop sensor right now. I'm happy with it, it's the best quality lens I have for my camera at this point, and produces a quality bokeh, which is difficult-to-impossible to add into photos.

Complaints by the haters:

-- Well, one of which is that this lens is expensive for a f/1.4. Ok, that is true; but it's well made, durable, and is impressive in size for sure.

-- It's not as sharp as [insert lens here]. Well I can sharpen photos in Aperture and Color Efex to the point to where the photo looks like a cartoon, even with a "kit lens". Unfortunately sharpness is somewhat of an argument of years gone by. In the film SLR days sharpness was a huge deal, but today most if not all of that can be corrected/applied by post processing software. On the flip-side -- right now, it's difficult if not impossible to add in that buttery bokeh. I'm sure in time software will fix that as well in the future, but as of right now, it's not possible.

Overall:

This is a well made, durable, large sized lens. It renders very good bokeh in foreground, or background pictures. I highly recommend this lens. GET IT!

title: Very Good Radio with a Few Minor Flaws
text:
I'll start with a disclaimer. I just got my technician license about a month ago and this is my first and only radio so I don't have experience with other radios (other than reviews and comparisons). So with that out of the way here goes my review.

Knowing nothing about radios I selected this one because it was the #1 best seller on Ham Radio Outlet (it has since dropped to #2) and had very good reviews on eham.net. Plus I was familiar with the Kenwood name based on their car audio equipment. I have purchased two of them so far, one for the car and one for home.

Kenwood has always been known for good audio quality (for ham radio equipment at least) and I usually hear that I sound good with full quieting even at ~20-30 miles with low power (25 watts). It's also very sensitive when it comes to picking up distant stations. Of course this also has a lot to do with the type of antenna you have and it's position, height and RF propagation, but in my case I'm running a homemade 1/4 wave ground plane antenna (tuned to 146Mhz) in my attic, so it's about 12-15 feet off the ground. With that setup I'm able to pick up and transmit to a repeater about 50 miles away. It's a bit scratchy with the RX audio and I don't know how much power it's running, but it's still not too bad. The front facing speaker is good, but I had a speaker that I wasn't using that I plugged into the back speaker port that makes it sound better.

It's very easy to program and I didn't need any special software to program it. It did take a little while figure out some of the features like how to get a PL tone programmed in to memory (you have to tune the station, turn on CT or T, set the tone or CT, all while in VFO mode, and then put it in memory. Make when you select a tone to press the tuning knob to set it before moving on, that one took me a while to figure out). It also took me a while to figure out how to send a tone to a repeater but not have it on for receive, that's what the "T" setting is for. There's "T", "CT" and "DCS" "T" for tone, "CT" for CTCSS, and DCS. "CT" is for two-way CTCSS (or PL tone), the same tone RX and TX, "T" is for just sending a tone on TX but no tone squelch for RX. That wasn't very well documented in the manual. Before I figured this out, I had set CT in memory and the radio would squelch out everything (like it was supposed to) so I would switch from memory to VFO on the same frequency so I could hear the audio without the tone on VFO, and then back to memory so I could transmit the with the tone. It made life a lot easier when I figured that out. There are a number of repeaters in my area that have a TX only tone.

Another strength is that it scans quite fast. I currently have 22 memory channels and scans them in about 1 second or less (when there is no activity and it doesn't stop) and it can scan the whole 144-148 band pretty quick too.

My only complaints so far is that it only has two power settings high/low (25/65 watts). I would give it 5 stars if it had 2 more lower power settings, maybe something like 5/10/25/65 which is what many other mobile transceivers have. It's too bad there's not a mod out there that could accomplish that. Plus it's factory set to high power, I highly recommend setting it to low power unless you absolutely need high power. In addition, it would also be nice to be able to program the power level into memory. This radio has a global power level setting.

One thing to keep in mind though is that you'll need a hefty power supply if you're going to use this in a non-mobile environment. The manual says to get a minimum 14A power supply. I have a Pyramid PS14KX and so far so good (I don't key up all that much, and mostly on low power), but I plan to upgrade to an Astron RS-20A (or bigger) so that I've got more than enough. I was in a net where one person said they couldn't get this radio to transmit and it turned out it was because the power supply was too small (a couple amps or something like that).

Also if you plan to put it in your vehicle, make sure you hook it directly to the battery, since a cigarette lighter port isn't designed to draw 14 amps. Some will argue this, but I hooked mine directly to the battery in my Jeep to be safe. You just never know what kind of wiring was used in the vehicle and if it can handle the load that this radio will draw.

The speaker sounds okay, but here's a little trick. The radio has a speaker output on the back and takes a 3.5mm mono jack. Go on to craigslist or ebay and search for a decent center channel speaker for $20-30 (or whatever you want to pay) since those are tuned for voice audio. You could also use any speaker you have laying around. Then go to Radio Shack, get a 3.5 mm (or 1/8 inch) mono jack and some speaker wire (if you don't have those already), solder the wire to the jack and hook up your speaker and you'll get an instant audio upgrade over the speaker in the radio. You can use any speaker you want and it's a lot better than paying $80 for a ham radio speaker. This works best in your home, but I've also had success hooking that same jack into my car stereo using a tape adapter with a mono to stereo converter jack (found at Radio Shack). Just be careful with the volume on the radio if you do that, start all the way down and slowly bring it up until it sounds good otherwise you'll distort it.

UPDATE: A good speaker to pair with this (or any other rig) is the KLH 970A. It's a huge improvement over the stock speaker (if you're using it as a base rig) and it's somewhat rugged because it's an indoor/outdoor speaker. I also use it with my Kenwood handheld (TH-K20, also a good radio). If you happen to buy the Kenwood TM-V71A, I believe it has two speaker outputs (for it's two channels) so then you'll have a pair of the KLH's to use with it.

Overall it's been a great radio and I haven't had any problems thus far.

UPDATE: Not actually a review update, but as far as prices go, try Main Trading Company (mtcradio) seems to have one of the lower prices on this. I've seen as low as $137 (normal appears to be $149) and free shipping. Also check Ham City and Ham Radio Outlet, between those three you'll find the best price.

title: Very good protection at a reasonable price
text:
I needed a case that offered excellent protection, as we have a 3 year old who would be using our Nexus 7. So far the best test has been when the 3 year old stood up on the coffee table, lifted the N7 to head height, and dropped the device to the floor (before running away squealing, of course). The N7 bounced without a scuff to the device or the case.

This is a very thick silicone case. I've had silicone cases for other devices, and none of them really compare. This is the rubber room treatment. It should be noted that the case adds significant thickness and weight, but it offers excellent protection. It's not the kind of case I'd want on a device that was going in and out of my pocket, like a phone, but size is less of an issue for me on the tablet. Because the case protrudes so high up around the rim in front, it offers pretty good protection for the screen, too, as long as you drop it on something mostly flat.

The case also stays on well. My son hasn't been able to pull it off. It is in no way flimsy, unlike most silicone cases. Cutouts line up well. It's a good fit around the sides and around buttons and holes.

I went with the blue. It's very vivid. Pretty close to the picture on my screen.

The negatives are minor. The cover over the buttons makes it harder to press them. Pushing the power or volume takes a little extra force. The silicone that wraps around the back of the device (which is quite a bit thinner than the edges, but I don't think that's a negative, as it's not doing much work) isn't snug against the back. That means when you have your fingers on the back (like when you're holding it) you feel a little bit of play between the case and the device. It's the only thing that makes this case feel at all cheap. It's not a big deal, and I don't see how it affects functionality of the case, but it's there. Not a big enough deal for me to take off a star from the overall rating.

Overall I love the case. I looked around a lot, and I didn't see anything offering near the protection for the price. If you are looking for something beefy, and you don't mind the extra thickness and heft, I highly recommend it.

UPDATE:
I just wanted to provide a brief update after a couple months more use. Our Nexus 7 has become almost exclusively the 3 year old's device. My wife and I hardly touch it, except to add apps, charge it, and occasionally clean it. Our 1 year old also occasionally gets her hands and teeth on it. This thing has been dropped, THROWN, stepped on, chewed on, had food rubbed on... you name it. All many times. Really, this thing couldn't get much more abuse if we were trying. We've washed the case and screen a few times, and right after a wash, it all looks brand new. Not a scuff to be found. This is turning out to be one of the best products we've bought, especially at the price point when you compare to other tough cases.

One other note about the buttons. As other reviews and I have mentioned, the case does make the buttons a little harder to press, but my 3 year old still has no trouble pressing them. So for us it's just a minor inconvenience to push a little harder, but it doesn't affect the functionality.

title: Absolutely beautiful
text:
Bought this TV a few days ago and I am blown away by how gorgeous it is. Not just the image quality, but the hardware itself. The tiny bezel immediately sold me and after reading reviews I knew I wanted it. However I was a bit scared of getting one with the dreaded flashlight effect, but mine does not have that at all. This is one of the reasons I purchased it locally instead of via Amazon, so that I could exchange it much faster and not deal with shipping etc, if needed (luckily I didn't have any problems). The other reason being several local stores were selling it for the same price as Amazon so even with Prime, it was much faster to just buy locally (patience is not a virtue of mine).

The image quality it outstanding and the tiny bezel really makes the picture pop. It just looks like it's floating in mid-air. Absolutely love it.

I didn't know anything about how the "magic" remote actually worked, reviews here seem mixed, but I really like it. It's like a mouse for your computer but it doesn't matter where you point, or if it's pointing down, up, whatever - it still works, and being able to recenter it by shaking it is a nice touch. Entering in text is much faster than other typical methods too (e.g. on PS3 or Xbox, having to press left/right/down/etc to get to each character - this is much faster than that).

I've seen a few 3D movies and they don't really do anything for me, but wow, 3D games on the PS3 are insane! Currently I only have a few games that support 3D (WipEout HD, Motorstorm 3D Rift, and Uncharted 3) but the 3D adds a lot to the experience - especially racing games. Super super fun!

I appreciate that the set comes with 6 sets of glasses. Not that I have many "TV parties" but that has been a sticking point it seems since 3D TV's came out, that they typically only came with one or two pairs and extra pairs were super expensive. So it's nice that they include this many sets of glasses. And I like that they're passive instead of active so you never have to worry about batteries or resyncing. The glasses look pretty dorky but whatever :P

Having wifi built in along with some streaming apps is great. I was thinking about buying a Roku recently but now with this there is no need, since Netflix is built right in. I do wish they had Amazon Instant Video, previous LG models did, not sure why this one doesn't but not the hugest deal in the world since my PS3 can play it.

The internet browser is kind of slow but I don't care about that really, I've never spent much time with the browser in the PS3 so not planning to use this one much either. However it's nice to know it's there in case I do want to use it.

What I also like is if you're watching TV or something from another device (PS3 etc) [basically anything other than streaming video on the TV itself], you can still use the LG menu system to do other things and it keeps the show you're watching in a "picture in picture" window in the top left corner. It's just a nice touch. Unfortunately it doesn't work the streaming apps built in though (e.g. Netflix). If you want to use the menu system, it completely exits out. Not a huge deal but once you get used to it working fine with TV and PS3 etc, it's slightly annoying.

The only real complaint I have is with the 240hz - I really hate the effect this has on video, particularly movies. I knew this before I bought it, as I've seen it on other people's TV's, but I thought if I turned it off it would stay off. However it seems like whenever you change any other settings related to video (e.g. brightness), it always gets turned back on so then I have to go turn it off again, which takes about 5 clicks through the menus. I wish there was a way to turn it off permanently because I absolutely hate it and will never want to use it. But now that I have the TV calibrated to just how I like it, I don't expect that to be an issue very often going forward.

Overall, I completely love this TV!

title: RCA RC142 Large Display Clock Radio with USB Charging
text:
I needed a clock radio with an AUX input so came to Amazon to see what was available.

I bought a Westclox Tech AM/FM clock radio from Amazon. The Westclox radio was poorly made, would not pick up even the strongest of stations - even the station with a radio tower 2 miles from me. The AUX input on the Westclox did not turn off via the sleep function. I am in the process of returning that unit to Amazon.

In the meantime, I still needed a clock radio with an AUX input. Went to Walmart and found the RCA RC142 radio.

I thought the Westclox was poorly made but the RCA RC142 was worse. The On/Off button was stuck down - I had to move it from side to side to get it to pop up to the start position so that I could turn it on or off.

The time set button would not select the lock position so the display stayed on the time set for Alarm 1.

Reception was poor - once again I could not pick up the local station whose tower was 2 miles away.

Tuning required a magnifying glass to see the frequencies printed on the tuning button. There is no vernier so you have little idea of what frequency you are tuning to.

The instruction sheet was written in about 10 different languages in very small print.

I hate it when I have to sift through multiple languages to find how to work something.

It seems that any RCA device I have purchased in the recent past has been poorly made and prone to premature failure. I took it back to Walmart and got my money back but I still needed a clock radio with an AUX input.

I went back to the electronics section of Walmart to look for another radio. I found an Emerson Smart Set Dual alarm radio with line-in [[ASIN:B000WNUGXQ Emerson Dual Alarm Clock Radio Amfm Smartset]]. I was skeptical since like RCA, Emerson had once been a very good brand of radio but my recent experience with Emerson had been less that spectacular.

I got home with the Emerson, opened the box and found a carefully packaged device.

On opening the Packaging and removing the radio, I found that it appeared to be well built. The finish was good, the buttons were solidly installed. For $20 and change it was more than I expected.

I plugged it in and the correct time appeared on the screen - no messing around trying to find out how to set the time. (The correct time is programmed in for Eastern Time. You will need to adjust for other time zones)

The correct day and date were already programmed into the radio.

I do not think it is an atomic clock thing but rather a finely tuned clock circuit that produced such an accurate time on start up.

A button type battery comes installed to provide backup for when the power is out.

The instructions are written in English - only.

The AUX input is controlled by the sleep function.

The tuning frequencies appear on the display as you turn the tuning knob and the thing picks up a station 30 miles from where I live.

I suggest that you pass on the RCA and look at the Emerson if you need a clock radio.

title: Good price, and this is a good fast drive
text:
My log in to 'usable desktop' time on a Win 7, i5 desktop went from 45 seconds to about 15 seconds (after about five boot cycles). I replaced a WD 2TB Black with this Seagate 2TB SSHD. The WD Black is a good drive, I just wanted to move it into a different machine. I am glad I did now.

Boot up time is important, but much more important to me is overall disk speed and acoustics. As measured with a disk read/write tool, this drive measured sequential reads at 194 MB/s and writes at 138 MB/s. Unless you put your ear up against the computer, this drive is silent.

The only thing that might be viewed as a minus, is that this drive runs hot, temperature wise. It runs about as hot as the WD Black. It is definitely not for conserving power.

I will update this if any problems develop. At this point in time, I am 100% happy with this purchase.

title: Awesome keyboard. Good Mouse. Don't like the click wheel.
text:
This key boards easy, short, keystroaks are really confortable on the hands and wrists and allow for significantly increased typing speed.

They curve of the keyboard gives many ergonomic benfits but is subtle enought that it is much easier for ergo keyboard novices to adapt to than other ergo keyboard configurations.

Those mouse laster system works better than any I have used and I have used alot.

The Shape of the mouse for hand comfort is a phenominal compromise for multiple users that range from small to large hands.

However, I just dont understand why microsoft continues to put out mouses with click wheels that dont ratchet but instead have a continuous smooth scroll. It's so hard to transition between fine movements and long scrolling movements with this type of click wheel. It is so inconsistent with it's sensetivity, and you can just barely touch it when you are using a drop down menu in a web brouser and it will change your selection. They side scroll clicking function is vary vague and unsatisfying feeling. it's hard to explain but I just really dislike this click wheel. Logitech's click wheel cluch solution is far far superior. click a convenient toggle button and the wheel goes to a satsifying precice ratcheting motion. click it again and you get a free wheeling spin great for racting through long pages and documents.

The click wheel is almost bad enought for me to take away two starts, however for those that are not picky about click wheels, the rest of the package is fantastic, confortable, and quick to use.

title: Easy on the Ears
text:
Good product at a good price.

I use these to officiate at athletic events and communicate with other officials. I have done 400 to 500 events that take hours at a time. Sometimes I will do as many as 9 games in a weekend. I have found that ear buds, or ear pieces that hang off you ear can be extremely uncomfortable after hours of use. I never have that problem with these. So I actual buy the radios that match these headsets, instead of getting headsets to match the radio. I also like pushing a button on the radio to talk with these, rather than having to find a microphone on my collar and lifting it to speak. That leaves one hand free to make notes while speaking.

Some people and athletic associations do not like these because they are more visible than other alternatives. However, they fit nicely under a cap if that is allowed without harming comfort. The boom can be adjusted so that you can change ears for the speaker.

The earpiece has soft foam so that it does not hurt the ear after hours of use. However, after time the foam may rip or tear causing one to buy another one. At this price, that is a minor drawback to pay for the extra comfort these provide.

Be careful to match the headset to the actual radio you have purchased. This headset does not work with all radios.
