title: So so audio, definitely not for audio books
text:
I bought this because I am tired of fighting with the wire attached to my Aux in on my head unit when it is attached to my iPhone 4. I really wanted to get a [[ASIN:B004KPLS7K Griffin Technology BlueTrip AUX for iPhone and Smartphones]] but it is a bit pricey. So I opted to try this.

To be honest, this unit is a disgrace to my Bose system.

The sound quality was not that great, with a lot of static coming through. This is somewhat masked when you are playing music, but if you are attempting to play an audio book or maybe something orchestral you are going to be annoyed. And the bass is majorly lacking when using this unit.

The connection did not seem to be consistent. The audio would come through at what seemed to be clear but very frequently static would take over. Especially if you move the phone around.

I tried this with many different stations with the same results.

This unit will NOT transmit phone call audio to your speakers, which isn't a problem for me, but I wanted to test it so I could let you know if that's what you were planning to accomplish with this unit.

THIS IS A BIGGIE AND WHY I GAVE THIS UNIT A LOW RATING:

If you do not transmit any audio through this unit for about 15 seconds, it will disengage the connection between itself and the station you are tuned into and screeching loud static will play through without warning until you happen to play something to re-engage the connection.

If you don't understand what I mean, let me put it this way... You plug the unit into your iPhone, tune into the station you have set on the transmitter, and the connection is made between the unit and station. Now that the connection is made you hear silence (pending you have a good connection). Now you need to find a song to play. Well you better hurry up and play it within 15 seconds because if you don't the transmitter will go into standby and static will come blaring through your speakers. Quite alarming!

Volume control on the iPhone is disabled when the transmitter is connected. Some may think that you don't need volume controls on the iPhone because you can just use the head unit's volume. The problem is, the volume being transmitted seems to have been set low from this device. Even with my head unit volume turned all the way up, it is does not come close to the loudness of a CD, the Radio, or the Aux connection in my car.

I really wanted to like this because of all the good reviews and the concept was pretty neat. Plus I HATE wires everywhere! But this thing is useless.

I am not an audiophile nor am I picky, but you really cant enjoy music or audio books with this device.

I may have to suck it up and go for the Griffin. Either that or I'll just deal with the wired connection, but I will not deal with this.

ALSO! Since the price was so good I happened to buy 2 of these transmitters because a buddy of mines CD Player broke in his car with no Aux input. That being said, I received 2 completely different units odd enough. And the one wasn't meant for and did not work with an iPhone 4. The second one was packaged much nicer and it said right on the packaging that it did work with the iPhone 4. The button placement was also different on the 2 units.

That being said, if you do decide to purchase this device, this is one of those Amazon orders where 'you never know what your gonna get'. So good luck!

Hope this helps!

title: I sold my T3i and bought a Sony NEX -- no regrets!
text:
I sold my T3i in search of a compact camera that takes crisp pictures in RAW while also capable of shooting HD video-- without the weight, bulk, and "Hey, I'm a tourist!" look of the dSLR.

I thought I was going to go Olympus PM-2, but wanted a tilted screen. The PL-5 felt awkward and cheap. I also realized how much I prefer buttons and wheels for menus rather than poking around on a touchscreen.

I then looked at Fuji cameras, the X series -- beautiful and unique images, and the cameras felt great and solid in my hands -- but the lens selection is limited and VERY pricey. No thanks.

Enter Sony NEX. I haven't held any models aside from the NEX-3N, but it feels great and well-made. No obnoxious touchscreen, and a menu that's easy to understand.

I bought a NEX-3N body new from a dealer on Amazon for $190 and skipped the kit lens. I picked up a $30 RainbowImaging 35MM lens for portrait shots and coughed up $200 for a 19mm Sigma lens for landscapes.

I've only had the camera for three days, but I've been blown away by the quality of video when paired with the fun little 35mm lens. It truly looks like it was filmed with a dSLR -- and all for less than $250! I cannot wait to take this little guy on my travels.

The only thing I wish this camera really had was a mount for an external microphone, but I knew that before I made my purchase -- so I can't be too upset.

**EDIT: Bizarre flaw in this particular camera -- whenever you take a picture, it emits a fake shutter sound from the bottom speaker in addition to the actual shutter noise. It's quite loud, tacky, and cannot be disabled. Several NEX-3N owners have been campaigning for a firmware update, but Sony continues to claim it's the "real" shutter.

If you buy this item and you hear the solid tone from any of the bands, slow down immediately because it is probably a cop gunning you down. Most of my experiences have been last second brake slams to avoid a ticket has worked but after a while of never being sure, you will want an escort or valentine.

title: Rock Star Potential but Buggy Firmware
text:
This router should be a rock star based on its features list, but it's just a little above average because of connectivity issues related to the firmware. Hopefully, they will get the firmware software correct someday and this router can live up to its true potential. The good thing is that NetGear has been investing the time and money into updating the software for the WNDR3800. I originally bought the router because the previous wireless router was only getting about 1 Mbps throughput instead of the 18 Mbps I would get on a wired device. This new router allows me to get that same 18 Mbps throughput wirelessly. So I'm now getting the internet connection I pay for wirelessly. Yeah!

Features I like:
A handy feature that is available now and wasn't when I bought the router is the ability to set up a USB printer as an AirPrint device. This allows you to print directly from your iPad/iPhone/iTouch device. Just upgrade the router software and you'll have that feature. The NetGear Genie software is also nice. I especially like that you can see what channels your neighbor WiFi networks are using so that you can pick a different channel to prevent competition for the same air space. The network map is also a great feature that allows you to see who is on your network and what signal strength they are connected with.

Past Issues with Router:
All issues have been with the 2.4 Ghz networks. The 5.0 Ghz networks have worked flawlessly. After going through many firmware upgrades and downgrades, this router has been fairly stable for months running V1.0.0.24. When friends come over with their iPhones and connect to the Guest Network, it always seems like I have to reboot the router for them so they can connect. I tried the V1.0.0.34 software but had issues with two Android phones running 2.3.4. They had an issue with the batteries draining overnight because they were constantly trying to connect to the WiFi network. I downgraded to V1.0.0.24 and that problem went away. I've seen the battery drain issue with Apple's iOS 4.x too with my old router, so this isn't just an Android issue. As of this review, I see that firmware V1.0.0.40 is available and is supposed to address some of the past issues I've had so I'll have to try that version of the software and see if we can turn this router into a rock star afterall.

Customer support from Netgear:
Customer support was about average to work with. They did help me make some setting changes that helped and they are good about responding back to you within a day or two. It seems like most of their support staff is foreign which I don't like because there is a immediate language barrier that you have to fight through to solve highly technical issues. Also, when I was having the battery drain issues, they wanted to pass off their connectivity issues to Apple or Android. Just own up to the issue and solve it. I understand that Android and Apple may make software changes that affect how the router interfaces, but NetGear is in the business of connecting these devices so they need to handle that better. It seems like their software development is on-board with this thinking because they keep releasing software to resolve these issues, but the support team needs to get onboard too.

title: Install fix for an otherwise great modem
text:
Update: This comment refers to Firmware version CAC001-31.30L.8. There is a newer firmware version available circa November 2014. Perhaps this new firmware fixes the below issues, as at least one commenter to this review says it does. Upgrade to the new firmware by going into your router's management page and go to Utilities>Upgrade Firmware.

We've had two of these C1000A's, both with the same problem. New out of the box, they install easily, but once you've entered PPP username and pw into the router's config setup, it gets stuck there. You can't change it. So if you've moved to a new DSL service/account or have bought this used, you can't update it to match your new info. I spent nearly 2 hours with CenturyLink tech support and finally got to the bottom of the issue between both my and their troubleshooting.

To erase and be able to update PPP login info:
(Worked for my CenturyLink account, YMMV)

* Go to router's config page (192.168.0.1)
* Go to "Utilities"
* On left menu, choose "Restore Default", then click "Restore Modem to Factory Default State"
(note: hard reset with the reset button on the back did not work for me, it reset everything but PPP username/pw)
* Wait for modem to reboot
* Go to "Advanced Setup"
* On left menu, choose "WAN Settings", then verify:
* ISP Protocol is "auto select" and Protocol Selected is "PPPoE"
* Enter your PPP username and password as given to you from your ISP
* Verify or choose enable for "PPP Auto Connect" and disable for "PPP Credentials Not Required"
* IP Addressing Type should be "Dynamic IP" and DNS Type should be "Dynamic DNS"
* Click Apply

Your PPP settings should now be saved and stick!

If now your config menu says "connected to DSL" and "not connected to internet", try these two things:

* Wait 5 minutes and see if the Internet light on the modem turns green, if not then try:
* go to install.centurylink.net (follow the prompts)
(if the link is not showing above it is: install onedot centurylink onedot net)

The range is great, speed is great and other than the buggy firmware, this works great. I don't use most of the other fancy features of the modem. Hope they update the firmware soon. It would be nice to have a longer timeout for the config setup menu.

title: This is the one!
text:
After purchasing all the top zoom lenses (14-24,24-70, and even a Nikon Edge85 for 2600mm of glory)
I quickly realized the importance of glass in the elements as many do.

Moving to a 35mm prime and a 85mm prime (1.4) I figured I had everything I needed for solid professional images. Occasionally pulling out the 14-24 for that super wide yet large focal plane - it works great for tight conditions and shooting the stars.

Then I met the 24-pce. I wanted ultimately as much manual control over my cameras (D4, D800E) so the next logical step was perspective control. And this my friends, is the holy grail of "fun".

Not only can you get easy to stitch panoramas by just shifting, but because of the perspective control you can shift to ensure lines are straight from edge to edge - which is highly noticeable on something like the 14-24.

Finally I can take pictures that have solid lines from edge to edge, which opens the doors to so many creative shots from simple things like fence posts in a row to capturing the magnificent architecture/landscapes you want to be accurately shot.

4 stars because they could have done something different with knobs to allow the D800-E to mount with out first mounting to the D4 and rotating the lens to invert the TILT in order to properly slide/lock the lens to the body. This gets more disorienting when you can only rotate the glass one way because of the D800 hood, which keeps the buttons on their "opposite side" as you might be use to on a "D4" where the shift knob can be located at the top near the hood, instead of under the body. Equally when you try to loosen or tighten the shifting lock nut, when its under the hood it can be hard to deal with.

Overall the glass is very sharp and vibrant, it takes some basic understanding to operate the lens for a desired effect which might take more patience than most "ehem subjects" might have patience for.

Tripod is highly recommended, but if you are really good at placing that focal plane and spot checking a zoomed in portion for focus - its a possible carry around lens.

Other than the simple toon town characteristics people associate to this lens, its main function is to correct perspective - but in being able to shift the focus plane you gain some amazing new capabilities.

For example you can shift the lens down, leave the aperture WIDE OPEN, and you can get the rocks to the sunset in focus. On a traditional lens you would have to stop down to F22 to ensure the rock is sharp, and any tree's in the distance - but we all know what is lost shooting at F22 - so this is the major game changer for some of my creative shots requiring wider areas of focus.

All in all, for what elements exist in this optic and the capabilities - its a 5 star lens.

However, lens clarity needs to make a jump up.
If this glass does not operate well on a D800 because of focal clarity at the position of the sensor - then Nikon needs to come up with some better glass to make use of that pixel density. It has been disappointing having such an arsenal of glass and sensors - only to see massive blurring at the edges on the D800. So if this is to be a professional lens, it needs to perform in relationship for the professional bodies they are mounted to.

With the prices of SSDs dropping, I recently upgraded the hard drive on my laptop to a 256GB SSD. Anyone looking into switching to SSDs will quickly learn that you have to make sure you back-up your SSD since a SSD will generally not give you any warning of impending failure as a conventional hard drive often does. They just die, so you need to be prepared for a worst case scenario. Knowing that, I decided to use the hard drive I pulled from the laptop as an external back-up drive. Of course I needed a 2.5" enclosure to do that, resulting in this purchase.

The Acomdata enclosure perfectly meets my needs. It was very inexpensive and the quality well exceeds what I expected at this price point. As other reviewers have noted, the aluminum case does a nice job of dissipating heat. I also like the fact that the HDD is securely mounted on the enclosure's circuit board when installed, unlike the cheaper enclosures (and even some of the comparably prices ones).

I have not gone to the trouble of benchmarking performance but I have had no problems with data transfers either using the USB cable (provided) or the eSATA connection (the eSATA cable must be purchased separately). The USB cable provides two USB connectors going to the computer; one primary connector for power and data, and the other being an auxiliary power connector. At least in my case, I have not needed to use the auxiliary USB power connector. Likewise, using the eSATA connection, all I needed was the primary USB connector for power. I used the eSATA connection when I created my back-up 27GB SSD drive image and it worked like a champ.

Personally, I think the USB connection should be satisfactory for most situations (storing pictures, music and videos to free up space on the SSD) and I plan on using the eSATA connection only when I need to deal with either a lot of files or really big files such as the drive image just because I'd rather not deal with a lot of cables connected to my laptop.

Bottom line is this enclosure is a quality product that performs well at a very reasonable price. Highly recommended!

title: Not good enough, even for a child...
text:
I have not owned a telescope within at least the past 20 years. I have always had a large interest in space, especially planetary. So, you can imagine the level of anticipation that I had when my Celestron 70AZ arrived. Everything looked good (from a visual standpoint of the scope and tripod) upon arrival. However, there was one enormous drawback... No matter what I located in the evening sky the telescope failed to "hold" the object within it's view. No matter what I tried the scope always sank downward and lost sight of what I was trying to view. I was able to view Saturn, Venus and the Moon HOWEVER when I was able to the image always moved in the sight due to the fact that I physically had to try and hold the scope to stabilize it enough so the object was not lost. Also, when you do find an object such as Saturn, Jupiter or Venus do not expect to see a quality image through this scope. I tried it with a combination of several different lenses, a barlow lens and even planetary filters and could not make out any contrast of colors in Jupiter whatsoever. If all you are looking to view is the moon, this might be for you. Anything else, forget it, a decent pair of binoculars will yield quite similar results.

Bottom line: Due to the telescope not being able to hold onto an object I find it to be useless and therefor defective. I returned this scope and ordered a better one.

title: Ramsey SA-7 kit worked great on my 1951 five-tube AM radio...
text:
I purchased this kit locally at an electronics hobby store to use with my "All-American Five" 5-tube radio. The early tube radios need a really long antenna OR an RF pre-amp like this one. The radio now picks up three strong stations instead of only one before, and eight weak stations instead of only three before. That's using an indoor 35' L-shaped long-wire antenna. I used a 9-volt battery for the pre-amps' power source (you will need to supply your own battery connector). You can use up to 15 volts.

Note: You will have to solder one tiny surface mount resistor measuring 1x2 mm or so on the back side. That's the only real challenge in the kit, but with care, tweezers, and a clean iron you can do it. They will send you another resistor free if you botch it. You MUST have some means of securing the tiny 1" x 1.5" PC board while you are working on it.

Curiously, there are no mounting holes on the PC board, so if you wish to mount it in a box you will have to devise some means of suspending it in midair from it's input, output, and power leads.

The kit requires about 90 minutes if you take your time.

title: Excellent Unit with Killer Flaws
text:
Revised after owning 8 months, Second firmware upgrade. NO MORE KILLER FLAWS

DENON (Japan) SOUND?? Marked "Made in China" the unit relies on components from Korea (Samyoung Capacitors) A/D & D/A conversion is done on a chip by the Japanese company Renasas. The FM/AM Tuner module is by Hong Kong company KSE (not RDS enabled), and the Wired and Wireless is done by US Company SMSC. The word "Denon" appears NOWHERE on any of the internal circuit boards, like it does on my Japanese manufactured A/V Receivers. I therefore suspect the unit was designed in China by people who love iPODs and iPOD parties.

CONCLUSION: No Chinese components means to me, this is still a GOOD, fun and media enabling unit at a reasonable price point, despite the BAD and UGLY flaws discussed below [Now Fixed with my 2nd Firmware upgrade]. Other than Music Server mode, NO PC is required to enjoy the features of this unit, though your library will have to have been created most likely by some computer and the internet.

All functions are rock solid. For details, the manual for the Euro version is available at the Denon Website but not the US version. The Euro manual shows support for FM Radio Text (RDS, like iPOD Nano text During FM) but that SADLY only applies to the European Market. DENON PLEASE give the US units RDS - it is widespread in America now also, just ask Apple marketing!!.

See Comments for other product information.

APPLICATION: If you are tired of listening to Mobile music over computer and car speakers; and ear buds AND have a stereo listening room or a home theater (that you don't want to upgrade), this may be your answer. And, except for the BAD and UGLY below (now fixed MAY 2013), this unit addresses those living without an iPOD or equivalent. While Bluetooth or an iPOD dock, etc may get you connected to your stereo this goes beyond the dock and Sonos. Audio formats includeMp3 VBR; wav; FLAC and more.

By way of Wired or Wireless Ethernet, you get access to your Music Servers, Apple AirPlay on your local networked PC (DNLA server required as per WMP12 or 3rd party, DBpOWERamp, J River etc). I tested Gapless Music Server play with DBPowerAMPs Asset UPnP.

By way of Computer free Internet you get easy streaming access to the emerging Internet Radio/Online Radio (e.g. vTuner, Pandora, Napster etc); you will need a router of course but you probably already have that.

By way of a USB port, access to USB, HDD or SD Card audio. I tested a 750Gb 2.5 inch SATA HDD, with Fat32 by EASEUS Partition Master. And of course, you can play any audio on your iPOD including Audible books (a plus with me). NOTE: The USB/iPOD port is rated at a generous 1 amp and easily supports my SIIG USB 2.0 to SATA Enclosure JU-SA0C12-S1 with HDD.

By way of the local airwaves, you get AM and Good FM as in your car. NOTE: I bought a highly rated Pioneer analog stereo Tuner in 1974 for about $375 that did just AM/FM. That's $1612 in today's dollars - according to the US Bureau of Labor's CPI calculator. By the way, this units KSE Tuner module uses a Panasonic AN18208 AM/FM chip.

iTunes recognizes the DNP-720AE as a selectable set of "speakers" on your local network, so anything you choose to play in iTunes will override the units current programming (or wake up the 720 unit!) and play while displaying the "AirPlay" icon. WMP12 has a similar "Play To" function. Denon has an app to turn your wireless Apple iOS4.2-6 devices (e.g. iPOD Touch) into a local area controller for the unit (not tested).

THE [Not so] BAD [Revised May 2013]: Firmware Fixed? I originally wrote, "This maybe the worlds first MP3 player that does not support the standard Fast Forward and Reverse for any media type." I now see that the Display Time does respond to FF/RW but the Status symbol confusingly remains the "Play" arrow not the FF/RW double arrows. I can live with that.

THE [UN] UGLY[Revised May 2013]: Firmware Fixed? If you are used to LP, CD or late model iPOD playback then you are used to Gapless playback - no ADDED silence or gap between songs. For single play items this is an optional personal preference. If you want to hear THE original Gapless album (Beatles: Sgt Pepper; live albums; Darkside of the Moon) as intended, you will be happy to know the unit appears to now support gapless play back and no longer puts a 1 sec Gap between the first and second song. The gapless is only if the Denon is the Control Point. "Pushing" by way of DLNA (from PC etc)still results in gaps.

LIKES: Looks, sound quality and ease of use. Of course some songs I've never heard on a decent sound system so the bar maybe low on Sound Quality.

This is my first OLED display and I like it- excellent at any angle. The "O" stands for organic which derives from the bio-luminescence of sea creatures. Display info includes basic ID3 info and kbps info. No album art. Its no touch screen, but Denon really takes advantage of OLED with excellent and informative icons and text.

The vTuner is fun. It allows you to listen to Paris Radio and other places around the world including certain local stations. Pandora Internet Radio is currently free and easily accessed. The unit supports Firmware upgrades and adding "new features" but I suspect this is mostly adding or deleting Online services such as vTuner and Pandora or the newly rumored Apple Internet Radio.

HDD play: It loaded folders relatively quickly BUT that is because it does not spend time filtering out non Audio files. It will attempt to play any file and will SOMETIMES hang with a format error on ".jpg" files. So HDD filtering is better done by you back at the Computer - that's OK with me. Changing the file extension to ".skip" causes the unit to skip the song (e.g. .flac to .skip). The owner's manual says nothing about any limit on number of files and folders, but I am planning on 32 folders with 999 files each. It appears to play anything in FAT32 format (HDD, SD Card etc) and it displays all file extensions. Be aware the PC file transfers to any Fat32 device are slow, but once on the HDD they are quickly accessed by the Denon unit.

APRIL 2003 UPDATE (6 MOS OWNERSHIP):

I have confirmed the unit will play at least 370 GB of flac files on HDD, folder browsing only. I used (and recommend) dbPowerAMP software to convert CDs to flac with metadata. I also use dbPowerAMPs Asset product for DNLA Music Server to Denon and other DNLA clients.

For a full graphical interface, I use JRiver sw with either an NAD wireless DAC for portability or an Edirol ASIO DAC. That JRiver "Digital Jukebox" does not use the 720AE BUT if a future product added a feature allowing use of the DNP-720AE as a DAC for PC sources I'm interested (e.g. Cambridge Audio StreamMagic 6).

title: Sound Appeal or Dayton?
text:
My review is comparing this amp and another one which is basically the same, but made to a different standard of manufacture and quality. Both amplifiers share a similar feature set and exterior shape. The Sound Appeal 100-T is the cheaper version, while the Dayton Audio DTA-120 is the slightly more expensive version. Both are low-end amplifiers aimed at folks who require decent sound quality for not a lot of money.

Other reviewers have identified the issues I found with each one, but I want to list these differences here in a side-by-side.

OVERALL CONSTRUCTION. They're both appropriately solid for the price range (they're both in the same range, folks), but the Dayton wins out here. There is a scratchiness to the volume knob on the Sound Appeal, while the Dayton is smooth. The hardware on the back of the Dayton (audio connections) is a step up as well, but that's not to say there's anything wrong with the Sound Appeal's connectors.

VOLUME KNOB. So, on the Sound Appeal, you can't really turn the audio all the way down before turning it off. The audio goes so low, then stays there until you turn it off. Admittedly this is a low level, but listening late at night in a quiet apartment, I found that I wanted it to really a whisper and it couldn't do that without adjusting the output level being fed into it, which isn't always an option. On the other hand, the Dayton knob spends a large portion at the bottom of its range in silence, so you have to turn it a bit before the sound comes up. It does fade all the way to 0, though.

BACKGROUND HISS. The Sound Appeal amp wins here, because the noise is lower than on the Dayton. The Dayton has a hiss that is audible on my Snell KII's from 6" from the speaker (in daytime; probably audible from much further in a more silent environment), whereas from the same distance the hiss produced by the Sound Appeal is much lower.

LED LIGHTS. They're both too bright, but the Sound Appeal's light is more so. It's was capable of casting a blue shadow onto the wall across the room, so many will want to find a way to cover/blunt it. I use a piece of electrical tape stuck to wax paper and made into a conveniently round shape in a hole puncher. Unstick the tape and you have a perfectly circular sticker to place over that annoying blue light.

SOUND QUALITY. The Dayton seems brighter, but we're not talking about a scientific observation here.

I should say that in the end, it was a matter of choosing between being able to have the volume fade cleanly to 0 and having less background hiss. The slightly better construction probly tipped the scales and I chose to keep the Dayton, opting to have a noisier amp with better volume control. Both are 3-star products.

title: One of the best Bluetooth headsets so far ...
text:
I always wanted a good (Bluetooth or not) cordless headset, but always had issues with in-ear headset and over-the-ear headset. Specially with longer conversations they prove to add some additional torture to lengthy conversations, not to mention actual PAIN when wearing them.

I've tried numerous headsets ("ear" models) from good brands like Jabra, Plantronics, Ericsson, etc. None of them seem to work for me. I've also tried numerous "over-the-head" or "behind-the-head" models from cheap brands to reputable brands like Sony and Logitech. They all proved to be a pain to use. Typical issues include battery live to short, bulky, and still poor sound quality.

This model however truly surprised me.
It's lightweight, it feels very comfortable, great sound quality (both phone calls and music), great microphone (the other party didn't even hear that I was using a headset), love that it can be charged with a standard micro-USB charger (easy to get your hands on a second charger, or a car adapter), no flimsy and confusing buttons, paired right away (tried: MacBook Pro, iPad, and a HTC Android phone), gentle sound feedback with functions (volume control, next/prev song, start/end call), easy to switch on (unfold it) and off (fold it), compatible with non-Bluetooth devices (ie. Airplane), etc.

The only two cons I could come up with:

1) Every time I have to fold it, it feels like I'm going to break it. Others have mentioned this as well, so it wasn't a surprise. I wonder who will be the first one to report that they actual broke it.

2) A case/glove for travel would have been nice. The soft padding might need some attention if I would not put it in some kind of protective glove or case.

Right now I can highly recommend this headset for listening to music, and for making phone/Skype calls.

title: Perfect workbench tool
text:
Got this for quickly transferring data between laptop drives without having to mess with the screw-in boards of permanent cases. This is the perfect tool for upgrading to a 2.5" SSD in a computer with only one 2.5" drive bay. You can drop in the new drive, install a fresh OS, and then use migration tools to copy what you need over USB. Even though the connector fits on 3.5" drives as well, this cable is intended for 2.5" drives because no AC adapter is included to power the larger desktop drives, so keep that in mind.

The covers are more of a novelty--the whole point of this cable for me is to plug a drive in, transfer data over USB, and move on, not to use it as a low-cost external enclosure. The silicone cover slips on easily and provides some protection, but like all silicone cases, will collect lint and dust over time. The included hard case is a bit of a mystery. It's a plastic container and the SATA connector doesn't fit through the open end. Maybe I'm using it wrong.

I've had no problems with stability or data copying errors, and my drive only needed the main USB plug connected (the second offshoot plug is just there to provide more power). Very satisfied with this, especially with the low cost.

title: Sony A37 has much to offer
text:
I own the A100 and A700 from Sony and have found them to be worthwhile cameras with pros and cons like any other brand. Initially I was quite hesitant about getting one of their new mirrorless offerings.
Camera came a day later than I expected but hey it was the midst of the holiday season, so no big thing. These comments are not intended to be very technical/professional but from the viewpoint of a slightly above average user.

1. The relatively small size and weight (compared to the A100 and the A700) were a surpise despite the fact that several reviewers mentioned how compact it was. This is a big plus for me since I am getting old and carrying anything the size and weight of an A700 gets to be a burden. The difference in weight may not seem much but to someone with arthritis it is a benefit.
I thought about the NEx series and similar from Nikon but I really didn't want to get into changing lens mounts.
2. The convenience of built in movie mode cannot be understated. It was no fun carrying around an A700 and a PS to take movies. While certainly not the best movie camera it is heads and shoulders above my trusty PS and the convenience over-rides any loss in quality.
3. Image quality is at least equal to the A700 in my opinion. I know this is very subjective and highly dependent on non-camera body factors such as lens and subject etc. But for whatever it's worth I think the A37 offers the same quality photos as the A700.
4. There is no doubt the A37 has far more menu choices and modes than the A700 and its generation. The one I found most interesting was the auto panoramic mode. It does work and the stitch quality may not completely please the purist but for most cases it beats the dickens out of manual panorama photography.Besides that I found it to be fairly forgiving since a tripod is not a must have for this to work.
5. Burst mode is obviously significantly faster than the older generation of cameras but this is expected. This will be a major plus when I try to shoot pics of my grandkids.
6. Battery life is not spectacular but from the relatively small battery on the average I get an estimated 350+ shots. I would say not bad at all.
7. The 135mm lens the kit came with for $593 lives uo to the high ratings almost all the reviewers indicated.
8. In my opinion it handles low lighting with a bit more ease and accuracy than the A700. Keep in kind I have only had it for a few weeks.
9. I would give the built in flash the edge over the A700 built in flash. More even lighting and seems a tad more powerful. Again, subjective rating not scientifically measured.
10. Having the memory card and the battery in one compartment like many other brands makes more sense. I always had to fumble a tad with the A100 and A700 with the double compartments for battery and card.
11. The buffer seems to be quite efficient since you can shoot quite a bit before the camera slows down. I would recommend using Class 10 memory cards anyhow. Why spend so much and then use the cheapest memory cards.

Cons
1. The menu system is confusing at times. However that may be somewhat due to my reluctance to read thru the manual.
2. For such a small battery it certainly takes a long time to charge (250 minutes)! My Toshiba Thrive Tablet with a larger wattage takes half that time.
3. The LCD viewing screen does not provde an accurate enough preview of your shots. The color seems off and overexposed. Others have berated Sony about this.
4. Not sure this is a criticism but the A700 shots with several megapixels less in resolution have larger files sizes than the A37 files. Is this the result of higher JPG compression and a subsequent loss of quality? I don't know. But it does seem curious. Perhaps it is due to more efficient JPG compression software.
That's all for now. Maybe I'll update this review after I've ben using it for six months.

I sent them as much detail as I could - my OS (Win 7), my driver information, my keyboard details, and all the steps I had already taken. 5 days later I got an email from them asking if I had installed the driver!! Not only did I include that in my original email, but it is required information when I submit a ticket. So I responded appropriately.

2 days later I got another email asking if I had updated the firmware!! This is also required information when filling out a ticket.

Anyone sensing a theme here?

Needless to say, I have a useless piece of equipment sitting on my desk. If you buy it, I hope it works flawlessly for you because otherwise you are in for a lot of frustration.

title: Awesome in a 2011 Mustang GT!!
text:
The stock speakers in my 2011 Mustang GT always distorted at about half volume when playing Disturb's Down With The Sickness. My country music that had any amount of bass to it would do the same and so would Rock, Alternative, etc.

I bought these from Amazon and they arrived in no time! Super fast shipping!

The stock speakers are 2ohm speakers and I wanted to make sure I replaced them with the same Ohm rating, but a higher RMS rating. I plan on keeping the stock Shaker 500 head unit, which has a built in amp. I also plan on keeping the stock door subs for now. When I removed the stock door 5x7's, I was shocked at how light they were! They couldn't have weighed more than a pound TOGETHER! I then lifted on of these beautiful Infinity Kapa's out of the box and was amazed at the weight difference alone. One of these speakers easily weighs more than three of the stock speakers, which is a GOOD thing because the more magnet weight you have on a speaker, the cooler and better performing the speaker will be. Also, the tweeters on these Kapa's are an adjustable unit so you can direct where it fires within your car. These Kapa's are extremely well made and have a built in cross-over unit, that small, oblong black thing you see in the pictures. You just cut your factory plug off and then strip the wire a little and use the cross-over screws to attach your wiring. You don't even need the adapter wires you see for sale on here unless you plan to reinstall your factory speakers at some point.

Once installed, and they fit perfectly in all four locations in my Mustang, it was time to crank up the tunes! OMG! From genre to genre, my music was totally different! Suddenly, I could hear high's and mid's that I had never heard in my car! The stock subs were suddenly sounding quite clear for factory subs and helped to separate the bass from the higher tones to make for a wonderful listening environment. Now audiophiles would want to replace their stock head units and the door subs while adding an amp, but for me and my budget, these just cannot be beaten! There are ZERO negatives with these speakers. Seriously, no negatives AT ALL and I've been jamming out with them for almost a month.

Cliff's Notes: The quickest, easiest route to a tremendously better audio experience in your car without spending much money!

title: DO NOT BUY ~ Don't even take it for free
text:
It can't be said enough that this product is useless.

Imagine for a moment that the content you want is already free.

Now instead of using that content for free you have to pay $10 a year and watch additional advertising while navigating that content.

That's what this service is, it's quite literally a list of free sites collected from search engines with additional advertising and you are paying to watch the extra ads (that they are also getting paid to show you)

Learn to use google.com to find free internet shows/movies (or any number of other search engines which are also free) and you will find this content easily

By the way you will find 99% of this free content simply by going directly to Hulu, youtube and right here on Amazon; and you'll find the other 1% spread all over the web by using search engines to find it

If you are looking for specific shows, go directly to the network in your country that broadcasts it first, than if they don't have it, search for it. This dongle won't do it for you any faster and it will show you extra advertising just to slow you down

Not only is this thing not worth paying for, but it's not worth using even if it was given to you for free because it's just a bulky slower way of finding things that are already free (and that's when it works at all because it's also buggy and full of broken links that don't always work anyway)

This thing is nothing but a scam for stupid people who don't know search engines exist and haven't yet figured out that they do not have to use special hardware to find sites like Hulu online

On top of that; the "1000's of networks" they are advertising, it isn't something new or special, it's all the normal ones you already know about plus thousands of links to local network news broadcasts (most of which are not going to be relevant since they aren't local to you). If you are looking for those local news links: start with your local news website (or the local news of whatever you want to look up) because that is all you are going to find with this device, but you'll have to jump through some advertising to get there if you buy this instead of just opening your web browser and going there directly ~ for free

title: FINALLY!!  Worth the wait!
text:
I have been waiting (rather impatiently) for a good chocolate brown case for my new "iPad 3." I searched everywhere for a nice brown cover that not only looked good, but also had a smart cover function THAT WORKED on the new iPad. Amazing how difficult that is and even how rude some sellers are (one told me that they had no intention to fix their brown case for the iPad 2 to work for the iPad 3). I saw this case and liked it but it was only in black at the time and I saw all the reviews saying that the smart function didn't work for the new iPad. So I decided to wait until this issue was resolved in order to get the black one (not really the color I wanted but I was willing to settle as long as the case was good). When the cases had been fixed for the new iPad, I decided out of curiosity to contact Invellop to ask whether or not there would eventually be a brown option. I will say that indeed their customer service is excellent. I got a response in less than 24 hours and was told that yes there would be a brown case. Some colors were being released in the next two weeks. If the brown one didn't come out that week, it would be out the next. So, I did have to wait two more weeks. The day it came out (last Friday) I ordered it immediately. Shipping was great as I got it today (Monday)!
I LOVE IT!! The brown color is a beautiful chocolate brown and like the black (from what I can see in the pictures), it does look and feel like real leather. Additionally I will say this brown case would look great on a white iPad, but still looks nice on my black one!
Thank you very much Invellop for the great case, service and for delivering on your promise for the brown case! With the quality of this case, I may end up buying a black one anyway!

title: Liberation for 82-yr old Mom!
text: The Kindle Fire has liberated my 82-yr old mother from her depression and decline! What a Godsend! Mom loves to read, but her vision is declining and the text on the pages of most books is too small for her. She also has severe arthritis, so holding up a heavy book was not working. I wondered whether the Kindle Fire would work for her. It was a real gamble; my siblings thought I was crazy since she tried a computer years ago but was too intimidated to continue. To sweeten the pot, when I received the Kindle, before I wrapped it, I downloaded several good historical novels and mysteries, and set up an email and Amazon account for her. She was a little shocked when she opened the gift, but once she found how easy it is to open her books, email, etc, it has become her prize possession. She is now reading all the books she's heard about but missed. She adjusts the text size, the font, the brightness of the screen, so that she can read easily and comfortably without any trouble. It is so light weight, she can hold it, rest it on a lap pillow, prop it on a table. She takes it everywhere with her; its a lot easier to carry around than a book. Mom told me this weekend it is the best gift she has ever received, and she now feels liberated. She no longer drives, yet she can go to the Amazon bookstore anytime she wants! Next....music and movies! The Kindle Fire has brought my 82-yr old mom into the 21st century and she LOVES it!

title: Solid Case!
text:
Likes:
*Sturdy, with nicely rolled edges throughout that won't cut you.
* 3 external 5.25 drive bays is just right.
*No external 3.5" drive bays. Use an external card reader or adapter dongle.
*Side and front panels are hinged, easy to remove.
*Roomy enough for 9"x12" boards with SATA ports mounted sideways.
*"Sideways" HDD bays make drive swapping easier.
*2 of the 3 fan intakes are filtered.
*Quiet fans, more than adequate for stock usage and even mild overclocking.
*"Tool-Less" bays work nicely.
*Cutout behind the CPU area makes installing giant coolers very easy.
*Fan behind the CPU. Case makers ignored that excellent cooling opportunity for years.
*Looks great, very sleek and simple.
*No cheesy, bulbous "convenience panels" which cause a real birds nest of wires.
*My Hyper212+ cooler and Ripjaws RAM all fit just fine!
*Cable management is awesome! Never had such a clean and easy build!

Dislikes:
*Has too many (6)internal 3.5 bays. If you need more than 4 HDD's, get a full tower!
*Side doors should have captive thumb screws. Even Dell uses them.
* No 3.5" to 2.5 HDD bay adapters were included, the "mounting holes" are useless.
*Rear 120mm exhaust fan is too weak for overclocking, though perfect for stock usage.
*Fans should have come with 4 pin connectors for automatic fan control.
*2 of the120mm fan intake grills are unfiltered, rendering the other filters useless.
*The front headphone jack is too tight, and almost ruined my expensive ear buds. (fixt).
*Fan grills are stamped honeycomb, far less efficient than concentric wire grills.
*Need a cable management access hole for the EATX power cable.

I wish Antec would have designed in a separate ~7" wide by ~16" tall door for quick access to the internal drive bays. I also wish the sideways drive bays were handy USB3 and SATA hot docks. A push button latch to open the front door would have been nice. Instead, you have to remove the left side panel in order to remove the front panel. Huh? What was Antec thinking?

This is a great case. It's designed for the mid level enthusiast, and did not disappoint me on the important features. Some of my complaints were easily fixed. I moved the rear fan to beneath the CPU, added a stronger fan in its place, and also made all the fans system speed controlled. I am ordering a pair of 2.5" HDD mounting adapters for my SSD's. I am also contemplating cutting out the honeycomb grilles and replacing them with proper chromed wire grilles.

I know there seems to be a lot of negatives in my review, but most are very minor annoyances. In fact, many people may prefer what I perceive as annoyances. Buy this case, you won't regret it either way!

title: Amazon Shipping via CEVA
text:
Just wanted to pop in and add a note about shipping. Elsewhere on these product reviews and other Amazon forums, customers have complained about the shipping of such a large TV, and how it was unreliable, showed up days late, lack of communication, etc. I had the exact opposite experience, and because I was anxious about purchasing an item of this cost and size from Amazon, I felt I should add a positive review for others that are contemplating the purchase.

During the purchase process, I was offered a calendar to choose a delivery timeframe. The shipping company, CEVA, was fantastic: tracking updates were accurate, and when I called them directly to confirm my delivery time, they were very helpful. title: IF YOUR SCREEN BLINKS UNCONTROLLABLY WHEN YOU USE THIS, READ MY REVIEW!!
text:
When I first bought this, I read some reviews about how this product blinks uncontrollably even when plugged in correctly. I bought it anyway and hoped for the best since the majority of the reviews were positive. But when I received it I had the same problem as the others.....

My screen started to blink uncontrollably. After trying everything I actually found a solution. I found that when it blinks, it's because the resolution of the screen is set to something that your TV can't maintain, so as a result it starts to blink.

ALL YOU HAVE TO DO TO FIX THIS is right click on your desktop, click personalize, click display, and then click Adjust Resolution. (It may be a little frustrating to do this because of the annoying blinking.... but just keep a cool head, you'll get it eventually). It doesn't have to be a substantial change in the resolution, just try to move it up or down just a little bit until you get a resolution that your TV can maintain properly. And there you go!!! Your screen shouldn't blink anymore!! I hope people that are having this problem see this review!! And hopefully it solves the problem for you too, cause I haven't had a problem since!!! Good luck!!!

title: Excellent projector with room to grow
text: This is the first projector that I've purchased and I'm very impressed. When I bought it over a month ago there were no amazon reviews so I figured I'd return it if I wasn't satisfied. My only apprehension in buying this model was that some people complain about a "rainbow effect" with this type of projector. After using it daily for over a month now, I do notice it on occasion but only when quickly glancing away and then back at the screen. It's not distracting and doesn't take away from my viewing experience. I built a 4'x7' screen with blackout curtain fabric (widely available in fabric stores)and some cheap construction grade lumber. The picture is clear, bright and sharp in eco mode, which is the only projection mode that I use. I find myself searching for movies that can show off the lush colors and crisp image when I show friends my home theater (I was surprised to find that Rango is now my go-to movie for this). I was relieved to find that the fan noise is quite low and only increases slightly when viewing for more than a couple of hours at a time. The black levels are deep. The remote and menu options are easy to navigate. I have both HDMI inputs in use with my Roku and Chromecast and I wish that there were a couple more inputs for other devices e.g. bluray player, cable box, video games, etc. The internal speaker is pretty ridiculous to listen to if you're watching a 720p movie so if you purchase this projector you will need external speakers. I have mine hooked up to a cheap 2.1 multimedia speaker system and it sounds amazing. My next step will be purchasing 3D glasses and trying out 3D blu-ray films.

title: Easy to use. Extremely reliable.
text:
I originally bought this camera five months ago to replace a stolen [[ASIN:B004J3V7MO Canon PowerShot SX230 HS 12.1 MP CMOS Digital Camera with 14x Image Stabilized Zoom 28mm Wide-Angle Lens and 1080p Full-HD Video (Blue)]]. In those five months, this camera has not let me down at all.

First of all, it takes very high quality images for a non-SLR, which you should be able to see from all the sample images laying around this site and elsewhere. It's also very ergonomic and feels very comfortable to hold. My two favorite things about the physical design are the zoom lever and the flip-out, rotating LCD screen. The control dial is very nice too and operates smoothly. Also, the mode dial can rotate infinitely, meaning you can continue to turn it after reaching the last notch, instead of having to turn it in reverse to get back to the first selection. There is also a fully customizable self-timer option on the dial, which can really come in handy.

The in-camera controls are very intuitive. For most users, the Auto and Scene modes will speak for themselves and get the job done very well, with minimal controls for the user to deal with. Those who prefer to shoot in Manual mode and/or dive deep into the main menu will be delighted at the many options and customizations available. There are so many options to choose from, and the menu is easy to navigate.

Lastly, the zoom is excellent. 35x may be a bit excessive for most occasions, but the option is there, and the results it produces are great. All in all, this camera doesn't really have any flaws I can think of that would warrant anything less than a full five-star rating.

title: Top Quality Backpack- Great for College or Work!!
text:

The next pocket is great for binders and business/school supplies.
My primary purpose to purchase this backpack is for college in the fall. This backpack is great for the amount of space it has to offer. The shoulder straps are very comfortable and they don't rub into your neck. The straps are easy to adjust, which is important for me because I am short and I am always struggling to find a comfortable fit.
This is a top quality backpack. This would be great for school, college, work, even travelling. This is the first backpack I would recommend for anyone.

title: Reliable
text:
Compared to my old alarm system, the Vista 20P has proven to be much more reliable. I'm using it with a 6160RF keypad / transceiver, which is centrally located within the house. For entry detection, I use four door-mounted wireless 5816's and six 5800PIR wireless motion detectors, which have operated flawlessly thus far. No missed transmitted signals and no false alarms. I was having to put up with those occasional problems on my old system, but no more. The Vista 20P control panel and associated accessories seem to be well designed and reasonably priced. Mine did come with a 4AH battery, but I had already ordered a Yuasa NP7-12 7AH battery, so I used it instead. I added a 4204 relay board inside the 20P cabinet so that I could disable two garage door openers and light up an alarm status LED when the system is armed. Everything works well.

I agree with the previous reviewer's comment about 'not for the amateur' because of the steep learning curve when programming the 20P system. I am a previous hardware engineer with some software experience. I did a lot of Honeywell document reading and some internet searching to learn how to program the system, but once the proper commands were entered, everything works as it should. Not all of the programming info is located in a single document, so one must search. After finishing the programming, including authenticating ten detectors and four wireless key fob's, I have a high level of confidence in this Honeywell system. It is interesting to watch the 6160RF alphanumeric display while others are tripping the motion detectors and opening doors. It displays the customized zone name in addition to the zone number, which is a nice touch. My main suggestion for improvement would be to offer a simple step-by-step guide for programming, contained within a single document.

title: I'm giving it 5 stars.
text:
I went in with my eyes open--knowing that macro shots would not be in the G1x's bag of tricks. With the compact design and the large sensor, you can't get good focus up close. A small sensor will give you that, but sacrifice low light and soft background capability in the process.

I shoot mostly outdoor architecture and landscape shots, so I was pretty much looking for just this thing. I carry an S95 in my pocket pretty much everywhere I go, but when I'm out sightseeing, the G1x has replaced my T2i for most outings. I have a macro lens for that, so when I'm doing product photography I still have that covered.

Here's what I like about the G1x:

Love the control layout. For a Canon shooter this camera is already a known quantity before you take it out of the box. Easy to pick up all the controls without even touching the manual.

Works with eye-fi card and New Ipad like a charm. It's really fun quick-editing RAW on the spot with Photogene, posting straight to Flickr and sharing on facebook immediately while most others are getting their facebook images from their cellphone cameras. I've been doing this for a year now with the S95, and the G1x really shines here. I hope someone develops a next-gen RAW editor for iPad that really exploits the new processing power and retina display. I'd like a much more thorough sharpening subroutine and many more options for tonemapping. But all in all, the G1x and New iPad seem to be made for each other--smaller than a pro rig and with somewhat limited functionality, but very good in what they CAN do.

Really, really dig the lens. For a Canon, this thing is very sharp. Maybe I got a really good 'un, but man. I'm getting a lot more keepers with this than with the big rig. Strikes a good balance between speed and low distortion and zoom range. Puts a good image on that big sensor. I shoot in Av most of the time, and the built-in ND element inside that lens really slows down a shot and gives me some great effects. Great tripod camera.

I also notice the pics come out with much more smoothness and glow than from the S95/G12. The lens/sensor combo here doesn't give you Leica luminosity, but it's really good for a Powershot.

Low light performance is fine, but I would have been willing to put up with a bit more distortion for a faster lens. I know the whiz kids at Canon have reasons for every little decision they make on these things, and the compromise is evident. There is no one camera at this price that can give any one shooter everything he wants.

Also, did I mention this thing is BIG. I mean, hefty bag here. Feels great in the hand, doesn't let you forget you're shooting a non-DSLR, but really a solid chunk of camera.

Compared to the G12, this thing really rocks. Minus the macro ability. I don't use it for that, so I'm getting real joy from it so far. Can't wait for this summer's family reunion. I'll leave the monster and the lenses at home and just take this guy and his little S95 brother along. Can't wait to see my brother's face when we compare images from his Super Zoom to mine.

He'll want one of these.

title: Great DAC for the price
text:
I purchased the DAC-ITx on the strength of Peachtree's reputation and the Stereophile Class B rating of the previous generation DAC-IT. Initial listening was unconvincing - providing less involving musical listening than my previous DAC, an HRT iStreamer (which is a great device by the way). I have it connected into my Linn system via a Sonos Connect and a Cardas 75 ohm digital cable.

Well, things have changed now, and I now have the wonderful, involving musical experience I had been looking for. Music played through the system now draws you in, you hear the music, the tempo, a wealth of micro-informational details that make for an engaging, fascinating listening experience. I have not made A/B comparisons etc. of the DAC-ITx with other DACs, at some point we have to say enough splitting hairs, are you happy or not with the way is sounds. After some initial hesitation and doubt regarding the Peachtree, I'm now thrilled with this DAC's performance. Perhaps the digital cable needed some breaking-in time, or maybe the DAC itself, although that would be surprising. In any case, I have now "found the sound"... DAC-ITx is highly recommended.

title: Fast and Reliable AP
text:
I have used every product in the UniFi family and the UniFi AC is amazing. It is a very fast AP with very good range. 2.4GHz has much better range than 5GHz, but 5GHz has better throughput. If you want the faster speed throughout your home that the 5GHz band delivers you will probably need more than one of these. It is hard to say how many you will need because a lot of factors will come into play such as building materials in your home, etc..., but I would estimate 1 per 1,000 sqft for 5GHz. The 2.4GHz band will cover about twice the area.

I was able to test this and compare it with the standard UniFi AP. Here are some of the test results.

All tests were performed with a Mac Mini computer with 150Mbs Cox Cable Internet and a MicroTik CRS125 router.

Signal Source ----------------- DL Speed ---------- UL Speed
Hard Wire 142Mbs 42Mbs
5GHz - UAP-AC 68Mbs 38Mbs
2.4GHz - UAP-AC 38Mbs 26Mbs
2.4GHz - UAP 31Mbs 22Mbs
Standard 2.4GHz Router 28Mbs 22Mbs

These numbers are based on the average of 4 separate speed tests and then averaged. These may not be the most accurate tests and results will differ from different users, but it is a good real world idea of the speed variations on different WiFi setups.

title: Not good at all
text:
07/15/2015
I guess I can share my final comments on this piece of work.
First of all - the Netgear support is absolutely clueless. I know I mentioned that before, but I need to stress it again. The latest issue was caused by bad FW and nobody at Netgear even mentioned that. I just noticed that the latest version disappeared from their site, downgraded mine and most of the issues were gone. Unfortunately, not all the issues. The major problem for us is the inconsistent Wi-Fi signal. The coverage is great, but pretty much useless, as random Wi-Fi devices in the house sporadically dropping the connection.
Bottom line - going back to Linksys.

06/21/2015
Yeah. Had to remove one more star - pretty bad for $280 router. I have it now for 8 month and to get Wi-Fi connected I need to reboot it pretty much every day. It has been updated with the latest FW, QoS disabled and it's been sitting on the cooling pad from the day one. Wired Internet connection is still good, but both radios stop working more and more frequently.
Spent 2 hours on the phone with the Netgear support - although it was way over 90 days, they agreed to talk. First person had no clue. No clue whatsoever - he was going by the book and kept telling me that I need to change the IP - that's why I'm getting the radios to drop the connection.
After talking to supervisor, I was switched to the to the next level of support - that guy supposed to know more than the first one, but I'm afraid he was just following the different troubleshooting guide. He suggested to change the wireless channels and modify CTS/RTS and fragmentation. He could not explain why the previous settings were working fine for 7 month and told me that the settings have to tweaked every time the FW is updated (!) and that would be paid support (!). What a horrible experience, so far...

10/19/2014
Thanks to the great Amazon customer support, I got it replaced. Both bands seem to be more stable with better coverage.
Still can't get any Cisco bridges connected, but this time got R7000 connected as the bridge in a matter of minutes...
QoS is still a joke. The arbitration is very far from being "intelligent". By the way, it completely kills VoIP.

10/11/2014
For some strange reason, Netgear abandoned the "repeater" function on this router (for me it's a major show stopper). I spent some time with Netgear support and they have no immediate plans to get the "repeater" option back to the picture.
Now, I've been using for a little while and would like to drop another star.
First of all, the coverage in my house is just a little bit better than $100 cheaper R7000. And I'm talking about 2.4GHz coverage. 5GHz is pretty bad.
Secondly, the "intelligent" QoS seems to be pretty dumb and not flexible. Of all the devices in the house, it assigned the highest priority to the bridge, which is used once in a blue moon. The VOIP box and most heavily used computer are set to "low".
The rest of the devices are assigned very awkwardly as well.
I have three bridges in the house. All of them worked perfectly fine with R7000. With R7500, none of them can find 5GHz band broadcast on site survey, although 5GHz works fine with the phones and TVs. If I install R7000, everything is back to normal.
Tried to use R7000 as the repeater for R7500 as base with absolutely zero luck. Called and chatted with Netgear support. Two people assured me that R7000 can easily repeat R7500, but the last lady told me that it's not possible because R7500 "does not have MAC address". What a great support!

title: Finally - an essential tool for over the air DTV
text: The Winegard SensorPro is an essential tool for anyone tapping into the huge number of free, over the air TV services.  When the industry dropped analog a couple of years ago the task of peaking antennas became a serious challenge.  With analog, a channel could be peaked by simply watching a TV screen as the antenna was slowly rotated.  As the signal increased the snow level decreased.  Pick the spot with the lest snow and the antenna was peaked.  Not so with digital TV.  With digital, signals are either there and the pictures are flawless, or the signal is gone, over the digital cliff.  You simply cannot tell within that huge range,where the best signal is located.  The Sensor has a number of features.  You can scan to see what channels are 'out there'.  In the scan mode it will find signals without the need to tap individually, channel to channel.  Once the channels in your area have been inventoried you can go to the individual channel mode and pick each of them individually.  In this mode you can rotate, move, or adjust the antenna while watching the digital read out on the meter, choosing the spot that give the best signal.  Lock the antenna at that point, and the channel is peaked.  The unit also has an audio unit which provides an auditory peaking assist in case you can't watch the meter while peaking an antenna.  The only downside is that the unit is designed to be placed in a standard electrical outlet and so if you intend to use it as a stand-alone meter it means a trip to an electronics store to buy a box, battery holders, F-connector nuts, and a switch for power.  I purchased two, four cell AA battery holders and coupled them in series in order to provide the 12 VDC the unit needs to operate.  And then I used velcro to fasten them in place to the bottom of the plastic meter box I picked up from an electronics supplier.  A bit of drilling and soldering and the unit was up and running in a portable mode.

The "guided" typing suggestions just get in the way, but if you try to use them, you can no longer see what you have typed; the typing feature deletes what you have typed when you do almost anything; there is no obvious way to go from typing in the "user name" box in a typical log-in to the "password" box and what looks like obvious choices just delete what you spent five minutes typing into the "user name" box; etc. The memory on the device is so poor that you have to re-log-in to sites very frequently. The streaming seems to be a problem too when interrupted by commercials - the streaming doesn't pause while you're waiting for the commercial to end, so then you have to rewind using the clunky remote's pointer control.

Do NOT get this device if you plan on using the web browser feature. Get a cheaper device without it, or wait for them to figure out how to make it less-awful.

title: Chromebook is a GREAT BUY
text:
I purchased the Samsung Wi-Fi Chromebook because I needed something fast and portable. I have a large powerful Windows-running laptop for work so I didn't need another PC. I also satisfied my need for something Apple with an iPhone 4S (but I will be upgraded to the Samsung Galaxy Note 3 when my contract is up at the end of the year. Sorry, Apple, I don't want your ugly gold iPhone.) ANYWAY. I love this Chromebook. It is the best deal for the price. If you looking for a computer to give a teenager or a college kid it's great for that. Transferring between Google Docs and Microsoft Word (or the other programs) is simple, so that's not an excuse to not buy the Chromebook. It takes some time getting used to how everything runs but once you get it it is simple. If you love keyboard shortcuts, the Chromebook is full of them. This machine is versatile and sleek (it really looks like a MacBook Air but is a fraction of the cost). It is very light and portable. It has a good battery life and charges quickly. If you're already using Google Chrome as your browser, doing typical internet things is exactly the same.
Things I Do With The Chromebook:
-Watch TV/Netflix. Unplug the HDMI cable from your cable box and put it in the Chromebook. You can mirror the screens or use the TV as a second monitor. Anyway, I can stream movies quickly right on to the TV.
-Listen to music. I have a two Bluetooth speakers and the Chromebook connects right to them. With the Pandora app, you're good to rock out.
-Work. I can create docs using Google's apps, save them to the drive and then open them on my PC in a Microsoft program if necessary.
-Social media stuff. It's the same as on a traditional computer.
I know I'm not using the device to its full potential and there are so many more uses and applications. The reps at a Best Buy are great and will talk to you about how to make the Chromebook do what you want it to do.
I'm pretty sure I will be purchasing two more Chromebooks during the holiday season (on Amazon).
Happy browsing!
UPDATE: I've had this Chromebook for 10 months. It still works perfectly (minus the normal hiccups that would come from having my Chromebook set on the Beta channel. Dev scares me though.) ANYWAY a few weeks ago I had my Chromebook on the coffee table next to a glass of water. During the night, one of my cats knocked the glass over (yes, I am a cat lady). Since it was a busy few days at work, I didn't notice my Chromebook had been sitting in a puddle of water for two days (when I finally had time to sit in front of the TV again; remember I have separate work computer...). I was pretty disappointed. I knew I could buy another Chromebook...BUT this was my modded-out personalized Chromebook and I didn't want to reprogram all of my settings. I turned it over and let all of the water drip out. When I was sure there was no water left in it I plugged it in and let it charge up--when I plugged the charger in the light went on--this is a really good sign. I let it charge for about 2 hours. Then the moment of truth.....it WORKED. It turned on like nothing had happened. I was surprised, but not shocked. I know Samsung makes great products. I love this thing. . . I don't know what else to say.

title: For the price - excellent!
text:
*REVIEW UPDATED!*

I recently built myself a desktop, so of course it was time for a new monitor. I knew I wanted LED for the power savings alone (and the arguably better blacks/contrast) and LG has been a good brand to me over the years. When I found this monitor for less than one hundred dollars, I jumped on it!

SOME QUICK SPECS:
22" Display (21.5" viewable)
LED Backlighting
1920x1080P Resolution @ 60hz (16:9 ratio)
Standard VESA Mount
5,000,000:1 Contrast Ratio (marketing hype)
5ms Response Time

BUILD QUALITY
It is as good as any sub-$300 monitor - the stand is quite wobbly but honestly I haven't found a cheap monitor with a good stand yet! Part of the problem is that everything is plastic, so there is no real weight to it. Apart from that, I am not terribly displeased. *UPDATE* - the wobbling finally became enough to annoy me, so I put two of these monitors on a [[ASIN:B002R9HQLI VESA Dual Monitor Stand]] and it is much more manageable. Also, out of the box this monitor ONLY tilts around 20°, it does not swivel or raise up and down. Since I knew this going in to it I was not disappointed, however adding a VESA mount gives you a lot more flexibility!

ACCESSORIES/FUNCTIONALITY
In the box was the monitor and stand, power cable and DVI and VGA cables, this is pretty standard. It plugged in and was recognized in both Windows and OSX (I am on a hackintosh), and drivers were automatically installed. This monitor only has VGA and DVI inputs - however using an HDMI-DVI adapter you can also have 1080P HDMI input without any loss of quality. I am currently using the [[ASIN:B000BTGVUS Tripp Lite HDMI to DVI adapter]] and it works particularly well - I highly recommend it.

IMAGE QUALITY
I am a photographer by trade, doing all my work on Apple's IPS technology. That said, the image quality isn't bad for the price. Blacks are displayed nicely and colors are crisp and relatively true. Gradients fair rather less well, with clear (and annoying) banding on greyscale gradients, but again, this is to be expected in this price range and unless you are very particular about image quality, you probably won't notice. You should flat-out ignore the 5,000,000:1 contrast ratio claims - each company has their own measurement for this number and it is more often than not absolutely overstated. The contrast on this monitor is closer to a 4 year old HP that I had, which claimed 8000:1. Response time is standard for gaming at 5ms with no visible ghosting. Color balance took a little tweaking for my liking, however you can use either Apple or Window's built-in color calibration tool to help you hit that sweet spot. I had to up the native gamma just a hair as well as reduce some blue but apart from that it was really rather decent OOB.

THE BENEFITS OF LED
The first and foremost benefit of LED technology is the power savings. This monitor (as any other LED monitor) does draw less power, and even though you probably won't see much in terms of financial savings, over time this will contribute to less money out of your pocket (in conjunction with other measures taken at home). Being EnergyStar certified, you know that they can't do much to exaggerate the energy saving capabilities of this product. As far as visual benefits, however, I honestly have to say that there was no noticeable gain from LED over decent true LCD monitors. Many LED monitors tout better black reproduction and better contrast, but honestly as I mentioned above, I saw the same performance from an older HP monitor that was in this same price range. NOTE: This may be (and probably is) different the more you pay in the LED monitor line, I am specifically commenting on this monitor, not all LED monitors.
Still, having a very thin, power-saving monitor is worth the upgrade in my opinion.

OVERALL
For the money spent, you are getting 22" of clear colorful LED display, which is more than enough for most users. If you mostly use this monitor for email and looking at family photos, you will be incredibly happy with this monitor. If you use your computer for gaming and movie watching, you probably won't be disappointed. Graphics and photography? You should already know that non-IPS monitors are a bad idea anyway, however if budget is what drives you, you can deal with a little gray-scale banding right? Take a look at the other reviews for support of my statements!

For the money spent (and even the current price), this is a very decent monitor (I now own two).
4/5, a true "I like it" as defined by Amazon's star rating guidelines.
