title: IF PRO-JECT CANNOT GET THE AC MOTOR CORRECT, WHAT ELSE REALLY MATTERS??
text:
It has been rewarding to have so many people thank me for my review of the Pro-Ject Debut Carbon Turntable. I'm adding this addendum on the front of my review for those of you would decide to purchase this turntable as I did, "disregarding" the warnings everyone seems to be giving in regard to the terrible motor hum. IF YOU DECIDE TO PURCHASE THIS TURNTABLE, DO THIS TEST BEFORE YOU DO ANYTHING ELSE. YOU WILL NOT HEAR THE HUM UNTIL THE STYLUS IS PLACED ON THE RECORD! THE SECOND THE STYLUS IS PLACED ON THE RECORD (THE LEAD IN GROOVE) YOU WILL HEAR THE HUM. YOU WILL ALSO HEAR IT DURING VERY QUIET, SOFT MUSIC PASSAGES, YOU WILL HEAR IT BETWEEN TRACKS, AND YOU WILL HEAR IT AS THE STYLUS TRACKS OUT AT THE VERY END OF THE RECORD. LOUDER MUSIC MASKS THE MOTOR HUM, WHICH IS WHY PROBABLY SOME BUYERS HAVE NOT NOTICED IT. REMEMBER, LISTEN FOR THE HUM FROM YOUR SPEAKERS THE SECOND THE STYLUS IS PLACED ON THE LEAD IN GROOVES ON YOUR RECORD, AS THE MOTOR HUM IS TRANSFERRED FROM THE PLINTH AND THE PLATTER RIGHT INTO THE HEAD SHELL AND CARTRIDGE, RIGHT OUT YOUR SPEAKERS! BE SURE AND TEST BETWEEN TRACKS AND AS THE STYLUS TRACKS OUT AT THE END OF THE RECORD, IT'S HARD TO MISS THIS HUM!

I purchased this turntable in the piano black on September 3rd, 2014, and was certainly looking forward to enjoying the next few years with my new turntable and record collection. Let me share what I encountered when the new table arrived.
1. The box is very small, and it is obvious this company took every shortcut possible in packing it, with the platter on the very bottom of the box where any dropping would totally damage the platter. The box and packing are minimal to say the very least, and it is certainly not double boxed.
2. The turntable paint is the product's best feature, beautifully painted, whatever color you purchase.
3. The instructions are not very well written and the part about the tiny screw and resolving the arm needs to be written a different way when discussing vertical tracking angle.
4. The platter mat is absolutely terrible, it is literally not worth 2 cents. The mat is so thin it's problematic just keeping it in place and any static on your record, and the mat sticks to the record. I have never seen such a pathetic, worthless mat furnished on any turntable at any price.
5. The cartridge furnished with the table is fine, no problems there, probably a good fit for this level of turntable. I would warn everyone, be VERY careful when removing the stylus cover, and especiallly putting it back on, if you need to put it back on for any reason. It clicks in the back and it's just so very easy to damage that stylus, so be warned, watch your step.
6. The armrest on the player locks the arm in with a slight click, which is fine, but the armrest gets in the way, when you move the arm towards the record. The up and down movement is just not comfortable and it will cause you to drop the arm, something you will have to get used to.
7. The pickup bar on the headshell is far too small, and you WILL drop the arm at some point in time, it's just too small and you have to grab it with two fingers to hold it. Unlike most turntables, you can't just reach under the pickup and lift the arm, it will jump right off your finger. This is a pretty serious shortcoming as you will see if you order this product.
8. The anti-skate weight and the 1" piece of fishing line is just not that great and usually the line is placed on the second notch and there is an angle when placed on the second notch, where the line can easily slip off, it's just not the best design to say the least.
9. The clear dust cover is very nice, with the Pro-ject logo on the top, it's always nice to get a nice dust cover with your turntable without paying $300.00 for it.
10. Unfortunately this is where things get very bad for the Pro-ject Carbon Turntable, the motor. The motor is held in place by two screws and a rubber band and cushioned by two small Sorbothane absorbers, designed to absorb AC motor vibrations, and unfortunately the entire configuration does not work, period. That motor transfers a very noticable hum/buzz that is clearly heard through the speakers the second the stylus touches the record. This hum/buzz can be heard on any quiet music passages, between tracks, on the lead in on every record, as well as at the end of the record. This design flaw is written about all over the Internet and Pro-ject has been completely redesigning the Debut Carbon with a new DC motor to control this terrible hum the AC motor introduces. Hemley Designs Ltd has worked on a kit and is supplying that kit at a cost of about $40.00, however there is NO kit for the Debut Carbon. Henley Designs Ltd is the UK Distributor for Pro-ject and they are located in Oxfordshire. I have spoken to Mr. Bill Rudolph, the Analog Manager for Sumiko Audio as well as Paul Greene, the Service Depart Manager for Sumiko. I suggested doing a swap, my humming AC turntable for one of their new and improved DC versions of the Debut Carborn, and they would not assist me and said just return the table to the vendor. THERE ARE MANY PEOPLE THAT WOULD HAVE YOU BELIEVE THIS IS AN ISOLATED SITUATION WITH THE HUMMING AC MOTORS IN SEVERAL OF THE PRO-JECT TURNTABLES, BUT IF YOU WILL TAKE THE TIME TO LOOK ON THE INTERNET AND SEE ALL THE THOUSANDS OF CUSTOMERS TRYING TO FIGURE OUT A WAY TO STOP THEIR PRO-JECT DEBUT CARBON AND OTHER PRO-JECT TURNTABLES FROM HUMMING, YOU WILL ABSOLUTELY PUT ON THE PURCHASING BRAKES. Do a Google search on (Pro-ject Debut Carbon Humming Problems) and be informed. This is a neat, flashy little turntable, but someone did not do their homework on the motor, and produced a turntable with significant motor hum and buzzing, that NEVER stops, and you continually hear it, so don't do what I did, buy the turntable and hope for the best, because when it arrived, I GOT THE WORST, IT WAS TERRIBLE, and nothing I did helped at all, that hum is there and it will not go away. After speaking to both of the men referenced above, they made it clear they were not willing to swap my one day old AC turntable for the newer DC model which is just coming to the United States. I have no idea if the terrible hum problem has be lessened or solved, but I was told to simply send the table back to the Vendor, which gladly took it back, but I just expected so much more from Sumiko and Pro-ject. I fully understand the rationale behind keeping this humming problem very quiet, it would cost millions of dollars to make this right with so many Pro-ject turntables out there in the field humming. It's just simpler to make a new DC version, hope you get that hum out and stay as quiet as you can about the thousands or millions of Debut Carbons and other Pro-ject turntables with AC motors in the field humming away!

Happy listening!

title: Perfect For One Cord or Several Cables
text:
Product: Velcro Reusable Self-Gripping Cable Ties, 0.5 Inches x 8 Inches Long, Black, 100 Ties per Pack (91140) $6.98 (with Prime, shipping was included)

These are as close as it gets to the velcro straps you find on things like laptop cords. They look a little funny. They come in rolls like stamps. (This makes for easy storage.) The ends in between each strap are perforated but the perforations are not easy to see. When I tried to pull them apart, between not being clear on where the break was and the thinness of the fabric, I was afraid I was going to tear them. They aren't as fragile as they seem. They also grip better than I thought after looking at them - they are not the thick commercial grade velcro. They almost feel smooth. But they work just great.

I pulled the first one off from the center of the roll. Don't do that. Doing that left material around the end that goes in the slot and I kept trying to push the end into the slot before I realized. Once I pulled off the extra material, the end slips in easily and you can pull it tight around the cord.

The other end (with the slot) is particularly cool. When you push the tab into the slot and pull it tight, the material on the bottom of the slot grips the other side and keeps the strap tight and in one place on the cord. This makes it easy to then wrap the rest of the strap around more cables without having to hold the strap in place while holding the cables all at the same time.

They are 8" long but remember it has to wrap around once (one cable) which takes away 3/4 - 2" depending on the thickness of the cable. They are long enough for most anything around the house. The one thing that you might have to use multiple wraps for is an entertainment setup - TV, DVD, cable box, router, receiver, etc. - again, depending on the thickness of the cables.

The straps are as you would expect from Velcro. They grip very well and yet they come apart when you pull them apart. And, like all Velcro, they are reusable. The price can not be beat.

Here's my one and only complaint (imagine me pouting here). They only come in black. I wanted pretty colors.

title: Vis it worth it?
text: I can only give this light an "acceptable" rating. I have recently purchased six different models of similar size and with similar features. and the Vizeri can only claim mixed results when compared to lights at a fraction of the cost. Color is the one feature the Vis can claim a degree of superiority, it was slightly whiter than other lights, but this advantage was lost due to vastly inferior optics. The much vaunted reflector casts a swirl pattern and leakage (a bullseye pattern), defects completely absent from other lights. It should be noted that all the lights appear to use the same LED but even among identical lights there is a great degree of variability in color. The very best light I tested had an identical twin that was quite a bit more blue. The widest flood was far narrower for the Viz than others. Construction strength on all of these lights is extremely good, the materials and machining is excellent. One nice feature in favor of the Viz is a much dimmer low setting, but it was NOT the brightest light tested, although all use the same power source. None of the other lights claim to be waterproof, the one clear area of superiority for the Viz, and a feature I did not test. I would select the Vizeri only if water resistance is critical. It cost more than the other six lights combined.

title: Works Great On OS X Mountain Lion -- Late 2011 MBP
text:
I downloaded the new Alpha 2 display drivers from Display Link's website and the product works well. There are small issues that occur occasionally, which is to be expected in Alpha, but nothing serious that can't be fixed with a replug. Judging on the Alpha version, this product will be awesome with full driver release on OS X. I haven't tested on Windows yet.

The image quality of the display is equivalent to my primary display. However, there is a slight lag and compression artifacts on full screen video and heavy action windows, but for most everyday tasks there is no noticeable difference in response or quality. Note, I have USB 2.0, but it's still great quality. I would assume USB 3 would be perfect.

The product DOES work with two displays, even over USB 2. Currently I have one VGA monitor and one HDMI plugged in. The HDMI port DOES provide flawless audio, which is a plus because the Alpha drivers specifically mention not supporting sound. However, with two displays, there is a more noticeable lag introduced into both added displays. They are still usable, but not as responsive. This is due to USB 2 being too slow, USB 3 should solve the issue.

Finally, all the OS X Display controls and Sound controls in Settings work flawlessly with this device: Arrangement, Resolution, Refresh Rate, Volume, etc.

There is one issue with the USB 3.0 plug that is supplied with the product. When plugged into the USB 2 Macbook fully the product does not work, but if you pull the plug out slightly it works fine. I am assuming the extra contacts in the USB 3 connector are shorting against the Macbook. There are two solutions:

1) Don't insert the provided cable all the way into the Macbook --if the cable sheath with the SS logo sits against the Macbook's frame it's in too far
2) Use another USB 2 cable that fits in the device.

Final note: I am using this device's screen to write this review. :-)

title: Attention: Not a true DVI-D Dual Link cable
text:
As another reviewer here says, as far as I can tell, this is NOT a true DVI-D Dual link cable. I have a new high-res Catleap monitor (from Korea) that requires a DVI-D Dual link cable. It specifically does not support single DVI cables; though a single link cable will fit, the monitor will not display an image unless it is a true DVI-D Dual link cable.

My experiment: I bought this cable, got it yesterday, hooked it up--and my monitor will not display an image. The monitor itself is brand new, working perfectly with a shorter DVI-D Dual that I already own. So, like the one reviewer here said, while the configuration of the pins are Dual-link, they are not actually wired that way. In my opinion, this appears to be a single-link cable, even though the pins appear to be dual-link. I'm sending it back now. What a pain in the butt.

If your equipment specifies a DVI-D Dual-link cable, look elsewhere. If all you need is single-link, then this would probably suit.

title: Good results, but still not quite strong enough.
text:
I installed this antenna in our attic this weekend. Our house presents a unique challenge in that it is steel framed (outside walls and studs along with the trusses; interior studs are wooden). It was one of a handful built in our area by U.S. Steel in the 1950s as a sort of experiment. Anyway, we've been in our house for 3 years and have had good/bad results from a host of indoor antennas. Not wanting to give in and get cable, I ordered the Winegard 2 weeks ago and set about doing the install on Saturday.

The antenna was very easy to put together and is small enough that it easily fit through our attic door. Using our TV Fool report, I mounted it on the north gable with velcro strips, did some channel scans and moved it around until it was in the best position. The most-distant station (Fox) is 24 miles with some hilly areas between. It's on the edge of the TV Fool yellow band for our area. The Winegard was able to detect the 3 Fox channels available but was unable to pull it in during the day (I was able to watch some of The Simpsons after dark last night). All of the other local channels came in crystal-clear with nice strong signals.

Fox is the channel I really want, due to my favorite football team being in the NFC, but the range of the Winegard combined with the terrain made it a disappointment. Other than that, it's pulling in everything else, including one yellow band station we never got before, with ease.

Pros: easy to assemble, good price for the high quality, compact enough for most attics
Cons: not quite enough range for our situation. I'll probably be looking for something a bit stronger, but it will most-likely be another Winegard model.

title: Great accessory for E-M1
text:
Let's get price out of the way:

As with most vertical grip options, it's at a price we'd rather not have to fork over. However, when you consider that the E-M1 is actually over-priced in some ways this accessory is actually competitively priced for the most part. I happened to have credit points built up with Amazon that were automatically applied to this item when I ordered it so I got it for about $35 less. However, when I added it to my cart I thought I was paying full price and would have.

The price is also relatively good when you consider that Nikons, for example, (yes it's a larger camera, but the teach is the same) average $260 or so for OEM grips in their higher line. And the D800's grip is still an absurd $350! Even Fuji's featureless metal grip for the X-E1/2 that also happens to block the battery/SD door is nearly $100. It's just a piece of metal with a screw into the camera.

Now we come to a WEATHER SEALED vertical grip that's lightweight, has a storage space for the rubber stopper that you remove from the bottom of the camera, holds an extra battery, gives you both command dials from the standard orientation and a pair of customizable function buttons. Many OEM grips don't offer this much, esp. weathersealing. I've had several grips over the years with Canon and Nikon (Fuji doesn't offer them as of now) and this is the most feature-rich, namely because of the incorporated dials.

Size and Build:

The size is rather small for a grip, as you'd expect paired with a smallish m43 body. The construction is good as well. Not heavy duty feeling like a magnesium Nikon grip, etc., but it's is a lot smaller and competently solid feeling. The contact points and connection are solid and I feel, at least as of now, that this will hold up well.

Features:

It's loaded. You get all the stuff I mentioned above - two function buttons, two control dials, shutter release, vertical lock switch, extra battery and weather sealing. Some mention wanting an SD card slot area and honestly, this is a feature that the $1400 camera should have. Most grips with an extra SD slot (Pentax for example) serves only as storage and doesn't actually communicate with the body. A communication SD slot would be nice for sure, but it should really have been built into the E-M1. The only "feature" I wish it had was a double-sided locking screw. The dial to "screw" the grip to the camera is on the back only. On other brands, like Nikon, the wheel goes through the grip to the front side as well. This really helps in locking it down as you can grip the wheel from both sides - like tightening the lid on a jar. The back-only orientation isn't bad, but I do prefer the through wheel design offered by other vendors - despite it being somewhat unsightly.

Performance:

Very good and usable without adding too much bulk to the camera. You buy m43 because it's small and transforming it into a D4 kind of defeats the purpose. This is right where it should be in size and it works very well. My only quibble is that the function buttons, though properly located, are a bit low for my thumb reach. This ONLY stands out to me because it's the only thing I've noticed not being completely fluid. And, obviously, hands are all different so this won't bother many. It's certainly not a reason for me to ding the rating as Fn buttons aren't used on EVERY shot. Hint: I find setting the B-Fn 1 button to "zoom in" so you can check focus is very quick and handy. I set the top Fn on the camera to this as well.

Conclusion:

If you spent $1400 on the E-M1 then $200 for a fully-featured, weather sealed grip really shouldn't be that big of a deal. You'll get more function out of it than you'll likely miss that $200. At least that's the case for me. It's actually somewhat of a value in an over-priced OEM grip market and if you're someone who shoots a lot of portraits - or any vertical orientation - you can consider it a luxury item as it greatly increases extended shooting comfort. Pick up some Wasabi batteries off Amazon and throw one in the grip for double the run time and you're good to go. The tight function buttons and non-thru wheel locking mechanism that I mentioned earlier are simply personal preferences and really don't inhibit true functionality all that much. It's a 5 star in my book.

A solid accessory that will make you shooting life easier. If you are a grip-type shooter, go for it.

title: Please READ THIS - it might save your camera.
text:
This monopod works perfectly with a GoPro except for one glaring defect (that can be fixed). The wrist strap attaches to the bottom of the pole with a thin piece of monofilament fishing line, covered in black thread. This broke as I was climbing a boat ladder on vacation, and I got on board with only the wrist strap. I had 86'd the pole with my GoPro attached. If I had been in SCUBA gear I would have dove after it. Unfortunately, we were snorkeling and the boat was in deep water. I just watched my gear sink to the bottom of the ocean.

The fix: Use a large, thin split-ring (keyring) to attach the wrist strap to the monopod. Loop it through the strap, not the thin plastic hole near the thread. Spend a few cents on a keyring, and you just might save your camera.

title: Works great but do you need it if you're a traveller?
text:
As an amateur - I take my T4i out with me when I'm traveling (amusement parks, tourist destinations, parks, etc). I've had a spare battery I'd carry around with me in case I was away from the room for long periods of time or if I was just shooting a lot so I didn't think this would be something I'd need. A friend kept extolling the virtues of it and how my life would be complete with it (in so many words) so I thought I'd go for it. I've got a few trips with it under my belt now and I'd like to report on my experiences.

One thing to point out that I didn't notice in the other reviews is that the AA battery and Canon battery containers are separate from the grip. You can either choose one container or the other to put into the grip, not both. If you're traveling that means you have to take both with you. Since I travel light this meant it stayed home taking up dust. It's great if you're into rechargable AA's to avoid the canon battery costs but I was hoping to use it as an emergency back-up and if I'm traveling, I can't unless I want to take it along.

Also, when you pop your battery door off of your T4i to put this in, there's a storage slot for the door on the grip (very handy).

Pros:
-Better Grip. I don't have big hands so I can handle the T4i comfortably. I didn't think the extra grip would be that much of an advantage but turns out that it does. I ended up holding the camera from a lower position with my pinky resting on the grip edge. This ended up being a much more comfortable and stronger grasp of the camera.

-Extended shooting time. Since I was carrying the spare with me anyway it just made sense to have the grip to keep it there and extend the shooting time of the camera rather than wait for one battery to go out and then have to switch which might be in the middle of shooting.

-Vertical shooting. Very easier to do now as the grip makes it much convenience and I love the special controls on the vertical side but vertical shots make up about 1% of my total shots so it's not something I use all that often. (I thought having the vertical grip would result in me doing more vertical shots but it didn't. I just do too many landscapes)

-It adds balance weight to the camera. If you use a large/heavy lens (like the 17-55 EFs) on the camera this is going to add balance to the back which will make it easier to hold the camera steady. This came in handy with doing videos as I didn't "jiggle" the camera as much because the added weight counter-balanced slight movements. (Still get video shake when walking though... I miss video stabilization...)

Cons:
-It adds balance weight to the camera. The camera is heavier now so it's that much more weight on your neck. It's not a lot of weight but I did notice it as the day went on.

-It makes your camera bigger. To avoid baggage-charges/baggage-check fun, I tend to travel light with just one backpack if I can. I like taking the camera on the plane anyway for the same reason but also so I can grab some photos while in the air. The grip adds enough size to the camera that it makes it more difficult to fit at the top my backpack. Even when I do get it to fit it makes it more difficult to get out of the backpack under the seat in front of me when trying to get a shot.

So did it "make my life complete"? Jury's still out. It's a well built product and the extra grip is nice and convenient but I haven't decided if that overcomes the issues I had with the size and weight to continue using it.

title: Update number 2!!
text:
Update number 2.....I bought a 47" 7600 to replace my 8600. Aside from the lack of dual core and silver bezel on bottom with illuminated logo, I have found no differences......so far, I'm loving it....going to 4 stars just based on length of time I've had this new one....(1 week). No reboots....a little light bleeding but you're going to get that anyway. I'll update after 2-3 weeks of use! :-)

I will leave my full previous review below.....unfortunately, I must update with bad news....SEVERE rebooting issues have struck my set. It reboots every 2 minutes on all settings/inputs. I've owned the set a little over three weeks. Because my window of return is so small at this point, I will NOT call LG and have a tech come out. After extensive research tonight, it seems there is no fix. I've ordered a return through Amazon due to my time running out to do so. Disappointed. I loved the TV. I cannot recommend it anymore. This problem seems very very common.

I held off writing a review until I had the TV for 3 weeks.....I wanted to really learn how to use and adjust the unit before coming up with a knee-jerk review.

Pros: Very nice design and picture. The magic remote took some getting used to, but that's why I waited to write my review. I'm used to it and it's fantastic. The blacks are deep and the "smooth motion" makes blu ray images and HD broadcasting look like it's right in your room with you. If you don't like it, simply turn it off.....the picture remains crystal clear but you don't get the freaky OMG clarity that comes with it. Very very easy to hook up to my wireless network and start cruising around in within minutes out of the box. 3D is fun and the glasses are comfortable. The 2D to 3D is commendable actually.....I had my doubts, but it is less gimmicky than kind of cool. Works GREAT on Netflix streaming kids shows like Fanboy and Chum Chum......

Cons: reflective screen. I'm coming from a plasma, so it's not a HUGE issue for me, but I can see it as an issue for some coming from LCD. Blooming effect. title: Measured Read/Write speed EXACTLY as advertised
text:
I have tested dozens of flash memory cards in the past few years. Being a cheapskate, I usually stay with mid-price products, such as the [[ASIN:B007XZM6VG SanDisk Ultra]] series. When Amazon held a lightning deal on this [[ASIN:B00FRHTXR2 SanDisk Extreme 16 GB microSDHC Card]], I jumped on the opportunity to try the faster series, just to see what I've been missing.

I used a benchmark program called "CrystalDiskMark v3.01 x64" to measure, among other parameters, the Sequential Read and Write speed of this card. The card reader I used is the [[ASIN:B009D79VH4 Transcend USB 3.0 Card Reader (TS-RDF5K)]], plugged into an USB 3.0 port. This is important because if you use an USB 2.0 card reader or USB 2.0 port, the maximum speed will be severally handicapped.

My benchmark shows Sequential Read speed of 47MB/s and Write speed of 32MB/s. See the image I uploaded to 'Customer Images' section for details. The result is consistent with the manufacturer's spec of 45MB/s in Read and 30MB/s in Write. The Write speed, in particular, is about 2.5x faster than the Sandisk Ultra card (which can only deliver 13MB/s).

Of course, the real benchmark has to be done in a real life application. For that, I inserted the Sandisk Extreme microSDHC card (with SD adapter) into my Canon Rebel T1i DSLR, set it to save both RAW and JPEG formats, then took 10 consecutive shots in burst mode. This Sandisk Extreme card took just 14.1 sec to save all 250MB of data in my camera. In contrast, the Sandisk Ultra card took much longer at 23.8s, even though it also qualifies as a 'class-10'.

This is the fastest card I have tested to date. But as it turns out, the card I bought is actually the SLOWEST among the Sandisk 'Extreme' family. According to the manufacturer's spec:
- 'Extreme': Up to 45 MB/s read; 30 MB/s write
- 'Extreme PLUS': Up to 80 MB/s read; 50 MB/s write
- 'Extreme Pro': Up to 95 MB/s read; 90MB/s write

On the other hand, this Sandisk Extreme card performed exactly as advertised, so I cannot complain. Maybe one day I'll break down and try the 'PLUS' or 'Pro' next. For now I'm happy.

title: Swing and a big miss
text:
I'm blown away by all of the reviews by all of the major websites. These speakers are average at best. I still own my original, 12 year old Klipsch Promedia v.2-400 speakers. The Klipschs completely blow the Corsairs away. Corsair gave the speakers a DSP (evident by the "hall" effects) but you only get 5 EQ modes?!?!? Not one of them is adjustable. You can't even do a high-mid-low adjustment. You can only turn the sub level up and down. They put a mini-usb connector on the controller but no software for making your own EQ curves? On top of all of that the speakers use proprietary cables and connectors. Sure you could dial up Digikey and order the matching Molex connectors, but really?!? At least put banana jacks on the speakers and the sub so that people have the choice of using their own speaker cables.

As for the sound quality... Lacking. Severely lacking. There's a big gap between the 3" drivers and the sub. You get some mid-bas then boom-boom-boom from the sub. I spent hours playing with the level feeding the speakers, the EQ modes, and the sub level. There was just no polishing this turd. Sure, I could have put an EQ in line but that would add $100 to an already expensive set of speakers. I also could have used my soundcard's EQ but then my PC would sound good but that wouldn't help any of the other sources.

I ended up running over to my local Brick and Mortar and buying a set of Klipsch Promedia 2.1 speakers. They sounded 10X better than the Corsairs and the Klipsch's only have a sub adjustment, no EQ. The 2.1's still didn't sound as good as my v.2-400's but the 400's have a dual sub and more power. I had the Corsairs and the Promedia 2.1's set up right next to each other. It is night and day. AND the Promedias were fifty bucks cheaper.

One other nitpick... The Corsairs have three inputs. You can only select one at a time. There's no option to enable multiple inputs at once. That's lame. With the Klipsch's both inputs are mixed together and work at the same time. This is nice because I can have my TV and computer both plugged in. Watch TV and still hear my PC's notifications.

My recommendation to Corsair is to hop on eBay and buy a set of Klipsch Promedia v.2-400 speakers. Make up an EQ mode that sounds just like them. OR give users a 7 band parametric EQ or a 31-band EQ and let them do it themselves. Or let Room EQ Wizard talk to the speakers over the USB port!!!

Corsair could have made these SOO much better just with some software tweaks.

title: An all in one product with many features, but falls just short of perfect.
text:
Sometimes peripherals get complicated. You need a keyboard, mouse, charger for your iPad, and SD card reader, but your computer doesn’t have enough ports. Fortunately, KDLinks has made the KDLINKS Ultra Slim 10 Ports USB 3.0 All In One Hub Station, as a way to centralize your peripherals.

▶ Package Contents
• KDLINKS Ultra Slim 10 Ports USB 3.0 All In One Hub Station
• Micro USB 3.0 Cable
• Power Adapter
• User Manual

▶ Accessories
This device includes a 33” Micro USB 3.0 cable and a 4.5” x 2” x 1” inch power adapter. The micro USB 3.0 interface is a very different adapter than many of the other USB 3.0 hubs that I have reviewed which usually use a USB 3.0 A to B, or USB 3.0 B to B cable. This was probably done to keep the size of the hub small, but it compromises availability of the cable. I know an USB 3.0 A to B or B to B cable would be available at my local department store, but not a Micro USB 3.0 cable. I would need to purchase such a cable online. The power adapter cord is 44.5” inches to the brick, which is then attached to a two-prong 55” inch laptop power cable to plug into your wall outlet. I like what manufacturers are doing with these power adapters, as they prevent surge protectors from getting crowded, and giving you the most efficient way to de-clutter your work space.

▶ Specifications
• Product Model: KDLINKS UMF6B
• Product Nam: UMF6B Multi-function All in One expansion Dock
• Interface: USB 3.0
• Material: Plastic
• Color: Black/White
• Dimension: 164mm x 63 x 15mm
• Input Interface: Micro B Type
• Output Interface: 6 USB 3.0 Ports & 3 Charging Ports & 1 SD Card Reader
• Weight: 60g
• Support System: Windows ME/2000/XP/Vista/7/8; MAC 9.1 or above
• Approval: CE and FCC

▶ Hardware
The device is very small and light (6.4” x 2.5” x 0.6” inches; 2 ounces). This is one of the few hubs I can imagine putting into my pocket, although I wouldn’t have a need to. The device comes in a matt plastic black, which initially feel very cheap, but then you start noticing the subtle details in the design. This device has 1 5V/2.1A charging port and 6 USB 3.0 ports on the front, two 5V/2.1A ports on the left side, one SD card slot on the right side, and the power adapter, USB connector, and power on button on the backside. To differentiate the charging ports from USB 3.0 ports, there is text on the top “5V/2.1A”, and the USB ports are pointed down instead of up. Also on the top is the kdLinks logo, the text indicating the SD card slot “SD”, and the name of the “USB 3.0 HUB+FAST CHARGE”.

When I first looked at this device, I was a little overwhelmed, because there was a lot going on, as this was a small device with several functions; the first of its kind. You would usually buy a USB hub with a lot of ports, and maybe one charging port, but this device has much more than that. This hub, unfortunately, has a few aesthetic features that I didn’t like though. Although the hub tries to pride itself on being small, it creates a few shortcomings. The ports are horizontal instead of vertical and only about 0.25” apart, which potentially blocks multiple flash drives from being used. There is also only one LED light to indicate the “ON” state instead of several LED indicators to indicate whether a port is transferring data or not. This has a SD card slot but no micro SD card slot, which would require me to still use a USB card reader. This hub has a lot going for itself, but it falls short of perfect.

▶ Setup
This device is plug-and-play, which is very straight forward.

1. Plug the power adapter into your wall outlet and USB 3.0 cable into your USB 3.0 port (For best results, otherwise a USB 2.0 port is also suitable).
2. Your computer should automatically recognize and install proper drivers, if necessary.

▶ Testing
I performed five tests with this device: Fit of ports, Multimeter, Fast charge, USB 3.0 transfer speed, and SD Card transfer speed. These tests are done to evaluate the quality of the product, and if the functionality matches the quality of other products.

• Fit of ports
I tested the 6 USB 3.0 ports, 3 Charging ports, and 1 SD card slot. I fit the appropriate ports with the appropriate card/cable, and found each to fit perfectly. All ports fit very snugly without any issues.

• Multimeter
The multimeter test attempts to test the voltage and current the device uses at the beginning and end of the test. Sometimes, devices remain the same current throughout the test, and sometimes the current lowers toward the end. It is nice to know if the power source is giving out less power by the end of the test. The current is the ampere the device is taking in, with max current the maximum amount of ampere the device is capable of taking in. The voltage is the amount the power source is capable of giving, with min voltage the lowest possible amount of the power source giving.

- 5%
Current: 1.13A
Voltage: 4.97V
Max Current: 1.21A
Max Voltage: 4.83V

- 98%
Current: 0.52A - 0.76A (fluctuated)
Voltage: 5.10V
Max Current: 0.76 (fluctuated)
Max Voltage: 4.98V

These are very high results for my Nexus 7 at this percentage. Usually, you can expect 0.40 – 0.60A, but to get a rating of almost double to triple that amount proves the efficiency of the charger.

• Fast Charge
The fast charge test attempts to find the efficiency and performance of the power source.

Time – Nexus 7 charge %
10:32PM - 5%
10:44PM - 10%
11:03PM - 20%
11:24PM - 32%
11:45PM - 43%
12:03AM - 54%
12:27AM - 67%
12:45AM - 77%
1:03AM - 89%
1:33AM - 100%

Nexus 7 Battery Size x Amount Charged = Total Charge
3950mA * (0.95) = 3752.5mA

Total Charge / Time (hours) = Charge per Hour
3752.5mA/3h = 1250.83mA per Hour

This device charges at 1250mA per an hour, which considering my OEM wall charger only charges at approximately 700mA per an hour, this is an amazingly fast result for a USB charger,. These results conclude this charger does indeed charge fast.

• USB 3.0/SD Card Transfer Speeds
For testing the transfer speed, or the read and write of the USB ports, I used a program called “CrystalDiskMark”, a storage benchmarking software. I can compare the original results to my current results and see if the claims of “High speed USB 3.0” ad “High speed SD card reader” are true. For these tests I used my Silicon Power Rugged Armor A80 1 TB (R: 116MB/s; W: 115MB/s) and SP 32GB SDHC Class 10 UHS-1 Superior Card (R: 91MB/s; W: 47MB/s).

These tests concluded that both the USB 3.0 port and SD card reader matched its claim and are capable of performing at fast speeds. These are excellent results.

▶ Final Thoughts
This device has a lot going for itself, as it can do multiple things while fitting in your pocket, but falls short of perfect for desktops. I would buy, and recommend this product to anyone needing more than a USB hub, and give this product a 5 star rating, but hope that kdLinks makes an improved version of this product.

Pros:
+ A very portable and versatile product, capable of replacing a charging hub and SD card reader.
+ Tests showed ports fit well, charger ports are very fast, and USB 3.0/SD Card reader are capable of providing fast transfer speeds.
+ Power adapter brick doesn’t directly plug into wall outlet.

Cons:
- Its strength in portability compromises some functionality. No micro SD slot, uses horizontal design, and only one LED indicator.
- Uses micro USB 3.0 interface, which is great in terms of keeping the hub small, but compromises availability if the cable ever needed replaced.

I was provided a sample in exchange for a thorough and honest review.

title: Fixed boot-up/start screen loop problem
text:
Just received this tablet as a Christmas gift for my daughter. Was very upset to find that upon start up, it was hopelessly locked in a loop on the splash page, running the Lenovo logo graphic over and over and...over...and over....and... Yeah. It never would get past that loop no matter what I tried.
After several hours of searching the Internet, I finally found a fix on one post on the Lenovo community forum. The simple solution was to press the volume-down button and the power button at the same time, and hold them until the tablet started. This ran the tablet through some kind of updating sequence, auto restarted it and then prompted me to do the expected 1st use set up that is normally required on a new device such as this. Soon it was up and running, with no problems. Christmas is saved.
Now, I should warn you...the forum poster who gave these instructions was advising someone who had this problem on a diff model lenovo tablet that he had been using for a long time before this loop issue happened to him. The poster said this process (holding the aforementioned keys down) would prompt the tab to take him through a FACTORY RESET). It didn't do that with mine obviously. Maybe because it had never been used? Maybe because I was trying it on a different model? I have no way of knowing. I also cant tell you what it will do with your tab if you try it. All I can tell you is what it did for me. I was extremely grateful for the tip, and had to share it.

title: HDE bags not as good as others
text:
Four months ago I bought a set of these bags from "Bluecell" for $16. Quality was very decent. Not as nice as LensCoat pouches, but only 1/3 the price... and plenty functional for many uses. The set I got from HDE (including a "Bluecell" velcro tie, so I thought it was exactly the same) a month ago was slighter less money, but quality was inferior. Whereas the the "Bleucell" version had nice flat, edge-butted seams, the HDE version used face-to-face overlapping seam construction that left a thick ridge of material inside the cylinder of the pouch. Also, the polypro strap protruded into the bottom of the bag with a sharp edge from the heat-cut. There were a few other details where corners were cut.

Note that both brands have non-stretching fabric for the collar that the drawstring runs through. While neoprene is very stretchy, the non-stretch collar constricts the size of what you put in it. (LensCoat uses stretchy collar material, hence a more versatile -- and more expensive -- pouch. LensCoat neoprene is not stinky like these from Hong Kong)

At $10, these are a decent value and plenty good for protecting many kinds of items, but for lenses, I'd rather pay $5 more and have a pouch that did not have material protruding into the inside.

text:

You don't need to download this unknown software. The software mentioned in the earlier review is not in the Apple App store, so I don't recommend using it. Particularlly because you can modify these setting without any additional software.

Here is how to read and adjust these settings on your own:
In finder, search for and open Terminal
In the terminal window type: defaults read com.apple.BluetoothAudioAgent (this will show your current settings)

If you choose to adjust them, in the same terminal window type: defaults write com.apple.BluetoothAudioAgent "Apple Bitpool Min (editable)" 40

Just replace min with max and 40 with whatever value you desire

title: Some Empty Promises...
text:
I'm going to use this review to correct some misleading descriptions about the Kindle Paperwhite. These are all things I noticed very quickly and it's frustrating. An overrated product.

Backlight: This is nowhere near what it is described as. As readers have mentioned, the backlight is uneven at the bottom of the screen. It gives the Paperwhite a cheesy, unnatural look. The backlight CANNOT be turned off, so the uneven lighting is permanent. The light is a blotchy electric blue. This color is not reading friendly (kindle designers must not read much).

Screen: Fingerprints collect all over the place. There's no glass so skin oils stay put. Certain angles render text unreadable. Isn't this what e-readers are supposed to avoid? Surface is gray, reflective, and text looks pretty dull - big and small. Slllooowwww touch response, feels ancient. Experience is harsh, selections unusable at times. iPhone/Galaxy users, prepare for a let down.

Look and Feel: Flimsy construction. On the plus side, it's lightweight, much better than a tablet. Page-turns fade comfortably with few instances of inverting contrast. You cannot change the screen savers (again..cheesy).

The bottom line is you'll really have to fool yourself into liking this thing. Reading is an activity that deserves quality craftsmanship. Bookmaking has a long history of high standards. The e-reader industry doesn't. Stop playing cheap Amazon. You'll have to be easily impressed to keep this...

title: Pretty impressed with this antenna
text: Had this up for a while now, did some comparisons with my old monster Yagi type antenna and this Antennacraft unit proved itself. I'm in a deep fringe area, usually can't get one channel with my old antenna un-amplified. Boosted signal on a couple channels went from 70 (Sony TV diagnostic readout) on the old antenna to 90. Daytime reception improved dramatically too. Only minor drawback to this unit is that it is mechanically unbalanced. Quite a bit heavier on one end, possibly not a good thing with the rotator (rotor), maybe not. Assembly is pretty simple, instructions good, hardware supplied as needed. Hoping the plastic element brackets hold up in the sunlight, had problems with this on the old antenna with similar looking pieces. We do have the full cable package but they don't carry some channels I want to watch, maybe due to FCC coverage limits, this antenna pulls them in pretty decent. Excellent reception from 45 to 60 miles in the So. Ohio hill country, decent reception up to 85 miles or so in good conditions with 1000kw stations.  Nice to see the Made in USA on the box and the manufacturer doesn't make the usual absurd claims about 150 mile range etc. Heck of a deal here on Amazon.  Looks trick too.

title: An honest comparison with the Roku 3.
text:
Full disclosure, I have owned and enjoyed every iteration of the Roku streaming box, and currently own and use a Roku 3. Additionally, I have owned and enjoyed every Amazon Fire tablet ever made, and have been a prime member for as long as the service has been offered. I buy and consume almost all of my digital media from Amazon, with the only exceptions being that I subscribe to Hulu Plus, and use Pandora to stream music. Having used the new Fire TV for 24 hours now, the following is my honest comparison.

Advantage Roku 3:

*Channel selection: This isn't even close. Roku offers over 1200 channels and games, compared to only 180 for Fire TV. While most of the Roku channels are completely senseless, all of the important channels are present. The Roku 3 also finally includes a YouTube channel, and also includes Blaze TV, which is missing on the Fire TV (please keep your political comments to yourself, as this is not the Huffpost blog).

*User interface: The Roku 3 interface is cleaner and more simple, while the Fire TV interface is really attempting to push Amazon Prime content. This is not a knock on Amazon, so much as it is a comment on the clutter of the Fire TV interface.

*Headphone jack in the remote: Why other streaming products fail to see the value in this is beyond me.

Advantage Fire TV:

*Voice search through the remote: While this feature only works with Amazon content, it is very helpful for navigation purposes. If you use Amazon instant video for your streaming service, this feature will save you serious time and headaches by not having to type in search queries with the remote control. Every time I have used this function it has worked flawlessly.

*Additional film information: Amazon is creating a real advantage in this regard. If you use Amazon Instant Video as your streaming service, you can pair Five TV with your HDX tablet and have all the information regarding any film right at your finger tips. Information about the actors, director, supplemental material, etc. No other streaming service offers anything remotely close to this level of detail.

*Speed and power: Let me be 100% clear on this point. If you use Amazon Instant Video as your streaming service, everything in your existing library and watch list will play immediately. By immediately I mean in less than a second! Amazon is leveraging it's massive server infrastructure and pre-queuing all of your content, as well as any content it recommends for you. Unfortunately, this speed advantage only works with Amazon content.

*Gaming: Fire TV will accommodate a much more detailed gaming experience than the Roku 3. You can purchase a very competent gaming controller for only $40. If you are looking for the ultimate gaming experience, the Xbox or PS whatever is obviously the way to go.

*Future software upgrades: Fire TV is built on the Android platform, which has very obvious advantages. Channel developers who already have functioning Android apps will be able to very cheaply convert to the Fire TV platform. I fully expect Fire TV to experience very quick channel growth. Additionally, I think this factor makes Fire TV a better value than Roku 3. While it costs more upfront, the life of the Fire TV box will be much longer than the Roku product. Roku requires a new box for any significant upgrade of the technology, while the Fire TV box can be significantly upgraded with software enhancements.

In conclusion, If you already use Amazon Instant Video than Fire TV is a no brainer. It offers a massive upgrade over what you will get using the Instant Video app on another platform. If you already own a Roku product, and do not use Amazon Instant Video, than I do not recommend you buy Fire TV. If you have yet to purchase a streaming device, and are looking to start using a streaming subscription service, than I hope you find this review helpful.

I'd be happy to answer any questions.

Tuck

title: Samsung S3 to 2008 Saab stock
text:
My car (2008 Saab 9-3) has an Aux port on the stock radio, but I have a huge problem. My Galaxy S3 tries to be "smart" with head phone detection and at the same time, my audio unit tries to be "smart" with Aux In connections. The S3 won't play audio through the Aux cable because it doesn't detect anything receiving on the other side, and my audio unit will disconnect from the Aux input back to radio because it doesn't detect any input.

I can get it to work if I have sound playing through my phone and plug the aux cable in at the right time and it will play for a song, but after a second and a half of silence, they disconnect from each other.

Then I found this! I connect via bluetooth to the dongle that goes in the 12v socket, and just connect the Aux cable (included) from the Tunelink to my radio and it works without a hitch. They have a nice feature in the app to suggest FM stations to tune to based on your location if you need the FM transmitter portion, but I plan on only using the Aux connection.

Sound quality is the same as Aux (when I can get it to work). Also, the volume works better too. My volume indicator is just a bar graph without numbers, but basically at 10% the sound from FM radio stations is loud enough, but through the Aux from my phone to the Audio unit, I had to use about 60-70% volume. So when they disconnected after a song, I would have to quickly lower the volume or lose my ear drums :O! With the Tunelink, the volume is nice and clear at 30%, so much more room for turning up low songs to hear them better and what not.

The picture indicates a green glow, but mine is blue. The packaging was green and it does indicate it is the android version. It also includes a USB charging port, so that is convenient as well.

title: Good, but too slow to be a 5D3 replacement
text:
I bought the 6D to replace my lost 5D Mark III because I didn't want to spend a huge amount on another camera and since I just shoot for fun I though the 6D would be adequate. Overall, it is but not in all ways. The body is a bit smaller and lighter, which is good, and the top of the body that is plastic instead of magnesium alloy in the 5D3 is not noticeable at all, nor is the plastic instead of the glass LCD screen cover. I can't really tell the difference. The LCD is slightly smaller (0.2" or so) but not a big deal to me. The viewfinder shows 97% instead of 100% but that doesn't make a big difference to me either (since the pics include everything that I can see plus a bit more). I welcome the simpler autofocus system of the 6D (never fully learned how to use the complex AF system on the 5D3). The low light performance seems to be really good, and I've read that it's slightly superior on the 6D anyway. The wifi is nice addition on the 6D since it lets you have better control over wifi uploads than when using an eye-fi card (since you can pick what to upload from your computer and not your camera).

The only thing I don't like is that the 6D is slightly but significantly slower at focusing and shooting. With my 5D3, I could pick up my camera and start shooting away shot after shot in rapid succession (each shot separately) without almost any delay. With the 6D, there is that split second (probably less than half a second) delay between shots that is much more noticeable and annoying than I anticipated. Not sure if it's just slower AF or also a slower shutter mechanism (probably just AF) but it's noticeable and a hindrance, especially since I need to shoot fast when taking pics of my fast-moving kid.

Anyway, the 6D is a nice full frame DSLR overall for the casual photographer but the slower AF/shooting is something that you should check out for yourself before plunking down the money to buy one (I got mine at that popular auction site and so I can't readily return it). I may eventually end up selling it and getting another 5D3, or I may wait for the eventual 5D4 or 6D2 if either improves the AF speed.

Following the well written instructions, I went in and turned off my TV's speakers, and was enjoying the surround sound amplification in minutes.

Comparisons... I had a Harmon Kardon receiver with individual satellite speakers spaced much further apart, plus a subwoofer, and I do think the widely spaced array and higher power output from the receiver provided a better overall sonic experience. But the footprint was huge - the receiver fills an entire foot-high slot in my entertainment center, whereas the Bose occupies no space in there at all. The Bose subwoofer is huge, though, but luckily still fit in the space we had for it. Check your measurements before purchasing.

Aside: the Bose remote was the easiest-to-set-up remote I've ever used. It works with my Charter Cable, Vizio TV, and Sony BluRay/DVD/Internet video player with ease. All my other remotes had failed on one component or another. Bose also had only one code to enter for any given component/manufacturer. Kudos to Bose on making that experience so easy!

All in all I'm extremely satisfied with this unit. The footprint of the bar is tiny, and the sound is brilliant... it won't be as widely spaced as satellites scattered around your room, but will absolutely be a significant upgrade to your TV.

title: If it had a manual focus mode and used AA batteries it would be practically perfect!
text:
After the whole world had gone digital (except for me), I finally sold my extensive Olympus collection, consisting of 3 bodies and an arsenal of lenses, said goodbye to film, and bought my first digital camera - a Fuji SL7000. With a whopping 6-megapixel processor (pretty standard for the time), I used it to photograph my sister's wedding. The results were impressive. In 2008 I bought an Olympus UZ-570 (10-megapixels and a 20x zoom) for a trip to Africa, and I used that camera for six years until last month when I bought the Fuji SL1000.

What can I say? The SL1000 packs a wallop in the zoom lens department! At 2 1/2 times the power of my Olympus "ultra zoom," the 50x zoom on the Fuji is a 1200mm equivalent in a DSLR system, eliminating a lot of weight to lug around and a lot of time and money saved by not having to buy expensive lenses and change them constantly. I did not want to return to the days of a 40-pound camera bag. The SL1000 and everything else I need fits neatly into a holster style case that I can wear on my hip.

Photo quality is excellent, even at full zoom, with the camera compensating for shake. Video quality is equally good, and the stereo sound recording is amazing! The menu is intuitive, modes are logical and allow for a great deal of creativity whether you are a pro photographer or a newbie. I photograph snakes and other reptiles, and the SL1000's macro ability is phenomenal.

I was disappointed that the SL1000 (and most of the new Fuji lineup) doesn't have a manual focus option. When I was in Africa, there were times when a lion was in tall grass and my Olympus would automatically focus on the grass, giving me a blurry lion. This was easily corrected by switching to manual focus mode. This is not possible with the Fuji, and could be problematic for anyone who spends time at the zoo photographing through glass, chain link, bars, etc., or who just prefers to be in total control by being able to focus on their own.

Best features besides the lens include a hot shoe, an adjustable diopter (for folks who find it awkward to wear glasses while looking through a viewfinder), an adjustable screen for up and down (but not sideways) viewing, dual zoom controls, and a neat assortment of special effects, all packed into a solid, lightweight, compact camera.

One of my main criteria for choosing digital cameras in the past was the ability to use AA batteries which are inexpensive and available everywhere. Battery type was the main reason for choosing the SL7000 and the UZ570. I compromised with this camera because I wanted the zoom, and I wish the technicians at Fuji would try to be more consistent in making all of their cameras AA compatible. Right now it's about half and half. (Are you listening, Fuji?) Proprietary batteries are a pain in the butt! They are expensive, require a charger, and are difficult to charge away from home, especially in foreign countries.

Overall, this is an excellent camera choice for anyone who wants a simple-to-use camera that yields excellent results.

I ordered a 3rd recently that didn't seem to work well, so I followed up with this. With that said I can't say anything about this as far as long term. So far it seems to switch perfectly fine.

One problem with it is how the lights on the front were designed. They're all blue and the same kind of light. There is a light for power, output, and the 3 inputs. The remote sensor window (between the power and output lights) actually gets some radiant light from the others and almost appears as a light itself, so you see this array of lights across the front that all look the same which makes it difficult, especially from a distance, to see which inputs are active. If there are some inputs that are active, but not selected they are red. This does help when discerning which line is active. This isn't a deal breaker of course.

If I would have designed it, I would have made the power light more distinguishable from the others, and there would be no output light. An output light is redundant.

The other problem I have isn't really a problem with the device itself. I have to unplug my comcast box from power or this device sees it as an active signal, making the device appear 'more on' than in a resting state. It also interferes with the auto switching. Other TV type devices do the same thing from what I've read. They are 'always on'. This isn't a big deal since I often unplug it anyway because it produces a lot of heat just sitting there. I realized this could have been the issue with my last two devices acting 'faulty' and might have not been faulty at all. Too late, I already threw them away.

Edit: solved my issue with the lights. Just cut out little circles using black electrical tape and covered the power and output lights since I don't need to know that information. If either of those aren't working, then neither does my picture - not to mention if I see lights for inputs, then I know it's powered on. It's now a lot less distracting and easier to see what line is on.

Also, wanted to note the benefit to using alternate lighting for active ports that aren't being used (via red light). You can still see whats active even if it's not selected. It was because of that is how I knew my comcast box is 'always on'.

title: Yes, it is Cat 5 and has twisted pairs
text: I used this cable to wire a home network and therefore had to put new connectors on the ends of the cable.  I found the cable to have twisted pairs unlike what others have found apparently.  The cable inside is copper stranded.  This means that each individual wire inside is made up of a couple dozen individual copper threads instead of a single copper wire.  A previous reviewer attacked this as being nonstandard but the truth is that it's a common practice to have stranded wire to use in tight spaces because it's more flexible especially in applications like a networking cabinet with many short connections.  If you are going to be putting new connectors on this cable just be sure you have the connector that is designed for stranded wire instead of solid wire.  Stranded wire connectors are designed to pierce each individual wire straight up the middle and therefore make it's connection in the middle of the strand.  Solid wire connectors will be designed to cut the sheath of each wire with something like a V-shape in order to make connection with the solid wire at the bottom of that V.  I wired my home and found this cable to work great especially in one area where I had to go under the carpet.  I was able to get it to lay very easily between the pad and the tack strip and I can't even tell it's there at all.

title: Roku streaming is not as free or easy as you think.  Disappointing.
text:
I purchased the Roku 3 to avoid having cable costs at my vacation home. I have DirectTV at home and didn't want to pay for another cable bill. I chose the Roku 3 over Google Chromecast as it received very high reviews and it offered (on the box and their website) access to the channels I want to use. I also liked the flexibility to connect both wirelessly and hardwired.

The Roku 3 was initially easy to set up. Took a few minutes to update software - be patient. I thought it was locking up, but it was just churning away.

I learned you have to set up each channel for use - at least those that matter. I was hoping to get a device that would let me use HBOGo, Amazon Prime, FoxNow, NBC, ABC and CBS. But all I can use is the Amazon Prime. Yes, it has dozens of free channels, but frankly, I'm not into watching other people bird watch, fish, golf, hike, make cabinets, etc. I just wanted to get to the news, stream a couple of TV shows and a movie every now and then. Here's what I found out.

1. Each time you select a channel and start to use it, you have to go to the internet and set up your connection to that channel by entering an access code. The access code only works if you currently are paying for a subscription to that channel AND if your TV (like Samsung) or TV Service Provider (live FioS or a cable company) ALLOW it. Yes, ALLOW it. If your TV or service provider don't allow it, you can't get to that channel. You get directed to a standard screen that tells you to send an email or otherwise contact your service provider to tell them you want this and to enter an agreement with that channel. Really?

2. You can't stream the major networks. Fox will allow you to stream their shows but only if your TV or Service Provider allow it. I have DirectTV - not on their list. Couldn't find channels for ABC, CBS or NBC. Did find one for PBS and they allow streaming, but first you have to log in and provide an email account.

3. You can stream Amazon Prime. I assume the same for independent services such as Hulu Plus. You can't stream regular Hulu. You have to enter your account info. Nothing unexpected there.

4. You can't stream HBOGo - the main reason I purchased this. Yes, the cover says they can and all the reviews say this is the only device that can do it. But you have to have a Service Provider that allows it. I have DirectTV - not on their list. So while I pay for HBO and can stream it on other devices, I can't on the Roku 3. That's right, you can't stream that which you already pay for, even though the box says you can.

5. Otherwise, I like the size, set up is easy and the iPhone app is easier to use than the remote.

Maybe the Roku 3 is for you - if you already pay for services for channels from approved providers, then it will work for you. I intend to return it and purchase a Google Chromecast. HBOGo, Amazon Prime, basic Hulu and the major networks all allow for streaming off their devices to computers and iPads.

title: Best self shot camera and much more.
text:
The Samsung NX Mini 20.5MP CMOS Smart WiFi & NFC Compact Interchangeable Lens Digital Camera with 9-27mm Lens and 3" Flip Up LCD Touch Screen is an amazing camera in such a small package.

The 20.5MP CMOS sensor offers great capture and fairly low noise at even fairly high 1600 ISO lets you take photos anywhere, any time. (ISO can be selected up to 12800)
The built in flash offers plenty of illumination but also included is a removable pop up flash for really lighting up a room. My only complaint here is that it seems you must navigate the menus to disable the built in flash with no button or touch screen option to instantly disable.

As with other Samsung cameras there are a host of options. I tend to stick with program mode as it offer the best control. But 17 built in scenes including waterfall, fireworks, sunset, parties, food, etc. all make quick work of setting up a no fuss shot. Built in panorama stitching was remarkably good with little artifacts and the on screen guide was easy to follow. There is a best face mode from group shots, if everyone stand fairly still you can take a series of shots and pick the best smile for each person for the final composition.
In selfie mode you have the option to operate the shutter with auto smile detection, wink detection, or normal shutter button.

When shooting fast action I found the shutter speed able to freeze some really fast action. in good light you can stop at 1/16000 sec shutter speed and with a burst of 10 frames/sec for 3 seconds can capture a moment you never saw with your naked eye.

While there are not a lot of buttons or dials, the touch screen is fairly easy to use and is visible is all but the most direct sunlight.

Startup time is quick with a top of the small and not really obvious power button located next to the similar looking wifi/direct link button. You can also power on the device by flipping up the real panel into "selfie mode". In either case though, you will need to rotate the lens out of its lock position.

In wide angle 9mm you will capture an image that reaches just a bit into your peripheral vision so you can get a pretty wide angle shot, full telephoto seems like about a 6x zoom and Optical Image Stabilization helps when you don't have a tripod.

Although the lens is interchangeable, this is a new NX-M mount and there really isn't much to choose from other than this 9-27mm zoom and a 9mm pancake lens.

In addition to 20MP photos the NX Mini offers full HD 1080p 30fps movie mode with a dedicated button to start recording. I found the video recording to be quite good and operating the zoom while filming was not difficult.

Built in Wifi works really well with the ability to upload to many shares such as facebook, dropbox, picasa, flickr, even email directly from the camera. Built in editing to remove redeye, change filters, crop, etc. lets you tweak the photo before you share it.

title: Great Little Lightweight Phones for the $7 Paid When I Got Them!!
text:
I have been using these little phones since I discovered them many years ago. They are so lightweight and the sound is outstanding for their category. If they cost $29.99 they'd still be a deal. At $7 bucks they're a steal.

These are great for general listening (MP3) or for movies or TV off the laptop. They are so light you don't even know they're on your head, and because they are open, they don't irritate the insides of your ears like earbuds. You can also hear other noise in the room if it's loud enough, which is handy if you want to be able to hear someone call, catch the phone ringing, or whatever.

The range if these phones is terrific as so many in the category are either tinny from too much high-end, muddy from reproducing bass poorly, or they lack mid-range all together. Not so with these little Sonys. They out-perform themselves by delivering clean sound across all frequencies.

No small-diameter earphone is going to be able to reproduce bass-rattling low frequencies like a woofer or external speak does, or even a larger, standard studio style headphone. But for everyday use there is nothing to beat them, or even come close. They will promptly become your favorite digital headphones.

UPDATE: As of Dec 2, 2013 the price on these is $64.99!!!! I have been buying these headphones for at least 10 yrs, have owned 4 pairs, and I paid $5.99 - $7.00!!!! The model number is still the same exact model number I bought from Amazon (that this review was based on) that I paid $7 for. That's just a rip off. If they could make a profit for so many years at $7... now to jump to $64??? I will never buy them again unless this is some kind of typo!!

title: 8 months in and still doing fine.
text:
After sorting through all the case options for the Nexus 10 on Amazon, I settled on this one and have been using it for 8 months. It holds up well to general use and does a good job protecting the Nexus 10.

Once you manage to shimmy your Nexus into this case, and it is a tight fit, your tablet is firmly in place and isn't going anywhere.

As with most fabric cases that are glued, durability may be an issue. After general use for 8 months, my case developed an opening in the cover near the fold by the "poetic" logo. With a small application of glue, though, this problem is easily taken care of.

For protection, this case has been solid. I have dropped my Nexus a handful of times; the tablet has always come away with nary a scratch, and the case even forgoes minor damage. This surprised me after my tablet met with the concrete on one unfortunate occasion, and the case didn't have any marks to show for it.

Overall ,this case has been a great investment and has held my Nexus 10 snugly in its protective grasp for going on 8 months.

Pros:
- Slim. This case doesn't add much bulk to the Nexus 10.
- Protective. As slim as it is, this case has saved my tablet from nasty falls on multiple occasions
- Magnets. The case does a reasonably well job of holding itself closed.
- Folding cover. By folding the cover, the tablet can stand up pretty good.
- Looks. This case is attractive and avoids being gaudy.

Cons:
- Button cutouts. It can be difficult to get at the volume buttons.
- Glued construction. Not as sturdy as sewn, but can be easily mended.
- Tendency to develop loose threads around the cover and along the back. Can be easily trimmed.
- Tight fit. Although it holds the Nexus securely, it can be a tight fit if you ever want to remove your tablet.

title: Read this, these are what you want! Recommended setup below!
text:
I have been holding off writing my review as I wanted to break these in and get a feel for what I think.

Installation: Took me a full day, and a few more days of tinkering with sound settings and placement in the living room. It was pretty easy, I bought the recommended banana plug adapters, made wiring a breeze, and I bought the 100ft 16g wire spool as well I recommend slightly longer spool of wire if you have a lot of distance to cover, I ran out thanks to one mistake on my length. I purchased the Atlantic Satellite speaker stands along with this and MAN do they look good in the man cave holding these puppies up!

Recommended hardware:
Atlantic Satellite 77305018 2 Speaker Stands (Black)
VideoSecu 5 Black Deluxe Speaker Mount Brackets for Walls and Ceilings 1XZ
RCA AH16100SR 100 Ft. 16-Gauge Speaker Wire
Mediabridge ULTRA Series Subwoofer Cable (25 Feet) - Dual Shielded
Denon AVR-X1000 5.1 Receiver (bought from crutchfield got a free iphone dock work 300 bucks)
Monoprice 109436 High-Quality Copper Speaker Banana Plugs - 5-Pair

Sound Quality: After getting the placement where I wanted everything and mounted on the walls I tried a Blu-ray movie. I think it was Inception. Holy crap. Action scenes shake the living room and the upstairs of the house, I now know to expect being yelled at for cranking it too loud. Playing Dead Rising 3 on the Xbox one is scary alone because you will hear growling coming from the rear speakers behind you! Trying Call of Duty brought smiles to all my friends faces who pulled the trigger, as base exploded through the room and vibrations from the controller collided together! Yes the sound quality of this set matched with my Denon receiver is astounding! Such a good value, my father gave me flak over the waste of money and how I should buy Bose, well now he has stopped that nonsense and come to appreciate my setup! Win!

Tips: If you go my route with the Denon Receiver, it does NOT have on board wifi. I am sorry about that one I did not know, but I simply threw an Ethernet cable from the box to my pc which is 2 feet away so whenever the PC is running the Denon has the wifi through it. The Apple Airplay is a win! Oh another tip! If you have the Xbox One and need a place to put your Kinect Sensor it is the EXACT same width as your center channel speaker, so I wall mounted my front three speakers and placed the Kinect Sensor ontop of my center channel and its flawless!

CONS: You will spend money. Once you start tinkering you will want to spend more money. Your friends will never leave. You will never go outside. Your family will hate you. Your neighbors will hate you. Your tv speakers will plot to assassinate you, but die from neglect.

I say buy these. I NEVER buy something this expensive without my research, and you can trust me I put weeks and weeks into studying these up from CNET and other reputable reviewers, checked the products that best match up, and spent time getting it right. THIS is what you want.
