title: Ten Stars out of Five
text:
BACKGROUND
A little over two months ago, I began my search for a new desktop PSU. I started by pulling up Amazon’s top 100 best sellers list. The top 20 were overwhelmingly dominated by just one brand, so I began drilling down there. Almost immediately I found myself unhappy with the state of affairs reported for these units due to their many problems (e.g., abundant multiple DOAs and RMAs in succession; units which apparently ran well for a few days or weeks and then died, some peacefully, some with sparks or light as of a short circuit, a few by explosion, taking out with them everything in the desktop case. Frustrated, I turned to other brands as they caught my attention. The story with these was largely similar: too many problems, little evidence of any real QC, lots of hype, and apparent realization of claims only by random chance. By now at least three weeks had elapsed and I was angry. Was the entire PSU area one large crap field? I asked myself.

I went back to the top 20 list again and noticed for the first time just a single entry for EVGA. (I didn’t know the brand. I’m not a gamer.) This quickly led me to the desktop 750 watt G2 (generation 2) PSU. (I later found that the G2 series was introduced around mid-2013.) At that time it had 35 reviews and a rating of 4.9. In a few days I had carefully read them all, spot-checked other product reviews in the EVGA line-up, and knew I had found my needle in the haystack!

As I write this review, there are 236 reviews with a product rating of 4.7. Not all the reviews pertain to the G2 line (reflecting Amazon’s policy of aggregating reviews from all family lines). Some include units from about a year ago when for a short time there actually appears to have been a manufacturer assembly error with the 1000 watt and 1300 watt units in the G2 and P2 families. EVGA’s G2 and P2 PSUs are designed and made by the regarded Taiwan OEM Super Flower Company, which also provides PSUs for a hand full of other labels, including Enermax, NZXT, and Sentey. (I had already noticed by my own analysis of the reviews, before I was aware of the episode of manufacturing error, that the higher wattage units seemed to be having a disproportionate number of the more serious problems.) That was a very valid issue then, but the negative reviews (they have no expiration) still weigh down the products being made now, after correction of the issue around 1 October 2013. One or two reviews concern rebate issues, not PSU quality issues. Some of the reported problems may even have been at least partially self-inflicted. Nevertheless, with a larger sample, valid problems now have arisen (even a few of the kind which take out everything in the desktop). And what shall I say? The occurrence of incidents in the G2 PSU line is by my analysis considerably lower than with other brand offerings competing near this price point, but unfortunately not entirely absent: there remains a residual luck-of-the-draw element. Perhaps faulty installation or other latent problems with the PC receiving the new PSU were even factors in a few cases. While understanding the anger and pain which will be the lot of those who experience it, I must write based on my own experience, and I begin to do so below.

The Quick-Look SUMMARY VERSION Review

The (essentially) totally-quiet operation of the PSU cooling fan and the lack of any coil whine have been abundantly documented in other reviews and need not be dealt with again here.

The subjective quality apparent in the cables, the PSU, and even the packaging is the last word from every angle from which I can think to judge. (I have no test equipment or technical know-how to perform quantitative measurements.) There have been no performance issues or idiosyncrasies so far (after one month) with my installation. To me, this PSU seems over-the-top and I am thoroughly impressed and completely delighted. For peace of mind and many additional reasons, tangible and intangible, ten stars out of five are what I would award if I could.

A JonnyGURU review made this salient observation: “EVGA tends to under-promise and over-deliver.” For at least once in your life, discover what it’s like to be overwhelmed with quality instead of hokum and to wallow in excellence. The next production run may not attain to the current production run, so grab this PSU now while it is still available.

The LONG VERSION Review

The product presents in a handsome black corrugated cardboard box entirely encased in shrink wrap. The box is opened by cutting (use a small X-acto knife) a tough plastic QA seal located over an interlocking cardboard tab at the bottom center of one of the smallest faces. The box has a black plastic carrying handle centered in this smallest face. Once the QA seal is cut, that smallest face lifts up (open), permitting the entire top (one of the largest faces) to hinge open.

What one then sees can be described as not only beautiful but (almost) breath-taking. Everything inside the box (including ALL inside surfaces of the box and the soft-ish foam packing material) is black. High quality and meticulous attention to detail seem everywhere apparent. It seems no exaggeration to state that every minutia of this product and its presentation has been carefully conceived, designed, and executed. For once, it looks like QC has been both real and at a high level. (At the time I actually made the purchase, the reviews (over 50) for this product were hovering closer to 5.0 than to 4.9. There were no 3-star, 2-star, or 1-star reviews. No smoke, sparks, or explosions; at that time, no DOAs or RMAs.)

The PSU itself comes in a very nice (black) nylon case (with gold EVGA lettering) with a closing flap secured with a Velcro closure. This nylon case ships inside the cardboard box suspended between two (black) foam end-caps. Slipped in on top of the PSU nylon case and under the two end-caps is the handsome (black-covered) 36-page 5-language manual (quality paper, die-cut, quality printing) also downloadable from www.EVGA.com. A large and handsome (black) nylon case (with gold EVGA lettering) is provided for storage of unused/uninstalled cables and has a closing flap secured with a Velcro closure. Like everything else in the box, it bespeaks of quality.

The first thing I inspected (by lengthy fondling and caressing) was the (black) PSU. The construction of the unit is solid. The fit and finish of all edges and corners are perfect, as are all surfaces. No cosmetic blemishes of any kind were found anywhere. The craftsmanship here is immaculate. There is even a small clear plastic disk over the stylized EVGA “E” in the center of the fan grill to protect its metallic finish and luster from tarnish. Affixed by static cling, this lifts cleanly and easily. (Don’t overlook its removal. I’ve wondered whether the few “fan noise” complaints reported might be due to that little plastic disk being sucked up into the fan area.)

ALL the cables (except the 6” Floppy Disk Drive “adapter,” if one can label that a “cable”) are encased in handsome (black) woven nylon sleeving.
ALL the cables at the PSU interface are latching.
ALL the cables at the other end (the attached-device interface) are latching EXCEPT as follows:
- The 15-pin SATA power cable connectors are non-latching. Depending upon your particular configuration of SATA devices, additional (extension) cabling may be needed.
- The peripheral cable’s Molex connectors (regular size) are non-latching. As above, depending upon your particular configuration of peripheral devices, additional (extension) cabling may be needed.
- The 2-pin part of the 6-pin + 2-pin VGA power cables is non-latching (it is too narrow for a latch; the 6-pin part is latching).
- The Floppy Disk Drive adapter cable (about 6” and connecting to a peripheral cable Molex connector [regular size]) is non-latching at both of its ends.

I inspected EACH cable by lengthy fondling and caressing. As before, everything I saw bespeaks of quality. There were no “oh-oh!” moments. Neither the cables nor their connectors feel in any way “cheap.” In fact, the cables have a reassuring hefty feel to them. All connectors SEEMED soundly attached.

Note that the “main cable” or motherboard-powering cable consists at the PSU interface of two separate parts: a 10-pin (left-most) part and an 18-pin (right-most) part. Both parts (latching) must be connected to the 28-pin PSU interface. The motherboard connector (latching) at the other end of this cable is a solid (non-breakable) 24-pin entity. It is NOT of the 20-pin + 4-pin variety. If you happen to have a 20-pin motherboard connector, you will need to obtain an inexpensive 24-pin to 20-pin adapter/adapter cable.

Note that JonnyGURU reviews (see references later) for the 1000 watt and 850 watt versions pointed out modular cable “connector contact issues” with his motherboard cable. (“The ATX [motherboard] cable in particular had a few loose connections in it that produced some voltage swings when I pushed on it.” That is, pushing in on the wiring harness where it enters the plastic connector [whether at the PSU interface or at the motherboard interface is not clear; it could be either or both] caused very small voltage fluctuations and thus the theoretical potential of losing/corrupting data due to power fluctuations.) I had already done my install before I knew about this review/problem. Even though I’ve had no problem so far, I thought to myself “it-wouldn’t-hurt-to-have-a-high-quality-spare-motherboard-cable-lying-around; they-can’t-be-that-expensive.” Perhaps I didn’t employ the best/correct descriptive terminology, but in several quick Internet searches I found no individual replacement motherboard cables! (mobo extension cables, yes; complete whole modular sets, yes)

There is ± 2% voltage regulation of the three regulated positive voltages (+ 12, + 5, and + 3.3). This degree of “tightness” is relatively rare (especially at this price point) and is indicator of the high quality of this PSU. Many top-of-the-line PSUs regulate to ± 3%. The ATX standard only requires ± 5% here. (The + 5 standby voltage need be only nominally regulated.)

DC-to-DC Converter technology has been used in PCs in various places for quite some time. This means that the regulated + 5 volt and + 3.3 volt currents are derived directly from the + 12 volt current rail of the PSU. This is more energy-efficient than having dedicated + 5 volt and + 3.3 volt transformer taps along with their voltage regulators. There is less waste heat to dissipate. This design technology maximizes the + 12 volt rail current output, permits faster dynamic current response, and increases system stability. It undoubtedly also is a large contributor to the tight ± 2% positive voltage regulation.

The EVGA G2 and P2 PSU series are based on the Super Flower Leadex (SFL) platform designed and built by the well-regarded Super Flower Company OEM based in Taiwan. The Super Flower brand can be imported from Europe but is itself not directly available in North America. In essence, in the current time frame, the EVGA G2 and P2 series ARE (exclusively?) the Super Flower product in the USA. I commend the following JonnyGURU reviews which cover many technical considerations and measurements (though his final ratings are somewhat subjective and informally breezy, and his write-ups are characterized by chronic, annoying, and puerile inner monologues, apparently as of a frustrated standup comic). Anyone interested in the EVGA G2 series of PSUs should read ALL of the following reviews to get an enlarged picture both of the G2 series and of the SFL products on which they are based. (The budget-targeted EVGA B2 product – ultimately SFL-based, though at a budget level – is included for contrast because I found the review.)

JonnyGURU review links
SFL 1300 watt http://www.jonnyGURU.com/modules.php?name=NDReviews&op=Story&reid=367
SFL 750 watt http://www.jonnyGURU.com/modules.php?name=NDReviews&op=Story&reid=370
EVGA G2 1300 watt http://www.jonnyGURU.com/modules.php?name=NDReviews&op=Story&reid=349
EVGA G2 1000 watt http://www.jonnyGURU.com/modules.php?name=NDReviews&op=Story&reid=346
EVGA G2 850 watt http://www.jonnyGURU.com/modules.php?name=NDReviews&op=Story&reid=377
EVGA G2 750 watt http://www.jonnyGURU.com/modules.php?name=NDReviews&op=Story&reid=380
EVGA B2 750 watt http://www.jonnyGURU.com/modules.php?name=NDReviews&op=Story&reid=393

The EVGA 750 watt G2 PSU (which more than meets my needs) is the smallest in the G2 family, which runs up by several models to 1600 watts. I don’t see how it gets better than this at any reasonable price I can afford to pay for a PSU. And it comes with an industry-unprecedented 10 year warranty, still another indicator of its quality and additionally indicative of what EVGA/SFC have poured into this G2 series, earlier manufacturing error episode (SFC’s fault) aside.

We were a little hesitant from the reviews, but decided on it anyway, the price was right and we have an LG TV and are pleased with that. I was a little intimidated when we opened the box because there was so much stuff. It was package very nicely and I LOVE the fact that all of the wires and cords are labeled and labeled on BOTH ends of it. The wireless receiver was SO easy, we plugged it in and it automatically connected with the receiver. Just an FYI, the Blue Ray player is the receiver as well, I didn't read that in the description but prob missed over it. We were able to connect the receiver to our wireless router incredibly easy. I mainly purchased this unit for the speakers, so I could listen to music while doing all the fun chores around the house, so I first tried the system with Pandora. I am SOOO happy with the sounds quality. I really like the different settings, either all of the speakers can be on, the two tall ones, the two wireless ones, all but the sub, etc, it's really cool. That might be a standard feature but this is my first "real" home theater system so I was pleasantly surprised. All in all I would highly recommend this product to anyone in the home theater system market with a $600ish price point. From opening the box to final speaker placement it took about 30minutes, of which half of it was unpacking the carefully packaged items. Very pleased.

Also, from one reviewer to another, when writing a review let's all remember to review the product; just because you received a product damaged doesn't mean it's a bad product. I've had my share of damaged product received and when I receive the replacement item it's worked out just fine.

title: A must for gaming needs.
text:
A shame that Lenovo phased out all of the Ideapad Y series, as I happen to have a Y500 with GT750M graphics. Not a bad machine by the way, but this piece of hardware makes your laptop even better. With SLI (and a little change on the BIOS for that to work), it grants you an additional 2GB of graphics power... I've been in the lookout for this upgrades this year and Lenovo didn't make it easy, but I finally bought it elsewhere.

First things first: Bear in mind that this product was thought with Windows 8 in mind and it's a bit perplexing that it doesn't work on 8.1 on the go, but thankfuly Lenovo made available a download for a necessary one-time BIOS upgrade on this card for Nvidia SLI to work on the newer OS. Also, you need some extra power for your PC, and that's why you need that bulky 170w AC Adapter brick from Lenovo too.

But after that, it's all charm.

For what it's worth, it makes the job done. Modern games benefits of the extra power on High+ setting @ 1080p, with some managing to get to Ultra: Max Payne 3, Far Cry 3, Tomb Raider (2013 reboot, even though Lara's TressFX hair still looks like MGS2 Snake's bandana in some instances as it was thought with AMD in mind), Deus Ex: Human Revolution, Mortal Kombat Komplete Edition, Borderlands 2 and most Unreal Engine 3 games. I haven't tested the whole 4GB VRAM on more recent games like Battlefield 3, The Witcher 2 Enhanced Edition and Watch Dogs (though this one I'm aware it's badly optimized for PC BTW), but in more older games like Valve's with Source Engine and even F.E.A.R. with those darn soft shadows, performance is (you guess it) flawless.

However, there are some thing to consider

First, it's not hot-swappable, and this has to do with the Ultrabay design and implementation on my laptop and all of the Ideapad Y series with similar solutions. Each time i want to put back the GPU and forth, i have to it turn and remove the battery.

Second, did i already mention this needs a more powerful AC adapter (170w) from Lenovo? This may scare away most people who, like me, wants to crank up their Y500s.

I wish Amazon allowed me to rank this 4.5 out of five stars; still I'm really happy I finally upgraded my Y500 with this card. it's hard to find, so get it for a reasonable price if you find one even used. You will be happy... and consider upgrading your RAM to 16GB for maximum performance.

Still, if Lenovo hadn't phased it out too soon...

P.S.: My laptop setup is a Lenovo Ideapad Y500 with Windows 8.1, Intel Core i7 3630QM @ 2.4GHz, and Corsair Vengeance with 16GB RAM (2x8GB DDR3 1600 MHz PC3 12800). Factory setup came with 12GB RAM, DVD burner on the Ultrabay slot and Nvidia GeForce GT750M graphics with 2GB... Hope you get the picture and this review helpful.

text:
The Dino-Lite works great. I received it a couple days ago and have no complaints. The main reason I bought it was to study my coins. If you buy it you will need a stand to help steady it to look at an object from a little greater distance than just setting the microscope right on top of it. I purchased the Dino-Light MS09B stand for $34. It's not worth the money and it's only good for looking at small objects that can be placed directly next to the stand. OK here is what you do:

1. Buy a cheap office lamp that has a flex stand.
2. Remove the light fixture and extension cord.
3. Attach a 1" 2-hole pipe strap to the end of the light fixture by drilling a hole through the center of the strap and mounting it on the flex stand.

Yes I know it won't look "professional" or there may be other ways to do it, but I went a cheap route. Total cost - under $8 and a little time.

title: Happy with Purchase!!
text:
Update 06/14/12: Still going strong! I liked it so much that I bought another one to put in a friend's computer I was fixing. Worked like a charm!!! Definitely impressed.

Update 04/29/12: I had this graphics card for a couple of months now and I have to say I am impressed. Remember, I do not use this card for gaming so I cannot test that aspect but I can tell you it handles any kind of video I try to throw at it. I was so happy I bought it for another computer of mine (also not used for gaming).

This product replaced a 2008 (3 year old) VisionTek ATI Radeon HD 4870 512 MB GDDR5 PCI Express Video Card 900244 in a 2007 (4 year old) Gateway Desktop PC. I originally had the VisionTek ATI Radeon HD 4870 for mid-range gaming (Crysis, Far Cry 2, Battlefield 2) but I no longer use this computer to game. So when that video card started failing (bright pink/green pixels all over my 24" Gateway FHD2401 monitor), I bought the EVGA GeForce GT 520 1024 MB DDR3 PCI Express 2.0 DVI/HDMI/VGA Graphics Card, 01G-P3-1521-KR.

The card arrived in 2 days (I'm a Amazon Prime Member) for the crazy price of $48.27 minus a mail-in rebate of $10 for a grand total of $38.27. My local Best Buy wanted $55.98 for it plus I had to wait 2-5 business days to get it since they did not have it in stock so Amazon was the clear winner in my decision making.

The video card is 5.7 inches long which fit in my desktop perfectly considering I had up to 8 inches for a component in my PCI-E slot.

Installation was extremely easy:

Prepare your desktop computer. Unplug your monitor, mouse, keyboard and other devices from the desktop computer tower. Leave the tower plugged into the surge protector. Lay the tower on its side and remove the cover. If possible, work on your desktop computer in a non-carpeted area to reduce static electricity.

Find a free expansion slot for the graphics card. If this is the first time you have removed the cover, you will probably see several free slots. You may need to remove an exterior slot cover to make room for the card. This will expose the connection ports on the graphics card to the back of the desktop computer. Remove the graphics card from its packaging, holding the video card by its edges. Never touch the sides of the video card or you may damage it with static electricity from your body. Press the graphics card gently but firmly into the expansion slot. If the graphics card requires an additional power supply, connect it now using the user manual provided with the card.

Install drivers and software for the graphics card. Plug your monitor, keyboard and mouse into the desktop computer and turn it on. Your graphics card usually comes with a CD for installing this software. If it's not included, you may need to download the software from the manufacturer's website. Consult your user manual to learn how.

Test your installed graphics card. After installing the graphics card software, you may need to unplug your monitor and plug it directly into the graphics card port in the newly exposed expansion slot. Follow instructions in your user manual to check your desktop computer settings. You should be able to check your computer's list of installed hardware to confirm the installation, usually labeled under display adapters. Play a high resolution video or game to test out your new graphics card settings. Adjust them according to your user manual.

title: I won't order anymore of them...
text:
First, I'm not sure that they should be able to claim "triple wall construction" when only 2 sides (the front and rear panels where the holes are cut out for handles) are constructed that way. The 3 remaining walls on the main box (long sides and bottom) although sturdy are only double wall.

Second, while the box itself is sturdy and well constructed, the lid appears to have been an afterthought. It's only single layer corrugated, and the corners are of an "Insert Tab-A into Slot-A" construction and don't hold together well. I've added clear packing tape to mine to keep the corners together or else the tabs slip out of the slots whenever I handle the lid.
After folding the boxes they held 55 slim jewel CD cases or 135 plastic sleeves with discs in them. I don't have any of the older style thick CD cases to try in there, but those are generally twice as thick as the slim cases so I'd guess about 25 may fit snug.

Finally, it might be a good idea for them to print the box's folding diagram on a separate sheet of paper. Mine were printed on the bottom of the box. And since they're not really that clear (just 5 drawings numbered I-V with no wording) it makes referring to the drawing during construction impractical. Fortunately, I'd ordered 2 so I was able to lay one flat and view the diagram while I folded the other.

"Diskeeper Ultimate CD Storage Box" isn't worth $10 per box, especially with so many other offerings around.

-Slaughter

title: Most enterprise-y SOHO router I have ever seen
text:
I got 2 of these as an upgrade from my Linksys WRT320n.

Almost all the walls in our house act as part of a faraday cage -- the original 1931 construction has stucco walls (even the interior), which contain a wire mesh. Renovated rooms have aluminum studs. Because of this, there were several rooms that were total dead zones with the WRT320n.

Even in the default configuration, and without any other 802.11ac devices, the RT-AC66u made a tremendous difference in connection speed and reliability, completely eliminating the dead zones. Then I found an option in the "Professional" tab of the wireless settings, which allows you to adjust the transmit power of this router. I increased it from the default of 80mW to 200mW on each band. I can now connect to my WiFi one house from the end of the block!

Transfer speeds over my LAN are now ~175Mbps when in the same room as the router, over 802.11n, on both 2.4 and 5GHz. From other areas of the house, I am mostly getting 75-100Mbps, where I was rarely getting above 10Mbps outside the room with my old router. In my front yard which was also a dead zone with the old router, as well as rooms that were previously dead zones, I now get over 50Mbps. This is especially convenient with my cell-phone GPS. I have Llama on the cell turning on WiFi only when I am home to save battery. Before I would always have to manually turn off WiFi when I got in the car, because it would see the driveway using the same cell tower as if in the house and try to use WiFi where there is no signal. Now the driveway gets a strong signal which speedtest.net rates as 55Mbps down 35Mbps up. On a single antenna cell phone.

The configurability and feature set of this router is also top notch.
* Easy single-option switch to go between normal SOHO router use, access point mode, and WiFi extender/bridge mode.
* Up to 3 guest networks on each band, with their own security settings
* Traffic monitoring, including both real-time and daily graphs, both for the WAN port, and broken down by wired vs. 2.5 vs. 5GHz
* Can function as a telnet/SSH server (the router is actually running linux)
* Parental control to make the internet only available to certain clients during certain hours. (and similar option for guest networks)
* Can connect drives to USB ports to make the router a file server.
* Can stream media from your LAN to the internet through Android/iOS apps.
* Rich port forwarding/firewall settings, and logging
* Can act as a VPN server
* Network testing tools through router admin pages.

Also, a large portion of the firmware is open source (I've read the standard Asus firmware is branched from DDWRT). There is a more advanced version maintained by "Merlin" with an even larger feature set.

Only a few down sides:
1. Only allows one machine to use the admin interface at a time. Won't let you log in to it from a new IP until you click "Logout" from the old IP (or reboot the router).
2. There is no easy way to bandwidth-restrict guest networks. The only way I could figure out is if you assign static IPs to all your own devices, and then bandwidth restrict the DHCP dynamically assigned IP range using the non-intuitive QoS settings.
3. Many/most options make you wait awhile after changing them and hitting apply. A lot cause clients to get disconnected during this wait. Many more than it should really. For example, why does changing DNS servers disconnect currently connected clients?
4. My 5 year old likes to play with the external antennas and I am worried he will eventually break them off or at least strip the threading with how they are screwed on.

title: Sony STR DN 1040
text:
Background:
Sharp 70 inch flat screen
Sony BD player
Comcast cable box
HP tower PC
PS3
Xbox 360
7.1 speakers- Pioneer SP-FS52 towers, 2 sets of SP-BS22 bookshelf, SP-C22 center speaker

The room is a 15x14 room w/12ft cathedral ceiling.

I have no need for a zone 2 as I have other systems available where needed. I also have everything hardwired so there is no need for wi-fi, even though it is nice that Sony included it on the 1040.

After my 2 ½ year old Pioneer 1120 receiver died an early death, I decided to pick up the Sony 1040. I chose Sony as I have had good luck with them, in the past, as far as reliability is concerned and bad luck with the Pioneer receivers (had a 1021 center ch. died after 15 months). So now will be going with Sony for the time being. Also, the Sony has two year warranty compared to the one year with Pioneer.

The 1040 was very easy to install and the automated system to adjust the speaker levels is very quick and easy to perform. The user interface is simple and easy to use. A firmware update was required and went through very smoothly with no issues, takes about 25 minutes or so (remember I am hardwired). It provides enough power for my system and sound performance is the same as my dead Pioneer, which is to say very good.

Things I wish it had are:
• Volume display shown on the TV
• User interface shown over top of your movie/TV show. Would make lip sync adjustments easier (as is it’s a PITA)
• Adjustable soft mute
• Album Art displayed when using Airplay
• 2 additional Speaker terminals for dedicated High/Wide Front speakers. (this is so that I can switch back and forth from 7.1 and 5.1 with High Front speakers. I really miss that from the Pioneer recv.)
• A decent app to control the receiver from your smartphone or IPAD. The Pioneer apps are super.

If you pay full boat for this receiver, I don’t think it’s worth it. But if you get a deal near $400 it would be a very good value for the money.

Four Stars.

title: Updated after 1 yr, 1 flaw away from 5 stars, still a great value!
text:
--- Update of review after 1 year of use (12/13) ---

I had two major gripes about this radio, the volume level that would revert to 10 at power up and the rear speakers increasing in music volume when the GPS was giving directions on the front speakers. The first one has been solved by a setting on the hidden settings menu. This has made a world of difference to my enjoyment of the radio as I can set the equalizer to what I want instead of what would be quiet enough at a volume setting of 10. I never did find a solution for the navigation audio problem other then changing the balance to all front speakers but I have gotten use to doing it. In my year of use, I never had any other problems, I never even had to do a reset. The nav software has a really nice feature that lets you instantly redirect around accidents which I have used on several occasions. Also I have yet to encounter an address for which it could not find. I'm upping the rating from 3 stars to 4 since it has been reliable and the start up volume problem has been fixed. If I could of solved the other nav/music volume problem I would of given it 5 stars. It's a great value and I recently bought another one for my wife's car.

--- End update ------

I find it strange that the reviews for this radio are all over the place with no common complaints. I wonder if there are multiple versions out there. Anyway here are some points based on my experience with it.

1 The radio body is double din in size but the faceplate is oversized. To get it to fit in my dash (2002 subaru wrx) I had to trim the faceplate above on top and on bottom. The trimming on the bottom was needed because the faceplate moves but the top is required just because it is too large even if it did not move.

2) There is no installation instructions, just a sticker on top that tells you what the wires do. The color coding on the pigtail is thankfully standardized so wiring is actually easy.

3) I don't have steering wheel controls on my car but it is easy to wire and setup if you do. There is an extra ground for the two available buttons. Once that is grounded then ground either one of the "key" wires activates whatever option you choose in the setup menu. Neat feature, I wish I had controls!

4)I purchased a rear view camera with this radio and it works perfectly. The wire from the radio that triggers the rear view camera should be wired to the positive wire of your backup lights.

5) My radio always starts set at volume 10 which is LOUD. This is just plain stupid. I don't think there is a fix for this as I believe it to be in the firmware and Pyle (Pyramid CO.) has no track record of releasing updates. I deal with it by setting my radio to "AUX IN" before turning it off. I have nothing connected to my Aux in so when it restarts I have the opportunity to turn down the volume before turning the radio on. Why it can remember that I left the radio set to Aux In but not the volume level is beyond me.

6) The nav system is poorly integrated with the radio functions and the navigation software supplied has problems. I read T. Dinnalls review (THANK YOU!) and took his advice and upgraded the IGO Prima software which fixed the key press/volume problem he mentions because this version of the software allows you to turn off the key press sound. If however did not fix the problem of the rear speakers not muting when the navigation software has something to say. In fact not only do they not mute, they turn up (probably to setting 10) and blast both music and the voice command so you can't here either. The work around for this was to set the fader all the way forward so that the rear speakers are completely turned off. BTW, I have the speakers connected to the speaker wires, not to the preamp, no idea what the preamp output does but maybe it works correctly on them and that is why not everyone complains, I don't know. Anyway, it's a shame because the navigation system otherwise works well and the radio sounds pretty good with all four speakers going. Oh, I have no idea what the subwoofer output does in this circumstance either.

7) The dvd works great, good picture quality and easy controls. I have the wire that goes to the parking brake grounded so the dvd player works while moving. My child's car seat is right in the middle of the back seat so she has a good view of it.

8) The Bluetooth telephone connection works great too, Very easy to set up and good sound out of it. The phone connection does properly mute the radio to all four speakers so it's all good.

9) The iphone plug is in the back of the radio and not secured very well, make sure you put a stain relief on the cable so you don't accidentally pull it out of the radio.

That is about it for now, the two major flaws I found was the volume starting a level 10 every time and the rear speakers volume during navigation. The oversize double din was annoying but not a deal breaker. I think both problems reside in firmware so I don't think there will ever be a fix for it. It drives me nuts as these seem to be simple problems to fix and really bring down what would otherwise be a very nice radio at a very nice price. I'm keeping mine (since I cut up the dash trim and all) but won't recommend it to anyone else unless they fix those issues

text:
The Good -

The Bad -
The dongle is generally weak and cannot take a beating at all it will easily break.
This is not a good mobile unit as the dongle is not discrete and can take damage easily.
The range on the device is not as advertised. I can get about 9-18 ft on a good day, nowhere near 40ft claimed on the box.
The Battery life is about 2/3 as long as advertised. Since day 1, I can get about 4-5 hours of use before I have to throw back on the charge.
The Unit does not operate while plugged in and charging. This puts you at a great disadvantage if you plan on using it every day in a mission critical environment. Hastily changing skype settings to use an old desktop microphone is the most annoying part of my workday.

The Ugly -
Personally, this unit is not a good fit for me personally. I am on Skype for work all day, and I'm chained to the desktop in my livingroom until I can find a better replacement unit that can reach through walls, and stay operational for a full 10-12 hour workday.

title: Suprisingly potent for small sealed enclosure
text:
Looking very slick in gloss black and descent reviews I purchased these to downsize and replace towers in family room (Toddler needs more toy room and getting too curious poking tower drivers). However hooking these up to mid/high end THX Onkyo receiver, I was terribly disappointed, perhaps because of high expectations bias and size of room, these just wouldn't put out enough air pressure at 30 watts rms to meet volume requirements (to the critics: I knew this before purchasing, was just hoping). So whilst seeking an alternative I placed these in the master bedroom on dresser and am powering them with the Lapei 2020 A+ (with upgraded 6amp power supply) and these little cubes came alive! Extremely clear, great soundstage, linear and efficient (for sealed). Frequencies under 65 hertz drops quickly but don't even notice with the beautiful timbre produced in the rest of the spectrum. Never used Coaxials for home use but have to say it is something I may consider for future purchases; only disadvantage is losing efficiency/area/vas of mid woofer cone. Also, am tipped a bit more to the sealed, versus ported argument; due to linearity and critical bass of these.
As an added caution, when opening the packaging, the inside of the top cardboard flap says (as memory servers) in large print: Caution: Tweeter Fragile. And that is not a 'oh, whatever!' statement, one poke and these crimple like a Pontiac Sunfire body panel. Since there are no covers.. I accidently bushed with a knuckle and it crimpled in a bit, managed to pull out but with permanent crease, then, as I mentioned toddler before (not kid friendly), I made the mistake of putting one down for a few secs and the toddler said "thumb.. button!?!" I looked down and she had turned the nice titanium dome into crimpled aluminum foil, haha, upset until she offered me her favourite toy as a peace offering. I pulled it back out but looks terrible, still sounds okay but much more grainy and frequency peaks around 3-5k hz. Such is life.
Thanks for reading,
Simon

title: You may love it, but I found it just too hard to deal with it's problems
text:
This is a hard camera to review, as the strengths (low ISO image quality) are so strong and the weaknesses (they are legion) are so hard to cope with. If you've used a recent Sigma and more or less liked it, you probably will love this. Most other users however will likely return it.

I had the chance to use this as a part of a novel free trial program from Sigma. Basically you bought the camera with a prearranged return for a full refund. I suppose I could have kept it, but honestly, I was happy to return it. It was just too hard to use. Why was it hard to use? Horrible ergonomics, limited battery life, slow performance (though admittedly better than earlier Sigma/Foveon efforts), bad screen, no evf, no 3rd party RAW support (with none pending), and horrible software (needed because of the lack of 3rd party support).

Poor ergonomics: Sometimes weird designs are a form follows function fresh take. This isn't that. It's large, hard to hold, has uncomfortable edges, and get's rather warm. The buttons are in the wrong place or do the wrong thing.

Horrible battery life: Bad. 100-150 shots at best, and that's from a camera without a flash and with a screen I dreaded to use. Based on the heat and complicated sensor output, there must be some hard working processing. Either way, it's a bit of a pain.

It's slow: While it's faster than earlier bodies, it's still slow to process images. It's also slow to acquire AF, and as the screen is poor (horrible in in the bright light that the sensor craves), it can be hard to see what's in focus.

As noted above the screen is poor, especially in bright light. It also doesn't pivot or swivel, and there's no real EVF option. I'm starting to wonder who this camera is for. The slow moving deliberate artists who might make the most of this camera would benefit from an outstanding screen/EVF (ala Fuji X-T1) to verify critical focus in the field.

RAW support: Worst in class. While Nikon, Canon, Fuji, etc... users may be critical of the results of using one conversion program or another, they have choices. Most also have first party supported or built applications that are at least mediocre. Even Nikon's lamentable new raw software is a million times better than what Sigma offers, and here there is no support from Adobe, PhaseOne, Sillypix, etc... The good news is that the out of body JPGs are now rather nice.

There's a lot wrong with this camera, but the image quality is amazing. The transition to the new Foveon sensor design hasn't lost the special wonderful image quality of previous generations, and one can create images with this camera that few others, even medium format, could match. The lens is rather nice too.

Sadly this camera is a niche camera. The 5 star reviewers used the same camera, but if you're used to the Sigma workflow and love having the best image quality, this is a 5 star camera. For most photographers, you may be better off getting a Fuji X100s and take 2-3x as many pictures, pic the best, and use any number of editing tools to get great results. You'd be less frustrated, it would fit in a coat pocket, and you'd miss far fewer shots. If you can try it for yourself, go for it. You may love it.

title: TV is ok, but...
text:
Well, I work at Sears in electronics so I get to play around with all the new TV's and see which by my opinion is the better one and what I don't like about the other. Well I played around with LG Google TV for awhile, and I thought it was a good TV and recommended it to my brother. After he bought it, I went over and played with the settings to get the TV the right picture and the sound to be balanced out right since he didn't want a sound bar (yet).
Well a few weeks later he told me that the remote wasn't working the right way. So I came over, played around with it and it worked and was also broken at the same time. To explain, the remote is a two in one, part remote on one side and keyboard on the other. So some buttons were sacrificed and merged into others. How my brother noticed is that the 3D/Mute button wasn't working, it would only mute the TV and would no longer put anything in 3D. So I had to contact LG twice, the first time the guy I spoke to was rude and would not listen to me at all. I told him it was the remote that was the problem, but he continued to make me do random tests on the TV and ask me stupid questions that had nothing to do with what I told him. When I told him it was the remote, not anything to do with the cable signal, not anything to do with the movie I wanted to watch in 3D, not anything to do with how old/new the HDMI is, or what update the TV has... it all remote. He then snapped at me, and hung up the phone.
Called back, explained myself again and what happen before with whoever I was talking to and 2 weeks later I got a new remote and all was well in the world... till now.
The TV will not stay connected to the router, and at first it was every once in awhile that it will drop, says it lost it's connection to router. We at first thought that it was the router, till we realized that everything else worked that was connected to it. The laptop, iPad, iPods and the other smart TV in the living room worked just fine, it was only the LG that would drop the signal.
So I contacted LG about the problem I was having again, and they said and I quote "We can't guarantee a constant signal when hooked up to WiFi"
But the router is literally on the other side of the wall, and the house is a small two bedroom... so there shouldn't be an issue. But they refused to help in anyway, they just shrugged their shoulders and repeated themselves saying it is the TV that's the problem but that I should connect it with a cable.
After that, I refuse to tell anyone to buy an LG till they fix the issue and I will let all my customers know that I wouldn't touch it. I did let them know of that, and they were fine with it. They really didn't care, so I feel everyone else should know this.

However, I will give you an honest opinion about everything else such as picture, 3D, sound...

The picture isn't that bad, I still think plasma have a better picture and color, but for a cheap LED it wasn't that bad. However, the black levels was a little poor, and shadows came out looking blue at first. I played with the settings a little, and made it better but still wasn't as deep as some plasma that I like or some higher end LEDs. If I were going to get an LED, I would get one with Local Dimming. The dimming helps with black levels and shadow detailing, so if you are looking at this TV I would go with the GA7600, which has 240hz and dimming. I did put the picture in Vivid and I noticed it helped allot with some of the stuff I was looking at, however when I played Married With Children it made the clothes washed out and blend together. You couldn't see detailing at all, so I had to switch it to Standard to get a somewhat ok picture. I would recommend the ST60 plasma for an amazing picture, deep inky blacks, and better color.

The sound is very poor, I have 5.1 surround sound and coming from that to this it was just bad. I like to have bass in my music, I like to hear sounds around me and like things to sound clear. The sound probably is what other TVs sound like, but I had to turn the volume really high just to get it to sound loud and hear definition in the music and vocals. So I would recommend a sound bar with a wired subwoffer just so the sound quality improves.

The 3D, is really good. I came from a 2011 Samsung Plasma which I thought was good, but I had problems with the 3D. This LG has Passive 3D, which is what movie theaters use. The other type of 3D is active, which is battery powered glasses that sync with the TV. However, with cheap active 3D you get what is called ghosting, which I can't stand. This would be my first Passive 3D I tested and I loved it, I know with passive you lose some resolution but that I hardly noticed and can live with when watching 3D. I rather it look like 720p than having a two ghostly hands trying to pop out of the TV.
I haven't seen what a high class active 3D looks like, and when I do see what a high class active 3D looks like I will update. My fav movie to test out for 3D is either "My Bloody Valentin 3D" "Fright Night 3D" also I like to test out and see how a video games that has the option in the menu to be played in 3D looks like. When I played Doom 3 in 3D on my old plasma it was extremely ghosty, almost everything had a second image and just looked bad. However, on this it looked great. I bought this Onkyo back in late 2008 for $440. At first, it sounded and worked well. But over time, the HDMI connections began to fail. At first, I noticed it would take a few minutes for the unit to switch between my cable box and my DVD player. As time went on, it would take as long as 15 to 30 minutes to get the DVD player "talking" to the Onkyo. The Onkyo would display NO SIGNAL on the front panel when connected to the DVD player and you could not use the DVD player when this happened. Then, a few weeks later, you could not connect the DVD player at all - the Onkyo would simply refuse to recognize it. Next, the Onkyo stopped working with the cable box as well. The sound began to drop out and eventually I could not use the Onkyo with the cable box either. I stopped using the Onkyo altogether.

At this point, I'm looking to open up the unit and replace cheap faulty capacitors which are causing the problems. If I can bring my Onkyo back to life, that will be great, but my next receiver will be a better brand. I will never buy Onkyo again.

title: almost five stars
text:
Samsung Galaxy Tab 2

Before buying the Tab 2, I read several Consumers Reports articles on tablets. (Oct 2012 and Feb 2013) I wanted a tablet so that I could read ebooks, surf the internet, read email, take an occasional picture, view pictures imported from other devices, and maybe do a little GPS navigation. I did not want a monthly bill for a 3G/4G connection. The Kindle Fire HD has a good price, superior speakers, but has no GPS or camera. The Google Nexus is highly rated and inexpensive, but has only a front camera - good for Skype but not for taking pictures. The iPad Mini is highly rated but expensive and lacks GPS. I had some difficulty discerning the pros/cons of the Galaxy Tab 7.0 Plus and the Galaxy Tab 2. The Galaxy Tab 7.0 Plus is actually a year older than the Tab 2 and runs an older version of Android (3.2), but costs quite a bit more. The only significant advantage I found in it is that is more internal storage - either 16GB or 32GB. However, you can buy a Tab 2 with 8GB and install a 32GB micro SD card at a lower cost than a Tab 7.0 Plus. The front camera on the Tab 2 has less resolution - 640 x 480 - but that is plenty for Skype, I think. CR also rated the Toshiba Excite and Toshiba Thrive. The Excite is highly rated but very expensive. The Thrive is a bit lower rated than the Google and Samsung models, yet costs more. So there you have it - I chose the Tab 2 and got a good sale price.

I had a strange experience when I went to buy it. The salesman tried real hard to get me to get an iPad - to the point of bullying me, I'd say. He said he had a Samsung and got rid of it and got an iPad instead. Maybe that was the truth, maybe not. I pointed out that the iPad doesn't have GPS, and he said that GPS doesn't work well on a tablet anyway. He said that the Samsung would not work with iTunes, which is true. With the Galaxy, you can either sync music and photos with Windows Media Player or Kies, which is free software that Samsung provides at their web site. I have used iTunes with other MP3 devices, and I tried both Windows Media Player and Kies. They both work fine, but maybe not as well as iTunes. Kies helps you install firmware and software updates on your Tab 2 or other Samsung device. It is supposed to be able to import playlists from iTunes, but I did not succeed at that. I created my own playlists in Kies. Maybe the salesman figured that since I was twice as old as him, I couldn't figure out the Tab 2. Or maybe he wanted a bigger commission.

The most pleasant surprise was that the Tab 2 prompted me to enter my Google username and password, and that immediately made my Gmail, Google Calendar, and Google+ accounts available and synchronized.

The most unpleasant surprise came when I tried to print an email from the Tab 2. I was informed that I could only print on a Samsung printer. Well I am not going to get Samsung printer. I read on another review that the EasyPrint app makes it possible to print to other printers - I'll try it.

I was annoyed that the Gallery app has an icon to make it easy to upload pictures to Google+, but not Facebook.

It has voice recognition, so when you want to enter text, there is a microphone icon. Click it, and speak, and the words you speak go into the text box. Works pretty well, and is fun.

Everything I read said it had Android 4.0, but mine has 4.1. Apparently the change was made at the end of 2012.

The Tab 2 is slippery and hard to hold on to. I keep mine in a cover all the time, which takes care of that. I didn't find many covers that were custom sized for the Tab 2, so I got a universal sized one, which works fine, but is a bit larger than necessary, so it won't fit into any of my pockets.

It has blue tooth, but I haven't made use of it yet. It would be good with a blue tooth keyboard. My Chevy Equinox allows blue tooth phones to connect to the sound system, but not tablets. It also has an infra-red light, and Peel software, to make it a remote control for your TV, DVR, etc, which I have not tried.

This was my first Android device. There is no user manual on the device, or in the box, but a decent user manual can be downloaded from the Samsung web site. It is reasonably easy to figure out how to do things on the Tab 2. If you are new to Android, you have to try things and see what they do.

I'd give it five stars if they would add a capability to print to any wifi printer and an icon for uploading pictures to Facebook.

title: This is a quality card with a great feature set and a free game the deal is awesome when OC'd its 670 performance
text:
My system specs:
AMD 8120 FX 8 core processor
Gigabyte UD3 AM3+ board
16 gig or Corsair DDR3 RAM
Samsung SSD 830 drive
Windows 7 64 bit
*Included as performance may very from system to system. MY statement are solely related to the system I've listed above.

This video card is replacing a crossfired Radeon 6870 setup. After doing alot of homework I found that this card performs as well as this setup but at a fraction of the power. In fact this card draws so little power replacing my 6870 would make a bit difference in electric cost savings over the next two years now that I've upgraded. Using some simple math and killowatt per hour rating from my electric company over two years I save 170 in electric cost.
Not bad....now lets move on to the good stuff you want to hear. But I did want ot be fair for the "green" guys out there that like to see efficiency in a product also.

The included EVGA Precision X Tuner automatically boosts the clocks for you to 1110 got the GPU which is more than the already factory clock out of the box and it runs quite stable. Be aware that the precision X tuner does have the ability in the setting to be able to display the GPU, MEM, temperature , etc in the game real time and for EVGA awesomeness they gave us the ability to see it on a Logitech LCD panel. Another +1 for EVGA. The end results are earth shattering performance in DX11 games with just a single GPU. With my Radeon 6870 setup i was using a GTX 430 as a hybrid physX card with special drivers. So for myself I could still retain the 430 to use with the new EVGA 660 as a dedicated PHysX card and for CUDA.

I was impressed that in The Secret World i was able to obtain at ULTIMATE settings in DX11 mode with everything maxed out a steady 45-50 frames per second. The game is drop dead gorgeous with smooth game play on this card With my Crossfire 6870's I was getting 34-40 fps and I had to knock down the tesselation as it was causing some performance hits in some areas of the game The 660 from EVGA no matter what I threw at it remained steady at 45 -50 fps. This card is very stable out of the box and it played my new favorite game flawlessly. I went through some dual crossfire driver and profile pains initially with my 6870 crossfire setup but to AMD's defense so did Nvidia players. Please note I've used AMD cards for 8 years, prior to that a couple of Nvidia cards and 3dfx I have a long history of 3d gaming cards. I hope you don't feel there's bias I go with the card with the best feature set and performance per dollar with decent power draw. Some may care about some of not at all. My review will tell you about all sides of the coin including overclocking.

I also , have, a Vizio 3D 42" television and I will say I was disappointed that nvidia does not include the 3d TV play. To Nvidia's defense ATI does have a solution of the Tridef software which was 25 dollars for AMD users. *NOTE* to AMD users moving to an Nvidia card. Your key from Tridef is an AMD card key. You will be required to purchase another key as it does recognize the AMD discounted key.

Now, after the warning I gave on the Tridef software activation and after seeing how Tridef performs with ATI and Nvidia I can tell you that Tridef does the better job for both companies. I don't recommend getting Nvidia 3D Play if you get this card for stereoscopic 3d. I do recommend another card dedicated to Physx although you can use the 660 as well you may not enjoy the performance hit that it would take on your game when you like to run everything at full eyecandy.

To sum up, the EVGA SC+ card does a fine job at performance, out of the box and Nvidia's recent drivers deliver great performance with not many bugs that I've seen so far. For a new card I'm impressed at the reliability and stability.
Im even further shocked that it is outperforming my 6870 crossfire rig in most of my DX11 games about 20 percent on average. Now just to mention, but for us 3d gamers it's not so important, but I did notice moving from my 6870's my desktop seemed to produce a noticeable crisper display on my Vizio 3d led tv.
The colors also seemed more natural not as vibrant as it was on my AMD 6870. The AMD does have setting to correct things like that but I think Nvidia nailed the default setting for 2D out of box. Furthermore, in some cases with AMD I've always run into scaling issues on my HDTV's where out of the box the default driver setting leave me a 1/2 inch border requiring me to scale the display to fit the border correctly. Out of the box my 660 didn't have any such issues. It detected my display and it was sized properly right out the box. I do think little things like this is very important for me to review on potential buyers.

Next, the installation was so simple. However, I did use Drivercleaner.net to wipe out all instances of ATI software and registry entried prior to installing as I've heard about conflicts. SO I suggest that you clean out first.
Uninstall all Nvidia and ATI AMD software in the cotrol panel. Then set your video controller to Standard Display. Then run a cleaner on your system before installing your new card.

Finally, the cards price at 339.00 may sound steep to you. But right now it comes with Borderlands 2 and the current price model they set for the 660 is definitely hooking some buyers as it did me. I was using AMD cards for 8 years and this card just appealed to me for all the reasons in this review. After i bought the game within just 3 days I got an email from Nvidia giving me the code redeem on STEAM. Yes, be aware the game is a STEAM code not DRM free if that upsets some of you then think twice as I wanted to share that I had to get the STEAM code. That doesn't bother me. The plus side of this bonus is that you do get the pre-order items as it comes up as the Pre-order not just the standard version of the game. Now the price retail of Borderlands 2 is 59.99. This EVGA SC+ card is 339.99. So in essense you get the card for 279.99!! This is 100 less that a Radeon 7950 and little over a hundred less than a 670. In OC mode using Precision X software this card is putting out identicle maybe 5-10 percent less at times than the 670 when the performance is boosted by Precision X.

You can't beat this deal. It's 670 performance for over a hundred less. It's main competitor the 7870 with the Borderlands 2 included is just not a good deal for AMD at this time. The card is awesome, this game deal included is awesome, the card is stable, the drivers are stable and in conclusion i'm trying to find a way to ding a star because usually there's something catchy or something that just doesn't work. And the new features of adaptive refresh which I've used is so nice to not see anymore tears in the screen due to the refresh rate changes the feature works great. TXAA be aware at 4X in Secret World my performance significantly dropped but i had to tone it down to 2X TXAA and this game is the only game that uses it. You'll get a gorgeous picture no jaggies or tears between TXAA and adaptive refreh rate feature. I suspect this will improve with time.

I can't find big problems folks this is the card at the best price point with a great game included. If you can look past it being a STEAM download the deal your getting just cannot be beat. EVGA hit the bulls eye with this one.
You will be pleased with the card and be sure you run the Precision X included software it does boost performance up to 10-20 percent. I hope you find the review useful. I did not run all types of benchmarks due to the fact that you can find those around the web. My review was to give you what it does in the real world with a recent game and how easy it was to boost the clock with the included app and the expected performance you'll get when moving from a previous generation of Nvidia or AMD cards. If you already have a SLI or crossfire rig you will get some improvement with just a single GPU but don't expect much more. In that case you may want to skip this generation from AMD and Nvidia. But for single card users expect a nice 50 percent jump in performance and being able to run all games you got in DX11 at 1080P over 40 fps average.

I hope this helps you make your decision as I wanted to give it a few days before spilling my brain out.

title: The camera is great...set up and customer service...meh.
text:
I was pretty pumped when I had this camera out of the box, set up, and could see my living room on my computer within 10 min. The picture is fantastic and the sound is adequate. I purchased this for dual purposes...nanny cam and to keep an eye on our house due to a recent string of break ins in our neighborhood. Using the app on my android phone, there is little to no delay/lag time. The pan and tilt feature works well. I can see well enough for around 20-25 feet, day and night. All in all, I am very satisfied with the camera.

The reason I did not give it 5 stars...I realized rather quickly that the 10 min set up was too good to be true. I installed the app onto my phone and it worked great....as long as I was on my network. So, I took out the very basic instructions that were included with the camera and completed the steps to view remotely. The instructions show you how to set the ip address, gateway, etc for the camera. They do not go any further than that. They don't tell you that you need to make some changes to your router, or what the address is for viewing your camera remotely.

After searching the internet and ultimately calling the foscam tech support, I realized that this is by design. The tech support was helpful and quick, though not very personable. Regardless, he accessed my pc remotely and had it all set up within 5 min. It was then that he practically forced me (tried to) to leave a 5 star review on amazon. He actually went to the website, pulled up the page to leave a review and entered 5 stars. Then he was trying to tell me what to write! I informed him that while I appreciated his service, I would be leaving my review on my own time.

So, overall, very happy with my product purchase. Not happy with the lack of set up instructions and the pushy tech rep. Foscam should provide better guidance out of the box and let the product/support speak for itself. If you do both of those things right, a customer will leave good feedback. You don't have to force people to do so. Not cool.

title: Love These Radios! Highly Reccomend
text:
I originally purchased one pair to stay in contact with my lead man on our shift in a manufacturing facility. Our department is extremely noisy, as we have numerous machines stamping out metal parts, forklifts beeping and driving by. I use the AVPH3 surveillance headset because my job entails that I use both hands working with pneumatic tools to set the dies to stamp the parts. When my Lead calls, I have no trouble hearing him, and answer him with the push-to-talk button clipped to my shirt.

After we used the 1st pair for a few days, we realized just how much more efficient we were working, so I ordered a second pair to give to operators so that we can be in constant contact with each other. Now, if there is a problem with one of the machines, I can ask them what the problem is, and avoid wasted time walking the 50 to 75 yards to survey the problem, and then walk back to get the necessary tools to fix the problem.

The in-ear headset also doubles as a sound-reducing ear plug, but still allows me to communicate with the crew. However, the clear plastic behind-the-ear spiral looks rather CIA/Secret Service, and I have had to put up with some ribbing from some of the other workers in the plant. If they only knew just how comfortable, and, convenient this headset is, they wouldn't rib for long.

Midland Radios has long been a leader in radio manufacturing, and that was one big selling point for my purchase. These are NOT cheap little toys, but, well-constructed, solid radios.

I would suggest to follow the instructions to give the units a 24 hour initial charge, and then to charge them only as needed, every 2 days or so.

All in all, I am very pleased with the quality, the performance, and the range that these radios provide. We may even decide to purchase a third set.

title: Extends the range, but with a wrinkle
text:
I live in an L-shaped house, where the AT&T U-verse router (2Wire 3801HGV) sits at the vertex. Needless to say, at the far ends of the house, signal is weak to nonexistent. So, I followed the quick setup sheet packaged with the repeaters (one for each end of the house), and BAM! In less than 5 minutes, we now have strong signal throughout the property.

The wrinkle? Let's say I'm at one end of the house, which is covered by a repeater. I have great signal on my smartphone, laptop, etc. But if I move that same smartphone/laptop to another part of the house (covered by the router or the other repeater), I can't access the internet. If I reset my client network connection (turn smartphone/laptop Wi-Fi off and on again), I'm back online...till I move to another part of the house that's covered by a different device.

Still, I'll take this over not having any coverage at all. But I suspect that the quick setup I did is the culprit, because the repeaters weren't set to clone the MAC address of the router. If I logged into each repeater and made them clone the router's MAC address, this might remedy the issue. I'll report back either way.

title: Bigger color screen not an improvement....
text:
I bought this as an update to my Sansa Clip+, hoping that the bigger screen would be an improvement. I'm going to keep this really simple and just share some observations of the new clip.

THE SCREEN "UPGRADE":
--The font is noticeably bigger, so less text will be shown even with a bigger screen. So much for being able to see more.
--The battery icon is a faint green color that doesn't contrast very well over the semi-transparent status bar and the various ugly backgrounds (which change at random, absent album art).
--Wish you could pick one background and stick to it, especially since they give you the option of turning album art off (an option which doesn't work, btw).
--The track progress bar is a thin line with a small dot denoting progress.
--The one improvement I actually like is that the clock is shown in the upper left hand corner. In the Clip+, you can set the clock but never see it unless you navigate to settings (huh?!).
--Menus navigate differently; The main menu scrolls Left/Right now, and you have to use the select button to select it before you can navigate further.
--Startup takes 2-3 seconds longer.

FORM FACTOR:
--Since the new screen is about twice as tall, they cut the height of the control inputs by 1/4 to 1/3. Something to get used to that feels awkward at first.
--They moved the back button to the left side of the player, which may be less awkward for some.
--PC connection port is now Micro USB instead of the Mini USB of the Clip+
--Overall size of the player is increased a tad, maybe 1/8" on H&W dimensions.
--Some new color choices, though all but the black are a two-tone where the nav "square" is silver.

PACKAGING:
--Blister box sealed up like Ft. Knox. Actually scratched the side of the player by cutting too close when I tried to cut the little square behind the player out. My own fault, but it shouldn't be quite so difficult to get one's new purchase out to play with. There's actually a funny video out there illustrating this with the Clip Zip's packaging.

Final Thoughts:
Overall, I think this player is worth the price and a decent buy. The interface is my biggest complaint. While it may be 1.1" and full color, I find the implementation to be inferior. I am giving the Clip Zip 3 stars because I think the designers missed an opportunity to really improve the readout. I think if they would have kept the same font size as the Clip+(or given the option to change it) it would have made a big difference for me. Having a track name cut off and having to wait for it to scroll to see what you're listening to is REALLY annoying. Perfect example: |Piano Sonata No|. I kid you not; that's exactly how little it shows. Any long track title or list of tracks with similar titles will prove a pain. I would have preferred if they just kept the black and cyan readout with a bigger screen to show more info at once.

title: Upgrade your old Canon SLR
text:
My dilemma: I bought a T3i for vacation, but my son will try to lay claim to it. My solution was to buy this body (with battery and charger) and use my existing lenses from my old film SLR. The old EF lenses are compatible with this camera! I really like it as well, but it's quite the upgrade from my old SLR and the string of point-and-shoots I've had since then.

Pros:
Super cheap for a DSLR
It takes better pics at 6.3MP than my 12MP point-and-shoot that cost me 3x more.
It's a DSLR... it is very configurable.

Cons:
It's old technology -- 6.3MP
The LCD doesn't display the pic until you've taken it, meaning I have nose grease all over the back.
It uses CompactFlash memory -- typical for its era.
Would like it to have the option to take a string of 3-5 pics via timer.

If you're considering using older SLR accessories, here are some pointers:
Old EF lenses are compatible, though it is designed for use with the newer EF-S lenses.
EF lenses increase the effective zoom by about 1.6x. That means my old 80-200mm lens turns out to be 128-320mm!!! It also means my old 35-80 lens is 55-128mm, meaning I'm always zoomed in some. To do macro shots, get a 18-55mm EF-S lens.
EF lenses don't have image stabilization. That's a sweet feature, especially when zoomed in to 320mm. Consider a tripod when zooming in close
My old external flash was not compatible. Some are supposed to be compatible but mine was an "EZ" model that wasn't. Your mileage may vary.

title: Canon does it very well
text:
I remember at the launch of this camera body, how reviewers hammered Canon for "downgrading" the XXD series with the 60D. After all, it was the first body to do away with the magnesium alloy for plastic.. OH NO! Actually, I think it saved some weight, and who throws around their camera gear anyway? I do, actually. I am a professional wedding photographer, and sometimes I have to shed one setup for another quickly. Yet, this baby was a great, inexpensive backup to my 7D, and complement to our full frame 5D II rigs.

As far as the focusing system is concerned, sometimes fewer AF points are a better option. For instance, when shooting in low light with a shallow depth of field at f1.2, I would much rather have the quickness of selecting a single point from just 9 instead of the 19 on the 7D. And the difference between image quality in the two bodies is negligible in my opinion. Plus the swivel screen comes in handy when creating more artistic angles from on the floor or up very high, shooting over someones shoulder, etc. I wish the full frame cameras from Canon offered the swivel screen.

In all, this is a camera that works well for the amateur who wants to put the camera in auto mode and shoot away, to the seasoned pro who is looking for a quick draw, low-light, artistic shot. Nice job again, Canon! Excited for the new 6D!

title: Decent Price For Decent Quality
text:
I frequently give presentations at work which includes a laptop and an old Panasonic LCD projector. I always felt it was concise and practical, but the new 3M Mobile projector is great for lots of reasons. Instead of using a small suitcase around, all I need is this 3M Mobile Projector and my laptop, iPhone or iPad. I prefer my laptop as I have all my PowerPoint presentations on it.

It is true plug-n-play. Hook your laptop (device) up with the HDMI cable and turn the power on. This means you connect it to your laptop's HDMI slot. Note that this set does NOT include the [[ASIN:B008H7UAIK Digital AV HDMI Adapter to HDTV for Apple New iPad 2 3 iPhone 4S 4G iPod Touch]], which you absolutely need to connect from your HDMI cable end to a 30-pin adapter or a lightning USB port. This is the only way to use your iPhone or iPad with the HDMI cord. This would have raised the price of this product by about twenty-five or thirty dollars and I think its a mistake to exclude it.

The speaker is adequate, in that, if you are in a small room you can hear. Most of my work I present vocally anyway. You do have the opportunity to plug in a remote speaker if you want. The actual '60 lumens' is also adequate, but you need to have a fairly dark room for great clarity (and it is very clear). There are several adapter plugs for world-wide use and a tiny wafer remote. You don't have to use the remote, but is a,n 'okay' convenience (its very small and not the easiest to read). I cannot address the battery life at this point and will update, but I always have the power plugged in during presentation. I think anyone will be surprised at how much power and ease of use one gets with this Mobile projector.

title: Love it so far, but........
text:
I have to say that Amazon's estimate of 10 hrs of usage on a fully charged battery is more than a little ambitious. Granted I've been downloading a lot of apps since mine arrived 3 days ago, but I've had it plugged in (standard micro-USB wall charger....the supposedly "fast" charger I ordered specifically for the Fire hasn't arrived yet) more than I've had it in use. It remains to be seen how that works once things level off and I'm done adding, trying out, and removing apps and have things arranged the way I want them.

After using my Kindle Touch (which I still love, by the way) for so long, the heft of this new one is taking some getting used to....certainly not a deal breaker. I think I'm really going to like the ability to read in bed without a reading light once I figure out how to prop it up comfortably. The readability is wonderful, page changes are smooth and fast.....absolutely no complaints about the Fire as an ereader. Video and sound are both absolutely wonderful, though I'm more than a little disappointed at the inability to view Flash video......I guess I'll get used to that or maybe Amazon will come up with a work-around in the foreseeable future, but I miss being able to watch videos on my favorite news and magazine sites. I'm also a bit put out that Google Play is inaccessible for Kindle.....there are a couple of apps that I've been using on my cell phone that I'd LOVE to use on my Fire, too, but alas, that is not possible and I haven't found anything available on Amazon that comes close enough to replacing them.....yet. Hopeful that this will change soon, though, as new Kindle apps pop up every day.

All that said, I'm still learning all the delightful things I can do with my new Fire above and beyond its function (my primary reason for having a Kindle) as an ereader. I absolutely love my new Fire and will certainly use it on a daily basis and take it everywhere I go. I'm an avid reader and an Amazon Prime member. I have a hunch there will be some movie & TV watching being done, too. As much as I have enjoyed my Kindle Touch, I think I am really going to enjoy the bigger, beautiful display on the Fire HD. Overall, I'm very happy with my new best friend.

title: Great while the configuration lasted
text:
My search for the holy grail of range extenders doesn't look like it will end here. I've tried other makes and models before and have been disappointed with their performance. I have two key issues with this particular WD model:

1. After successfully configuring the product and testing out the performance, I couldn't get more than three dots of signal strength even when the extender was in the same room as my main computer. Maybe I expect too much, but when all of my devices that I'm testing are within three feet of each other and there are signal problems, I'm not very pleased.
2. Only a day or two after going through the configuration process my connection (and therefore extended signal transmission) were lost. Reconfiguration and troubleshooting loomed large to get things back to where they were the day before. I quickly lost the energy required to maintain this sort of support and attention, which meant the end of my relationship with the WD extender.
