title: Decent for music, not for phone calls
text:
I purchased one of these lightly used off craigslist. As other reviewers have said, the microphone built into the faceplate is not just bad, it's WORSE than useless. I tested it parked in the driveway with the engine idling, and while I can hear other people through my speakers fine during calls, all they hear is engine noise or just loud bass, even though during a call the stereo stops all music. I intend to relocate the microphone to somewhere that won't pick up chassis vibration and will actually pick up my voice, probably somewhere near the speedometer.

Other than the horrible microphone this is a decent unit for the price. I don't care about CDs - I honestly can't remember the last time i listened to one. Everything is either mp3 or streaming now. For music, bluetooth works great. Pairing was super easy once my phone actually "found" the stereo, and now my phone automatically pairs with it within 2-3 seconds of starting the car. It would be nice if it showed some text from the phone like song title, but I love how you can use the play/pause and next/back buttons right on the stereo instead of fumbling for your phone. I have not tested the aux input, but really, how can you screw that up? I expect it to work just like every other aux port on the planet. Bluetooth is so much easier though, so I might never use the aux port.

I like how the display is NOT a epileptic seizure-inducing flash riot, and there's not a ton of chrome to attract a thief's attention - it kinda looks like a boring factory unit, which is good for me. I like having an actual volume knob, which some stereos don't have - I hate when a loud song/commercial comes on and it scares us all, or I'm listening to talk radio or an audiobook and need to turn it up quickly so I don't miss something quiet. Sound quality is decent, though it could use a little more treble. With the factory original and then a Kenwood stereo, I left the treble adjustment at zero. With this unit, I had to turn treble up all the way (to 7) to get similar sound. Based on that, I expect most folks will be left wanting for highs. On the other hand, bass is good (through my factory 6x9's - no subs in my car).

The way this thing reads directories and subdirectories on the SD card is rather odd. It's fast to read my old 2gb SD card (I've heard some of the early mechless units were very slow to read SD/USB before they started playing), but it orders the directories strangely. It seems to just grab a list of every folder that has mp3s in it, then alphabetize those, rather than sticking to the carefully-created directory structure already on the card. For example, let's say you had something like this:
\Classical\Beethoven
\Classical\Orff
\Classical\Tchaikovsky
\Rock\Aerosmith
\Rock\Led Zeppelin
\Rock\RHCP

You'd expect that if you had shuffle turned off, you'd hear Beethoven first, because "classical" comes before "rock", but you'd be wrong. It plays Aerosmith first. Then when you press DIR+ to go up a directory, you'd think, ok, it started in rock\aerosmith, so I should hear Zep next... again, wrong. In this example, each time you press DIR+ you'll get folders in this order: Aerosmith, Beethoven, Led Zeppelin, Orff, RHCP, Tchaikovsky, then back around to Aerosmith. I didn't test to see what it would do with MP3s in the root folder, since I like things organized, but you have to agree this is a pretty stupid way to handle folders - you might as well just dump everything in the root and have a big mess, or else rename all your folders so that they WILL sort properly, and keep them at most one level deep... ie: \Classical-Beethoven\ and \Rock-Aerosmith\ --- at least that way they'd stay in the correct order. Of course if you use folders like I do, where each album is yet another subfolder inside the artist folder, that is a very time-consuming project with very little gain. I could probably write a script to do it, but I shouldn't have to.

I've had no luck using the USB port with a thumb drive. With the SD card inserted, it seems to completely ignore anything you put in the USB port. With no SD card in, it briefly flashes USB on the screen when i plug in my 16gb Kingston thumb drive, but it won't stay on USB when i try to switch modes, and thus won't use the USB stick. I'll try another drive but I'm not holding my breath. I thought I would be able to use these small old drives to have certain genres on them - one for classical, one for rock, etc, but right now it looks like that's not an option. If other USB sticks don't work, I plan to buy a 64gb sd card and try that in this deck. That way I won't have anything sticking out of the face, and I can fit ALL of my music on there and just leave it in there 24/7 and forget about it. I'd probably invest the time renaming folders so they'll sort right, but I feel like I shouldn't have to.

Others have noted that there's no clock. There is one, but it doesn't always show up - you have to hold BAND to make it show for a few seconds before it goes back to whatever it was showing before. I don't care though since there's already a clock on my dashboard - I don't need a second one.

The Good:
screen is easy to read, even in bright sunlight
lack of CD player makes the unit small and lightweight - easier to handle during install, and less moving parts to fail
easy install, just like any standard stereo
simple, un-flashy design
actual volume knob which reacts quickly
reads SD cards fast, changes tracks fast too
play/pause, next and back buttons will also control phone via bluetooth
phone automatically links almost immediately after starting the car (once it's paired of course)

The Bad:
faceplate feels a little cheap and sometimes hard to snap back on
buttons sometimes rattle
needs more treble - highs are weak
text is hard to read on screen for track info because it has so few characters and scrolls too quick
directory sorting is moronic
USB doesn't seem to work at all (maybe mine's defective)
manual is a poorly translated mess which doesn't really help you understand functions
Boss doesn't seem to know their own products - some places (including the box!!) say it has a CD player, and there's even a Laser warning sticker on the chassis, even though there's obviously no laser inside

The Ugly:
built-in mic is actually worse than useless - the only way you can use it for calls is if you're parked with the engine turned off... at that point, there's no need for handsfree anymore.

Verdict:
If you don't care about handsfree calling, don't use CDs anymore, and don't need/want flashy displays that turn the inside of your car into a rave every night, this could be a good value device for you. If you want bling, good handsfree, or a cd player, look elsewhere.

UPDATE February 2015:
I have noticed a little bit of alternator whine during quiet songs. I can probably cure this by adding a dedicated chassis ground between the chassis of the stereo and the body/frame of the car. the ground lead from the head unit is small gauge - maybe 18awg - so i'm not surprised it allows noise.

Also noticed that on warm/hot days, the faceplate doesn't sit flat against the radio, and so sometimes the display doesn't work at all, and other times it only displays garbage - scrambled characters, and no buttons work. Sometimes it even goes nuts from the partial/intermittent connection and turns up the volume all teh way. I discovered that if I press the lower left corner of the face into the radio, it will fix the display and allow the buttons to work again... till the face sort of clicks loose again or it cools down enough to work normally. the audio part still works, and my phone still automatically pairs, but not being able to adjust volume or change tracks is kind of annoying. and the random full blast thing is VERY annoying. but it happens pretty rarely, so isn't the end of the world, especially considering how little I paid for this radio.

title: The perfect solution for me!
text:
I went through a couple of neck straps and along the way found that I really wanted a sling solution. After some research, I found Peak Design's Leash. I mulled it over for a couple of months, watched all the videos on their website and looked at the video reviews on YouTube. I periodically checked some out other straps and finally decided on the Leash. My due diligence was rewarded as this is one awesome piece of gear!

Pros

Slim and strong
Comfortable
Performs exactly as described by the vendor (an ambitious little startup, btw)
Well-engineered - it has only what is needed to do the job, nothing more. No extra material, no bulky connections, etc.

Cons
There really aren't any cons as far as I can tell. The only thing I've found - and it is a minor thing - is that my thumbs are a little fat so the clips do not push and slide out quite as easily as demonstrated in the video. I'm sure the woman in the video has done it a thousand times more than me (and definitely has smaller thumbs) so I figure after a while it'll work just fine. It's really picking a nit.

Lessons Learned
Do exactly what the video says and it is amazing how well the camera sits where it should. Make sure the Peak Design logo is facing forward. Make sure you attach the anchors to the correct points for the desired camera position (I wanted the camera to face lens down so I connected one to the bottom plate and one to the left strap mount - other positions require different attachment points).

Bonus!
I don't have the capture plate system, so I connected the bottom anchor to the ring of my Manfrotto 498RC2 ballhead mount that I leave on my camera all the time. The anchors are so small that I don't have to remove the bottom one when I mount my camera on my tripod. The cord is very thin and it fits in the groove of my plate and the anchor sits out of the way. It works so well I almost think it was designed to work that way. And it does not impede the camera movement on the tripod in any way. It all works exactly as I hoped it would!

My advice
Look at the Peak Design Demo video and read about how it works. If it looks like what you want to do with your camera, buy the leash. For me it works exactly as described in the video (all the videos, really), so I am comfortable recommending this selection approach to others.

Footnote: I was impressed by their kickstarter demo. The small company is composed of some really smart people with good ideas. They are dedicated to making good products and are passionate about their work. I appreciate that.

title: Why get any other DVR?
text:
I know this will be long, so I will present this in pro's & con's, a summary of my background a little, a summary of my experiences, and then a more detailed follow up on some of those pro's/con's - for those that like to read.

PROs
* Season Pass and the Season Pass Manager
* 4 channels for recording
* Storage space for shows, over 300hrs of HDTV
* Easy setup
* HDTV user interface is very nice
* Picture in Picture during when viewing TIVO menu
* Search features for finding TV programs
* App for your phone to access the TIVO (only at home though)

CONs
* Price, this is a big one
* Std TV interface is functional (old TIVO sytle)
* Search feature for external programs, such as Amazon Prime movies

BACKGROUND

I have had a TIVO Series 2 for a very long time, I think I'ts been over 10yrs now. Probably after they shortly came out. I was not an early adopter of DVRs, but after that TIVO, my life has changed...well, it changed for other reasons, but at least I was not a slave to what day and time a TV show came on the air....at the time, I refused to miss Stargate unless I really had too, most any other show I may feel bad about it, but would get over it.

So I'm not really what I would call a avid TV watcher. My wife and I have shows we love to watch, but with TIVO, we watch them when we have the time. We usually watch some TV during the week, but could go a week not watching a single show. Hence our need for storage space on any DVR we have.

MY EXPERIENCE

In general, TIVO allows one to easily set a show to record. Only need to know the name, not the channel, time, or day. Though you can only find it if it plays in the next 13 days, as that's all the sched info it keeps. It says 14 days, but that gets clipped for a number of reasons.

I also love the ability to skip over commercials. Sure, if you love commercials, you can still watch them, as the unit does not automatically skip over them. And you have to push the 30sec skip button a number of times at each commercial break, but it's a skill my wife and I have learned quite well. For us, the person closest to the remote, has the job of advancing to the end of the commercial, but the skill really comes from stopping before you get a preview of the show and don't get any spoilers.

I really love the season pass, where once you tell it to record a show as season pass, you never again have to remember when it comes on during the year, but once set, you don't have to even care when the season (or half season) starts back up, or for that matter, what day, time, or channel it is even on. I'll tell people about a show, and they ask when or what channel it is on...don't know, but the name of the show is ..... On TIVO, that's all you need. You only need part of the name, and not the first word. i.e. type in house, and you could get House, or Warehouse 13. Not bad huh. The older TIVO required the words in order (except for The, A, etc). I very nice improvement.

This new TIVO season pass has some really nice features when in HDTV display mode, such as indicating which show has shows coming up or not, and a summary of the settings for that show.

On this unit, over my older one, the user interface (HDTV) has huge improvements, and the 4 channels, wow, 4 channels is soooo nice. I occasionally have 2 shows recording at once, and that is because I have a couple new stations recording at the same time, but the season pass only keeps one show (so just that days is on there).

MORE DETAILS (than you probably need)

Cost:

Ok, price is probably one reason you question peoples sanity on buying a TIVO, especially with the life time service fee (the units, and not yours BTW). And really, the only negative about the product, and I dinged it a half star (a few other things mentioned below bumped it up to a full star).

I live in COX country, and when I had to convert from tv to HDTV, I had to make a decision, stay with TIVO or not. After a number of questions at COX, doing the math, and a bit of thinking, TIVO was an obvious option. Why?

Cost over three years for both units: COX was a little cheaper, and smaller space, also only two channels recorded at one time.

Small space, and knowing our needs, factoring in an external drive (which COX does not officially support, but I hear it is possible), pretty much wiped out the cost difference. Keep in mind, if you live in COX country (at least in San Diego, Ca), you will need a channel card ($5 monthly fee) and free converter box. So your center will have a box half the size of the TIVO in it, though you only need access to it until you get it fully set up.

So in the end, the units were about the same price at 3 years, with a lifetime, the price point was 4 years or so. But after that time, I don't lay out another dime. I had my last TIVO so long, I can't remember when I bought it....ten years ago?, maybe longer. Though I did have to replace the drives as they wore out, via [...] it is not hard, clear instructions, and many price points. Something to consider if you keep the TIVO for a long time, being at some point you will need to service it, or go through the expense again. The rest of the unit basically never wore out on the old TIVO, but the drives do run 24/7.

Also, after putting out that much money after 4 years, I can take it with me if I move to another area.

Interface:

I did use it in std TV mode for awhile until we bought the HDTV a month or so later. While the std TV mode is good, and what I'm used too, wow, what a difference in HDTV. I love that you get a pic in pic while browsing, and I like the phone app to use the TIVO while watching the TV...though honestly, we don't use it much. But, if we loose the remote....

There are also more features for finding, and better navigation through the menus.

My Shows menu has more info, such as those show groups that have new shows, and not just repeats in them. Also, and I never thought I would say this, but the season pass manager is very much improved. Some things are just soooo simple, but very nice. Such as greying out the titles that do not have any recordings coming up, and on the right, it shows the settings for a quick preview.

13 vs 14 days schedule data:

Ok, so the TIVO logs in at night, downloads the data....14 days worth. But if you are looking up a show in the evening, you have lost most of a day. So if you know a show is coming up, that you have not set a season pass for, then you need to count 13 days rather than 14.

A note on programming data:

Garbage in, garbage out. Occasionally, and I mean the rare case occasionally, TIVO will record appear to miss a show, or record the wrong one. TIVO does not actually generate the information. The station that sets the schedule is wrong, so is TIVO. Again this is rare, but if it happens, you will know why. Sometimes last minute changes to the schedule, say an election or a super bowl, or breaking news. Also, sometimes the stations get lazy, and just use a generic name for a show, so TIVO may think it's new, because they didn't flag it as a rerun.

Skipping commercials:

This would the next big improvement, after # of channels, which was mentioned above. Skipping commercials is so powerful to your time. My older TIVO unit skipped over 30sec interval. Hit the button 6 times (3min commercial block), and bingo, you are still watching your show. This unit is slightly annoying, in that you get to watch the commercial in speed mode - 30 sec in 3 seconds. It's a little confusing, as I'm looking for the show, not commercials. Maybe something I will get more used to after a few more months. But kind of an annoyance for me after having the other TIVO for so long.

Setup:

Rather simple for most of it, but you can't scan for channels on a cable network. Just have to skip that during setup, even though it makes you think you need to do it. I don't know what else to say here, it's just easy, follow the screen prompts. Switching from std to HDTV was relatively painless, though not realizing my new receiver was not quite set to the correct input didn't help. As I had been using in non-HDTV, I didn't set the input to HDMI1, but to AV1, and didn't get a picture, surprise surprise. That one took longer than I will admit. Again, this was not the TIVO, but the receiver and healthy dose of user error.

Other services:

And of course the TIVO hooks up to external music and movie sources. I have Amazon Prime, so I use Amazon for movies. I don't personally like the search and purchase feature, opting to buy online and tell Amazon to send it to the TIVO. This works well for me, and download typically starts in about 5min, but not right away.

One odd flaw;

When switching between live tv and the TIVO screen (where the channel or recorded show you were watching shows up in the pic in pic), the sounds cuts out for a few seconds. Annoying, but ok.

title: Good Engineering at its best.
text:
Wow, what a nice enclosure. As people have noted, it is not cheap, but it is about as well designed as anything I have bought in the computer area. It's small, rugged, and has both Firewire 800 support and high speed USB. If you have a Macbook, having FW800 allows you to boot from an external disk and still have decent performance. I bought a new hard drive for my laptop, and the old hard drive, exactly as it was, is now in this enclosure so I can save it as a bootable image in case somethign happens to my new drive. This case is about as small as you could possibly get and still fit a 2.5" drive. It comes with an external power supply, but that does not seem to be required if you use FW800 interface. Maybe you need it if you daisy-chain FW drives, which this enclosure allows.

As someone noted, it comes with a "short" FW800 cable (maybe 18"), but thats long enough for my uses which will be as a baclup clone of my internal drive. Time Machine is great, but nothing beats having a fully bootable external drive with all your software installed. The case has a small power switch so it does not draw power from the laptop if you are not using the drive. It has a nice blue LED that shows power and disk usage. I think the heatsink style aluminum case will help keep the unit at a reasonable temperature while you use the drive. I hope that the person who did the actual industrial and circuit board design is getting some money from each of these units sold, because that person did an outstanding job of designing this enclosure.

title: Waterproof & automated tracker that measures your heart rate
text:
UPDATE: Android app is available now in beta at last! Jaybird is releasing new updates to the software still to improve many shortcomings, but this review is describing how the band itself works. It would've been better if their app was completely polished up from the launch, but that doesn't mean this tracker doesn't work. Do feel free to ask any questions here!
------------

Jaybird Reign is an automated activity tracker that keeps track of your activities 24/7 and is fully waterproof. There have been many fitness bands in the market but this is one of the first ones that will just track you accurately without any physical buttons. I've been an owner of Fitbit Flex and Force before, and I didn't like how I would have to hold the button to let it know I'm sleeping or about to start a workout. Jaybird's Reign boasts in accurate tracking that is automated and I can vouch that it actually works, and is fully waterproof, whoa.

The lights that you see after tapping on the tracker four times will vary depending on your setting from the app, but there are two things that you can see. First, your activity status, that shows how much you've been active out of your set goal in a day. Secondly, the red light that stays lit indicates the hour, and position of the blinking red light indicates minutes in interval of nearest five. There's a dimple on one end of the pod and in the middle to show you where 6th and 12th LED is. For example, if the bottom three dots are red and the 6th dot is blinking, that means it's 3:30 pm/am. (3 solid dots are 3 hours and 6*5 is 30 min) It's kind of hard to tell especially in the dark but it's better than having none I suppose.

I found the battery life to last long enough to never worry about the tracker dying on me. Jaybird advertises Reign to last about 5 days, and you can see the tracker's battery life through the app on your phone. There's no percentage or a number so it can be hard to tell, but the tracker would blink in red every so often when the battery is low. Then I would hook it up to the charger while I'm eating dinner or something and it'd be good to go for another week.

How well does it hold up against water? Very well, and I really like that it's fully waterproof and it stays on me through many hot showers and swimming pool full of chlorine, great. Most of other trackers in the market are water-resistant and not waterproof, but there's no need to worry at all with the Reign. I tapped on it four times to get the tracker under the water, and it lit up without a problem. One interesting find was that I kept triggering the lights to show up while showering. As I put shampoo and move my hands all over my hair, moving my hands rapidly kept lighting it up. While it doesn't really bother me at all or maybe I just need to wash up more gently, but a long shower would probably hurt the battery life for me.

Pros
- Automated activity/sports tracking, no need to press buttons
- Fully waterproof, not just water-resistant
- Comfortable enough to wear it 24/7
- Tells you how much sleep you need tonight
- Go-Zone (heart rate variability) knows your body better than you do
- Comes with variety of sizes and bands

Cons
- No motor for vibrations
- Can be difficult to read time from the LED lights
- Two minute wait for Go-Zone can seem long
- Unable to check past data (for now)

Check out the full review on Normal Consumer. Thanks for reading!

title: A Nice Soundbar for $300
text:
This Yamaha 152BL is the second soundbar in my house and I've used it for about one month. My first soundbar that I use in my basement AV setup is a Sonos so that it is connected wirelessly to all my other Sonos speakers (totally awesome by the way). But Sonos commands a big price premium for their strong wireless technology so the Sonos soundbar set me back about $700.

So now I'm using this Yamaha on a second TV and it's a nice unit, particularly for $300 and sounds about the same to my layman ears as my Sonos soundbar. The Yamaha was very plug-and-play easy for my situation - just plug the optical cable from the soundbar into the tv and that's it (other than also plugging it into a wall outlet). The Yamaha and tv are then in synch on audio except the soundbar speakers are much better / more powerful than the wimpy stock speakers that need to fit inside a flat panel tv. One tip I almost always forget after setup - once you're using the soundbar be sure to go into tv menu and turn those speakers off so they don't muddle the bar's superior sound.

Like I mentioned I think the Yamaha's sound is good as far as soundbar's go (ie; way better than stock tv speakers). Soundbars will never be the true 7.1 surround sound because the soundbar is physically only in front of you. Most soundbars will attempt to extend some surround sound aspect and I think this Yamaha does as decent a job as any (eg; when I'm watching some scenes I do hear some sound coming from far left or far right of tv). And while soundbars will have better bass than stock tv speakers they will also never replicate the bass of a 35 pound dedicated subwoofer. BTW, this Yamaha soundbar (like my Sonos) has a jack for a dedicated subwoofer for the true bass-heads. Also this soundbar has other output speaker jacks so several rear speakers could be connected to increase surround sound aspect.

As for bluetooth, I tried it with my phone to see if it worked and it did as was fairly easy to use. But I have a bunch of bluetooth speaker devices and I've given up on the hassle of fiddling with them individually (hence the inspiration for me to blanket my house with sonos speakers that can all play in synch with one touch).

Overall in summary I think this Yamaha soundbar is a solid value at $300 and I've had a good experience with it thus far - 5 stars from me in consideration of price/value.

text:
Range is poor. Even with new batteries, a motion detector that is about 20 feet away, loses communication with
the control center. A couple door sensors about the same distance frequently lost communication.

If two sensors (in the same zone or in different zones) are triggered within a few seconds of each other, and
then reset, the control unit gets confused and a zone will continue to flash. Sometimes, cycling one of the
previously tripped sensors will cancel the flashing, sometimes not.

If one sensor is tripped and quickly reset, the corresponding zone light on the control unit may continue to
flash.

If a zone 4 device it tripped, the mute function will suppress the alert beep, but only for about an hour.
Then the mute button has to be pushed again (or the device reset). I could not find mention of this in the
documentation.

The F.A.Q.s describe resetting, in some situations, by arming, then dis-arming the system. Many of the resets
I had to perform, while investigating erroneous LED flashes, required removal of power including batteries.
Inconvenient!

My opinion is that this system is not suitable for a house. Might be suitable for small apartments. The
capability of this system is too primitive for practical use.

title: Good headphones
text:
From the first review on this site, I worried that these headphones would be too bass heavy. I don't find that to be the case, certainly well within the realm of personal preference. As a matter of fact if you are a bass head you may find these a little too neutral for your taste. I made a preset for iTunes that's basically flat with just a tiny boost to the mid vocal range. The phones are very efficient, requiring me to turn the volume way down. Sound is clear Individual instruments are distinct.

I got these and plugged them into my laptop and set iTunes to run through my library for 30 hours to break them in. I honestly didn't listen to them before that, as I was very busy that day. When did put them on, I was quite pleased. I love detail in music, which the Monster earphones deliver. The mids may be a tiny bit weak. Again, nothing the equalizer can't fix. Highs are clear but not too forward. Just once, I cranked the volume up to check for distortion. None at any volume I'm willing to subject myself to. BTW, the packaging is classy. Unboxing the phones was like opening an Apple product.

I've been using open on-ear phones and over the ear ones, not closed on-ear phones, so was a bit worried about comfort. The cans swivel. The phones are not heavy, and disappear from awareness quickly, at least for a couple of hours. They stay comfortably on my ears, even when I walk around, but they are not too tight. After about three hours, I started to feel a bit of discomfort from the set. I shouldn't have been sitting for that long anyway. The discomfort wasn't bad, just noticeable and I could wear the phones again a couple of hours later. That just may be a problem inherent in on-ear headphones. They are nice and light.

Another issue that on-ear phones have is that they don't block out external noises quite as well as over the ear ones do. I did find the noise blocking more than adequate. Again, how much isolation from the environment you want is a personal thing. I'm happy with these. The phones have one cord that comes into the left side. I like that.

As a middle aged guy, I'm not looking for earphones as a fashion statement and was initially put off but the design. I got over that. They are distinctive but not over the top. The plug is 1/8 inch, so needs an adaptor to plug into standard stereo equipment (not included). One interesting design choice is to make the cord detachable. The cord has a double male plug. The straight end has a button that mutes music and switches on a microphone for use with an iPhone.

As with any Monster product, MSRP is a bit high. I'd say that these phones are of equal quality to others with similar suggested prices, like the Sennheiser and Sony ones I own. Those, however, have been heavily discounted and can be had for much less. That's my only consideration about recommending these. The are good earphones, but not better than other brands in the price range. On the other hand, they may appeal to your fashion sense.

Knocked off 1 star for build quality, and 1 star for over-priced. Build quality is ok. The aluminum is well-shaped but the stamp of manufacturer name and model name, which are both prominently displayed on the top center, had a fingerprint smudge on it, and the rubber pads designed to rest between the top of the stand and the bottom of my rMBP were not positioned correctly and are a bit cheap, causing metal on metal contact. I pulled them off and repositioned, and also added some scotch tape to some of the contact points where I could easily observe the laptop metal was coming in contact with the metal of the stand. Dissapointing. Shouldn't need to re-engineer when it is 12oz of aluminum which priced at $39.99. Only other complaint is the aluminum is a bit brighter and the bead-blasted finish a bit different than the specific shade and finish of Apple products. That's a nit, but if you are expecting it to match your Apple products 100% its not quite there.

Overall though, sitting in the stand and using the stand to type and use my keyboard everyday is a joy. It is, IMO, the perfect angle and height for the keyboard. That's the #1 thing I wanted, and the #2 thing was aluminum matching look, which is close enough. So final thought- very good, but not great, and probably $10 over-priced.

title: Impressed! (a 2003 camera in 2012 technology...)
text:
This camera is nearly a decade old. This review was written in March 2012 and this camera came out in 2003.
I bought it because I was interested in beginning photography, and didn't want to spend too much. So I bought an older model to get the feel.

I read countless reviews before buying this camera.
I am very impressed. A family member of mine has a Canon XSi that I have used a few times, and I honestly think this camera is much better quality.

-The first thing I noticed when I opened the box was that it was very small, very narrow.
-In reviews, I read that this camera has a tiny view finder, equivalent to viewing "a postage stamp at the end of a tunnel." I do not find this to be accurate. Sure, it would be nice for the viewfinder to be a tad larger, but its current size is perfectly manageable.
-I was worried about the 8MP compared to the modern 12MP or so. I shouldn't have even hesitated. The detail on this thing is quite good. I uploaded three photos. One of paint splatters to show off its colour. Second of the Santa Fe railyard to show off its nice contrast. Third of a tree to show off its detail. Those pictures were taken with a 28-80 lens, rather than the kit lens.

-One thing that really bugs me truly is the small LCD. I barely get an example of the image with that thing. The only true way I can determine if an image is good is when I upload it to my computer. Newer models have larger LCDs, some 3 inches, which I'm pretty sure is twice the one on the XT!
-The memory cards for this thing are different than current models, and can go up into the $40's for only a few GB!(sandisk compact flash) Luckily mine came with one, but be warned.
-Sometimes the shutter-release-button (not so great on my terminology yet) sticks. I'll hold it half-down to focus, and it won't take the picture when I try to push it down fully. Happens probably 3/10 shots. Mostly why I gave this 4 stars instead of 5.

So if you're a beginner, this camera is perfect for you.

title: Love It For Dedicated Theater....3D Is AWESOME!
text:
I was looking for a projector to upgrade my home theater and wanted something mainly for 3d movies (I LOVE a good 3d movie) and something that doesn't cost an arm and a leg. After reading just about every website and every review known to man, I narrowed my choice down to the Optoma HD131XE and this BenQ W1070. The choice between the two seemed, at first, difficult. As I continued reading, it seems the only advantage for the Optoma are the deeper black levels. However, after digging deeper, the reason for the supposedly deeper blacks on the Optoma is due to the fact that it uses a lower wattage bulb; not something I want...plus, you could just throw a cheap 10$ N2 filter on the BenQ and bam, problem solved (essentially that's what the optoma mimics with it's lower powered bulb).
Furthermore, the choice between the two became even easier to make after I read that the Optoma uses a 4x business style RGBCMY color wheel that artificially enhances whites and creates a marketing gimmick higher lumens rating. Meanwhile the BenQ uses a 6x true movie theater style RGBRGB color wheel. That alone decided it for me.
I mounted my BenQ to the ceiling and have watched a couple 3d movies and another 2d. I have to say, omg...wow, this thing is really insane. The blacks are not that dark, but who the heck cares? The image off a bluray (not the same if streaming from internet or any other file) is so sharp and the colors are just...wow! I had to play with the 3d to figure things out, but once I did I found myself sitting there and trying to shoo away the objects popping out; especially on Gravity when Sandra Bullock is crying (so cool). Compared to the cinema, in my dedicated theater sitting 9 feet away from 105" screen and 5.1 surround; I prefer my 3d experience, I think the image is WAY sharper than what passive 3d can deliver. Oh, and if you're worried about image brightness? I have no idea why you'd want a brighter image? In fact, I prefer wearing my Sainsonic even watching 2d, just to dim the brightness a little.
Last thing, I had a friend over who installs professional and higher end theaters. He said he deals with BenQ but never recommends because of the price and truthfully, he's never even demoed one. His thoughts after coming over? He's going to buy one for his home:).
Bottom line, I'm glad I spent the extra 90$ on this projector over the Optoma. I know, just based on the color wheel and bulb strength, that I'm getting a better image and peace of mind that I made the right choice. Had I purchased the Optoma I would have constantly been watching for washed out images and wondering if I made the best choice. Pull the trigger on the BenQ, you won't be disappointed!

Gamers, I don't play much but my son loves to play his kids games on xbox 360 and compared to the 50" LCD TV, this thing looks even better.

One more thing: it's difficult to find material that will max out what this thing can do. I hate streaming video via netflix or VUDU because, even though they say "trueHD" their file size is like 2GB compared to 50GB off a bluray. If you want the best image on this thing, you need a good bluray player.

title: Excellent and inexpensive case

Highly recommended!

title: Well rounded sound
text:
Let me start off by saying I built a new home and pre-wired a 7.2 surround sound setup. The room is 20'L x15'W x10'H. I did not want towers or bookshelf speakers. I wanted my front right and left speakers installed in the wall directly beside my TV, and all the other speakers mounted in the ceiling, with the exception of my subs which are to be located on the floor of the wall where the TV is located. I knew going in to my plans that my wife would flip if I had any kind of speaker set up that was obtrusive. Keeping that in mind, I wanted speakers that were less noticeable. I also wanted durable speakers in the mid price range. Nothing too expensive, but not too cheap either. Especially since I would be cutting holes in the wall and ceiling.

So I started with the purchase of a Yamaha receiver, the RX V-673. It allows for a zone 2 speaker setup for my back porch, along with all the bells and whistles of airplay through my iPhone and an app to control everything.

These speakers were my first speakers to add to my setup. I did a lot of research because I was worried about the sound balance since I would be using these as my right and left front speakers. I read all the reviews and knew that the screens on these speakers would not be flat, as one person said it had a dimension to it. And they were correct. This speaker could have a flatter screen (grill cover), but for some reason yamaha decided to add the curvature at the top and bottom, which makes these speakers very noticeable on my front wall. So while my wife was out of town, I installed these and got chewed out when she got back, because admittedly, they are a little on the obtrusive side. They are paintable, but I recommend a lot of patience. If you have a wall color like me that is hard to match with a spray paint, then I recommend watering down the paint and use multiple coats of paint to get the grill covers the color you need them to be. The small holes will get clogged with paint otherwise and it's extremely difficult to get the paint out of the holes. When paint did clog holes, I just pushed the paint brush down through the holes repeatedly and they disappeared.

As for the installation, I recommend using a drywall hand saw or jabsaw as it's called, and go slow. Use the template that's provided because it is accurate. I already had insulation in the wall, but if you don't, you might want to add some just behind the speakers. The longest part of the install was actually measuring on both sides of the TV so that the speakers were perfectly centered. Cutting the drywall and hanging the speaker took less than 5 minutes on each speaker.

As for sound, I was thoroughly impressed. I turned the volume up to as comfortably loud as I could and they never distorted. Listening to music or movies, these speakers provide a crisp, clear sound with all the highs and mids as you might expect from these types of speakers. They have thump for the low registers, but let me just say that these speakers are NOT made to rattle the glass windows in your room with bass. They will rattle your glass because of how loud they can reach, but booming bass is the subs job, not these speakers. I'm no audiophile, but I really don't think I would notice a better sound that would justify spending more money when this one does more volume and sound quality than I will ever need anyway.

I added a BIC F-12 sub not long after i installed these two speakers. So all I currently have is a 2 ch speaker setup with that monster ours sub from BIC. My first movie test was Man of Steel. Oh WOW, these speakers delivered, more than I could have ever hoped for. My wife made me turn them down because I wanted to really push them, and they held up without distorting. In my opinion, if you can turn a speaker to a volume that makes it uncomfortable to listen to, and it can still go louder, that's a good speaker! Oh, and that BIC 12" sub, it would shatter my windows if I didn't adjust the volume down on it, because the bass coming from that speaker shakes my furniture.

I highly recommend these speakers on sound quality and value. If you have a wife that doesn't like obtrusive wall speakers, you might want to pass on these, lol. As for the rest of my setup, I'm still working on it, but I will definitely have to find better hidden speakers for the ceiling.

Very poor design. Two weeks later, I managed to lose it. After an exhaustive search online, I finally found this one, which is started as being for the Turcom. (A number of others looked like they might work but there was no mention of Turcom.) It finally arrived a few days ago, and I am thrilled with. The construction is far better. The top and bottom screw together, whereas the original was just a push together design. The battery compartment is clearly marked for negative/positive, and is very secure. I haven't done a lot of close design work with it yet, but general usage, it's great. Very responsive. The functions of the buttons and tip are the same as the original.

The only downside - and this applies to all tablet pens - is that it is black, thus easy to lose. Quick fix? Christmas wrapping paper wrapped snug around the upper segment. It's reflective paper too, so it will stand out when light hits it. Hopefully some the reps from various pen makers will see this and take the hint!

title: Powerful ! Works for me as both a professional videographer and an enthusiast
text:
I'm a working professional videographer, but no i don't put the same expectations on a camera like the hero4 that i do on my other bigger cameras. Up until now I've been using a hero 3 black for both professional and personal uses. Considering my satisfaction with the hero3, picking up a hero4 was inevitable

**UPDATE: Took off a star for questionable issue: While i haven't come across any major glitches, it does seem to hiccup here and there (my hero3 did the same), the heat that comes off it can be more than warm, but it seems others are experiencing rather hot temperatures. While not entirely reassuring, i've heard some folks have positive experiences dealing with gopro on their overheating matters. We'll have to wait and see, so be sure to buy from a reputable dealer!

What i like about the hero 4 black:

-4K at usable framerates (hero3 could only do 15fps)
-Sweet 120fps slow motion at 1080
-More wireless connectivity(some hiccups, but can work)
-More slowmotion
-Sharpness is satisfactory
-Lowlight is decent enough
-More manual control

What's not to like?

-Battery still not great
-No rear touchscreen
-Doesn't make bacon pancakes
-Doesn't banish ISIS members to the phantom zone(that place jor-el banished general zod to)

New manual controls:

Finally, you can make exposure adjustments! For instance: for night timelapses, you usually want longer exposure times/shutter speed, and you can now do it with this little cam. I need to play with this more to see how well it really performs

No screen:

Many people are very confused as to why the silver edition has it but the black does not. Yea, it's odd and i would have much preferred the flagship get the screen, that being said, i've gotten along very well with my screen-less hero 3, because i have a cautious understanding of the angles it can capture at narrow/medium/wide settings. I'll usually use it as a backup/bonus angle that i don't plan to rely on.That, and it has the phone app in case i need to verify i'm getting the angle i need. The new hero4 has even more connectivity and despite the lack of a screen, as long as you have some digital device with you, it can likely connect and give you a live view.

My bottom line about the screen? You can always add a screen to the black, you cannot add the black features to the silver. The wifi connectivity suits me fine for framing.

Size/weight:

Not much change! That's a good thing, still works with most of all the accessories/etc...

Battery life:

Seems nothing improved over the hero3, still under an hour per charge. Wasabi has a decent extended battery for the hero3, grab that up once they make it for the hero4.

Heat

Possible concern: Can get very warm depending on the settings, and i've seen some users experience very hot temperatures. we'll have to see if this becomes a widespread thing, considering the hero's size, you can't imagine much heat dissipation designed into there. My main concern is the longevity of the device given the heat. heat wears electronics down, reducing their life, if this thing's average temperature is 130degrees, how long will it live? Might be a valid concern, but can't tell without real long testing.

Resolution and Framerates:

Of course the big headline feature is 4k, and that's probably what you're going to buy this thing mainly for. 4k allows for lots of reframing in editing if you're still planning on outputting to 1080. The 4k from the hero4 looks pretty satisfying, maybe not as sharp as bigger/professional cameras, but this is a tiny actioncamera, and i don't see it reasonable to hold it to quite the same standards. for a $500 pocket camera, it's plenty good.

Slow motion keeps getting better on the gopros, there's not much else to say except that you're now getting 1080 at 120fps. Something rare in a camera in this price range, my rx10 which is around a grand can only do 120fps at 720.

Bitrate:

4k gives you up to 60mpbs, which may sound low, but other more expensive cameras use a similar setup and get nice results, and the gopro does pretty well here as well. THe main area where you can see breakup in the codec is fast motion throughout the entire frame, but since all the angles are wide, and many of the details small, the breakup is pretty well controlled. Not perfect, but IMO plenty acceptable for this tiny camera.

Summary, competitors:

If you want 4k in a tiny, rugged camera, the hero4 is on a list of its own. While there are other cameras out there, the overall package gopro has with the hero4 black is impressive, and whether you're a professional or just an enthusiast, it'll get you some nice shots.

title: Do not believe positive reviews (I suspect review stacking going on here)
text:
This was very expensive at $80.00

We expected it to work and work well for many years. (at the very least the DVD player)

However, we were sadly mistaken.
1: After almost exactly one year, the DVD play stopped working altogether. It plays for about 90 seconds, then freezes while the disk over-spins inside and it never finds tracking on the disk again. This is the same result no matter what dvd is put in.

2: The USB port only finds the USB stick "sometimes". When it does, it will not play MP4 or AVI files whatsoever.

3: The screen is quite bad and not even standard 480p proper resolution. It is often blurry and you can almost count the lines of resolution. The color has never matched correctly either.

The bottom line is this... Items of this price should always last at least 4 years, and not just over a year before they die completely. You see all sorts of glowing reviews on so many products like these on Amazon, but I am finding more and more often that those glowing reviews are simply False. I suspect more and more people are posting fake reviews on more and more products. Amazon needs to setup an internal review shop and test some of these products on their own. I just might start to believe a product is decent, if it is actually tested by Amazon first. I pray for a better review process and verification program overall.

People like us spend thousands upon thousands here annually, but am starting to get ripped off more and more by these shoddy products being pushed on unsuspecting customers who tend to rely on the reviews they read before purchasing these products.

title: Decent modem
text: I've had this modem for 2 weeks now and so far so good. The modem runs consistently utilizing DOCSIS 3.0. Setup was a breeze. After I called Comcast to give them the MAC address and serial number access was immediate. The speed is decent and so far I haven't had any problems with it reseting itself or losing connection. This will save me $7 a month on modem rental fees. I've read some of the negative comments about this modem. This is an electronic item so some are going to be defective. That's an easy fix. Exchange it for another one. But I'm getting the feeling that some of these issues lie with the ISP's infrastructure. Cable companies bombard the TV claiming high speed availability for everyone. That just ain't so. The cable company's ability to deliver those speeds most of the time lie somewhere in the middle and depend on the ISP's ability to handle their internet traffic. Old, outdated wiring can affect speeds and connectability as well. So my advice, get it and see how it works with your ISP. If it doesn't work, send it back to Amazon. Their return policy is AWESOME!!

title: HORRIBLE keyboard
text:
If you value a good keyboard and usability, DO NOT BUY THIS LAPTOP!

I don't disagree with the specs and performance ratings other reviewers have posted -- the machine is relatively fast and durable. However, HP really dropped the ball when it comes to usability with this laptop's design.

KEYBOARD:
HP put so much attention on creating a keyboard that fit a grid, that they totally ignored usability. One of the key principles of design is to "chunk" things to make them easier to identify/remember/etc. That's why phone numbers and social security numbers have hyphens in them; it's easier to remember three chunks of small numbers than one large number. This is also why for as long as keyboards had function keys (F1 - F12), there were groups of four keys with a space between them. This keyboard, however, has every single key right next to each other, violating the principle of chunking. There's no space between the [Esc] and [F1], [F4] and [F5], or even between the arrow keys and the [Ctrl] key. Everything is jammed into a grid, making it VERY difficult to feel for keys. I've always touch-typed and now find myself having to look at the keyboard to read labels on keys.

The arrow keys are laid out across three cells on the "grid", with the Up and Down keys jammed into a single cell -- that's right, the Up and Down are only half-size, jammed together in the space for a single key. However, the Left and Right arrow keys are full-sized with a space between them and the Up/Down keys. It's just plain AWKWARD!

Typing on this reminds me of typing on an iPad -- it's okay for short messages, but you wouldn't want to write a book on it.

CHASSIS:
The chassis does seem durable and has a nice metal feel to it. However, they did away with the rounded-over front edge below the keyboard. So, type on it for a while and your wrists will have little sore marks from the sharp edge of the chassis.

INDICATOR LIGHTS:
I think HP swung the pendulum WAY too far to the other side with addressing customer feedback on LED indicator lights. If you saw the predecessors to this laptop (the HP 8440P, etc.), you'd know that one of the customer complaints was the insanely bright LED indicator lights -- they would blind you while using the laptop. So, HP took customer feedback and went to the other extreme! The indicator lights ARE NOT VISIBLE!

The indicator lights (power, HDD, WiFi, charge) are TINY little pinholes with tiny LED's behind them. They are smaller than 0.5 mm! The only way to see them is to position yourself directly inline with the LED and stare into the pinholes. ABSOLUTELY USELESS!!!

TOUCHPAD: (The only good thing)
The touchpad is the only thing that seems to be done well. It is over-sized (4"x2"), supports gestures (two fingers cause scroll, etc.), and can be easily disabled. If you double-tap the tiny dot on the top-left corner of the touchpad, it disables the touchpad. If you double-tap again, it re-enables it. Also, your thumb won't affect the touchpad -- if you rest your thumb or slide it across the touchpad, the touchpad ignores it. Nice for people who hate touchpads because of accidental movement with resting thumbs. VERY NICELY DONE.

SCREEN:
The screen has a strong blueish-green cast to it without a lot of color fidelity. I had to go into advanced settings and adjust the gamma settings to .7 and other color settings to get the right color fidelity.

title: Garmin 510 is better than other reviewers mention
text:
First off, I felt the need to leave a review on the Garmin 510 (with HR, Cadence, & extra out front mount) for several reasons. Many of the reviews here on Amazon can often be misleading- I will explain. I was debating between getting the 500 bundle or even 800 at a lower price since the release of the 510 & 810, but here is why I didn't. The Edge 510 bundle comes with the HR band, cadence sensor, the out front mount (which Garmin and others charge $40+ for), standard stem or bar mount, plus the bluetooth connectivity which includes "Live Tracking" with the Garmin Connect App on your smartphone. The advantages on the 510 over the 500 are simple: Color Touch Screen (500 is physical buttons, black and white screen), the actual screen on the 510 is larger (which is a happy medium size wise between the 500 and 800), easy selection of different bikes if you move the unit from one to another, and easy to use customization of the screens that can be more cumbersome on the 500.

This entire review can be summed up by watching this really cool video on YouTube video, but the review explains each feature in detail: [...]

Many reviewers mention that an upgrade to the 510 is not worth the investment- if you already have a 500, this may be a solid argument. If you have a 200, Garmin Watch, or no GPS at all, maybe an old school speed sensor and cadence computer- the Garmin 510 kit is worth every penny.

REASONS TO BUY THE EDGE 510 BUNDLE:

1) The screen is great, all other's who complain its hard to read are full of it- the screen does not have the sharp contrast of the 500, but it is full color, and its plenty bright (adjustable) and easy to read. Secondly, the color screen is a whole lot nicer to look at- kind of like the difference between an old DOS and a new Windows screen.

2) While it takes a little time to figure out how to program the various screens with Data to your needs, its easy once you figure it out. Also, you have to push the physical "ride" or "play" button on the front of the unit even after tapping "RIDE" onscreen, which is no big deal, you just have to do it, or your unit will not begin your ride or the timer. I think many of the complaints on the 510 come from users who either didn't read the manual, or lack some basic technology skills when it comes to phones, computers, tablets, or anything else. While the user interface on the 510 is still somewhat crude (in the early stages) compared to an iPhone, but it still is incredibly sophisticated, and is perfect for a very usable GPS computer on a road or mountain bike.

3) Bluetooth Connectivity, and Garmin "LiveTrack": This feature is touted by many buyers of this unit as not worthwhile, or a waste of technology for cyclists. BOGUS, the Bluetooth feature on the 510 and 810 are AWESOME. Here is why: my wife or friends can watch my rides live on their computers, tablets, or phones while I'm actually in route- in REAL TIME. We all know how tough it can be to ride a century in the summer heat, and potentially dangerous with cars, trucks, and just bad roads. What a perfect way to let your loved ones know where you are at any given moment? OK some of you are going to say there are already APPS for Android and iPhones that have this feature, and you don't need to waste $400 to buy a Garmin to get it. HERE IS WHERE YOUR WRONG: Anyone who has used these APPS knows that having your GPS turned on full time on your phone (which all APPS that track require) kills your phone battery, often times before your ride ever nears completion. The Garmin unit lets you turn off your phone GPS, all you need turned on is the Bluetooth so your Garmin can stay connected. While this may seem like a solution in search of a problem, it actually works very well. I took a 8 hour ride today, turned off my phone GPS, and at the end of the ride, the Garmin was still at 50% charge, and my phone was at 50% charge (iPhone 5). I could have potentially rode another 5-8 hours with both units turned on, Bluetooth on, and the Garmin Connect App running in the background all the while "Live Tracking" my entire ride.

4) FINALLY: One last feature (may seem trivial, but I think its pretty darn cool) that makes this unit a game changer is the automatic updates at the completion of your ride to Garmin Connect online. As soon as you hit the end ride button (and SAVE on screen) the Garmin unit uploads all the details of your entire ride to the Garmin Connect website for you and everyone to see (if you set it up that way) !!! OK, many of you are going to say that "Garmin Connect" sucks compared to STRAVA, so why would I want to automatically upload my ride to Garmin Connect? You would be right, except for a really cool third party plug in online called: "GARMIN SYNC" here's the website: [...]

I have listed the website here because it took me some time to find it. This website does one simple thing: It uploads your entire ride data from Garmin Connect directly into STRAVA!!! (AUTOMATICALLY.) You don't have to do a thing, once you set it up, every time your Garmin unit uploads your ride to Garmin Connect, this little plug in "pushes" your ride information to STRAVA, and I don't mean some half baked version, I MEAN THE ENTIRE RIDE- Including: Miles ridden, Time traveled, average heart rate, max heart rate, average speed, max speed, cadence, calories, energy output, power, suffer score (Strava Premium only) !! As far as I can tell, there is no difference between the "Auto" upload of a ride, or the old school plug the Garmin into your computer and upload to STRAVA method. Now some might make the argument they have to plug their Garmin in to charge it anyway, so why not plug into a computer to charge and upload your ride at the same time, why do I need the auto uploads? Here are a couple scenarios I can think of why this is useful: If your traveling, and don't want to bring a laptop to upload your rides, you don't need to. Also, at what point is plugging a device into your computer to upload anything going to become a thing of the past completely: sooner than later. iPhone IOS already does all of its updates from iPhones without ever having to plug them in anymore, not set up, backups, downloads, etc. Why shouldn't other devices be so simple?

5) Last but not least: While my review may seem long winded, there are so many great features of the 510 and 810, I felt it was necessary to review what they are, and what makes them better than the 500 or 800. If you use a smartphone, and can find your way around, these Garmin units are fantastic. I'm not a Garmin employee, or one of Garmin Sync, I'm just an average Joe who is massive cycling junkie, and I think the ride information provided by these Garmin models gives the average "Joe" information that used to only be available to pro cyclists, and that makes them fun in their own right. Why would anyone buy old technology when the new stuff is so much cooler? (assuming it works- and these work really well...)

6) I have purchased several different bar mounts for my iPhone to be able to use the cycle "APPS" that allow your phone to be used as a bike computer. They all are a pain, even an iPhone 5 which is smaller than most of the new Android phones on the market is still too big to mount on your handlebar, plus it just looks stupid. You have to turn the screen brightness up so high that if the GPS being on doesn't kill your battery, the screen brightness will. The beauty of the Garmin plus your phone is they just work together, very well I might add. You get the cool Garmin mounted out front, with its long life battery, and the phone stays in your jersey pocket, all the while tracking your ride in REAL time- its the best of both worlds. You get to save your phone's battery so you can use it a real emergency, which is why you carry it while riding your bike anyway.

CONS: The only con I can think of is that the learning curve is a little longer than the standard 500, or certainly the 200. If you want a super basic GPS without any of the "special" features I mention above, the Edge 200 or 500 will be fine. But based on my research, the 500 is usually only $50-$75 cheaper than the 510, and you don't get the "out front" mount I mention above- so the price is pretty close in the end.

But the price was also quite a bit more. I wasn't willing to spend an extra $500 for the Samsung.

This Sharp is priced well and I am mostly happy with the picture quality. My one criticism involves watching sports. When a ball (or any other object) is moving quickly across the screen, it looks like a weird blur on my TV. I believe another reviewer mentioned something about that, suggesting that you can correct this with the settings. I will play with it and update if I find anything.

If I were to do it all over again, I would still go with this TV.

____***** UPDATE 8/24/12 *****____
I found the "motion enhancement" option under "picture settings". I played with the three choices (high/low/off) and it looks noticeably better when set to "off". When watching football, with motion enhancement turned on, the ball becomes a strange blinky blur when it is thrown quickly. Basketballs don't usually move fast enough across the screen to cause the blur. I don't watch baseball, but I am sure it would be a problem to. I don't know what benefit motion enhancement offers, but I really dislike what it does to sports viewing. With this said, although turning this feature off is an improvement, I can't recommend this TV if sports are important to you. Even with the off setting, the fast motion picture quality is still not as good as I would like it to be. From what I hear, a 240hz (or higher) tv will have better fast motion picture quality.

_____***** Update on 10/2/12 *****_____
If you have this tv, make sure you play with the picture settings. Lately I have noticed that the picture quality with all of the pre-programmed options was a bit lacking. I played with the settings, and now it looks much nicer. I made several changes, but the biggest improvements came from lowering the backlight a little, increasing the reds a bit and raising the sharpness all the way.

title: Classy Protection
text:
Shipped fast and in perfect condition. Bulkier than another case I have on my first gen iPad but that case also doesn't stand up very well while trying to watch Netflix; the bottom is slightly rounded. The Cyber Acoustics case has a slightly backwards lean (a good thing!) and a wider base and doesn't fall forward onto the table.

Two cons... had a heck of a time putting the case on! The corners have more flex to them than you'd think though so just be persistent and you'll eventually get the case on -- but you're NOT going to want to remove it again!

Second con -- and this would be true of any case like this -- when you're trying to use the camera or FaceTime, the front cover is in the way. So rather than hold the case like an open book and have the left side flop around, I just fold the flap back and tuck it in, like you're going to watch a movie, and hold it that way to FaceTime or shoot.

I wish the case wasn't so bulky because it really adds to the weight, but I got it for ultimate protection -- and it does that very well. The inside strap is a nice addition, though I rarely carry my iPad in a glassfront-exposed position.

Little bits of lint and fuzz do tend to accumulate on the inside of the front cover that closes against the glass but I just brush it off with a *slightly* damp paper towel.

The sleep/wake function works great with the case, though I've only had it about a month. People reported the front cover wouldn't stay closed after a while but I haven't had that issue yet. Plus you have the two corner straps if it ever came to that.

All ports are accessible, though the sleep/wake button at the top is a little harder to access due to the rubberized corner there. sometimes hard to do a screenshot. Overall, my new 64gb Retina display iPad feels cushioned and protected -- and that was my goal. Would highly recommend!

title: Open Letter to Jeff Bezos - FIRE PRAISE
text:
Mr Bezos,

I'm not sure you get to read these emails, but I hope that this one makes it through to you.

I have been a huge fan of Amazon since its inception in the mid 90's. That's when few people would agree we would ever "shop" online. I remember how odd the name sounded when it launched, yet I was drawn to watch it survive. Ive watched Amazon mature, make mistakes, learn, turn, and prosper. I literally did all my holiday shopping online this year and with 5 children that's a lot of transactions. I'm happy to say that most of my shopping was done with Amazon. I always feel safe with Amazon, knowing (a) Amazon stands behind me, and (b) I get to see what others think about the products you sell. Even when I am researching a product, I ALWAYS look to see what Amazon shoppers think. Amazon draws a quality shopper in my opinion.

In any event, I was able to purchase a Kindle Fire for my wife for her Birthday (Jan 1). She is an avid reader, not so much into technology, but she loves to read. I was skeptical ordering it, being a true lover of technology myself, but knew if she didnt like it we could return it. I will have to say you have hit a home run with this device, she is thrilled with the Fire. The size is "perfect", the screen flawless and the navigation intuitive. It took me only a minute or two (Grinch speak) to become fluent in "Kindle". I have read and watched a lot of reviews online and in print on the Fire and have listened to the argument whether this device could "kill" the iPad. After holding this in my hands, I dont know why the discussion even needs to take place. It's doing things the iPad cannot, and the user experience is rich. This device is a totally new category, rather, a more refined one; following in the footsteps of its previously released cousins. The vision of Amazon is to be congratulated, for in my opinion, you have a clear winner with the Fire. I cant see it going anywhere but up in its ownership.

I admire companies with "vision" and as broad as Amazon is, you have definitely a visionary aspect to your company. While everyone else has been chasing "fruit", Amazon has done its own thing, which almost always reflects vision and knowledge of its customer. For that, I congratulate you and Amazon on the Kindle Fire. My only regret is not being able to order one for myself, but maybe next year. With 7 of us in the house, every penny counts, and Amazon helps us stretch our buying dollar a long ways. (Thank you!)

Thanks for listening, and I look forward to watching the Kindle family grow and continue to blaze new trails.

Sincerely,

Charles Hall - North Augusta, SC

[[VIDEOID:moD5PVXAD4DKIE]]I was skeptical when viewing the listing for this item. Although I own a few Opteka products, the gearless design was not what I was looking for when choosing a DSLR follow focus. But I never did like the geared design of most follow focuses, so I decided to give this product a whirl. I was glad I did. This thing is solidly built of metal and plastic and nothing feels cheap or unprofessionally made. I like the way the wheel unit is slidable along a side axis to make it useable with various width of lenses. And the nine inch rods are a little short to use with a matte box or flags unit, so you might want to use longer rods if going this route. I already have a lens gear that I will test with this unit later today, and will put in an update. I gave the Opteka follow focus four stars for the build quality alone. If it works successfully with the lens gear I have, I will update to five stars. Good job, Opteka!
UPDATE: I tried the Opteka follow focus with my focus gear and it was very clumsy attempting to just get the gear on the lens. I gave up after five minutes. But after just a few moments of monkeying with the follow focus, I was able to get it working with the f/1.8 Canon prime lens that I just bought on Amazon. Again, working without a gear. So this truly is a gearless follow focus. So, you earned five starts, Opteka!

Another Update: I filmed this shot using the Opteka gearless follow focus. Notice that there is little to no jiggle when the shot focuses from one object to another in this shot. I did have the camera (Canon 60D) locked down on a tripod, but I did take my hand off the follow focus knob each time I re-focused.

title: easy install,clear picture,factory finish,sturdy,wire harness long enough for  ALL truck beds
text: so i n=bought a 2014 f150...standard cab,long bed...126" wheel base...just the cheapest truck with very few options...one option I wanted was a back up camera....so after searching local shops,and on-line, I finally decided on this one. I went from a short bed ranger to a long bed f150 and found it difficult to back in to places with any type of speed or accuracy....so I bought this and the BOYO 3.5" rearview mirror/screen...couldn't be happier. this camera seemed simple when I opened the box...I took the six torx 30 bolts out of the truck tailgate,then looked at the factory handle and thought...."oh boy" lock rods,lock,handle ect....how do I do this? then I saw 2 10mm bolts.....so I removed those and the tailgate handle gently was removed quicker than the time it took to write this review...the lock rods stayed in place, the key lock thingy was only held in by a simple u shaped spring...with in under 5 minutes the key lock and handle were in and the 2 10mm nuts were tightened..very very easy! then using an open coat hanger I taped the wire to the hanger and fished it though the tailgate opening.plenty of wire! the wire connects to another supplied harness...the red/black get rerouted back to the drivers tail lamp assembly removed by 2 8mm bolts...and red/black get connected to the reverse light.....the center light, on is black/ground..and the other is reverse light power....very easy.then routing the wire harness along side factory harness and securing with supplied tie wraps..I then removed the kick plate (carefully) and routed the wire harness into the cab through the parking brake groumet...seems a bit tricky, but use a razor blade to cut a slit in the gromet ,you will see the spot/plenty of room...the slit will reseal and keep out water...the wire harness is plenty long enough for any and all f150...xtened f150,4 door,and long bed.now here is the great part...the wire harness now in the kick panel is a yellow video rca,,,,AND a green reverse light OUTPUT!!! no searching where to connect inside the truck! the green wire is magically connected to the reverse lights you connected in the back at the tail light! now just plug in the video rca...and connect the green wire that says light output to the lcd screen input! that easy!! the camera looks nice,feels sturdy,operated nice,has guide lines that are pretty accurate,does not glitch or roll,and is able to see at night!!!very clear image and the handle itself feels and looks factory! the whole install took about 45 minutes..MOST of the time was spent routing the wire alongside the factory harness and clipping off the cable ties ends and wrapping the wire harness with tape the last 12" where it entered the truck through the parking brake gromet so it doesn't hang down and gets snagged on something this winter...for the price I could find anything better,no need to drill holes,only needed a t30 and a 10mm socket,a razor blade,and a roll of electric tape.

title: It's OK for what it IS and that is bare bones basic
text:
It's a trip back in time from my perspective or back about 12 years ago when cell phones were starting to evolve into limited multi capabilities. I got this phone for emergency backup to my main Smartphone (Galaxy Note II) and it's been a task in attempting to remember all the old functions and navigation from the early cell phone days. Having to actually read the manual to discover the myriad functions I clumsily got through the various set ups to include voice mail, making calls, sending texts, building the address book with current contacts and that sort of thing which is second nature easy on the modern device.

A word of caution: One can easily insert the Sim card backwards as I did on my initial attempt. Going back, I re-placed it with the notch in the card matching the notch on the inner lining of the phone itself. Had I carefully read the instructions, I would have known this but haste made for frustration. The same could be said for setting up the phone with the basic functions so a word to the wise there. The call quality is very good and once back up to 'old speed', the various navigation movements can be done with minimal drama.

I plan on carrying the a157 fulltime in my main vehicle along with the appropriate mobile charger for those times I might forget taking my Note II with me OR when one of the phones is outside its calling zone. The a157 is AT&T while my other phone is with Sprint. I elected to bite the bullet and take the 10cents a call package, paying the $100 for a full year so I wouldn't have to renew the thing every few months or so. AT&T dings you for EVERYTHING on this unit! Checking voice mail? Ding. Setting up voice mail? Ding. It does provide a current standing after every usage as to where you stand with the financials so that's somewhat helpful.

Summing up, it's an okay phone and if what you want or need is the basic stuff or, like me, a seldom used backup, I think you'll be okay with it too.

title: This is a fantastic flash, with little options
text:
If you're looking to add a little flexibility to your flash photography this is a great option. It's compatible with nearly every Nikon camera and does a great job with fill flash as well as bounce flash. It has no manual controls what so ever. You can only "adjust" flash intensity through the camera body. The only control on the back is the power switch.

If all you're looking to do is add flash capability to a pro body, a body with a broken built in flash or a film camera this is a great option for you.

If you want to get creative with your flash in any way i.e. wireless triggers, manual exposure settings etc I would recommend you look elsewhere.

There are plenty of other flashes out there that will provide you with all the essential functions of a hot shoe mounted flash for less money than that of a branded (Nikon, Canon etc) with maybe just a few exceptions.

The [[ASIN:B00BBWNOJK Yongnuo YN-560 III Speedlite Flash for Canon & Nikon - GN58 - Built in 2.4Ghz trigger/transceiver with full support for RF602/603 triggers.]] will do everything you need with the exception of iTTL metering. This can actually help you learn about how to properly use flashes and adjust their output to suit your shot's overall feel and theme. Not to mention it has a whole host of other features not even found in Nikon flashes twice the price!

The [[ASIN:B001ZT3DOU Vivitar Digital TTL Auto-Focus Flash for Nikon - Black (DF383NIK)]] will do everything the SB400 will and more for about the same money. It may not be a Nikon, but at least you've got the ability to customize the shot now.

Overall, the SB400 is a perfectly capable unit, but, in the long run, I wish I had just done a bit more research before I purchased this one. It's great, but only for a finite spectrum of use.

title: wow.  wow!
text:
important: follow the IC Diamond manufacturer's instructions, which is on their website. When applying, I did their suggested method, which was putting a glob in the center and pressing down, and not lifting up again - I know it's tempting to lift it up to observe the coverage, but just don't do it. It ruins the airless/bubbleless contact effect that the "glob method" creates. I also made sure that the surfaces were completely clean, carefully cleaning several times over so no resedue of inferior products would get in the way.

when the product arrived, I peeled off the label. Along the translucent barrel were little measurement lines. I also saw that there was hardly anything in the tube. Looked like enough for 5 or 6 applications, max. So don't waste it! You can go and buy the version with more in it, it's just more expensive. But I only had a couple applications I needed to do anyway:

used it on an old Dell GX280 with fans screaming at 50% processor use - works silently now. I even loaded up several big programs, putting the processor to the torture test: computer started freezing up with all the huge tasks, processor 100% for an hour, no screaming fan! It's a definite difference.

also used it on my Gateway FX P7805-U, which was slowing down during game play before. I had a silver compound on processor and a thermal pad on the GPU. I used the IC DIAMOND on the processor and a copper shim with IC DIAMOND in between the shim/cooling assembly and shim/GPU. Game does not slow up, or if it does, it must be hardly at all. I mean, my system has my limits, but it just doesn't seem to slow up anymore, from what I was assuming was a heating problem.

I actually in the end was so impressed I ordered the aformentioned larger capacity version, to have on hand for other computers/friends' computers.
