title: The best so far
text:
I have been buying screen protectors for years for various devices. What I have learned is that paying a higher price does not necessarily mean you get a better product. I paid big bucks for big, name brand screen protectors that were not so great. The iLLumiShield at this point is the best I have used. What I like most is the way it traps a very minimal amount of bubbles. And the bubbles that are trapped are very easy to squeeze out. Once on the screen you can hardly tell it is there. My finger slides effortlessly across the screen unlike some others that feel like some sort of adhesive is on them. It's as easy as the bare glass. I'm glad I found iLLumiShield and will use them next time I buy devices they make screen protectors for.

A couple of pointers that always help me install screen protectors. Use the hinge method that is demonstrated on a few YouTube videos. If you have to take the screen off to re-positioning it (which you shouldn't have to do with the hinge method) do not use your fingernail to lift the protector. Once you bend the edge it will not lay flat again. So use a piece of tape to lift it off. Also if you get a dust particle stuck under the protector, lift is as I mentioned with tape and take another piece of tape to remove the dust.

title: I love it!
text:
I've never owned a monitor stand of any kind before, so take that into consideration when reading my praise. In short, I absolutely love this stand and wish I would had purchased one years ago. Not only can I place my monitors where I want them, but I now have all that usable space _beneath_ the monitors for stuff like textbooks and misc papers I'm working on.

_I_ have no complaints, but I've heard others mention (and show via video) trimming/cutting the pole to reduce the height so it doesn't stick up so much. For me, it's a non-issue.

I absolutely love it; have I said that yet? I have two [[ASIN:B005BZNDS0 ASUS VS247 LCD monitors]] attached to it and really enjoy all of the adjustment options such as tilt, height (via pole) and the ability to flex the arms to place the monitors exactly where I wish to use them. There are also cable clips beneath the arms to help with cable management, but I haven't used them so I can't say how well they work.

My desk dimensions:

* Depth: 32"
* Width: 62"
* Table-top thickness: 1.25"

The clamp for the table-top is adjustable in regards to tension (turn knobs) and also for grip (thickness of your desktop). The secret hoarder inside of me is trying to rationalize buying a second one, even if I don't have an immediate purpose for it, just in case I want another later. I can't praise this stand enough. :P

P.S.

I've had this stand for about two weeks as of this review date and have zero complaints.

Edit: A year later and these are still solid; no issues and hopefully many more years of service ahead.

title: Great bag, good size, excellent protection!
text:
I just received this bag and I'm very pleased. I was really afraid this bag might be too big, it really isn't. The product dimensions for this bag are a bit misleading. It's listed as 21.3" wide but that's from strap to strap. The actual body is only about 16-17" wide. This is a FAR BETTER size than anticipated. It does measure about 11" inches tall and it's a little wider when filled at about 6-7" inches.

The interior of this bag is roomy and built in padded camera box will fit at least 2 lenses plus the DSLR. There are spaces on either side of the camera box for additional lenses in their own cases OR anything else. I was able to fit my Canon 6D DSLR with attached 24-105mm f/4L lens in the camera box. My second 16-35mm lens could fit in the box at the same time but it's a bit of a squeeze. Instead, my 50mm 1.4 and my 40mm pancake lens fit in the box along with the camera quite easily. I was able to put the 4th lens next to the box and there's still room for a speedlight and other camera accessories in the bag. The pocket has a nice RFID blocking pocket to protect you passport or credit cards while traveling. The one noticeable thing the bag is lacking is pockets for memory cards. This isn't a deal killer for me. I have a small memory card pouch I use and it fits nicely between the box and the exterior of the bag and keeps them out of the way.

The body is expandable and this will make an extra 2 inches or so for a tablet, small notebook or iPad/tablet.

I've been a fan of Pacsafe bags for a couple of years now. I also own the shoulder bag AND the 25L backpack. Their bags offer what I consider some of the best protection for your belongings compared to anything else on the market. Not only do they make really well made bags, I've taken mine to the ends of the earth and back (just back from Patagonia walking on glaciers and then hiking in the Andes) but they held very well.

Like most of their product line he body of the bag has slash resistant mesh built in and the straps have metal cabling to make them stronger and slash resistant as well. The best thing about these bags are the zippers which all can be closed with a clip to make pickpocketing from the bag nearly impossible. One of my favorite features of these bags are the handles and the built in clips which makes it easy to secure my bags while seated at a restaurant or cafe. If you clip the bag around the arm of a chair or the table it's nearly impossible to walk away with the bag.

If you travel anywhere and gear security is a concern, this is the bag for you!

title: Loved it while it worked
text:
I really, really love this mouse. I love that it folds flat and I can stick it in the pocket of my laptop sleeve and it doesn't create this huge inconvenient lump like other mice. I love the feel, the scrolling and the small nano transceiver that conveniently hugs the bottom of the mouse via magnet for storage. Although some say this is a negative, I always store the mouse in the pocket of my laptop sleeve, which lays flat against my laptop, so the transceiver has nowhere to go, really. I have had this mouse for about a year, I think. It got very light use, as I mainly only pulled it out when I was doing a lot of mousing/clicking/dragging that would be much easier to do with a mouse rather than my touch pad.

Today, it stopped working! Updated everything at microsoft.com/hardware and replaced the batteries, took out the usb, turned off, restarted comp, etc etc. The blue light goes on and my computer recognizes the device and says it is ready to use. However, it just doesn't work... A quick search told me that a lot of people have had issues like this with this mouse. So, sadly, I'm on the search for another mouse that is just as flat as this one... For the price, this isn't worth it given that I bought this mouse for $35 and you can buy a wireless mouse from a good brand for half to a third of the price of this one. I'm sad to say I have looked a bit and can't find anything this flat. If anyone knows of another good alternative, PLEASE comment and let me know. :(

title: Horrible, do not buy!!!
text:
After installing then original card in my Galaxy S3, the card would unmount and mount again and again through out the day. This created horrible battery life. Then within a week all the data on the card became corrupted. I formatted it in FAT32 hoping this would solve the problem only to have the same thing happen again. Then I tried once more with exFat, only to get the same data corruption. I contacted Sandisk and they replaced the card.

Card #2 did the same thing within two weeks. I decided I might use the card in my SLR since it was a no go in my phone. However, it was slower than the three other class 10 cards I owned and the two other class 6 cards I own. I tested them with both a Windows program, a Mac program, and in the SLR itself. My slowest class 6 card from Transcend would take 18 pictures in burst mode before slowing down. Sandisk's "Ultra" card would only take 14.

This problem is well known, just look at the reviews here or Google the card. So when I talked to Sandisk, I asked that they replace the card with of equal value from one of their different line of cards. I talked with a representative at length and she escalated the next level of support to see if this alternative was possible. I was assured that the same representative would contact me shortly by phone so I would not have to go through the whole process of explaining things again from the beginning. Seven hours later I got a call from a different representative who knew nothing of the problem, requiring me to explain everything from the beginning. He said all Sandisk could do was send another of the same card. He assured me that the problem with the card had been fixed and that Sandisk's products were reliable. Funny, the representative told me the exact same thing a month ago when they shipped me card #2. I have 9 other SD cards (two of the micro SDXC variety) and none of them have had any problems. Yet, the two Sandisk cards of this variety have both failed. Please, please buy a different card so you can avoid my experience!

title: Sleek, Snappy, and Slim!
text:
[Original review with updates]

If you're looking for a laptop that fits the description of the title I wrote above, this is it!

I've had this laptop for about 4 days now and after playing around with it and adjusting the settings to my liking, I'm in love with this machine!

The display, is fantastic. The matte screen + the resolution makes this a wonderful choice for watching movies or working outdoors. Everything is very responsive and runs extremely smoothly and quiet for the most part. The instant on is an awesome feature as well. I never realized how much I would need something like this until I got this laptop. Now I can't imagine going back to my old one with its slow restart and resuming speed.

I never owned the previous Zenbook UX31e so I can't compare, but from what I've heard, the Zenbook Prime UX31a has fixed some of the keyboard issues that people were complaining about with the older model. I don't know if it's true since I haven't tried typing on the older model, but I have no problems typing on this.

With that said, I just wanted to address a couple of issues that people have been mentioning on various sites on the web.

1. Backlight bleeding [updated] - If you're extremely lucky, you'll get a unit with hardly noticeable backlight bleeding. My first unit that I had to send back due to problems with wifi was great, but the unit I received after that had terrible backlight bleeding. My sister has also ordered the same ultrabook and she has had terrible bleeding on hers too. ASUS needs apply better quality control to their products and figure out a way to fix this it seems. However, if you're not going to be watching movies with dark screens or do things like photo editing, you'll probably have no issues with the backlight bleeding for you won't see it, if you aren't looking for it! For those who will be watching movies in the dark (unless you have your brightness setting on low or you're running off the battery saving power plan) you'll definitely see the bleeding that can distract. If you get a screen with little bleeding, KEEP IT! Don't exchange it in hopes that you'll get a PERFECT screen with absolutely no bleeding because you won't. I totally regret sending my first unit back, but I had to with the wifi issue which seemed to be a hardware issue.

2. Fan noise - this seems to be a hit and miss for people as well. So far, mine has been relatively quiet. However between yesterday and today the fan was running for long periods of times at full speed. I looked into the resources list and found out that the bluetooth device manager was acting up for no reason, so once I killed that, the laptop has gone back to being almost silent again. I'm in a quiet room right now and I can't hear it at all. So if you think the fan is acting up for no reason, go into your task manager and look through the resources list.

UPDATE - My sister received a unit with a fan noise issue that some on the web have been describing. Her fan was spinning at max speed, extremely loudly for 5-15 second periods every minute for no reason at all. If you're experiencing this issue, send it back. It is not something that should be happening.

3. Keyboard Flex - this issue seems to be more reported among UX32VD purchasers, but just in case people were wondering, I cannot get the keyboard to flex at all on my UX31A unless I'm intentionally pushing down with a lot of force, which would probably end up breaking the laptop before you experience the amount of flexing people have been worried about.

So if you're looking for a light, extremely portable machine that still packs enough power to carry out your everyday tasks and a bit more with a great screen that's matte (which will cut out glare associated with glossy displays) you just can't get any better than this ultrabook. However, if you're looking for a laptop you can replace parts with, such as upgrading the RAM and such, but still want the look and feel of this model, check out the Zenbook Prime UX32VD.

P.S. I got the ADATA Sandforce SSD as well. It seems so far everyone who has received this model at least has gotten the ADATA rather than the Sandisk unlike previous generation Zenbooks.

-
[6/28/2012 UPDATE - I started noticing a wi-fi issue. I noticed that it started getting slower and slower at connecting to the internet. I would have to wait an extra 20 seconds or so for the wi-fi to connect after I revived it from standby (this is 20 seconds after windows had all loaded up). Not something I noticed when I had first gotten it. Then today, we changed our internet service provider. The Zenbook Prime struggled very hard to connect when the 2 other laptops in our house connected with no problem. Once it managed to connect, the connection was so slow, I couldn't even load a google search. I tried to restore everything to the factory condition just to see if that would help with anything in case the driver settings somehow got messed with (although highly unlikely), but then it got stuck on and endless cycle of restarting and shutting down with no way to stop it unless I force shut it down. It was absolutely bizarre.

As this is a new laptop, it shouldn't be having issues like this to start with, so it's going back. I still love this thing though, so I'll be ordering the same model again and hope that the new one will have the fantastic no bleed screen + perfectly lit up keys + no dead pixels like my current one, but without the wi-fi issue and the endless rebooting! Will update when I get the new one.

[6/30/2012 UPDATE - Just got my new one today as Amazon is amazing with their customer service and overnighted the replacement to me! Anyways, this one had the other wifi issue that people had been talking about in the later reviews here and on the UX31A-AB71 page. The wifi connection arrived disabled to start with, and I had to manually go into the driver settings to enable it. Once that was enabled, I was able to connect but the connection was extremely slow and the wifi dropped off and on. The wireless adapter seems to be unstable when using N setting on routers.

Thanks to user 'foot attack' who pointed out this work around the connectivity issues with N-routers, I was able to get it working with my other router. If your router is on the N mode, change it to the G mode through your router settings and see if that works. I tried setting up the internet connection with my other router with the N enabled and noticed that the connectivity issue was only solved once I switched back to G through the router settings. Quite annoying, I hope ASUS will be able to fix this soon with a new update as N-routers are pretty much the standard these days.

So far so good on the replacement laptop minus the N wifi connection issue. The only thing driving me insane right now is my space bar is squeaky! Hopefully it'll stop squeaking on its own, or I guess I'll have to try putting some oil under it to see if it helps. Oh, also, the trackpad/touchpad on this replacement seems much easier to physically click on than my previous one, which I had to press on really firmly to get the click to register.

P.S. There is backlight bleeding this time on the new unit while my previous unit had a perfect screen :( , but you only see it on dark screens so oh wells, doesn't matter.

Nevermind, turned up the brightness setting and tried watching a movie on it. The bleeding is really really bad. It totally distracted from the movie whenever the scene was a bit dark. I could have dealt with little backlight bleeding, but not this.

[7/8/2012]
I loved almost all features about this laptop except for the sensitivity of the touchpad and the backlight bleeding (Out of the 4 units my sister and I've had between us for this laptop, only one had little backlight bleeding that didn't distract. Rest of the units had pretty bad bleeding with other issues on top of it. ASUS needs to take into the issue of quality control with this model for we've experienced random issues on top of major backlight bleeding. However besides those two factors, this notebook is definitely one of my favorites I've ever owned. It's quiet, responds instantly, and the display is amazing (when not watching a movie with dark screens in a dark room), and looks ultra sleek and feels extremely well made.

However, I've gotten tired of trying to receive the perfect unit, so I've sent my second unit back for a refund and will probably wait until later on in the future to repurchase. My sister, however, is a bit more patient than I am, and is waiting for a new unit.

title: A good, solid family computer
text:
So right off the bat, I'm going to tell you this a review coming from the standpoint of a *family computer.* We have two children, ages 6 and 8 (that's grades 1 and 3). Some years ago, before the kids were even of a computer age, my husband and I got frustrated with our Dell all-in-one desktop that ran Windows Vista, dumped the darned thing, and went to tablets and laptops of our own. Well, now it's time to have a family desktop again because the kids are of an age that it's just needed. So that is the viewpoint this review is coming from so keep this in mind as it may or may not be helpful to you (example, if you're a dedicated gamer or a stockbroker looking for a power computer, this may be a great computer for you, but my review might not tell you everything you need to know so look at other reviews!).

Okay, that said, this thing is HUGE. I know, I know, it said 27" but holy cow, I didn't realize the full impact of that until I hefted this thing out of the box. It's at least 30lbs. Because it's an All-in-One and because, as I'm sure you've seen from the photos and videos of this computer here on this page, the monitor is movable into different positions, the base has to be *very* stable and heavy to keep it secure and yes it is. I wrestled it on to the desk in the family room and, whew, that was my workout for the day.

As a 43 year old, I've set up far more than my fair share of computers in my lifetime and thank God they just keep getting easier. (Yay for technology.) HP has certainly kept up to speed in this regard. Honestly, I set it on the desk, peeled off the protective plastic cover from the screen, plugged it in the wall and I was connected to my home wireless network in *less than 5 minutes.* I'm not exaggerating. As I said earlier, the last Windows product I used was Vista (this is the part where you all feel sorry for me), so the new Windows 8.1 took me a couple of days to familiarize myself with. I won't do a review of Windows here since that's just the OS that HP chose to put on there, not the HP product itself, but suffice to say it was easy to work with and just seemed to me Microsoft's attempt to make itself relevant again by using apps. It's all good.

The machine itself: let's see, we covered big and heavy, which isn't a bad thing. Let's talk about that movable monitor. As you can see from the product page, it basically has the 3 positions. First one is like any normal monitor. Which I presume is what most adults would want it to be. Again, it's huge. And, by the way, has absolutely gorgeous color and clarity. (Nicer than a lot of TVs I've owned in my life, lol.) Because it's so big, if I were using this as a normal computer monitor for myself and my husband, we'd want it sitting farther back on the desk because of it's huge size (as my mother used to say, "You'll ruin your eyesight!").

But with the kids and the touchscreen, we wanted it easier for them to actually touch the screen, so we brought the monitor lower so that the bottom edge is flush against the desk. If you had shorter kids or a shorter chair, you could even bring the monitor lower, so that it hangs off the front of the desk if you wanted to. Anyway, the kids can touch the screen easy this way, reaching the apps or whatever. Our desk happens to have one of those small keyboard shelves that pull out so they can then type (yes, I still make them type things properly sometimes....I know, I know, mean mom) which is why I just have the bottom flush with the desk.

The third monitor position they advertise is flat on it's back, where you could use it like a tablet looking down at it. Frankly, I do not understand this one at all. Maybe another user/reviewer could explain this one to me.

But moving right along. I mentioned that it's a touch screen. As anyone who has small kids knows, this can be both a pro and a con. It's nice to be able to touch the app they want, but dear lordy....there's something about eight year old boys and boogers. They are magnetically attracted to each other. Gah. Thankfully, I can report that the screen cleans up easily.

The computer comes with a bunch of paperwork advertising HP's integration of "Leap Motion" technology, which is a technology that allows the computer to recognize hand motions and directions in the air just *in front* of the computer rather than actually touching the screen, but in tiny print at the bottom it says "on select models only." Please be aware this is NOT one of those models.

Here's some stuff important to parents: there are a lot of USB ports (yay!), three of them altogether and one of those is powered so it can charge something plugged into it even when the computer is turned off. It should go without saying, but maybe not so I'll say it here, that this computer is blazing fast. After the initial updates are done when you first set it up, which is always the case, the start-up time on this is very quick.

It comes with a meh keyboard and mouse....if I were the primary user, I'd replace them, but since the kids don't care, I don't. The mouse isn't even needed, given the touchscreen, in fact. It also comes with an external DVD-RW drive for you. The speakers are really, really good (so invest in a really good pair of headsets).

The webcam is so-so. Can't say I was impressed by the quality there, but that's a minor issue for me.

The bottom line for this *family* is that this is a pretty darned good computer. The gimmick, of course, is the adjustable monitor. So you have to ask yourself if that's something that you'd find useful or cool. We certainly did in this house with the kids. The plus side is that even if you got the computer and found the other positions of the monitor didn't work for you, you can always set it up as a "traditional" monitor, no harm no foul. So there's really no risk involved there. It's got a gorgeous screen and very nice sound. Techies are going to really want to get into the nuts and bolts of it, of course, but they knew from the beginning of my review that this wasn't written for them. So happy computer hunting everyone and good luck....

title: It's a Bose, are you kidding?! Buy this!!!
text:
I know I need to write more than, "OMG, you HAVE to buy this!!!" so I will do so for your benefit, my dear fellow music lovers. But seriously, you can just stop reading now and BUY IT RIGHT NOW. You will not regret it!!!

As a teen in the 80s, I listened to heavy metal and rock on my Sony stereo system if I was home and awake, continuously. My dad bought the best of the best, from the receiver to the diamond-needle turntable to the speakers and beyond, and I learned early on how to tell whether a music system could produce high-quality sound. Even after I became a DJ in college and CDs became popular, I preferred my records because my system produced such amazing sound.

When my 1984 Sony receiver bit the dust in a lightning strike a few years ago, I actually cried. Nothing could produce that sound quality...until now. (And I still have my old 100-watt speakers that do sound amazing with a $20 amplifier we recently bought here on Amazon.) I've never bought a Bose because of the cost and because, well, as someone spoiled by killer 80s metal, most music today sucks so I didn't see it as worth the investment. But oh, my friends, this Bose SoundTouch 20 Series is worth every penny and then some, whether you are rocking out or enduring your 17-year-old's inexplicable taste in dub step. If a music system can actually make dub step tolerable (in short increments), you know it's good.

Set-up was easy as can be. We installed the apps on our phones and our computers in just seconds. We plugged the Bose in, turned it on, and started cranking some tunes. We blasted some Bruno Mars (hey, a girl can expand her musical horizons!) and wow, was it crisp (except the parts that are supposed to sound distorted). I then tested it with my standard music system test song, Dokken's super-crunchy "Mr. Scary." It features searing guitar, solid bass and killer drums. I was blown away. It was equally amazing with the bass-heavy "Balls to the Wall" by Accept. Very full, rich sound. There was no song it couldn't handle. I felt at times like I was at the concert or in the studio. I got this system free in exchange for doing a review, but really, if something happened to it, I'd buy a replacement in a heartbeat (drumbeat?).

Bottom line on the sound? BRILLIANT. If you care nothing else about awesome features, the sound alone is enough reason to spend $400 on this thing. I used to work with rock bands at gigs and in the studio and I know sound systems. For $400, you cannot beat this sound. If you are a serious music lover, you will NOT be disappointed. Trust me.

Ok, now on to features. With the Bose apps, you can tap into Spotify, Pandora, online radio, your computer's music library, local radio, even global radio. In seconds, I was able to find my favorite radio station 4 hours away, 98Rock in Baltimore, and start playing it through the Bose. In the mood for South African music? Go for it! It struggled with Pandora when I searched for Accept's song, and it wasn't finding things accurately or quickly, but that was only happening with Pandora and could be a problem on their end. To have it see your music library on a PC, you just sync it with Windows Media Player, and then sync that with the Bose app. You can even turn the unit on with the app. Sick, right??? When I installed the app on my computer, it recognized our IP address and already had my husband's login set up, so I could just log in and start playing music. I could have added my own ID and likely will (he likes 70s classic rock like America and Steely Dan, eww, but the first song he played after syncing our computer cache of music was an 80s Rush song, so he's still a keeper), but I could immediately hop in and start playing music.

You can easily set up a playlist for a party and just be good to go. There's a remote control, 6 presets (which can do local radio, online radio, etc.), and you can either use the app on your phone/MP3 device or plug it in directly to the Bose and play music from there. The only trouble I ran into is that the Speck case on my iPhone 5 blocked the aux plug from going all the way in, so if I want to plug my phone into the Bose, I have to take the case off. When I did so, I was already playing music through the computer app, and when I started a song on my phone, it didn't switch over. I had to switch the Bose to Aux for it to pick up the new music source. Not a big deal and it kinda makes sense.

Really, I can't find a single complaint about this system. I have always wanted a Bose (I did buy my husband Bose speakers for his computer years ago) and am SO glad I finally have one. GET IT GET IT GET IT. 'Nuf said.

title: Decent Cans...Good Price...add $30 Bose cable
text:
In this review, I will give you my first impressions of these decent noise canceling headphones and suggest a $30 mod that will improve the overall experience of these using these cans.

Summary:
I received my ATH-ANC27 headphones today from Amazon, so keep in mind these are my initial impressions and nitpicks. I researched this model considerably online before purchasing. The overwhelming consensus online is that these are a good bargain for a good pair of noise canceling headphones. I find the user reviews here on Amazon, rather than the "expert" bloggers, to be more accurate and representative. They offer decent sound quality, acceptable comfort, and quite good noise canceling. There is a reason Bose QC15's are the gold standard in noise canceling headphones. At this price point, they are worth keeping but they are not competitive with the Bose QC15.

Unboxing

First, the packaging was very easy to open and get started. It seems ridiculous to mention this, but today most electronic components are sealed in impenetrable plastic sarcophagi which have undoubtedly resulted in countless ER-trip-worthy lacerations (I refuse to open them without the presence a sober adult, capable of driving me to the hospital just in case). Included in the package were some nice touches: a nice carrying case, a velcro sleeve for holding the several included audio adapters, a 2.5mm to 3.5mm jack-to-jack cable, and an alkaline AAA battery (so many devices forgo the battery or may as well have by including an utterly worthless "heavy duty" zinc carbon battery). The unboxing was expedient except for the battery installation which required a quick glance at the manual. A quick setup guide on the right ear piece battery cover would eliminate this.

Build

The build quality is above what I expected for a sub sixty dollar set of noise canceling cans. The padding is fair quality. The "leather" is a little plasticky. The plastic parts on the headband don't feel fragile but I don't expect them to last years (hey, neither did my Bose AE's). The ON/OFF switch is a little stiff and junky feeling. They look decent in the case but the profile is large making them look a little goofy on the cranium. The cable and adapters appear to be gold plated. The cable is a little thin and has a nearly useless "locking" mechanism (a protruding rubber key on the jack) to keep them in the left ear but the perfect length to stick an iPhone in your pocket (I'm 6'2") and I'm all for a single stereo cable. All-in-all, they are built very well for the price.

Noise Canceling

The first thing you'll do after installing the battery is turn on noise canceling without music. The first thing you'll notice is not the silence, but the soft white noise ("hissing") in the background. It's not obnoxious to me, but it is noticeable. The seal on the headphones is not good. My Bose AE2's passively cancel out much more noise with a better seal than the ANC27's will in passive mode (i.e., OFF). In a quiet environment the noise canceling is negligible. I went into the laundry room, turned on the fan and the washer and the dryer and flipped on and off the switch...on...off...on...off. The low frequency noise cancelation is very impressive. For air travel, these would be superb. The high frequency noise cancelation was adequate but not great. Bose QC15's also do a much better job at low frequency cancelation (which is what you really want for most noises). I went out to the garage and used some power tools (e.g. a belt sander to mod a Bose cable, see below). Again, great noise cancelation. For $60, I am very impressed. Are they Bose QC15 quality? Nope. Are they close? Hard to say. I'll do a side by side comparison tomorrow. But I suspect the answer is: for 20% of the cost you get 80-90% of the value. There is a reason Bose QC15s are the industry's gold standard. The noise cancelation is the selling point for these headphones and their strongest suit...if you don't mind the white noise background which vanishes when listening to music.

Audio Quality

The sound quality is not the strongest suit of these headphones. With noise canceling OFF these cans sound terrible. WIthout active noise canceling, the sound is muddled, distorted, sloppy. They sound like a cheap pair of noise canceling headphones. That is with noise canceling OFF. With noise canceling ON, the sound is more crisp, clean, and clear. Unmistakably better audio quality with the use of a AAA battery. I will not use these headphones without noise canceling. I'll go so far as to carry a few spare AAA's in the case to avoid the temptation. That said, the noise quality is not great even with the noise canceling ON. The mids range from okay to very weak depending on the song. I have been listening to over an hour of my favorite songs and I find myself often distracted by the lack of distinct mid-frequency voices, especially when they are the dominant melody (e.g., guitar or vocal solos). The bass ranges from clear and clean to boomy and excessive. If you like bass, these have enough. The highs are clear...clear enough to distinguish 128kbps vs 192+kbps mp3 encoding. Compared to Bose AEs, AE2s, and QC15s which, like all Bose products I've owned, offer excellent, clean, crisp, clear, flat performance across all bands, the ANC27s sound will leave you wanting. They are far from the worst and best headphones I've used. Again, (variations on a theme) the performance is good for $57 noise canceling headphones.

Comfort

The ANC27s are not comfortable. I have a large head (7 5/8 - 7 3/4) but small ears. They fit, but barely. My ears touch the foam inserts inside the cavity, which at first is not noticeable but leads to mild fatigue in as little as 30 mins. They are also hot. They do not breath well, they are tight, and the plasticky leather is not nearly as comfortable as Bose AE style cans. I suspect I can wear these for a 2-3 hour flight but I suspect that I'll be glad to take them off at the end. I can wear my Bose AE2s and QC15s for hours, all day even without discomfort (they may be a little warm but its not worth taking off). Comfort is, in my mind, the worst part of these headphones but the sound quality is a close second.

Suggested Improvement

The obvious improvement for these headphones almost goes without saying: they need a cable with an inline mic with remote. The good news is you can make one with a Bose AE2i replacement cable [[ASIN:B0059F3EXG AE2 inline remote and microphone cable]]. The bad news it costs $30. The worst news, you need to grind off the rubber fitting. I tried this tonight by using my benchtop belt sander. I was careful and took my time and the entire experiment lasted 2 minutes. It worked with my iPhone 4 and ANC27's. Attempt at your own risk and use appropriate PPE and don't say I didn't warn you. But it's worth $30 to me to be able to remotely control my volume, music, and have a phone conversation with the ANC27s on.

Bottom Line

The less than stellar (Incubus is on right now) sound quality and discomfort of the ANC27 headphones earned them an honest 3 stars. These headphones may be a 5 star for value but I wanted to present a sincere and honest review of the ANC27's performance. Bose QC15's would be a 5 star. I nearly gave them 4 stars but I figured I can upgrade them later if I feel like it. I'm sure I'd want to downgrade the 4 star to a 3 star in the future as the excitement of a new toy further decays.

Worth the $$$? You decide.

Do you want the gold standard QC15 quality, quiet, and comfort (get it?)? Spend $300.

Want a cheap alternative that performs at about 50-75% the level of QC15s at 20% of the price? ANC27s will do that.

title: Great cover for the Kindle Fire!
text:
When I bought my Kindle Fire, I did a lot of research on cases and covers, and I finally decided on the Sena Magia, because it had many of the features that were important to me.

First of all, the Sena Magia has a great thin profile that doesn't add a lot of bulk or heft to the Kindle itself. Also, when open, the cover folds back flat and flush with the case. A lot of the cases I saw would open up in an awkward position, with the cover folded back in a seemingly unnatural way. Not so with the Magia.

The magnetic closure is quick and convenient, and I like the "quick snap" action of the closure that holds the cover in place. As a bonus, the magnetic closure also works in reverse, holding the cover open when folded to the backside. I didn't want to fiddle with button closures or "strap and loop" closures because in my mind they are not nearly as fast or simple.

There are also magnets usefully hidden elsewhere on the case. When rolling the front cover up into its triangle-shaped stand (like an iPad cover), a pair of magnets hold the triangle-base to the back. There's also a magnet on the back cover to prevent the closure from flopping around when the cover is in stand mode, or when you just don't feel like folding the cover completely back.

The Magia's genuine leather is well-constructed and high quality material. If you're going to hold something in your hands for a long period of time, you're going to want genuine leather, which absorbs your skin's natural oils a lot better than fake leather. After a couple of hours, fake leather--otherwise known as polyurethane (PU) leather, faux leather, premium simulated leather, etc.--will feel just like plastic. But just like any other leather product, the Magia may require some "breaking-in" to properly mold itself to the Kindle. Leaving the Magia closed and on its face overnight seemed to do the trick for me.

I was a little concerned about the Magic Tape adhesive and how it would actually work, but I was pleasantly surprised. The Magic Tape holds the Kindle in place pretty snuggly, and I stuck and un-stuck the Kindle to the Magia a few times. As promised, it did not lose its stickiness and did not leave any messy residue on my Kindle. I wouldn't recommend constantly sticking and removing the Kindle from the Magia, because dust and particles will undoubtedly collect on the Magic Tape and reduce the stickiness, but it's definitely good for a few re-positionings. And it allows the face of the Kindle to remain clear of any unsightly retaining straps or sleeves that other cases might have.

I would also note that the Sena Magia is really more of a cover than a case (hence the "cover" in the official name). I think the Magia would provide minimal protection if I dropped the Kindle on its corner onto a concrete floor from six feet up, but it does protect my Kindle from small bumps and scratches encountered in regular daily use.

Finally, the Sena logo is printed in foil and stuck to the front cover in the lower right-hand corner. It's a little bit garish, and I wonder if some of the logo's letters will come off after a while. I'd much rather have a more subtle embossed logo stamped into the cover, but it's not too bad as it is now.

With the current suggested retail price at 35% of the cost of a brand new Kindle Fire, I think it might be a bit expensive, but discounts to the MSRP found on Amazon.com or elsewhere make it much more reasonable.

I also considered the Spigen SGP Stehen case, which is similar but seems to provide a little bit more edge protection to the Kindle Fire, but because of its lack of genuine leather material and magnetic closures, I stuck with the Sena Magia.

All in all, I think the Sena Magia is a great product and recommend it highly to those looking for a quality cover/case for their Kindle Fire.

title: WARNING:TurnOffCheckSupplyLevels
text:
First, this unit needs to have Internet access to download printer drivers. Second, I could not print if the ink level was "low" on an HP Photosmart. I plan to use this print server when I travel so that I can print from an iPad or iPhone to whatever printer is available. I wanted to test the unit first. So I turned off the wireless connection on my HP Photosmart Premium C310 as a TEST to see if the unit worked. This disabled the built in support in the printer for AirPrint. I then connected the server to my printer over USB and to the Internet over ethernet. The unit recognized the printer and downloaded the C310 driver. I could not print from my iPad or Mac Pro. Finally, I logged on to the print server using a web browser. I checked the firmware and the logs. The logs kept saying the print jobs had been canceled. I went to Printers --> List --> Gear Icon --> Set Printer Options --> xPrintServer --> Check Supply Levels --> OFF --> Save Changes. Now I can print! Who would of thunk the printer generated low ink level warnings were the culprit. You should be able to log on to a factory set XPrintServer Home from a web browser at:

Address: xPrintServer.local
ID: admin
Password: PASS

title: Bookshelf speaker sound at a fraction of the size
text:
"They look bright, and they sound bright!" That's what's in the product description and it's definitely true. I'm using these as desktop speakers and they sound fantastic with a little bit of EQ.

"They look bright"...I was attracted to the form factor of these speakers: 7"x7"x7"...small enough to fit on a desk but with technical specs similar to those of larger bookshelf speakers.

The "they sound bright" part is magnified in the near field, but that's the nature of acoustics. I have the high end EQ'd down a little to make them sound more natural at a close range.

There's a few things that I think are important to note:
- The product sheet (at the time of this review) rates the frequency response down to 60 Hz +/- 3dB, 45 Hz +/- 6dB. I think that those are pretty accurate measurements, so if you're wanting the full bass spectrum, these should be paired with a sub.
- If you are not wall-mounting these, you're on your own for vibration isolation. No rubber feet included. I used some felt pads that are designed for furniture legs on the bottom of the speakers.
- THESE SPEAKERS ARE RATED AT 4 OHMS. That is something to keep in mind when pairing with an amp, as many amps state an 8 ohm per speaker minimum load. There's a lot of helpful information out there on this topic.

title: Be Productive or Playful--the W510 is Upto Both
text:
For a disclaimer I didn't buy this from Amazon--about 8-9 days ago when I ordered the Acer Iconia W510 was not in stock at Amazon. I got mine delivered from another site on Monday-about 5 days ago.
To sum up the experience so far: This device is what I have been waiting for a long time. This is my 4th tablet in last few years. Two are/were Androids. And one Window-based Acer W500. So I am not unfamiliar with tablets. I also know that there can't be one tablet which will fit all needs for all users. But this one is perfect for me, despite minor issues, to the point of giving this device a 5-star rating here.
Here are my reasons for the rating:
1) A very long battery life! I have yet to push this to the claimed 18 hours but I can already tell that a 'normal' daily use of email, Office, some You Tube, some web surfing etc should not be a problem--10 hours should be easy to achieve. This means a full workday without carrying power cords etc. Certainly can't say that about my Acer W500.
2) Light weight: The tablet portion is only 1.3 lbs. Adding the keyboard doesn't make it much heavier--this is essentially along the lightest of the ultra-books but significantly cheaper AND with a stellar battery life which no ultrabook can match! Also, not many ultra books are out there which have detachable touch-screens.
3) Full Windows experience. Yes, that is important to me and probably to the roughly billion PC users who may be considering an affordable tablet in the Windows environment. Forget about the negative reviews of an split OS--switching between Windows Metro and desktop is not a big deal especially considering that you can do so much in the desktop environment until Metro applications catch up. Microsoft has just given us two Operating System in one device without extra charges. I am most happy with that.
4) Some so-called critics have questioned the keyboard as being too small. I assure you that the keyboard is more than adequate. I am typing this Review using the W510. Yesterday I scored 40 WPM in an online typing test website--and I am not a great typist. Yes, you can accidentally hit a wrong key because of the small keyboard but how can you not have such occasional mistakes in a small keyboard like this one's? Need a bigger keyboard then get a bigger tablet!
5) Internet Explorer 10. For the first time in several years IE has become my main browser again. IE 10 is very good. And supports Flash even in the Metro for some websites, which means you will have the full You Tube experience. I also saw an Amazon Instant Prime video in Metro and that worked fine inside Flash after installing an update to Flash in the desktop mode. So forget if there are no 'apps' for these two sites yet!
6) While Netflix should work in the desktop mode the 'app' is truly good! Love it.
7) Multiple ways to use the tablet/keyboard: That is a big, big plus! The tablet is so light it is a perfect for late night Kindle reading. The keyboard gives you a notebook experience. The 'tent' mode helps to place on your tummy in bed and browse the web. The display mode should be good for meetings.
8) Performance. It is adequate enough for most casual needs. I don't think I am going to install Photoshop or Visual Studio on it but people say that full Office works fine. Forget about those low 'bench-mark' or Windows Experience Index low numbers. This is an adequate device.
9) Multi-media support. You can watch any content in this device! As I said above Netflix, Amazon streaming, and You Tube work fine. But one big advantage is that if you have home ripped movies they too will work. I have some dozens of videos in a network drive and this has no problem finding and playing 2+ gb movies from the drive. I couldn't say the same about the two Android tablets or even the Google TV devices I have--they need configurations and even then don't always work.
Now to a few Cons:
Occasionally the keyboard docks misbehaved--sometimes pressing the 'backspace' a couple of times, for example, erased 10-15 characters. Not a huge problem--I did score 40 wpm in the typing test. 2-3 times the tablet became completely unresponsive for no apparent reasons and had to be rebooted. Once I lost sound after the tablet woke up from Sleep and had to reboot. I am assuming those are Windows 8 related issues and some 'fix' will come in future.

*** First Update to my review on 16 December 2012***
The device continues to be a great 'value' for the money. The battery life has been tested to 16 hours according to one online review! My own experience is that I simply don't bother to take the power-cord to work with me along with the W510 because I am confident that I would not need to plugin the device.
**To those having the track-pad problem it may help to install the Acer Driver Package for W510 from Acer website. I don't have the problem. But I haven't seen the need to use the track pad much so far.**
**Also look up Chippy's just-posted review of Acer W510 on the Ultra Mobile PC website--in my opinion it is the most comprehensive one out there.**
I continue to have occasional freezes and sound getting lost. Some diagnostic done using WhoCrashed software points toward software (drivers) issues.
Oh, take this device to a public area and place it in the 'tent' mode--it will arouse some attention and even questions--people are VERY impressed by the multiple ways one can use this device.
NFC works with my Nokia Lumia 920.

*** Update 3 Feb. 2013***
Still love this tablet. The more I think about and use the 4 different ways of using it (tablet, tent-mode, notebook, and display modes) the more I think it would be very hard to live with other, more limited form factors. The battery life remains a big plus. I simply don't bother to look at the battery power status most of the time and never carry the power cord to work along. Anyway, here are some more thoughts: The keyboard getting stuck problem is fixed since I applied Acer's Driver Package 2.04 a few days ago. I did have one scare recently: The tablet stopped charging and I thought the power cord/adapter had gone bad. Called Acer Support who, surprisingly, sent out a replacement cord within 4 days delivered without any charges. But it turned out that the power plug was slightly out of place with its adapter part (these are two detachable parts) and simply removing and re-attaching fixed the problem. Anyway, kudos to Acer. Also, may be it was because of the Package 2.04 and/or other Windows 8 Updates, but the tablet has not crashed even once in days--a welcome development.
*** Update 12 Sept. 2014** Almost two years later still loving this baby. Can't find a (faster) alternate which has same form factor and battery life. I will keep looking.

title: No More Zeiss
text: I bought my first pair of Zeiss Victories in 2000, when they first came out.  A few months after I got them, on the first day of a trip to Peru, I found that the top of the binoculars had come loose on one side and was flapping like a trap door.  I used duct tape to hold the top down, got the binoculars repaired after the trip, but never trusted them again and switched to Swarovski ELs.  Last year, when I finally had enough of the slow focus on the Swarovskis, I decided to give Zeiss another chance, figuring that after ten years, the product had improved.  I was very happy with the new Victory FLs - fast focus, great optics, comfortable in the hand, good close focus.  And after seven months, the locking mechanism on one of the eyepieces broke.  I am very careful handling my binoculars; there was no reason for the eyepiece to break except that it was badly designed.  I sent the binoculars to Zeiss for repair.  After waiting for two and a half weeks with not a word from them, I called and was told it would be another week before they would ship them back to me.  I am now not only unimpressed with Zeiss products; I am equally unimpressed with their customer service.  If I ever buy optical equipment in the future, it won't be from Zeiss.

title: Lean, mean toting machine.
text:
I am pretty stoked on this bag. It is small, very lightweight and comfortable to wear. It fits my NEX-3N with two extra prime lenses or one telephoto with room to spare. It is very easy to swing around to your front while you're wearing it to get access to your gear. I even had it on over a winter coat this weekend with no issues. The water bottle holder is handy, and you could probably use it to hold a compact tripod instead, were you so inclined. There are one or two minor drawbacks but they're not deal breakers. One - The front pouch is pretty shallow, as you can see from the photo with the phone sticking out, and there are no dividers or pockets for your accessories. It is big enough for my charger, USB cord, a couple of cards and some other odds and ends, they just kinda float around in there. Two, you can only wear this over your right shoulder. Not a big deal, just a heads-up. The main pouch is big enough to hold a light jacket or something. There is a zippered mesh pocket inside the main compartment, running the entire back side of the front panel. It doesn't strike me as being really useful but it's there. I guess you could keep slim/non-bulky object divided from other stuff in the main compartment. There is the padded zippered pouch along the back for a tablet. I don't own one so I probably won't get much use out of that compartment. It's not quite big enough for my 14" laptop. It might hold a 10" netbook or a 12" super compact. Probably nothing bigger or thicker than that.

Bottom line, it's way more comfortable and convenient to wear than a camera bag with a shoulder strap, and screams "steal me" much less. It's less bulky and a lot lighter and easier to get into than a full backpack. If you're into traveling light with a small DSLR or a Four Thirds with room for some other stuff to get you through the day, this pack is for you.

Update 1/2015:

The inside mesh pouch has proved to be more handy than I would have thought. It nicely holds a flat velcro wallet with my lens filters and a collapsible flash diffuser. It's come in rather handy. I've also since purchased a 7" tablet which fits in the main compartment with more than enough room. I've used this bag as a carry on a few times now and it's been great. Camera gear, tablet, headphones, a book and/or magazine(s), some snacks and a water bottle. It's perfect. I still wish the outer pouch was a bit bigger but it's such a trivial concern now that I'm bumping my rating to five stars.

title: Perfect for a Small Bedroom
text: I just bought this VSB207 at Sam's Club for a great price.  There is one audio cable in the box: red and white RCA connectors at one end and a 3.5 connector at the other end. After I plugged in the connections I had some humming to begin with until I stopped it by resecuring all connections tightly AND moving the power cord around until the humming stopped.  I'm giving it 5 stars because: 1) it works perfectly in a small bedroom, 2) has a low profile which fits nicely next to my 26" LED TV without blocking the TV sensors, 3) it is simple to set up, 4) it has a connection to add a powered sub woofer, and 5) it is inexpensive without being "cheap."  I would not buy this sound bar expecting to be blown away by the sound.  This unit clarifies/amplifies speech and ambient noise in movies and TV shows.  It does not come with a manual. I don't believe one is needed since it's such a simple unit.  Instead, it does come with a quick start guide with several pages illustrating its few connections and features.  Of note, I did not see where the guide said "plug the the 3.5 connector into the TV headphone jack."  I did that intuitively and used the RCA connections on the back of the sound bar.  Once I set up the unit using the sound bar remote to turn on SRS WOW HD (very nice sound boost) and to establish the input location - #1 input for the sound bar RCA connections, I no longer needed the remote to control the sound volume.  I can use my TV remote to change channels AND control sound volume.  There is a #2 input on this unit which is a 3.5 jack, presumably to allow a "reverse" connection if your TV does not have a headphone jack but does have RCA connectors. Long story short - since flat panel TVs no longer come with decent speakers, something else has to boost sound quality.  That's what this sound bar does without breaking the bank.

title: Adjustment Finicky / picky on switched load(s) attached.
text:
Really want to like this power strip, it's the right size and has more always-on sockets than competitors' but sadly no cigar.

As others mentioned, the controller adjustment may not work under all circumstances. To me, I would adjust it to work in the morning, leave it on all day, and at night it would not turn off. Re-adjust again, works, turn it off, then the next morning, it doesn't work again. Am feeling like there is a thermal drift that's affecting the control circuitry. Thermal Drift = As electronics heat up, certain characteristics can change, which in a well-designed device, this would be self-regulating. My morning vs night settings were a full 1/4 turn of the knob so I don't think it needs only a more precise knob as someone posted. Am also a little disconcerted that at one point the strip did not trigger on until I plugged in the switched load, this tells me that what you plugged in as switched load(s) affect how the power strip performs, confirmed by the documentation that asks for at least a 25 watt incandescent and a 5 watt fluorescent.

My old Radio Shack smart power strip (no longer made) is relay-based, there is a click when it turns on and accepts any switched load. Old tech, but in a way more versatile.

But hey if everything looks OK to you, try it. Amazon will send UPS out to pick up the return if it doesn't work.

title: Yes to Graphics, Maybe to Sketchup, No to AutoCAD
text:
Yes to Graphics, Maybe to Sketchup, No to Autocad.
I decided that I needed to purchase a graphics tablet during the last week of December while I was working on my portfolio. The deadline for submission was the Jan 3 and I was creating diagrams and graphics for my submission. The realization occurred after I spent 5 hours trying to diagram a site plan with a mouse when the same graphic could have been accomplished under an hour using a graphics tablet. Thus, I began my search for a graphics tablet. The first brand I went to was Wacom. I recently saw some of these fancy LCD and I noticed that they just released a new line of tablets so I decided to take the plunge.

I initially decided to purchase the larger version (Wacom Bamboo Create) with the bigger equals better mentality; however, I was quick to realize that it was way too big. For a size comparison, it was approximately the same size as my 13 inch Macbook Pro, maybe even wider. I sent it back to Amazon and got the smaller version.
I've been using the tablet for a few days and the Wacom Capture is great. I am running a late-2009 13 inch Macbook Pro with 8 gigs of ram. The OS I am using is Windows 7 via Bootcamp. The size of the tablet is approximately the size of a sheet of 8.5x11 inch paper with a drawing area of something like a small Moleskin book. The finish and feel is kind of luxurious and it really took me by surprise. When I unboxed it, I was in awe of how nice it felt from a piece of hardware. Very impressive.

The first thing I did after unboxing it was go to the Wacom website and download the latest software and drivers for the Create. I didn't even bother opening up the included CDs since I never use the free software with any of the things I buy. I installed both of the available downloads from the site and then proceeded to restart the computer. Everything went smoothly and then I plugged in the tablet. It registered and off I went. I adjusted some of the settings in the Windows' Control Panel and including settings that another reviewer mentioned regarding the response. I restarted again so everything is registered and working fine.

The first 15 to 20 minutes of using it, I was completely thrown off. I was just shifting the pen over the tablet and it kept selecting things. If the pen is touching the tablet, it selects things. If it is hovering over the active area on the tablet, it moves the pointer. Tapping on the pen would signify a click and holding it down for a while will active the `right-click' menu. The initial setup of the tablet is aligned to the screen of the computer. Click the top corner of the active tablet area will cause the point on the screen to jump to the respective location on the screen. This was immensely annoying because I was not accustomed to it. I recommend switching the tablet to "Mouse" mode instead of "Pen" for the initial use to get acquainted to the new tablet. The option can be found at the "Bamboo Preferences" via "Pop Up Menu."

After getting a taste of the tablet, I opened up Photoshop and started making lines and marks on a blank piece of paper. It's pretty responsive and it worked really well. I then proceeded to test it on Illustrator. It was fantastic. I was able to create diagrams and draw things very accurately. Both CS4 Photoshop and Illustrator worked flawlessly with no noticeable lag. I then opened up a blank Word document and started drawing on it. There was a good chunk of lag probably because it was not meant to handle drawing data efficiently. For graphics, this tablet is effective and works efficiently.

Being a student and intern architect, I spend a ton of my time using AutoCAD, Sketchup and Revit when I am not creating or editing graphics. I started off by testing out AutoCAD with it, and then Revit. I find the tablet struggling with it. I didn't seem to find any additional lag while I was using the tablet in both of these performance intensive software; however, I did end up spending way too more time doing the simplest things on the tablet. The biggest issue/nightmare in CAD drafting or building a model is not having the 3rd mouse button with a scroll wheel. Zooming in and out of areas and objects takes forever. It's like drafting with a touchpad for those who have tried it - It's not fun at all. In the end, I spent more time zooming in and out of the drawings/model than I did creating content. I haven't figured out a good way to navigate in these two programs, but with practice I can see how this is tolerated if the tablet was to be used. For Sketchup, I think this tablet works significantly better than compared to AutoCAD and Revit. The reason for this is due how Sketchup operates. I've set one of my keys on the Wacom pen as the "Middle" button, allowing me to pan across the screen relatively easily. Despite this, however, the tablet still suffers the limitations of zooming in and out. All these programs work, but not that well compared to a 3-Button mouse with a scroll wheel. Also, use "Mouse" model for these software will make your life significantly easier.

Summary:
If you're working in the building design profession and produce a lot of graphics work, you should get this tablet. It will save a ton of time. If you only do technical drawings and don't do graphics often, stick with the 3 button scrolling mouse be completed faster.

Notes:
- As the other reviewers mentioned, the cord for the tablet is short. It's about 5 feet long I think. If this is a problem, you can always buy a longer cable or reuse an old one. It uses a micro USB cable and a longer cable is pretty cheap.
- I am right handed and 95% of my typing is done with my left hand. I feel very awkward and out of place when I the tablet is next to the right side of my mac. It creates a gap between my laptop keyboard, the cables from the tablet, and tablet that is fairly wide. Since I need access to my keyboard 90% of the time, I decided to make this gap between the tablet and my keyboard as small as possible. I decided that the most ergonomic and efficient position is to flip the orientation of the tablet. In other words, change the settings to "Left Handed". This way, the gap between keyboard and tablet is very minimal.
- There is no eraser on the opposite end of the pen and there is no need for it. I find it easier to just set a button as "Eraser" and clicking on the button when the need arises. It's much faster than flipping the pen around to erase.
- Some people use this as a touchpad. I'm on a laptop so I will never use the tablet as a touchpad. I keep the option of using it as a touchpad off at all times. This allows me to lay my hand on the tablet while I'm drawing.

title: Gets Local Channels Without Jitters, Not Distant Stations
text:
I live in an urban area with good television coverage but am using the antenna on a side of the building opposite the local television station transmitters. I have three walls separating me from the transmitters. I watch TV on a computer and have tried it with a mini-tuner, with old-fashioned large rabbit ears & UHF loop, and with the Terk HDTVa.

I ran a signal analysis report at TVFool.com and compared my reception to what I could get with all three antennas. At most, what the Terk HDTVa did, even with the amplifier on, was to eliminate 90% of jitters on stations which I already received. It improved reception of the "green" stations but didn't give me any of the yellow or red ones. It did not give me anywhere near the 45-mile range mentioned, but then again, my position is on the side of the building farthest from the transmitters. I did get two new stations which I was not able to get before, including a station which is 22 miles away. But reception for that station is poor, requires the antenna to be in a very specific position, and still has a great deal of jitters.

This antenna is appropriate for improving reception of local stations which you already receive. You can enjoy your local stations reliably, without worrying too much about jitters, and perhaps receive an extra station or two if it is relatively close by. That's about it.

Both VHF and UHF reception is good. The cable is built into the antenna and cannot be detached. It tucks in to the bottom of the antenna and, it is true, it is easy to tip the antenna over.

If you have stations in the VHF band that you want to receive (broadcast on "real" channels 2-13), this antenna will take up a great deal of space as you will have to extend the rabbit ears. But then again, you would have to do that with most other VHF antennas. I haven't been able to find an indoor, tabletop VHF antenna that does not use rabbit ears.

title: Decent noise cancelling hurt by terrible sound
text:
I have tried many different brands of active noise cancelling headphones but have not found one that meets all of my needs for a set of headphones. I find that most active noise cancelling headphones do one thing and only one thing great and it varies depending on which brand/model you try. The Creative headphones here fall somewhat outside of that statement in that they don;t do one thing great. They do a few things just OK.

Let me start with comfort, these headphones are very comforatble and can be worn for hours at a time. This makes them perfect for long flights or long train rides. Add in the long battery life and and ability to use them without the noise cancelling on and they rank above any of the various Bose headphones I've tried. There are alternatives that are just as comforatble such as those from Sennheiser or Audio Technica.

The Noise cancelleing feature falls in the middle of others I've tried. First, let me state this up front, Bose must have souled their souls to be able to produce active noise cancellation as well as they have. No one does it better. They are incredible compared to all others. My issue with Bose is that my ears tend to feel the pressuer from the technology used. Somewhat uncomfortable if you have bloced ears or fighting a cold. Creative does a decent job of changing the way ambient sounds come through the headphones. They don't really block the sounds, but rather make them less harsh. It is still easy to hear people around you unlike Bose where it is freakishly quiet. Compared to Senns or Audio Technica, and I would rate the Creatives as a step above. And I get no pressure impact on my ears like a I do with Bose.

Sound was terribly disappointing. With the noise cancelling off, the sound is very muddy and low. Running an Ipod just doesn't have enough juice to make these sound good. I tried EQ'ing them several ways but the sound did not improve. Once you turn the noise cancelling on you do get a boost in sound quality but it is far behind the Senns and even the Bose (and I hate the way Bose sounds). Again, the sound was very muddy with little distinction between highs and lows. I tried using a headphone amplifier (Fiio E7) with the Ipod lineout cord but it actually made the sound worse. This was a first for me as usially I get better results. I left the headphones burn in for over 20 hours hoping for some improvement but it never happened. Unless I have a bad set, these are just not as good as Sennheiser or Bose from an audio standpoint.

Since I've been lucky enough to try a lot of headphones over the last year, I've come to realize that if you are trying to combine good noise cancellation and quality sound, you will never be able to do it. Finding something that offers noise isolation (passive rather than active) is much more doable and their are a lot of great options out there. If you goal is to minimize surrouding noise in places like planes trains and automobiles and music is not a priority, then these Creatives are a good choice from a price and performance perspective.

title: Updated - Lots of features for a fair price
text:
I was looking for 3 things in my replacement clock radio.
1. A red display
2. FM sensitivity for weak stations
3. Dual alarms

The Timex T736S had everything I wanted and some fun extras.

First, why was I looking for a red display? Our body's circadian rhythms are regulated by light, blue light in particular. Exposure to blue or white light from a clock or other light source at night confuses the body into thinking it is daytime. This confusion causes hormonal changes related to sleep and behavior disorders and is implicated in development of breast cancer. It turns out that few clock radios on the market today have red displays. This display is red, large and readable. The projector is red too. One point for the Timex.

The radio function on this Timex works well. I bought this unit specifically to pick up an FM station with problematic reception. I did have to be creative with the wire FM antenna curling it just right, but the station came in loud and clear. Point two for the Timex.

Dual alarm functions have spoiled me. One setting for weekdays and one for weekends. This radio makes it easy to set and forget. It's also easy to turn the alarms on or off from the front of the unit, another plus. Until I used the clock radio to wake up the first time, I didn't realize that the radio starts soft building to your wake up volume setting. That is much less jarring in the morning. So the Timex met my three main points when shopping for a clock radio.

But there is much more. This clock radio sets the clock as soon as you plug it in. It was close, but I had to adjust it about 4 minutes initially. It has been on time since.

Battery backup is included to prevent losing your settings during power outages, and it will alarm even when the power is out. The radio audio is not hi-fi, but is a step above my last clock radio.

Radio tuning is analog not digital, so it is not precise. The digital readout may or may not show the actual frequency of the station. You have to tune by ear, not the dial reading. But the good news is that it picks up stations very well in both AM and FM.

A neat value added feature is sound effects. You can lull yourself to sleep or wake up with the sound of the surf or one of three other sounds. If you need some white noise to go to sleep, this is your answer.

The projector clock really does project 30 feet. I can easily read the time in the middle of the night without my glasses using the readout projected on the ceiling. I guess the projected numbers are at least 2' tall on a 12' ceiling. The projector is adjustable for most possible installations. The room does need to be completely dark to see the projected time.

Quirks or limitations: If you go to sleep with radio then you wake with radio. The same is true for the sound effects. You can't mix and match. As with most analog radio tuners, finesse is required with antenna position and dial movement to get some stations. The switch to turn off the projector sometimes takes two or three tries.

Considering all of the features, this clock radio is a great value. I am very pleased with mine so far.

Update August 22,2012

I have updated my review to 5 stars. The Timex clock radio has functioned beautifully and has performed as advertised. The projection feature, not critical to me when I bought it, is wonderful. It is so easy to see the time at night even without glasses. The battery backup works flawlessly in what seem to be more frequent power outages here. Research continues to pile up linking night time light pollution with melatonin suppression and increased risk of cancer. While any light is a problem, the red part of the light spectrum is the least offensive. So I feel even more comfortable with the red display on this unit.

Update October 21, 2013

I still give this clock radio 5 stars. There have been zero issues with operation or function.

title: THE long-distance champion
text: Is... is it ethical to fall in love with a router? Line of sight between where my router sits and where my computer sits is only about 80 feet, BUT this "line" goes through several walls, some brick, and up one floor. To defeat the problem of being on a different floor, I hooked my wireless card up to the outlet leading to an unused VHF/UHF yagi combo in my attic, but then the signal travels through about 60 feet of RG-6 coaxial cable. So, naturally, I had a lot of trouble finding a router that would work for me. I tried newer D-Link and Netgear models that boasted of high range Wireless N signals, and both ultimately failed to atmospheric interference and could never keep a connection for very long. Enter the WRT54GL, September 2011. It may be the only model in the world capable of delivering a clean signal throughout my house. Setting it up with DD-WRT was ridiculously easy, and less than an hour after unpacking the router, I was back on my feet. The signal is not very strong where my computer is, but despite that, it is a remarkably clean signal. I easily get 15-20 Mbps and the connection stays up 24/7. Even with the modified firmware, I don't have to overclock anything or even increase the broadcast power beyond its factory default. It has been powered on for almost half a year now, carrying on many lively conversations with my wireless card, and hasn't needed one reboot. If you're looking for Wireless G, this is the router to try first.

title: T3i vs. T2i --- Body only vs. Kit
text:
Since there are so many great reviews already that go in depth about the actual T3i, I am going to gear mine more towards what I struggled with the most when making my decision:

1) Should I get the T3i over the T2i?
2) Do I purchase the body only or the kit?

I had a hard time deciding if I wanted to spend extra money for the flip out screen, but I'm so glad I did. I am a videographer and this thing is amazing with video (even better with fast lenses of course). Being that I shoot video, the fold out screen has been very useful in seeing what I am shooting whether the camera is high or low, for example, I am able to have the camera mounted on a monopod and lift it up over the dance floor at a wedding... Without the adjustable screen, many of my shots would be useless. Much of the research I did, didn't make a big deal of this, but I definitely think it worth the difference in price, if not more. If you just shoot photos, it may not be as necessary, but I'm sure it will still help more than you expect.

If you're a professional photographer, you may want to skip the rest of this review. If you're new to DSLRs, DON'T GET THE KIT!!! I know its very tempting because as soon as your new toy comes in, you want to play with it. To do so you obviously need a lens. Well to say the least, I wish I listened to everyone and put the money into better lenses than these. If you haven't looked into lenses yet, be prepared for sticker shock, because many of them cost much more than the camera itself. I know it's a bit overwhelming at first, but your pictures and video will be much better AND your lenses will retain their value whereas your camera body will not. To be honest, if you are just getting into photography(and no video), I would say save some money on the body and buy a used canon xsi and put the rest into a lens or two. It's sad to say but they will outlive your camera body (as long as you care for them) and if for some reason you decide you want to stop shooting, they can easily be sold for close to what you bought them for.

The canon 50mm 1.8f is an amazing value for about $100-$120 (see the product link at the bottom) which I would strongly recommend over the kit lens. If you're planning on doing professional photography in the future, you may want to get the 1.4f, $300 - $400, if you have the money because it's a faster lens with better construction, and the focus ring is much nicer. It is important to note that the 50mm lens is a prime lens (meaning no zoom) so you would have to walk closer or further from the subject to manually zoom.

If you want a zoom lens, I would recommend a couple things... Research "Aperture" and understand what the "f" number is when purchasing a lens(a constant aperture throughout the range is preferable, yet more costly). Also I would recommend doing some research on Tamron and sigma brand lenses. Although canon lenses are definitely the best, the price tag definitely reflects it. I have decided to go with sigma lenses myself, but that's not really the point of this review so I won't go any further than to say if you have lens questions, feel free to use the comment section of this review and I can share everything that I've learned researching them. I am by no means an expert but I will do my best to assist.

Sorry for that rant, yet I see these reviews as a way of helping others learn from my mistakes and benefiting from my research. Back to the T3i, It is an amazing camera for the price and I would definitely recommend it (Body Only =). Hope this helps!!!
