text:
Pasted from my comments on Maximum PC's online review of this product - the review that inspired my purchase:

"I bought this drive because of this glowing review. Later, I began seeing references elsewhere that what I spent $600 on is TLC, not MLC as the review led me to believe. Samsung's website describes this as incorporating their "new 3 bit MLC NAND..." I logged into my Samsung account and wrote their customer support for clarification, but after three weeks passed without a reply, I called them on the phone and got confirmation that EVO SSD's are TLC. No wonder it has a three year warranty.

I love Maximum PC and have relied on their reviews over many years, but I wouldn't have wasted $600 on TLC had Josh Norem made that clear. Now I'm using an SSD in maximum reliability mode so that my TLC NAND doesn't burn out in a few years and don't enjoy blistering speed. What I did was essentially like buying a car advertised as having DOHC, which everyone thinks is double overhead camshaft, and find out after the fact that it's really diameter overhead camshaft. I'm disappointed with Maximum PC and Samsung. Don't trust everything you read in Maximum PC."

SLC (single level cell) SSD's are the longest lasting NAND and are super expensive - meant for enterprise solutions. MLC (multi level cell) NAND is 2 bits per cell, won't last as long as SLC, and have been marketed to the general public for years. TLC (triple level cell) is new and has the lowest expected life span.

title: Eh
text:
They get the job done. The packaging is great, the rings are great, but the filter holder is a little flimsy.

The filters themselves are plastic. Optically, they aren't amazing, but they get the job done. Quality doesn't degrade too much to the point that it's irreparable in PS. The ND filters, especially the darker ones, introduce a very strong magenta color cast to your picture. This is especially evident when stacking multiple ND filters. Some global correction may work to fix the color cast, but they really should be clear. This is great to get some starter work done, but otherwise take your money to SR, BW, Lee, etc and get some high quality filters from them.

I'm personally somewhat happy with this set. I won't return them, but I know that they'll all need more postwork. If you're not a PS or LR person who does not retouch much, avoid these. Otherwise, prepare to make some corrections to your images.

title: Just another love story: Trite, but true
text:
Getting the right lens for my camera, a difficult love match.

I have used SLR film cameras since 1968. I was an animal portrait specialist.

When 35mm film began to evaporate from the store shelves I finally switched to digital cameras but could not afford eight thousand dollars, or more, for a good d-SLR; so I made do with upper tier point and shoots .... learning the digital ropes while waiting for prices to come into reach for me.

16 months ago I finally made the plunge to digital SLR, with a Canon 7D [[ASIN:B002NEGTTW Canon EOS 7D 18 MP CMOS Digital SLR Camera with 3-Inch LCD (Body Only)]]. I had mixed first reactions. I loved how it felt and looked like a "Real Camera" but I was afraid I had waited too long to try a digital SLR, attempting to put it together and figure it out, near blew my mind. It was overwhelmingly complicated, compared to my old Canon F1.

And vastly more difficult to master than my [[ASIN:B002LITT42 Canon PowerShot S90 10MP Digital Camera with 3.8x Wide Angle Optical Image Stabilized Zoom and 3-Inch LCD]] or my Kodak [[ASIN:B00132MMVE Kodak Easyshare Z1012 10.1 MP Digital Camera with 12xOptical Image Stabilized Zoom]] my two primary point and shoot cameras.

I bought several "L" lenses for my 7D, [[ASIN:B0001G6U48 Canon EF 28-300mm f/3.5-5.6L IS USM Lens]] [[ASIN:B00004XOM3 Canon EF 100mm f/2.8 Macro USM Lens for Canon SLR Cameras]][[ASIN:B000AZ57M6 Canon EF 24-105mm f/4 L IS USM Lens for Canon EOS SLR Cameras]] hoping each time to recapture the clarity and flavor of my long ago lover, my 35mm Canon F1.

But none came close; and I placated my wounded soul by concentrating on Corel and Adobe and Canon's software tools that can tease second rate digital patterns into near 35mm quality images.

I contented myself that way for some while. But ...

... nagging at me were the occasional raves I saw in Amazon and dpreview and other digital photography forums.

Stories of people taking 35mm film, or slide quality pictures, consistently, day after day.

Some were using lesser cameras than mine, some used my 7D but with those inferior and untrustworthy EF-S lenses!!!

Full frame, medium frame and cropped: new concepts for my fossilized mind to sift and sort and try to grasp.

Was it possible? Was she, my sweet little 7D, was she begging for a mate more suited to her cropped cmos sensor and EF-S receptacle?

So I got a [[ASIN:B003A6H27K Sigma 17-50mm f/2.8 EX DC OS HSM FLD Large Aperture Standard Zoom Lens for Canon Digital DSLR Camera]]

and they melded as if Heaven itself had ordered it! I was ecstatic, little dSLR 7D was blissfully snapping pieces of virtual 35mm film and drooling all over herself. All that was lacking was a decent distance-gulping zoom lens. Then I noticed on the Sigma-Photo website that they were releasing a new revised 18-200mm F3.5 6.3II DC OS FLD. The older version lacked the OS and FLD and a goodly number of reviewers panned it. The new version was SO NEW that no one had yet reviewed it at all.

Still riding the endorphin high of unlikely fulfillment, I once again closed my eyes to danger and abandoned my wallet to woo [[ASIN:B005QJOIP8 Sigma 18-200mm F3.5-6.3 II DC OS HSM Canon Mount]]

Well, how do you spell satisfaction? I spell it fast and accurate and cute as a button!

This little zoom lens did not come wrapped in a leather zip pouch, just nested in a paper-mache shell, but she has a pretty little lipstick-red band, just like a Canon L lens; unlike them, she is light and nimble. 7D acts like its just the right sort to have and to hold; to love and to cherish till torque wrests them apart.

If you own a Canon 7D and are wondering why life seems lacking light, color and clarity; look for one of the lenses specific to the EF-S mount in the 7D body.

The two I have in my 7D's bed are exactly what the preacher sang to the choir for.

I still miss a lot of potentially great shots, just like the old days. But I got a couple of dozens 35mm Kodachrome quality photos today.

Color me satisfied.

PS: so what became of my expensive, high falutin, Canon EF "L" lenses?

I mated them to a [[ASIN:B001G5ZTLS Canon EOS 5D Mark II 21.1MP Full Frame CMOS Digital SLR Camera (Body Only)]]

To my delight, they too seemed a marriage preordained.

Hee hee hee ...

Who could ah knowed ;-)

title: Stunning!
text: This device absolutely WORKS!  It enhances the source material so vividly you can see pimples, hair follicles, wrinkles, clothing details, and extraordinary color way better.  I have it hooked up to an Epson 3010 3D HD projection theater system displaying on a ridiculously large 120" Elite screen about 10 feet from my viewing position, and it even improved the quality of the reference standard "Avatar" BluRay, adding details and color and contrast to faces and mechanical details with no artifacts.  Even the 3D version was enhanced and there appeared to be more depth.  It's almost TOO good, and you may have to adjust the "gain" or whatever down a bit from 100% to about 80-90% using the remote control, but it can do that.  I found going much past 100% gain for a BluRay is a bit too much, though and some hair fibers start to look too bright.  The manufacturer says that feature is mainly for gaming.  The greatest improvement though, is on broadcast TV, which, even coming from digital Verizon FiOS, is still significantly enhanced.  Again, it's completely adjustable and it's ALWAYS better on rather than off.  Its almost as if an extra focusing mechanism or a much more expensive lens was added to the Epson projector (which is already an excellent display system at around $1300).  If you don't believe it, turn it on and off and you will see the difference.  I know the design is not square like other AV components, but this thing is so cool and effective at what it does, I actually glued it on the wall to display the HDMI wires (and power cord) going in and out of it and the light-up circuitry inside the tinted see-through plastic case.  It adds a different kind of almost "retro" high-tech effect to the Home Theater.  (I almost wished it hummed!)  BTW, the "Darbee" logo is NOT persistent on the TV image, i.e., fiddle around with the menu's and you can get it to fade away after adjusting the on-screen controls.  The printed instructions are very basic so it's easier to just use the remote and adjust it to your liking.  Finally, what amazes me is that this device was DESIGNED and BUILT in the USA, and is of exceptional build quality.  This is true American genius, folks.  For this price, you are getting the computational equivalent of a much more expensive focus lens or image processing system that essentially turns a mid-range Home Theater projector into something far more.  It's not 4K, but if you can clearly see increased brightness, color, contrast, depth, pimples, wrinkles, hair follicles, mechanical details, and dandruff on a 120" inch screen ten feet away for $300, what's the difference??  Highly recommended!!

title: Great noise-cancelling headset
text:
By "noise cancelling" I mean that the boom mike clearly picks up your voice, but unlike a regular "stick" microphone it does not pick up all the background room noise - You might get a little if the noise is particularly loud, but things like air-conditioning or hard drives or CPU fan noise doesn't come through. (The fan noise from an HP server starting up might come through but that sounds like a jet taking off). My point is that I used to use a stick mike and one of the things I found annoying was that you could hear when the air from the heating vent started or stopped, and you could hear the hard drive.

Comfort-wise, the length of the band can be adjusted if your ears are farther apart, and the foam cushions make it possible to wear these a few hours without pinching my ears. (Your experience may differ, but I've had ear phones that were either too tight or pads that were too small or inadequate cushion - these were comfortable to wear for 5-6 hours).

The boom mike will swivel from +120 degrees to -120 degrees, so you can wear the mike on your left or right side by swiveling it around.

Volume-wise these headsets seemed a bit quieter than my speakers, so I had to crank the volume up on the PC. The cord has a built-in volume adjustment, but I left this cranked up all the way.

On the other end of this particular model it has two 3.5mm plugs - one green, and one pink. I chose this particular model because it had those separate connectors -the green "headset" connector goes into my computer's output, and I use the pink connector on a Sony PVR so that I can record my voice separately. But you could easily plug both cables into the front audio jacks found on most PCs.

I left off one star because the range of audio isn't as good as a professional mike and the construction doesn't seem that strong, but for the price this is an excellent product - I am currently using this as an entry level mike in the field of computer videos.

title: Amazing earpieces & sound, disappointing cable
text:
I'd give 5 stars for the earphones themselves hands down, but let's face it, the iPhone mic cable is the only reason to buy this particular version of the Shure SE215-CL, but be warned that the cable for iPhone is black, not clear like the earphones, and the mic/control assembly is friggin' huge. Also, ergonomically, the buttons are remarkably hard to identify by feel. While the center button is recessed as to set it apart, the volume up down buttons are flush, and there's enough non moving plastic surrounding them that you have to be fairly precise in hitting them.The iPhone mic cable lacks the the reenforced moldable section for wrapping around the ear. both cables are incredibly long. this is nice if you want to tuck it under a coat and still have enough slack to pull your iPhone out of your jeans pocket and change tracks, but in almost every other situation its way to much (and i'm 6'2").

Pros:
- amazing sound
- strong isolation
- great fit and finish
- plain clear audio cable included in addition to black iPhone mic cable
- over ear wire keeps things secure.
- comfortable, even with pressure on ear (e.g. helmet/ pillow)

cons:
- extreme sound isolation makes ones own speech sound a bit strange when on the phone.
- not as easy to slip on and off as regular (non-over-ear) buds.
- extra long cable length gets in the way more than it's useful.
- iPhone mic cable is black, not clear like the buds
- iPhone mic cable has clunky controls (about 2 inches long) that aren't any easier to use for their size, and look outdated.

Upshot:
the color mismatch is an annoyance, but not a deal breaker, and a non-issue if you're getting the black ones. if you mostly use your iPhone headphones for listening to music, definitely get the 215s. If on the other hand, you do a lot of talking on the phone while wearing your iPhone headphones, you may want to look for something that's not as sound isolating so your own voice doesn't sound like you're under water.

title: Rock Solid Communication
text:
I needed a serial cable to communicate to an Allen Bradley Micrologix PLC and my laptop does not have a RS-232 serial port. I read about some bad experiences people have had with other adapters. It seemed that the general consensus has been to stick with the FTDI chipset adapters.

After looking through some products and reviews, I came across this item. In my opinion, the LED lights to indicate activity was good feature to have for any troubleshooting.

My computer uses the 64-bit version of Windows 7. When I plugged the adapter in, the OS recognized it and downloaded the drivers via Windows update. It defaulted to COM7, so I changed it to COM1 and connected it to the PLC. I auto-configured a DF1 channel in RSLinx Classic and immediately discovered it using RSWho.

I've had it connected to the PLC all day and there have been no issues in the communication. I checked the diagnostics for the channel and there were no bad packets, timeouts, or retries.

This seems like a great product.

title: Not BAD for the price
text:

The EZ Vinyl Converter is extremely limited in what it does, but it appears to do that fairly well, BUT it does not really allow any user configuration AND it ONLY captures to 192kbps MP3, no option to capture at higher quality or to WAV or other format. And it requires you to have Apple iTunes installed or it apparently cannot export the captured music to the harddrive.

Gain setting was WAY too LOW as shipped, it needed to be adjusted, and the USB port and the Gain Control are awkwardly located and not easily accessible, especially if trying to adjust the gain while watching the meters when recording

However, the signal is free of anyking of hum (unlike the ART phono to USB adapter we tried and re-turned due to extremely excessive 60 cycle hum even though the ART unit was strictly powered by USB and everything was grounded and double checked)

The recommend a minimum of 3.5grams tracking, but don't really give you any way to accurately set that up. A simple pivoting balance type scale set up for 3.5grams would have been nice and could be mass produced probably for less than 50cents, so not providing one is something that should have been done

All in all, not a bad product, but not a GREAT product either. For the cost, I can recommend it IF you are aware of the caveats/limitations

title: SSD's are hard to review until you had them for a bunch of years...
text:
SSDs are usually splendid until they die.

Even slow ones are plenty fast for most users, so the only real issues are DOA, incompatibility and early death.

So, if you get one that is compatible with your system, not DOA and the Manufacturer looks like its going to still be around in a few years, it should be an automatic 5 star rating.

While Crucial (Micron) SSD's are usually among the top performing drives, where differences aren't really that large, there are some caveats to look out for, when buying SSD's: there are some laggards among SSDs you want to avoid, there are some risky chip designs that might break down / loose data sooner than others, and there are certain drives that perform particularly well in some metric or other, which you should choose if you have very specific applications that can benefit from that particular metric. I presume those people know what to pick and don't really need details or advice.

I use mine in a higher-end laptop, which I use for DAW recording/editing, CAD and the occasional game.

I have no complaints. Its fast and it hasn't lost anything yet.

If it does keel over before 500GB becomes so obsolete that I end up replacing it before 5 years are up, I'll update this review and drop some stars, depending on how long it went...

So, 5 stars for lack of reason to deduct any ;-)

title: only because I got a better deal on it
text:
I recently purchased the UN55H7150 after doing a ton of research. It came down to this and the LG55LB7100. Both TV's were rated very well by consumer reports so I went with the Samsung, only because I got a better deal on it. After getting it home and setting it up all was well.

The second day we were watching TV when all of the sudden these adds appeared on the bottom of the screen. You had to grab the remote and exit out of the adds to go back to watching the full screen TV. Well a few minutes, they popped up again. So after doing this several times I had had enough and brought this TV back. I am not going to spend a bunch of money on a quality TV only to be bombarded by adds while we are trying to watch TV. I spoke to the sales person who informed me Samsung has an agreement with an advertisement company to push these adds out over the internet. Apparently when you click "AGREE" in the internet portion of the TV set up, you are agreeing to this. So if you want to use the "Smart" features of your new TV, you have to agree to this. When I asked the salesperson how to fix the problem, I was told "Return the Samsung." Other than this extremely annoying, poor business practice, the TV had a good picture and I think would have been a good TV.

So I jut wanted to make sure people are aware that this is going on. I had no idea because not one sale person at several stores that I visited ever mentioned this issue. I think it is completely unacceptable for Samsung to do this to its consumers. I went back and purchased the LG and I am glad I did. The picture quality is just as good, if not better and there are no pop up adds to fight with. I can honestly say that because of this experience I will never buy another Samsung product unless they remedy this issue.

Thanks

title: I love this radio. It's one I wouldn't mind having two of.
text:
I have owned a Voyager V1 dynamo and solar radio for about two weeks now. It is an AM/FM/SW receiver with the ability to be powered four ways. The Voyager V1 comes with a rechargeable Ni-MH power pack installed in the radio, but not plugged in. Mine came charged and after I plugged the pack in the radio it worked. The Ni-MH pack can be charged from a computer USB output to the mini USB input on the radio, or, as I found, from my cell phone charger that has the Mini USB output. Bonus, my cell phone can be charged back in an emergency from the radio which has a standard USB output to charge a cell phone. There is also a crank dynamo that can recharge the run down rechargeable pack. The solar panel on top of the radio will slow charge or maintenance charge the radio. It also can use three AAA batteries. I should never be without power to use this "green" radio.

I love to DX in the evening hours on the AM band to see how far away I can receive a listenable program signal. For a radio of any size this small radio is a joy. Last night, I received the powerhouse 100KW station WSN 650, and 50KW WLAC 1510 from Nashville, TN, - WTVN 610, only 5KW, Columbus, OH, - two Philadelphia, PA stations KYW 1060 and WPHT 1210 both 50KW, - completely the opposite direction ,WHO 1040 50KW, Des Moines, IA., - and WKZO 590 only 5KW from Kalamazoo, MI., and this morning broadcasting only in daytime hours, WMIC 660 and just 1KW from Sandusky, MI. Where am I? - metro Detroit, right in the heart of lots of powerful local radio activity. This radio has good AM reception.

FM radio is equally strong and, while not stereo, provides power to both earphones if you use them. The FM/SW antenna is only 14 inches long fully extended, but it does the job. Most local FM stations don't need it folded out.

SW - shortwave listening is for me much like listening to AM. I look for distant English broadcasts between 10:00 pm and 12:00 am Eastern Daylight time, which is 2:00-4:00 UTC - Universal time. This week I have heard CRI Beijing, China, RTI radio Taiwan, The Voice of Vietnam, Radio Romania, and many religious broadcasters from all over. At daytime hours, it is possible to pickup broadcast from Australia. All of these stations broadcast world news and sports from an international viewpoint. It's two SW bands cover 5.8Mhz to 18.20Mhz, very useful.

The sound quality from the speaker is excellent, seeming bigger than it's size. Music from earphones that I bought separately provide solid quality sound.

This radio fits well in the hand and is about the size of a small paving brick and seems just as solid. It is marketed for everyday use and emergency use, it could fit in a backpack or cargo pants pocket, great for camping and it has a built in three LED lamp. I have used it everyday since receiving it from Electronnix through Amazon.

Can you tell, I love this radio! A great buy at a very good price. I think it's made by Kaito. This is one radio that I wouldn't mind having two of. I have the gray one, but it is the same as the green.

title: Gives a Rough Approximation of Reality but Support Is Worst I've Ever Seen
text:
After further use of the Tracker, I am lowering my review again for two reasons.

1) Concern over security/privacy issues;
2) Deteriorating Customer Support.

1) After some problems synching the Tracker, I decided to remove the Fitbit wireless dongle from my laptop. The Tracker continued to synch. My wife removed her Fitbit wireless dongle from her laptop. The Tracker synched again. One Fitbit support person told me that it would synch with any wireless Bluetooth device within a certain radius. With two basic mobile phones (not SMART), and one iPad with Bluetooth disabled, I began to suspect it was synching through a neighbor's Bluetooth device. Another Fitbit support person told me it could only synch when paired to another device. Since Fitbit said it had been synching all day and neither of us had the wireless dongles in our laptops, the conclusion seemed inescapable to me. It was never paired with any but the dongle in my laptop. The Bluetooth capability in both our laptops is disabled.

Since a Bluetooth device first sends out an unencrypted header including ID information (MAC) when looking for another one, I began to wonder about security. I found that other Fitbit community users had commented on their Tracker synching while walking down the street or in a building more than 60 feet away from another device. Since personal information, including your height, weight, and age are stored on Fitbit's Cloud, I am no longer comfortable with that possible privacy invasion, so I removed my online profile and simply keep track in a spreadsheet.

On Fitbit agent maintains that the Tracker cannot synch to a non-paired device. Another one says it will synch to any Bluetooth active. I tell them I have definitive proof it will. Things were left at an impasse.

2) Another contradictory response from Fitbit support came in response to my comment (echoing many more) that the Tracker overestimated steps--I logged an 85 percent over counting using the recommended test of counting off 100 steps. I did this multiple times. One agent said if the sleep setting was "sensitive" the Tracker would log any movement while walking as steps. Another agent said that was not so. The last advice from Support was to do a manual reset. That temporarily fixed the problem but the count is still slowly incrementing. I was offered a replacement, but then I would have to re-enable my online account, so I have rejected that. I thought I could just do resets occasionally when the count got badly off, but another Support agent said they do not recommend that because it could damage the device. This is contradicted by an FAQ, which recommends resetting to fix problems.

And Fitbit still sends me surveys on how they are doing!

I am lowering my review a star from sheer frustration with Fitbit Customer Support. After begging Support to please take the time to read and understand my problem or stop sending unrelated responses, I got this email: "Need more help? CLICK HERE or reply to this email to tell us how we can further assist."

Really, Fitbit Customer Support is more annoying than the occasional glitches with the device itself!

Pros: Smaller than most pedometers like Omron; Synchronizes automatically (sometimes).
Cons: Data is not individualized as it would be with a good Pedometer where you can set your stride length; No way to maintain results on your own PC or Mac unless you manually copy data to something like a spreadsheet. Your cumulative health record is only available online, which seems a privacy risk. Default settings assume you want to share all data with various online social media and others. You can change this.

The FitBit One counts steps whether walking or riding in a car (and stairs if driving up a hill if you live in hilly areas). Therefore the steps and stairs reported results do not necessarily relate to what you actually did as exercise. Since you cannot input your stride length, the translation from steps to miles has to be only a rough approximation. By the nature of the tracking system, the calories burned also have to be only rough approximations as well.

The alleged sleep functions are more meaningless for what they claim to do than the physical activity results. The sleep tracking is not tracking sleep; instead it tracks movement. So if you lie quietly for say ten minutes before getting to sleep, Fitbit will report that as sleep. If you wake up or get up briefly during the night and then lie quietly for awhile before dropping off, that last segment will be reported as sleep as well.

As for differentiating between "Awake" and "Restless," Fitbit does some unexplained calculation of how much movement qualifies as actually awake and how much as simply restless movement while asleep. There are two options in the sleep mode: Normal and Sensitive. The difference seems to be that in Sensitive mode, it only takes the slightest of movements to qualify as restless. Thus, a night on Sensitive mode might report 163 episodes of restless sleep, while on Normal mode 17 episodes of restless sleep. How does the user have any idea what this means as far as real sleep quality? The "Sleep Efficiency" report, which potentially could be the most useful, can vary widely depending on what counts as restless.

As for Customer Support, in my experience it ranks up there with the worst of computer software support. What you will get is round after round of email exchanges from people supposedly eager to help you but who do not bother to read (or fully understand) your issue. Support uses a lot of boilerplate as well, where after reading a few words of your request, someone apparently pushes a function key or other shortcut to print out that they think answers your question--which usually has no relationship to your problem. You might ask, for example, why after setting up your account and having the log in remember your email and password, you still have to log in each time when you view the "Dashboard." The first answer probably will be boilerplate instructions on how to log in.

If you are going to spend the money for this device, my advice is to just accept it for what it purports to be. Do not bother asking for help or explanation unless you simply cannot get it to run at all. Otherwise you will spend a lot of frustrating time trying to get an idea across to support.

title: Skeptic Turned Believer!
text: I was so disappointed when I noticed my diamond stud earrings had etched the glass of my new iPhone 5S that I'd had no more than one month that I was desperate for a remedy. I searched online endlessly and was very skeptical about all the remedies posted, including this one. My friend mentioned to me that she used this product on a fairly deep scratch on her iPhone glass and she was very happy with the results, so after a week of hmm'ing and haw'ing, I went ahead and purchased it, figuring since my scratches weren't nearly that deep (or so I thought), that I'd get great results. The first couple rounds with this product I really didn't see any progress. Turned out what I thought were just minor surface scuffs from my earrings were cuts or scratches deeper than I thought. I almost gave up, but the key really is patience. Between tasks at work I'd apply a few more drops and buff away. It took a good 45 minutes total, but the results have been fantastic. I can barely see the scratches at this point (I really have to hold my phone at just the right angle in just the right light to see them), I'm sure if I were to apply the product a few more times I wouldn't see them at all, but I'm very happy with how it's turned out at this point. The key to this product is patience, using the right cloth, putting a little elbow grease into it, and do not expect results within the first few applications, you WILL need to go at this for a while, but all in all I highly, HIGHLY recommend this product, and I was as skeptical (if not more) as they get. To add: This product will remove the oleophobic(??) coating, but that is to be expected if you're trying to "remove" (ie: fill in) scratches. Is it really noticeable? No. Trying to clean fingerprints once a bit of that coating was removed was a non-issue for me as my goal was just to get the scratches reduced as much as possible and put a screen protector on.

title: It does what it's supposed to...kind of (TL;DR)
text:
*If you don't want to read all this, scroll to the bottom for pros/cons list*

These bluetooth headphones are really great in terms of doing what they're supposed to do: making clear phone calls, comfortably fitting in the ear, easy to use. I know people who have complaints that the previous versions have inconvenient button placement, or that the earphones disconnect from the magnets too easily. I really haven't had too many problems with the Tone Ultra.

The connectivity is pretty good; better than I expected. I can walk up to about 10 feet away from the phone before it starts dropping in sound quality, which isn't too bad, since I usually keep my phone close by. If I keep a direct line of sight with my phone, such as if I put it on a bookshelf, I can go up to about 20 feet away before it starts breaking up sound. I might just have a great phone carrier too :) However there are times when the microphone stops working mid-conversation and I have to disconnect and reconnect the headset. Annoying but workable, but not worth what I paid for it.
Overall a great headset!

I'm not sure if I'm the only person who has this problem, but sometimes the phone doesn't respond to the buttons on the headset. For example, if I'm listening to music, sometimes there's a lag when I press the "next" button, or the "pause" button, and sometimes my phone doesn't respond at all, even though the music is still playing through the headset, which means it's still connected. I found it really easy to fix; I just have to press pause on my phone, and then using the headset buttons will work again. Maybe it's a phone problem? I have a Galaxy S4.

HOWEVER, I am really tiffed about this one thing: YOU CAN'T EVEN TELL IF THE NOISE CANCELLATION FEATURE IS ON OR NOT. Basically, the noise cancellation feature doesn't really make a difference in the call quality nor in music audio playback. I've tried testing it by making phone calls in Costco, and while driving, and it really doesn't make a difference. For benefit of the doubt, I can't say that it doesn't work at all, but IF it did, you really can't tell the difference. Don't pay extra if the ANC is the only reason why you'd pay extra for this headset!

TL;DR

Pros
- comfortable around the neck
- ergonomic, user-friendly design
- clear phone calls and music playback with adjustable volume
- great battery life; I recharge everyday after work and have never gone below medium battery level status.
- connectivity; about 10 feet away from device

Cons
- ANC DOESN'T MAKE NOTICEABLE DIFFERENCE IN SOUND QUALITY, you can't even tell if it's on or not
- microphone sometimes stops working during phone calls
- button lag

title: Legendary sound and clarity
text:
I'm a huge audio enthusiast so I'm always chasing the next thing in quality. I went from Audio technica m-50 to sennheiser hd 25-1 ii. Each purchase gave me a sense of enjoyment but also a sense of need to move a step up. For some reason every time I purchase headphones I'm blown away by the sound but also not completely satisfied. It wasn't until I purchased some really nice speakers that I understood that I like the fullness of speakers and the actual way our ears perceive sound.

Now these things still don't reproduce the low ends that are capable on speakers that you can feel all over your body but these are legendary in detail retrieval. After owning everything under the sun I can say that these keep me satisfied with having just the next level of detail retrieval over other headphones. The m50 and sennheiser hd25 just seem to be missing something to my ears even when they sound amazing. The soundstage and imaging just cannot compete with speakers.

With that said, I do feel that these do a better job that the other two that I own. I feel as if they are another level above my headphones. My speakers aren't so clear on detail retrieval. The imaging may not be as great as the speakers but the sense of detail retrieval makes me feel as if I can see the drummer in front of me tapping the hi hats into rhythm. Sure it may be a simulation as most music is digital now a days but the fact is these things shine where others dont. Speakers, or headphone you will be hard pressed to find something that can bring out this level of clarity in music.

Im a very analytical person and I love to hear every little detail in my music. Sometimes these headphones do a little too much and make the music enjoyable because I am so distracted with all the different elements going on. Some people may or may not like this. If you purchase these you will know what I mean. Every recording you have ever heard on the radio a million times you should revisit just for fun. Youll be surprise how intricate the production was done. These things WILL bring out all the little details.

Also don't use cheap source. You can really hear the level of quality in your audio files from mp3 to wav. If you love music and you want to hear it in a completely different way that you have heard before get these.

I also want to note that these are very nuetral and detailed headphones. I do music production and I love this quality in my headphones. It may not be for everyone however if you don't enjoy having your music presented in such a manner.

NETGEAR -- I see that you have been responding to negative posts here. If you can help me resolve my issue, I would be more than happy to give you more stars and keep my router. If not, I will unfortunately have to return it.

I've had other issues too. One click backup of the SD card is flaky at best. It sometimes works, sometimes not. And now I have a backed-up folder that I cannot delete because it keeps telling me permission denied. I was only backing it up to test the feature. Very frustrating.

For the record, the basic router functionality did work out of the box. No issues with wifi -- both 2.5 and 5GHz worked fine.

Edit to add: I also had a lot of trouble with using a 3TB hard drive. I picked a drive that was on their approved list -- only to find out that their router will format a 3TB hard drive to only 2 TB (it treats it as a 2TB drive, so you lose essentially 1/3 of the drive). Went to their forum page and figured out that I had to format it using a PC or something else. That was a huge pain since I only have an iMac and laptop -- no PC to stick the bare drive into. Finally had to have a friend format it for me with their PC, which included having to upgrade drivers to handle a 3TB drive. title: Blu Tooth Issues resolved - Updated
text:
Bought this device as second Android screen for my Samsung Galaxy S4 smart phone. Got with the black strap. So far it is working ok. There were some initial troubles in pairing this device with my phone via NFC. After several attempts, gave up on NFC pairing and went with blu tooth pairing. Blu tooth pairing is holding good till now. I have moved this watch away from the phone by significant distance and did not face any re-pairing type annoyances yet.

The watch face is wider than the length by few mm. I went with this watch instead of Samsung gear because I have small hands and I thought this will fit better than Samsung gear. The Gear is longer and narrower than Sony SW2. This watch sits perfect on my hand with no constant sliding in any direction. I have to use the last hole on the strap though.

I did not go with Samsung Gear because, as of now it will not work with my S4. I was also not keen on camera, extra cost and non-replaceable straps.

The resolution on SW2 is decent, but Samsung Gear resolution is much better. I did not compare them side by side, but I am fine with Sony SW2 resolution. I purchased one app so far to enable me to dial numbers from the phone (just for coolness factor).

The SW2 has one button on the side (like a regular watch) and it has 3 soft buttons (back, home and apps type button - still trying to figure this one out). You cannot press the soft buttons directly without pressing side button first. One the other side, there is a micro usb port to charge the watch.

Sony SW2 Smart Connect Liveware is the software that need to be installed on the phone first. It happens when the watch is paired with phone. One can also download the s/w from google play store directly as well. Once the Liveware s/w is installed the watch comes to life. The liveware s/w gives options to installs apps on the watch directly. There are few to select from.

The screen response is decent. It is not blazing fast, but generally responsive. I have installed Gmail, Messages, phone app, dial pad so far. They all work fine. The gmail app shows the gmail on your watch, messages shows texts on watch on so on. The dialpad allowed me to dial a number from the watch.

My biggest complaint about this watch is its standby brightness. It is very low and it is difficult to read the time without pushing the side button. The black watch face (shown in some pictures) is absolutely not readable. I have switched to white background, which made it marginally better. Pushing the side button, brightens up the screen and makes the time very readable. I think this is a big miss for Sony SW2. The watch should always tell time clearly without the need to push additional buttons. Hopefully this will get fixed via s/w update in near future.

My second issue is that there are no apps to allow multiple timezones to be displayed on the watch. As a watch linked to smartphone, I think this should have been made available out of the box. It should have allowed the travelers to switch timezones with a simple swipe action. This would have made it really useful for people traveling in multiple time zones regularly. I hope an app gets released by Sony or some third party to address this gap. There is a timezone app in the market, which allows to set a single timezone.

I will keep testing and post any updates.

Pros:

- fits on my small hand
- looks good
- wide and flexible strap
- Decent resolution
- Some useful apps

Cons:

- Standby display brightness is very low making it very difficult to tell time without pushing the side button
- Cannot pair via NFC (may be it is a galaxy s4 issue)
- Very few free apps. Most of the apps are at least 0.99
- No hotmail app
- Mail app listed by liveware is not compatible with the watch
- No world clock app yet
- Watch froze once so far, Had to reset (by pushing and holding power button for 15 second)

Update : 10/4/2013

The device is always paired over blu tooth. As some else pointed out, NFC is just for easier pairing. I think the issue was, when I tried pair it by NFC tapping, it did not download the liveware software. However when I paired it using blu tooth manually, it started downloading liveware software. I stand corrected on the NFC pairing. Thanks for pointing it out. However, theI am downgrading it 1 star because this device impacts the call quality on my blu tooth paired car phone system (honda odyssey). When this device is paired, the phone calls have become scratchy, barely audible over the other blu tooth paired headset.

Update : 10/11/2013

The blue tooth issue has been resolved after taking to an android expert. Basically on the phone I have to turn off sending Media Audio over BT, but only send Call Audio over BT. This resolved the call quality issues I had with Odyssey Handsfree Link BT.

title: Excellent lossless capture, but...
text:
The Blackmagic Intensity Extreme captures excellent high quality video, just like it is supposed to. In the raw format, with 1080p 60 frames / second, expect to burn nearly 10Gb of disk space for every minute of capture. (Ouch!) Thunderbolt makes that kind of data transfer rates possible without any trouble.
Using ProRez 4.2.2 -LT the disk burn rate drops to about 1GB / minute.

Looses 1 star because...
It would be nice if the provided software would support various video compression. I don't always need Raw or Pro Rez video. Especially if I am doing a long capture, like an hour or two. H.264 would be great. The disk demand is too high to be practical for long captures.

Looses another star because...
No timed capture. I can't believe they don't give the user the ability to start the capture and stop automatically after a preset time. Otherwise, if the user is not there to press the button, this thing just runs until the disk is full, which doesn't take long. I am finding it difficult to find any software package that does timed capture. I don't understand why this function is not available.

Looses yet another star because...
The instructions and Blackmagic's website say it works with "most' software... I can't make it work with Debut, Final Cut Pro X, iMovie or even VLC. My video source is typically 1080p at 59.94fps or 720p at the same frame rate. In these other software packages, i either can't select 59.94fps (60 is the only selection) or the unit isn't even listed as a video source. In Debut, I can select 1080p at 59.94fps, but all i get is blackness and after a minute, it tells me it can't connect to the source. So, without a scaler, i am stuck with using the somewhat limited Blackmagic Media Express.

I haven't decided if I am going to send it back or not... I am going to spend a few more hours trying to get it working and I am still looking for some 3rd party video capture software that will do what I need to do.

title: Nice quality and lightweight - but too many design flaws
text:
I traveled around SE Asia for 6 weeks using this bag. It has quality craftsmanship and is lightweight. I bought it because it had (i) those straps on the outside that can hold an item outside the bag, and (ii) because it had a little pouch area where you could place a small laptop/ipad without it banging around.

The good:

1- It is super lightweight and really can hold a lot. If you are using this as an overnight bag, you will be able to fit much.
2- Quality craftsmanship. Whatever this material is, it stands up to everything I threw at it.

The bad:
1- If you're using this as a day bag, it's inconvenient. It is missing small interior pockets. It has some, but they are so tight, that you really can't place much inside. The one outside is huge (as long as the bag), and this doesn't allow you to easily get at your sunglasses or ipod or whatever quickly.
2- One of the worst parts of the bag is that if you are carrying something using the straps on the outside (in my case I carried a pair of scuba fins), you can't access the outside pocket as the fins (or skateboard or whatever) blocks this pocket.
3- There is a small side pocket - but it too is super tight and small - and doesnt really suffice to hold anything of any size (and this includes a water bottle!). If they could just add a small, but usable, outside pocket, it would make this bag much better.
4- The shoulder straps are uncomfortable. Once I had 7-8kg in the bag, they sort of cut into your shoulders. You just have to grin and bear it - there is no way to adjust and no padding to assist.
5- The straps on the outside are adjustable - BUT - they do have a limit. And sadly, the limit was reached for my fins. Also, the straps do not stay tight - the come loose and require constant re-tightening or whatever you are holding in them falls out.

Its sad really, because this bag had such a great start. But it's like the person who created this bag didn't travel with it. When you add up all the small things, you realize it's not as usable as you'd like.

title: Don't try this camera on your BABY!
text:
1. I can't take a good photo of my kids, on AUTOMATIC, without 10 tries telling them repeatedly to "HOLD STILL."
2. SO, if I change to 1/250 or higher, I can get a good shot, but only in GREAT lighting conditions. which bring us to #3..
3. You can't take a good low light shot, on automatic, without using the flash (it won't auto-focus)
4. But, the flash on this camera does not automatically go off!! (you have to click the button to "raise" it)
5. And if you use the flash, you cannot have the shutter speed at 1/250!!!! You're back to square one with a blurry photo.

So, hear me (all professional photographers can silently tip-toe past):
An average layman like myself cannot get a decent photo of their children (or anything moving) just turning on the camera and using it.

See for yourself: I uploaded the first photo I took after taking this out of the box, charging battery and turning it on. See customer images on product page.

Hear me! In order to take a non-blurry shot of anything not static, you will have to turn on the camera and then CHANGE the shutter speed.
However, now this is important:
You cannot use the flash with a shutter speed of 1/250 !!!

So, if you purchase the Nikon 1, you will ONLY be taking non-blurry photos of your children in bright light (and this is after changing shutter speed). You will not be getting any decent shots of children otherwise.

As a mother, I need to be able to turn on the camera and get the shot when my baby is starting to stand, without changing the settings. I can do this on my DSLR. There is absolutely no way on the Nikon 1, that you will QUICKLY get the shot. The Nikon 1 sounds so appealing because of the claims about how fast it is! This is why I bought it, and really wanted to love it. But you will not get the shot FAST, if you have to change settings first. And if it's not the brightest light, you will need to turn on the flash, but that is an added step, and usually you will not have realized that you needed to turn it on until you are staring down at the dark photo you just took of that sweet but foregone smile. Not to mention you can't have a fast shutter speed with the flash turned on, so you had better hope that baby enjoys holding perfectly still after dusk!!
Got it?

Now I understand I am probably not the primary intended user for the Nikon 1 (someone who mostly just wants automatic settings). So the reason for the 2 star rating is this: There is no way Nikon should ever be charging this hefty pricetag on a camera that simply cannot take good low-light shots. Right? I am not saying this is a terrible camera. I am sure someone who knows what they are doing could use this bad boy proficiently (you know, in good light!) BUT. $750 for a non-DSLR camera that has irritating navigation, requires excellent lighting, and too big to put in a pocket? There are so many options out there. In my opinion, this is simply not a good choice for the money.

What I don't understand, is who the target audience is. If you are looking to adjust settings manually, for this price you should be considering a DSLR. If you were simply leery of the size of a DSLR, please realize this is not a small enough camera that you will be putting it into your pocket. You will still be "lugging" it around. And for the compromised quality (of a DSLR) and difficult navigation, I just don't think you would be satisfied. Of course, just my opinion.

So, for me, my solution is to keep my DSLR, for when I need the nice photos. And then purchase a quality point and shoot (I have a [[ASIN:B005MTME3U Canon S100]] on the way) for when I am going somewhere that I don't want to lug around the DSLR, or I want to take a video. This puppy is going BACK.

In summary...
Mark my words: If you are taking lots of photos of children on a Nikon 1 and you don't end up frustrated, I'll take you to lunch.

title: Probably the device Microsoft had in mind for Windows 8
text:
Indeed, the rumors are true: it's a solid, aluminum beast with a nice screen and as-advertised battery life. It's practically silent and very handy. It's a great machine, and I'm enjoying working on it.

Now, here are the things you should know about it:
The challenge to the convertible design is that everything of any importance has to go in the screen, so the screen is heavier than the keyboard dock. As a result it can't lean back that far in the dock, which means that viewing angles when placed on a lap are suboptimal.
On the other hand, it doesn't have to be plugged into the dock for the (radio) keyboard to work. Obviously, that means that you can place the screen and keyboard separately for superior ergonomics. Less obviously, that means that you can turn the screen on its side (undocked) and work on documents in 1080x1920 full-page mode (=Sweet). If only there were a stand available! Also less obviously, it feels as if the keyboard/mouse radio polling is less frequent under CPU load. The keypresses come through, but the trackpad (which has a very heavy and loud mouseclick) is squirrely. Translation: I have had better trackpads for gaming on netbooks. If you want to consider even light gaming, throw in an extra twenty bucks for a decent mouse...Then plug that into the only available USB port. Without one, XCOM is practically unplayable, FTL is a pain. The Stanley Parable doesn't require much in the line of mouse clicks, and works fine.
Also, add to the 13.3" screen an inch and a half of bevel on each side. This is a big beast.
The keyboard made the interesting choice of putting a row of keys (home pgup pgdn end) to the right of the enter key. Expect a day of swearing at it before you get accustomed to it.
Finally, the charger is an Apple-style "box with a plug" for a brick with a cable running to the PC. So it's nonstandard, and will be a pain dropping into a power strip.

Upgrading to Windows 8.1 was a bit of a pain. Microsoft could never figure out that pixel density varies greatly across devices, and this case is no different. Their solution to high-density screens like that of the T300LA is to artificially scale the image. As a result, when you upgrade to Windows 8.1, Windows effectively renders a 1280x760 screen, then multiplies half the pixels to give you a full-HD experience as crisp as a pickled egg. Asus' support page even has the advice to turn this off. So you're left with a high-density 1920x1080 desktop where everything looks a little tiny (but nice and clear).
Further, the Intel Dual Band Wireless-N 7260 card has some issues with dropping the connection (going to "Limited Connectivity" after a fiew minutes), and I think I encountered those. After all, this machine was dropping the connection with some frequency -- far more often than the other 16 or so tablets, phones and PCs running Linux, iOS, Android and Windows on the same network. I'm not sure what resolved it: on my end, I knocked it down to 802.11g; my host discovered a conflict with the neighbors, and changed channels, and the cable provider's neighborhood drop caught fire and was replaced. Now it works fine, and I'm back at 802.11n.

Truth be told, the biggest problem I have with this machine is Windows 8. This monstrosity of an OS system seems to have been cobbled together by tone-deaf middle managers intent on driving talented teams to insanity. So it's a very pretty OS designed for a machine that's half-desktop, half-touchscreen tablet. And, when using it on a half-desktop, half-touchscreen tablet, you'll want to ditch Metro and use classic shell. The screen can handle ten fingers at once; you'll want to give Metro just one of them.

title: HB4008 and HB7003 are both great options to consider
text:
Disclosure of Material Connection: I received these products for free so that I could provide product feedback to the company and post a product review. I was not required to write a positive review and I do not rate products higher than they should have been. I am disclosing this in accordance with the Federal Trade Commission's requirements.

Since multiple products are bundled under the same entry, this review covers two models ( HB4008 and HB7003 ). The pictures are for the HB4008.

// HB4008 Review //

NOTE: This is a review of Inateck Model HB4008 - Hub with: 3 port USB 3.0 + SD Card Reader + OTG Support

To test the hub, I used my DROK USB tester to measure the current required. Here is the current it required for various items:

- USB hub with nothing attached pulled 0.1A
- Adding a wired mouse made it increase to 0.11A
- Adding a wifi adapter and thumb drive pushed it up to 0.25A

So even with the hub, a mouse, a thumb drive and wifi adapter the total current was only 0.25A which is under the limits for both USB 2 and USB 3. I was even able to get an external USB hard drive to work, but when I connected two drives it started to cause problems - which is to be expected since that is too much for one port. If you plan to use an external USB hard drive, make sure you limit the other devices to lower current devices or just get a powered hub.

After that test, I put my microSD card into the included adapter and was able to read files from the memory card with no problem. I even used the OTG adapter on my Nexus 7 tablet and was able to use my mouse on my tablet. I didn't test any memory cards or thumb drives since my Nexus 7 is not rooted and out the box it doesn't really support mass storage devices.

To test performance, I used Ubuntu to do a benchmark on an external USB 3.0 case ( Inateck FE2005 ) directly connected and via the hub -- no noticeable impact to the benchmark.

Here are the main points I noticed about this product:

Easy of Use: As with any hub, it was pretty simple - connect it to your device (computer, smartphone or tablet) and then connected the USB devices you want to use into the hub.

Versatile: In addition to acting as the normal USB 3.0 hub, it comes with an OTG adapter for use on microUSB devices (such as a smartphone or tablet) and has a built-in SD reader (includes SanDisk microSD adapter) allowing you to use various memory cards.

Portable: The hub itself is about the size of a candy bar, and does not require a separate power adapter so it is easy to use as a "grab and go" device.

Bottom line: If you are looking for a portable USB 3.0 hub than can work with memory cards, and with various devices (such as smartphones and tablets) this is a great option.

// HB7003 Review - 7-port portable USB 3.0 hub with BC1.2 charging

I recently received an Inateck 7-port portable USB 3.0 Hub with BC1.2 charging ( Model HB7003 ) for a product review. The package came with the hub, the power adapter and a USB cable.

The hub itself is actually not that big, and feels very light. In addition to acting as just a hub, it supports BC1.2 charging. Basically normal USB 3.0 can support 0.9A output but the BC1.2 standard can support more ( I believe 1.5A ). With the BC1.2 charging capability, this essentially makes it a 7 port hub and 7 port USB charger.

To test the hub functionality, I wanted to see what impact (if any) it had on the performance of an external hard drive. I used Ubuntu ( booted from CD ) to do hard drive benchmarks. I first tested with the drive connected directly and then tested again with the hub between the computer and the drive. The hub had no real impact on the measured average read/write and seek times.

To test the power output it was a bit more tricky. Using my DROK load tester, I was getting around 0.8A on my Nexus 7 which is right around the USB 3 spec. However, when I removed the DROK tester and directly connected the Nexus 7 to the hub there was an increase of about 0.2A (measured using an app called Ampere. That would put it at around 1.1A, which is over the USB 3 spec and likely the BC1.2 standard kicking in.

Using my USB 1A/2A adjustable load, I was actually able to max the port out at 2A. I think the BC1.2 standard just tells the attached device that it can safely pull more than the 0.9A rating for USB 3.

Here are the main points I noticed about this product:

Compact: This hub is pretty small, smaller than another 7-port USB 3.0 hub I tested. For travel, you should be able to use this hub to also charge devices letting you reduce the amount of devices you need to drag along.

Performance: The hub did not demonstrate any real impact to the benchmark tests performed on an external USB hard drive.

Bottom line: If you are looking for a solid USB 3.0 hub, this ones seems to do the job without impacting performance as an added bonus can also act as a charger for your devices including BC1.2 compliant devices that can charger at a higher rate than normal USB devices.

title: Not bad optics for the price, but don't expect too much.
text:
SUPER FAST DELIVERY!
Celestron is better know for their telescopes, and indeed their top of the line scopes are pretty good. Their low end telescopes suffer from shaky mountings and cheap eyepieces.

Now, about this microscope: Decent optics for the price, and a serviceable small "starter kit" suitable for the curious with a tight budget. Keep in mind that with "toy" microscopes, the higher powers are about useless. Keep the magnification under 150x, and you will do okay.

Pros:
1. Price is good, under $30.
2. Fair to good optics.
3. 2 very adequate light sources.
4. Seems fairly durable. (Note! There are 4 little rubber feet that will need to be properly glued on with superglue. Don't lose them!)

Cons:
1. Internal reflections: As a telescope maker, Celestron should know better. All internal surfaces of an optical instrument should be flat black, with no internal reflections. (I may take this apart someday and try to fix it.)
2. Nothing is parafocal. When you zoom the eyepiece or rotate the turret to change power, it has to be re-focused. Not critical for a "toy" but compounded by "con #3" below, it's a little annoying.
3. Rotating the turret to change power also results in a slight misalignment - what was centered before is now off center. taken together with "#2 con" it becomes difficult to change magnification.
4. Although a minor complaint, there are no cover glasses provided for the 2 blank slides, and the well slide is plastic.

Given that this is intended to be a toy and it has a great price, I give this scope 4/5 stars based on the value for your dollar. Well recommended for a curious child. However, if intended for an adult or if you can spend 2x as much, go for the "My First Lab Duo-Scope Microscope" [[ASIN:B000NOU54O My First Lab Duo-Scope Microscope]] for about $55.

(Don't forget 2-aaa and 2-aa batteries for the light sources.)

title: Thrilled with my purchase
text:
I've had the 60 inch model of the VT60 for just about 2 weeks now and I couldn't be happier with it. Initially, I was looking at purchasing the ST60 series, but when I saw this TV go on sale for just a couple hundred more than the ST60, I decided to splurge and use the money I had planned on spending on speakers and go for the VT60 model. The colors are incredible and the black levels are outstanding. I've been watching a mix of Cable TV, streaming content, BluRay movies, and Blu-Ray 3-D, some Xbox 360 gaming and I'm continually impressed. The depth of the 3D is better than I had imagined, since I wasn't able to view this TV at any retail store. They all said they don't have them on display because of cost. Lame excuse, but with all the positive reviews I decided to make the purchase. Only negative I can think of on this is that I wish it had 4 HDMI ports instead of just the 3, but that's a minor issue.
The touch remote is kinda goofy and I don't use the voice controls at all. The WiFi and Apps are very snappy and quick to respond and I like that I'm able to have multiple custom home screens. The built-in speakers are also quite good, though at some point I'm planning on getting a surround sound system so that the sound quality can match the picture quality. In the meantime, I'm content with the sound.
Some folks have complained about fan noise, but I can hardly hear the fans, even with the volume muted. Unless, of course, you put your head behind the TV... but who watches TV from there?
I've tweaked the picture settings based on a CNET review, but so far it looks very similar to the THX Cinema settings.
As far as the 3-D glasses are concerned, the included pair have been used in watching two movies in addition to a more expensive and rechargeable Panasonic branded pair. I also purchased a $20 Samsung pair. Comparing each of them, they all seem to display the picture in the same quality, so it's just a matter of comfort. I have prescription glasses, so the Samsung 3-D glasses fit over my glasses better than the others. Those without glasses seem to like the fit of the rechargeable Panasonic 3-D glasses better.

title: Finally stay in ear – awesome ear buds!
text:
I have tried several BT ear buds in the past including expensive Bose ones but have returned them as they always tend to fall off from the ear. So when I received these I was skeptical as well. When I first tried them out I was in a hurry to clean/blow off all the fall leaves in my yard so was in a real hurry before it got dark but wanted to listen to some music while I was at it.

So I thought how hard it could be putting on some ear phones on! Wrong! I read the included folded one piece ‘quick guide’ which was useless, and so was the other included ‘detailed’ manual. I wanted to try the over-the-ears secure-fit sports configuration. I just could not do it – the whole thing was a big mess, so thought I’d have to return it and I was going to give it a two-star review as this thing just did not want to work. In any case I used my existing headphones and did the leaves!

Few days later after calming down I went to the online manual:

http://helpguide.sony.net/mdr/as800bt/v1/en2/print.html

read it carefully and I was finally able to set it up. Initially I had done everything wrong. Sony also has another online link:

http://helpguide.sony.net/mdr/as800bt/v1/h_uc/index.html

but don’t use this, use the first one which gives a lot more details. Basically you need to reverse the Right unit with the Left Arc and vice-versa. Also the Arc has to go in exactly as the manual says. It is actually pretty easy to do if you pay attention and read. So before you think of returning it to the store, give it another try as these headphones, once you get them working are just awesome.
I have tried all kinds of things with my head to see if I could get them to pop-out of my ears but I could not. So these are the perfect Sports earphones. They are also Splash Proof. They are extremely comfortable as well. Kudos to the Sony engineers on the design. They are also very sleek looking and high-tech in the sense that the Arc Supporters that fit inside of your ear lobe and the Adjustment band etc are unique features and only be found on this head set. The earbuds are designed such that they point down and go inside the ear canal while the Arc supporters cling on to your outer ear. Because they fit so tight and comfortably they tend to be somewhat ‘noise-cancelling’ although that is not a feature of these ear buds.

The set comes with 4 different ear bud sizes and 3 different Arc supporters. The SS (smallest) ear bud and the S (Smallest) Arc Supporter worked for me. These different sizes should fit anybody I would say. Also it comes with a small carrying case – how perfect!

I paired this with my Sony Xperia Z1 phone using the NFC function and that was a breeze. Also pairing with an IPAD and IPOD was a breeze as well and worked right away. My Xperia Z1 came with its own wired ear phones and I thought those were great but try these on and the sound quality is many times better. However the volume level on the wired ear-phones were higher than this BT set (I do listen to very loud music though so for an average person these would be more than adequate).

Controlling functions (such as volume, next/previous track) is done thru one single button on the Right side ear phone (i.e. one click to answer an incoming call, two presses to increase the volume etc). It works well, however I had an issue with using this on my Sony Xperia Z1 phone. The next/previous track does not work with the Xperia Z1 as it requires AVRCP for Bluetooth. And unbelievably The Xperia Z1 does not have that support – although this might be an issue from Android. The same functionality works fine with my IPAD or IPOD (Although the sound quality is better thru the Xperia Z1 compared to the IPOD/IPAD).
Answering a call works extremely well. The call quality is really good and the other party said they could not notice any difference compared to using the phone directly.

The batteries seem to last forever (although user manual said 4.5 hours) and are quick to charge. The Bluetooth reception with the device that plays it has a limited distance of 30 feet according to the user manual but it seems to work even up to about 45 feet or more. Once disconnected, when you walk towards the device it will connect automatically.

In conclusion I have to say that I have finally found the perfect ear buds that do not fall off. It has excellent sound quality and functionality. WARNING: If you get a pair be sure to get a second pair as your significant other is bound to swipe them off of you!

UPDATE September 2014

Ok I figured out how to mirror my iPhone on to the head unit screen.

1- In the setting, the connection must be set as iPhone via bluetooth. Connect your phone to the head unit with the cable. (all cables must be connected as described above.)
2- In the main menu, go to iPod.
3- Open whatever app you want on your iPhone. Netflix, Youtube, Navigation, ...
4- On the iPod control tab (where you usually forward or reverse the tracks) look for "Apps", press on the text.
5- You will see your iPhone screen on the head unit. You can't control the iPhone from Pioneer though.
6- You can change the mirrored screen size from the options available on the screen. Look for "Normal". You can make it full screen, etc.

title: Same review I left on eBay and I'd still buy this phone.
text: I was apprehensive to jump from a BB 9900 series running OS7 (not iOS 7, BB OS7) to a Z10 running BB10 because for me the 9900 had a good OS and I loved the physical keyboard.  It also had phenomenal build quality.  I didn't have any interest in changing platforms either.  I've used but not owned an iP4, 4S and 5 and came away unimpressed to say the least.  I also currently own a Sony Xperia SL running Android 4.2 (I think that's the version loaded, it's either that or 4.1, either way, it's been demoted to a toy for the kids for the most part).  It's a nice phone with a decent OS but messaging is lackluster.  Plus I'm not a fan of the stock keyboard.  After several months of indecision and instead of using my upgrade discount, I decided to find an unlocked Z10 on eBay.  As soon as I received the unit, I charged it up and was ready to play.  I had to wait to receive a new SIM card so I used it on Wi-Fi for several days which worked perfectly.  For any reviews where the user is put off by the gesture based UI or couldn't grasp it, I simply don't understand.  I had the phone in my hand for less than a minute and all but mastered it.  Swipe up, down, left, right, flick words into emails, BBM; the whole thing for me was very intuitive.  I pick up the Xperia some days trying to swipe everything on it, then I realize I have to deal with lowly back and home buttons.  BBRY gets a lot of flack for their app selection but once again, I don't care a lot about apps.  I've browsed through Google Play countless times just seeing what apps are available and truthfully, for me, it's annoying.  There is simply too much junk to filter through.  Along the line of not caring much for apps, I always read, well there isn't a native Instagram for BB10.  I loaded Instragram on my Xperia the first day I got the phone, which has been at least 9 months now.  I have used that app a total of three times because I have no use for it.  I also don't play games on my phones.  I have enough stuff to do without playing Candy Crush or Angry Birds all day.  My main uses for a phone - calls, messaging and internet.  The Z10 and BB10 pretty much leaves the other major OSes in the dust with those.  While I apparently don't represent the norm anymore, for me, a BB still handles my needs for a mobile device.  And once again, as has been my experience with the BBs I've owned, the build quality is quite good.  I especially like the textured back panel.  If I do have one complaint, the camera and camera options could use a bit of improvement.  Hopefully those are addressed with 10.2.  Sorry for the lengthy review.

title: Not quite ready for my home
text:
This was my first DVR, I should mention. I bought this product with a hope that I wouldn't be chained to my TV whenever programming came on that I wanted to watch at inopportune times. It absolutely works to record your favorite shows for viewing at a later date. Unfortunately, I had some problems with the machine that marred my experience and ultimately had me sending it back for a refund. I'll list the pros and cons below, but I also wanted to point out something incredibly archaic about when I tried to cancel my subscription with the company:

When I went to the website, I was surprised to find that you cannot cancel through the Internet ("for your security", they cite). They force you to call them up, only to be confronted with someone who is essentially a sales rep to act as a potential roadblock. I told her my problems with the device, and then was hit with a speech about why TiVo is so great and why I should contact tech support instead of cancelling. I politely waited for her to finish and then told her that I had already returned the unit to Amazon. I was then met with a moment of silence and then a quick 'okay, please hold'. Two minutes later, my account was cancelled.

The call went smoother than I anticipated, but it was still awkward having to do something that can and should easily be done online. If you can activate/renew online, you should just as easily be able to cancel online.

Pros:
▪ Fairly easy to navigate interface
▪ Decent size hard drive and recording time
▪ Controller looks and feels good and has a good layout
▪ Quite a few connectors in the back of the box
▪ eSATA external hard drive upgrade option

Cons:
▪ Live TV muddied my SD picture quality to the point where some text was unreadable
▪ Lacks built-in wifi in favor of expensive adapters
▪ Various settings can be difficult to locate and are scattered between menus
▪ Noticeable compression in video playback
▪ Fast forwarding and rewinding at speeds greater than 1 have annoying playback results
▪ No option to link my Amazon digital video account to it
▪ $15 monthly charge; $500 for the life of the box itself
▪ Displays ads despite the monthly fee
▪ Inability to cancel your account online; forced telephone call
