title: Very Nice RCA 10.1 Tablet/Case/Keyboard
text:
I saw this RCA tablet/keyboard combo over a week and a half ago at my local Walmart. I took a couple of days to check out the specs and reviews and then bought it a week ago. I wanted to see if I made a mistake buying a ASUS TF103C over a month ago for almost twice the price of this RCA. I didn't, but this tablet/keyboard is a very nice device. I am impressed with the tablet, but not with the keyboard/case.

TABLET: A very nice, bright, screen. Not hi-res but very pleasing to use if you can view it straight on. Off-angle viewing is poor. In landscape mode, tilting the screen up or down significantly lightens or darkens the screen with only 20-30 degrees of movement. Not IPS like the ASUS. It has Bluetooth and HDMI out, but not GPS. Memory is about standard for this price point - 1 GB RAM and 16 GB Internal memory. Speed is fairly fast (Antutu Benchmark= 18,612 and Quadrant Standard= 5,315. But regardless of speed tests, this tablet feels snappy and web page loads are fast. In this week of operation, I have had no freezes, no slowdowns, and no glitches.

Other reviews have said that they could not run several Apps and Games. I downloaded 20 Apps and Games from my more than 300 Apps that I have on my other tablets. All ran without a hitch and looking at the compatibility of this device and all my other Apps says the vast majority of Apps will run fine. Most of the Apps that would not download were specific to ASUS or Samsung or required GPS or phone hardware.

DOCUMENTATION: RCA really did this right! It has a excellent 19 page printed User Manual and a Quick Connect Guide with excellent illustrations. And there is a screen icon and the first tab in the browser that will bring up a RCA help web page.

CASE AND KEYBOARD: Here is where it falls down. I have large hands and find the keyboard cramped and the keystroke soft. In addition, if you have it on your lap, the keyboard flexes. I would not suggest using this for more than light typing. The case is nice except that if you want to put it on your lap, you cannot angle the tablet easily because the kickstand falls between your legs. It almost requires the use of a lap desk (and the lap desk supports the keyboard better - reduces the flex). The connection to the tablet using Bluetooth worked fine for me and there is a good troubleshooting guide, but many people have problems consistently making a Bluetooth connection (and now you have two devices to keep charged). The ASUS has a physical connection which I prefer.

BATTERY: The specs say 6 hours of battery life. That is very conservative. I kept waiting for the battery to run down to 15% and it seemed to take a long time. So I ran "Battery+" from the App store. The following were the battery run times (tablet Bluetooth on but not connected to the keyboard and screen brightness about 70%):
Music playback = 24 hrs, 38 min.
Video Playback = 12 hrs, 30 min.
Internet Browsing = 12 hrs, 30 min.
Talk time(VoIP) = 9 hrs, 59 min.
Reading = 13 hrs, 45 min.

CONCLUSION: For the price, this is a very nice tablet/case/keyboard combination. If you are not going to do extensive typing and you can live with the poor off-angle viewing, this combo may be very good for you. If these things will bother you, get a better hi-res tablet with a IPS screen and a separate bigger and better Bluetooth keyboard for $30-$50 more.

UPDATE******************************************************************************************************************************

I don't think that this is the same tablet that is now offered that I reviewed. The tablet/keyboard/case that I reviewed was a RCA Pro 10 Edition. Model RCT6103W46. The specs now shown here are different than what I reviewed

title: Not too bad for the price.
text:
I bought this radio to replace a Kenwood CD player that had a USB input on the front. I used the USB port much more than the CD, so when I found out they sold media receivers such as this one I was happy. It is lighter and smaller than a regular CD player. That made installation in my GMC pickup better because of the shallow opening.

This radio does what it's supposed to do. However there are several things about it that are annoying. I agree with several other reviews that complain about the clock, or lack of view of the clock. When you hold the clock button it displays for about 10 seconds and then goes away. Very annoying because I am in my truck a lot and I constantly look over to see the time. I guess I will have to buy a small stick on clock, but how will I see it at night ?

Another annoying feature is the display. It is constantly flashing and scrolling information. Some of which is not unnecessary. This should be an option, to decide what information you want displayed. I will try to upload a video of this. I will also put up a picture of the radio installed in my GMC pickup. I use a mini USB thumb drive that only sticks out less than half an inch. I will eventually change to a SD card. The USB drive is 8GB and I have over 1000 songs in about 55 folders and it's not even half full. No more stacks of scratched CDs laying around in my truck ! This would be great for a semi too, I have tons of comedy cd's on mp3 and that could keep me entertained for hours. Not to mention downloadable podcasts that could be put on USB/SD.

Pros:
-Light and small
-Easy to install
-USB and SD slots
-Display is bright
-Volume knob is large and easy to turn, not small like some radios

Cons
-Clock and display annoying
-Navigation could be easier, changing folders for example requires long pressing buttons
-No remote (for less than $40 I guess that's ok)
-Sound quality is not as good as factory stereo, but acceptable
-The included wiring harness has a confusing extra plug. Had to clip it off to use my Scosche connector for my truck. Not a big
deal if you are a little technically inclined.

Conclusion:
For less than $40, it's ok. I wanted something cheap to put in my older truck that would play mp3's. I might upgrade it to a better name brand someday, or if I buy a newer vehicle, but for now it does the job. I was very happy to find out that they were making media players for vehicles.
If you are looking for something to play USB/SD cards and don't want to spend $80 plus, I would recommend the Boss media receiver.

title: Returned It After One Day
text:
I got the second gen Nexus 7 tablet at Staples and was excited to use it since it would be my first Android tablet. When I booted up the device, I was prompted to connect to a WiFi network. Several seconds after I connected, the tablet shut off without warning and rebooted. This happened two more times while I was trying to log into my Google account. While this was happening, the battery notification indicated that there was 30% battery life left. I grabbed the charger and let it charge to 100% before doing anything else. After it fully charged, I used it for the rest of the night without incident. I did notice however that the battery notification lingered at 100% battery life for a while. During the next day when the battery dropped to 40%, the tablet started to shut off and reboot again. It happened randomly and without warning. I googled the problem and saw several forums stating a battery problem with the last generation Nexus 7. Solutions to fix this would involve popping off the back of the tablet, re-seating the battery, and calibrating the battery. I assumed the battery issue affecting the last gen Nexus 7 was affecting my particular second gen Nexus 7 tablet. I didn't want to deal with this problem so I returned it to Staples after one day.

I'm hoping that I got a faulty one and this isn't really an issue affecting everyone. I really enjoyed the high resolution screen, the great build quality, and the responsiveness of the tablet. I'll wait a few months and maybe buy it again when it's cheaper.

title: Worst product you could possibly buy for streaming media
text:
I'm shocked this product currently has 4 stars on Amazon. Netgear must be pumping in false reviews. I've spent the last month on a hunt for the best media solution in my family room. I'm looking for easy usability, great audio and video quality, and the ability to play my own video files, hbo go, netflix, hulu, and other stuff would be a great bonus.

The Netgear Push2TV was my 4th stop in this horrible media journey. It looked very promising before ever using it. Ease of use would be great from the laptop while on my couch, I could easily bring up netflix, hulu and hbo go or bring up my own video files VERY easily. This was actually all true. Unfortunately, none of this mattered because the streaming quality was awful.

Setup was a piece of cake, and the ability to mirror your computer to your TV with ease or use as an extended desktop was awesome. Unfortunately, things went very bad once I started streaming video. I first went to HBO Go and tested it out with an episode of Newsroom. It couldn't handle smooth video. It was incredibly choppy, even stopping at certain points. The audio cut in and out as well. I even went as far as placing the computer right next to the adapter for the strongest signal possible, and it still had the same issues. I then went to Netflix and experienced the exact same issue when watching Breaking Bad in HD. Choppy with bad audio. I turned off HD and it got a little better, but the motion was still smearing A LOT. Plus, I'm not looking to watch things in horrible definition. The product is advertised to be 1080p. And it is, but it's a 1080p chopfest. I also tested it out on youtube, vevo, and hulu. All similar horrible results.

I've now attempted using AppleTV and returned it due to lack of options. Then I ran XBMC on an old laptop and ease of use is an issue. I tried Plex with a mac mini hooked up to the TV which was great, but again, very difficult to manage from the couch and control everything. I then went to a Samsung Bluray player w/apps and plex but it was insanely slow, and now this Netgear piece of garbage. Without a doubt, the Netgear Push2TV with Intel WiDi has the potential to be the easiest to use among them all, but fails miserably at streaming 1080p video.

Do not buy this device if you plan to use it as a way to watch internet streaming services on your TV. It's awful.

title: Very good camera.
text:
I purchased this for photos of North Montana, Glacier Park, and Yellowstone. I am pleased overall with the camera. I took 1300 photos when all was said and done.

Positives:
* Clarity and detail of photos were beyond my expectations.
* Landscape Mode is MOST EXCELLENT. Better than any other camera I have owned.
* The Zoom (to include the digital) is just as great as described.
* The stability feature is fantastic. Of the 1300 photos, only perhaps a dozen carried a blur from my shaky hands. The rest were stabilized, even at max zoom.
* Panorama worked well in assist mode. Pleased.
* Low light mode? AWESOME. I took a couple of photos of the moon with Jupiter alongside that were simply amazing. The same with landscapes at dusk with very little light left. Low light mode was amazing.

Negatives:

* Auto-shoot mode was weak and I could not count on it to provide a quality photo. More of these were blurred than should have been..especially accounting for the 'wait' for focus.
* Temperature effected the camera (I am not an expert or a pro photographer, so I don't know exactly what to expect...maybe this is normal): Outside temperatures of 36f down to 32f effected the focus/zoom horribly. The camera would not focus auto or manual. Only after zooming in and out perhaps two dozen times did the camera 'warm up' and begin to act normally. This was a problem on an all day trek where, although clear skies, the temperature stayed within the above-mentioned ranges. (When the temperature was 40f or above...no issues whatsoever.)

I would have loved to give 5-stars, but my experience with Auto-Mode and the very bad time with the lower temperature situation pulled me down to a 4.

That said, I WOULD RECOMMEND this all day long to the outdoor casual or amateur photographer (indoors as well). I believe 100% that it was worth the cost.

title: Excellent Quality for Home Use
text:
For home use where banana plugs probably won't be removed and inserted 50 times, these plugs should do the job. I don't know if they would last for commercial, heavy use applications. Amazon could've provided a nice you tube installation video. Instead, you might need to look at equivalent banana plug videos.
Here is what I did to install the wires into the plugs.
I unscrewed the inside piece apart from the plug. Then I stripped about a half inch of wire and twisted the braids. Then inserted the wire into the back of the plug then curled the bare wire and fed it out the side hole. Next, I screwed in the back piece into the front piece but not too tight. Then I gently tugged on the wire to limit the excess sticking out of the side hole. Then I used (2) channel lock pliers to grip both pieces of the plug and tighten them very tight. If necessary trim the excess bare wire with quality sharp wire cutters and bend over the wire in order to avoid any chance of a short. I bought the shrink tubing some recommended in another post for covering the bare wire but I haven't used them yet. My Denon AVR-2313 receiver has a significant distance between speaker posts plus I trimmed the bare wire pretty close so I'm not too concerned about a short. P.S. I used 16 guage wire but you could probably go a little thicker (14 guage) for a really good fit.

title: This is a great TV
text:
The Sony W900A looks spectacular, both aesthetically and in terms of picture quality. It has an extremely small bezel with a smooth matte finish, which looks extremely classy and minimizes the amount of space it takes up. There is a small silver box underneath the TV which displays the Sony logo and a soft light that glows and pulses as you move through the settings.

The picture is awesome. I'm pretty picky with this stuff (my other TV is a Panny plasma from last year) and I can see no flaws in the image. Blacks are deep, colors pop, and I see no banding, clouding, or uniformity issues. Everything I've seen looks great, but sports are a special standout. The menu settings are clear and easy to navigate so calibration is a breeze. Setting up the internet was also no problem at all.

The TV ships with a number of apps, and I've only tried out Netflix and Youtube. It works fine, though - very fast and smooth. I'm not sure what CPU they are using in there, but it seems like a capable one. The Netflix streaming also works well, resolving to high definition faster than what I have seen on the PlayStation 3 app.

I do have one nitpick - I couldn't get ARC to work. ARC is a feature of the new HDMI standard that allows the TV to pass audio back to the receiver through the HDMI Out - this simplifies connections, especially for modern "smart TVs" like the one in question. I could not get audio to work no matter what I did. I am not sure if it is because of the TV or the receiver, which is a few years old and on the lower end (Onkyo SR508). Instead, I was able to get sound through Netflix and Youtube instead by hooking up an optical cable to the receiver. I think we are getting 5.1 through that, so it is okay in the end, but ARC would have been a nice, convenient feature.

This set is a huge hit in this house. This is well worth looking into if you want a higher-end TV and are willing to spend the premium. Overall, I can definitely see where the extra money you have to spend on a TV like this versus the lower end models go.

text:
The Window Experience Index went from 3.7 to 4.6 after I installed this video card for Windows 7 (x64).
I have pretty ancient configuration of my PC Desktop.
Intel Duo CPU E4500 - 2.2GHz
4 GB RAM
ECS 945GCT-M (V1.0) LGA 775 Intel Micro ATX - Motherboard ,which has 2 PCI-e slots and this video card worked perfect with Blue one (x4 bandwidth). But did not work with red one though.
After driver instalation from CD-ROM, I've upgraded through Catalyst Manager to latest version (2013) of driver, then ran Catalyst Control Center, clicked at "My VGA Display", selected "Properties (VGA Display)" and unchecked in "Monitors data" the "Use Extended Display Identification Data", left "Maximum resolution" as it was by default (1920x1080) and set the "Maximum refresh rate" to 100GHz. After that I had no problems to set desirable resolution for my pretty old AOC monitor without overlapping or flattening Desktop picture. 1280x800 worked just fine.
I have now for $30 clear contrast picture from corner to corner.
ATI video cards never failed on me, unless it getting old.
Before this Video Card I tried GIGABYTE GeForce NVIDIA 210 Silent 1GB DDR3. This was a nightmare. I tried 6 different versions of drivers directly from NVIDIA Web site. None of them worked. And I did not want that kind of card with standard low resolution VGA driver. So I sent it back.
But MSI Radeon HD5450 worked just fine. If you have an old computer 5-6 year old and you need a video card upgrade for any Graphic Animation purpose (like a Toonboom) or just need to replace your old video card, this one would be the right choice.

text:
First, I should start by saying that this product does work, but it took some tinkering with. Partly, this is my fault because I have 64-bit Windows 7 and didn't notice that it wasn't listed on the supported OS, something I should have seen. I always read reviews first and saw that other users with Windows 7 got it to work, so I thought I'd try.

Outside of that, the reason I'm giving this a low rating is because there is no support whatsoever. Anything that goes wrong, expect the responsibility of fixing it to be on you. That means, if you do not know how to mess with settings and find/install drivers, and you happen to have Windows 7 or later, don't waste your money. My package came with the item and just the item; there was no install disc, no manual, no receipt, no instructions or trouble-shooting info, and since it's a generic item, good luck tracking down the original manufacturer. Furthermore, while I understand the nature of generic merchandise, it seems ridiculous to me that a product wouldn't support Windows 7. If you're going to be a reputable product, you need to maintain support for the newest OS. Windows 8 is out now, so Windows 7 isn't even "new."

So, with all of that out of the way, if you're looking to get this working with Windows 7 64-bit, you'll want to download a bluetooth driver from another company. For me, I used Toshiba's Bluetooth Stack driver and that seemed to do the trick, but there could certainly be plenty more out there that will work.

Good luck.

title: BUYER BEWARE: There is no System Restore on this model!
text:
I bought the Dell Inspiron Duo with the intention of using it as a replacement for my two-year-old netbook, with added touch-screen capabilities that I hoped would let me browse the Internet more effectively, take notes in my classes, and draw. I had it less than a week before I had to give up in disgust and return it. Now, for people who want to use this for other things, this might still be just fine, but I ran into several issues that make me unwilling to ever endorse this device to anyone.

The first and foremost concern, and this was the deal-breaker that made me pack it up and ship it back, is that System Restore effectively doesn't exist on the machine. You can't roll your system settings back to prior restoration points if you run into trouble, and that's just unacceptable for any Windows computer on the market. Had I known that up front, I NEVER would have bought the machine, because that is a serious, potentially fatal, design defect. The reason for the defect is simple: the drive uses FAT32 formatting, and Windows 7 apparently doesn't support System Restore for FAT32. Why Dell put such a drive in the machine, knowing about this incompatibility, is beyond my comprehension. Also, don't expect a restoration CD or partition, because there isn't one. You have to make your own and then hope for the best. This was another nasty surprise for me because I've never bought a computer that didn't come with one or the other, and nothing in the product information indicated this kind of fundamental lack. Most computer manufacturers will sell you boot discs if needed, but I wasn't able to find any on Dell's site; in fact, I could barely find any support for, or mention of, the Inspiron Duo at all. I think they've been quietly sweeping this one back under the rug.

Another thing that turned me off of this machine once I had it was the Windows Experience Index. The base score is 2.9. The Processor's score is 3.1, the RAM scores 4.5, Graphics get 2.9, Gaming Graphics get 3.0, and the Primary Hard Disk gets the best score of all, 5.9, in spite of its glaring issues. I've never encountered such a poor-scoring unit, but this also explains why none of the big-box stores have these models on their floors; they would never, ever sell if people could actually try them before buying. This also explains why I had so many troubles with the unit in the few days I tried to work with it.

The display IS lovely, but a side-effect of the dense resolution is that touch gets very imprecise. If you don't hit exactly the right spot on the screen, you'll very easily end up doing something unexpected and unwanted (and my hands are SMALL, and the best stylus of several I tried had even worse troubles than my fingers). I re-calibrated the screen several times with no appreciable effect. Many of the OS's bells and whistles also directly interfered with touch input, and my attempts to write and draw frequently got broken up while the system ignored my input in favor of using its memory to make a ripple effect or hide task buttons. Its ability to interpret my writing was slowly improving, but I had to write in really large letters, bigger than the input utility was designed to handle, just to get them legible. (It was while I was searching for a way to fix this problem that I discovered the System Restore issue.) The screen is just too high-resolution to actually use it for writing or drawing, which meant that two of the three reasons I had wanted a touch screen in the first place had gone out the window and the third would do so as well if I reduced the resolution. There are potential fixes for some of these problems, but most of them aren't actually contained in Windows 7 Home Premium. You have to upgrade to Professional or higher in order to get them, so expect to shell out at least another $75, minimum, on top of what you've already paid, if you need to customize the touch screen (and you will if you want to do more than just navigate and tap). I probably would have done that, except, well... no system restore, like I said.

Weight is a problem, at least for me, because it's really not something you can comfortably hold in your hands for long periods of time in spite of what they say. Dell clearly expects everybody to get the dock to go with it, and that dock does restore some other surprising lapses in functionality. Without it, all you get are two USB ports and an audio-out port (that microphone they mention is the webcam microphone, by the way, not an actual port!) so add the cost of the dock to your budget plan if you're really set on buying this. Even with the dock, you won't have a video-out port, so plan on shelling out some more money to get a USB-to-VGA or USB-to-HDMI converter if you want to run a PowerPoint presentation, or play to your TV. Space that COULD have been used to give us more ports is instead taken up by a nonfunctional SIM card slot, which isn't actually supported by the motherboard or CPU. Pretty as it is - and it IS a pretty little machine - it's entirely impractical. Someone came up with a nice physical design but then started cutting corners all over the place to try to make it competitive, and turned it into a mess in the process. After spending an hour doodling and practice-writing with the device, my hands really, really hurt. There's no way I could use it in a two-hour lecture class, which HAD been one of my plans.

And then there's lag. Everything is super-slow. The worst lag comes from the screen itself, when you rotate from landscape to portrait and back. Expect the screen to go completely dark for a few seconds, then flicker, then reappear looking horrible and warped before finally realigning itself in its new position. Expect it to radically reorder your desktop icons while it does this. And expect this to happen a lot, if you accidentally tilt the screen even a little. If you're like me you might end up shutting the rotation off and asking yourself, yet again, why this is a tablet if you can't actually use it as one.

Maybe things will improve with Windows 8, but even so, this won't be the machine for it. It has too much wrong with it on a fundamental level unless your only plans for it involve consuming entertainment media (which, I will admit, looks and sounds lovely on the Duo). It just can't handle higher-powered productivity applications, and there are plenty of lighter, faster, and less expensive alternatives on the market if you just want to watch YouTube or NetFlix.

But don't EVER buy a Windows machine that doesn't have a functional System Restore on it. That's just outright dangerous, and it's made me really wary of ever buying another computer from Amazon again.

title: Photographing Minis (Ugh!- Well, actually, not anymore.)
text:
Love this camera! I cannot tell you how awesome this camera is. I am not a tech geek, just a miniature artist. Taking photos of minis is really hard. I work in one inch scale, which is traditionally considered dollhouse size (not Barbie dollhouse size; smaller). It has been really hard to get good close up shots of tiny details, like the pips in an apple that is no larger than a pea. This camera has completely fixed that for me. It takes amazing close up shots, capturing every detail and nuance in my pieces. It has a number of great auto settings, including one specifically for shooting food (which happens to come in handy for me). It is very easy to use.

I'm having fun with the extra things that came in the bundle, too. I LOVE the spider tripod; again perfect for the weird camera angles I need to shoot miniature sized items. It's not a big tripod, less than eight inches tall, but it's very versatile. I did some math: the camera, the memory card and the tripod alone would have cost more than this bundle. Obviously, I bought the bundle. I don't know if I'll use everything that came with it, but so far, I've used more than half the things. I had no problem using the camera case, except when I tried to put the camera away before removing the quick release connector from the tripod (that was my mistake). But that quick release function on the tripod is something I already can't live without. The case holds the camera just fine, with plenty of room in the two front pockets for the USB cord and an extra battery/memory card. The battery charged in a few hours(plugged into a power strip) the first time I used the camera. The quality of the photos overall is fantastic. If you're looking to upgrade to a camera that will give you better quality images, regardless of the size of the things you're shooting, this is it.

title: Makes your photos look like a pro
text:
You can find a list of features in many places. Here are the day-to-day things I've noticed.

Pros:
- Auto+ mode is *smart*. It will do the right thing most of the time.
- The SCN mode has right number of "modes": portrait, sunset, etc and they all work great.
- The viewfinder can be adjusted so you won't need to find your reading glasses.
- Videos are pretty. Auto focus makes it really nice, but noise from autofocus can be an issue especially with 3rd party lens.
- Focus is FAST. I was always missing shots with my last camera. Not any more.
- Auto ISO does this crazy cool thing where it takes snaps multiple photos in a fraction of a second, then combines them into a single, low-light, low grain picture.

Cons:
- Heavy (but rugged). Consider getting a high quality "sling camera strap" (search amazon)
- Custom Sony flash connector. You'll need a $10 adapter to use your existing flash.
- Batteries don't last long, get extras.
- HDR, while cool is slow. Auto+ will sometimes decide it's the right thing to do, but then you're stuck waiting for the processor to combine images.
- No time lapse. I miss this fun feature, but if you buy a $30 Remote Timer Control and combine images on your computer then you can do it. Just not easy/fun.
- Shutter click is louder than expected.

Recommendations:
1. Get the camera with the Sony lens "kit" (bundled together).
It's worth $700, but the bundle only charges you $600. I've used multiple lens with with A77 and the "stock" one is excellent. Fast focus and solid performer. You can always sell it on eBay for a profit if you don't want it.

2. If you want a camera to take everywhere, then this is NOT the one.
If it's too heavy and big, then go check out the (currently back-ordered) Sony NEX-7. It's basically the same camera but in a smaller form factor.

3. Get a SDHC UHS-I Memory Card. The A77 will take advantage of its 80mb/s write speeds for video and continuous shooting mode. Search Amazon for DDSDELITE633-16GB. Here's a video showing the speed difference over a class-10 card:
[...]

The kindle keyboard was nice too, but the back felt thin, and you could feel components inside the unit popping as you would reposition your hand. Otherwise no other complaints.

But this kindle knocked it out of the park. The construction is much improved. The materials are nice. The screen is very easy to read, and the back-lighting is pleasant. Overall feel is high quality. Touch recognition is improved. And the new features are appreciated and inspired.

The only con I give this unit is for audiobook listeners. This device no longer has built-in speakers or an audio jack. But if you are like me and don't use audiobooks, you won't miss them.

I was very excited to see this unit, and I recommend this kindle for any kindle user, both over other e-reader brands, and other kindle products.

title: Give this modem lots of air beneath it to keep it cool and it will work great!
text:
Our last modem died so we ended up buying this one to replace our old modem and router. After I set up (~30min) the modem and router it worked great! And then a couple hours later the connection died and I was thinking "OH CRAP!" When I picked up the modem I noticed the bottom of the was REALLY hot and suspected this was why it lost connection.

We found a wire frame to put the modem up on so it could have ~6" of air beneath it to keep it cool. Since then it hasn't had ANY problems at all. No lost connections and works super fast!

So just remember to give this modem lots of air beneath it to keep it cool and it will work great for you.

title: Great performance, but runs super hot and loud!
text:
I was really excited to receive this after my 7950 crapped out. As soon as I received it, I put it through its paces.

The good:
+Very fast, factory overclocked at 1100mhz, runs most games fast enough that you can't notice lag or studder
+3 fans, large heatsink
+Separate VRM heatsink and VRM back plate
+2 position Bios switch
+Anti flex metal brace

The bad
-Runs HOT, Crysis 3 runs around 70C with case lid off. Can be 73-74 with case lid on. the VRM backplate was scorching to touch.
-Runs LOUD, gaming at around 60 degrees ambient the fans run at 70-76% and they are screaming jets. By far the loudest thing in my case. Without headphones, it's unbearable
-Voltage locked (core and mem), core voltage is at 1.200v and can't be changed unless you flash or mod bios with VBE7
-No VRM sensors
-HUGE, the card butts against my HDD bracket and I have to install and remove it at an angle. I have a Coolermaster Scout 2, a pretty large case.
-My ASIC quality in GPU-Z was 60.1% (might be my bad luck, your mileage will vary).

I did my tests on a warm evening, around high 70s ambient temps. Running Furmark 1080p 15min bench with my case lid open.

Temps maxed out at 75C, at which point the 1100mhz boost cut off (within 2 minutes of testing) and the card throttled to 1000mhz base clock. Temps then settled at 71C for the rest of the benchmark. Fans ran at 76% and were extremely loud. The score was around 3119.

I tried to set the power limit to +20% just to see if the boost can be maintained. During the next test with same parameters, the boost cut off too, but maintained for a little longer like 3 minutes before throttling down to 1000mhz. Also temps maxed out at 80/81C! After the boost cut out, temps dropped to 75C for the rest of the test. The fans jumped to 100% (crazy loud) and after the throttling, down to 90% (still hugely loud).

I repeated these tests a few times and got the same results.

Considering the heat, fan noise, and voltage, I doubt it's overclockable by much. 80C and 100% fan speed on stock 1100mhz clocks is really the maximum heat and fan speed that can be safe. Granted Furmark really puts your card through the ringer, this is a worst case scenario. Also I want to add that my case lid was off during the tests. I'm actually too afraid to conduct the test with case lid on. Imagine playing a game with this thing, with case lid on and on a hotter day like high 80s-90C. This card would probably clear way higher than 80C. I touched my finger on the VRM backplate to see if it was warm, and it was BURNING. I would say, it is not safe overclocking this card at all. Maybe if you swap out the cooler for a waterblock, used some exotic liquid metal paste, and flash the bios to undervolt it you can go ahead with a 100+ overclock with safe temps. If you are buying this card, consider that it is factory overclocked and there's really not much else you can do to modify it. Maybe you will get lucky and a get ASIC %. However, mine doesn't seem to be that great :(

title: Excellent keyboard, good battery life, horrible bluetooth range.
text:
This is essentially the same "island style" keyboard included in the current generation of Thinkpads, including the latest generation trackpoint. The typing experience is probably 90 or 95% as good as the laptop, dinged only by how small and light the keyboard is, so it likes to move around. The battery will last for 2-3 days of moderate use before needing a quick recharge. The major letdown is the radio range. I sit about 3 feet from my laptop in its dock, and if I move the keyboard even a few inches further away, the mouse begins to lag or even stop working. If I go a full 4 feet away, even the keyboard stops working. I know bluetooth is a short range protocol, but the range rating on the BT radio inside the laptop is 10 meters, so you'd think the keyboard could manage at least 2 meters (~6.5 feet).

I've ordered the wired USB version of the keyboard as a replacement for this extremely disappointing implementation.

title: Super zoom super cool.
text: I bought this camera to pacify my wife. I have the big brother D600 with expensive lenses, and she felt left out, so I got her this. I am an avid photographer, she is along for the ride. Basically she wanted a camera with a view finder and manual operation as well as auto controls, and the P510 met the requirements. Having owned other Nikon compacts I knew the P510 would take great photographs, but I felt it was no match for my outfit. We went out to a wildlife preserve to photograph birds. I set up by camera on its stable tripod, 300mm prime lens, tuned in the optimal exposure and composition, and took my best shots. Meanwhile she was shooting out the window, or walking around snapping at whatever presented itself. When we got home I loaded both sets of pictures and knew right away I was in trouble. She caught the detailed orange eyes of a sandhill crane, I did not. She caught the windblown feather detail of a yellow headed blackbird, I did not. We will be printing some of her photographs to hang on the wall, there will be none of mine. With a lighter and more agile camera she was able to take advantage of the moment while I was stuck on the tripod. Lesson learned. All I got to say is Wow!. I would recommend this camera for anybody who wants a compact camera without the lens bag, and full auto or full manual or anything in between. I would even recommend it as an accessory for a more advanced photographer so they can see what the shot should have looked like.

title: This is an excellent Computer case worth the price!
text:
I have bought a lot of cases over the years, but this one is the best in the size and price class I have had so far!
I will try to keep this simple and not include the details that otehrs have also gone deeper into..... other reviews I mean.
1: It is SO easy to get this to run super-cool - just buy the second 200mm fan for it to be placed in the top opening for it; you will love it.
2: We have a "room" for our projects and computers. The place where this needed to go had been a real problem in the past for cooling.
3: It needed good positive pressures from the fans installed and not the usual "puff" of the typical fans you see in most computer cases.
4: The placement of the front 200mm fan is ideal for getting clean cool air, and with the one mounted in the top - it's EXCELLENT!
5: The price is reasonable, and though it is about 1" wider than many of the cases you see, it allows for a tad bit more room, better cooling flow, and...

7: It is a clean cool looking case too! The lighting effects are subdued and sharp looking. I like the top front start and USBs... excellent.
8: Though it has the 2 big fans in mine now, it is NOT excessivley noisey or a problem - annnnd, it does run cool even with the high powered CPU (148 watts).
I hope this adds some cogent remarks that will help anyone in making the choice here: choose with confidence knowing that if you have just a little bit of extra space for the slightly larger box size, you will get a LOT for your money: the extra fan is only $10. Amazon
Enjoy, Gary (Dee's Geek)

Update on 14Jan 2013: This one has been so good this past year that I have now bought a second one for a system upgrade to my work computer. I also bought a couple of the CoolMax 120mm fans in the "blue" color and swapped out the single red 120 for two blue 120's. I like it in blue (humor). It takes about 2.5 minutes to change out the front fan it comes with.... so easy.
This case is even better in my estimation than my big AZZA case!!(It has 7 of the smaller sized fans and this is even better!) The Hard drive side installation is so easy with the sata hard drives and the 90* sata cable ends. The system for attaching the slip-bars to the side of the HDs, then sliding them into place so they click and lock in is unique in the industry and works SO easily! It has such versatility built into it, that even if you want to use 6 3.5" HDs and have a couple of 2.5s you can do it if your board will allow it all. It is very well made, it is however about an inch wider than most cases to allow the side mounting.... a minor consession in my book for what you get..... the case cooling with 2 - 120mm fans is excellent!! title: Six cameras running on BlueIris NVR - 1000% better than my analog system
text: I am currently upgrading from an older analog system and after an incident where I could not see sufficiently to identify the person involved in a crime, I decided it was time to spend a little extra money and upgrade to a better quality camera system.  I looked around on the web at different forums, youtube and some blogs and found good feedback on this camera (IPC-HDB3200C) and ordered one.  My intention was to build a system like I had with my analog DVR system, instead with just with a Network Video Recorder on a PC we no longer used.  What I liked about the camera was that it was one wire - a single CAT5 cable, while I did have to pull out my old coax cable and replace it with the CAT5, I was able to use my coax as a pull string for the new cable.  Then it was just a matter of putting on the CAT5 jack and plugging it into my trendnet POE switch.  I found I was able to configure everything from within the web UI, though if you want to view video through the web interface (such as during setup) you will need Internet Explorer, though you can still configure the camera if you don't install the ActiveX control.  I'll spare you all the functionality in the UI as there is a youtube video that goes through nearly all of the features, though my firmware was slightly newer / different than the one on the youtube video.  I got the camera all configured and then working with BlueIris, a $50 PC based software application which worked perfectly to store all the video (added a 2TB drive) and providing me a method to access recorded content and to also access live video via my Android phone and my wife's iPhone.  I won't kid you - setting up IP cameras does require some technical understanding that the average person might not have (terminating CAT5 cables if you pull your own, networking with POE, software configuration, RTSP configuration) - though this would apply to all IP cameras as it is just part of the process.  So, don't think this (or any IP cam) is just a drop in solution, you'll need to know your stuff.  I just finished purchasing another six cameras for the rest of the house.  A hint here - though my cameras came with 3.6mm lenses, you can find additional "mega pixel board" lenses as another reviewer mentioned on the web and I was able to get some tighter areas (FOV) with even more clarity (front and back doors and next to the side of the house.)  So far so good, they have worked great and even considering they don't have IR (I didn't want to have to deal with all the extra wiring/power issues), low light resolution is pretty good - I can clearly see better through these cameras at night than I can with my own naked eye at night.

title: Default Samsung 6100-series picture quality settings are pretty awful.
text:
I just set up a Samsung UN40ES6100.
The default Samsung UN40ES6100 picture quality settings are pretty awful.

The basic problem is that the default settings have too much contrast, brightness and color saturation.
They produce a picture that seems intended to "pop" in the store, but is actually very unrealistic, un-natural, almost cartoonish.
There are many examples of this, but perhaps the best is that grass (e.g.: football field) is far too unrealistically bright glowing (almost fluorescent) green than it should be.
Samsung could easily have done better.

The default Picture Mode setting on the UN40ES6100 I just set up was "Standard" (the other three choices are "Dynamic," "Natural" and "Movie"). There are also a looooot of additional settings (especially in the Advanced Settings) that allow changes to be made to many different attributes that affect the picture color and quality. Most of which are available only if the Picture Mode is set to one of the other choices besides "Dynamic" or "Natural."

Unless you want to spend hours tweaking all those settings, I suggest changing Picture Mode to "Dynamic" or "Natural" even though that will cause the Advanced Settings to be unavailable, because it will also make fine tuning a lot simpler. One reason for this is that changes to many of the advanced settings are inter-related; changing one causes changes to other aspects of picture quality. This can turn the process of dialing in the correct image quality using the advanced settings into a time consuming struggle. You can still to get excellent image quality with Picture Mode set to "Dynamic" or "Natural."

The "Dynamic" Picture Mode appears to have artificial dynamic contrast expansion on the quarter-tone to three quarter-tone range (the middle part of the contrast range, e.g.: maybe the 30%-to-70% range is expanded out to maybe 20%-to-80%), at the expense of shadow and highlight detail (e.g.: the 0%-to-30% brightness range is compressed to 0%-to-20% and the 70%-to-100% brightness range is compressed to 80%-to-100%), to make the image have a more "punchy" look. This dynamic aspect of this range expansion is that it appears to vary somewhat depending on the image on screen at any given time. Sometimes this causes very slight, but noticeable shifts in the image brightness. In comparison, the "Natural" Picture Mode doesn't appear to have this contrast adjustment, so compared to "Dynamic" it looks more natural, less punchy, with slightly better highlight detail and noticeably better shadow detail.

In all four "Picture Modes" the default Picture options: "Color Tone" setting is "Cool" and I am pretty sure that is wrong for just about every situation. Color Tone: "Cool" makes whites a little too blue and also introduces a greenish/bluish color cast to highlight & shadow areas that should be close to neutral (e.g.: causes a greenish color cast in men's beard stubble). Color Tone: "Cool" also causes grass (e.g.: football field) to be even more unrealistically bright glowing green than it should be. It should be changed to "Standard." The other two choices (Warm 1 and Warm 2) are not available with Picture Mode set to "Dynamic" and are probably undesirable anyway, because Warm 1 and Warm 2 introduce a noticeable color cast into what should be neutral highlights (unless compensated for in white balance; an example of how changing one advanced setting affects something else).

- - - - - - - - - -

So the easiest way to make the Samsung UN40ES6100 look a lot better and more realistic is use either of the following settings as a starting point:

Picture Mode: Dynamic
Backlight: 15 or less (Reduces backlight bleed-thru "clouds." Lower backlight setting may require slightly higher brightness)
Contrast: 70 to 80 (default is 100. Helps compensate for "Dynamic" Picture Mode's artificially expanded mid-tone contrast)
Brightness: 35 to 40
Sharpness: 35 to 45 (default is 55. Depends on personal preference; sharper picture = more noticeable sharpening artifacts)
Color: 35 to 45 (closer to 35 is more natural, but some people like over-saturated colors)
Tint: should be within 2 of the default 50-50 setting; e.g.: 48-52 or 52-48
Picture options-> Color Tone: Standard

Picture Mode: Natural
Backlight: 15 or less
Contrast: 95 to 100 (definitely requires a higher setting than the "Dynamic" Picture Mode)
Brightness: 45
Sharpness: 35 to 45
Color: 40 to 45
Tint: should be within 2 of the default 50-50 setting; e.g.: 48-52 or 52-48
Picture options-> Color Tone: Standard

In summary, either of these two setups should give a pretty good result:
Set Picture Mode to Dynamic; significantly reduce backlight, contrast, brightness, sharpness & color saturation; set Color Tone to Standard
or
Set Picture Mode to Natural; significantly reduce backlight, brightness, sharpness & color saturation; set Color Tone to Standard

Also, the "ECO" settings (System->"Eco Solution") should be turned off, because they cause the screen routinely change brightness when it should not, with the net result being that it looks like flickering.

- - - - - - - - - -

These settings should get you pretty close to having an excellent - but realistic looking - picture quality, especially for Over The Air HDTV signals. I had to use slightly different settings for the HDMI signal coming from my HTPC DVR (which itself has an even more extensive set of image adjustments available in the video card software). When you throw in the adjustments that are possible on each other device that sends a signal to the TV set (which itself has independent settings for each input and signal type), it's easy to see why the overall complexity increases very quickly.

If possible, I'd start with the most consistent possible source - an OTA HDTV signal, and I'd use the live local HDTV news broadcast as the guide, because they seem to have the best control over lighting in their studios and the signal is live.

It is also important to note that these video quality settings are tied EACH video input and/or signal type. This means that not only will settings made for HDMI1 *NOT* automatically apply to any the other input (i.e.: you have to repeat the adjustment process for EACH and every input), but also if you are using the antenna connection, the settings can be different for each different signal type as well (HDTV, SDTV, analog, etc.), and this also applies to aspect ratio control - which is a good thing, because it allows different picture quality and aspect ratio settings for each different signal type coming in via the same antenna connection. The settings for SmartHub/Netflix/HuluPlus, etc. are also different too, so you need to check the values for each app you use.

- - - - - - - - - -

After setting up the new Samsung 6100 TV set, I had to re-configure my home theater audio system. Normally, I would have used an external powered woofer/subwoofer, and let the TV's internal speakers take care of the mid-range and treble, but there's a problem in this case:

The Samsung 6100 external audio output is fixed volume, which means the internal volume control does not affect the volume of the external audio output.

Not only that, none of the other audio adjustments (including the 6100's equalizer, sound effects, and "Automatic Volume" volume leveler) are applied to the external audio output either. Since the internal speakers are wimpy, and even worse, down-firing (which makes them muffled), I had to disable them entirely and use only an external speaker system.

I can't believe that Samsung did not provide a setting to make the external audio output variable with the TV's volume setting, especially considering that would be a fairly standard way for some people who don't have elaborate sound systems to improve upon the dinky internal speakers, and also considering that competing products like the Vizio M420SL provide a setting to make the external audio volume change with the TV's volume setting.

title: Best case period, for the Nexus 7. Not without a flaw though...
text:
I'll try to keep this short and sweet. Hands down, this is the best case available for the Nexus 7, but it's not without a flaw.

The build quality and materials are top notch, much better than I was expecting. The case is definitely black, not the gray it appears in the picture (this was a good thing for me).

The molded back-piece that the tablet clicks into is perfectly sized for a snug and secure fit. Magnets hold the flip cover nicely. The magnet embedding in the front cover works great as well, turning on and off the screen with ease while causing no issues when folded back. The inside of the flip cover has a nice soft lining that protects the screen and helps with finger prints.

The outer shell is a hard plastic, but within that is a softer rubberized plastic that covers the back of the tablet. This gives the case a little texture and grip which is really nice touch.

Speaker grill, headphone jack, usb port, and microphone are all perfectly cutout to allow access with the cover open or closed. Power button and volume rocker are also perfectly cut out, however, I can see how some people could have issue with this. For me personally, I like the way they're recessed and protected. Overall build quality and product design: 9/10

Now, my one and only issue with this case - the front cover. There is so much play in the placement of the front cover that the edges are never lined up flush with the body of the case when close. When closed naturally (just flipped closed), the front cover over-hangs the body of the case by nearly 1/4 of an inch. You can kind of push it back so it's flush, but naturally it slides back to over-hang. This is a bit annoying and detracts from the polish of the overall case. I think this cover was designed this way to allow it to be folded back flush against the back cover while holding. Unfortunately, the "hinge" just allows a bit too much play. Maybe there will be one last revision to fix this minor issue. If not, I'm still happy with this case and will use it until it wears out.

title: Perfect for my needs

title: Phenomenal cosmic powers! Itty bitty living space!
text:
I do the same thing w/ the Surface Pro 3 that I used to so with my regular notebook: carry it between work and home, where an external keyboard, mouse, and screen await it. Otherwise the SP3 is like a laptop used in meetings and, um, on my lap. The extra appeal comes when the keyboard is detached. About 4 times a week the SP3 is an awesome tablet, used for presentations. The tablet disappears from the crowd's view when laid on a lectern, yet is light enough to carry comfortably in one hand when approaching the audience.

My nice, 3 pound notebook has about the same specs as the 1.8 pound Surface Pro 3. The notebook now lives on a counter, relegated to the role of backup PC. The SP3 is front and center.

The SP3 is a standout among tablets because it runs Win8.1 with a reasonable, productive screen size, incredibly low weight, and a full i5 processor. In addition to Office, I use a resource-hungry niche software package. The SP3's muscles manage the heavy-lifting without breaking a sweat.

Microsoft fooled me: I had jumped for a SP2 about 6 weeks prior to the SP3's release. Most pundits anticipated the release of a "Surface Mini," not the larger-sized Surface 3. Now I'll unload the SP2 out the back door...or let it replace my once-treasured notebook as a backup PC.

There is one SP3 glitch that remains unresolved: scaling. Connecting an external monitor can have unexpected results, particularly with Powerpoint 2013. It's a minor issue, though, given the power and engineering in the PS3's little silver sliver of a package.

Oh, and did I mention the price? One I tricked the 256gb SSD SP3 out with type cover, case, and video adaptor and taxes I was down about $1600. That's a premium price, but then the SP3 is a primo PC.

title: Good Case With One Nagging Issue
text:
I ordered this case from Acase along with my Transformer Pad Infinity after looking at a number of cases available on Amazon. This one seemed like it was what I was looking for because I had a similar case for my Acer 7" tablet. I wanted something just for the tablet since I haven't decided to buy the dock yet.

For the most part, I like the case although I almost sent it back in the beginning. It has no instructions, and I had a hard time figuring out how to get my tablet in the case. If you are also puzzled, fold the case as if it has the tablet already inside in one of the viewing positions. Now slide the top of it through the middle brackets that hold it in place and up to the top corners. It does not "snap" in place if you hold it and the tablet flat. I only have one other minor complaint with this case. It does not fold completely flat if you are not using it in one of the stand positions. This makes it somewhat awkward to hold for reading or thumb typing.

In the end, it is very difficult to find exactly what you are looking for in a case without seeing it in person first. I can say that the build/materials of this case are solid, and I have no durability concerns. All of the ports and speakers are accessible. I just wish it was a few millimeters thicker at the fold so that it would lay flat. It would probably also be good if Acase included some basic instructions because I'm sure I'm not the first person to be puzzled about how to actually get the tablet in there. Hopefully this gives you an idea of what you can expect from this case.

title: Supernormal
text:
I have had this lens on my EOS SL-1 for a month now.
It is bigger than I would like but it delivers extremely good results.
There is a Lightroom plug-in to correct the distortion and the chromatic aberration which can be notable in backlit subjects at full aperture.

The depth of field is -as expected- quite narrow at f/1.4 which again means that you have to understand how to use the autofocus to get the right areas sharp. I am pretty sure that there are more people who do not understand how focusing works than there are faulty lenses around.

You get flare shooting at the sun, of course. As with most fast lenses it is a good idea to keep the lens hood on. It is cheaper to replace than the front lens element, also.

The build quality is convincing. I thought the material is metal but it is some composite that does not change dimensions with temperature.

I do not love mechanic things but this piece of engineering got me quite excited.
Shooting with a normal (48mm full frame 135 equivalent) lens makes you move to frame your shot and stop down and open up the diaphragm to isolate the subject. It feels like taking photos, I like it!

title: Why should you buy this camera?
text:
I bought this camera on a whim - something I could carry with me all the time for quick shots, in place of my more expensive cameras.

When I opened it up, I noticed right away the power on button is not protected. So if you should power it on by mistake like in a bag/coat/purse etc - there is a good change you can damage the lens as it telescopes out. A web search found several users that have lens opening issues - but to be fair any camera with a telescoping lens is at risk, but the power button on this camera makes it pretty easy.

There is way more image noise in the image than I expected. The lower the light, the more the noise. Image sharpness and overall quality are so so. The long zoom is not very good for sharpness and forget the digital zoom for anything other than curiosity.

In all honesty this camera produces SLIGHTLY better images than a cellphone. The zoom makes this a better camera than a cellphone, but not by much.

For the money it's ok - it's best for 4x6 prints, a cheap trip camera and web sharing. I am returning mine as I know the lens opening will be an issue.

** I just realized that you can turn the camera on with the lens cap on and it does not pop the lens cap off like some cameras do - so if this happens you can jam the lens.

title: Love It!
text:
I decided to replace my Linksys WRT610N router (which was having dropouts, especially when streaming Netflix using my Roku box). I also wanted an improved range of coverage.

I first purchased the E4200V1. After purchasing I noticed there was a V2. So why not try it as well before making a final decision??? I bought one, and was able to try both routers, swapping them in and out, trying to decide which to keep.

I could not detect any difference between the two in terms of range of coverage, or transfer rate. However, for sure, both the V1 and V2 were noticably better in range and transfer rate when compared to my WRT610N.

The setup was unbelievably easier than any of the several routers I've owned in the past. It took no more than 5 minutes, and I was up and running... no problems... a relief indeed.

Both the V1 and V2 fixed my Netflix/Roku dropouts. I decided on keeping the V2 (though more expensive) because of it's added capabilities - a desire to future proof my network.

I have 3 computers, 2 iPhones, 1 iPad, a Roku, Apple TV, SlingBox, a WEB based Sony TV, and a few other internet connect devices... all hooked up and running seemlessly. I have zero problems. Linksys, you've earned my 2 thumbs up award.

I'm very happy with my E4200V2, and believe it to be one of my better technology purchases of late.

title: Works but poor description is misleading (Max output is +15dB)
text: The product description on this is a little deceiving. I bought this because I wanted to boost my signal before a splitter because you generally get a 6db drop when you split a signal.  I figured boosting by 11dB would more than compensate for the loss.  What they don't tell you anywhere is that this amp goes into compression at +15dB. I was hoping to get the signal close to +30dB. Since my signal was at +20dB the amp did absolutely nothing and actually degraded it a little (since you are adding noise from the amplifier).  So if you are trying to boost a signal below 10dB. this amp will work for you. anything above and you're out of luck. I would recommend going with a 30dB preamp instead.

title: Decent camera that tries to do a lot of things but sometimes it chokes
text:
Update: 2019-01-06
Thank you D-Link. Your camera provided decent monitoring service for around 4 years but I finally decided to retire it. The main reason was micro SD card failures.
I have replaced the micro SD card twice throughout these 4 years and I used the same brand too: SanDisk 32GB the red and gray one. The last failure was just about a week ago. It was strange because the camera says the card is not formatted. Just weeks ago I was going over old recordings and also confirmed the camera was making live recordings. I suspect the card failure is like that computer message about doing a proper software eject before the actual physical eject of USB removable storage. I had to unplug the camera power because of moving things around and I think the sudden power loss must have caused the problem. About a year ago, I used the same method I documented here in my original review to create scripts to turn off or on recording. Essentially I made it a one-click process instead of going through the camera's admin interface and navigating through the menu system to turn off or on recording. I forgot to activate my "turn off recording to card" script before unplugging the camera power.
The camera was however well built. It went through rains, hot and cold weather, and some strong winds. The lens unfortunately did suffer one very microscopic water leak. I silicone sealed the entire lens ring and haven't noticed water inside the lens since. The back parts that protected the card and the power cable and network plug worked excellent. Despite the unfortunate water leak, I still think D-Link did a very good job building an outdoor camera.
Over the years I did notice D-Link discontinued this camera and unfortunately never had a replacement. As a result, prices shot up exponentially. I think D-Link focused mainly on indoor cameras. I did consider those cameras but I needed an outdoor camera. So I continued using this camera until something of interest caught my attention. In my original review, I essentially didn't like the video quality and despite my efforts to get around it I still wanted something better.
Surprisingly the last card failure forced my hand. In the days before the failure, I was testing out a camera I bought for myself and another as a secret santa gift and I liked this new camera very much. It is an indoor camera but there are third party companies making outdoor cases specifically for this camera. So when the failure happened, I bought another of that camera, picked an outdoor case and mounted it in my now retired D-Link camera's spot. It's been about a week now and has gone through rains and slight to medium winds and is still holding up. That camera is the Wyze Cam and the case I got is the black Frienda brand.
Thank you D-Link. I enjoyed the DCS-2332L despite the ups and downs. If you ever make outdoor cameras again I will consider it.

I heard about IP wireless outdoor cameras and after a search I chose D-Link's DCS-2332L. I took the time to read through the manual and was impressed by the features.

Based on the manual, it looked like 5 stars because it met my expectations. I wanted a camera to monitor things at home, record in high quality, notify me of motion, and integrate with my network via WiFi. This camera appeared to do the trick and it had a good price point.

After using it, I am giving it 3 stars. The camera does provide the features but I think it seems to try its best to deliver all of them but in the end chokes on almost all of them including the most important one.

The problem is the monitoring. During night time and other random times, the recordings suddenly go haywire. The file sizes suddenly bloat about 6 times. The frame rate decreases. And this is if there are recordings. I've seen some files with very small sizes, in terms of kilobytes. I record in 60 second clips so obviously something is wrong and not working correctly. I don't know if this is related but when I get video clip notifications either day or night, the clips either don't play or play very badly. When they play badly, it starts out fine for only a couple seconds then it becomes very slow and choppy and finally stops. I haven't had much success getting around these problems but I have found that restoring the camera to factory defaults sometimes helps. Even then, that's not an option because it would mean un-mounting the camera, plugging the camera into the router, re-applying configuration settings, testing the recording and if it's ok finally re-mounting the camera. Yikes!

On the positive, the camera is well made and the packaging presents it very nicely. The camera feels very sturdy; there's no loose parts. The box is compact and I like the nice magnetic flap on the front with marketing information. I can re-purpose those magnets. I stick lots of stuff on the fridge door.

The camera also comes with an adjustable stand and screws for mounting. These things are nice and I made use of them.

The camera can record video at 30 frames/sec, produce clear video during the day and the early part of the night, detect motion and email that motion in the form of pictures or one video clip. Unfortunately I think it's during this process that things don't run smoothly.

My first knock is on the recordings' file sizes. I chose H.264, 1280x800, 30 frames/sec, Excellent video quality and save to SD in 60 second clips. The file sizes initially ranged from 10-16MB. The camera also saves a jpg file with each recording which is about 70KB. So with a 32GB card, the recordings last about a day before they're erased.For some reason, and one reason appears to be night time, suddenly the sizes can shoot way up to over 100MB! I've seen sizes in the range of 20MB to over 100MB. Additionally the frame rate drops to around 15-20 / sec. Restoring the camera to factory defaults seems to "fix" it but it's painful to un-mount the camera, plug it into the router, re-apply my settings, re-mount the camera and test the camera to see that it's not recording in big sizes again. This doesn't help because the problem eventually comes back.

My second knock is the motion detection clips. They played fine initially but I think when the camera started recording at higher than expected file sizes, the clips would have strange errors. On the computer, it would say the clip's index needs to be re-built but it can try to play it as is. On the mobile, the clip would play fine for the first few seconds but then would slow down and then stop. Sometimes the clips don't even play. Additionally the file name of the clip is a long sequence of numbers. Turns out it's the UNIX time stamp. That's not exactly helpful if I want to match it up with the recordings to get a fuller video of what happened. The recordings' file names have the year, month, day and 24-hour time. I understand I can also get the date/time from the email and also imprinted on the clip itself on the top left corner but why create a layer of confusion by using the UNIX time stamp when it doesn't correlate with the recordings' file names?

My third knock is with email notifications: Sometimes I get an attachment with an "evt" log file. This 65 byte file contains nothing important. I wish there's a way to tell the camera *not* to send it.

My fourth knock is with configuration. Using Windows and IE is almost the best. This is because the motion detection configuration uses ActiveX. The camera does provide a Java plugin for Macs but the Java version only provides live video preview so no motion detection. I was using XP and IE7 and made the mistake of upgrading to IE8. That caused the live video, motion detection and other pages containing video preview to not work. Luckily XP's Add/Remove Programs allowed me to remove IE8 and I guess by default reverted back to IE7. I say almost the best because one of the buttons, the talk button, doesn't work.

My fifth knock is night vision. It's not so useful when it's almost dark. Viewing the live video with MPEG4 encoding is mostly random gray blocks moving around. Changing the encoding to H.264 seems to help but the video seems to go in and out to the point that it's choppy. I am also recording in H.264 so I wonder if the problem is because the camera can't both record and view a live video in H.264 encoding.

My sixth knock as mentioned in the fourth knock is the speaker button to activate two-way audio appears to only work when using "mydlink Lite" Android app. In XP/IE7, nothing happens. Also the two-way audio works like a CB radio. Having the microphone and speaker buttons enabled at the same time in app causes an unpleasant continuous crackling and static noise.

My seventh knock is the HTTPS feature. It's nice that D-Link includes it but it is just slow. If the camera's hardware is more powerful to deliver it, I would use it, but then again I would want the more powerful hardware to go towards the monitoring and delivering a consistent service.

In summary, I had high hopes for this but unfortunately I think D-Link dropped the ball. I am giving the camera 3 stars though because the camera for the most part does work and I do need something now to monitor so this will have to do for now. I was hoping that if this camera worked out, I would get more to monitor other parts of the home but now I have to wait and see on what the market offers.

Update March 28, 2014:
After experimenting for a while, I've found certain configurations that I feel optimizes usage that I like to share. I was really frustrated with the product when I wrote my original review. Now after finding out certain things that worked, I am content and I hope this helps people who experienced the same. If I could, I would increase my rating by half a star.

So for the large file size problem from 24/7 recording at high quality in 60 second clips that I mentioned, I found a way to bring it down to about 25MB by adjusting the image settings. For the email motion detection clips that had playback problems, I found a certain quality and time length that worked.

Below are the details to fix those problems:

For the size problem, it appears to happen during the evening up to about early morning. It's only during the day that the file sizes drop down to about 15MB. I found out that if I change the image settings during the evening then the file sizes stabilize to about 25MB. This is a huge benefit from the crazy 100+MB. This is what I change: Denoise to 255 and Brightness to 6. Unfortunately when early morning starts , those settings aren't so great for image quality so I revert back to the default. Since I don't want to do these two things every day, I found out I can do this programmatically by inspecting what gets sent to the camera's webserver.

The URL to change Denoise to 255 is:
<camera-host> / vb.htm ? denoise=255
(added spaces to bypass review filtering and don't forget http in front)
URL to change Brightness to 6:
same as above, but replace denoise with "brightness=6"
URL to revert to default image settings
same as above, but use "imagedefault=1"

On the computer, I use 'curl' to issue those URLs. I also used the '-u' option to include my camera's login and password. I tried combining Denoise and Brightness to one URL, but the camera's webserver wouldn't have it. Next I put those curl commands into two shell scripts: a night one and a day one. Finally I add those two scripts into crontab. The night one starts around 730p and the day one starts around 730a.

Since I didn't want to leave the computer on 24/7 for this, I decided to make use of an Android phone, which is almost on 24/7. The apps I used are: (all of them free versions and don't require phone rooting or mods)
1. Non-root BusyBox by Burrows Applications LLC
This is for the 'wget' command. I couldn't find 'curl' but this also works.
2. SManager by DEVWOM
This is for scheduling the scripts to run.
3. Any Terminal app
This is for creating/editing the scripts and moving it to a proper directory if needed. I used 'vi' to edit. I found out later that editing can also be done through SManager.

'wget' is different from 'curl', so I needed to use these options:
format:
wget --auth-no-challenge --user=<...> --password=<...> -q -O - <the URL>
Since 'wget' is from BusyBox, I had to do this before using wget:
export PATH=$PATH:/data/data/burrows.apps.busybox/app_busybox/

To schedule the scripts, I start SManager. Then I choose the three dots virtual button, select 'Advanced', select 'Scheduler', and choose 'Add a new task'. I select the 'Repeat' line. This opens up a new screen. I select 'Time' and then choose the time I want to start the script. Next I select either the '-' or '+' button for 'Run each:'. This basically enables the 'Until' line. I select that and choose the same time as 'Time'. All this does is tell SManager to run the script every day at that 'Time'. I select the 'Ok' button. Then I select 'Add Script...' and then 'Name' and finally 'Save' after identifying a script to run and naming the task.

For resolving the email clips playback problem, I used these video settings:
H.264, 640x360, 15 fps, Good Fixed Quality
In 'Setup'->'Event Setup'->'Media', I created this video profile:
3 seconds Pre-Event recording, 6 seconds Maximum duration, 5000 Kbytes Max. file size
This creates clips averaging about a megabyte. Sometimes it can be less than half or it can go over but for the most part it hovers around a megabyte. This is perfect for not killing the phone data plan but most importantly the clips don't have playback problems.

For motion detection, I originally used the default Sensitivity but I think that created a lot of false positives mainly because of the lighting triggering the motion. I've now lowered it to 25. I also make use of the motion detection boxes and decided on 30 Percent.

Another reviewer, Wayne, talked about using RP-SMA extension cables so I want to acknowledge him for that. I mount my camera outside and reception was on the fringes. Using a home-made foil helped a bit but that won't work with high winds and rain that could sometimes turn the antenna around and the foil would block the camera or ruin the foil. Using the extension cable helped a lot by bringing the antenna inside for better reception. Thanks Wayne!

title: Corruption in the wings!!! or firmware.
text:
This review is for the wd30ezrx 3T drive.
I have had many drives from western digital, seagate, IBM, and Hitachi over the years. My failure rate has been low for all of them because I always condition my power and keep the drives cool.
I've had 2 drives bad out of the box when WD was going from 512 to 4k sectors but until now I have never had a western digital drive go bad in warranty that was working when it arrived.
I bought this drive in June 2012. I used it as a backup drive nightly. It was on a Sata3 port and mounted right next to the cooling fan.
Yesterday while I was copying some files it gave and error and stopped. It wasn't even visible in disk manager.

After a little research, it seems that firmware problems are famous with Western Digital WD30EZRX hard drive. Firmware modules are located on the service area on the platters. For some reason if one or more modules get corrupted, Western Digital WD30EZRX hard drives become inaccessible. If you attempt to access drives with firmware corruption, you will see error messages like boot failure, no operating system found, S.M.A.R.T or other BIOS errors. It is impossible to fix these errors by Do-it-Yourself data recovery. So you will have to RMA the drive and loose and data you had on it or use a professional data recovery service.

If your drive is working well for you now great! I hope it continues to do so without firmware corruption for a long time.
I can NOT recommend this drive for anything because of it's unpredictability.

Western Digital is usually very reliable. But they have let the quality control down on these drive just like the EARS(512to4k) drives.

title: Form versus Function
text:
Pros:
1. Most gaming mice I've seen look like they were designed by people who think the more impractical it looks, the better. This mouse looks quite nice and practical. The operative word here is "looks" however and I will get to that in a moment.
2. It looks fantastic and once night falls the blue streak it leaves behind is endlessly charming and I've been making unnecessary gestures just to see the trail. I have also been losing more often than usual but it is a fair trade off. It really does look that cool.
3. That start up sound it makes is a very nice touch.

Cons:
1. It looks very nice but then again, so do Apple's ambidextrous mice and this one is about as comfortable to use as those except with the added bonus of a sharp edge at the back which, although lending it the look of a light cycle, also makes it annoying to use for more than 5 minutes at a time.

Thoughts:
At the end of the day you most likely are not going to be admiring how nifty your mouse looks like and more likely to be staring intently at the screen and wondering why your team isn't following you and why you are dead. The displeasure of losing a game is only intensified by the throbbing in the fleshy part of your palm due to that sharp edge at the back. Only buy this mouse if:
1. You really like how it looks
2. That's about it actually
I'm going to be using this as a spare mouse and keeping my old one as my main.
