title: New 2014 version v. Old 1980s version
text:
When I saw recently in SONY's on-line store (store.sony.com/over-the-head/cat-27-catid-All-Over-Head-Headphones;pgid=m2lmcD9xx_pSRp3Bc5rNsKM_0000uLEOXrV1;sid=JA3P7quxLCbd7vj0oz9r6jO77TaBK2KKasjJt9Lj) that the MDR-V6 headphones have been re-issued as "new" in 2014, and that Amazon is an authorized dealer, I ordered a new pair to back up my original "Made in Japan" V6 cans that I've had forever as a recording engineer.

The current ones are "Made in Thailand" and the box carries a 2014 copyright. The new 2014 version sounds close to my excellent Japanese originals that I used for monitoring/mixing/mastering in my recording studio. Evaluated using the headphone circuit of my vintage Harman/Kardon PM660 amplifier and recording studio original lossless digital masters as the source, and measured against my studio reference AKG Austrian made K701s, I find the new V6 are not as well balanced across the audio spectrum as the K701 headphones. The 2014 V6 has a noticeable boost in the low bass - educated guess, about +5dB centered broadly around 70Hz (or say about +5dB between 50Hz and 150Hz) - making them a bit less suitable for studio applications than the K701s, and making them about +2dB or +3dB higher in the low bass than my vintage MDR-V6 headphones were when new. The 2014 V6 has excellent mid and high range reproduction, has very good image placement/sound stage, and no audible distortion, but does not reproduce the low end of my master recordings quite as faithfully due to the slight bass boost.

The fit of the new V6 for me is snug without being tight or uncomfortable. Leakage is minimal, if at all, at anything less than levels that will damage hearing; and the isolation from external sounds is very good. Fitment is good, and the stitching on the leather headband is well done. But physically they seem just a tad "different" somehow. The originals have the feel of solid construction. Although the new ones look to be put together well, they just don't give that same sense of being as solid and durable.

Earpads look like the pleather that's been problematic in the past for flaking. Another minor gripe - the cable of the new headphones was so tightly packed into the box that the coils were deformed in several places - but I was able to get the cable back in shape.

So I've knocked off one star because of my subjective feeling about the physical qualities, and being a bit less suitable for studio applications than the AKG K701s. I'd have to determine exactly where and how much low bass needs to be EQ'd down to use these as highly accurate reference cans. That shouldn't be with headphones billed as "studio monitors", and it's a departure from the signature of the original "Made in Japan" V6 headphones, which, when new, were essentially flat over the majority of the audio spectrum (+/- 3dB between 25Hz and 10kHz), as true studio monitor headphones should be.

This 2014 version of the V6 is still very good for home listening enjoyment (they also sound darn good with my Samsung Galaxy S4 smartphone), but some may want to turn the bass control down a bit (about 3dB or so) on the sound source; or consider replacing the OEM pleather earpads with Auray Deluxe EarPads, which tame the low end by about 3dB between 50 Hz and 150Hz (the trade-off though is a high end boost by about 4dB to about +7dB at 10kHz).

An alternative headphone is the SONY MDR 7506, which has a flat frequency response (+/- 3dB between 25Hz and 10kHz).

Consider looking elsewhere if you need a tool for critical recording studio applications.

title: 5 Years of Heavy Use and No Problems
text:
I've been very impressed with this TV for more than 5 years. I would highly recommend it if it were still for sale.

I purchased mine directly through sharpusa.com in early September 2007. I got a special deal through my company (Sharp was a client), 50% off at the time, for a total of $1,000. I got it a bit earlier than retail stores and Sharp's website didn't even acknowledge the model at the time I got it. It may have been from the batch of models that they send to reviewers.

I immediately did a full calibration on my TV and it has looked perfect for 5 years with:

- No dead pixels
- No banding
- No ghosting
- No dimming back-light
- No sudden shut-off issues
- No sound issues
- No HDMI or other input issues (VCR, DVD, PS3, BluRay, XBox 360, Wii, etc...)
- No issues of any kind, whatsoever, no how

We have used the TV at home for a total of several thousand hours. Sometimes we leave the TV on all day and all night (by mistake) and we haven't had a single issue.

We have also moved 3 times with the TV with no issues with flexing or breakage during transport, nor any issues with the display afterwards.

There were some firmware updates for the TV. I have no idea what they changed but they certainly didn't hurt the TV. It was easy enough as downloading the firmware package to a USB thumbdrive and selecting the update feature in the menu.

The only time I ever thought that the TV was going out was when my PS3 would take 10 minutes to show up on screen with the image flickering black on and off faster and faster until it stayed on the HDMI signal. Well, much to my delight the problem was the HDMI cable (go figure). Swapping that out with a $2 monoprice cable solved the problem. I'll never buy an HDMI cable in the store again.

It sucks that a few people have suffered through faulty models. I'm honestly sad to hear it because I love mine so much. I have no reason to get rid of it. I have it calibrated just how I want it and I see no reason to replace it. When it breaks I'm going to have a hell of a time finding a replacement to my liking.

As for price, the list price was $2,000 at release (according to SharpUSA) and I got it for $1,000. I thought that was a great deal at the time. However, I just bought my mom a 47" LG 3D TV for $400 at a retail store this month. What an amazing advancement in cost-cutting.

If anyone is interested in my calibration settings, send me a comment and I'll list them all out.

UPDATE 2014/06/10
---------------------------------------------------
nearly 7 years and still going strong. Moved twice since last review. Not a single issue.

title: Functions OK but interface kills it
text:
This device will correctly do everything that you would expect. It is entirely serviceable in its various modes: playing radio, IPOD integration, Pandoa linking, Bluetooth link. The Bluetooth link was easy to setup as I recall initially - something that can't be said for other devices.

However, the entire device is brought down by interface design. I have had this for a year and the annoyances have grown to me over time, not something I am getting used to. To start with, standard design (principle of least surprise) would usually demand that the large prominent circular button on the left be the POWER button and that rotation of this button ALWAYS control the volume. Instead, pushing this leads to a byzantine labyrinth of sub-menus. To further complicate it, while in these sub-menus, rotation of the knob cycles through the choices in these menus and does NOT affect volume. Thus, often if you are trying to rapidly decrease volume for some reason, you end up accidentally pushing the button and falling into one of the menus. So you are rapidly turning to decrease volume, but you are stuck on these misc. menus instead. Further, it is not obvious at all how to exit up the stack and RETURN to volume control. I still don't know if there is actually a way to turn the unit off.

Many of these sub-menus are very esoteric and don't need to be accessed this way. The other buttons are also fairly small and easy to miss, particularly in the dark (the back lighting isn't as noticeable as it could be). The whole thing is just way too complex and not usable at all.

I get that they cram a lot of functionality in here in a small space and need a way to "control" it. But other devices manage to do a better job without violating decades of ingrained knowledge in consumers on how the most prominent buttons should behave.

I am writing this review because I do not have another place to voice how bad this product is. To set the stage and show I am a techie I want to state I have a Masters in Computer Engineering.

I travel a lot and this product fit into a "perfect sweet spot" of giving me my own private internet in public hot spots such as hotels or airports. Another purpose was to provide me with an additional layer of protection at home by giving me another firewall to protect my network.

A profile is what the device saves so it can reconnect when revisiting a network location such as going to the same Starbucks location. I reached the unpublished limit of 10 yesterday. I read alot of comments on wireless issues but people must understand that wireless and throughput issues are largely a function of your router, not the camera. I have this coupled with an e4200 linksys router so disconnects and throughput issues are non-existent.
Low light sensitivity is very good however the motion detector doesn't seem to work as well in low light conditions. Video quality is satisfactory but not excellent. However, I did not purchase this camera to watch my front door in 1080p.
For those of you having difficulty setting up the motion detector email functionality use port 587 as your smtp port and you will have no issues.
I cannot give the camera 5 stars as there is one severe issue with this product. Some important parameters for the motion detector require Active X to tweak them. This means you are required to use Internet Explorer only. For a Linux user like myself (or Chrome, Firefox users) this means when you want to change the motion detector sensitivity and you have to go hunting for a PC with Internet Explorer. Why these features could not have been coded into the firmware like the rest of the settings is beyond me. The days of Internet Explorer dominance are over, Linksys/Cisco really should offer support for other browsers.
The power cord for the camera is also far too short making installation challenging, make sure you buy an extension cord with this product.
Despite this one deficiency this is an excellent security camera, you will be happy with your purchase.

title: Great cover ... for a week or so
text:
I looked at lots of different cases for our new Nexus 7 tablets before settling on this one based on very positive early reviews. And I have to admit, I loved the cases when they first arrived. They felt very sturdy, quite well-made and, with the magnetic catches and sleep/wake functionality, even better than the official case from Google/Asus. We ordered two of these, one in blue and one in black, for our new tablets at a time when they were $25 each, which itself was a supposedly discounted price. My first minor complaint came immediately after they arrived; despite looking quite different in the pictures on Google, in all but the brightest light the blue and the black might just as well have been the same color. So much for easily telling the two apart.

However, the color issue was trivial in comparison with the problems that followed. After only a couple weeks of very light around-the-house-only usage, the leather "hinge" on each case began to get very floppy, quickly to the point where the case would no longer function as a stand because everything collapsed. This wasn't a huge deal for us, because we used the stand function rarely (I don't think my wife ever did, in fact) and though it was disappointing, especially considering how much we had paid, it wasn't enough to be worth complaining about.

However, not long after that we noticed the edges starting to peel, as countless others have since noted here in their reviews -- not badly, mind you, because we have been very gentle with the cases. Then a couple weeks ago I noticed mine was cracked where the plastic surrounds the power and volume buttons. Odd, I thought, considering it had NEVER been dropped, slammed, kicked or otherwise abused in any way. So, knowing that there was a three-year warranty, this was the defect that finally pushed me to ask for a replacement. The manufacturer agreed right away, probably because they knew full well how many people were having quality issues with this case.

I waited a few days for a replacement, which came with a prepaid return label so I could send the broken one back. When I pulled the replacement out of the package, I thought they had sent the wrong model. This new one had a wafer-thin cover compared with the sturdy heft of the one I was planning to return. Instead of a finished edge, the front and back were just stamped/crimped together to the point that there was actually a sharp edge that although not quite lethal would easily leave a mark on my skin. I immediately contacted the manufacturer again and explained that I thought they had sent the wrong case, that this looked like a much lesser model. They explained that this was in fact the correct one, that it had been redesigned due to the peeling edge issue. I quickly decided that it wasn't worth keeping the lightweight piece of junk they had sent as a replacement so I used the return label to send it back instead of the broken one, then carefully superglued the original back together. I've since been issued a refund for both cases through Amazon's A-to-Z Guarantee and we're once again searching for a more durable case. If I weren't hooked on the magnetic gizmos I'd plunk down $20 x 2 on a couple of the official cases, but I can't quite bring myself to do it. So the search will continue.

In the meantime, the best I can do is warn people to stay far, FAR away from this model. Not only is the old design defective, were you to get some old stock from the warehouse, but the redesigned version is even worse and I guarantee you could find one a lot better for less money from the Chinese vendors on eBay -- not that you should, but if you are bent on wasting money on a disposable case you might as well pay less for one that will last just as long ... not that that's saying much.

title: Sorry I waited so long to buy these
text:
I almost never do reviews but there is so much conflicting information out there on these that I felt compelled to add my two cents to the mix.

First and foremost the sound quality. It's why we buy them right? These sound great. Better than great. My first reaction was "Holy S***!!". I couldn't believe how great these sound. These are desktop speakers. I sit in the sweet spot. The sound is rich and the bass goes deep enough that I never feel it's lacking. The inner detail on recordings is exceptional. I am hearing things I don't hear on my big rig system. Now I guess if you buy these expecting to play them at head banger sound volumes you might be disappointed. I don't do that. Probably never will. At reasonable sound levels these sound great. I have a speaker system in the same room that was double the price but these are such a joy to listen to that I have been listening to these almost none stop since I got them. I am sorry I waited so long to pull the trigger on these.

Next up is the concern about these hissing. I don't hear anything from these. I am 61 so okay my hearing is a little shot. But these are also in my office where there are two computers and a ethernet switch along with some NAS drives. In other words lots of fans from other devices. If these speakers are contributing noise I ain't hearing it. No concern there.

Next up the remote. I don't use it. I am sitting three feet from the speakers. Why do I need a remote? I can do everything the remote can do with my keyboard except turn them off which I never do. The speakers will go into standby if I turn off the computer or put it to sleep. Good enough.

Complaints? Just one. The DAC in this as far as I can tell can't do sample rates at 96Hz or 192Hz like the newer DACs. That was a bit of a disappointment but then again the sound quality is so good that it hardly seems to matter. They do sound best when seated in the sweet spot. Off axis listening is not as good as sitting in the middle. These look and sound great and get my highest recommendation for desktop speakers. A little spendy but worth every penny. Go get yourself a pair and enjoy the music.

text:

This is what you do...
Start by charging the unit for an hour or so because the battery is probably empty.
Turn the unit on by pressing the button at the top, left corner.
At the main page press View Map
Press the speed readout in the bottom right corner
Press and hold the Speedometer until the debug screen shows (10 seconds)
Select Demo Mode
Click Disable Demo Mode
Return to the debug screen
Select GPS Simulator Mode
Select Off and click OK

Piece of cake, right?

title: Good for the price.
text:
I got this radio to add to my go box after weighing the price of this with the features of the PRO520XL. I've had access to both radios now for a little bit, and unfortunately regret not going for the PRO520XL.

Aside from the style, the 520 is actually smaller than this lower-end model. This model forgoes an RF gain knob, which is essential for tuning down to the noise floor for distant stations. The issue is particularly compounded by poor mounting techniques such as clip or mag-mount antennas. Reading the specs for each radio before deciding revealed that the 520's receiver sensitivity was brilliant compared to this one, so in most cases distant stations hear me long after I stop hearing them.

Another stark comparison of this radio with it's bigger brother is the weight. The 520's chassis is solidly constructed steel from top to bottom, where the 505 opts for cheaper plastic. After noticing an incredible drop in the noise floor when placing my magmount on top of the radio, I further realised another big "nono" in the radio's design; cracking it open revealed that there was no shielding whatsoever apart from the side mounting rails. I haven't tested for leaked RF yet, but I've already begun adding adhesive tin foil in an effort to provide some shielding and quell the noise this thing absorbs. It's a fairly simple process, but be sure to use a sheet of acetate (transparency film works) between the circuit board and the conductive metal to prevent shorts.

If installing any CB radio permanently, I recommend wiring the radio directly to the battery or jump points. Be sure to install an inline fuse *at the battery*, or an electrical fire is a real danger. Since this radio has an inline 2A fuse, a 2A fuse at the battery would be ideal, but 2A blades aren't common. 5A is more common and will work fine for this wiring gage. Remember, the fuse at the radio will NOT protect you from a fire if the short is between the battery and the fuse. Using it this way instead of an accessory port adapter takes care of most alternator noise and interference issues.

title: Review from iPad Convert
text:
Updated Review: Ok, so when I just got this tablet, it was a 5/5 for me. I loved the zippiness, the use of the S-Pen, true multitasking, and the increased screen real estate. However, three months later, I am selling my Galaxy Note Pro 12.2 and switching to something smaller. Here's why:

Size --> The size is a doubled-edged sword for this tablet. While I love the versatility and being able to multitask like a beast, I have also found that I use it very infrequently because of the size. It is difficult to use as a book reader on a bus or in an airplane, and the reading apps that are on it: Kindle, Kobo, etc display things very funkily on the stretched screen. At a certain point, I felt like I was reading a scroll more than I was reading a book because of how long the screen is when held in portrait mode. The size and length of the device also makes it awkward to hold one-handed, and I found myself taking it out less and less, to the point where it was relegated to being a solely movie-watching device for when I was at home, which kind of destroyed the purpose of having a tablet to begin with.

Screen --> It is still a beautiful beautiful screen, but something is up with Samsung's colors. I didn't notice it much at first until I started to compare the colors with my smartphone (an Apple iPhone 6 Plus) that the yellow was almost always off. Even when highlighting in the Kindle App, a yellow highlight mark would show up as mustard yellow. Hardly a deal breaker, but it gets annoying, especially considering how this thing is supposed to be "pro."

S-Note --> I still loved having the S-Pen and being able to jot down notes on the device as I would with paper, but with time, realized that it was another one of those functions I only ever used once a week at most. It's cool to show off, but it gets old, and the experience is not nearly as good as real pen and paper. It's just not as satisfying, unfortunately.

Android --> I love Android. I owned a Galaxy Note 2 and loved it, and seriously considered a Galaxy Note 4 for a few weeks before pulling the plug on an iPhone 6 Plus, but Android is simply not the greatest for tablets. I already talked about how book apps, even popular ones like the Kindle App, simply stretched either horizontally or vertically to accommodate the screen size, and I found that with a lot of other apps too, such as the Wall Street Journal App, etc. You don't run into this problem with iOS, so for now, I would say that Android is still lacking where tablets are concerned.

Value --> I loved the idea of a potential laptop AND tablet replacement (at least for things like multitasking, writing, graphic design work, worksheets, etc), but this Galaxy Note Pro is not it. After playing around with Hancom Office, I found several deficiencies to it that were just too much to stomach using it. While the programs in Hancom look like their Microsoft counterparts, its the finer details that show how poorly executed the programs really are: opening a document in any Hancom program would take easily a minute, and after saving said document, they were difficult to locate. I tried to save a document I had written in Hancom to my dropbox folder, and even though it registered that they were saved, I couldn't find it in Dropbox. I thought that this could be a problem on Dropbox's end, until I realized I had no problem uploading documents to dropbox in other apps, and pictures to dropbox as well. The selling point of the Galaxy Note Pro is that it is a professional middle ground between a fun and frilly tablet, and a professional workhorse laptop, but sadly it is neither. I kind of wish I had sprung a few extra bucks for the Surface Pro 3, which seems to have accomplished what the Samsung has not.

Overall, I still think there is an audience for the Galaxy Note Pro, but that audience is a lot smaller niche than most would expect. In Short: If you like the android tablet experience and want something that is great for taking notes by hand, drawing by hand, and multitasking over multiple screens, and also don't mind the weight, dimensions, and somewhat off-coloring, then this is the device for you.

title: Amazing beginner's lens
text:
So if you're anything like me, you probably bought the kit lens with your DSLR because it's fairly inexpensive and having a lens is a necessity right? Well if you haven't learned yet as I did, the kit lens really aren't worth having if you plan on producing nice pictures. You're much better off puting the $50-$100 towards better lenses.

Its a true shock when entering the world of photography to see that most lenses cost more than camera bodies! However, this particular lens brings amazing value at it's price point and although it is a prime (no zoom) I would recommend this a 100 times over the kit lens.

It is a fast lens at 1.8f which will give you nice bokeh (shallow depth of field)and will work quite well in low light situations. If you're not familiar with shallow depth of field, take a look at some of the pictures others have posted above and you'll see many that have something in focus and the background is out of focus. This is a really nice effect and makes your pictures look much more professional.

If you do a lot of manual focusing (or video) the focus ring is pretty cheap and not fluid at all, yet at around $100 you really can't ask for more. The body is all plastic, but again, there must be sacrices somewhere to achieve this price point.

This lens gets 4 stars from me because of the last two points, but only because I've since used many other lenses that I can see where spending the extra money helps (especially since I do a lot of manual focusing), however if I were to rate this compared to the kit lens, ten stars all the way. Feel free to ask any questions through the comments and I'd be glad to help. Although I'm not an expert, I've done a lot of research and if my experience can help you in any way, I'd love to share what I've learned! Hope this helps!

title: FIRE THE CABLE COMPANY!!!!!
text: First if you are a huge ESPN fan and sports freak getting rid of cable is not for you.  I really could care less for sports so saving 140 bucks a month and about $17,000 in 10 years was a no brainer! I live in East Orlando and only live 8-9 miles from our broadcast towers.  The antenna is not a large footprint and is easy to set up and install.  If you have Satellite TV you can hook it up to your existing dish mount and into your existing cables even better if you have HDTV because the cables should be shielded RG6 that helps in cutting down in the noise in your cables and allows the signal to travel farther. You can check if your mount has a direct line of site to your locations antenna farm by using [...]  or [...] plus both sites will tell you what channels you should be able to receive. Make sure you ground your antenna and RG6 cables from lighting strikes.  Remember if you don’t get all your channels you think you should be getting try adjusting the aim of the antenna, this is old schools stuff so the aim is critical so it might take you a few tries.  If you have newer cables or installing high quality quad shielded RG6 most likely you will not need an antenna power booster (amp).  If you are using older cables, have a weak signal, have mutable cable splits, or have 50ft or longer runs you might need the power amp.  I went and got a few quotes to install this and the cheapest was $250.00 (to include the cost of the antenna) I did the entire install within a few hours and I would call my experience as beginner/basic.  Just use youtube on how to install RG6 cables and antennas and you will be good to go.  I didn’t give the antenna 5 stars because even though it performs great, install is a breeze, and the mount is really great the quality of the construction of the antenna is about average but it does have a warranty and hey its 50 bucks to include 2 day shipping on Amazon prime! Living without cable and cable bill is really great and I encourage everyone to do it, with high speed internet who needs cable?  If anyone want to know how I “cut the cord” or how I did it send me a message I will help anyone escape the slavery of cable TV!

title: Startech's implementation of RAID fails anytime any drive in the array fails
text:
Quick summary:
Their implementation of RAID (fail the whole array anytime any drive fails) is completely flawed in my humble opinion. I will be avoiding their products in the future.

Details:
My background - I've worked as an engineer at Compaq, HP, and Cisco helping customer design and deploy large scale server farms since 1998. Let's just say I've used array controllers (and configure RAID) more times than I really care to admit to because I might start realizing I need a life. Anyways, I digress.

I purchased this low cost disk array to provide a simple/cheap RAID 1 array for home use. Out-of-box experience was acceptable. I wasn't impressed by the method of configuring RAID levels (removing a tab on the rear and doing finger gymnastics using toggle buttons on the front and back simultaneously). I have a one handed friend that can't use this product, for example. I also wasn't impressed that I couldn't visit the manufacturers website and download a user manual. All that's available online is something equivalent to a "getting started" guide. So, if you buy it, don't lose the CD they give you with the manual. Its the only one you'll have. I also wasn't pleased to experience a bug in the product where the RAID array kept randomly disappearing from one of my home servers (as if it was unplugged). I was using USB 3.0. I dumbed it down to 2.0 (slower speed) and problem went away. I was too busy to figure out why or call support. I just needed the array up and running. All of the issues above were "acceptable" to me because it was too much of a hassle to return it and the price was ok. If what I wrote above was the only issues I had, I probably wouldn't be writing this review.

Well, "today" happened. Today, one of the drives in my RAID 1 set failed (thanks Seagate). But I was ok with it because THIS is why I went to the trouble of setting up the storage using RAID 1...even though a drive failed, my data should still be available. Well, reality struck....StarTech doesn't seem to think a RAID 1 array should continue functioning if one of the HDDs fails. What does their product do? It takes the RAID 1 drive offline. Your stuff is still there on the remaining drive and they COULD allow the RAID 1 array to be active (in a non-redundant state) until you replace the failed drive...but they don't. Unfortunately, their mentality is that RAID 1 arrays with a failed drive should go offline because they need to protect your data for you?!?! Unlike all other array controllers that exist in the world that continue to present the drive as a functioning drive even if a drive fails...StarTech doesn't. If you HAVE to get to the data on the remaining drive, you have to remove the drive from their RAID enclosure and plug it directly into your computer. No, Im not joking. StarTech thinks that all the other RAID array controller vendors in the world are wrong and that "Those raid controllers are not truly protecting your data if they allow you to access the drive in raid 1 when there is only 1 disk" (direct from Jeff Worville at StarTech). I guess HP, Compaq, Dell, IBM, Cisco, etc. are all doing it wrong then and StarTech is the only one doing it right.

I bought this product for RAID 1 benefits...if a drive fails, the server is none the wiser and the volume stays available. I replace the failed drive as quickly as possible to provide redundancy again. Unfortunately, StarTech's products DO NOT FUNCTION THE WAY THE REST OF THE WORLD DOES in regards to RAID technology. Its an utter fail...coming straight from a reluctantly self-described IT geek.

Here's the transcript of my chat session today. I wouldn't want to take anything they said out of context. You judge for yourself before buying this product (read from the bottom up):
------------------------------------------------------

title: Pretty good, for the most part
text:
I'm breaking my review into two parts: GoogleTV versus Roku/AppleTV and The Sony NSZ-GS7 itself.
GoogleTV versus Roku/AppleTV:
I've had Roku, AppleTV and wanted GoogleTV for one reason: The browser - a feature Roku and AppleTV don't offer. Roku has a great selection of channels, but you're locked in to whatever channels they provide. AppleTV is VERY limited in it's content selection as they want you to buy all your content from them via iTunes. Can't even get Amazon on AppleTV, where you can on Roku and GoogleTV. Not to mention movies for rent in iTunes are generally $1 more (versus Amazon or other) and movies to buy are more expensive too. GoogleTV's browser sets you free to stream or watch content from just about any site (however, some sites do block the browser, not sure why). I was concerned how the browser would scale/look on a TV, but it's awesome. Additionally, my goal was to have one device to watch all of my content like personal DVD library (I ripped them using DVDFab), photos, home videos, and streaming content. GoogleTV is the one device that has allowed me to accomplish that goal. I can finally say I am unplugged from cable and disks. The only downside I've realized thus far with GoogleTV is purely aesthetic because the Netflix interface is not near as slick as AppleTV or Roku. Actually ,it's kind of clunky. Also if you access Netflix from the integrated GoogleTV & Movies app, and then try and access Netflix directly (like after watching a movie and then trying to watch another) Netflix is unresponsive. You have to reboot. I quickly got over it though based on the other positives that far outweigh this one downside.

The Sony NSZ-GS7:
The remote is, well, awesome. I love it. Not to mention I installed the GoogleTV remote app on my android phone and can control from there. I also installed the GoogleTV remote app on my wife's iPad so given one of those devices is always near we never have to search for the remote. The hardware's performance has been pretty solid with just a couple exceptions. It seems to lock up from time to time, but it is rather infrequent. I've had to hard reset it maybe 2-3 times in the couple months I've had it. Again, given all the positives, I can live with it. I was contemplating the Vizio box for $99, but given a lot of the reviews said the small form factor cause it to overheat, I chose to go with the Sony ($70 more) for the reliability of the brand overall. Thus far I've not been disappointed.

Overall, if they could fix the Netflix integration issue (probably as simple as a software update), make the interface more slick/intuitive and solve the occasional hardware lock up I would give this box and GoogleTV 5 stars. That said, given my goal of having only one device to play all my media, this box (and GoogleTV) take the cake and leave Roku and AppleTV in the dust.

title: Great Product, Super Cusomer Support. Give it a Try!!
text:
Getting close to a candidate for a hearing aid with about a 20% loss due to loud rock music (I'm 52 years old and have subjected myself to playing on very loud stages and didn't adequately protect my ears, but it was fun! lol) Tough to hear conversation especially in a a classroom because I am an instructor and also need the TV way up which is annoying to everyone else so instead of going the expensive hearing aid way I decided to check out the low end/cost solutions and glad I did. These work great and the customization with the app makes all the difference so I am able to hear speech and the TV much better.

The Bluetooth feature is what really sold it for me so it doesn't appear like a hearing aid but a more socially familiar bluetooth phone device. This is the only reason I did not give it 5 stars since it lacks the sound and peculiarly, the volume of a regular bluetooth or at least the one I was used to using which was the Motorola H730 which is the loudest I've found. I am also told my voice sounds "tinny" to the end user when I speak. So I had to order the H730 and only use the CS10 when I need it to hear better so it was a bit of a disappointment NOT to be able to use this universally as I had hoped. Maybe with with enough reviews about this condition ( and I've noticed a few) they will improve the circuitry to take care of this problem and I wouldn't hesitate to updgrade because the unit does what it does well and the price point is so reasonable.

Also a bit of advice: take the time to get a good fit in the ear because the more secure it is the better your low frequency,the more natual it will sound and the volume increases. I use in ear monitors on stage when I paly in my band so I was used to this but most users will not be aware that the fit makes a big difference in how the sound will come out.

Also I must tell you the customer service and the way this company stands behind this product is superb! I had a problem with the battery fit on the unit and they sent me a whole new unit express mail in 2 days no questions asked!

So buy with confidence and give a try. I would say you have an excellent chance of being very pleased witht this product!

title: Looks good, but too many shortcomings
text:
I bought this when it was new, for over $1000. I felt like it definitely wasn't worth it at that price. For significantly less (i.e the current pricing), I probably would think differently, although I still think there are better systems.

Pros:
- Looks nice.
- Pretty fast.
- Backlit keyboard.
- Works as either a laptop or a tablet.

Cons:
- Kind of heavy for its size.
- The batteries die in less than a week when it's just sitting there totally powered off.
- When used as a laptop on your lap, it feels off-balance (because the screen section is heavy - since it's actually full-fledged tablet), and the sharp edges of the bottom hinge dig into your thighs.
- If you use the "classic" desktop mode and apps (instead of the new Windows 8 tiled "modern" UI), you'll probably run into some software which will have trouble with the high-res screen. For instance Google Chrome can't show its controls and menus at a consistent usable size (but web pages themselves look OK if you zoom them in a bit).
- Uneven backlighting creates bright spots on the left and right edges. It's especially noticeable when the image is fairly dark.
- The on-screen keyboard frequently pops up even when the real keyboard is connected.

title: The 7 Beeps of Death
text:
While this is a decent laptop in the low end of the price range (while it is working), many owners have experienced a processor/motherboard crash with no warning somewhere between 6 and 18 months of operation. This crash is characterized by a black screen, no boot, and the continuously repeating 7 beeps of death.

Dell should have recalled this model after so many owners have experienced this problem (the tech boards are full of reports on this). Instead, Dell has chosen to ignore the faulty parts. Even those who had this problem while their laptop was still under warranty have had the same problem after Dell replaced the motherboard.

While I would suggest you try another model, since Dell has been stunningly irresponsible in addressing the problems of the M5030, I suggest you buy another brand altogether. I won't buy another Dell product.

title: The microphone sound great the speed of it is lightning fast (press the ...
text:
I, and my wife, are astonished of the clarity of this camera. From research and reading reviews, I decided to purchase this product with a 64Gb 80Mb/s card (to place the camera in "PRO" mode - 1080/60FPS) where it performed greater than our expectations. The microphone sound great the speed of it is lightning fast (press the record button while it's off and it will turn on and start record in less than 3 seconds). The image stabilization circuit is a big plus, I don't know how anyone can work without it. Sony definitely knows what they are doing with video products!

The directions read like stereo instructions, so I was able to get a handling on it rather quickly, however, there are some modes that I have not worked with yet (timer and real-time streaming). I not quite sure why they have you go to a different menu to enable the "PRO" mode, as they could have integrated it with the "VMODE" menu - with a rejection if the card was not compatible (or better yet not listing the "PRO" mode if the card was not compatible).

The "water proof" case that comes with it is not really designed for underwater video. I see it as more to protect it in the snow, rain, around a pool, and to prevent scratches of the lens. Yes, they have other products to protect the lens, however, I can see the included case as an "all around" general protector of the camera and lens. The case has a built-in tripod mount, additionally, you can run the camera without the "water proof" case with the included tripod adapter.

I've only worked with the free program (PMHOME) just a little bit and have not been able to figure it out yet (like the GPS overlay), so I will update when I get a chance. I work almost exclusively in Linux, so I'm not sure if I will even use it. Some have reported that you cannot delete video nor pictures from the camera without performing a "format". This is not true. It is true that you cannot accomplish this function from within the camera software, nor the PMHOME software, however, you can open a file manager and search through the card when the camera is connected to a computer and manually delete the files. This is MUCH more preferable then formatting the card as these cards have a finite number of writes (so if you "write" the image then "format" the card, then "write" a new image - that's three writes).

The camera that I purchased already had the updated firmware, so I did not need to make any changes.

-Update 1 (1 month from purchase)

The camera continues to impress! Learned more tricks and now have added a "selfipod" adapter. Have recorded about 10 hours worth of video so far. Here is what I have found:

- Check the lens (du). Seems simple enough, however, a few times I have placed it in the case without checking the lens and left smears on it. I have also neglected to check the case lens as well (oops).
- When dealing with a "selfipod" be very careful of grip as slight grip change can and will transfer down the pole to the camera where it WILL be picked up by the very sensitive Mic's.
- Having a high quality/high speed card really helps.
- The "MyMemories" phone software tends to hang on connection - not sure why, just says "connecting...'. When it works, it works well, just not consistent. I'm not sure if it is a problem with the actual camera or the phone software.
- I've seen some complaints about the mounting capability - The camera includes a standard tripod mount! This means that if you can (and you will) find a standard camera mount, this camera will work with it! Grant you, it's funny to see this little camera on a full size tripod or the selfipod taking a foot print of half the size of the mount itself, but it does work - just like a regular camera.
- I LOVE the feature of taking 10 pictures in 2 seconds. No more blink problems.
- Taking still pictures is a little strange because you don't know what you are going to get, however, remember that even if you are not centered you can crop to center the shot.

More later!

title: Great mid-camera.
text:
Bought this used for $400+. I'm no pro, or amateur - just a guy sick and tired of point-and-shoots.

Pros:
You can get lens adapters, to fit other lenses (Canon, Nikon, etc)
Size is fantastic. I literally have used this on bicycle rides, strapped around my shoulder on my back.
"Intelligent Auto" button is a life-saver. I showed my wife how to use that, and now she can take good photos all the time. I enjoyed it as well, because initially I was still learning how to use the camera's different settings, etc. So I didn't have to wait until I learned everything, if I wanted a good photo of something, I just used the auto, and it's always pretty decent.
Photos are usually fantastic.
Used this with tripod, and took fireworks-over-water photos that I would never have thought that I would be capable of taking.

Cons:
The kit lens is good, but limiting (to be expected).
The other panasonic micro-4/3's lenses are more expensive than their non-micro-4/3 counterparts. You're paying extra for the form factor basically.
Low light scenes can be difficult to capture properly - DSLR's could do better, but then again this is a different genre all together.

Overall:
If you're looking for a non-point-and-shoot that will take excellent photos, large enough photos for displaying on your 40" TV, printing onto canvas, etc; and you're not wanting to spend $1000+ on all the big bulky gear of a full DSLR, then this is the style camera you want. Spend $400 on a used one of these, then in a few years if you're looking to grow, just simply buy a new lens and work with that. If you're not a tech hungry person who is always buying the latest and greatest, then you could buy this camera, and literally get 20+ years of use out of it.

title: Poorly Designed
text:
I have an Olympus 6200PC & love it. I needed another one, but Olympus doesn't manufacture it anymore. They make a newer model that has NO way to download recordings to a computer so the newer model is useless!

Unable to get another 6200PC, I looked over all the available Olympus recorders and purchased the Olympus DM-620 because the controls are the most similar to the 6200PC while still retaining the ability to transfer recordings to a computer. Not all the Olympus recorders have this ability. I hate tiny, complicated control buttons and especially dislike having a pause or stop button right next to the record button where it is too easy to hit the wrong button by mistake. The DM-620 has those buttons fairly well apart from each other. However, the 3 little black buttons above the Stop & Record buttons require a fingernail in order to use them.

Unfortunately, the DM-620 is really awful! First, the menus are not user friendly. Second, the playback volume -- even set on high -- is not loud enough, nor of good quality. Next, when you want to play back only one certain recording, the machine does not stop at the end of that recording but continues on to the next separate recording without any indication that it has moved to a new recording -- no beep -- no delay -- just goes right on. It will play every separate recording until you stop it -- just as though they are all the same recording.

I thought the playback volume and continuous playback problems were manufacture flaws and took the recorder back to Staples for an exchange. Nope! The second Olympus DM-620 was exactly like the first. Playback sound is awful and not very loud. Playback of a recording does not stop at its end, but continues to the next recording and the next, etc. Both units performed the same way so I have to conclude the DM-620 was designed to perform this way.

Also, as mentioned in another review, the machine "names" each successive recording in a manner that makes no sense and does not seem to include the folder name (there are Folders A, B, C, D & E available to record in and each folder can hold dozens of different recordings). This makes it impossible to find a specific recording after moving them to a PC.

THEN, I had problems using it as an MP3 player. I put some music files on a mini memory card. The first unit that was returned to the store would only play one song at a time and stop. I tried every setting in the menu I could find and it still only played one song, then I'd have to manually start another song. The 2nd DM-620 did the same thing -- played one song and stopped -- but I was able to finally set the menu so it played continuously. Of course, the volume on both units--whether used to play a voice recording or music - wasn't loud enough. This probably isn't a concern when playing music because most people will use ear buds.

LOST FILES. For some reason, both the 1st and 2nd units I purchased showed there were no music files on the mini card where there were lots of files. I moved the files around so they were not in sub folders -- apparently the DM-620 won't play music in sub-folders -- but both machines said there were no files where I knew there were files. Also, I had problems getting it to play in 'shuffle' mode.

Finally, this model has a recorded voice telling you what the machine is doing. The voice has a British accent -- not everybody likes a British accent ! Thank the Gods this feature can be disabled !

Whoever designed this model (Olympus DM-620) had to be on drugs. I took the 2nd unit back for a refund. Guess I'll look for a different brand.

I wish Olympus would re-issue the 6200PC or include the ability to move files to a computer on all models.

title: Poor Front Panel Design - VERY POOR Customer Service
text:
The front panel USB / Audio IO connector is very flimsy. Sometimes, when inserting a USB plug, the circuit board on the back side of the front panel will dislodge from it's mounting bracket. This is not a manufacturing defect, it's a design flaw.

In the unit I purchased, there was a broken wire in the cable that connects the front panel USB to the mother board. I can see the broken wire near the connector that plugs into the mother board. The broken wire causes audio popping and hiss when USB and audio devices are simultaneously plugged into the front panel - like when synchronizing an ipod and using a gaming headset. I emailed NZXT customer support 3 times over a 2 week period and they totally ignored me - I never heard back from them once. If you have a problem with your case, don't expect to get any help from the manufacturer!

The Cooler Master HAF 912 costs $20.00 more but is a much better deal in my opinion. The HAF 912 has room for an extra large video card, includes mounting hardware for 3 SSD drives, and has a robust, sturdy front panel design. I own 4 HAF 912s and never had a single problem with any of them. The only redeeming quality of this NZXT case is it's low price; but, you get what you pay for: Junk.

text: This is my first L series Lens.  I own other canon lenses that are tack sharp that perform wonders in their own right.  I read all the rave about this lens among a few others so I simply started with what I could afford. At first, I wanted to scream because not many of my shots came out sharp and at one point, I even thought my 85 mm prime lens is "better than this".  BUT.. with some time, and learning from the shared settings from other owners, my photos are now fantastic.  I am in AWE of the beautiful color and contrast. I recommend this lens to everyone, especially the budget conscious who are still wanting professional looking photos. With the right set up and lighting, you too will experience the beauty of the glass lens. You will kick yourself for not owning this lens sooner. It bothers me when I read negative reviews based on the users inadequate training or knowledge of a product. Had I reviewed it off my first few photos, I would have misguided a lot of readers by saying this lens is overrated. Just give it time if you are not experiencing razor sharp images.  Don't just review the photos on your camera, instead review them on your computer to see your dislikes (if any) then consult with someone knowledgeable about settings specific for this lens. You can be a professional photographer but lack the proficiency with an individual lens and that certainly makes the difference. This lens is worth every penny and you will not be disappointed. Yes, the many positive reviews this lens is getting are VERY accurate!! You'll work harder in dimmer light but again, with a little tweaking of you settings, that won't matter a bit. All the photos I have taken since receiving guidance and training, have ALL received compliments. Now that's the real "show and tell".

title: A surprise everyone should know about
text:
Normally when you hear about a new amazing product from apple, now Microsoft as well there is a big presentation that thousands tune in to watch live. They are the largest advertising for the product to fans and will almost convince you need it. There is however a rare occasion when a device just sells itself. This tablet is the first tablet dell has made that is worth buying. Of course, in buying something you always need to assess how you will use it. If you are buying a tablet to play cheap apps, well this probably is not for you. Android and IOS will both contain a significantly richer amount of touch based native apps.

However, if you are like me and see that tablets are restricted computers, then you may be on the right page. This tablet will do everything your iPad, or android will, minus those apps. Music? I am currently listening to the desktop iTunes application, but have access to metro apps and every other x86 movie player I care to download. Also have visual studio running in the background and am using Google chrome to write this. Point is, this device runs windows 8.1 beautifully allowing you so much more possibilities than its competitors.

To this devices' credit though, windows is a different review than the tablet itself. Therefore here are the best parts, and its drawbacks.

Pros:

1. The screen

As many others have stated, the screen is beautiful, a true joy to look. Despite its lower resolution screen it looks stunningly sharp and colors shine.

2. The sound quality

An amazing surprise from the device was just how loud it could actually go. It is not the best audio quality out there, however, it is something to be proud of. External speakers for this device could almost be a crime.

3. Processor

Hello Intel, welcome back in the race. Bay Trail is as zippy and promising as the previews have noted.

4. Windows 8.1

Full windows 8 is by far the largest plus of this device. The tablet is not as user friendly as IOS or android, but it gives you a world of possibilities the other do not.

5. The device itself

It is great size, just light enough. The bezel is a great size and fits in your hand snugly. In addition, the grip on the back makes holding the device with one hand comfortable and easily doable.

Cons:

1. Only micro usb out/in

This means if you would like to connect a usb powered hard drive you will need a micro usb to usb converter. It is possible to convert to hdmi as well, however, good luck charging the device while doing so. Any output will most likely be expensive and engineered to work.

2. Cameras

They are nothing to be proud of. After messing with them a little they took mostly blurry pictures with a few nicer ones. Looks like you will really need to try to get a good picture. It is a con simply because everything else is so perfect, anything normal sticks out.

3. Heat

Looks like the device will get warm whenever the Intel chip starts reaching 1.8 GHz. It is not awful, however, as it has no fan, and I have not yet tried anything I would consider CPU intense (like gaming) yet and I have already experienced this, it looks like it could be a problem.

With that said, the device really is a great product. What a surprise from Dell and good for them. It is truly everyone should know about, even if it is not the device for you.
